seo.prose: A scaffold of world history built from the PeriodO period gazetteer: every scholarly period definition placed at real coordinates on a globe, stacked outward by date, and linked forward in time both within a region and across regions by conquest, colonisation and transmission.
seo.title: World History Scaffold, 5000 BC – AD 2000
seo.description: Historical periods from PeriodO with coordinates, start and end years, and directed time-forward links, ready to receive museum objects as widgets.

knowledgeTree.positionNote: radius = (5000 + y) / 500 + 100 where y is the signed year (BC negative): 100 at 5000 BC, 110 at 1 BC, 114 at AD 2000. Nodes are placed at their tStart; radiusStart and radiusEnd give the full extent if you want to draw each period as a radial segment.
knowledgeTree.edgeNote: 'succeeds' = the next period in the same place, forming that place's vertical chain through time. 'conquers'/'colonises' = one polity contacted or attacked another, kept only where the two periods overlap in time. 'transmits' = a later period borrowed an idea or technology from an earlier one. All three come from the source gazetteer. 'contemporary' edges carry "inferred": true and were added here to reconnect otherwise isolated nodes: they record that two periods overlapped in time and either shared a named place or lay within 1200 km of one another. They are proximity inferences, not attested contacts. PeriodO's 'contains' taxonomy and same-place 'succeeds' continuity were removed, as neither asserts contact or borrowing.
knowledgeTree.ingestNote: To add a museum object, match its place and date against tStart/tEnd and lat/lon, then append it to that node's widgets array.

Early Bronze (Israel, 3499 BC–2249 BC).label: Early Bronze
Early Bronze (Israel, 3499 BC–2249 BC).prose:
[Levant, 3499 BC–2249 BC] Early Bronze. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The southern Levant saw its first experiment with urban life: villages grew into walled towns with temples, palaces, granaries and planned streets at places like Arad, Megiddo and Bet Yerah. Olive oil and wine were produced for export, and trade with Egypt was intense enough that Egyptian rulers' names appear on jars in Canaan. Around 2500–2300 BC the towns were abandoned and people returned to villages and pastoralism, a collapse still debated by archaeologists.

Late Bronze (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC).label: Late Bronze
Late Bronze (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Canaan was an Egyptian province of walled city-states, each with its ruler answering to a pharaoh's garrison and paying tribute. The Amarna letters capture their rivalries and pleas for help, while Cypriot, Mycenaean and Egyptian goods in the tombs show how deeply the region was tied into eastern Mediterranean trade. Widespread destructions and the appearance of new groups, including the earliest mention of Israel, close the age.

Iron IIC (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).label: Iron IIC
Iron IIC (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Levant, 699 BC–585 BC] Iron IIC. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Judah alone remained, a client of Assyria and then of Babylon, with Jerusalem swollen by refugees and the Negev and Shephelah reorganised for trade and agriculture. Literacy is unusually visible in ostraca from Arad and Lachish, written as the Babylonian armies closed in. The period ends with the destruction of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple and the deportation of 586 BC.

EB II (Israel, 3099 BC–2649 BC).label: EB II
EB II (Israel, 3099 BC–2649 BC).prose:
[Levant, 3099 BC–2649 BC] EB II. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Towns hardened into walled cities with gates, towers and public buildings — Arad in the Negev is the classic example, laid out with streets and a water reservoir. Trade with Old Kingdom Egypt and Byblos flourished, and mass-produced pottery points to craft specialists rather than households making their own. This is the first urban age in the southern Levant.

EB III (Israel, 2649 BC–2249 BC).label: EB III
EB III (Israel, 2649 BC–2249 BC).prose:
[Levant, 2649 BC–2249 BC] EB III. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Urban life reached its height, with massive fortifications at places like Megiddo, Bet Yerah and Yarmuth, and imported Khirbet Kerak ware showing links to communities from the Caucasus. Then, over a few generations, city after city was abandoned or burned. Debate over whether drought, over-extension or the collapse of Egyptian trade did it continues today.

Neolithic (Israel, 8499 BC–4499 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Israel, 8499 BC–4499 BC).prose:
[Levant, 8499 BC–4499 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

LB I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC).label: LB I
LB I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1549 BC–1399 BC] LB I. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Canaan came under Egyptian imperial control after Thutmose III's campaigns, and the fortified towns of the previous age were left smaller, poorer and often unwalled. Local rulers governed as vassals, sending tribute and hostages to the Nile. Imported Cypriot and Mycenaean pottery in the tombs shows how thoroughly the region was plugged into eastern Mediterranean trade.

MB IIC (Israel, 1599 BC–1549 BC).label: MB IIC
MB IIC (Israel, 1599 BC–1549 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1599 BC–1549 BC] MB IIC. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The last phase of the great Canaanite towns, still prosperous but heading for collapse. Egyptian resurgence under the early Eighteenth Dynasty and the expulsion of the Hyksos coincide with widespread destructions and abandonments, after which the surviving cities re-emerge smaller and under Egyptian imperial control.

Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).label: Iron IIA
Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Levant, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron IIA. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Monumental building returns: fortified gates, palaces and administrative centres at sites like Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, traditionally credited to Solomon and hotly debated ever since. Pharaoh Sheshonq I campaigned through the region around 925 BC, leaving a list of conquered towns at Karnak. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature.

Iron I (Israel, 1199 BC–999 BC).label: Iron I
Iron I (Israel, 1199 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1199 BC–999 BC] Iron I. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The world of Canaanite city-states and Egyptian garrisons fell apart, and settlement shifted to hundreds of small unwalled villages in the central highlands — the archaeological horizon from which Israel emerges. On the southern coast, newcomers usually identified with the Philistines founded cities with distinctly Aegean-flavoured pottery, architecture and diet. It was a poorer, more fragmented age than the one before it, but the political map it produced would last for centuries.

Neo-Babylonian (Israel, 585 BC–538 BC).label: Neo-Babylonian
Neo-Babylonian (Israel, 585 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Levant, 585 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. this date: see also Mazar, 1992. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Judah under Babylonian rule was a diminished, largely rural province, its capital and temple in ruins and its royal house deported. Excavations show towns in the south and the Shephelah abandoned or shrunken while some settlements north of Jerusalem, around Benjamin, carried on. This bleak interval ended when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and permitted exiles to return.

EB I (Israel, 3499 BC–3099 BC).label: EB I
EB I (Israel, 3499 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[Levant, 3499 BC–3099 BC] EB I. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Villages across Canaan grew larger and more organised, with the first planned settlements, olive and vine cultivation, and copper working on a serious scale. Trade with Egypt in the run-up to its unification brought Canaanite jars south and Egyptian goods north, and some sites show Egyptian residents living among locals. It set the stage for the region's first true cities.

Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Iron IIB
Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Levant, 899 BC–699 BC] Iron IIB. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Israel under the Omrides and then Jeroboam II became a substantial regional power with ivory-decorated palaces at Samaria, before Assyrian armies destroyed it and deported its population in 720 BC. Judah survived as a vassal, and Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BC is documented from both sides — by Assyrian palace reliefs and by the excavated siege ramp and mass grave. Royal administration is visible in stamped jar handles and standardised weights.

LB IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–1199 BC).label: LB IIB
LB IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1299 BC–1199 BC] LB IIB. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Egyptian control over Canaan tightened under Seti I and Ramesses II, with governors' residences and garrison towns at places like Beth Shean and Lachish. Then, around 1200, the whole system unravelled: cities burned, Egypt withdrew, and international trade networks collapsed across the eastern Mediterranean. Out of the aftermath came the Philistine settlements on the coast and the villages of the highlands that would become Israel.

Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

MB IIA (Israel, 1924 BC–1699 BC).label: MB IIA
MB IIA (Israel, 1924 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1924 BC–1699 BC] MB IIA. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Urban settlement revived along the coastal plain and in the valleys, with new towns founded, bronze metallurgy in wide use and fast-wheel pottery of high quality. Contacts with Middle Kingdom Egypt and with Byblos are visible in imported goods and in Egyptian execration texts naming Canaanite chiefs. Levantine settlers moving into the Nile Delta at this time laid the groundwork for the Hyksos.

Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I (Israel,.node: Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I (Israel, 2249 BC–1924 BC)
Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I (Israel,.label: Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I
Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I (Israel,.prose:
[Levant, 2249 BC–1924 BC] Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

A non-urban interval between two ages of cities: people lived in small unwalled villages, campsites and copper-working camps, and buried their dead in vast shaft-tomb cemeteries. Bronze daggers and javelins and a distinctive hand-finished pottery mark the material culture, but there are no fortifications, palaces or writing. The debate over whether these were newcomers from the north or the descendants of the collapsed Early Bronze towns is still unresolved.

MB IIB (Israel, 1699 BC–1599 BC).label: MB IIB
MB IIB (Israel, 1699 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1699 BC–1599 BC] MB IIB. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The peak of Canaanite urban civilisation, when cities such as Hazor grew enormous and were ringed by huge sloping earthen ramparts and fosses. Palaces, temples and rich warrior burials with bronze weapons and scarabs reflect a stratified society tied into a trade network reaching Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia. In Egypt the Hyksos kings, of Levantine origin, ruled the Delta from Avaris.

Pottery Neolithic A (PNA) (Israel, 6299.label: Pottery Neolithic A (PNA)
Pottery Neolithic A (PNA) (Israel, 6299.prose:
[Levant, 6299 BC–4999 BC] Pottery Neolithic A (PNA). Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The first phase in which southern Levantine villagers made and used fired pottery, associated with the Yarmukian and Jericho IX assemblages. Settlements were smaller and more scattered than the crowded pre-pottery towns, with pit houses, storage pits and a mixed economy of cereals and herded sheep, goats, pigs and cattle. Distinctive incised herringbone designs filled with red paint, and coffee-bean-eyed clay figurines, make its material culture instantly recognisable.

Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3499 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Levant, 4499 BC–3499 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Hellenistic (Israel, 331 BC–52 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Israel, 331 BC–52 BC).prose:
[Levant, 331 BC–52 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Pottery Neolithic B (PNB) (Israel, 4999.label: Pottery Neolithic B (PNB)
Pottery Neolithic B (PNB) (Israel, 4999.prose:
[Levant, 4999 BC–4499 BC] Pottery Neolithic B (PNB). Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The later Pottery Neolithic in the southern Levant, largely the Wadi Rabah horizon, when villages grew again and pottery became finer: burnished dark wares, bow-rim jars and carinated bowls. Farmers began exploiting olives and other tree crops alongside cereals and herds, and stamp seals and small quantities of copper hint at growing exchange and ownership. Much of what defines the following Chalcolithic villages is already taking shape here.

Middle Bronze II (Israel, 1924 BC–1549 B.label: Middle Bronze II
Middle Bronze II (Israel, 1924 BC–1549 B.prose:
[Levant, 1924 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze II. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

The main urban phase of Bronze Age Canaan, when cities such as Hazor, Megiddo, Lachish and Ashkelon were fortified with earthen ramparts and equipped with palaces and temples. Bronze weaponry, scarabs and imported ceramics show wide trade contacts with Egypt, Cyprus and Syria. Egyptian campaigns following the expulsion of the Hyksos ended the era in destruction.

LB IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–1299 BC).label: LB IIA
LB IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–1299 BC).prose:
[Levant, 1399 BC–1299 BC] LB IIA. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

This is the world of the Amarna letters, the cuneiform correspondence in which the mayors of Jerusalem, Megiddo, Shechem and Byblos beg the pharaoh for troops and accuse each other of treachery. Canaan was a patchwork of small city-states under an Egyptian umbrella, with garrisons at key points and caravans moving along the coastal road. Temples with Egyptian and Syrian features, and rich imported pottery, reflect a cosmopolitan elite.

Persian (Israel, 538 BC–331 BC).label: Persian
Persian (Israel, 538 BC–331 BC).prose:
[Levant, 538 BC–331 BC] Persian. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. See map as ill. 227, page 392. Period definition from Life in biblical Israel — King, Philip J., 2001.

Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and Judah became Yehud, a small tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire. Under governors and an increasingly powerful priesthood, much of the Hebrew Bible took shape and Aramaic became the everyday language. Coins, imported Greek pottery and administrative seal impressions show a province tied into imperial and Mediterranean networks.

Early Minoan III Period (Crete, 2200 BC–.node: Early Minoan III Period (Crete, 2200 BC–2051 BC)
Early Minoan III Period (Crete, 2200 BC–.label: Early Minoan III Period
Early Minoan III Period (Crete, 2200 BC–.prose:
[Crete, 2200 BC–2051 BC] Early Minoan III Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

A transitional phase on Crete, thinly represented at most sites but crucial: population and wealth were gathering at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, and white-on-dark painted pottery marks a break with earlier styles. Within a few generations these centres would build the first palaces, so this is the run-up to Minoan civilisation proper.

Late Minoan III Period (Crete, 1410 BC–1.node: Late Minoan III Period (Crete, 1410 BC–1051 BC)
Late Minoan III Period (Crete, 1410 BC–1.label: Late Minoan III Period
Late Minoan III Period (Crete, 1410 BC–1.prose:
[Crete, 1410 BC–1051 BC] Late Minoan III Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete after the palaces, run by Mycenaean-influenced elites who wrote Greek in Linear B and buried their dead in chamber tombs and painted clay coffins. Pottery became standardised and repetitive, part of an Aegean-wide 'koine' shared from the Peloponnese to Cyprus. The era closes with the collapse of the palace world, when islanders abandoned the coasts for defensible mountain sites and the island slid toward the Iron Age.

Bronze Age Period (Crete, 3100 BC–1051 B.label: Bronze Age Period
Bronze Age Period (Crete, 3100 BC–1051 B.prose:
[Crete, 3100 BC–1051 BC] Bronze Age Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The era on Crete when small farming communities grew into the palace-centred societies of Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, with storerooms of giant jars, workshops, archives and elaborate wall paintings. Seafaring linked the island to Egypt, the Levant and the Cyclades, and Cretan styles in pottery, metalwork and stone vases travelled with the trade. It closes with the arrival of Mycenaean rulers and the shift to Greek-language Linear B record keeping.

Early Minoan II Period (Crete, 2650 BC–2.node: Early Minoan II Period (Crete, 2650 BC–2201 BC)
Early Minoan II Period (Crete, 2650 BC–2.label: Early Minoan II Period
Early Minoan II Period (Crete, 2650 BC–2.prose:
[Crete, 2650 BC–2201 BC] Early Minoan II Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Prosperity peaked before the palaces: villages grew into tightly packed complexes of rooms, storage jars multiplied, and metalworkers turned out daggers, tools and jewellery. Potters mastered the mottled surfaces of Vasiliki ware, and stone-carvers produced vessels of banded marble and breccia. Imports and imitations link Crete to the Cyclades, Egypt and the Levant, showing seafaring contacts well established.

Late Roman Period (Crete, AD 250–AD 399).label: Late Roman Period
Late Roman Period (Crete, AD 250–AD 399).prose:
[Crete, AD 250–AD 399] Late Roman Period. Parent period: Roman. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.

Late Minoan II Period (Crete, 1460 BC–14.node: Late Minoan II Period (Crete, 1460 BC–1411 BC)
Late Minoan II Period (Crete, 1460 BC–14.label: Late Minoan II Period
Late Minoan II Period (Crete, 1460 BC–14.prose:
[Crete, 1460 BC–1411 BC] Late Minoan II Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

A short, distinctive phase in which Knossos stood alone as the surviving palace, under rulers who used Greek and the Linear B script for their records. Weapons in tombs and a taste for formal, imposing 'Palace Style' jars point to Mycenaean control of the island's administration. The Linear B archives from this era give the first detailed written picture of Aegean economy and religion.

Early Byzantine II Period (Crete, AD 700.label: Early Byzantine II Period
Early Byzantine II Period (Crete, AD 700.prose:
[Crete, AD 700–AD 899] Early Byzantine II Period. Parent period: Early Byzantine. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Settlement contracted and people moved to defensible upland sites as Arab raiding intensified across the eastern Mediterranean. In the 820s Andalusian exiles seized the island and founded the Emirate of Crete with its capital at Chandax, modern Heraklion, which raided Aegean shipping for well over a century until Nikephoros Phokas reconquered the island in 961.

Byzantine Period (Crete, AD 400–AD 1199).label: Byzantine Period
Byzantine Period (Crete, AD 400–AD 1199).prose:
[Crete, AD 400–AD 1199] Byzantine Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.

Middle Minoan III Period (Crete, 1700 BC.node: Middle Minoan III Period (Crete, 1700 BC–1676 BC)
Middle Minoan III Period (Crete, 1700 BC.label: Middle Minoan III Period
Middle Minoan III Period (Crete, 1700 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1700 BC–1676 BC] Middle Minoan III Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Following the destruction of the first palaces, Cretan builders raised new and more elaborate complexes with light-wells, ashlar facades and painted plaster walls. Administration switched to the Linear A script, and the island's ceramic and architectural styles spread outward to Thera and the Cyclades.

Roman Period (Crete, 100 BC–AD 399).label: Roman Period
Roman Period (Crete, 100 BC–AD 399).prose:
[Crete, 100 BC–AD 399] Roman Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

Venetian Period (Crete, AD 1200–AD 1749).label: Venetian Period
Venetian Period (Crete, AD 1200–AD 1749).prose:
[Crete, AD 1200–AD 1749] Venetian Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Venice bought and then conquered the island after the Fourth Crusade, governing it from Candia as its most valuable overseas colony and using it as the main way-station on the sea route to the Levant. Heavy taxation and land seizures provoked repeated revolts by Cretan nobles and villagers, but over time Venetian and Greek elites merged, producing the icon workshops that trained El Greco and a flowering of Cretan literature and drama. Ottoman armies took the island in a long war ending with the surrender of Candia in 1669.

Late Minoan I Period (Crete, 1675 BC–146.node: Late Minoan I Period (Crete, 1675 BC–1461 BC)
Late Minoan I Period (Crete, 1675 BC–146.label: Late Minoan I Period
Late Minoan I Period (Crete, 1675 BC–146.prose:
[Crete, 1675 BC–1461 BC] Late Minoan I Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete's Neopalatial civilisation at its most confident, with rebuilt palaces, harbour towns, frescoed villas and a distinctive naturalistic art of plants, sea creatures and ritual scenes. Cretan goods and fashions spread through the Cyclades and reached Egypt and the Near East. The volcanic destruction of Akrotiri on Thera and a subsequent wave of destructions across Crete bracket its end.

Early Iron Age Period (Crete, 1050 BC–70.node: Early Iron Age Period (Crete, 1050 BC–701 BC)
Early Iron Age Period (Crete, 1050 BC–70.label: Early Iron Age Period
Early Iron Age Period (Crete, 1050 BC–70.prose:
[Crete, 1050 BC–701 BC] Early Iron Age Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

After the collapse of Mycenaean-controlled Crete, islanders moved to defensible upland refuges like Karphi before settling again in the lowlands. Cremation burial, iron tools and a distinctive Protogeometric and Geometric pottery tradition spread, while Phoenician traders and Near Eastern craftsmen brought new metalworking and imagery, visible in the bronze shields and cauldrons dedicated in the Idaean Cave. By the end of the period, Cretan communities such as Dreros and Praisos had become small city-states with written laws.

Early Minoan I Period (Crete, 3100 BC–26.node: Early Minoan I Period (Crete, 3100 BC–2651 BC)
Early Minoan I Period (Crete, 3100 BC–26.label: Early Minoan I Period
Early Minoan I Period (Crete, 3100 BC–26.prose:
[Crete, 3100 BC–2651 BC] Early Minoan I Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Cretan communities began to bury their dead in collective tholos tombs and caves, a practice that would continue for a thousand years and tie families to particular places. Copper tools and daggers appear, and potters produced the burnished chalices of Pyrgos ware and the red-streaked jugs of Agios Onouphrios type. Settlement expanded into new parts of the island, including the eastern coasts.

Early Minoan Period (Crete, 3100 BC–2051.label: Early Minoan Period
Early Minoan Period (Crete, 3100 BC–2051.prose:
[Crete, 3100 BC–2051 BC] Early Minoan Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The Cretan Bronze Age begins: metalworking spreads, seaborne contact with the Cyclades, Egypt and the Levant intensifies, and communities bury their dead together in stone tholos tombs used over many generations. Villages such as Myrtos and Vasiliki show specialised craft production and storage on a scale not seen before. Everything that made the later palaces possible—surplus, trade, seals, social ranking—accumulated during these centuries.

Middle Minoan I Period (Crete, 2050 BC–1.node: Middle Minoan I Period (Crete, 2050 BC–1851 BC)
Middle Minoan I Period (Crete, 2050 BC–1.label: Middle Minoan I Period
Middle Minoan I Period (Crete, 2050 BC–1.prose:
[Crete, 2050 BC–1851 BC] Middle Minoan I Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete shifted from a landscape of villages and communal tombs to one dominated by large court-centred complexes, with the first palaces founded at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia. Peak sanctuaries on mountaintops drew crowds leaving clay figures of people and animals, and potters adopted the wheel and brighter polychrome styles.

Hellenistic Period (Crete, 323 BC–101 BC.label: Hellenistic Period
Hellenistic Period (Crete, 323 BC–101 BC.prose:
[Crete, 323 BC–101 BC] Hellenistic Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.

Archaic Period (Crete, 700 BC–481 BC).label: Archaic Period
Archaic Period (Crete, 700 BC–481 BC).prose:
[Crete, 700 BC–481 BC] Archaic Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The island's many small city-states — Knossos, Gortyn, Dreros, Lyktos — produced the earliest surviving Greek law inscribed on stone, and a strong tradition of hammered bronze work and Daedalic sculpture that influenced sculptors on the mainland. Votive deposits in the Idaean Cave and the temples of Dreros and Prinias show a distinctive local blend of Greek and Near Eastern forms. Crete then turned inward, staying out of the Persian Wars and playing little part in the classical politics that followed.

Final Neolithic Period (Crete, 4500 BC–3.label: Final Neolithic Period
Final Neolithic Period (Crete, 4500 BC–3.prose:
[Crete, 4500 BC–3101 BC] Final Neolithic Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

After several thousand years in which Knossos was almost the only substantial settlement on Crete, people began founding new sites across the island, from upland refuges to coastal points facing the Aegean. Pottery, stone tools and the first metal objects show growing contact with the islands and Anatolia. The population and connections built up in these centuries fed directly into the Early Minoan communities that followed.

Middle Minoan II Period (Crete, 1850 BC–.node: Middle Minoan II Period (Crete, 1850 BC–1701 BC)
Middle Minoan II Period (Crete, 1850 BC–.label: Middle Minoan II Period
Middle Minoan II Period (Crete, 1850 BC–.prose:
[Crete, 1850 BC–1701 BC] Middle Minoan II Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The mature phase of Crete's first palaces, with large-scale storage of oil and grain, workshops for seal-cutting and metalwork, and administrative records kept in Cretan Hieroglyphic. Kamares pottery, wheel-thrown and painted in white and red on a dark ground, was exported to Egypt and the Levant. The period ended in destruction, after which the palaces were rebuilt on a larger plan.

Early Byzantine Period (Crete, AD 400–AD.label: Early Byzantine Period
Early Byzantine Period (Crete, AD 400–AD.prose:
[Crete, AD 400–AD 899] Early Byzantine Period. Parent period: Byzantine. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete began this stretch as a rich, densely settled Christian province of grain estates and mosaic-floored basilicas centred on Gortyn, and ended it in upheaval. Earthquakes, plague and the collapse of Mediterranean security shrank its cities, and in the 820s Arab settlers took the island and founded the Emirate of Crete. Byzantine rule was only restored in 961.

Middle Byzantine Period (Crete, AD 900–A.label: Middle Byzantine Period
Middle Byzantine Period (Crete, AD 900–A.prose:
[Crete, AD 900–AD 1199] Middle Byzantine Period. Parent period: Byzantine. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Byzantine forces retook the island from its Arab emirate in 961, and a wave of church building, monastic foundation and resettlement followed. Fresco-painted small churches survive in the hundreds from these centuries, and noble families were transplanted from Constantinople to secure the island. Venetian rule replaced Byzantine after the Fourth Crusade.

Classical Period (Crete, 480 BC–324 BC).label: Classical Period
Classical Period (Crete, 480 BC–324 BC).prose:
[Crete, 480 BC–324 BC] Classical Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete's Bronze Age glory was long gone; the island was now a mosaic of quarrelsome city-states such as Knossos, Gortyn and Lyttos, largely outside the great power struggles of mainland Greece. Its most famous monument is the Gortyn law code, inscribed on stone and preserving detailed rules on inheritance, marriage and the status of slaves. Cretan archers and mercenaries were in demand abroad, and the island had a reputation for piracy.

Middle Minoan Period (Crete, 2050 BC–167.label: Middle Minoan Period
Middle Minoan Period (Crete, 2050 BC–167.prose:
[Crete, 2050 BC–1676 BC] Middle Minoan Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The age of Crete's first palaces, when Knossos, Phaistos and Malia became court-centred complexes combining storerooms, shrines and workshops under central management. Writing appears in the form of Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A, seal-stones proliferate, and the wheel-made polychrome Kamares ware becomes one of the finest ceramics of the Bronze Age Mediterranean. Earthquake destruction around 1700 BC was followed by even more ambitious rebuilding.

Ottoman Period (Crete, AD 1650–AD 1899).label: Ottoman Period
Ottoman Period (Crete, AD 1650–AD 1899).prose:
[Crete, AD 1650–AD 1899] Ottoman Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

Late Minoan Period (Crete, 1675 BC–1051.label: Late Minoan Period
Late Minoan Period (Crete, 1675 BC–1051.prose:
[Crete, 1675 BC–1051 BC] Late Minoan Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

The final chapter of Bronze Age Crete, opening with the island's palatial civilisation at its most confident - Marine Style pottery, frescoed halls, wide trade with Egypt and the Levant - and running through the eruption of Thera and the fiery destructions of the country villas. Mycenaean Greeks took control at Knossos and kept accounts in Linear B, the earliest readable Greek. The period closes with palaces abandoned, populations retreating to mountain refuges, and Crete entering the Iron Age.

Early Byzantine I Period (Crete, AD 400–.label: Early Byzantine I Period
Early Byzantine I Period (Crete, AD 400–.prose:
[Crete, AD 400–AD 699] Early Byzantine I Period. Parent period: Early Byzantine. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete was a peaceful and prosperous province, exporting grain and wine and studded with large three-aisled basilicas; Gortyn, its capital, held one of the island's great churches at Ayios Titos. Rural settlement was dense and widely dispersed across the island. Earthquakes, plague and the wider crises of the seventh century brought the boom to an end.

Modern Period (Crete, AD 1900–AD 2015).label: Modern Period
Modern Period (Crete, AD 1900–AD 2015).prose:
[Crete, AD 1900–AD 2015] Modern Period. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Crete entered the century in political limbo, an autonomous state under great-power supervision, and was formally joined to Greece in 1913. German paratroopers seized the island in the fierce battle of 1941, and the brutal occupation and mountain resistance that followed are still central to local memory. Since the 1960s mass tourism and intensive olive and greenhouse agriculture have reshaped the coast, while excavation at Knossos, Phaistos and elsewhere turned the Minoan past into a national and international symbol.

Early Roman Period (Crete, 100 BC–AD 249.label: Early Roman Period
Early Roman Period (Crete, 100 BC–AD 249.prose:
[Crete, 100 BC–AD 249] Early Roman Period. Parent period: Roman. Period definition from Priniatikos Pyrgos Periodization — Frank Lynam, 2015.

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

Roman (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 394).label: Roman
Roman (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 394).prose:
[Egypt, 29 BC–AD 394] Roman. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Naqada I-early II (Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 B.label: Naqada I-early II
Naqada I-early II (Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 B.prose:
[Upper Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 BC] Naqada I-early II. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Farming villages along the Upper Egyptian Nile produced the distinctive black-topped red pottery and finely worked flint and stone vessels that define early predynastic culture. Cemeteries show growing gaps in wealth, with some graves crowded with imported goods and others nearly bare. These centuries laid the demographic and cultural groundwork from which the first Egyptian kingdoms emerged.

Maadi/Buto I (Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 BC).label: Maadi/Buto I
Maadi/Buto I (Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 BC).prose:
[Lower Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 BC] Maadi/Buto I. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

The distinctive culture of Lower Egypt before unification, known from settlements at Maadi near Cairo and Buto in the Delta, with subterranean houses, large storage jars and a plain, practical material culture very different from the elaborate graves of Upper Egypt. Copper from Sinai, imported Levantine pottery and donkey transport show these communities acting as Egypt's gateway to Palestine. They were eventually absorbed as Upper Egyptian Naqada culture expanded northwards.

Persian Period (Egypt, 524 BC–401 BC).label: Persian Period
Persian Period (Egypt, 524 BC–401 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 524 BC–401 BC] Persian Period. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.

Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2669 BC–2167 BC).label: Old Kingdom
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2669 BC–2167 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2669 BC–2167 BC] Old Kingdom. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

Early A-group (Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 BC).label: Early A-group
Early A-group (Egypt, 3999 BC–3399 BC).prose:
[Lower Nubia, 3999 BC–3399 BC] Early A-group. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Farming and herding communities in Lower Nubia buried their dead with fine black-topped pottery and imported Egyptian jars, showing they were already trading up and down the Nile with Predynastic Egypt. They handled the flow of ivory, ebony, incense and gold coming north from inner Africa, which made control of this stretch of river valuable. Their rising prosperity foreshadows the wealthy Terminal A-Group rulers later crushed by early Egyptian kings.

Buto II (Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC).label: Buto II
Buto II (Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC).prose:
[Lower Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC] Buto II. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Occupation layers at Tell el-Fara'in in the north-western Nile Delta, the key site for the Lower Egyptian culture that developed separately from the Naqada communities of the south. Excavations reached these levels only by pumping out groundwater, recovering local pottery and light mudbrick and reed architecture from a marshland town. The material shows a Delta world with its own traditions and its own contacts across the northern Sinai.

Second Persian Period (Egypt, 342 BC–331.label: Second Persian Period
Second Persian Period (Egypt, 342 BC–331.prose:
[Egypt, 342 BC–331 BC] Second Persian Period. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Artaxerxes III reconquered Egypt after some six decades of independence, ending native rule under Nectanebo II and installing the short-lived Thirty-first Dynasty of Persian satraps. Achaemenid control was resented, remembered for the plundering of temples, and it collapsed almost at once when Alexander the Great arrived and was welcomed as a liberator. Egypt would not be ruled by an Egyptian again for over two thousand years.

Naqada IIIb (Egypt, 3149 BC–2949 BC).label: Naqada IIIb
Naqada IIIb (Egypt, 3149 BC–2949 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 3149 BC–2949 BC] Naqada IIIb. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

The "Dynasty 0" rulers - Scorpion, Ka, Narmer - extended control over the whole Nile valley, and the famous Narmer Palette commemorates the union of Upper and Lower Egypt in the imagery kings would reuse for three millennia. Serekh-marked pottery from Palestine shows Egyptian interests reaching the Levant. State formation was essentially complete by the end of the phase.

Predynastic (Egypt, 4499 BC–2949 BC).label: Predynastic
Predynastic (Egypt, 4499 BC–2949 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 4499 BC–2949 BC] Predynastic. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Farming villages along the Nile grew into competing chiefdoms with cemeteries, craft workshops and long-distance trade in lapis, cedar and gold. Naqada-culture potters, flint-knappers and stone-vase makers reached extraordinary technical heights, and the imagery on their palettes and painted jars — kings smiting enemies, sacred boats, animal standards — is already the visual language of pharaonic Egypt. It ends with the unification of the Nile Valley under a single ruler.

Naqada IIIc (Egypt, 2949 BC–2799 BC).label: Naqada IIIc
Naqada IIIc (Egypt, 2949 BC–2799 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2949 BC–2799 BC] Naqada IIIc. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

The First Dynasty ruled from a new administrative centre at Memphis while burying its kings in great mudbrick tombs at Abydos, surrounded by rows of sacrificed retainers. Writing moved from simple labels to full accounting and royal annals, and standardised jar sealings track a working state economy. It is the moment Egypt becomes a recognisably pharaonic society.

Badarian (Middle Egypt) (Egypt, 4499 BC–.label: Badarian (Middle Egypt)
Badarian (Middle Egypt) (Egypt, 4499 BC–.prose:
[Middle Egypt, 4499 BC–3999 BC] Badarian (Middle Egypt). UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Villages along the desert edge near el-Badari produced Egypt's earliest well-defined farming culture, growing emmer and barley, herding cattle, sheep and goats, and weaving linen. They are best known for exquisitely thin, rippled black-topped red pottery, ivory combs and spoons, and copper and glazed steatite beads. Their cemeteries, set apart from the living and stocked with grave goods, contain the seeds of the funerary beliefs that later defined pharaonic Egypt.

Late Naqada II (Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC).label: Late Naqada II
Late Naqada II (Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC).prose:
[Upper Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC] Late Naqada II. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Egypt's late predynastic villages were consolidating into a handful of powerful centres at Hierakonpolis, Naqada and Abydos, with rulers buried in outsize tombs stocked with imported goods. Decorated pottery showing boats, standards and figures reflects an emerging shared iconography of power. Contacts with Mesopotamia and the Levant brought in cylinder seals and motifs that fed directly into the imagery of the first pharaohs.

Early Dynastic (Egypt, 2949 BC–2669 BC).label: Early Dynastic
Early Dynastic (Egypt, 2949 BC–2669 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2949 BC–2669 BC] Early Dynastic. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1085 B.label: Third Intermediate Period
Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1085 B.prose:
[Egypt, 1085 BC–663 BC] Third Intermediate Period. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

A long stretch of divided rule in which no single king controlled the whole Nile valley. Pharaohs of Libyan descent ruled the Delta while Thebes answered to a priestly dynasty of Amun, and royal tombs were tucked into the temple enclosure at Tanis - one of the few Egyptian royal burials found nearly intact. Kushite kings from Nubia later reunified the country, only for Assyrian invasion to end the period and usher in the Saite revival.

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1547 BC–1085 BC).label: New Kingdom
New Kingdom (Egypt, 1547 BC–1085 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1547 BC–1085 BC] New Kingdom. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Buto IV (Egypt, 3149 BC–2949 BC).label: Buto IV
Buto IV (Egypt, 3149 BC–2949 BC).prose:
[Lower Egypt, 3149 BC–2949 BC] Buto IV. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Continued life of the Delta town at Tell el-Fara'in as Egypt came together under its earliest dynasties, now fully within the material world of the unified state. Buto's importance was lasting: it became the cult seat of the cobra goddess Wadjet and, paired with Nekhen in the south, one of the two symbolic capitals invoked in royal titles for three thousand years.

Neolithic (Egypt, 5999 BC–4499 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Egypt, 5999 BC–4499 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 5999 BC–4499 BC] Neolithic. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Middle A-group (Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC).label: Middle A-group
Middle A-group (Egypt, 3399 BC–3299 BC).prose:
[Lower Nubia, 3399 BC–3299 BC] Middle A-group. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Nubian communities along the Nile south of the First Cataract herded cattle, made fine thin-walled painted pottery, and traded with the Egyptian towns downstream. Increasing quantities of Egyptian jars, copper and stone vessels in their graves show how tightly they were tied into the exchange of incense, ivory, gold and ebony from the south. Their wealth, and eventually their independence, would be extinguished as the unified Egyptian state pushed into Lower Nubia.

Buto III (Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC).label: Buto III
Buto III (Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC).prose:
[Lower Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC] Buto III. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

The levels at Tell el-Fara'in in which the distinctive Lower Egyptian material culture gives way to pottery and tools in the Upper Egyptian Naqada style. This is the clearest stratigraphic evidence anywhere for the cultural absorption of the Delta into a single Egyptian tradition, the process that preceded political unification under the first kings.

Naqada IIIa (Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC).label: Naqada IIIa
Naqada IIIa (Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC).prose:
[Upper Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC] Naqada IIIa. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Rival centres at Abydos, Hierakonpolis and Naqada consolidated into larger territorial powers ruled by kings whose names appear on jars and labels. Tomb U-j at Abydos, packed with hundreds of imported wine jars and small bone tags bearing the earliest known hieroglyphic signs, marks the beginning of Egyptian writing. Bureaucracy, taxation and royal display all take recognisable shape here.

Naqada IIId (Egypt, 2799 BC–2669 BC).label: Naqada IIId
Naqada IIId (Egypt, 2799 BC–2669 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2799 BC–2669 BC] Naqada IIId. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

The Second Dynasty saw political friction - possibly a north-south split - reflected in the shifting royal names and burial places, ending with Khasekhemwy's massive brick funerary enclosure at Abydos. Stone architecture, quarrying and the organisation of labour advanced sharply. Within a generation these skills produced Djoser's Step Pyramid and the age of pyramid building.

Late Period (Egypt, 663 BC–331 BC).label: Late Period
Late Period (Egypt, 663 BC–331 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 663 BC–331 BC] Late Period. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2167 B.label: First Intermediate Period
First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2167 B.prose:
[Egypt, 2167 BC–2039 BC] First Intermediate Period. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Central authority collapsed after the long reign of Pepi II, and Egypt broke into competing regional powers - provincial governors ruling as local dynasts, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Low Nile floods, famine and disorder colour the literature written afterwards, but tomb goods and inscriptions show provincial workshops and local elites flourishing. Funerary practices once reserved for kings spread to lesser officials, laying groundwork for the Coffin Texts. The Theban victory that ended the era produced the reunified Middle Kingdom.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

A divided Egypt, with the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the Delta from Avaris, a rump Theban kingdom in the south, and the Kushite kings of Kerma pressing the frontier. Trade with the Levant and the Aegean flourished at Avaris even as pharaonic art and building shrank. The Theban wars of liberation under Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and finally Ahmose reunified the country and launched the New Kingdom.

Later occupation of the Delta town at Tell el-Fara'in, spanning the early centuries of the pharaonic state. The site's waterlogged setting has preserved settlement remains of a kind rarely recovered in the Delta, where most ancient towns lie buried beneath river silt or modern fields.

Alexander took Egypt from the Persians without a fight, was welcomed as a liberator, consulted the oracle of Ammon at Siwa and founded Alexandria on the coast. After his death his general Ptolemy took control of the country as satrap, keeping the Egyptian administrative machinery but installing a Greek-speaking ruling class at its head.

In Lower Nubia a wealthy elite emerged, best known from the large tombs at Qustul with their incense burners, imported Egyptian wine jars and stone vessels. Control of trade in gold, ebony, ivory and incense flowing north made these rulers rich enough to rival their contemporaries in Upper Egypt. Their culture disappears abruptly around the time Egypt unified, apparently swept aside by early pharaonic expansion up the Nile.

Alexander's general Ptolemy seized Egypt after his death and founded a Greek-speaking dynasty that ruled from Alexandria for nearly three centuries. The city became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean, with its Library, Museum and lighthouse, while the countryside kept its temples and priesthoods - pharaonic architecture built by kings with Macedonian names. The line ended with Cleopatra VII, whose defeat alongside Mark Antony delivered Egypt to Rome.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.

Crete's Bronze Age glory was long gone; the island was now a mosaic of quarrelsome city-states such as Knossos, Gortyn and Lyttos, largely outside the great power struggles of mainland Greece. Its most famous monument is the Gortyn law code, inscribed on stone and preserving detailed rules on inheritance, marriage and the status of slaves. Cretan archers and mercenaries were in demand abroad, and the island had a reputation for piracy.

The unravelling of Old Europe's tell-dwelling farming societies. The great painted-pottery cultures of the Carpathian and Danubian lands broke up, copper metallurgy and settlement patterns changed, and new communities appear with cord-decorated pottery, more herding, horse bones and burials under mounds - developments long linked to contact with, or movement from, the Pontic steppe, and leading directly into the Bronze Age.

Illyrian communities in what is now Albania shifted from hillforts to genuine towns with fortification walls, streets and public buildings, minting coins and absorbing goods and ideas from the Greek colonies at Apollonia and Epidamnos. Local dynasts built up kingdoms strong enough to fight Macedon. The urban centres of this era became the foundation for the later Roman cities of Illyricum.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Bulgaria spent much of this stretch inside the Byzantine Empire after the fall of the First Bulgarian state, then broke free in 1185 to build a Second Empire ruled from Tarnovo, whose churches, painted tombs and silver coinage mark a confident revival. Ivan Asen II briefly made it the dominant power in the Balkans before Mongol raids, noble feuding and territorial splintering wore it down. Ottoman armies took Tarnovo and then Vidin, ending Bulgarian independence for nearly five centuries.

The Zarubintsy culture occupied the middle Dnipro and Prypiat, its fibulae, pottery and fortified settlements showing strong Celtic La Tène influence transmitted through Central Europe. Bastarnae and other groups moved through the region, and Sarmatian horsemen displaced the Scythians on the open steppe, confining the last Scythians to Crimea. Trade with the Greek Black Sea cities and, increasingly, with Rome brought coins and wine amphorae far inland.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

Rome absorbed the old Mauretanian kingdom into the province of Tingitana, holding the northern plains and coast while the interior remained beyond direct control. Towns like Volubilis, Lixus and Tingis grew rich on olive oil, grain and the export of wild animals, leaving mosaics, bronzes and forums that are still the best-preserved ancient ruins in the country; the army largely withdrew in the later third century, though a coastal foothold persisted.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.

Copper Age communities in the Ljubljana Marshes built pile-dwelling villages on wooden platforms above the wetlands, leaving waterlogged deposits that preserve wood, textiles and tools normally lost. From one of them comes the oldest known wooden wheel and axle, evidence that wheeled transport was in use here in the late fourth millennium. Copper tools, Bell Beaker pottery and long-distance contacts mark the transition towards the Bronze Age.

Rome pushed north-east from the colony at Aquileia into the world of the Iron Age Alpine and Adriatic peoples, trading before it conquered. Local hillforts and cemeteries fill with Italic wine vessels, coinage and weapons, showing communities drawn into Mediterranean commerce well before annexation. By the time of Augustus the region had been incorporated outright, and the town of Emona was founded to hold the route into Italy.

Illyria and Epirus settled into provincial life under the early emperors, with the Via Egnatia carrying traffic from the Adriatic ports of Dyrrachium and Apollonia towards Macedonia and Constantinople's future site. Roman colonies, forums, theatres and aqueducts reshaped older Greek and Illyrian towns such as Buthrotum, and Latin spread inland alongside Greek on the coast. Local elites bought into Roman citizenship and civic building.

The Chernyakhov culture spread across the forest-steppe — a mixed population of Goths, Sarmatians and local farmers using wheel-made pottery, Roman coins and imported wine. Gothic power was shattered by the Huns around 375, sending refugees into the Roman Empire and beginning the migrations that reshaped Europe. The Greek cities of the coast shrank and the Bosporan Kingdom faded, while Slavic groups emerge into visibility in the written sources for the first time.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

Burial under earthen mounds, often used and reused over centuries by the same groups, is the defining feature of the period and continued long afterwards, which is why archaeologists have argued about its links to the later Illyrian tribes.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

The age when the Illyrian south was drawn into the Hellenistic world: fortified cities such as Byllis, Amantia and Phoinike were built with monumental walls, theatres and stoas, coinage circulated widely, and local dynasts ruled alongside the Greek colonies of the coast. It closed with Rome's defeat of Macedon and the capture of the Illyrian king Gentius, which brought the region under Roman control.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

The western empire dissolved into barbarian kingdoms: Ostrogothic rule under Theoderic preserved much of Roman administration at Ravenna, until Justinian's twenty-year Gothic War devastated the peninsula and the Lombards seized the north in 568. Cities shrank, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and bishops and monasteries took over civic leadership. It was also an age of extraordinary art - Ravenna's mosaics - and of the Rule of St Benedict.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Italy shifted from scattered farming hamlets to dense, organised settlements: pile-built villages around the northern lakes, the embanked terramare of the Po plain, and transhumant herding communities in the Apennines. Bronze axes, swords and fibulae circulated along routes linking the peninsula to central Europe, the Aegean and Mycenaean traders who reached southern coasts and Sicily. The collapse of the terramare and the spread of cremation urnfields at the end of the era set up the Villanovan and Etruscan world.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

Byzantine control over the Albanian lands was repeatedly challenged by Bulgarians, Normans crossing from Italy, Venetians and Serbs, and the coastal cities of Durrës and Vlora changed hands again and again. Out of this contest emerged the first native polities, the Principality of Arbanon and later the Angevin Kingdom of Albania, and the earliest written references to Albanians as a distinct people. Fortified towns, Orthodox churches with fresco cycles and Catholic cathedrals on the coast reflect a land caught between Rome and Constantinople.

From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Vandal raiders and later Byzantine garrisons touched the Mediterranean coast, but the interior went its own way. This was the political landscape the Arab armies would encounter in the following century.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Byzantine authority over the Serbian lands gave way to independent principalities and then, under the Nemanjić dynasty, to a kingdom and briefly an empire under Stefan Dušan. Wealth from silver mines paid for fresco-covered monastery churches such as Studenica and Gračanica, some of the finest medieval painting in Europe. The empire fragmented after Dušan's death, and the defeat at Kosovo in 1389 opened the way to Ottoman domination.

Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Greek settlers from Miletos and other Ionian cities planted colonies along the northern Black Sea shore — Berezan, Olbia, Panticapaeum, Theodosia — turning the coast into a frontier of the Greek world. They exported grain, fish and slaves southward and imported wine, oil and painted pottery, while dealing daily with the Scythian nomads of the steppe. The mixing produced the distinctive Graeco-Scythian art and the wealthy city-states that shaped the region for the next thousand years.

A state formed when Scandinavian Rus rulers and Slavic tribes came together along the Dnipro trade route from the Baltic to Byzantium, with Kyiv as its capital. Volodymyr's conversion in 988 brought Byzantine Christianity, Cyrillic literacy, stone churches and law codes such as the Ruska Pravda; Yaroslav the Wise married his daughters into half the courts of Europe. Princely rivalries split the realm into competing principalities, and the Mongol storming of Kyiv in 1240 ended its unity, though its churches, chronicles and dynastic memory shaped everything that followed.

Copper objects and new prestige goods appear alongside a long-established way of life based on herding, farming and coastal foraging. Communal burials and the distinctive Bell Beaker pottery found on the Atlantic coast show that Morocco's communities were tied into exchange networks reaching across the Strait of Gibraltar to Iberia.

Runaway peasants and frontiersmen on the lower Dnipro formed self-governing warrior communities, fortified at the Zaporozhian Sich, raiding Ottoman coasts and electing their own hetmans. Khmelnytsky's 1648 rising against Polish rule created a Cossack state, then drew Muscovy into the region and set off decades of war known as the Ruin. Cossack autonomy was steadily eroded by St Petersburg until Catherine II destroyed the Sich in 1775 — but the era became the central myth of Ukrainian national identity.
