The unravelling of Old Europe's tell-dwelling farming societies. The great painted-pottery cultures of the Carpathian and Danubian lands broke up, copper metallurgy and settlement patterns changed, and new communities appear with cord-decorated pottery, more herding, horse bones and burials under mounds - developments long linked to contact with, or movement from, the Pontic steppe, and leading directly into the Bronze Age.

In the far northwest of Africa the Bronze Age is thin and hard to see: metal remained rare, and communities largely continued older herding and farming ways of life. Its clearest traces are the rock engravings of the High Atlas, where daggers, halberds and axes of unmistakably European type were pecked into the stone, and Bell Beaker pottery that shows contact across the Strait of Gibraltar. Together they hint at exchange linking Morocco with Iberia long before written history.

Enver Hoxha's communist party took power at the end of the Second World War and held Albania in Europe's most rigid isolation — collectivised farms, banned religion, hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers, and successive ruptures with Yugoslavia, the USSR and finally China. The regime collapsed in 1990–91, followed by mass emigration, the ruinous pyramid-scheme crisis of 1997 and a difficult transition to a market economy.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.

Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Occupation and partisan warfare in the Second World War were followed by socialist Yugoslavia and, in 1991, independence after a ten-day war.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Slavic migrations and the collapse of the late Roman urban network reduced most inland towns to hilltop refuges, while Durrës survived as a Byzantine stronghold and the seat of a theme. Christianity persisted but the region became a border zone fought over by Byzantium and the expanding Bulgarian empire. Archaeologically it is a thin, difficult period of scattered cemeteries and reused fortifications, from which the medieval Albanian population emerges.

Emona (Ljubljana) and Celeia (Celje) were laid out on grid plans with walls, drains and cemeteries, and local elites adopted Latin names and Roman gods alongside their own. The route made the region a corridor for armies and, later, for invaders heading into Italy.

Livestock, grain storage and long-distance exchange in obsidian and fine wares mark the shift from scattered settlement to established communities.

Latin inscriptions, funerary monuments and imported goods show a provincial elite living in Roman style alongside a strongly local population.

The western empire dissolved into barbarian kingdoms: Ostrogothic rule under Theoderic preserved much of Roman administration at Ravenna, until Justinian's twenty-year Gothic War devastated the peninsula and the Lombards seized the north in 568. Cities shrank, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and bishops and monasteries took over civic leadership. It was also an age of extraordinary art - Ravenna's mosaics - and of the Rule of St Benedict.

Mines at Las Médulas and Río Tinto, oil shipped in amphorae whose sherds built Rome's Monte Testaccio, and grand cities at Mérida, Italica and Tarraco date from these centuries, as does the spread of Christianity in the later part of the span.

Copper tools, Bell Beaker pottery and long-distance contacts mark the transition towards the Bronze Age.

Sarmatian horsemen dominated the steppe while the Zarubintsy communities of the forest-steppe farmed and traded northward. Roman denarii, wheel-made tableware and wine amphorae turn up hundreds of kilometres beyond any frontier, a measure of how far imperial goods reached.

Copper metallurgy spread across the Iberian peninsula alongside the first walled settlements, such as Los Millares in the southeast, with bastioned enclosures, collective tholos and megalithic tombs, and rich grave goods of ivory, ostrich eggshell and Atlantic amber. Communal burial and long-distance exchange point to societies growing more unequal and more organised, while irrigation and metalworking reshaped the countryside. Near its end came the Bell Beaker phenomenon, whose distinctive drinking vessels and archer's kit turn up from Portugal to central Europe. The fortified towns and copper daggers of these centuries set the stage for the Bronze Age El Argar culture.

Illyrian communities in the interior fortified hilltop settlements and buried their leading families under tumuli with weapons, bronze ornaments and imported goods. Greek pottery and metalwork arriving from the Adriatic colonies show these groups plugged into wider Mediterranean trade, and some settlements begin to take on genuinely urban form. It is the world in which the Dardanian and other Illyrian polities that later fought Macedon and Rome took shape.

Mounted nomads from the Asian steppe shattered the Gothic kingdoms of the Pontic region and set whole peoples fleeing westward across the Danube, the trigger for the great migrations that broke the western Roman Empire. For a few decades a Hunnic confederation, culminating under Attila, extracted tribute from Constantinople and terrorised Gaul and Italy. Their legacy in the region is archaeological — cauldrons, gold-sheathed saddles, artificially elongated skulls — rather than institutional, as the empire dissolved after Attila's death.

With Roman authority gone, the lands north of the Danube passed through the hands of Gepids, Avars, Slavs, Bulgars and finally the Magyars, who arrived at the end of the ninth century. Towns disappeared in favour of small farming villages with sunken-floored houses and hand-made pots, though hoards of Byzantine coins show trade never wholly stopped. The Slavic settlement of the region and the arrival of the Hungarians in the plain set the ethnic map that later Transylvanian history was built on.

After the Mongol conquest the lands were reshaped politically: Galicia-Volhynia flourished briefly as a kingdom, then was divided as the Grand Duchy of Lithuania absorbed most of the Rus' principalities and Poland took the west. Castles, brick churches and chartered towns with Magdeburg-law privileges mark the period, alongside the Crimean Khanate's rise in the south. It closes with the Union of Lublin, which folded these territories into a single Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

Mounted nomads from the steppe built a powerful confederation that dominated the region for centuries, extracting tribute from farming populations and trading grain to the Greek colonies of the Black Sea coast in exchange for wine and luxury goods. Their royal kurgans, some the size of small hills, held gold pectorals, sword scabbards and vessels showing scenes of Scythian life, much of it made by Greek craftsmen for Scythian patrons. Herodotus described their customs, horse sacrifices and burial rites in detail, and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed him.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Herding of sheep, goats and cattle, together with pottery and cultivated grain, spread across the Moroccan coast, the Rif and the Atlas, taking hold among populations descended from earlier hunter-gatherers. Cardial-impressed pottery in the north points to contact across the Strait with Iberia, while cave sites and shell middens show a mixed economy of farming, herding, fishing and gathering. Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.

The town of Ulpiana, raised to municipal status under Trajan, acquired baths, walls and a forum, and roads linked the region to the Adriatic and the Danube. Latin inscriptions, funerary monuments and imported goods show a provincial elite living in Roman style alongside a strongly local population.

Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

The Roman provinces along the lower Danube and in Thrace became a frontier zone under constant pressure, with Goths, Huns and other groups crossing the river while emperors fortified cities and roads. Christianity spread fast: basilicas and bishoprics appeared at Serdica, Philippopolis and elsewhere, and Serdica hosted a major church council. After the empire split, these lands fell to the eastern half, setting up their long Byzantine future.

The union of Castile and Aragon under the Catholic Monarchs, the fall of Granada and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 created a single confessional monarchy that immediately became an Atlantic empire. American silver funded Habsburg wars in the Netherlands, Italy and Germany while sustaining the literary and artistic Golden Age of Cervantes, Velázquez and the great cathedrals. Decline, the loss of the Portuguese crown and a war of succession brought in the Bourbons and a century of centralising reform.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Arab armies brought Islam to the Maghreb in the seventh century, and Morocco became the base of a succession of dynasties: the Idrisids, who founded Fez, then the Almoravids and Almohads, whose Berber empires ruled from the Sahara to central Spain. Trans-Saharan caravans carried gold, salt and slaves north, funding mosques, madrasas and walled cities. The Marinids and their successors held the country while Christian kingdoms completed the reconquest of Iberia, pushing Portuguese and Spanish forces onto the Moroccan coast.

The Greek cities of the northern Black Sea — Olbia, Chersonesos and the Bosporan kingdom around the Kerch strait — reached their commercial peak, shipping grain to the Aegean and burying their rulers in monumental tumuli. Scythian power on the open steppe gave way to a smaller kingdom in the Crimea and to incoming Sarmatians, keeping the cities under constant pressure. In the 1st century BC the region was pulled into the wars of Mithridates VI and then into the Roman sphere.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

Ottoman rule reshaped Albanian society over more than four centuries: Skanderbeg's long resistance in the fifteenth century became the founding national legend, but after his death the highlands and coastal towns were absorbed into the empire's provincial system. Large numbers converted to Islam, Albanians rose to the highest offices in Istanbul and Cairo, and semi-independent pashas such as Ali of Tepelena carved out near-sovereign domains. Mosques, bridges, bazaars and hillside citadels from these centuries still dominate towns like Berat and Gjirokastër.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

The Danube frontier was consolidated under the first Roman emperors, with legions stationed at Singidunum and Viminacium and a road network binding the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia to Italy. Veteran colonies, mining districts and river forts drew in traders and settlers, and Latin, Roman law and urban planning spread among local Illyrian, Celtic and Thracian communities. The region's importance grew until it eventually produced emperors of its own.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Rome passed from the assassination of Commodus into a century of civil war, plague and currency collapse, then was rebuilt by Diocletian and Constantine as a more bureaucratic, militarised state with new capitals and a Christian emperor. Italy itself lost its privileged position — the court moved to Milan and then Ravenna — and Rome was sacked by the Goths in 410. Visitors see the shift in art too, from naturalistic portraiture to the frontal, hieratic style that leads into Byzantine imagery.

Isin II (Iran, 1099 BC–899 BC).label: Isin II
Isin II (Iran, 1099 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1099 BC–899 BC] Isin II. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The second dynasty of Isin ruled Babylonia after the collapse of Kassite power, its most famous king, Nebuchadnezzar I, raiding deep into Elam and carrying home the statue of Marduk that Elamite armies had taken. That victory was celebrated in poetry for centuries and pushed Marduk to the head of the Babylonian pantheon. For Elam it marked the end of a period of dominance and the beginning of a long dark age in the written record.
Isin II (Iran, 1099 BC–899 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Early Dynastic II (Iran, 2749 BC–2599 BC.label: Early Dynastic II
Early Dynastic II (Iran, 2749 BC–2599 BC.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2749 BC–2599 BC] Early Dynastic II. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

A middle phase in which independent city-states hardened into rivals, each with its patron deity, temple estate and palace. Later Mesopotamian tradition placed its legendary kings, including Gilgamesh of Uruk, in roughly this era. Temple sculpture of wide-eyed worshippers in fringed skirts, made to stand in perpetual prayer on behalf of the donor, belongs to this world.
Early Dynastic II (Iran, 2749 BC–2599 BC.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 599 BC–549 BC).label: Neo-Elamite II
Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 599 BC–549 BC).prose:
[Elam, 599 BC–549 BC] Neo-Elamite II. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Elam's final decades, following the Assyrian sack of Susa, when fragmented kingdoms and princes ruled the lowlands while Persian groups established themselves in Anshan and the highlands. Elamite scribal and administrative traditions passed directly to these newcomers, and within a lifetime Cyrus the Great had absorbed the whole region into Persia.
Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 599 BC–549 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3499.label: Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite
Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3499.prose:
[Elam, 3499 BC–2699 BC] Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. This period corresponds to Proto-Literate period in Mesopotamia. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

At Susa and across the Iranian plateau, administrators adopted an accounting script of their own — Proto-Elamite — written on clay tablets that record livestock, grain and labour but remain largely undeciphered. The system spread remarkably far east, to Tepe Yahya and Shahr-i Sokhta, tracing a network of trading centres handling metal, stone and textiles. When it fell out of use, writing in Iran lapsed for centuries before Elamite cuneiform appeared.
Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3499.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Bronze Age (Iran, 2899 BC–1199 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Iran, 2899 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Iran, 2899 BC–1199 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Early Dynastic III (Iran, 2599 BC–2333 B.label: Early Dynastic III
Early Dynastic III (Iran, 2599 BC–2333 B.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2599 BC–2333 BC] Early Dynastic III. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The richest phase of the early city-state era, ending with conquest by Sargon of Akkad. Royal inscriptions become genuinely historical — border disputes between Lagash and Umma are recorded in detail — and cuneiform is used for literature, hymns and law. The Royal Cemetery of Ur, with its lyres, gold headdresses and mass retainer burials, dates to these centuries.
Early Dynastic III (Iran, 2599 BC–2333 B.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 599 BC–499 BC).label: Neo-Babylonian
Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 599 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 599 BC–499 BC] Neo-Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Judah under Babylonian rule was a diminished, largely rural province, its capital and temple in ruins and its royal house deported. Excavations show towns in the south and the Shephelah abandoned or shrunken while some settlements north of Jerusalem, around Benjamin, carried on. This bleak interval ended when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and permitted exiles to return.
Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 599 BC–499 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Achaemenid (Iran, 549 BC–299 BC).label: Achaemenid
Achaemenid (Iran, 549 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Elam, 549 BC–299 BC] Achaemenid. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Cyrus the Great and his successors welded Iran, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Egypt into the largest empire the world had yet seen, governed through satraps, royal roads and a standardised silver coinage. Persepolis and Susa displayed the empire's wealth in carved processions of tribute-bearers from every subject people. Alexander's invasion brought it down, but its administrative model outlived it.
Achaemenid (Iran, 549 BC–299 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–899 BC).label: Middle Elamite
Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Elam, 1499 BC–899 BC] Middle Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Elam's most powerful era, when kings ruling from Susa and Anshan wrote in Elamite rather than Akkadian and built on a monumental scale. Untash-Napirisha founded the sacred city of Chogha Zanbil with its huge stepped ziggurat, still the best-preserved in the world, and later Shutrukid rulers sacked Babylon and carried off the stele of Hammurabi's laws and the victory monument of Naram-Sin as trophies for Susa. Assyrian and Babylonian counterattacks eventually broke the dynasty.
Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–899 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Late Uruk (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC).label: Late Uruk
Late Uruk (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–3099 BC] Late Uruk. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The world's first cities took shape in the Mesopotamian lowlands, and their institutions, goods and administrators reached deep into the Iranian plateau and Khuzestan. Mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and the earliest clay tablets with proto-cuneiform signs mark the birth of bureaucratic record-keeping. When the Uruk network contracted, Susa and its neighbours went their own way, developing the Proto-Elamite script and state.
Late Uruk (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999.node: Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC)
Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999.label: Susa I archaeological period
Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999.prose:
[Elam, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Susa I archaeological period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. This period designates prehistoric Susa and corresponds to Ubaid period in Mesopotamia. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Susa's earliest urban phase, dominated by a monumental mud-brick terrace and an extensive cemetery beside it. Its painted funerary beakers, with geometric animals stretched to fit the vessel, are icons of Iranian prehistory, and the copper tools and seals buried with them point to emerging craft specialisation and social hierarchy on the Susiana plain.
Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Kassite (Iran, 1599 BC–1099 BC).label: Kassite
Kassite (Iran, 1599 BC–1099 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–1099 BC] Kassite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

After the Hittite raid that toppled Hammurabi's dynasty, Kassite kings—outsiders of uncertain origin—ruled Babylonia for close to four centuries, the longest single dynasty in Mesopotamian history. They stabilised the south, corresponded as equals with Egypt's pharaohs in the Amarna letters, built the new capital of Dur-Kurigalzu, and left the carved kudurru stones that recorded royal land grants.
Kassite (Iran, 1599 BC–1099 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Ur III (Iran, 2099 BC–1999 BC).label: Ur III
Ur III (Iran, 2099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC] Ur III. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The Third Dynasty of Ur built a tightly administered state that reached across the Iranian lowlands, holding Susa and planting garrisons and governors in the Zagros foothills. Its scribes produced tens of thousands of accounting tablets recording livestock, labour and grain in obsessive detail, the densest bureaucratic archive of the ancient world. The empire fell when Elamite forces sacked Ur, an event lamented in Sumerian poetry for centuries afterwards.
Ur III (Iran, 2099 BC–1999 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Old Babylonian (Iran, 1799 BC–1699 BC).label: Old Babylonian
Old Babylonian (Iran, 1799 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1799 BC–1699 BC] Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.
Old Babylonian (Iran, 1799 BC–1699 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Jamdat Nasr (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC).label: Jamdat Nasr
Jamdat Nasr (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Jamdat Nasr. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The phase between the first Uruk cities and the Early Dynastic world, marked by distinctive polychrome painted jars and by the spread of proto-cuneiform tablets recording rations, land and livestock. Writing was still pictographic and administrative rather than literary, but the bureaucratic habits of temple economies were taking shape. Sites across the Iranian plateau show how far Mesopotamian styles and accounting practices travelled.
Jamdat Nasr (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Prehistoric (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC).label: Prehistoric
Prehistoric (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Elam, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Prehistoric. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Late Chalcolithic communities on the Iranian plateau and in Khuzestan used mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, copper metallurgy and clay tokens and seals to track goods. Susa emerged as a major centre in close contact with Mesopotamian Uruk, and the accounting systems developed here fed directly into the invention of writing.
Prehistoric (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC).label: Neo-Elamite I
Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Elam, 899 BC–599 BC] Neo-Elamite I. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The first phase of Elam's revival, when local rulers reasserted themselves in Susiana and the highlands and began intervening in Babylonian politics against Assyria. Written sources are thin and largely Assyrian, but rock reliefs and rebuilt sanctuaries show royal ambition returning after centuries of obscurity.
Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Neo-Assyrian (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC).label: Neo-Assyrian
Neo-Assyrian (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 899 BC–599 BC] Neo-Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Assyrian armies pushed repeatedly into the Zagros in these centuries, campaigning for horses, tribute and control of the trade routes across the Iranian plateau, and leaving royal inscriptions and reliefs that give the first written glimpses of the Medes and Persians. Local fortified centres and elite burials, such as those at Hasanlu and Ziwiye, reflect both Assyrian pressure and the wealth it drew in. The eventual Median coalition that helped destroy Assyria grew out of this long confrontation.
Neo-Assyrian (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Early Uruk (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC).label: Early Uruk
Early Uruk (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Early Uruk. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Southwestern Iran was drawn into the orbit of the emerging urban world of lowland Mesopotamia, adopting its mass-produced, undecorated pottery, its architecture and its systems of accounting with clay tokens and seals. Susa and its neighbours on the Susiana plain grew into centres with monumental buildings and clear differences in wealth. The exchange of highland metal, stone and timber for lowland goods set up a relationship that shaped Elamite civilisation for millennia.
Early Uruk (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Early Dynastic I (Iran, 2899 BC–2749 BC).label: Early Dynastic I
Early Dynastic I (Iran, 2899 BC–2749 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2749 BC] Early Dynastic I. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The opening phase of the southern Mesopotamian sequence that follows the Jemdet Nasr period, felt across the Susiana plain as well. Cities pulled inward behind massive fortification walls — Uruk's is the most famous — as competing centres emerged from the earlier Uruk world. Seal designs shift to dense, repetitive 'brocade' patterns, and cuneiform writing is still largely a tool of accountants rather than storytellers.
Early Dynastic I (Iran, 2899 BC–2749 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Old Elamite (Iran, 2699 BC–1499 BC).label: Old Elamite
Old Elamite (Iran, 2699 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Elam, 2699 BC–1499 BC] Old Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. unsure why GeoDia listed this twice, both inaccurate to the text (2400-2200 B.C. & 2200-2000 B.C.). Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

In the highlands and plains of southwestern Iran, the rulers of Awan, Simashki and later the Sukkalmah dynasty of Susa alternated between war and marriage alliances with the Mesopotamian kingdoms next door. Elamite armies sacked Ur and carried off its last king, and later hauled Babylonian monuments home as trophies. The period produced a distinctive script and language unrelated to any neighbours, and a religious tradition centred on Inshushinak and Napirisha.
Old Elamite (Iran, 2699 BC–1499 BC).source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

Early Bronze Age II (Sicily, 1999 BC–149.node: Early Bronze Age II (Sicily, 1999 BC–1499 BC)
Early Bronze Age II (Sicily, 1999 BC–149.label: Early Bronze Age II
Early Bronze Age II (Sicily, 1999 BC–149.prose:
[Sicily, 1999 BC–1499 BC] Early Bronze Age II. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.
Early Bronze Age II (Sicily, 1999 BC–149.source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Thapsos (Sicily, 1499 BC–1199 BC).label: Thapsos
Thapsos (Sicily, 1499 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 1499 BC–1199 BC] Thapsos. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of eastern Sicily, known from the coastal settlement on the Thapsos peninsula near Syracuse, where rectangular houses arranged around courtyards replaced older round huts. Its cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs have yielded Mycenaean, Cypriot and Maltese pottery, showing that Sicilian communities were plugged into long-distance Mediterranean trade centuries before Greek colonists arrived. The wealth of imported goods suggests local elites grew rich as middlemen on the sea routes between the Aegean and the western Mediterranean.
Thapsos (Sicily, 1499 BC–1199 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Middle Bronze Age (Sicily, 1499 BC–1199.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Sicily, 1499 BC–1199.prose:
[Sicily, 1499 BC–1199 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Sicily, 1499 BC–1199.source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Pantalica North (Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC).label: Pantalica North
Pantalica North (Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC] Pantalica North. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

The great necropolis above the Anapo gorge belongs to this phase: thousands of chamber tombs cut into limestone cliffs, serving communities that had abandoned the open coast for defensible inland ridges after the collapse of Mycenaean trade. Grave goods of bronze fibulae, mirrors and wheel-made red-slipped pottery show workshops still working to a high standard, and the so-called Anaktoron, a large megalithic building on the plateau, suggests a chief's residence. Later Greek writers remembered a native king Hyblon here, and these hill communities were the Sikel population Greek colonists met when they landed at Syracuse.
Pantalica North (Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Castelluccian (Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 BC).label: Castelluccian
Castelluccian (Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 BC] Castelluccian. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

The Early Bronze Age culture of southeastern Sicily, known from hilltop villages and, above all, from cemeteries of rock-cut tombs whose entrances were sometimes closed with slabs carved in spirals. Its potters painted dark geometric bands on pale burnished vessels, and carved bone plaques found in graves resemble objects from the Aegean and Malta, evidence that Sicily sat on early Mediterranean exchange routes.
Castelluccian (Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Late Copper Age (Sicily, 2999 BC–2499 BC.label: Late Copper Age
Late Copper Age (Sicily, 2999 BC–2499 BC.prose:
[Sicily, 2999 BC–2499 BC] Late Copper Age. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

The last pre-Bronze Age centuries on the island, associated with the Malpasso and Sant'Ippolito styles, when communities buried their dead in rock-cut chamber tombs and worked small amounts of copper. Pottery and metal types show contacts with the Italian mainland, Malta and the wider Mediterranean. Out of this grew the Castelluccio culture, with its fortified villages and carved tomb facades.
Late Copper Age (Sicily, 2999 BC–2499 BC.source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Cassabile (Sicily, 899 BC–733 BC).label: Cassabile
Cassabile (Sicily, 899 BC–733 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 899 BC–733 BC] Cassabile. Table 1 lists more phase names by sites. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

Named after a vast necropolis of rock-cut chamber tombs in the limestone gorges near Syracuse, this early Iron Age phase of eastern Sicily follows the hilltop settlement pattern of Pantalica. Its people made distinctive bronze fibulae, mirrors and basins, and their metalwork shows contact with Italy and the wider Mediterranean on the eve of Greek colonisation. Within a generation or two of its close, Corinthian and Chalcidian settlers were founding cities on the same coast.
Cassabile (Sicily, 899 BC–733 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Finocchito (Sicily, 733 BC–649 BC).label: Finocchito
Finocchito (Sicily, 733 BC–649 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 733 BC–649 BC] Finocchito. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

An indigenous Sikel culture of southeastern Sicily, named after a hilltop settlement inland from Syracuse, with rock-cut chamber tombs, elaborate bronze fibulae and distinctive painted pottery. Its people lived alongside the first Greek colonists on the coast, and their graves fill with imported Greek cups and wine equipment. The mixture shows how quickly local elites absorbed Greek habits in the generations after colonisation.
Finocchito (Sicily, 733 BC–649 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Early Bronze Age (Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 B.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 B.prose:
[Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Sicily, 2499 BC–1499 B.source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Iron Age II (Sicily, 733 BC–449 BC).label: Iron Age II
Iron Age II (Sicily, 733 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 733 BC–449 BC] Iron Age II. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

Greek settlers pushed out from Syracuse and Naxos to found a chain of colonies around the coast, while Phoenicians held the western tip at Motya and Panormus. The indigenous Sikels, Sikanians and Elymians adopted Greek pottery, building styles and writing even as they lost land, and Sikel resistance culminated in Ducetius' short-lived confederation. Sicily's grain, its tyrants and its rivalry with Carthage made the island a major player in the wider Mediterranean world.
Iron Age II (Sicily, 733 BC–449 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Late Bronze Age (Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC).label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Sicily, 1199 BC–899 BC).source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Early Bronze Age I (Sicily, 2499 BC–1999.node: Early Bronze Age I (Sicily, 2499 BC–1999 BC)
Early Bronze Age I (Sicily, 2499 BC–1999.label: Early Bronze Age I
Early Bronze Age I (Sicily, 2499 BC–1999.prose: [Sicily, 2499 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze Age I. Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.
Early Bronze Age I (Sicily, 2499 BC–1999.source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Early Iron Age (I) (Sicily, 899 BC–733 B.label: Early Iron Age (I)
Early Iron Age (I) (Sicily, 899 BC–733 B.prose:
[Sicily, 899 BC–733 BC] Early Iron Age (I). Period definition from Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age — Leighton, Robert, 1958-, 1999.

Indigenous Sicilian communities lived in hilltop villages with rock-cut chamber tombs, producing the painted geometric pottery of the Pantalica South and Finocchito styles. Contact with Phoenician and Greek traders intensified through the period, bringing new goods and ideas. It ends with the founding of the first Greek colonies, which transformed the island's population, economy and politics.
Early Iron Age (I) (Sicily, 899 BC–733 B.source: Sicily before history : an archaeological survey from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age

Late Iron Age (Galicia, 399 BC–99 BC).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (Galicia, 399 BC–99 BC).prose:
[Galicia, 399 BC–99 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from The Celts in Iberia: An Overview — Alberto J. Lorrio, 2005.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.
Late Iron Age (Galicia, 399 BC–99 BC).source: The Celts in Iberia: An Overview

Early Iron Age (Galicia, 799 BC–399 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Galicia, 799 BC–399 BC).prose:
[Galicia, 799 BC–399 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from The Celts in Iberia: An Overview — Alberto J. Lorrio, 2005.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.
Early Iron Age (Galicia, 799 BC–399 BC).source: The Celts in Iberia: An Overview

Hasmonean (Syria, 164 BC–63 BC).label: Hasmonean
Hasmonean (Syria, 164 BC–63 BC).prose:
[ancient Near East, 164 BC–63 BC] Hasmonean. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. see also Mazar, 1992. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible. Volume III, Alexander to Constantine — Meyers, Eric M., 2012.

The dynasty founded by the Maccabees, who drove Seleucid forces from Jerusalem and rededicated the Temple, then turned rebellion into an independent Jewish state. Its rulers combined the high priesthood with kingship, expanded into Galilee, Idumaea and beyond, and forcibly converted conquered populations. Dynastic civil war invited Roman intervention, and Pompey's capture of Jerusalem ended real independence.
Hasmonean (Syria, 164 BC–63 BC).source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible. Volume III, Alexander to Constantine

Cultura de Hallstatt (Germany, 599 BC–44.label: Cultura de Hallstatt
Cultura de Hallstatt (Germany, 599 BC–44.prose:
[Suroeste de Alemania, 599 BC–449 BC] Cultura de Hallstatt. Spatial coverage: France, Germany, Switzerland. Come back later to this source to mine / match to formal p.175-222 & Celtic art periods p.431-450 (SB scanned) though the latter is mainly references to other writers. Period definition from Los celtas : Hispania y Europa — 1993.

The Iron Age culture of the Celtic heartland, named after an Austrian salt-mining town whose brine preserved miners' tools, clothing and bodies. Chieftains were buried under great mounds with four-wheeled wagons, bronze cauldrons and imported Greek and Etruscan wine vessels, evidence of trade running from the Mediterranean deep into temperate Europe. Its wealthy hillfort princedoms gave way to the La Tène culture and the Celtic world that Rome later confronted.

Late Neolithic (Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC).label: Late Neolithic
Late Neolithic (Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC).prose:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic. Applies to "Mainland Greece in general", including Thessaly and the Peloponnese. Period definition from The Greek Neolithic: A New Review — Jean-Paul Demoule, 1993.

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.
Late Neolithic (Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC).source: The Greek Neolithic: A New Review

Final Neolithic (Greece, 4499 BC–3199 BC.label: Final Neolithic
Final Neolithic (Greece, 4499 BC–3199 BC.prose:
[Greece, 4499 BC–3199 BC] Final Neolithic. Applies to "Mainland Greece in general", including Thessaly and the Peloponnese. Period definition from The Greek Neolithic: A New Review — Jean-Paul Demoule, 1993.

Farming communities spread out from the old tell villages of the plains into caves, hilltops and small coastal sites, and herding became a bigger part of the economy. Copper and silver objects appear alongside new pottery styles such as the Attica-Kephala group, and contacts across the Aegean intensified. These centuries laid the groundwork for the metal-using, seafaring societies of the Early Bronze Age.
Final Neolithic (Greece, 4499 BC–3199 BC.source: The Greek Neolithic: A New Review

Early Classic (Mexico, AD 250–AD 600).label: Early Classic
Early Classic (Mexico, AD 250–AD 600).prose:
[Mesoamerica, AD 250–AD 600] Early Classic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Early Classic Period (CA. 250-600 AD)", page 121. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Teotihuacan grew into one of the largest cities in the world, its grid of apartment compounds housing perhaps a hundred thousand people, while its traders, soldiers and iconography reached as far as the Maya lowlands. In the Maya area, dynasties recorded their own histories in stone with the Long Count calendar, and Monte Alban dominated Oaxaca. It is the era in which Mesoamerican urbanism, divine kingship and long-distance politics reached their first full expression.
Early Classic (Mexico, AD 250–AD 600).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Middle to Late Formative (Mexico, 599 BC.node: Middle to Late Formative (Mexico, 599 BC–299 BC)
Middle to Late Formative (Mexico, 599 BC.label: Middle to Late Formative
Middle to Late Formative (Mexico, 599 BC.prose:
[Mesoamerica, 599 BC–299 BC] Middle to Late Formative. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Middle to Late Formative Period (CA. 600-300 BC)", page 119. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Olmec power on the Gulf coast faded and new centres took its place: San José Mogote gave way to hilltop Monte Albán, Zapotec carved stones recorded conquests and dates, and the first big Maya towns rose in the lowlands. Writing, the 260-day calendar and monumental plazas spread across Mesoamerica, along with obsidian and jade exchange over hundreds of kilometres. This is when the political template of later Mesoamerican cities was set.
Middle to Late Formative (Mexico, 599 BC.source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Early Formative (Mexico, 1199 BC–899 BC).label: Early Formative
Early Formative (Mexico, 1199 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Mesoamerica, 1199 BC–899 BC] Early Formative. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Early Formative Period (CA. 1200-CA. 900 BC) Early Mesoamerican Civilization Begins", page 118. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Villages along the Gulf coast and in the highlands grew into the first Mesoamerican societies with hereditary rank, and San Lorenzo became a genuine ceremonial centre. Olmec sculptors carved colossal basalt heads and were-jaguar figures, and their imagery spread through exchange networks reaching Oaxaca, the Valley of Mexico and Chiapas. Maize agriculture, pottery styles and the earliest ballcourts all take recognisable form here.
Early Formative (Mexico, 1199 BC–899 BC).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Formative period (Mexico, 999 BC–AD 250).label: Formative period
Formative period (Mexico, 999 BC–AD 250).prose:
[Mesoamerica, 999 BC–AD 250] Formative period. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Widespread evidence for sedentism marked the start of the Formative period 1000 BC-250 AD", page 116. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Mesoamerica's village era, when settled maize farming, pottery and permanent hamlets spread across the region and quickly gave rise to something more. Olmec centres on the Gulf coast raised earthen mounds and colossal stone heads, and later Preclassic cities such as Cuicuilco, El Mirador and early Monte Albán built pyramids, developed writing and calendars, and organised long-distance trade in jade and obsidian. Nearly everything that defines Classic Maya and Teotihuacan civilisation was worked out here first.
Formative period (Mexico, 999 BC–AD 250).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Late Postclassic (Mexico, AD 1400–AD 152.label: Late Postclassic
Late Postclassic (Mexico, AD 1400–AD 152.prose:
[Mesoamerica, AD 1400–AD 1521] Late Postclassic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Late Postclassic Period (CA. 1400-1521 AD)", page 125. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

The Aztec Triple Alliance, led from Tenochtitlan, extended tribute demands across much of central Mexico, feeding a capital of well over a hundred thousand people built on an island in a lake. Markets, causeways, chinampa gardens and the twin-shrine Templo Mayor made it one of the largest cities in the world at the time. It ended abruptly with the Spanish siege of 1521, after which the city was dismantled and rebuilt as Mexico City.
Late Postclassic (Mexico, AD 1400–AD 152.source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Late Archaic (Mexico, 3999 BC–1999 BC).label: Late Archaic
Late Archaic (Mexico, 3999 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Mesoamerica, 3999 BC–1999 BC] Late Archaic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "The Late Archaic Period (4000-2000 BC)", page 116. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.
Late Archaic (Mexico, 3999 BC–1999 BC).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Late Classic (Mexico, AD 600–AD 900).label: Late Classic
Late Classic (Mexico, AD 600–AD 900).prose:
[Mesoamerica, AD 600–AD 900] Late Classic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Late Classic Period (CA. 600-900 AD)", page 122. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

The height of Classic Maya civilisation, when dozens of rival city-states — Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán, Yaxchilán — raised temple-pyramids and carved stelae recording dynastic history in hieroglyphs, the richest written record of the ancient Americas. With Teotihuacan's collapse, central Mexico fragmented and centres like Cholula, Xochicalco and El Tajín rose in its place, while Monte Albán was abandoned. In the ninth century the southern lowland cities stopped building and recording dates and were largely emptied, one of archaeology's most debated collapses.
Late Classic (Mexico, AD 600–AD 900).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Late Formative (Mexico, 299 BC–AD 1).label: Late Formative
Late Formative (Mexico, 299 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Mesoamerica, 299 BC–AD 1] Late Formative. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Late Formative Period (CA. 300 BC-1 AD)", page 120. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

The Mesoamerican highlands and Maya lowlands filled with their first true cities — Monte Albán terracing its mountaintop, Cuicuilco and then Teotihuacan growing in the Basin of Mexico, and El Mirador raising vast platform pyramids. Hieroglyphic writing, the Long Count calendar and carved monuments celebrating rulers all appear in recognisable form. Much of the political and religious grammar of later Classic civilisation is set here.
Late Formative (Mexico, 299 BC–AD 1).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Middle Formative (Mexico, 899 BC–599 BC).label: Middle Formative
Middle Formative (Mexico, 899 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Mesoamerica, 899 BC–599 BC] Middle Formative. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Middle Formative Period (CA. 900-CA. 600 BC)", page 118. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Olmec civilisation reached its height at La Venta, with earthen pyramids, colossal basalt heads and buried offerings of jade, while an Olmec-influenced art style spread across highland and coastal Mesoamerica. Villages grew into ranked centres at places like Chalcatzingo and in the Valley of Oaxaca, where Monte Albán was founded and the earliest Mesoamerican writing and calendar signs appear. Much of what later Maya and Zapotec kingdoms did with kingship, ritual and art begins here.
Middle Formative (Mexico, 899 BC–599 BC).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Terminal Formative (Mexico, AD 1–AD 250).label: Terminal Formative
Terminal Formative (Mexico, AD 1–AD 250).prose:
[Mesoamerica, AD 1–AD 250] Terminal Formative. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Terminal Formative Period (CA. 1-250 AD)", page 121. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

The centuries when Mesoamerican societies crossed from village-based chiefdoms into true urban states. Monumental centres such as Teotihuacan and Monte Albán expanded rapidly, hieroglyphic writing and the Long Count calendar came into use, and populations concentrated into planned cities with pyramids, plazas and ball courts.
Terminal Formative (Mexico, AD 1–AD 250).source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Middle Postclassic (Mexico, AD 1200–AD 1.label: Middle Postclassic
Middle Postclassic (Mexico, AD 1200–AD 1.prose:
[Mesoamerica, AD 1200–AD 1400] Middle Postclassic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Middle Postclassic Period (CA. 1200-1400)", page 124. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

With Tula fallen, central Mexico fractured into competing city-states settled by migrating groups from the north, each claiming Toltec ancestry to justify its rule. Alliances, tribute and dynastic marriage drove constant warfare in the Basin of Mexico, and a marshy island settlement founded in the 1320s – Tenochtitlan – began its rise. In Yucatan, Mayapan dominated a league of Maya towns, and Mixtec lords in Oaxaca recorded their genealogies in painted screenfold books.
Middle Postclassic (Mexico, AD 1200–AD 1.source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Initial Formative (Mexico, 1999 BC–1199.label: Initial Formative
Initial Formative (Mexico, 1999 BC–1199.prose:
[Mesoamerica, 1999 BC–1199 BC] Initial Formative. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Initial Formative (Preclassic) Period (2000-1200 BCE): Early Mesoamerica", page 116. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

Villages of a few hundred people spread across Mesoamerica, living on maize, beans and squash and making the first widespread pottery. Permanent houses, storage pits and cemeteries appear, and with them the first signs of differences in wealth and status between households. These small communities set the stage for the Olmec centres and the ceremonial architecture that followed.
Initial Formative (Mexico, 1999 BC–1199.source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Epiclassic and Early Postclassic (Mexico.label: Epiclassic and Early Postclassic
Epiclassic and Early Postclassic (Mexico.prose:
[Mesoamerica, AD 750–AD 1200] Epiclassic and Early Postclassic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua. "Epiclassic and Early Postclassic Periods (CA. 750-1200 AD)", page 124. Period definition from The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology — 2012.

With Teotihuacan burned and the southern Maya cities abandoned, power in Mesoamerica fragmented among fortified hilltop centres such as Xochicalco and Cacaxtla, and then coalesced around Tula and Chichén Itzá. Warfare, long-distance trade and militarised imagery of eagles, jaguars and feathered serpents spread widely, and the movements of Nahua-speaking peoples in these centuries set up the political map the Aztecs would later inherit.
Epiclassic and Early Postclassic (Mexico.source: The Oxford handbook of Mesoamerican archeology

Israelite Age (Syria, 1199 BC–585 BC).label: Israelite Age
Israelite Age (Syria, 1199 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Land of Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC] Israelite Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Spatial_coverage_label per page 139 quote, "Therefore, 'the archaeology of the Land of Israel is preferable.'" Also on page 141: "the author proposes...the other two terms, 'Canaanite Age' and 'Israelite Age' to replace 'Bronze Age' and 'Iron Age.'" Sourced from Mazar, 1992, page 29 note 14: "M. Dothan in BAT, pp. 136-41.". Period definition from Biblical archaeology today : proceedings of the International Congress on Biblical Archaeology, Jerusalem, April 1984. — International Congress on Biblical Archaeology (1984 : Jerusalem), 1985.

The Iron Age in the Levant, when Aramaean, Phoenician, Israelite and neo-Hittite kingdoms filled the vacuum left by the collapse of the Bronze Age empires, writing in alphabetic scripts and trading across the Mediterranean. Assyrian armies absorbed them one by one from the ninth century, deporting populations and reorganising the region into provinces. The era closes with Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem and the exile.
Israelite Age (Syria, 1199 BC–585 BC).source: Biblical archaeology today : proceedings of the International Congress on Biblical Archaeology, Jerusalem, April 1984.

Early Canaanite Age (Syria, 3249 BC–2499.label: Early Canaanite Age
Early Canaanite Age (Syria, 3249 BC–2499.prose:
[Land of Israel, 3249 BC–2499 BC] Early Canaanite Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Spatial_coverage_label per page 139 quote, "Therefore, 'the archaeology of the Land of Israel is preferable.'" Also on page 141: "the author proposes...the other two terms, 'Canaanite Age' and 'Israelite Age' to replace 'Bronze Age' and 'Iron Age.'" Sourced from Mazar, 1992, page 29 note 14: "M. Dothan in BAT, pp. 136-41.". Period definition from Biblical archaeology today : proceedings of the International Congress on Biblical Archaeology, Jerusalem, April 1984. — International Congress on Biblical Archaeology (1984 : Jerusalem), 1985.

The term used in Syrian and Levantine scholarship for the region's first urban age, when fortified towns with temples and palaces appeared across the interior and coast. Ebla's palace archives, written in cuneiform on thousands of clay tablets, reveal a kingdom trading in textiles and metals and negotiating with Mari and Akkad. Its destruction, and the emptying of many towns, closed the era.
Early Canaanite Age (Syria, 3249 BC–2499.source: Biblical archaeology today : proceedings of the International Congress on Biblical Archaeology, Jerusalem, April 1984.

Middle Canaanite Age (Syria, 1999 BC–124.label: Middle Canaanite Age
Middle Canaanite Age (Syria, 1999 BC–124.prose:
[Land of Israel, 1999 BC–1249 BC] Middle Canaanite Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Spatial_coverage_label per page 139 quote, "Therefore, 'the archaeology of the Land of Israel is preferable.'" Also on page 141: "the author proposes...the other two terms, 'Canaanite Age' and 'Israelite Age' to replace 'Bronze Age' and 'Iron Age.'" Sourced from Mazar, 1992, page 29 note 14: "M. Dothan in BAT, pp. 136-41.". Period definition from Biblical archaeology today : proceedings of the International Congress on Biblical Archaeology, Jerusalem, April 1984. — International Congress on Biblical Archaeology (1984 : Jerusalem), 1985.

A long span covering the walled city-states of the Middle Bronze Age and their absorption into the empires that followed. Rampart-girt towns such as Ebla, Qatna and Hazor first flourished on inland trade, then became pawns fought over by Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites, with local kings writing to pharaohs in Akkadian. It ends as the palace system frays on the eve of the great Late Bronze Age collapse.
Middle Canaanite Age (Syria, 1999 BC–124.source: Biblical archaeology today : proceedings of the International Congress on Biblical Archaeology, Jerusalem, April 1984.

Victorian (England, AD 1837–AD 1901).label: Victorian
Victorian (England, AD 1837–AD 1901).prose:
[England, AD 1837–AD 1901] Victorian. Dating to the reign of Queen Victoria (1837 CE to 1901 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The age that gave England most of its familiar built landscape: red-brick terraces, mills and pumping stations, railway viaducts, board schools and Gothic Revival churches and town halls. Archaeologically it is a period of mass-produced things — transfer-printed ceramics, glass bottles, clay pipes, tinned food — that let sites be dated almost to the decade. It is also the period when antiquarianism hardened into archaeology, with the first systematic excavations and county societies.

Later Prehistoric (England, 3999 BC–AD 4.label: Later Prehistoric
Later Prehistoric (England, 3999 BC–AD 4.prose:
[England, 3999 BC–AD 43] Later Prehistoric. For monuments that can be identified only to a date range from Neolithic to Iron Age. Circa -4000 BCE to 43 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

This long stretch covers the arrival of farming, the raising of Stonehenge and thousands of barrows, the spread of bronze and then iron, and the hillforts and tribal kingdoms the Romans found on arrival. Landscapes were permanently reshaped: forests cleared, fields laid out, boundaries dug that still show in aerial photographs. Metalwork hoards dropped into rivers and bogs, and richly furnished burials, hint at beliefs and hierarchies that left no written record.

Edwardian (England, AD 1902–AD 1910).label: Edwardian
Edwardian (England, AD 1902–AD 1910).prose:
[England, AD 1902–AD 1910] Edwardian. The period covering the reign of Edward VII (1902 CE to 1910 CE). Do not use for the reigns of Edwards I-VI. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The decade after Victoria's death is remembered for its social confidence: grand hotels, motoring, department stores and a loosening of Victorian formality among the wealthy. It also saw suffragette militancy, strikes, the beginnings of state welfare provision and a fight over the power of the House of Lords. Its architecture and fashions read today as the last flourish before the First World War.

Iron Age (England, 799 BC–AD 43).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (England, 799 BC–AD 43).prose:
[England, 799 BC–AD 43] Iron Age. This period follows on from the Bronze Age and is characterized by the use of iron for making tools and monuments such as hillforts and oppida. The Iron Age is taken to end with the Roman invasion. Circa -800 BCE to 43 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Early Medieval (England, AD 410–AD 1066).label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (England, AD 410–AD 1066).prose:
[England, AD 410–AD 1066] Early Medieval. This dates from the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain (c. 410) to the Norman invasion in 1066 and is to be used for monuments of post Roman, Saxon and Viking date. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Jacobean (England, AD 1603–AD 1625).label: Jacobean
Jacobean (England, AD 1603–AD 1625).prose:
[England, AD 1603–AD 1625] Jacobean. Dating to the reign of James I of England (VI of Scotland). (1603 CE to 1625 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

England under its first Stuart king, newly joined in one person's crown with Scotland. The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 and the sour relations between king and Parliament set the terms of later conflict, while the reign produced the King James Bible, Shakespeare's last plays and the dark tragedies of Webster and Middleton. Overseas, the first permanent English colony took root at Jamestown and the East India Company opened its first factories.

Post Medieval (England, AD 1540–AD 1901).label: Post Medieval
Post Medieval (England, AD 1540–AD 1901).prose:
[England, AD 1540–AD 1901] Post Medieval. Begins with the dissolution of the monasteries (c.1540) and ends with the death of Queen Victoria (1901). Use more specific period where known. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Beginning with the dissolution of the monasteries and the Reformation's stripping of parish churches, these centuries carried England through civil war, the growth of an Atlantic empire, enclosure of open fields, and industrialisation. Excavations of the period yield mass-produced goods - tin-glazed and transfer-printed pottery, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes, machine-made nails - that let sites be dated to within a decade or two. Landscapes changed as thoroughly as objects: hedged fields, canals, railways, mines and terraced workers' housing all belong to this span.

Mid 20th Century (England, AD 1933–AD 19.label: Mid 20th Century
Mid 20th Century (England, AD 1933–AD 19.prose: [England, AD 1933–AD 1966] Mid 20th Century. The second third of the 20th Century of the common era (1933 CE to 1966 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Early 20th Century (England, AD 1901–AD.label: Early 20th Century
Early 20th Century (England, AD 1901–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1901–AD 1932] Early 20th Century. The first third of the 20th century of the common era (1901 CE to 1932 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Edwardian confidence — motor cars, ocean liners, mass newspapers and militant campaigns for women's suffrage — was shattered by the First World War, which killed nearly three quarters of a million British servicemen. Afterwards came votes for women, the first Labour government, the General Strike of 1926 and the slump that followed the 1929 crash. Cinema, radio and suburban housing estates reshaped how ordinary people lived.

Early Iron Age (England, 799 BC–299 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (England, 799 BC–299 BC).prose:
[England, 799 BC–299 BC] Early Iron Age. The earliest subdivision of the Iron Age. Circa -800 BCE to -300 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

Georgian (England, AD 1714–AD 1830).label: Georgian
Georgian (England, AD 1714–AD 1830).prose:
[England, AD 1714–AD 1830] Georgian. Dating to or characteristic of the reigns of any of the first four kings of Great Britain called George (1714 CE to 1830 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The century of the four Georges gave England sash windows, brick terraces, classical proportion and squares laid out to speculative plans, from Bath to Bloomsbury. Beneath the elegance ran rapid change: turnpikes and canals, coal, iron and cotton mills, a booming consumer market in ceramics and tea, and a slave-based Atlantic trade that funded much of it. Excavated Georgian sites are rich in mass-produced tablewares, clay pipes and imported goods.

Medieval (England, AD 1066–AD 1540).label: Medieval
Medieval (England, AD 1066–AD 1540).prose: [England, AD 1066–AD 1540] Medieval. The Medieval period or Middle Ages begins with the Norman invasion (1066) and ends with the dissolution of the monasteries (c.1540). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Bronze Age (England, 2599 BC–699 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (England, 2599 BC–699 BC).prose:
[England, 2599 BC–699 BC] Bronze Age. This period follows on from the Neolithic and is characterized by the increasing use of Bronzework. It is subdivided in the Early, Middle and Late Bronze Age. Circa -2600 BCE to -700 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Elizabethan (England, AD 1558–AD 1603).label: Elizabethan
Elizabethan (England, AD 1558–AD 1603).prose:
[England, AD 1558–AD 1603] Elizabethan. Dating to the reign of Elizabeth I of England (1558 CE to 1603 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The years of Elizabeth I, when the Protestant church settlement bedded down, the Spanish Armada was scattered, and English ships began raiding and trading across the Atlantic. London's population swelled and its new purpose-built playhouses gave Shakespeare and Marlowe their audiences. Portraiture, prodigy houses and elaborate court ritual made the queen herself the central image of the age.

Cold War (England, AD 1946–AD 1991).label: Cold War
Cold War (England, AD 1946–AD 1991).prose:
[England, AD 1946–AD 1991] Cold War. The period of political and military opposition between the major Superpowers (USA and USSR) and their allies. Known as the Cold War as there were no direct military conflicts between the two main protagonists (1946 CE to 1991 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain emerged from the Second World War bankrupt and dependent on American aid, then rebuilt as a nuclear power and NATO's chief European partner, testing its own bomb in 1952. Airfields, radar chains, bunkers and early-warning stations spread across the countryside, while conscription, civil defence drills and CND protests shaped public life. Empire was dismantled at speed even as the country tied itself to Washington and, eventually, to Europe.

Late 20th Century (England, AD 1967–AD 2.label: Late 20th Century
Late 20th Century (England, AD 1967–AD 2.prose:
[England, AD 1967–AD 2000] Late 20th Century. The final third of the 20th century of the common era (1967 CE to 2000 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.
