Coal mines, shipyards and textile mills closed in quick succession, and the economy tilted towards services, finance and North Sea oil while unemployment reshaped whole regions. Postwar migration from the Caribbean and South Asia made cities visibly multicultural, motorways and tower blocks rewrote the built landscape, and Britain joined the European Community in 1973. Computers, plastics and supermarket packaging fill the archaeological record of these decades.

Middle Bronze Age (England, 1599 BC–1199.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (England, 1599 BC–1199.prose:
[England, 1599 BC–1199 BC] Middle Bronze Age. The second subdivision of the Bronze Age. Circa -1600 BCE to -1200 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

Mesolithic (England, 9999 BC–3999 BC).label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (England, 9999 BC–3999 BC).prose:
[England, 9999 BC–3999 BC] Mesolithic. The Middle Stone Age, falling between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic; marks the beginning of a move from a hunter gatherer society towards food producing society. Circa -10000 BCE to -4000 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Late Bronze Age (England, 1199 BC–699 BC.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (England, 1199 BC–699 BC.prose:
[England, 1199 BC–699 BC] Late Bronze Age. The third and latest subdivision of the Bronze Age. Circa -1200 BCE to -700 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Stuart (England, AD 1603–AD 1714).label: Stuart
Stuart (England, AD 1603–AD 1714).prose:
[England, AD 1603–AD 1714] Stuart. Dating to the reign of the Stuart kings of England including the Commonwealth inter-regnum (1603 CE to 1714 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

England under the Stuarts swung violently between royal claims to divine right and parliamentary resistance, producing civil war, the execution of Charles I, a decade of republic under Cromwell, and then restoration. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 settled the argument by installing William and Mary on parliamentary terms, and the Bill of Rights that followed set limits on the crown that still underpin British constitutional practice. It was also the age of Shakespeare's late plays, the King James Bible, the Royal Society, plague and the Great Fire of London, and the first permanent English colonies in America.

Early Neolithic (England, 3999 BC–3299 B.label: Early Neolithic
Early Neolithic (England, 3999 BC–3299 B.prose:
[England, 3999 BC–3299 BC] Early Neolithic. The earliest subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age. Circa -4000 BCE to -3300 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Farming, pottery and domesticated animals arrived in Britain, and within a few generations people were building monuments: earthen long barrows over the bones of the dead, ditched causewayed enclosures for gatherings and feasts, and deep flint mines. Woodland was cleared for cereals and pasture, beginning the long transformation of the British landscape. These communities laid the groundwork for the great henge and stone circle building that followed.

Neolithic (England, 3999 BC–2199 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (England, 3999 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[England, 3999 BC–2199 BC] Neolithic. The New Stone Age, this period follows on from the Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic and is itself succeeded by the Bronze Age. This period is characterized by the practice of a farming economy and extensive monumental constructions. Circa -4000 BCE to -2200 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Middle Iron Age (England, 299 BC–99 BC).label: Middle Iron Age
Middle Iron Age (England, 299 BC–99 BC).prose:
[England, 299 BC–99 BC] Middle Iron Age. The second subdivision of the Iron Age. Circa -300 BCE to -100 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Hillforts, enclosed farmsteads and grain storage pits dominated the landscape, and roundhouse communities produced increasingly regionalised pottery and fine metalwork in flowing La Tène style. Many hillforts were abandoned or slimmed down to fewer, larger centres, hinting at the consolidation of the tribal groupings Roman writers would later name. Bodies and objects placed deliberately in disused pits offer a glimpse of ritual life.

Early Prehistoric (England, 999999 BC–39.label: Early Prehistoric
Early Prehistoric (England, 999999 BC–39.prose:
[England, 999999 BC–3999 BC] Early Prehistoric. For monuments which are characteristic of the Palaeolithic to Mesolithic but cannot be specifically assigned. Circa -1000000 BCE to -4000 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The long stretch of the Old and Middle Stone Age, when small bands of hunters followed herds across a landscape repeatedly transformed by advancing and retreating ice. Britain was periodically abandoned altogether and repopulated, at times joined to the continent by the dry plain of Doggerland. The traces are flint tools, butchered animal bone and rare human remains — the evidence of half a million years of intermittent occupation before farming.

Late Neolithic (England, 2899 BC–2199 BC.label: Late Neolithic
Late Neolithic (England, 2899 BC–2199 BC.prose:
[England, 2899 BC–2199 BC] Late Neolithic. The third and latest subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age. Circa -2900 BCE to -2200 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.

Middle Neolithic (England, 3299 BC–2899.label: Middle Neolithic
Middle Neolithic (England, 3299 BC–2899.prose:
[England, 3299 BC–2899 BC] Middle Neolithic. The second subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age. Circa -3300 BCE to -2900 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Communal long barrows and causewayed enclosures fell out of use, and people began building cursus monuments – enormous parallel-ditched avenues running for miles across the landscape – along with the first great henges. Pottery grew heavier and more elaborately decorated, and forest clearance and herding reshaped the countryside. The earthwork phase of Stonehenge belongs to the end of this stretch of time.

First World War (England, AD 1914–AD 191.label: First World War
First World War (England, AD 1914–AD 191.prose:
[England, AD 1914–AD 1918] First World War. Used to record buildings, defensive monuments and sites dating to, and associated with, the First World War (1914 CE to 1918 CE). For other types of building, such as houses, built during this period use Early 20th Century. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain's first experience of industrialised total war: conscription from 1916, Zeppelin and Gotha raids on civilian towns, rationing, and women entering munitions factories and transport in huge numbers. Nearly three-quarters of a million British servicemen died, and almost every town has a war memorial dating from the years just after. Trench systems, practice grounds, aerodromes and shell-filling factories left archaeological traces across the countryside.

Roman (England, AD 43–AD 410).label: Roman
Roman (England, AD 43–AD 410).prose:
[England, AD 43–AD 410] Roman. The Roman period traditionally begins with the Roman invasion in 43AD and ends with the emperor Honorius directing Britain to see to it's own defence in 410AD. Circa 43 CE to 410 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Prehistoric (England, 999999 BC–AD 43).label: Prehistoric
Prehistoric (England, 999999 BC–AD 43).prose:
[England, 999999 BC–AD 43] Prehistoric. For monuments that can be identified only to a date range from Palaeolithic to Iron Age. Circa -1000000 BCE to 43 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late Chalcolithic communities on the Iranian plateau and in Khuzestan used mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, copper metallurgy and clay tokens and seals to track goods. Susa emerged as a major centre in close contact with Mesopotamian Uruk, and the accounting systems developed here fed directly into the invention of writing.

Late Mesolithic (England, 6999 BC–3999 B.label: Late Mesolithic
Late Mesolithic (England, 6999 BC–3999 B.prose:
[England, 6999 BC–3999 BC] Late Mesolithic. The latest subdivision of the Mesolithic, or Middle Stone Age. Circa -7000 BCE to -4000 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Hunter-gatherers in dense post-glacial woodland made tiny geometric microliths set into composite arrows and worked the coasts, rivers and clearings with fire to draw in game. Rising seas finally drowned Doggerland during this period, cutting Britain off from the Continent and leaving its foragers on an island. Their world ended with the arrival of farming, and the debate over how much they contributed to what came next is still unresolved.

Hanoverian (England, AD 1714–AD 1837).label: Hanoverian
Hanoverian (England, AD 1714–AD 1837).prose:
[England, AD 1714–AD 1837] Hanoverian. Dating to the reign of the monarchs of the House of Hanover (1714 CE to 1837 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain under George I to William IV, when a German-speaking dynasty inherited the throne and real power drifted toward Parliament and the office of prime minister. The period saw the loss of the American colonies, victory over Napoleon, the Act of Union with Ireland, and the first railways and factory towns of industrialisation. Its wealth is visible in Georgian terraces, country houses, porcelain and mahogany furniture.

Early Bronze Age (England, 2599 BC–1599.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (England, 2599 BC–1599.prose:
[England, 2599 BC–1599 BC] Early Bronze Age. The earliest subdivision of the Bronze Age. Circa -2600 BCE to -1600 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

Tudor (England, AD 1485–AD 1603).label: Tudor
Tudor (England, AD 1485–AD 1603).prose:
[England, AD 1485–AD 1603] Tudor. Dating to the reign of the Tudor monarchs. (1485 CE to 1603 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Henry VII took the crown on Bosworth field and his dynasty then remade England: Henry VIII broke with Rome and dissolved the monasteries, Edward VI's regents imposed Protestantism, Mary I burned its adherents, and Elizabeth I settled a compromise church and saw off the Spanish Armada. Royal government grew stronger and more bureaucratic, printing spread, and enclosure and inflation reshaped the countryside. It is also the age of Shakespeare, Marlowe and the first English voyages to the Americas.

20th Century (England, AD 1901–AD 2000).label: 20th Century
20th Century (England, AD 1901–AD 2000).prose:
[England, AD 1901–AD 2000] 20th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 20th Century of the common era (1901 CE to 2000 CE). Previously recorded as 'Modern'. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Two world wars drained the country's wealth and manpower, and the empire that had underwritten its power was dismantled within two decades of 1945. Out of the wars came the welfare state and the National Health Service; out of decolonisation came migration from the Caribbean and South Asia that remade Britain's cities. Heavy industry and coal collapsed, seaside and mill towns emptied, and the country reinvented itself around finance, services and pop culture.

Second World War (England, AD 1939–AD 19.label: Second World War
Second World War (England, AD 1939–AD 19.prose:
[England, AD 1939–AD 1945] Second World War. Used to record buildings, defensive monuments and sites dating to, and associated with, the Second World War (1939 CE to 1945 CE). For other types of building, such as houses, built during this period use Mid 20th Century. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain fought from the first day to the last: evacuation at Dunkirk, the air battle over southern England, and the Blitz that gutted city centres from London to Coventry. Rationing, conscription of women into war work, and the evacuation of children reshaped everyday life, while cracking German codes at Bletchley Park quietly changed the war at sea. Victory came at the cost of exhaustion, debt and the beginning of the end of empire.

Late Iron Age (England, 99 BC–AD 43).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (England, 99 BC–AD 43).prose:
[England, 99 BC–AD 43] Late Iron Age. The third and latest subdivision of the Iron Age. Circa -100 BCE to 43 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Chalcolithic (England, 2499 BC–2199 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (England, 2499 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[England, 2499 BC–2199 BC] Chalcolithic. The transitional period at the end of the Neolithic when metal is first used to make tools and weapons. New burial rites and artefacts appear at the same time as these copper implements appear. Circa -2500 BCE to -2200 BCE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Flavian (England, AD 69–AD 96).label: Flavian
Flavian (England, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[England, AD 69–AD 96] Flavian. Referring to the reigns of the emperors Vespasian (69-79 ), Titus (79-81 CE), and Domitian (81-96 CE), that coincided with the dynasty established after the death of Nero in 69 CE. Circa 69 CE to 96 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Under Vespasian, Titus and Domitian, Roman armies pushed conquest to its furthest extent in Britain: Wales and northern England were subdued, legionary fortresses built at Chester, Caerleon and York, and Agricola campaigned deep into Scotland, winning at Mons Graupius. Towns acquired forums, baths and street grids, and Fishbourne-style villas appeared in the south. Much of the province's characteristic pottery and coin dating hinges on this well-documented building boom.

Hadrianic (England, AD 117–AD 138).label: Hadrianic
Hadrianic (England, AD 117–AD 138).prose:
[England, AD 117–AD 138] Hadrianic. Referring to the reign of Hadrian, 117 to 138 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The decades when Rome stopped trying to conquer the north of Britain and drew a line instead: a wall of stone and turf from the Tyne to the Solway, with milecastles, turrets, forts and a great ditch behind it. It reshaped the frontier economy, drawing soldiers, traders and their families into new settlements, and it remains the most visible Roman monument in Britain.

Antonine (England, AD 138–AD 192).label: Antonine
Antonine (England, AD 138–AD 192).prose:
[England, AD 138–AD 192] Antonine. Referring to the reign of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius and his successors (from 138 CE) until the late 2nd century. Circa 138 CE to 192 CE. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman Britain under Antoninus Pius and his successors, when the frontier was pushed north to the newly built turf-and-timber Antonine Wall between the Forth and Clyde before being pulled back to Hadrian's Wall a generation later. Towns and villas flourished, and the era's distinctive samian pottery and coin issues make it one of the most closely dated horizons in British archaeology. It ends with the disorder following Commodus's assassination.

Severan (England, AD 193–AD 235).label: Severan
Severan (England, AD 193–AD 235).prose:
[England, AD 193–AD 235] Severan. Referring to the Severan dynasty who were Emperors of Rome in 193-235 C.E. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Septimius Severus brought a huge army to Britain, campaigned deep into Scotland and died at York in 211, and the province was afterwards split in two to limit the power of its governors. Frontier forts along Hadrian's Wall and the northern roads were rebuilt in stone, and York and London flourished as provincial capitals. It was a boom time for the towns and villas of the south, funded by military spending and a garrison whose soldiers could now legally marry.

Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 410–AD 1066).label: Anglo-Saxon
Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 410–AD 1066).prose:
[England, AD 410–AD 1066] Anglo-Saxon. Both a political and cultural term: applied to the distinctive culture and artistic styles that evolved from the merging of native traditions with those of Germanic tribes who had migrated from northern Europe. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

After Roman administration collapsed, settlers from across the North Sea — Angles, Saxons, Jutes and others — mixed with the British population and built a patchwork of small kingdoms that gradually consolidated into Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria. Missionaries from Rome and Ireland converted the elites, bringing literacy, monasteries and works like Bede's history and Beowulf. Viking invasions from the 790s nearly swept the kingdoms away before Alfred and his heirs forged a single English realm, which fell to William of Normandy in 1066.

Early Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 410–AD 66.label: Early Anglo-Saxon
Early Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 410–AD 66.prose:
[England, AD 410–AD 660] Early Anglo-Saxon. The first part of the period which saw the arrival of Anglo-Saxon culture (circa 410 CE to 660 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Germanic-speaking settlers from across the North Sea mixed with the surviving British population, and a landscape of Roman towns and villas gave way to timber halls, sunken-featured buildings and cemeteries full of brooches, weapons and cremation urns. Small competing chiefdoms hardened into kingdoms such as Kent, East Anglia, Mercia and Northumbria, whose rulers displayed their wealth in burials like Sutton Hoo. The period closes with conversion to Christianity, the arrival of literacy and the Synod of Whitby.

Mid Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 660–AD 899).label: Mid Anglo-Saxon
Mid Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 660–AD 899).prose:
[England, AD 660–AD 899] Mid Anglo-Saxon. The middle part of the Anglo-Saxon period which saw the development of the Seven Kingdoms - the Heptarchy (circa 660 CE to 899 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

England's kingdoms consolidated into a handful of large powers, Christianity became universal, and coinage and long-distance trade revived through coastal emporia such as Ipswich, Hamwic and Lundenwic. Monasteries became major landowners and centres of literacy, producing manuscripts like the Lindisfarne Gospels. The period closes with Viking armies dismantling most of those kingdoms and Alfred's Wessex rebuilding around fortified burhs.

Late Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 899–AD 106.label: Late Anglo-Saxon
Late Anglo-Saxon (England, AD 899–AD 106.prose:
[England, AD 899–AD 1066] Late Anglo-Saxon. The final part of the Anglo-Saxon period which began with the reign of Edward the Elder and ended with the Norman Conquest(circa 899 CE to 1066 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Alfred's successors conquered the Danelaw and forged a single English kingdom, governed through shires, hundreds and a remarkably efficient royal coinage reminted every few years. Burhs matured into real towns with markets and mints, monastic reform rebuilt the church, and Viking pressure returned to put the Danish king Cnut on the throne in 1016. The line of development was cut short at Hastings in 1066.

1st Century (England, AD 1–AD 100).label: 1st Century
1st Century (England, AD 1–AD 100).prose:
[England, AD 1–AD 100] 1st Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 1nd Century of the common era (1 CE to 100 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman armies landed in AD 43 and turned southern Britain into a province, meeting fierce resistance — most famously Boudica's revolt, which burned Colchester, London and St Albans. Within a generation there were paved roads, planned towns with forums and baths, coinage and a Latin-using elite, while much of rural life carried on in roundhouses as before. It is the moment written history begins for Britain.

Early 1st Century (England, AD 1–AD 32).label: Early 1st Century
Early 1st Century (England, AD 1–AD 32).prose:
[England, AD 1–AD 32] Early 1st Century. The first third of the 1st Century of the common era. (1 CE to 32 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Southern Britain was ruled by Iron Age dynasties who minted inscribed coins, imported Roman wine and silverware, and built sprawling earthwork centres like Camulodunum, where Cunobelin styled himself king. Rome had not yet invaded, but its influence already shaped politics, taste and trade, and exiled British princes lobbied emperors for support. These decades set up the Claudian conquest that would follow in AD 43.

Mid 1st Century (England, AD 33–AD 66).label: Mid 1st Century
Mid 1st Century (England, AD 33–AD 66).prose: [England, AD 33–AD 66] Mid 1st Century. The second third of the 1st Century of the common era (33 CE to 66 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 1st Century (England, AD 67–AD 100).label: Late 1st Century
Late 1st Century (England, AD 67–AD 100).prose:
[England, AD 67–AD 100] Late 1st Century. The final third of the 1st Century. (67 CE to 100 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

After Boudica's revolt was crushed, Roman armies pushed into Wales, the north and briefly deep into Scotland under Agricola, leaving a chain of forts and military roads. Behind the frontier, towns with forums, baths and grid streets took shape, and villas began to appear in the countryside. Finds of samian pottery, wine amphorae and coinage show how quickly imported goods reached even modest British households.

2nd Century (England, AD 101–AD 200).label: 2nd Century
2nd Century (England, AD 101–AD 200).prose:
[England, AD 101–AD 200] 2nd Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 2nd Century of the common era (101 CE to 200 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain was a settled Roman province: Hadrian's Wall was built across the north from AD 122, the Antonine Wall briefly pushed the frontier to the Forth-Clyde line, and towns like London, York and Cirencester acquired forums, baths and masonry walls. Villas, roads, coinage and imported pottery spread through the lowlands while the army held the north and Wales. Much of what visitors recognise as 'Roman Britain' - inscriptions, mosaics, writing tablets - dates from these hundred years.

Early 2nd Century (England, AD 101–AD 13.label: Early 2nd Century
Early 2nd Century (England, AD 101–AD 13.prose:
[England, AD 101–AD 132] Early 2nd Century. The first third of the 2nd Century of the common era (101 CE to 132 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman Britain settled into provincial routine, with forums, baths and stone town houses replacing timber, and pottery and coin flowing along a maturing road network. In 122 Hadrian visited and ordered a wall built across the north, fixing the empire's edge in stone and turning the frontier into a permanent military zone with its own garrison towns. The wall remains the most visible Roman monument in Britain.

Mid 2nd Century (England, AD 133–AD 166).label: Mid 2nd Century
Mid 2nd Century (England, AD 133–AD 166).prose: [England, AD 133–AD 166] Mid 2nd Century. The second third of the 2nd Century of the common era (133 CE to 166 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 2nd Century (England, AD 167–AD 200.label: Late 2nd Century
Late 2nd Century (England, AD 167–AD 200.prose:
[England, AD 167–AD 200] Late 2nd Century. The final third of the 2nd Century of the common era (167 CE to 200 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The Antonine Wall in Scotland was given up and Hadrian's Wall resumed its role as the northern frontier, garrisoned by units drawn from across the empire. Many British towns raised earth ramparts and gates in these years, a sign of insecurity or civic ambition or both. The province's governor Clodius Albinus stripped troops from Britain in 196 to make his failed bid for the throne, and the frontier suffered for it.

3rd Century (England, AD 201–AD 300).label: 3rd Century
3rd Century (England, AD 201–AD 300).prose:
[England, AD 201–AD 300] 3rd Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 3rd Century of the common era (201 CE to 300 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman Britain grew rich and comparatively quiet while the rest of the empire lurched through civil wars, plague and invasion; villas, mosaics and walled towns spread across the south. The province was split in two for easier control, and coastal forts went up against seaborne raiders. For a decade Britain broke away entirely under Carausius and Allectus, who struck their own coins and ruled an independent North Sea empire before Constantius reconquered it.

Early 3rd Century (England, AD 201–AD 23.label: Early 3rd Century
Early 3rd Century (England, AD 201–AD 23.prose:
[England, AD 201–AD 232] Early 3rd Century. The first third of the 3rd Century of the common era (201 CE to 232 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Septimius Severus brought an army to Britain and campaigned deep into Scotland, dying at York in 211; his sons abandoned the northern conquests and split the province in two, Britannia Superior and Inferior. The 212 edict granting citizenship to nearly all free provincials transformed legal status across the island. Towns were walled, villa estates prospered, and the army became a permanent economic force in the north.

Mid 3rd Century (England, AD 233–AD 266).label: Mid 3rd Century
Mid 3rd Century (England, AD 233–AD 266).prose: [England, AD 233–AD 266] Mid 3rd Century. The second third of the 3rd Century of the common era (233 CE to 266 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 3rd Century (England, AD 267–AD 300.label: Late 3rd Century
Late 3rd Century (England, AD 267–AD 300.prose:
[England, AD 267–AD 300] Late 3rd Century. The final third of the 3rd Century of the common era (267 CE to 300 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain broke away under Carausius and then Allectus, who ruled an independent maritime empire with their own coinage until Constantius reconquered the island in 296. Forts of the Saxon Shore were built or strengthened along the south and east coasts against seaborne raiders. Debased coinage and huge buried hoards from this period reflect the wider inflation and insecurity of the third-century empire, even as villa estates in the south prospered.

4th Century (England, AD 301–AD 400).label: 4th Century
4th Century (England, AD 301–AD 400).prose:
[England, AD 301–AD 400] 4th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 4th Century of the common era (301 CE to 400 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman Britain's most prosperous and most anxious century: grand mosaic-floored villas were built in the west and south while towns shrank and coastal forts were strengthened against Saxon, Irish and Pictish raiders. Christianity became the official religion, leaving behind chi-rho mosaics, lead baptismal tanks and hoards like Water Newton, though pagan temples were still being built. The raids of 367 and the steady withdrawal of troops for continental wars left the province exposed by the century's end.

Early 4th Century (England, AD 301–AD 33.label: Early 4th Century
Early 4th Century (England, AD 301–AD 33.prose:
[England, AD 301–AD 332] Early 4th Century. The first third of the 4th Century of the common era (301 CE to 332 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Diocletian's reorganisation turned Britain into a group of small provinces under a vicarius, with new bureaucracy, taxation in kind and reformed coinage. In 306 Constantine was proclaimed emperor by the troops at York, a British acclamation that led to the empire's conversion to Christianity; British bishops attended the Council of Arles in 314. Villas in the south reached their most lavish phase, with mosaics and bath suites.

Mid 4th Century (England, AD 333–AD 366).label: Mid 4th Century
Mid 4th Century (England, AD 333–AD 366).prose: [England, AD 333–AD 366] Mid 4th Century. The second third of the 4th Century of the common era (333 CE to 366 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

[England, AD 367–AD 400] Late 4th Century. The final third of the 4th Century of the common era (367 CE to 400 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The 'Barbarian Conspiracy' of 367 saw Picts, Scotti and Saxons overwhelm the frontier before Count Theodosius restored order and rebuilt defences. Christianity became the official religion and temples were abandoned, while some southern villas reached their most luxurious phase with mosaic floors. Troops were repeatedly withdrawn for continental wars, and the flow of new coin to Britain was about to stop altogether.

5th Century (England, AD 401–AD 500).label: 5th Century
5th Century (England, AD 401–AD 500).prose:
[England, AD 401–AD 500] 5th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 5th Century of the common era (401 CE to 500 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman government ended and Britain fragmented into small territories run by warlords, bishops and surviving town elites; coinage, pottery industries and stone building largely disappeared within a generation. Germanic-speaking settlers from across the North Sea established farms and cremation cemeteries in the east, while British kingdoms held the west and north. Almost everything we know comes from archaeology and from Gildas's furious sermon about the ruin of Britain — the shadowy period that later produced the Arthur legends.

Early 5th Century (England, AD 401–AD 43.label: Early 5th Century
Early 5th Century (England, AD 401–AD 43.prose:
[England, AD 401–AD 432] Early 5th Century. The first third of the 5th Century of the common era (401 CE to 432 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Imperial government unravelled: troops were withdrawn for continental wars, the coin supply dried up, and around 410 Britain was told to see to its own defence. Towns emptied of their public functions, pottery industries and the cash economy collapsed within a generation, and local warlords and landowners filled the gap. Germanic settlers were already arriving on the east coast when Germanus of Auxerre visited in 429 to combat heresy.

Mid 5th Century (England, AD 433–AD 466).label: Mid 5th Century
Mid 5th Century (England, AD 433–AD 466).prose: [England, AD 433–AD 466] Mid 5th Century. The second third of the 5th Century of the common era (433 CE to 466 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 5th Century (England, AD 467–AD 500.prose:
[England, AD 467–AD 500] Late 5th Century. The final third of the 5th Century of the common era (467 CE to 500 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Roman administration, coinage and mass-produced pottery had vanished, and life reverted to timber buildings, local exchange and small-scale power. Anglo-Saxon settlers were established across eastern and central Britain, burying their dead with brooches, weapons and cremation urns, while British kingdoms held the west. Later tradition places the British victory at Mount Badon somewhere in these decades, checking the westward advance for a generation.

6th Century (England, AD 501–AD 600).label: 6th Century
6th Century (England, AD 501–AD 600).prose:
[England, AD 501–AD 600] 6th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 6th Century of the common era (501 CE to 600 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Small Anglo-Saxon kingdoms took shape across eastern and central Britain, their elites buried with weapons, brooches and imported glass, while British kingdoms survived in the west and Ireland's monasteries flourished. Plague swept the post-Roman world in the 540s and the climate downturn of 536 hit harvests hard. The century closed with Augustine's mission landing in Kent in 597 and the beginning of the conversion.

Early 6th Century (England, AD 501–AD 53.label: Early 6th Century
Early 6th Century (England, AD 501–AD 53.prose:
[England, AD 501–AD 532] Early 6th Century. The first third of the 6th Century of the common era (501 CE to 532 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain was a patchwork of British kingdoms in the west and north and expanding Germanic settlements in the east, with no coinage, no towns in the Roman sense and burial rites that separate the two worlds archaeologically. Gildas, writing in this era, denounced British rulers and recalled a victory at Mons Badonicus that had checked the Saxon advance. It is the least documented century in English history and the seedbed of the Arthurian legend.

Mid 6th Century (England, AD 533–AD 566).label: Mid 6th Century
Mid 6th Century (England, AD 533–AD 566).prose: [England, AD 533–AD 566] Mid 6th Century. The second third of the 6th Century of the common era (533 CE to 566 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

[England, AD 567–AD 600] Late 6th Century. The final third of the 6th Century of the common era (567 CE to 600 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Small warrior kingdoms - Kent, East Anglia, Bernicia, Wessex - were hardening into recognisable states with royal dynasties and tributary hinterlands. Kentish kings traded and intermarried with Merovingian Francia, and gold coins, garnet jewellery and imported glass appear in their graves. In 597 Augustine landed in Kent on a mission from Pope Gregory, beginning the conversion of the English and the return of literacy and stone building.

7th Century (England, AD 601–AD 700).label: 7th Century
7th Century (England, AD 601–AD 700).prose:
[England, AD 601–AD 700] 7th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 7th Century of the common era (601 CE to 700 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

England's kings converted to Christianity, some more than once, bringing literacy, stone churches and monasteries founded from both Rome and Iona; the Synod of Whitby in 664 settled the contest in Rome's favour. The Sutton Hoo ship burial captures the wealth and long-distance connections of these new dynasties. Northumbria and Mercia emerged as the dominant powers, and the first English law codes were written down.

Early 7th Century (England, AD 601–AD 63.label: Early 7th Century
Early 7th Century (England, AD 601–AD 63.prose:
[England, AD 601–AD 632] Early 7th Century. The first third of the 7th Century of the common era (601 CE to 632 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Augustine's mission from Rome converted Kent, and Æthelberht issued the first law code written in English; missionaries then worked north as kings weighed baptism against political advantage. Royal power grew rich and theatrical, seen most spectacularly in the Sutton Hoo ship burial with its helmet, garnet jewellery and Mediterranean silver. Edwin of Northumbria's baptism in 627 brought the north into the Christian orbit.

Mid 7th Century (England, AD 633–AD 666).label: Mid 7th Century
Mid 7th Century (England, AD 633–AD 666).prose:
[England, AD 633–AD 666] Mid 7th Century. The second third of the 7th Century of the common era (633 CE to 666 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

A generation in which the English kingdoms committed to Christianity and Mercia rose to dominance under Penda and his successors. Missionaries from Iona and from Rome competed for influence until the Synod of Whitby settled the question in Rome's favour, and Theodore of Tarsus soon after began knitting the scattered churches into a single organisation. Rich furnished burials of the kind found at Sutton Hoo were giving way to churchyard graves, and the first stone churches and monasteries appeared.

Late 7th Century (England, AD 667–AD 700.label: Late 7th Century
Late 7th Century (England, AD 667–AD 700.prose:
[England, AD 667–AD 700] Late 7th Century. The final third of the 7th Century of the common era (667 CE to 700 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Conversion was largely complete and monasteries such as Lindisfarne, Jarrow and Whitby became centres of learning, manuscript production and stone architecture. Kings issued written law codes, minted silver sceattas, and founded trading settlements at London, Ipswich and Southampton where Continental goods came ashore. Furnished burial faded out, replaced by churchyard graves, so wealth becomes visible in reliquaries and illuminated books rather than grave goods.

8th Century (England, AD 701–AD 800).label: 8th Century
8th Century (England, AD 701–AD 800).prose:
[England, AD 701–AD 800] 8th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 8th Century of the common era (701 CE to 800 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Northumbrian monasteries produced Bede's history and manuscripts such as the Lindisfarne Gospels, and English missionaries like Boniface and scholars like Alcuin carried that learning to the Continent. Offa of Mercia dominated southern England, minted a reformed silver coinage, dealt with Charlemagne as an equal and built the great dyke facing Wales. Trading settlements at London, Ipswich and Hamwic grew — and in 793 Viking raiders sacked Lindisfarne.

Early 8th Century (England, AD 701–AD 73.label: Early 8th Century
Early 8th Century (England, AD 701–AD 73.prose:
[England, AD 701–AD 732] Early 8th Century. The first third of the 8th Century of the common era (701 CE to 732 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Northumbria was at its intellectual height: Bede was writing at Jarrow, monastic scriptoria produced the Lindisfarne Gospels, and English scholars and missionaries such as Boniface carried learning to the Continent. Minster churches spread across the countryside, trading places like Ipswich and London's Lundenwic handled Frankish goods, and small silver sceattas circulated widely. Mercia was steadily building the dominance it would hold under Offa.

Mid 8th Century (England, AD 733–AD 766).label: Mid 8th Century
Mid 8th Century (England, AD 733–AD 766).prose:
[England, AD 733–AD 766] Mid 8th Century. The second third of the 8th Century of the common era (733 CE to 766 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The high point of Mercian power, when Æthelbald and then Offa held overlordship of the southern English kingdoms and issued charters and coin in their own names. Silver sceattas circulated in quantity through trading settlements like Lundenwic and Hamwic, tying England into North Sea commerce. English monks such as Boniface were meanwhile at work converting the Continental Saxons and reforming the Frankish church.

Late 8th Century (England, AD 767–AD 800.label: Late 8th Century
Late 8th Century (England, AD 767–AD 800.prose:
[England, AD 767–AD 800] Late 8th Century. The final third of the 8th Century of the common era (767 CE to 800 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Offa of Mercia dominated southern Britain, corresponded with Charlemagne, built the great dyke facing Wales and issued the fine silver penny that became the standard English coin for centuries. Trade through the wics at London and Ipswich linked England to Frankish markets, and scholars like Alcuin of York were exported to the Continent. The Viking raid on Lindisfarne in 793 announced a new and violent age.

9th Century (England, AD 801–AD 900).label: 9th Century
9th Century (England, AD 801–AD 900).prose:
[England, AD 801–AD 900] 9th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 9th Century of the common era (801 CE to 900 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Viking raids became conquest: the Great Heathen Army destroyed the kingdoms of Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia, and Scandinavian settlers took land across the north and east under the Danelaw. Alfred of Wessex survived, bought time, built fortified burhs and a navy, and promoted translation of Latin works into English. Out of that emergency came the framework of a single English kingdom and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

Early 9th Century (England, AD 801–AD 83.label: Early 9th Century
Early 9th Century (England, AD 801–AD 83.prose:
[England, AD 801–AD 832] Early 9th Century. The first third of the 9th Century of the common era (801 CE to 832 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Mercian overlordship faded after Coenwulf's death, and in 825 Egbert of Wessex crushed the Mercians at Ellendun, beginning the rise of the dynasty that would eventually unite England. At the same time Viking raiders struck coastal monasteries and trading sites with increasing boldness, and defence against them became a royal obligation. Charters, minsters and market ports show a wealthy society about to be tested.

Mid 9th Century (England, AD 833–AD 866).label: Mid 9th Century
Mid 9th Century (England, AD 833–AD 866).prose:
[England, AD 833–AD 866] Mid 9th Century. The second third of the 9th Century of the common era (833 CE to 866 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Viking raiding turned from summer hit-and-run attacks into overwintering and conquest, culminating in the arrival of the Great Heathen Army in 865. Within a few years Northumbria, East Anglia and much of Mercia had fallen, leaving Wessex as the only surviving English kingdom. Coin hoards buried in these decades and never recovered are among the clearest archaeological traces of the disruption.

Late 9th Century (England, AD 867–AD 900.label: Late 9th Century
Late 9th Century (England, AD 867–AD 900.prose:
[England, AD 867–AD 900] Late 9th Century. The final third of the 9th Century of the common era (867 CE to 900 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The Viking Great Army destroyed the kingdoms of Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia, and Danish settlers took land across the north and east. Alfred of Wessex survived, defeated Guthrum at Edington, and built a network of fortified burhs, a reformed army and a fleet, along with a programme of translating books into English. The partition into English and Danelaw territory left lasting marks on law, place names and the language itself.

10th Century (England, AD 901–AD 1000).label: 10th Century
10th Century (England, AD 901–AD 1000).prose:
[England, AD 901–AD 1000] 10th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 10th Century of the common era (901 CE to 1000 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The kings of Wessex turned their military recovery against the Vikings into a single kingdom of England, with Æthelstan the first to rule the whole country and a network of fortified burhs, shires and royal mints binding it together. A monastic reform movement led by Dunstan and Æthelwold rebuilt the great abbeys and produced some of the finest manuscript art of the age. Renewed Danish raids at the century's end undid much of the stability the West Saxon kings had built.

Early 10th Century (England, AD 901–AD 9.label: Early 10th Century
Early 10th Century (England, AD 901–AD 9.prose:
[England, AD 901–AD 932] Early 10th Century. The first third of the 10th Century of the common era (901 CE to 932 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Edward the Elder and his sister Æthelflæd of Mercia pushed north and east from Wessex, taking fortified burhs from Danish armies one by one. Their work produced something new: a single kingdom of the English, which Æthelstan completed by seizing York. English kings now ruled peoples who had never obeyed Wessex before.

Mid 10th Century (England, AD 933–AD 966.label: Mid 10th Century
Mid 10th Century (England, AD 933–AD 966.prose: [England, AD 933–AD 966] Mid 10th Century. The second third of the 10th Century of the common era (933 CE to 966 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 10th Century (England, AD 967–AD 10.prose:
[England, AD 967–AD 1000] Late 10th Century. The final third of the 10th Century of the common era (967 CE to 1000 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Edgar's peaceful, unified kingdom gave way under Æthelred to a second age of Viking assault, with fleets extorting ever larger payments of silver. The Benedictine reform movement, led by Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald, remade English monasteries and produced magnificent illuminated manuscripts and a flowering of vernacular writing. The defeat at Maldon in 991 and the Danegeld that followed set the kingdom on the path to Danish conquest.

11th Century (England, AD 1001–AD 1100).label: 11th Century
11th Century (England, AD 1001–AD 1100).prose:
[England, AD 1001–AD 1100] 11th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 11th Century of the common era (1001 CE to 1100 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

England changed hands twice in fifty years: first to the Danish king Cnut, who ruled it as part of a North Sea empire, then to William of Normandy in 1066. The conquest replaced almost the entire landholding class, brought castles and a French-speaking aristocracy, and was recorded in the extraordinary land survey of Domesday Book. Stone cathedrals and abbeys were rebuilt on a vast scale, and England was pulled firmly into the orbit of continental Europe.

Early 11th Century (England, AD 1001–AD.label: Early 11th Century
Early 11th Century (England, AD 1001–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1001–AD 1032] Early 11th Century. The first third of the 11th Century of the common era (1001 CE to 1032 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Renewed Viking assaults overwhelmed Æthelred the Unready, who bought them off with vast Danegeld payments and then fled. Cnut of Denmark took the throne in 1016 and ruled England as part of a North Sea empire, keeping English law and churchmen while planting Danish earls. England was, briefly, Scandinavian.

Mid 11th Century (England, AD 1033–AD 10.label: Mid 11th Century
Mid 11th Century (England, AD 1033–AD 10.prose: [England, AD 1033–AD 1066] Mid 11th Century. The second third of the 11th Century of the common era (1033 CE to 1066 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 11th Century (England, AD 1067–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1067–AD 1100] Late 11th Century. The final third of the 11th Century of the common era (1067 CE to 1100 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The Normans made their conquest permanent: castles rose over English towns, the north was devastated and depopulated, and almost the entire native aristocracy was dispossessed in favour of a French-speaking elite. The Domesday survey of 1086 recorded who held what with a thoroughness no other medieval European ruler attempted. Vast new cathedrals and abbeys in the Romanesque style, Durham above all, replaced the Anglo-Saxon churches.

12th Century (England, AD 1101–AD 1200).label: 12th Century
12th Century (England, AD 1101–AD 1200).prose:
[England, AD 1101–AD 1200] 12th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 12th Century of the common era (1101 CE to 1200 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

After the civil war between Stephen and Matilda known as the Anarchy, Henry II built an empire stretching from Northumberland to the Pyrenees and laid the foundations of the English common law with itinerant royal justices and juries. Towns and markets multiplied, Cistercian monks colonised the uplands with sheep runs, and the first stirrings of Gothic architecture appeared. The murder of Thomas Becket in 1170 made Canterbury one of Europe's great pilgrimage destinations.

Early 12th Century (England, AD 1101–AD.label: Early 12th Century
Early 12th Century (England, AD 1101–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1101–AD 1132] Early 12th Century. The first third of the 12th Century of the common era (1101 CE to 1132 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Henry I ruled a Norman England of stone castles, cathedral building and increasingly sophisticated royal administration — the Exchequer's audits date from his reign. The drowning of his only legitimate son in the White Ship in 1120 left the succession to his daughter Matilda. Barons who had sworn to accept her turned to Stephen instead, and civil war followed.

Mid 12th Century (England, AD 1133–AD 11.label: Mid 12th Century
Mid 12th Century (England, AD 1133–AD 11.prose: [England, AD 1133–AD 1166] Mid 12th Century. The second third of the 12th Century of the common era (1133 CE to 1166 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 12th Century (England, AD 1167–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1167–AD 1200] Late 12th Century. The final third of the 12th Century of the common era (1167 CE to 1200 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Henry II's itinerant justices and standardised writs laid the foundations of the English common law, while his quarrel with Thomas Becket ended in murder in Canterbury Cathedral and a shrine that drew pilgrims for centuries. England was one part of a sprawling Angevin domain stretching to the Pyrenees, and its king's absences on crusade left government to ministers and made administration more professional. Towns won charters, coin and trade multiplied, and the Exchequer's records begin to run continuously.

13th Century (England, AD 1201–AD 1300).label: 13th Century
13th Century (England, AD 1201–AD 1300).prose:
[England, AD 1201–AD 1300] 13th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 13th Century of the common era (1201 CE to 1300 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Conflict between kings and barons produced Magna Carta and then, after Simon de Montfort's rebellion, the first parliaments to include knights and townsmen. Edward I conquered Wales and ringed it with castles, and began the long wars with Scotland. Friars arrived to preach in the fast-growing towns, and the wool trade tied English farming to Flemish looms.

Early 13th Century (England, AD 1201–AD.label: Early 13th Century
Early 13th Century (England, AD 1201–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1201–AD 1232] Early 13th Century. The first third of the 13th Century of the common era (1201 CE to 1232 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

King John lost Normandy to the French, quarrelled with the Pope until England was placed under interdict, and taxed his barons until they rebelled. The result was Magna Carta in 1215, a peace deal that failed immediately but established the idea that the king was subject to law. John's death left a child, Henry III, on the throne under a regency that reissued the charter.

Mid 13th Century (England, AD 1233–AD 12.label: Mid 13th Century
Mid 13th Century (England, AD 1233–AD 12.prose: [England, AD 1233–AD 1266] Mid 13th Century. The second third of the 13th Century of the common era (1233 CE to 1266 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 13th Century (England, AD 1267–AD 1.label: Late 13th Century
Late 13th Century (England, AD 1267–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1267–AD 1300] Late 13th Century. The final third of the 13th Century of the common era (1267 CE to 1300 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Edward I conquered Gwynedd and ringed it with the great castles of Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech, then turned north to begin the long, ruinous war with Scotland. To pay for it he summoned parliaments that included knights and townsmen alongside barons and clergy, a habit that hardened into constitutional practice. His reign also brought a torrent of statute law and, in 1290, the expulsion of England's Jewish community.

14th Century (England, AD 1301–AD 1400).label: 14th Century
14th Century (England, AD 1301–AD 1400).prose:
[England, AD 1301–AD 1400] 14th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 14th Century of the common era (1301 CE to 1400 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The Black Death of 1348-49 killed perhaps a third to a half of the population, shattering the old manorial economy, driving up wages and helping provoke the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. War with France dragged on for decades, paid for by new taxes and fought by archers whose victories at Crécy and Poitiers became national legend. English replaced French in the courts and, in Chaucer's hands, became a literary language, while Wycliffe's followers began questioning the church.

Early 14th Century (England, AD 1301–AD.label: Early 14th Century
Early 14th Century (England, AD 1301–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1301–AD 1332] Early 14th Century. The first third of the 14th Century of the common era (1301 CE to 1332 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Edward II's favourites, his defeat by Robert Bruce at Bannockburn and his eventual deposition by his own wife made this a wretched period for the English crown. Torrential rains brought the Great Famine of 1315-17, killing perhaps a tenth of the population. The young Edward III seized power from his mother's regime and turned England towards war in France.

Mid 14th Century (England, AD 1333–AD 13.label: Mid 14th Century
Mid 14th Century (England, AD 1333–AD 13.prose: [England, AD 1333–AD 1366] Mid 14th Century. The second third of the 14th Century of the common era (1333 CE to 1366 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.
