Late 14th Century (England, AD 1367–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1367–AD 1400] Late 14th Century. The final third of the 14th Century of the common era (1367 CE to 1400 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

A generation living in the shadow of repeated plague saw wages rise, labour laws imposed to hold them down, and in 1381 a mass rising that took London and killed the archbishop. English replaced French in the courts and at court, and Chaucer, Langland and the Gawain poet wrote for a newly confident vernacular readership, while Wyclif's followers attacked the wealth of the church and put the Bible into English. The century closed with Richard II deposed and murdered, and a usurping dynasty on the throne.

15th Century (England, AD 1401–AD 1500).label: 15th Century
15th Century (England, AD 1401–AD 1500).prose:
[England, AD 1401–AD 1500] 15th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 15th Century of the common era (1401 CE to 1500 CE). For sites and buildings constructed in the Tudor period, double-index with Tudor. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Defeat in France ended the long war with almost nothing to show for it, and the aristocracy turned on itself in the dynastic conflict remembered as the Wars of the Roses, ending with Henry Tudor's victory at Bosworth in 1485. Wool gave way to woven cloth as the country's great export, and gentry and merchants built the grand parish churches and timber houses that still survive. Caxton set up a printing press at Westminster in 1476, putting books in English into circulation for the first time.

Early 15th Century (England, AD 1401–AD.label: Early 15th Century
Early 15th Century (England, AD 1401–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1401–AD 1432] Early 15th Century. The first third of the 15th Century of the common era (1401 CE to 1432 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Henry IV spent his reign defending a throne he had usurped, against Welsh rebellion under Owain Glyndŵr and repeated baronial plots. His son Henry V revived the French war and won Agincourt in 1415, coming close to uniting the two crowns before dying young. An infant king and a slow unravelling in France followed.

Mid 15th Century (England, AD 1433–AD 14.label: Mid 15th Century
Mid 15th Century (England, AD 1433–AD 14.prose: [England, AD 1433–AD 1466] Mid 15th Century. The second third of the 15th Century of the common era (1433 CE to 1466 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 15th Century (England, AD 1467–AD 1.label: Late 15th Century
Late 15th Century (England, AD 1467–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1467–AD 1500] Late 15th Century. The final third of the 15th Century of the common era (1467 CE to 1500 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The last spasms of the dynastic wars carried Edward IV to a settled second reign, then Richard III to the throne and to defeat at Bosworth, after which Henry VII rebuilt royal finances and crushed pretenders. Caxton set up his press at Westminster, putting printed English books into circulation for the first time. Merchants pushed into the Atlantic, and John Cabot sailed from Bristol to a landfall in North America.

16th Century (England, AD 1501–AD 1600).label: 16th Century
16th Century (England, AD 1501–AD 1600).prose:
[England, AD 1501–AD 1600] 16th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 16th Century of the common era (1501 CE to 1600 CE). For sites and buildings constructed in the Tudor style double-index with Tudor or Elizabethan. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Henry VIII's break with Rome dissolved the monasteries, transferred enormous wealth to the crown and gentry, and began a century of religious upheaval that swung between Protestant and Catholic before settling under Elizabeth I. Population rose sharply, prices soared, and enclosure of common land pushed people towards the towns. The defeat of the Spanish Armada, the first ventures across the Atlantic, and the London playhouses of Shakespeare and Marlowe all belong to the reign's later years.

Early 16th Century (England, AD 1501–AD.label: Early 16th Century
Early 16th Century (England, AD 1501–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1501–AD 1532] Early 16th Century. The first third of the 16th Century of the common era (1501 CE to 1532 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Henry VIII's early reign was one of jousts, French wars and Cardinal Wolsey's magnificence, funded by the fortune his father had hoarded. Humanist learning arrived with Erasmus and More, and printed books spread fast. By the 1520s the king's failure to get a papal annulment was pushing England towards a break with Rome.

Mid 16th Century (England, AD 1533–AD 15.label: Mid 16th Century
Mid 16th Century (England, AD 1533–AD 15.prose: [England, AD 1533–AD 1566] Mid 16th Century. The second third of the 16th Century of the common era (1533 CE to 1566 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 16th Century (England, AD 1567–AD 1.label: Late 16th Century
Late 16th Century (England, AD 1567–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1567–AD 1600] Late 16th Century. The final third of the 16th Century of the common era (1567 CE to 1600 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Elizabeth's long reign settled a Protestant church broad enough to be tolerated by most and hated by some, while Catholic plots, the execution of Mary Queen of Scots and open war with Spain kept the regime nervous. The defeat of the Armada in 1588 became a founding national legend; privateers preyed on Spanish shipping, colonisation was attempted in Ireland and tried and failed at Roanoke. It was also the age of the purpose-built playhouse, of Marlowe and the young Shakespeare, and of a population growing faster than the food supply.

17th Century (England, AD 1601–AD 1700).label: 17th Century
17th Century (England, AD 1601–AD 1700).prose:
[England, AD 1601–AD 1700] 17th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 17th Century of the common era (1601 CE to 1700 CE). For sites and buildings constructed in the Elizabthan, Stuart or Jacobean Style double-index with the appropriate term. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Quarrels between crown and parliament over money and religion escalated into civil war, the execution of Charles I in 1649 and a decade of republican rule, before the monarchy returned in 1660 and was again reshaped by the Glorious Revolution of 1688. Plague and the Great Fire devastated London in the 1660s, and the rebuilt city became a commercial capital served by joint-stock companies, coffee houses and the new Bank of England. The Royal Society gave institutional form to experimental science, and colonies in the Caribbean and North America made England a slave-trading Atlantic power.

Early 17th Century (England, AD 1601–AD.label: Early 17th Century
Early 17th Century (England, AD 1601–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1601–AD 1632] Early 17th Century. The first third of the 17th Century of the common era (1601 CE to 1632 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne, joining the crowns and sponsoring the Bible translation that bears his name; the Gunpowder Plot came two years into his reign. Merchants and settlers pushed outwards to Virginia, Plymouth and India. Under Charles I, disputes over taxation and religion hardened until he dismissed Parliament altogether in 1629.

Mid 17th Century (England, AD 1633–AD 16.label: Mid 17th Century
Mid 17th Century (England, AD 1633–AD 16.prose: [England, AD 1633–AD 1666] Mid 17th Century. The second third of the 17th Century of the common era (1633 CE to 1666 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 17th Century (England, AD 1667–AD 1.label: Late 17th Century
Late 17th Century (England, AD 1667–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1667–AD 1700] Late 17th Century. The final third of the 17th Century of the common era (1667 CE to 1700 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

London rose again from the Great Fire in brick and stone, with Wren's churches and St Paul's as the showpieces, while coffee houses, newspapers and the young Royal Society spread new ideas. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced James II with William and Mary and bound the crown to Parliament; the Bank of England followed in 1694 to fund war with France. Household archaeology from these decades is rich in clay pipes, wine bottles with sealed necks and the first English delftware and Chinese porcelain in ordinary homes.

18th Century (England, AD 1701–AD 1800).label: 18th Century
18th Century (England, AD 1701–AD 1800).prose:
[England, AD 1701–AD 1800] 18th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 18th Century of the common era (1701 CE to 1800 CE). For sites and buildings constructed in the Stuart or Georgian periods double-index with the appropriate term. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Georgian England grew rich on Atlantic trade, colonial expansion and a booming market in consumer goods, while enclosure and new crop rotations remade the countryside and pushed people toward the towns. Canals, coke-smelted iron, steam engines and mechanised spinning laid the groundwork for industrial production in the century's later decades. Everyday material culture changed dramatically: tea drinking, cheap printed cottons, mass-produced Staffordshire ceramics and clay pipes turn up in enormous quantities on sites of the period. Politically it was the century of the Union with Scotland, Hanoverian rule, the Jacobite risings and the loss of the American colonies.

Early 18th Century (England, AD 1701–AD.label: Early 18th Century
Early 18th Century (England, AD 1701–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1701–AD 1732] Early 18th Century. The first third of the 18th Century of the common era (1701 CE to 1732 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Marlborough's victories at Blenheim and Ramillies made Britain a first-rank European power, and the 1707 Act of Union merged the English and Scottish parliaments. Anne's death brought in the Hanoverians and a failed Jacobite rising. The South Sea Bubble's collapse in 1720 ruined thousands and lifted Robert Walpole into the long dominance that shaped the office of prime minister.

Mid 18th Century (England, AD 1733–AD 17.label: Mid 18th Century
Mid 18th Century (England, AD 1733–AD 17.prose: [England, AD 1733–AD 1766] Mid 18th Century. The second third of the 18th Century of the common era (1733 CE to 1766 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 18th Century (England, AD 1767–AD 1.label: Late 18th Century
Late 18th Century (England, AD 1767–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1767–AD 1800] Late 18th Century. The final third of the 18th Century of the common era (1767 CE to 1800 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Steam engines, coke-fired ironworks and a new canal network turned the Midlands and North into the world's first industrial landscape, while enclosure redrew the countryside into hedged fields. Britain lost the American colonies and then went to war with revolutionary France, even as its Atlantic trade and slave-worked plantations poured in capital. Sites of the period yield the mass-produced results: Wedgwood creamware, transfer-printed plates and factory bricks.

19th Century (England, AD 1801–AD 1900).label: 19th Century
19th Century (England, AD 1801–AD 1900).prose:
[England, AD 1801–AD 1900] 19th Century. Use for phases and events dating to the 19th Century of the common era (1801 CE to 1900 CE). For sites and buildings constructed in the Georgian or Victorian periods double-index with the appropriate term. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Steam, iron and coal turned England into the world's first industrial society: railways spread across the country from the 1830s, factory towns swelled, and by mid-century most people lived in urban places. Reform came in fits and starts, through the Reform Acts, factory and public health legislation, and the growth of trade unions, alongside grinding poverty, cholera and the workhouse. Britain's empire and global trade reached their greatest extent, and mass-produced goods, from transfer-printed china to bottled patent medicines, fill archaeological deposits of the period.

Early 19th Century (England, AD 1801–AD.label: Early 19th Century
Early 19th Century (England, AD 1801–AD.prose:
[England, AD 1801–AD 1832] Early 19th Century. The first third of the 19th Century of the common era (1801 CE to 1832 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain fought and won a long war against Napoleonic France, then turned inward to the strains of industrial growth: steam-powered mills, booming manufacturing towns, agricultural distress and radical agitation that culminated in the Peterloo massacre. The first public railways opened, Catholic emancipation passed, and the Great Reform Act of 1832 redrew the electoral map to give the new industrial cities a voice. It is the moment when an agrarian, aristocratic country began to look like a modern urban one.

Mid 19th Century (England, AD 1833–AD 18.label: Mid 19th Century
Mid 19th Century (England, AD 1833–AD 18.prose: [England, AD 1833–AD 1866] Mid 19th Century. The second third of the 19th Century of the common era (1833 CE to 1866 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Late 19th Century (England, AD 1867–AD 1.label: Late 19th Century
Late 19th Century (England, AD 1867–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1867–AD 1900] Late 19th Century. The final third of the 19th Century of the common era (1867 CE to 1900 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain was the workshop and banker of the world, its cities swollen by railways and its empire near its greatest extent. Reform acts widened the vote, school boards taught the poor to read, and sewers, gasworks and terraced by-law housing reshaped urban life after decades of cholera and slums. Excavated backyards from these years are full of cheap factory china, glass bottles and tinned food - the debris of the first consumer society.

Caroline (England, AD 1625–AD 1649).label: Caroline
Caroline (England, AD 1625–AD 1649).prose:
[England, AD 1625–AD 1649] Caroline. Dating to the reign of King Charles I (1625 CE to 1649 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The reign of Charles I, remembered for a refined court culture of Van Dyck portraits, masques and poets, and for the political collapse beneath it. Eleven years of personal rule without Parliament, funded by disputed levies, and Archbishop Laud's imposition of ceremonial worship provoked rebellion first in Scotland and then in England. It ended with civil war, the king's trial and his public execution outside his own banqueting house.

Cenozoic (England, 64999999 BC–AD 2026).label: Cenozoic
Cenozoic (England, 64999999 BC–AD 2026).prose:
[England, 64999999 BC–AD 2026] Cenozoic. The youngest era of the Phanerozoic. It follows the Mesozoic, extending from about 65 million years ago to the present. During the Cenozoic, flora and fauna evolved toward their present state and the continents assumed their modern configuration. The Cenozoic comprises two periods: the Tertiary (with its five epochs) and the Quaternary. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The era that began when the asteroid impact and its aftermath wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs, leaving mammals and birds to fill the empty ecological space. India collided with Asia to raise the Himalaya, grasslands spread as the world cooled, and by the last few million years ice sheets were advancing and retreating across the northern continents. Primates evolved within it, and every human being who has ever lived belongs to its final sliver.

Phanerozoic (England, 541999999 BC–AD 20.label: Phanerozoic
Phanerozoic (England, 541999999 BC–AD 20.prose:
[England, 541999999 BC–AD 2026] Phanerozoic. The Phanerozoic is the current eon in the geologic time scale. It extends from approximately 542 million years ago until the present and is marked by the rapid expansion and evolution of life forms allowed by the development of plants carrying out photosynthesis, thus releasing oxygen into the atmosphere. It contains the Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic eras. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The eon of visible life, beginning with the Cambrian explosion of hard-shelled animals and running to the present day. Its rocks contain almost the whole fossil record a museum visitor would recognise — trilobites, ammonites, dinosaurs, mammals — punctuated by five mass extinctions that repeatedly reset the direction of evolution. It also covers the greening of the land, the assembly and breakup of Pangaea, and the ice ages during which humans appeared.

Early Roman (England, AD 43–AD 138).label: Early Roman
Early Roman (England, AD 43–AD 138).prose:
[England, AD 43–AD 138] Early Roman. The first subdivision of the Roman period corresponding roughly with the period between the Roman Invasion (43CE) and the end of the Hadrianic period (138CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The Claudian invasion turned southern Britain into a province: legions pushed north and west, client kings were absorbed, and the revolt of Boudica was crushed. Towns with forums, baths and grid streets appeared where none had existed, roads linked new civitas capitals, and villas began to dot the countryside. By the end of the period the frontier had settled at Hadrian's Wall.

English Civil War (England, AD 1642–AD 1.label: English Civil War
English Civil War (England, AD 1642–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1642–AD 1651] English Civil War. The period of the mid 17th Century which saw a series of civil wars between Royalists and Parliamentarians (1642 CE to 1651 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Quarrels between Charles I and Parliament over taxation, religion and the limits of royal authority broke into armed conflict, drawing in Scotland and Ireland and killing a larger share of the population than the First World War would. Parliament's New Model Army won, and in 1649 the king was tried and beheaded in Whitehall — an act without precedent in Europe. The republic that followed did not last, but the principle that a monarch could be held accountable to law did.

High Medieval (England, AD 1001–AD 1400).label: High Medieval
High Medieval (England, AD 1001–AD 1400).prose:
[England, AD 1001–AD 1400] High Medieval. The period of European history that lasted from the 11th to the 14th Century (1001 CE to 1400 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Norman lords replaced the English aristocracy, filling the landscape with motte-and-bailey castles and rebuilding almost every cathedral in stone. Population and towns grew, common law and Parliament took shape around conflicts like Magna Carta, and universities appeared at Oxford and Cambridge. The expansion broke in the fourteenth century under famine and the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third to a half of the population.

Holocene (England, 11999 BC–AD 2026).label: Holocene
Holocene (England, 11999 BC–AD 2026).prose:
[England, 11999 BC–AD 2026] Holocene. The second epoch of the Quaternary and the most recent geologic interval of time. It extends from about 12,000 BCE to the present. It coincides with the late and post-Stone Age history of the human species. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The warm interval since the last glaciation, in which rising seas cut Britain off from the continent and drowned the plain now beneath the North Sea. Tundra gave way to birch, pine and then dense mixed woodland; hunter-gatherers were followed by farmers, and every monument, field system, town and road in the country belongs to this sliver of geological time. Its later part is marked worldwide by human alteration of climate, soils and species.

Interregnum (England, AD 1649–AD 1660).label: Interregnum
Interregnum (England, AD 1649–AD 1660).prose:
[England, AD 1649–AD 1660] Interregnum. The period between the execution of Charles I and the restoration of the monarchy in 1660. During this time the monarchy was replaced by a political structure known as the Commonwealth led by the Lord Protector, Oliver Cromwell (1649 CE to 1660 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

With Charles I executed and monarchy and the House of Lords abolished, England was governed first as a republic by the Rump Parliament and then by Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector, with an army that repeatedly overrode the assemblies it created. Theatres closed, radical religious sects flourished, Ireland and Scotland were conquered and forcibly united with England. The experiment collapsed within two years of Cromwell's death, and the restored Stuarts dated their reign as though it had never happened.

Interwar (England, AD 1919–AD 1939).label: Interwar
Interwar (England, AD 1919–AD 1939).prose:
[England, AD 1919–AD 1939] Interwar. The period of the 20th Century that begins with the end of the FIrst World War and ends with the start of the Second World War (1919 CE to 1939 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain emerged from the Great War victorious, indebted and short of a generation of young men, and spent the following two decades wrestling with mass unemployment, the General Strike, the slump and the slow retreat from the gold standard. It was also the age of the wireless and the cinema, suburban semis and arterial roads, votes for all women in 1928, and the abdication crisis. Rearmament and the failure of appeasement brought it to a close.

Late Medieval (England, AD 1333–AD 1565).label: Late Medieval
Late Medieval (England, AD 1333–AD 1565).prose:
[England, AD 1333–AD 1565] Late Medieval. The period of European history that lasted from the 14th to the Mid 16th Century (1333 CE to 1565 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Bulgaria spent much of this stretch inside the Byzantine Empire after the fall of the First Bulgarian state, then broke free in 1185 to build a Second Empire ruled from Tarnovo, whose churches, painted tombs and silver coinage mark a confident revival. Ivan Asen II briefly made it the dominant power in the Balkans before Mongol raids, noble feuding and territorial splintering wore it down. Ottoman armies took Tarnovo and then Vidin, ending Bulgarian independence for nearly five centuries.

Late Roman (England, AD 235–AD 410).label: Late Roman
Late Roman (England, AD 235–AD 410).prose:
[England, AD 235–AD 410] Late Roman. The final subdivision of the Roman period corresponding to the period between the end of the Severan Period and 410 CE (Circa. 235 CE to 410 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

Mid Roman (England, AD 138–AD 235).label: Mid Roman
Mid Roman (England, AD 138–AD 235).prose:
[England, AD 138–AD 235] Mid Roman. The second subdivision of the Roman period corresponding to the period between the start of the Antonine period (138CE) and the end of the Severan period (235CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Britain settled into provincial routine after the frontier had been fixed: Hadrian's Wall was manned, the Antonine advance into Scotland tried and abandoned, and the province divided in two under Severus. Towns gained stone walls, villas multiplied in the south, and industries such as the Black Burnished and Nene Valley potteries supplied markets across the island. It is the era that has left most of the mosaics, bathhouses and street grids visitors see today.

Quaternary (England, 2599999 BC–AD 2026).label: Quaternary
Quaternary (England, 2599999 BC–AD 2026).prose:
[England, 2599999 BC–AD 2026] Quaternary. The Quaternary is the second major division of geologic time in the Cenozoic era, following the Tertiary period. It extends from about 2.6 million years ago to the present. It is divided into Pleistocene and Holocene epochs. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

The most recent stretch of geological time, defined by repeated ice ages in which glaciers advanced and retreated across northern Europe, sea levels rose and fell by more than a hundred metres, and mammoth, reindeer and woolly rhinoceros ranged over the continent. It is also the age of humanity: the whole story of stone tools, cave painting, farming and cities falls inside it.

Regency (England, AD 1811–AD 1820).label: Regency
Regency (England, AD 1811–AD 1820).prose:
[England, AD 1811–AD 1820] Regency. The period between 1811 and 1820, following the relapse of George III, when his son George, Prince of Wales, was appointed Prince Regent to discharge royal functions. Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

With George III permanently incapacitated, his son ruled as Prince Regent — a spendthrift patron of architecture and fashion presiding over a country exhausted by war. These years saw the defeat of Napoleon, the first great wave of industrial unrest and the Peterloo massacre, alongside Nash's terraces and the Brighton Pavilion, the novels of Jane Austen and the poetry of Byron, Shelley and Keats. The contrast between elegant drawing rooms and hungry, radicalised manufacturing towns defines the period's reputation.

Restoration (England, AD 1660–AD 1685).label: Restoration
Restoration (England, AD 1660–AD 1685).prose:
[England, AD 1660–AD 1685] Restoration. The period following the reinstatement of the Stuart Monarchy in 1660. Often used to refer to the reign of Charles II (1660 CE to 1685 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Charles II returned to a throne left vacant by the collapse of the Cromwellian regime, and the theatres, maypoles and court pleasures suppressed under the Puritans came back with him. The regicides were hunted down, but a broad amnesty kept the peace; meanwhile London endured plague and the Great Fire, and rose again in brick and Portland stone. It was a brilliant period for science and the stage, with the Royal Society chartered and women appearing on the English stage for the first time.

Viking (England, AD 800–AD 1050).label: Viking
Viking (England, AD 800–AD 1050).prose:
[England, AD 800–AD 1050] Viking. Defined as the period of initial settlement following on from a period of Viking (raiding) activities and initial contact. (800CE to 1050 CE). Period definition from Historic England Periods — Historic England, 2014.

Raids on coastal monasteries from the 790s turned into invasion: the Great Heathen Army destroyed most English kingdoms, and only Wessex under Alfred survived, dividing the country with the Danelaw. Scandinavian settlers reshaped the north and east — place-names, land divisions, law and everyday speech — and made York a booming trading city. Later came a second wave and a Danish king, Cnut, ruling England as part of a North Sea empire.

Neo-Hittite (Turkey, 1199 BC–799 BC).label: Neo-Hittite
Neo-Hittite (Turkey, 1199 BC–799 BC).prose:
[ancient Middle East, 1199 BC–799 BC] Neo-Hittite. Period definition from The Hittites and their contemporaries in Asia Minor — Macqueen, J. G. (James G.), 1986.

When the Hittite Empire collapsed, small successor kingdoms in southeastern Anatolia and northern Syria kept its royal names, gods and hieroglyphic Luwian script alive for another four centuries. Places like Carchemish, Malatya and Karatepe produced distinctive stone reliefs and gateway sculptures blending Hittite, Aramaean and Assyrian styles. These states were the main conduit for Bronze Age Anatolian traditions into the Iron Age world before Assyria annexed them one by one.
Neo-Hittite (Turkey, 1199 BC–799 BC).source: The Hittites and their contemporaries in Asia Minor

Early Bronze Age II (Turkey, 2599 BC–229.node: Early Bronze Age II (Turkey, 2599 BC–2299 BC)
Early Bronze Age II (Turkey, 2599 BC–229.label: Early Bronze Age II
Early Bronze Age II (Turkey, 2599 BC–229.prose:
[ancient Middle East, 2599 BC–2299 BC] Early Bronze Age II. Period definition from The Hittites and their contemporaries in Asia Minor — Macqueen, J. G. (James G.), 1986.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.
Early Bronze Age II (Turkey, 2599 BC–229.source: The Hittites and their contemporaries in Asia Minor

Uruk (Warka) Period (Iraq, 3499 BC–3099.label: Uruk (Warka) Period
Uruk (Warka) Period (Iraq, 3499 BC–3099.prose:
[Ur, 3499 BC–3099 BC] Uruk (Warka) Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

Named after the great mound at Warka, this is the era when temple complexes, large-scale irrigation and the first bureaucratic tools appear in southern Iraq. Clay tokens and sealings gave way to inscribed tablets, and craft production became specialised and industrial in scale. Everything later Mesopotamian civilisation depended on, cities, writing, kingship, took shape here.
Uruk (Warka) Period (Iraq, 3499 BC–3099.source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Neo-Babylonian Period (Iraq, 625 BC–538.label: Neo-Babylonian Period
Neo-Babylonian Period (Iraq, 625 BC–538.prose:
[Ur, 625 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

Babylon's brief imperial heyday, when Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II turned the wreckage of Assyria into a southern-based empire and poured its wealth into rebuilding the city's temples, walls and processional street. Scribes copied and curated older Sumerian and Akkadian learning while astronomers compiled the diaries that made Babylonian astronomy famous. Persian conquest ended political independence but left the city and its priesthoods flourishing.
Neo-Babylonian Period (Iraq, 625 BC–538.source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Neo-Sumerian Period (Iraq, 2112 BC–2005.label: Neo-Sumerian Period
Neo-Sumerian Period (Iraq, 2112 BC–2005.prose:
[Ur, 2112 BC–2005 BC] Neo-Sumerian Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

A last flowering of Sumerian kingship under the Third Dynasty of Ur, with a centralised state, standardised weights and calendars, and a documentary record of unmatched density. Its ziggurats at Ur, Uruk and Nippur still stand as the period's most visible monuments, and its royal hymns and law code were copied by students for centuries. Collapse around 2000 BC ushered in the Amorite kingdoms and the rise of Babylon.
Neo-Sumerian Period (Iraq, 2112 BC–2005.source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Ubaid Period (Iraq, 4499 BC–3499 BC).label: Ubaid Period
Ubaid Period (Iraq, 4499 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Ur, 4499 BC–3499 BC] Ubaid Period. Neo-Assyrian 717-612 B.C. was listed in GeoDia but not found in the book on page 20. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

The later stages of southern Mesopotamia's first farming culture, when villages such as Eridu and Tell al-'Ubaid grew into substantial settlements with monumental temples and craft specialists. Irrigated cereal farming, boats and long-distance contacts along the Gulf underpinned an increasingly unequal society, and its distinctive painted pottery turns up far beyond the alluvium. The trajectory leads directly into the urban explosion at Uruk.
Ubaid Period (Iraq, 4499 BC–3499 BC).source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Early Dynastic Period (Iraq, 2899 BC–236.label: Early Dynastic Period
Early Dynastic Period (Iraq, 2899 BC–236.prose:
[Ur, 2899 BC–2369 BC] Early Dynastic Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

Mesopotamia's cities came into their own: walled, densely populated, and ruled by kings who built temples and fought their neighbours. Writing spread beyond the storeroom into royal boasts, legal contracts and literature, giving the earliest named individuals in history. Excavated palaces, royal tombs and temple statuary from Ur, Lagash and Kish give an unusually vivid picture of daily and ceremonial life.
Early Dynastic Period (Iraq, 2899 BC–236.source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Jemdet Nasr Period (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 B.label: Jemdet Nasr Period
Jemdet Nasr Period (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 B.prose:
[Ur, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

The last stage before Sumer's city-states emerged, marked by bold polychrome pottery and by clay tablets whose pictographic signs were on their way to becoming cuneiform. Temples and their storehouses dominated the economy, and cylinder seals were used to control goods moving in and out. Excavated tablets from the type site list officials, rations and a network of cooperating southern cities.
Jemdet Nasr Period (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 B.source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Isin-Larsa Period (Iraq, 2019 BC–1599 BC.label: Isin-Larsa Period
Isin-Larsa Period (Iraq, 2019 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Ur, 2019 BC–1599 BC] Isin-Larsa Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

After the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur, no single king held the south: Isin and Larsa each claimed the old imperial titles and fought a long struggle for control of the canals, cities and temples between them. Amorite dynasties took power in city after city, law codes such as Lipit-Ishtar's were promulgated, and the scribal schools produced the Sumerian literature we now read even as Sumerian died out as a spoken tongue. Larsa eventually won, only to be swallowed by Hammurabi's Babylon.
Isin-Larsa Period (Iraq, 2019 BC–1599 BC.source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Akkad Period (Iraq, 2369 BC–2229 BC).label: Akkad Period
Akkad Period (Iraq, 2369 BC–2229 BC).prose:
[Ur, 2369 BC–2229 BC] Akkad Period. Period definition from Discovering the royal tombs at Ur. — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1969.

Sargon of Akkad unified the quarrelling Sumerian city-states under one crown, creating what is usually called the world's first empire, with a standing army, appointed governors and a capital whose site is still unfound. Akkadian, a Semitic language, spread as the language of government beside Sumerian, and royal art turned to celebrating the king himself — most famously in Naram-Sin's victory stele. Weakened by revolts and pressure from the Gutians, the empire fell apart within about two centuries but became the model every later Mesopotamian ruler invoked.
Akkad Period (Iraq, 2369 BC–2229 BC).source: Discovering the royal tombs at Ur.

Early Helladic I (Messenia, 3099 BC–2649.label: Early Helladic I
Early Helladic I (Messenia, 3099 BC–2649.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 3099 BC–2649 BC] Early Helladic I. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Small farming hamlets in the southwest Peloponnese take up metal and new pottery shapes, the first mainland stage of the Bronze Age. Settlements were modest and scattered, with burials in simple pits and cists rather than monumental tombs. It provides the baseline against which the wealthier, more centralised communities of the following centuries stand out.
Early Helladic I (Messenia, 3099 BC–2649.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Archaic Period (Messenia, 699 BC–479 BC).label: Archaic Period
Archaic Period (Messenia, 699 BC–479 BC).prose:
[ancient Pylos, 699 BC–479 BC] Archaic Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The island's many small city-states — Knossos, Gortyn, Dreros, Lyktos — produced the earliest surviving Greek law inscribed on stone, and a strong tradition of hammered bronze work and Daedalic sculpture that influenced sculptors on the mainland. Votive deposits in the Idaean Cave and the temples of Dreros and Prinias show a distinctive local blend of Greek and Near Eastern forms. Crete then turned inward, staying out of the Persian Wars and playing little part in the classical politics that followed.
Archaic Period (Messenia, 699 BC–479 BC).source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Roman Period (Messenia, 30 BC–AD 400).label: Roman Period
Roman Period (Messenia, 30 BC–AD 400).prose:
[ancient Pylos, 30 BC–AD 400] Roman Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.
Roman Period (Messenia, 30 BC–AD 400).source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Dark Age (Messenia, AD 600–AD 900).label: Dark Age
Dark Age (Messenia, AD 600–AD 900).prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 600–AD 900] Dark Age. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the Justinianic plague and Slavic and Avar incursions, the towns and villas of the southwestern Peloponnese largely vanish from the record: coinage becomes scarce, imported pottery dries up, and settlement retreats to hilltops and coastal refuges. Byzantine control over the interior was nominal for generations, and much of the population is thought to have shifted to herding and subsistence farming. It is one of the emptiest stretches in the archaeology of an otherwise densely documented region.
Dark Age (Messenia, AD 600–AD 900).source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Early Modern Era (Messenia, AD 1800–AD 1.label: Early Modern Era
Early Modern Era (Messenia, AD 1800–AD 1.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1800–AD 1950] Early Modern Era. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The southwestern Peloponnese passed from Ottoman rule into the new Greek state after the revolution of the 1820s and the naval battle in Navarino Bay. Currant and olive exports tied the region to European markets, and when prices collapsed, tens of thousands emigrated to America. Two world wars, occupation and civil war closed the era, leaving a landscape of half-emptied villages.
Early Modern Era (Messenia, AD 1800–AD 1.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Early Helladic III (Messenia, 2199 BC–20.label: Early Helladic III
Early Helladic III (Messenia, 2199 BC–20.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 2199 BC–2049 BC] Early Helladic III. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the destructions, Messenian settlements were smaller and simpler, with apsidal houses and new dark-on-light painted pottery of the Tiryns type. Population and long-distance contacts contracted sharply. The pottery and building traditions of this phase carry directly into the Middle Helladic period.
Early Helladic III (Messenia, 2199 BC–20.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Frankish Period (Messenia, AD 1204–AD 14.label: Frankish Period
Frankish Period (Messenia, AD 1204–AD 14.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1204–AD 1430] Frankish Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Western knights partitioned the Peloponnese after the sack of Constantinople and ruled it as a feudal principality, granting fiefs to French and Italian lords and raising castles over the ancient landscape. Greek Orthodox villagers lived under Latin barons, and Venetian ports like Methoni and Koroni handled the trade. Byzantine forces based at Mystras gradually reversed the conquest, taking the last Frankish holdings by the 1430s.
Frankish Period (Messenia, AD 1204–AD 14.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Neolithic (Messenia, 5999 BC–3099 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Messenia, 5999 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[ancient Pylos, 5999 BC–3099 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.
Neolithic (Messenia, 5999 BC–3099 BC).source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Early Helladic II (Messenia, 2649 BC–219.label: Early Helladic II
Early Helladic II (Messenia, 2649 BC–219.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 2649 BC–2199 BC] Early Helladic II. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The most prosperous stage of the early mainland Bronze Age in Messenia, marked by larger settlements, standardised wheel-influenced pottery and active exchange around the Aegean. Elsewhere in the Peloponnese this is the age of monumental corridor houses and sealing systems, and Messenian sites participate in the same expanding economy. Its end came with disruption and abandonment at many sites.
Early Helladic II (Messenia, 2649 BC–219.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Helladic IIIA (Messenia, 1399 BC–12.label: Late Helladic IIIA
Late Helladic IIIA (Messenia, 1399 BC–12.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1399 BC–1299 BC] Late Helladic IIIA. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The height of Mycenaean expansion, with palaces functioning, chamber-tomb cemeteries filling, and standardised stirrup jars and kylikes shipped to Egypt, the Levant and Italy. Hittite records of a kingdom called Ahhiyawa probably refer to these Greeks, dealing as equals with the great powers of the Near East.
Late Helladic IIIA (Messenia, 1399 BC–12.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Second Ottoman Period (Messenia, AD 1715.label: Second Ottoman Period
Second Ottoman Period (Messenia, AD 1715.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1715–AD 1827] Second Ottoman Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Ottoman forces swept the Venetians out of the Morea in a single campaign in 1715, ending the brief experiment in Venetian rule and restoring the pashaliks and tax-farms. Local Greek notables and armed klephts filled much of the gap in provincial control, and the Russian-backed Orlov revolt of 1770 was crushed with Albanian irregulars. The period closed in war: Ibrahim Pasha's devastating campaign through Messenia, the destruction of the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827, and the French expedition that secured Greek independence.
Second Ottoman Period (Messenia, AD 1715.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Helladic II (Messenia, 1599 BC–1399.label: Late Helladic II
Late Helladic II (Messenia, 1599 BC–1399.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1599 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic II. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Chieftains stopped digging shaft graves and began building tholoi, great stone beehive chambers approached by long passages, a display of labour and permanence. Mycenaean goods spread through the Aegean and mainlanders took control of Knossos, where Linear B was adapted to write Greek.
Late Helladic II (Messenia, 1599 BC–1399.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Middle Byzantine (Messenia, AD 900–AD 12.label: Middle Byzantine
Middle Byzantine (Messenia, AD 900–AD 12.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 900–AD 1204] Middle Byzantine. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the disruptions of the early medieval centuries, imperial administration and the church reasserted control over the southwest Peloponnese, and new bishoprics, monasteries and small cross-in-square churches were built. Settlement and agriculture expanded, and Slavic-speaking populations in the interior were gradually Christianised and absorbed. The period ends with the Fourth Crusade, after which Frankish lords carved up the Morea.
Middle Byzantine (Messenia, AD 900–AD 12.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Classical Period (Messenia, 479 BC–322 B.label: Classical Period
Classical Period (Messenia, 479 BC–322 B.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 479 BC–322 BC] Classical Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Crete's Bronze Age glory was long gone; the island was now a mosaic of quarrelsome city-states such as Knossos, Gortyn and Lyttos, largely outside the great power struggles of mainland Greece. Its most famous monument is the Gortyn law code, inscribed on stone and preserving detailed rules on inheritance, marriage and the status of slaves. Cretan archers and mercenaries were in demand abroad, and the island had a reputation for piracy.
Classical Period (Messenia, 479 BC–322 B.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Roman Period (Messenia, AD 400–AD 7.label: Late Roman Period
Late Roman Period (Messenia, AD 400–AD 7.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 400–AD 700] Late Roman Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.
Late Roman Period (Messenia, AD 400–AD 7.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Venetian Rule (Messenia, AD 1686–AD 1715.label: Venetian Rule
Venetian Rule (Messenia, AD 1686–AD 1715.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1686–AD 1715] Venetian Rule. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Francesco Morosini's campaigns in the Morea War took the Peloponnese from the Ottomans, and Venice governed it as the Kingdom of the Morea. Engineers rebuilt the harbour fortresses of Methoni, Koroni and Navarino, while officials compiled detailed censuses and land registers that remain among the richest sources on rural Greek life. The experiment lasted barely a generation: an Ottoman army swept the peninsula in 1715 and Venetian power in mainland Greece ended for good.
Venetian Rule (Messenia, AD 1686–AD 1715.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Helladic IIIB (Messenia, 1299 BC–11.label: Late Helladic IIIB
Late Helladic IIIB (Messenia, 1299 BC–11.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1299 BC–1179 BC] Late Helladic IIIB. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The palaces reached their fullest form, with the Lion Gate and the huge walls of Tiryns raised and Linear B scribes tallying grain, textiles, chariots and rowers. Late in the phase came fire, abandonment and hurried defensive works, ending in the destruction of every mainland palace and the loss of writing.
Late Helladic IIIB (Messenia, 1299 BC–11.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

First Ottoman Period (Messenia, AD 1460–.label: First Ottoman Period
First Ottoman Period (Messenia, AD 1460–.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1460–AD 1684] First Ottoman Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Ottoman conquest ended Byzantine and Frankish rule in the southwest Peloponnese, absorbing it into an empire governed through timar landholdings, tax registers and provincial garrisons. Churches gave way to mosques in the towns, coastal Koroni and Methoni changed hands with Venice, and much of the population settled into farming villages recorded in Ottoman defters. It closed when Venetian forces under Morosini swept through the Morea.
First Ottoman Period (Messenia, AD 1460–.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Byzantine Period (Messenia, AD 1261.label: Late Byzantine Period
Late Byzantine Period (Messenia, AD 1261.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1261–AD 1453] Late Byzantine Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the Byzantines retook Constantinople, the southwest Peloponnese stayed a patchwork: Frankish barons of the Principality of Achaea held castles like Methoni and Koroni ports fell to Venice, while the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, ruled from Mystras, pushed steadily westward. The result is a landscape of fortified towns, Latin and Greek churches side by side, and Venetian harbours built for the trade in oil, silk and currants. Ottoman raids and the Venetian-Ottoman wars closed the era, leaving the region's castles to be reused for centuries.
Late Byzantine Period (Messenia, AD 1261.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Helladic I (Messenia, 1679 BC–1599.label: Late Helladic I
Late Helladic I (Messenia, 1679 BC–1599.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1679 BC–1599 BC] Late Helladic I. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 3: Tyler Conlin and Morgan Newton. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

The moment mainland Greece grew rich: the Mycenae shaft graves were cut, filled with gold death masks, inlaid daggers, amber and ostrich eggs, evidence of warrior chiefs with long-distance connections. Fine matt-painted and lustrous decorated pottery shows Minoan Crete's influence being absorbed and reworked into something distinctly mainland.
Late Helladic I (Messenia, 1679 BC–1599.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Geometric Period (Messenia, 899 BC–699 B.label: Geometric Period
Geometric Period (Messenia, 899 BC–699 B.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

In the southwest Peloponnese this is a thinly settled landscape of small villages, a long way from the palace society that had ruled from Pylos in the Bronze Age. Sanctuaries and cemeteries show local communities reforming and Corinthian and Argive pottery arriving through trade. By the period's end Sparta was pressing across the Taygetos mountains, and Messenia's conquest and centuries of helot servitude lay just ahead.
Geometric Period (Messenia, 899 BC–699 B.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Late Helladic IIIC (Messenia, 1179 BC–10.label: Late Helladic IIIC
Late Helladic IIIC (Messenia, 1179 BC–10.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1179 BC–1059 BC] Late Helladic IIIC. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Life after the palaces: no kings, no scribes, no frescoes, but surviving communities at Tiryns, Lefkandi, Perati and in the islands, some prospering briefly. Painters produced lively pictorial vases of ships and warriors, and refugees and traders kept Aegean contacts alive. A final decline led into the Protogeometric period and the Iron Age.
Late Helladic IIIC (Messenia, 1179 BC–10.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Early Byzantine Period (Messenia, AD 400.label: Early Byzantine Period
Early Byzantine Period (Messenia, AD 400.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 400–AD 600] Early Byzantine Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Crete began this stretch as a rich, densely settled Christian province of grain estates and mosaic-floored basilicas centred on Gortyn, and ended it in upheaval. Earthquakes, plague and the collapse of Mediterranean security shrank its cities, and in the 820s Arab settlers took the island and founded the Emirate of Crete. Byzantine rule was only restored in 961.
Early Byzantine Period (Messenia, AD 400.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Frankish Morea (Messenia, AD 1205–AD 143.label: Frankish Morea
Frankish Morea (Messenia, AD 1205–AD 143.prose:
[ancient Pylos, AD 1205–AD 1430] Frankish Morea. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the Fourth Crusade, French knights conquered the Peloponnese and held it as the Principality of Achaea, planting castles and feudal fiefs over a Greek countryside. The Byzantines clawed back the southeast from Mystras and eventually absorbed the whole peninsula, completing the reconquest around 1430. The period left a striking hybrid landscape of Gothic-influenced towers and churches, and a verse Chronicle of the Morea written to justify the conquerors' claims.
Frankish Morea (Messenia, AD 1205–AD 143.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Dark Age (Messenia, 1099 BC–899 BC).label: Dark Age
Dark Age (Messenia, 1099 BC–899 BC).prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1099 BC–899 BC] Dark Age. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the Justinianic plague and Slavic and Avar incursions, the towns and villas of the southwestern Peloponnese largely vanish from the record: coinage becomes scarce, imported pottery dries up, and settlement retreats to hilltops and coastal refuges. Byzantine control over the interior was nominal for generations, and much of the population is thought to have shifted to herding and subsistence farming. It is one of the emptiest stretches in the archaeology of an otherwise densely documented region.
Dark Age (Messenia, 1099 BC–899 BC).source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Middle Helladic (Messenia, 2049 BC–1679.label: Middle Helladic
Middle Helladic (Messenia, 2049 BC–1679.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 2049 BC–1679 BC] Middle Helladic. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 3: Tyler Conlin and Morgan Newton. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Mainland Greece at its poorest and plainest: modest villages of mudbrick houses, burials in simple cist graves and tumuli, and the grey wheel-made pottery known as Minyan ware. Messenia's communities were small and dispersed, with little sign of the wealth or hierarchy to come. Towards its end, richer graves and imported Cretan goods signal the emergence of the warrior elites who would build the Mycenaean palace at Pylos.
Middle Helladic (Messenia, 2049 BC–1679.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark.node: Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark Age (Messenia, 1059 BC–899 BC)
Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark.label: Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark Age
Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 1059 BC–899 BC] Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark Age. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

After the burning of the palace at Pylos, the densely settled Mycenaean landscape here emptied out dramatically—site numbers collapse and the region becomes one of the starkest examples of post-palatial depopulation in Greece. What remains are scattered small settlements and cist burials, with pottery that slowly drifts from tired Mycenaean shapes toward Protogeometric forms. Messenia stayed thinly occupied until Spartan expansion reshaped it centuries later.
Submycenaean and Early Iron Age or Dark.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

Hellenistic Period (Messenia, 322 BC–30.label: Hellenistic Period
Hellenistic Period (Messenia, 322 BC–30.prose:
[ancient Pylos, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic Period. Period definition from Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino — 1998.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.
Hellenistic Period (Messenia, 322 BC–30.source: Sandy Pylos : an archaeological history from Nestor to Navarino

La Tène D (Germany, 119 BC–49 BC).label: La Tène D
La Tène D (Germany, 119 BC–49 BC).prose:
[La Tène (north-west Switzerland), Mosel-Rhineland, 119 BC–49 BC] La Tène D. Spatial coverage: Germany, Switzerland. check map references. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The final Iron Age phase, dominated by the oppida: huge walled towns with streets, workshops, mints and imported Roman wine. Political life sharpened into named tribes with magistrates and coinage, and the archaeological record ends with the Gallic Wars and the absorption of the region into the Roman world.

Hallstatt A (Germany, 1199 BC–999 BC).label: Hallstatt A
Hallstatt A (Germany, 1199 BC–999 BC).prose:
[west-central Austria, 1199 BC–999 BC] Hallstatt A. Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

Despite the name, these are Late Bronze Age generations in Reinecke's scheme: the Urnfield world, where the dead were cremated and their ashes buried in pots in vast flat cemeteries. Bronzesmiths worked sheet metal into helmets, cuirasses and buckets, and fortified hilltop settlements multiplied across southern Germany.

La Tène C (Germany, 249 BC–119 BC).label: La Tène C
La Tène C (Germany, 249 BC–119 BC).prose:
[La Tène (north-west Switzerland), Bohemia, Marne-Champagne, Mosel-Rhineland, 249 BC–119 BC] La Tène C. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, France, Germany, Switzerland. check map references. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The middle La Tène, when the long slashing sword hung from an iron chain belt becomes the standard warrior's equipment and cremation begins to replace inhumation over much of the region. Large open settlements and craft centres grew, gold and silver coinage struck in imitation of Macedonian and Roman types came into use, and trade with the Mediterranean intensified. The decorated scabbards of this phase, in the so-called Sword Style, are among the finest Celtic metalwork.

Early Christian (Britain, Ireland) (Unit.label: Early Christian (Britain, Ireland)
Early Christian (Britain, Ireland) (Unit.prose:
[Caledonia, Ireland, AD 300–AD 500] Early Christian (Britain, Ireland). Spatial coverage: Ireland, United Kingdom. Maps pages 116, 119. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

Christianity took root in the western provinces and on the Irish fringe while Roman authority in Britain collapsed. The archaeology is thin but telling: small church buildings, chi-rho monograms scratched on silver and plaster, inscribed memorial stones, and cemeteries laid out east-west without grave goods. These threads survived the end of Roman rule and fed into the monastic culture of the following centuries.

Anglo-Saxon (East Britain) (United Kingd.label: Anglo-Saxon (East Britain)
Anglo-Saxon (East Britain) (United Kingd.prose:
[East Britain, AD 500–AD 800] Anglo-Saxon (East Britain). Maps pages 110-111. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The eastern side of the island, closest to the Continent, is where Germanic-style settlement shows earliest and most densely in the archaeology: timber halls, sunken-featured buildings, and cremation and furnished inhumation cemeteries full of brooches, beads and weapons. Kingdoms such as Kent, East Anglia and Lindsey grew rich on cross-Channel trade, a wealth displayed in the Sutton Hoo ship burial. Conversion to Christianity from the 590s changed burial practice and brought stone churches, coinage and the first trading towns.

Hallstatt C (Germany, 749 BC–599 BC).label: Hallstatt C
Hallstatt C (Germany, 749 BC–599 BC).prose:
[west-central Austria, 749 BC–599 BC] Hallstatt C. Spatial coverage: Austria, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

Iron becomes the ordinary metal for weapons and tools, and a new warrior display emerges: long iron slashing swords, and burials under mounds containing four-wheeled wagons and horse gear. Salt extraction at Hallstatt reached its height, and the goods buried in its miners' graves show trade reaching to the Mediterranean and the Baltic.

Viking (United Kingdom, AD 800–AD 1000).label: Viking
Viking (United Kingdom, AD 800–AD 1000).prose:
[Britain, Ireland, AD 800–AD 1000] Viking. Spatial coverage: Ireland, United Kingdom. Map page 131. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

Raids on coastal monasteries from the 790s turned into invasion: the Great Heathen Army destroyed most English kingdoms, and only Wessex under Alfred survived, dividing the country with the Danelaw. Scandinavian settlers reshaped the north and east — place-names, land divisions, law and everyday speech — and made York a booming trading city. Later came a second wave and a Danish king, Cnut, ruling England as part of a North Sea empire.

Romano-Celtic (Italy, 49 BC–AD 300).label: Romano-Celtic
Romano-Celtic (Italy, 49 BC–AD 300).prose:
[Mediolanum, River Po, Rome, 49 BC–AD 300] Romano-Celtic. Map page 60. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

Covers the Celtic-speaking populations of the north Italian plain after Rome absorbed them, when Transpadane communities gained citizenship and reorganised themselves as Roman towns. Gaulish names, dress ornaments and cults persisted for generations beneath a Latin surface, and centres like Mediolanum and Aquileia grew into major cities.

La Tène A (Germany, 479 BC–399 BC).label: La Tène A
La Tène A (Germany, 479 BC–399 BC).prose:
[La Tène (north-west Switzerland), Bohemia, Marne-Champagne, Mosel-Rhineland, 479 BC–399 BC] La Tène A. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, France, Germany, Switzerland. check map references. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The opening phase of the La Tène Iron Age, when a wealthy elite in the Rhine, Moselle and Marne regions buried its dead with two-wheeled chariots, gold neck-rings and imported Etruscan and Greek wine service. Out of contact with those Mediterranean imports came the Early Style of Celtic art, which took palmettes, lotus buds and lion masks and reworked them into the swirling, ambiguous designs seen on the Glauberg and Reinheim finds. The old Hallstatt hillfort centres further west collapsed at about this time, and power shifted north.

Hallstatt B (Germany, 999 BC–749 BC).label: Hallstatt B
Hallstatt B (Germany, 999 BC–749 BC).prose:
[west-central Austria, 999 BC–749 BC] Hallstatt B. Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The later Urnfield phase, still bronze-using, with cremation cemeteries, hoards of scrap and finished metalwork, and hilltop enclosures. Iron begins to appear in small quantities as an exotic material, and salt mining at Hallstatt itself gets under way, setting up the wealth of the centuries to come.

Hallstatt D (Germany, 599 BC–479 BC).label: Hallstatt D
Hallstatt D (Germany, 599 BC–479 BC).prose:
[west-central Austria, 599 BC–479 BC] Hallstatt D. Spatial coverage: Austria, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The climax and collapse of Hallstatt society. Fortified "princely seats" like the Heuneburg, with its Mediterranean-style mudbrick wall, controlled trade in Greek wine, bronze vessels and coral, while nearby mounds held spectacular burials such as the woman of Vix with her huge Greek bronze krater. Long swords gave way to short daggers, and by the end of the phase the centres were abandoned and the La Tène style was taking shape.

La Tène Iron Age (Germany, 479 BC–49 BC).node: La Tène Iron Age (Germany, 479 BC–49 BC)
La Tène Iron Age (Germany, 479 BC–49 BC).label: La Tène Iron Age
La Tène Iron Age (Germany, 479 BC–49 BC).prose:
[La Tène (north-west Switzerland), Bohemia, Marne-Champagne, Mosel-Rhineland, 479 BC–49 BC] La Tène Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, France, Germany, Switzerland. check map references. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The second half of the Iron Age north of the Alps, named for a lakeside deposit of weapons in Switzerland and recognised by its flowing, abstract ornament on metalwork. Communities in southern and central Germany built hillforts and later oppida, worked iron on an industrial scale, and traded intensively with the Mediterranean. Toward its end, Germanic groups pressed south and Roman armies advanced to the Rhine and Danube.

Hallstatt Iron Age (Germany, 1199 BC–479.label: Hallstatt Iron Age
Hallstatt Iron Age (Germany, 1199 BC–479.prose:
[west-central Austria, 1199 BC–479 BC] Hallstatt Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Austria, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The whole sequence Reinecke labelled Hallstatt A–D, running from the late Bronze Age Urnfield cemeteries through the adoption of iron to the wealthy princely centres of the sixth century. Over these centuries central Europe shifted from broadly egalitarian cremation cemeteries to towering burial mounds stuffed with wagons, gold and Mediterranean wine services. Its end coincides with the rise of La Tène art and the Celtic migrations that would take warriors as far as Rome and Delphi.

La Tène B (Germany, 399 BC–249 BC).label: La Tène B
La Tène B (Germany, 399 BC–249 BC).prose:
[La Tène (north-west Switzerland), Bohemia, Marne-Champagne, Mosel-Rhineland, 399 BC–249 BC] La Tène B. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, France, Germany, Switzerland. check map references. Period definition from Atlas of the Celts — Twist, Clint., 2001.

The phase of the great Celtic migrations, when war bands from the north moved into the Po valley, the middle Danube and the Balkans; the sack of Rome and the raid on Delphi belong to these generations. Large flat cemeteries of inhumations replace the earlier princely tumuli, with men buried with sword, spear and shield and women with brooches and rings. Metalworkers developed the Waldalgesheim or Vegetal Style, a flowing tendril ornament that spread across Europe with astonishing uniformity.

Highland villages multiply and the Philistine cities of the southern coast reach their height, producing the locally made bichrome pottery that marks their distinctive culture. Iron working spreads, and Egyptian presence in Canaan finally ends. By the close of the period, larger centres and the first signs of centralised authority are visible.

The world of Canaanite city-states and Egyptian garrisons fell apart, and settlement shifted to hundreds of small unwalled villages in the central highlands — the archaeological horizon from which Israel emerges. On the southern coast, newcomers usually identified with the Philistines founded cities with distinctly Aegean-flavoured pottery, architecture and diet. It was a poorer, more fragmented age than the one before it, but the political map it produced would last for centuries.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

The immediate aftermath of the Late Bronze Age collapse: Egyptian control of Canaan unravelled, great cities like Hazor lay in ruins, and international trade networks that had linked the eastern Mediterranean for centuries went quiet. Small new settlements appear in the highlands with simple pillared houses and collared-rim storage jars. Material culture is markedly impoverished, but the population map is being redrawn.

Judah alone remained, a client of Assyria and then of Babylon, with Jerusalem swollen by refugees and the Negev and Shephelah reorganised for trade and agriculture. Literacy is unusually visible in ostraca from Arad and Lachish, written as the Babylonian armies closed in. The period ends with the destruction of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple and the deportation of 586 BC.

The peak and then the collapse of Egypt's empire in Canaan. Local kings corresponded with the pharaoh in cuneiform, Egyptian officials occupied residences at key towns, and imported Mycenaean and Cypriot wares filled elite tombs. Within a generation or two around 1200 BC the cities burned, Egyptian rule ended, and the political map of the Levant was redrawn.

Farming villages coalesced into large unwalled settlements, and olive and vine cultivation, donkey caravans and copper from the Arabah began to knit the region into wider trade. Egyptian traders and settlers established themselves in the southern coastal plain, leaving pottery and serekhs of the earliest pharaohs, including Narmer. Out of this came the region's first true towns.

The later Pottery Neolithic in the southern Levant, largely the Wadi Rabah horizon, when villages grew again and pottery became finer: burnished dark wares, bow-rim jars and carinated bowls. Farmers began exploiting olives and other tree crops alongside cereals and herds, and stamp seals and small quantities of copper hint at growing exchange and ownership. Much of what defines the following Chalcolithic villages is already taking shape here.

A non-urban interval between two ages of cities: people lived in small unwalled villages, campsites and copper-working camps, and buried their dead in vast shaft-tomb cemeteries. Bronze daggers and javelins and a distinctive hand-finished pottery mark the material culture, but there are no fortifications, palaces or writing. The debate over whether these were newcomers from the north or the descendants of the collapsed Early Bronze towns is still unresolved.

Canaan revived after a long rural interlude, with substantial cities ringed by massive earthen ramparts and glacis, and a material culture of fine wheel-made pottery, bronze weapons and scarab seals. Trade linked the coast to Egypt, Cyprus and Syria, and Canaanite settlers in the Nile Delta eventually gave rise to Hyksos rule in Egypt. Many of the biblical cities - Hazor, Megiddo, Jericho, Shechem - reached their greatest size in these centuries.

Following the fall of the fortified Middle Bronze Age towns, Canaan became a patchwork of small Egyptian-dominated city-states paying tribute to the pharaohs. Urban life was thinner than before, but international trade thrived, bringing Cypriot and Aegean pottery, and Egyptian scarabs and statuary appear in local temples.

Canaan was an Egyptian province of walled city-states, each with its ruler answering to a pharaoh's garrison and paying tribute. The Amarna letters capture their rivalries and pleas for help, while Cypriot, Mycenaean and Egyptian goods in the tombs show how deeply the region was tied into eastern Mediterranean trade. Widespread destructions and the appearance of new groups, including the earliest mention of Israel, close the age.

The southern Levant saw its first experiment with urban life: villages grew into walled towns with temples, palaces, granaries and planned streets at places like Arad, Megiddo and Bet Yerah. Olive oil and wine were produced for export, and trade with Egypt was intense enough that Egyptian rulers' names appear on jars in Canaan. Around 2500–2300 BC the towns were abandoned and people returned to villages and pastoralism, a collapse still debated by archaeologists.

In the Middle Bronze Age the Levant filled with fortified city-states, ringed by massive earthen ramparts and glacis and ruled by kings who exchanged letters and gifts with Mari, Egypt and Aleppo. Bronze weaponry, painted Levantine pottery, scarabs and rich tomb goods reflect a prosperous merchant world running along the coast from Ugarit and Byblos southwards. It was in this milieu that the first alphabetic writing appeared, the ancestor of the Phoenician, Greek and Latin alphabets.

The centuries between the collapse of the Late Bronze Age palace world and the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem. Egyptian control of Canaan ended, Philistine towns took shape on the coast, small kingdoms including Israel, Judah, Moab, Ammon and the Aramaean states emerged inland, and alphabetic writing spread. Assyrian and then Babylonian armies swallowed them all, ending with the fall of Jerusalem and the Judaean exile.

The land of Canaan moved from its first walled towns in the Early Bronze Age, through the collapse and pastoral interlude that followed, to the powerful fortified city-states of the Middle Bronze Age with their sloping earthen ramparts and chariot-owning elites. In the Late Bronze Age these cities became vassals of Egypt, and the Amarna letters preserve their rulers' pleading correspondence with the pharaoh. The whole system unravelled around 1200 BC, clearing the ground for the Philistines, Israelites and Arameans of the Iron Age.

Massive mudbrick fortifications went up at Arad, Bet Yerah, Megiddo and elsewhere, enclosing temples, palaces and streets in the southern Levant's first genuine urban centres. Olive oil and wine flowed to Egypt, and imported Khirbet Kerak ware shows contacts stretching to the Caucasus. The system unravelled in the later third millennium, when the towns were emptied and the countryside reverted to villages and herding.

Monumental building returns: fortified gates, palaces and administrative centres at sites like Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, traditionally credited to Solomon and hotly debated ever since. Pharaoh Sheshonq I campaigned through the region around 925 BC, leaving a list of conquered towns at Karnak. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature.

The age of the kingdoms — Israel in the north, Judah in the south, alongside Philistine, Phoenician, Aramaean and Transjordanian neighbours. Cities gained casemate walls, gateways, palaces and rock-cut water tunnels; Hebrew inscriptions, seals and ostraca show a functioning bureaucracy. Assyrian conquest ended Samaria in 720 BC, and Babylon ended Jerusalem in 586 BC, deporting Judah's elite.

As Egyptian and Hittite power receded, the coastal cities of Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad turned to the sea, building a trading network that eventually reached Spain. Their greatest export was the alphabet, an efficient consonantal script that Greeks and later Romans adapted. Cedar, purple-dyed cloth, ivory and metalwork made these small city-states wealthy without any territorial empire.

The first phase in which southern Levantine villagers made and used fired pottery, associated with the Yarmukian and Jericho IX assemblages. Settlements were smaller and more scattered than the crowded pre-pottery towns, with pit houses, storage pits and a mixed economy of cereals and herded sheep, goats, pigs and cattle. Distinctive incised herringbone designs filled with red paint, and coffee-bean-eyed clay figurines, make its material culture instantly recognisable.

Israel under the Omrides and then Jeroboam II became a substantial regional power with ivory-decorated palaces at Samaria, before Assyrian armies destroyed it and deported its population in 720 BC. Judah survived as a vassal, and Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BC is documented from both sides — by Assyrian palace reliefs and by the excavated siege ramp and mass grave. Royal administration is visible in stamped jar handles and standardised weights.
