Roman authority in Hispania gave way to Germanic kingdoms, above all the Visigoths, who ruled from Toledo, absorbed the Suevi and eventually converted from Arianism to Catholicism. Cities shrank, coinage and trade contracted, and the church became the chief institution of learning, producing figures such as Isidore of Seville. The period closed with the Muslim invasion of 711, which swept the Visigothic state away in a few campaigns.

Roman II (Cyprus, AD 150–AD 249).label: Roman II
Roman II (Cyprus, AD 150–AD 249).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 150–AD 249] Roman II. Jamieson, 2007 (Ian Potter Museum exhibition). Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Cypriot cities reached their most lavish phase, with grand houses whose mosaic floors set out mythological scenes still visible at Paphos. The island's Jewish community was destroyed in the revolt of AD 116, and Christian congregations grew steadily thereafter. Prosperity rested on copper, agriculture and a position on the shipping routes between Syria, Egypt and the Aegean.

Jüngere Kupferzeit (Austria, 3000 BC–220.label: Jüngere Kupferzeit
Jüngere Kupferzeit (Austria, 3000 BC–220.prose: [Austria, 3000 BC–2201 BC] Jüngere Kupferzeit. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Neolithikum (Germany, 5600 BC–4001 BC).label: Neolithikum
Neolithikum (Germany, 5600 BC–4001 BC).prose:
[Germany, Switzerland, Czech Republic, Liechtenstein, 5600 BC–4001 BC] Neolithikum. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. no source provided. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Agriculture spread across the German lands, beginning with Bandkeramik longhouse villages on the loess and continuing through Rössen and Michelsberg communities with their hilltop enclosures. Forests were cleared, pottery and polished stone axes became commonplace, and populations concentrated in permanent settlements for the first time. Long-distance exchange in flint, stone axes and Spondylus shell shows these farmers were far from isolated.

Vroege Bronstijd (Netherlands, 2000 BC–1.label: Vroege Bronstijd
Vroege Bronstijd (Netherlands, 2000 BC–1.prose:
[Netherlands, 2000 BC–1801 BC] Vroege Bronstijd. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Copper-alloy tools and ornaments reached the Low Countries through long-distance exchange, though flint remained in everyday use and metal stayed scarce and prestigious. Farming communities lived in small dispersed settlements and still buried their dead under barrows raised in earlier centuries, reusing an ancestral landscape of mounds.

Historie (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1950).label: Historie
Historie (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1950).prose: [Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1950] Historie. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Klasike/Qytetare ilire (Albania, 480 BC–.label: Klasike/Qytetare ilire
Klasike/Qytetare ilire (Albania, 480 BC–.prose:
[Albania, 480 BC–337 BC] Klasike/Qytetare ilire. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Illyrian communities in what is now Albania shifted from hillforts to genuine towns with fortification walls, streets and public buildings, minting coins and absorbing goods and ideas from the Greek colonies at Apollonia and Epidamnos. Local dynasts built up kingdoms strong enough to fight Macedon. The urban centres of this era became the foundation for the later Roman cities of Illyricum.

pozni srednji vek (Slovenia, AD 1300–AD.label: pozni srednji vek
pozni srednji vek (Slovenia, AD 1300–AD.prose:
[Slovenia, AD 1300–AD 1499] pozni srednji vek. ZRC SAZU, Institute of Archaeology. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The Counts of Celje rose from provincial nobility to princes of the Empire and in-laws of kings, before dying out in 1456 and leaving the Habsburgs to absorb the Slovene lands. Towns like Ptuj, Škofja Loka and Ljubljana grew on trade and mining, while Gothic churches with vivid wall paintings went up in the countryside. From the 1460s Ottoman raiding parties swept through repeatedly, forcing villagers to build fortified church refuges that still stand.

Bronze Age (Poland, 1800 BC–401 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Poland, 1800 BC–401 BC).prose:
[Poland, 1800 BC–401 BC] Bronze Age. ARENA1/ADS. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Mezolit (Albania, 10000 BC–4001 BC).label: Mezolit
Mezolit (Albania, 10000 BC–4001 BC).prose: [Albania, 10000 BC–4001 BC] Mezolit. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Neolithikum (Austria, 5600 BC–4001 BC).prose:
[Austria, 5600 BC–4001 BC] Neolithikum. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Agriculture spread across the German lands, beginning with Bandkeramik longhouse villages on the loess and continuing through Rössen and Michelsberg communities with their hilltop enclosures. Forests were cleared, pottery and polished stone axes became commonplace, and populations concentrated in permanent settlements for the first time. Long-distance exchange in flint, stone axes and Spondylus shell shows these farmers were far from isolated.

Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III (Cyprus,.label: Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III
Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III (Cyprus,.prose:
[Cyprus, 850 BC–751 BC] Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III. Jamieson, 2007 (Ian Potter Museum exhibition). Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Wealth returned in force: rich tombs, imported Levantine and Egyptian luxuries, and orientalising motifs appearing on Cypriot pots alongside the old geometric designs. Phoenician Kition flourished and the island's kingdoms grew powerful enough that, soon after, ten of their kings would submit to the Assyrian empire. The period ends as Cypro-Archaic art takes over, full of figures, animals and floral ornament.

Senmodern tid (Sweden, AD 1789–AD 2000).label: Senmodern tid
Senmodern tid (Sweden, AD 1789–AD 2000).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1789–AD 2000] Senmodern tid. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

From the age of revolution to the end of the twentieth century, a poor agrarian kingdom on Europe's edge became one of the world's richest societies. Timber, iron ore and engineering drove industrialisation, while more than a million people emigrated to America; later came universal suffrage, neutrality through two world wars, and the construction of the welfare state.

неолитот (Republic of Macedonia, 7000 BC.label: неолитот
неолитот (Republic of Macedonia, 7000 BC.prose:
[Macedonia, 7000 BC–4501 BC] неолитот. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The earliest farmers here settled the Pelagonia and Ovče Pole basins, building mudbrick villages that grew into low tells at Anzabegovo, Vršnik, Porodin and Velušina. Their painted and dark burnished pottery, and the distinctive house-shaped altars topped with human faces, link them to the Balkan-Anatolian farming world. These communities introduced wheat, sheep and permanent settlement to the region and set the pattern for millennia of village life.

бронзова епоха (Bulgaria, 3400 BC–1101 B.label: бронзова епоха
бронзова епоха (Bulgaria, 3400 BC–1101 B.prose:
[Bulgaria, 3400 BC–1101 BC] бронзова епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Life shifted from the crowded farming tells of the Copper Age toward fortified settlements and, increasingly, burial mounds raised over individual graves, a sign of new social hierarchies and mobile, herding-oriented groups. Bronze metallurgy tied the region into long-distance exchange with the Aegean and central Europe, seen in hoards of tools, weapons and gold vessels such as those from Valchitran. These are the centuries in which the populations later known as Thracians took form.

Mittlere Bronzezeit (Austria, 1600 BC–13.label: Mittlere Bronzezeit
Mittlere Bronzezeit (Austria, 1600 BC–13.prose:
[Austria, 1600 BC–1301 BC] Mittlere Bronzezeit. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The age of the Tumulus culture, when the dead across much of central Europe were buried under round earthen mounds with bronze daggers, pins and spiral ornaments. Bronzeworking became routine rather than exotic, supplied by long-distance trade in copper from the Alps and tin from further west, and cemeteries show clear differences in wealth between graves. The tradition ends as cremation and urnfield burial spread, remaking funerary practice across the continent.

хеленистичкиот период (Republic of Maced.label: хеленистичкиот период
хеленистичкиот период (Republic of Maced.prose:
[Macedonia, 350 BC–AD 29] хеленистичкиот период. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

After Alexander's conquests the Macedonian homeland was ruled by the Antigonids from Pella, exporting Greek urban forms, coinage and language across a vastly enlarged world. Defeat at Pydna in 168 BC dismantled the kingdom, and Rome absorbed it as a province in 148 BC, though Greek civic culture continued unbroken. Excavated tombs, painted stelae and hoards of silver coin from this era show a society still wealthy and outward-looking under new masters.

poznorimska doba (Slovenia, AD 300–AD 59.label: poznorimska doba
poznorimska doba (Slovenia, AD 300–AD 59.prose:
[Slovenia, AD 300–AD 599] poznorimska doba. ZRC SAZU, Institute of Archaeology. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The province of Noricum and the approaches to Italy became a militarised frontier, defended by the Claustra Alpium Iuliarum, a system of walls and forts across the mountain passes. Populations moved from open valley towns to fortified hilltop settlements with early Christian churches, and Emona's basilica shows how thoroughly Christianity had taken hold. The Battle of the Frigidus in 394 was fought here, and within two generations imperial control had dissolved before Ostrogothic and then Lombard power.

Vikingatid (Sweden, AD 800–AD 1050).label: Vikingatid
Vikingatid (Sweden, AD 800–AD 1050).prose:
[Sweden, AD 800–AD 1050] Vikingatid. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Swedish Vikings looked east, following the rivers of Russia to Novgorod, Kiev, the Caspian and Byzantium, and bringing back the Arab silver dirhams found by the tens of thousands in Gotland hoards. Birka and later Sigtuna grew as trading towns, and hundreds of rune-stones were raised across the Mälaren region, many commemorating men who died on eastern voyages. The period closes with the slow arrival of Christianity and the consolidation of a Swedish kingdom.

Evul Mediu Târziu (Romania, AD 1601–AD 1.label: Evul Mediu Târziu
Evul Mediu Târziu (Romania, AD 1601–AD 1.prose:
[Romania, AD 1601–AD 1820] Evul Mediu Târziu. Romanian Academy. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Following the collapse of Michael the Brave's brief union, Transylvania passed from Ottoman-backed autonomy to Habsburg rule, while Wallachia and Moldavia fell under governors appointed from Constantinople. Greek-speaking Phanariot princes ran the two principalities as tax farms, and peasant burdens grew heavy enough to provoke risings such as Horea's in 1784. Baroque churches, boyar houses and the first printed books in Romanian belong to these years.

középső rézkor (Hungary, 4000 BC–3601 BC.label: középső rézkor
középső rézkor (Hungary, 4000 BC–3601 BC.prose:
[Hungary, 4000 BC–3601 BC] középső rézkor. Hungarian National Museum. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Copper metallurgy matured: heavy shaft-hole axes and hammer-axes were cast, buried with men in the cemeteries of the Bodrogkeresztúr culture. People abandoned the big Neolithic tells for smaller, scattered settlements, moving more often with growing herds of cattle. The change in burial and settlement marks a society organised increasingly around herds, mobility and personal status displayed in metal.

късна римска епоха (Bulgaria, AD 284–AD.label: късна римска епоха
късна римска епоха (Bulgaria, AD 284–AD.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 284–AD 394] късна римска епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Diocletian's reorganisation cut the region into small provinces, and Serdica became a favourite residence of Constantine, who is said to have called it his Rome. Christianity moved from persecuted sect to state religion; the Council of Serdica met in 343, and large basilicas replaced temples. The Gothic victory at Adrianople in 378 showed how fragile the Danube frontier had become, and barbarian groups were settled inside the provinces rather than kept out.

Bas-Empire (France, AD 300–AD 499).label: Bas-Empire
Bas-Empire (France, AD 300–AD 499).prose:
[France, AD 300–AD 499] Bas-Empire. INRAP. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The reforms of Diocletian and Constantine reshaped Gaul into smaller provinces run by an expanded bureaucracy, with Trier serving as an imperial capital. Cities shrank behind hastily built walls, villas were fortified or abandoned, and Christianity moved from tolerated cult to the religion of the state, leaving bishops as the effective leaders of urban life. By the end of the period Frankish and Visigothic settlers were established inside the frontier.

Modern (Poland, AD 1500–AD 2000).label: Modern
Modern (Poland, AD 1500–AD 2000).prose:
[Poland, AD 1500–AD 2000] Modern. ARENA1/ADS. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

римска епоха (Bulgaria, AD 15–AD 394).label: римска епоха
римска епоха (Bulgaria, AD 15–AD 394).prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 15–AD 394] римска епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Rome absorbed Thrace and the Danube lands into a network of provinces, garrison towns and paved roads, founding cities such as Nicopolis ad Istrum and monumentalising Philippopolis and Serdica with theatres, baths and forums. The Danube became a fortified frontier and a corridor for trade, armies and, eventually, invaders. Over these four centuries the region was Romanised, Christianised and repeatedly raided, ending as the embattled frontier of a divided empire.

Nieuwe Tijd Vroeg (Netherlands, AD 1500–.label: Nieuwe Tijd Vroeg
Nieuwe Tijd Vroeg (Netherlands, AD 1500–.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 1649] Nieuwe Tijd Vroeg. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The Reformation and the revolt against Spanish rule split the Low Countries, and the northern provinces emerged as an independent Republic. Amsterdam exploded outward along its new canal rings, the VOC and WIC pushed Dutch shipping into Asia and the Atlantic, and drained lakes turned into geometric polder farmland. The archaeology of the era is unusually rich: brick cellars, waterlogged waste pits full of glass and majolica, and the wrecks of the ships that carried it all.

ранна бронзова епоха (Bulgaria, 3200 BC–.label: ранна бронзова епоха
ранна бронзова епоха (Bulgaria, 3200 BC–.prose:
[Bulgaria, 3200 BC–1901 BC] ранна бронзова епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Tell settlements were reoccupied — Ezero is the type site — now with fortification walls and a metal industry using tin and arsenical bronze. Wheeled vehicles, horses and mound burials point to steppe contacts from the north, while pottery and metal forms link the region to Troy and northwest Anatolia. Society became more warlike and more hierarchical, laying the basis for the Thracian world of later centuries.

kora bronzkor (Hungary, 2700 BC–1901 BC).label: kora bronzkor
kora bronzkor (Hungary, 2700 BC–1901 BC).prose:
[Hungary, 2700 BC–1901 BC] kora bronzkor. Hungarian National Museum. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Metalworking became a serious industry in the Carpathian Basin, with tin bronze, standardised axe and dagger types and long-distance exchange running towards the Aegean and the Baltic. Groups such as Nagyrév, Hatvan and Makó built the first tell settlements, occupied for centuries and rising above the plain on the debris of earlier houses. Fortified sites and weapon-rich burials point to competition over the copper and gold routes.

Järnålder (Sweden, 500 BC–AD 1050).label: Järnålder
Järnålder (Sweden, 500 BC–AD 1050).prose:
[Sweden, 500 BC–AD 1050] Järnålder. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Sweden's long Iron Age runs from the first bog-iron smelting through the Roman trade contacts that brought glass, bronze vessels and gold to Scandinavian graves, then the boat burials and helmets of the Vendel elite, and finally the Viking centuries of raiding, silver hoards and trade routes to Byzantium and the Caliphate. It is the period of runic writing, of hillforts and great hall complexes like Uppåkra and Gamla Uppsala. It closes as Christian kingship takes hold and Sweden enters the written record of medieval Europe.

Neolítico Final (Spain, 2700 BC–2301 BC).label: Neolítico Final
Neolítico Final (Spain, 2700 BC–2301 BC).prose:
[Spain, 2700 BC–2301 BC] Neolítico Final. Institute of Heritage Sciences, Spanish National Research Council (CSIC Incipit). Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The closing phase of the Neolithic, when settlements grew larger, ditched and walled enclosures appeared, and copper metallurgy began to be practised alongside older stone technologies. Collective burial in megalithic tombs and artificial caves reached its peak, with rich grave goods hinting at emerging differences in status. Within a few generations these communities would build the fortified Chalcolithic towns of the south.

Völkerwanderungszeit (Germany, AD 375–AD.label: Völkerwanderungszeit
Völkerwanderungszeit (Germany, AD 375–AD.prose:
[Germany, Switzerland, Czech Republic, Liechtenstein, AD 375–AD 567] Völkerwanderungszeit. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. no source provided. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Roman Noricum and Pannonia unravelled as Goths, Huns, Lombards and others moved through and settled the Danube provinces. Towns shrank to fortified hilltop refuges, the frontier garrisons dissolved, and the population that stayed mixed with the newcomers. The period ends with the Lombards leaving for Italy and Avars and Slavs filling the space behind them.

IJzertijd (Netherlands, 800 BC–13 BC).label: IJzertijd
IJzertijd (Netherlands, 800 BC–13 BC).prose:
[Netherlands, 800 BC–13 BC] IJzertijd. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Iron, smelted locally from bog ore, replaced imported bronze and put decent tools in far more hands. People lived on small family farms with byre-houses, laid out rectangular Celtic field systems, and in the northern salt marshes began raising dwelling mounds above the tides. The period closes with Roman armies on the Rhine and the Low Countries divided between an occupied south and a free north.

Epoca Mijlocie a Bronzului (Romania, 230.node: Epoca Mijlocie a Bronzului (Romania, 2300 BC–1601 BC)
Epoca Mijlocie a Bronzului (Romania, 230.label: Epoca Mijlocie a Bronzului
Epoca Mijlocie a Bronzului (Romania, 230.prose:
[Romania, 2300 BC–1601 BC] Epoca Mijlocie a Bronzului. Romanian Academy. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The height of Carpathian bronze culture, when fortified settlements with ditches and ramparts anchored the landscape and workshops turned out decorated axes, swords and disc ornaments. Groups such as Otomani, Wietenberg, Monteoru and Tei left rich cremation cemeteries and gold work, evidence of chiefs who controlled metal and its long-distance exchange.

Eisenzeit (Austria, 800 BC–1 BC).label: Eisenzeit
Eisenzeit (Austria, 800 BC–1 BC).prose:
[Austria, 800 BC–1 BC] Eisenzeit. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Iron working spread through the region, first in the Hallstatt culture, whose chieftains were buried with wagons, gold and imported Mediterranean wine vessels, then in the La Tene culture with its swirling ornamental art. Hilltop strongholds grew into fortified towns with coinage, workshops and long-distance trade, while Germanic-speaking groups consolidated north of the Celtic zone. The era closes with Caesar's conquest of Gaul, which pushed the Roman frontier to the Rhine.

Epoca Romană (Romania, AD 107–AD 274).label: Epoca Romană
Epoca Romană (Romania, AD 107–AD 274).prose:
[Romania, AD 107–AD 274] Epoca Romană. Romanian Academy. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Trajan's two wars destroyed the Dacian kingdom and turned it into a province settled with colonists from across the empire, whose Latin speech is the ancestor of Romanian. Gold from the Apuseni mines, salt, roads, forts and cities such as Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa and Apulum made Dacia prosperous, though its exposed position beyond the Danube led Rome to abandon it after some 165 years.

Epoca Timpurie a Bronzului (Romania, 350.node: Epoca Timpurie a Bronzului (Romania, 3500 BC–2301 BC)
Epoca Timpurie a Bronzului (Romania, 350.label: Epoca Timpurie a Bronzului
Epoca Timpurie a Bronzului (Romania, 350.prose:
[Romania, 3500 BC–2301 BC] Epoca Timpurie a Bronzului. Romanian Academy. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Tell-dwelling Neolithic villages gave way to more mobile, stock-raising communities, some of them burying their dead under earth mounds in the steppe manner. Coțofeni, Glina and Schneckenberg groups worked copper and the first bronze, and the newly dispersed settlement pattern and warrior burials mark a real break with the farming world that preceded them.

Prima Epocă a Fierului (Romania, 1050 BC.node: Prima Epocă a Fierului (Romania, 1050 BC–451 BC)
Prima Epocă a Fierului (Romania, 1050 BC.label: Prima Epocă a Fierului
Prima Epocă a Fierului (Romania, 1050 BC.prose:
[Romania, 1050 BC–451 BC] Prima Epocă a Fierului. Romanian Academy. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Iron tools and weapons became common across the Carpathians and lower Danube, and communities shifted toward fortified hilltop settlements. Hallstatt-style pottery, horse harness and elite burials mark increasingly stratified societies, the ancestors of the Getae and Dacians. Greek colonies on the Black Sea coast opened the region to Mediterranean trade in its later centuries.

Haut Empire (France, 50 BC–AD 299).label: Haut Empire
Haut Empire (France, 50 BC–AD 299).prose:
[France, 50 BC–AD 299] Haut Empire. INRAP. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The Roman Principate as it played out in Gaul: legionary campaigns gave way to a peaceful, thoroughly urbanised province of chartered towns, amphitheatres, aqueducts and paved roads radiating from Lyon. Gaulish elites took Roman names and offices, villas covered the countryside, and local potteries and glassworks supplied markets across the western empire. Gaulish gods survived in Roman dress, and Christianity arrived in the Rhône valley before the period closed.

bakrena doba (Slovenia, 2800 BC–801 BC).label: bakrena doba
bakrena doba (Slovenia, 2800 BC–801 BC).prose:
[Slovenia, 2800 BC–801 BC] bakrena doba. ZRC SAZU, Institute of Archaeology. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The centuries when copper metallurgy took hold between the Alps and the Adriatic hinterland, adding cast axes, daggers and ornaments to a still largely Neolithic farming world. This is the era of the Ljubljana Marshes pile-dwelling villages, whose waterlogged timbers preserved a wooden wheel with its axle — among the oldest known anywhere.

Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499).label: Antiquité
Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499).prose:
[France, 600 BC–AD 499] Antiquité. INRAP. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The long stretch in which Gaul moved from Iron Age chiefdoms trading with Mediterranean merchants to a fully Roman province and then to a Christianised, increasingly fragmented late-imperial society. It covers Greek colonial contact on the southern coast, Caesar's conquest, the Gallo-Roman towns with their forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, and the arrival of Frankish and Visigothic settlers. Most of France's monumental ancient remains, from Nîmes to Vienne, belong to it.

Stormaktstiden (Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1721).label: Stormaktstiden
Stormaktstiden (Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1721).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1721] Stormaktstiden. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

For a century Sweden punched far above its population, seizing the Baltic coastlands and intervening decisively in the Thirty Years' War under Gustavus Adolphus, whose mobile artillery and drilled infantry reshaped European warfare. Conquests in Livonia, Ingria and northern Germany turned the Baltic into something close to a Swedish lake, funded by copper, iron and war contributions. The state built to sustain this - conscription by farm district, a professional bureaucracy, thorough parish record-keeping - long outlived the empire itself, which collapsed after Charles XII's defeat by Russia and Denmark in the Great Northern War.

Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC).label: Chalcolithique
Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC).prose:
[France, 3000 BC–2201 BC] Chalcolithique. INRAP. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Copper working spread through late Neolithic communities in France, while the great megalithic tomb-building traditions continued and collective burial in hypogea and gallery graves reached its height. Toward the close of the period, Bell Beaker pottery and archery equipment arrived from the wider European network, bringing new metalworking skills and burial customs that led into the Bronze Age.

Römische (Austria, AD 1–AD 374).label: Römische
Römische (Austria, AD 1–AD 374).prose:
[Austria, AD 1–AD 374] Römische. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The centuries when the Rhine and Danube marked the edge of the Roman world and the lands beyond looked in. Behind the limes grew cities like Cologne, Trier and Mainz, with stone architecture, wine, baths and coinage; outside it, Germanic groups traded, served in the army and coalesced into larger confederations. Sustained raiding from the third century onward eroded the frontier long before it finally gave way.

Mesjetë /Bizantine (Albania, AD 1000–AD.label: Mesjetë /Bizantine
Mesjetë /Bizantine (Albania, AD 1000–AD.prose:
[Albania, AD 1000–AD 1588] Mesjetë /Bizantine. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Byzantine control over the Albanian lands was repeatedly challenged by Bulgarians, Normans crossing from Italy, Venetians and Serbs, and the coastal cities of Durrës and Vlora changed hands again and again. Out of this contest emerged the first native polities, the Principality of Arbanon and later the Angevin Kingdom of Albania, and the earliest written references to Albanians as a distinct people. Fortified towns, Orthodox churches with fresco cycles and Catholic cathedrals on the coast reflect a land caught between Rome and Constantinople.

Kupferzeit (Austria, 4250 BC–2201 BC).label: Kupferzeit
Kupferzeit (Austria, 4250 BC–2201 BC).prose:
[Austria, 4250 BC–2201 BC] Kupferzeit. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Copper working spread through central Europe alongside farming villages, and metal objects began to mark out status in a way pottery and stone never had. These centuries saw the Michelsberg and Corded Ware traditions, then Bell Beaker burials with their distinctive drinking vessels and archery gear, plus the first ox-drawn wagons and ploughs. The Alpine ice mummy known as Ötzi, carrying a copper axe, belongs to this world.

neolitik (Slovenia, 5000 BC–2801 BC).label: neolitik
neolitik (Slovenia, 5000 BC–2801 BC).prose:
[Slovenia, 5000 BC–2801 BC] neolitik. ZRC SAZU, Institute of Archaeology. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Farming spread into Slovenia along two routes, from the Adriatic and from the Pannonian plain, bringing domestic animals, cereals, pottery and polished stone tools. Caves in the Karst preserve early herding deposits, while open settlements and, later, the pile dwellings of the Ljubljana Marshes show permanent villages. By the end of the span copper working had begun, blurring the line into the Copper Age.

Metaaltijden (Netherlands, 2450 BC–13 BC.label: Metaaltijden
Metaaltijden (Netherlands, 2450 BC–13 BC.prose:
[Netherlands, 2450 BC–13 BC] Metaaltijden. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The blanket term for the Bronze and Iron Ages in the Low Countries, from the arrival of metal-using Bell Beaker and barrow-building communities to the Roman conquest. Farmsteads with byre-houses, urnfield cemeteries and field systems spread across the sandy uplands, while bronze and later iron circulated through long-distance exchange networks reaching Britain, the Alps and central Europe. Bog deposits of swords, ornaments and human bodies hint at the ritual side of these societies.

Klockbägarkultur (Sweden, 3000 BC–2000 B.label: Klockbägarkultur
Klockbägarkultur (Sweden, 3000 BC–2000 B.prose:
[Sweden, 3000 BC–2000 BC] Klockbägarkultur. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Bell Beaker material — distinctive bell-shaped drinking cups, archers' wristguards, barbed arrowheads and the first copper objects — reached southern Scandinavia, above all Scania and the Limfjord region, marking new contacts with western Europe. In Sweden it blends with local Late Neolithic traditions rather than replacing them, and is closely tied to the flourishing of skilled flint dagger production. It signals the beginning of metal-using society in the north.

ранна желязна епоха (Bulgaria, 1100 BC–5.label: ранна желязна епоха
ранна желязна епоха (Bulgaria, 1100 BC–5.prose:
[Bulgaria, 1100 BC–501 BC] ранна желязна епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons as the tribal groups later known as Thracians took shape, burying their dead under thousands of mounds and worshipping at rock-cut sanctuaries and pit fields. Fine wheel-made and channelled pottery, horse gear and bronze fibulae fill the graves. Greek colonists founded Apollonia, Mesambria and Odessos on the Black Sea coast, and the exchange that followed helped turn Thracian chieftaincies into kingdoms.

Middle Bronze Age (Cyprus, 1800 BC–1651.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Cyprus, 1800 BC–1651.prose:
[Cyprus, 1800 BC–1651 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Jamieson, 2007 (Ian Potter Museum exhibition). Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

Spätmittelalter (Germany, AD 1250–AD 149.label: Spätmittelalter
Spätmittelalter (Germany, AD 1250–AD 149.prose:
[Germany, Switzerland, Czech Republic, Liechtenstein, AD 1250–AD 1499] Spätmittelalter. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. no source provided. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The Habsburgs supplanted the Babenbergs and Ottokar of Bohemia to make the Austrian duchies their family base, gradually accumulating Tyrol, Carinthia and Carniola. Towns grew on the Danube trade, mining brought silver and salt wealth, and universities and Gothic building flourished. By the reign of Maximilian I, dynastic marriage had turned a regional principality into the core of a European empire.

újkor (Hungary, AD 1526–AD 2000).label: újkor
újkor (Hungary, AD 1526–AD 2000).prose:
[Hungary, AD 1526–AD 2000] újkor. Hungarian National Museum. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The long Habsburg peace after the Rákóczi uprising was settled by treaty. Depopulated lands in the south and centre were resettled by German, Serb and Slovak colonists, estates were reorganised, and Vienna governed through a compliant Hungarian nobility. From the 1820s a reform generation pushed Hungarian language, industry and constitutional rights, leading to the revolution of 1848, its defeat by Austrian and Russian armies, and the negotiations that would produce the Compromise of 1867.

Ältere Eisenzeit (Austria, 800 BC–451 BC.label: Ältere Eisenzeit
Ältere Eisenzeit (Austria, 800 BC–451 BC.prose:
[Austria, 800 BC–451 BC] Ältere Eisenzeit. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

This is the Hallstatt period, named after the Upper Austrian site whose prehistoric salt mines and vast cemetery gave the culture its name — the mines preserve wooden tools, leather sacks and miners' clothing in astonishing detail. Salt and iron made local elites rich, and they were buried in mounds with four-wheeled wagons, bronze vessels, weapons and imported goods from Italy and the Mediterranean. Objects like the Strettweg cult wagon show a distinctive ritual imagination on the eve of the Celtic La Tène world.

Mesjetë e hershme (Albania, AD 565–AD 99.label: Mesjetë e hershme
Mesjetë e hershme (Albania, AD 565–AD 99.prose:
[Albania, AD 565–AD 999] Mesjetë e hershme. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Slavic migrations and the collapse of the late Roman urban network reduced most inland towns to hilltop refuges, while Durrës survived as a Byzantine stronghold and the seat of a theme. Christianity persisted but the region became a border zone fought over by Byzantium and the expanding Bulgarian empire. Archaeologically it is a thin, difficult period of scattered cemeteries and reused fortifications, from which the medieval Albanian population emerges.

Bronzezeit (Germany, 2200 BC–801 BC).label: Bronzezeit
Bronzezeit (Germany, 2200 BC–801 BC).prose:
[Germany, Switzerland, Czech Republic, Liechtenstein, 2200 BC–801 BC] Bronzezeit. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland. no source provided. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Alpine copper from mines such as the Mitterberg fed a metal industry that supplied much of central Europe, and the Danube corridor carried goods and ideas in both directions. Burial fashions track the era's phases: rich flat graves early on, then great tumuli, then the cremation cemeteries of the Urnfield period. Salt digging began in the Hallstatt valley in these centuries, laying the foundation for the wealth of the Iron Age chieftains who followed.

елинистическа епоха (Bulgaria, 323 BC–AD.label: елинистическа епоха
елинистическа епоха (Bulgaria, 323 BC–AD.prose:
[Bulgaria, 323 BC–AD 15] елинистическа епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Alexander's successors fought over the region: Lysimachus campaigned against the Thracians, invading Celts established a kingdom at Tylis, and Thracian dynasts built genuinely urban capitals such as Seuthopolis with grid plans and coin mints. Monumental tombs with domed chambers and painted walls, most famously at Kazanlak, show rulers borrowing Greek art to advertise their own status. Roman intervention grew steadily until the client kingdoms were absorbed outright.

класическа епоха (Bulgaria, 500 BC–323 B.label: класическа епоха
класическа епоха (Bulgaria, 500 BC–323 B.prose:
[Bulgaria, 500 BC–323 BC] класическа епоха. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Persian armies crossed Thrace on their way to Greece, and in their wake the Odrysian dynasty of Teres and Sitalkes built the first large Thracian state, taxing and trading with Athens and the coastal colonies. Painted Greek pottery, coinage and imported wine amphorae reached inland residences, while local goldsmiths produced the rhyta and pectorals found in aristocratic tombs. It ended with conquest: Philip II of Macedon subdued the Thracian kings, and Alexander drew their cavalry into his eastern campaigns.

античност (Bulgaria, 500 BC–AD 609).label: античност
античност (Bulgaria, 500 BC–AD 609).prose:
[Bulgaria, 500 BC–AD 609] античност. National Institute of Archaeology with Museum, Automated Information System "Archaeological Map of Bulgaria". Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Thracian kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, grew rich on metalwork and trade with the Greek cities founded along the Black Sea coast, then fell under Macedonian and finally Roman control. Under Rome the region filled with cities such as Serdica, Philippopolis and Augusta Traiana, linked by roads carrying armies to the eastern frontier, and later Christianity reshaped its towns with basilicas. Gold and silver treasures from Thracian tombs and the painted burial chambers of their nobles are among the most spectacular survivals.

Antonine (Roman Empire, AD 138–AD 192).label: Antonine
Antonine (Roman Empire, AD 138–AD 192).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 138–AD 192] Antonine. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Roman Britain under Antoninus Pius and his successors, when the frontier was pushed north to the newly built turf-and-timber Antonine Wall between the Forth and Clyde before being pulled back to Hadrian's Wall a generation later. Towns and villas flourished, and the era's distinctive samian pottery and coin issues make it one of the most closely dated horizons in British archaeology. It ends with the disorder following Commodus's assassination.
Antonine (Roman Empire, AD 138–AD 192).source: The Romans, from village to empire

High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193).label: High Empire
High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193] High Empire. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

From Nerva to Commodus, the empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan and then settled into consolidation behind fixed frontiers like Hadrian's Wall. Cities across the provinces filled with baths, aqueducts and forums, provincials rose to the throne, and law and citizenship spread widely. The Antonine plague and Commodus's murder in 192 exposed how much depended on a single life, ushering in civil war.
High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Hadrianic (Roman Empire, AD 117–AD 138).label: Hadrianic
Hadrianic (Roman Empire, AD 117–AD 138).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 117–AD 138] Hadrianic. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

The decades when Rome stopped trying to conquer the north of Britain and drew a line instead: a wall of stone and turf from the Tyne to the Solway, with milecastles, turrets, forts and a great ditch behind it. It reshaped the frontier economy, drawing soldiers, traders and their families into new settlements, and it remains the most visible Roman monument in Britain.
Hadrianic (Roman Empire, AD 117–AD 138).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Late Roman (Roman Empire, AD 235–AD 410).label: Late Roman
Late Roman (Roman Empire, AD 235–AD 410).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 235–AD 410] Late Roman. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.
Late Roman (Roman Empire, AD 235–AD 410).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Archaic (Italy, 579 BC–479 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Italy, 579 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Roman Empire, 579 BC–479 BC] Archaic. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Italy, 579 BC–479 BC).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Trajanic (Roman Empire, AD 98–AD 117).label: Trajanic
Trajanic (Roman Empire, AD 98–AD 117).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 98–AD 117] Trajanic. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

The reign of Trajan, remembered as Rome's high-water mark: the Dacian wars, the eastern campaigns, and the flood of wealth that funded the Forum of Trajan, Trajan's Markets, the harbour at Portus and a state scheme to support poor children. Sculpture of these years, above all the continuous narrative frieze of Trajan's Column, sets the standard for Roman historical relief, and the emperor's correspondence with Pliny in Bithynia gives an unusually candid view of how the provinces were actually governed.
Trajanic (Roman Empire, AD 98–AD 117).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Orientalizing (Italy, 724 BC–579 BC).label: Orientalizing
Orientalizing (Italy, 724 BC–579 BC).prose:
[Roman Empire, 724 BC–579 BC] Orientalizing. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Rich hillforts and enormous burial mounds in the Dolenjska region mark a wealthy Hallstatt-era elite trading with Italy and the eastern Alps. Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. The imagery borrows from Etruscan and Near Eastern art but tells local stories.
Orientalizing (Italy, 724 BC–579 BC).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Severan (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235).label: Severan
Severan (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235] Severan. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Septimius Severus brought a huge army to Britain, campaigned deep into Scotland and died at York in 211, and the province was afterwards split in two to limit the power of its governors. Frontier forts along Hadrian's Wall and the northern roads were rebuilt in stone, and York and London flourished as provincial capitals. It was a boom time for the towns and villas of the south, funded by military spending and a garrison whose soldiers could now legally marry.
Severan (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Augustan (Germany, 11 BC–AD 14).label: Augustan
Augustan (Germany, 11 BC–AD 14).prose:
[Roman Empire, 11 BC–AD 14] Augustan. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Under Augustus, Roman armies pushed across the Rhine and campaigned deep into Germania, founding bases such as Haltern, Oberaden and Waldgirmes - the last with a forum, suggesting plans for a civil province. The annihilation of three legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 ended that project and fixed the Rhine as the frontier. Excavated camps, coin hoards and the battlefield at Kalkriese give an unusually sharp archaeological picture of a short, decisive episode.
Augustan (Germany, 11 BC–AD 14).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Julio-Claudian (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 6.label: Julio-Claudian
Julio-Claudian (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 6.prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 69] Julio-Claudian. Includes the year of the four emperors for purposes of timeline continuity. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

The line of emperors descended from or adopted into the families of Augustus and Livia, spanning Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. Under them the improvised rule of one man hardened into a permanent monarchy with a court, a praetorian guard and an imperial bureaucracy; Britain was invaded, Egypt's grain fed Rome, and the succession repeatedly turned on poisonings, adoptions and palace intrigue. The line ended with Nero's suicide and a year of civil war.
Julio-Claudian (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 6.source: The Romans, from village to empire

Republican (Roman Empire, 271 BC–141 BC).label: Republican
Republican (Roman Empire, 271 BC–141 BC).prose:
[Roman Empire, 271 BC–141 BC] Republican. GeoDia had 9 separate entries for Republican (unclear), each with different spatial coverages. Could add back later if figure out page sources. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.
Republican (Roman Empire, 271 BC–141 BC).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Imperial (Roman Empire, 26 BC–AD 476).label: Imperial
Imperial (Roman Empire, 26 BC–AD 476).prose:
[Roman Empire, 26 BC–AD 476] Imperial. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Augustus kept the forms of the Republic while holding its powers alone, and the arrangement lasted five centuries. Roads, aqueducts, standard coinage and Roman law knit together territory from Britain to the Euphrates, mass-produced goods travelled the length of the Mediterranean, and Latin and Greek became the vehicles of law, literature and eventually Christianity. Civil war, plague, currency collapse and pressure on the frontiers reshaped the state repeatedly before the western half dissolved into Germanic kingdoms.
Imperial (Roman Empire, 26 BC–AD 476).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Gallic Empire (France, AD 260–AD 274).label: Gallic Empire
Gallic Empire (France, AD 260–AD 274).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 260–AD 274] Gallic Empire. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

As the empire buckled under invasion and civil war, the commander Postumus was proclaimed emperor and Gaul, Britain and Spain broke away into a separate state with its own senate, consuls and coinage. It was less a rebellion against Rome than a regional bid to defend the Rhine frontier when the central government could not, and for fourteen years it largely succeeded. Aurelian defeated the last of its rulers at Chalons and reunited the empire, one step in the recovery from the third-century crisis.
Gallic Empire (France, AD 260–AD 274).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Flavian (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96).label: Flavian
Flavian (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96] Flavian. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Under Vespasian, Titus and Domitian, Roman armies pushed conquest to its furthest extent in Britain: Wales and northern England were subdued, legionary fortresses built at Chester, Caerleon and York, and Agricola campaigned deep into Scotland, winning at Mons Graupius. Towns acquired forums, baths and street grids, and Fishbourne-style villas appeared in the south. Much of the province's characteristic pottery and coin dating hinges on this well-documented building boom.
Flavian (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96).source: The Romans, from village to empire

Augustan (Roman Empire, 26 BC–AD 14).prose:
[Roman Empire, 26 BC–AD 14] Augustan. Period definition from The Romans, from village to empire — Boatwright, Mary Taliaferro., 2004.

Herakleid (Turkey, 1184 BC–679 BC).label: Herakleid
Herakleid (Turkey, 1184 BC–679 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 1184 BC–679 BC] Herakleid. chronological table on p. 4. Period definition from The Corinthian, Attic, and Lakonian pottery from Sardis — Schaeffer, Judith Snyder, 1937-, 1997.

The dynasty that Greek tradition, above all Herodotus, credited with ruling Lydia from Sardis for over five centuries, claiming descent from Herakles. Its history is largely legend, ending with the tale of King Candaules, who displayed his wife naked to his bodyguard Gyges and was killed for it. Gyges' seizure of the throne began the Mermnad line and Lydia's rise as a genuine historical power.
Herakleid (Turkey, 1184 BC–679 BC).source: The Corinthian, Attic, and Lakonian pottery from Sardis

Υστερομινωική IB (Crete, 1479 BC–1424 BC.label: Υστερομινωική IB
Υστερομινωική IB (Crete, 1479 BC–1424 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1479 BC–1424 BC] Υστερομινωική IB. full credits: 

Mαραγκού, Λ. (εκδ.), Μινωικός και ελληνικός πολιτισμός από τη Συλλογή Μητσοτάκη, Ίδρυμα Ν.Π. Γουλανδρή-Μουσείο Κυκλαδικής Τέχνης, Αθήνα 1992, σ. 26. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

The high point of Minoan artistry and the moment of catastrophe: potters produced the exuberant Marine Style with its octopuses and argonauts, and craftsmen filled villas across the island with fine goods. Then, in a short span, Knossos aside, nearly every palace, town and country house on Crete was destroyed by fire. Whether the cause was invasion, revolt or the aftershocks of the Thera eruption is still argued, but Crete never again ran itself the same way.

Νεολιθική (Greece, 6799 BC–3199 BC).label: Νεολιθική
Νεολιθική (Greece, 6799 BC–3199 BC).prose:
[Greece, 6799 BC–3199 BC] Νεολιθική. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

Farmers arriving from Anatolia brought wheat, sheep, goats and pottery, and Thessaly filled with mudbrick villages that piled up over generations into tells like Sesklo and Dimini. Populations grew, figurines of full-bodied women were modelled by the thousand, and obsidian from Melos shows boats crossing open water routinely. Everything later Greek — settled village life, land ownership, the agricultural year — starts here.

On the mainland this was a long, modest stretch of village life — grey Minyan pottery, simple houses — while Crete built palaces and Cycladic towns prospered. Towards its end the shaft graves at Mycenae suddenly reveal warlords buried with gold masks, weapons and amber, evidence of chiefs enriched by trade and raiding. Those graves mark the beginning of Mycenaean power.

After centuries of poverty, Greek communities grew again, and potters covered vases with meanders, triangles and files of silhouette figures — the first Greek narrative art in three hundred years. The alphabet was adapted from Phoenician traders, the Homeric poems took shape, and sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filled with bronze dedications. Huge grave-marker amphorae from the Dipylon cemetery in Athens are the signature objects.

The great rebuilt palaces of Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros ran a Crete of fresco-painted halls, bull-leaping, elaborate seals and export trade reaching Egypt and the Levant. The Thera eruption fell within this span, and its aftermath coincides with mounting disruption. It closes with widespread destructions and the arrival of Mycenaean Greeks, whose Linear B tablets record administration at Knossos.

The last flicker of Minoan pottery tradition, made by communities living in defensible upland refuges like Karphi and in reoccupied lowland sites after the palaces were long gone. Cremation and chamber-tomb burial spread, iron begins to replace bronze for weapons, and Cretan potters slowly absorb the new Protogeometric styles from the mainland. It marks the point where Bronze Age Crete becomes Early Iron Age Crete.

Ύστερη Γεωμετρική (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC.label: Ύστερη Γεωμετρική

A century of rapid change, visible above all in the huge Dipylon vases of Athens with their rows of mourners and chariots, the first Greek narrative art. Population and sanctuary offerings surged, colonists sailed west to Italy and Sicily, the alphabet was adapted from Phoenician script, and the epic tradition behind Homer took shape. The city-state emerges here as the basic unit of Greek life.

The last stretch of the Stone Age in the Aegean, when the first copper objects appear alongside stone tools and villages spread onto islands and coastal headlands that had been thinly settled before. Burial caves and cemeteries such as those at Alepotrypa and Kephala show growing concern with the dead and with display, while herding, olive and vine cultivation and sea travel expanded. These centuries set up the metal-using, seafaring societies that would flower in the Early Bronze Age Cyclades and Crete.

Ύστεροι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι (Greece, 1049 B.label: Ύστεροι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι
Ύστεροι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι (Greece, 1049 B.prose:

The recovery phase after the Mycenaean collapse, when iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons and cremation became common. Pottery took on the disciplined compass-drawn circles of the Protogeometric style, and sites like Lefkandi show a wealthy chieftain's household with contacts reaching to Cyprus and the Levant. Small communities were regrouping in ways that would soon produce the Greek polis.

Μέση Βυζαντινή (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204).label: Μέση Βυζαντινή

The empire shrank to a Christian rump defending Anatolia and the Aegean, lost and then regained the Balkans, and tore itself apart over icons before restoring them. Greece filled with small, elegantly proportioned domed churches covered in mosaic and fresco — Hosios Loukas, Daphni, Nea Moni — while Slav settlement and Byzantine reconquest reshaped the countryside. It ends abruptly when the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and Frankish lords parcelled out Greek lands.

Αρχαϊκή (Greece, 799 BC–479 BC).label: Αρχαϊκή
Αρχαϊκή (Greece, 799 BC–479 BC).prose:

City-states hardened into recognisable political communities: written law, coinage, hoplite armies, and colonies planted from the Black Sea to Spain. Monumental stone temples and the stiff, smiling kouros statues appear, while Ionian thinkers began asking what the world was made of. The era closes with the Persian invasions, whose defeat set up Athens' golden age.

Bronze metallurgy, the potter's wheel, the sail and cultivation of the olive and vine transformed Aegean life. In the Cyclades, marble folded-arm figurines and long boats carved on frying-pan vessels show island communities trading widely; on the mainland, substantial buildings like the House of the Tiles at Lerna suggest emerging leaders. Widespread destructions around 2200 BC ended this first burst of complexity.

Oθωμανική (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).label: Oθωμανική
Oθωμανική (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).prose:

Ottoman rule over the Greek lands followed the fall of Constantinople, organising the Orthodox population as a religious community under its patriarch while Venetian outposts were gradually conquered. Trade in the empire's ports and in western Europe created a wealthy Greek merchant class, and mountain bands preserved a culture of resistance celebrated in later folk song. The revolution that began in 1821 grew out of this world.

Νεότερη Νεολιθική Ι (Greece, 5299 BC–479.label: Νεότερη Νεολιθική Ι
Νεότερη Νεολιθική Ι (Greece, 5299 BC–479.prose:

Villages spread and diversified, with black burnished and painted wares, more elaborate houses, and the beginnings of copper working in the northern Aegean. Regional pottery styles sharpen, suggesting communities that increasingly saw themselves as distinct. Sesklo-type settlements in Thessaly are the best-known examples.

After the destruction of Knossos, Crete had no palaces; power scattered to smaller centres and hilltop refuges. Mycenaean Greek influence dominated in burial customs, pottery and the Linear B script, and religion shifted to shrines with strange upraised-armed clay goddess figures. The period ends with island-wide flight to defensible mountain sites as the Bronze Age world collapsed.

The first Cretan palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia: sprawling complexes of storerooms, workshops and courts that concentrated grain, oil and craft production. Writing appeared in the form of Cretan hieroglyphs and seals, and potters produced eggshell-thin polychrome Kamares ware. It is the moment Crete became Europe's first state-level society.

Υστερομινωική IIIΓ (Crete, 1189 BC–1069.label: Υστερομινωική IIIΓ

After the fall of the Mycenaean palace system, Cretans abandoned open coastal towns and moved to defensible hilltops and mountain refuges such as Karphi, Vrokastro and Kavousi. Settlements grew small and self-sufficient, long-distance trade shrank, and pottery decoration fragmented into local styles, though shrines with distinctive goddess figures with upraised arms kept older religious traditions alive. These unsettled generations bridge the collapse of the Bronze Age world and the emergence of Iron Age Crete.

Settlements grew denser and some were ringed with ditches and enclosures, as at Dimini, hinting at competition over land and stored surplus. Metal objects appear more often, matt-painted and polychrome pottery styles proliferate, and long-distance exchange in obsidian, Spondylus shell and fine stone links the Aegean to the Balkans.

Μέση Γεωμετρική (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC).label: Μέση Γεωμετρική

Geometric decoration reached its most disciplined phase, with banded meanders and hatched motifs covering whole pots in tightly controlled zones. Athens led production, and rich burials with imported gold and eastern goods show trade routes reopening across the Aegean and towards the Levant. The wealthy Lefkandi burials belong to this world of re-emerging elites.

Υστερομινωική II (Crete, 1424 BC–1389 BC.label: Υστερομινωική II

With the other Cretan centres in ruins, Knossos alone flourished, now under rulers who wrote administrative records in Greek using the Linear B script. Rich "warrior graves" filled with swords, boars'-tusk helmets and bronze vessels appear around the city, and potters made the grand, formal Palace Style storage jars. It is the clearest evidence that Mycenaeans from the mainland had taken control of Crete.

Πρώιμη Βυζαντινή (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).label: Πρώιμη Βυζαντινή

Constantine's new capital shifted the empire's centre east, and Greece became a Christian province of prosperous cities filled with basilicas built from recycled temple stone. Athens' philosophical schools were closed in 529, the old sanctuaries fell silent, and Justinian's reconquests briefly restored Roman reach. Plague, Slav and Avar incursions and the loss of the East to the Arabs ended it, leaving a much diminished, Greek-speaking empire.

εποχή του Χαλκού (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 B.label: εποχή του Χαλκού
εποχή του Χαλκού (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 B.prose:

Two thousand years in which Greece went from farming villages to literate palace states and back again. Cycladic islanders carved marble figurines, Cretan rulers built the Minoan palaces, and Mycenaean lords raised citadels at Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos, kept accounts in Linear B and traded across the Mediterranean. Their collapse around 1200 BC ended writing and monumental building in Greece for centuries, but left the legends of Troy and the heroes that Homer would later work into epic.

Ελληνιστική (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).label: Ελληνιστική
Ελληνιστική (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Greece, 322 BC–30 BC] Ελληνιστική. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

Alexander's generals carved his empire into rival kingdoms, and Greek language, coinage and city planning spread from Egypt to the Hindu Kush. Mainland Greece became a province of a much bigger world, its cities eclipsed by Alexandria, Antioch and Pergamon, where libraries, mechanics and astronomy flourished. Art turned emotional and theatrical — writhing giants, wrinkled fishermen, the Laocoön — before Rome absorbed the last kingdom with Cleopatra's death.

Πρώιμοι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι (Greece, 1099 B.label: Πρώιμοι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι
Πρώιμοι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι (Greece, 1099 B.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–1049 BC] Πρώιμοι Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

The immediate aftermath of the Mycenaean collapse: palaces gone, Linear B writing forgotten, populations scattered into small settlements. Pottery of this Submycenaean phase is crude and derivative, but graves show iron beginning to replace bronze. Some communities moved overseas, seeding the Greek settlement of the Anatolian coast.

Νεότερα Χρόνια (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).label: Νεότερα Χρόνια
Νεότερα Χρόνια (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).prose:

Revolution against Ottoman rule produced a small independent kingdom that spent the next century expanding towards the borders of today. Catastrophic defeat in Asia Minor in 1922 brought over a million refugees and ended three thousand years of Greek life in Anatolia; occupation, civil war, mass emigration and a colonels' dictatorship followed. Athens grew from a dusty town of a few thousand into a metropolis holding a third of the country.

Ύστερη Βυζαντινή (Greece, AD 1204–AD 145.label: Ύστερη Βυζαντινή
Ύστερη Βυζαντινή (Greece, AD 1204–AD 145.prose:
[Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453] Ύστερη Βυζαντινή. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

Byzantium after the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and split the empire among Latin lords. The Palaiologan emperors recovered the capital in 1261 but ruled a shrinking, impoverished state hemmed in by Serbs, Venetians and finally Ottomans, even as painters and scholars produced some of Byzantium's most admired mosaics, frescoes and classical scholarship. The fall of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Roman state and sent Greek learning westwards.

Ύστερη Χαλκοκρατία (Greece, 1549 BC–1099.label: Ύστερη Χαλκοκρατία
Ύστερη Χαλκοκρατία (Greece, 1549 BC–1099.prose:
[Greece, 1549 BC–1099 BC] Ύστερη Χαλκοκρατία. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

The age of the Mycenaean palaces, when rulers at Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns and Thebes ran redistributive economies recorded in Linear B, built cyclopean walls and tholos tombs, and traded across the eastern Mediterranean. Greek-speaking elites took over Crete after the Minoan collapse and appear in Hittite and Egyptian records. Around 1200 BC the palaces burned, the script was forgotten, and the system never returned.

Πρώιμη Γεωμετρική (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC.label: Πρώιμη Γεωμετρική
Πρώιμη Γεωμετρική (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC.prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–849 BC] Πρώιμη Γεωμετρική. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

The earliest confident phase of recovery after the Dark Age, when Athenian potters replaced Mycenaean flourishes with taut, austere designs — a few bands of meander on a black-glazed body. Cremation burial became standard in Athens, and iron working replaced bronze for tools and weapons. Small in output, but it sets the visual language of the next two centuries.

Ρωμαϊκή (Greece, 26 BC–AD 324).label: Ρωμαϊκή
Ρωμαϊκή (Greece, 26 BC–AD 324).prose:
[Greece, 26 BC–AD 324] Ρωμαϊκή. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

Greece became a backwater of provinces admired for its past — Roman emperors and aristocrats came to study, be initiated at Eleusis and endow buildings, as Hadrian and Herodes Atticus did at Athens. Old sanctuaries were maintained as tourist attractions while Corinth was refounded as a Roman colony and prospered on trade. Paul preached here, planting Christian communities that would eventually replace the gods the tourists came to see.

Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC.label: Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι
Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Σκοτεινοί χρόνοι. full credits:. Period definition from Hellenic History on the Internet — Foundation of the Hellenic World, 2000.

With the Mycenaean palaces destroyed, writing, monumental building, fresco and long-distance trade disappeared for generations, and the population fell sharply. Iron gradually replaced bronze, communities became small and mobile, and Greeks settled across the Aegean in Ionia. Out of this thinly documented stretch came the oral tradition that eventually produced Homer, and the small chiefdoms that grew into the polis.

Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1299.label: Late Helladic IIIA
Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1299.prose:
[Greece, 1399 BC–1299 BC] Late Helladic IIIA. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley. — Pedley, John Griffiths., 2007.

The height of Mycenaean expansion, with palaces functioning, chamber-tomb cemeteries filling, and standardised stirrup jars and kylikes shipped to Egypt, the Levant and Italy. Hittite records of a kingdom called Ahhiyawa probably refer to these Greeks, dealing as equals with the great powers of the Near East.
Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1299.source: Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley.

Archaic (Greece, 799 BC–499 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Greece, 799 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Greece, 799 BC–499 BC] Archaic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley. — Pedley, John Griffiths., 2007.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Greece, 799 BC–499 BC).source: Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley.

Dark Age (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC).label: Dark Age
Dark Age (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Dark Age. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley. — Pedley, John Griffiths., 2007.

After the Justinianic plague and Slavic and Avar incursions, the towns and villas of the southwestern Peloponnese largely vanish from the record: coinage becomes scarce, imported pottery dries up, and settlement retreats to hilltops and coastal refuges. Byzantine control over the interior was nominal for generations, and much of the population is thought to have shifted to herding and subsistence farming. It is one of the emptiest stretches in the archaeology of an otherwise densely documented region.
Dark Age (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC).source: Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley.

Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1549 BC.label: Middle Helladic
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1549 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1549 BC] Middle Helladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley. — Pedley, John Griffiths., 2007.

Mainland Greece at its poorest and plainest: modest villages of mudbrick houses, burials in simple cist graves and tumuli, and the grey wheel-made pottery known as Minyan ware. Messenia's communities were small and dispersed, with little sign of the wealth or hierarchy to come. Towards its end, richer graves and imported Cretan goods signal the emergence of the warrior elites who would build the Mycenaean palace at Pylos.
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1549 BC.source: Greek art and archaeology John Griffiths Pedley.

Flavian (United Kingdom, AD 69–AD 96).label: Flavian
Flavian (United Kingdom, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 69–AD 96] Flavian. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

Under Vespasian, Titus and Domitian, Roman armies pushed conquest to its furthest extent in Britain: Wales and northern England were subdued, legionary fortresses built at Chester, Caerleon and York, and Agricola campaigned deep into Scotland, winning at Mons Graupius. Towns acquired forums, baths and street grids, and Fishbourne-style villas appeared in the south. Much of the province's characteristic pottery and coin dating hinges on this well-documented building boom.
Flavian (United Kingdom, AD 69–AD 96).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

Gallo-Belgic (Germany, 149 BC–54 BC).label: Gallo-Belgic
Gallo-Belgic (Germany, 149 BC–54 BC).prose:
[Germany, 149 BC–54 BC] Gallo-Belgic. Spatial coverage: France, Germany, United Kingdom. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

The gold staters struck by the Belgic tribes between the Seine and the Rhine, copied at increasing removes from the coins of Philip II of Macedon until the horse and chariot dissolve into abstract lines. They were traded and carried across the Channel in quantity, giving Britain its first coinage, and their distribution maps the alliances and refugee movements that Caesar encountered. Their production peaked in the decades of political turmoil before the Roman conquest of Gaul.
Gallo-Belgic (Germany, 149 BC–54 BC).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

Hallstatt (Germany, 749 BC–449 BC).label: Hallstatt
Hallstatt (Germany, 749 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Germany, 749 BC–449 BC] Hallstatt. Spatial coverage: France, Germany. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

Central Europe's Early Iron Age, named after the Austrian salt-mining village whose cemetery yielded a thousand richly furnished graves. Iron replaced bronze for weapons and tools, while chieftains were buried under great mounds with four-wheeled wagons, horse harness, and wine-drinking gear imported from Greek and Etruscan traders. Hilltop "princely seats" such as the Heuneburg and Mont Lassois show wealth concentrating in a few hands before the whole system gave way to the La Tène world.
Hallstatt (Germany, 749 BC–449 BC).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

High Empire (United Kingdom, AD 96–AD 19.label: High Empire
High Empire (United Kingdom, AD 96–AD 19.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 96–AD 192] High Empire. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

From Nerva to Commodus, the empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan and then settled into consolidation behind fixed frontiers like Hadrian's Wall. Cities across the provinces filled with baths, aqueducts and forums, provincials rose to the throne, and law and citizenship spread widely. The Antonine plague and Commodus's murder in 192 exposed how much depended on a single life, ushering in civil war.
High Empire (United Kingdom, AD 96–AD 19.source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

Bronze Age (France, 1799 BC–669 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (France, 1799 BC–669 BC).prose:
[France, 1799 BC–669 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: France, Italy, Switzerland. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (France, 1799 BC–669 BC).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410).label: Roman
Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410).prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410] Roman. Spatial coverage: France, Germany, United Kingdom. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.
Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

La Tene (France, 449 BC–54 BC).label: La Tene
La Tene (France, 449 BC–54 BC).prose:
[France, 449 BC–54 BC] La Tene. Spatial coverage: France, Germany. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

The second Iron Age of temperate Europe, named for a lakeside site in Switzerland but defined here by the Celtic peoples of Gaul. Its craftsmen developed a flowing, abstract art of spirals and stylised animals applied to sword scabbards, torcs, brooches and wine flagons, much of it inspired by imported Mediterranean goods. Gaulish war bands raided Rome and Delphi; centuries later the great walled oppida fell to Caesar's legions.
La Tene (France, 449 BC–54 BC).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

Iron Age (France, 669 BC–54 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (France, 669 BC–54 BC).prose:
[France, 669 BC–54 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: France, Germany, Italy, Switzerland. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (France, 669 BC–54 BC).source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

Julio-Claudian (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD.label: Julio-Claudian
Julio-Claudian (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 69] Julio-Claudian. Period definition from Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire — Scullard, H. H. (Howard Hayes), 1903-1983., 1979.

The line of emperors descended from or adopted into the families of Augustus and Livia, spanning Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. Under them the improvised rule of one man hardened into a permanent monarchy with a court, a praetorian guard and an imperial bureaucracy; Britain was invaded, Egypt's grain fed Rome, and the succession repeatedly turned on poisonings, adoptions and palace intrigue. The line ended with Nero's suicide and a year of civil war.
Julio-Claudian (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD.source: Roman Britain : outpost of the Empire

First Period (Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC).label: First Period
First Period (Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC] First Period. "First Period (or period of the old empire), from the earliest times (say 2700 b. c.) to 2080.." page 17.
"Ancient Egypt comprised three divisions, — Lower Egypt, or the Delta ; Middle Egypt, or the Heptanomis ; Upper Egypt, or the Thebais." with map, page 13.
