First Period (Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC).source: Outlines of the world's history, ancient, mediæval, and modern, with special relation to the history of civilization and the progress of mankind

Second Period (Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 BC).label: Second Period
Second Period (Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 BC).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 BC] Second Period. "Second Period (or period of the Hyk'sos rule), from 2080 to 1527." page 17.
"The Second Period is the era covered by the rule of the Hyksos, or Shepherd Kings, and lasts for about five centuries (2080 - 1525 b.c.)."

Second Period (Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 BC).source: Outlines of the world's history, ancient, mediæval, and modern, with special relation to the history of civilization and the progress of mankind

Third Period (Egypt, 1526 BC–524 BC).label: Third Period
Third Period (Egypt, 1526 BC–524 BC).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 1526 BC–524 BC] Third Period. "Third Period (or period of the new empire), from 1527 to 525." page 17.
"The revival of Egyptian independence by the expulsion of the 'Shepherds' introduces us to the Third Period, or that of the New Empire. This continues for about one thousand years (1527-525 b.c.)..." page 19.

Third Period (Egypt, 1526 BC–524 BC).source: Outlines of the world's history, ancient, mediæval, and modern, with special relation to the history of civilization and the progress of mankind

âge du Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–16.node: âge du Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–1600 BC)
âge du Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–16.label: âge du Bronze ancien
âge du Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–16.prose:
[France, 2200 BC–1600 BC] âge du Bronze ancien. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Copper-alloy metallurgy took hold across the region, with tin-bronze daggers, axes and pins produced and traded along river and coastal routes. Communities were still small and dispersed, but the demand for tin and copper drew them into long-distance exchange networks reaching Cornwall, the Alps and central Europe. Burials begin to single out individuals with weapons and ornaments, a hint of hardening social hierarchies.

âge du Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–800.node: âge du Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–800 BC)
âge du Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–800.label: âge du Bronze final
âge du Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–800.prose:
[France, 1400 BC–800 BC] âge du Bronze final. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Bronze production reached industrial scale: founders' hoards of hundreds of broken axes and swords were buried, and standardised types circulated over vast distances. Cremation in urnfields replaced older burial customs, and fortified hilltop sites multiplied. It is the world just before iron, and its metalwork traditions fed directly into the first Iron Age chiefdoms.

premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–450 B.node: premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–450 BC)
premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–450 B.label: premier âge du Fer
premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–450 B.prose:
[France, 800 BC–450 BC] premier âge du Fer. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Iron replaced bronze as the everyday working metal, and Hallstatt-period elites in eastern and central Gaul built hilltop strongholds that controlled trade up the Rhône and Seine. Their power shows in spectacular burials under great mounds, furnished with four-wheeled wagons, gold torcs and imported Greek and Etruscan bronzes and wine vessels, the Vix krater being the most famous. This traffic in Mediterranean luxuries drew the region into a wider commercial world and set the stage for the Celtic societies of the following centuries.

Moyen Âge (France, AD 476–AD 1492).label: Moyen Âge
Moyen Âge (France, AD 476–AD 1492).prose:
[France, AD 476–AD 1492] Moyen Âge. by Isabelle Catteddu. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

A thousand years running from the collapse of Roman authority through Merovingian and Carolingian kingdoms to the age of cathedrals, and on into the plague, the Hundred Years' War and recovery under Charles VII and Louis XI. Latin Christianity, feudal lordship and the manorial countryside gave the era its framework, while towns, guilds and universities gradually grew inside it. By its end a recognisably French kingdom, language and royal state had emerged.

Période moderne (France, AD 1492–AD 1789.label: Période moderne
Période moderne (France, AD 1492–AD 1789.prose:
[France, AD 1492–AD 1789] Période moderne. by Didier Dubant et Gilles Bellan. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

France emerged from the Italian Wars with a taste for Renaissance art and architecture - the châteaux of the Loire, Leonardo at Amboise - then tore itself apart in decades of Catholic-Protestant conflict resolved by the Edict of Nantes. The Bourbon monarchy afterwards built the most centralised state in Europe, culminating in Louis XIV at Versailles, with a global empire in Canada, the Caribbean and India. Enlightenment writing, fiscal crisis and social resentment brought the whole edifice down in 1789.

âge du Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–140.node: âge du Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–1400 BC)
âge du Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–140.label: âge du Bronze moyen
âge du Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–140.prose:
[France, 1600 BC–1400 BC] âge du Bronze moyen. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Settlements became more permanent and field systems more organised, while metalworkers turned out palstave axes, rapiers and elaborate ornaments in growing quantities. Burial under barrows, often with weapons, marked out warrior elites. The scale of bronze circulation in this phase shows communities firmly locked into continental exchange networks.

âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–52 BC).label: âge du Fer
âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–52 BC).prose:
[France, 800 BC–52 BC] âge du Fer. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Iron, cheap and widely available, replaced bronze for tools and weapons and changed who could arm and equip themselves. Princely burials, Mediterranean wine imports and later the fortified oppida trace the rise of Celtic chiefdoms with coinage, towns and craft specialisation. It ends with Caesar's conquest, which folded Gaul into the Roman world.

âges des Métaux (France, 2200 BC–52 BC).label: âges des Métaux
âges des Métaux (France, 2200 BC–52 BC).prose:
[France, 2200 BC–52 BC] âges des Métaux. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

An umbrella term for the millennia between the last farming communities using stone tools and the Roman conquest, covering both the Bronze and Iron Ages. Metal changed everything it touched: agriculture, warfare, trade routes and the way status was displayed. By its close, hillforts and oppida had grown into something close to towns.

Néolithique (France, 6000 BC–2100 BC).label: Néolithique
Néolithique (France, 6000 BC–2100 BC).prose:
[France, 6000 BC–2100 BC] Néolithique. by Françoise Bostyn. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Herding of sheep, goats and cattle, together with pottery and cultivated grain, spread across the Moroccan coast, the Rif and the Atlas, taking hold among populations descended from earlier hunter-gatherers. Cardial-impressed pottery in the north points to contact across the Strait with Iberia, while cave sites and shell middens show a mixed economy of farming, herding, fishing and gathering. Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.

second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–50 BC).node: second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–50 BC)
second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–50 BC).label: second âge du Fer
second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–50 BC).prose:
[France, 450 BC–50 BC] second âge du Fer. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

The La Tène era, when Gaulish societies developed a distinctive curvilinear art style, struck their own gold and silver coinage, and traded wine and slaves with the Mediterranean. In its last centuries people concentrated in oppida – large fortified towns with workshops, mints and imported goods – until Caesar's campaigns of the 50s BC brought the whole territory under Rome.

âge du Bronze (France, 2200 BC–800 BC).label: âge du Bronze
âge du Bronze (France, 2200 BC–800 BC).prose:
[France, 2200 BC–800 BC] âge du Bronze. by Pierre Jacquet. Period definition from INRAP: Chronologie Generale — INRAP, 2007.

Copper and tin alloyed into bronze pulled the region into long-distance exchange networks running from Cornwall and Brittany to central Europe and the Mediterranean. Warrior elites were buried under tumuli with daggers and axes, and later centuries produced enormous hoards of scrap and finished metalwork, deliberately buried or thrown into rivers. By the closing phase, cremation in urnfields, fortified hilltop sites and mass-produced socketed axes point to the more crowded, competitive world that iron would inherit.

Reign of King Roger II (Italy, AD 1130–A.node: Reign of King Roger II (Italy, AD 1130–AD 1154)
Reign of King Roger II (Italy, AD 1130–A.label: Reign of King Roger II
Reign of King Roger II (Italy, AD 1130–A.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1130–AD 1154] Reign of King Roger II. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

Exploiting a disputed papal election to obtain a crown, Roger welded Sicily and southern Italy into a centralised kingdom with a treasury, a law code issued at Ariano, and a navy that took cities along the North African coast. His Palermo court mixed Latin, Greek and Arabic: the geographer al-Idrisi compiled a world map and description for him, and the mosaics and muqarnas ceiling of the Cappella Palatina show the fusion in built form. The kingdom he made lasted, in one dynasty or another, until Italian unification.

Norman Conquest of Sicily (Italy, AD 106.label: Norman Conquest of Sicily
Norman Conquest of Sicily (Italy, AD 106.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1060–AD 1091] Norman Conquest of Sicily. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

A few hundred Norman adventurers under Robert Guiscard and his brother Roger took Sicily piece by piece from its divided Muslim emirs, beginning at Messina and ending thirty years later at Noto. The result was not expulsion but a hybrid state: Arabic, Greek and Latin used side by side in the chancery, Muslim tax officials, Byzantine mosaicists and Islamic craftsmen working for Christian kings. Out of it came the Kingdom of Sicily and monuments like the Cappella Palatina and Monreale, which look like nothing else in medieval Europe.

Regency of Queen Margaret of Navarre (It.node: Regency of Queen Margaret of Navarre (Italy, AD 1166–AD 1172)
Regency of Queen Margaret of Navarre (It.label: Regency of Queen Margaret of Navarre
Regency of Queen Margaret of Navarre (It.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1166–AD 1172] Regency of Queen Margaret of Navarre. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

The widow of William I ruled Sicily for her adolescent son, releasing political prisoners and trying to broaden the narrow circle of court power. Her promotion of her French kinsman Stephen du Perche as chancellor and archbishop of Palermo provoked a violent backlash from the island's barons and officials, and he was driven out. The turbulence exposed how fragile the balance between Norman, Greek and Arab factions at the Palermo court had become.

Joint Rule of Kings Tancred and Roger II.node: Joint Rule of Kings Tancred and Roger III (Italy, AD 1192–AD 1193)
Joint Rule of Kings Tancred and Roger II.label: Joint Rule of Kings Tancred and Roger III
Joint Rule of Kings Tancred and Roger II.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1192–AD 1193] Joint Rule of Kings Tancred and Roger III. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

Tancred of Lecce, an illegitimate grandson of Roger II, had seized the Sicilian throne against the claims of the Hohenstaufen emperor Henry VI, and crowned his son as co-king to secure the succession. The plan collapsed when the young Roger died within the year, followed months later by Tancred himself, leaving an infant heir and a divided kingdom. Henry VI marched south and took Sicily in 1194, ending Norman rule on the island.

Reign of Count Roger I (Italy, AD 1072–A.node: Reign of Count Roger I (Italy, AD 1072–AD 1101)
Reign of Count Roger I (Italy, AD 1072–A.label: Reign of Count Roger I
Reign of Count Roger I (Italy, AD 1072–A.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1072–AD 1101] Reign of Count Roger I. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

The youngest of the Hauteville brothers finished the thirty-year conquest of Sicily from its Muslim rulers and then governed the island as its Great Count. Rather than displacing the Arab and Greek population, he kept their administrators, taxes and languages, tolerated Islam and Orthodoxy, and rebuilt the Latin church around a privilege from the pope that gave him unusual control over it. The hybrid state he assembled became the basis for the wealthiest kingdom in twelfth-century Europe.

Reign of King William II (Italy, AD 1172.node: Reign of King William II (Italy, AD 1172–AD 1189)
Reign of King William II (Italy, AD 1172.label: Reign of King William II
Reign of King William II (Italy, AD 1172.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1172–AD 1189] Reign of King William II. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

Known as "the Good," William II presided over a peaceful, prosperous Sicily and poured its wealth into building — above all the cathedral of Monreale, whose acres of gold mosaic are the high point of Norman-Arab-Byzantine art. He married Joan, daughter of Henry II of England, campaigned against Byzantium and Egypt, and married his aunt Constance to the Hohenstaufen heir Henry. Dying childless, he unintentionally handed his kingdom to the German emperors, ending Norman rule.

Reign of King Tancred (Italy, AD 1190–AD.label: Reign of King Tancred
Reign of King Tancred (Italy, AD 1190–AD.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1190–AD 1194] Reign of King Tancred. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

An illegitimate grandson of Roger II elected king to keep the German Hohenstaufen out, Tancred spent his short reign fighting Henry VI's invasions and rebellious barons. He also had to manage Richard the Lionheart, who wintered at Messina on his way to the Third Crusade, sacked the city and extracted a large payment. Tancred's death, followed within months by his young heir's deposition, delivered Sicily to Henry VI and ended Norman rule.

Reign of Count Roger II (Italy, AD 1112–.node: Reign of Count Roger II (Italy, AD 1112–AD 1130)
Reign of Count Roger II (Italy, AD 1112–.label: Reign of Count Roger II
Reign of Count Roger II (Italy, AD 1112–.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1112–AD 1130] Reign of Count Roger II. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

Taking personal control of Sicily as a teenager, Roger built a professional administration staffed by Greeks and Arabs, developed a fleet, and waited for the Hauteville line on the mainland to fail. When his cousin died without heirs he seized Apulia and Calabria, uniting the Norman conquests in southern Italy under one ruler over the objections of the papacy. The union of island and mainland set up his coronation as king.

Reign of King William I (Italy, AD 1154–.node: Reign of King William I (Italy, AD 1154–AD 1166)
Reign of King William I (Italy, AD 1154–.label: Reign of King William I
Reign of King William I (Italy, AD 1154–.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1154–AD 1166] Reign of King William I. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

William I of Sicily, remembered by hostile chroniclers as "the Bad," inherited Roger II's rich Norman kingdom and spent his reign holding it together: baronial revolts, the lynching of his powerful minister Maio of Bari, Byzantine landings in Apulia, and war with the papacy and the German emperor. He beat them all off, and the Treaty of Benevento won papal recognition of the Sicilian crown. His court at Palermo kept its extraordinary mix of Latin, Greek and Arabic officials, artists and scholars, seen today in the mosaics and muqarnas ceilings of the Cappella Palatina.

Regency of Countess Adelasia (Italy, AD.label: Regency of Countess Adelasia
Regency of Countess Adelasia (Italy, AD.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1101–AD 1112] Regency of Countess Adelasia. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

Adelaide del Vasto governed Norman Sicily for her young sons after the death of Roger I, holding together a conquest state whose Muslim, Greek and Latin subjects vastly outnumbered its Norman rulers. She moved the centre of government to Palermo, which became the kingdom's capital, and relied heavily on Greek and Arabic-speaking officials. Her later marriage to Baldwin I of Jerusalem ended in humiliating annulment, but the claim to Antioch it generated was used by her son for decades.

Reign of King William III (Italy, AD 119.node: Reign of King William III (Italy, AD 1194–AD 1194)
Reign of King William III (Italy, AD 119.label: Reign of King William III
Reign of King William III (Italy, AD 119.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1194–AD 1194] Reign of King William III. Period definition from Norman Sicily Project — Dawn Marie Hayes, 2017.

A child king crowned amid the scramble for the Sicilian throne after the Norman line failed. Within months Emperor Henry VI took Palermo, deposed him, and shipped him off to captivity in Germany, where he vanished from the record. His removal ended the Hauteville dynasty and joined Sicily to the Hohenstaufen empire.

Early Bronze Age (Syria, 3299 BC–1999 BC.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Syria, 3299 BC–1999 BC.prose:
[Palestine, 3299 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

Middle Bronze Age (Syria, 1999 BC–1549 B.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Syria, 1999 BC–1549 B.prose:
[Palestine, 1999 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

monarchic period (Syria, 999 BC–585 BC).label: monarchic period
monarchic period (Syria, 999 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Palestine, 999 BC–585 BC] monarchic period. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

Aramaean kingdoms - Damascus, Hamath, Bit-Agusi and their rivals - ruled from walled capitals with palaces, carved orthostats and monumental inscriptions in alphabetic Aramaic, a script that would spread across the Near East. They fought and allied with Israel, Phoenicia and the Neo-Hittite states before Assyrian armies annexed them one by one. Babylonian campaigns finished the job, ending independent kingship in the region.

Israelite Period (Syria, 1199 BC–299 BC).label: Israelite Period
Israelite Period (Syria, 1199 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Palestine, 1199 BC–299 BC] Israelite Period. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

Spans the Iron Age kingdoms of the Levant through the Babylonian conquest and the two centuries of Persian rule that followed. Under the Achaemenids the region was a satrapal backwater but a prosperous one: exiles returned to rebuild the Jerusalem temple, Phoenician ports flourished, and Greek pottery and coinage flooded in. It ends with Alexander's conquest and the arrival of Hellenistic rule.

Iron Age (Syria, 1199 BC–299 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Syria, 1199 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Palestine, 1199 BC–299 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Early Canaanite Period (Syria, 3299 BC–1.label: Early Canaanite Period
Early Canaanite Period (Syria, 3299 BC–1.prose:
[Palestine, 3299 BC–1999 BC] Early Canaanite Period. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. see also Mazar, 1992. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

The Levant's first cities rose, thrived and fell within this span: walled towns with temples, palaces and craft quarters, connected by trade in oil, wine, timber and metals to Egypt and Mesopotamia. Ebla in inland Syria is the outstanding example, its cuneiform archives naming hundreds of trading partners. By the end, drought, warfare and the fall of Old Kingdom Egypt and the Akkadian empire had scattered many communities into villages and pastoral camps.

Late Bronze Age (Syria, 1549 BC–1199 BC).label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Syria, 1549 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Palestine, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Middle Canaanite (Syria, 1999 BC–1549 BC.label: Middle Canaanite
Middle Canaanite (Syria, 1999 BC–1549 BC.prose:
[Palestine, 1999 BC–1549 BC] Middle Canaanite. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

The Middle Bronze Age of the Levant and inland Syria, when fortified city-states ringed by massive earthen ramparts dominated the landscape and Amorite dynasties ruled at Mari, Aleppo, Qatna and Ebla. Trade in tin, textiles and wine tied the region to Mesopotamia, Egypt and Crete, and Levantine settlers in the Nile Delta eventually became Egypt's Hyksos rulers. Visitors will recognise the period's fine burnished pottery, bronze duckbill axes and the alphabet's earliest experiments in the region's scripts.

Late Canaanite (Syria, 1549 BC–1199 BC).label: Late Canaanite
Late Canaanite (Syria, 1549 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Palestine, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Canaanite. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

The Late Bronze Age Levant, when Canaanite city-states such as Ugarit, Qatna and Alalakh were caught between the Egyptian New Kingdom, Mitanni and the Hittites, paying tribute and playing one great power against another. Palaces held archives in cuneiform — the Amarna letters preserve the correspondence — and ports handled Cypriot copper, Mycenaean pottery and Egyptian luxuries; at Ugarit scribes wrote the world's earliest alphabetic texts. Around 1200 BC the palaces burned and the system collapsed, clearing the way for the Iron Age kingdoms of Syria and Israel.

Old Syrian Period (Syria, 1999 BC–1549 B.label: Old Syrian Period
Old Syrian Period (Syria, 1999 BC–1549 B.prose:
[Palestine, 1999 BC–1549 BC] Old Syrian Period. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

Amorite-ruled city-states such as Aleppo (Yamhad), Qatna, Ebla and Mari dominated inland Syria, each with its palace, temples and treaty networks binding it to neighbours and rivals. The royal archive at Mari, with its thousands of letters, reveals diplomacy, prophecy and the workings of a Bronze Age court in extraordinary detail. Distinctive glyptic art and monumental temples of this age were swept aside by Hittite raids and the rise of Mitanni.

Middle Syrian (Syria, 1549 BC–1199 BC).label: Middle Syrian
Middle Syrian (Syria, 1549 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Palestine, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Middle Syrian. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

Syria became the contested ground between great powers – Mitanni, then the Hittites pressing south and Egypt pushing north – with local kingdoms surviving as vassals playing one overlord against another. Cosmopolitan ports and river towns such as Ugarit and Emar grew wealthy on trade, and at Ugarit scribes reduced cuneiform to a thirty-sign alphabet. The whole system collapsed around 1200 BC amid destruction, migration and the fall of the Hittite empire.

New Syrian Period (Syria, 1199 BC–299 BC.label: New Syrian Period
New Syrian Period (Syria, 1199 BC–299 BC.prose:
[Palestine, 1199 BC–299 BC] New Syrian Period. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. Period definition from The biblical world — 2002.

With the collapse of the Bronze Age empires, Syria fragmented into Aramaean and Neo-Hittite kingdoms such as Damascus, Hamath, Guzana and Carchemish, whose rulers built columned palaces guarded by carved stone orthostats and wrote in alphabetic Aramaic. One by one they were swallowed by the Assyrian empire, then passed to Babylon and to Persia. Aramaic outlived every one of these conquerors to become the common language of the Near East.

Later Uruk period (Iraq, 3399 BC–3099 BC.label: Later Uruk period
Later Uruk period (Iraq, 3399 BC–3099 BC.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 3399 BC–3099 BC] Later Uruk period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

Southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities, with Uruk itself sprawling over hundreds of hectares around monumental temple platforms. Accounting needs drove the invention of writing: clay tablets of pictographic signs recording rations, livestock and labour. Uruk-style pottery, architecture and cylinder seals appear from Syria to Iran, evidence of colonies or trading outposts reaching far up the rivers.

Mitanni (Iraq, 1499 BC–1349 BC).label: Mitanni
Mitanni (Iraq, 1499 BC–1349 BC).prose:
[Babylonia, 1499 BC–1349 BC] Mitanni. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

A Hurrian-speaking kingdom that dominated northern Syria and Mesopotamia from a capital, Washukanni, still not securely located. Its chariot aristocracy and horse-training expertise made it a great power on par with Egypt, Babylon and Hatti; Mitanni princesses married into the Egyptian royal house, and its kings correspond as equals in the Amarna letters. Hittite attacks and Assyrian expansion dismembered it, and Assyria inherited its territory.

Second Dynasty of Isin (Iraq, 1156 BC–10.node: Second Dynasty of Isin (Iraq, 1156 BC–1025 BC)
Second Dynasty of Isin (Iraq, 1156 BC–10.label: Second Dynasty of Isin
Second Dynasty of Isin (Iraq, 1156 BC–10.prose:
[Babylonia, 1156 BC–1025 BC] Second Dynasty of Isin. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Dynasty IV from Isin. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

After an Elamite raid carried off the last Kassite king and the statue of Marduk, a line of rulers from Isin took the Babylonian throne. Its greatest king, Nebuchadnezzar I, invaded Elam and brought the god home in triumph - an event celebrated in poetry that helped raise Marduk to the head of the Babylonian pantheon. The dynasty's later reigns were eroded by Aramaean incursions and famine, and Babylonia sank into a long period of weakness.

Old Babylonian period (Iraq, 2003 BC–177.label: Old Babylonian period
Old Babylonian period (Iraq, 2003 BC–177.prose:
[Babylonia, 2003 BC–1779 BC] Old Babylonian period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

After the collapse of the Ur III state, Amorite dynasties took over the old cities, with Isin, Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari competing until Hammurabi of Babylon defeated them all. His law stele is the most famous product of an era that also gave us letters, contracts and school exercises in unprecedented quantity. Scribes of this time copied and shaped the Sumerian literary canon and the earliest full version of the Gilgamesh epic, and worked out mathematics that anticipated the Pythagorean theorem.

Ubaid (Iraq, 6199 BC–4099 BC).label: Ubaid
Ubaid (Iraq, 6199 BC–4099 BC).prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 6199 BC–4099 BC] Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

The first widespread village culture of southern Mesopotamia, marked by pale greenish painted pottery, mudbrick houses of tripartite plan and small temples rebuilt again and again on the same spot, most famously at Eridu. Irrigation let farmers work the dry alluvium, herds and fishing filled out the diet, and communities grew large enough to support differences in status visible in burials and buildings. Ubaid pottery and styles spread north into Syria and Anatolia and down the Gulf, setting the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.

Jemdet Nasr period (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 B.label: Jemdet Nasr period
Jemdet Nasr period (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 B.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

A short but pivotal span in southern Mesopotamia when writing moved from crude tokens of quantity toward a flexible script, and when large temple institutions organised farming and craft production. Painted polychrome jars are its signature find. The cities that grew during it, Uruk, Ur, Kish and others, became the rival powers of the Early Dynastic age.

Akkadian Empire (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC).label: Akkadian Empire
Akkadian Empire (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC).prose:
[Sumer, Akkad, northern Levant, eastern Anatolia, Zagros, 2333 BC–2192 BC] Akkadian Empire. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

Sargon's conquest of Sumer produced the first state to hold the whole of southern Mesopotamia and much of the north under one ruler, garrisoned by soldiers who 'ate bread' at the king's table. Trade reached Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha, temple estates were reorganised, and the king's daughter Enheduanna composed hymns that are the earliest poetry attributed to a named author. Its fall left a memory of universal empire that Ur, Babylon and Assyria all tried to revive.

Neo-Assyrian period (Iraq, 779 BC–608 BC.label: Neo-Assyrian period
Neo-Assyrian period (Iraq, 779 BC–608 BC.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 779 BC–608 BC] Neo-Assyrian period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

The last and most powerful century and a half of Assyrian rule, when kings from Tiglath-pileser III to Ashurbanipal governed a vast provincial empire from Nineveh and moved whole populations to break resistance. Palace reliefs, royal correspondence and scholarly archives from this time make it one of the best documented periods of the ancient Near East. Overextension, civil war and a Median-Babylonian alliance brought the whole structure down within a generation.

Early Uruk period (Iraq, 4099 BC–3399 BC.label: Early Uruk period
Early Uruk period (Iraq, 4099 BC–3399 BC.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 4099 BC–3399 BC] Early Uruk period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient Mesopotamia : new perspectives — McIntosh, Jane., 2005.

Villages in southern Mesopotamia swelled into the world's first cities, with Uruk itself outgrowing every rival. Mass-produced bevel-rimmed bowls, probably used to pay rations, signal an economy in which temples and their administrators organised labour on a large scale. The bookkeeping devices of this era - seals, tokens and clay envelopes - developed directly into the earliest writing.

Early Archaic (Italy, 599 BC–549 BC).label: Early Archaic
Early Archaic (Italy, 599 BC–549 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 599 BC–549 BC] Early Archaic. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.

Late Archaic (Italy, 519 BC–469 BC).label: Late Archaic
Late Archaic (Italy, 519 BC–469 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 519 BC–469 BC] Late Archaic. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.

Late Classical (Italy, 399 BC–299 BC).label: Late Classical
Late Classical (Italy, 399 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 399 BC–299 BC] Late Classical. Brendel earlier calls this period "Etruscan Art of the Fourth Century", but then only refers to art of this period as "Classical" or "Late Classical", with the same temporal boundaries. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

In the Greek cities of the south, this was the era of grand Apulian and Lucanian red-figure vases, tomb painting, and lavish burials, even as Oscan and Lucanian peoples took over cities like Poseidonia. Central Italy saw Etruscan power ebb and Rome fight its way through the Latin and Samnite wars, absorbing neighbours and building the first roads and aqueducts. By the end of the century the peninsula's future belonged to Rome rather than to the Greek or Etruscan cities.

Classical (Italy, 479 BC–329 BC).label: Classical
Classical (Italy, 479 BC–329 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 479 BC–329 BC] Classical. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.

Middle Archaic (Italy, 549 BC–519 BC).label: Middle Archaic
Middle Archaic (Italy, 549 BC–519 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 549 BC–519 BC] Middle Archaic. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

Villanovan Geometric (Italy, 799 BC–724.label: Villanovan Geometric
Villanovan Geometric (Italy, 799 BC–724.prose:
[Etruria, 799 BC–724 BC] Villanovan Geometric. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

In the later Villanovan phase, geometric ornament borrowed from the Greek world spreads across pottery and bronzework, a sign of the contacts opened by Euboean traders at Pithekoussai and Cumae. Graves become sharply unequal: a few contain imported vases, elaborate armour and the first writing in Italy, while proto-urban centres consolidate into the cities of historical Etruria.

Hellenistic (Italy, 299 BC–99 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Italy, 299 BC–99 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 299 BC–99 BC] Hellenistic. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Classical (Italy, 449 BC–399 BC).label: Classical
Classical (Italy, 449 BC–399 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 449 BC–399 BC] Classical. Brendel also calls this period "Response to Greek Classical Art" (259). Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.

Orientalizing (Italy, 679 BC–599 BC).label: Orientalizing
Orientalizing (Italy, 679 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 679 BC–599 BC] Orientalizing. Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

Rich hillforts and enormous burial mounds in the Dolenjska region mark a wealthy Hallstatt-era elite trading with Italy and the eastern Alps. Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. The imagery borrows from Etruscan and Near Eastern art but tells local stories.

Transitional (Italy, 479 BC–449 BC).label: Transitional
Transitional (Italy, 479 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 479 BC–449 BC] Transitional. Brendel also calls this period "Proto-Classical" (e.g. 283ff). Period definition from Etruscan art — Brendel, Otto, 1901-1973., 1995.

The decades between the Archaic and the fully Classical in Greek and South Italian art, when the stiff smiling kouroi give way to the grave, heavy-limbed figures of the Severe Style. Vase painters abandon Archaic mannerisms for freer poses and foreshortening, and sculptors begin to model bodies that shift their weight and turn in space.

Middle Lydian (Turkey, 679 BC–546 BC).label: Middle Lydian
Middle Lydian (Turkey, 679 BC–546 BC).prose:
[Lydia, 679 BC–546 BC] Middle Lydian. R's Middle Lydian period is coterminous with the Mermnad dynasty: chronological chart on p. 12. Period definition from The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander — Roosevelt, Christopher H. (Christopher Havemeyer), 1972-, 2009.

Under the Mermnad kings from Gyges to Croesus, Lydia grew from a western Anatolian kingdom into the dominant power between the Aegean coast and the Halys river, taxing the Greek cities and funding lavish dedications at Delphi. Its craftsmen refined electrum from the Pactolus river and struck it into stamped, standardised lumps, effectively inventing coinage. Sardis fell to Cyrus the Great, and Lydia's wealth, its coinage and its road system passed to the Persian Empire.
Middle Lydian (Turkey, 679 BC–546 BC).source: The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander

Early Lydian (Turkey, 1199 BC–679 BC).label: Early Lydian
Early Lydian (Turkey, 1199 BC–679 BC).prose:
[Lydia, 1199 BC–679 BC] Early Lydian. From chronological table on p. 12; = Lydian "Early Iron Age". Period definition from The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander — Roosevelt, Christopher H. (Christopher Havemeyer), 1972-, 2009.

In the centuries after the Hittite empire fell, the communities of the Hermus valley in western Anatolia rebuilt around the citadel of Sardis. Excavation there has revealed successive Iron Age occupation layers with local painted wares and evidence of gold-bearing streams, beneath the later royal city. This obscure phase precedes the Mermnad kings, whose wealth and invention of coinage made Lydia famous.
Early Lydian (Turkey, 1199 BC–679 BC).source: The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander

Late Lydian (Turkey, 546 BC–333 BC).label: Late Lydian
Late Lydian (Turkey, 546 BC–333 BC).prose:
[Lydia, 546 BC–333 BC] Late Lydian. From chronology chart on p. 12; = Achaemenid period. Period definition from The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander — Roosevelt, Christopher H. (Christopher Havemeyer), 1972-, 2009.

After Cyrus defeated Croesus, Sardis became the western capital of the Persian empire — seat of a satrap, terminus of the Royal Road, and the place where Persian tribute and Greek diplomacy met. Lydian language, burial mounds and pottery continued alongside imported Achaemenid luxury goods and administrative practice. The city was handed over to Alexander without a fight, ending Persian rule.
Late Lydian (Turkey, 546 BC–333 BC).source: The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander

Late Bronze Age (Turkey, 1599 BC–1199 BC.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Turkey, 1599 BC–1199 BC.prose:
[Lydia, 1599 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander — Roosevelt, Christopher H. (Christopher Havemeyer), 1972-, 2009.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Turkey, 1599 BC–1199 BC.source: The archaeology of Lydia, from Gyges to Alexander

Archaic Age (Greece, 619 BC–479 BC).label: Archaic Age
Archaic Age (Greece, 619 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Greece, 619 BC–479 BC] Archaic Age. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Out of the poverty of the Dark Age came an explosion of activity: the alphabet adapted from Phoenician, colonies planted from Spain to the Black Sea, and the city-state emerging as the standard political unit. Massed hoplite warfare tied citizenship to military service, tyrants seized power in city after city, and Athens moved through Solon's reforms and the Peisistratids to Cleisthenes' democracy. It ended in the Persian invasions, whose defeat at Salamis and Plataea left the Greeks with a sense of themselves that shaped everything after.

Dark Ages (Greece, 1099 BC–799 BC).label: Dark Ages
Dark Ages (Greece, 1099 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–799 BC] Dark Ages. GeoDia had Late Period 664 and 760 B.C. to 332 B.C. (unclear). Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

The centuries after the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, when writing disappeared from Greece along with monumental building, fresco painting and long-distance trade. Populations fell and dispersed into small villages, but iron working spread, cremation burial became common, and Protogeometric pottery shows a new visual order emerging. Out of this reduced world came the alphabet, the city-state and the oral tradition that would be written down as the Homeric epics.

Israelite (Israel, 1199 BC–923 BC).label: Israelite
Israelite (Israel, 1199 BC–923 BC).prose:
[Israel, 1199 BC–923 BC] Israelite. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Lebanon, West Bank. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Small unwalled villages spread across the central highlands, with pillared four-room houses, terraced fields and collar-rim storage jars, marking the emergence of a distinct people in the hill country as Egyptian control of Canaan faded. Tradition remembers this as the age of the judges and then of Saul, David and Solomon, when Jerusalem became a royal centre. The united monarchy split into Israel and Judah at the end of the period, a division that shaped the biblical narrative.

Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1639.label: Second Intermediate Period
Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1639.prose:
[Egypt, 1639 BC–1531 BC] Second Intermediate Period. GeoDia had 1795-1550 B.C., and Hyksos from 1650-1550 B.C. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

A divided Egypt, with the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the Delta from Avaris, a rump Theban kingdom in the south, and the Kushite kings of Kerma pressing the frontier. Trade with the Levant and the Aegean flourished at Avaris even as pharaonic art and building shrank. The Theban wars of liberation under Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and finally Ahmose reunified the country and launched the New Kingdom.

Villanovan period (Italy, 899 BC–759 BC).label: Villanovan period
Villanovan period (Italy, 899 BC–759 BC).prose:
[Etruria, 899 BC–759 BC] Villanovan period. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

The earliest Iron Age culture of central Italy, known above all from its cemeteries: ashes placed in distinctive biconical urns, sometimes in miniature clay huts that model the thatched houses of the living. Scattered hilltop villages gradually clustered into the sites that would become Tarquinia, Vulci, Veii and Bologna, and bronze- and iron-working supported growing trade with Sardinia, Greece and the Levant. Most scholars now see these people not as newcomers but as the direct ancestors of the Etruscans, caught at the moment before cities appeared.

Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2599 BC–2129 BC).label: Old Kingdom
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2599 BC–2129 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2599 BC–2129 BC] Old Kingdom. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

Bronze Age (Sumer, 2999 BC–999 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Sumer, 2999 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Sumer, 2999 BC–999 BC] Bronze Age. GeoDia had Amarna 1352-1336 B.C. (Egyptian capital) and Bronze Age 3150-1070 B.C. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Hellenistic Age (Greece, 335 BC–30 BC).label: Hellenistic Age
Hellenistic Age (Greece, 335 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Greece, 335 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic Age. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Alexander's campaigns broke the Persian Empire and scattered Greek settlers, soldiers and administrators from Egypt to the Indus; after his death his generals carved the conquests into rival monarchies. Greek became the common language of trade and learning across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, and cities such as Alexandria and Pergamon eclipsed old Athens as centres of science, libraries and monumental art. Rome absorbed the pieces one by one, ending with Egypt in 30 BC.

Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC).label: Middle Kingdom
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC] Middle Kingdom. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

Hittite (Turkey, 1849 BC–1199 BC).label: Hittite
Hittite (Turkey, 1849 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 1849 BC–1199 BC] Hittite. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

An Indo-European-speaking people built a state around Hattusa on the Anatolian plateau, first known from the tablets of Assyrian merchants and then from their own cuneiform archives. They fielded light chariots, wrote some of the earliest surviving law codes and international treaties, and preserved older Hattian and Hurrian gods alongside their own. Their capital's rock-cut sanctuaries and lion gates, and a royal archive of tens of thousands of clay tablets, make them one of the best-documented Bronze Age powers.

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC).label: New Kingdom
New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Old Palace Period (Crete, 1999 BC–1599 B.label: Old Palace Period
Old Palace Period (Crete, 1999 BC–1599 B.prose:
[Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Old Palace Period. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Crete's earliest palaces served as hubs where grain, oil and wine were gathered and redistributed, and where seal-stones and early writing were used to track it all. Minoan pottery and metalwork from this era turn up in Egypt and the Levant, evidence of an island economy reaching well beyond the Aegean. Peak sanctuaries and cave shrines show a religious life closely tied to the landscape.

First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2129 B.label: First Intermediate Period
First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2129 B.prose:
[Egypt, 2129 BC–2039 BC] First Intermediate Period. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Central authority collapsed after the long reign of Pepi II, and Egypt broke into competing regional powers - provincial governors ruling as local dynasts, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Low Nile floods, famine and disorder colour the literature written afterwards, but tomb goods and inscriptions show provincial workshops and local elites flourishing. Funerary practices once reserved for kings spread to lesser officials, laying groundwork for the Coffin Texts. The Theban victory that ended the era produced the reunified Middle Kingdom.

New Palace Period (Crete, 1599 BC–1424 B.label: New Palace Period
New Palace Period (Crete, 1599 BC–1424 B.prose:
[Crete, 1599 BC–1424 BC] New Palace Period. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

The great age of the Minoan palaces, when Knossos and its rivals were vast multi-storey complexes of storerooms, workshops, light wells and ceremonial halls. Cretan ships, pottery and craftsmen reached Egypt and the Levant, and Linear A writing recorded palace accounts still undeciphered today. Frescoes and seal-stones from this period supply nearly everything we picture when we think of Minoan civilisation.

Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3099 BC–2599 BC).label: Early Dynastic
Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3099 BC–2599 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 3099 BC–2599 BC] Early Dynastic. GeoDia had 3000-2613 B.C. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

Assyrian (Syria, 1299 BC–604 BC).label: Assyrian
Assyrian (Syria, 1299 BC–604 BC).prose:
[Euphrates, Cyprus, southern Anatolia, Palestine, Syria, Egypt, 1299 BC–604 BC] Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Gaza, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Assyrian armies pushed west repeatedly into Syria, absorbing the Aramaean and Neo-Hittite states one by one until the region became a patchwork of provinces governed from Nineveh and Kalhu. Deportation was used as policy, shuffling populations across the empire and spreading Aramaic as a common tongue. Syrian cities supplied tribute in ivory, purple cloth and horses, and the ivory-carving workshops of Arslan Tash and elsewhere produced some of the finest luxury objects of the age.

Third Intermediate period (Egypt, 1059 B.label: Third Intermediate period
Third Intermediate period (Egypt, 1059 B.prose:
[Egypt, 1059 BC–663 BC] Third Intermediate period. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Centralised royal power dissolved into competing dynasties, with kings in the Delta, high priests governing the south from Thebes, and Libyan chiefs carving out territories of their own. Temple treasuries and reused royal burials became the focus of wealth, and metalwork inlaid with gold and silver reached a peak. Kushite rulers from Sudan reunified Egypt for a time, before Assyrian armies ended the arrangement.

Classical Age (Greece, 479 BC–403 BC).label: Classical Age
Classical Age (Greece, 479 BC–403 BC).prose:
[Greece, 479 BC–403 BC] Classical Age. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

With the Persians repulsed, Athens converted a defensive alliance into a maritime empire and spent its tribute on the Parthenon, on drama festivals and on the world's most radical experiment in citizen democracy. Sophists, Socrates, Herodotus and the tragedians all worked in this intense half-century. Rivalry with Sparta erupted into the Peloponnesian War, which ended in plague, defeat and the dismantling of Athenian power.

Mycenaean (Greece, 2199 BC–1099 BC).label: Mycenaean
Mycenaean (Greece, 2199 BC–1099 BC).prose:
[Greece, 2199 BC–1099 BC] Mycenaean. added. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Mainland Greece moved from farming villages to fortified palace centres at Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns, ruled by warrior elites buried with gold masks, weapons and imported luxuries. Their scribes kept accounts in Linear B, the earliest written Greek, recording rations, livestock and offerings to gods later worshipped in the classical world. The palaces burned around 1200 BC and writing vanished with them, but memories of these citadels survived to become the world of Homer's epics.

Orientalizing Period (Greece, 729 BC–629.label: Orientalizing Period
Orientalizing Period (Greece, 729 BC–629.prose:
[Greece, 729 BC–629 BC] Orientalizing Period. Period definition from Egypt, Greece and Rome — Freeman, Charles., 2004.

Greek artists absorbed the visual language of the Near East, filling vases and bronzes with lions, sphinxes, and floral ornament borrowed from Phoenician and Syrian models. Trading posts and colonies carried the exchange in both directions, and Corinth grew rich exporting the resulting painted pottery. Alongside the imagery came the alphabet and Eastern myths that resurface in Hesiod and Homer.

DAI (Greece, 1074 BC–974 BC).label: DAI
DAI (Greece, 1074 BC–974 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1074 BC–974 BC] DAI. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 3: Tyler Conlin and Morgan Newton. Period definition from The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective — W. A. McDonald.

The first phase of the Greek Dark Age, defined at excavations such as Nichoria in Messenia, when the Mycenaean world had broken down into small scattered communities. Populations were low, writing had been lost, and people lived in modest apsidal huts, herding animals and working iron rather than bronze.
DAI (Greece, 1074 BC–974 BC).source: The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective

DAIII (Greece, 799 BC–749 BC).label: DAIII
DAIII (Greece, 799 BC–749 BC).prose:
[Greece, 799 BC–749 BC] DAIII. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 3: Tyler Conlin and Morgan Newton. Period definition from The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective — W. A. McDonald.

The closing phase of the Greek Dark Age, when population rose sharply, sanctuaries began receiving substantial dedications, and Greeks were sailing to Italy and the Levant. The alphabet was adopted from Phoenician traders, monumental Geometric vases were painted with funeral scenes, and the first city-states took shape.
DAIII (Greece, 799 BC–749 BC).source: The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective

DAII (Greece, 974 BC–799 BC).label: DAII
DAII (Greece, 974 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Greece, 974 BC–799 BC] DAII. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 3: Tyler Conlin and Morgan Newton; note that this period subsumes a separate period "Dark Age II/III" that Conlin and Newton drew from McDonald and Coulson, and date 850-800 B.C. Period definition from The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective — W. A. McDonald.

The long middle stretch of the Greek Dark Age, when small communities grew into more stable villages with large central buildings that may have housed a chief and his household. Contacts with Crete, Cyprus and the Levant slowly resumed, and Protogeometric pottery with its compass-drawn circles spread out from Athens across the Aegean.
DAII (Greece, 974 BC–799 BC).source: The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective

Late Geometric (Greece, 749 BC–699 BC).label: Late Geometric
Late Geometric (Greece, 749 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 749 BC–699 BC] Late Geometric. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 3: Tyler Conlin and Morgan Newton. Period definition from The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective — W. A. McDonald.

Greek vase painters abandoned pure pattern for people: funeral processions, chariots, warships and duelling warriors crowd the huge Dipylon grave markers of Athens. The same decades saw the alphabet adopted, sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filling with dedications, colonists sailing west to Italy and Sicily, and the emergence of the polis — the world in which the Homeric poems took shape.
Late Geometric (Greece, 749 BC–699 BC).source: The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective

DAII/III (Greece, 849 BC–799 BC).label: DAII/III
DAII/III (Greece, 849 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Greece, 849 BC–799 BC] DAII/III. Period definition from The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective — W. A. McDonald.

A transitional phase in Dark Age Greece as village communities became larger and more organised, with wealthier burials, growing metalwork and reviving overseas contact - the groundwork for the sanctuaries, colonies and city-states of the following century.
DAII/III (Greece, 849 BC–799 BC).source: The Dark Age at Nichoria: A Perspective

Late Classical (Sicily, 399 BC–322 BC).label: Late Classical
Late Classical (Sicily, 399 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 399 BC–322 BC] Late Classical. Period definition from Uplands of ancient Sicily and Calabria : the archaeology of landscape revisited — 2007.

In the Greek cities of the south, this was the era of grand Apulian and Lucanian red-figure vases, tomb painting, and lavish burials, even as Oscan and Lucanian peoples took over cities like Poseidonia. Central Italy saw Etruscan power ebb and Rome fight its way through the Latin and Samnite wars, absorbing neighbours and building the first roads and aqueducts. By the end of the century the peninsula's future belonged to Rome rather than to the Greek or Etruscan cities.
Late Classical (Sicily, 399 BC–322 BC).source: Uplands of ancient Sicily and Calabria : the archaeology of landscape revisited

Hellenistic (Sicily, 322 BC–240 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Sicily, 322 BC–240 BC).prose:
[Sicily, 322 BC–240 BC] Hellenistic. Period ends with Roman annexation of Sicily, 241 B.C. Period definition from Uplands of ancient Sicily and Calabria : the archaeology of landscape revisited — 2007.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.
Hellenistic (Sicily, 322 BC–240 BC).source: Uplands of ancient Sicily and Calabria : the archaeology of landscape revisited

Roman Republic (Italy, 508 BC–26 BC).label: Roman Republic
Roman Republic (Italy, 508 BC–26 BC).prose:
[Rome, 508 BC–26 BC] Roman Republic. Period definition from Epigraphische Datenbank Heidelberg — Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, 2017.

After expelling its kings, Rome developed a government of elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and citizen assemblies, and an army of property-owning citizens. It absorbed Italy, destroyed Carthage and took the Greek east, becoming the dominant Mediterranean power within two centuries. The wealth and slaves that flooded in wrecked the old order, producing land crises, political violence and the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Caesar. Its institutions and its collapse became the standard reference point for later republics.

Late Roman Republic (Italy, 145 BC–26 BC.label: Late Roman Republic
Late Roman Republic (Italy, 145 BC–26 BC.prose:
[Rome, 145 BC–26 BC] Late Roman Republic. Broader:Roman Republic. Period definition from Epigraphische Datenbank Heidelberg — Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, 2017.

Conquests from Spain to Syria poured wealth, slaves and grain into Italy while the political system built for a city-state buckled: land reform turned violent, generals recruited armies loyal to themselves, and civil war became routine. Sulla, Pompey, Caesar, Antony and Octavian each pushed the constitution further until it stopped functioning. The result was Augustus and one-man rule, dressed in the language of the restored Republic.

Style Attique à Figures Noires (Greece,.node: Style Attique à Figures Noires (Greece, 599 BC–499 BC)
Style Attique à Figures Noires (Greece,.label: Style Attique à Figures Noires
Style Attique à Figures Noires (Greece,.prose:
[Attique (Grèce), 599 BC–499 BC] Style Attique à Figures Noires. "Nous ne citerons ici que les publications générales les plus récentes qui présentent une vue d'ensemble sur la fabrication classique du VIe et du Ve siècle, pour les vases à figures noires et à figures rouges. Voir pour la France: Pottier, 'Catalogue des vases du Musée du Louvre, IIIe partie, l'École Attique.--Perrot, 'Hist. de l'art', tome X.--Dugas, article 'Vasa' du 'Dict. des Antiq.' de Saglio.--Pour l'Angleterre: Walters-Birch, 'History of ancient Pottery', tome I.--Pour l'Italie: Ducati, 'Storia della ceramica greca' (en cours de publication).--Pour l'Allemagne: Furtwaengler-Reichhold-Hauser, 'Griechische Vasenmalerei'.--Hoeber, 'Griech. Vasen'.--Buschor, 'Griech. Vasenmalerei'.--Pfuhl, 'Malerei und Zeichnung der Griechen'.". Period definition from Corpus vasorum antiquorum, France. Fascicule 2, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 2 — 1923.

Athenian potters painted figures in glossy black silhouette on the orange clay, incising interior detail with a needle and adding touches of white and purple - a technique perfected in the sixth century and exported all over the Mediterranean. Painters such as Exekias and the Amasis Painter signed their work and pushed the medium toward genuine narrative, giving us some of the earliest named artists in Europe. Because these vases travelled in trade and were buried in Etruscan tombs, they now supply much of what we know about Greek myth, dress, drinking parties and athletics.
Style Attique à Figures Noires (Greece,.source: Corpus vasorum antiquorum, France. Fascicule 2, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 2
