Style Proto-Élamite, Deuxième Période (I.source: Corpus vasorum antiquorum, France. Fascicule 2, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 2

Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.label: Late Cycladic I
Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Cycladic I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The moment captured at Akrotiri on Thera: a prosperous multi-storey town with paved streets, plumbing and walls painted with boxing boys, saffron gatherers and a fleet of ships. Cretan weights, script and pottery shapes show how deeply the islands were tied into the Minoan world, without being ruled by it. A volcanic eruption buried the town under metres of pumice, preserving it and ending the phase abruptly.
Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan III (palaces) (Greece, 1389.label: Late Minoan III (palaces)
Late Minoan III (palaces) (Greece, 1389.prose:
[Aegean, 1389 BC–1079 BC] Late Minoan III (palaces). Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Palace administration ended with the final destruction of Knossos, and Crete settled into a pattern of scattered towns under Mycenaean cultural influence. Burial in rock-cut chamber tombs with painted larnakes became standard, and mass-produced pottery circulated across the Aegean and to Cyprus. The general Bronze Age collapse pushed communities up into remote, defensible sites, closing the Minoan world.
Late Minoan III (palaces) (Greece, 1389.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Minoan III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999 B.label: Early Minoan III
Early Minoan III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999 B.prose:
[Aegean, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Early Minoan III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

A quieter, poorly understood stretch between the collapses of the Early Bronze Age and the sudden appearance of the palaces. Potters adopted white-painted decoration on dark burnished surfaces, hieroglyphic-style seals began to circulate, and settlement concentrated at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia—the very sites where monumental courts would soon rise.
Early Minoan III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan IIIA2 (Greece, 1359 BC–1299.label: Late Minoan IIIA2
Late Minoan IIIA2 (Greece, 1359 BC–1299.prose:
[Aegean, 1359 BC–1299 BC] Late Minoan IIIA2. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The high point of Cretan participation in eastern Mediterranean trade, when Cretan stirrup jars carrying oil and wine reached Egypt, Cyprus and Sardinia and Aegean names appear in Egyptian inscriptions. Settlements such as Chania and Kommos flourished as ports while Knossos declined. Chamber tombs with painted larnakes spread across the island, marking a broad, prosperous elite rather than a single royal centre.
Late Minoan IIIA2 (Greece, 1359 BC–1299.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Helladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.label: Early Helladic III
Early Helladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.prose:
[Aegean, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

After the destructions, Messenian settlements were smaller and simpler, with apsidal houses and new dark-on-light painted pottery of the Tiryns type. Population and long-distance contacts contracted sharply. The pottery and building traditions of this phase carry directly into the Middle Helladic period.
Early Helladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan IIIC (Greece, 1189 BC–1079 B.label: Late Minoan IIIC
Late Minoan IIIC (Greece, 1189 BC–1079 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1189 BC–1079 BC] Late Minoan IIIC. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The refuge era: Cretans moved to steep, defensible inland sites such as Karphi, Vrokastro and Kavousi Kastro, leaving the great coastal centres empty. Writing and centralised administration vanished, but potters produced lively new octopus and pictorial styles, and iron began to appear alongside bronze. Out of these small upland communities came the settlement pattern and cults of Early Iron Age Crete.
Late Minoan IIIC (Greece, 1189 BC–1079 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Minoan (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC).label: Middle Minoan
Middle Minoan (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Minoan. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Crete's first palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, huge multi-storey complexes built around a central court, packed with storage magazines for oil and grain and workshops for craft production. Administrators kept accounts on clay in Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A, potters threw eggshell-thin Kamares ware painted in white and red on black, and Cretan goods travelled to Egypt and the Levant. Earthquakes levelled the palaces around 1700 BC; they were rebuilt grander still.
Middle Minoan (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.label: Middle Cycladic III
Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.prose:
[Aegean, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Cycladic III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Cretan influence becomes overwhelming: Minoan pottery, weights, loomweights and even Linear A writing appear in island towns, and local products imitate palatial styles. The transformation carries directly into the frescoed, richly furnished Akrotiri destroyed by the eruption of Thera in the following period.
Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Helladic
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Helladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Mainland Greece at its poorest and plainest: modest villages of mudbrick houses, burials in simple cist graves and tumuli, and the grey wheel-made pottery known as Minyan ware. Messenia's communities were small and dispersed, with little sign of the wealth or hierarchy to come. Towards its end, richer graves and imported Cretan goods signal the emergence of the warrior elites who would build the Mycenaean palace at Pylos.
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1189 B.label: Late Minoan IIIB
Late Minoan IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1189 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1299 BC–1189 BC] Late Minoan IIIB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

A period of steady output and shrinking horizons: pottery workshops kept producing the standard Aegean repertoire, but decoration grew formulaic and long-distance contacts thinned. Chania emerged as the island's leading centre, exporting inscribed stirrup jars whose Linear B labels record oil shipments. The phase ends amid the wider destructions that brought down the Mycenaean palaces on the mainland.
Late Minoan IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1189 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan IB (Greece, 1499 BC–1424 BC).label: Late Minoan IB
Late Minoan IB (Greece, 1499 BC–1424 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1499 BC–1424 BC] Late Minoan IB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Potters produced the celebrated Marine Style, with octopuses and nautili wrapped around jars and flasks, and stone vases and seals reached a technical peak. Then almost every settlement, villa and palace on the island except Knossos was burned or abandoned in a single horizon of destruction. Whether the cause was earthquake, revolt, invasion or the long aftermath of the Thera eruption is still argued.
Late Minoan IB (Greece, 1499 BC–1424 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Bronze Age (Greece, 1999 BC–1599.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Greece, 1999 BC–1599.prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Greece, 1999 BC–1599.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 B.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 B.prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan IA (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC).label: Late Minoan IA
Late Minoan IA (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Minoan IA. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Palaces and villas across Crete were richly decorated with frescoes, and potters favoured flowing floral designs on light grounds. Minoan style dominated the southern Aegean, visible in the wall paintings of Akrotiri on Thera, which was buried by the volcano's eruption in this phase. Debate over the eruption's date and its consequences for Crete remains one of the sharpest arguments in Aegean archaeology.
Late Minoan IA (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Minoan (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Minoan
Early Minoan (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Minoan. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Bronze Age Crete before the palaces: farming communities grew in size and wealth, buried their dead collectively in circular tholos tombs and rock shelters, and began working copper, bronze, gold and fine stone. Distinctive mottled Vasiliki ware, elaborate stone vases and engraved seals appear, along with imports showing contact with Egypt, the Levant and the Cyclades. The accumulating wealth and administrative habits of these centuries made the first Cretan palaces possible.
Early Minoan (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.label: Middle Cycladic II
Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.prose:
[Aegean, 1899 BC–1699 BC] Middle Cycladic II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The mature phase of island town life, when Phylakopi, Ayia Irini and Akrotiri were compact, densely built settlements with organised streets and defences. Painted pottery, including jugs decorated with birds and flowers, shows Cycladic workshops absorbing Cretan taste while keeping their own style, and Melian obsidian and trade in metals kept the islands prosperous.
Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.label: Middle Helladic II
Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.prose:
[Aegean, 1899 BC–1699 BC] Middle Helladic II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Mainland Greek villages of small mudbrick houses, cist-grave cemeteries and plain, wheel-made grey 'Minyan' pottery, materially far poorer than Minoan Crete across the sea. Communities like Lerna, Asine and Kolonna on Aegina were farming settlements with modest hierarchies, though Aegina's fortified town shows some were already trading widely. The apparent simplicity is deceptive: this is the society out of which Mycenaean Greece grew.
Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).label: Late Cycladic
Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1079 BC] Late Cycladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The Bronze Age islands at their most connected, when Cretan influence in architecture, script, fresco and fashion gave way after about 1450 BC to Mycenaean control from the mainland. Towns like Akrotiri on Thera, Phylakopi on Melos and Ayia Irini on Keos were substantial harbour settlements with shrines, drainage and painted rooms. The eruption of Thera, the rise of Mycenaean palatial trade and the upheavals around 1200 BC all fall within this span.
Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Cycladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.label: Early Cycladic III
Early Cycladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.prose:
[Aegean, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Early Cycladic III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The islands lost their earlier prominence as trade shifted toward Crete and the mainland; many cemeteries went out of use and figurine production largely ceased. Settlement contracted onto fewer, often defensible sites, a reorganisation that preceded the rise of Minoan influence in the Aegean.
Early Cycladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Cycladic
Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Cycladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

After the fragmented villages of the earlier islands, Cycladic life concentrated into a few substantial, sometimes walled towns — Phylakopi on Melos, Ayia Irini on Kea, Akrotiri on Thera — living off obsidian, trade and the sea. Potters produced matt-painted jars and beaked jugs decorated with birds and spirals, and Cretan goods and habits arrived in growing quantity. The Minoan connection deepened until the islands became cultural satellites of Crete, setting the stage for the frescoed town buried by the Thera eruption.
Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan II (Greece, 1424 BC–1389 BC).label: Late Minoan II
Late Minoan II (Greece, 1424 BC–1389 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1424 BC–1389 BC] Late Minoan II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Knossos alone functioned as a palace, and its rulers were Greek-speaking Mycenaeans who kept inventories on clay tablets in Linear B — the earliest readable Greek. Burials changed too, with 'warrior graves' containing swords, helmets and boar's-tusk gear appearing around the city. Pottery turned formal and imposing in the Palace Style, adapting old Minoan motifs to a stiffer, more heraldic taste.
Late Minoan II (Greece, 1424 BC–1389 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic IIB (Greece, 1449 BC–1399.label: Late Helladic IIB
Late Helladic IIB (Greece, 1449 BC–1399.prose:
[Aegean, 1449 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic IIB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Pottery decoration grew more restrained and standardised, a sign of workshops producing for a wider market. Mycenaean influence over Crete tightened, and mainland centres were on the verge of building the palaces that would define the following century.
Late Helladic IIB (Greece, 1449 BC–1399.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).label: Late Minoan
Late Minoan (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1079 BC] Late Minoan. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Crete's palace civilisation reached its most brilliant phase — frescoed halls, marine-style pottery, bronze work and trade reaching Egypt and the Levant — before a run of disasters. The eruption of Thera, then island-wide destructions, left Knossos alone in charge, now under Greek-speaking Mycenaean rulers who kept their accounts in Linear B. The palace system finally failed altogether, and Cretans retreated to defensible hilltop villages as the wider Bronze Age world collapsed.
Late Minoan (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Bronze Age (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC.prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1079 BC] Late Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Minoan I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 BC).label: Early Minoan I
Early Minoan I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Early Minoan I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The opening phase of the Cretan Bronze Age, when new burial customs appeared: circular stone tholos tombs in the south and burial caves elsewhere, used by whole communities over generations. Dark burnished Pyrgos ware and red-on-buff Agios Onouphrios pottery mark the period, alongside the first regular use of copper. Change came gradually from the preceding Neolithic, with some sites showing signs of newcomers arriving on the island.
Early Minoan I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Minoan III (Greece, 1699 BC–1599.label: Middle Minoan III
Middle Minoan III (Greece, 1699 BC–1599.prose:
[Aegean, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Minoan III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The palaces were rebuilt after destruction, larger and more architecturally sophisticated, with light-wells, gypsum-faced walls and the first true frescoes. Linear A replaced hieroglyphic writing for administration, and Cretan influence spread through the Aegean islands. This is the threshold of the Neopalatial heyday, and the town of Akrotiri on Thera was flourishing under strong Cretan influence.
Middle Minoan III (Greece, 1699 BC–1599.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Helladic
Early Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The mainland Greek Bronze Age begins: bronze tools and weapons, donkeys and sailing craft, and settlements engaged in Aegean-wide exchange. Its most striking buildings are the 'corridor houses' such as the House of the Tiles at Lerna — large, tiled, administratively organised structures, sealed storerooms and all — which suggest emerging central authority. Widespread destructions and abandonments end the period, and the mainland enters the poorer Middle Helladic era.
Early Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Minoan II (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 B.label: Middle Minoan II
Middle Minoan II (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1799 BC–1699 BC] Middle Minoan II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The high point of the first palaces, when Phaistos and Knossos ran centralised storage and craft production and kept records with seals and Cretan Hieroglyphic script. Kamares ware reached its technical peak, thin as an eggshell and painted with swirling white, red and orange designs, and it turns up in Egypt and along the Levantine coast as evidence of Cretan trade. The phase closed with widespread destruction, probably by earthquake.
Middle Minoan II (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Minoan IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199 B.label: Early Minoan IIB
Early Minoan IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199 B.prose:
[Aegean, 2399 BC–2199 BC] Early Minoan IIB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

A prosperous phase that ended badly: Vasiliki, Myrtos and other settlements burned or were abandoned, and the pattern of Cretan habitation shifted. Before that, potters produced elegant spouted jugs and teapots, and seal-carving in ivory and bone spread as a way of marking property. The disruptions cleared the ground for the reorganisation that led to the first palaces.
Early Minoan IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Minoan IA (Greece, 1999 BC–1899 B.label: Middle Minoan IA
Middle Minoan IA (Greece, 1999 BC–1899 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Middle Minoan IA. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The last phase before the palaces, when Cretan communities were growing fast and burying their dead in collective tombs, while mountaintop peak sanctuaries filled with clay votive offerings. Potters experimented with light-on-dark polychrome painting, the direct ancestor of the famous Kamares ware.
Middle Minoan IA (Greece, 1999 BC–1899 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.label: Middle Helladic I
Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Middle Helladic I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The opening of a subdued era on the Greek mainland, following widespread destruction and abandonment at the end of the Early Bronze Age. Settlements are small and simply built, grave goods are few, and the characteristic burnished grey Minyan pottery becomes standard — a material culture that gives little hint of the Mycenaean wealth to come.
Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan II (palaces) (Greece, 1424 B.label: Late Minoan II (palaces)
Late Minoan II (palaces) (Greece, 1424 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1424 BC–1389 BC] Late Minoan II (palaces). Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Only Knossos still operated as a palace centre, run by an administration writing Greek in Linear B and drawing tribute in wool, textiles, grain and chariots from across the island. Rich burials with weapons and armour suggest a mainland-style warrior elite had taken control. Its tall Palace Style storage jars, with stylised octopuses and papyrus, are the signature pottery of the phase.
Late Minoan II (palaces) (Greece, 1424 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.label: Late Helladic I
Late Helladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Helladic I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The moment mainland Greece grew rich: the Mycenae shaft graves were cut, filled with gold death masks, inlaid daggers, amber and ostrich eggs, evidence of warrior chiefs with long-distance connections. Fine matt-painted and lustrous decorated pottery shows Minoan Crete's influence being absorbed and reworked into something distinctly mainland.
Late Helladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.label: Late Helladic II
Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1499 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Chieftains stopped digging shaft graves and began building tholoi, great stone beehive chambers approached by long passages, a display of labour and permanence. Mycenaean goods spread through the Aegean and mainlanders took control of Knossos, where Linear B was adapted to write Greek.
Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Cycladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.label: Early Cycladic I
Early Cycladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Early Cycladic I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The earliest phase of island culture in the Bronze Age Aegean, known largely from small cist-grave cemeteries of the Grotta-Pelos type rather than from settlements. Grave goods include schematic 'violin-shaped' marble figurines and simple dark burnished pottery, the beginnings of a distinctive Cycladic tradition.
Early Cycladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Minoan IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399 B.label: Early Minoan IIA
Early Minoan IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399 B.prose:
[Aegean, 2699 BC–2399 BC] Early Minoan IIA. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Cretan communities grew into substantial villages like Myrtos Fournou Korifi and Vasiliki, with sophisticated potting—the mottled red-and-black Vasiliki ware—and imported gold, ivory and Cycladic marble figurines showing the island plugged into wider Aegean exchange. Collective burial in circular tholos tombs on the Mesara plain and house tombs in the east reached its height. Much of what would define palatial Crete—craft specialisation, seal use, seaborne trade—was already taking shape.
Early Minoan IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1189 BC–1079.label: Late Helladic IIIC
Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1189 BC–1079.prose:
[Aegean, 1189 BC–1079 BC] Late Helladic IIIC. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Life after the palaces: no kings, no scribes, no frescoes, but surviving communities at Tiryns, Lefkandi, Perati and in the islands, some prospering briefly. Painters produced lively pictorial vases of ships and warriors, and refugees and traders kept Aegean contacts alive. A final decline led into the Protogeometric period and the Iron Age.
Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1189 BC–1079.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.label: Middle Helladic III
Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.prose:
[Aegean, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Helladic III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The moment mainland Greece began to pull ahead. Warrior burials filled with bronze weapons, gold and imported Cretan goods — above all Grave Circle B at Mycenae — reveal families accumulating wealth and advertising it in death for the first time. Within a couple of generations these lineages would build the shaft-grave dynasties and palatial citadels of the Mycenaean world.
Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Cycladic
Early Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Cycladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The islands of the Aegean supported small farming and fishing communities that became skilled sailors and metalworkers, moving obsidian, copper and marble around the sea. They are best known for the marble folded-arm figurines placed in graves, pared down to abstract simplicity and much admired by modern artists. Their trading networks laid the groundwork for the later Minoan and Mycenaean maritime world.
Early Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Sub-Mycenaean (Greece, 1079 BC–999 BC).label: Sub-Mycenaean
Sub-Mycenaean (Greece, 1079 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1079 BC–999 BC] Sub-Mycenaean. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The bleak aftermath of the palatial collapse, known mainly from small cemeteries of simple cist graves around Athens, Salamis and Argos, with clumsy undecorated pots and modest bronze pins and fibulae. Population, settlement size and long-distance contact all shrank sharply, and Linear B writing disappeared entirely. It is the trough between the Mycenaean world and the Protogeometric recovery, and a key exhibit in debates about how societies lose complexity.
Sub-Mycenaean (Greece, 1079 BC–999 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Helladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.label: Early Helladic I
Early Helladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.prose:
[Aegean, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Early Helladic I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Small farming hamlets in the southwest Peloponnese take up metal and new pottery shapes, the first mainland stage of the Bronze Age. Settlements were modest and scattered, with burials in simple pits and cists rather than monumental tombs. It provides the baseline against which the wealthier, more centralised communities of the following centuries stand out.
Early Helladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1389 B.label: Late Cycladic II
Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1389 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1499 BC–1389 BC] Late Cycladic II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The generations after the Theran eruption, when island settlements rebuilt on a smaller scale and Minoan influence gave way to Mycenaean. Pottery, burial customs and imports increasingly point towards the mainland palaces rather than Crete. Phylakopi and Ayia Irini remained the main harbours, now nodes in a Mycenaean-run trade network.
Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1389 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Minoan IB (Greece, 1899 BC–1799 B.label: Middle Minoan IB
Middle Minoan IB (Greece, 1899 BC–1799 B.prose:
[Aegean, 1899 BC–1799 BC] Middle Minoan IB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The first palaces were built at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, each a large complex of storerooms, workshops and shrines wrapped around a rectangular central court. Administration begins to leave traces in clay sealings and early Cretan Hieroglyphic signs, and fine polychrome Kamares pottery comes into its own.
Middle Minoan IB (Greece, 1899 BC–1799 B.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic IIIA1 (Greece, 1399 BC–136.label: Late Helladic IIIA1
Late Helladic IIIA1 (Greece, 1399 BC–136.prose:
[Aegean, 1399 BC–1369 BC] Late Helladic IIIA1. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Mycenaean pottery became remarkably uniform across the mainland and islands, suggesting tightly organised production. Palace building was underway, and Aegean goods reached Amarna in Egypt in quantity.
Late Helladic IIIA1 (Greece, 1399 BC–136.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Cycladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.label: Early Cycladic II
Early Cycladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.prose:
[Aegean, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Early Cycladic II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The high point of Cycladic culture, when settlements such as Chalandriani on Syros grew and fortified sites appeared. Craftsmen produced the famous canonical folded-arm figurines, marble bowls, and metal tools and weapons, while frying-pan vessels engraved with ships attest to long-distance voyaging.
Early Cycladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic IIA (Greece, 1499 BC–1449.label: Late Helladic IIA
Late Helladic IIA (Greece, 1499 BC–1449.prose:
[Aegean, 1499 BC–1449 BC] Late Helladic IIA. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Palatial-style jars and elegant Ephyraean goblets show mainland potters mastering and transforming Minoan design. Wealth concentrated in a few centres whose rulers were buried in early tholos tombs, and Mycenaean exports began appearing regularly in the eastern Mediterranean.
Late Helladic IIA (Greece, 1499 BC–1449.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1189.label: Late Helladic IIIB
Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1189.prose:
[Aegean, 1299 BC–1189 BC] Late Helladic IIIB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The palaces reached their fullest form, with the Lion Gate and the huge walls of Tiryns raised and Linear B scribes tallying grain, textiles, chariots and rowers. Late in the phase came fire, abandonment and hurried defensive works, ending in the destruction of every mainland palace and the loss of writing.
Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1189.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Minoan IIIA1 (Greece, 1389 BC–1359.label: Late Minoan IIIA1
Late Minoan IIIA1 (Greece, 1389 BC–1359.prose:
[Aegean, 1389 BC–1359 BC] Late Minoan IIIA1. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

A short phase in which Mycenaean administrative habits were fully embedded on Crete, with Greek-language Linear B accounting and warrior burials with bronze weapons. Pottery grew more uniform and less inventive than the marine and floral styles of earlier generations. Scholars still argue over whether the palace at Knossos was destroyed at the start of this phase or survived into the next.
Late Minoan IIIA1 (Greece, 1389 BC–1359.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).label: Late Helladic
Late Helladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1599 BC–1079 BC] Late Helladic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The Mycenaean age on the Greek mainland: shaft graves heaped with gold masks and weapons give way to vast tholos tombs, then to citadels at Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos with cyclopean walls and frescoed palaces. Scribes kept accounts in Linear B, the earliest written Greek, and Mycenaean pottery travelled from Egypt to Sardinia. The palaces burned around 1200 BC, and the memory of their kings survived, distorted, in Homer.
Late Helladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Helladic IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399.label: Early Helladic IIA
Early Helladic IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399.prose:
[Aegean, 2699 BC–2399 BC] Early Helladic IIA. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The high point of the early mainland Bronze Age. Communities at Lerna, Tiryns, Kolonna and Thebes built large tiled "corridor houses", stamped hundreds of clay sealings to control stored produce, and imported obsidian, metal and finished goods from the islands and Anatolia. Historians see here the first attempts at centralised authority on the Greek mainland, several centuries before Mycenaean palaces.
Early Helladic IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Helladic IIIA2 (Greece, 1369 BC–129.label: Late Helladic IIIA2
Late Helladic IIIA2 (Greece, 1369 BC–129.prose:
[Aegean, 1369 BC–1299 BC] Late Helladic IIIA2. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

Mycenaean exports peaked, with mainland pots found from Sardinia to Syria and in the rubbish of Akhenaten's city. At home the great citadels took shape and rulers commissioned frescoes, roads and drainage on a scale never before attempted in Greece.
Late Helladic IIIA2 (Greece, 1369 BC–129.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Sub-Minoan (Greece, 1079 BC–999 BC).label: Sub-Minoan
Sub-Minoan (Greece, 1079 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Aegean, 1079 BC–999 BC] Sub-Minoan. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The last phase of Cretan Bronze Age culture, after the palaces had gone: pottery still recognisably Minoan in shape but coarser and looser in decoration, made by communities that had largely withdrawn to defensible upland refuges such as Karphi. Metal is scarcer, settlements smaller, writing gone. Out of this thinned-out world came the Cretan communities of the Early Iron Age.
Sub-Minoan (Greece, 1079 BC–999 BC).source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1389 BC–1079.label: Late Cycladic III
Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1389 BC–1079.prose:
[Aegean, 1389 BC–1079 BC] Late Cycladic III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The islands under mainland Mycenaean culture, with megaron-plan buildings and a sanctuary at Phylakopi holding clay idols, and fortification walls going up as conditions worsened. Around 1200 BC the palatial system collapsed and many sites were burned, abandoned or reduced to villages. Scattered communities carried on into the early Iron Age, with new cemeteries and the first signs of the later island city-states.
Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1389 BC–1079.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Early Helladic IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199.label: Early Helladic IIB
Early Helladic IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199.prose:
[Aegean, 2399 BC–2199 BC] Early Helladic IIB. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

A short, unsettled phase in which new pottery of the Lefkandi I–Kastri type, with Anatolian-looking shapes such as tankards and depas cups, spreads across the Aegean. It closes with the burning of the House of Tiles at Lerna and destructions at other major sites, ending the corridor-house world.
Early Helladic IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.label: Middle Cycladic I
Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.prose:
[Aegean, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Middle Cycladic I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age — 2008.

The islands settle into fewer, larger communities as the scattered hamlets of the Early Bronze Age are abandoned. Local potters develop matt-painted wares with dark geometric designs on pale slip, while imports show contact with Crete and the Greek mainland is still modest.
Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.source: The Cambridge companion to the Aegean Bronze Age

English New York (New York, AD 1661–AD 1.label: English New York
English New York (New York, AD 1661–AD 1.prose:
[New England and New York, AD 1661–AD 1776] English New York. Spatial coverage: New York, Vermont. The Dutch colony of New Netherland was taken without a fight in 1664 and renamed for the Duke of York, though the Dutch language, Reformed church and landholding families persisted for generations. English rule kept the great Hudson Valley manors and the Iroquois alliance known as the Covenant Chain, which made Albany the hinge of northern diplomacy and the fur trade. New York City grew into a diverse, commercially minded port unlike any other in British America.

Pizarro's small force captured and executed the Inca Atahualpa and seized an empire already weakened by civil war and smallpox, though Inca resistance held out at Vilcabamba for forty years. The silver mountain of Potosí, worked by rotating mita labour drafts, made Peru the treasury of the Spanish world and connected Andean villages to a global economy. Andean communities adapted, preserving language, kin groups and huaca worship beneath a Catholic surface, while colonial Cuzco and Lima developed their own painting and architecture.

The Marinids and then the Wattasids ruled Morocco from Fez, endowing the city with the madrasas, fountains and libraries that still define its old quarters and making it a centre of Maliki learning. They fought for control of the Maghreb and briefly intervened in Spain, but lost ground steadily as Portugal and Castile seized Ceuta, Tangier and the Atlantic ports. Their decline opened the way for the Saadian sharifs.

Macedonians (Egypt, 330 BC–29 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 330 BC–29 BC] Macedonians. From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Egypt", pp. 89-90: "They seem to have been subject to Cyrus about 534, but, probably rebelling, were reduced by Cambyses in 525; and although Egypt several times revolted, it was always recovered by the Persians, and was part of that empire when Alexander the Great put an end to it in 331 B.C. In 30 B.C. it was reduced to a Roman province, and continued a part of the Roman empire, till it was conquered by the Saracens in 640.". Period definition from A new chart of history. The three centuries in which Egypt was ruled by a Greek-speaking dynasty descended from Alexander's general Ptolemy. Alexandria became the largest city of the Mediterranean, home to the Library, the Museum and the Pharos lighthouse, while the kings presented themselves to Egyptians as pharaohs and to Greeks as Hellenistic monarchs. The line ended with Cleopatra VII and the Roman annexation of Egypt.

Begun as a proprietary grant to court favourites of Charles II, with settlement spreading from the Albemarle Sound and the new port of Charles Town. The northern half developed as a scattered society of small farms, naval stores and pine tar, chronically short of good harbours and often in revolt against its proprietors; it was split off formally and later taken over by the Crown. Piracy, Tuscarora warfare and disputes over land and quitrents shaped a famously ungovernable colony.

The Andean highlands saw the rise of the Inca state from a small polity around Cuzco into an empire stretching from Ecuador to Chile, tied together by paved roads, storehouses, terraced fields and labour tribute rather than money or writing. Rule was administered through knotted-cord khipu records and resettled populations. A ruinous succession war left the empire divided when Pizarro landed in 1532.

Cambyses' conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy of the Achaemenid empire, counted by later Egyptians as the Twenty-Seventh Dynasty. Persian kings styled themselves pharaohs, restored temples and finished a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea, but heavy taxation and distant rule bred repeated revolts, and Egypt regained independence for some sixty years before a brutal reconquest. Alexander the Great took the country from the Persians in 332 BC to general welcome.

A regime run by manumitted slave-soldiers, in which command was won by training and faction rather than inheritance. Cairo under their rule became the richest city of the Islamic world, a centre of scholarship and trade that absorbed refugees and craftsmen after the Mongol sack of Baghdad. Their lavish stone mosques and domed tombs remain the signature architecture of medieval Egypt.

After the collapse of John Law's speculative Company of the Indies, the young colony centred on New Orleans settled into a plantation economy worked by thousands of enslaved Africans shipped mainly from Senegambia, whose skills and culture shaped Louisiana rice, indigo and Creole society. Governance ran on the Code Noir and on uneasy diplomacy with the Choctaw, Natchez and Chickasaw; the Natchez war of 1729 nearly destroyed the colony. Ceded secretly to Spain, it left behind French law, language and a durable Creole identity.

The Zayyanid (Abd al-Wadid) dynasty ruled western Algeria from Tlemcen, a walled city that grew rich as the Mediterranean terminus of trans-Saharan caravans carrying gold, slaves and salt. Squeezed between Marinid Morocco and Hafsid Tunis, its rulers survived by paying tribute, switching allegiances and trading with Genoa and Aragon. Spanish coastal conquests and then Ottoman corsairs ended the kingdom in the sixteenth century.

Beginning with the Pilgrims at Plymouth and expanding with the Puritan migration to Massachusetts Bay, these colonies were built around town congregations, family farms and an unusual commitment to literacy and schooling. Harvard, printing presses and town meetings appeared within a generation; so did the expulsion of dissenters and the devastating wars with the Wampanoag, Pequot and Abenaki. Its merchant fleets, fisheries and traditions of local self-government made Boston the seedbed of the American Revolution.

Spanish ships, soldiers and friars turned the Florida peninsula into the northern frontier of an American empire, founding St Augustine and a chain of Franciscan missions among the Timucua, Guale and Apalachee. Epidemic disease, forced labour drafts and raids by English-backed Creek slavers destroyed the mission populations within a few generations. Archaeologically the period shows up as olive jars, majolica and iron tools mixed into Native pottery assemblages.

The decade after the fall of Montreal, when Britain took over the French colony along the St Lawrence and had to work out how to govern some 70,000 Catholic, French-speaking subjects. Military rule gave way to civil administration under the Royal Proclamation of 1763, which also drew a line barring settlement west of the Appalachians and angered colonists to the south. The accommodations made here set Canada on a separate path from the Thirteen Colonies.

The Jurchen chieftains of Manchuria overthrew their Khitan Liao overlords, then drove the Song court out of northern China, capturing two emperors and taking the Yellow River plain. Ruling from Zhongdu, on the site of modern Beijing, they governed a Chinese population with a mix of tribal military households and Confucian bureaucracy. Mongol armies ground the dynasty down over twenty years, ending it in 1234.

Rome absorbed the kingdom of Mauretania after its last king was killed by Caligula, creating the province of Tingitana in the far north-west. Volubilis, Lixus and Tingis prospered on olive oil, grain and wild animals for the arena, and a chain of forts held the frontier against unsubdued tribes. In the later third century Rome pulled back to a coastal strip, leaving inland cities to carry on without imperial troops.

Following Henry Hudson's 1609 voyage, Dutch traders built posts on the Hudson to tap the beaver trade with the Mohawk and Mahican, founding Fort Orange and, on Manhattan, New Amsterdam. New Netherland stayed small and commercial rather than agricultural, but it was unusually mixed in language and religion, and it wedged itself between the English colonies of New England and the Chesapeake. Wars with Native neighbours and constant friction with English settlers weakened it before an English fleet took the colony in 1664 and renamed it New York.

The Tanguts, a people of Qiangic origin from the Tibetan borderlands, rose from frontier commanders to found the Western Xia state, which held the Gansu corridor and the Silk Road oases against Song China, the Liao and the Jin. They devised their own complex script, patronised Buddhism lavishly and left libraries of printed texts at Khara-Khoto. Genghis Khan's Mongols destroyed the state in 1227, and its rulers and language largely vanished from Chinese historiography.

Dynasties claiming descent from the Prophet — first the Saadians, then the Alaouites — rallied resistance to Portuguese coastal garrisons and built a Moroccan state independent of Ottoman control. Their high point came at the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578 and Ahmad al-Mansur's astonishing march across the Sahara to destroy the Songhai Empire and seize the gold and salt trade of the Niger. Later sultans, above all Moulay Ismail with his slave army and vast palace at Meknes, made Morocco the only part of North Africa never absorbed by the Ottomans.

Founded by settlers from Tyre, Carthage grew into the dominant maritime power of the western Mediterranean, running trade networks from Iberia to West Africa and controlling much of Sicily, Sardinia and the North African coast. Its temples, tophet precinct and harbours reflect a Phoenician culture that adapted and prospered far from its homeland. Three wars with Rome ended with the city burned and its territory turned into the province of Africa.

The centuries in which Arab armies moving west from Egypt overran the Maghreb, and Berber populations converted to Islam in large numbers while repeatedly rebelling against Umayyad governors and their tax demands. Kharijite doctrines took deep root, and the great revolt of 740 broke caliphal control of the far west for good. Out of the resulting patchwork came the Idrisids, who founded Fez and established the first enduring Muslim dynasty in Morocco.

Founded as a philanthropic and military experiment — a refuge for the deserving poor and a buffer between South Carolina and Spanish Florida — with initial bans on slavery, rum and large landholdings. The trustees' rules collapsed under pressure from settlers who wanted plantations, slavery was legalised in 1751, and Georgia became a royal colony run much like its neighbour. Its rapid conversion to a rice and slave economy shows how hard it was to sustain an alternative model in the colonial South.

Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish soldier sent to govern Egypt for the Abbasid caliphs, kept the tax revenues for himself, built an army of slave soldiers and made the country effectively independent for the first time in centuries. He founded a new capital quarter at al-Qata'i and the great congregational mosque that still bears his name, and extended his rule over Syria. His successors could not hold it, and an Abbasid army retook Egypt in 905.

Sugar, and later the gold and diamonds of Minas Gerais, were worked overwhelmingly by enslaved Africans, making Brazil the largest destination of the Atlantic slave trade. A period in which political authority in Tibet passed from the kings of Tsang to the Fifth Dalai Lama, installed in 1642 with the military backing of the Mongol leader Gushri Khan. The Ganden Phodrang government that resulted fused monastic and secular rule, built the Potala Palace and made the Gelug school dominant. It ends as Mongol and then Manchu armies made Tibet a theatre of wider Inner Asian rivalry, on the eve of the Dzungar seizure of Lhasa.

Coastal towns and ports kept some Mediterranean trade going while the interior slipped out of any central control. The whole area passed nominally to Byzantium after the Vandal defeat, but effective power stayed with Berber chiefdoms.

Missionaries, coureurs de bois and soldiers pushed French claims to the Mississippi, while seigneurial land tenure and the Catholic parish shaped rural life. Conquest by Britain ended French rule but not French Canada: the language, law and church survived to define Quebec.

The fall of Tenochtitlan replaced the Aztec empire with the Viceroyalty of New Spain, built literally on top of it: cathedrals over temples, encomiendas over tribute districts. Epidemics cut the indigenous population by perhaps ninety per cent, while silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato financed Spain's wars and flowed on to China through Manila. A new colonial society of castas, haciendas and baroque churches took shape, along with hybrid indigenous-Christian art and devotion.

Saladin ended the Shi'i Fatimid caliphate in Egypt and founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt, Syria and the Yemen, restoring Sunni orthodoxy and building madrasas to teach it. His defeat of the Crusaders at Hattin in 1187 recovered Jerusalem and triggered the Third Crusade; his successors alternated between war and truces with the Frankish states. Reliance on Turkish slave soldiers proved fatal to the family, and in 1250 those Mamluks seized power for themselves.

After the near-collapse of Jamestown, the colony survived on tobacco, which reshaped everything: land hunger, a scattered pattern of riverside plantations, and a growing demand for bound labour. The first representative assembly in English America met in 1619, the same year the first Africans were landed at Point Comfort; over the following century law hardened servitude into hereditary racial slavery. Its planter elite would supply an extraordinary share of the leaders of American independence.

William Penn's charter created a colony run on Quaker principles: religious liberty, an elected assembly, and treaties rather than war with the Lenape. Cheap land and toleration drew Germans, Scots-Irish and others in huge numbers, and Philadelphia became the largest city in British America and a centre of printing, science and trade. The peaceable frontier eventually broke down as settlers pushed west, but the colony's pluralism shaped the later United States.

A proprietary colony granted to the Catholic Calvert family, settled from the ships Ark and Dove, and intended partly as a haven where Catholics could worship without penalty. Its 1649 Act Concerning Religion was an early legal guarantee of toleration among Christians, though it was repeatedly overturned as Protestants came to dominate. Economically it was a tobacco colony like Virginia, dependent first on indentured servants and then increasingly on enslaved Africans.

Pedro de Valdivia's expedition founded Santiago and a string of southern towns, but the Mapuche destroyed them in the great rising of 1598 and pushed the colony back to the Bío-Bío river. For nearly two centuries Chile was a poor, militarised frontier province of the Viceroyalty of Peru, supplying wheat, hides and tallow and paying for a standing army against an unconquered indigenous south. Its distinctive mestizo rural society, the inquilino estate system, took shape in these years.

The Dutch West India Company held the sugar-rich northeast from its capital at Recife, running plantations with enslaved African labour and briefly seizing Portuguese slaving posts in Angola to feed them. Under governor Johan Maurits of Nassau the colony drew painters like Frans Post and Albert Eckhout, naturalists, and a Sephardic Jewish community that built the Americas' first synagogue. Planter revolt and Portuguese arms ended it at the battles of Guararapes; the departing Dutch carried sugar expertise and capital to the Caribbean, and some of the Recife Jews to New Amsterdam.

Esarhaddon and then Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt, sacking Memphis and eventually Thebes and carrying off its treasures - a shock recorded in both Assyrian annals and the Hebrew Bible. Assyrian control depended on local Delta princes as vassals, one of whom, Psamtik I, soon parlayed the arrangement into independence. The occupation was brief but it ended Kushite rule over Egypt for good.

Ethiopian royal tradition, set down most fully in the Kebra Nagast, held that the kings of Ethiopia descended from Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, who was said to have brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. The claim gave Ethiopian monarchy a biblical charter that later rulers invoked for centuries. Whatever its historical basis, it shaped how Ethiopians and outsiders alike understood the kingdom's legitimacy.

The Solomonic line, claiming descent from Solomon and Sheba, ruled a mobile Christian kingdom whose court moved between camps rather than a fixed capital. It fought a devastating war with the Muslim sultanate of Adal under Ahmad Gragn in the 1500s, survived with Portuguese musketeers, then expelled Jesuit missionaries and turned inward. From the 1630s the kings settled at Gondar and built stone castles and churches there, before royal power dissolved into the rule of regional warlords.

The end date coincides with the death of Ramesses XI and the beginning of the the Third Intermediate Period. That the spatial reference is to lower Egypt/the Delta is inferred from the arrangement of this bar in the timeline. Period definition from A new chart of history. To Benjamin Franklin LL. Egyptians (Egypt, 1199 BC–944 BC).prose: [Egypt, 1199 BC–944 BC] Egyptians. Although this range overlaps with the "Shepherd Kings" and includes a period in which Egypt seems to control the "Ethiopians" between 1010 and 955 BC, Priestley's references are not clear enough to parse into multiple periods in different places, so the "Egyptian" segment here encompasses the entire chronological range but excludes Sudan and Ethiopia. Priestley is probably differentiating between Lower Egypt and the Delta (where he places the Shepherd Kings), Upper Egypt (always ruled by Egyptians), and the northern parts of Nubia, where Egypt made incursions at the end of the New Kingdom. United-States (Maine, AD 1776–AD 1800).label: United-States
United-States (Maine, AD 1776–AD 1800).prose:
[Nova Scotia, New England & New York, Pensilvania Maryland and Virginia, Carolina and Georgia, AD 1776–AD 1800] United-States. Spatial coverage: Delaware, Georgia, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York. The addition of "United-States" to a chart that otherwise seems to be the version published in 1769 can be explained as a later addition; we have not verified that this appears in the charts published in 1792, but those also had different credits for the writer and draftsperson. The inclusion of Nova Scotia in the United States is presumably an error. Period definition from A new chart of history. To Benjamin Franklin LL. D.F.R.S. this chart is in testimony of esteem & friendship, inscribed by his most obliged humble servt. Joseph Priestley. — Joseph Priestley, 1769.

Maine spent these years as the northern district of Massachusetts, its coast recovering from wartime raids and shipping disruption. Lumber, shipbuilding and the coasting trade drove a rapid push of settlement inland and downeast, onto lands still claimed by the Wabanaki. Frustration with distant government in Boston began the agitation that would end in separate statehood in 1820.
United-States (Maine, AD 1776–AD 1800).source: A new chart of history. To Benjamin Franklin LL. D.F.R.S. this chart is in testimony of esteem & friendship, inscribed by his most obliged humble servt. Joseph Priestley.

Patans (India, AD 1530–AD 1587).prose: [Visapour, AD 1530–AD 1587] Patans. From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v.
