Japanese monarchy (Japan, 659 BC–AD 1188.label: Japanese monarchy
Japanese monarchy (Japan, 659 BC–AD 1188.prose:
[Japan, 659 BC–AD 1188] Japanese monarchy. From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Japan", pp. 86-87: "Sin-onu, an ecclesiastic, is said to have founded the Japanese monarchy, about 660 B.C. but in 1188 Jerotimo put an end to the supreme ecclesiastic authority, and became the first secular monarch of Japan.". Period definition from A new chart of history. To Benjamin Franklin LL. D.F.R.S. this chart is in testimony of esteem & friendship, inscribed by his most obliged humble servt. Joseph Priestley. — Joseph Priestley, 1769.

The traditional chronology of Japan's imperial line, reckoned from the legendary Emperor Jimmu and running through the courts of Asuka, Nara and Heian. Over these centuries the throne absorbed Chinese-style law, writing and Buddhism, then gradually surrendered practical power to Fujiwara regents, retired emperors and finally warrior houses. By the end of the span the emperor was a sacred figurehead in Kyoto while real authority lay with the shogunate.
Japanese monarchy (Japan, 659 BC–AD 1188.source: A new chart of history. To Benjamin Franklin LL. D.F.R.S. this chart is in testimony of esteem & friendship, inscribed by his most obliged humble servt. Joseph Priestley.

Regal (Rome, 752 BC–508 BC).label: Regal
Regal (Rome, 752 BC–508 BC).prose:
[Rome, 752 BC–508 BC] Regal. Period definition from The archaeology of early Rome and Latium — Holloway, R. Ross, 1934-, 1994.

Rome's first two and a half centuries under a line of seven kings, from the legendary Romulus to the Etruscan Tarquins. Tradition credits this era with the city's basic institutions — the Senate, the religious calendar, the census and the division of citizens into voting classes — and with the draining of the Forum and building of the great Capitoline temple. The expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus left Romans with a lasting horror of one-man rule that shaped their politics for the next five hundred years.
Regal (Rome, 752 BC–508 BC).source: The archaeology of early Rome and Latium

Latial Iron Age (Lazio, 1019 BC–579 BC).label: Latial Iron Age
Latial Iron Age (Lazio, 1019 BC–579 BC).prose:
[Lazio, 1019 BC–579 BC] Latial Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of early Rome and Latium — Holloway, R. Ross, 1934-, 1994.

The villages on the hills of Latium, including the huts on Rome's Palatine, grew into the communities that classical writers remembered as the age of kings. Cremation burials with miniature hut-shaped urns give way over time to richly furnished inhumations with imported Greek and Etruscan goods, showing new wealth and social ranking. It is the archaeological backdrop to Rome's own foundation legends.
Latial Iron Age (Lazio, 1019 BC–579 BC).source: The archaeology of early Rome and Latium

Iron Age (Italy, 752 BC–579 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Italy, 752 BC–579 BC).prose:
[Italy, 752 BC–579 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of early Rome and Latium — Holloway, R. Ross, 1934-, 1994.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Italy, 752 BC–579 BC).source: The archaeology of early Rome and Latium

Proto-Villanovan (Italy, 1199 BC–899 BC).label: Proto-Villanovan
Proto-Villanovan (Italy, 1199 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Italy, 1199 BC–899 BC] Proto-Villanovan. Period definition from The archaeology of early Rome and Latium — Holloway, R. Ross, 1934-, 1994.

Communities across the peninsula switched to cremating their dead and burying the ashes in biconical urns set in flat urnfields, a practice linked to wider changes sweeping Bronze Age Europe. Bronze-working reached a high technical peak, with sheet-metal vessels, razors and fibulae traded over long distances. These cemeteries lead directly into the Villanovan culture and, through it, to the Etruscan cities.
Proto-Villanovan (Italy, 1199 BC–899 BC).source: The archaeology of early Rome and Latium

Villanovan (Italy, 899 BC–749 BC).label: Villanovan
Villanovan (Italy, 899 BC–749 BC).prose:
[Italy, 899 BC–749 BC] Villanovan. Period definition from The archaeology of early Rome and Latium — Holloway, R. Ross, 1934-, 1994.

The Early Iron Age of Etruria and the Bologna region, and the direct ancestor of Etruscan civilisation. The dead were cremated and their ashes placed in distinctive biconical urns, sometimes in pottery models of thatched huts, capped with a bowl or a bronze helmet. Scattered Bronze Age hamlets drew together into large plateau settlements that would become Tarquinia, Vulci, Veii and Cerveteri, while ironworking and long-distance trade grew rapidly.
Villanovan (Italy, 899 BC–749 BC).source: The archaeology of early Rome and Latium

Seleucid Monarchy (Turkey, 300 BC–83 BC).label: Seleucid Monarchy
Seleucid Monarchy (Turkey, 300 BC–83 BC).prose:
[Greater Armenia, 300 BC–83 BC] Seleucid Monarchy. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

Seleucus I and his heirs ruled the largest of the kingdoms carved from Alexander's empire, stretching at its height from the Aegean to the Hindu Kush and governed through a lattice of Greek-style cities planted among older Near Eastern populations. In Anatolia they contended with Ptolemies, Attalids and Galatians, and after defeat by Rome at Magnesia in 190 BC they lost the peninsula altogether. Repeated dynastic civil wars shrank the state to a rump in Syria until Rome and Armenia swept it away.

Third Armenian Monarchy (Turkey, AD 66–A.label: Third Armenian Monarchy
Third Armenian Monarchy (Turkey, AD 66–A.prose:
[Greater Armenia, AD 66–AD 400] Third Armenian Monarchy. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

The Arsacid line of Armenian kings, beginning when Tiridates travelled to Rome to receive his crown from Nero, a settlement that made Armenia a buffer state fought over by Rome and its eastern rivals for centuries. Around 301 Trdat III accepted Christianity from Gregory the Illuminator, giving Armenia a claim to be the first Christian kingdom. Roman and Sasanian pressure eventually partitioned the country, but the period also produced the Armenian alphabet and a literate church culture that outlasted the monarchy.

Abbasid Caliphate (Turkey, AD 750–AD 772.label: Abbasid Caliphate
Abbasid Caliphate (Turkey, AD 750–AD 772.prose:
[Greater Armenia, AD 750–AD 772] Abbasid Caliphate. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads and rebuilt the caliphate around Baghdad, mixing Arab, Persian and Central Asian talent in a cosmopolitan court. Anatolia at this moment was a militarised frontier, raided each summer and fortified by both Muslim and Byzantine garrisons.

proto-Armenian Satrapy of Greater Armeni.node: proto-Armenian Satrapy of Greater Armenia (Turkey, 611 BC–549 BC)
proto-Armenian Satrapy of Greater Armeni.label: proto-Armenian Satrapy of Greater Armenia
proto-Armenian Satrapy of Greater Armeni.prose: [Greater Armenia, 611 BC–549 BC] proto-Armenian Satrapy of Greater Armenia. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Kingdom was ruled by Romans between 17 A.D.-43 A.D. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

Artaxiad Monarchy (Turkey, 199 BC–AD 14).label: Artaxiad Monarchy
Artaxiad Monarchy (Turkey, 199 BC–AD 14).prose:
[Greater Armenia, 199 BC–AD 14] Artaxiad Monarchy. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

Founded when Artaxias I broke free of Seleucid control, this dynasty built Armenia into a substantial kingdom, briefly stretching under Tigranes the Great from the Caspian to the Mediterranean before Roman legions under Lucullus and Pompey cut it back. Hellenistic culture mixed with Iranian religious and courtly traditions at capitals like Artashat and Tigranakert. The dynasty's later kings ruled as clients caught between Rome and Parthia, a squeeze that defined Armenian politics for centuries.

Arsacid period (Turkey, AD 63–AD 428).label: Arsacid period
Arsacid period (Turkey, AD 63–AD 428).prose:
[Greater Armenia, AD 63–AD 428] Arsacid period. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

Armenia, including its lands in eastern Anatolia, was ruled by a Parthian-descended royal house installed under a settlement between Rome and Persia. The period saw the kingdom become officially Christian, the creation of the Armenian alphabet, and a flowering of translation and church-building. Caught between two empires, the realm was eventually divided between them and the monarchy suppressed.

Fourth Armenian Monarchy (Turkey, AD 885.label: Fourth Armenian Monarchy
Fourth Armenian Monarchy (Turkey, AD 885.prose:
[Greater Armenia, AD 885–AD 1045] Fourth Armenian Monarchy. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

Armenia regained a king when the Bagratid Ashot I was recognised by both the caliph and Byzantium, ending two centuries of direct foreign rule. Trade wealth paid for a building boom, above all at the capital Ani, whose cathedral and walls made it one of the great cities of the age, and for a revival of Armenian manuscript art and historiography. Rival princely lines fragmented the realm, and Byzantine annexation left it exposed to the Seljuk invasions that followed.

post-Arsacid period (Turkey, AD 428–AD 5.label: post-Arsacid period
post-Arsacid period (Turkey, AD 428–AD 5.prose:
[Greater Armenia, AD 428–AD 580] post-Arsacid period. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

With the deposition of the last Arsacid king in 428, Armenia lost its own monarchy and was governed by Persian-appointed marzbans, with the western portion under Roman control. Religious pressure from Zoroastrian Persia provoked the revolt that culminated at Avarayr in 451, and although the Armenians lost the battle they won the right to keep their Christian faith. The same era saw the newly invented Armenian alphabet fuel an extraordinary burst of translation and original writing that preserved Armenian identity without a state.

Orontid First Monarchy (Turkey, 694 BC–3.label: Orontid First Monarchy
Orontid First Monarchy (Turkey, 694 BC–3.prose:
[Greater Armenia, 694 BC–300 BC] Orontid First Monarchy. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

The Orontids governed Armenia first as satraps for the Persian kings, supplying cavalry and tribute, and gradually turned the office into a hereditary dynasty. They built and ruled from centres such as Armavir, blending Iranian court practice with local traditions. Their line outlasted the Achaemenid collapse and shaped Armenian kingship long afterwards.

Arab period (Turkey, AD 653–AD 1150).label: Arab period
Arab period (Turkey, AD 653–AD 1150).prose:
[Greater Armenia, AD 653–AD 1150] Arab period. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Studies in Christian Caucasian history — Toumanoff, Cyrille., 1963.

Muslim armies pushed into Anatolia within a generation of Muhammad's death, and the Taurus mountains hardened into a fortified frontier — the thughur — where Arab and Byzantine raiders traded annual campaigns for centuries. Border emirates like Tarsus and Melitene grew rich on raiding and ransom, while Byzantine society reorganised around defensible themes and hilltop refuges. The pattern only broke when Byzantine armies rolled the frontier back in the tenth century, and later when the Seljuk Turks made the whole plateau a new kind of contested ground.

Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2040 BC–1782 BC).label: Middle Kingdom
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2040 BC–1782 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2040 BC–1782 BC] Middle Kingdom. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

Late Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 2700 BC–2400.label: Late Chalcolithic
Late Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 2700 BC–2400.prose:
[Cyprus, 2700 BC–2400 BC] Late Chalcolithic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The final stage of Cyprus's distinctive Chalcolithic villages, best seen at Kissonerga-Mosphilia and Lemba, where people lived in circular mudbrick and stone houses, carved picrolite ornaments and used the island's first copper in small quantities. Settlements grew larger and some buildings stand out in size and contents, hinting at emerging differences in status. The tradition ended as the Philia culture introduced cattle, the plough, extramural cemeteries and serious copper metallurgy, launching the Cypriot Bronze Age.

Middle Roman Period (Egypt, AD 135–AD 25.label: Middle Roman Period
Middle Roman Period (Egypt, AD 135–AD 25.prose:
[Egypt, AD 135–AD 250] Middle Roman Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt settled into its role as Rome's granary, its wheat shipped annually to feed the capital while a Greek-speaking urban elite ran the towns and a heavily taxed peasantry worked the land. Hadrian's new city of Antinoopolis, the papyrus archives of the Fayum and the painted mummy portraits all belong to these generations. Plague, rural unrest and mounting fiscal pressure gradually eroded the prosperity of the countryside.

Chalcolithic (Turkey, 6400 BC–3000 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Turkey, 6400 BC–3000 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 6400 BC–3000 BC] Chalcolithic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Cypro Classical II (Cyprus, 400 BC–310 B.label: Cypro Classical II
Cypro Classical II (Cyprus, 400 BC–310 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 400 BC–310 BC] Cypro Classical II. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The last phase of the independent city-kingdoms, when Cypriot rulers backed Alexander at the siege of Tyre and supplied him with fleets. Within a generation the kingdoms were abolished and the island absorbed into Ptolemaic Egypt, ending more than a thousand years of local dynastic rule.

Hellenistic I (Cyprus, 310 BC–150 BC).label: Hellenistic I
Hellenistic I (Cyprus, 310 BC–150 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 310 BC–150 BC] Hellenistic I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The island's ancient city-kingdoms were abolished and Cyprus became a Ptolemaic possession governed from Egypt, valued for its copper, timber and shipbuilding. Nea Paphos replaced Salamis as the administrative capital, and Alexandrian styles in sculpture, mosaics and burial architecture reshaped island culture. Greek language and Ptolemaic coinage displaced the old Cypro-syllabic script and local dynasties.

Early Islamic Period (Egypt, AD 641–AD 1.label: Early Islamic Period
Early Islamic Period (Egypt, AD 641–AD 1.prose:
[Egypt, AD 641–AD 1100] Early Islamic Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Amr ibn al-As took the country from Byzantium in AD 641 and founded Fustat beside the Nile, the nucleus of what became Cairo. For centuries the population remained largely Coptic Christian while Arabic slowly displaced Greek and Coptic in government and daily speech; papyri from these years record taxes, complaints and letters in all three languages. Autonomous rulers, first the Tulunids and then the Fatimids, made the country an independent power again, founding Cairo in 969 and the mosque-university of al-Azhar soon after.

Iron Age IIB (Israel, 900 BC–700 BC).label: Iron Age IIB
Iron Age IIB (Israel, 900 BC–700 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 900 BC–700 BC] Iron Age IIB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The kingdoms of Israel and Judah flourished side by side, leaving palaces at Samaria, water systems at Megiddo and Hezekiah's tunnel in Jerusalem, along with the earliest substantial Hebrew inscriptions. Assyrian conquest ended the north in 722 BC, scattering its people; Judah endured as a tribute-paying vassal after Sennacherib's assault on Lachish, a siege carved in stone for a Nineveh palace wall.

Philia (Cyprus, 2400 BC–2300 BC).label: Philia
Philia (Cyprus, 2400 BC–2300 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 2400 BC–2300 BC] Philia. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The horizon in which Cyprus shifted decisively toward metal: copper working expanded, cattle and the plough appeared, and new pottery and burial customs suggest contact with Anatolia and possibly incomers. Settlements like Marki and Vasilia show the island moving from village self-sufficiency toward the trade in copper that would make it famous. It forms the bridge between the Chalcolithic and the Cypriot Bronze Age.

Intermediate Bronze Age (Syria, 2200 BC–.label: Intermediate Bronze Age
Intermediate Bronze Age (Syria, 2200 BC–.prose:
[Syria, 2200 BC–2000 BC] Intermediate Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The great walled cities of the third millennium — Ebla, Mari and their neighbours — shrank or were abandoned, monumental building stopped, and much of the population shifted toward mobile pastoralism and small settlements. Archaeologists link the collapse to a sharp arid episode and the disruption of long-distance trade, while texts of the era speak of Amorite groups moving through the region. Urban life revived after 2000 BC on very different political foundations.

Early Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 4000 BC–3400.label: Early Chalcolithic
Early Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 4000 BC–3400.prose:
[Cyprus, 4000 BC–3400 BC] Early Chalcolithic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Copper begins to appear alongside stone tools on the island, and villages of round houses spread into new areas of the interior and south coast. Excavated sites show pit-dwellings, elaborate cemeteries, and the first picrolite figurines with outstretched arms that would become a Cypriot signature. It marks the shift from the long Neolithic isolation toward the metal-using societies that followed.

Ceramic Neolithic B (Israel, 5000 BC–450.label: Ceramic Neolithic B
Ceramic Neolithic B (Israel, 5000 BC–450.prose:
[Israel, 5000 BC–4500 BC] Ceramic Neolithic B. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The later Pottery Neolithic of the southern Levant, associated with the Wadi Rabah tradition — dark burnished bowls, bow-rim jars and incised decoration made by villagers farming grain and herding sheep, goats and cattle. Settlements are modest and scattered compared with the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic towns that preceded them, but the material culture leads directly into the copper-using Chalcolithic.

Iron Age III (Turkey, 700 BC–547 BC).label: Iron Age III
Iron Age III (Turkey, 700 BC–547 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 700 BC–547 BC] Iron Age III. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Lydia rose to dominate western Anatolia from Sardis, striking some of the world's first coins and drawing wealth from the Pactolus river, while Phrygia declined after Cimmerian raids. In the east, Urartu was worn down and the Assyrian empire fell, leaving Medes and Babylonians to divide the spoils. The era closed abruptly when Cyrus the Great took Sardis and made Anatolia Persian.

Ceramic Neolithic (Cyprus, 4600 BC–4000.label: Ceramic Neolithic
Ceramic Neolithic (Cyprus, 4600 BC–4000.prose:
[Cyprus, 4600 BC–4000 BC] Ceramic Neolithic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After a long gap in the settlement record, Cypriot villages reappear with pottery for the first time — first dark combed wares, then the red-on-white painted pottery of the Sotira culture. Communities such as Sotira Teppes lived in clusters of small rounded houses, farming, herding and fishing in near-total isolation from the mainland. The tradition ends abruptly, and the island's next inhabitants build in a noticeably different style.

Roman Republic (Turkey, 133 BC–31 BC).label: Roman Republic
Roman Republic (Turkey, 133 BC–31 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 133 BC–31 BC] Roman Republic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After expelling its kings, Rome developed a government of elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and citizen assemblies, and an army of property-owning citizens. It absorbed Italy, destroyed Carthage and took the Greek east, becoming the dominant Mediterranean power within two centuries. The wealth and slaves that flooded in wrecked the old order, producing land crises, political violence and the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Caesar. Its institutions and its collapse became the standard reference point for later republics.

Late Hellenistic Period (Lebanon, 200 BC.label: Late Hellenistic Period
Late Hellenistic Period (Lebanon, 200 BC.prose:
[Lebanon, Syria, 200 BC–63 BC] Late Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Seleucid power collapsed into dynastic civil war, and the old Phoenician harbour cities — Tyre, Sidon, Berytus — bought or seized autonomy, minting their own coins and trading across the Mediterranean. Greek civic institutions and temple architecture were grafted onto older Canaanite religious traditions, producing the hybrid sanctuaries later rebuilt on a colossal scale at Baalbek. Pompey's arrival ended the experiment, folding the coast into the Roman province of Syria.

Frankish/Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD 109.label: Frankish/Ayyubid Periods
Frankish/Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD 109.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 1099–AD 1291] Frankish/Ayyubid Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Two centuries in which crusader states and Muslim powers fought over, divided and shared the same small country. The Latin Kingdom built castles, harbours, churches and industrial sugar mills; Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 took Jerusalem back for the Ayyubids and reduced the Franks to a coastal strip governed from Acre. The Mamluk capture of Acre in 1291 ended Latin rule on the mainland, leaving fortresses like Belvoir, Montfort and Caesarea as the period's most visible remains.

Fatimid/Mameluke Periods (Israel, AD 129.label: Fatimid/Mameluke Periods
Fatimid/Mameluke Periods (Israel, AD 129.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 1291–AD 1516] Fatimid/Mameluke Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After the fall of Acre the Mamluk sultans of Cairo ruled Palestine, deliberately razing the coastal ports to prevent any Crusader return and shifting life inland to Jerusalem, Safed and Hebron. They endowed those towns with madrasas, markets, fountains and khans, and organised the postal and pilgrimage roads that crossed the country until the Ottoman conquest.

Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 324–AD 1453.label: Byzantine Period
Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 324–AD 1453.prose:
[Turkey, AD 324–AD 1453] Byzantine Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.

Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 3000 BC–270.node: Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 3000 BC–2700 BC)
Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 3000 BC–270.label: Early Bronze Age II
Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 3000 BC–270.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 3000 BC–2700 BC] Early Bronze Age II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.

Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2000 BC–180.node: Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2000 BC–1800 BC)
Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2000 BC–180.label: Middle Bronze Age I
Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2000 BC–180.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 2000 BC–1800 BC] Middle Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Towns and cities were re-established across the southern Levant after centuries of largely village and pastoral life, with fortifications, wheel-made pottery and true bronze metallurgy returning. Coastal sites looked north to Byblos and the Syrian world for trade and inspiration. This revival set the framework of Canaanite city-states that Egyptian and biblical sources would later describe.

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1570 BC–1070 BC).label: New Kingdom
New Kingdom (Egypt, 1570 BC–1070 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1570 BC–1070 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Early Bronze Age IV (Israel, 2200 BC–200.node: Early Bronze Age IV (Israel, 2200 BC–2000 BC)
Early Bronze Age IV (Israel, 2200 BC–200.label: Early Bronze Age IV
Early Bronze Age IV (Israel, 2200 BC–200.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 2200 BC–2000 BC] Early Bronze Age IV. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The walled towns of the preceding centuries were abandoned, and people scattered into small villages, seasonal camps and cemeteries across the steppe and hill country. Metalwork and distinctive hand-made pottery continued, but writing, monumental building and centralised authority vanished for some two hundred years. Often called the Intermediate Bronze Age, it forms the gap between the region's first urban experiment and the revival of city life under the Middle Bronze Age Canaanites.

Later Islamic Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD.label: Later Islamic Period
Later Islamic Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 1291–AD 1516] Later Islamic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After the fall of Acre ended the crusader states, the coastal cities were deliberately dismantled and depopulated to deny future invaders a foothold, while inland towns and the pilgrimage routes flourished under Mamluk rule. Cairo-appointed governors endowed Jerusalem and Hebron with madrasas, hospices and fountains in the striped stonework and stalactite vaulting typical of Mamluk architecture. Sugar mills, soap works and caravanserais tied the region into a trade network reaching from the Nile to Damascus, until Ottoman armies took over in 1516.

Ottoman (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1878).label: Ottoman
Ottoman (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1878).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1878] Ottoman. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

Ceramic Neolithic A (Syria, 6000 BC–5000.label: Ceramic Neolithic A
Ceramic Neolithic A (Syria, 6000 BC–5000.prose:
[Syria, 6000 BC–5000 BC] Ceramic Neolithic A. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Farming villages that had long lived without pots began firing them in quantity, and the new medium quickly became a canvas: painted and burnished wares spread across the north Syrian plains. It is the world in which the Halaf tradition, with its exquisite polychrome bowls, took shape, and pottery styles start to reveal networks of contact stretching hundreds of kilometres.

Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2663 BC–2181 BC).label: Old Kingdom
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2663 BC–2181 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2663 BC–2181 BC] Old Kingdom. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

Roman (Cyprus, 30 BC–AD 330).label: Roman
Roman (Cyprus, 30 BC–AD 330).prose:
[Cyprus, 30 BC–AD 330] Roman. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Ceramic Neolithic A (Lebanon, 6000 BC–50.label: Ceramic Neolithic A
Ceramic Neolithic A (Lebanon, 6000 BC–50.prose:
[Lebanon, 6000 BC–5000 BC] Ceramic Neolithic A. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Farming villages that had long lived without pots began firing them in quantity, and the new medium quickly became a canvas: painted and burnished wares spread across the north Syrian plains. It is the world in which the Halaf tradition, with its exquisite polychrome bowls, took shape, and pottery styles start to reveal networks of contact stretching hundreds of kilometres.

Persian Period (Turkey, 547 BC–333 BC).label: Persian Period
Persian Period (Turkey, 547 BC–333 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 547 BC–333 BC] Persian Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.

Middle Cypriot I and II (Cyprus, 1950 BC.node: Middle Cypriot I and II (Cyprus, 1950 BC–1750 BC)
Middle Cypriot I and II (Cyprus, 1950 BC.label: Middle Cypriot I and II
Middle Cypriot I and II (Cyprus, 1950 BC.prose:
[Cyprus, 1950 BC–1750 BC] Middle Cypriot I and II. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cypriot villages of this time still lived by farming and herding, burying their dead in rock-cut chamber tombs with distinctive Red Polished and White Painted pottery, including elaborate composite vessels and clay models of ploughing and ritual scenes. Copper production grew steadily, and contact with Syria and Egypt increased, though the island had no cities yet.

Middle Bronze Age III (Israel, 1650 BC–1.node: Middle Bronze Age III (Israel, 1650 BC–1500 BC)
Middle Bronze Age III (Israel, 1650 BC–1.label: Middle Bronze Age III
Middle Bronze Age III (Israel, 1650 BC–1.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 1650 BC–1500 BC] Middle Bronze Age III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The last phase of Canaanite urban splendour, when the great fortified towns were still functioning but increasingly under pressure. Egyptian expulsion of the Hyksos and subsequent campaigns into Asia brought destructions and abandonments at many sites. What followed was a Canaan of smaller towns under Egyptian imperial control.

Cypro Geometric I (Cyprus, 1050 BC–950 B.label: Cypro Geometric I
Cypro Geometric I (Cyprus, 1050 BC–950 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 1050 BC–950 BC] Cypro Geometric I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After the collapse of the Bronze Age palaces, Cyprus reorganised around new coastal towns and adopted iron for everyday tools earlier than most of the Mediterranean. Chamber tombs with painted pottery show continuity with the past alongside a wave of Aegean settlers whose Greek dialect took root on the island.

Predynastic (Egypt, 6000 BC–3150 BC).label: Predynastic
Predynastic (Egypt, 6000 BC–3150 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 6000 BC–3150 BC] Predynastic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Farming villages along the Nile grew into competing chiefdoms with cemeteries, craft workshops and long-distance trade in lapis, cedar and gold. Naqada-culture potters, flint-knappers and stone-vase makers reached extraordinary technical heights, and the imagery on their palettes and painted jars — kings smiting enemies, sacred boats, animal standards — is already the visual language of pharaonic Egypt. It ends with the unification of the Nile Valley under a single ruler.

British (Cyprus, AD 1878–AD 1960).label: British
British (Cyprus, AD 1878–AD 1960).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1878–AD 1960] British. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Britain took over administration of the island from the Ottomans as a strategic base guarding the route to Suez, annexing it outright in 1914 and making it a crown colony in 1925. Colonial rule sharpened the divide between Greek Cypriot demands for union with Greece and Turkish Cypriot opposition. The EOKA insurgency of the 1950s ended in independence, with Britain retaining sovereign military bases.

Early Islamic Period (Israel, AD 638–AD.label: Early Islamic Period
Early Islamic Period (Israel, AD 638–AD.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 638–AD 1099] Early Islamic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Amr ibn al-As took the country from Byzantium in AD 641 and founded Fustat beside the Nile, the nucleus of what became Cairo. For centuries the population remained largely Coptic Christian while Arabic slowly displaced Greek and Coptic in government and daily speech; papyri from these years record taxes, complaints and letters in all three languages. Autonomous rulers, first the Tulunids and then the Fatimids, made the country an independent power again, founding Cairo in 969 and the mosque-university of al-Azhar soon after.

Iron Age IIA (Israel, 1000 BC–900 BC).label: Iron Age IIA
Iron Age IIA (Israel, 1000 BC–900 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 1000 BC–900 BC] Iron Age IIA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Villages grew into fortified towns with gates, palaces and storehouses, and the first real state institutions appear in the southern Levant. Scholars argue bitterly over whether these remains belong to a Solomonic kingdom or to the later Omride dynasty, and radiocarbon dating has become central to the fight. Distinctive red-slipped, burnished pottery marks the horizon at sites from Megiddo to Beersheba.

First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2181 B.label: First Intermediate Period
First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2181 B.prose:
[Egypt, 2181 BC–2040 BC] First Intermediate Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Central authority collapsed after the long reign of Pepi II, and Egypt broke into competing regional powers - provincial governors ruling as local dynasts, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Low Nile floods, famine and disorder colour the literature written afterwards, but tomb goods and inscriptions show provincial workshops and local elites flourishing. Funerary practices once reserved for kings spread to lesser officials, laying groundwork for the Coffin Texts. The Theban victory that ended the era produced the reunified Middle Kingdom.

PPNB (Israel, 5000 BC–4500 BC).label: PPNB
PPNB (Israel, 5000 BC–4500 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 5000 BC–4500 BC] PPNB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Villages grew into substantial settlements of rectangular, multi-roomed houses, some of them among the largest communities anywhere at the time. Goats, sheep, cattle and pigs were brought under domestication to join the cereal crops, and lime plaster was used for floors, vessels and the famous modelled skulls in which the faces of the dead were reconstructed over bone. Long-distance exchange in obsidian and shell tied distant communities together before many of these sites were abandoned.

Middle Hellenistic Period (Turkey, 235 B.label: Middle Hellenistic Period
Middle Hellenistic Period (Turkey, 235 B.prose:
[Turkey, 235 BC–187 BC] Middle Hellenistic Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Anatolia was carved up between the Seleucid king Antiochus III, the rising Attalid dynasty at Pergamon, and Galatian and local principalities. Antiochus's defeat by Rome at Magnesia and the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BC pushed Seleucid power back beyond the Taurus and handed most of the peninsula to Pergamon and Rhodes. Pergamon spent its new wealth on the library, sculpture and monumental terraces that made it a showcase of Hellenistic art.

Hellenistic Period (Egypt, 332 BC–31 BC).label: Hellenistic Period
Hellenistic Period (Egypt, 332 BC–31 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 332 BC–31 BC] Hellenistic Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.

Intermediate Bronze Age (Israel, 2200 BC.label: Intermediate Bronze Age
Intermediate Bronze Age (Israel, 2200 BC.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 2200 BC–2000 BC] Intermediate Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The great walled cities of the third millennium — Ebla, Mari and their neighbours — shrank or were abandoned, monumental building stopped, and much of the population shifted toward mobile pastoralism and small settlements. Archaeologists link the collapse to a sharp arid episode and the disruption of long-distance trade, while texts of the era speak of Amorite groups moving through the region. Urban life revived after 2000 BC on very different political foundations.

Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 167 BC–.label: Late Hellenistic Period
Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 167 BC–.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, 167 BC–63 BC] Late Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Seleucid power collapsed into dynastic civil war, and the old Phoenician harbour cities — Tyre, Sidon, Berytus — bought or seized autonomy, minting their own coins and trading across the Mediterranean. Greek civic institutions and temple architecture were grafted onto older Canaanite religious traditions, producing the hybrid sanctuaries later rebuilt on a colossal scale at Baalbek. Pompey's arrival ended the experiment, folding the coast into the Roman province of Syria.

Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1500 BC–1400.node: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1500 BC–1400 BC)
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1500 BC–1400.label: Late Bronze Age I
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1500 BC–1400.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 1500 BC–1400 BC] Late Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Canaan's towns recovered slowly from the upheavals that ended the Middle Bronze Age, now under Egyptian overlordship after repeated pharaonic campaigns. Settlements were smaller and rarely walled, and the wealth that remained came from trade: painted bichrome jugs, Cypriot base-ring flasks and Aegean vessels found their way into local tombs and temples.

Cypro Archaic I (Cyprus, 750 BC–600 BC).label: Cypro Archaic I
Cypro Archaic I (Cyprus, 750 BC–600 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 750 BC–600 BC] Cypro Archaic I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cyprus was divided among a set of rival city-kingdoms - Salamis, Kition, Paphos and others - that paid tribute first to Assyria and traded freely with Phoenicia, Egypt and the Greek world. Sanctuaries filled with thousands of terracotta votive figures, and royal tombs at Salamis held chariots, horse burials and bronze cauldrons that recall scenes from Homer.

Ummayyad/Abbasid Periods (Israel, AD 638.label: Ummayyad/Abbasid Periods
Ummayyad/Abbasid Periods (Israel, AD 638.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 638–AD 1099] Ummayyad/Abbasid Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Muslim rule replaced Byzantine after the 630s; Jerusalem gained the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa, and Ramla was founded as a new provincial capital. Churches and synagogues continued in use, but pilgrimage patterns, coinage and trade routes reoriented toward Damascus and then Baghdad. Under the later Abbasids and their Fatimid rivals the region grew unstable, and it ended with the Crusader conquest of Jerusalem in 1099.

Cypro Archaic II (Cyprus, 600 BC–480 BC).label: Cypro Archaic II
Cypro Archaic II (Cyprus, 600 BC–480 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 600 BC–480 BC] Cypro Archaic II. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The island's kingdoms passed under Egyptian and then Persian control while their art absorbed Egyptian and Greek models, producing the distinctive limestone statues with Greek-style smiles and Egyptian kilts. Rich sculpture, painted 'free-field' pottery and monumental sanctuaries mark a prosperous period that ended as Cypriot cities were drawn into the Persian Wars.

Iron Age II (Turkey, 850 BC–700 BC).label: Iron Age II
Iron Age II (Turkey, 850 BC–700 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 850 BC–700 BC] Iron Age II. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Greek settlers pushed out from Syracuse and Naxos to found a chain of colonies around the coast, while Phoenicians held the western tip at Motya and Panormus. The indigenous Sikels, Sikanians and Elymians adopted Greek pottery, building styles and writing even as they lost land, and Sikel resistance culminated in Ducetius' short-lived confederation. Sicily's grain, its tyrants and its rivalry with Carthage made the island a major player in the wider Mediterranean world.

Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1782.label: Second Intermediate Period
Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1782.prose:
[Egypt, 1782 BC–1570 BC] Second Intermediate Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

A divided Egypt, with the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the Delta from Avaris, a rump Theban kingdom in the south, and the Kushite kings of Kerma pressing the frontier. Trade with the Levant and the Aegean flourished at Avaris even as pharaonic art and building shrank. The Theban wars of liberation under Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and finally Ahmose reunified the country and launched the New Kingdom.

Ceramic Neolithic B (Lebanon, 5000 BC–45.label: Ceramic Neolithic B
Ceramic Neolithic B (Lebanon, 5000 BC–45.prose:
[Lebanon, 5000 BC–4500 BC] Ceramic Neolithic B. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The later Pottery Neolithic of the southern Levant, associated with the Wadi Rabah tradition — dark burnished bowls, bow-rim jars and incised decoration made by villagers farming grain and herding sheep, goats and cattle. Settlements are modest and scattered compared with the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic towns that preceded them, but the material culture leads directly into the copper-using Chalcolithic.

Cypro Geometric II (Cyprus, 950 BC–900 B.label: Cypro Geometric II
Cypro Geometric II (Cyprus, 950 BC–900 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 950 BC–900 BC] Cypro Geometric II. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

A short, quiet phase of consolidation in which the island's settlements stabilised and pottery workshops developed the concentric-circle and cross-line styles that would define Cypriot ceramics. Contact with the Levant resumed, setting the stage for Phoenician colonists at Kition.

Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 332 BC.label: Early Hellenistic Period
Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 332 BC.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, 332 BC–167 BC] Early Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Alexander's conquest ended two centuries of Persian rule and pulled the southern Levant into the contest between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek cities, gymnasia, coinage and language spread along the coast and into Jerusalem's elite, provoking tensions over Judaean religious practice. The period closes with Antiochus IV's decrees and the Maccabean revolt.

Middle Bronze Age (Turkey, 2000 BC–1600.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Turkey, 2000 BC–1600.prose:
[Turkey, 2000 BC–1600 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

Ottoman Period (Turkey, AD 1453–AD 1922).label: Ottoman Period
Ottoman Period (Turkey, AD 1453–AD 1922).prose:
[Turkey, AD 1453–AD 1922] Ottoman Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

Late Cypriot II A-B (Cyprus, 1450 BC–132.node: Late Cypriot II A-B (Cyprus, 1450 BC–1325 BC)
Late Cypriot II A-B (Cyprus, 1450 BC–132.label: Late Cypriot II A-B
Late Cypriot II A-B (Cyprus, 1450 BC–132.prose:
[Cyprus, 1450 BC–1325 BC] Late Cypriot II A-B. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cypriot copper underwrites a boom in imports: Mycenaean and Levantine pottery, ivory and precious metal fill tombs at Enkomi and other coastal towns. This is the era when the island's rulers dealt with Egypt as the kingdom of Alashiya, and when Cypro-Minoan writing came into regular use.

Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).label: Byzantine Period
Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 324–AD 638] Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.

Middle Roman Period (Turkey, AD 138–AD 2.label: Middle Roman Period
Middle Roman Period (Turkey, AD 138–AD 2.prose:
[Turkey, Lebanon, Syria, AD 138–AD 250] Middle Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt settled into its role as Rome's granary, its wheat shipped annually to feed the capital while a Greek-speaking urban elite ran the towns and a heavily taxed peasantry worked the land. Hadrian's new city of Antinoopolis, the papyrus archives of the Fayum and the painted mummy portraits all belong to these generations. Plague, rural unrest and mounting fiscal pressure gradually eroded the prosperity of the countryside.

Intermediate Bronze Age (Lebanon, 2200 B.label: Intermediate Bronze Age
Intermediate Bronze Age (Lebanon, 2200 B.prose:
[Lebanon, 2200 BC–2000 BC] Intermediate Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The great walled cities of the third millennium — Ebla, Mari and their neighbours — shrank or were abandoned, monumental building stopped, and much of the population shifted toward mobile pastoralism and small settlements. Archaeologists link the collapse to a sharp arid episode and the disruption of long-distance trade, while texts of the era speak of Amorite groups moving through the region. Urban life revived after 2000 BC on very different political foundations.

Early Bronze Age I (Israel, 3500 BC–3000.node: Early Bronze Age I (Israel, 3500 BC–3000 BC)
Early Bronze Age I (Israel, 3500 BC–3000.label: Early Bronze Age I
Early Bronze Age I (Israel, 3500 BC–3000.prose: [Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 3500 BC–3000 BC] Early Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Ceramic Neolithic B (Syria, 5000 BC–4500.label: Ceramic Neolithic B
Ceramic Neolithic B (Syria, 5000 BC–4500.prose:
[Syria, 5000 BC–4500 BC] Ceramic Neolithic B. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The later Pottery Neolithic of the southern Levant, associated with the Wadi Rabah tradition — dark burnished bowls, bow-rim jars and incised decoration made by villagers farming grain and herding sheep, goats and cattle. Settlements are modest and scattered compared with the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic towns that preceded them, but the material culture leads directly into the copper-using Chalcolithic.

Late Cypriot II C (Cyprus, 1325 BC–1200.node: Late Cypriot II C (Cyprus, 1325 BC–1200 BC)
Late Cypriot II C (Cyprus, 1325 BC–1200.label: Late Cypriot II C
Late Cypriot II C (Cyprus, 1325 BC–1200.prose:
[Cyprus, 1325 BC–1200 BC] Late Cypriot II C. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cypriot towns are rebuilt on a grand scale, with ashlar masonry, planned street grids, sanctuaries and workshops tying copper production directly to temple and elite quarters at Enkomi and Kition. It is the island's most prosperous and urbanised moment — and the one immediately preceding the upheavals that swept the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC.

Late Cypriot III (Cyprus, 1200 BC–1050 B.label: Late Cypriot III
Late Cypriot III (Cyprus, 1200 BC–1050 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 1200 BC–1050 BC] Late Cypriot III. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Destructions and abandonments hit the coastal towns, and the island is resettled and rebuilt in a noticeably Aegean idiom: locally made Mycenaean-style pottery, megaron-plan buildings, new sanctuaries at Kition and Enkomi. Greek-speaking newcomers appear to have arrived and stayed, laying the basis for the later Greek city-kingdoms, while Cypriot smiths became early masters of iron.

Late Period (Egypt, 525 BC–332 BC).label: Late Period
Late Period (Egypt, 525 BC–332 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 525 BC–332 BC] Late Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

Late Roman Period (Egypt, AD 250–AD 330).label: Late Roman Period
Late Roman Period (Egypt, AD 250–AD 330).prose:
[Egypt, AD 250–AD 330] Late Roman Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.

Frankish (Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 1489).label: Frankish
Frankish (Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 1489).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 1489] Frankish. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Richard the Lionheart seized the island during the Third Crusade and sold it on; the Lusignan family then ruled it as a Latin kingdom for three centuries. A French-speaking aristocracy sat atop a Greek Orthodox population, building Gothic cathedrals at Nicosia and Famagusta and mountain castles like St Hilarion, while Italian merchants made the ports rich on sugar, cotton and the eastern trade. Genoese and Mamluk pressure wore the kingdom down until Venice took over in 1489.

Iron Age I (Turkey, 1200 BC–850 BC).label: Iron Age I
Iron Age I (Turkey, 1200 BC–850 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 1200 BC–850 BC] Iron Age I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The Hittite empire disappeared and Anatolia fragmented into small, often illiterate societies, with monumental hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions kept alive only by the Neo-Hittite successor states of the south-east. Phrygians moved into the central plateau and settlement clustered on defensible mounds, while in the east the tribal groups later unified as Urartu began to coalesce. From this fractured landscape came the kingdoms - Phrygia, Urartu, Lydia and the Syro-Hittite city-states - that dominated the following centuries.

Hellenistic II (Cyprus, 150 BC–30 BC).label: Hellenistic II
Hellenistic II (Cyprus, 150 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 150 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic II. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Ptolemaic rule continued but weakened as Egypt itself fell into dynastic crisis and Roman interference. Rome annexed the island in 58 BC, briefly restored it to Cleopatra, and finally absorbed it for good - a shift from Alexandrian to Roman orbit that reoriented Cypriot trade and administration westward.

Early Byzantine (Cyprus, AD 330–AD 647).label: Early Byzantine
Early Byzantine (Cyprus, AD 330–AD 647).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 330–AD 647] Early Byzantine. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The island prospered as a wealthy province of the Eastern Roman Empire, its cities rebuilt with grand basilicas whose floors were laid with mosaics and whose bishops claimed independence from Antioch. Salamis, refounded as Constantia, and Kourion and Paphos flourished despite earthquakes. Arab naval raids from the 640s ended this security and opened centuries in which Cyprus was contested and shared between Byzantium and the caliphate.

Herodian Period (Israel, 37 BC–AD 70).label: Herodian Period
Herodian Period (Israel, 37 BC–AD 70).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, 37 BC–AD 70] Herodian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Herod the Great, installed by Rome as king of the Jews, spent his reign building on a spectacular scale: the vastly enlarged Temple Mount platform, the harbour city of Caesarea Maritima, the desert palaces at Masada and Herodium. Under him and his heirs Judaea was a client kingdom balanced uneasily between Roman power and Jewish religious life, the setting for the events of the Gospels. It ended with revolt against Rome and the burning of the Temple in AD 70.

Middle Bronze Age II (Israel, 1800 BC–16.label: Middle Bronze Age II

[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 1800 BC–1650 BC] Middle Bronze Age II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The high point of Canaanite urbanism, when cities were surrounded by huge sloping ramparts and fosses, and palaces, temples and craft workshops flourished. Trade connected the region to Egypt, Cyprus and inland Syria, and scarabs, cylinder seals and fine painted pottery circulated widely. Cities of this era, such as Hazor, were among the largest ever built in the southern Levant.

Early Cypriot (Cyprus, 2300 BC–1950 BC).label: Early Cypriot
Early Cypriot (Cyprus, 2300 BC–1950 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 2300 BC–1950 BC] Early Cypriot. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The Bronze Age opens on Cyprus with a new material culture, probably introduced by settlers from Anatolia: rectangular houses, cattle and the plough, and distinctive red polished pottery. Copper extraction began in earnest, setting the island on the path to becoming the Mediterranean's main source of the metal. Extramural chamber-tomb cemeteries with elaborate offerings replace earlier burial customs.

Iron Age IIC (Israel, 700 BC–586 BC).label: Iron Age IIC
Iron Age IIC (Israel, 700 BC–586 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 700 BC–586 BC] Iron Age IIC. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Judah alone remained, prospering under Assyrian overlordship as an exporter of oil and wine before the empire crumbled. Attempts at independence brought Babylonian retaliation, and Jerusalem was burned and its population exiled. The exile that followed reshaped Judaean religion and produced much of the biblical literature that survives.

Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1069 B.label: Third Intermediate Period
Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1069 B.prose:
[Egypt, 1069 BC–525 BC] Third Intermediate Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

A long stretch of divided rule in which no single king controlled the whole Nile valley. Pharaohs of Libyan descent ruled the Delta while Thebes answered to a priestly dynasty of Amun, and royal tombs were tucked into the temple enclosure at Tanis - one of the few Egyptian royal burials found nearly intact. Kushite kings from Nubia later reunified the country, only for Assyrian invasion to end the period and usher in the Saite revival.

Early Hellenistic Period (Turkey, 333 BC.label: Early Hellenistic Period
Early Hellenistic Period (Turkey, 333 BC.prose:
[Turkey, 333 BC–235 BC] Early Hellenistic Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Alexander's conquest ended two centuries of Persian rule and pulled the southern Levant into the contest between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek cities, gymnasia, coinage and language spread along the coast and into Jerusalem's elite, provoking tensions over Judaean religious practice. The period closes with Antiochus IV's decrees and the Maccabean revolt.

Ceramic Neolithic A (Israel, 6000 BC–500.label: Ceramic Neolithic A
Ceramic Neolithic A (Israel, 6000 BC–500.prose:
[Israel, 6000 BC–5000 BC] Ceramic Neolithic A. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Farming villages that had long lived without pots began firing them in quantity, and the new medium quickly became a canvas: painted and burnished wares spread across the north Syrian plains. It is the world in which the Halaf tradition, with its exquisite polychrome bowls, took shape, and pottery styles start to reveal networks of contact stretching hundreds of kilometres.

Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 330–AD 641).label: Byzantine Period
Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 330–AD 641).prose:
[Egypt, AD 330–AD 641] Byzantine Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.

Early Hellenistic Period (Lebanon, 332 B.prose:

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

Middle Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 2.label: Middle Roman Period
Middle Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 2.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, AD 132–AD 250] Middle Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt settled into its role as Rome's granary, its wheat shipped annually to feed the capital while a Greek-speaking urban elite ran the towns and a heavily taxed peasantry worked the land. Hadrian's new city of Antinoopolis, the papyrus archives of the Fayum and the painted mummy portraits all belong to these generations. Plague, rural unrest and mounting fiscal pressure gradually eroded the prosperity of the countryside.

Venetian (Cyprus, AD 1489–AD 1571) [p0m6.label: Venetian
Venetian (Cyprus, AD 1489–AD 1571) [p0m6.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1489–AD 1571] Venetian. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Venice took formal control of the island after the last Lusignan queen, Caterina Cornaro, was persuaded to abdicate, running it as a colony geared to sugar, cotton and grain exports. Facing the Ottoman threat, Venetian engineers threw up the massive walls of Nicosia and Famagusta that still ring both cities. The Ottoman invasion of 1570 took Nicosia in weeks; Famagusta held out for nearly a year before falling in 1571.

Late Bronze Age (Turkey, 1600 BC–1200 BC.prose:

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Egyptian rule over Canaan was at its tightest, with garrisons, grain taxes and a scatter of local kings squabbling in the letters sent to Akhenaten's court. Cities such as Hazor, Megiddo and Lachish held rich temples and imported luxuries. The era closes in fire and disruption, followed by the appearance of Philistine settlers on the coast and new villages in the hills.

Late Byzantine (Cyprus, AD 965–AD 1191).label: Late Byzantine
Late Byzantine (Cyprus, AD 965–AD 1191).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 965–AD 1191] Late Byzantine. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Nikephoros Phokas's reconquest in 965 ended centuries of contested Arab-Byzantine condominium and made Cyprus a securely imperial province again, governed from Nicosia and Famagusta. Wealth from grain, sugar and trade paid for the mountain monasteries and churches whose frescoes are the island's greatest medieval treasure. It ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island in 1191, beginning three centuries of Latin rule.

Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3150 BC–2663 BC).label: Early Dynastic
Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3150 BC–2663 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 3150 BC–2663 BC] Early Dynastic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

Ceramic Neolithic B (Jordan, 5000 BC–450.label: Ceramic Neolithic B
Ceramic Neolithic B (Jordan, 5000 BC–450.prose:
[Jordan, 5000 BC–4500 BC] Ceramic Neolithic B. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The later Pottery Neolithic of the southern Levant, associated with the Wadi Rabah tradition — dark burnished bowls, bow-rim jars and incised decoration made by villagers farming grain and herding sheep, goats and cattle. Settlements are modest and scattered compared with the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic towns that preceded them, but the material culture leads directly into the copper-using Chalcolithic.

Neo Babylonian Period (Israel, 586 BC–53.label: Neo Babylonian Period
Neo Babylonian Period (Israel, 586 BC–53.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 586 BC–539 BC] Neo Babylonian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After Nebuchadnezzar II's armies burned Jerusalem and its temple, Judah ceased to exist as a kingdom and became a Babylonian province administered from Mizpah, with much of its elite deported to Babylonia. Settlement in the Judean hills thinned sharply, while the exile communities produced much of the writing and editing that shaped the Hebrew Bible. The experience of loss and displacement reframed Israelite religion around law, memory and a temple-less devotion that would outlast the empire that caused it.

Middle Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 3600 BC–270.label: Middle Chalcolithic
Middle Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 3600 BC–270.prose:
[Cyprus, 3600 BC–2700 BC] Middle Chalcolithic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cyprus at its most distinctive before metals took hold: villages of round, mud-and-timber houses at Erimi, Lemba and Kissonerga, with wells, storage pits and cemeteries set apart from the living. Craftworkers carved blue-green picrolite into cruciform figurines with outstretched arms, worn as pendants and buried with the dead, and modelled clay figures of women giving birth. The island stayed largely self-contained, developing its own idiom while the mainland moved into the Bronze Age.

Cypro Geometric III (Cyprus, 900 BC–750.label: Cypro Geometric III
Cypro Geometric III (Cyprus, 900 BC–750.prose:
[Cyprus, 900 BC–750 BC] Cypro Geometric III. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Phoenicians established themselves at Kition and rebuilt its great temple, while local centres grew into the kingdoms that would dominate the island for centuries. Trade with the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant revived strongly, and Cypriot copper again moved widely across the eastern Mediterranean.

Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.prose:

Seleucid power collapsed into dynastic civil war, and the old Phoenician harbour cities — Tyre, Sidon, Berytus — bought or seized autonomy, minting their own coins and trading across the Mediterranean. Greek civic institutions and temple architecture were grafted onto older Canaanite religious traditions, producing the hybrid sanctuaries later rebuilt on a colossal scale at Baalbek. Pompey's arrival ended the experiment, folding the coast into the Roman province of Syria.

Early Roman Period (Lebanon, 63 BC–AD 13.prose:

Intermediate Bronze Age (Jordan, 2200 BC.label: Intermediate Bronze Age
Intermediate Bronze Age (Jordan, 2200 BC.prose:
[Jordan, 2200 BC–2000 BC] Intermediate Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The great walled cities of the third millennium — Ebla, Mari and their neighbours — shrank or were abandoned, monumental building stopped, and much of the population shifted toward mobile pastoralism and small settlements. Archaeologists link the collapse to a sharp arid episode and the disruption of long-distance trade, while texts of the era speak of Amorite groups moving through the region. Urban life revived after 2000 BC on very different political foundations.

PPNA (Israel, 6000 BC–5000 BC).label: PPNA
PPNA (Israel, 6000 BC–5000 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 6000 BC–5000 BC] PPNA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The first villages of the Levant belong to this phase: round mud-brick houses, communal storage and the beginnings of cultivated wheat, barley and pulses, still without pottery. Jericho's stone tower and wall and the carved pillars of Göbekli Tepe further north show unprecedented investment in building. Hunting and gathering continued alongside the new crops, and the groundwork was laid for full farming economies.

Cypro Classical I (Cyprus, 480 BC–400 BC.label: Cypro Classical I
Cypro Classical I (Cyprus, 480 BC–400 BC.prose:
[Cyprus, 480 BC–400 BC] Cypro Classical I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cypriot kings manoeuvred between Persian overlords and Greek liberators, most famously Evagoras of Salamis, who Hellenised his court and challenged Persia directly. Coinage, Greek-style sculpture and Attic imported pottery spread through the island as its elites aligned themselves increasingly with the Aegean world.

Arab Conflict (Cyprus, AD 647–AD 965).label: Arab Conflict
Arab Conflict (Cyprus, AD 647–AD 965).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 647–AD 965] Arab Conflict. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Beginning with Mu'awiya's naval raids, Cyprus was fought over between the Byzantine empire and the caliphate and for long stretches held in an unusual condominium, its tribute divided between the two powers and neither garrisoning it permanently. The island's harbours and forests made it strategically valuable to both fleets, and coastal towns were repeatedly sacked and populations deported. Nikephoros Phokas's reconquest in 965 restored full Byzantine control.

Persian Period (Israel, 539 BC–332 BC).label: Persian Period
Persian Period (Israel, 539 BC–332 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 539 BC–332 BC] Persian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.

Chalcolithic (Israel, 4500 BC–3500 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Israel, 4500 BC–3500 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 4500 BC–3500 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I (Cypru.node: Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1750 BC–1450 BC)
Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I (Cypru.label: Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I
Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I (Cypru.prose:
[Cyprus, 1750 BC–1450 BC] Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The decisive shift on Cyprus, when villages gave way to towns, fortifications were built across the island, and copper became an export industry. Coastal centres such as Enkomi were founded to ship metal abroad, Cypriot pottery turns up throughout the eastern Mediterranean, and the island — probably the Alashiya of cuneiform letters — begins corresponding with the great powers as a kingdom in its own right.

Hasmonean Period (Israel, 167 BC–37 BC).label: Hasmonean Period
Hasmonean Period (Israel, 167 BC–37 BC).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, 167 BC–37 BC] Hasmonean Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Judaean self-rule under the descendants of Judas Maccabeus, who held both the crown and the high priesthood and pushed the kingdom's borders out to something close to the biblical ideal. Its politics produced the rival factions of Pharisees and Sadducees and, in the desert, the community associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls. Fratricidal quarrels among the last Hasmoneans opened the door to Rome and to Herod, who married into the family and then destroyed it.

Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 3000 BC–2000 B.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 3000 BC–2000 B.prose:
[Turkey, 3000 BC–2000 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

Early Roman Period (Egypt, 31 BC–AD 135).prose:
[Egypt, 31 BC–AD 135] Early Roman Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.
