Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).label: Ottoman Period
Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 1516–AD 1917] Ottoman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2700 BC–22.node: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2700 BC–2200 BC)
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2700 BC–22.label: Early Bronze Age III
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2700 BC–22.prose:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 2700 BC–2200 BC] Early Bronze Age III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Fortified towns in the southern Levant reached their peak, with thick town walls, temples, palaces and the huge circular storage structure at Beth Yerah. Distinctive burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, related to northern traditions, spreads through the region. By the close of the period nearly all these towns had been abandoned, and urban life vanished for centuries.

Late Iron Age (Spain, 549 BC–205 BC).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (Spain, 549 BC–205 BC).prose:
[Spain, 549 BC–205 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of the Iberians — Ruiz, Arturo., 1998.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Iron Age (Spain, 799 BC–549 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Spain, 799 BC–549 BC).prose:
[Spain, 799 BC–549 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of the Iberians — Ruiz, Arturo., 1998.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Freedpeople moved into wage labour, sharecropping and turpentine and timber camps, while the Ku Klux Klan and paramilitary intimidation worked to reverse their gains. The disputed 1876 election, decided partly on Florida's returns, ended federal protection and opened the way to white Democratic 'Redemption'.

The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. The Potawatomi, pushed west out of the Great Lakes by treaty and removal, were settled near the Missouri River bluffs in the 1830s and moved on again within a generation, leaving the name attached to the county. Sites of this span include trading posts, mission and agency buildings, emigrant trail camps and early farmsteads.

Their descendants met the first French explorers and traders, and the archaeological trail leads directly to the historic Ioway, Oto, and Ho-Chunk nations.

Canals, coke-smelted iron, steam engines and mechanised spinning laid the groundwork for industrial production in the century's later decades. Everyday material culture changed dramatically: tea drinking, cheap printed cottons, mass-produced Staffordshire ceramics and clay pipes turn up in enormous quantities on sites of the period. The upper Mississippi became a contested frontier as British traders and their Sauk, Fox and Winnebago allies fought American attempts to plant forts and control the river. American expeditions were beaten back at Campbell's Island and Credit Island, and Black Hawk fought alongside the British — a grievance that resurfaced in the 1832 war that bears his name. More engagements were fought on its soil than anywhere else - Manassas, the Peninsula, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, the Wilderness, the long siege of Petersburg - and its western counties broke away in 1863 to enter the Union as a separate state. Dakota bands hunted, fished and gathered wild rice across the lakes and prairies of the region, drawn into the French fur trade from the seventeenth century and later pushed westward by Ojibwe expansion and American settlement. Treaties in the 1830s and 1851 stripped away their land in the area, and the killings at Spirit Lake in 1857 hastened their removal. Village sites, burial mounds and trade goods from the period document both the older lifeway and its rapid disruption.

A Late Archaic hunter-gatherer complex of the mid-Mississippi valley, recognised by long Sedalia lanceolate points and heavy chipped-stone gouges and adzes used for woodworking. Groups moved seasonally between upland camps and river bottoms, harvesting nuts, deer and freshwater mussels, and cemeteries with red ochre burials show growing attachment to particular places. It belongs to the long build-up towards settled river-valley life and early native plant cultivation.

Also known as the Fox, this Algonquian-speaking people were pushed west from the Great Lakes by decades of brutal warfare with the French and their allies, and later by U.S. treaties that stripped them of land in Illinois and Iowa. Removed to Kansas in the 1840s, many refused to stay: in 1857 they pooled money from annuities and horse sales and bought back land along the Iowa River, becoming one of the few Native nations to own its territory outright rather than hold it in reservation trust. That settlement near Tama still exists, and its origin story is the reason Meskwaki archaeology in Iowa spans the whole colonial and early modern era.

Covers the long presence of people of African descent in Florida, from enslaved and free Africans in Spanish St Augustine to Fort Mose, the first legally sanctioned free black town in what became the United States. Later came plantation slavery under British and American rule, alliance and intermarriage with the Seminoles, emancipation, and the segregated communities of the Jim Crow era. Archaeological sites range from slave quarters and cemeteries to twentieth-century town lots.

Excavated in the 1940s ahead of the flooding of Kentucky Lake, its overlapping house and stockade patterns gave archaeologists one of the clearest pictures of how such fortified communities grew, burned and were rebuilt - and of the endemic warfare that shaped life in the late prehistoric Southeast.

Maize farming along the river bottoms supported the largest towns north of Mexico, built around flat-topped earthen mounds and open plazas. Cahokia, across the river from modern St Louis, grew to many thousands of people with a hundred mounds and a woodhenge of cedar posts, and its shell-tempered pottery and shell-and-copper regalia circulated across half a continent. Sites such as Indian Knoll have yielded thousands of burials, along with dog interments, spearthrower weights and ornaments of copper from the Great Lakes and shell from the Gulf. Iowa farmers entered the slump already burdened by debt from the collapse of wartime crop prices, and the 1930s brought foreclosures, bank failures and corn selling below the cost of growing it. Anger boiled over in the Farm Holiday movement, when farmers blockaded roads, dumped milk and confronted judges to halt forced sales. New Deal programmes — crop price supports, the Rural Electrification Administration, soil conservation and WPA construction — reshaped the countryside and left buildings, roads and murals still in use.

Members of the Religious Society of Friends, who worshipped in silence without clergy or ritual and refused oaths, war and social deference. Friends were among the earliest and most persistent American abolitionists, and their meetinghouses and farms in the Midwest served as stations on the Underground Railroad. Their plain furniture, unadorned buildings and burial grounds with uniform markers reflect a deliberate rejection of display.

The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

The copper came mainly from Lake Superior deposits and travelled hundreds of miles through exchange networks. Over time metal shifted from tools toward ornaments and grave goods, marking growing distinctions in status among burials.

Postwar prosperity remade the state: suburbs spread around Washington, Richmond and Hampton Roads, interstates cut through old farmland, and federal and military payrolls became a mainstay of the economy. Segregation was dismantled in the face of fierce official resistance, with schools closing rather than integrating before the courts forced the issue; in 1990 Virginia inaugurated the first elected Black governor in the United States. By the 1990s the northern counties were a hub of computing and telecommunications, and much of the archaeology of this era is about tract housing, shopping centres and demolished rural landscapes.

The half-century in which colonial Virginia reached its height and then turned against Britain. Settlement filled the piedmont and the valley, tobacco inspection laws reshaped the export trade, and the Seven Years' War brought frontier fighting, debt and new imperial taxes. Genteel material culture spread widely in these decades, with white salt-glazed stoneware, creamware and tea equipage marking sites of the period, while the enslaved population grew and became largely American-born.

Farming towns on the Ohio and Wabash built flat-topped mounds around open plazas, ringed themselves with palisades, and grew maize on the floodplains. Angel Mounds near Evansville was one of the largest, home to perhaps a thousand people and tied by trade and shared ritual style to Cahokia and other Mississippian centres. Shell-tempered pottery, chiefly burials and hierarchy between towns mark the region's most complex pre-contact societies.

Groups still moved seasonally but returned to favoured spots year after year, and some began tending native seed plants. The Meskwaki (called Fox by the French) appear in written records from the 1670s and spent the next century resisting French campaigns aimed at destroying them, eventually allying with the Sauk. Treaties in the 1830s and 1840s stripped them of Iowa land and forced removal to Kansas, but groups drifted back and in 1857 bought land outright near Tama - an unusual case of a tribe purchasing its own settlement rather than holding a federal reservation. Archaeological traces of these movements include village sites, trade goods and burials scattered across eastern Iowa.

They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Tobacco, timber and coal drove the economy, while good-roads campaigns and the first automobiles began breaking rural isolation. Communities dispersed, merged and moved, laying the groundwork for the Creek, Cherokee and other historic nations. Because each paddle left a traceable signature, archaeologists can track individual paddles across distant sites and reconstruct networks of exchange and marriage. Communities built low burial and platform mounds and combined foraging with early cultivation of native seed plants.

These middens contain some of the earliest cemeteries in North America, with burials accompanied by atlatl weights, bone tools and marine shell traded from the Gulf coast. Sites from these centuries mix traditional material culture with glass beads, brass kettles, gunflints and horse gear, showing how deeply the fur trade reshaped daily life. Lewis and Clark set out from here in 1804, St. Louis grew into the hub of the western fur trade, and the New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-12 shook the region violently. Iowa passed from Michigan and Wisconsin territorial government to its own territory in 1838 and to statehood in 1846, as settlers broke the tough prairie sod and laid out county towns. By 1860 railroads had reached the Missouri River and the state's farming economy was established.

A long stretch in which people of the Eastern Woodlands adopted pottery, built burial mounds, and gradually shifted from foraging to cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder, with maize arriving late. Trade networks moved copper, marine shell and exotic stone across half a continent, and Hopewell-style earthworks and elaborate grave goods appear in the middle centuries. By its end, settled villages, the bow and arrow and maize agriculture had set the stage for the town-building societies that followed.

Cahokia, across the river from modern St Louis, grew to many thousands of people with a hundred mounds and a woodhenge of cedar posts, and its shell-tempered pottery and shell-and-copper regalia circulated across half a continent. The great centres were largely abandoned before Europeans arrived, leaving mounds that later settlers refused to credit to Native builders.

They ran their own woollen mills, farms and craft shops with remarkable self-sufficiency until members voted in 1932 to end communal life and reorganise as a business corporation. Postwar Virginia was transformed by federal spending, as Pentagon and government work turned the northern counties into sprawling commuter suburbs and shifted political power away from the rural Southside. The Byrd Organization's policy of Massive Resistance closed public schools rather than desegregate them after Brown v. Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.

Early Woodland communities of the Ohio Valley and its fringes who built conical earthen burial mounds and buried their dead with copper bracelets, tubular pipes and carved stone tablets. They gathered and cultivated native seed plants, made some of the region's first pottery, and traded for exotic materials over long distances. Their mound-building and ritual exchange laid the groundwork for the far larger Hopewell networks that followed.

Maize farming along the Mississippi and its tributaries supported larger, more permanent villages, and communities began raising flat-topped earthen mounds around open plazas. Shell-tempered pottery, the bow and arrow, and a new emphasis on hereditary leadership all spread in these centuries. The trend culminated in Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico, just across the river from Missouri's American Bottom settlements.

The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. Tobacco planting spread across the tidewater on the backs of indentured servants and, increasingly, enslaved Africans brought directly from the Atlantic trade; laws passed in these decades made slavery hereditary and racial. Falling tobacco prices and land pressure fed the discontent behind Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, which burned Jamestown and ended with frontier attacks on Native communities. The capital moved to Williamsburg in 1699, and the colony's brick houses, imported ceramics and household goods show a settled gentry class taking shape.

A long stretch in which people of the Eastern Woodlands adopted pottery, built burial mounds, and gradually shifted from foraging to cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder, with maize arriving late. Trade networks moved copper, marine shell and exotic stone across half a continent, and Hopewell-style earthworks and elaborate grave goods appear in the middle centuries. By its end, settled villages, the bow and arrow and maize agriculture had set the stage for the town-building societies that followed.

Bows replaced spearthrowers, and shell-tempered pots and triangular arrow points are the typical finds. Communities dispersed, merged and moved, laying the groundwork for the Creek, Cherokee and other historic nations. Pottery came into everyday use, communities grew more settled, and people began burying their dead in earthen mounds and tending native seed crops long before maize arrived. Distinctive complicated-stamped and check-stamped wares mark the period in the region, and long-distance exchange brought exotic materials into local burial ceremonies. The bow and arrow appeared late in the sequence, and rising populations along the rivers set the stage for the mound-building towns that followed.

Britain took the territory after 1763 and many French families crossed the Mississippi rather than live under it. George Rogers Clark's capture of Kaskaskia in 1778 brought the region into the American Revolution.

Earthlodge farmsteads scattered through the loess bluffs above the Missouri River, part of the Central Plains tradition. Families lived in square, timber-framed lodges dug partly into hillsides, growing maize, beans and squash in bottomland gardens and hunting bison on the prairies. The settlements were abandoned as drier conditions set in, with these groups moving on to become part of the later Plains village peoples.

The era of Mississippian town life in the lower Ohio valley, centred on the great walled settlement at Angel Mounds with its plazas, flat-topped earthen mounds and thousands of residents supported by maize agriculture. Such towns were the largest communities the region had ever seen, ruled by chiefs whose authority was expressed in mound architecture and shell-tempered pottery traded far along the rivers. They were abandoned well before Europeans arrived, leaving the valley to the dispersed Native communities encountered in the historic period.

Royal government collapsed in 1775, and Virginia declared rights and independence the following year; the war reached the colony directly with raids, the Yorktown campaign and Cornwallis's surrender in 1781. Thousands of enslaved Virginians fled to British lines seeking freedom, while the state's leaders went on to shape the federal Constitution. The capital moved to Richmond, the Anglican church was disestablished, and planters increasingly turned worn tobacco fields over to wheat.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

Orr phase (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673).prose:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673] Orr phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The last archaeological phase of Oneota in northeastern Iowa and adjacent Minnesota and Wisconsin, recognised by its thin shell-tempered pottery and, at later sites, European trade goods. Its villages are generally accepted as the direct remains of the Ioway, making it one of the clearest links between an archaeological culture and a named historic tribe.

[Indiana, AD 1650–AD 1900] Historic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Opens with the first European descent of the Mississippi and covers French lead mining and river villages, Spanish administration, and then American statehood, steamboats and railroads. Sites from these centuries include trading posts, farmsteads, Civil War fortifications and industrial works, and are studied with documents and maps alongside the ground itself. Native communities persisted and were pushed out during the same span, so the archaeology records both settlement and dispossession.
Historic (Indiana, AD 1650–AD 1900).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Newtown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000).label: Newtown
Newtown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000).prose:
[Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Newtown. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Late Woodland farming hamlets of the central Ohio Valley, living in small circular villages after the great Hopewell earthwork and mound-building tradition had faded. Their people made cord-marked jars, took up the bow and arrow, and leaned increasingly on maize alongside native seed crops. Out of these communities grew the later Fort Ancient villages of the region.
Newtown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Fox (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950).label: Fox
Fox (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950).prose:

The Meskwaki (called Fox by the French) were pushed west out of the Great Lakes by two brutal French campaigns of extermination in the 1710s and 1730s, and later ranged the Mississippi valley alongside the Sauk. Removed to Kansas after the 1842 treaty, a group of them did something almost unique in Native American history: they pooled money and bought their land back, purchasing acreage on the Iowa River in 1857 to found the Meskwaki Settlement, which their descendants still hold.
Fox (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Chicago rebuilt after the 1871 fire with steel-framed buildings, and the state's railroads, stockyards, coal mines and steel mills drew waves of European migrants into fast-growing industrial towns. Labour conflict was intense, from the Haymarket affair to the Pullman strike. Archaeologically, the period shows in worker housing, factory sites and mass-produced consumer goods.
Early Industrial (Illinois, AD 1871–AD 1.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.
Early Woodland (Missouri, 1000 BC–500 BC.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

The stretch when people of the Gulf coastal plain and its river valleys began making and using pottery in quantity - first fibre-tempered, later sand-tempered wares - while still living largely by hunting, fishing and gathering. Settlements grew more permanent and long-distance exchange in stone and other goods expanded, setting up the burial-mound societies of the Woodland period that followed.

Marked by check-stamped versions of the region's chalky pottery, this was a time of larger, more organised communities with platform and burial mounds and clear social ranking, influenced by but distinct from Mississippian chiefdoms inland. Fishing and shellfish remained the economic base rather than intensive maize farming. Its final generations were the Timucua chiefdoms met by French and Spanish expeditions.

Communities along the Ohio and its tributaries lived in small settlements, made thick grit-tempered pots, and buried their dead under earthen mounds. They grew squash, sunflower and native seed crops while still hunting and gathering heavily, and they traded for copper, marine shell and fine cherts through the exchange networks that linked Adena and Hopewell centres. The label is used when artefacts show only that a site falls somewhere in this broad ceramic-and-mound era.

1880 to 2008 (Iowa, AD 1880–AD 2008).prose:
[Iowa, AD 1880–AD 2008] 1880 to 2008. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A span that runs from the height of small-farm, small-town Iowa to the present-day landscape of consolidated grain and livestock operations. Steam and horse power gave way to tractors, hybrid seed and centre-pivot machinery; interstate highways and grain terminals replaced the local depot and creamery. Standing buildings and archaeological deposits from these years document ordinary rural and urban life, from farmstead outbuildings and privies to factory sites and demolished neighbourhoods.
1880 to 2008 (Iowa, AD 1880–AD 2008).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

19th Century (South Carolina, AD 1800–AD.label: 19th Century
19th Century (South Carolina, AD 1800–AD.prose:
[South Carolina, AD 1800–AD 1900] 19th Century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Steam, iron and coal turned England into the world's first industrial society: railways spread across the country from the 1830s, factory towns swelled, and by mid-century most people lived in urban places. Reform came in fits and starts, through the Reform Acts, factory and public health legislation, and the growth of trade unions, alongside grinding poverty, cholera and the workhouse. Britain's empire and global trade reached their greatest extent, and mass-produced goods, from transfer-printed china to bottled patent medicines, fill archaeological deposits of the period.

Used for remains clearly of Mississippian type but not assignable to a named phase. Mississippian communities built platform mounds and plazas, farmed maize intensively on river bottomlands, made shell-tempered pottery, and were organised into ranked chiefdoms that rose and collapsed repeatedly. Western Kentucky sat within this world, linked by the Ohio and Mississippi rivers to centres like Cahokia and Angel.

A subdivision of the long Weeden Island ceramic sequence in the Florida panhandle and adjacent Southeast, tracked through changing decoration on mound and village pottery. Ritual life centred on sand burial mounds accompanied by caches of elaborately modelled and perforated vessels. Settlement remained tied to rich coastal and river-valley food sources rather than to intensive farming.
Weeden Island 4 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Railroads, drainage of the Everglades and aggressive land promotion turned a thinly settled state into a destination, with a speculative boom in the 1920s that collapsed spectacularly before the 1926 hurricane and the Depression. Military airfields and training bases in the 1940s brought in hundreds of thousands of servicemen, many of whom returned to stay. Sites from these decades range from Mediterranean Revival resorts and packing houses to New Deal camps and wartime airstrips.

The era of maize farming, flat-topped earthen mounds and hereditary chiefs in the Southeast. Towns like Etowah were laid out around plazas and mounds, ringed by palisades, and their elites were buried with copper plates, engraved shell and stone effigies bearing a shared body of religious imagery. The chiefdoms were still functioning when Hernando de Soto marched through in 1540, and collapsed rapidly afterwards under the diseases and disruption that followed.
General Mississippian (Georgia, AD 900–A.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

The span covers Iowa's transformation from newly railroaded farm country into an industrialised agricultural landscape. Horse-drawn work gave way to tractors and combines, rural electrification and paved highways closed the distance between farm and town, and hybrid corn and chemical fertiliser multiplied yields while steadily reducing the number of people needed to produce them. Hundreds of small towns and one-room schools shrank or disappeared, and the farm crisis of the 1980s accelerated consolidation into far fewer, far larger operations.
1870-1998 (Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1998).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Villages of the Oneota tradition along the central Des Moines River valley, whose people combined maize, bean and squash gardening with bison hunting and fishing. They left thick middens, storage and refuse pits, and distinctive shell-tempered pottery with trailed decoration. These communities are widely regarded as ancestral to the historic Ioway, and the sequence closes at the point when French explorers first reached the region.
Moingona (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

A Plains Woodland pottery complex of the Missouri valley and its eastern margins, known from cord-roughened jars decorated with single-cord impressions around the rim. Its people lived in small settlements, hunted bison and deer, gathered wild plants and built low burial mounds, and stand between the earlier Woodland mound-builders and the later village farmers of the Plains.

A long span covering the shift from the early maize-farming Great Oasis hamlets to the Oneota villages that dominated the region until Europeans arrived. Oneota people made shell-tempered globular pots, lived in large seasonal settlements, and combined horticulture with bison hunting and wild rice gathering; their descendants include the Ioway, Otoe and Ho-Chunk. The end date marks the arrival of Marquette and Jolliet on the Mississippi.

The Yuchi spoke a language unrelated to any other, a linguistic isolate that hints at a long and separate history in the Southeast. Pushed from the Savannah River country by war and slave raiding, they resettled among the Creek towns while keeping their own square grounds, ceremonies and identity. They survived removal to Indian Territory as a distinct people despite being counted as Creeks.

The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

A Late Woodland community pattern in the upper Mississippi valley, known from cord-impressed jars and the small triangular arrowheads that archaeologists still call Madison points. The bow had replaced the spearthrower, and people lived in scattered hamlets, hunting, fishing and tending small plots of native seed crops. These were the last generations before maize agriculture and Oneota village life reshaped the region.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.

A warmer, drier climate expanded prairie at the expense of forest, pushing groups toward river valleys and increasing the importance of bison hunting. Ground and polished stone tools, grinding equipment for seeds and nuts, and the first substantial storage pits show a more scheduled, resource-specific way of life. Deeply buried sites in alluvial valleys preserve much of what is known about this time.

A continuation of the St. Johns way of life in which decorated wares from neighbouring traditions, including complicated-stamped and check-stamped pottery from the Gulf side, begin to appear alongside the local chalky ceramics. Sand burial mounds became more common, showing growing attention to formal treatment of the dead.

For Virginia these decades brought a huge federal and military build-up, with Norfolk's naval and shipbuilding complex, Quantico, Fort Eustis and Langley reshaping whole districts, and drawing workers into rapidly built housing. Between the wars came the collapse of tobacco and farm prices, Depression relief and New Deal projects such as the Blue Ridge Parkway and Shenandoah National Park, and the beginnings of colonial restoration at Williamsburg. Archaeologically it is the period of concrete bases, worker housing, motor roads and abandoned farmsteads.

Woodland communities in the Southeast made pottery stamped with carved wooden paddles bearing intricate curvilinear designs, each paddle so distinctive that archaeologists can trace individual pots — and the social ties behind them — across hundreds of kilometres. They built low burial mounds and participated in the wider exchange networks that carried exotic stone, copper and mica through the Hopewellian world. Village life was based on fishing, shellfish, hunting and gathered plants rather than farming.

Shell-mound people of the central Florida Gulf coast, living off fish, shellfish and estuary resources rather than farming, and piling up the vast middens and ridges that still mark the shoreline. They buried their dead in sand mounds with shell and bone tools, and their plain sand-tempered pottery marks the long transition from Archaic life to the later Manasota and Weeden Island traditions.
Perico Island (Florida, 500 BC–AD 800).source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Late Woodland (South Carolina, AD 500–AD.prose:
[South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1150] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

Spans Illinois from the arrival of French missionaries and traders in the Illinois Country through statehood, prairie farming, and industrial Chicago. The archaeology includes French colonial villages of vertical-log houses, Native towns full of trade goods, lead-mining camps, steamboat wrecks, canal works and factory neighbourhoods. It tracks the transformation of tallgrass prairie into one of the most heavily engineered landscapes in the country.

Exchange with the St Johns and Okeechobee regions is visible in the pottery, and the concentration of labour at a few places suggests leaders able to command it.

Iowa's towns grew up along the Mississippi and Missouri and then along the rail lines, filling with German, Irish, Scandinavian and Czech immigrants who brought breweries, churches and fraternal halls. Urban lots from this era yield privy and cellar fills packed with bottles, ceramics and butchered bone, the everyday debris of households before municipal sewers and trash collection.

late Middle Woodland (Iowa, AD 50–AD 300.label: late Middle Woodland

[Iowa, AD 50–AD 300] late Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The great Hopewell exchange networks that had carried obsidian, mica and copper into the river valleys began to unravel, and elaborate mound burial grew simpler. Villages along the Mississippi and its tributaries stayed put longer, relying on fish, mussels and cultivated native seeds. What followed was a more local, dispersed way of life without the earlier long-distance ceremonial connections.

Their sites keep the familiar shell-tempered pottery and bison-scapula hoes but now include trade silver, iron axes and gun parts, letting archaeologists tie an archaeological tradition directly to named living nations. That link makes Oneota one of the clearest cases in North America of an excavated culture matched to its descendants.

Two world wars drained the country's wealth and manpower, and the empire that had underwritten its power was dismantled within two decades of 1945. Out of the wars came the welfare state and the National Health Service; out of decolonisation came migration from the Caribbean and South Asia that remade Britain's cities. Heavy industry and coal collapsed, seaside and mill towns emptied, and the country reinvented itself around finance, services and pop culture.

The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. After the collapse of their settlement at Nauvoo, a remnant established a colony in Iowa where property was held in common, decisions were made by vote, and meals were taken together in a communal dining hall. Repeated schisms between older and younger members eventually broke it up, but it lasted longer than almost any other secular commune in America.

The Wahpekute, whose name is usually rendered 'shooters among the leaves', occupied the prairie and woodland edge of southern Minnesota and northern Iowa. Their seasonal round combined bison hunting, fishing and gathering with fur trading at posts along the rivers, and archaeological traces include camp sites, trade goods and burial places. Treaty cessions and the violence of the 1850s and 1862 ended their presence in the region.

The new capital at Williamsburg took shape, with the Capitol, the Governor's Palace and the college giving the colony a monumental centre for the first time. Direct shipments from Africa peaked in these years, and slavery became the normal basis of tobacco production across the tidewater. It was also the era of Chesapeake piracy, ended with Blackbeard's death in 1718, and of the first serious settlement pressure west of the fall line.

English settlement at Jamestown put a permanent European foothold on the Chesapeake, and within a few decades tobacco planting had reshaped the whole region: land taken from the Powhatan paramount chiefdom, indentured servants and then enslaved Africans brought in to work it. Epidemic disease, trade in copper, glass beads and guns, and two devastating wars broke Algonquian political power by the 1640s. Archaeologically it is a period of hybrid sites, where Native pottery turns up alongside English pipes and ironwork.

Coastal and riverine shell-mound dwellers here made some of the earliest pottery in North America, thick vessels tempered with Spanish moss and palmetto fibre, often decorated with incised lines. The pots appear alongside enormous accumulations of oyster and clam shell, evidence of settled, resource-rich lives without agriculture. Their invention of ceramics spread widely across the Southeast.

Everything left behind by newcomers to Georgia after Spanish entradas opened the interior — Spanish missions on the coast, English trading posts and forts, plantations worked by enslaved Africans, then farms, mills, railroads and towns. The archaeology here runs from potsherds and wine bottles to slave quarters, Civil War earthworks and tenant-farm sites. It is the material record of how a Native landscape became a colonial and then an industrialising one.

Virginia went from prosperous slave state to the central theatre of the Civil War, with campaigns from Manassas to Appomattox destroying property and displacing whole communities. Emancipation freed roughly half a million people and the western counties left to form West Virginia. The years after 1865 brought military occupation, a new state constitution, and the beginnings of sharecropping and Black churches, schools and towns.

A catch-all label for material belonging to the Fort Ancient tradition that cannot be pinned to a particular phase. Fort Ancient people lived in circular villages around open plazas along the middle Ohio and its tributaries, farming maize, beans and squash, hunting deer and elk, and making shell-tempered pottery. Their descendants encountered European goods - glass beads, brass - before they ever met Europeans face to face.

The archaeological sequence of southwest Florida's estuaries, ending with the Calusa encountered by Spanish ships. These people never farmed maize seriously: fish, shellfish and other estuarine resources were rich enough to support dense, permanent towns, monumental shell mounds, canals and a powerful chiefdom that extracted tribute from much of the peninsula. Waterlogged sites such as Key Marco preserved wooden masks, carved animal figureheads and nets that almost never survive elsewhere.

Virginia emerged from the war with a wrecked economy and a transformed labour system, as freedpeople bargained over wages, founded churches and schools, and briefly held office before disfranchisement. Railroads, coalfields in the southwest, tobacco factories in Richmond and Danville and shipbuilding at Newport News pulled the state toward industry and cities. The 1902 constitution imposed poll taxes and literacy tests that stripped Black and many poor white Virginians of the vote, locking in segregation for half a century.

German pietists of the Community of True Inspiration, persecuted at home, crossed to America and eventually built seven villages on the Iowa River where land, workshops and meals were shared in common. Their woollen mills, furniture shops and disciplined farming made the colonies prosperous and largely self-sufficient, with worship in plain meeting houses and no ordained clergy. Communal ownership ended in the Depression, when members reorganised the enterprise as a corporation.

The Community of True Inspiration began as a pietist movement in German-speaking Europe, guided by prophets who spoke inspired testimonies, and emigrated to escape conscription and state church pressure. Its members finally settled seven villages on the Iowa River, holding all property in common, eating in communal kitchens and running woollen mills and farms together. The communal system was voted out in 1932 and reorganised as a joint-stock company, though the church and the villages survive.

Jamestown was planted in 1607 and very nearly failed, with the 'starving time' winter of 1609-10 reducing the settlement to a handful of survivors. John Rolfe's success with West Indian tobacco after 1612 gave the colony an export crop, and with it came scattered riverside plantations, the first representative assembly in 1619, and the first documented Africans in the colony. The Powhatan attack of 1622 killed a quarter of the settlers and led to the Virginia Company losing its charter.

A Middle Woodland culture of the Florida panhandle coast, whose people fished and gathered shellfish in the bays and built low sand burial mounds. Their pottery carries the swirling complicated-stamped designs of Swift Creek potters in Georgia, made with carved wooden paddles. Copper, mica and panpipes found in the mounds show the community was plugged into the long-distance Hopewell exchange network reaching to the Ohio valley.

A late Middle Woodland complex marked by thick, cord-roughened jars and the disappearance of the elaborate Hopewell mortuary ceremonialism and long-distance trade that had preceded it. Communities lived in small, scattered settlements along river valleys, gathering wild plants, hunting and tending native seed crops. It represents the quieter, more locally focused world that followed the collapse of the Hopewell interaction sphere.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

Farming societies of the Southeast organised as chiefdoms, living in palisaded towns around plaza-and-mound complexes and growing maize, beans and squash. Moundville on the Black Warrior River is the outstanding example, with its ranked burials, engraved stone palettes and copper ornaments. Hereditary rank, craft specialists and long-distance exchange in marine shell and copper mark a decisive break from earlier village life.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

War with France on the Ohio frontier drew Virginia into imperial conflict and left the colony taxed, indebted and quarrelsome; two decades later its planters were leading the break with Britain. The Revolution ended with the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781, and afterwards Virginians wrote much of the new republic's constitutional framework while leaving slavery intact and expanding. Evangelical revivals unsettled the Anglican establishment, the capital moved to Richmond in 1780, and planters began shifting from exhausted tobacco land toward wheat.

The archaeology of European-descended settlement: fortified stations and log cabins, then farmsteads, mills, distilleries, iron furnaces and river towns. Excavated cellars, wells and refuse pits show how imported ceramics, glass and hardware spread inland, and how enslaved African Americans lived and worked on those same properties. The Sauk, an Algonquian-speaking people pushed westward out of the Great Lakes country, established villages along the Mississippi and its tributaries and lived by a cycle of maize farming, summer bison hunts on the prairies and winter trapping for the fur trade. Their expulsion from lands east of the Mississippi triggered the Black Hawk War of 1832, after which treaty cessions stripped away their Iowa holdings within two decades. Their sites are recognisable from trade silver, gunflints, glass beads and European kettles mixed with traditional tools.

Virginia went from frontier war against the French and their allies to the leadership of the Revolution, supplying Washington, Jefferson, Madison and Henry. Tobacco debts to British merchants sharpened planter hostility to imperial taxation, and Dunmore's offer of freedom to enslaved men who joined the Crown exposed the contradiction at the heart of the cause. Yorktown ended the war on Virginia soil, and Virginians then drafted much of the federal Constitution.

Covers the Native nations of the Missouri region from the first French descent of the Mississippi onward — Osage, Missouria, Illinois, Kansa and, later, peoples pushed west by removal. Sites from these centuries mix traditional material culture with glass beads, brass kettles, gunflints and horse gear, showing how deeply the fur trade reshaped daily life. The period ends with dispossession: by the 1830s most of these nations had been forced out of the state entirely.

Angel Mounds near Evansville was one of the largest, home to perhaps a thousand people and tied by trade and shared ritual style to Cahokia and other Mississippian centres. Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. Founded by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés to expel French Huguenots and guard the treasure fleets, it became the capital of Spanish Florida and the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the United States. Repeatedly burned and besieged by English raiders, it was rebuilt around the coquina-stone Castillo de San Marcos, and it sheltered a free Black community at Fort Mose. Virginia settled into a tobacco economy run on indentured labour, with planters claiming headrights of land for every servant they imported and pushing settlement up the rivers onto Powhatan and other Native land. Parliament's Navigation Acts tied the colony's crop to English ships and merchants, squeezing prices just as small planters were finishing their terms and finding the best land already taken. Africans were present in growing numbers, and colonial courts were beginning to treat their servitude as lifelong and hereditary. Excavated house sites from these decades are typically earthfast timber buildings, cheaply built by people who expected to move on.

A half-century that carried Virginia from Depression-era farms to a suburban, federally employed society. War industry and military bases swelled the Hampton Roads and Washington regions, cars and interstates dispersed settlement, and the tobacco-and-agriculture economy shrank. The same span saw the long confrontation over school desegregation, from the Brown decision through Massive Resistance to court-ordered busing.

The long-lived archaeological tradition of northeastern Florida, recognised by its distinctive chalky pottery made with freshwater sponge spicules. Its people never took up serious farming, instead thriving on fish, shellfish and wild plants, and leaving behind enormous shell middens and burial mounds along the river and coastal lagoons. Their descendants were the Timucua encountered by French and Spanish colonists in the sixteenth century.

Florida's hunter-fisher-gatherers adapted to rising seas and expanding wetlands, exploiting shellfish, fish and marsh plants in enormous quantity. Waterlogged sites preserve what usually rots away - woven fabrics, wooden tools, and at Windover the brains of people buried in a peat pond some 7,000 years ago. Along the St. Johns and the coast they piled shell mounds and, late in the period, made some of the earliest pottery in North America.

Over these millennia groups returned repeatedly to rich river and shoal locations, building up the deep shell middens that later became burial places. Excavations in these settings often cut through layered fills where hand-blown bottles and transfer-printed ceramics give way to machine-made glass, tin cans and mass-produced goods shipped in by rail.

Ceramic vessels, earthen burial mounds and a growing reliance on cultivated native seed plants distinguish this era from the Archaic centuries before it. Adena-related communities in the Ohio Valley raised conical mounds and log-tomb burials over their dead, accompanied by copper, mica and marine shell obtained through long-distance exchange. The bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, marked archaeologically by a sudden shift to small triangular points, and maize became a real part of the diet. Populations grew and gathered into larger villages, some fortified; in the northeast, groups built the animal-shaped effigy mounds. These changes set the stage for the Oneota and Mississippian farming societies that followed.

Iowa's farms mechanised in these decades, with tractors and combines displacing horses and hired hands and steadily enlarging the average holding. A collapse in commodity prices after the First World War brought rural bankruptcies and bank failures well before the Depression deepened them, prompting New Deal price supports, soil conservation programmes and rural electrification. Wartime demand and postwar hybrid seed then pushed yields higher, while small towns and one-room schools began the long decline that followed.

Exhausted tobacco soils pushed many Virginians west and turned the state into the country's main exporter of enslaved people to the cotton South, a trade run out of Richmond and Alexandria. Gabriel's conspiracy in 1800 and Nat Turner's rebellion in 1831 provoked harsh new restrictions and a legislative debate on slavery that ended with the institution reaffirmed. Canals, turnpikes and the first railroads opened the piedmont and valley, wheat replaced tobacco on many farms, and Richmond's mills and ironworks made it an industrial exception in the South.

A Late Woodland complex of the prairie lake country, known from small campsites, cord-roughened pottery and low burial mounds. People hunted bison and deer, gathered wild plants, and moved seasonally between lake and prairie, with the bow and arrow largely replacing the spearthrower. It precedes the arrival of maize-farming villages in the region.

Part of the Central Plains tradition, these were dispersed homesteads of large square earthlodges set above river valleys, combining maize horticulture with bison hunting. Deep bell-shaped storage pits, cord-roughened jars and bone tools are the characteristic remains. The settlements were abandoned in the fourteenth century, with populations apparently moving north and west.

The Sauk and the Meskwaki (called Fox by the French) became close allies after French campaigns nearly destroyed the Meskwaki in the 1730s, and thereafter shared villages, hunting grounds and treaty negotiations. Together they controlled the lead-mining country of the upper Mississippi and traded heavily with British and American merchants. Removal followed the Black Hawk War, though a group of Meskwaki later bought land back in Iowa and remain there today.

Woodland communities in the Gulf coastal plain raised earthen mounds and buried their dead with extraordinary pottery — effigy vessels shaped as birds, animals and human heads, made to be broken and deposited rather than used. Complicated-stamped and Weeden Island wares from these ceremonies travelled through long-distance exchange networks across the Southeast. The scale of the mound-building shows people organising large labour projects long before maize farming and chiefdoms arrived.

In the early 1800s Cherokees adopted a written syllabary, printed a newspaper, and built a constitutional government — and were forced west anyway on the Trail of Tears. The founding decades: a fortified trading post at Jamestown, catastrophic mortality from disease and hunger, and the discovery that Virginia tobacco could be sold at a profit in London. The Virginia Company collapsed after the Powhatan attack of 1622 and the colony passed to royal control in 1624, while planters spread up the rivers and imported indentured servants by the shipload. Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

Returning servicemen, cheap federal mortgages and the GI Bill fuelled a rush into new suburbs ringing Chicago while industry converted back to consumer production. The second wave of the Great Migration brought tens of thousands of Black southerners to the city, into neighbourhoods hemmed in by restrictive covenants and, soon, by high-rise public housing. Almost everything about the modern Illinois landscape - subdivisions, shopping strips, expressways - was set in motion in these few years.

Mound building and the far-flung exchange of the Hopewellian centuries largely ceased, while native seed crops were joined and then overtaken by maize. Out of these local traditions grew the Fort Ancient and Mississippian villages of the following centuries.

The Potano were a Timucua-speaking people of north-central Florida, farmers of maize, beans and squash who lived in dispersed villages of round thatched houses linked to the archaeological Alachua tradition. They fought Hernando de Soto's army in 1539 and later accepted Spanish Franciscan missions, where labour drafts and epidemics thinned their numbers. Raids by Carolina colonists and their Creek allies at the start of the eighteenth century shattered the surviving mission towns and ended the Potano as a distinct people.

Maize, bean and squash farmers who lived in scattered clusters of square earthlodges along the streams of the central Plains, storing crops in deep bell-shaped pits and hunting bison on foot. In western Iowa their easternmost settlements are the Glenwood earthlodges above the Missouri River.
