Ubaid (Syria, 5799 BC–3999 BC).label: Ubaid
Ubaid (Syria, 5799 BC–3999 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 5799 BC–3999 BC] Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The first widespread village culture of southern Mesopotamia, marked by pale greenish painted pottery, mudbrick houses of tripartite plan and small temples rebuilt again and again on the same spot, most famously at Eridu. Irrigation let farmers work the dry alluvium, herds and fishing filled out the diet, and communities grew large enough to support differences in status visible in burials and buildings. Ubaid pottery and styles spread north into Syria and Anatolia and down the Gulf, setting the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.
Ubaid (Syria, 5799 BC–3999 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1599 BC–999 BC).label: Middle Assyrian
Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1599 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–999 BC] Middle Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Dates different in GeoDia. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Assyria emerged from vassalage to Mitanni to become a great power, its kings conquering northern Mesopotamia and, under Tukulti-Ninurta I, briefly capturing Babylon itself. An efficient provincial administration, meticulous royal archives and the Middle Assyrian Laws - unusually harsh, especially toward women - date from this era. Weakened by Aramaean pressure after 1100 BC, the kingdom nevertheless kept the institutions that its Neo-Assyrian successors used to build an empire.
Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1599 BC–999 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC).label: Early Dynastic
Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2333 BC] Early Dynastic. in chronological discussion on p. 56, provides "ca." before date. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.
Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC).label: Akkadian
Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 2333 BC–2192 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.
Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Uruk (Iraq, 3749 BC–3149 BC).label: Uruk
Uruk (Iraq, 3749 BC–3149 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 3749 BC–3149 BC] Uruk. in chronological discussion on p. 55, provides "ca." before date. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities in this period, with Uruk itself swelling to a size no settlement had reached before. Monumental temple platforms, mass-produced bevel-rim bowls for rationed labour, cylinder seals for accounting and finally the earliest writing all appear together, the machinery of a society organised around institutions rather than kin. Uruk-style material spread up the Euphrates into Syria and Anatolia, whether by colony, trade or imitation.
Uruk (Iraq, 3749 BC–3149 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Sassanian (Iraq, AD 227–AD 651).label: Sassanian
Sassanian (Iraq, AD 227–AD 651).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, AD 227–AD 651] Sassanian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.
Sassanian (Iraq, AD 227–AD 651).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Neo Assyrian (Syria, 999 BC–604 BC).label: Neo Assyrian
Neo Assyrian (Syria, 999 BC–604 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 999 BC–604 BC] Neo Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Assyrian kings drove west from the Tigris to take the cities of Syria one by one, turning Aramaean and Neo-Hittite kingdoms into taxed provinces under Assyrian governors and deporting whole populations to break resistance. Aramaic spread as the common language of administration and trade across the empire. When Nineveh fell in 612 BC the provinces passed rapidly to Babylon, and later to Persia.
Neo Assyrian (Syria, 999 BC–604 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3149 BC–2899 BC).label: Jemdet Nasr
Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3149 BC–2899 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 3149 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr. in chronological discussion on p. 55, provides "ca." before date. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Named for a mound in central Iraq, this phase sits between Uruk and the Early Dynastic city-states. Distinctive polychrome painted jars in red and black appear alongside the earliest archives of proto-cuneiform tablets, which record grain, livestock and labour rather than stories. Settlements across southern Mesopotamia show a shared culture of seals, accounting and temple economies, the administrative machinery that would soon underpin Sumerian kingship.
Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3149 BC–2899 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Parthian (Syria, 125 BC–AD 227).label: Parthian
Parthian (Syria, 125 BC–AD 227).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 125 BC–AD 227] Parthian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. 226 A.D. in GeoDia. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The Arsacid empire out of Iran pressed to the Euphrates, making Syria the frontier zone of a rivalry with Rome that lasted nearly three centuries. Crassus lost his army and his head at Carrhae in 53 BC, and later Parthian raids and Roman counter-invasions repeatedly swept the caravan cities between the two powers. That contested ground was also enormously profitable: Palmyra, Dura-Europos and the Euphrates routes grew rich handling silk and spices moving between the empires, and their art blends Greek, Iranian and Semitic styles.
Parthian (Syria, 125 BC–AD 227).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Chalcolithic (Syria, 5799 BC–3749 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Syria, 5799 BC–3749 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 5799 BC–3749 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Does not seem to be present in this work. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.
Chalcolithic (Syria, 5799 BC–3749 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 624 BC–538 BC).label: Neo-Babylonian
Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 624 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 624 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian. In GeoDia as "Median". Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Judah under Babylonian rule was a diminished, largely rural province, its capital and temple in ruins and its royal house deported. Excavations show towns in the south and the Shephelah abandoned or shrunken while some settlements north of Jerusalem, around Benjamin, carried on. This bleak interval ended when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and permitted exiles to return.
Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 624 BC–538 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2111 BC–2003 BC).label: Neo-Sumerian
Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2111 BC–2003 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 2111 BC–2003 BC] Neo-Sumerian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. In chronological discussion on p. 56, refers to this as the Third Dynasty of Ur. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The Third Dynasty of Ur reunited southern Mesopotamia after the Akkadian collapse and ran it through an extraordinarily detailed bureaucracy that has left tens of thousands of accounting tablets. Ur-Nammu and Shulgi built the great stepped ziggurats, issued one of the earliest law collections and promoted Sumerian as a language of high culture even as Akkadian took over daily speech. The state fell to famine, Amorite pressure and an Elamite attack, but its scribal schools shaped Mesopotamian literature for a thousand years.
Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2111 BC–2003 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1599 BC).label: Old Assyrian
Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Old Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian grouped together under one heading on p. 340. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Merchants from Assur ran a long-distance trade network carrying tin and woollen textiles by donkey caravan into Anatolia, exchanging them for silver and gold. Their archives at the Kanesh trading colony preserve thousands of clay letters, contracts and lawsuits, including those of women managing textile production at home. Shamshi-Adad I briefly welded northern Mesopotamia into a kingdom before Hammurabi's Babylon overshadowed it.
Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1599 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Hellenistic (Turkey, 330 BC–125 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Turkey, 330 BC–125 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 330 BC–125 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.
Hellenistic (Turkey, 330 BC–125 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC).label: Old Babylonian
Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Old Babylonian. Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian grouped together under one heading on p. 340. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.
Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Persian (Iraq, 538 BC–330 BC).label: Persian
Persian (Iraq, 538 BC–330 BC).prose:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 538 BC–330 BC] Persian. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. In GeoDia as "Achaemenid". Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and Judah became Yehud, a small tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire. Under governors and an increasingly powerful priesthood, much of the Hebrew Bible took shape and Aramaic became the everyday language. Coins, imported Greek pottery and administrative seal impressions show a province tied into imperial and Mediterranean networks.
Persian (Iraq, 538 BC–330 BC).source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

Republican (Spain, 132 BC–26 BC).label: Republican
Republican (Spain, 132 BC–26 BC).prose:
[Spain, 132 BC–26 BC] Republican. Beginning-date corresponds with the end of the Celtiberian wars; outside of the Celtiberian homeland, the Republican period in Spain begins 218 B.C. (Second Punic War). Period definition from The romanization of central Spain : complexity, diversity, and change in a provincial hinterland — Curchin, Leonard A., 1950-, 2004.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.
Republican (Spain, 132 BC–26 BC).source: The romanization of central Spain : complexity, diversity, and change in a provincial hinterland

Archaic (Spain, 629 BC–499 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Spain, 629 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Iberia, 629 BC–499 BC] Archaic. See also Dominguez in C. Sanchez & G.R. Tsetskhladze, 2001. Greek Pottery from the Iberian Peninsula. Period definition from Greek Trade in Iberia: The Extent of Interaction — Paloma Cabrera, 1998.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Spain, 629 BC–499 BC).source: Greek Trade in Iberia: The Extent of Interaction

Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 BC).label: Jemdet Nasr
Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 BC).prose:
[Uruk, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr. See also Charvat 2002. Period definition from The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies — Adams, Robert McC. (Robert McCormick), 1926-, 1972.

Named for a mound in central Iraq, this phase sits between Uruk and the Early Dynastic city-states. Distinctive polychrome painted jars in red and black appear alongside the earliest archives of proto-cuneiform tablets, which record grain, livestock and labour rather than stories. Settlements across southern Mesopotamia show a shared culture of seals, accounting and temple economies, the administrative machinery that would soon underpin Sumerian kingship.
Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 BC).source: The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies

Early Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–3199 BC).label: Early Uruk
Early Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–3199 BC).prose:
[Uruk, 3499 BC–3199 BC] Early Uruk. See also Liverani 2006. Period definition from The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies — Adams, Robert McC. (Robert McCormick), 1926-, 1972.

Southwestern Iran was drawn into the orbit of the emerging urban world of lowland Mesopotamia, adopting its mass-produced, undecorated pottery, its architecture and its systems of accounting with clay tokens and seals. Susa and its neighbours on the Susiana plain grew into centres with monumental buildings and clear differences in wealth. The exchange of highland metal, stone and timber for lowland goods set up a relationship that shaped Elamite civilisation for millennia.
Early Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–3199 BC).source: The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies

Late Uruk (Iraq, 3199 BC–3099 BC).label: Late Uruk
Late Uruk (Iraq, 3199 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[Uruk, 3199 BC–3099 BC] Late Uruk. See also Liverani 2006. Period definition from The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies — Adams, Robert McC. (Robert McCormick), 1926-, 1972.

The world's first cities took shape in the Mesopotamian lowlands, and their institutions, goods and administrators reached deep into the Iranian plateau and Khuzestan. Mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and the earliest clay tablets with proto-cuneiform signs mark the birth of bureaucratic record-keeping. When the Uruk network contracted, Susa and its neighbours went their own way, developing the Proto-Elamite script and state.
Late Uruk (Iraq, 3199 BC–3099 BC).source: The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p0.label: New Kingdom
New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p0.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1069 B.label: Third Intermediate Period
Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1069 B.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 1069 BC–711 BC] Third Intermediate Period. unsure why GeoDia start_label said 2055 B.C. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

A long stretch of divided rule in which no single king controlled the whole Nile valley. Pharaohs of Libyan descent ruled the Delta while Thebes answered to a priestly dynasty of Amun, and royal tombs were tucked into the temple enclosure at Tanis - one of the few Egyptian royal burials found nearly intact. Kushite kings from Nubia later reunified the country, only for Assyrian invasion to end the period and usher in the Saite revival.

First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2133 B.label: First Intermediate Period
First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2133 B.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 2133 BC–2039 BC] First Intermediate Period. Robins' chronology is being used in preference to Freeman's, since it seems to represent the general textbook situation more accurately. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Central authority collapsed after the long reign of Pepi II, and Egypt broke into competing regional powers - provincial governors ruling as local dynasts, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Low Nile floods, famine and disorder colour the literature written afterwards, but tomb goods and inscriptions show provincial workshops and local elites flourishing. Funerary practices once reserved for kings spread to lesser officials, laying groundwork for the Coffin Texts. The Theban victory that ended the era produced the reunified Middle Kingdom.

Roman emperors (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 395).label: Roman emperors
Roman emperors (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 395).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 29 BC–AD 395] Roman emperors. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egypt became the emperor's private preserve, governed by a prefect and closed to senators, its harvests shipped north to feed Rome. Emperors from Augustus onward appear on temple walls at Dendera, Esna and Philae in pharaonic costume, offering to Egyptian gods in hieroglyphs. Alexandria stayed a vast, restive city of Greeks, Jews and Egyptians, while everyday papyrus documents record how Roman taxation and law reshaped village life.

Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC).label: Middle Kingdom
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC] Middle Kingdom. unsure why GeoDia start_label said 2055 B.C. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1639.label: Second Intermediate Period
Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1639.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 1639 BC–1531 BC] Second Intermediate Period. unsure why GeoDia end_label said 1550 B.C. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

A divided Egypt, with the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the Delta from Avaris, a rump Theban kingdom in the south, and the Kushite kings of Kerma pressing the frontier. Trade with the Levant and the Aegean flourished at Avaris even as pharaonic art and building shrank. The Theban wars of liberation under Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and finally Ahmose reunified the country and launched the New Kingdom.

Late Period (Egypt, 711 BC–331 BC).label: Late Period
Late Period (Egypt, 711 BC–331 BC).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 711 BC–331 BC] Late Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

Early Dynastic Period (Egypt, 2919 BC–26.label: Early Dynastic Period
Early Dynastic Period (Egypt, 2919 BC–26.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 2919 BC–2648 BC] Early Dynastic Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Mesopotamia's cities came into their own: walled, densely populated, and ruled by kings who built temples and fought their neighbours. Writing spread beyond the storeroom into royal boasts, legal contracts and literature, giving the earliest named individuals in history. Excavated palaces, royal tombs and temple statuary from Ur, Lagash and Kish give an unusually vivid picture of daily and ceremonial life.

Predynastic Period (Egypt, 4999 BC–2919.label: Predynastic Period
Predynastic Period (Egypt, 4999 BC–2919.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 4999 BC–2919 BC] Predynastic Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Nile Valley societies moved from village agriculture to hierarchical chiefdoms with wealthy elite burials and specialised craft production. Trade linked Egypt to Nubia, the Levant and Mesopotamia, and rulers began using standardised symbols of power that would become the pharaonic crowns and regalia. Its close saw the political unification that launched dynastic Egypt.

Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2648 BC–2133 BC).label: Old Kingdom
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2648 BC–2133 BC).prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 2648 BC–2133 BC] Old Kingdom. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

Graeco-Roman Period (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 39.label: Graeco-Roman Period
Graeco-Roman Period (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 39.prose:
[Ancient Egypt, 331 BC–AD 395] Graeco-Roman Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Ptolemaic kings and then Roman prefects governed the Nile valley from Alexandria, running the country as an enormously profitable estate exporting grain, papyrus and glass. Traditional temple religion flourished under Greek and Roman patronage at Edfu, Dendera and Philae even as Greek became the language of government, and mixed Greek-Egyptian burial customs produced the strikingly lifelike Fayum portraits. The period closes with Egypt as a heartland of early Christianity and monasticism.

Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC) [p077fc.label: Iron IIA
Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC) [p077fc.prose:
[Bethsaida, 999 BC–924 BC] Iron IIA. Period definition from Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century — Savage, Carl E., 2011.

Monumental building returns: fortified gates, palaces and administrative centres at sites like Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, traditionally credited to Solomon and hotly debated ever since. Pharaoh Sheshonq I campaigned through the region around 925 BC, leaving a list of conquered towns at Karnak. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature.
Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC) [p077fc.source: Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century

Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–721 BC).label: Iron IIB
Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–721 BC).prose:
[Bethsaida, 899 BC–721 BC] Iron IIB. Period definition from Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century — Savage, Carl E., 2011.

Israel under the Omrides and then Jeroboam II became a substantial regional power with ivory-decorated palaces at Samaria, before Assyrian armies destroyed it and deported its population in 720 BC. Judah survived as a vassal, and Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BC is documented from both sides — by Assyrian palace reliefs and by the excavated siege ramp and mass grave. Royal administration is visible in stamped jar handles and standardised weights.
Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–721 BC).source: Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century

Iron III (Israel, 585 BC–538 BC).label: Iron III
Iron III (Israel, 585 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Bethsaida, 585 BC–538 BC] Iron III. this date: see also Mazar, 1992. Period definition from Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century — Savage, Carl E., 2011.

The decades of the Babylonian Exile, when Jerusalem lay ruined and administration shifted north to Mizpah. Excavation shows the Judean heartland around Benjamin largely continuing while the city, the Shephelah and the Negev were emptied and burnt. It was in these years that exiled scribes reshaped Judah's traditions, and it ends with Cyrus's capture of Babylon and the permission to return.
Iron III (Israel, 585 BC–538 BC).source: Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century

Yugoslav War, 1991-1995 (Slovenia, AD 19.label: Yugoslav War, 1991-1995
Yugoslav War, 1991-1995 (Slovenia, AD 19.prose:
[Yugoslavia, AD 1991–AD 1995] Yugoslav War, 1991-1995. Spatial coverage: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro, Republic of Macedonia, Serbia, Slovenia. Extracted from heading "Yugoslav War, 1991-1995". Added to LCSH in 2003, revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Slovenia's declaration of independence triggered a ten-day conflict with the Yugoslav People's Army that ended with the federal troops' withdrawal and few casualties compared with what followed. The republic escaped the far bloodier wars in Croatia and Bosnia and turned quickly towards Europe. The break-up it began ended the multinational Yugoslav state built after the Second World War.

Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Tarragona, AD 19.label: Bombardment, 1937-1939
Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Tarragona, AD 19.prose:
[Tarragona (Spain), AD 1937–AD 1939] Bombardment, 1937-1939. Extracted from heading "Tarragona (Spain)--History--Bombardment, 1937-1939". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Republican-held port was hit again and again by Italian aircraft flying from Majorca and by warships offshore, aimed at the harbour, railway and the road link to Barcelona. Civilian districts were wrecked and much of the population fled; the raids ended only when Nationalist troops overran Catalonia.

Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD.label: Henry V, 1106-1125
Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1106–AD 1125] Henry V, 1106-1125. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry V, 1106-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Salian emperor came to power by deposing his own father, then spent years fighting the papacy over who could invest bishops with ring and staff. The struggle ended in the Concordat of Worms of 1122, a compromise that separated spiritual from secular investiture and set the pattern for church-state relations in Europe. His death without an heir opened the contest between Welf and Hohenstaufen families that shaped German politics for the next century.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Rome, AD 1943–AD.label: Bombardment, 1943-1944
Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Rome, AD 1943–AD.prose:
[Rome (Italy), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Rome (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2007, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

Naval Revolt, 1893-1894 (Brazil, AD 1893.label: Naval Revolt, 1893-1894
Naval Revolt, 1893-1894 (Brazil, AD 1893.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1893–AD 1894] Naval Revolt, 1893-1894. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--Naval Revolt, 1893-1894". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Officers of the Brazilian navy turned their guns on Rio de Janeiro in an attempt to unseat President Floriano Peixoto, only four years after the monarchy had been overthrown. The rebellion fused monarchist sympathies, naval resentment of the army-dominated republic, and the southern federalist war in Rio Grande do Sul. Its defeat entrenched army primacy in Brazilian politics and cleared the way for the civilian oligarchic republic that followed.

Medieval period, 1066-1485 (England, AD.label: Medieval period, 1066-1485
Medieval period, 1066-1485 (England, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1066–AD 1485] Medieval period, 1066-1485. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Medieval period, 1066-1485". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Norman Conquest imposed a new French-speaking aristocracy, castles and a reordered church, and produced Domesday Book, the most detailed survey of any early medieval kingdom. Over four centuries came Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament, the growth of towns and the wool trade, Gothic cathedrals, the Black Death that killed perhaps a third or more of the population and broke the grip of serfdom, and the long wars in France. The dynastic bloodletting of the Wars of the Roses ends the period at Bosworth.

Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–A.label: Charles V, 1519-1556
Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1519–AD 1556] Charles V, 1519-1556. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Charles V, 1519-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected emperor with money borrowed from the Fuggers, he confronted Luther at the Diet of Worms and spent the rest of his reign unable to contain the Reformation while also fighting France in Italy and the Ottomans on the Danube and in the Mediterranean. He beat the Lutheran princes at Mühlberg in 1547 but could not make the victory stick, and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 conceded that each prince would determine his territory's religion. Worn out, he abdicated and split his inheritance between his son and his brother, ending the dream of a single universal Christian empire.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Delaware, AD 1775.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Delaware, AD 1775.prose:
[Delaware, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Delaware--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.26 of LCSH 1987, and p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Wars of Independence, 1809-1825 (Bolivia.label: Wars of Independence, 1809-1825
Wars of Independence, 1809-1825 (Bolivia.prose:
[Bolivia, AD 1809–AD 1825] Wars of Independence, 1809-1825. Extracted from heading "Bolivia--History--Wars of Independence, 1809-1825". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The juntas of Chuquisaca and La Paz in 1809 were among the earliest revolts in Spanish America, and they were crushed brutally. Upper Peru then endured sixteen years of grinding guerrilla warfare by local 'republiquetas' while regular armies from Buenos Aires failed repeatedly to hold the highlands. Liberation came from outside, with Sucre's campaign after Ayacucho; the new republic took the name Bolivia in Bolívar's honour.

Augustus III, 1734-1763 (Poland, AD 1734.label: Augustus III, 1734-1763
Augustus III, 1734-1763 (Poland, AD 1734.prose:
[Poland , AD 1734–AD 1763] Augustus III, 1734-1763. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Augustus III, 1734-1763". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His accession followed a war fought by France, Russia and Austria over who should be king of Poland, which tells you how far sovereignty had slipped. He spent almost all his reign in Dresden, leaving Poland to feuding magnate families while the Sejm was paralysed by the liberum veto - a single deputy could dissolve it, and repeatedly did. The drift left the Commonwealth defenceless against the partitions that began a decade after his death.

Civil War, 1965- (Chad, AD 1965–AD 2015).label: Civil War, 1965-
Civil War, 1965- (Chad, AD 1965–AD 2015).prose:
[Chad, AD 1965–AD 2015] Civil War, 1965-. Extracted from heading "Chad--History--Civil War, 1965-". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A tax revolt in the north grew into the FROLINAT rebellion against a southern-dominated government, and the fighting never fully stopped. Libya occupied the Aouzou Strip and backed rival factions, France repeatedly intervened, and the 1987 "Toyota War" saw Chadian pickup-mounted troops rout Libyan armour. Successive rulers took power by force, and rebellions from the east and north continued into the twenty-first century.

Shimabara Uprising, 1637-1638 (Japan, AD.label: Shimabara Uprising, 1637-1638
Shimabara Uprising, 1637-1638 (Japan, AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 1637–AD 1638] Shimabara Uprising, 1637-1638. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Shimabara Uprising, 1637-1638". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Overtaxed peasants and persecuted Christians on the Shimabara Peninsula and Amakusa islands rose behind the teenage figurehead Amakusa Shirō and held the ruined castle of Hara against a huge shogunal army, which finally starved and stormed it, killing the defenders almost to the last person. A Dutch ship shelled the walls from the sea, proof of Protestant usefulness. The shock hardened Tokugawa policy: the Portuguese were expelled, Christianity was hunted with picture-treading tests, and Japan's seclusion was locked in place for two centuries.

Bar Kokhba Rebellion, 132-135 (Israel, A.label: Bar Kokhba Rebellion, 132-135
Bar Kokhba Rebellion, 132-135 (Israel, A.prose:
[Jews, AD 132–AD 135] Bar Kokhba Rebellion, 132-135. Spatial coverage: Israel, State of Palestine. Extracted from heading "Jews--History--Bar Kokhba Rebellion, 132-135". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Spatial coverage extent inferred from knowledge of the Bar Kokhba revolt against the Romans, and the limited geographic identifier of "Jews". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Simon bar Kokhba led a disciplined revolt against Rome that ran an independent Judaea for some three years, minting coins dated to "the freedom of Israel" and issuing orders preserved on letters found in Dead Sea caves. Hadrian sent his best general, Julius Severus, who reduced the rebels stronghold by stronghold, ending at Betar; ancient sources describe catastrophic slaughter and depopulation. Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina, rebuilt Jerusalem as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from it, closing the era of Jewish armed nationalism and pushing Judaism decisively towards the rabbinic study of law.

Civil War, 1960-1965 (Democratic Republi.prose:
[Democratic Republic of the Congo, AD 1960–AD 1965] Civil War, 1960-1965. Extracted from heading " Congo (Democratic Republic)--History--Civil War, 1960-1965". Added to LCSH in 1986.
