Independence from Belgium was followed within weeks by army mutiny, the secession of mineral-rich Katanga, and the murder of Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba. UN peacekeepers intervened on an unprecedented scale — Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash during the mission — while the Cold War powers backed rival factions. The crisis ended with Mobutu Sese Seko's coup and a kleptocratic dictatorship lasting three decades.

Trajan, 98-117 (Roman Empire, AD 98–AD 1.label: Trajan, 98-117
Trajan, 98-117 (Roman Empire, AD 98–AD 1.prose:
[Rome, AD 98–AD 117] Trajan, 98-117. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Trajan, 98-117". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under the first emperor born in the provinces, Rome reached its greatest territorial extent, absorbing Dacia and its gold, and briefly Armenia and Mesopotamia. Dacian plunder paid for a spectacular building programme - the Forum and Markets of Trajan, baths, a new harbour at Portus and roads across the empire - while the spiral frieze of Trajan's Column turned a military campaign into the most detailed picture of the Roman army ever carved.

Victoria, 1837-1901 (United Kingdom, AD.label: Victoria, 1837-1901
Victoria, 1837-1901 (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1837–AD 1901] Victoria, 1837-1901. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Victoria, 1837-1901". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain's longest reign until Elizabeth II covered the country's transformation into the world's first industrial superpower: railways, steamships, telegraphs, factory towns and a population that doubled. Abroad it meant the Raj, the scramble for Africa and an empire spanning a quarter of the globe; at home, reform acts that widened the vote, public health and schooling laws, and fierce arguments about poverty, faith and evolution. The monarchy itself was reinvented as a symbol of domestic respectability and imperial unity.

Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045 (Armenia, AD.label: Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045
Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045 (Armenia, AD.prose:
[Armenia, AD 885–AD 1045] Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.5 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ashot I secured recognition as king from both the caliph and Byzantium, restoring an Armenian monarchy after centuries of foreign governors. The Bagratid century brought a building boom — above all at the capital Ani, the "city of a thousand and one churches" — along with flourishing trade, manuscript painting and the historians who recorded it. Family partitions weakened the kingdom, and Byzantine annexation left Armenia without defenders when the Seljuks arrived a generation later.

Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654 (Netherlands,.label: Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654
Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654 (Netherlands,.prose:
[Netherlands, Great Britain, AD 1652–AD 1654] Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654. Spatial coverage: England, Netherlands. Extracted from heading "Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A war fought almost entirely at sea, sparked by English navigation laws aimed at Dutch carrying trade and by disputes over salutes in the Channel. Fleets of the Commonwealth under Blake met Tromp's convoys in a series of huge line-of-battle engagements that helped invent modern naval tactics. The English blockade throttled Dutch commerce and forced peace terms, but the underlying commercial rivalry was untouched.

French intervention, 1860-1861 (Lebanon,.label: French intervention, 1860-1861
French intervention, 1860-1861 (Lebanon,.prose:
[Lebanon, AD 1860–AD 1861] French intervention, 1860-1861. Extracted from heading "Lebanon--History--French intervention, 1860-1861". Added to LCSH in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After massacres of Maronite Christians by Druze in Mount Lebanon and the killing of thousands in Damascus, France landed an expeditionary force at Beirut with the consent of the other European powers and the Ottoman government. The intervention produced the Règlement Organique, which made Mount Lebanon an autonomous district under a Christian governor answerable to Istanbul. That settlement gave the region decades of relative peace and entrenched the practice of allotting office by religious community.

Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884 (China, AD.label: Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884
Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 874–AD 884] Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884. Extracted from heading "China--History--Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Huang Ch'ao Rebellion, 874-884." appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A failed examination candidate turned salt smuggler led a rebel army the length and breadth of China, sacking Guangzhou - where tens of thousands of Arab, Persian and Jewish merchants were reportedly massacred, wrecking the southern sea trade - and then taking Chang'an itself. The Tang emperor fled to Sichuan and only recovered his capital with the help of Turkic cavalry. The dynasty survived on paper for another twenty years, but real power had passed permanently to regional warlords.

Vladimir, 972-1015 (Russia, AD 972–AD 10.label: Vladimir, 972-1015
Vladimir, 972-1015 (Russia, AD 972–AD 10.prose:
[Kievan Rus, AD 972–AD 1015] Vladimir, 972-1015. Spatial coverage: Belarus, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Ukraine. Extracted from heading "Kievan Rus--History--Vladimir, 972-1015". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975 (source uses term "Russia"). Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Vladimir seized Kiev with Varangian help, ruled a sprawling realm of Slavic and Finnic tribute-payers, and then made the decision that redirected the region's history: he accepted Byzantine Christianity, married the emperor's sister, and had the people of Kiev baptised in the Dnieper. Pagan idols were thrown down, Greek clergy and Church Slavonic books arrived, and stone churches such as the Tithe Church rose in the capital. The choice tied the Rus to Constantinople rather than Rome, shaping the alphabet, art and religion of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864 (Vietnam.label: Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864
Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864 (Vietnam.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1862–AD 1864] Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864". Added to LCSH in 1993, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Nguyễn court ceded three southern provinces to France, the officer Trương Định refused the order to disband and kept fighting from the marshes of Gò Công, acclaimed by villagers as "Great General Pacifier of the West". His guerrilla bands harried French posts until he was betrayed and killed. The revolt showed that resistance to colonial rule in Cochinchina would come from local militias rather than the throne.

Louis XI, 1461-1483 (France, AD 1461–AD.label: Louis XI, 1461-1483
Louis XI, 1461-1483 (France, AD 1461–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1461–AD 1483] Louis XI, 1461-1483. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XI, 1461-1483". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The 'Universal Spider', who preferred bribery, spies and patient diplomacy to battle, and wove alliances that undid his enemies. His long duel with Charles the Bold ended when the Burgundian duke died at Nancy, allowing Louis to seize the duchy; Anjou, Maine and Provence also fell in to the crown. He encouraged trade and fairs, organised a royal courier service, and left France far more unified and centrally governed than he found it.

Boleslaus II, 1058-1079 (Poland, AD 1058.label: Boleslaus II, 1058-1079
Boleslaus II, 1058-1079 (Poland, AD 1058.prose:
[Poland , AD 1058–AD 1079] Boleslaus II, 1058-1079. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Boleslaus II, 1058-1079". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bolesław the Bold revived royal power after decades of collapse, intervening in Hungary and Rus and having himself crowned king in 1076 with papal backing during the Emperor's quarrel with Rome. Three years later he had Bishop Stanislaus of Kraków killed, a scandal that cost him the throne and sent him into exile. The murdered bishop became Poland's national saint, and the crown was lost again for another generation.

Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43 (Vietnam.label: Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43
Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43 (Vietnam.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 39–AD 43] Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two aristocratic sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, raised the Lac lords against Han Chinese officials and briefly ruled some sixty-five citadels across the Red River delta. General Ma Yuan crushed them and dismantled the old Vietnamese aristocracy, tightening direct Chinese rule for centuries. The sisters became the enduring emblem of Vietnamese independence and are still honoured with temples and a national holiday.

Gothic period, 414-711 (Spain, AD 414–AD.label: Gothic period, 414-711
Gothic period, 414-711 (Spain, AD 414–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 414–AD 711] Gothic period, 414-711. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Gothic period, 414-711". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Visigoths settled in Hispania after their wanderings through Gaul and built a kingdom centred on Toledo, ruling a Hispano-Roman majority under their own kings. Their conversion from Arian to Catholic Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 fused crown and church, and the resulting law code, the Liber Iudiciorum, shaped later Iberian law. Internal succession disputes left the kingdom brittle, and it collapsed within a few years of the Muslim landing of 711.

Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Denmark, AD 16.label: Frederick III, 1648-1670
Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Denmark, AD 16.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1648–AD 1670] Frederick III, 1648-1670. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick III, 1648-1670". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign began with a disastrous war against Sweden that cost Denmark Scania and the provinces east of the Sound, permanently fixing the modern Scandinavian border. But when Copenhagen's citizens helped hold the city under siege, he used the crisis to break the nobility: in 1660-61 the elective monarchy was abolished and the King's Law of 1665 made him one of the most absolute rulers in Europe, on paper at least. He was also a passionate collector, founding the royal library and Kunstkammer.

Fyodor III, 1676-1682 (Russia, AD 1676–A.label: Fyodor III, 1676-1682
Fyodor III, 1676-1682 (Russia, AD 1676–A.prose:
[Russia , AD 1676–AD 1682] Fyodor III, 1676-1682. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Fyodor III, 1676-1682". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Theodore, 1678-1682" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign under a young and often ill tsar that nonetheless pushed through real reform, above all the abolition of mestnichestvo, the system that assigned offices by aristocratic pedigree rather than ability. Taxation was simplified, the war with the Ottomans over Ukraine was brought to a truce, and Western learning gained ground at court. His death without an heir triggered the succession crisis and streltsy revolt that brought his half-brother Peter the Great to the throne.

Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254.label: Interregnum, 1254-1273
Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1254–AD 1273] Interregnum, 1254-1273. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Interregnum, 1254-1273". Added to LCSH in 1986. Note that many of the periods for the Holy Roman Empire are reduplicated under the "Germany--History" heading, but are given different URIs. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the last Hohenstaufen emperors fell, no king could make his authority felt in Germany; rival foreign candidates, Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile, were elected and largely ignored. Princes, bishops and cities filled the vacuum, fortifying, coining and warring on their own account, and leagues formed to keep the roads safe. The election of Rudolf of Habsburg ended the drift, but the crown never recovered the ground lost to the territorial princes.

Turkish Wars, 1453-1571 (Veneto, AD 1453.label: Turkish Wars, 1453-1571
Turkish Wars, 1453-1571 (Veneto, AD 1453.prose:
[Venice, AD 1453–AD 1571] Turkish Wars, 1453-1571. Extracted from heading "Venice (Italy)--History--Turkish Wars, 1453-1571". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The fall of Constantinople set Venice against an expanding Ottoman Empire in a series of long, costly wars for its maritime empire. Negroponte fell in 1470, the Morean strongholds and finally Cyprus followed, and even the great victory at Lepanto in 1571 brought no territory back. Venice increasingly turned to its mainland Italian possessions as the eastern trade routes slipped away.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Ukraine, AD 1905–.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Ukraine, AD 1905–.prose:
[Ukraine, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Ukraine--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 118 of LCSH 1986 and p.100 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Philadelphia, AD.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Philadelphia, AD.prose:
[Philadelphia (Pa.), AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Philadelphia (Pa.)--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.91 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789 (Turkey, AD 177.label: Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789
Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789 (Turkey, AD 177.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1774–AD 1789] Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign opened with the humiliating treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, which handed Russia a foothold on the Black Sea and a claim to speak for Ottoman Orthodox subjects. Efforts to modernise the army and navy with French advisers began in earnest, but a new war with Russia and Austria was already going badly when he died.

Muromachi period, 1336-1573 (Japan, AD 1.label: Muromachi period, 1336-1573
Muromachi period, 1336-1573 (Japan, AD 1.prose:
[Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573] Muromachi period, 1336-1573. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Muromachi period, 1336-1573". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1990. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ashikaga Takauji's shogunate presided over a country where real power drained steadily to provincial military governors and, later, to self-made warlords. It was nevertheless the age of Noh drama, linked verse, the tea ceremony and the Golden and Silver Pavilions, funded partly by licensed trade with Ming China. Portuguese ships arrived in 1543 with firearms, and Jesuit missionaries followed, opening Japan's first sustained contact with Europe just as the old order was breaking apart.

Insurrection, 1868-1878 (Cuba, AD 1868–A.label: Insurrection, 1868-1878
Insurrection, 1868-1878 (Cuba, AD 1868–A.prose:
[Cuba, AD 1868–AD 1878] Insurrection, 1868-1878. Extracted from heading "Cuba--History--Insurrection, 1868-1878". Added to LCHS in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ten Years' War began with Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freeing his slaves and calling for independence, and turned into a grinding guerrilla campaign that devastated the eastern countryside and killed perhaps 200,000 people. It ended in a negotiated peace rather than victory, but it forged a generation of fighters, hastened the abolition of slavery, and left the unfinished business that produced the 1895 war of independence.

Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C. (China, 220 BC.label: Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C.
Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C. (China, 220 BC.prose:
[China, 220 BC–206 BC] Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C.. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C.". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate lable "Ch'in dynasty, 221-207 B.C." appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fifteen years that reorganised China: the warring states abolished, walls between them torn down and frontier walls joined, a single script and currency imposed, and the empire divided into commanderies staffed by officials answerable to the throne. The First Emperor's tomb complex near Xi'an, with its thousands of individually modelled terracotta soldiers, gives a startling picture of the regime's scale and ambition. Rebellion broke out within a year of his death and the Han took over the machinery he had built.

Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945 (Burma, A.label: Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945
Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945 (Burma, A.prose:
[Burma, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.12 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Japanese forces drove the British out within months, aided by the Burma Independence Army under Aung San, and installed a nominally independent state under Ba Maw in 1943. Reality meant harsh military rule, forced labour on the Thailand–Burma railway, and severe shortages. Aung San's forces switched sides in 1945, and the wartime rupture of British authority made a return to colonial rule impossible.

Federal Revolution, 1898-1899 (Bolivia,.label: Federal Revolution, 1898-1899
Federal Revolution, 1898-1899 (Bolivia,.prose:
[Bolivia, AD 1898–AD 1899] Federal Revolution, 1898-1899. Extracted from heading "Bolivia--History--Federal Revolution, 1898-1899". Added to LCSH and revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short civil war between the Conservative establishment in Sucre and Liberals based in La Paz, fought partly with the support of Aymara peasant forces under Pablo Zárate Willka. The Liberals won, La Paz became the seat of government and congress, and the indigenous allies were then turned on and their leaders executed.

Charles IV, 1788-1808 (Spain, AD 1788–AD.label: Charles IV, 1788-1808
Charles IV, 1788-1808 (Spain, AD 1788–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 1788–AD 1808] Charles IV, 1788-1808. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Charles IV, 1788-1808". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who preferred hunting to governing left affairs to his wife's favourite, Manuel Godoy, just as the French Revolution broke out next door. Spain's alliance with Napoleonic France ended in the destruction of its fleet at Trafalgar and then in French armies occupying the country. Forced to abdicate at Bayonne in favour of Napoleon's brother, he went into exile as Spain rose in the Peninsular War. Goya, his court painter, left the era's unsparing record.

James I, 1603-1625 (England, AD 1603–AD.label: James I, 1603-1625
James I, 1603-1625 (England, AD 1603–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1603–AD 1625] James I, 1603-1625. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--James I, 1603-1625". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Scottish king who inherited England from the childless Elizabeth, uniting the two crowns in one person though not the two states. He survived the Gunpowder Plot, quarrelled repeatedly with Parliament over money and royal prerogative, and commissioned the Bible translation that carries his name. He preferred peace abroad and favourites at home, and both choices stored up trouble for his son.

English Conquest, 1166-1186 (Ireland, AD.label: English Conquest, 1166-1186
English Conquest, 1166-1186 (Ireland, AD.prose:
[Ireland, AD 1166–AD 1186] English Conquest, 1166-1186. Extracted from heading "Ireland--History--English Conquest, 1166-1186". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.61 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The exiled king of Leinster, Diarmait Mac Murchada, recruited Cambro-Norman lords to help him regain his kingdom, and they came with mailed cavalry and archers. Richard de Clare ('Strongbow') took Waterford and Dublin, and Henry II crossed over in 1171 to assert lordship over both the newcomers and the Irish kings. It began eight centuries of English involvement in Ireland, and left a lasting patchwork of fortified manors, boroughs and Gaelic territories.

Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898 (India, AD 189.label: Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898
Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898 (India, AD 189.prose:
[India, AD 1897–AD 1898] Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898. Extracted from heading "India--History--Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2015. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A British Indian expedition of some 40,000 troops sent into the Afridi and Orakzai highlands after the great Pathan uprising had overrun the Khyber forts. The storming of the Dargai Heights, where the Gordon Highlanders took heavy losses, became one of the most celebrated actions of the frontier wars. The tribes were never decisively beaten, and the campaign helped convince the British to govern the north-west frontier through subsidies and militias rather than occupation.

Interregnum, 1410-1412 (Aragon, AD 1410–.label: Interregnum, 1410-1412
Interregnum, 1410-1412 (Aragon, AD 1410–.prose:
[Aragon, AD 1410–AD 1412] Interregnum, 1410-1412. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--Interregnum, 1410-1412". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975; revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Martin I died without a legitimate heir, leaving six claimants and the real possibility of civil war across Aragon, Valencia and Catalonia. Rather than fight it out, delegates from the three realms met at Caspe and chose Ferdinand of Antequera by arbitration — a rare instance of a medieval succession settled by committee. It brought the Castilian Trastámara dynasty to Aragon and set the two crowns on the path that led to their union under Ferdinand and Isabella.

Regency, 1715-1723 (France, AD 1715–AD 1.label: Regency, 1715-1723
Regency, 1715-1723 (France, AD 1715–AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1715–AD 1723] Regency, 1715-1723. Extracted from heading "France--History--Regency, 1715-1723". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Philippe d'Orléans governed for the child Louis XV and deliberately unwound the late king's system, moving the court back to Paris, easing censorship and briefly handing government to councils of nobles. His backing of John Law's bank and Mississippi Company produced Europe's first modern stock bubble and its spectacular collapse, which left France suspicious of paper money for generations. Socially, it is remembered as a loosening — libertine, sceptical and fond of small elegant rooms — that opened the way to the Enlightenment.

Charles I, 1866-1914 (Romania, AD 1866–A.label: Charles I, 1866-1914
Charles I, 1866-1914 (Romania, AD 1866–A.prose:
[Romania, AD 1866–AD 1914] Charles I, 1866-1914. Extracted from heading "Romania--History--Charles I, 1866-1914". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.98 of LCSH 1987, and p.83 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Prussian Hohenzollern prince was imported to rule the young union of Moldavia and Wallachia, and stayed for nearly half a century. He led Romanian troops alongside Russia against the Ottomans, winning full independence in 1878 and a royal crown in 1881, then presided over railways, banks, a new constitution and the fairy-tale castle at Peleș. His secret alliance with Austria-Hungary and Germany became untenable in 1914, and he died weeks after the war began.

Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600 (.node: Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600 (Roman Empire, AD 30–AD 600)
Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600 (.label: Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600
Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600 (.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, Rome, AD 30–AD 600] Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600. Spatial coverage: Byzantine Empire, Roman Empire. Extracted from heading "Church history--Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2010. Spatial coverage description given as "Church". Spatial coverage inferred from state of Church in this time period. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A small Jewish messianic movement grew into the official religion of the Roman Empire. Persecution, martyrdom and fierce internal argument over the nature of Christ gave way after Constantine to imperial patronage, great basilicas, monasteries and the ecumenical councils that fixed doctrine. The bishops of Rome, Constantinople, Antioch and Alexandria built the institutional church that would outlast the empire in the West.

Louis XV, 1715-1774 (France, AD 1715–AD.label: Louis XV, 1715-1774
Louis XV, 1715-1774 (France, AD 1715–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1715–AD 1774] Louis XV, 1715-1774. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XV, 1715-1774". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inherited the throne as a five-year-old and reigned for nearly six decades, in which France fought the Wars of the Polish and Austrian Successions and then lost Canada and its Indian holdings in the Seven Years' War. Wealth and population grew and the Enlightenment flourished in Paris salons, but the monarchy quarrelled endlessly with the parlements over taxes and lost much of its prestige. He acquired Lorraine and Corsica, and left his grandson a kingdom with unreformed finances and a critical, increasingly hostile reading public.

German occupation, 1915-1918 (Lithuania,.label: German occupation, 1915-1918
German occupation, 1915-1918 (Lithuania,.prose:
[Lithuania, AD 1915–AD 1918] German occupation, 1915-1918. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--German occupation, 1915-1918". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.72 of LCSH 1987, and p.58 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

German armies drove the Russians out and placed the country under the military administration of Ober Ost, which requisitioned timber, food and labour and controlled movement with permits. Berlin encouraged a Lithuanian council, the Taryba, hoping for a client state, but it declared full independence in February 1918 and made the claim stick once Germany collapsed.

Fernando I, 1412-1416 (Kingdom of Aragon.label: Fernando I, 1412-1416
Fernando I, 1412-1416 (Kingdom of Aragon.prose:
[Aragon, AD 1412–AD 1416] Fernando I, 1412-1416. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--Fernando I, 1412-1416". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975; revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Castilian prince chosen as king of Aragon by the Compromise of Caspe, an arbitration by nine electors that settled a disputed succession without civil war and installed the Trastámara dynasty in Aragon. His short reign tied the two crowns' ruling houses together, a link that led to the union under his grandson Ferdinand the Catholic. He also helped end the Great Schism by withdrawing support from the Aragonese antipope Benedict XIII.

Jin dynasty, 1115-1234 (China, AD 1115–A.label: Jin dynasty, 1115-1234
Jin dynasty, 1115-1234 (China, AD 1115–A.prose:
[China, AD 1115–AD 1234] Jin dynasty, 1115-1234. Extracted from heading "China--History--Jin dynasty, 1115-1234". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Chin dynasty, 1115-1234" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by the Jurchen of Manchuria, who overthrew the Khitan Liao and then drove the Song out of northern China, capturing Kaifeng and two emperors in 1127. Ruling from Beijing over a mostly Chinese population, the Jin blended steppe military organisation with Chinese bureaucracy, taxation and examinations. Their destruction by the Mongols after decades of war opened the way for Khubilai Khan's conquest of the rest of China.

George I, 1714-1727 (United Kingdom, AD.label: George I, 1714-1727
George I, 1714-1727 (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1714–AD 1727] George I, 1714-1727. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George I, 1714-1727". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A German prince from Hanover took the British throne because he was the nearest Protestant heir, passing over dozens of Catholic Stuarts and provoking the Jacobite rising of 1715. Uninterested in day-to-day government and often absent in Hanover, he left business to ministers, and Robert Walpole's rise in the wake of the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720 pushed Britain toward rule by a prime minister and cabinet.

Vitellius, 69 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 69.label: Vitellius, 69
Vitellius, 69 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 69.prose:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 69] Vitellius, 69. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Vitellius, 69". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed emperor by the Rhine legions, Vitellius won the throne by beating Otho at Bedriacum and lost it within months to the armies backing Vespasian. His brief reign, remembered by hostile sources mainly for gluttony, ended with street fighting in Rome, the burning of the Capitol and his own lynching. He was the third of the four emperors of 69, the year that proved an emperor could be made outside Rome by whichever army moved fastest.

Henry IV, 1589-1610 (France, AD 1589–AD.label: Henry IV, 1589-1610
Henry IV, 1589-1610 (France, AD 1589–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1589–AD 1610] Henry IV, 1589-1610. Extracted from heading "France--History--Henry IV, 1589-1610". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Protestant king of Navarre inherited the French crown but had to conquer his kingdom, finally entering Paris only after converting to Catholicism. His Edict of Nantes gave Huguenots legal toleration and fortified towns, ending nearly forty years of religious war, and with Sully he restored royal finances, roads and canals. Stabbed by a Catholic fanatic in a Paris street, he became the founding figure of the Bourbon dynasty and, in popular memory, the good king who wanted a chicken in every pot.

Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C (Greece, 734.label: Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C
Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C (Greece, 734.prose:
[Greece, 734 BC–459 BC] Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sparta's long conquest of fertile Messenia across the Taygetus mountains turned an entire neighbouring people into helots, state-owned serfs who farmed Spartan land. The wealth freed Spartan citizens to train as full-time soldiers, but the constant threat of helot revolt shaped Spartan society into the militarised, inward-looking state it became. The great revolt after the earthquake of 464 BC dragged in Athens and helped poison relations between the two cities on the road to the Peloponnesian War.

Ramiro I, 1035-1063 (Spain, AD 1035–AD 1.label: Ramiro I, 1035-1063
Ramiro I, 1035-1063 (Spain, AD 1035–AD 1.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1035–AD 1063] Ramiro I, 1035-1063. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Ramiro I, 1035-1063". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The illegitimate son of Sancho the Great of Navarre inherited a small mountain county and turned it into the Kingdom of Aragon, expanding at the expense of his brothers and pressing south against the Muslim taifa of Zaragoza. He was killed besieging Graus, but the kingdom he founded became one of the great powers of medieval Iberia and the Mediterranean.

French occupation, 1918-1946 (Lebanon, A.label: French occupation, 1918-1946
French occupation, 1918-1946 (Lebanon, A.prose:
[Lebanon, AD 1918–AD 1946] French occupation, 1918-1946. Extracted from heading "Lebanon--History--French occupation, 1918-1946". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.72 of LCSH 1987, and pg.58 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied victory over the Ottomans brought French troops to the coast and, under a League of Nations mandate, the creation of Greater Lebanon - the old autonomous mountain enlarged with Beirut, Tripoli, the Bekaa and the south, and with it a far more mixed population. A 1926 constitution introduced a republic whose offices were shared out by sect, the framework Lebanese politics still runs on. Independence was declared during the Second World War and confirmed when French troops finally withdrew.

Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221 (Anatolia, AD 1.label: Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221
Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221 (Anatolia, AD 1.prose:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1218–AD 1221] Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Fifth, 1218-1221". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rather than march on Jerusalem, the crusaders attacked Egypt, the heart of Ayyubid power, and besieged the Nile port of Damietta for eighteen months before taking it. The sultan al-Kamil twice offered to trade Jerusalem for their withdrawal; the papal legate Pelagius refused, and Francis of Assisi crossed the lines to preach to the sultan in person. The army then advanced upriver, was trapped by the Nile flood, and had to surrender everything it had won.

Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254.label: Interregnum, 1254-1273
Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254.prose:
[Germany , AD 1254–AD 1273] Interregnum, 1254-1273. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Interregnum, 1254-1273". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the last Hohenstaufen emperors fell, no king could make his authority felt in Germany; rival foreign candidates, Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile, were elected and largely ignored. Princes, bishops and cities filled the vacuum, fortifying, coining and warring on their own account, and leagues formed to keep the roads safe. The election of Rudolf of Habsburg ended the drift, but the crown never recovered the ground lost to the territorial princes.

Jangalī movement, 1914-1921 (Iran, AD 19.label: Jangalī movement, 1914-1921
Jangalī movement, 1914-1921 (Iran, AD 19.prose:
[Iran, AD 1914–AD 1921] Jangalī movement, 1914-1921. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Jangalī movement, 1914-1921". Added to LCSH in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A guerrilla movement based in the forests of Gilan, led by Mirza Kuchak Khan, which fought Russian and British intervention and the weakness of the Tehran government, calling for constitutional rule and an end to foreign control. With Bolshevik backing it proclaimed a short-lived Soviet republic in Gilan in 1920, then fractured over communist land policy. Reza Khan's army crushed it, and Kuchak Khan froze to death fleeing into the mountains.

Frederick I, 1523-1533 (Denmark, AD 1523.label: Frederick I, 1523-1533
Frederick I, 1523-1533 (Denmark, AD 1523.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1523–AD 1533] Frederick I, 1523-1533. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick I, 1523-1533". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He took the throne after the nobles deposed his nephew Christian II, promising to defend the Catholic Church and then quietly doing the opposite. At the Diet of Odense in 1527 he granted Lutheran preachers protection and let the reform movement spread through the towns. His death without a settled succession triggered the civil war known as the Count's Feud, out of which the Danish Reformation was imposed outright in 1536.

Tokugawa period, 1600-1868 (Japan, AD 16.label: Tokugawa period, 1600-1868
Tokugawa period, 1600-1868 (Japan, AD 16.prose:
[Japan, AD 1600–AD 1868] Tokugawa period, 1600-1868. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Tokugawa period, 1600-1868". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Sekigahara the Tokugawa shoguns imposed two and a half centuries of peace, holding the daimyo in check through hostage residence in Edo and closing the country to most foreign contact. Cities grew enormous, a merchant class prospered, and with it came kabuki, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, haiku and a highly literate urban public. Commodore Perry's warships exposed the regime's weakness, and its fall in 1868 launched Japan's headlong modernisation.

Arab rebellion, 1936-1939 (State of Pale.label: Arab rebellion, 1936-1939
Arab rebellion, 1936-1939 (State of Pale.prose:
[Palestine, AD 1936–AD 1939] Arab rebellion, 1936-1939. Extracted from heading "Palestine--History--Arab rebellion, 1936-1939". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A general strike against British rule and Jewish immigration escalated into three years of armed insurgency across the countryside, with rural bands attacking police posts, railways and the Haifa oil pipeline. Britain answered with mass detentions, house demolitions and thousands of troops, and by 1939 the Arab leadership was exiled or dead and the villages disarmed. The revolt won the 1939 White Paper limiting Jewish immigration, but it also shattered Palestinian Arab political organisation on the eve of the decisive decade.

Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Emden, AD 1943–A.label: Bombardment, 1943-1945
Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Emden, AD 1943–A.prose:
[Emden (Lower Saxony, Germany), AD 1943–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1943-1945. Extracted from heading "Emden (Lower Saxony, Germany)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1945". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A North Sea port and shipyard town on the Ems, it was attacked for its harbour and submarine construction and lost the overwhelming majority of its old buildings, with the centre effectively erased in a single raid in September 1944. Postwar reconstruction produced an almost entirely modern town on a medieval street plan.

Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Germany, AD 1576–A.label: Rudolf II, 1576-1612
Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Germany, AD 1576–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1576–AD 1612] Rudolf II, 1576-1612. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Rudolf II, 1576-1612". Added to LCSH in 1986. Identical entries exist under both "Germany--History" and "Austria--History", but with separate URIs. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Habsburg emperor moved his court to Prague and turned it into a magnet for astronomers, alchemists, painters and collectors – Tycho Brahe and Kepler worked under his patronage, and his cabinet of curiosities was the most famous in Europe. Politically he was indecisive and increasingly withdrawn, letting confessional tensions in the empire fester until his own family forced him to cede power. The Letter of Majesty he granted Bohemian Protestants in 1609, and its later breach, helped set up the revolt that began the Thirty Years' War.

Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C (Greece, 403.label: Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C
Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C (Greece, 403.prose:
[Athens, 403 BC–402 BC] Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C. Extracted from heading "Athens (Greece)--History--Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Athens surrendered to Sparta, a pro-Spartan oligarchy of thirty men took control and ruled by execution, exile and confiscation, killing perhaps 1,500 citizens in a matter of months. Democratic exiles under Thrasybulus seized the Piraeus and overthrew them within a year. The restored democracy issued an amnesty, but the memory of the terror shaped Athenian politics and coloured the trial of Socrates, who had ties to several of the ringleaders.

Ferdinand II, 1619-1637 (Austria, AD 161.label: Ferdinand II, 1619-1637
Ferdinand II, 1619-1637 (Austria, AD 161.prose:
[Austria, AD 1619–AD 1637] Ferdinand II, 1619-1637. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Ferdinand II, 1619-1637". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Jesuit-educated hardliner whose determination to restore Catholicism to the Habsburg lands turned the Bohemian revolt into a European war. Victory at White Mountain let him execute or dispossess the Czech nobility and rebuild Bohemia as a Catholic, German-speaking crown land; his Edict of Restitution of 1629 then demanded the return of church property across the Empire and drove Protestant princes and Sweden into arms against him. He raised, and eventually murdered, the mercenary commander Wallenstein, whose private armies showed how war had become a business.

Qing dynasty, 1644-1912 (China, AD 1644–.label: Qing dynasty, 1644-1912
Qing dynasty, 1644-1912 (China, AD 1644–.prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1912] Qing dynasty, 1644-1912. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qing dynasty, 1644-1912". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Ch'ing dynasty, 1644-1912" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and p.16 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Manchu invaders from beyond the Great Wall seized Beijing and went on to rule the largest Chinese empire ever assembled, pushing control deep into Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet. A long boom under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors tripled the population and filled palaces with porcelain, painting and encyclopedic scholarship, while ordinary men were made to shave their foreheads and wear the queue as a sign of submission. The nineteenth century brought opium, foreign gunboats, the catastrophic Taiping Rebellion and forced treaty ports, and the dynasty's collapse ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule.

Russian Conquest, 1831-1859 (Caucasus, A.label: Russian Conquest, 1831-1859
Russian Conquest, 1831-1859 (Caucasus, A.prose:
[Caucasus, Northern (Russia), AD 1831–AD 1859] Russian Conquest, 1831-1859. Extracted from heading "Caucasus, Northern (Russia)--History--Russian Conquest, 1831-1859". Added to LCSH in 2016, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Russia's push into the mountains of Dagestan and Chechnya met a religious and military resistance movement led by Imam Shamil, who welded the highland communities into an Islamic state. Decades of fortress-building, forest-clearing and scorched-earth campaigning ended with Shamil's surrender at Gunib, followed by mass deportations and emigration of Muslim highlanders to the Ottoman Empire – a displacement still remembered across the Caucasus and Turkey.

Xuantong, 1908-1912 (China, AD 1908–AD 1.label: Xuantong, 1908-1912
Xuantong, 1908-1912 (China, AD 1908–AD 1.prose:
[China, AD 1908–AD 1912] Xuantong, 1908-1912. Extracted from heading "China--History--Xuantong, 1908-1912". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Hsuan t'ung, 1908-1912" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The nominal reign of the infant Puyi, last of the Qing, ending with the abdication of February 1912 and the founding of the Republic. Reform came too late to save the dynasty: railway nationalisation protests and the army mutiny at Wuchang triggered province after province to declare independence. Puyi kept his title and the Forbidden City for another twelve years as a private citizen-emperor.

Partition period, 1763-1796 (Poland, AD.label: Partition period, 1763-1796
Partition period, 1763-1796 (Poland, AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1763–AD 1796] Partition period, 1763-1796. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Partition period, 1763-1796". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under Stanisław August Poniatowski, a cultured king installed with Russian backing, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth attempted reform and was dismembered for it. Russia, Prussia and Austria took slices in 1772 and 1793; the Constitution of 3 May 1791, Europe's first modern written constitution after America's, provoked invasion; Kościuszko's rising of 1794 was crushed. The third partition of 1795 removed the state from the map entirely, and Polish national identity survived for over a century without any Polish state.

Hannibal's War, 1644-1645 (Norway, AD 16.label: Hannibal's War, 1644-1645
Hannibal's War, 1644-1645 (Norway, AD 16.prose:
[Norway, AD 1644–AD 1645] Hannibal's War, 1644-1645. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Hannibal's War, 1644-1645". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Named after Hannibal Sehested, the Danish king's governor in Norway, this was the Norwegian front of the wider war between Denmark-Norway and Sweden. Norwegian troops raided across the border into Jämtland and Värmland with some success, but the peace settled at Brömsebro handed Jämtland and Härjedalen to Sweden for good. The campaign is remembered for Sehested's attempt to build a self-financing Norwegian army and administration.

Ivan IV, 1533-1584 (Russia, AD 1533–AD 1.label: Ivan IV, 1533-1584
Ivan IV, 1533-1584 (Russia, AD 1533–AD 1.prose:
[Russia , AD 1533–AD 1584] Ivan IV, 1533-1584. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Ivan IV, 1533-1584". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned as Russia's first tsar, Ivan the Terrible conquered the khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan, opening the Volga and the road to Siberia, and issued a new law code while summoning the first assembly of the land. His later years turned savage: the oprichnina, a private terror corps, tore through the nobility and sacked Novgorod, and a long, failed war for the Baltic drained the country. He struck his own heir dead in a rage, leaving a weak successor and the collapse into the Time of Troubles.

Claudius, 41-54 (Roman Empire, AD 41–AD.label: Claudius, 41-54
Claudius, 41-54 (Roman Empire, AD 41–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 41–AD 54] Claudius, 41-54. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Claudius, 41-54". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed emperor by the Praetorian Guard after Caligula's murder, Claudius was dismissed as a stammering scholar but proved an energetic administrator. He invaded Britain in AD 43, annexed Thrace and Mauretania, built the harbour at Portus and a great aqueduct system for Rome, and gave freedmen real power in a growing imperial bureaucracy. His death, widely rumoured to be poisoning by Agrippina, brought Nero to the throne.

Frederick I, 1720-1751 (Sweden, AD 1720–.label: Frederick I, 1720-1751
Frederick I, 1720-1751 (Sweden, AD 1720–.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1720–AD 1751] Frederick I, 1720-1751. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Frederick I, 1720-1751". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Hessian prince who gained the Swedish throne through marriage and promptly surrendered most royal power to the Riksdag, opening the parliamentary "Age of Liberty" in which the Hat and Cap factions governed. His reign saw a disastrous war with Russia that cost more Finnish territory, while the king himself was better known for hunting and mistresses than for ruling. Real authority lay with the Council and the estates, a constitutional experiment unusual in eighteenth-century Europe.

Angeli, 1185-1204 (Byzantine Empire, AD.label: Angeli, 1185-1204
Angeli, 1185-1204 (Byzantine Empire, AD.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1204] Angeli, 1185-1204. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Angeli, 1185-1204". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three emperors of the Angelos family presided over the unravelling of the Byzantine state: revenues collapsed, provincial governors went their own way, and a Bulgarian revolt permanently detached the Balkans north of the Balkan range. Dynastic infighting — a brother blinding a brother, then a fugitive prince offering money for restoration — drew the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople. In 1204 the crusaders stormed and sacked the city, ending eight centuries of unbroken imperial rule there.

American Occupation, 1915-1934 (Haiti, A.label: American Occupation, 1915-1934
American Occupation, 1915-1934 (Haiti, A.prose:
[Haiti, AD 1915–AD 1934] American Occupation, 1915-1934. Extracted from heading "Haiti--History--American Occupation, 1915-1934". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.54 of LCSH 1987, and p. 43 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

US Marines landed after the lynching of President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam and stayed for nineteen years, taking control of customs revenue, rewriting the constitution to permit foreign land ownership, and building roads and hospitals with forced corvée labour. Peasant resistance under Charlemagne Péralte was crushed, and thousands died. The occupation left behind a centralised, US-trained Garde d'Haïti that dominated national politics for decades afterwards, and a bitter nationalist memory that shaped Haitian intellectual life.

Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Indonesi.label: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945
Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Indonesi.prose:
[Indonesia, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Japanese occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.48 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch colonial regime collapsed in weeks, and Japan governed the archipelago as three separate military zones, extracting oil, rice and hundreds of thousands of romusha forced labourers. To mobilise support it released and promoted nationalists such as Sukarno and Hatta and trained Indonesian militias like PETA. When Japan surrendered, those leaders and those armed units declared independence, and the Dutch never regained control.

Indian occupation, 1969-1971 (California.label: Indian occupation, 1969-1971
Indian occupation, 1969-1971 (California.prose:
[California, AD 1969–AD 1971] Indian occupation, 1969-1971. Extracted from heading "Alcatraz Island (Calif.)--History--Indian occupation, 1969-1971". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Activists of the group Indians of All Tribes landed on the abandoned Alcatraz prison island and held it for nineteen months, claiming it under a treaty provision on surplus federal land and demanding a cultural centre and university. The occupation drew national press, made Red Power visible to a mass audience, and helped push Washington away from the termination policy toward tribal self-determination. Painted slogans from the occupiers survive on the buildings and are now preserved as historic fabric.

Casimir IV, 1447-1492 (Poland, AD 1447–A.label: Casimir IV, 1447-1492
Casimir IV, 1447-1492 (Poland, AD 1447–A.prose:
[Poland , AD 1447–AD 1492] Casimir IV, 1447-1492. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Casimir IV, 1447-1492". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Casimir Jagiellon spent thirteen years fighting the Teutonic Knights, and the Second Peace of Toruń in 1466 handed Poland Gdańsk, Malbork and access to the Baltic while making the Order's remaining state a Polish fief. To pay for the war he conceded the Nieszawa statutes, entrenching the nobility's right to be consulted, a step towards the szlachta democracy of later centuries. His sons wore the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary as well, making the Jagiellonians the dominant dynasty of central Europe.

Federal Wars, 1858-1863 (Venezuela, AD 1.label: Federal Wars, 1858-1863
Federal Wars, 1858-1863 (Venezuela, AD 1.prose:
[Venezuela, AD 1858–AD 1863] Federal Wars, 1858-1863. Extracted from heading "Venezuela--History--Federal Wars, 1858-1863". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.106 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The bloodiest conflict in Venezuela's republican history, pitting Federalists demanding regional autonomy and land reform against the Caracas Conservative order. Guerrilla campaigns across the plains killed perhaps a tenth of the population; the Treaty of Coche ended the fighting and produced a federal constitution that changed less on the ground than its slogans promised.

Soviet occupation, 1979-1989 (Afghanista.label: Soviet occupation, 1979-1989
Soviet occupation, 1979-1989 (Afghanista.prose:
[Afghanistan, AD 1979–AD 1989] Soviet occupation, 1979-1989. Extracted from heading "Afghanistan--History--Soviet occupation, 1979-1989". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Soviet troops entered to prop up a faltering communist government and found themselves fighting a decade-long guerrilla war against mujahideen fighters armed and financed by the United States, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Roughly a million Afghans died and five million fled abroad, while Soviet casualties and costs corroded confidence in Moscow. The withdrawal left behind a shattered country, a well-armed militia culture and networks of foreign volunteers that would shape the following decades.

Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592 (Vietnam, AD 1527.label: Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592
Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592 (Vietnam, AD 1527.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592] Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A palace guard commander seized the Vietnamese throne from the failing Lê rulers, holding the Red River delta and winning grudging recognition from Ming China. Loyalists proclaimed a restored Lê emperor in the south under the Nguyễn and Trịnh families, and the country split into rival regimes for two generations of civil war. Driven out of Thăng Long, the last of the family clung on in the mountains at Cao Bằng.

Maximus, 455 (Roman Empire, AD 455–AD 45.label: Maximus, 455
Maximus, 455 (Roman Empire, AD 455–AD 45.prose:
[Rome, AD 455–AD 455] Maximus, 455. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Maximus, 455". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Petronius Maximus seized power after conniving at the murder of Valentinian III, then reigned barely eleven weeks. Forcing the dead emperor's widow into marriage broke the western court's fragile arrangements with Gaiseric, whose Vandal fleet sailed for Rome; Maximus was lynched by a mob as he fled, days before the city was sacked. The episode shows how thoroughly the western throne had become the plaything of court factions and barbarian fleets.

Qi dynasty, 479-502 (China, AD 479–AD 50.label: Qi dynasty, 479-502
Qi dynasty, 479-502 (China, AD 479–AD 50.prose:
[China, AD 479–AD 502] Qi dynasty, 479-502. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qi dynasty, 479-502". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised later that year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Southern Qi was the shortest-lived of the southern dynasties ruling from Jiankang on the Yangtze, a span of barely two decades marked by murderous succession struggles within the ruling Xiao clan. Despite the turmoil the court was a centre of Buddhist patronage and literary refinement, and the tonal experiments of the Yongming poets shaped the rules of later Chinese verse. A cousin of the last emperor seized the throne and founded the Liang, continuing the same aristocratic culture under a new name.

Clement V, 1305-1314 (Vatican City, AD 1.label: Clement V, 1305-1314
Clement V, 1305-1314 (Vatican City, AD 1.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1305–AD 1314] Clement V, 1305-1314. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Clement V, 1305-1314". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Gascon elected under heavy French pressure, Clement never went to Rome and settled the papal court at Avignon, beginning nearly seventy years of French-dominated papacy. He bowed to Philip IV in suppressing the Knights Templar at the Council of Vienne, and their leaders were burned in Paris. The move damaged papal prestige and helped set up the later Great Schism.

Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873 (Fr.label: Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873
Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873 (Fr.prose:
[France, AD 1871–AD 1873] Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873. Extracted from heading "France--History--Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After defeat by Prussia, German troops remained garrisoned across the north and east while France paid off a five-billion-franc indemnity. The money was raised faster than Bismarck expected, through hugely oversubscribed public loans, and the last soldiers withdrew in September 1873. The experience left Alsace-Lorraine lost, the young Third Republic scarred, and a grievance that shaped French politics until 1914.

Edmund, 855-870 (England, AD 855–AD 870).label: Edmund, 855-870
Edmund, 855-870 (England, AD 855–AD 870).prose:
[Great Britain, AD 855–AD 870] Edmund, 855-870. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edmund, 855-870". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edmund ruled East Anglia until the Great Heathen Army of the Danes overwhelmed his kingdom and killed him. Legend turned his death into martyrdom by arrows and beheading, and his shrine at Bury St Edmunds became one of the richest pilgrimage sites in England. He was venerated as a patron saint of the kingdom long before St George displaced him.

Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438 (Romania, AD.label: Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438
Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438 (Romania, AD.prose:
[Transylvania (Romania), AD 1437–AD 1438] Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438. Extracted from heading "Transylvania (Romania)--History--Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hungarian and Romanian serfs in Transylvania rose at Bobâlna against the bishop's tithe and tightening manorial demands, defeating noble forces before being ground down. The threat drove the nobility, the Székely and the Saxon towns into a mutual defence pact, the Union of the Three Nations, which became the constitutional basis of Transylvania for centuries. It froze the largely Orthodox Romanian peasantry out of political life, a grievance still cited in nationalist argument four hundred years later.
