The Dutch colonial regime collapsed in weeks, and Japan governed the archipelago as three separate military zones, extracting oil, rice and hundreds of thousands of romusha forced labourers. To mobilise support it released and promoted nationalists such as Sukarno and Hatta and trained Indonesian militias like PETA. When Japan surrendered, those leaders and those armed units declared independence, and the Dutch never regained control.

Social War, 90-88 B.C (ancient Rome, 89.node: Social War, 90-88 B.C (ancient Rome, 89 BC–87 BC)
Social War, 90-88 B.C (ancient Rome, 89.label: Social War, 90-88 B.C
Social War, 90-88 B.C (ancient Rome, 89.prose:
[Rome, 89 BC–87 BC] Social War, 90-88 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Social War, 90-88 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rome's Italian allies, who had supplied its armies for generations without gaining citizenship, rose in revolt, minted their own coinage and set up a rival capital. Rome won the war but conceded the cause, extending citizenship to the peninsula's free populations. The result was an Italy legally unified under Rome — and a generation of commanders and veteran armies that would soon be turned against the Republic itself.

Ivan VI, 1740-1741 (Russia, AD 1740–AD 1.label: Ivan VI, 1740-1741
Ivan VI, 1740-1741 (Russia, AD 1740–AD 1.prose:
[Russia , AD 1740–AD 1741] Ivan VI, 1740-1741. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Ivan VI, 1740-1741". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed emperor at two months old, he reigned only through regents before a palace coup by the guards put Peter the Great's daughter Elizabeth on the throne. The deposed baby was hidden away, his portraits and coins withdrawn from circulation, and he grew up in solitary confinement at Shlisselburg fortress, barely aware of who he was. He was killed by his guards in 1764 during a botched attempt to free him.

Maria I, 1777-1816 (Portugal, AD 1777–AD.label: Maria I, 1777-1816
Maria I, 1777-1816 (Portugal, AD 1777–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1777–AD 1816] Maria I, 1777-1816. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Maria I, 1777-1816". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Her accession ended the domineering rule of the Marquis of Pombal, who was dismissed and put on trial while exiled nobles returned to court. Devout and increasingly incapacitated by mental illness, she left government to her son John as regent, and when Napoleon's armies invaded, the whole court sailed for Brazil under British escort. She died in Rio de Janeiro, a Portuguese queen who spent her last years ruling from South America.

Vladislaus I, 1305-1333 (Poland, AD 1305.label: Vladislaus I, 1305-1333
Vladislaus I, 1305-1333 (Poland, AD 1305.prose:
[Poland , AD 1305–AD 1333] Vladislaus I, 1305-1333. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus I, 1305-1333". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Władysław the Elbow-high spent decades in exile and rebellion before piecing the fragmented Polish duchies back together and having himself crowned in Kraków in 1320 — the first coronation in the old capital and the formal end of nearly two centuries of division. His reign was consumed by war with the Teutonic Knights over Pomerania and by alliance-building with Hungary and Lithuania. He left his son Casimir a kingdom that was smaller than the old Poland but was once again a kingdom.

Rebellion, 1914-1915 (South Africa, AD 1.label: Rebellion, 1914-1915
Rebellion, 1914-1915 (South Africa, AD 1.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1914–AD 1915] Rebellion, 1914-1915. Extracted from the heading "Africa, South--History--Rebellion, 1914-1915". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.1 of LCHS 1975; revised 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As South Africa's government prepared to invade German South West Africa on Britain's behalf, Afrikaner officers and former Boer generals, including De Wet, Beyers and Maritz, took up arms in protest. Botha and Smuts, themselves Boer War commanders, put the rising down within months with commando forces of their own. The episode split Afrikaner politics between those reconciled to the British Empire and a nationalist current that would later grow into the National Party.

Christian I, 1448-1481 (Norway, AD 1448–.label: Christian I, 1448-1481
Christian I, 1448-1481 (Norway, AD 1448–.prose:
[Norway, AD 1448–AD 1481] Christian I, 1448-1481. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Christian I, 1448-1481". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Oldenburg king, elected in Denmark and then accepted in Norway, he spent his reign chasing an expensive union with Sweden and borrowing to pay for it. Short of cash for his daughter's dowry, he pledged Orkney and Shetland to the Scottish crown in 1468–69 — a loan never repaid, which is why those islands are Scottish today. He also secured papal permission for the University of Copenhagen, founded in 1479.

Civil War, 1989-1996 (Liberia, AD 1989–A.label: Civil War, 1989-1996
Civil War, 1989-1996 (Liberia, AD 1989–A.prose:
[Liberia, AD 1989–AD 1996] Civil War, 1989-1996. Extracted from heading "Liberia--History--Civil War, 1989-1996". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles Taylor's incursion from Côte d'Ivoire toppled Samuel Doe and then fragmented into a war of warlord factions, notorious for drugged child soldiers and looting of timber, rubber and iron. A West African intervention force, ECOMOG, fought for years to contain it. Elections in 1997 made Taylor president, but the underlying conflict resumed within two years and spilled into Sierra Leone.

Insurrection, 1925-1927 (Syria, AD 1925–.label: Insurrection, 1925-1927
Insurrection, 1925-1927 (Syria, AD 1925–.prose:
[Syria, AD 1925–AD 1927] Insurrection, 1925-1927. Extracted from heading "Syria--History--Insurrection, 1925-1927". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Great Syrian Revolt began among the Druze of the Hawran under Sultan al-Atrash and spread to Damascus, Hama and the countryside, uniting rural fighters with urban nationalists against the French Mandate. France responded with aerial bombardment and artillery fire on Damascus, destroying whole quarters and shocking international opinion. The rebellion was defeated but became the founding episode of modern Syrian nationalism.

Augustus II, 1697-1733 (Poland, AD 1697–.label: Augustus II, 1697-1733
Augustus II, 1697-1733 (Poland, AD 1697–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1697–AD 1733] Augustus II, 1697-1733. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Augustus II, 1697-1733". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony, converted to Catholicism to win the Polish crown and then dragged the Commonwealth into the Great Northern War against Sweden, losing the throne to Stanisław Leszczyński before Russian arms restored him. Real power drained to the magnates and to Russia, whose troops came and went as they pleased. He is better remembered in Dresden, where he built baroque palaces and founded the Meissen porcelain works after his alchemists cracked the Chinese formula.

House of Habsburg, 1477-1556 (Netherland.label: House of Habsburg, 1477-1556
House of Habsburg, 1477-1556 (Netherland.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1477–AD 1556] House of Habsburg, 1477-1556. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--House of Habsburg, 1477-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Mary of Burgundy's marriage to Maximilian of Austria carried the Low Countries into Habsburg hands, and under Charles V - born in Ghent - they were governed as part of an empire stretching to Spain and the Americas. Antwerp became the commercial capital of Europe, while the Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 bound the Seventeen Provinces together as a single inheritance. Charles's abdication in 1556 handed them to his Spanish son Philip II, a transfer that within a dozen years produced open revolt.

Henry VII, 1308-1313 (Germany, AD 1308–A.label: Henry VII, 1308-1313
Henry VII, 1308-1313 (Germany, AD 1308–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1308–AD 1313] Henry VII, 1308-1313. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry VII, 1308-1313". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A count of Luxembourg elected as a compromise candidate, he secured Bohemia for his family and then led the first imperial expedition to Italy in decades, seeking to revive the emperor's authority there. Dante hailed him as Italy's saviour and wrote him into the Paradiso; the Guelf cities and the pope resisted him. He died of fever near Siena before he could break Florence, and the imperial dream in Italy died with him.

Henry V, 1413-1422 (England, AD 1413–AD.label: Henry V, 1413-1422
Henry V, 1413-1422 (England, AD 1413–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1413–AD 1422] Henry V, 1413-1422. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry V, 1413-1422". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short, relentlessly focused reign that revived the English claim to the French crown and won the archers' victory at Agincourt in 1415. Systematic conquest of Normandy followed, and the Treaty of Troyes made Henry heir to France and regent for the mad Charles VI. He died of dysentery at thirty-five, leaving a nine-month-old son to hold together a dual monarchy that soon collapsed.

English Invasion, 1780-1781 (Nicaragua,.label: English Invasion, 1780-1781
English Invasion, 1780-1781 (Nicaragua,.prose:
[Nicaragua, AD 1780–AD 1781] English Invasion, 1780-1781. Extracted from heading "Nicaragua--History--English Invasion, 1780-1781". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A British scheme to cut Spanish America in two by seizing the San Juan River and Lake Nicaragua, opening a route to the Pacific. The force, which included a young Horatio Nelson, took Fort San Juan but was destroyed by malaria and dysentery rather than by fighting; the survivors withdrew after losing most of their men. It stands as one of the costliest British failures of the American Revolutionary War.

European intervention, 1861-1867 (Mexico.label: European intervention, 1861-1867
European intervention, 1861-1867 (Mexico.prose:
[Mexico, AD 1861–AD 1867] European intervention, 1861-1867. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--European intervention, 1861-1867". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.77 of LCSH 1987, and p.62 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

France, Britain and Spain landed troops after Mexico suspended payments on its foreign debt; the others withdrew, but Napoleon III pressed on and installed the Habsburg archduke Maximilian as emperor. Benito Juárez's republican government never surrendered, and the improbable Mexican victory at Puebla on 5 May 1862 became a national holiday. French withdrawal under American pressure left Maximilian to be captured and shot at Querétaro, ending monarchy in Mexico for good.

Revolution, 1647-1648 (Naples, AD 1647–A.label: Revolution, 1647-1648
Revolution, 1647-1648 (Naples, AD 1647–A.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1647–AD 1648] Revolution, 1647-1648. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Revolution, 1647-1648". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A new tax on fruit set off a rising in the Naples markets led by the fisherman Masaniello, who briefly held the city before being murdered. The revolt widened into a broader assault on Spanish rule and noble privilege, and a Neapolitan Republic was proclaimed with French encouragement. Spanish forces under Don Juan José of Austria retook the city, but the episode became a byword across Europe for the sudden power of an urban crowd.

Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845 (B.label: Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845
Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845 (B.prose:
[Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil), AD 1835–AD 1845] Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845. Extracted from heading "Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil : State)--History--Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cattle ranchers and gaúcho militias in Rio Grande do Sul rebelled against imperial taxes on their salted beef and hides, and declared the Riograndense Republic. The war spread into Santa Catarina and drew in the young Giuseppe Garibaldi, who learned his trade as a guerrilla and sailor in its service. It was the longest and most dangerous of the revolts against the Brazilian Empire, ending in a negotiated peace that left the province in the empire but confirmed its distinct identity.

Duarte, 1433-1438 (Portugal, AD 1433–AD.label: Duarte, 1433-1438
Duarte, 1433-1438 (Portugal, AD 1433–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1433–AD 1438] Duarte, 1433-1438. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Duarte, 1433-1438". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Edward, 1433-1438" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The scholarly son of John I, who wrote on ethics and horsemanship and codified Portuguese law, inherited a kingdom already committed to Atlantic expansion. His reign is remembered for the catastrophic assault on Tangier, where the army was trapped and his brother Fernando was left behind as a hostage to die in Moroccan captivity. Duarte died of plague barely a year later, leaving a six-year-old heir and a disputed regency.

Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Austria, AD 1576–A.label: Rudolf II, 1576-1612
Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Austria, AD 1576–A.prose:
[Austria, AD 1576–AD 1612] Rudolf II, 1576-1612. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Rudolf II, 1576-1612". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Rudolph II, 1576-1612" appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987, and p.6 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Habsburg emperor moved his court to Prague and turned it into a magnet for astronomers, alchemists, painters and collectors – Tycho Brahe and Kepler worked under his patronage, and his cabinet of curiosities was the most famous in Europe. Politically he was indecisive and increasingly withdrawn, letting confessional tensions in the empire fester until his own family forced him to cede power. The Letter of Majesty he granted Bohemian Protestants in 1609, and its later breach, helped set up the revolt that began the Thirty Years' War.

Miguel I, 1828-1834 (Portugal, AD 1828–A.label: Miguel I, 1828-1834
Miguel I, 1828-1834 (Portugal, AD 1828–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1828–AD 1834] Miguel I, 1828-1834. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Miguel I, 1828-1834". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Dom Miguel seized his niece's throne and ruled as an absolutist, backed by the church and much of the countryside, abolishing the liberal charter and persecuting his opponents. The result was the Liberal Wars, in which his brother Pedro landed with a constitutionalist army; Miguel's defeat sent him into permanent exile and settled Portugal's future as a constitutional monarchy.

Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066 (Englan.label: Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066
Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066 (Englan.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1042–AD 1066] Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward returned from long exile in Normandy to rule an England still shaped by its Danish conquest, balancing the power of Earl Godwine's family against Norman favourites. He poured resources into rebuilding Westminster Abbey, where he was buried and later venerated as a saint. Dying childless, he left a disputed succession that brought Harold Godwinson, Harald Hardrada and William of Normandy into collision in 1066.

Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–A.label: Charles V, 1519-1556
Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1519–AD 1556] Charles V, 1519-1556. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Charles V, 1519-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected emperor with money borrowed from the Fuggers, he confronted Luther at the Diet of Worms and spent the rest of his reign unable to contain the Reformation while also fighting France in Italy and the Ottomans on the Danube and in the Mediterranean. He beat the Lutheran princes at Mühlberg in 1547 but could not make the victory stick, and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 conceded that each prince would determine his territory's religion. Worn out, he abdicated and split his inheritance between his son and his brother, ending the dream of a single universal Christian empire.

Republic, 1836-1846 (Texas, AD 1836–AD 1.label: Republic, 1836-1846
Republic, 1836-1846 (Texas, AD 1836–AD 1.prose:
[Texas, AD 1836–AD 1846] Republic, 1836-1846. Extracted from heading "Texas--History--Republic, 1836-1846". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

For a decade Texas was an independent state with its own president, army, currency and diplomats in Washington, London and Paris, after Anglo settlers and Tejano allies broke away from Mexico at San Jacinto. Mexico never accepted the loss, the treasury was chronically broke, and frontier war with the Comanche was constant. Annexation by the United States ended the experiment and triggered the U.S.–Mexican War.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Kansas, AD 1861–AD.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Kansas, AD 1861–AD.prose:
[Kansas, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Kansas--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.69 of LCSH 1987, and p.67 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Ethelred II, 979-1016 (England, AD 979–A.label: Ethelred II, 979-1016
Ethelred II, 979-1016 (England, AD 979–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 979–AD 1016] Ethelred II, 979-1016. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Ethelred II, 979-1016". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign remembered for renewed Viking assaults, met with enormous payments of silver that flooded Scandinavia with English coin and left a rich numismatic record of the king's frequently changing coin types. Æthelred's ordered massacre of Danes in 1002 and the campaigns of Swein Forkbeard drove him briefly into exile in Normandy, a connection that would matter greatly in 1066. His death left England open to Cnut's conquest and a generation of Danish rule.

Henry IV, 1056-1106 (Germany, AD 1056–AD.label: Henry IV, 1056-1106
Henry IV, 1056-1106 (Germany, AD 1056–AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1056–AD 1106] Henry IV, 1056-1106. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry IV, 1056-1106". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign was consumed by the Investiture Controversy, the struggle with Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops — a contest about the very basis of royal authority. Excommunicated and facing revolt, he crossed the Alps in winter to stand penitent at Canossa and win absolution, then returned to depose Gregory and install an antipope. Decades of civil war followed, and he died deposed by his own son, with imperial prestige in Germany permanently weakened.

Robert III, 1390-1406 (Scotland, AD 1390.label: Robert III, 1390-1406
Robert III, 1390-1406 (Scotland, AD 1390.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406] Robert III, 1390-1406. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Robert III, 1390-1406". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Lamed by a horse-kick and reckoned unfit to rule, he left government largely to his brother and other kinsmen while the kingdom slid towards factional violence; his heir David died in suspicious captivity at Falkland. His surviving son James was captured by the English at sea in 1406, news that reportedly killed the king and left Scotland under regents for eighteen years.

Frederick William I, 1713-1740 (Germany,.label: Frederick William I, 1713-1740
Frederick William I, 1713-1740 (Germany,.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1713–AD 1740] Frederick William I, 1713-1740. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick William I, 1713-1740". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The "Soldier King" turned Prussia into a barracks state, more than doubling the army, creating a disciplined salaried bureaucracy in the General Directory, and running the treasury with obsessive thrift while stamping out court luxury. He introduced compulsory schooling in principle, settled Protestant refugees on empty land, and collected exceptionally tall recruits for his Potsdam Giants. Brutal to his son, he nonetheless bequeathed him a full treasury and Europe's best-drilled army — the tools with which Frederick the Great made Prussia a great power.

Southern Han kingdom, 917-971 (China, AD.label: Southern Han kingdom, 917-971
Southern Han kingdom, 917-971 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 917–AD 971] Southern Han kingdom, 917-971. Extracted from heading "China--History--Southern Han kingdom, 917-971". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A regional state centred on Guangzhou, founded by the Liu family after the Tang collapse, which grew rich on the sea trade bringing Arab and Southeast Asian merchants to its harbour. Later rulers were remembered for extravagance and for staffing the government with eunuchs. Song forces conquered it, ending independent rule on China's southern coast.

Afonso III, 1248-1279 (Portugal, AD 1248.label: Afonso III, 1248-1279
Afonso III, 1248-1279 (Portugal, AD 1248.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1248–AD 1279] Afonso III, 1248-1279. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Afonso III, 1248-1279". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alfonso III, 1248-1279" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Seizing the throne from his brother, he completed the Portuguese Reconquista by taking the Algarve, giving the kingdom the borders it still has. He moved the capital to Lisbon and summoned townsmen to the Cortes, drawing the merchant class into royal government for the first time. His reign also began the long argument with Castile over who owned the newly won south.

Restoration, 1660-1688 (England, AD 1660.label: Restoration, 1660-1688
Restoration, 1660-1688 (England, AD 1660.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1660–AD 1688] Restoration, 1660-1688. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Restoration, 1660-1688". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From the return of Charles II to the flight of his brother James II, the restored monarchy tried and failed to settle the religious question that had caused the Civil Wars. The Exclusion Crisis over a Catholic heir split politics into the first recognisable Whig and Tory parties, and James's Catholicising policies finally provoked the invitation to William of Orange. The era's culture was worldly and inventive: Wren's churches, Dryden's verse, Newton's mathematics, and comedies far bawdier than anything before or after.

Robert II, 996-1031 (France, AD 996–AD 1.label: Robert II, 996-1031
Robert II, 996-1031 (France, AD 996–AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 996–AD 1031] Robert II, 996-1031. Extracted from heading "France--History--Robert II, 996-1031". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as Robert the Pious, he spent his reign shoring up the still-fragile Capetian hold on a kingdom where great counts and dukes were the real powers, and secured the succession by crowning his son in his lifetime. His excommunication over an uncanonical marriage showed how far reforming churchmen could now press a king, and his reign coincided with the Peace of God movement and the first burnings for heresy in the medieval West.

Baudouin I, 1951-1993 (Belgium, AD 1951–.label: Baudouin I, 1951-1993
Baudouin I, 1951-1993 (Belgium, AD 1951–.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1951–AD 1993] Baudouin I, 1951-1993. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Baudouin I, 1951-1993". Added to LCSH and revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the throne as a young man after his father's wartime conduct forced an abdication, and spent his reign as a stabilising figure in a country pulling apart along linguistic lines. His reign saw the abrupt independence of the Congo in 1960 and the long constitutional reforms that turned Belgium into a federal state. A devout Catholic, he briefly stood aside from his royal duties in 1990 so an abortion law could be signed without his name on it.

Separatist movement, 1918-1924 (Germany,.label: Separatist movement, 1918-1924
Separatist movement, 1918-1924 (Germany,.prose:
[Rhineland (Germany), AD 1918–AD 1924] Separatist movement, 1918-1924. Extracted from heading "Rhineland (Germany)--History--Separatist movement, 1918-1924". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In the chaos after defeat, activists in the Rhineland and Palatinate, encouraged by French occupation authorities who wanted a buffer state, proclaimed short-lived independent republics. The movement peaked during the hyperinflation and Ruhr occupation of 1923, when Rhenish Republic governments briefly seized town halls. It collapsed under popular hostility, violent counter-attacks and the withdrawal of foreign backing, but the episode fed nationalist grievance narratives for years.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Russia, AD 1917–A.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Russia, AD 1917–A.prose:
[Soviet Union, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Estonia, Georgia (country), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia. Extracted from heading "Soviet Union--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.108 of LCSH 1987, and on p.87 of LCSH 1975 (source uses term "Russia"). Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Revolution, 1918-1923 (Turkey, AD 1918–A.label: Revolution, 1918-1923
Revolution, 1918-1923 (Turkey, AD 1918–A.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1918–AD 1923] Revolution, 1918-1923. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Revolution, 1918-1923". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the Ottoman capital under Allied occupation and Anatolia parcelled out for partition, Mustafa Kemal built a rival government in Ankara and fought off the Greek invasion. Victory tore up the Treaty of Sèvres and produced Lausanne, new borders, and a massive population exchange with Greece. The sultanate and then the caliphate were abolished, and a secular nation-state replaced a six-hundred-year empire.

French occupation, 1923-1925 (Germany, A.label: French occupation, 1923-1925
French occupation, 1923-1925 (Germany, A.prose:
[Ruhr (Germany), AD 1923–AD 1925] French occupation, 1923-1925. Extracted from heading "Ruhr (Germany : Region)--History--French occupation, 1923-1925". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Citing missed reparations deliveries of coal and timber, French and Belgian troops seized the Ruhr industrial basin. The German government called for passive resistance and printed money to pay idled workers, tipping the currency into hyperinflation that wiped out savings and fed extremist politics, including Hitler's failed Munich putsch. The crisis was defused by the Dawes Plan, which rescheduled reparations and brought American loans, and the troops went home.

Louis XIV, 1643-1715 (France, AD 1643–AD.label: Louis XIV, 1643-1715
Louis XIV, 1643-1715 (France, AD 1643–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1643–AD 1715] Louis XIV, 1643-1715. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XIV, 1643-1715". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Sun King turned France into Europe's dominant power and the model of absolute monarchy, governing without a chief minister and drawing the nobility to a gilded life at Versailles. Colbert's economic management, a huge standing army and Vauban's fortresses paid for near-constant warfare that ended in exhaustion during the War of the Spanish Succession. Revoking the Edict of Nantes drove hundreds of thousands of Protestants abroad; French language, cuisine and classical art meanwhile set the standard for courts everywhere.

Paul V, 1605-1621 (Vatican City, AD 1605.label: Paul V, 1605-1621
Paul V, 1605-1621 (Vatican City, AD 1605.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1605–AD 1621] Paul V, 1605-1621. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Paul V, 1605-1621". Added to LCSH in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Camillo Borghese's pontificate pressed papal jurisdictional claims hard, most famously in the losing quarrel with Venice, and it also produced the first formal warning to Galileo in 1616 that Copernicanism was not to be held. In Rome he finished the job on St Peter's, adding Maderno's nave and façade, and rebuilt the ancient Trajanic aqueduct to feed the Acqua Paola fountain. Borghese family patronage, and the collections gathered by his nephew Scipione, seeded one of Europe's great art collections.

Sancho I, 1185-1211 (Portugal, AD 1185–A.label: Sancho I, 1185-1211
Sancho I, 1185-1211 (Portugal, AD 1185–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1185–AD 1211] Sancho I, 1185-1211. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Sancho I, 1185-1211". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sancho I earned the nickname 'the Populator' by filling a thinly held frontier with settlers, granting town charters and backing the new military orders to hold land against Almohad raids. He briefly took Silves in 1189 with the help of passing northern crusaders, only to lose it two years later. His long quarrels with the bishops over royal taxation of church property set the pattern for a century of crown–clergy conflict in Portugal.

House of Burgundy, 1384-1477 (Netherland.label: House of Burgundy, 1384-1477
House of Burgundy, 1384-1477 (Netherland.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1384–AD 1477] House of Burgundy, 1384-1477. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--House of Burgundy, 1384-1477". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Through marriage, purchase and inheritance the Valois dukes of Burgundy assembled Flanders, Brabant, Holland, Hainaut and their neighbours into a single princely bloc, imposing central councils and taxes on famously independent towns. Their court was the richest in Europe, paying for Van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden, polyphonic music, and the Order of the Golden Fleece. The experiment collapsed when Charles the Bold was killed at Nancy in 1477, but the united Low Countries he left behind became the core of the later Netherlands and Belgium.

Maximilian I, 1493-1519 (Germany, AD 149.label: Maximilian I, 1493-1519
Maximilian I, 1493-1519 (Germany, AD 149.prose:
[Germany , AD 1493–AD 1519] Maximilian I, 1493-1519. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Maximilian I, 1493-1519". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He gained the rich Burgundian Netherlands by marriage and then arranged his children's and grandchildren's marriages so shrewdly that his grandson Charles inherited Spain, the Low Countries, Austria and the Americas. At home he pushed through imperial reforms, an imperial court of justice and a common peace, though the Empire remained loosely governed and he was chronically short of money. He fought long and inconclusive wars in Italy, promoted the Landsknecht infantry, and used printed images and books to build his own legend.

Interregnum, 1696-1697 (Poland, AD 1696–.label: Interregnum, 1696-1697
Interregnum, 1696-1697 (Poland, AD 1696–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1696–AD 1697] Interregnum, 1696-1697. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1696-1697". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of John III Sobieski, the victor of Vienna, opened an election in which foreign money flowed freely and two candidates were proclaimed at once: the French prince de Conti and Augustus the Strong of Saxony. Augustus reached Kraków first and was crowned, beginning a Saxon connection that lasted, with interruptions, for two thirds of a century and left the Commonwealth increasingly at the mercy of its neighbours.

Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496 (I.label: Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496
Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496 (I.prose:
[Italy, AD 1494–AD 1496] Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The French king marched an army the length of Italy to claim the throne of Naples, taking the city almost without a fight and exposing how vulnerable the Italian states were to a large modern army with mobile siege artillery. His success frightened Venice, Milan, the Pope and Spain into the League of Venice, which fought him at Fornovo as he retreated. The venture opened more than sixty years of Italian Wars and made the peninsula a battleground for foreign powers.

Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775 (Russia.label: Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775
Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775 (Russia.prose:
[Russia , AD 1773–AD 1775] Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775". Added to LCSH in 2003; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Yemelyan Pugachev, a Don Cossack deserter, claimed to be the murdered Tsar Peter III and drew Cossacks, serfs, Old Believers, Bashkirs and Ural factory workers into the largest popular revolt in Russian history. Rebel armies took Kazan and threatened the Volga heartland before Catherine II's troops, freed up by peace with the Ottomans, crushed them; Pugachev was quartered in Moscow. The shock hardened Catherine against reform, tightened noble control over serfs, and led to the reorganisation of provincial government to prevent anything similar.

Peter I, 1689-1725 (Russia, AD 1689–AD 1.label: Peter I, 1689-1725
Peter I, 1689-1725 (Russia, AD 1689–AD 1.prose:
[Russia , AD 1689–AD 1725] Peter I, 1689-1725. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Peter I, 1689-1725". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peter the Great dragged Russia into the European state system by force of will, building a navy, remodelling the army, shaving beards and taxing those who kept them, and founding a new capital on Baltic marshland at enormous human cost. Victory over Sweden at Poltava broke the northern balance of power and made Russia a great power; in 1721 he took the title of emperor. His reforms of administration, the church and the nobility set the framework of the Russian state for two centuries, and the argument over whether the westernisation was salvation or violence has never stopped.

Allied occupation, 1945-1955 (Austria, A.label: Allied occupation, 1945-1955
Allied occupation, 1945-1955 (Austria, A.prose:
[Austria, AD 1945–AD 1955] Allied occupation, 1945-1955. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Allied occupation, 1945-1955". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Austria was split into American, British, French and Soviet zones, with Vienna similarly quartered and patrolled by joint four-power teams. Treated as Hitler's first victim rather than an enemy state, the country kept its own government throughout and avoided the permanent partition that befell Germany. The State Treaty of 1955 withdrew all foreign troops in exchange for a pledge of permanent neutrality.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Belarus, AD 1905–.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Belarus, AD 1905–.prose:
[Belarus, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Belarus--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Grand duchy, 1806-1918 (Germany, AD 1806.label: Grand duchy, 1806-1918
Grand duchy, 1806-1918 (Germany, AD 1806.prose:
[Hesse (Germany), AD 1806–AD 1918] Grand duchy, 1806-1918. Extracted from heading "Hesse (Germany)--History--1806-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Napoleon dismantled the Holy Roman Empire, several German princes were promoted to grand dukes, creating states such as Baden, Hesse and the Mecklenburgs. They kept their crowns through the German Confederation and then as constituent states of Bismarck's empire, each with its own court, army contingent, constitution and postage stamps. All of them fell together in the revolution of November 1918.

Christian III, 1534-1559 (Denmark, AD 15.label: Christian III, 1534-1559
Christian III, 1534-1559 (Denmark, AD 15.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1534–AD 1559] Christian III, 1534-1559. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian III, 1534-1559". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He won the throne in the civil war known as the Count's Feud and immediately arrested the Catholic bishops, confiscating church lands for the crown in 1536. The Lutheran Reformation was imposed from above, with a new church order drawn up with help from Wittenberg and the first complete Danish Bible printed in 1550. Royal finances and royal power both grew enormously on the back of former monastic estates.

Antislavery movement, 1830-1863 (Massach.label: Antislavery movement, 1830-1863
Antislavery movement, 1830-1863 (Massach.prose:
[Boston, Massachusetts, AD 1830–AD 1863] Antislavery movement, 1830-1863. Extracted from heading "Antislavery movements--Massachusetts--Boston". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised 1994. Earlier established form "Boston (Mass.)--History--Antislavery movement, 1830-1863" used as primary label, because it includes dates. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Boston became the engine room of radical abolition, with William Lloyd Garrison launching The Liberator in 1831 and demanding immediate, uncompensated emancipation rather than gradual reform. Black activists, women's antislavery societies, fugitive-slave rescues and speakers like Frederick Douglass made the state a centre of both organising and violent backlash. The movement's pressure helped push a reluctant nation toward emancipation, and Massachusetts raised the first Black regiments of the Civil War.

Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD.label: Henry VI, 1190-1197
Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1190–AD 1197] Henry VI, 1190-1197. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry VI, 1190-1197". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Barbarossa's son married the heiress of Norman Sicily and seized the island kingdom, briefly encircling the papacy with Hohenstaufen power from the Baltic to Palermo. He financed the effort partly with the enormous ransom extorted from Richard the Lionheart, captured on his way home from crusade. His sudden death at thirty-one, leaving a three-year-old heir, wrecked his plan to make the empire hereditary and plunged Germany into civil war.

Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C (Greece, 3.node: Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C (Greece, 354 BC–345 BC)
Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C (Greece, 3.label: Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C
Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C (Greece, 3.prose:
[Greece, 354 BC–345 BC] Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dispute over sacred land at Delphi escalated when the Phocians seized the sanctuary and melted down its treasures to hire mercenary armies. The decade of fighting exhausted the central Greek states and gave Philip II of Macedon his opening to intervene as the god's champion. His victory won Macedon a seat on the Delphic council and effective leadership in Greek affairs, a step towards the conquest of Greece itself.

John III Sobieski, 1674-1696 (Poland, AD.label: John III Sobieski, 1674-1696
John III Sobieski, 1674-1696 (Poland, AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1674–AD 1696] John III Sobieski, 1674-1696. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--John III Sobieski, 1674-1696". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier elected king on the strength of his victories over the Ottomans, he is famous for the ride to Vienna in 1683, where his winged hussars broke the Turkish siege in the largest cavalry charge in history. The victory made him a hero of Christendom and marked the beginning of the Ottoman retreat from central Europe. At home he failed to strengthen the monarchy against a fractious nobility, and built the palace of Wilanów as a private retreat.

Bombardment, 1939-1945 (Wilhelmshaven, A.label: Bombardment, 1939-1945
Bombardment, 1939-1945 (Wilhelmshaven, A.prose:
[Wilhelmshaven (Germany), AD 1939–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1939-1945. Extracted from heading "Wilhelmshaven (Germany)--History--Bombardment, 1939-1945". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Germany's principal North Sea naval base and warship yard was attacked by the RAF within days of the war's outbreak — among the very first bombing raids of the conflict — and was also the target of the first American heavy-bomber raid on Germany in January 1943. Repeated attacks on its docks, U-boat pens and shipbuilding left the town shattered by 1945.

Stephen, 1135-1154 (England, AD 1135–AD.label: Stephen, 1135-1154
Stephen, 1135-1154 (England, AD 1135–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1135–AD 1154] Stephen, 1135-1154. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Stephen, 1135-1154". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Stephen seized the English throne on his uncle Henry I's death, breaking the oath he had sworn to support Henry's daughter Matilda. The result was two decades of civil war known as the Anarchy, with rival courts, unlicensed castles and a chronicler's famous complaint that Christ and his saints slept. It ended with a settlement making Matilda's son Henry II the heir, founding the Plantagenet dynasty.

Troubles, 1968-1998 (Northern Ireland, A.label: Troubles, 1968-1998
Troubles, 1968-1998 (Northern Ireland, A.prose:
[Northern Ireland, AD 1968–AD 1998] Troubles, 1968-1998. Extracted from heading "Northern Ireland--History--1968-1998". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2017. Actual primary title "Northern Ireland--History--1968-1998" was replaced with variant. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Civil rights marches by Northern Ireland's Catholic minority met violent resistance, and within a few years the province was locked into a conflict between republican paramilitaries, loyalist gunmen, the police and the British Army. Around 3,500 people died in bombings, shootings and riots that reached Britain and the Republic as well. The Good Friday Agreement ended it with power-sharing institutions, a compromise that left the border question deliberately unresolved.

Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534 (China, AD.label: Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534
Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 386–AD 534] Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.16 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by the Tuoba Xianbei, this was the state that finally ended a century of warlordism in northern China. Its emperors sponsored Buddhist carving at Yungang and Longmen, ordered a great persecution of Buddhism and then reversed it, and moved the capital to Luoyang as part of a programme of Chinese-style reform. Mutiny among the neglected northern garrisons brought it down in the 530s.

Isabel I, 1474-1504 (Kingdom of Castile,.label: Isabel I, 1474-1504
Isabel I, 1474-1504 (Kingdom of Castile,.prose:
[Castile, AD 1474–AD 1504] Isabel I, 1474-1504. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile, Spain. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Isabel I, 1474-1504". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1998. Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Isabella's contested accession and her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon joined the two great Iberian crowns in a personal union that became the foundation of Spain. Her reign brought the fall of Granada in 1492, ending Muslim rule in Iberia, the establishment of the Spanish Inquisition and the expulsion of the Jews, and royal backing for Columbus's voyage west. She also curbed the Castilian nobility, reformed the coinage and courts, and left a monarchy strong enough to build an empire.

Civil War, 1992-2006 (Algeria, AD 1992–A.label: Civil War, 1992-2006
Civil War, 1992-2006 (Algeria, AD 1992–A.prose:
[Algeria, AD 1992–AD 2006] Civil War, 1992-2006. Extracted from heading "Algeria--History--Civil War, 1992-2006". Added to LCSH in 2012, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The army cancelled elections that the Islamic Salvation Front was poised to win, and the country descended into a decade of insurgency and massacre. Armed Islamist groups and state forces both targeted civilians, and journalists, intellectuals and whole villages were slaughtered in what Algerians call the "black decade". An amnesty policy under President Bouteflika wound the conflict down while leaving responsibility for perhaps 150,000 deaths largely unexamined.

Dirty War, 1976-1983 (Argentina, AD 1976.label: Dirty War, 1976-1983
Dirty War, 1976-1983 (Argentina, AD 1976.prose:
[Argentina , AD 1976–AD 1983] Dirty War, 1976-1983. Extracted from heading "Argentina--History--Dirty War, 1976-1983". Added to LCSH in 2003, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A military junta seized power and set out to eliminate 'subversion' through clandestine detention centres, torture and the killing of thousands of people who simply disappeared, some thrown alive from aircraft into the sea. Babies born to detained women were taken and given to other families, a crime still being unravelled by DNA testing today. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo circled the square in white headscarves demanding answers, and the regime's collapse after defeat in the Falklands led to a democratic government that put its own former commanders on trial.

Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C (ancient Rom.node: Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C (ancient Rome, 87 BC–62 BC)
Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C (ancient Rom.label: Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C
Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C (ancient Rom.prose:
[Rome, 87 BC–62 BC] Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three wars between Rome and Mithridates VI of Pontus, who exploited resentment of Roman tax-farmers by orchestrating the massacre of tens of thousands of Italians across Asia Minor. Sulla, Lucullus and finally Pompey campaigned against him, and the fighting spilled into Greece and Armenia before Mithridates died a fugitive in the Crimea. Victory left Rome in direct control of Anatolia and Syria, and gave Pompey the wealth and clientele that fed the politics of the late Republic.

Chimurenga War, 1966-1980 (Zimbabwe, AD.label: Chimurenga War, 1966-1980
Chimurenga War, 1966-1980 (Zimbabwe, AD.prose:
[Zimbabwe, AD 1966–AD 1980] Chimurenga War, 1966-1980. Extracted from heading "Zimbabwe--History--Chimurenga War, 1966-1980". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.132 of LCSH 1987, and p.110 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Guerrilla armies of ZANU and ZAPU, based in Zambia and Mozambique and supplied by China and the Soviet bloc, fought the white minority government that had unilaterally declared independence from Britain. Fighting spread from border skirmishes to a rural war of ambushes, protected villages and cross-border raids that wore down the Rhodesian state and its economy under sanctions. The Lancaster House settlement ended it with elections that brought Robert Mugabe to power and created Zimbabwe.

Ava kingdom, 1364-1527 (Burma, AD 1364–A.label: Ava kingdom, 1364-1527
Ava kingdom, 1364-1527 (Burma, AD 1364–A.prose:
[Burma, AD 1364–AD 1527] Ava kingdom, 1364-1527. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Ava kingdom, 1364-1527". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded on the Irrawaddy by Thado Minbya, Ava saw itself as the heir of Pagan and spent decades trying to reconquer the Mon kingdom of Pegu in the south in the long, inconclusive Forty Years' War. Its court produced a golden age of Burmese poetry and chronicle writing even as Shan raids and rebellious vassals ate away at its power. Shan confederates sacked the city in 1527, splintering upper Burma.

Claudius II, 268-270? (Roman Empire, AD.label: Claudius II, 268-270?
Claudius II, 268-270? (Roman Empire, AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 268–AD 270] Claudius II, 268-270?. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Claudius II, 268-270?". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-emperor raised by the army during the worst years of imperial breakdown, when Gaul and Palmyra had broken away and plague and invasion were constant. He won a crushing victory over the Goths at Naissus, earning the title Gothicus, before dying of plague after barely two years. His short reign began the run of tough Illyrian emperors who eventually put the empire back together.

Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609 (Po.label: Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609
Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609 (Po.prose:
[Poland , AD 1606–AD 1609] Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A legal revolt, or rokosz, in which nobles led by Mikołaj Zebrzydowski took up arms against Sigismund III Vasa, accusing him of scheming for absolute rule and of Jesuit and Habsburg sympathies. The king won the battle at Guzów in 1607 but had to pardon the rebels and abandon his reform plans. The outcome entrenched the szlachta's veto over royal power, weakening central authority in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for the rest of its existence.

Luís I, 1861-1889 (Portugal, AD 1861–AD.label: Luís I, 1861-1889
Luís I, 1861-1889 (Portugal, AD 1861–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1861–AD 1889] Luís I, 1861-1889. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Luís I, 1861-1889". Added to LCSH in 2013, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cultured constitutional monarch who translated Shakespeare into Portuguese while parliament governed through the rotation of two rival parties. His reign saw railways and telegraphs spread, the death penalty and slavery in the colonies abolished, and Portugal stake ambitious claims in Africa that would soon collide with British interests.

Peter I, 1782-1830 (Montenegro, AD 1782–.label: Peter I, 1782-1830
Peter I, 1782-1830 (Montenegro, AD 1782–.prose:
[Montenegro, AD 1782–AD 1830] Peter I, 1782-1830. Extracted from heading "Montenegro--History--Peter I, 1782-1830". Added to LCSH in 2005. Alternate label "Petar I, 1782-1830" appears on p.79 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Petar I Petrović-Njegoš ruled as prince-bishop, combining spiritual and political authority over a fractious set of clans. He beat back two Ottoman invasions at Martinići and Krusi, issued Montenegro's first written law code, and worked to replace blood feud with a central court. Canonised after his death as St Peter of Cetinje, he is treated as the founder of the modern Montenegrin state.

Joachim Murat, 1808-1815 (Naples, AD 180.label: Joachim Murat, 1808-1815
Joachim Murat, 1808-1815 (Naples, AD 180.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1808–AD 1815] Joachim Murat, 1808-1815. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Joachim Murat, 1808-1815". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's cavalry marshal and brother-in-law ruled Naples as king, abolishing feudal dues, imposing the Napoleonic Code and reorganising the army and administration. When the empire collapsed he tried to rally Italians to his cause with a call for national unity, was defeated at Tolentino, and was shot by firing squad. His brief reign left southern Italy with reformed institutions and an early taste of Italian nationalism.

Anschluss movement, 1918-1938 (Austria,.label: Anschluss movement, 1918-1938
Anschluss movement, 1918-1938 (Austria,.prose:
[Austria, Germany, AD 1918–AD 1938] Anschluss movement, 1918-1938. Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany. Extracted from heading "Anschluss movement, 1918-1938". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Habsburg empire dissolved, the German-speaking rump declared itself part of Germany, only to be forbidden union by the peace treaties and left as a small, economically shaky republic. Support for Anschluss ran across the political spectrum for years, but the 1930s brought paramilitary street fighting, a brief civil war, an authoritarian corporate state and the murder of Chancellor Dollfuss by Nazis. Under German military pressure Austria was annexed in March 1938, greeted by cheering crowds in Vienna and followed at once by persecution of Austrian Jews.

Vladislaus III, 1434-1444 (Poland, AD 14.label: Vladislaus III, 1434-1444
Vladislaus III, 1434-1444 (Poland, AD 14.prose:
[Poland , AD 1434–AD 1444] Vladislaus III, 1434-1444. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus III, 1434-1444". Added to LCSH in 1999; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned as a boy in Poland and later elected king of Hungary as well, Władysław was pushed by papal legates into leading crusading campaigns against the advancing Ottomans in the Balkans. He broke a sworn truce to march on Varna, where his army was destroyed and the young king was killed and his body never found. The defeat ended serious Western efforts to halt the Ottomans before Constantinople fell nine years later.

Sigismund I, 1506-1548 (Poland, AD 1506–.label: Sigismund I, 1506-1548
Sigismund I, 1506-1548 (Poland, AD 1506–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1506–AD 1548] Sigismund I, 1506-1548. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Sigismund I, 1506-1548". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sigismund the Old ruled a Jagiellonian Poland-Lithuania at its height, defeating the Teutonic Order and turning its state into the secular, vassal Duchy of Prussia at the Homage of 1525. His Italian queen, Bona Sforza, brought Renaissance architects, artists and cooks to Kraków, and Wawel Castle was rebuilt as an arcaded Italianate palace. Beneath the splendour, the gentry were already pressing for reform of royal lands and offices, a movement that would shape the next reign.

Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710.label: Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710
Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710.prose:
[France, AD 1702–AD 1710] Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710. Extracted from heading "France--History--Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710". Added to LCSH and revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Protestant peasants and artisans of the Cévennes rose against the dragoons and priests sent to enforce Catholic conformity after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Fighting in small bands led by prophets and lay preachers, they held off royal armies far larger than themselves in a brutal guerrilla war of burned villages. The revolt failed but forced a de facto tolerance in the mountains, and its visionary preachers carried French prophetic Protestantism to London and beyond.

Charles I, 1516-1556 (Spain, AD 1516–AD.label: Charles I, 1516-1556
Charles I, 1516-1556 (Spain, AD 1516–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 1516–AD 1556] Charles I, 1516-1556. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Charles I, 1516-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Flemish-raised teenager inherited Castile, Aragon, Naples and the Indies, and within three years added the Holy Roman Empire, binding Spain into a dynastic system stretching from the Low Countries to Vienna. Castilian towns rose against the foreign king in the Comuneros revolt and were crushed; meanwhile Cortés took Mexico and Pizarro Peru, and American silver began funding endless European wars. Exhausted, he divided the inheritance and retired to a monastery at Yuste, leaving Spain to his son and the imperial title to his brother.

Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312 (Kingdom of Cast.label: Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312
Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312 (Kingdom of Cast.prose:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1295–AD 1312] Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the throne as a child amid rival claims and noble rebellion, and survived largely through the political skill of his mother, María de Molina, who held the kingdom together during the regency. As an adult he campaigned against Granada and captured Gibraltar in 1309, the first Christian seizure of the rock. His sudden death at twenty-six earned him the nickname "el Emplazado", the Summoned, from the legend that condemned men had called him to divine judgement.

Charles III, 898-922 (France, AD 898–AD.label: Charles III, 898-922
Charles III, 898-922 (France, AD 898–AD.prose:
[France, AD 898–AD 922] Charles III, 898-922. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles III, 898-922". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as the Simple, meaning straightforward rather than stupid, he made the bargain that created Normandy, granting land around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo in exchange for baptism and defence of the Seine. He briefly recovered Lotharingia for the West Frankish crown. His reliance on a favoured counsellor alienated the great magnates, who deposed him in 922; he died a prisoner at Péronne.

Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925 (Iran, AD 1794–.label: Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925
Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925 (Iran, AD 1794–.prose:
[Iran, AD 1794–AD 1925] Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by Agha Mohammad Khan after decades of civil war, the Qajar state reunified Iran and made Tehran its capital, but lost the Caucasus to Russia and spent the nineteenth century balancing Russian and British ambitions. Concessions sold to foreigners, notably over tobacco, triggered mass protest led by merchants and clerics, and in 1906 forced the shah to accept a constitution and parliament. Qajar visual culture is instantly recognisable: life-size oil portraits of bejewelled princes, painted lacquer boxes, and the pioneering photographs of Nasir al-Din Shah's court.

Sixtus V, 1585-1590 (Vatican City, AD 15.label: Sixtus V, 1585-1590
Sixtus V, 1585-1590 (Vatican City, AD 15.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1585–AD 1590] Sixtus V, 1585-1590. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Sixtus V, 1585-1590". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.89 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A ferocious reformer who hanged bandits by the hundred to restore order in the Papal States and rebuilt the papal government, fixing the College of Cardinals at seventy and dividing the Curia into permanent congregations — a structure that lasted for centuries. He remade Rome physically too, cutting straight avenues between the pilgrimage basilicas, raising the Vatican obelisk in a famous feat of engineering, and pushing the dome of St Peter's to completion. Visitors to Rome still walk his street plan.

Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673 (Poland,.label: Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673
Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673 (Poland,.prose:
[Poland , AD 1669–AD 1673] Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected as a compromise candidate by the lesser nobility, this weak and inexperienced king presided over factional paralysis in the Commonwealth. An Ottoman invasion in 1672 forced the humiliating Treaty of Buchach, ceding Podolia and promising tribute to the sultan. He died in 1673, one day before his hetman Jan Sobieski smashed the Turks at Chocim, a victory that carried Sobieski to the throne.

Mahmud I, 1730-1754 (Turkey, AD 1730–AD.label: Mahmud I, 1730-1754
Mahmud I, 1730-1754 (Turkey, AD 1730–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1730–AD 1754] Mahmud I, 1730-1754. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mahmud I, 1730-1754". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Placed on the throne by the Patrona Halil uprising that ended the pleasure-loving Tulip Period, he then quietly disposed of the rebels. With the French convert Humbaraci Ahmed Pasha he began drilling artillery units on European lines, and his armies fought Russia and Austria to a successful close, regaining Belgrade in the Treaty of Belgrade of 1739. It was the Ottomans' last clearly victorious war for a century.

German occupation, 1941-1944 (Belarus, A.label: German occupation, 1941-1944
German occupation, 1941-1944 (Belarus, A.prose:
[Belarus, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Belarus--History--German occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

Aurelian, 270-275 (Roman Empire, AD 270–.label: Aurelian, 270-275
Aurelian, 270-275 (Roman Empire, AD 270–.prose:
[Rome, AD 270–AD 275] Aurelian, 270-275. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Aurelian, 270-275". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Aurelian inherited an empire split three ways and put it back together in five years, crushing the Palmyrene realm of Zenobia in the east and reclaiming the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west. He also drove back Juthungi and Vandals, abandoned Dacia as indefensible, reformed the debased coinage and ringed Rome itself with the walls that still bear his name. Murdered by his own officers, he had bought the empire the breathing space Diocletian would use.

Mehmed III, 1595-1603 (Turkey, AD 1595–A.label: Mehmed III, 1595-1603
Mehmed III, 1595-1603 (Turkey, AD 1595–A.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1595–AD 1603] Mehmed III, 1595-1603. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mehmed III, 1595-1603". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Mohammed III, 1595-1603" appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign opened with the execution of nineteen brothers, the most extreme application of the Ottoman fratricide law and effectively its last. He personally led the army to victory at Mezőkeresztes in 1596 during the long, grinding war with Habsburg Austria in Hungary. At home the Celali revolts spread through Anatolia, and power increasingly shifted toward the palace household and the sultan's mother.

Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960 (China, AD 9.label: Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960
Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960 (China, AD 9.prose:
[China, AD 951–AD 960] Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960. Extracted from heading "China--History--Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Later Chou dynasty, 951-960" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Five Dynasties, and the one that laid the groundwork for reunification. Emperor Shizong reformed the army, curbed monastic landholding and campaigned successfully against the Southern Tang and the Khitan. His death left a child on the throne, and his general Zhao Kuangyin took power to found the Song.

Alfonso X, 1252-1284 (Kingdom of Castile.label: Alfonso X, 1252-1284
Alfonso X, 1252-1284 (Kingdom of Castile.prose:
[Castile, AD 1252–AD 1284] Alfonso X, 1252-1284. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso X, 1252-1284". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Learned King turned his court into a workshop of translation and compilation, producing the Siete Partidas law code, astronomical tables used across Europe, histories of Spain and the world, and the Cantigas de Santa María. He promoted Castilian over Latin for official writing, shaping the language itself. His ruinously expensive campaign to be elected Holy Roman Emperor failed, and he ended his reign deposed in all but name by his rebellious son.

Barons' War, 1263-1267 (England, AD 1263.label: Barons' War, 1263-1267
Barons' War, 1263-1267 (England, AD 1263.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1263–AD 1267] Barons' War, 1263-1267. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Barons' War, 1263-1267". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Simon de Montfort and a faction of English nobles took up arms against Henry III over his refusal to abide by the reforms he had sworn to at Oxford. After capturing the king at Lewes in 1264, Montfort ruled in his name and summoned a parliament that included townsmen as well as barons and knights — a precedent later cited in the growth of the Commons. Royal victory at Evesham in 1265 killed Montfort and dismembered his body, but the settlement that followed conceded much of what the rebels had demanded.

Uprising of 1357-1358 (France, AD 1357–A.label: Uprising of 1357-1358
Uprising of 1357-1358 (France, AD 1357–A.prose:
[Paris, AD 1357–AD 1358] Uprising of 1357-1358. Extracted from heading "Paris (France)--History--Uprising of 1357-1358". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With King John II a prisoner of the English after Poitiers, the kingdom's government broke down: the Paris merchants' provost Etienne Marcel seized control of the capital and forced reforms on the dauphin, while in the countryside north of Paris peasants rose in the bloody revolt known as the Jacquerie. Both movements were crushed within months, the Jacquerie with great slaughter and Marcel by assassination. The episode showed how badly the Hundred Years' War had strained French royal authority, and it hardened noble attitudes toward the peasantry for generations.

Charles II, 840-877 (France, AD 840–AD 8.label: Charles II, 840-877
Charles II, 840-877 (France, AD 840–AD 8.prose:
[France, AD 840–AD 877] Charles II, 840-877. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles II, 840-877". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The youngest son of Louis the Pious fought his brothers for a share of the Carolingian inheritance, settling it at Verdun in 843 with the western kingdom that became France. His reign was harried by Viking fleets on the Seine and Loire, bought off with tribute and eventually met with fortified bridges. He was a lavish patron of manuscripts and scholars, and took the imperial crown in 875; the concessions he made to his counts helped turn offices into hereditary lordships.

Brother-in-law of the previous emperor, Basiliscus drove Zeno out of Constantinople and held the throne for about twenty months. He alienated the capital by issuing an encyclical repudiating the Council of Chalcedon, lost the support of the church and the crowd, and was deposed when Zeno returned; he and his family were shut up in a Cappadocian fortress and left to die.

Wars with Persia, 1576-1639 (Turkey, AD.label: Wars with Persia, 1576-1639

A long contest between the Ottoman sultans and Safavid Iran, fought over Iraq, the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia and sharpened by the Sunni–Shia divide. Fortunes swung dramatically: the Ottomans seized Tabriz and Georgian territory, then Shah Abbas I reconquered almost everything, before Murad IV retook Baghdad in 1638. The Treaty of Zuhab fixed a frontier close to the modern Iraq–Iran border and held, more or less, for centuries.

Henry III, 1574-1589 (France, AD 1574–AD.label: Henry III, 1574-1589

Returning from Poland to a kingdom torn by religious war, he tried to steer between militant Catholics and Huguenots and was distrusted by both, mocked for his favourites and his court ceremonial. When the Catholic League forced him out of Paris he had the Duke of Guise assassinated, then allied with his Protestant heir Henry of Navarre to besiege his own capital. A friar stabbed him to death in camp, ending the Valois dynasty.

Christian IX, 1863-1906 (Denmark, AD 186.label: Christian IX, 1863-1906
Christian IX, 1863-1906 (Denmark, AD 186.prose:

His accession was the spark for the Second Schleswig War, in which Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864 — a defeat that shrank the country to roughly its modern shape. At home he backed conservative governments that ruled by provisional decree for two decades before finally conceding parliamentary rule in 1901. His children married into the British, Russian, Greek and Norwegian royal houses, earning him the nickname "father-in-law of Europe".

Tang dynasty, 618-907 (China, AD 618–AD.label: Tang dynasty, 618-907

Founded by the Li family after the Sui collapse, the Tang built a centralised bureaucracy on recruitment by examination and projected power across the Tarim Basin and into Korea. Its capital was a planned metropolis of a million people and a magnet for foreign religions and goods; Empress Wu Zetian ruled it as China's only reigning female emperor. After the An Lushan revolt the court survived on compromise with provincial commanders until peasant rebellion finished it.

Northern Expedition, 1926-1928 (China, A.label: Northern Expedition, 1926-1928
