Chiang Kai-shek led Nationalist armies north from Guangdong against the warlords who had carved up China since 1916, taking Wuhan, Shanghai and finally Beijing. Midway through the campaign he turned on his Communist allies in the bloody Shanghai purge of 1927, splitting the revolutionary coalition and beginning a civil war that ran for two decades. The result was a Nationalist government at Nanjing whose authority over much of the country remained more nominal than real.

William I, 1871-1888 (Germany, AD 1871–A.label: William I, 1871-1888
William I, 1871-1888 (Germany, AD 1871–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1871–AD 1888] William I, 1871-1888. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--William I, 1871-1888". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As the first emperor of a united Germany, Wilhelm presided over a state that within twenty years became Europe's leading industrial and military power. Real direction came from Bismarck, whose government fought the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf, banned socialist organisations, and then introduced the world's first national sickness, accident and old-age insurance. The old emperor's death opened the way to his grandson and the collapse of the Bismarckian system.

Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C (Eg.label: Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C
Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C (Eg.prose:

Ramesses III fought off Libyan invasions and the Sea Peoples, recording the battles on the walls of Medinet Habu, but his reign also saw the first recorded labour strike, by the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, and a harem conspiracy that may have killed him. The eight later Ramesses presided over inflation, failing harvests and the systematic looting of the royal tombs, documented in remarkable court papyri. By the end, the high priests of Amun at Thebes were effectively independent, and the New Kingdom dissolved.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Kyrgyzstan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Kyrgyzstan, AD 19.prose:
[Kyrgyzstan, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Kyrgyzstan--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD.label: Henry V, 1106-1125
Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1106–AD 1125] Henry V, 1106-1125. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry V, 1106-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Salian emperor came to power by deposing his own father, then spent years fighting the papacy over who could invest bishops with ring and staff. The struggle ended in the Concordat of Worms of 1122, a compromise that separated spiritual from secular investiture and set the pattern for church-state relations in Europe. His death without an heir opened the contest between Welf and Hohenstaufen families that shaped German politics for the next century.

Vladislaus II, 1138-1146 (Poland, AD 113.label: Vladislaus II, 1138-1146
Vladislaus II, 1138-1146 (Poland, AD 113.prose:
[Poland , AD 1138–AD 1146] Vladislaus II, 1138-1146. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus II, 1138-1146". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The eldest son of Bolesław III inherited the position of senior duke under his father's succession testament, meant to keep Poland united under one overlord. Instead his attempt to subdue his half-brothers failed, he was driven into exile in Germany, and the seniority principle collapsed almost at once. Poland spent the next 175 years split among rival branches of the Piast family.

Diadochi, 323-276 B.C (Macedonia, 322 BC.label: Diadochi, 323-276 B.C
Diadochi, 323-276 B.C (Macedonia, 322 BC.prose:

Alexander's generals spent nearly fifty years fighting over his empire, and the wars destroyed his family: his mother, wife and both sons were all killed. Attempts to hold the whole conquest together failed at battles like Ipsus, and the territory settled into rival Macedonian kingdoms in Egypt, Asia and the homeland itself. Macedonia was fought over, invaded by Gauls in 279, and only stabilised when Antigonus Gonatas secured the throne for his dynasty.

Anti-Kine-Killing Movement, 1880-1894 (I.label: Anti-Kine-Killing Movement, 1880-1894

Cow protection societies spread across north India and the Punjab, collecting signatures, prosecuting butchers and staging mass meetings against the slaughter of cattle by Muslims and by British army contractors. Backed by Arya Samaj preachers and rural notables, the campaign built one of the first mass-mobilising Hindu political networks, complete with printed tracts and touring lecturers. It also hardened religious boundaries, erupting in serious riots in 1893 that shaped communal politics for decades.

Sophia ruled Russia as regent for her young brother Ivan V and half-brother Peter, an unusual position for a woman in Muscovy, and governed with her favourite Vasily Golitsyn. Her government signed a permanent peace with Poland and the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Qing China, but two costly failed campaigns against the Crimean Tatars drained her support. Peter overthrew her in 1689 and confined her to a convent, beginning his own reign.

Charles II, 1665-1700 (Spain, AD 1665–AD.label: Charles II, 1665-1700

Physically frail and childless, the last Spanish Habsburg inherited at four and spent his life the object of court factions and foreign diplomacy. Spain's European position slipped as Louis XIV nibbled at the Netherlands and Franche-Comté, and the great question of the age became who would inherit the empire when he died. His final will left everything to a French Bourbon prince, triggering the War of the Spanish Succession and a general European conflict.

Anastasius I, 491-518 (Byzantine Empire,.label: Anastasius I, 491-518
Anastasius I, 491-518 (Byzantine Empire,.prose:

A former palace official chosen as emperor in his sixties, Anastasius overhauled Byzantine finance: he abolished the hated chrysargyron tax on trades, reformed the copper coinage into a usable small-change system, and left an enormous surplus in the treasury. He fought a war with Persia, fortified Dara, and built the Long Walls of Thrace. His Miaphysite sympathies provoked riots and Vitalian's revolt, leaving religious division as his main legacy.

Revolution, 1963-1974 (Guinea-Bissau, AD.label: Revolution, 1963-1974

Amílcar Cabral's PAIGC turned the swamps and forests of Portuguese Guinea into the most effective of the African liberation wars, running schools, clinics and courts in liberated zones while fighting. Portuguese generals admitted the war was unwinnable; Cabral was assassinated in 1973, months before the party declared independence unilaterally. The strain of this war more than any other pushed Portuguese officers into the coup that ended their own dictatorship.

Mieszko the Old, duke of Greater Poland, held the senior throne at Kraków during the era when Poland was split among Piast dukes. His heavy-handed rule, coin debasements and tight control of officials provoked the nobles and clergy, who expelled him in favour of his younger brother — an early demonstration that Polish magnates could unmake a ruler.

After the Central Powers drove the Russians out, the conquered Polish lands were split into a German zone around Warsaw and an Austro-Hungarian zone administered from Lublin. The occupiers requisitioned food, timber and labour, but also permitted Polish schools and courts and, in 1916, proclaimed a nominal Kingdom of Poland to recruit soldiers. Those half-measures gave Polish politicians institutions to seize when the empires collapsed in November 1918.

Spent his reign hammering the robber barons of the Île-de-France into submission, making the small royal domain around Paris genuinely governable for the first time. He allied with the towns and the Church, and his adviser Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis both shaped policy and wrote his life. He secured Aquitaine for his son by marriage to Eleanor just before his death, laying groundwork for the later expansion of Capetian power.

The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

Discontent with Roman taxation, procuratorial abuses and religious provocation exploded into open war; the rebels drove Roman forces from Jerusalem and struck their own coins, but fell into bitter factional fighting. Vespasian and then Titus reconquered the country, and in 70 the Temple was burned and Jerusalem destroyed, with the last holdouts at Masada falling in 73. The loss of the Temple transformed Judaism into a religion of synagogue, text and rabbinic law, and furnished Rome with the triumphal imagery of the Arch of Titus.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

Charles XIII, 1809-1818 (Sweden, AD 1809.label: Charles XIII, 1809-1818
Charles XIII, 1809-1818 (Sweden, AD 1809.prose:

An elderly, childless placeholder installed after officers deposed his nephew in a coup, he presided over the loss of Finland to Russia after six centuries of Swedish rule. In exchange Sweden got a new constitution dividing power between king and Riksdag that lasted until 1974, and Norway, seized from Denmark in 1814. Needing an heir, the Swedes elected a French marshal, Jean Baptiste Bernadotte, who ran the country long before he inherited the crown.

Inheriting the War of the Spanish Succession from his father, this emperor pushed the Habsburg cause hard, backing Marlborough and Prince Eugene in the campaigns that broke French power in Italy and the Low Countries. At home he sought terms with the Hungarian rebels of Ferenc Rakoczi. His sudden death from smallpox at thirty-two upended everything: his brother Charles inherited both Austria and the Spanish claim, and the allies, unwilling to see one man rule such an empire, began negotiating the peace of Utrecht.

Revolution, 1848-1849 (Slovenia, AD 1848.label: Revolution, 1848-1849
Revolution, 1848-1849 (Slovenia, AD 1848.prose:

The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

French occupation, 1803-1813 (Germany, A.label: French occupation, 1803-1813
French occupation, 1803-1813 (Germany, A.prose:

The Imperial Recess swept away ecclesiastical principalities and most free cities, consolidating hundreds of statelets into a few dozen; three years later the Holy Roman Empire was abolished and Napoleon's client states formed the Confederation of the Rhine. Satellite kingdoms like Westphalia received the Civil Code, religious equality and the end of serfdom, while conscription and the Continental System bred resentment. Defeat at Leipzig ended French control but left a simplified map and reform agenda that shaped nineteenth-century Germany.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Kentucky, AD 1775.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Kentucky, AD 1775.prose:

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

A Transylvanian prince elected king of Poland alongside Anna Jagiellon, remembered above all as a soldier. His campaigns drove Ivan the Terrible out of Livonia and secured the northern frontier, funded by a reformed army and newly organised registered Cossacks. He also founded the university at Vilnius, still one of the region's great institutions.

Henry II, Richard I and John ruled an empire stretching from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, held together by an itinerant court and constant war. Henry's reforms — royal justices touring the shires, juries, the writ system — laid the foundations of English common law, though his quarrel with Thomas Becket ended in murder in Canterbury Cathedral. John lost Normandy and Anjou to the French king and, taxed to the limit, faced a baronial revolt that produced Magna Carta in 1215.

The Ottoman government deported and destroyed its Armenian population, killing around a million people through massacres, forced marches into the Syrian desert and starvation. An ancient community was erased from most of Anatolia, and the survivors formed a worldwide diaspora. The events shaped the modern concept of genocide - Raphael Lemkin cited them when coining the word - and remain politically contested to this day.

Turkish rule, 1571-1878 (Cyprus, AD 1571.label: Turkish rule, 1571-1878

After the conquest from Venice the Latin church was dismantled and the Orthodox archbishop became the recognised leader of the Christian population, collecting taxes as well as souls. Muslim settlement created the island's mixed communities, and periodic revolts and heavy taxation marked the centuries. Britain took over the administration in 1878 while the Sultan retained nominal sovereignty.

A devastating epidemic, described by Bishop Cyprian of Carthage, swept the Roman world from the late 240s, reportedly killing thousands a day in the capital and carrying off at least one emperor. It struck alongside civil war, currency debasement and frontier invasions, thinning the army and the tax base during the Crisis of the Third Century. Christian communities won converts by caring for the sick, while the state blamed the disaster on neglect of the old gods and persecuted them for it.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

Raised to the throne by a janissary revolt after catastrophic defeats in Hungary, this sultan inherited an empire in retreat, with the Habsburgs taking Belgrade and rebellion spreading in the provinces. His reign is remembered chiefly for handing power to the grand vizier Fazıl Mustafa Köprülü, whose tax reforms and counterattack recovered Belgrade in 1690 before he fell in battle the following year.

From Ivan III to Boris Godunov, Moscow absorbed Novgorod and the other Russian principalities, threw off tribute to the Horde, and remade itself as an imperial capital with a new Kremlin and a claim to the Byzantine inheritance. Ivan IV took the title of tsar, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan, and opened Siberia to Russian expansion, while his terror and endless Livonian war exhausted the country. The line ended in dynastic failure and the Time of Troubles.

England's first undisputed queen regnant seized the throne from the supporters of Lady Jane Grey and set about undoing the Protestant Reformation, restoring papal authority and the Latin mass. Nearly three hundred Protestants were burned, including Archbishop Cranmer, which earned her the name Bloody Mary in later Protestant memory. Her marriage to Philip of Spain was deeply unpopular, it produced no child, and the war it dragged England into cost the loss of Calais, the last English foothold in France.

A cosmopolitan and unstable decade and a half, remembered for "Taishō democracy": party governments, mass movements, a lively press, and the modern girl in Western dress on the streets of Ginza. Japan profited from the First World War and joined the League of Nations as a great power, but economic slumps, the 1923 Kantō earthquake and rising anxiety about socialism set the stage for the militarism of the following reign.

A martial king who fought Sweden to a costly draw in the Northern Seven Years' War, then turned to profiting from the Sound dues and rebuilding. He raised Kronborg at Elsinore as a Renaissance showpiece guarding the strait, and famously gave the island of Hven and a generous income to Tycho Brahe, whose observatory at Uraniborg became the finest in Europe.

Charles XII, 1697-1718 (Sweden, AD 1697–.label: Charles XII, 1697-1718
Charles XII, 1697-1718 (Sweden, AD 1697–.prose:

Attacked at eighteen by a coalition of Denmark, Poland and Russia, he spent the rest of his life in the field and never returned to Stockholm. Brilliant early victories at Narva and elsewhere ended in disaster at Poltava, followed by five surreal years as a guest-prisoner of the Ottoman sultan. A bullet through the head at a Norwegian fortress ended both the king and Sweden's age as a great power.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Remembered as Pedro the Just, he rode a circuit of the kingdom hearing complaints and punishing corrupt officials, and clashed with the Church over clerical immunity. His reign is inseparable from the story of Inês de Castro, the Galician noblewoman his father had murdered: on taking the throne he hunted down her killers and had them executed, and built the paired tombs at Alcobaça that still face each other. A decade of peace and full treasuries left Portugal prosperous when his son Fernando inherited it.

The Grand Duchy was overrun in a day and, unlike other occupied states, was treated as German soil and attached to the Gau Moselland. French was banned, names were Germanised, and young men were conscripted into the Wehrmacht, prompting a general strike in 1942 that was answered with executions and deportations. The government-in-exile in London kept the country's legal existence alive until liberation in September 1944.

The Anglo-Irish Treaty split the independence movement, and former comrades in the IRA turned on each other over partition and the oath to the Crown. The pro-Treaty Free State government, better armed and backed by London, won, but at the cost of executions, assassinations including Michael Collins's, and bitterness that shaped Irish party politics for generations. Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael trace their origins directly to the two sides.

The count who defeated his mother's supporters, took the title of king and fought a long campaign against both Leon and the Almoravids to make Portugal a separate realm. With the help of passing crusader fleets he captured Lisbon in 1147, pushing the frontier to the Tagus. Papal recognition in 1179 confirmed the independence of the kingdom he had created.

Kublai Khan's accession turned the Mongol conquest of China into a Chinese-style empire, complete with a new capital at Dadu, a Chinese dynastic name and a grand extension of the Grand Canal. His authority was contested by rival Mongol khans, and his fleets failed disastrously against Japan and Java. A century later, plague, famine, ruinous paper currency and the Red Turban revolts destroyed the dynasty.

Revolt in the Peloponnese and the islands grew into a savage war of massacre and reprisal, with Ottoman forces reinforced by Egyptian troops who retook Missolonghi and overran the Morea. European philhellenes, Byron among them, made the Greek cause a romantic sensation, and the destruction of the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino by British, French and Russian squadrons decided the outcome. A small independent Greek kingdom emerged — the first successful nationalist secession from Ottoman rule, and a template for the Balkans.

Under Frederick Barbarossa, Henry VI and Frederick II the Staufen ruled Germany, imperial Italy and eventually Sicily, and pursued a vision of universal empire that brought them into repeated, ruinous conflict with the papacy and the Lombard cities. Their courts fostered chivalric culture, Minnesang, and in Frederick II's Palermo a famously cosmopolitan mix of Latin, Greek and Arabic learning. The dynasty's extinction left Germany without an effective king and its princes and towns permanently stronger.

A brief and troubled reign, remembered for concessions to leagues of angry nobles and for an ordinance offering serfs on royal lands their freedom in exchange for payment. He died suddenly, leaving a pregnant widow; the baby lived only days, and the crown passed to his brother rather than his daughter. That decision, justified afterwards by appeals to Salic law, barred women from the French throne and later helped trigger the Hundred Years' War.

The Tudor victory at Bosworth conventionally opens the modern era in England, followed by the break with Rome, the dissolution of the monasteries and the redistribution of church lands that remade the countryside. Civil war and the execution of a king in the 1640s, union with Scotland, and overseas trade and colonies set the stage for industrialisation, when coal, iron and cotton turned a largely rural society into the world's first urban industrial one. Empire, two world wars and post-war immigration and deindustrialisation complete the sequence.

American occupation, 1906-1909 (Cuba, AD.prose:

When a disputed election and Liberal revolt toppled President Estrada Palma, Washington invoked the Platt Amendment and installed Charles Magoon as provisional governor. American administrators reorganised the courts, public works and the army, and supervised new elections before withdrawing. The episode showed how thoroughly Cuban sovereignty was hedged by the right of US intervention.

Augustus's victory ended a century of civil war and replaced the Republic with rule by one man dressed in republican language. The next three centuries brought the Pax Romana: an integrated Mediterranean economy, mass urbanisation, citizenship extended to all free inhabitants in 212, and monumental building from Hadrian's Wall to the Euphrates. It ended in the crisis of the third century, when plague, inflation, frontier invasions and a rapid succession of soldier-emperors nearly broke the state.

Son-in-law of Emperor Sigismund, he inherited Hungary and Bohemia and was elected German king, briefly uniting the three crowns before dying of dysentery on campaign against the Ottomans. His election began an unbroken Habsburg grip on the imperial title that lasted until the eighteenth century.

Succeeding as a child, he lost the northern English counties his grandfather David I had gained, doing homage to Henry II and even campaigning with him in France. At home he faced repeated risings in Galloway and the Gaelic west, and continued the settlement of Anglo-Norman families on Scottish land. He died unmarried at twenty-three, leaving the crown to his brother William the Lion.

Seizing the throne from his twelve-year-old nephew, who vanished with his brother into the Tower, he ruled barely two years amid rumour and rebellion. Defeat and death at Bosworth ended both the Plantagenet dynasty and the Wars of the Roses, putting the Tudors in power and giving Shakespeare his most notorious villain. The discovery of his skeleton beneath a Leicester car park in 2012 confirmed the scoliosis of the hostile legend.

As Holy Roman Emperor he presided over a Germany of hundreds of near-sovereign principalities, working through the permanent Imperial Diet at Regensburg and rallying the princes against French expansion in the Rhineland. Habsburg victories over the Ottomans and the elevation of allies - the elector of Brandenburg to king in Prussia, the elector of Saxony to king of Poland - reshaped the political map of central Europe.

An Albanian officer in the Ottoman army made himself governor of Egypt and secured his position by massacring the Mamluk elite in the Cairo citadel in 1811. He built a conscript army and navy, monopolised long-staple cotton for export, founded factories, schools and medical services, and conquered Sudan and much of Syria before the European powers forced him back. His dynasty ruled Egypt until 1952, and the great mosque bearing his name still dominates the Cairo skyline.

The Peace of Westphalia restored him to a Lower Palatinate wrecked by thirty years of war, with a newly created eighth electorate to replace the one his father had lost. He rebuilt Heidelberg and revived its university, brought in settlers to repopulate emptied villages, and allowed unusual religious latitude. His daughter Liselotte's marriage into the French royal house later gave Louis XIV the pretext to claim the Palatinate and devastate it again.

A movement of martial-arts practitioners, the Yihetuan or 'Boxers', attacked missionaries, Chinese Christians and foreign property in north China, and the Qing court gambled on backing them. The siege of the Beijing legations brought an eight-nation expeditionary army that looted the capital and imposed a crushing indemnity. The humiliation discredited the dynasty and pushed it into late reforms that came too late to prevent the 1911 revolution.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

With French revolutionary rule rejected by Pasquale Paoli, the island was placed under the British crown as the Anglo-Corsican Kingdom, with a viceroy and an elected parliament. Nelson lost the sight of an eye at the siege of Calvi during its capture. The experiment lasted barely two years before French successes in Italy forced a British evacuation.

Made king as a baby when Mary, Queen of Scots was deposed, he survived kidnappings and rival regents to rule in his own right, curbing the power of the nobility and arguing for the divine right of kings in print. His inheritance of the English throne in 1603 united the crowns and shifted his court to London. The King James Bible and the plantation of Ulster both date from his reign.

Bombardment, 1944-1945 (United Kingdom,.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1944–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1944-1945. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Bombardment, 1944-1945". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From June 1944 the country was struck by pilotless V-1 flying bombs and then by V-2 rockets, which arrived without warning at supersonic speed and could not be intercepted. They killed thousands, triggered a second mass evacuation from London, and announced the age of the guided missile — the technology and many of the engineers passed straight into the Cold War rocket programmes.

Third Seminole War, 1855-1858 (Florida,.label: Third Seminole War, 1855-1858
Third Seminole War, 1855-1858 (Florida,.prose:
[Florida , AD 1855–AD 1858] Third Seminole War, 1855-1858. Extracted from heading "Seminole War, 3rd, 1855-1858". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1990. Note that alternate label "Seminole Wars" includes the First and Second Seminole Wars as well. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the wars to force Seminoles out of Florida began with surveying parties intruding on Billy Bowlegs's lands in the Big Cypress. It was fought as a guerrilla campaign of raids and army sweeps through swamp and hammock rather than pitched battles. Most surviving Seminoles were shipped west to Indian Territory, but a few hundred stayed hidden in the Everglades, ancestors of Florida's Seminole and Miccosukee communities today.

Saxon House, 919-1024 (Germany, AD 919–A.label: Saxon House, 919-1024
Saxon House, 919-1024 (Germany, AD 919–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 919–AD 1024] Saxon House, 919-1024. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Saxon House, 919-1024". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry the Fowler and his Ottonian successors turned the east Frankish kingdom into the dominant power of Latin Europe, breaking the Magyar raids at the Lechfeld in 955 and reviving the imperial title when Otto I was crowned in Rome in 962. Bishops and abbots were used as instruments of royal government, tying church and crown together in a bond that would explode into the Investiture Contest a century later. The dynasty's manuscripts, ivories and great churches mark a deliberate revival of Carolingian and Byzantine imperial style.

John VI, 1816-1826 (Portugal, AD 1816–AD.label: John VI, 1816-1826
John VI, 1816-1826 (Portugal, AD 1816–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1816–AD 1826] John VI, 1816-1826. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John VI, 1816-1826". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had fled Napoleon's armies to Rio de Janeiro in 1807 and became king there, ruling a transatlantic monarchy in which Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal with Portugal. Recalled by the Liberal Revolution of 1820, he returned to Lisbon and swore to a constitution, leaving his son Pedro in Brazil — who promptly declared independence. His last years were spent caught between constitutionalists and the absolutist plots of his wife and younger son Miguel.

Popes at Avignon, 1309-1378 (Vatican Cit.label: Popes at Avignon, 1309-1378
Popes at Avignon, 1309-1378 (Vatican Cit.prose:
[Papacy, Avignon, AD 1309–AD 1378] Popes at Avignon, 1309-1378. Spatial coverage: France, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papacy--History--1309-1378". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Seven successive popes governed the Church from the Rhône rather than Rome, building a fortified palace and an efficient, money-hungry bureaucracy under heavy French influence. Critics from Petrarch to Catherine of Siena denounced the move as a Babylonian captivity, and the papacy's prestige suffered even as its administration grew more sophisticated. Gregory XI's return to Rome was followed almost at once by the Great Schism, with rival popes in both cities for another forty years.

Insurrection, 1804-1813 (Serbia, AD 1804.label: Insurrection, 1804-1813
Insurrection, 1804-1813 (Serbia, AD 1804.prose:
[Serbia, AD 1804–AD 1813] Insurrection, 1804-1813. Extracted from heading "Serbia--History--Insurrection, 1804-1813". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Serbian villagers led by Karađorđe rose against the renegade janissaries who had seized control of the Belgrade pashalik, and the revolt grew into a war for autonomy from the Ottoman Empire. For a few years the rebels ran their own assembly, courts and school in Belgrade, with intermittent Russian support. When Russia made peace with the Sultan in 1812, Ottoman armies crushed the rising and its leaders fled, but the idea of a Serbian state survived.

Middle Ages, 843-1555 (Netherlands, AD 8.label: Middle Ages, 843-1555
Middle Ages, 843-1555 (Netherlands, AD 8.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 843–AD 1555] Middle Ages, 843-1555. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--Church history--To 1500". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. From the division of the Carolingian empire to the abdication of Charles V, the Low Countries grew from frontier counties and bishoprics into the richest urban region north of the Alps. Peasants and lords diked and drained the peat and marsh, creating the polder landscape; Bruges, Ghent, Antwerp and the Holland towns grew fat on cloth, herring and shipping. The Burgundian dukes gathered the separate provinces into one dynastic state, setting the stage for the revolt that followed.

Antirightist Campaign, 1957-1958 (China,.label: Antirightist Campaign, 1957-1958
Antirightist Campaign, 1957-1958 (China,.prose:
[China, AD 1957–AD 1958] Antirightist Campaign, 1957-1958. Extracted from heading "China--History--Antirightist Campaign, 1957-1958". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After briefly inviting criticism during the Hundred Flowers period, Mao turned on those who had spoken out, labelling hundreds of thousands of intellectuals, teachers, writers and officials as 'rightists'. Those denounced lost jobs and party membership and were often sent to labour camps or rural exile for two decades. The campaign silenced expert dissent just as the Great Leap Forward was launched, removing the very people who might have warned against it.

Papal Interdict, 1199-1200 (France, AD 1.label: Papal Interdict, 1199-1200
Papal Interdict, 1199-1200 (France, AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1199–AD 1200] Papal Interdict, 1199-1200. Extracted from "France--History--Papal Interdict, 1199-1200". Added to LCSH in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Innocent III suspended public worship across the French kingdom to force Philip II Augustus to take back his repudiated Danish wife, Ingeborg. Churches closed, the dead went unburied in consecrated ground and marriages could not be solemnised, punishing a whole population for a king's marital politics. Philip yielded enough to have the interdict lifted, but kept Ingeborg confined for another decade; the episode showed how far a determined pope would go to make sacraments an instrument of political pressure.

Charles IV, 1347-1378 (Germany, AD 1347–.label: Charles IV, 1347-1378
Charles IV, 1347-1378 (Germany, AD 1347–.prose:
[Germany , AD 1347–AD 1378] Charles IV, 1347-1378. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Charles IV, 1347-1378". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Luxembourg prince raised in Paris made Prague the capital of the Empire, founding its university in 1348, laying out the New Town and beginning the cathedral and the bridge that carries his name. His Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the imperial election in the hands of seven named princes, settling a question that had caused centuries of civil war and standing as constitutional law until 1806. He worked by diplomacy, marriage and purchase rather than campaigns, and left Bohemia the richest realm in central Europe.

Fernando I, 1367-1383 (Portugal, AD 1367.label: Fernando I, 1367-1383
Fernando I, 1367-1383 (Portugal, AD 1367.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1367–AD 1383] Fernando I, 1367-1383. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Fernando I, 1367-1383". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three costly wars against Castile over a claim to its throne left Portugal exhausted, and the king's alliance with England produced early treaties of the partnership that would become the world's longest-standing. His marriage to Leonor Teles and the betrothal of his only heir to the king of Castile raised the prospect of Portugal being absorbed by its neighbour. His death without a son opened the 1383-85 crisis, resolved by popular revolt, victory at Aljubarrota and the accession of the House of Aviz.

Albert I, 1298-1308 (Germany, AD 1298–AD.label: Albert I, 1298-1308
Albert I, 1298-1308 (Germany, AD 1298–AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1298–AD 1308] Albert I, 1298-1308. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Habsburg who seized the German throne by deposing and killing Adolf of Nassau in battle, then spent his reign clawing back crown lands and taxing the Rhine tolls, which set the electors and cities against him. He was murdered by his own nephew, and the crown passed out of Habsburg hands for a generation.

Allied occupation, 1945-1952 (Japan, AD.label: Allied occupation, 1945-1952
Allied occupation, 1945-1952 (Japan, AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 1945–AD 1952] Allied occupation, 1945-1952. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Allied occupation, 1945-1952". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

General MacArthur's headquarters governed a defeated Japan through its own bureaucracy, imposing a new constitution that renounced war and stripped the emperor of sovereignty. Land reform, union rights, votes for women and the breakup of the zaibatsu were pushed early; as the Cold War hardened, the emphasis shifted to economic recovery and anti-communism. The San Francisco peace treaty restored sovereignty while leaving American bases and a security alliance in place.

Christian III, 1537-1559 (Norway, AD 153.label: Christian III, 1537-1559
Christian III, 1537-1559 (Norway, AD 153.prose:
[Norway, AD 1537–AD 1559] Christian III, 1537-1559. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Christian III, 1537-1559". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Reformation reached Norway by conquest rather than persuasion: the last Catholic archbishop fled Trondheim with the shrine's treasures, and Nidaros lost its independent church province. In the same settlement Norway was declared a subordinate part of the Danish realm, its council abolished, and government conducted from Copenhagen. Church silver and monastic lands passed to the crown, and Danish became the written language of administration.

Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca..node: Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca. 650 B.C (Egypt, 1070 BC–649 BC)
Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca..label: Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca. 650 B.C
Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca..prose:
[Egypt, 1070 BC–649 BC] Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca. 650 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Third Intermediate Period, ca. 1071-ca. 650 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Egypt fractured after the New Kingdom: pharaohs at Tanis in the Delta ruled alongside a line of powerful Amun priest-generals at Thebes, and Libyan military families eventually took the throne outright. Political weakness went with striking artistic output, including elaborate bronze inlay work and lavishly decorated coffins for a new style of burial. The disunity invited outsiders, and Nubian kings from Kush swept north to rule the whole country before the Assyrians invaded.

Shunzhi, 1644-1661 (China, AD 1644–AD 16.label: Shunzhi, 1644-1661
Shunzhi, 1644-1661 (China, AD 1644–AD 16.prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1661] Shunzhi, 1644-1661. Extracted from heading "China--History--Shunzhi, 1644-1661". Added to LCSH in 2000. The Manchu conquest of China proper, run for most of it by the regent Dorgon in the name of a child emperor. Resistance in the south was ground down city by city, with notorious massacres at Yangzhou and Jiading, and the queue order forced Han men to adopt Manchu hairstyle as a mark of submission. The dynasty simultaneously adopted Ming institutions and the examination system, presenting itself as the legitimate heir to the mandate.

Richard I, 1189-1199 (England, AD 1189–A.label: Richard I, 1189-1199
Richard I, 1189-1199 (England, AD 1189–A.prose: [Great Britain, AD 1189–AD 1199] Richard I, 1189-1199. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Richard I, 1189-1199". Added to LCSH in 1986. Venetian rule, 1204-1669 (Crete, AD 1204.label: Venetian rule, 1204-1669
Venetian rule, 1204-1669 (Crete, AD 1204.prose:
[Crete (Greece), AD 1204–AD 1669] Venetian rule, 1204-1669. Extracted from heading "Crete (Greece)--History--Venetian rule, 1204-1669". Added to LCSH in 1990, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Venice bought and fought its way into Crete after the Fourth Crusade, ruling the island from Candia as its most valuable overseas colony, with Venetian nobles settled on confiscated estates and repeated Cretan revolts against them. Over time the two cultures fused, producing the Cretan school of icon painting that trained El Greco and a flowering of Greek literature in Italian metres. Its end came with the Cretan War and the twenty-one-year siege of Candia, one of the longest in European history.

Ismail, 1863-1879 (Egypt, AD 1863–AD 187.label: Ismail, 1863-1879
Ismail, 1863-1879 (Egypt, AD 1863–AD 187.prose:
[Egypt, AD 1863–AD 1879] Ismail, 1863-1879. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Ismail, 1863-1879". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and p.23 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Khedive Ismail spent lavishly to make Egypt 'part of Europe': the Suez Canal opened, Cairo gained boulevards and an opera house, railways and cotton exports boomed, and Egyptian armies pushed deep into Sudan. The money came from European loans at ruinous rates, and when the cotton boom collapsed the state went bankrupt, forcing the sale of Egypt's canal shares to Britain and the imposition of foreign debt controllers. Ismail's deposition at the sultan's behest set the stage for the Urabi revolt and the British occupation.

John II Comnenus, 1118-1143 (Byzantine E.label: John II Comnenus, 1118-1143
John II Comnenus, 1118-1143 (Byzantine E.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1118–AD 1143] John II Comnenus, 1118-1143. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--John II Comnenus, 1118-1143". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Praised even by hostile writers as the finest of the Komnenian emperors, he spent almost every campaigning season in the field. He annihilated the Pecheneg threat, checked the Hungarians and Serbs, recovered territory in Anatolia from the Danishmendids, and forced the Crusader prince of Antioch to acknowledge Byzantine overlordship. With his wife Piroska he founded the great Pantokrator monastery in Constantinople, part hospital, part imperial mausoleum.

Miloš Obrenović, 1814-1839 (Serbia, AD 1.label: Miloš Obrenović, 1814-1839
Miloš Obrenović, 1814-1839 (Serbia, AD 1.prose:
[Serbia, AD 1814–AD 1839] Miloš Obrenović, 1814-1839. Extracted from heading "Serbia--History--Miloš Obrenović, 1814-1839". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Miloš led the Second Serbian Uprising and then, by patient bargaining rather than battle, extracted from the sultan an autonomous principality with himself as hereditary prince. He built a state almost from nothing — borders, taxes, a church hierarchy, the first schools and printing press — while ruling as a shrewd autocrat and pig-trader, until the constitutionalist opposition forced his abdication.

Mahmud II, 1808-1839 (Turkey, AD 1808–AD.label: Mahmud II, 1808-1839
Mahmud II, 1808-1839 (Turkey, AD 1808–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1808–AD 1839] Mahmud II, 1808-1839. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mahmud II, 1808-1839". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruled through the loss of Greece, the near-secession of Egypt under Muhammad Ali, and Russian armies reaching Edirne — and answered by rebuilding the state from the top down. In 1826 he destroyed the Janissary corps outright, then created a European-style army, a modern ministry system, a state newspaper and a new dress code topped by the fez. His reforms laid the direct foundation for the Tanzimat era that followed.

Philip I, 1060-1108 (France, AD 1060–AD.label: Philip I, 1060-1108
Philip I, 1060-1108 (France, AD 1060–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1060–AD 1108] Philip I, 1060-1108. Extracted from heading "France--History--Philip I, 1060-1108". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long, unglamorous Capetian reign spent consolidating a small royal domain around Paris and Orléans while great magnates like the dukes of Normandy overshadowed the crown. Philip's excommunication over his abduction of Bertrade de Montfort kept him out of the First Crusade. Quiet accumulation of land and rights during these decades gave his successors the base for later royal power.

Pedro I, 1094-1104 (Kingdom of Aragon, A.label: Pedro I, 1094-1104
Pedro I, 1094-1104 (Kingdom of Aragon, A.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1094–AD 1104] Pedro I, 1094-1104. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Pedro I, 1094-1104". Added to LCSH in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruling Aragon and Pamplona together, he pushed the frontier down out of the Pyrenean valleys into the Ebro plain. His victory at Alcoraz in 1096 delivered Huesca, the first major Muslim city taken by the Aragonese and soon their capital, and Barbastro followed in 1100. He fought as a crusader in spirit and in fact, joining the Cid's campaigns near Valencia, and left the kingdom positioned for his brother Alfonso the Battler's conquest of Zaragoza.

Revolution, 1915-1916 (China, AD 1915–AD.label: Revolution, 1915-1916
Revolution, 1915-1916 (China, AD 1915–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1915–AD 1916] Revolution, 1915-1916. Extracted from heading "China--History--Revolution, 1915-1916". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Yuan Shikai, president of the young republic, had himself proclaimed emperor, and the backlash destroyed him. Yunnan rose in the National Protection War, province after province declared independence from Peking, and Yuan abandoned the throne within months and died soon after. His death removed the one figure holding the military together, and China slid into more than a decade of warlord rule.

Insurrection, 1849-1851 (Cuba, AD 1849–A.label: Insurrection, 1849-1851
Insurrection, 1849-1851 (Cuba, AD 1849–A.prose:
[Cuba, AD 1849–AD 1851] Insurrection, 1849-1851. Extracted from heading "Cuba--History--Insurrection, 1849-1851". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Narciso López, a Venezuelan-born former Spanish officer, launched a series of filibustering expeditions from the United States to detach Cuba from Spain, recruiting American volunteers and flying the flag he designed — still Cuba's today. The landings drew little local support and López was garroted in Havana in 1851, but the episodes exposed how closely Cuban independence was entangled with American annexationist ambitions and the politics of slavery.

Edward VII, 1901-1910 (United Kingdom, A.label: Edward VII, 1901-1910
Edward VII, 1901-1910 (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1901–AD 1910] Edward VII, 1901-1910. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward VII, 1901-1910". Added to LCSH in 1986. After sixty years waiting as Prince of Wales, Edward gave his name to a decade of conspicuous wealth, motor cars, country-house weekends and steadily rising social tension. He worked at royal diplomacy, helping to warm relations with France in the Entente Cordiale as Europe divided into armed blocs. Behind the glamour lay suffrage campaigns, labour unrest and a constitutional clash over the House of Lords.

Ivan Asen I, 1186-1196 (Bulgaria, AD 118.label: Ivan Asen I, 1186-1196
Ivan Asen I, 1186-1196 (Bulgaria, AD 118.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1186–AD 1196] Ivan Asen I, 1186-1196. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Ivan Asen I, 1186-1196". Appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987, added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With his brother Peter, Ivan Asen led a rebellion of Bulgarians and Vlachs against Byzantine taxation, defeated successive imperial armies and restored an independent Bulgarian state with its capital at Tarnovo. The Second Bulgarian Empire he founded would dominate the Balkans in the following century. He was murdered by a boyar conspirator at the height of his success.

Siege, 1940-1943 (Malta, AD 1940–AD 1943.label: Siege, 1940-1943
Siege, 1940-1943 (Malta, AD 1940–AD 1943.prose:
[Malta, AD 1940–AD 1943] Siege, 1940-1943. Extracted from heading "Malta--History--Siege, 1940-1943". Added to LCSH and revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Malta lay astride the Axis supply route to North Africa, and Italian and German aircraft bombed it almost continuously, at times more heavily than anywhere else on earth. Islanders lived in rock shelters on starvation rations while convoys were sunk trying to reach them; the arrival of the tanker Ohio, lashed between destroyers, in August 1942 kept the island fighting. Submarines and aircraft flying from Malta savaged Rommel's supplies, and the whole population was awarded the George Cross.

War of Independence, 1285-1371 (Scotland.label: War of Independence, 1285-1371
War of Independence, 1285-1371 (Scotland.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1285–AD 1371] War of Independence, 1285-1371. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--War of Independence, 1285-1371". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.101 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of Alexander III and then his infant heiress left Scotland without a king and open to Edward I's claim of overlordship, touching off generations of war. Wallace's revolt, Robert Bruce's victory at Bannockburn and the Declaration of Arbroath forced England eventually to recognise Scottish independence, though fighting flared again under David II. The struggle forged a durable sense of Scottish nationhood and the Auld Alliance with France, and ended with the first Stewart king on the throne.

Murad IV, 1623-1640 (Turkey, AD 1623–AD.label: Murad IV, 1623-1640
Murad IV, 1623-1640 (Turkey, AD 1623–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1623–AD 1640] Murad IV, 1623-1640. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Murad IV, 1623-1640". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Enthroned as a child amid janissary revolts, he seized personal control in his twenties and ruled by terror, executing officials, banning tobacco, coffee and alcohol and reportedly prowling the streets in disguise to enforce it. He restored fiscal discipline and army obedience, then led the campaigns that retook Baghdad from the Safavids in 1638. The treaty he signed at Zuhab fixed the Ottoman-Iranian border close to where the Iraq-Iran line runs today.

Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C (Greec.node: Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C (Greec.label: Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C
Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C (Greec.prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Geometric period, ca. 900-700 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Greece recovering after the dark age, with Athens leading a pottery style of strict bands and meanders that eventually admitted human figures — chariot processions, laid-out corpses, rowers and warriors. Sanctuaries, bronze dedications and hero cults multiplied, the alphabet arrived from Phoenicia, and Greeks founded settlements from Ischia to Syracuse. The city-state and the earliest written Greek poetry both belong to these two centuries.

Civil War, 1993-2005 (Burundi, AD 1993–A.label: Civil War, 1993-2005
Civil War, 1993-2005 (Burundi, AD 1993–A.prose:
[Burundi, AD 1993–AD 2005] Civil War, 1993-2005. Extracted from heading "Burundi--History--Civil War, 1993-2005". Added to LCSH in 2011, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The assassination of Burundi's first democratically elected Hutu president set off a decade of massacres and guerrilla warfare between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebel movements, killing some 300,000 people and driving hundreds of thousands into exile. Fighting spilled across borders and became entangled with the Rwandan genocide and the wars in eastern Congo. The Arusha peace process gradually brought rebel factions into a power-sharing government, ending with elections and a former guerrilla leader as president.

Rebellion, 1831-1832 (Brazil, AD 1831–AD.label: Rebellion, 1831-1832
Rebellion, 1831-1832 (Brazil, AD 1831–AD.prose: [Brazil, AD 1831–AD 1832] Rebellion, 1831-1832. Extracted from heading "Brazil, Northeast--History--Rebellion, 1831-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

United Kingdom, 1815-1822 (Brazil, AD 18.label: United Kingdom, 1815-1822
United Kingdom, 1815-1822 (Brazil, AD 18.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1815–AD 1822] United Kingdom, 1815-1822. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--United Kingdom, 1815-1822". Added to LCSH in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the Portuguese court exiled in Rio after fleeing Napoleon, Brazil was raised from colony to a kingdom equal in status with Portugal. Ports opened to foreign trade, printing presses and academies appeared, and Rio functioned as the seat of a European monarchy. Portuguese attempts to reverse this after the king's return home pushed the resident prince Pedro to declare independence in 1822.

Eric XIV, 1560-1568 (Sweden, AD 1560–AD.label: Eric XIV, 1560-1568
Eric XIV, 1560-1568 (Sweden, AD 1560–AD.prose:

The eldest son of Gustav Vasa inherited a newly consolidated Sweden and pushed it into the Baltic, seizing Reval and fighting the long Northern Seven Years' War against Denmark. A learned, artistically gifted and deeply suspicious man, he courted Elizabeth I of England unsuccessfully and then descended into paranoia, personally taking part in the killing of imprisoned Sture nobles. His brothers deposed him in 1568; he died in captivity, probably poisoned.

Louis I, 814-840 (Germany, AD 814–AD 840.label: Louis I, 814-840
Louis I, 814-840 (Germany, AD 814–AD 840.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 814–AD 840] Louis I, 814-840. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Charlemagne's only surviving son inherited the whole Frankish empire and tried to keep it whole, decreeing in 817 that his eldest son would rule above his brothers. The birth of a fourth son wrecked the plan and plunged the empire into revolts in which Louis was twice deposed by his own children, once forced into public penance. The wars he failed to end concluded three years after his death with the Treaty of Verdun, splitting the Carolingian world into the kernels of France and Germany.

Anglo-French War, 1793-1802 (France, AD.label: Anglo-French War, 1793-1802
Anglo-French War, 1793-1802 (France, AD.prose:
[Europe, France, AD 1793–AD 1802] Anglo-French War, 1793-1802. Spatial coverage: Europe, France. Extracted from heading "Anglo-French War, 1793-1802". Added to LCSH and revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain entered the wars of the French Revolution after the execution of Louis XVI and the French move into the Low Countries, and stayed at war for nine years, funding coalitions on the continent while its navy swept French shipping from the seas. Nelson's victories at the Nile and Copenhagen secured British command of the Mediterranean and stranded Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition. The Peace of Amiens in 1802 proved only a fourteen-month breathing space before the Napoleonic Wars.

Bourbon Restoration, 1814-1868 (Spain, A.label: Bourbon Restoration, 1814-1868
Bourbon Restoration, 1814-1868 (Spain, A.prose:
[Spain, AD 1814–AD 1868] Bourbon Restoration, 1814-1868. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Bourbon Restoration, 1814-1868". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ferdinand VII returned from French captivity, tore up the liberal Constitution of 1812 and restored absolute rule, setting off half a century of struggle between liberals and reactionaries. Most of Spain's American empire broke away during these decades, and disputes over the succession fed the Carlist civil wars. The reign of Isabella II ended in the 1868 revolution that briefly drove the dynasty out.

Diocletian, 284-305 (Roman Empire, AD 28.label: Diocletian, 284-305
Diocletian, 284-305 (Roman Empire, AD 28.prose:
[Rome, AD 284–AD 305] Diocletian, 284-305. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Diocletian, 284-305". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Diocletian ended fifty years of usurpations and invasions by rebuilding the empire from the top down: power was shared among four rulers, provinces were multiplied and grouped into dioceses, the army was enlarged and the tax system rebuilt on regular assessments. His Edict on Maximum Prices tried and failed to control inflation, and his final years brought the most systematic persecution Christians had yet faced. He then did what no emperor had done — abdicated and retired to his palace at Split, leaving a system that fell apart within a year of his death.

Tamoio Confederation, 1554-1567 (Brazil,.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1554–AD 1567] Tamoio Confederation, 1554-1567. Extracted from heading "Tamoio Confederation, 1554-1567". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2016. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Tupinambá peoples around Guanabara Bay and the coast to the south banded together to resist Portuguese enslavement and land seizure, allying with the French colonists of France Antarctique. For over a decade the confederation held the region, killing settlers and blockading Portuguese positions. Its defeat, aided by Jesuit-brokered splits among the indigenous groups, cleared the way for the expulsion of the French and the founding of Rio de Janeiro.

Konrad III, 1138-1152 (Germany, AD 1138–.label: Konrad III, 1138-1152
Konrad III, 1138-1152 (Germany, AD 1138–.prose:
[Germany , AD 1138–AD 1152] Konrad III, 1138-1152. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Konrad III, 1138-1152". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Hohenstaufen to rule Germany, elected against Welf opposition and never crowned emperor in Rome. His feud with Henry the Proud and the Welf dynasty hardened into the Guelph–Ghibelline division that split German and Italian politics for generations. He led the German army on the disastrous Second Crusade, and on his death the crown passed to his far abler nephew, Frederick Barbarossa.

Civil War, 1876-1877 (Colombia, AD 1876–.label: Civil War, 1876-1877
Civil War, 1876-1877 (Colombia, AD 1876–.prose:
[Colombia, AD 1876–AD 1877] Civil War, 1876-1877. Extracted from heading "Colombia--History--Civil War, 1876-1877". Added to LCSH in 2008, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as the war of the schools, it began when Conservatives and clergy in Cauca and Antioquia rose against the Liberal government's secular, compulsory public education. Liberal forces won at Los Chancos and Garrapata, confirming radical control and bringing fresh anticlerical reprisals. The defeat pushed Conservatives toward the alliance with dissident Liberals that produced Rafael Núñez's Regeneration a few years later.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Uzbekistan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Uzbekistan, AD 19.prose:
[Uzbekistan, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Uzbekistan--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Civil War, 1999-2003 (Liberia, AD 1999–A.label: Civil War, 1999-2003
Civil War, 1999-2003 (Liberia, AD 1999–A.prose:
[Liberia, AD 1999–AD 2003] Civil War, 1999-2003. Extracted from heading "Liberia--History--Civil War, 1999-2003". Added to LCSH and revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A second round of warfare engulfed Liberia as rebel coalitions closed in on Monrovia and Charles Taylor's government, itself born of the earlier war, collapsed. Child soldiers, mutilation and plunder of timber and diamonds characterised the fighting, which bled into neighbouring Sierra Leone. Taylor's exile and later conviction for war crimes opened the way to a transitional government and Africa's first elected woman head of state.

Gempei Wars, 1180-1185 (Japan, AD 1180–A.label: Gempei Wars, 1180-1185
Gempei Wars, 1180-1185 (Japan, AD 1180–A.prose:
[Japan, AD 1180–AD 1185] Gempei Wars, 1180-1185. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Gempei Wars, 1180-1185". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A five-year civil war between the Taira, who had seized control of the imperial court, and the Minamoto clan and their eastern warrior allies. It ended with the Taira destroyed in the sea battle of Dan-no-ura and the child emperor Antoku drowned with them. Minamoto no Yoritomo built a separate military government at Kamakura from the victory, beginning nearly seven centuries of rule by shoguns, and the war became the great subject of Japanese epic in the Tale of the Heike.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Indiana, AD 1775–.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Indiana, AD 1775–.prose:
[Indiana, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Indiana--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.57 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Christian VI, 1730-1746 (Denmark, AD 173.label: Christian VI, 1730-1746
Christian VI, 1730-1746 (Denmark, AD 173.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1730–AD 1746] Christian VI, 1730-1746. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian VI, 1730-1746". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A devout Pietist, he shut the theatres, banned Sunday amusements and made confirmation compulsory in 1736, backing it with a drive for rural schools so children could read the catechism. In 1733 he tied peasants to the estates where they were born, the stavnsbånd, to guarantee landowners a supply of soldiers and labour. Despite his austerity he spent lavishly on building, replacing the old castle with the first Christiansborg Palace.

The rise of the Zulu kingdom under Shaka set off a chain of wars, displacements and state-building across southern Africa. Refugee and raiding armies such as Soshangane's Nguni followers pushed north into Mozambique, where they founded the Gaza kingdom and dominated the Portuguese trading settlements along the coast. Whole regions were depopulated while new centralised kingdoms formed, redrawing the political map that European colonisers would encounter a generation later.

Urraca, 1109-1126 (Kingdom of Castile, A.label: Urraca, 1109-1126
Urraca, 1109-1126 (Kingdom of Castile, A.prose:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1109–AD 1126] Urraca, 1109-1126. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Urraca, 1109-1126". Urraca inherited León-Castile from her father Alfonso VI and ruled in her own right, the first woman to do so in a Christian Spanish kingdom. Her marriage to Alfonso the Battler of Aragon was meant to unite the realms but collapsed into open war, with bishops, nobles and townsmen switching sides and Galicia backing her young son. She held the kingdom together long enough to pass it to him as Alfonso VII, who would claim the title of emperor.

Leo VI, 886-911 (Byzantine Empire, AD 88.label: Leo VI, 886-911
Leo VI, 886-911 (Byzantine Empire, AD 88.prose:

Nicknamed 'the Wise', he oversaw the completion of the Basilika, a vast Greek recasting of Justinian's law that remained the empire's legal foundation for centuries, and issued the Book of the Eparch regulating Constantinople's guilds. His reign saw heavy losses to Arab raiders, including the sack of Thessalonica in 904. His four marriages, undertaken in the search for an heir, provoked a bitter church crisis and only ended when the future Constantine VII was legitimised.

Boris III, 1918-1943 (Bulgaria, AD 1918–.label: Boris III, 1918-1943
Boris III, 1918-1943 (Bulgaria, AD 1918–.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1918–AD 1943] Boris III, 1918-1943. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Boris III, 1918-1943". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the throne with his country defeated and stripped of territory, survived coups, political assassinations and peasant revolt, and by the mid-1930s ruled through a personal, royal dictatorship. Aligning with Germany brought back Macedonia and Thrace without much fighting, but he refused to send troops against the Soviet Union and, under public and parliamentary pressure, blocked the deportation of Bulgaria's own Jews; he died abruptly after a meeting with Hitler, leaving a child heir and a country facing occupation.

Ludwig IV, 1294-1347 (Germany, AD 1294–A.label: Ludwig IV, 1294-1347
Ludwig IV, 1294-1347 (Germany, AD 1294–A.prose:

Louis the Bavarian rose from ruling a divided Wittelsbach duchy to become king of Germany and, in 1328, Holy Roman Emperor. His long fight with the Avignon papacy, which excommunicated him and denied his election, drew thinkers like Marsilius of Padua and William of Ockham to his court to argue that imperial authority came from the electors, not the pope. That argument was written into the constitutional practice of the empire.

Fuad, 1917-1936 (Egypt, AD 1917–AD 1936).label: Fuad, 1917-1936
Fuad, 1917-1936 (Egypt, AD 1917–AD 1936).prose:
[Egypt, AD 1917–AD 1936] Fuad, 1917-1936. Extracted from heading "Egypt-- History--Fuad, 1917-1936". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.30 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fuad ruled first as sultan and then, after Britain's unilateral declaration of 1922, as king of a nominally independent Egypt still occupied by British troops. His reign was a three-way struggle between the palace, the nationalist Wafd party and the British Residency, with constitutions granted, suspended and rewritten as the balance shifted. The unresolved questions of Sudan, the Suez Canal and foreign privilege passed to his son Farouk and poisoned Egyptian politics until the 1952 revolution.

Louis V, 986-987 (France, AD 986–AD 987).label: Louis V, 986-987
Louis V, 986-987 (France, AD 986–AD 987).prose:
[France, AD 986–AD 987] Louis V, 986-987. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis V, 986-987". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Carolingian ruler of the West Franks, on the throne barely a year before dying childless after a hunting accident. The magnates passed over his uncle and elected Hugh Capet instead, beginning a dynasty that would hold the French crown in the direct or collateral line for eight centuries.

Elizabeth II, 1952- (United Kingdom, AD.label: Elizabeth II, 1952-
Elizabeth II, 1952- (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1952–AD 2015] Elizabeth II, 1952-. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Elizabeth II, 1952-". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign that began with rationing still in force and ended in the age of the internet, spanning the dismantling of the British Empire and the transformation of the Commonwealth into a voluntary association. The monarchy survived by shedding political power and remaking itself as a televised national institution, from the coronation broadcast of 1953 onward. Her longevity made her the constant against which fifteen prime ministers and enormous social change were measured.

Spartan and Theban Supremacies, 404-362.node: Spartan and Theban Supremacies, 404-362 B.C (Greece, 403 BC–361 BC)
Spartan and Theban Supremacies, 404-362.label: Spartan and Theban Supremacies, 404-362 B.C

[Greece, 403 BC–361 BC] Spartan and Theban Supremacies, 404-362 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Spartan and Theban Supremacies, 404-362 B.C". Victory over Athens left Sparta dominant, but its garrisons and harmosts made it widely hated, and Persian gold funded rivals against it. Epaminondas shattered the myth of Spartan invincibility at Leuctra in 371 and freed Messenia, breaking Sparta's economic base forever. Thebes' own supremacy died with him at Mantinea, leaving a power vacuum that Macedon would fill within a generation.

Persia's seizure of Herat, which Britain regarded as a buffer protecting India, brought a British expeditionary force ashore in the Gulf at Bushehr and Khorramshahr. Persia capitulated quickly and, by the Treaty of Paris, renounced all claim to Herat and recognised Afghan independence. The episode fixed Afghanistan as the separate cushion state at the heart of the Anglo-Russian 'Great Game'.

While Trajan's armies were fighting in Mesopotamia, Jewish communities rose in Cyrene, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia in a series of ferocious revolts. Roman suppression, associated with the general Lusius Quietus, devastated the ancient Jewish populations of Alexandria, Cyrenaica and Cyprus. The revolt helped force Rome's retreat from its eastern conquests and set the stage for the Bar Kokhba war a generation later.

Sikh War, 1845-1846 (India, AD 1845–AD 1.label: Sikh War, 1845-1846
Sikh War, 1845-1846 (India, AD 1845–AD 1.prose:

After Ranjit Singh's death the Lahore court collapsed into faction and its army crossed the Sutlej, meeting the East India Company in a series of brutally close-run battles at Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal and Sobraon. British victory brought the Treaty of Lahore: a huge indemnity, a shrunken army, the loss of the Jalandhar Doab, and Kashmir sold off to Gulab Singh. A British resident now sat in Lahore, and full annexation followed after a second war three years later.
