Two rival imperial lines, one installed in Kyoto by the Ashikaga shoguns and one holding out in the mountains of Yoshino, each claiming the throne and the regalia. Six decades of shifting warfare let provincial military governors accumulate land and power at the expense of the court and the old estates. Reunification under Ashikaga Yoshimitsu left the emperors as figureheads and the shoguns as real rulers - and inspired the war tales and the beginnings of Noh theatre.

Zrinski-Frankopan Conspiracy, 1664-1671.label: Zrinski-Frankopan Conspiracy, 1664-1671
Zrinski-Frankopan Conspiracy, 1664-1671.prose:
[Croatia, AD 1664–AD 1671] Zrinski-Frankopan Conspiracy, 1664-1671. Extracted from heading "Zrinski-Frankopan Conspiracy, Croatia, 1664-1671". Added to LCSH in 2003, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Croatian and Hungarian nobles, furious that Vienna had signed a humiliating peace with the Ottomans after winning the battle of Saint Gotthard, plotted to break free of Habsburg rule and sought backing from France, Venice and even the Sultan. The plan collapsed; Petar Zrinski and Fran Krsto Frankopan were beheaded at Wiener Neustadt and their vast estates confiscated, wiping out two of Croatia's greatest noble houses. Their execution became a founding episode of Croatian national memory in the nineteenth century.

Civil War, 1996-2006 (Nepal, AD 1996–AD.label: Civil War, 1996-2006
Civil War, 1996-2006 (Nepal, AD 1996–AD.prose:
[Nepal, AD 1996–AD 2006] Civil War, 1996-2006. Extracted from heading "Nepal--History--Civil War, 1996-2006". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Maoist rebels launched a 'People's War' from Nepal's western hills, building parallel governments in the countryside while the army held the towns; around 17,000 people died. The palace massacre of 2001 and a royal power grab drained support for the monarchy, and mass street protests eventually forced the king to yield. The peace deal brought the Maoists into parliament and led to the abolition of the world's last Hindu kingdom.

Bombardment, 1940-1944 (Naples, AD 1940–.label: Bombardment, 1940-1944
Bombardment, 1940-1944 (Naples, AD 1940–.prose:
[Naples (Italy), AD 1940–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1940-1944. Extracted from heading "Naples (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1940-1944". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The most heavily bombed city in Italy, struck first by British raids and then by hundreds of American attacks on its port and rail yards, which killed thousands and drove much of the population into caves and cellars. The wreckage, hunger and German reprisals that followed Italy's armistice provoked the popular uprising of the Four Days of Naples in September 1943, which drove the Germans out just before the Allies arrived.

Revolution, 1863-1864 (Lithuania, AD 186.label: Revolution, 1863-1864
Revolution, 1863-1864 (Lithuania, AD 186.prose:
[Lithuania, AD 1863–AD 1864] Revolution, 1863-1864. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--Revolution, 1863-1864". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The January Uprising against Russian rule was more radical here than in Poland, drawing in peasants freed only two years earlier and led in part by Konstanty Kalinowski, who published an underground paper in Lithuanian-Belarusian peasant speech. Governor Muravyov, remembered as 'the Hangman', crushed it with executions, mass deportations to Siberia and the confiscation of gentry estates. Russia then banned printing Lithuanian in Latin letters, producing forty years of book smuggling that turned literacy itself into national resistance.

István II, 1116-1131 (Hungary, AD 1116–A.label: István II, 1116-1131
István II, 1116-1131 (Hungary, AD 1116–A.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1116–AD 1131] István II, 1116-1131. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--István II, 1116-1131". Added LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Stephen II inherited the Hungarian throne as a teenager and spent his reign fighting Bohemians, Venetians and Byzantines, losing ground in Dalmatia. He died childless, and the crown passed to his blinded cousin Béla, a legacy of the dynastic mutilations of the previous generation.

Sino-Japanese War, 1937-1945 (Japan, AD.label: Sino-Japanese War, 1937-1945
Sino-Japanese War, 1937-1945 (Japan, AD.prose:
[Japan, China, AD 1937–AD 1945] Sino-Japanese War, 1937-1945. Spatial coverage: China, Japan. Extracted from heading "Sino-Japanese War, 1937-1945". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A clash at the Marco Polo Bridge escalated into full-scale invasion, with Japanese forces taking Shanghai, Nanjing and much of the coast and interior while Chinese governments withdrew to Chongqing. The massacres at Nanjing, the bombing of civilian cities and the biological warfare programme made it one of the most destructive campaigns of the century. After Pearl Harbor it merged into the wider Pacific War, and its memory still shapes relations between the two countries.

Cabanagem, 1835-1840 (Brazil, AD 1835–AD.label: Cabanagem, 1835-1840
Cabanagem, 1835-1840 (Brazil, AD 1835–AD.prose:
[Pará (Brazil), AD 1835–AD 1840] Cabanagem, 1835-1840. Extracted from heading "Pará (Brazil : State)--History--Cabanagem, 1835-1840". Added to LCSH in 1989, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the bloodiest revolts in Brazilian history, when the poor of the Amazon - riverbank labourers, Indigenous people and free blacks living in the palm-thatched cabanas that gave the movement its name - rose against the landowners and merchants of Belém and twice took the city. Erupting during the fragile Regency, it briefly severed the Amazon province from the empire. Imperial forces retook the region with extraordinary savagery, and perhaps a third of Grão-Pará's population died.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman rule in the west and the Renaissance saw Latin Christendom take shape: monasteries preserved and reworked classical learning, kingdoms hardened into states, and lords, peasants and towns settled into new legal relationships. Population and cultivated land grew steadily until plague and famine reversed it in the fourteenth century. Cathedrals, universities, guilds, parliaments and the vernacular literatures of Europe all date from this span.

Fyodor I, 1584-1598 (Russia, AD 1584–AD.label: Fyodor I, 1584-1598
Fyodor I, 1584-1598 (Russia, AD 1584–AD.prose:
[Russia , AD 1584–AD 1598] Fyodor I, 1584-1598. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Fyodor I, 1584-1598". Added to LCSH and revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The pious and sickly son of Ivan the Terrible reigned while his brother-in-law Boris Godunov effectively governed. The Russian church won its own patriarchate in 1589, peasants' freedom of movement was further restricted, and a war with Sweden recovered Baltic ground lost by Ivan. Fyodor died childless, extinguishing the Rurikid dynasty that had ruled for seven centuries and opening the way to the Time of Troubles.

Alfonso V, 1416-1458 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: Alfonso V, 1416-1458
Alfonso V, 1416-1458 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1416–AD 1458] Alfonso V, 1416-1458. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Alfonso V, 1416-1458". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Magnanimous spent most of his reign away from Spain, fighting a twenty-year campaign to win Naples, which he entered in triumph in 1442. From there he ruled a Mediterranean empire stretching from Sicily and Sardinia to Catalonia and made his court a magnet for humanist scholars. His absence left Aragon and Catalonia to deputies and mounting social tension.

War of 1807-1814 (Norway, AD 1807–AD 181.label: War of 1807-1814
War of 1807-1814 (Norway, AD 1807–AD 181.prose:
[Norway, AD 1807–AD 1814] War of 1807-1814. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--War of 1807-1814". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Dragged into the Napoleonic wars when Britain seized the Danish fleet, Norway was cut off by the Royal Navy's blockade from the grain it imported from Denmark, and years of hunger followed. When the losing side was carved up, the Treaty of Kiel handed Norway to Sweden, but Norwegians refused to be transferred and wrote their own constitution at Eidsvoll in 1814. A short Swedish campaign forced a union of crowns, yet the constitution survived and became the foundation of the modern Norwegian state.

Sebastião, 1557-1578 (Portugal, AD 1557–.label: Sebastião, 1557-1578
Sebastião, 1557-1578 (Portugal, AD 1557–.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1557–AD 1578] Sebastião, 1557-1578. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Sebastião, 1557-1578". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Sebastian, 1557-1578" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sebastian came to the Portuguese throne as a three-year-old and grew into a devout, crusading young king who dreamed of conquest in North Africa. In 1578 he led the flower of the Portuguese nobility into Morocco and was killed at Alcácer Quibir, where the army was destroyed and thousands were held for ransom. With no heir, the crown passed within two years to Philip II of Spain, and for generations Portuguese believed the lost king would return - a messianic hope that became known as Sebastianism.

Qianlong, 1736-1795 (China, AD 1736–AD 1.label: Qianlong, 1736-1795
Qianlong, 1736-1795 (China, AD 1736–AD 1.prose:
[China, AD 1736–AD 1795] Qianlong, 1736-1795. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qianlong, 1736-1795". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Ch'ien lung, 1736-1795" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sixty years on the throne, ten self-proclaimed 'great campaigns', and an empire stretched to its widest limits across Central Asia and the southwest frontier. The emperor's tastes shaped the look of Qing luxury: jade carvings, enamelled porcelain, European-style palaces at the Yuanmingyuan, and a colossal literary compilation project that doubled as a purge of subversive texts. He abdicated to avoid outreigning his grandfather, leaving a treasury drained by war and a court dominated by the corrupt favourite Heshen.

Tatar Conquest, 1643-1644 (China, AD 164.label: Tatar Conquest, 1643-1644
Tatar Conquest, 1643-1644 (China, AD 164.prose:
[China, AD 1643–AD 1644] Tatar Conquest, 1643-1644. Extracted from heading "China--History--Tartar Conquest, 1643-1644". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The moment the Ming dynasty fell: rebel armies under Li Zicheng took Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself, after which a Ming general opened the Shanhai Pass to the Manchu forces European writers called Tartars. The Qing entered the capital and began a conquest of China that would last another four decades and a dynasty that lasted until 1912.

Mustafa III, 1757-1773 (Turkey, AD 1757–.label: Mustafa III, 1757-1773
Mustafa III, 1757-1773 (Turkey, AD 1757–.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1757–AD 1773] Mustafa III, 1757-1773. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mustafa III, 1757-1773". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A ruler who tried to shore up Ottoman finances and modernise the army, hiring European advisers such as the Baron de Tott to reform the artillery and found a school of mathematics for gunners. Against his own better judgement he was pushed into war with Catherine the Great's Russia in 1768, a conflict that saw the Ottoman fleet burned at Cesme and Russian armies overrun the Danubian provinces. He died before the humiliating peace was signed.

Medieval Greece (Greece, AD 323–AD 1453).label: Medieval Greece
Medieval Greece (Greece, AD 323–AD 1453).prose:
[Greece, AD 323–AD 1453] Medieval Greece. Extracted from variant term "Medieval Greece" associated with heading "Greece--History--323-1453". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Greek lands spent these centuries as the core of the Byzantine Empire, Orthodox in faith and Greek in language, weathering Slavic settlement, Arab raids and the loss of the countryside to insecurity before a revival from the ninth century. The Fourth Crusade of 1204 shattered the empire and left a patchwork of Frankish duchies, Venetian ports and Byzantine successor states like the Despotate of the Morea, whose castles still crown the landscape. Mystras became a late centre of learning whose scholars carried Greek texts to Renaissance Italy before the Ottoman conquest.

British occupation, 1882-1936 (Egypt, AD.label: British occupation, 1882-1936
British occupation, 1882-1936 (Egypt, AD.prose:
[Egypt, AD 1882–AD 1936] British occupation, 1882-1936. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--British occupation, 1882-1936". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.30 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British forces bombarded Alexandria and crushed the Urabi revolt, beginning an occupation that was never formally a colony but ran the country through financial advisers and a consul-general. Cotton exports, irrigation works and the Suez Canal tied Egypt to the imperial economy while nationalist pressure grew, erupting in the 1919 revolution. Nominal independence in 1922 and the 1936 treaty left British troops in place along the canal.

First Republic, 1889-1930 (Brazil, AD 18.label: First Republic, 1889-1930
First Republic, 1889-1930 (Brazil, AD 18.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1889–AD 1930] First Republic, 1889-1930. Extracted from first variant to heading "Brazil--History--1889-1930". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A military coup deposed Emperor Pedro II and replaced the monarchy with a federal republic modelled on the United States. Politics settled into the café com leite bargain between the coffee planters of São Paulo and the cattle interests of Minas Gerais, with elections managed by rural bosses. Mass European and Japanese immigration and a coffee export boom transformed the south, until the 1930 revolution brought Getúlio Vargas to power.

Shona Revolt, 1896-1897 (Zimbabwe, AD 18.label: Shona Revolt, 1896-1897
Shona Revolt, 1896-1897 (Zimbabwe, AD 18.prose:
[Zimbabwe, AD 1896–AD 1897] Shona Revolt, 1896-1897. Extracted from heading "Zimbabwe--History--Shona Revolt, 1896-1897". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Shona communities rose against the British South Africa Company's rule, killing settlers and attacking farms and mines, in a rebellion overlapping with a parallel Ndebele revolt. Spirit mediums, notably Nehanda Nyakasikana and Kaguvi, gave the risings coordination and legitimacy; both were hanged in 1898 after the uprising was crushed by company columns and dynamite attacks on cave strongholds. Zimbabwean nationalists later named it the First Chimurenga, casting the guerrilla war of the 1960s and 70s as its continuation, and Nehanda became a national icon.

Mongol Invasion, 1237-1241 (Russia, AD 1.label: Mongol Invasion, 1237-1241
Mongol Invasion, 1237-1241 (Russia, AD 1.prose:
[Kievan Rus, AD 1237–AD 1241] Mongol Invasion, 1237-1241. Spatial coverage: Belarus, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Ukraine. Extracted from heading "Kievan Rus--History--Mongol Invasion, 1237-1241". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Batu Khan's tumens crossed the frozen rivers in winter and destroyed the Rus principalities one by one - Ryazan, Vladimir, and in 1240 Kyiv, whose ruin shocked chroniclers across Europe. The princes' inability to unite left them paying tribute to the Golden Horde and travelling to the khan's camp for permission to rule. Power drifted north and east to Moscow and Tver, reshaping the political centre of gravity in the Russian lands for centuries.

Bourbons, 1700- (Spain, AD 1700–AD 2015).label: Bourbons, 1700-
Bourbons, 1700- (Spain, AD 1700–AD 2015).prose:
[Spain, AD 1700–AD 2015] Bourbons, 1700-. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Bourbons, 1700-". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of the last Spanish Habsburg brought a French Bourbon, Philip V, to the throne and triggered the War of the Spanish Succession. The new dynasty imported French administrative models, abolished the separate laws of the Aragonese realms and pursued Enlightenment reforms under Charles III. Interrupted by Napoleon, two republics and the Franco dictatorship, the line returned in 1975 and presided over Spain's transition to democracy.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (New York, AD 1775.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (New York, AD 1775.prose:
[New York, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "New York (State)--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.83 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Frederick IX, 1947-1972 (Denmark, AD 194.label: Frederick IX, 1947-1972
Frederick IX, 1947-1972 (Denmark, AD 194.prose:
[Denmark , AD 1947–AD 1972] Frederick IX, 1947-1972. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick IX, 1947-1972".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A tattooed former naval officer who presided over Denmark's transformation into a modern welfare state, its entry into NATO and the abandonment of neutrality, and the vote to join the European Community shortly before his death. The 1953 constitution he signed abolished the upper house, made Greenland an integral county rather than a colony, and changed the succession law so that his eldest daughter could inherit the throne as Margrethe II.

Personal Rule, 1629-1640 (England, AD 16.label: Personal Rule, 1629-1640
Personal Rule, 1629-1640 (England, AD 16.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1629–AD 1640] Personal Rule, 1629-1640. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Personal Rule, 1629-1640". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles I dissolved Parliament and governed for eleven years without one, raising money through revived feudal dues, forced loans and above all ship money, a tax on inland counties that John Hampden famously refused to pay. Archbishop Laud's insistence on altar rails, ceremony and uniformity alarmed Puritans and drove emigration to New England. The attempt to impose an English prayer book on Scotland triggered the Bishops' Wars, and the cost of fighting them forced Charles to recall Parliament in 1640, opening the road to civil war.

Norman period, 1066-1154 (England, AD 10.label: Norman period, 1066-1154
Norman period, 1066-1154 (England, AD 10.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1066–AD 1154] Norman period, 1066-1154. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Norman period, 1066-1154". Added to LCSH in 1986. William of Normandy's victory at Hastings replaced the English landholding class almost entirely with a French-speaking aristocracy within a generation. Castles of earth and timber, then stone, went up across the country, great Romanesque cathedrals were rebuilt on a new scale, and the Domesday survey of 1086 recorded who held what in unprecedented detail. The era closed in the civil war between Stephen and Matilda, remembered as the Anarchy, and passed to the Angevin kings with Henry II.

Constans II, 641-668 (Byzantine Empire,.label: Constans II, 641-668
Constans II, 641-668 (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 641–AD 668] Constans II, 641-668. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Constans II, 641-668". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign spent absorbing the shock of the Arab conquests, which stripped away Egypt and pushed on into North Africa, while a Muslim fleet first challenged Byzantium at sea. Constans reorganised what was left into military districts run by soldier-farmers, tried to silence the bitter dispute over Christ's wills by banning discussion of it, and eventually moved his court west to Syracuse, where he was murdered in his bath.

Rebellion of Stepan Razin, 1667-1671 (Ru.label: Rebellion of Stepan Razin, 1667-1671
Rebellion of Stepan Razin, 1667-1671 (Ru.prose:
[Russia , AD 1667–AD 1671] Rebellion of Stepan Razin, 1667-1671. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Rebellion of Stepan Razin, 1667-1671. Added to LCSH in 2003. Alternate label "Rebellion of Stenka Razin, 1667-1671" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Don Cossack raider turned rebel leader, Razin moved from plundering the Caspian coast to leading a mass uprising of Cossacks, runaway serfs and Volga peoples against landlords and tsarist officials. His forces took Astrakhan, Saratov and Samara before being broken at Simbirsk; Razin was executed in Red Square. He became a folk hero in song and legend, and the revolt exposed how deeply the new burdens of serfdom and state taxation were resented along the frontier.

Manuel II Palaeologus, 1391-1425 (Byzant.label: Manuel II Palaeologus, 1391-1425
Manuel II Palaeologus, 1391-1425 (Byzant.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1391–AD 1425] Manuel II Palaeologus, 1391-1425. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Manuel II Palaeologus, 1391-1425". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A scholar-emperor who ruled a city rather than an empire, spending years touring Paris and London in person to beg Western monarchs for help against the Ottomans. Constantinople was saved only by Timur's shattering of Sultan Bayezid at Ankara in 1402, buying half a century of reprieve. His writings and letters are among the finest late Byzantine prose, and his diplomacy of playing rival Ottoman princes against one another kept the walls standing a little longer.

John IV, 1640-1656 (Portugal, AD 1640–AD.label: John IV, 1640-1656
John IV, 1640-1656 (Portugal, AD 1640–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1640–AD 1656] John IV, 1640-1656. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John IV, 1640-1656". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Duke of Braganza was pushed onto the throne by a coup that ended sixty years of Spanish Habsburg rule, launching a war of independence that lasted long after his death. He had to fight simultaneously to recover Brazil and Angola from the Dutch, and to win recognition from France, England and the papacy. A serious musician and collector, he assembled one of Europe's great music libraries, later destroyed in the Lisbon earthquake.

Alfonso III, 866-910 (Spain, AD 866–AD 9.label: Alfonso III, 866-910
Alfonso III, 866-910 (Spain, AD 866–AD 9.prose:
[Leon, AD 866–AD 910] Alfonso III, 866-910. Extracted from heading "Leon (Kingdom)--History--Alfonso III, 866-910". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alfonso the Great pushed the Asturian frontier south to the Duero and organised the resettlement of the emptied lands, laying the groundwork for the kingdom of León. His court produced chronicles that traced Asturian kingship back to the Visigoths, an origin story that shaped how later Spanish monarchies justified themselves. Forced to abdicate, he divided the realm among his sons.

Nicholas I, 1825-1855 (Russia, AD 1825–A.label: Nicholas I, 1825-1855
Nicholas I, 1825-1855 (Russia, AD 1825–A.prose:
[Russia , AD 1825–AD 1855] Nicholas I, 1825-1855. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Nicholas I, 1825-1855". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign opened with the Decembrist officers' revolt and closed with defeat in the Crimea, and everything between was shaped by his determination that neither should be possible. He built the Third Section secret police, imposed censorship and the doctrine of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality, crushed the Polish rising and marched into Hungary in 1849 as the 'gendarme of Europe'. The Crimean War exposed how far the empire's serf economy and army had fallen behind the West, forcing his son into emancipation and reform.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Kazakhstan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Kazakhstan, AD 19.prose:
[Kazakhstan, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Kazakhstan--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1994, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca..node: Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca. 1550 B.C (Egypt, 1782 BC–1549 BC)
Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca..label: Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca. 1550 B.C
Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca..prose:
[Egypt, 1782 BC–1549 BC] Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca. 1550 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Second Intermediate Period, ca. 1783-ca. 1550 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Beginning with the collapse of the Twelfth Dynasty's stable succession, this long era saw dozens of short-lived kings, the loss of the Delta to the Hyksos rulers of Avaris, and the rise of Kerma in Nubia. Monumental building nearly ceased, and much of what survives comes from cemeteries and settlements rather than temples. The period ended when Ahmose expelled the Hyksos and founded the Eighteenth Dynasty.

John I, 1385-1433 (Portugal, AD 1385–AD.label: John I, 1385-1433
John I, 1385-1433 (Portugal, AD 1385–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1385–AD 1433] John I, 1385-1433. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John I, 1385-1433". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1988. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Illegitimate son of a king and Master of the Order of Avis, he was raised to the throne by a popular revolt and confirmed it by victory over Castile at Aljubarrota. His long reign founded the Avis dynasty, sealed the Treaty of Windsor with England — the oldest alliance still in force — and in 1415 took Ceuta in North Africa, the opening move of Portuguese overseas expansion. His sons included Henry the Navigator; the monastery at Batalha was built to commemorate his victory.

Carlos I, 1889-1908 (Portugal, AD 1889–A.label: Carlos I, 1889-1908
Carlos I, 1889-1908 (Portugal, AD 1889–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1889–AD 1908] Carlos I, 1889-1908. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Carlos I, 1889-1908". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Charles I, 1889-1908" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign opened with the humiliation of the British Ultimatum over African territory, which discredited the monarchy in the eyes of a growing republican movement. Two state bankruptcies and his decision to back João Franco's dictatorship deepened the crisis, and the king and his heir were shot dead in an open carriage in Lisbon. The monarchy fell two years later.

Revolution, 1798-1799 (Rome, AD 1798–AD.label: Revolution, 1798-1799
Revolution, 1798-1799 (Rome, AD 1798–AD.prose:
[Rome (Italy), AD 1798–AD 1799] Revolution, 1798-1799. Extracted from heading "Rome (Italy)--History--Revolution, 1798-1799". Added to LCSH in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

French troops entered Rome, proclaimed a Roman Republic on the classical model with consuls and tribunes, and carried Pope Pius VI away to die in exile in France. Papal treasures and works of art were shipped north, and the church's temporal government was dismantled almost overnight. The republic was unpopular and short-lived, collapsing when Neapolitan and allied forces returned, but the papacy's claim to worldly rule never fully recovered.

South African Incursions, 1978-1990 (Ang.label: South African Incursions, 1978-1990
South African Incursions, 1978-1990 (Ang.prose:
[Angola, AD 1978–AD 1990] South African Incursions, 1978-1990. Extracted from heading "Angola--History--South African Incursions, 1978-1990". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

South African forces mounted repeated cross-border raids into southern Angola against SWAPO's guerrilla bases, beginning with the deadly attack on Cassinga camp, while backing UNITA against the Angolan government. The fighting drew in Cuban troops and Soviet advisers and escalated into conventional battles around Cuito Cuanavale in 1987-88. Stalemate there helped produce the New York Accords, Cuban withdrawal and Namibian independence.

Christian IV, 1588-1648 (Norway, AD 1588.label: Christian IV, 1588-1648
Christian IV, 1588-1648 (Norway, AD 1588.prose:
[Norway, AD 1588–AD 1648] Christian IV, 1588-1648. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Christian IV, 1588-1648". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A restlessly energetic builder-king whose long reign left more physical marks on Norway than any other's: Kongsberg's silver mines, Røros copper, and the towns of Kristiansand and Christiania, the latter laid out on a grid after Oslo burned in 1624. He gave Norway its first printed law code in Norwegian in 1604 and took a personal interest in northern trade and the Arctic. His wars against Sweden and his disastrous intervention in the Thirty Years' War drained the treasury and cost territory.

Leopold III, 1934-1951 (Belgium, AD 1934.label: Leopold III, 1934-1951
Leopold III, 1934-1951 (Belgium, AD 1934.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1934–AD 1951] Leopold III, 1934-1951. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Leopold III, 1934-1951". Added to LCSH and revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His decision to surrender the Belgian army to the Germans in May 1940 and remain in the occupied country, rather than join his government in exile, split the nation. Held by the Germans and then kept out of Belgium after liberation, his possible return became the bitterly contested 'Royal Question', dividing Flemish from Walloon and Catholic from socialist. A referendum narrowly favoured him, but strikes and shootings followed, and he abdicated in favour of his son Baudouin.

George VI, 1936-1952 (United Kingdom, AD.label: George VI, 1936-1952
George VI, 1936-1952 (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1936–AD 1952] George VI, 1936-1952. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George VI, 1936-1952". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.50 of LCSH 1987, and p.40 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reluctant king who took the throne when his brother abdicated, he became a symbol of resistance by staying in bombed London through the Blitz. His reign covered the Second World War, the founding of the welfare state, and the independence of India and Pakistan, which turned the empire into the Commonwealth.

Uprising, 1520-1521 (Kingdom of Castile,.label: Uprising, 1520-1521
Uprising, 1520-1521 (Kingdom of Castile,.prose:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1520–AD 1521] Uprising, 1520-1521. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Uprising, 1520-1521". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Comuneros revolt: Castilian cities, angry at a young Habsburg king who spoke no Spanish, packed his court with Flemings and taxed them to buy an imperial crown, formed their own governing junta and briefly claimed to speak for the realm. Royal forces crushed the rebel army at Villalar and beheaded its leaders the next day. The defeat broke the political independence of the Castilian towns and left the Cortes a weak assembly, clearing the way for the absolutist monarchy that funded Charles V's European wars.

Bombardment, 1944-1945 (Tokyo, AD 1944–A.label: Bombardment, 1944-1945
Bombardment, 1944-1945 (Tokyo, AD 1944–A.prose:
[Tokyo (Japan), AD 1944–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1944-1945. Extracted from heading "Tokyo (Japan)--History--Bombardment, 1944-1945". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From June 1944 the country was struck by pilotless V-1 flying bombs and then by V-2 rockets, which arrived without warning at supersonic speed and could not be intercepted. They killed thousands, triggered a second mass evacuation from London, and announced the age of the guided missile — the technology and many of the engineers passed straight into the Cold War rocket programmes.

Foreign intervention, 1857-1861 (China,.label: Foreign intervention, 1857-1861
Foreign intervention, 1857-1861 (China,.prose:
[China, AD 1857–AD 1861] Foreign intervention, 1857-1861. Extracted from heading "China--History--Foreign intervention, 1857-1861". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Second Opium War brought British and French forces to Canton and then north to the capital, forcing the Treaties of Tianjin and the Convention of Peking. China had to open more ports, legalise the opium trade, admit foreign envoys and missionaries into the interior, and cede Kowloon; the Summer Palace was looted and burned in reprisal. Coming while the Taiping rebellion raged in the south, the defeat exposed the Qing state's weakness and prompted the first self-strengthening reforms.

Christian V, 1670-1699 (Norway, AD 1670–.label: Christian V, 1670-1699
Christian V, 1670-1699 (Norway, AD 1670–.prose:
[Norway, AD 1670–AD 1699] Christian V, 1670-1699. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Christian V, 1670-1699". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited the new hereditary absolutism and gave it working form, issuing the Norwegian Law of 1687 — a clear, systematic code that governed Norwegians for generations. A new titled nobility of counts and barons was created to bind the elite to the crown, and offices were increasingly filled by professionals rather than magnates. His war against Sweden brought hard fighting on the Norwegian frontier under the popular commander Ulrik Frederik Gyldenløve.

Bombardment, 1940-1941 (London, AD 1940–.label: Bombardment, 1940-1941
Bombardment, 1940-1941 (London, AD 1940–.prose:
[London (England), AD 1940–AD 1941] Bombardment, 1940-1941. Extracted from heading "London (England)--History--Bombardment, 1940-1941". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Night after night for months, German bombers set the docks, the East End and the City ablaze, killing some 20,000 Londoners and destroying or damaging more than a million homes. Life reorganised itself around shelters, blackout and fire-watching, and the endurance of the population became a central image of British wartime identity — and a precedent, later returned with interest, for attacking cities from the air.

John V Palaeologus, 1341-1391 (Byzantine.label: John V Palaeologus, 1341-1391
John V Palaeologus, 1341-1391 (Byzantine.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1341–AD 1391] John V Palaeologus, 1341-1391. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--John V Palaeologus, 1341-1391". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A boy emperor whose accession triggered civil war, he spent fifty years being deposed and restored by rivals, his own son and his grandson while the empire disintegrated around him. The Ottomans crossed into Europe during these quarrels and took Gallipoli and Adrianople; John ended as a tribute-paying vassal of the sultan. He travelled to Italy and personally converted to Catholicism in Rome in the hope of Western aid, and got almost none.

Carlist War, 1833-1840 (Spain, AD 1833–A.label: Carlist War, 1833-1840
Carlist War, 1833-1840 (Spain, AD 1833–A.prose:
[Spain, AD 1833–AD 1840] Carlist War, 1833-1840. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Carlist War, 1833-1840". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Ferdinand VII died leaving an infant daughter, his brother Don Carlos claimed the throne and much of the Basque country, Navarre and rural Catalonia rose for him. What began as a succession dispute became a savage guerrilla struggle between clerical traditionalism and urban liberalism, killing perhaps two hundred thousand people. The liberal victory entrenched the army in Spanish politics and left grievances that would reignite twice more.

Jiaqing, 1796-1820 (China, AD 1796–AD 18.label: Jiaqing, 1796-1820
Jiaqing, 1796-1820 (China, AD 1796–AD 18.prose:
[China, AD 1796–AD 1820] Jiaqing, 1796-1820. Extracted from heading "China--History--Jiaqing, 1796-1820". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Chia ch'ing 1796-1820" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and p.16 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Assuming full power only after his father Qianlong's death, this emperor purged the notorious favourite Heshen and tried to restore honest administration and a solvent treasury. Rebellion in the interior, piracy at sea and a growing illegal opium trade drained his resources; even the Forbidden City was briefly stormed by sectarian rebels in 1813. The confident expansion of the previous century was over.

Sancho Ramírez, 1063-1094 (Spain, AD 106.label: Sancho Ramírez, 1063-1094
Sancho Ramírez, 1063-1094 (Spain, AD 106.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1063–AD 1094] Sancho Ramírez, 1063-1094. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Sancho Ramírez, 1063-1094". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sancho Ramírez turned a small Pyrenean county into a serious kingdom, adding Navarre in 1076 and pressing steadily down the valleys towards the Ebro. He placed Aragon under papal protection, replaced the old Mozarabic liturgy with the Roman rite, and issued the celebrated charter of Jaca that drew merchants and pilgrims across the mountains. He was killed by a crossbow bolt while besieging Huesca, a city his son took three years later.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Ohio, AD 1861–AD 1.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Ohio, AD 1861–AD 1.prose:
[Ohio, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Ohio--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.87 of LCSH 1987, and p.85 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Sverre, 1177-1202 (Norway, AD 1177–AD 12.label: Sverre, 1177-1202
Sverre, 1177-1202 (Norway, AD 1177–AD 12.prose:
[Norway, AD 1177–AD 1202] Sverre, 1177-1202. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Sverre, 1177-1202". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A priest from the Faroes who claimed royal descent, took over the ragged Birkebeiner rebels and fought his way to the Norwegian throne against the established aristocracy. He held power by favouring lesser men and royal servants over the old magnates, and was excommunicated for defying the archbishop over church independence. His saga, partly composed in his presence, is one of the great works of Norse historical writing.

Regulator Insurrection, 1766-1771 (North.label: Regulator Insurrection, 1766-1771
Regulator Insurrection, 1766-1771 (North.prose:
[North Carolina, AD 1766–AD 1771] Regulator Insurrection, 1766-1771. Extracted from heading "North Carolina--History--Regulator Insurrection, 1766-1771". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Farmers in the North Carolina backcountry organised against sheriffs and court officials who overcharged fees, rigged taxes and seized land for debt, at first through petitions and then by shutting down courts by force. Governor Tryon marched the eastern militia west and broke them at Alamance, hanging several leaders. The grievances — corrupt local government and an unresponsive assembly dominated by the coastal elite — carried straight into the divisions of the Revolution a few years later.

Demotic, ca. 650 B.C.-450 A.D (Egypt, 64.label: Demotic, ca. 650 B.C.-450 A.D
Demotic, ca. 650 B.C.-450 A.D (Egypt, 64.prose:
[Egypt, 649 BC–AD 450] Demotic, ca. 650 B.C.-450 A.D. Extracted from heading "Egyptian language--Demotic, ca. 650 B.C.-450 A.D". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A fast, heavily abbreviated cursive script that replaced hieratic for everyday Egyptian writing — contracts, tax receipts, letters, legal codes — and eventually carried a rich literature of tales, wisdom texts and astronomical and magical handbooks. It stayed in use through Persian, Ptolemaic and Roman rule, gradually giving way to Greek and then Coptic. Its appearance on the Rosetta Stone alongside hieroglyphs and Greek was central to the decipherment of ancient Egyptian.

Occupation, 1939-1945 (Poland, AD 1939–A.label: Occupation, 1939-1945
Occupation, 1939-1945 (Poland, AD 1939–A.prose:
[Poland , AD 1939–AD 1945] Occupation, 1939-1945. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Occupation, 1939-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.79 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Invaded from west and east in September 1939, Poland was carved up between Germany and the Soviet Union, its western provinces annexed and the rest ruled as the General Government. Elites were targeted for execution, millions were deported for forced labour, and the country became the site of the extermination camps where most of Europe's murdered Jews died. An underground state and Home Army sustained resistance through the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943 and the Warsaw Uprising of 1944, both crushed; roughly a fifth of the population did not survive.

Anjou dynasty, 1268-1442 (Naples, AD 126.label: Anjou dynasty, 1268-1442
Anjou dynasty, 1268-1442 (Naples, AD 126.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1268–AD 1442] Anjou dynasty, 1268-1442. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Anjou dynasty, 1268-1442". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles of Anjou, backed by the papacy, destroyed the last Hohenstaufen heirs and made Naples the seat of a French dynasty and the leading Guelf power in Italy. The revolt of the Sicilian Vespers tore Sicily away to Aragon within a generation, leaving the Angevins ruling the mainland south, where Robert the Wise's court patronised Petrarch and Boccaccio and Naples grew into one of Europe's largest cities. Disputed successions and the chaotic reign of Joanna II ended in Alfonso of Aragon's conquest, uniting Naples and Sicily under Spanish rule.

Lusignan dynasty, 1192-1474 (Cyprus, AD.label: Lusignan dynasty, 1192-1474
Lusignan dynasty, 1192-1474 (Cyprus, AD.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1192–AD 1474] Lusignan dynasty, 1192-1474. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--Lusignan dynasty, 1192-1474". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A French crusader family bought Cyprus from Richard the Lionheart and ruled it as a Latin kingdom for nearly three centuries, transplanting feudal law, Gothic cathedrals and a Catholic hierarchy onto a Greek Orthodox island. After the fall of Acre in 1291 the island became the last crusader foothold in the east and a rich hub of trade between Europe and Syria. Genoese and Venetian pressure eroded the dynasty until Cyprus passed to Venice.

James III, 1460-1488 (Scotland, AD 1460–.label: James III, 1460-1488
James III, 1460-1488 (Scotland, AD 1460–.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1460–AD 1488] James III, 1460-1488. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--James III, 1460-1488". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cultivated, reclusive king who quarrelled with his brothers, debased the coinage and relied on favourites, alienating the magnates who expected a share of government. Orkney and Shetland came to Scotland during his reign through his marriage to Margaret of Denmark, and his portrait coinage is among the first realistic royal likenesses in Britain. He died after a rebel army led in his teenage son's name defeated him near Stirling.

Tengyō Revolt, 938-940 (Japan, AD 938–AD.label: Tengyō Revolt, 938-940
Tengyō Revolt, 938-940 (Japan, AD 938–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 938–AD 940] Tengyō Revolt, 938-940. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Tengyō Revolt, 938-940". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Taira no Masakado seized government offices across the eastern provinces and proclaimed himself a "New Emperor", while Fujiwara no Sumitomo raided shipping in the Inland Sea. The court had no army of its own and had to hire rival provincial warriors to put them down; Masakado was killed in battle in 940 and later worshipped as a vengeful deity in Edo. The episode is often taken as the moment the samurai emerged as an independent political force.

Civil War, 1991-2002 (Sierra Leone, AD 1.label: Civil War, 1991-2002
Civil War, 1991-2002 (Sierra Leone, AD 1.prose:
[Sierra Leone, AD 1991–AD 2002] Civil War, 1991-2002. Extracted from heading "Sierra Leone--History--Civil War, 1991-2002". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Revolutionary United Front, backed by Charles Taylor of Liberia, invaded to seize the diamond fields and became infamous for amputating civilians' limbs and conscripting children. The state effectively collapsed, and the war was sustained by "blood diamonds" traded for weapons. British military intervention and a large UN mission ended it; the resulting Special Court convicted Taylor of aiding the atrocities.

World War, 1914-1918 (Earth, AD 1914–AD.label: World War, 1914-1918
World War, 1914-1918 (Earth, AD 1914–AD.prose:
[World, AD 1914–AD 1918] World War, 1914-1918. Extracted from heading "World War, 1914-1918". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Industrial warfare on a scale no one had planned for: machine guns, artillery, gas and barbed wire locked armies into trench lines across France and Belgium while fighting spread to Russia, the Middle East, Africa and the oceans. Around nine million soldiers died, and the strain destroyed the Russian, Ottoman, Habsburg and German empires. The peace settlements redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East and left grievances that fed the next war twenty years later.

Revolution, 1789-1790 (Belgium, AD 1789–.label: Revolution, 1789-1790
Revolution, 1789-1790 (Belgium, AD 1789–.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1789–AD 1790] Revolution, 1789-1790. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Revolution, 1789-1790". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inspired by resistance to Joseph II's sweeping reforms of the Church and the courts, the Austrian Netherlands rose in the Brabant Revolution and declared the United Belgian States. Conservative clericals and democratic radicals could not agree on what the new country should be, and their split doomed it within a year. Austrian troops restored imperial rule under Leopold II, but the episode supplied Belgium with a name, a flag and a memory that mattered in 1830.

Otto I, 936-973 (Germany, AD 936–AD 973).label: Otto I, 936-973
Otto I, 936-973 (Germany, AD 936–AD 973).prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 936–AD 973] Otto I, 936-973. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Crowned at Aachen on Charlemagne's throne, Otto subdued rebellious dukes, crushed the Magyars at the Lechfeld and ended their raids on the West, then took the imperial crown in Rome. He built his power on bishops and abbots appointed by the king, whose lands and troops served the crown but could not be inherited – a system that shaped German politics for centuries. His coronation is conventionally the founding of the Holy Roman Empire.

Caesar's heir Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus seized power as a triumvirate, hunting down their enemies in bloody proscriptions - Cicero among the victims - and crushing the assassins at Philippi. The alliance then curdled into a contest between Octavian in Italy and Antony allied with Cleopatra in Egypt. Victory at Actium and the fall of Alexandria left one man in control of the Roman world and ended the Republic in all but name.

Genoa governed Corsica for four centuries, much of it through the Bank of Saint George, exploiting the island for timber, grain and taxes while fortifying its coastal towns against Barbary raiders. Rebellion was near-constant, and from the 1750s Pasquale Paoli ran an independent Corsican republic with its own constitution that impressed Enlightenment Europe. Exhausted, Genoa sold its claim to France, which invaded the following year — Napoleon was born a French subject months later.

Indochinese War, 1946-1954 (Vietnam, AD.label: Indochinese War, 1946-1954
Indochinese War, 1946-1954 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Indochina, Vietnam, AD 1946–AD 1954] Indochinese War, 1946-1954. Spatial coverage: Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam. Extracted from heading "Indochinese War, 1946-1954". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

France's attempt to restore colonial rule after the Second World War collided with Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh, beginning a war of ambushes, jungle bases and eventually set-piece battles. It ended with the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu overrun and the Geneva Accords splitting the country at the 17th parallel. The partition, and the American commitment to the southern state that followed, led directly to the far larger war of the 1960s.

Constantine I, 1913-1917 (Greece, AD 191.label: Constantine I, 1913-1917
Constantine I, 1913-1917 (Greece, AD 191.prose:
[Greece, AD 1913–AD 1917] Constantine I, 1913-1917. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Constantine I, 1913-1917". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975 under "Greece, Modern". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He took the throne on his father's assassination, fresh from commanding the Greek armies that seized Salonika and Epirus in the Balkan Wars. His insistence on neutrality in the First World War, against the pro-Allied prime minister Venizelos, split the country into rival governments in the so-called National Schism, and Allied pressure forced him out in 1917.

Christian X, 1912-1947 (Denmark, AD 1912.label: Christian X, 1912-1947
Christian X, 1912-1947 (Denmark, AD 1912.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1912–AD 1947] Christian X, 1912-1947. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian X, 1912-1947".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In the Easter Crisis of 1920 he dismissed a government he disliked, provoked mass protests and a threatened republic, and had to back down — the last time a Danish monarch tried to pick a ministry. The same year a plebiscite returned North Schleswig to Denmark, and he rode across the old border on a white horse. During the German occupation his daily rides through Copenhagen made him a quiet emblem of national defiance, and in 1944 Iceland dissolved its union with the crown.

Occupation, 1941-1944 (Greece, AD 1941–A.label: Occupation, 1941-1944
Occupation, 1941-1944 (Greece, AD 1941–A.prose:
[Greece, AD 1941–AD 1944] Occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Occupation, 1941-1944". Added in to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975 under "Greece, Modern". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Germany, Italy and Bulgaria divided the country between them after the spring 1941 invasion, stripping food and resources and triggering a famine that killed tens of thousands in Athens during the first winter. The Jewish community of Thessaloniki, one of the oldest in Europe, was almost entirely deported to Auschwitz. Armed resistance movements grew powerful in the mountains but fell out among themselves, so that liberation led almost directly into civil war.

Alfonso XII, 1465-1468 (Kingdom of Casti.label: Alfonso XII, 1465-1468
Alfonso XII, 1465-1468 (Kingdom of Casti.prose:
[Castile, AD 1465–AD 1468] Alfonso XII, 1465-1468. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso XII, 1465-1468". A boy set up as rival king by nobles who staged the mock deposition of Henry IV at Ávila, burning his effigy in front of the assembled court. The revolt split Castile into two royal camps for three years. His sudden death at fourteen shifted the opposition's hopes onto his sister Isabella, and so towards the union with Aragon.

Revolution, 1848-1849 (Austria, AD 1848–.label: Revolution, 1848-1849
Revolution, 1848-1849 (Austria, AD 1848–.prose:
[Austria, AD 1848–AD 1849] Revolution, 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Revolution, 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

Louis IX, 1226-1270 (France, AD 1226–AD.label: Louis IX, 1226-1270
Louis IX, 1226-1270 (France, AD 1226–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1226–AD 1270] Louis IX, 1226-1270. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis IX, 1226-1270". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A pious and formidably effective king who curbed private warfare, sent investigators to check his own officials, and made the royal court the final appeal for the whole kingdom, giving France a reputation for even-handed justice. He built the Sainte-Chapelle to house the Crown of Thorns and made Paris a centre of Gothic art and learning. Two crusades ended badly, with capture in Egypt and death of disease at Tunis; canonised in 1297, he became the model Christian king.

Anglo-Dutch War, 1780-1784 (Netherlands,.label: Anglo-Dutch War, 1780-1784
Anglo-Dutch War, 1780-1784 (Netherlands,.prose:
[Netherlands, Great Britain, AD 1780–AD 1784] Anglo-Dutch War, 1780-1784. Spatial coverage: Netherlands, United Kingdom. Extracted from heading "Anglo-Dutch War, 1780-1784". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain declared war on the Dutch Republic for trading with the American rebels and preparing to join the League of Armed Neutrality. The once-formidable Dutch navy had been neglected and could barely protect its own convoys; British squadrons took Dutch posts from the Caribbean to India and trade was paralysed. The war exposed the Republic's decline as a great power and triggered the political crisis that led to the Patriot revolt.

Leopold I, 1657-1705 (Austria, AD 1657–A.label: Leopold I, 1657-1705
Leopold I, 1657-1705 (Austria, AD 1657–A.prose:
[Austria, AD 1657–AD 1705] Leopold I, 1657-1705. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Leopold I, 1657-1705". Appears on pg.6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on pg.7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His long reign was a two-front struggle: against the Ottomans, who besieged Vienna in 1683 before being routed, and against Louis XIV's France on the Rhine. The counter-offensive that followed 1683 drove the Turks out of Hungary and Transylvania, transforming the Habsburgs into a genuine Danubian great power. He died with the War of the Spanish Succession, fought over his family's claim to the Spanish throne, still undecided.

Revolution, 1924-1925 (Brazil, AD 1924–A.label: Revolution, 1924-1925
Revolution, 1924-1925 (Brazil, AD 1924–A.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1924–AD 1925] Revolution, 1924-1925. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--Revolution, 1924-1925". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Junior army officers, the tenentes, rose against the coffee-planter oligarchy that controlled the republic, seizing São Paulo for three weeks before being bombarded out of it. Survivors joined Luís Carlos Prestes and marched some 25,000 kilometres through the interior without being defeated, becoming a legend among reformers. The movement failed militarily but supplied both the ideas and the men for the 1930 revolution that brought Vargas to power.

William II, 1888-1918 (Germany, AD 1888–.label: William II, 1888-1918
William II, 1888-1918 (Germany, AD 1888–.prose:
[Germany , AD 1888–AD 1918] William II, 1888-1918. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--William II, 1888-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last German emperor dismissed Bismarck within two years and steered a "new course" of naval building, colonial ambition and blustering diplomacy that alienated Britain, France and Russia in turn. Germany under him was a scientific and industrial powerhouse, but the alliance system his policy helped harden collapsed into world war in 1914, after which the generals eclipsed him entirely. He abdicated as the front broke in 1918 and fled to the Netherlands, ending the Hohenzollern monarchy.

Allied intervention, 1918-1920 (Russia,.label: Allied intervention, 1918-1920
Allied intervention, 1918-1920 (Russia,.prose:
[Soviet Union, AD 1918–AD 1920] Allied intervention, 1918-1920. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Estonia, Georgia (country), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia. Extracted from heading "Soviet Union--History--Allied intervention, 1918-1920". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.108 of LCSH 1987, and on p.87 of LCSH 1975 (source uses term "Russia"). Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British, French, American, Japanese and other troops landed at Archangel, Murmansk, Vladivostok and the Black Sea, first to keep war supplies from the Germans and revive an eastern front, then increasingly to prop up White armies against the Bolsheviks. The forces were small, poorly coordinated and unpopular at home, and they withdrew without changing the outcome of the civil war. The episode left a lasting Soviet conviction that the capitalist powers meant to strangle the revolution.

Kangxi, 1662-1722 (China, AD 1662–AD 172.label: Kangxi, 1662-1722
Kangxi, 1662-1722 (China, AD 1662–AD 172.prose:
[China, AD 1662–AD 1722] Kangxi, 1662-1722. Extracted from heading "China--History--Kangxi, 1662-1722". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in same year. Alternate identifier selected from "Earlier Established Forms" due to its use of the older Wade-Giles method of transliteration. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the longest reigns in Chinese history, in which Manchu rule was made secure and greatly expanded — the southern feudatories defeated, Taiwan taken, Russia held at the Amur, and Tibet brought under influence. Tax quotas were frozen, canals and dykes repaired, and Chinese scholars drawn into vast state-funded compilations. The reign's kilns at Jingdezhen produced the famille verte and monochrome wares that define the period's look.

Partition, 1919-1922 (Poland, AD 1919–AD.label: Partition, 1919-1922
Partition, 1919-1922 (Poland, AD 1919–AD.prose:
[Upper Silesia, AD 1919–AD 1922] Partition, 1919-1922. Spatial coverage: Czech Republic, Poland. Extracted from heading "Silesia, Upper (Poland and Czech Republic)--History--Partition, 1919-1922". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The frontiers of the newly restored Polish republic were settled piecemeal by war, plebiscite and diplomacy rather than by any single treaty. Polish forces fought the Soviets to the gates of Warsaw and back again, seized Vilnius, and clashed with Czechoslovakia over Cieszyn, while Allied commissions ran votes in Upper Silesia and East Prussia. The industrial heart of Upper Silesia was divided between Poland and Germany in 1922, leaving grievances that Berlin would exploit two decades later.

Southern Tang kingdom, 937-975 (China, A.label: Southern Tang kingdom, 937-975
Southern Tang kingdom, 937-975 (China, A.prose:
[China, AD 937–AD 975] Southern Tang kingdom, 937-975. Extracted from heading "China--History--Southern Tang kingdom, 937-975". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Southern T'ang kingdom, 937-975" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the Ten Kingdoms of the fragmented post-Tang south, controlling the rich Yangzi valley from its capital at Jinling. Its rulers styled themselves heirs of the Tang and built a brilliant court culture of painting, calligraphy and song lyrics, most famously under Li Yu, who surrendered to the Song and died a captive. Its fall was a decisive step in the Song reunification of China.

Victor Emmanuel I, 1802-1821 (Sardinia,.label: Victor Emmanuel I, 1802-1821
Victor Emmanuel I, 1802-1821 (Sardinia,.prose:
[Sardinia, AD 1802–AD 1821] Victor Emmanuel I, 1802-1821. Extracted from heading "Sardinia (Italy)--History--Victor Emmanuel I, 1802-1821". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the mainland in French hands, the king ruled from Cagliari in Sardinia until the fall of Napoleon returned him to Turin, enlarged by the former Republic of Genoa. His restoration was thorough and backward-looking, reinstating the laws, offices and privileges of 1798 as though the intervening years had not happened. When soldiers and students rose in 1821 demanding a constitution, he abdicated rather than grant one.

German occupation, 1940-1945 (Denmark, A.label: German occupation, 1940-1945
German occupation, 1940-1945 (Denmark, A.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1940–AD 1945] German occupation, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--German occupation, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark was seized in a few hours and then governed with unusual lightness: the king stayed, parliament sat, and the country was presented as a model protectorate supplying food to Germany. Cooperation collapsed in August 1943 amid strikes and sabotage; when deportation of Denmark's Jews was ordered that October, the resistance and ordinary citizens ferried some 7,000 people to safety in Sweden.

Henry IV, 1056-1106 (Germany, AD 1056–AD.label: Henry IV, 1056-1106
Henry IV, 1056-1106 (Germany, AD 1056–AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1056–AD 1106] Henry IV, 1056-1106. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry IV, 1056-1106". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign was consumed by the Investiture Controversy, the struggle with Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops — a contest about the very basis of royal authority. Excommunicated and facing revolt, he crossed the Alps in winter to stand penitent at Canossa and win absolution, then returned to depose Gregory and install an antipope. Decades of civil war followed, and he died deposed by his own son, with imperial prestige in Germany permanently weakened.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Michigan, AD 1861–.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Michigan, AD 1861–.prose:
[Michigan, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Michigan--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.78 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Severans, 193-235 (Roman Empire, AD 193–.label: Severans, 193-235
Severans, 193-235 (Roman Empire, AD 193–.prose:
[Rome, AD 193–AD 235] Severans, 193-235. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Severans, 193-235". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dynasty founded in civil war by a North African general and sustained by the influence of a remarkable line of Syrian women, above all Julia Domna and Julia Maesa. Its emperors bought the army's loyalty with pay rises and granted citizenship to almost every free provincial, while spending lavishly on building in Rome and Lepcis Magna. The murder of the last Severan by mutinous troops in 235 began the crisis of the third century.

Maximinus, 235-238 (Roman Empire, AD 235.label: Maximinus, 235-238
Maximinus, 235-238 (Roman Empire, AD 235.prose:
[Rome, AD 235–AD 238] Maximinus, 235-238. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Maximinus, 235-238". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A career soldier of provincial origin raised to the purple by mutinous troops on the Rhine, Maximinus Thrax was the first emperor never to set foot in Rome as ruler. His heavy taxation to fund frontier warfare provoked revolt in Africa and the Senate's open defiance, and he was murdered by his own men outside Aquileia. His accession and death mark the opening of the third-century crisis, half a century of usurpation, inflation and invasion.

Civil War, 1936-1939 (Spain, AD 1936–AD.label: Civil War, 1936-1939
Civil War, 1936-1939 (Spain, AD 1936–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 1936–AD 1939] Civil War, 1936-1939. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Civil War, 1936-1939". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A failed military coup against the Republic hardened into a three-year war between Nationalists under Franco and a Republican coalition of liberals, socialists and anarchists. Germany and Italy supplied Franco with aircraft and troops while the Soviet Union and the International Brigades backed the Republic, making the conflict a rehearsal for the Second World War — Guernica's bombing became its emblem. Franco's victory brought a dictatorship that lasted until 1975.

Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Rhode Is.label: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775
Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Rhode Is.prose:
[Rhode Island, AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "Rhode Island--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.97 of LCSH 1987, and p.95 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Charles VI, 1711-1740 (Austria, AD 1711–.label: Charles VI, 1711-1740
Charles VI, 1711-1740 (Austria, AD 1711–.prose:
[Austria, AD 1711–AD 1740] Charles VI, 1711-1740. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Charles VI, 1711-1740". Appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had fought to make himself king of Spain and never quite gave up the idea, keeping Spanish ceremonial at Vienna while ruling the Austrian lands, Hungary, Naples, Milan and the former Spanish Netherlands. With no surviving son, he spent decades persuading the European powers to accept the Pragmatic Sanction guaranteeing his daughter Maria Theresa's inheritance. Prince Eugene's victories over the Ottomans took Belgrade, though much was lost again by 1739; the promises about the succession proved worthless within months of his death, when Prussia invaded Silesia.

Peasant Uprising, 1994- (Mexico, AD 1994.label: Peasant Uprising, 1994-
Peasant Uprising, 1994- (Mexico, AD 1994.prose:
[Chiapas (Mexico), AD 1994–AD 2015] Peasant Uprising, 1994-. Extracted from heading "Chiapas (Mexico)--History--Peasant Uprising, 1994-". Added to LCSH in 1994, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

On the day the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation seized towns in Chiapas, demanding land, indigenous rights and democracy. Fighting lasted less than two weeks before public pressure forced a ceasefire, but the movement kept going, building self-governing communities and using communiqués, the internet and the masked figure of Subcomandante Marcos to reach a global audience. It reframed indigenous rights as a national issue in Mexico and became a template for later anti-globalisation movements.

Sigurd Jorsalafari, 1103-1130 (Norway, A.label: Sigurd Jorsalafari, 1103-1130
Sigurd Jorsalafari, 1103-1130 (Norway, A.prose:
[Norway, AD 1103–AD 1130] Sigurd Jorsalafari, 1103-1130. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Sigurd Jorsalafari, 1103-1130". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sigurd earned his byname, 'Jerusalem-farer', by sailing a fleet from Norway through the Mediterranean, fighting Muslim forces in Iberia and the Balearics, helping the crusaders take Sidon, and returning overland via Constantinople. He was the first European king to go on crusade in person, and the voyage gave the young Norwegian kingdom huge prestige. At home he strengthened the Church, enforced the tithe and founded the bishopric at Stavanger.

War with France, 1798-1800 (United State.label: War with France, 1798-1800
War with France, 1798-1800 (United State.prose:
[United States, AD 1798–AD 1800] War with France, 1798-1800. Extracted from heading "United States--History--1797-1801". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An undeclared naval conflict, fought largely in the Caribbean, broke out after French privateers began seizing American ships and French officials demanded bribes to open negotiations — the XYZ Affair. It prompted the creation of a permanent US Navy and the Marine Corps, and at home the Federalists' Alien and Sedition Acts, which crippled them politically. The 1800 settlement quietly dissolved the 1778 alliance with France, setting the pattern of American non-entanglement.

Louis XIII, 1610-1643 (France, AD 1610–A.label: Louis XIII, 1610-1643
Louis XIII, 1610-1643 (France, AD 1610–A.prose:
[France, AD 1610–AD 1643] Louis XIII, 1610-1643. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XIII, 1610-1643". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Came to the throne as a child under his mother's regency and later governed alongside Cardinal Richelieu, whose policy he consistently backed against court plots. Together they broke the Huguenots' military power at La Rochelle, curbed the great nobles and dragged France into the Thirty Years' War against the Habsburgs. The intendants and centralised machinery they built up became the foundation of the absolute monarchy his son inherited.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Arkansas, AD 1861–.prose:
[Arkansas, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Arkansas--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.5 of LCSH 1987, and p.4 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.
