Wars of 1918-1921 (Poland, AD 1918–AD 19.prose:
[Poland , AD 1918–AD 1921] Wars of 1918-1921. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Wars of 1918-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.79 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Polish state reconstituted after 123 years of partition had no agreed borders and fought on every side to fix them: risings in Greater Poland and Silesia, a war with the West Ukrainian republic over Lviv, clashes with Czechoslovakia and Lithuania. The largest struggle was with Soviet Russia, whose advance was broken outside Warsaw in August 1920, halting the Red Army's march towards Germany. The Treaty of Riga in 1921 set an eastern frontier deep in Belarusian and Ukrainian lands.

Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Germany, AD 1940.label: Bombardment, 1940-1945
Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Germany, AD 1940.prose:
[Germany , AD 1940–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Bombardment, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British night raids and American daylight raids grew into a round-the-clock campaign that destroyed the centres of Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and dozens of other cities, killed several hundred thousand civilians and made millions homeless. It absorbed a vast share of German industry and manpower in air defence, and it left a moral argument about area bombing that has never been settled.

Charles VI, 1711-1740 (Germany, AD 1711–.prose:
[Germany , AD 1711–AD 1740] Charles VI, 1711-1740. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Charles VI, 1711-1740". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had fought to make himself king of Spain and never quite gave up the idea, keeping Spanish ceremonial at Vienna while ruling the Austrian lands, Hungary, Naples, Milan and the former Spanish Netherlands. With no surviving son, he spent decades persuading the European powers to accept the Pragmatic Sanction guaranteeing his daughter Maria Theresa's inheritance. Prince Eugene's victories over the Ottomans took Belgrade, though much was lost again by 1739; the promises about the succession proved worthless within months of his death, when Prussia invaded Silesia.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Russia, AD 1917–A.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Russia, AD 1917–A.prose:
[Siberia, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Siberia (Russia)--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.103 of LCSH 1987, and p.90 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Charles Robert, 1308-1342 (Hungary, AD 1.label: Charles Robert, 1308-1342
Charles Robert, 1308-1342 (Hungary, AD 1.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1308–AD 1342] Charles Robert, 1308-1342. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Charles Robert, 1308-1342". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Angevin claimant from Naples spent years fighting Hungary's warlord oligarchs before making himself master of the kingdom and rebuilding royal authority on new foundations. He reorganised the treasury, took a share of the Slovak gold and silver mines, and struck a gold florin that made Hungary one of Europe's richest crowns. His court at Visegrád hosted the 1335 congress with the Polish and Bohemian kings, which settled disputes and opened trade routes bypassing Vienna.

Valentinian I, 364-375 (Roman Empire, AD.label: Valentinian I, 364-375
Valentinian I, 364-375 (Roman Empire, AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 364–AD 375] Valentinian I, 364-375. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Valentinian I, 364-375". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-emperor who took the throne and immediately split the empire's administration, handing the east to his brother Valens while he held the west from Milan and Trier. His reign was spent campaigning on the Rhine and Danube and building an unprecedented chain of forts, watchtowers and river defences along those frontiers. He also legislated against corruption and appointed defenders of the plebs, though his temper was notorious – he is said to have died of a stroke while shouting at a German embassy.

Ottoman Empire, 1288-1918 (Turkey, AD 12.label: Ottoman Empire, 1288-1918
Ottoman Empire, 1288-1918 (Turkey, AD 12.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1288–AD 1918] Ottoman Empire, 1288-1918. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Ottoman Empire, 1288-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From a small warband on the Byzantine frontier, the Ottomans took Bursa, crossed into Europe, and after the capture of Constantinople in 1453 governed an empire reaching from Hungary to Yemen. Janissary infantry, a salaried bureaucracy and land grants to cavalry underpinned the state, while trade routes and pilgrim roads to Mecca ran through its provinces. Territorial losses, reform movements such as the Tanzimat and the Young Turk revolution marked its last century, which closed with defeat in 1918 and the empire's dismemberment.

Michael, 1613-1645 (Russia, AD 1613–AD 1.label: Michael, 1613-1645
Michael, 1613-1645 (Russia, AD 1613–AD 1.prose:
[Russia , AD 1613–AD 1645] Michael, 1613-1645. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Michael, 1613-1645". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A sixteen-year-old chosen by an assembly of the land, Michael Romanov ended the Time of Troubles and founded a dynasty that would rule Russia for three centuries. His reign was largely one of recovery: peace with Sweden and Poland, rebuilding of state finances, the extension of serfdom, and continued Cossack-led expansion across Siberia. Real power lay for much of it with his father, Patriarch Filaret, who governed as co-ruler.

Italian Risorgimento (Italy, AD 1815–AD.label: Italian Risorgimento
Italian Risorgimento (Italy, AD 1815–AD.prose:
[Italy, AD 1815–AD 1870] Italian Risorgimento. Extracted from first variant for heading "Italy--History--1815-1870". Added to LCHS in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A generation of conspirators, soldiers and diplomats turned a peninsula of duchies, papal territories and Austrian provinces into a single kingdom. Mazzini supplied the ideology, Garibaldi and his Thousand the drama in Sicily and Naples, and Cavour the calculating Piedmontese statecraft and French alliance that made it stick. Rome was taken in 1870, ending the Papal States and leaving the popes self-declared prisoners in the Vatican for the next sixty years.

Portuguese rule, 1469-1637 (Ghana, AD 14.label: Portuguese rule, 1469-1637
Portuguese rule, 1469-1637 (Ghana, AD 14.prose:
[Ghana, AD 1469–AD 1637] Portuguese rule, 1469-1637. Extracted from heading "Ghana--History--Portuguese rule, 1469-1637". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.46 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Portuguese ships reached the gold-bearing coast and in 1482 built São Jorge da Mina at Elmina, the first large European fortress in tropical Africa, to funnel gold from Akan states into Lisbon's treasury. Trade ran both ways: Portugal bought gold and sold cloth, metalware and, increasingly, enslaved people carried from elsewhere on the coast. Dutch competition eroded the monopoly through the early 1600s and ended it when Elmina fell in 1637, opening the era of rival European forts crowding the shoreline.

Al-Aqsa Intifada, 2000- (Gaza Strip, AD.label: Al-Aqsa Intifada, 2000-
Al-Aqsa Intifada, 2000- (Gaza Strip, AD.prose:
[Gaza, West Bank, AD 2000–AD 2015] Al-Aqsa Intifada, 2000-. Spatial coverage: Gaza Strip, Israel, State of Palestine, West Bank. Extracted from heading "Al-Aqsa Intifada, 2000-". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A second Palestinian uprising erupted in late 2000 and turned far more lethal than the first, with suicide bombings, Israeli reoccupation of West Bank cities and the building of the separation barrier. Israel withdrew its settlers and soldiers from Gaza in 2005; Hamas won elections the following year and seized full control of the Strip in 2007, prompting a long blockade. Repeated rounds of war in 2008–09, 2012 and 2014 devastated Gaza's infrastructure and left the territory politically severed from the West Bank.

Caligula, 37-41 (Roman Empire, AD 37–AD.label: Caligula, 37-41
Caligula, 37-41 (Roman Empire, AD 37–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 37–AD 41] Caligula, 37-41. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Caligula, 37-41". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rome's third emperor began his reign amid popular relief after Tiberius and ended it murdered by his own Praetorian guardsmen. Ancient writers, hostile almost to a man, left stories of cruelty, extravagance and self-deification that have shaped his reputation ever since; more solidly, he pushed imperial ceremonial towards outright monarchy, drained the treasury on building and games, and annexed Mauretania. His assassination raised the question of whether the Republic could be restored, and the guard's answer, proclaiming his uncle Claudius, showed that the army now made emperors.

Ansei Purge, 1858-1860 (Japan, AD 1858–A.label: Ansei Purge, 1858-1860
Ansei Purge, 1858-1860 (Japan, AD 1858–A.prose:
[Japan, AD 1858–AD 1860] Ansei Purge, 1858-1860. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Ansei Purge, 1858-1860". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The shogunal regent Ii Naosuke signed commercial treaties with the Western powers without imperial sanction and installed his own candidate as shogun, then jailed, exiled or executed those who objected. Among the victims was the teacher Yoshida Shōin, whose students went on to lead the overthrow of the shogunate. Ii himself was cut down by swordsmen outside Edo Castle's Sakurada Gate, a killing that shattered the shogunate's aura of authority.

Abdul Mejid, 1839-1861 (Turkey, AD 1839–.label: Abdul Mejid, 1839-1861
Abdul Mejid, 1839-1861 (Turkey, AD 1839–.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1839–AD 1861] Abdul Mejid, 1839-1861. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Abdul Mejid, 1839-1861". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The sultan who proclaimed the Tanzimat reforms, promising equality before the law for Muslims and non-Muslims, new law codes, and a reorganised bureaucracy and army. His reign brought the Crimean War alliance with Britain and France, the first Ottoman foreign loans, and European-style palaces like Dolmabahçe.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Maryland, AD 1861–.label: Civil War, 1861-1865

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Arcadius, 395-408 (Byzantine Empire, AD.label: Arcadius, 395-408
Arcadius, 395-408 (Byzantine Empire, AD.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 395–AD 408] Arcadius, 395-408. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Arcadius, 395-408". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Theodosius' elder son inherited the eastern half of the empire as a teenager and never really governed it; power passed among the praetorian prefect Rufinus, the eunuch Eutropius, the Gothic general Gainas and the empress Eudoxia. Constantinople survived Gothic pressure by diplomacy and money rather than battle, while the east's tax base and cities held up as the west began to fray. The reign is best remembered for the clash between the court and John Chrysostom, the outspoken bishop driven into exile and death.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Terni, AD 1943–A.label: Bombardment, 1943-1944
Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Terni, AD 1943–A.prose:
[Terni (Italy), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Terni (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2015. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

Frederick VII, 1848-1863 (Denmark, AD 18.label: Frederick VII, 1848-1863
Frederick VII, 1848-1863 (Denmark, AD 18.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1848–AD 1863] Frederick VII, 1848-1863. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick VII, 1848-1863".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inherited absolute power and gave it up within a year, signing the June Constitution of 1849 that made Denmark a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. His reign was dominated by the Schleswig-Holstein question: a three-year war with the German duchies and their allies ended in Danish victory, but the settlement was fragile. Childless, he was the last of the Oldenburg line, and the disputed succession after his death gave Bismarck the opening for the war of 1864.

Charles IX, 1560-1574 (France, AD 1560–A.label: Charles IX, 1560-1574
Charles IX, 1560-1574 (France, AD 1560–A.prose:
[France, AD 1560–AD 1574] Charles IX, 1560-1574. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles IX, 1560-1574".Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the throne at ten with his mother Catherine de' Medici holding real power, in a France splitting along confessional lines. Attempts at compromise between Catholics and Huguenots collapsed into repeated civil wars, and in August 1572 the killing of Protestant leaders in Paris spilled into the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, thousands dead in the capital and provinces. He died at twenty-three, the wars unresolved.

Basil II Bulgaroctonus, 976-1025 (Byzant.label: Basil II Bulgaroctonus, 976-1025
Basil II Bulgaroctonus, 976-1025 (Byzant.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 976–AD 1025] Basil II Bulgaroctonus, 976-1025. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Basil II Bulgaroctonus, 976-1025". Added to LCSH in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After surviving years of revolt by the great military families, Basil spent decades grinding down the Bulgarian state, earning the name 'Bulgar-slayer' — tradition says he blinded thousands of prisoners after Kleidion. He annexed Bulgaria, secured Armenia and Georgia, curbed the landed aristocracy in favour of the peasantry that paid the taxes, and recruited the Varangian Guard from Rus mercenaries. He left the empire at its greatest extent since antiquity, and a full treasury that his successors squandered.

Yongzheng, 1723-1735 (China, AD 1723–AD.label: Yongzheng, 1723-1735
Yongzheng, 1723-1735 (China, AD 1723–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1723–AD 1735] Yongzheng, 1723-1735. Extracted from heading "China--History--Yongzheng, 1723-1735". Added to LCSH in 2000. A short, severe reign between two long ones, spent auditing the treasury, punishing corrupt officials and stripping power from the Manchu princes who had rivalled him for the throne. Fiscal reform folded the head tax into land tax and funded local government openly rather than through unofficial levies. Porcelain, painting and lacquer made for his court are admired for restraint and technical perfection.

Third Reich, 1933-1945 (Germany, AD 1933.label: Third Reich, 1933-1945
Third Reich, 1933-1945 (Germany, AD 1933.prose:
[Germany , AD 1933–AD 1945] Third Reich, 1933-1945. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--1933-1945". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Variant used as primary label because it identifies the period by name as well as date range. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hitler's dictatorship dismantled the Weimar Republic within months, replacing parliamentary politics with one-party rule, secret police and mass propaganda. Rearmament and territorial aggression triggered the Second World War, while state antisemitism escalated into the industrialised murder of six million Jews and millions of others. Its total defeat left Germany divided, occupied and confronting the legal and moral reckoning of the Nuremberg trials.

Mongolian Invasions, 1231-1270 (Korean P.label: Mongolian Invasions, 1231-1270
Mongolian Invasions, 1231-1270 (Korean P.prose:
[Korea, AD 1231–AD 1270] Mongolian Invasions, 1231-1270. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Mongolian Invasions, 1231-1270". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Six major Mongol campaigns battered Goryeo over four decades while the Choe military dictators sheltered on Ganghwa Island, leaving the mainland peasantry to bear the devastation. Monks carved the Tripitaka Koreana's eighty thousand woodblocks as a plea for divine protection; the great Hwangnyongsa pagoda burned. Goryeo eventually submitted and entered a long period of Mongol domination, marriage alliances and tribute, resisted to the last by the Sambyeolcho rebels.

Robert I, 1306-1329 (Scotland, AD 1306–A.label: Robert I, 1306-1329
Robert I, 1306-1329 (Scotland, AD 1306–A.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1306–AD 1329] Robert I, 1306-1329. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Robert I, 1306-1329". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Robert the Bruce killed his rival, took the crown in defiance of Edward I, and spent years as a hunted guerrilla before turning the tide. His victory at Bannockburn in 1314 and the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320 secured recognition of Scottish independence, sealed by treaty in 1328, and made him the founding hero of the Scottish national story.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Rhode Island, AD 1.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Rhode Island, AD 1.prose:
[Rhode Island, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Rhode Island--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.97 of LCSH 1987, and p.95 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

British rule, 1867-1942 (Malaysia, AD 18.label: British rule, 1867-1942
British rule, 1867-1942 (Malaysia, AD 18.prose:
[Malaya, AD 1867–AD 1942] British rule, 1867-1942. Extracted from heading "Malaya--History--British rule, 1867-1942". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Straits Settlements passed from Indian to Colonial Office control, and British residents were soon installed in the Malay states, leaving sultans as ceremonial rulers. Tin mining and rubber plantations made the peninsula one of the empire's most profitable possessions and drew in huge Chinese and Indian labour migrations that reshaped its population. Japanese invasion in 1941-42 shattered British prestige and set the stage for decolonisation.

Charles VIII, 1483-1498 (France, AD 1483.label: Charles VIII, 1483-1498
Charles VIII, 1483-1498 (France, AD 1483.prose:
[France, AD 1483–AD 1498] Charles VIII, 1483-1498. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles VIII, 1483-1498". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His march into Italy to claim the throne of Naples began the Italian Wars, a struggle between France, Spain and the Habsburgs that consumed the peninsula for sixty years. The campaign was a military stroll and a political failure, but the French returned dazzled by Italian art, gardens and architecture, importing Renaissance taste wholesale. He died at twenty-seven after striking his head on a door lintel at Amboise.

Turkic Mongol domination, 1045-1522 (Arm.label: Turkic Mongol domination, 1045-1522
Turkic Mongol domination, 1045-1522 (Arm.prose:
[Armenia, AD 1045–AD 1522] Turkic Mongol domination, 1045-1522. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Turkic Mongol domination, 1045-1522". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.5 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the Bagratid kingdom absorbed by Byzantium and Ani soon lost to the Seljuks, Armenia passed through centuries of rule by incoming steppe powers — Seljuk, Mongol, Timurid, and the Turkmen Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu. Invasion, heavy taxation and depopulation pushed many Armenians to emigrate, notably to Cilicia, the Crimea and later Poland. Monastic scriptoria nonetheless kept producing illuminated manuscripts, and local princely houses survived in the mountains.

Anna, 1730-1740 (Russia, AD 1730–AD 1740.label: Anna, 1730-1740
Anna, 1730-1740 (Russia, AD 1730–AD 1740.prose:
[Russia , AD 1730–AD 1740] Anna, 1730-1740. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Anna, 1730-1740". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Invited to the throne on conditions that would have handed power to a council of magnates, Anna publicly tore up the document and restored full autocracy. Her reign is remembered for the dominance of German favourites around Ernst Biron, a feared secret chancery, costly wars against the Ottomans and Poland, and a court of extravagant spectacle, including a palace built of ice. She left the crown to an infant grand-nephew, opening a scramble that put Peter the Great's daughter Elizabeth on the throne.

Revolution, 1910-1920 (Mexico, AD 1910–A.label: Revolution, 1910-1920
Revolution, 1910-1920 (Mexico, AD 1910–A.prose:
[Mexico, AD 1910–AD 1920] Revolution, 1910-1920. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--Revolution, 1910-1920". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.77 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Francisco Madero's call to arms against the thirty-year dictatorship of Porfirio Diaz unleashed a decade of civil war in which Emiliano Zapata's land-hungry villagers in the south and Pancho Villa's cavalry in the north fought, and then fought each other and the constitutionalists. Perhaps a million people died. The 1917 Constitution that emerged promised land redistribution, labour rights and state ownership of subsoil resources, and the victors built the single party that governed Mexico for the rest of the century.

Francis II, 1559-1560 (France, AD 1559–A.label: Francis II, 1559-1560
Francis II, 1559-1560 (France, AD 1559–A.prose:
[France, AD 1559–AD 1560] Francis II, 1559-1560. Extracted from heading "France--History--Francis II, 1559-1560". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A sickly fifteen-year-old who came to the throne when his father was killed in a tournament, and died of an ear infection seventeen months later. He was married to Mary, Queen of Scots, and his brief reign put her Guise uncles in command of France, whose harsh treatment of Protestants provoked the failed Amboise conspiracy. His death handed power to his mother Catherine de' Medici on the eve of the Wars of Religion.

Revolution of 1848-1849 (Rome, AD 1848–A.label: Revolution of 1848-1849
Revolution of 1848-1849 (Rome, AD 1848–A.prose:
[Rome, AD 1848–AD 1849] Revolution of 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Revolution of 1848-1849". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 85 of LCSH 1975 under Rome (City). Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With Pope Pius IX fled to Gaeta after the assassination of his minister Rossi, radicals proclaimed a Roman Republic and abolished the temporal power of the papacy. Mazzini led its triumvirate and Garibaldi organised its defence, and for a few months Rome experimented with universal male suffrage and land reform. A French army sent by Louis-Napoleon crushed it after a siege, restoring the pope and making Rome a symbol for the Italian national movement.

William IV, 1830-1837 (United Kingdom, A.label: William IV, 1830-1837
William IV, 1830-1837 (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1830–AD 1837] William IV, 1830-1837. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--William IV, 1830-1837". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The "Sailor King" came to the throne in his sixties after a career in the navy and an unroyal domestic life, and immediately faced a constitutional crisis over parliamentary reform. He reluctantly agreed to create peers if needed, which forced the Lords to pass the Great Reform Act of 1832, redistributing seats and widening the franchise. His short reign also brought the abolition of slavery across most of the British Empire, factory legislation and the new Poor Law, and ended with the accession of his niece Victoria.

Hashemite Kingdom, 1921-1958 (Iraq, AD 1.label: Hashemite Kingdom, 1921-1958
Hashemite Kingdom, 1921-1958 (Iraq, AD 1.prose:
[Iraq, AD 1921–AD 1958] Hashemite Kingdom, 1921-1958. Extracted from heading "Iraq--History--Hashemite Kingdom, 1921-1958". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Created by Britain out of three Ottoman provinces, the new kingdom was handed to Faisal, the Hashemite prince who had led the Arab Revolt and been expelled from Syria. Formal independence came in 1932, but British bases, advisers and oil interests remained, fuelling nationalist anger through the Second World War and after. A military coup in 1958 killed the young King Faisal II and his family and ended the monarchy.

War of 1807-1814 (Denmark, AD 1807–AD 18.label: War of 1807-1814
War of 1807-1814 (Denmark, AD 1807–AD 18.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1807–AD 1814] War of 1807-1814. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--War of 1807-1814".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Dragged into the Napoleonic wars when Britain seized the Danish fleet, Norway was cut off by the Royal Navy's blockade from the grain it imported from Denmark, and years of hunger followed. When the losing side was carved up, the Treaty of Kiel handed Norway to Sweden, but Norwegians refused to be transferred and wrote their own constitution at Eidsvoll in 1814. A short Swedish campaign forced a union of crowns, yet the constitution survived and became the foundation of the modern Norwegian state.

Austrian rule, 1814-1866 (Veneto, AD 181.label: Austrian rule, 1814-1866
Austrian rule, 1814-1866 (Veneto, AD 181.prose:
[Venice (Italy), AD 1814–AD 1899] Austrian rule, 1814-1866. Extracted from heading "Venice (Italy)--History--Austrian rule, 1814-1866". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Congress of Vienna handed Venice and its mainland to Austria as half of the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia, governed by imperial bureaucrats and garrisons. Venice rose in 1848 under Daniele Manin and held out for seventeen months of blockade, bombardment and cholera before surrendering. Austria kept the province until defeat by Prussia in 1866 forced its cession, and a plebiscite joined the Veneto to the new Kingdom of Italy.

Turkish rule, 1430-1913 (Greece, AD 1430.label: Turkish rule, 1430-1913
Turkish rule, 1430-1913 (Greece, AD 1430.prose:

Ottoman administration over the Greek lands began with the fall of Thessaloniki and lasted, in the north, until the Balkan Wars. Greeks lived under the millet system, with the Patriarchate given authority over the Orthodox population, while Phanariot families rose to power in Constantinople and the Danubian provinces. Klepht bands, island shipping fortunes and Enlightenment ideas fed the revolution of 1821, after which the Ottoman frontier retreated northward in stages.

Soviet occupation, 1940-1941 (Latvia, AD.label: Soviet occupation, 1940-1941
Soviet occupation, 1940-1941 (Latvia, AD.prose:
[Latvia, AD 1940–AD 1941] Soviet occupation, 1940-1941. Extracted from heading "Latvia--History--Soviet occupation, 1940-1941". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under ultimatum, the country admitted Soviet troops, staged a rigged election and was incorporated into the USSR. Property was nationalised, the officer corps and political class arrested, and some 15,000 people deported eastward in a single June night in 1941. The German advance swept the Soviets out within days, leaving a legacy of trauma that fed both collaboration and later resistance.

Chremonidean War, 267-262 B.C (Greece, 2.label: Chremonidean War, 267-262 B.C
Chremonidean War, 267-262 B.C (Greece, 2.prose:
[Greece, 266 BC–261 BC] Chremonidean War, 267-262 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Chremonidean War, 267-262 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Athens and Sparta, encouraged and subsidised by Ptolemy II of Egypt, tried to shake off Macedonian domination of Greece. Antigonos Gonatas blockaded Athens into surrender, killed the Spartan king Areus in battle, and installed garrisons in the city and its ports. Athens lost control of its own foreign policy for a generation, and Macedonian mastery of the mainland was confirmed.

Jane I, 1343-1382 (Naples, AD 1343–AD 13.label: Jane I, 1343-1382
Jane I, 1343-1382 (Naples, AD 1343–AD 13.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1343–AD 1382] Jane I, 1343-1382. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Jane I, 1343-1382". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.65 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Queen of Naples and countess of Provence, she inherited at seventeen and ruled for nearly four decades through four marriages, papal quarrels and civil war, dogged by suspicion over the murder of her first husband. She sold Avignon to the papacy, and her backing of the Avignon claimant during the Great Schism cost her dearly. Deposed by her cousin Charles of Durazzo, she was smothered in prison.

Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713 (Massachuset.label: Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713
Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713 (Massachuset.prose:
[Massachusetts, AD 1702–AD 1713] Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713. Extracted from heading "Massachusetts--History--Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.90 of LCSH 1987, and p.88 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The North American front of the War of the Spanish Succession, fought between English colonists and New France with Native allies decisive on both sides. Frontier settlements bore the worst of it: the raid on Deerfield in 1704 left dozens dead and more than a hundred captives marched north to Canada. The peace at Utrecht handed Britain Acadia, Newfoundland and Hudson Bay, setting up the final struggle for the continent.

Frederick VI, 1808-1839 (Denmark, AD 180.label: Frederick VI, 1808-1839
Frederick VI, 1808-1839 (Denmark, AD 180.prose:
[Denmark , AD 1808–AD 1839] Frederick VI, 1808-1839. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick VI, 1808-1839".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As crown prince regent from 1784 he pushed through the great agrarian reforms that ended the peasants' bondage to the estate and redistributed land into individual farms. As king he backed Napoleon, saw Copenhagen bombarded and the fleet seized by Britain, endured state bankruptcy in 1813 and lost Norway in 1814. The later reign was quiet, paternalistic and censorious, though it created advisory provincial assemblies that would nurture the coming liberal movement.

Iwai Rebellion, 527-528 (Japan, AD 527–A.label: Iwai Rebellion, 527-528
Iwai Rebellion, 527-528 (Japan, AD 527–A.prose:
[Japan, AD 527–AD 528] Iwai Rebellion, 527-528. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Iwai Rebellion, 527-528". Added to LCSH in 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A powerful chieftain of northern Kyushu rose against the Yamato court, reportedly in league with the Korean kingdom of Silla, and cut the sea route by which Yamato armies reached the peninsula. Yamato crushed him after more than a year of fighting and then tightened its grip on Kyushu, planting royal estates and the administrative base that became the Dazaifu. The episode marks a step in the hardening of Yamato from a loose alliance of clans into a state.

John III, 1567-1592 (Sweden, AD 1567–AD.label: John III, 1567-1592
John III, 1567-1592 (Sweden, AD 1567–AD.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1567–AD 1592] John III, 1567-1592. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--John III, 1567-1592". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He seized the throne from his mentally unstable brother Erik XIV and imprisoned him. Married to a Polish Catholic princess, he pushed a Catholic-flavoured liturgy known as the Red Book on the Swedish church, provoking lasting resistance from Lutheran clergy. He fought a long war with Russia over Estonia, and his son Sigismund was elected king of Poland, entangling the two realms.

German occupation, 1914-1918 (France, AD.label: German occupation, 1914-1918
German occupation, 1914-1918 (France, AD.prose:
[France, AD 1914–AD 1918] German occupation, 1914-1918. Extracted from heading "France--History--German occupation, 1914-1918". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ten northern departments, containing much of France's coal, iron and textile industry, spent the whole war behind German lines. Civilians faced requisitions, forced labour gangs, curfews and hostage-taking, while factories were stripped of machinery and orchards felled during the 1917 retreat to the Hindenburg Line. The devastated zone left behind shaped French demands for reparations and a decade of reconstruction.

House of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, 1654-1718 (S.label: House of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, 1654-1718
House of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, 1654-1718 (S.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1654–AD 1718] House of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, 1654-1718. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--House of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, 1654-1718". Added to LCSH in 2007, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Christina's abdication brought her cousin Charles X Gustav to the throne, and three warrior kings followed: the march across the frozen Belts that humbled Denmark, Charles XI's reduktion of noble estates that funded a genuinely absolutist state, and Charles XII's long duel with Russia, Poland and Denmark. Poltava in 1709 broke the Swedish army, and the king's death before a Norwegian fortress in 1718 ended both the line and Sweden's career as a great power.

Joseph I, 1705-1711 (Austria, AD 1705–AD.label: Joseph I, 1705-1711
Joseph I, 1705-1711 (Austria, AD 1705–AD.prose:
[Austria, AD 1705–AD 1711] Joseph I, 1705-1711. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Joseph I, 1705-1711". Appears on p. 6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inheriting the War of the Spanish Succession from his father, this emperor pushed the Habsburg cause hard, backing Marlborough and Prince Eugene in the campaigns that broke French power in Italy and the Low Countries. At home he sought terms with the Hungarian rebels of Ferenc Rakoczi. His sudden death from smallpox at thirty-two upended everything: his brother Charles inherited both Austria and the Spanish claim, and the allies, unwilling to see one man rule such an empire, began negotiating the peace of Utrecht.

Allied occupation, 1945-1990 (Berlin, AD.label: Allied occupation, 1945-1990
Allied occupation, 1945-1990 (Berlin, AD.prose:
[Berlin, AD 1945–AD 1990] Allied occupation, 1945-1990. Extracted from heading "Berlin (Germany)--History--1945-1990". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The ruined capital was carved into four sectors deep inside the Soviet zone, an arrangement that turned the city into the front line of the Cold War. Stalin's blockade of the western sectors was defeated by an eleven-month airlift; the Wall went up in 1961 to stop the flow of East Germans westward. Four-power rights formally lapsed only with reunification, after the Wall was opened in 1989.

Konbaung dynasty, 1752-1885 (Burma, AD 1.label: Konbaung dynasty, 1752-1885
Konbaung dynasty, 1752-1885 (Burma, AD 1.prose:
[Burma, AD 1752–AD 1885] Konbaung dynasty, 1752-1885. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Konbaung dynasty, 1752-1885". Added to LCSH in 1987; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by Alaungpaya, the last Burmese royal house reunified the country, sacked the Siamese capital of Ayutthaya in 1767 and pushed west into Manipur and Assam. That westward expansion collided with British India and produced three Anglo-Burmese wars, each stripping away provinces, until the deposition of King Thibaw in 1885 ended Burmese independence. The dynasty also built Mandalay and left the great glazed and gilded monastic architecture that survives there.

Turkish Wars, 15th Century (Albania, AD.label: Turkish Wars, 15th Century
Turkish Wars, 15th Century (Albania, AD.prose:
[Albania, AD 1400–AD 1499] Turkish Wars, 15th Century. Extracted from heading "Albania--History--Turkish Wars". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.2 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ottoman armies pushed into the Albanian highlands and met sustained resistance led by Skanderbeg, who held Krujë through repeated sieges and became a symbol of Christian defiance across Europe. After his death in 1468 the country was progressively subdued, and Venetian coastal holdings fell one by one. Thousands fled across the Adriatic, founding the Arbëresh communities still found in southern Italy.

Julian, 361-363 (Roman Empire, AD 361–AD.label: Julian, 361-363
Julian, 361-363 (Roman Empire, AD 361–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 361–AD 363] Julian, 361-363. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Julian, 361-363". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last non-Christian Roman emperor, raised a Christian but converted in secret to the old gods and Neoplatonic philosophy. Once in sole power he restored the temples, cut state subsidies to the church, barred Christians from teaching classical literature, and tried to reorganise paganism into a rival charitable priesthood. He was killed on campaign in Persia after eighteen months, and the pagan revival died with him.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Azerbaijan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Azerbaijan, AD 19.prose:
[Azerbaijan, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Azerbaijan--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Medieval Church period, 1057-1567 (Scotl.label: Medieval Church period, 1057-1567
Medieval Church period, 1057-1567 (Scotl.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1057–AD 1567] Medieval Church period, 1057-1567. Extracted from heading "Scotland--Church history--To 1500". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Scotland's church was reorganised on continental lines: dioceses and parishes were fixed, Augustinian, Cistercian and later friar houses were founded, and great buildings like Melrose, Glasgow Cathedral and St Andrews rose. The church claimed independence from York and Canterbury, answering directly to Rome as a 'special daughter'. The period closes with the Reformation of 1560 and the deposition of Mary, Queen of Scots, after which monastic estates were carved up and many churches stripped.

Raoul, 923-936 (France, AD 923–AD 936).label: Raoul, 923-936
Raoul, 923-936 (France, AD 923–AD 936).prose:
[France, AD 923–AD 936] Raoul, 923-936. Extracted from heading "France--History--Raoul, 923-936". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Duke of Burgundy, elected king of the Franks after Charles the Simple was deposed and imprisoned by rebellious magnates. His reign was consumed by fighting Viking raiders on the Seine and Loire and Hungarian horsemen in the east, and by the reality that the great regional princes now made and unmade kings. His death allowed the Carolingian line to be restored, though the Robertian family he served would eventually supply the Capetian dynasty.

Corinthian War, 395-386 B.C (Greece, 394.label: Corinthian War, 395-386 B.C
Corinthian War, 395-386 B.C (Greece, 394.prose:
[Greece, 394 BC–385 BC] Corinthian War, 395-386 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Corinthian War, 395-386 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sparta's heavy-handed dominance after winning the Peloponnesian War drove Corinth, Thebes, Argos and a reviving Athens into an alliance against it, bankrolled by Persian gold. Athens rebuilt its Long Walls and its fleet, and the Spartan navy was smashed at Cnidus, but the war ended with Persia switching sides and dictating the King's Peace, which handed the Greek cities of Asia Minor back to the Great King.

Robert I, 922-923 (France, AD 922–AD 923.label: Robert I, 922-923
Robert I, 922-923 (France, AD 922–AD 923.prose:
[France, AD 922–AD 923] Robert I, 922-923. Extracted from heading "France--History--Robert I, 922-923". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A great magnate of the Seine and Loire, he was raised up by nobles who had lost patience with the Carolingian Charles the Simple, and crowned in rebellion against him. He was killed within months at the battle of Soissons, but his family's power endured: his grandson Hugh Capet founded the dynasty that would rule France for centuries.

Revolution, 1791-1804 (Haiti, AD 1791–AD.label: Revolution, 1791-1804
Revolution, 1791-1804 (Haiti, AD 1791–AD.prose:
[Haiti, AD 1791–AD 1804] Revolution, 1791-1804. Extracted from heading "Haiti--History--Revolution, 1791-1804". added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 54 of LCSH 1987, and p. 43 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Enslaved people in France's richest sugar colony rose in the north and, under Toussaint Louverture and then Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeated French, Spanish and British armies in turn. Slavery was abolished, restored by Napoleon and abolished again by force of arms, and in 1804 Haiti declared independence as the first Black republic and the second independent state in the Americas. The victory terrified slaveholding societies everywhere and pushed France to sell Louisiana.

Bombardment, 1936-1938 (Majorca, AD 1936.label: Bombardment, 1936-1938
Bombardment, 1936-1938 (Majorca, AD 1936.prose:
[Majorca (Spain), AD 1936–AD 1938] Bombardment, 1936-1938. Extracted from heading "Majorca (Spain)--History--Bombardment, 1936-1938". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Held by the Nationalists after a Republican landing failed, the island became a fortified air base from which Italian squadrons flew against Barcelona, Valencia and the Catalan coast. In return it drew Republican air and naval attacks on Palma and its harbour, making a Mediterranean holiday island one of the first places to experience the shuttle of modern aerial warfare.

Great War, 1843-1852 (Uruguay, AD 1843–A.label: Great War, 1843-1852
Great War, 1843-1852 (Uruguay, AD 1843–A.prose:
[Uruguay, AD 1843–AD 1852] Great War, 1843-1852. Extracted from heading "Uruguay--History--Great War, 1843-1852". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.106 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Uruguay's Colorados and Blancos fought a civil war that drew in Argentina, Brazil, Britain and France, with Montevideo besieged for nearly nine years while the countryside was held by the opposing side. Giuseppe Garibaldi commanded an Italian legion in the defence of the city, an apprenticeship for his later campaigns in Italy. The war entrenched the two-party division that shaped Uruguayan politics for the next century.

Conrad II, 1024-1039 (Germany, AD 1024–A.label: Conrad II, 1024-1039
Conrad II, 1024-1039 (Germany, AD 1024–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1024–AD 1039] Conrad II, 1024-1039. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Conrad II, 1024-1039". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first of the Salian emperors, elected when the Ottonian line died out, and a ruler who leaned on lesser knights and ministeriales rather than the great dukes. He secured hereditary rights for minor vassals in Italy, strengthening a service nobility loyal to the crown. His acquisition of the kingdom of Burgundy joined the three crowns of Germany, Italy and Burgundy under one emperor.

Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686.node: Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686 B.C (Egypt, 3099 BC–2685 BC)
Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686.label: Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686 B.C
Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686.prose:
[Egypt, 3099 BC–2685 BC] Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Early Dynastic Period, ca. 3100-ca. 2686 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Egypt's first kings welded the Nile valley and Delta into one realm and invented the apparatus to run it — hieroglyphic writing, a royal court at Memphis, provincial administration and a calendar tied to the flood. Elaborate tombs at Abydos and Saqqara, sealed with jars of wine and oil from far afield, show wealth flowing to the crown. The artistic and religious language established now underpins everything that follows, including the pyramids of the next dynasty.

Canudos Campaign, 1893-1897 (Brazil, AD.label: Canudos Campaign, 1893-1897
Canudos Campaign, 1893-1897 (Brazil, AD.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1893–AD 1897] Canudos Campaign, 1893-1897. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--Canudos Campaign, 1893-1897". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In the drought-stricken backlands of Bahia, the wandering preacher Antônio Conselheiro gathered thousands of poor settlers into a religious community that the new Brazilian republic branded a monarchist threat. Three military expeditions were beaten back before a massive fourth force levelled the settlement and killed most of its inhabitants. Euclides da Cunha's eyewitness account, Os Sertões, turned the slaughter into a founding critique of Brazil's divide between coast and interior.

Heraclius, 610-641 (Byzantine Empire, AD.label: Heraclius, 610-641
Heraclius, 610-641 (Byzantine Empire, AD.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 610–AD 641] Heraclius, 610-641. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Heraclius, 610-641". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Seizing power amid catastrophe, he clawed back the Byzantine east from the Persians in a series of daring campaigns, recovering the True Cross and destroying Sassanian power. Within a decade of that triumph, exhausted armies lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arab conquests at Yarmuk and after. His reign marks the point where the East Roman state becomes recognisably Byzantine: Greek replaced Latin as the language of government, and the emperor took the title basileus.

Honorius, 395-423 (Roman Empire, AD 395–.label: Honorius, 395-423
Honorius, 395-423 (Roman Empire, AD 395–.prose:
[Rome, AD 395–AD 423] Honorius, 395-423. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Honorius, 395-423". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The western half of the Roman Empire under a weak emperor who ruled from the marshes of Ravenna while his generals and rivals fought over the provinces. In these years Alaric's Goths sacked Rome, Roman troops left Britain for good, and Vandals, Sueves and Alans crossed the frozen Rhine into Gaul and Spain. By his death barbarian kingdoms were settled on imperial soil as supposed allies, an arrangement from which the west never recovered.

William I, 1066-1087 (England, AD 1066–A.label: William I, 1066-1087
William I, 1066-1087 (England, AD 1066–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1066–AD 1087] William I, 1066-1087. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--William I, 1066-1087". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Norman duke who won England at Hastings and then spent twenty years holding it, crushing revolts and devastating Yorkshire so thoroughly in the Harrying of the North that the damage still showed a generation later. He replaced almost the entire English landholding class with Normans, planted castles in every major town, and tied land to military service. The Domesday survey of 1086 counted the resulting kingdom manor by manor and remains the most detailed record of any early medieval European state.

Revolution, 1922-1923 (Paraguay, AD 1922.label: Revolution, 1922-1923
Revolution, 1922-1923 (Paraguay, AD 1922.prose:
[Paraguay, AD 1922–AD 1923] Revolution, 1922-1923. Extracted from heading "Paraguay--History--Revolution, 1922-1923". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rival factions of Paraguay's ruling Liberal Party turned their quarrel over the presidency into open war, with army units splitting between the government in Asunción and the rebels. The fighting devastated an already poor country and was settled by government victory, leaving the political system unstable a decade before the Chaco War with Bolivia.

Charles Albert, 1831-1849 (Sardinia, AD.label: Charles Albert, 1831-1849
Charles Albert, 1831-1849 (Sardinia, AD.prose:
[Sardinia, AD 1831–AD 1849] Charles Albert, 1831-1849. Extracted from heading "Sardinia--History--Charles Albert, 1831-1849". Added to LCSH in 2003; appears on p.101 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The king of Piedmont-Sardinia who granted the Statuto Albertino in 1848, a constitution that would serve as the basic law of united Italy until 1946. He led Piedmont into war against Austria during the revolutions of 1848, and after defeat at Novara abdicated in favour of his son Victor Emmanuel II, leaving Piedmont as the state around which Italian unification would form.

Kamakura-Momoyama periods, 1185-1600 (Ja.label: Kamakura-Momoyama periods, 1185-1600
Kamakura-Momoyama periods, 1185-1600 (Ja.prose:
[Japan, AD 1185–AD 1600] Kamakura-Momoyama periods, 1185-1600. "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Japanese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A broad art-historical sweep from the rise of samurai rule through the fractured Muromachi centuries to the warlord unifiers of the late sixteenth century. It covers Zen ink painting and dry-landscape gardens, the tea ceremony and Noh theatre, the arrival of Portuguese traders and firearms, and finally the gilded screens and towering castles built by Nobunaga and Hideyoshi.

War of the Emboabas, 1707-1709 (Brazil,.label: War of the Emboabas, 1707-1709
War of the Emboabas, 1707-1709 (Brazil,.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1707–AD 1709] War of the Emboabas, 1707-1709. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--War of the Emboabas, 1707-1709". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The gold strikes of Minas Gerais drew a flood of newcomers from Portugal and Brazil's northeast, whom the Paulista pioneers who had found the deposits derided as 'emboabas' and tried to drive out. The fighting ended with the Paulistas defeated and the Portuguese Crown stepping in to impose order, creating a new captaincy and a machinery of taxation over the richest gold region in the world. Displaced Paulistas pushed west, opening Goiás and Mato Grosso.

Non-cooperation movement, 1920-1922 (Ind.label: Non-cooperation movement, 1920-1922
Non-cooperation movement, 1920-1922 (Ind.prose:
[India, AD 1920–AD 1922] Non-cooperation movement, 1920-1922. Extracted from heading "India--History--Non-cooperation movement, 1920-1922". Added to LCSH in 1990, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Gandhi's first all-India mass campaign asked Indians to withdraw from the Raj rather than confront it: to boycott British courts, schools, titles, elections and cloth, and to spin their own khadi instead. Joined to the Khilafat agitation, it brought Hindus and Muslims into the same protest and turned the Congress from a debating body of lawyers into a mass organisation with village branches. Gandhi called it off after a mob burned policemen alive at Chauri Chagra, insisting that nonviolence was not negotiable — a decision that disillusioned many but set the template for the campaigns that followed.

Long March, 1934-1935 (China, AD 1934–AD.label: Long March, 1934-1935
Long March, 1934-1935 (China, AD 1934–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1934–AD 1935] Long March, 1934-1935. Extracted from heading "China--History--Long March, 1934-1935". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Encircled and nearly destroyed by Nationalist armies, the Chinese Communists broke out of their southern base and marched thousands of kilometres through mountains, marshland and hostile territory to reach a refuge in the northwest. Most who set out died on the way. At a conference in Zunyi during the retreat Mao Zedong secured leadership of the party, and the ordeal became the founding legend of the People's Republic.

Ba Đinh Uprising, 1886-1887 (Vietnam, AD.label: Ba Đinh Uprising, 1886-1887
Ba Đinh Uprising, 1886-1887 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1886–AD 1887] Ba Đinh Uprising, 1886-1887. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Ba Đinh Uprising, 1886-1887". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A stronghold of three fortified villages in Thanh Hóa province held out for months against French artillery and infantry, the most famous set-piece battle of the Cần Vương ("Aid the King") resistance that followed the French seizure of the Nguyễn court. Its defenders, led by Đinh Công Tráng and Phạm Bành, dug bamboo-and-mud ramparts behind flooded paddy fields and were finally burned out; the survivors scattered into guerrilla bands. The defeat showed that scholar-gentry loyalist warfare could not stop colonial firepower, and later Vietnamese nationalists looked back on it as a founding act of anti-French struggle.

French Protectorate, 1912-1956 (Morocco,.label: French Protectorate, 1912-1956
French Protectorate, 1912-1956 (Morocco,.prose:
[Morocco, AD 1912–AD 1956] French Protectorate, 1912-1956. Extracted from heading "Morocco--History--1912-1956". Added to LCSH and revised in 2000. The primary variant does not include a label for the period, so we have used the two variants that do include labels. Different parts of the country itself were under French and Spanish control at the same time, which explains the two apparently contradictory labels. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Treaty of Fes left the sultan on his throne while France took control of the army, finances and foreign policy, with Spain holding the north and Tangier internationalised. Lyautey's administration built ville nouvelle districts alongside preserved medinas, laid railways and ports, and fought a long war of 'pacification' in the Atlas and the Rif that lasted into the 1930s. Nationalist agitation and the sultan's exile turned Mohammed V into a symbol of independence, achieved when the protectorate was dissolved.

Acacian Schism, 484-519 (Roman Empire, A.label: Acacian Schism, 484-519
Acacian Schism, 484-519 (Roman Empire, A.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, Rome, AD 484–AD 519] Acacian Schism, 484-519. Spatial coverage: Byzantine Empire, Roman Empire. Extracted from heading "Schism, Acacian, 484-519 ". Added to LCSH in 1986. Spatial coverage description given as "Church", coverage inferred from state of Church in this time period. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A thirty-five-year rupture between the churches of Rome and Constantinople, triggered by the emperor Zeno's Henotikon, a compromise formula meant to reconcile opponents of the Council of Chalcedon. Popes excommunicated the patriarch Acacius; eastern emperors refused to back down. The split hardened the divide between Chalcedonian and Miaphysite Christians and gave an early rehearsal of the later East-West schism.

Empire, 284-476 (Roman Empire, AD 284–AD.label: Empire, 284-476
Empire, 284-476 (Roman Empire, AD 284–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 284–AD 476] Empire, 284-476. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Empire, 284-476". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Diocletian rebuilt a shattered empire with co-emperors, a bigger bureaucracy, a mobile field army and price controls, and Constantine added a Christian church backed by the state and a new capital at Constantinople. Power drifted east while the western provinces absorbed Goths, Vandals and Franks as settlers, soldiers and then rulers. By 476 a western emperor had become an irrelevance, and a Germanic king in Italy simply dispensed with the office.

Haakon Gamli, 1217-1263 (Norway, AD 1217.label: Haakon Gamli, 1217-1263
Haakon Gamli, 1217-1263 (Norway, AD 1217.prose:
[Norway, AD 1217–AD 1263] Haakon Gamli, 1217-1263. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Haakon Gamli, 1217-1263". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Haakon IV ended over a century of Norwegian civil war and presided over what later historians called the kingdom's golden age: a stable royal succession, a professional court, stone castles and cathedrals, and translated French romances read aloud in the hall. Iceland and Greenland submitted to the Norwegian crown in his reign, giving Norway its greatest extent. He died in Orkney on his way home from an inconclusive campaign against the Scots.

Otho I, 1832-1862 (Greece, AD 1832–AD 18.label: Otho I, 1832-1862
Otho I, 1832-1862 (Greece, AD 1832–AD 18.prose:
[Greece, AD 1832–AD 1862] Otho I, 1832-1862. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Otho I, 1832-1862". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975 under "Greece, Modern". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Great Powers handed the throne of the new Greek kingdom to a seventeen-year-old Bavarian prince, who arrived with German troops, German advisers and a regency that governed in his name. Athens – then a village among ruins – was made the capital and rebuilt on a neoclassical plan, while resentment at foreign officials and the king's refusal of a constitution boiled over in the bloodless coup of 1843. Continued frustration with his rule and his failed adventures in the Crimean War led to his deposition and exile.

Boeotian War, 378-375 B.C (Greece, 377 B.label: Boeotian War, 378-375 B.C
Boeotian War, 378-375 B.C (Greece, 377 B.prose:
[Greece, 377 BC–374 BC] Boeotian War, 378-375 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Boeotian War, 378-375 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Theban exiles murdered the pro-Spartan junta and expelled the Spartan garrison from their citadel, and the war that followed pitted a revived Boeotian federation, backed by Athens, against Sparta's hegemony over Greece. Athens used the crisis to build a second naval confederacy, promising members they would not be treated as subjects this time. Sparta failed to crush Thebes, whose Sacred Band and new tactics were tested here before shattering the Spartan army at Leuctra a few years later.

Alexander I, 1801-1825 (Russia, AD 1801–.label: Alexander I, 1801-1825
Alexander I, 1801-1825 (Russia, AD 1801–.prose:
[Russia , AD 1801–AD 1825] Alexander I, 1801-1825. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Alexander I, 1801-1825". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Came to the throne over his murdered father's body, flirted with liberal reform, then found himself Napoleon's chief antagonist: allied at Tilsit, invaded in 1812, and riding into Paris as the man who broke the Grande Armée. At the Congress of Vienna he redrew Europe and pushed his mystical Holy Alliance, but turned conservative at home, and his sudden death triggered the Decembrist revolt.

Capetians, 987-1328 (France, AD 987–AD 1.label: Capetians, 987-1328
Capetians, 987-1328 (France, AD 987–AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 987–AD 1328] Capetians, 987-1328. Extracted from heading "France--History--Capetians, 987-1328". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.28 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hugh Capet's family held the French crown for over three centuries by a mixture of luck, fertility and the habit of crowning the heir during the father's lifetime. From a small domain around Paris they grew into rulers who seized Normandy and the south, built up royal courts and taxation, and made the Ile-de-France the centre of Gothic architecture and scholastic learning. The line's failure of male heirs in 1328 triggered the dynastic dispute behind the Hundred Years War.

New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847 (New Zealand.label: New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847
New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847 (New Zealand.prose:
[New Zealand, AD 1843–AD 1847] New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847. Extracted from heading "New Zealand--History--New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847". Added to LCSH in 2004. Sources cited: Belich, J. The New Zealand wars and the Victorian interpretation of racial conflict, 1986: p. 204 (three local outbreaks of conflict took place between 1843 and 1847) p. 212 (The period 1847-60 was one of peace between Māori and Pākehā); Oxford hist. of N.Z., 1981: p. 148 (The central role of land in the wars between Māori and Pāehā has often been remarked; sometimes they have been called the Land Wars); The New Zealand Wars web site, Sept. 19, 2003 (The New Zealand Wars were fought in New Zealand between 1843 and 1872) what's in a name (the Maori Wars; the Land Wars; Nga Pakanga Nu Nui o Aotearoa; Nga pakanga o Aotearoa; the Anglo-Maori Wars; the Colonial New Zealand Wars; new Zealand Civil Wars; the overwhelmingly favourite name used these days is undoubtedly the New Zealand Wars). Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first armed clashes over land and sovereignty after the Treaty of Waitangi: the Wairau confrontation with settlers from Nelson, then Hōne Heke's repeated felling of the British flagstaff at Kororāreka and the northern campaign that followed, and fighting in the Hutt Valley and Whanganui. Māori built and abandoned purpose-designed gunfighter pā that absorbed artillery fire and frustrated British troops. The wars settled nothing, and left both sides rehearsing tactics for the far larger conflicts of the 1860s.

Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000.node: Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D (United States, 999 BC–AD 1000)
Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000.label: Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D
Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000.prose:
[eastern North America, 999 BC–AD 1000] Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D. "Here are entered works on the prehistoric culture of eastern North America which extended to the eastern Great Plains and existed ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D. prior to contact with European influences.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Eastern North American societies took up pottery, buried their dead in mounds, and cultivated native starchy and oily seeds long before maize became a staple. Exchange networks carried Great Lakes copper, Gulf Coast shell and Rocky Mountain obsidian to ceremonial centres in the Ohio Valley. The bow and arrow spread in the later centuries, and rising populations and maize farming led on to the Mississippian towns.

Civil War, 1944-1949 (Greece, AD 1944–AD.label: Civil War, 1944-1949
Civil War, 1944-1949 (Greece, AD 1944–AD.prose:

As German occupation ended, the communist-led resistance and the British- then American-backed government army fought for control of the country. It was among the first open confrontations of the Cold War: the crisis prompted the Truman Doctrine and large-scale US aid. The government's victory kept Greece in the Western bloc, but left a divided society and decades of anti-communist repression.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Yuan Shikai's death left the Chinese republic with no centre: regional militarists with private armies fought shifting coalitions while a nominal government in Beijing sold offices and loans to foreigners. Amid the disorder came the May Fourth movement, the New Culture debates and the founding of the Communist Party. The Nationalists' Northern Expedition subdued or absorbed most of the warlords by 1928, though many kept their armies within the new order.

Elizabeth I steered England to a Protestant settlement that was deliberately broad enough to keep most of her subjects inside the church, while refusing to marry and so leaving the succession open for forty-five years. Her reign saw the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the first English ventures into the Atlantic and the founding of the East India Company. It was also the age of Shakespeare, Marlowe and Spenser, when English became a literary language of the first rank.

The May Revolution in Buenos Aires unseated the viceroy in the name of the captive Spanish king, and the provinces of the Río de la Plata slid from autonomy into open separation, formally declared at Tucumán in 1816. Campaigns north into Upper Peru failed repeatedly, so San Martín built an army at Mendoza and took the war over the Andes to Chile instead. Independence was won, but the question of whether Buenos Aires or the provinces would rule opened decades of civil war.

Based in the northwest, the Yuwen emperors built an army of farmer-soldiers and a cohesive Guanlong aristocracy that would supply the ruling houses of the Sui and Tang. A state suppression of Buddhism in 574 stripped the monasteries of land, wealth and monks. Victory over the Northern Qi in 577 united the north, and four years later the dynasty was overthrown from within.

Germanic rule, 962-1268 (Italy, AD 962–A.label: Germanic rule, 962-1268
Germanic rule, 962-1268 (Italy, AD 962–A.prose:

Otto I's imperial coronation in Rome bound the German crown to Italy, and for three centuries emperors marched south to claim it. The result was chronic conflict: the Investiture Contest with the papacy, the northern communes' leagues against Frederick Barbarossa, and the Guelf and Ghibelline factions that split Italian cities. It ended with the execution of the last Hohenstaufen, Conradin, leaving Italy a patchwork of independent city-states and papal and Angevin territories.

Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832 (France, A.label: Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832
Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832 (France, A.prose:

Peasants and rural gentry in western France rose against the revolutionary government's conscription levy and its attack on the Catholic Church, fighting a guerrilla war under the white flag of the Bourbons. The Republic's response — the "infernal columns" that burned farms and killed indiscriminately — left well over a hundred thousand dead and is still argued over as an early case of state mass killing. Smaller risings flared up again under Napoleon and the Restoration, keeping the west a symbol of counter-revolution deep into the nineteenth century.

Wars of Independence, 1809-1830 (Ecuador.label: Wars of Independence, 1809-1830

Quito's junta of August 1809 claimed to be the first cry of independence in Spanish America, and its leaders were massacred a year later. Liberation finally came with Sucre's victory on the slopes of Pichincha above Quito in 1822, after which the territory joined Bolívar's Gran Colombia. When that union fell apart in 1830, Ecuador emerged as a separate republic.

Qin-Han dynasties, 221 B.C.-220 A.D (Chi.label: Qin-Han dynasties, 221 B.C.-220 A.D
Qin-Han dynasties, 221 B.C.-220 A.D (Chi.prose:

Four centuries in which the idea of a unified Chinese empire was invented and then made durable. The Qin supplied the bureaucratic apparatus; the Han softened it with Confucian learning, an examined officialdom and state ritual, pushed the frontier into Central Asia and opened the Silk Road, and presided on paper, lacquer, silk and iron. Han tombs are among archaeology's richest sources, and later Chinese would call themselves the Han people ever after.

Pedro V, 1853-1861 (Portugal, AD 1853–AD.label: Pedro V, 1853-1861

A young, conscientious king who put his energy into modernising a poor country: railways and telegraph lines were laid, roads and hospitals built, and he spent his own fortune on public works and famine relief. His refusal to leave Lisbon during an epidemic cost him his life at 24, and his death was mourned as a national tragedy. The reforming impulse of his reign, driven by the ministries of the Regeneração, outlived him.

French armies crossed the Pyrenees and put Joseph Bonaparte on the throne, triggering a brutal war of sieges, massacres and irregular "guerrilla" fighting that gave the word to the world. With the king a prisoner, patriot juntas filled the vacuum and a rump parliament at Cádiz drafted a liberal constitution in 1812. British and Portuguese forces under Wellington ground the French out, but Spanish America had meanwhile begun governing itself and never fully returned to Madrid's control.

Murad III, 1574-1595 (Turkey, AD 1574–AD.label: Murad III, 1574-1595
Murad III, 1574-1595 (Turkey, AD 1574–AD.prose:

The sultan never left Istanbul on campaign, and power shifted toward the palace household - his mother and consort, the chief eunuchs and grand viziers who rose and fell rapidly. A long war seized Caucasian territory from the Safavids at ruinous cost, while debased silver coinage and inflation fed janissary mutinies and provincial unrest. His reign also opened formal trade with England and produced some of the finest Ottoman illustrated manuscripts.

Spain fought the Thirty Years' War, lost Portugal, faced revolt in Catalonia, and finally conceded Dutch independence in 1648 and defeat to France in 1659. The Count-Duke of Olivares's attempt to make all the kingdoms share the burden of war triggered the crises that broke Habsburg dominance. Yet the same decades produced Velázquez, Zurbarán and Calderón in a golden age of art.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Tajikistan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Tajikistan, AD 19.prose:

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

A band of Andalusi exiles seized the island and founded an emirate at Chandax, today's Heraklion, ringed by a great ditch that gave the city its name. For over a century the island was the base for fleets that raided the Aegean and the Greek mainland, and Byzantium mounted repeated failed expeditions to dislodge them. Nikephoros Phokas finally took Chandax after a winter siege in 961, reopening the sea lanes and making his reputation as the empire's greatest soldier.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Some fifty emperors and usurpers in fifty years, most raised by their troops and killed by them, while Persian and Germanic invasions broke through the frontiers and the empire briefly split into three. Silver coinage collapsed, cities threw up walls, and long-distance trade contracted. Aurelian and finally Diocletian restored order, but the reformed state that emerged was more militarised, more bureaucratic and no longer ruled from Rome.
