As administrator of the Palatinate for his young nephew, this Wittelsbach prince reversed his brother's Lutheran policy and re-established Calvinism, making Heidelberg a centre of the Reformed faith. He also sent mercenary armies to support the Huguenots in France and the Dutch rebels, tying the Palatinate to the militant Protestant cause across Europe.

The dates here follow the traditional chronology of later Chinese historians, who dated the dynasty from Tang's overthrow of the Xia to King Wu's victory at Muye. Archaeology at Erligang and Anyang has since shown a real state of walled cities, bronze foundries and chariot warfare, whose oracle-bone inscriptions are China's earliest deciphered writing. The gap between the transmitted dates and the excavated evidence is itself a good illustration of how ancient chronologies get built and revised.

Seizing the treasury and crown within days of his brother William Rufus's death in the New Forest, Henry issued a Charter of Liberties promising to end abuses — a document later quarried for Magna Carta. He captured Normandy from his elder brother Robert, imprisoning him for life, and built up a professional royal administration whose exchequer accounts are the first of their kind in Europe. The drowning of his only legitimate son in the White Ship left the succession to his daughter Matilda, and his death was followed by nearly twenty years of civil war.

James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne, uniting the crowns and commissioning the King James Bible, while English colonists took root in Virginia, New England and the Caribbean. Quarrels over taxation, royal prerogative and religion hardened under Charles I, who ruled for eleven years without Parliament before war broke out across the three kingdoms. It ended with the king tried and beheaded in Whitehall — an event without precedent in Europe.

The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

Britain took the island from France to shut down the privateers preying on East India Company shipping in the Indian Ocean. The Treaty of Paris confirmed British possession while allowing the French-speaking planters to keep their language, law and Catholic religion. The sugar economy expanded sharply, and after the abolition of slavery the island became the first great destination for indentured labourers from India.

Ethiopia dissolved Eritrea's federal autonomy and annexed it, and armed resistance began almost at once, later dominated by the disciplined and famously self-reliant EPLF. Three decades of fighting, including the great sieges and trench warfare around Nakfa, outlasted both Haile Selassie and the Derg. The EPLF took Asmara in 1991 and a referendum confirmed independence in 1993, making Eritrea Africa's newest state at the time.

José Gabriel Condorcanqui, claiming descent from the last Inca and taking the name Tupac Amaru II, executed a colonial official and set off the largest rebellion in Spanish America before independence. Tens of thousands of Andean villagers joined, driven by tribute demands, forced labour and the hated repartimiento of goods. The rising was crushed with public torture and dismemberment, and the crown banned Inca dress, portraits and titles, trying to erase the memory it had drawn on.

A restlessly energetic builder-king whose long reign left more physical marks on Norway than any other's: Kongsberg's silver mines, Røros copper, and the towns of Kristiansand and Christiania, the latter laid out on a grid after Oslo burned in 1624. He gave Norway its first printed law code in Norwegian in 1604 and took a personal interest in northern trade and the Arctic. His wars against Sweden and his disastrous intervention in the Thirty Years' War drained the treasury and cost territory.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

French armies swept away the old confederation of cantons and imposed a single centralised state on the French model, with one citizenship, one currency plan and an end to the rule of privileged towns over subject territories like Vaud and Aargau. The experiment was deeply unpopular, bankrupt and repeatedly overturned by coups, and Napoleon abandoned it with the Act of Mediation, restoring the cantons. But its abolition of feudal dues and subject status was never fully reversed, and it set the terms for the modern Swiss federal state.

A Stoic philosopher who spent most of his reign on campaign, defending the Danube frontier against Marcomanni and Quadi while plague brought back from the East thinned the army and the cities. His private notebook, the Meditations, written in camp, became one of the most widely read works of ancient philosophy. By naming his son Commodus as heir he ended the run of adoptive emperors, and later writers dated Rome's decline from his death.

Lê Lợi drove out the occupying Ming armies and founded a dynasty that gave Vietnam its most influential law code and a thoroughly Confucian bureaucracy under Lê Thánh Tông. Southward expansion crushed the Cham kingdom and pushed Vietnamese settlement toward the Mekong delta. From the sixteenth century the emperors reigned as figureheads while the Trịnh lords in the north and Nguyễn lords in the south ran a divided country.

A charming, hard-drinking king who left government largely to able ministers, above all J. H. E. Bernstorff and A. G. Moltke, and Denmark enjoyed peace and profitable neutral trade while wars raged elsewhere. The reign built the Frederiksstaden district of Copenhagen with the Amalienborg palaces and the Marble Church, founded academies of art and sciences, and dispatched the celebrated scientific expedition to Arabia from which only Carsten Niebuhr returned.

French occupation, 1798-1800 (Malta, AD.label: French occupation, 1798-1800

Napoleon, sailing for Egypt, took the island in a few days and ended more than 250 years of rule by the Knights of St John. His administration abolished slavery and the nobility, reorganised courts and schools, and stripped churches of their silver - which provoked a general Maltese uprising that penned the French into Valletta. Blockaded by British and Maltese forces, the garrison starved into surrender, and the island passed to Britain.

Joseph, 1750-1777 (Portugal, AD 1750–AD.label: Joseph, 1750-1777

A king who largely left government to his formidable minister, the Marquis of Pombal. The reign was defined by the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, which destroyed the capital and was answered with a rationally planned, quake-resistant new city centre; by the expulsion of the Jesuits from Portugal and its empire; and by the crushing of noble opposition, the reorganisation of colonial trade and the ending of slavery within mainland Portugal.

Louis XII, 1498-1515 (France, AD 1498–AD.label: Louis XII, 1498-1515
Louis XII, 1498-1515 (France, AD 1498–AD.prose:

Pursued the family claim to Milan and the Neapolitan crown, conquering Milan but eventually losing it after Pope Julius II turned the Holy League against him. At home he cut taxes and reformed justice, earning the title 'Father of the People' from the Estates. His Italian wars drew French armies deep into a Renaissance world whose art, architecture and manners they carried back north.

With Constantinople in Latin hands after the Fourth Crusade, Theodore Laskaris had himself crowned emperor at Nicaea and built the most effective of the Byzantine successor states. John III Vatatzes turned it into a prosperous, well-governed realm with a strong army and full treasury, steadily reclaiming territory in Anatolia and the Balkans. The dynasty ended when the child John IV was pushed aside and blinded by Michael Palaiologos, who two years later walked into the recovered capital.

Interregnum, 1572-1573 (Poland, AD 1572–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1572–AD 1573] Interregnum, 1572-1573. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1572-1573". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of Sigismund II Augustus ended the Jagiellonian line and turned the Polish–Lithuanian throne into an elective office chosen by the assembled nobility. The nobles used the vacancy to bind their next king with conditions: the Warsaw Confederation guaranteed religious peace between Catholics and Protestants, and the Henrician Articles set out rights the monarch had to swear to uphold. Henry of Valois was elected, and the Commonwealth's peculiar noble republic took shape.

Palermo rose against Bourbon rule from Naples, demanding the restoration of the island's separate constitution and parliament, while liberal officers in Naples forced King Ferdinand to accept the Spanish constitution of 1812. The Sicilian movement split between autonomists and those wanting union with the mainland revolutionaries, and both were crushed when Austrian troops marched south on the orders of the Congress of Laibach. The episode hardened Sicilian resentment of Naples that resurfaced in 1848 and again in 1860.

Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814 (Europe, A.label: Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814
Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814 (Europe, A.prose:

With the Grande Armée destroyed in Russia, Prussia, Russia, Austria, Sweden and Britain combined against Napoleon in Germany, and the enormous Battle of the Nations at Leipzig drove the French back over the Rhine. The allies invaded France and entered Paris, forcing Napoleon's abdication and exile to Elba. In Germany the campaign was remembered as a national awakening, feeding a nationalism the restored princes then spent decades trying to contain.

The dynasty founded by Chandragupta and brought to its height by Ashoka united nearly the whole subcontinent under one administration for the first time, with a treasury, road network and bureaucracy described in the political treatise called the Arthashastra. Ashoka's patronage carried Buddhism far beyond India, and his lion capital from Sarnath is now the emblem of the Republic of India. The empire unravelled after his death and ended when the last king was assassinated by his own general.

Second Empire, 1852-1870 (France, AD 185.label: Second Empire, 1852-1870
Second Empire, 1852-1870 (France, AD 185.prose:
[France, AD 1852–AD 1870] Second Empire, 1852-1870. Extracted from heading "France--History--Second Empire, 1852-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Louis-Napoleon converted his presidency into an empire by coup and plebiscite, ruling first through authoritarian control of press and parliament and later through cautious liberalisation. It was France's boom era: railways and investment banks, free-trade treaties, Haussmann's boulevards driven through medieval Paris, and world's fairs to display it all. Foreign adventure undid it - Crimea and Italy brought prestige, Mexico humiliation, and the Prussian war ended with the emperor's capture at Sedan and the birth of the Third Republic.

Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807 (United State.label: Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807
Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807 (United State.prose:
[United States, AD 1805–AD 1807] Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807. Extracted from heading "Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Aaron Burr, lately vice-president and notorious for killing Alexander Hamilton in a duel, gathered men and boats on the Ohio for a venture whose aim is still argued over: invading Spanish Mexico, or detaching the western territories from the Union. Betrayed by his co-conspirator General Wilkinson, he was arrested and tried for treason before Chief Justice John Marshall. The acquittal set a deliberately narrow standard for treason in American law, requiring witnesses to an overt act.

Henry I, 1031-1060 (France, AD 1031–AD 1.label: Henry I, 1031-1060
Henry I, 1031-1060 (France, AD 1031–AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1031–AD 1060] Henry I, 1031-1060. Extracted from heading "France--History--Henry I, 1031-1060". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The third Capetian king ruled a domain barely larger than the lands around Paris and Orléans, while dukes and counts around him — above all the Normans — grew far stronger. His repeated campaigns against the young William the Bastard of Normandy ended in defeat at Mortemer and Varaville, confirming Norman independence a decade before the conquest of England. His marriage to Anne of Kiev brought an unusual link between the French court and the Rus.

Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-43.node: Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439 (China, AD 304–AD 439)
Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-43.label: Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439

Non-Han peoples - Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Qiang and Jie - founded a rapid succession of short-lived states across northern China after the Jin court fled south. Mass migration carried Han elites to the Yangtze while Buddhism spread rapidly under rulers who patronised monks like Kumārajīva and Fotudeng. The Northern Wei finally reunified the north, beginning the long fusion of steppe and Chinese traditions that shaped the later Sui and Tang.

Jacobite Rebellion, 1745-1746 (Scotland,.prose:

Charles Edward Stuart landed in the Hebrides with almost nothing, raised the Highland clans, took Edinburgh and routed a government army at Prestonpans before marching to within 130 miles of London. The retreat ended on Culloden Moor, where his exhausted army was destroyed in under an hour. The aftermath was systematic: punitive laws against Highland dress and weapons, the dismantling of clan chiefs' powers, roads and forts driven through the glens, and the end of armed Stuart hopes.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Maryland, AD 1775.label: Revolution, 1775-1783

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

[Argentina , AD 1806–AD 1807] English Invasions, 1806-1807. Extracted from heading "Argentina--History--English Invasions, 1806-1807". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975. Two British attempts to seize Buenos Aires and Montevideo while Spain was allied to Napoleon. The viceroy fled, and the city was retaken and then defended by locally raised militias fighting from rooftops — an experience that showed the colonists they could act without Spain and gave them arms and leaders. Within four years those same militias were central to the revolution of 1810.

Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C (Egypt,.node: Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C (Egypt, 2648 BC–2574 BC)
Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C (Egypt,.label: Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C
Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C (Egypt,.prose:
[Egypt, 2648 BC–2574 BC] Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

This is the moment monumental stone architecture begins in Egypt: Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by Imhotep, replaced mudbrick mastabas with a six-tiered mountain of limestone inside a vast walled complex. A strong central administration, backed by expeditions to Sinai for copper and turquoise, made such projects possible. The techniques and ambitions worked out here led directly to the true pyramids of the following dynasty.

Decius, 249-251 (Roman Empire, AD 249–AD.label: Decius, 249-251
Decius, 249-251 (Roman Empire, AD 249–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 249–AD 251] Decius, 249-251. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Decius, 249-251". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign remembered for one decree: every inhabitant of the empire was ordered to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate proving it, producing the first systematic, empire-wide persecution of Christians and a wave of martyrdoms and apostasies that split the church for decades. Surviving papyrus libelli from Egypt record ordinary people certifying their compliance. Decius then marched against the Goths and was killed with his son at Abritus, the first Roman emperor to die in battle against a foreign enemy.

Republic, 1931-1939 (Spain, AD 1931–AD 1.label: Republic, 1931-1939
Republic, 1931-1939 (Spain, AD 1931–AD 1.prose:
[Spain, AD 1931–AD 1939] Republic, 1931-1939. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Republic, 1931-1939". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Second Republic arrived when Alfonso XIII left after republican victories in municipal elections, and it attempted rapid change: land reform, women's suffrage, regional autonomy for Catalonia, secular schooling and the separation of Church and state. Polarisation between left and right ran through elections, strikes and the 1934 Asturias rising. A military rebellion in 1936 became the Spanish Civil War, ending in Franco's dictatorship and a long exile for the republic's supporters.

Athelstan, 925-940 (England, AD 925–AD 9.label: Athelstan, 925-940
Athelstan, 925-940 (England, AD 925–AD 9.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 925–AD 940] Athelstan, 925-940. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Athelstan, 925-940". Added to LCSH in 2011, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Athelstan took Northumbria, received the submission of Welsh and Scottish rulers, and at Brunanburh in 937 beat a coalition of Norse, Scots and Strathclyde Britons - leaving him the first king who could plausibly be called king of all England. He issued law codes, reformed the coinage to a single national design, and ran a court that drew scholars and foreign envoys, marrying his sisters into the ruling houses of Europe. The kingdom he assembled outlasted him.

Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD.label: Henry VI, 1190-1197
Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1190–AD 1197] Henry VI, 1190-1197. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry VI, 1190-1197". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Barbarossa's son married the heiress of Norman Sicily and seized the island kingdom, briefly encircling the papacy with Hohenstaufen power from the Baltic to Palermo. He financed the effort partly with the enormous ransom extorted from Richard the Lionheart, captured on his way home from crusade. His sudden death at thirty-one, leaving a three-year-old heir, wrecked his plan to make the empire hereditary and plunged Germany into civil war.

A boy of ten inherited Castile and never reached adulthood, the kingdom being fought over by regents and the powerful Lara family. He died at thirteen when a roof tile fell on his head while playing. The crown passed to his sister Berenguela, who promptly handed it to her son Ferdinand III — the man who would unite Castile with León and conquer Córdoba and Seville.

A Muslim army crossing from North Africa destroyed the Visigothic kingdom in a single campaign season, and within a few years most of the peninsula was al-Andalus. Córdoba under the Umayyads became the largest and most learned city in western Europe, a place where Arabic science, Hebrew poetry and Roman engineering met; after the caliphate fractured into taifa kingdoms, Christian realms pressed south, and the last emirate, Granada, fell in 1492. Its legacy runs through the Alhambra, the vocabulary of Spanish, and the transmission of Greek philosophy and mathematics back into Latin Europe.

Gustav III, 1771-1792 (Sweden, AD 1771–A.label: Gustav III, 1771-1792
Gustav III, 1771-1792 (Sweden, AD 1771–A.prose:

A theatrical, French-educated king who seized back royal power in a bloodless coup in 1772, ending Sweden's parliamentary 'Age of Liberty'. He founded the Swedish Academy and the Royal Opera, promoted a distinctive neoclassical style in art and architecture, and pushed through religious toleration and a currency reform, while his war on Russia and his autocratic drift alienated the nobility. He was shot at a masked ball in his own opera house, a killing later retold on stage by Verdi.

The shortest-lived of the four Southern Dynasties, ruling a diminished realm on the lower Yangtze while the militarised north grew steadily stronger. Its conquest by Sui forces marked the end of the long north–south split and the beginning of a reunified empire.

After Beijing fell and the last Ming emperor hanged himself, loyalist courts were proclaimed in succession at Nanjing, Fuzhou, Guangzhou and finally in the southwest, each undermined by factional quarrels as Qing armies advanced. Resistance drew in the Ming general Zheng Chenggong, who raided the coast and later took Taiwan from the Dutch. The last claimant, the Yongli emperor, fled to Burma and was handed over and executed, ending Ming rule.

Physically and mentally impaired after a childhood illness, he reigned while others governed, and it was under his nominal rule that Portugal won the decisive victories of Ameixial and Montes Claros that secured independence from Spain. His marriage was annulled, his wife married his brother, and in 1667 that brother deposed him and ruled as regent. He spent his last years confined, first in the Azores and then at Sintra.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched two massive invasions aimed at conquering Ming China through Korea, overrunning much of the peninsula before stalling. Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet, including armoured 'turtle ships', cut Japanese supply lines, while Ming armies and Korean irregulars ground the invaders down. Korea was left devastated — its population, farmland, palaces and artisan workshops wrecked — and the war helped topple the Toyotomi regime in Japan.

Civil War, 1879-1884 (South Africa, AD 1.label: Civil War, 1879-1884
Civil War, 1879-1884 (South Africa, AD 1.prose:
[Zululand, AD 1879–AD 1884] Civil War, 1879-1884. Extracted from heading "Zululand (South Africa)--History--Civil War, 1879-1884". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.132 of LCSH 1987, and p.110 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After British troops destroyed the Zulu kingdom's independence in 1879, Zululand was carved into thirteen chiefdoms, setting rival factions against one another. The restoration of King Cetshwayo in 1883 triggered open warfare between his uSuthu followers and Zibhebhu's Mandlakazi, who sacked the royal homestead at Ulundi; Cetshwayo died the following year. His son Dinuzulu bought Boer help with land, creating the short-lived New Republic and opening the way to full colonial annexation.

Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

The first prince of newly autonomous Bulgaria, a German-born nephew of the Russian tsarina who quickly fell out with his Russian patrons. He backed the 1885 union with Eastern Rumelia, doubling the country's size, and defeated Serbia's attempt to overturn it. Pro-Russian officers kidnapped him in 1886 and forced his abdication, an early demonstration of how far Bulgarian politics would be pulled between St Petersburg and Vienna.

Caesar, Pompey and Crassus struck a private alliance to push their agendas past a hostile Senate, dividing the great provincial commands among themselves. It funded Caesar's conquest of Gaul and Crassus's fatal expedition against Parthia. When Crassus died at Carrhae and the marriage tie between Caesar and Pompey lapsed, the arrangement dissolved into civil war.

Peloponnesian War, 431-404 B.C (Greece,.label: Peloponnesian War, 431-404 B.C

A twenty-seven-year struggle between Athens' maritime empire and Sparta's land alliance that drew in most of the Greek world and ended with Athens starved into surrender, its walls pulled down and its fleet gone. Plague, the disastrous Sicilian expedition and repeated coups hollowed out the Athenian democracy even as Thucydides was writing its history. The war exhausted the city-states and opened the way for Theban and then Macedonian dominance.

Insurrection, 1815-1817 (Serbia, AD 1815.label: Insurrection, 1815-1817
Insurrection, 1815-1817 (Serbia, AD 1815.prose:
[Serbia, AD 1815–AD 1817] Insurrection, 1815-1817. Extracted from heading "Serbia--History--Insurrection, 1815-1817". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A second rising, led by Miloš Obrenović, avoided outright war for independence and pressed instead for negotiated concessions. The Ottomans conceded a measure of self-government under Serbian officials, tax collection and an assembly, laying the foundations of the autonomous principality recognised in the 1830s. Miloš consolidated his position by having the returned Karađorđe killed, beginning a dynastic feud between the two families that shaped Serbian politics for a century.

Coming to the throne at eleven amid a regency and anti-Jewish pogroms across Castile, he grew into a ruler who curbed the great nobles and rebuilt royal finances despite chronic ill health. He sent embassies far afield, including Ruy González de Clavijo's famous journey to the court of Timur at Samarkand. His reign also saw the first Castilian-sponsored ventures into the Canary Islands, an early step towards Atlantic empire.

Great Trek, 1836-1840 (South Africa, AD.label: Great Trek, 1836-1840
Great Trek, 1836-1840 (South Africa, AD.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1836–AD 1840] Great Trek, 1836-1840. Extracted from heading "Africa, South--History--Great Trek". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.1 of LCSH 1975; revised 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Thousands of Dutch-speaking farmers loaded ox-wagons and left the British Cape Colony, driven by resentment at British administration, the abolition of slavery and pressure for land. Their advance into the interior brought violent collisions with the Ndebele and the Zulu, most famously at Blood River, and produced the short-lived Natalia republic and the later Boer states of the Transvaal and Orange Free State. The trek became the founding myth of Afrikaner nationalism and reshaped the political map of southern Africa.

Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375 (Armenian Ki.node: Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375 (Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, AD 1080–AD 1375)
Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375 (Armenian Ki.label: Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375
Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375 (Armenian Ki.prose:
[Cilicia, AD 1080–AD 1375] Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375. Extracted from heading "Cilicia--History--Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.22 of LCSH 1987. Revise in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Driven from their homeland by Seljuk invasions, Armenians founded a new state on the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia, where it became an indispensable ally, supplier and staging ground for the Crusader states. Its rulers married into Frankish families, adopted western titles and court fashions, and traded through the port of Ayas with Genoa and Venice. Cilician manuscript illumination, especially the work of Toros Roslin, is the high point of Armenian art; the kingdom fell to the Mamluks.

Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934 (China.label: Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934
Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934 (China.prose:
[China, AD 1930–AD 1934] Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934. Extracted from heading "China--History--Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934". Added to LCSH in 2012, revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Chiang Kai-shek launched five successive offensives to destroy the Communist base areas in Jiangxi and elsewhere. The first four were beaten off by guerrilla tactics, but the fifth used blockhouses, blockades and German military advice to strangle the Jiangxi Soviet. The Red Army broke out in October 1934 and began the Long March, a retreat that nearly destroyed it but brought Mao Zedong to the leadership.

Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C..label: Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D.
Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C..prose:
[Armenia, 188 BC–AD 1] Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D.. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D.". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.4 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Artaxias broke free of Seleucid control and founded a dynasty that unified the Armenian highlands and built new capitals such as Artaxata. Under Tigranes the Great the kingdom briefly stretched from the Caspian to the Mediterranean, absorbing what was left of the Seleucid empire - until Roman armies under Lucullus and Pompey cut it back down. Thereafter Armenia became the perpetual buffer and battleground between Rome and Parthia.

Bombardment, 1942-1945 (Kakegawa, AD 194.label: Bombardment, 1942-1945
Bombardment, 1942-1945 (Kakegawa, AD 194.prose: [Kakegawa-shi (Japan), AD 1942–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Kakegawa-shi (Japan)--History--Bombardment, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Philip V, 1700-1746 (Spain, AD 1700–AD 1.label: Philip V, 1700-1746
Philip V, 1700-1746 (Spain, AD 1700–AD 1.prose:
[Spain, AD 1700–AD 1746] Philip V, 1700-1746. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Philip V, 1700-1746". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A French Bourbon grandson of Louis XIV whose accession triggered the War of the Spanish Succession, which cost Spain the Netherlands, Naples and Gibraltar. Victory at home let him abolish the separate laws of Aragon and Catalonia and impose centralised, French-style government. Spain shrank in Europe but its administration and navy were rebuilt.

Anne, 1702-1714 (United Kingdom, AD 1702.label: Anne, 1702-1714
Anne, 1702-1714 (United Kingdom, AD 1702.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1702–AD 1714] Anne, 1702-1714. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Anne, 1702-1714". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Stuart monarch presided over the union of the English and Scottish parliaments, creating the kingdom of Great Britain, and over Marlborough's victories at Blenheim and Ramillies in the War of the Spanish Succession. Bitter Whig and Tory rivalry, fought out in a newly unlicensed press and in the queen's own household, shaped modern party politics. None of her many pregnancies produced a surviving heir, so the crown passed by statute to the Protestant house of Hanover and Jacobite claimants were left to rebel.

Six Dynasties, 220-589 (China, AD 220–AD.label: Six Dynasties, 220-589
Six Dynasties, 220-589 (China, AD 220–AD.prose:
[China, AD 220–AD 589] Six Dynasties, 220-589. Extracted from heading "China--History--220-589". Added to LCSH in 1986. Primary title "China--History--220-589" too generic, so variant "Six Dynasties, 220-589" substituted for primary identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nearly four centuries of political fragmentation after the Han, when successive southern courts at Jiankang faced a shifting patchwork of northern regimes. Buddhism became a mass religion in China during these years, cave temples were carved, and the great families of the south turned their estates into centres of art and letters. The disunity ended only when the Sui conquered the south, but the cultural forms invented here shaped the Tang.

Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706 (Russia, A.label: Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706
Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706 (Russia, A.prose:
[Russia , AD 1705–AD 1706] Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Streltsy soldiers, townspeople and Old Believers in the Volga delta rose against Peter the Great's taxes, forced shaving of beards and Western dress codes, killing the governor and running the city by an elected council. It took Field Marshal Sheremetev and regular troops to retake Astrakhan. The revolt showed how deeply Peter's reforms cut against ordinary Russians, and it distracted the state at a dangerous moment in the Great Northern War.

Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D (Eg.label: Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D
Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D (Eg.prose:
[Egypt, 331 BC–AD 640] Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D". Added to LCSH in1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and on p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From Alexander's arrival to the Arab conquest, Egypt was governed by Greek-speaking rulers: first the Ptolemies, then Roman and Byzantine officials. Alexandria became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean with its Library and Museum, while the countryside kept farming, worshipping and writing much as before, now recorded in Greek on papyrus. Christianity took hold early and deeply here, giving rise to the Coptic church and to desert monasticism.

Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632 (Sweden, AD 1.label: Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632
Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632 (Sweden, AD 1.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1632] Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.112 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Gustavus Adolphus turned a peripheral Baltic kingdom into a great power, overhauling the army with mobile field artillery, disciplined musket volleys and conscription, and reforming administration and taxation with his chancellor Axel Oxenstierna. His intervention in the Thirty Years' War rescued the Protestant cause in Germany and won stunning victories at Breitenfeld and the Lech, until he was killed leading a cavalry charge at Lützen. The blood-stained buff coat and horse relics of that battle became national relics, and his campaigns set the template for European warfare for a century.

War of the Pacific, 1879-1884 (Bolivia,.label: War of the Pacific, 1879-1884
War of the Pacific, 1879-1884 (Bolivia,.prose:
[Bolivia, Chile, Peru, AD 1879–AD 1884] War of the Pacific, 1879-1884. Spatial coverage: Bolivia, Chile, Peru. Extracted from heading "War of the Pacific, 1879-1884". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dispute over taxes on Chilean-run nitrate works in the Atacama escalated into war between Chile and the allied Bolivia and Peru. Chilean naval supremacy and an advance that reached Lima delivered total victory, and Bolivia lost its entire coastal province — leaving it landlocked, a grievance still pursued in international courts. Chile gained the nitrate fields that funded its state for a generation.

Louis XVI, 1774-1793 (France, AD 1774–AD.label: Louis XVI, 1774-1793
Louis XVI, 1774-1793 (France, AD 1774–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1774–AD 1793] Louis XVI, 1774-1793. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XVI, 1774-1793". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A well-meaning but indecisive king inherited a bankrupt treasury and a society straining against noble privilege. His attempt to solve the debt crisis by calling the Estates-General in 1789 unleashed the French Revolution, which stripped him of power, turned him into 'Citizen Louis Capet', and ended with his execution by guillotine. His reign closes a thousand years of French absolute monarchy and opens the modern age of republics and mass politics.

War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Estonia,.label: War of Independence, 1918-1920
War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Estonia,.prose:
[Estonia, AD 1918–AD 1920] War of Independence, 1918-1920. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--War of Independence, 1918-1920". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987, and p.25 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Days after declaring independence, the new Estonian state had to fight off an invasion by Soviet Russia, and later German Baltic forces in the south, with help from Finnish volunteers and a British naval squadron. The Treaty of Tartu in 1920 saw Soviet Russia renounce all claims to Estonia — the first such recognition it granted anyone. Radical land reform, breaking up the Baltic German estates, followed as a reward to the soldiers who had fought.

Casimir I, 1040-1058 (Poland, AD 1040–AD.label: Casimir I, 1040-1058
Casimir I, 1040-1058 (Poland, AD 1040–AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1040–AD 1058] Casimir I, 1040-1058. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Casimir I, 1040-1058". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Casimir the Restorer inherited a wrecked kingdom: pagan revolt, peasant uprising and a Bohemian raid had gutted the church and burned Gniezno. With German and Kievan backing he rebuilt the Piast monarchy from Kraków, which became the effective capital in place of the ruined Wielkopolska centres, and re-established bishoprics and monasteries. His patchwork recovery is why Poland survived as a state at all in the eleventh century.

Civil War, 1945-1949 (China, AD 1945–AD.label: Civil War, 1945-1949
Civil War, 1945-1949 (China, AD 1945–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1945–AD 1949] Civil War, 1945-1949. Spatial coverage: China, Taiwan. Extracted from heading "China--History--Civil War, 1945-1949". Added to LCSH in 1985, revised in 2014. Spatial coverage extend expanded to include Taiwan based off knowledge of the Chinese Civil War and Chiang Kai-Shek and the Kuomintang's flight to Taiwan after their defeat. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With Japan defeated, the truce between Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists and Mao Zedong's Communists collapsed into full-scale war across the Chinese mainland. Communist forces, helped by land reform in the countryside and Nationalist inflation and corruption, swept south in a series of huge campaigns. The Nationalists retreated to Taiwan, the People's Republic was proclaimed in 1949, and the two governments' rivalry remains unresolved.

Henry III, 1573-1574 (Poland, AD 1573–AD.label: Henry III, 1573-1574
Henry III, 1573-1574 (Poland, AD 1573–AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1573–AD 1574] Henry III, 1573-1574. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Henry III, 1573-1574". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The French prince chosen in Poland-Lithuania's first free royal election had to swear to the Henrician Articles, a contract guaranteeing noble privileges, religious toleration and regular parliaments, with the right of rebellion if he broke them. Those articles became the constitutional foundation of the Commonwealth for two centuries. He lasted only months before slipping out of Kraków by night on learning that he had inherited the French throne.

Middle Ages, 500-1500 (Europe, AD 500–AD.label: Middle Ages, 500-1500
Middle Ages, 500-1500 (Europe, AD 500–AD.prose:
[Europe, AD 500–AD 1500] Middle Ages, 500-1500. Extracted from heading "Biography--Middle Ages, 500-1500". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2005. Variants include the term "Medieval", but since individual headings use either "Medieval" (as for Social History) or "Middle Ages" (as here), we have entered them as two separate definitions. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A thousand years bracketed by the end of the western Roman Empire and the voyages and printing presses that opened the modern age. Christianity spread to the edges of the continent, Latin remained the language of learning while vernaculars found their first writers, and the manor, the town charter and the university all took form. Visitors usually recognise it through its buildings - castles, monasteries and Gothic cathedrals - but its lasting legacies include universities, banking and representative assemblies.

James II, 1685-1688 (England, AD 1685–AD.label: James II, 1685-1688
James II, 1685-1688 (England, AD 1685–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1685–AD 1688] James II, 1685-1688. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--James II, 1685-1688". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

England's last Catholic king inherited a broadly loyal country, crushed Monmouth's rebellion, then squandered support by packing the army and universities with Catholics and suspending the penal laws by prerogative. The birth of a Catholic son turned a temporary problem into a dynasty, and leading politicians invited William of Orange to intervene. James fled to France, and the Revolution settlement that followed made Parliament, not the crown, the final authority.

Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598 (France.label: Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598
Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598 (France.prose:
[France, AD 1562–AD 1598] Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598. Extracted from heading "France--History--Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598". Added to LCSH in 2011; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Eight rounds of civil war between Catholic and Calvinist (Huguenot) factions tore the French kingdom apart, mixing religious hatred with a struggle among the Guise, Bourbon and Valois houses for control of a weak crown. The St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, when thousands of Protestants were killed in Paris and provincial towns, became the era's defining atrocity. The fighting ended when the Protestant Henry of Navarre converted, took the throne as Henry IV, and issued the Edict of Nantes granting Huguenots limited toleration and fortified towns — a pragmatic settlement that put royal order above confessional unity.

Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815 (F.label: Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815
Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815 (F.prose:
[France, AD 1799–AD 1815] Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815. Extracted from heading "France--History--Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.39 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's coup ended the Revolution's parliamentary phase and replaced it with one-man rule, crowned as empire in 1804. He gave France a lasting legal code, prefects, lycées and the Bank of France, and gave Europe fifteen years of war that redrew its map and spread revolutionary law wherever his armies went. Russia, Spain and finally Waterloo undid him, but the institutions largely survived the restoration of the monarchy.

Ferdinand I, 1037-1065 (Spain, AD 1037–A.label: Ferdinand I, 1037-1065
Ferdinand I, 1037-1065 (Spain, AD 1037–A.prose:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1037–AD 1065] Ferdinand I, 1037-1065. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Ferdinand I, 1037-1065". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

By inheriting Castile and taking León at the battle of Tamarón, he joined the two realms and made himself the dominant Christian ruler in Iberia. He forced the Muslim taifa kings to pay him tribute, wealth that funded churches and the growing cult of Santiago, then split his lands among his sons and set off the wars that Alfonso VI would eventually win.

Oscar II, 1872-1907 (Sweden, AD 1872–AD.label: Oscar II, 1872-1907
Oscar II, 1872-1907 (Sweden, AD 1872–AD.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1872–AD 1907] Oscar II, 1872-1907. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Oscar II, 1872-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cultivated monarch, patron of the sciences and sponsor of the mathematics prize that prompted Poincaré's work on the three-body problem, he presided over Sweden's industrial takeoff, mass emigration to America, and the rise of parliamentary politics. He arbitrated international disputes abroad while struggling at home with Norwegian demands, finally accepting the dissolution of the union in his last years.

Pogroms, 1919-1920 (Ukraine, AD 1919–AD.label: Pogroms, 1919-1920
Pogroms, 1919-1920 (Ukraine, AD 1919–AD.prose:
[Ukraine, AD 1919–AD 1920] Pogroms, 1919-1920. Extracted from heading "Pogroms--Ukraine". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in 1994. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

During the Russian Civil War, Ukrainian territory saw the worst anti-Jewish violence before the Holocaust, carried out by Directory troops, Denikin's White forces, peasant warlords such as Hryhoriv and, less often, Red Army units. Estimates of Jewish dead run from tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand, with whole shtetl communities destroyed. The killings shaped Jewish emigration, self-defence movements and the assassination of Symon Petliura in Paris in 1926.

Alfonso VI, 1065-1109 (Spain, AD 1065–AD.label: Alfonso VI, 1065-1109
Alfonso VI, 1065-1109 (Spain, AD 1065–AD.prose:
[Castile, AD 1065–AD 1109] Alfonso VI, 1065-1109. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso VI, 1065-1109". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His capture of Toledo in 1085 handed Christian Spain the old Visigothic capital and made the taifa kings his tributaries. Alarmed, they invited the Almoravids from North Africa, who crushed him at Sagrajas and turned the tide back; the frontier warlord Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, made his own career in the gap. Alfonso styled himself emperor of all Spain and brought the Roman liturgy and Cluniac monks into his realms.

Uprisings, 1846-1848 (Poland, AD 1846–AD.label: Uprisings, 1846-1848
Uprisings, 1846-1848 (Poland, AD 1846–AD.prose:
[Wielkopolska (Poland), AD 1846–AD 1848] Uprisings, 1846-1848. Extracted from heading "Wielkopolska (Poland)--History--Uprisings, 1846-1848". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Partitioned Poland's conspirators tried twice to rise. The 1846 Kraków rising ended in disaster when Galician peasants, encouraged by Austrian officials, massacred the very landowners who were leading the revolt; the Free City of Kraków was annexed by Austria in punishment. Two years later the European revolutions brought renewed risings in Poznań and Galicia, also defeated, though serfdom was abolished in Galicia as a consequence. The lesson drawn by later nationalists was that independence would need the peasantry on its side.

Christian VIII, 1839-1848 (Denmark, AD 1.label: Christian VIII, 1839-1848
Christian VIII, 1839-1848 (Denmark, AD 1.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1839–AD 1848] Christian VIII, 1839-1848. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian VIII, 1839-1848".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had already been elected king of Norway in 1814 under the Eidsvoll constitution, a short-lived independence he was forced to surrender to Sweden. Danish liberals expected him to grant a constitution too, but he governed as an absolute monarch and only conceded reform on his deathbed. His reign ended just as the Schleswig question boiled over into war and Denmark's absolute monarchy gave way to the Constitution of 1849.

Insurrection, 1866-1868 (Crete, AD 1866–.label: Insurrection, 1866-1868
Insurrection, 1866-1868 (Crete, AD 1866–.prose:
[Crete (Greece), AD 1866–AD 1868] Insurrection, 1866-1868. Extracted from heading "Crete (Greece)--History--Insurrection, 1866-1868". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cretan Christians rose against Ottoman rule demanding union with Greece, and the war became a cause célèbre across Europe after the defenders of Arkadi Monastery blew up their own powder magazine rather than surrender. The revolt failed militarily but won administrative concessions, and it set the pattern of periodic Cretan risings that kept the island's status an open European question for decades.

British occupation, 1811-1816 (Indonesia.label: British occupation, 1811-1816
British occupation, 1811-1816 (Indonesia.prose:
[Indonesia, AD 1811–AD 1816] British occupation, 1811-1816. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--British occupation, 1811-1816". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.48 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain seized Java and the other Dutch possessions during the Napoleonic Wars, installing Thomas Stamford Raffles as lieutenant-governor. He overhauled the land revenue system, curbed forced deliveries, commissioned surveys of Javanese antiquities including Borobudur, and published a History of Java. The islands were returned to the Netherlands after Napoleon's defeat.

Civil War, 1970-1975 (Cambodia, AD 1970–.label: Civil War, 1970-1975
Civil War, 1970-1975 (Cambodia, AD 1970–.prose:
[Cambodia, AD 1970–AD 1975] Civil War, 1970-1975. Extracted from heading "Cambodia--History--Civil War, 1970-1975". Added to LCSH in 2006; appears on p.15 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Lon Nol deposed Prince Sihanouk, the country was drawn fully into the Vietnam War, with American bombing of the countryside on an enormous scale. The Khmer Rouge grew from a small maquis into an army capable of taking Phnom Penh in April 1975. Their victory opened four years of forced evacuation, execution and starvation in which roughly a quarter of the population died.

Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Milan, AD 1940–A.label: Bombardment, 1940-1945
Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Milan, AD 1940–A.prose:
[Milan (Italy), AD 1940–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Milan (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British night raids and American daylight raids grew into a round-the-clock campaign that destroyed the centres of Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and dozens of other cities, killed several hundred thousand civilians and made millions homeless. It absorbed a vast share of German industry and manpower in air defence, and it left a moral argument about area bombing that has never been settled.

Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771 (Sweden, A.label: Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771
Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771 (Sweden, A.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1751–AD 1771] Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who reigned with almost no power during Sweden's Age of Liberty, when the Riksdag and the rival Hat and Cap parties governed the country. His attempt to reclaim royal authority failed so completely that ministers stamped documents with a facsimile of his signature when he refused to sign. The frustrations of his reign set the stage for his son Gustav III's coup and the return of royal absolutism.

Maximilian II, 1564-1576 (Germany, AD 15.label: Maximilian II, 1564-1576
Maximilian II, 1564-1576 (Germany, AD 15.prose:
[Germany , AD 1564–AD 1576] Maximilian II, 1564-1576. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Maximilian II, 1564-1576". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Habsburg emperor of famously ambiguous religion, sympathetic to Lutheran ideas yet never breaking with Rome, he presided over an unusually tolerant interlude in the Empire and allowed Protestant nobles wide latitude in Austria. He kept the peace with the Ottomans at a price, paying tribute for Hungary, and cultivated humanists, botanists and collectors at his court. The confessional compromise he embodied collapsed under his more militantly Catholic successors.

Carolingian rule, 774-887 (Italy, AD 774.label: Carolingian rule, 774-887
Carolingian rule, 774-887 (Italy, AD 774.prose:
[Italy, AD 774–AD 887] Carolingian rule, 774-887. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Carolingian rule, 774-887". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 63 of LCSH 1987 as "Carlovingian rule". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charlemagne answered the pope's appeal by conquering the Lombard kingdom and taking its iron crown, ending two centuries of Lombard rule in the north. Frankish counts and bishops reshaped landholding and church life, while the alliance with Rome laid the foundations of the Papal States. Later Carolingians ruled Italy weakly from Pavia, and their extinction left the peninsula to competing local dynasties.

Papal rule, 1506-1797 (Bologna, AD 1506–.label: Papal rule, 1506-1797
Papal rule, 1506-1797 (Bologna, AD 1506–.prose:
[Bologna (Italy), AD 1506–AD 1797] Papal rule, 1506-1797. Extracted from heading "Bologna (Italy)--History--Papal rule, 1506-1797". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Julius II marched on the city in person and drove out the Bentivoglio family, bringing Bologna into the Papal States as its wealthiest possession after Rome. A cardinal legate ruled alongside a local senate of aristocratic families, and the arrangement funded the university, the great building projects of the Archiginnasio and San Petronio, and the painting workshops of the Carracci and Guido Reni. Charles V was crowned emperor here in 1530; the whole structure fell in 1797 when Napoleon's armies folded the city into a new Italian republic.

Bonaparte's first Italian campaign swept away Austrian and ducal government, and Milan became the capital of a series of French satellite states, culminating in the Kingdom of Italy with Napoleon as king. Church lands were sold, the Napoleonic Code and conscription imposed, roads and administration modernised on the French model. The experience of a single Italian state under one law outlived the empire and fed the nationalist movement of the following decades.

Rebellion of Lubomirski, 1665-1666 (Pola.label: Rebellion of Lubomirski, 1665-1666

A powerful magnate, condemned and stripped of office by the royal court, raised an army and beat the king's forces in the field, most decisively at Matwy. His victory killed John Casimir's plan to elect a successor during his own lifetime and to reform the paralysed Polish parliament. The Commonwealth kept its free elections and liberum veto, and the noble anarchy that followed left it defenceless before its neighbours a century later.

Alexios I salvaged an empire that had lost Anatolia to the Seljuks, buying help with trade privileges to Venice and appeals west that helped launch the First Crusade. His successors recovered coasts and prestige, ran a court culture of literature and learning, and tied the aristocracy to the throne by marriage. The system depended on strong emperors, and after Manuel I's death it unravelled fast, leaving the empire exposed to 1204.

Charles XI, 1660-1697 (Sweden, AD 1660–A.label: Charles XI, 1660-1697
Charles XI, 1660-1697 (Sweden, AD 1660–A.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1660–AD 1697] Charles XI, 1660-1697. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles XI, 1660-1697". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After a humiliating war he turned on the aristocracy, clawing back the crown lands they had been granted in the Great Reduction and having parliament declare him an absolute monarch answerable only to God. The confiscated estates funded the allotment system, which settled soldiers on farms and gave Sweden a standing army it could actually pay for. His reign ended in the catastrophic famine of the 1690s, which killed perhaps a third of the Finnish population.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Pennsylvania, AD 1.label: Civil War, 1861-1865

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

War of 1860-1861 (Italy, AD 1860–AD 1861.label: War of 1860-1861
War of 1860-1861 (Italy, AD 1860–AD 1861.prose:
[Italy, AD 1860–AD 1861] War of 1860-1861. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--War of 1860-1861". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Garibaldi sailed for Sicily with a thousand red-shirted volunteers, toppled the Bourbon kingdom in a few months, and handed the south to Victor Emmanuel II rather than claim it himself, while Piedmontese troops marched down through the Papal States to meet him. In March 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed, uniting nearly the whole peninsula under one crown for the first time since antiquity. Rome and Venice remained outside, and the abrupt annexation of the south left resentments and a brigand war that lasted years.

Cyprus Crisis, 1974- (Cyprus, AD 1974–AD.label: Cyprus Crisis, 1974-
Cyprus Crisis, 1974- (Cyprus, AD 1974–AD.prose:

A coup by the Greek military junta against President Makarios triggered a Turkish invasion that left the north of the island under Turkish control and displaced roughly a third of the population in both directions. A UN-patrolled buffer zone still cuts across the island and through Nicosia, the last divided capital in Europe. Repeated negotiations, including the rejected 2004 Annan Plan, have failed to reunify it, and the abandoned resort of Varosha remains sealed behind fences.

Charles I, 1625-1649 (England, AD 1625–A.label: Charles I, 1625-1649
Charles I, 1625-1649 (England, AD 1625–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1625–AD 1649] Charles I, 1625-1649. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Charles I, 1625-1649". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king convinced of his divine right ruled eleven years without Parliament, raising money through ship money and other levies that many considered illegal, and pushed ceremonial reforms that Puritans read as creeping popery. Attempts to impose a prayer book on Scotland forced him to recall Parliament, and the quarrel escalated into civil war across the three kingdoms. Defeated twice, he was tried by his own subjects and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall — an event without precedent in Europe. His art collection, one of the finest ever assembled, was sold off by the victors.

Conrad II, 1024-1039 (Germany, AD 1024–A.label: Conrad II, 1024-1039
Conrad II, 1024-1039 (Germany, AD 1024–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1024–AD 1039] Conrad II, 1024-1039. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Conrad II, 1024-1039". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first of the Salian emperors, elected when the Ottonian line died out, and a ruler who leaned on lesser knights and ministeriales rather than the great dukes. He secured hereditary rights for minor vassals in Italy, strengthening a service nobility loyal to the crown. His acquisition of the kingdom of Burgundy joined the three crowns of Germany, Italy and Burgundy under one emperor.

Sharif Hussein of Mecca rose against Ottoman rule with British money, weapons and liaison officers including T. E. Lawrence, while his son Faisal led irregular forces north along the Hejaz railway. The revolt tied down Ottoman troops and culminated in the entry into Damascus in 1918 and a short-lived Arab government there. Its promises of independence collided with the Sykes-Picot agreement and the mandates, a grievance that shaped Arab politics for the rest of the century.

The last Roman emperor, ruling a city surrounded by Ottoman territory and containing perhaps 50,000 people. He accepted union with the Roman church to buy western help that never adequately came, and refused Mehmed II's offer of surrender. He died fighting on the walls when the Ottomans broke through, ending an imperial line traced back to Augustus.

Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (United S.label: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775
Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (United S.prose:

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Known as the Pastry War after a French baker's damage claim, this was a naval blockade and bombardment of Veracruz mounted to force Mexico to pay debts to French residents. It cost Santa Anna a leg - which he later had buried with military honours - and restored his political career. Mexico paid up, and the affair exposed how vulnerable the young republic was to gunboat diplomacy.

Club War, 1596-1597 (Finland, AD 1596–AD.label: Club War, 1596-1597
Club War, 1596-1597 (Finland, AD 1596–AD.prose:

Peasants in Ostrobothnia and Savonia, worn down by the billeting and requisitions of Klaus Fleming's cavalry during the long war with Russia, rose in revolt armed largely with clubs and farm tools. They were also pawns in the struggle between Duke Charles and King Sigismund for the Swedish crown. Fleming's professional troops slaughtered them in a series of one-sided battles, and thousands of rebels died.

Genkō Incident, 1331-1333 (Japan, AD 133.label: Genkō Incident, 1331-1333
Genkō Incident, 1331-1333 (Japan, AD 133.prose:

Emperor Go-Daigo's second attempt to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate began with betrayal and defeat — he was besieged at Kasagi and exiled to the Oki Islands — but guerrilla resistance by Kusunoki Masashige and others kept the revolt alive. When the shogunate's own generals turned, Ashikaga Takauji seized Kyoto and Nitta Yoshisada burned Kamakura, wiping out the Hōjō. The result was the short-lived Kenmu Restoration and, soon after, sixty years of civil war between two rival imperial courts.

Portuguese rule ended abruptly after the Carnation Revolution, and FRELIMO took power in a country whose settler population and technicians had largely fled. A Marxist-Leninist state faced an insurgency by RENAMO, backed by Rhodesia and then apartheid South Africa; the war killed around a million people, displaced millions more, wrecked railways, schools and clinics, and left the countryside strewn with landmines. Peace talks in Rome ended the fighting and led to multiparty elections.

The Catholic Monarchs ruled Castile and Aragon jointly while keeping each kingdom's institutions intact, tamed the great nobles, and used the new Inquisition as an instrument of royal as much as religious authority. In a single year, 1492, they took Granada, expelled the Jews and sent Columbus west, decisions that ended Muslim rule in Iberia and opened an Atlantic empire. Their marriage alliances placed Habsburg Charles V in line for the whole inheritance, linking Spain to central Europe.

Age of Tyrants, 560-510 B.C (Greece, 559.node: Age of Tyrants, 560-510 B.C (Greece, 559 BC–509 BC)
Age of Tyrants, 560-510 B.C (Greece, 559.label: Age of Tyrants, 560-510 B.C

Across the Greek world single rulers seized power in cities that had been run by quarrelling aristocratic clans — Peisistratos and his sons at Athens, Polycrates on Samos — usually with popular backing against the nobility. Tyrants built temples, harbours and water systems, patronised poets, and promoted festivals that gave their cities a common civic identity. Their fall, when Hippias was driven out of Athens, opened the way to Cleisthenes' reforms and the beginnings of democracy.

A guerrilla resistance to French rule in the Red River Delta, named for the tangled reed marshes its fighters used as a refuge. Led principally by Nguyễn Thiện Thuật under the royalist Cần Vương banner, small bands ambushed patrols and tax collectors across Hưng Yên and Hải Dương for nearly a decade. Its slow strangulation by French columns and local auxiliaries marked the exhaustion of scholar-gentry armed resistance in the north.

Philip III, 1598-1621 (Spain, AD 1598–AD.label: Philip III, 1598-1621
Philip III, 1598-1621 (Spain, AD 1598–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 1598–AD 1621] Philip III, 1598-1621. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Philip III, 1598-1621". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Government by favourite, as the Duke of Lerma ran Spain while the king hunted and attended court festivals. Peace with England and a truce with the Dutch eased the wars, but inflation, debased copper coinage and the expulsion of some 300,000 Moriscos damaged the economy. It was also the age of Cervantes, Lope de Vega and El Greco.

Romania entered the Russo-Turkish war on Russia's side, and its troops proved decisive at the long siege of Plevna. Victory converted formal Ottoman suzerainty into full sovereignty, recognised by the Congress of Berlin in 1878, though the price included surrendering southern Bessarabia to Russia in exchange for Dobruja. Within three years the principality was proclaimed a kingdom.

A boy of thirteen was raised to the purple after the chaotic 'Year of the Six Emperors', and the empire was effectively run by his praetorian prefect Timesitheus. His reign brought a brief lull in the third-century crisis before a Persian campaign on the Euphrates ended in his death and the accession of Philip the Arab; his coinage, struck in huge quantities, is among the most common Roman issues found across the provinces.

A failed examination candidate who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ raised an army in south China and founded the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace, capturing Nanjing and holding much of the Yangzi valley for over a decade. The war that followed killed perhaps twenty million people, making it the deadliest civil conflict in history. Its suppression by provincial armies under men like Zeng Guofan shifted military power away from the Qing centre and into regional hands, a change the dynasty never reversed.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Rhode Island, AD.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Rhode Island, AD.prose:

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Eudes, 888-898 (France, AD 888–AD 898).label: Eudes, 888-898
Eudes, 888-898 (France, AD 888–AD 898).prose:

Odo, count of Paris and hero of the city's defence during the Viking siege of 885-86, was elected king of the West Franks in preference to the Carolingian heir. His reign showed that the crown could pass by the choice of the magnates to a man who could actually fight, and his family, the Robertians, would eventually become the Capetian dynasty. He spent his years contesting the throne with the young Charles the Simple and fending off further Norse raids.

Caracas deposed its captain-general and in 1811 declared the first independent republic in Spanish America, which an earthquake and royalist counterattack destroyed within a year. Bolívar's proclamation of "war to the death", the switching allegiance of the llanero horsemen, and the British Legion turned the tide, and Carabobo in 1821 broke Spanish power on land. The final Spanish force surrendered after the naval battle on Lake Maracaibo, leaving a country exhausted, depopulated and dominated by its victorious generals.

Spanish dynasty, 1580-1640 (Portugal, AD.prose:

When the Portuguese royal line died out, Philip II of Spain claimed the throne and joined the two Iberian crowns and their global empires in a personal union. Portugal kept its own laws and institutions, but its ships, colonies and trade routes became targets in Spain's wars, and the Dutch seized much of Asia, Brazil and the African slave forts. Resentment at the costs of Castilian wars produced the 1640 revolt that put the House of Braganza on the throne and began a long war of independence.

Twice within a decade the rising Manchu state struck south into Korea to secure its flank before attacking Ming China. The second campaign ended with King Injo emerging from the besieged fortress of Namhansanseong to kowtow to the Qing emperor at Samjeondo, sending his sons as hostages and breaking Joseon's loyalty to the Ming. The humiliation shaped Korean politics and thought for generations, feeding both resentment of the Qing and debate over how to strengthen the kingdom.

One of the southern states that broke away as northern China convulsed, ruled from Chengdu behind the mountain barriers of Sichuan. Sheltered from war, its court became a refuge for poets and painters and produced the first great anthology of ci lyric verse. Its ruler surrendered after a brief campaign by the newly founded Song.

Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925 (China, AD.label: Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925
Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925 (China, AD.prose:

When the Tang dynasty fell, the general Wang Jian made himself emperor in Sichuan, whose mountains sheltered it from the wars convulsing the north. Poets, painters and officials fled there, and the court became a refuge for Tang culture and a centre of early printing. Wang's dissolute son lost it to the Later Tang armies in barely two months.

Revolution, 1954-1962 (Algeria, AD 1954–.label: Revolution, 1954-1962
Revolution, 1954-1962 (Algeria, AD 1954–.prose:

The FLN's coordinated attacks on All Saints' Day 1954 opened a war that France fought as an internal matter, since Algeria was legally part of the republic and home to a million European settlers. Torture, massacres and the Battle of Algiers made the conflict a moral crisis in France, bringing down the Fourth Republic and returning de Gaulle to power. Independence came in 1962 after the Évian Accords, followed by the flight of nearly the entire settler population.

French rule, 1797-1815 (Bologna, AD 1797.label: French rule, 1797-1815
French rule, 1797-1815 (Bologna, AD 1797.prose:

Papal government ended abruptly as the city was folded into Napoleon's Cispadane and then Cisalpine republics and finally the Kingdom of Italy. Monasteries were suppressed and their property sold, the university and academies reorganised, and paintings by Raphael and the Carracci carted off to Paris - some never returned. Restoration handed the city back to the pope, but the taste of secular, code-based government left a lasting appetite for change that surfaced in the risings of the following decades.

Three Chinese generals who had helped the Manchus conquer the Ming were rewarded with near-independent southern domains; when the young Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish them, Wu Sangui and his allies revolted and for a time held most of southern China. Eight years of war ended in Qing victory and the elimination of the semi-autonomous feudatories, followed by the conquest of Taiwan in 1683. The victory secured Qing rule over all of China and confirmed Kangxi as one of its most effective emperors.

Leopold I, 1831-1865 (Belgium, AD 1831–A.label: Leopold I, 1831-1865
Leopold I, 1831-1865 (Belgium, AD 1831–A.prose:

A German prince chosen to head the newly independent Belgian state, he gave the young constitutional monarchy credibility and secured its recognition and guaranteed neutrality through the 1839 Treaty of London. Uncle and mentor to both Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, he acted as an unofficial broker among Europe's courts, and Belgium industrialised rapidly under his rule while escaping the revolutions of 1848.

Berlin Blockade, 1948-1949 (Berlin, AD 1.prose:
[Berlin (Germany), AD 1948–AD 1949] Berlin Blockade, 1948-1949. Extracted from heading "Berlin (Germany)--History--Blockade, 1948-1949". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Soviet forces cut every road, rail and canal route into the western sectors of the city, hoping to force the Western Allies out. Instead, British and American aircraft flew in coal, flour and everything else a city of two million needed, landing at times every few minutes for nearly a year. The blockade failed, but it hardened the split between East and West, hastened the creation of two German states and led directly to the founding of NATO.

Crowned in the cradle in both England and France, he grew into a pious, politically hopeless king who suffered periods of catatonic mental collapse. Under him the English lost everything in France but Calais, and the resulting recriminations between court factions hardened into the Wars of the Roses. His deposition by Edward IV began three decades of dynastic bloodletting.

Movement to Protect the Constitution, 19.node: Movement to Protect the Constitution, 1917-1923 (China, AD 1917–AD 1923)

After the Beiyang government in Beijing dissolved parliament, Sun Yat-sen led dissident legislators south to Guangzhou and set up a rival regime claiming to defend the 1912 provisional constitution. Dependent on southern warlords who repeatedly turned on him, the movement failed to reunify the country, and China remained split among militarists. Its failure convinced Sun to build a disciplined party and army of his own, with Soviet help - the seed of the Nationalist Party's later Northern Expedition.

Frederick I, 1797-1816 (Germany, AD 1797.label: Frederick I, 1797-1816
Frederick I, 1797-1816 (Germany, AD 1797.prose:
[Württemberg (Germany), AD 1797–AD 1816] Frederick I, 1797-1816. Extracted from heading "Württemberg (Germany)--History--Frederick I, 1797-1816".
