The Württemberg ruler who rode Napoleon's coattails from duke to elector to king, doubling his territory with secularised church lands and absorbed imperial cities and free knights' estates. He dissolved the duchy's old representative estates and ruled as an autocrat over a newly enlarged, centralised state. Switching sides in 1813, he kept his crown at the Congress of Vienna, so a kingdom built by French power survived Napoleon's fall.

Revolution, 1830-1832 (Lithuania, AD 183.label: Revolution, 1830-1832
Revolution, 1830-1832 (Lithuania, AD 183.prose:
[Lithuania, AD 1830–AD 1832] Revolution, 1830-1832. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--Revolution, 1830-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.72 of LCSH 1987, and p.58 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Insurrection against Russian rule spread from Warsaw into the former Grand Duchy, where noble-led detachments and peasant volunteers seized much of the countryside before regular Russian forces retook Vilnius and drove survivors into Prussia. The defeat brought sweeping punishment: Vilnius University was closed, estates were confiscated, and thousands went into exile, where Polish-Lithuanian emigre politics took root. The suppression pushed national feeling out of the manor houses and towards a new generation of writers and, eventually, peasant activists.

Francis I, 1515-1547 (France, AD 1515–AD.label: Francis I, 1515-1547
Francis I, 1515-1547 (France, AD 1515–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1515–AD 1547] Francis I, 1515-1547. Extracted from heading "France--History--Francis I, 1515-1547". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who opened his reign by winning Milan at Marignano and spent the rest of it losing ground to Emperor Charles V, including a year as Charles's prisoner after the disaster at Pavia in 1525. He shipped Italian Renaissance style into France wholesale — Leonardo da Vinci died in his service, and Chambord and Fontainebleau went up on his orders — while allying with the Ottoman sultan against fellow Christians, to Europe's scandal. His 1539 ordinance made French, not Latin, the language of law and administration.

Egypt's imperial age began when Ahmose drove out the Hyksos and reunited the country, opening the New Kingdom. Its rulers - Hatshepsut, the conqueror Thutmose III, the heretic Akhenaten and the boy-king Tutankhamun - pushed Egyptian power to the Euphrates and Nubia, filled Karnak with obelisks and cut royal tombs into the Valley of the Kings. The Amarna episode, when Akhenaten abolished the old gods for the sun-disc Aten and built a new capital in the desert, was reversed within a generation, but its startlingly naturalistic art survives.

Edward II, 1307-1327 (England, AD 1307–A.label: Edward II, 1307-1327
Edward II, 1307-1327 (England, AD 1307–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1307–AD 1327] Edward II, 1307-1327. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward II, 1307-1327". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward's reliance on favourites, first Piers Gaveston and then the Despensers, set him against his own barons and cost him the support of his queen. His defeat by Robert Bruce at Bannockburn in 1314 secured Scottish independence in practice. He was deposed by an invasion led by Isabella and Mortimer and died in captivity, the first English king forced from the throne.

John II, 1458-1479 (Kingdom of Aragon, A.label: John II, 1458-1479
John II, 1458-1479 (Kingdom of Aragon, A.prose:

He came to the Aragonese throne already old and already king of Navarre, and spent his reign fighting a decade-long Catalan civil war against his own subjects, losing Roussillon to France in the process. His real achievement was diplomatic: the marriage he arranged in 1469 between his son Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile united the two crowns and made modern Spain possible.

Caesar's two raids put Britain on Rome's map; Claudius invaded in earnest in AD 43 and the island became a frontier province, walled off from the north by Hadrian's Wall. Towns, roads, baths, villas, coinage and writing arrived with the army and the tax collector, alongside new gods and eventually Christianity. When the field army and the money went in the early fifth century the towns emptied fast, and the traditional date for the coming of the Anglo-Saxons closes the period.

Clement VII, 1523-1534 (Vatican City, AD.label: Clement VII, 1523-1534
Clement VII, 1523-1534 (Vatican City, AD.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1523–AD 1534] Clement VII, 1523-1534. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Clement VII, 1523-1534". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Medici pope whose shifting alliances between France and the Emperor brought disaster: imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527 and held him prisoner in the Castel Sant'Angelo. Unable to defy Charles V, he refused Henry VIII's annulment, pushing England out of the Roman church. He also commissioned Michelangelo's Last Judgement and backed Copernicus's early circulation of his heliocentric ideas.

Interregnum, 1383-1385 (Portugal, AD 138.label: Interregnum, 1383-1385
Interregnum, 1383-1385 (Portugal, AD 138.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1383–AD 1385] Interregnum, 1383-1385. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Interregnum, 1383-1385". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of Ferdinand I left only a daughter married to the king of Castile, and Lisbon's merchants and artisans revolted rather than accept absorption by Castile. John of Aviz, backed by the townsmen and the commander Nuno Álvares Pereira, was made king and destroyed a far larger Castilian army at Aljubarrota. The crisis founded the Aviz dynasty, sealed the alliance with England, and launched the voyages that became Portugal's overseas empire.

Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941 (Th.label: Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941
Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941 (Th.prose:
[Indochina, Thailand, AD 1940–AD 1941] Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941. Spatial coverage: China, France, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam. Extracted from heading "Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941". With France defeated in Europe, Thailand attacked French Indochina to reclaim territories in Laos and Cambodia ceded decades earlier. Thai troops made gains on land while the French navy won a sharp victory at Ko Chang; Japan then imposed mediation, handing Thailand the disputed provinces and drawing Bangkok firmly into Tokyo's orbit on the eve of the Pacific War.

Constitutional period, 1789-1809 (United.label: Constitutional period, 1789-1809
Constitutional period, 1789-1809 (United.prose:

The new federal machinery was switched on and tested: Washington's first administration, the Bill of Rights, a national bank, a Supreme Court that had to invent its own authority. Bitter argument between Federalists and Jeffersonian Republicans produced the first party system and the first peaceful transfer of power between opponents. The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled the country's territory at a stroke.

French Colony, 1555-1567 (Brazil, AD 155.label: French Colony, 1555-1567
French Colony, 1555-1567 (Brazil, AD 155.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1555–AD 1567] French Colony, 1555-1567. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--French Colony, 1555-1567". Appears on p.10 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.12 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Villegagnon's expedition planted a fortified settlement on an island in Guanabara Bay - France Antarctique - drawing both Catholics and Calvinist refugees in an experiment that collapsed into religious quarrelling. Portuguese forces drove the French out and founded Rio de Janeiro to hold the bay for good. The episode produced Jean de Léry's famous account of the Tupinambá, one of the earliest ethnographic descriptions of Brazil.

Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1.node: Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1878 (South Africa, AD 1877–AD 1878)
Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1.label: Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1878

A brawl at a beer drink escalated into the ninth and last of the frontier wars between the Xhosa and the Cape Colony, drawing in both Gcaleka and Ngqika chiefdoms against colonial forces armed with breech-loading rifles. Xhosa defeat ended a century of resistance on the eastern frontier, killed the paramount chief Sarhili's independence and opened the Transkei to annexation. It was the opening move in the wider British campaign to subdue independent African polities across southern Africa.

Henry IV seized the crown from Richard II, and the usurpation shadowed the dynasty for sixty years. Henry V's victory at Agincourt and the treaty naming him heir to France marked the high point; under the pious, intermittently insane Henry VI those conquests evaporated and the nobility split into factions. Defeat at Towton in 1461 put the Yorkists on the throne and turned dynastic quarrel into the Wars of the Roses.

Grandson of Peter the Great, he came to the throne at eleven and was governed by rival aristocratic factions, first Menshikov and then the Dolgorukovs, who moved the court back to Moscow and let his grandfather's navy rot. He died of smallpox at fourteen on the day set for his wedding, ending the male line of the Romanovs and opening a succession crisis that the nobility briefly tried to exploit to limit the monarchy.

Proclaimed by his father's troops at York, he fought his way to sole rule and dismantled the tetrarchy that Diocletian had built. He legalised and then favoured Christianity, called the Council of Nicaea to settle its doctrine, and founded Constantinople as a new imperial capital that would outlast Rome by a thousand years. His reformed gold solidus underpinned Mediterranean trade for centuries.

Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916 (Austria, AD 1.label: Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916
Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916 (Austria, AD 1.prose:

Put on the throne at eighteen during the revolutions of 1848, he reigned for sixty-eight years while his empire was expelled from Italy and Germany, forced into partnership with Hungary in 1867, and steadily strained by its dozen nationalities. His Vienna tore down its walls for the Ringstrasse and became the city of Freud, Klimt and Mahler, even as the dynasty absorbed the suicide of his son and the assassination of his wife. His ultimatum to Serbia after the killing of his heir began the First World War.

Charles V, 1364-1380 (France, AD 1364–AD.label: Charles V, 1364-1380
Charles V, 1364-1380 (France, AD 1364–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1364–AD 1380] Charles V, 1364-1380. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles V, 1364-1380". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inheriting a kingdom humiliated at Poitiers and carved up by treaty, he recovered nearly all the lost territory without fighting a great battle, using Bertrand du Guesclin's raids, sieges and a rebuilt fleet to wear the English down. He reformed taxation and the coinage, fortified Paris and built the Bastille, and assembled a royal library of a thousand manuscripts, commissioning translations of Aristotle and Augustine into French. His careful, bookish style of kingship earned him the name the Wise.

Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979 (Iran, AD 192.label: Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979
Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979 (Iran, AD 192.prose:
[Iran, AD 1925–AD 1979] Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two shahs, father and son, remade Iran as a centralised modern state with a conscript army, railways, universities and a secularised legal system, financed increasingly by oil. Foreign involvement was constant, from the Anglo-Soviet occupation in 1941 to the CIA- and British-backed coup of 1953. The monarchy collapsed in 1979, replaced by an Islamic republic.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (West Virginia, AD.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (West Virginia, AD.prose:

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Maria Theresa, 1740-1780 (Austria, AD 17.label: Maria Theresa, 1740-1780
Maria Theresa, 1740-1780 (Austria, AD 17.prose:
[Austria, AD 1740–AD 1780] Maria Theresa, 1740-1780. Extracted from the heading "Austria--History--Maria Theresa, 1740-1780". Appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Her inheritance of the Habsburg lands was immediately challenged, and the wars that followed cost her Silesia to Prussia but proved the monarchy could survive as a single state. She rebuilt it with a standing army, a professional bureaucracy, tax reform and compulsory schooling, centralising power in Vienna at the expense of the provincial estates. Mother of Joseph II and Marie Antoinette, she used dynastic marriages as deliberately as she used armies.

Achinese War, 1873-1904 (Indonesia, AD 1.label: Achinese War, 1873-1904
Achinese War, 1873-1904 (Indonesia, AD 1.prose:
[Indonesia, AD 1873–AD 1904] Achinese War, 1873-1904. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Achinese War, 1873-1904". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.48 of LCSH 1975. The Dutch invasion of the sultanate of Aceh in northern Sumatra turned into the longest and bloodiest colonial war in the Netherlands' history, dragging on for three decades. Guerrilla resistance led by local chiefs and Islamic scholars was eventually broken by mobile counter-insurgency columns and the harsh methods of Van Heutsz. Its end completed Dutch control of the Indonesian archipelago and left a legacy of Acehnese separatism that lasted into the twenty-first century.

Babylonian captivity, 598-515 B.C (Iraq,.prose:

Nebuchadnezzar II's armies deported Judah's king, nobles, priests and craftsmen to Babylonia in successive waves, destroying Jerusalem and its Temple in 586 BC. In exile, Judeans kept their identity through sabbath, circumcision, genealogy and the collection of prophetic and legal texts, while prophets such as Ezekiel and Second Isaiah reimagined their god as ruler of all nations. Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed a return, and the rebuilt Second Temple marked the end of the episode that turned a national cult into a portable religion.

He restored royal authority after a period of civil war and had himself crowned Emperor of All Spain in León in 1135, claiming overlordship over the other Iberian rulers. He campaigned deep into Andalusia and took Almería, though it was soon lost to the Almohads. Dividing León and Castile between his two sons at his death undid much of what he had built.

Frederick I, 1152-1190 (Germany, AD 1152.label: Frederick I, 1152-1190
Frederick I, 1152-1190 (Germany, AD 1152.prose:
[Germany , AD 1152–AD 1190] Frederick I, 1152-1190. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Frederick I, 1152-1190". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Barbarossa spent his reign trying to make imperial authority real in Italy, launching six expeditions south and destroying Milan, only to be beaten by the Lombard League at Legnano in 1176 and forced to recognise the cities' liberties. At home he broke his greatest rival, Henry the Lion, and redistributed his duchies, cementing the princes' power. He drowned in a river in Anatolia on the Third Crusade, and German legend later had him sleeping in a mountain, waiting to return.

Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913 (Vietnam, AD.label: Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913
Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1913] Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peasant fighters in the forested hills north of Hanoi, led for most of three decades by Hoàng Hoa Thám (Đề Thám), waged guerrilla war against French colonial forces, negotiating truces and then resuming the fight. It outlasted every other armed resistance of its generation and tied down substantial French troops. Đề Thám's killing in 1913 ended it, but he became a national symbol for later anticolonial movements.

Francis II, 1792-1806 (Germany, AD 1792–.label: Francis II, 1792-1806
Francis II, 1792-1806 (Germany, AD 1792–.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1792–AD 1806] Francis II, 1792-1806. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. The last Holy Roman Emperor, whose reign was one long losing struggle against revolutionary and Napoleonic France. After the catastrophe of Austerlitz and Napoleon's creation of the Confederation of the Rhine, he laid down the crown in 1806 and dissolved an institution that had existed in some form for a thousand years. He carried on as Francis I of Austria, a title he had created for himself two years earlier.

Put on the throne at eighteen during the revolutions of 1848, he reigned for sixty-eight years while his empire was expelled from Italy and Germany, forced into partnership with Hungary in 1867, and steadily strained by its dozen nationalities. His Vienna tore down its walls for the Ringstrasse and became the city of Freud, Klimt and Mahler, even as the dynasty absorbed the suicide of his son and the assassination of his wife. His ultimatum to Serbia after the killing of his heir began the First World War.

Daoguang, 1820-1850 (China, AD 1820–AD 1.label: Daoguang, 1820-1850
Daoguang, 1820-1850 (China, AD 1820–AD 1.prose:
[China, AD 1820–AD 1850] Daoguang, 1820-1850. Extracted from heading "China--History--Daoguang, 1820-1850". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Tao kuang, 1820-1850" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987, and on p.16 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign spent watching Qing authority erode from within and without: opium imports drained silver from the economy, rebellions and floods strained the treasury, and the government's attempt to suppress the drug trade at Canton brought war with Britain. Defeat produced the 1842 Treaty of Nanjing, the cession of Hong Kong and the opening of treaty ports — the start of what Chinese historians call the century of humiliation. The emperor himself was frugal and cautious, and his indecision has often been blamed for the scale of the collapse that followed.

Rebellion, 1485-1487 (Naples, AD 1485–AD.label: Rebellion, 1485-1487
Rebellion, 1485-1487 (Naples, AD 1485–AD.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1485–AD 1487] Rebellion, 1485-1487. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Rebellion, 1485-1487". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The barons of the kingdom of Naples, backed by Pope Innocent VIII, rose against King Ferrante of Aragon's centralising taxation and his squeeze on feudal privilege. Ferrante offered terms, then arrested and executed the ringleaders at a wedding feast and confiscated their estates. The affair left the monarchy hated by the nobility and the kingdom fatally divided when the French invaded in 1494.

Antonines, 96-192 (Roman Empire, AD 96–A.label: Antonines, 96-192
Antonines, 96-192 (Roman Empire, AD 96–A.prose:
[Rome, AD 96–AD 192] Antonines, 96-192. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Antonines, 96-192". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius presided over the empire at its largest and, by later Roman reckoning, its most stable, with succession managed by adoption rather than birth. The century brought Trajan's Dacian and Parthian wars, Hadrian's frontier walls, monumental building across the provinces, and a flowering of Greek and Latin literature and philosophy. It closed badly, with plague, war on the Danube and the erratic reign of Commodus.

Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C (Egyp.node: Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C (Egypt, 2685 BC–2180 BC)
Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C (Egyp.label: Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C
Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C (Egyp.prose:
[Egypt, 2685 BC–2180 BC] Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Egypt's first long era of unified, centralised rule, remembered above all for pyramid building and for the officials' tombs clustered around royal cemeteries. Wall reliefs in those tombs show farming, fishing, brewing and craftwork in remarkable detail, the everyday world that supported the court. When central authority weakened under Pepi II's successors, the provinces went their own way and the country slid into the First Intermediate Period.

Charles V, 1506-1555 (Belgium, AD 1506–A.label: Charles V, 1506-1555
Charles V, 1506-1555 (Belgium, AD 1506–A.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1506–AD 1555] Charles V, 1506-1555. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Charles V, 1506-1555". Appears on p. 8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.9 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born in Ghent and Burgundian by upbringing, he ruled the Low Countries as their natural prince while governing half of Europe from elsewhere, leaving regents — his aunt Margaret and sister Mary — in charge at Mechelen and Brussels. He completed the Seventeen Provinces by conquest and inheritance and bound them together by the Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 as a single indivisible unit. Antwerp became the commercial capital of the world in these decades, while his edicts against Protestants sowed the grievances that later exploded into the Dutch Revolt. He abdicated in the palace at Brussels in 1555.

Wars of Independence, 1806-1830 (South A.label: Wars of Independence, 1806-1830
Wars of Independence, 1806-1830 (South A.prose:
[South America, AD 1806–AD 1830] Wars of Independence, 1806-1830. Extracted from heading "South America--History--Wars of Independence, 1806-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's overthrow of the Spanish king in 1808 left colonial cities governing themselves through juntas, and the improvised self-rule hardened into demands for full separation. Campaigns led by San Martín from the south and Bolívar from the north converged in Peru, with the royalist cause finished at Ayacucho in 1824. Bolívar's dream of a united Spanish America collapsed almost at once, leaving a patchwork of republics along old colonial administrative lines.

Gothic War, 535-555 (Italy, AD 535–AD 55.label: Gothic War, 535-555
Gothic War, 535-555 (Italy, AD 535–AD 55.prose:
[Italy, AD 535–AD 555] Gothic War, 535-555. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Gothic War, 535-555". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 63 of LCSH 1987; revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Justinian's armies, under Belisarius and later Narses, set out to recover Italy from the Ostrogoths and spent twenty years doing it. Rome changed hands repeatedly, the Gothic king Totila nearly reversed the conquest, and the campaigning wrecked the cities, aqueducts and senatorial society that had survived the fall of the western empire intact. Byzantine rule over the wasted peninsula lasted barely a decade before the Lombards walked in.

Hussite Wars, 1419-1436 (Czech Republic,.label: Hussite Wars, 1419-1436
Hussite Wars, 1419-1436 (Czech Republic,.prose:
[Bohemia (Czechoslovakia), AD 1419–AD 1436] Hussite Wars, 1419-1436. Extracted from heading "Bohemia (Czechoslovakia)--History--Hussite Wars, 1419-1436". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.10 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1993. Source refers to the Czech Republic as Czechoslovakia. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bohemian followers of the executed preacher Jan Hus rose against the Church and the Emperor Sigismund, beginning with the Defenestration of Prague and turning back five papal crusades. Jan Žižka's peasant armies pioneered war wagons and massed handguns, showing that disciplined infantry could destroy mounted knights. The conflict ended in a negotiated settlement allowing communion in both kinds, leaving Bohemia with a tolerated reformist church a century before Luther.

French occupation, 1881-1956 (Tunisia, A.label: French occupation, 1881-1956
French occupation, 1881-1956 (Tunisia, A.prose:
[Tunisia, France, AD 1881–AD 1956] French occupation, 1881-1956. Spatial coverage: France, Tunisia. Extracted from heading "Tunisia--History--French occupation, 1881-1956". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. "France--History--War with Tunisia, 1881" listed as a variant, so spatial coverage for France added. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A border incident with Algeria gave France the pretext to invade; the Treaty of Bardo and the Convention of La Marsa left the bey as figurehead while a French resident-general ruled. European settlers took the best farmland, phosphate mining and railways transformed the economy, and Tunis grew a new colonial city beside the medina. A modern nationalist movement, culminating in Bourguiba's Neo-Destour party, forced negotiations that led to independence.

Wallace's Rising, 1297-1304 (Scotland, A.label: Wallace's Rising, 1297-1304
Wallace's Rising, 1297-1304 (Scotland, A.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1297–AD 1304] Wallace's Rising, 1297-1304. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Wallace's Rising, 1297-1304". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A knight of modest rank, William Wallace led a popular revolt against Edward I's occupation and, with Andrew Moray, destroyed an English army trapped on a narrow crossing at Stirling Bridge. Defeat at Falkirk a year later ended his brief guardianship of Scotland, and after years as a fugitive he was betrayed, tried in Westminster Hall and butchered as a traitor. His refusal to submit made him a lasting symbol of resistance, and his revolt kept the fight alive until Robert Bruce took it up.

Heisei period, 1989- (Japan, AD 1989–AD.label: Heisei period, 1989-
Heisei period, 1989- (Japan, AD 1989–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 1989–AD 2015] Heisei period, 1989-. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Heisei period, 1989-". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Named for the reign of Emperor Akihito, it began with the bursting of the land and stock bubble and became known for the 'lost decades' of flat growth and falling prices. Earthquakes at Kobe and Tōhoku, the Fukushima nuclear accident and a rapidly greying population defined the domestic mood, even as Japanese animation, fashion and technology shaped global youth culture.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Florida, AD 1861–A.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Florida, AD 1861–A.prose:
[Florida , AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.78 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Batavian Republic, 1795-1806 (Netherland.label: Batavian Republic, 1795-1806
Batavian Republic, 1795-1806 (Netherland.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1795–AD 1806] Batavian Republic, 1795-1806. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--Batavian Republic, 1795-1806". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

French revolutionary armies crossed the frozen rivers in the winter of 1795 and the old Dutch Republic collapsed, its stadtholder fleeing to England. Patriot revolutionaries replaced the loose federation of provinces with a centralised state, wrote the first Dutch constitution and separated church from state, while remaining a satellite obliged to fund and fight France's wars. Napoleon dissolved it to install his brother Louis as King of Holland.

Ferdinand III, 1217-1252 (Kingdom of Cas.label: Ferdinand III, 1217-1252
Ferdinand III, 1217-1252 (Kingdom of Cas.prose:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1217–AD 1252] Ferdinand III, 1217-1252. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Ferdinand III, 1217-1252". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He permanently united the crowns of Castile and León and then drove the Reconquista deep into the south, taking Córdoba, Jaén, Murcia and finally Seville. Granada survived only as a tributary vassal, an arrangement that lasted two and a half centuries. Great mosques became cathedrals, Castilian settlers were planted across Andalusia, and the king was later canonised as San Fernando.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Georgia, AD 1775–.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Georgia, AD 1775–.prose:
[Georgia, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Georgia--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.42 of LCSH 1987, and p.40 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Henry VII, 1308-1313 (Germany, AD 1308–A.label: Henry VII, 1308-1313
Henry VII, 1308-1313 (Germany, AD 1308–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1308–AD 1313] Henry VII, 1308-1313. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry VII, 1308-1313". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A count of Luxembourg elected as a compromise candidate, he secured Bohemia for his family and then led the first imperial expedition to Italy in decades, seeking to revive the emperor's authority there. Dante hailed him as Italy's saviour and wrote him into the Paradiso; the Guelf cities and the pope resisted him. He died of fever near Siena before he could break Florence, and the imperial dream in Italy died with him.

Sigismund III, 1587-1632 (Poland, AD 158.label: Sigismund III, 1587-1632
Sigismund III, 1587-1632 (Poland, AD 158.prose:
[Poland , AD 1587–AD 1632] Sigismund III, 1587-1632. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Sigismund III, 1587-1632". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Vasa prince raised Catholic, Sigismund lost the Swedish crown to his uncle and spent decades trying to win it back, dragging the Commonwealth into long wars in the Baltic. His armies intervened in Russia's Time of Troubles and briefly held Moscow, while his court championed the Counter-Reformation and Jesuit education. He also shifted the royal seat from Kraków to Warsaw, making it Poland's capital in all but name.

John II, 1406-1454 (Castile and León, AD.label: John II, 1406-1454
John II, 1406-1454 (Castile and León, AD.prose:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1406–AD 1454] John II, 1406-1454. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--John II, 1406-1454". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cultivated, indecisive king whose long reign was effectively run by his favourite Álvaro de Luna, and torn by feuds with the ambitious Infantes of Aragon that culminated in the battle of Olmedo. The royal court became a centre of Castilian lyric poetry and early humanism. He finally abandoned Luna to the executioner's block; his daughter by his second marriage was Isabella the Catholic.

Three kingdoms-Sui dynasty, 220-618 (Chi.label: Three kingdoms-Sui dynasty, 220-618
Three kingdoms-Sui dynasty, 220-618 (Chi.prose:
[China, AD 220–AD 618] Three kingdoms-Sui dynasty, 220-618. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Four centuries of division between the fall of Han and the Sui reunification saw northern China ruled largely by dynasties of steppe origin and the south by successive courts at Nanjing. Buddhism took deep root, filling the landscape with cave temples at Yungang, Longmen and Dunhuang, while calligraphy, landscape poetry and celadon ceramics flourished. When the Sui reunited the country, they inherited a fused Chinese and Inner Asian elite and a Buddhist culture that shaped the Tang.

Wilhelmina, 1898-1948 (Netherlands, AD 1.label: Wilhelmina, 1898-1948
Wilhelmina, 1898-1948 (Netherlands, AD 1.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1898–AD 1948] Wilhelmina, 1898-1948. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--Wilhelmina, 1898-1948". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.81 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fifty years on the Dutch throne, from a girl-queen crowned at eighteen to a symbol of national resistance. She steered the Netherlands through neutrality in the First World War, then fled to London in 1940 and broadcast to occupied Holland over Radio Oranje, becoming a far more political monarch than the constitution imagined. She abdicated in favour of her daughter Juliana as the Indonesian revolution was dismantling the Dutch empire in the East.

William II, 1840-1849 (Netherlands, AD 1.label: William II, 1840-1849
William II, 1840-1849 (Netherlands, AD 1.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1840–AD 1849] William II, 1840-1849. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History-William II, 1840-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.81 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Willem II took the Dutch throne after his father abdicated, having earlier commanded troops at Waterloo and against the Belgian revolt. Alarmed by the revolutions sweeping Europe in 1848, he turned, in his own words, from conservative to liberal in a single night and allowed Thorbecke to draft a constitution that gave real power to parliament and made ministers answerable to it. That charter is the foundation of Dutch parliamentary democracy.

Henry IV, 1454-1474 (Kingdom of Castile,.label: Henry IV, 1454-1474
Henry IV, 1454-1474 (Kingdom of Castile,.prose:
[Castile, AD 1454–AD 1474] Henry IV, 1454-1474. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Henry IV, 1454-1474". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nicknamed 'the Impotent' by his enemies, he faced a nobility that staged a mock deposition of his effigy at Ávila and questioned whether his daughter Juana was really his. Forced to name his half-sister Isabella as heir, then to reverse himself, he left the succession unresolved at his death. The resulting civil war ended with Isabella and Ferdinand of Aragon on the throne and the union of the Spanish crowns.

Great Western Schism, 1378-1417 (Papal S.label: Great Western Schism, 1378-1417
Great Western Schism, 1378-1417 (Papal S.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1378–AD 1417] Great Western Schism, 1378-1417. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Schism, The Great Western, 1378-1417". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A disputed election left rival popes in Rome and Avignon, each with his own curia, cardinals and taxes, and each excommunicating the other; a council at Pisa made matters worse by adding a third. Kings and universities chose sides according to politics rather than doctrine, and the spectacle badly damaged the papacy's claim to spiritual authority. The Council of Constance finally deposed the claimants and elected Martin V, but the conciliar argument it started, and the disillusion it bred, fed into later calls for reform.

Dorian invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C (Gre.node: Dorian invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C (Greece, 1124 BC–1024 BC)
Dorian invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C (Gre.label: Dorian invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C
Dorian invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C (Gre.prose:
[Greece, 1124 BC–1024 BC] Dorian invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Dorian Invasions, ca. 1125-1025 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The traditional Greek explanation for the collapse of the Mycenaean world: waves of Dorian-speaking newcomers from the northwest overrunning the Peloponnese and driving refugees to Attica, the islands and Asia Minor. Ancient writers used it to explain the later map of Greek dialects and the claims of Sparta and Argos to ancestral rights. Archaeologists have found little sign of a single invasion, and most now see a slower, messier breakdown of palace society — but the story shaped how Greeks understood their own origins.

Lucius Septimus Severus, 193-211 (Roman.label: Lucius Septimus Severus, 193-211
Lucius Septimus Severus, 193-211 (Roman.prose:
[Rome, AD 193–AD 211] Lucius Septimus Severus, 193-211. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Lucius Septimius Severus, 193-211". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An African-born general who won the throne in the civil wars that followed Commodus's murder, he ruled frankly as a soldier's emperor, raising army pay and telling his sons to enrich the troops and ignore everyone else. He expanded the empire into Mesopotamia, doubled the size of Rome's garrison, and died at York while campaigning in Britain. His dynasty pushed the emperor's dependence on the army to the point that later succession crises became almost purely military affairs.

House of Valois, 1363-1477 (France, AD 1.label: House of Valois, 1363-1477
House of Valois, 1363-1477 (France, AD 1.prose:
[Burgundy, AD 1363–AD 1477] House of Valois, 1363-1477. Extracted from heading "Burgundy (France)--History--House of Valois, 1363-1477". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Source notes Burgundy is in modern France. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

John II gave the duchy of Burgundy to his youngest son Philip the Bold, creating a cadet branch that proved more dangerous than any foreign enemy. Enriched by the Flemish cloth towns, the dukes allied with England during the Hundred Years' War, sold Joan of Arc to her judges, and behaved as sovereigns in all but name. When Charles the Bold died at Nancy, Louis XI moved fast to seize the duchy itself for the crown.

Pogroms, 1881-1882 (Russia, AD 1881–AD 1.label: Pogroms, 1881-1882
Pogroms, 1881-1882 (Russia, AD 1881–AD 1.prose:
[Russia , AD 1881–AD 1882] Pogroms, 1881-1882. Extracted from heading "Pogroms--Russia". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The assassination of Alexander II unleashed hundreds of anti-Jewish riots across the southern provinces of the Pale of Settlement, with looting, arson, rape and killings that local authorities were slow to stop. The government responded not by protecting Jews but with the May Laws restricting where they could live and work. The violence triggered mass emigration to America and western Europe and gave a powerful impetus to Zionism and Jewish socialist politics.

James II, 1291-1327 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: James II, 1291-1327
James II, 1291-1327 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1291–AD 1327] James II, 1291-1327. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--James II, 1291-1327". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Aragon's king inherited Sicily but traded his claim in a papal bargain that granted him Sardinia and Corsica instead, then had to conquer Sardinia by force against Pisa and Genoa. He extended the crown's Mediterranean commerce, negotiated with the Mongols and the Mamluks, and profited from the suppression of the Templars. At home he strengthened the Corts and confirmed the union of his realms.

Revolution, 1911-1912 (China, AD 1911–AD.label: Revolution, 1911-1912
Revolution, 1911-1912 (China, AD 1911–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1911–AD 1912] Revolution, 1911-1912. Extracted from heading "China--History--Revolution, 1911-1912". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A bomb accident in Wuhan triggered a garrison mutiny, and within weeks province after province declared independence from the Qing. Sun Yat-sen returned to head a republic at Nanjing but handed the presidency to the general Yuan Shikai in exchange for the child emperor's abdication. Two thousand years of imperial rule ended, though the republic quickly fragmented into warlord rivalries, leaving the question of who would reunify China to be settled by later revolutions.

Erik Glipping, 1259-1286 (Denmark, AD 12.label: Erik Glipping, 1259-1286
Erik Glipping, 1259-1286 (Denmark, AD 12.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1259–AD 1286] Erik Glipping, 1259-1286. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Erik Glipping, 1259-1286". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign of near-constant conflict between crown, magnates and the Church, ending in one of the most famous unsolved crimes in Danish history. In 1282 Erik was forced to seal a coronation charter promising to hold a national assembly each year and not to imprison men without trial — the first written limitation on Danish royal power. Four years later he was stabbed to death in a barn at Finderup, and the nobles blamed for it were outlawed.

Shōwa period, 1926-1989 (Japan, AD 1926–.label: Shōwa period, 1926-1989
Shōwa period, 1926-1989 (Japan, AD 1926–.prose:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989] Shōwa period, 1926-1989. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Shōwa period, 1926-1989". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Six decades that contained both catastrophe and reinvention: ultranationalism and assassination in the 1930s, the war in China and the Pacific, atomic bombing and surrender, then occupation reforms, land redistribution and an export boom that made Japan an economic superpower. Visitors often note the contrast between the emperor as sacred war-time figurehead and the mild, marine-biologist figure of his later years. His death in 1989 coincided with the peak of the asset bubble that burst soon after.

Sigismund, 1411-1437 (Germany, AD 1411–A.label: Sigismund, 1411-1437
Sigismund, 1411-1437 (Germany, AD 1411–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1411–AD 1437] Sigismund, 1411-1437. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Sigismund, 1411-1437". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry appears under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Luxembourg emperor summoned the Council of Constance, which ended the Great Schism of rival popes and restored a single papacy. The same council burned Jan Hus despite Sigismund's safe-conduct, igniting the Hussite wars that consumed Bohemia for a generation and repeatedly defeated imperial armies. He was crowned emperor only in 1433, and his death without a male heir passed the imperial title to the Habsburgs for good.

War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Lithuani.label: War of Independence, 1918-1920
War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Lithuani.prose:
[Lithuania, AD 1918–AD 1920] War of Independence, 1918-1920. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--War of Independence, 1918-1920". Added to LCSH in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Days after declaring independence, the new Estonian state had to fight off an invasion by Soviet Russia, and later German Baltic forces in the south, with help from Finnish volunteers and a British naval squadron. The Treaty of Tartu in 1920 saw Soviet Russia renounce all claims to Estonia — the first such recognition it granted anyone. Radical land reform, breaking up the Baltic German estates, followed as a reward to the soldiers who had fought.

Austro-Turkish War, 1661-1664 (Austria,.label: Austro-Turkish War, 1661-1664
Austro-Turkish War, 1661-1664 (Austria,.prose:

An Ottoman army pushed up the Hungarian frontier and into Habsburg territory, taking the fortress of Nové Zámky before Raimondo Montecuccoli halted it at the Raab river near Saint Gotthard. The victory was thrown away at the negotiating table: the Peace of Vasvár confirmed Ottoman gains and left Hungarian nobles feeling betrayed by Vienna. Their resentment fed the Wesselényi conspiracy and decades of Hungarian revolt against Habsburg rule.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Estonia, AD 1905–.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Estonia, AD 1905–.prose:
[Estonia, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987, and on p.25 LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Konrad III, 1138-1152 (Germany, AD 1138–.label: Konrad III, 1138-1152
Konrad III, 1138-1152 (Germany, AD 1138–.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1138–AD 1152] Konrad III, 1138-1152. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. The first Hohenstaufen to rule Germany, elected against Welf opposition and never crowned emperor in Rome. His feud with Henry the Proud and the Welf dynasty hardened into the Guelph–Ghibelline division that split German and Italian politics for generations. He led the German army on the disastrous Second Crusade, and on his death the crown passed to his far abler nephew, Frederick Barbarossa.

Boniface IX, 1389-1404 (Vatican City, AD.label: Boniface IX, 1389-1404
Boniface IX, 1389-1404 (Vatican City, AD.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1389–AD 1404] Boniface IX, 1389-1404. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Boniface IX, 1389-1404". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruling from Rome while a rival pope claimed the office from Avignon, he devoted his pontificate to shoring up the Roman obedience and rebuilding papal authority over the city and the Papal States, fortifying the Castel Sant'Angelo and reducing the commune to obedience. He financed it by selling offices, indulgences and dispensations on a scale that scandalised contemporaries and gave ammunition to reformers, and his two jubilees drew huge crowds of paying pilgrims.

Post-exilic period, 586 B.C.-210 A.D (Is.label: Post-exilic period, 586 B.C.-210 A.D
Post-exilic period, 586 B.C.-210 A.D (Is.prose:

Jerusalem's temple was destroyed and its elite deported to Babylon; when Persian rule allowed a return, the community that rebuilt the temple was organised around priesthood, law and text rather than kingship. Under successive Persian, Hellenistic and Roman overlords, Judaism took recognisably later form - scripture edited and canonised, synagogues, competing sects - while revolts in AD 66-70 and 132-135 destroyed the second temple and depopulated Judaea. The period closes with rabbinic learning centred in Galilee and the compilation of the Mishnah.

Frederick II, 1740-1786 (Germany, AD 174.label: Frederick II, 1740-1786
Frederick II, 1740-1786 (Germany, AD 174.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1740–AD 1786] Frederick II, 1740-1786. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick II, 1740-1786". Frederick the Great seized Silesia from Austria within months of his accession and spent much of his life defending it, surviving the Seven Years' War against France, Austria and Russia by hard marching, luck and battlefield nerve. He made Prussia a great power, joined the first partition of Poland to link his lands, and governed as an "enlightened" autocrat: religious toleration, legal reform, drained marshes and new farming, alongside a rigid society of nobles and serfs. He wrote French verse, played the flute, corresponded with Voltaire, and made Sanssouci a byword for philosopher-kingship.

Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713 (New York, A.label: Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713
Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713 (New York, A.prose:

The North American front of the War of the Spanish Succession, fought between English colonists and New France with Native allies decisive on both sides. Frontier settlements bore the worst of it: the raid on Deerfield in 1704 left dozens dead and more than a hundred captives marched north to Canada. The peace at Utrecht handed Britain Acadia, Newfoundland and Hudson Bay, setting up the final struggle for the continent.

John III, 1521-1557 (Portugal, AD 1521–A.label: John III, 1521-1557
John III, 1521-1557 (Portugal, AD 1521–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1521–AD 1557] John III, 1521-1557. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John III, 1521-1557". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Portugal's Asian empire reached its widest extent under him, from Hormuz to the Moluccas, while at home the crown sank into debt. He turned seriously to Brazil, dividing it into hereditary captaincies and founding Salvador as its first capital, and he introduced the Inquisition to Portugal in 1536. He also sponsored the Jesuits' missions east, sending Francis Xavier to India and beyond.

Martin I, 1396-1410 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: Martin I, 1396-1410
Martin I, 1396-1410 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1396–AD 1410] Martin I, 1396-1410. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Martin I, 1396-1410". Added to LCSH in 2013, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as Martin the Humane, he ruled Aragon and, after his son's death in Sardinia, Sicily as well, presiding over a Mediterranean empire held together by Catalan shipping and merchant money. He died without a surviving legitimate heir, ending the centuries-old House of Barcelona. The succession crisis was settled by nine arbitrators at the Compromise of Caspe, which handed the crown to a Castilian Trastámara prince and bound Aragon's fate to Castile's.

Bombardment, 1944-1945 (Italy, AD 1944–A.label: Bombardment, 1944-1945
Bombardment, 1944-1945 (Italy, AD 1944–A.prose:

From June 1944 the country was struck by pilotless V-1 flying bombs and then by V-2 rockets, which arrived without warning at supersonic speed and could not be intercepted. They killed thousands, triggered a second mass evacuation from London, and announced the age of the guided missile — the technology and many of the engineers passed straight into the Cold War rocket programmes.

James V, 1513-1542 (Scotland, AD 1513–AD.label: James V, 1513-1542
James V, 1513-1542 (Scotland, AD 1513–AD.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1513–AD 1542] James V, 1513-1542. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--James V, 1513-1542". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned as a baby after his father's death at Flodden, he grew up amid factional struggles before taking power himself. He taxed the church heavily to pay for Renaissance palaces at Stirling and Falkland, founded the College of Justice, and cemented the French alliance through marriage to Madeleine of Valois and then Mary of Guise. His sudden death after the defeat at Solway Moss left the throne to his infant daughter Mary.

Revolution, 1832-1835 (Brazil, AD 1832–A.label: Revolution, 1832-1835
Revolution, 1832-1835 (Brazil, AD 1832–A.prose:
[Alagoas (Brazil), AD 1832–AD 1835] Revolution, 1832-1835. Extracted from heading "Alagoas (Brazil)--History--Revolution, 1832-1835". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In the unstable regency that followed Pedro I's abdication, revolts broke out across the provinces, among them the Cabanada in the backlands of Pernambuco and Alagoas, where poor farmers, Indigenous fighters and runaway slaves took up arms under Vicente Ferreira de Paula demanding the emperor's return. The rebels were worn down by scorched-earth campaigns rather than a single defeat. Such risings convinced elites in Rio that decentralisation was dangerous, and pushed them to strengthen central authority and crown the boy Pedro II early.

Peter III, 1276-1285 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: Peter III, 1276-1285
Peter III, 1276-1285 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1276–AD 1285] Peter III, 1276-1285. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Peter III, 1276-1285". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Married to the heiress of the Hohenstaufen claim to Sicily, he seized the island after the 1282 revolt known as the Sicilian Vespers, taking it from the French Angevins. The move launched a long Mediterranean war, brought papal excommunication and a French crusade against Aragon, and committed the crown to overseas empire. Aragon's naval power in the western Mediterranean dates from his reign.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Moldova, AD 1917–.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Moldova, AD 1917–.prose:
[Moldova, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Moldova--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Mehmed V, 1909-1918 (Turkey, AD 1909–AD.label: Mehmed V, 1909-1918
Mehmed V, 1909-1918 (Turkey, AD 1909–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1909–AD 1918] Mehmed V, 1909-1918. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mehmed V, 1909-1918". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Placed on the throne by the Young Turks after his brother's counter-revolution failed, he reigned as a constitutional figurehead while the Committee of Union and Progress governed. Under his nominal rule the empire lost Libya to Italy and nearly all its European territory in the Balkan Wars, then entered the First World War alongside Germany. His proclamation of jihad in 1914 was intended to raise Muslims across the British and French empires; it largely failed.

Middle Ages, 843-1517 (Germany, AD 843–A.label: Middle Ages, 843-1517
Middle Ages, 843-1517 (Germany, AD 843–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 843–AD 1517] Middle Ages, 843-1517. Extracted from heading "Germany--Religious life and customs--Middle Ages, 843-1517". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Beginning with the Treaty of Verdun, which split the Carolingian empire and left East Francia as the nucleus of Germany, this span covers the Ottonian and Salian emperors, the struggle between emperors and popes, and the eastward settlement of German-speaking farmers and townsmen. Free imperial cities and the Hanseatic League made trade a political force, while the empire itself stayed a patchwork of principalities rather than a unified state. It closes with Luther's challenge to the Church.

Asuka period, 592-645 (Japan, AD 592–AD.label: Asuka period, 592-645
Asuka period, 592-645 (Japan, AD 592–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 592–AD 645] Asuka period, 592-645. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Asuka period, 592-645". Added to LCSH in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The court in the Asuka valley absorbed Buddhism, Chinese script and continental statecraft, with Prince Shōtoku credited with the Seventeen Article Constitution and embassies sent to Sui China. Behind the reforms the Soga clan dominated the throne through marriage, until a palace coup in 645 destroyed them and opened the way to the Taika reforms. Gilt-bronze Buddhas and the temple complex at Hōryū-ji survive from these decades.

Severus Alexander, 222-235 (Roman Empire.label: Severus Alexander, 222-235
Severus Alexander, 222-235 (Roman Empire.prose:

A teenage emperor who ruled under the guidance of his mother Julia Mamaea and a council of senators, giving the empire a decade of comparatively restrained government after the scandals of Elagabalus. His reign faced a new and aggressive Persian power under the Sasanians, and an indecisive eastern campaign followed by an attempt to buy off German raiders destroyed his standing with the troops. Soldiers murdered him and his mother in camp near Mainz, ending the dynasty and beginning fifty years of military anarchy.

Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty, 66-428 (Arm.label: Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty, 66-428
Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty, 66-428 (Arm.prose:
[Armenia, AD 66–AD 428] Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty, 66-428. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty, 66-428". A branch of the Parthian royal house ruled Armenia in a compromise brokered with Rome, whose emperor Nero crowned Tiridates in a lavish ceremony. Squeezed between Rome and Persia, the kingdom nonetheless made two decisions of lasting consequence: the adoption of Christianity as the state religion in the early fourth century, and the invention of the Armenian alphabet by Mesrop Mashtots, which launched a national literature. Partitioned between the two empires and finally abolished, the dynasty left Armenia's church and script as its enduring institutions.

Three kingdoms, 220-265 (China, AD 220–A.label: Three kingdoms, 220-265
Three kingdoms, 220-265 (China, AD 220–A.prose:
[China, AD 220–AD 265] Three kingdoms, 220-265. Extracted from heading "China--History--Three kingdoms, 220-265".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Beginning with the formal end of the Han in 220, Wei, Shu and Wu each maintained courts, calendars and armies in a three-way stalemate broken only by Wei's conquest of Shu. In 265 the Sima family took the Wei throne to found the Jin dynasty. The period's generals and strategists, from Cao Cao to Zhuge Liang, became models of cunning and loyalty in Chinese storytelling.

Leo I, 457-474 (Byzantine Empire, AD 457.label: Leo I, 457-474
Leo I, 457-474 (Byzantine Empire, AD 457.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 457–AD 474] Leo I, 457-474. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Leo I, 457-474". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Thracian soldier raised to the purple by the Alan general Aspar, Leo eventually turned on his patron and had him killed, breaking the grip of Germanic and Alan commanders on the eastern army by recruiting Isaurian highlanders instead. He was the first emperor known to have been crowned by the patriarch of Constantinople, a precedent with long consequences. His enormous naval expedition against the Vandals in Africa in 468 ended in disaster and drained the treasury, while the western empire slid toward its final collapse.

Spanish rule, 1535-1714 (Lombardy, AD 15.label: Spanish rule, 1535-1714
Spanish rule, 1535-1714 (Lombardy, AD 15.prose:
[Lombardy, AD 1535–AD 1714] Spanish rule, 1535-1714. Extracted from heading "Lombardy (Italy)--History--Spanish rule, 1535-1714". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.73 of LCSH 1987, and p.58 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the last Sforza duke died without heirs, Milan passed to Charles V and then to the Spanish branch of the Habsburgs, making the duchy the pivot of Spain's military road linking Italy to the Netherlands. Milanese wealth in arms, silk and finance paid for distant wars, while plague and heavy taxation drained the countryside. Austria took the duchy in the War of the Spanish Succession, opening a new era of reform.

Song-Yuan dynasties, 960-1368 (China, AD.label: Song-Yuan dynasties, 960-1368
Song-Yuan dynasties, 960-1368 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 1368] Song-Yuan dynasties, 960-1368. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Four centuries covering China's commercial and technological flowering under the Song and its absorption into the Mongol world empire under the Yuan. Printing, paper currency, porcelain export and gunpowder date from the earlier half; the later brought overland caravan routes reopened across Eurasia, foreign administrators, Marco Polo's Cathay, and drama and vernacular literature flourishing while scholars were shut out of office. The period ends with rebellion, plague and the Ming restoration.

Soviet occupation, 1940-1941 (Estonia, A.label: Soviet occupation, 1940-1941
Soviet occupation, 1940-1941 (Estonia, A.prose:
[Estonia, AD 1940–AD 1941] Soviet occupation, 1940-1941. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--Soviet occupation, 1940-1941". Added to LCSH 2004; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under ultimatum, the country admitted Soviet troops, staged a rigged election and was incorporated into the USSR. Property was nationalised, the officer corps and political class arrested, and some 15,000 people deported eastward in a single June night in 1941. The German advance swept the Soviets out within days, leaving a legacy of trauma that fed both collaboration and later resistance.

American intervention, 1994-1995 (Haiti,.label: American intervention, 1994-1995
American intervention, 1994-1995 (Haiti,.prose:
[Haiti, AD 1994–AD 1995] American intervention, 1994-1995. Extracted from heading "Haiti--History--American intervention, 1994-1995". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Operation Uphold Democracy put some 20,000 US troops ashore to reverse the 1991 coup and restore the elected president Jean-Bertrand Aristide. An invasion was called off at the last hour when a delegation led by Jimmy Carter persuaded the junta to step down, so the landing was unopposed. A UN mission took over in 1995, and the Haitian army was disbanded.

XYZ Affair, 1797-1798 (United States, AD.label: XYZ Affair, 1797-1798
XYZ Affair, 1797-1798 (United States, AD.prose:
[United States, AD 1797–AD 1798] XYZ Affair, 1797-1798. Extracted from heading "XYZ Affair, 1797-1798". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

American envoys sent to calm a quarrel with revolutionary France were met by intermediaries - anonymised in the published dispatches as X, Y and Z - who demanded a bribe and a loan before talks could begin. Publication of the papers enraged the American public, produced the slogan of millions for defence but not one cent for tribute, and pushed the country into the undeclared naval Quasi-War. It also let the Federalists build a navy and push through the Alien and Sedition Acts, deepening the split with Jefferson's Republicans.

Latin Kingdom, 1099-1244 (Israel, AD 109.label: Latin Kingdom, 1099-1244
Latin Kingdom, 1099-1244 (Israel, AD 109.prose:
[Jerusalem, AD 1099–AD 1244] Latin Kingdom, 1099-1244. Spatial coverage: Israel, State of Palestine. Extracted from heading "Jerusalem--History--Latin Kingdom, 1099-1244". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The First Crusade's capture of Jerusalem created a Frankish state ruled by a transplanted French-speaking aristocracy over a mostly Muslim, Jewish and Eastern Christian population. Castles, churches and fortified towns went up along the coast and the interior, and Italian merchant colonies in the ports linked Europe to eastern trade. Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 broke its power; Jerusalem itself was lost, briefly regained by treaty, and finally taken in 1244.

Henry II, 1369-1379 (Castile and León, A.label: Henry II, 1369-1379
Henry II, 1369-1379 (Castile and León, A.prose:
[Castile, AD 1369–AD 1379] Henry II, 1369-1379. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Henry II, 1369-1379". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1998.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He won the throne by killing his half-brother Peter the Cruel in a tent at Montiel, ending a civil war that had drawn in English and French armies from the Hundred Years' War. To secure the loyalty of the nobles who had backed him he distributed enormous grants of land and revenue, the mercedes enriquinas, creating a new high aristocracy that would dominate Castile for generations. His Trastámara dynasty went on to rule Castile, Aragon and ultimately Spain.

Medieval period, 987-1515 (France, AD 98.label: Medieval period, 987-1515
Medieval period, 987-1515 (France, AD 98.prose:
[France, AD 987–AD 1515] Medieval period, 987-1515. Extracted from heading "France--History--Medieval period, 987-1515". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.28 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hugh Capet's election began a dynasty that turned a king with little more than the Île-de-France into the ruler of a consolidated kingdom, absorbing Normandy, Languedoc after the Albigensian Crusade, and eventually Burgundy's lands. These centuries produced Gothic architecture and the cathedral schools that became the University of Paris, the crusading movement, the Black Death, and the Hundred Years' War with its final French recovery under Joan of Arc's inspiration. By its close the monarchy had a standing army, permanent taxation and a court turning towards Italy and the Renaissance.

Uprising, 1992-1993 (Abkhazia, AD 1992–A.label: Uprising, 1992-1993
Uprising, 1992-1993 (Abkhazia, AD 1992–A.prose:
[Abkhazia, AD 1992–AD 1993] Uprising, 1992-1993. Spatial coverage: Abkhazia, Georgia (country). Extracted from heading "Abkhazia (Georgia)--History--Uprising, 1992-1993". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

War broke out when Georgian troops entered Abkhazia and Abkhaz forces, aided by North Caucasian volunteers and Russian military backing, drove them out. Sukhumi fell in 1993 and almost the entire ethnic Georgian population, some 200,000 people, was expelled. Abkhazia has functioned as a de facto separate state ever since, one of the frozen conflicts that has shaped Georgian politics and Russian leverage in the Caucasus.

Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066 (England, A.label: Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066
Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066 (England, A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 449–AD 1066] Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066". Added to LCSH in 1986. The starting date comes from Bede, who dated the arrival of Hengist and Horsa to 449 and cast it as the founding moment of the English people — a tidy story for what was in fact a long, uneven process of migration, assimilation and shifting identity. What followed was the emergence of English kingdoms and the English language, conversion to Christianity, a written law code tradition, and the creation of one of Europe's most efficiently governed kingdoms. It ended at Hastings, when the crown passed to a Norman duke.

Stanislaus II Augustus, 1764-1795 (Polan.label: Stanislaus II Augustus, 1764-1795
Stanislaus II Augustus, 1764-1795 (Polan.prose:
[Poland , AD 1764–AD 1795] Stanislaus II Augustus, 1764-1795. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Stanislaus II Augustus, 1764-1795". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last king of Poland, elected with Russian backing but a serious patron of the arts and a genuine reformer. His reign produced the National Education Commission and the Constitution of 3 May 1791, Europe's first modern codified constitution — and provoked the neighbouring powers into the partitions that erased Poland from the map. He abdicated in 1795 and died a pensioner in St Petersburg.

Canute, 1017-1035 (England, AD 1017–AD 1.label: Canute, 1017-1035
Canute, 1017-1035 (England, AD 1017–AD 1.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1017–AD 1035] Canute, 1017-1035. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Canute, 1017-1035". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cnut, a Danish conqueror, took the English throne after years of Viking warfare and then ruled it not as a raider but as a Christian king, upholding English law, endowing churches and issuing his own codes. England became the wealthiest part of a North Sea empire that also included Denmark and Norway. The union collapsed among his sons within seven years of his death, reopening the succession crisis that led to 1066.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Indiana, AD 1861–A.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Indiana, AD 1861–A.prose:
[Indiana, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Indiana--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.57 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. The monarchy returned after a decade of republican rule, and with it the theatres, the royal court and a taste for pleasure that earned the king his reputation. His reign saw the Great Plague, the Fire of London and Wren's rebuilding, the chartering of the Royal Society, and war with the Dutch. Fights over his Catholic brother's right to succeed produced the Exclusion Crisis and the first outlines of Whig and Tory parties; he ended his reign ruling without Parliament, and was received into the Catholic Church on his deathbed.

Two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno and Hatta declared Indonesian independence, and the returning Dutch found a republic already governing much of Java and Sumatra. Four years of guerrilla fighting, negotiated truces and Dutch "police actions" followed, alongside internal struggles including the crushing of a communist rising at Madiun. International pressure, especially from the United States, forced the Netherlands to transfer sovereignty at the end of 1949.

The king who transformed the French monarchy, seizing Normandy, Anjou and Maine from King John and crushing an imperial-English coalition at Bouvines in 1214. He paved and walled Paris, built the Louvre as a fortress, and replaced feudal improvisation with salaried officials and written records. France emerged as the strongest kingdom in western Europe.

Ne Win's coup replaced parliamentary government with a soldiers' council pursuing the "Burmese Way to Socialism": banks, trade and industry nationalised, foreigners expelled, the country closed to the outside world. One of Asia's richest rice exporters became a UN-designated least developed country while ethnic insurgencies burned on in the borderlands. Economic collapse and the demonetisation of banknotes triggered the 1988 uprising that ended the system, though the army kept power.

He inherited a realm at war with revolutionary France, lost repeatedly to Napoleon, and in 1804 invented a new title — Emperor of Austria — so that his dynasty would keep an imperial crown when the Holy Roman Empire was abolished two years later. He even married his daughter Marie Louise to Napoleon, then helped destroy him. After 1815 his chancellor Metternich made Vienna the headquarters of conservative Europe, policing censorship, secret police and the suppression of nationalist stirrings.

Alexander crossed into Asia and broke the Achaemenid empire in three battles — Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela — before taking Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, whose palace was burned. Darius III fled and was murdered by his own satrap, ending the dynasty that had ruled from the Indus to the Aegean. Alexander pressed on through Bactria to India, and the Iranian plateau passed to Greek and Macedonian rulers for the next two centuries.

Toba War, 1878-1907 (Indonesia, AD 1878–.label: Toba War, 1878-1907
Toba War, 1878-1907 (Indonesia, AD 1878–.prose:

Dutch forces pushed into the Batak highlands around Lake Toba, meeting decades of resistance led by the priest-king Sisingamangaraja XII, who was finally hunted down and killed in 1907. Conquest went hand in hand with German and Dutch missionary work, and the Toba Batak became one of the most thoroughly Christianised peoples of Indonesia. The war completed the extension of colonial rule over the Sumatran interior and remade Batak society, land tenure and religion.

Bombardment, 1940-1945 (London, AD 1940–.label: Bombardment, 1940-1945

British night raids and American daylight raids grew into a round-the-clock campaign that destroyed the centres of Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and dozens of other cities, killed several hundred thousand civilians and made millions homeless. It absorbed a vast share of German industry and manpower in air defence, and it left a moral argument about area bombing that has never been settled.

Civil War, 1990-1993 (Rwanda, AD 1990–AD.label: Civil War, 1990-1993

The Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed by descendants of Tutsi exiled since 1959, invaded from Uganda and fought the Habyarimana government to a stalemate. France backed the government while extremist militias and hate radio prepared the population for mass violence. The Arusha Accords of 1993 set out power-sharing, but the assassination of the president in April 1994 unleashed genocide instead.
