The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

The Jagiellonian king's reign is remembered less for its wars than for the Piotrków statutes of 1496, which tied peasants to the soil and handed the szlachta commercial privileges — a legal foundation of Poland's manorial serfdom. His 1497 expedition into Moldavia ended in disaster in the Bukovina forests, a defeat proverbially blamed for the death of the nobility. Meanwhile Lithuania was ruled separately by his brother Alexander, loosening the dynastic union.

Uprising of 1848-1849 (Hungary, AD 1848–.label: Uprising of 1848-1849
Uprising of 1848-1849 (Hungary, AD 1848–.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1848–AD 1849] Uprising of 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Uprising of 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The March revolution won Hungary its own responsible ministry, an end to serfdom and freedom of the press, but Habsburg attempts to reverse the gains led to open war and a declaration of independence under Lajos Kossuth. Honved armies held out through the winter and won a spring campaign, until Emperor Franz Joseph called in a Russian army of some 200,000 men. Surrender at Vilagos was followed by executions and a decade of centralised rule, yet the demands of 1848 shaped the compromise that created Austria-Hungary in 1867.

Classical period, 1500-1700 (Spain, AD 1.label: Classical period, 1500-1700
Classical period, 1500-1700 (Spain, AD 1.prose:

Habsburg rule turned the newly unified kingdoms into the hub of the first global empire, funded by silver shipped from Potosí and Mexico through Seville. That wealth paid for wars in the Netherlands, Italy and against the Ottomans, and for the writers and painters of the Golden Age, from Cervantes to Velázquez. By the end of the period, inflation, plague, debt defaults and the loss of Portugal and the northern Netherlands had drained the treasury and moved economic power north.

A famously austere and ferocious general who seized the throne and turned Byzantium onto the offensive, retaking Crete from Arab corsairs, then Cilicia, Cyprus and finally Antioch. He taxed the church and the cities hard to pay for the army and was loathed in Constantinople for it. His wife Theophano conspired with his nephew John Tzimiskes to murder him in his bedchamber.

A millenarian uprising in the poor, recently settled mountain borderlands of Hubei, Shaanxi and Sichuan, led by sectarians who awaited the coming of the Maitreya Buddha. Eight years of guerrilla warfare drained perhaps 100 million taels from the treasury and exposed the Manchu banner armies as ineffective, so the Qing came to rely on locally raised militias. The rebellion is usually taken as the point at which Qing power visibly began to slide, decades before the Opium Wars.

Father Hidalgo's call to arms in the parish of Dolores turned into a mass rising of Indians and mestizos, continued after his execution by Morelos and then, in guerrilla form, by Guerrero. The war ended not with an insurgent victory but with a deal: the royalist commander Iturbide switched sides, offering independence, Catholicism and equality between Spaniards and Mexicans. He crowned himself emperor, a regime that lasted barely a year before the republic replaced it.

Elected king in infancy, he held Sweden and Norway together in a personal union and bought Scania from a bankrupt Denmark. He gave Sweden its first realm-wide law code, replacing the patchwork of provincial laws, but debt, the Black Death and the loss of Scania turned the nobility against him; he was deposed in favour of Albert of Mecklenburg. His reign is a study in how fragile late medieval Scandinavian kingship was without aristocratic consent.

Mussolini's troops landed in April 1939 and put the Italian crown on the Albanian throne, ruling through a puppet government and using the country as a springboard for the failed invasion of Greece. Italy enlarged Albania with Kosovo and parts of Macedonia and Montenegro in 1941; when Italy capitulated in 1943 German forces took over. Resistance was dominated by Enver Hoxha's communist partisans, who took power at liberation and held it for the next forty-five years.

Persian and Greek Rule, 429-640 (Armenia.prose:

With the Arsacid monarchy abolished, Armenia was carved up between Sasanian Persia, which governed the larger eastern share through appointed marzpans, and the Byzantine empire in the west. Persian attempts to impose Zoroastrianism provoked the revolt of Vardan Mamikonian and the battle of Avarayr in 451; though defeated in the field, the Armenians won the right to keep their Christian faith, and the newly invented alphabet fuelled an outpouring of theology and history in Armenian. Nakharar noble houses ran the country between the two empires until Arab armies swept in.

Joseph II, 1780-1790 (Austria, AD 1780–A.label: Joseph II, 1780-1790
Joseph II, 1780-1790 (Austria, AD 1780–A.prose:
[Austria, AD 1780–AD 1790] Joseph II, 1780-1790. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Joseph II, 1780-1790". Appears on p. 6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p. 7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The most impatient of the enlightened despots issued some six thousand decrees in ten years: serfdom abolished, religious toleration extended to Protestants and Jews, contemplative monasteries dissolved, censorship relaxed, torture ended, and German imposed as the language of administration everywhere. The pace and the disregard for local privilege provoked open revolt in the Austrian Netherlands and near-rebellion in Hungary, and he died revoking much of his own work - a warning about reform from above that Europe noted just as the French Revolution began.

Messina rose against Spanish viceregal rule and taxation and invited in Louis XIV, who sent fleets and troops that fought Spanish and Dutch squadrons in the Sicilian channel. When France withdrew in 1678, the city was left to Spanish reprisals: its privileges were abolished, its senate dissolved, and its port trade ruined. Messina's commercial primacy in Sicily never recovered.

British India and the expanding Konbaung kingdom collided over the frontier states of Assam and Manipur, and the resulting campaign up the Irrawaddy proved the longest and costliest war British India had yet fought, killing far more troops through disease than combat. The Treaty of Yandabo stripped Burma of Arakan, Tenasserim, Assam and Manipur and imposed a crushing indemnity. It was the first of three wars that ended with the whole kingdom annexed in 1885.

Saladin, 1171-1193 (Egypt, AD 1171–AD 11.label: Saladin, 1171-1193

Salah al-Din, a Kurdish officer in Nur al-Din's service, ended two centuries of Ismaili Fatimid rule in Egypt and restored the country to Sunni allegiance, founding the Ayyubid dynasty. He united Egypt and Syria, crushed the crusader army at Hattin in 1187 and took Jerusalem, provoking the Third Crusade and his long duel with Richard the Lionheart. He fortified Cairo with the Citadel and a new wall, and his reputation for chivalry made him a legend in Europe as well as the Islamic world.

Japanese troops swept down the Malay peninsula and took Singapore in February 1942, the greatest military humiliation Britain ever suffered in Asia. Occupation brought the Sook Ching massacres of Chinese civilians, food shortages and inflation, while a largely Chinese communist guerrilla force fought back from the jungle. The shattering of British invincibility, and the sharpening of ethnic divisions under Japanese rule, shaped the independence struggle and the Emergency that followed.

Elected king of Germany in a disputed double election, Louis the Bavarian defeated his Habsburg rival in battle and then spent decades locked in conflict with the popes at Avignon, who refused to recognise him and placed his lands under interdict. He had himself crowned emperor in Rome by the citizens rather than the pope, a deliberate break with tradition. The polemicists he sheltered laid out early arguments for the separation of secular and church power.

Louis VII, 1137-1180 (France, AD 1137–AD.prose:

His marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine promised to double the royal lands, but the Second Crusade soured the relationship and the annulment of 1152 let her marry Henry Plantagenet, who soon ruled England and half of France. Louis spent the rest of his reign checking Angevin power by supporting Henry's rebellious sons, with limited success. He founded the reputation of the French crown as protector of the Church and fathered, late in life, the heir who would finally break the Angevin empire.

Henry I, 919-936 (Germany, AD 919–AD 936.label: Henry I, 919-936

The Saxon duke known as the Fowler was elected king of the East Franks after the Carolingian line there failed, and he governed by bargaining with the other dukes rather than commanding them. He bought a nine-year truce from the Magyars and used it to build fortified strongpoints and train heavy cavalry, then crushed them at Riade. By naming his son Otto sole successor he founded the Ottonian dynasty that would revive the imperial title in the West.

English colony, 1763-1784 (Florida, AD 1.label: English colony, 1763-1784
English colony, 1763-1784 (Florida, AD 1.prose:
[Florida , AD 1763–AD 1784] English colony, 1763-1784. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--English colony, 1763-1784". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.35 of LCSH 1987, and p.27 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain held Florida for two decades, splitting it into East and West and encouraging plantation settlement with land grants around St Augustine and along the Gulf. It became a loyalist refuge during the American Revolution, receiving thousands of exiles from Georgia and the Carolinas, until Spain retook Pensacola and regained the province by treaty. Almost the entire British population then evacuated, leaving little behind but surveys, roads and a brief boom in indigo.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Arezzo, AD 1943–.prose:

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

Boleslaus I, 992-1025 (Poland, AD 992–AD.label: Boleslaus I, 992-1025

Bolesław the Brave turned his father's newly Christian duchy into a European power, fighting long wars against the German emperors and briefly seizing Kiev. His meeting with Otto III at Gniezno in 1000 won Poland its own archbishopric and cut its dependence on German churchmen. Crowned king shortly before his death, he set the precedent that Poland was a kingdom, not a frontier province of the Empire.

He took power just as an vast Arab army and fleet closed on Constantinople, and the city's survival of the year-long siege of 717-718 - helped by Greek fire and a brutal winter - halted the Umayyad advance into Europe. He reorganised the empire's law in the compact Ecloga and reshaped provincial administration, then around 726 began restricting religious images, opening the iconoclast controversy that split Byzantine society and soured relations with Rome for over a century.

[Castile, AD 1284–AD 1295] Sancho IV, 1284-1295. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Sancho IV, 1284-1295". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sancho IV came to the throne by rebelling against his own father, Alfonso X, and by pushing aside his nephews, the Infantes de la Cerda, whose claim was arguably better. The shadow over his title shaped everything that followed: a marriage the papacy refused to recognise, constant baronial intrigue, and reliance on his formidable queen, María de Molina. His capture of Tarifa in 1292 gave Castile a foothold controlling the Strait of Gibraltar.

John, 1199-1216 (England, AD 1199–AD 121.label: John, 1199-1216
John, 1199-1216 (England, AD 1199–AD 121.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1199–AD 1216] John, 1199-1216. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--John, 1199-1216". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He lost Normandy, Anjou and most of the Angevin lands in France to Philip Augustus, then taxed England ferociously to fund a failed attempt to win them back. A quarrel with Pope Innocent III put the kingdom under interdict for six years until John surrendered his realm as a papal fief. Baronial fury at his exactions and arbitrary justice forced him to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215 — a document he immediately repudiated, plunging England into civil war and a French invasion that only his death resolved.

Flavians, 69-96 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD.label: Flavians, 69-96
Flavians, 69-96 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 96] Flavians, 69-96. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Flavians, 69-96". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three emperors - a father and two sons - who replaced the extinct Julio-Claudian line and rebuilt a state shattered by the Year of the Four Emperors. They expanded citizenship in the provinces, professionalised the bureaucracy, and left the Colosseum, the Arch of Titus and a rebuilt Rome as monuments. Their reigns also produced the destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum, which froze a Roman town for archaeologists.

Peninsular War, 1807-1814 (Spain, AD 180.label: Peninsular War, 1807-1814
Peninsular War, 1807-1814 (Spain, AD 180.prose:
[Spain, AD 1807–AD 1814] Peninsular War, 1807-1814. Extracted from heading "Peninsular War, 1807-1814". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's attempt to seize the Iberian thrones set off a popular uprising, a brutal guerrilla campaign and a long Anglo-Portuguese-Spanish counteroffensive that bled the French army for six years. The word 'guerrilla' entered European languages here, and Goya's Disasters of War recorded the atrocities. Occupation also cut Spain off from its American colonies, hastening their independence, while the Cortes of Cádiz produced Spain's first liberal constitution in 1812.

Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Charlest.label: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775
Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Charlest.prose:
[Charleston (S.C.), AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "Charleston (S.C.)--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.23 of LCSH 1987, and p.20 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Afghan Wars, 1838-1919 (India, AD 1838–A.label: Afghan Wars, 1838-1919
Afghan Wars, 1838-1919 (India, AD 1838–A.prose:
[India, AD 1838–AD 1919] Afghan Wars, 1838-1919. Extracted from heading "Afghan Wars". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three wars fought by British India against Afghanistan, driven by fear of Russian expansion towards the northwest frontier. The first ended in the annihilation of a retreating British army in the passes east of Kabul; the second imposed British control of Afghan foreign policy; the third, in 1919, ended it. The conflicts fixed the Durand Line as the border and taught successive empires how difficult Afghanistan is to hold.

Bombardment, 1942-1943 (Saint-Nazaire, A.label: Bombardment, 1942-1943
Bombardment, 1942-1943 (Saint-Nazaire, A.prose:
[Saint-Nazaire (France), AD 1942–AD 1943] Bombardment, 1942-1943. Extracted from heading "Saint-Nazaire (France)--History--Bombardment, 1942-1943". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The huge concrete U-boat pens built here made the port a prime Allied target, and repeated raids flattened almost the entire town while leaving the bunkers essentially intact — a stark lesson in the limits of bombing against hardened structures. The same docks had already drawn the celebrated commando raid of March 1942, which rammed an explosive-packed destroyer into the dry gate to deny it to the battleship Tirpitz.

Gustav VI Adolf, 1950-1973 (Sweden, AD 1.label: Gustav VI Adolf, 1950-1973
Gustav VI Adolf, 1950-1973 (Sweden, AD 1.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1950–AD 1973] Gustav VI Adolf, 1950-1973. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav VI Adolf, 1950-1973". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A scholar-king and practising archaeologist who dug in Italy, Greece and China, built major collections of Chinese art, and was respected enough to sit on academic bodies in his own right. His reign coincided with the height of the Swedish welfare state and with the debate that stripped the monarchy of political power in the 1974 constitution, passed just after his death. Public affection for him is often credited with saving the institution itself.

Edward IV, 1461-1483 (England, AD 1461–A.label: Edward IV, 1461-1483
Edward IV, 1461-1483 (England, AD 1461–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1461–AD 1483] Edward IV, 1461-1483. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward IV, 1461-1483". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward seized the throne for the House of York in the middle of the Wars of the Roses, lost it briefly to a Lancastrian revival, then won it back at Barnet and Tewkesbury. His later years brought relative stability, solvent royal finances and a court that patronised luxury goods and the new printing press of William Caxton. His sudden death left a boy heir and triggered the crisis that put Richard III on the throne.

Isabella II, 1833-1868 (Spain, AD 1833–A.label: Isabella II, 1833-1868
Isabella II, 1833-1868 (Spain, AD 1833–A.prose:
[Spain, AD 1833–AD 1868] Isabella II, 1833-1868. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Isabella II, 1833-1868". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign that opened with a disputed succession: her uncle Carlos's claim triggered the first of the Carlist civil wars, and the young queen's throne depended on the liberals who fought for her. Under a series of constitutions and generals-turned-politicians, Spain dissolved monasteries, sold off church and common lands, built its first railways and centralised the state, but governments rose and fell by coup. Scandal and misrule finally brought the Glorious Revolution of 1868, which drove her into exile in Paris and left Spain searching for a replacement monarch — a search that helped ignite the Franco-Prussian War.

Philip of Swabia, 1198-1208 (Germany, AD.label: Philip of Swabia, 1198-1208
Philip of Swabia, 1198-1208 (Germany, AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1198–AD 1208] Philip of Swabia, 1198-1208. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Philip of Swabia, 1198-1208". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Hohenstaufen claimant locked in a decade-long civil war with the Welf rival Otto IV, with Pope Innocent III arbitrating between them. The contest let princes and towns extract concessions and weakened royal authority in Germany. Philip's murder in Bamberg in 1208 was the first assassination of a German king.

Franconian House, 1024-1125 (Germany, AD.label: Franconian House, 1024-1125
Franconian House, 1024-1125 (Germany, AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1024–AD 1125] Franconian House, 1024-1125. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Franconian House, 1024-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Also called the Salians, these four emperors pushed imperial authority to its height and then broke it against the reformed papacy. Henry IV's clash with Gregory VII over who appointed bishops produced the humiliation at Canossa in 1077 and decades of civil war, settled only by the Concordat of Worms in 1122. Their vast cathedral at Speyer, built as a dynastic burial church, remains the largest Romanesque building in Europe.

World War, 1939-1945 (Earth, AD 1939–AD.label: World War, 1939-1945
World War, 1939-1945 (Earth, AD 1939–AD.prose:
[World, AD 1939–AD 1945] World War, 1939-1945. Extracted from heading "World War, 1939-1945". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The deadliest conflict in human history, fought across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Pacific, killing perhaps sixty million people, most of them civilians. It encompassed the Holocaust, the firebombing of cities, and the first use of atomic weapons. Its end left Europe divided between American and Soviet spheres, accelerated the collapse of European colonial empires, and produced the United Nations and the legal concept of crimes against humanity.

Filibuster War, 1855-1860 (Nicaragua, AD.label: Filibuster War, 1855-1860
Filibuster War, 1855-1860 (Nicaragua, AD.prose:
[Nicaragua, AD 1855–AD 1860] Filibuster War, 1855-1860. Extracted from heading "Nicaragua--History--Filibuster War, 1855-1860". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.84 of LCSH 1987, and p.69 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The American adventurer William Walker sailed into Nicaragua's civil war with a few dozen armed men, made himself commander and then president, ruled in English, and re-legalised slavery with an eye to annexation by the southern United States. An alliance of Central American states, backed by Cornelius Vanderbilt, who wanted his transit route back, drove him out in 1857; he was shot in Honduras after a final attempt in 1860. The episode is remembered across Central America as a founding national struggle and as a warning about North American expansion.

War of 1894-1895 (Mozambique, AD 1894–AD.label: War of 1894-1895
War of 1894-1895 (Mozambique, AD 1894–AD.prose:
[Mozambique, AD 1894–AD 1895] War of 1894-1895. Extracted from heading "Mozambique--History--War of 1894-1895". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Portugal, needing to make its paper claims real after the Berlin Conference, moved against the Gaza kingdom of Gungunhana, the last great independent power in southern Mozambique. Portuguese columns won at Coolela and Mouzinho de Albuquerque seized the king at Chaimite; Gungunhana was paraded through Lisbon and exiled to the Azores. Effective colonial rule, forced labour and chartered-company administration followed across the territory.

Azuchi-Momoyama period, 1568-1603 (Japan.label: Azuchi-Momoyama period, 1568-1603
Azuchi-Momoyama period, 1568-1603 (Japan.prose:
[Japan, AD 1568–AD 1603] Azuchi-Momoyama period, 1568-1603. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Azuchi-Momoyama period, 1568-1603". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Beginning with Nobunaga's march into Kyoto, three decades of ruthless campaigning ended a century of civil war and produced a unified Japan under Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Castles became monumental symbols of power, cities grew around them, and merchants, missionaries and European guns reshaped daily life. Hideyoshi's death, the failed Korean invasions and the battle of Sekigahara handed the country to Tokugawa Ieyasu.

Earlier Nine Years' War, 1051-1062 (Japa.label: Earlier Nine Years' War, 1051-1062
Earlier Nine Years' War, 1051-1062 (Japa.prose:
[Japan, AD 1051–AD 1062] Earlier Nine Years' War, 1051-1062. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Earlier Nine Years' War, 1051-1062". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long campaign in the far north of Honshu, where the court sent Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and his son Yoshiie to break the power of the Abe family in Mutsu. Victory took twelve years despite the name and depended heavily on switching alliances among northern warlords. It made the Minamoto the leading warrior house of eastern Japan and supplied generations of storytellers with heroic material.

Xianfeng, 1850-1861 (China, AD 1850–AD 1.label: Xianfeng, 1850-1861
Xianfeng, 1850-1861 (China, AD 1850–AD 1.prose:
[China, AD 1850–AD 1861] Xianfeng, 1850-1861. Extracted from heading "China--History--Xianfeng, 1850-1861". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Hsien feng, 1850-1861" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987, and p.16 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign consumed by crisis: the Taiping rebels seized the Yangzi valley and held Nanjing, while Britain and France fought the Second Opium War, occupied Beijing and burned the Summer Palace. The emperor fled to Rehe and died there, and the treaties signed in his name opened the interior to foreign trade, missionaries and diplomats. His death left a small child on the throne and brought the Empress Dowager Cixi to power.

Min kingdom, 909-945 (China, AD 909–AD 9.label: Min kingdom, 909-945
Min kingdom, 909-945 (China, AD 909–AD 9.prose:
[China, AD 909–AD 945] Min kingdom, 909-945. Extracted from heading "China--History--Min kingdom, 909-945". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the Ten Kingdoms that broke away as the Tang order collapsed, ruled from Fuzhou by the family of Wang Shenzhi, a warlord who had led migrants south into Fujian. Its rulers courted merchants and monks, dredging harbours and encouraging the maritime trade and tea cultivation that would make the Fujian coast wealthy for centuries. Fratricidal violence among Wang's heirs tore the state apart within a generation, and its territory was carved up by the Southern Tang and Wuyue.

Matthias, 1612-1619 (Germany, AD 1612–AD.label: Matthias, 1612-1619
Matthias, 1612-1619 (Germany, AD 1612–AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1612–AD 1619] Matthias, 1612-1619. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Matthias, 1612-1619". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.55 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had spent years intriguing against his brother Rudolf II, stripping him of territory before finally succeeding him, and then found himself unable to manage the religious settlement he had helped unsettle. Childless and ageing, he let the hardline Catholic Ferdinand of Styria be imposed on Bohemia, which provoked the Defenestration of Prague in 1618. The Thirty Years' War began in his last months on the throne.

Li Zicheng Rebellion, 1628-1645 (China,.label: Li Zicheng Rebellion, 1628-1645
Li Zicheng Rebellion, 1628-1645 (China,.prose:
[China, AD 1628–AD 1645] Li Zicheng Rebellion, 1628-1645. Extracted from heading "China--History--Li Zicheng Rebellion, 1628-1645". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Li Tzu ch'eng Rebellion, 1628-1645" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Famine, unpaid soldiers and a bankrupt treasury in the northwest fed a peasant uprising that grew into a rebel army under a former postal courier. Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644, prompting the last Ming emperor to hang himself on a hill behind the palace. His triumph lasted weeks: the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who drove Li out and founded the Qing dynasty.

John I, 1379-1390 (Castile and León, AD.label: John I, 1379-1390
John I, 1379-1390 (Castile and León, AD.prose:
[Castile, AD 1379–AD 1390] John I, 1379-1390. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--John I, 1379-1390". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His attempt to claim the Portuguese throne through marriage ended in catastrophe at Aljubarrota in 1385, where the Castilian chivalry was cut down and Portugal's independence secured for centuries. He also fought off an English invasion led by John of Gaunt, buying off the rival claim by marrying his heir to Gaunt's daughter. That heir was given the new title Prince of Asturias, still borne by Spanish crown princes.

Tiberius II, 578-582 (Byzantine Empire,.label: Tiberius II, 578-582
Tiberius II, 578-582 (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 578–AD 582] Tiberius II, 578-582. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Tiberius II, 578-582". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Tiberius abandoned his predecessor's ferocious tax collecting and unpopular religious persecutions, spending lavishly on the army and remitting taxes — a policy that made him popular and left the treasury empty. His generals won victories against Persia in the east while Avars and Slavs poured across the Danube into the Balkans, a settlement that would permanently change the region's population. On his deathbed he handed the empire to his best general, Maurice.

Meiji period, 1868-1912 (Japan, AD 1868–.label: Meiji period, 1868-1912
Meiji period, 1868-1912 (Japan, AD 1868–.prose:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912] Meiji period, 1868-1912. Source specifies in general note: Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Japanese. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Japan's transformation from a closed feudal society into an industrial nation-state, driven by the slogan 'rich country, strong army'. Class distinctions were abolished, Western dress and calendars adopted at court, and Shinto was reorganised as a state cult; the 1889 constitution created a parliament under a sovereign emperor. The costs fell heavily on rural taxpayers and on the displaced samurai, whose last armed protest was crushed at Satsuma in 1877.

Revolution, 1835-1836 (Texas, AD 1835–AD.label: Revolution, 1835-1836
Revolution, 1835-1836 (Texas, AD 1835–AD.prose:
[Texas, AD 1835–AD 1836] Revolution, 1835-1836. Extracted from heading "Texas--History--Revolution, 1835-1836". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.115 of LCSH 1987, and p.112 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Anglo-American settlers and Tejano allies rebelled against the centralising government of Santa Anna, and after the massacre at the Alamo and Goliad won a stunning victory at San Jacinto, capturing the Mexican president himself. The result was an independent Republic of Texas that Mexico never recognised. Its annexation by the United States in 1845 led directly to the Mexican-American War and the transfer of the entire Southwest, while the new republic's protection of slavery inflamed the American sectional crisis.

Civil War, 1642-1649 (England, AD 1642–A.label: Civil War, 1642-1649
Civil War, 1642-1649 (England, AD 1642–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1642–AD 1649] Civil War, 1642-1649. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Civil War, 1642-1649". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

King and Parliament went to war over control of the army, taxation and the church, splitting families and towns across the kingdom. Parliament's disciplined, well-paid New Model Army won decisively at Naseby, and radical currents in the ranks - Levellers debating manhood suffrage at Putney - pushed the settlement far beyond anything intended in 1642. The trial and public beheading of Charles I in January 1649 was unprecedented: a reigning monarch executed by his own subjects, and England declared a republic.

Zanj Rebellion, 868-883 (Iraq, AD 868–AD.label: Zanj Rebellion, 868-883
Zanj Rebellion, 868-883 (Iraq, AD 868–AD.prose:
[Iraq, AD 868–AD 883] Zanj Rebellion, 868-883. Extracted from heading "Iraq--History--Zanj Rebellion, 868-883". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

East African labourers, worked in gangs to clear salt flats in the marshes of southern Iraq, rose under a leader claiming descent from Ali and held the region for fifteen years. They built a fortified capital, defeated Abbasid armies repeatedly and sacked Basra. Suppressing them cost the caliphate enormously and is often seen as a turning point in its decline, and as one of the largest slave revolts in history.

Hồ dynasty, 1400-1407 (Vietnam, AD 1400–.label: Hồ dynasty, 1400-1407
Hồ dynasty, 1400-1407 (Vietnam, AD 1400–.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1400–AD 1407] Hồ dynasty, 1400-1407. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Hồ dynasty, 1400-1407". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hồ Quý Ly seized the throne from the exhausted Trần, moved the capital to a huge stone-walled citadel in Thanh Hóa, and pushed through radical reforms: paper currency, limits on landholding and slave-owning, examinations in the vernacular script, and a rebuilt army. The measures alienated the old aristocracy, and Ming China used the deposed Trần as a pretext to invade, capturing Hồ Quý Ly in 1407. Two decades of direct Chinese occupation followed, ended only by Lê Lợi's rebellion.

Christian V, 1670-1699 (Denmark, AD 1670.label: Christian V, 1670-1699
Christian V, 1670-1699 (Denmark, AD 1670.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1670–AD 1699] Christian V, 1670-1699. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian V, 1670-1699". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited the new hereditary absolutism and gave it working form, issuing the Norwegian Law of 1687 — a clear, systematic code that governed Norwegians for generations. A new titled nobility of counts and barons was created to bind the elite to the crown, and offices were increasingly filled by professionals rather than magnates. His war against Sweden brought hard fighting on the Norwegian frontier under the popular commander Ulrik Frederik Gyldenløve.

House of Valois, 1328-1589 (France, AD 1.label: House of Valois, 1328-1589
House of Valois, 1328-1589 (France, AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1328–AD 1589] House of Valois, 1328-1589. Extracted from heading "France--History--House of Valois, 1328-1589". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Valois inherited a quarrel over the French succession and spent their first century fighting it, losing at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt before Joan of Arc and gunpowder artillery turned the war and expelled the English. Consolidation followed: Burgundy and Brittany absorbed, a standing army, chateaux on the Loire, and adventurous wars in Italy that imported the Renaissance. The line ended in the Wars of Religion, with Henry III assassinated and the crown passing to the Bourbons.

Dinis, 1279-1325 (Portugal, AD 1279–AD 1.label: Dinis, 1279-1325
Dinis, 1279-1325 (Portugal, AD 1279–AD 1.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1279–AD 1325] Dinis, 1279-1325. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Dinis, 1279-1325". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Denis, 1279-1325" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denis is remembered as the farmer-king: he encouraged land clearance and settlement, planted the pine forest at Leiria to supply timber and hold back the dunes, and hired a Genoese admiral to build a royal navy. He fixed Portugal's border with Castile by the Treaty of Alcañices, made Portuguese rather than Latin the language of the chancery, founded the university that moved to Coimbra, and preserved the Templars' wealth by reconstituting them as the Order of Christ. His long reign gave the kingdom the institutions and coastline it would use to launch overseas expansion.

Brigand War, 1795-1797 (Saint Lucia, AD.label: Brigand War, 1795-1797
Brigand War, 1795-1797 (Saint Lucia, AD.prose:
[Saint Lucia, AD 1795–AD 1797] Brigand War, 1795-1797. Extracted from heading "Saint Lucia--History--Brigand War, 1795-1797". Added to LCSH in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

French revolutionary agents and freed slaves, the 'Brigands', drove the British from most of the island and held it under the tricolour after Paris abolished slavery. Ralph Abercromby's expedition retook the island in 1796, but resistance continued in the forested interior until the surviving fighters were enrolled into a British regiment. The war showed how quickly revolutionary emancipation could turn Caribbean plantation society upside down.

John II, 1350-1364 (France, AD 1350–AD 1.label: John II, 1350-1364
John II, 1350-1364 (France, AD 1350–AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1350–AD 1364] John II, 1350-1364. Extracted from heading "France--History--John II, 1350-1364". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign is defined by catastrophe at Poitiers, where he was captured by the Black Prince and carried off to England, leaving France to the Jacquerie peasant revolt and the reforming Estates General under Étienne Marcel. The Treaty of Brétigny bought his release with vast territorial concessions and a ransom so huge it required a new gold coin, the franc. When a hostage son escaped, he returned voluntarily to captivity in London and died there. His grant of Burgundy to his son Philip the Bold created a rival power that would haunt France for a century.

Hadrian, 117-138 (Roman Empire, AD 117–A.label: Hadrian, 117-138
Hadrian, 117-138 (Roman Empire, AD 117–A.prose:
[Rome, AD 117–AD 138] Hadrian, 117-138. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Hadrian, 117-138". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hadrian broke with his predecessor's expansionism, abandoning Trajan's eastern conquests and fixing the empire's edges with walls, palisades and roads. He spent much of his reign travelling the provinces, inspecting armies and funding building on a huge scale — the rebuilt Pantheon, his sprawling villa at Tivoli, the refounding of Athens as a cultural capital. His philhellenism, his grief for the drowned Antinous, and his brutal crushing of the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judaea all belong to the same complicated reign.

King Philip's War, 1675-1676 (United Sta.label: King Philip's War, 1675-1676
King Philip's War, 1675-1676 (United Sta.prose:
[United States, AD 1675–AD 1676] King Philip's War, 1675-1676. Spatial coverage: New England, United States. Extracted from heading "King Philip's War, 1675-1676". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Metacom, the Wampanoag leader the English called King Philip, led a broad Native coalition against New England colonists whose land hunger and legal encroachments had become intolerable. Proportionally the deadliest war in American history, it burned dozens of towns and killed thousands on both sides. Native defeat broke independent Indigenous power in southern New England, sending survivors into servitude, refuge communities, or flight north.

Rebellion, 1494-1509 (Tuscany, AD 1494–A.label: Rebellion, 1494-1509
Rebellion, 1494-1509 (Tuscany, AD 1494–A.prose:
[Pisa (Italy), AD 1494–AD 1509] Rebellion, 1494-1509. Extracted from heading "Pisa (Italy)--History--Rebellion, 1494-1509". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Charles VIII's French army marched through Tuscany, Pisa threw off nearly a century of Florentine rule and Florence itself expelled the Medici, turning to the republic of Savonarola and later Soderini. Fifteen years of intermittent war over Pisa drained Florentine finances and prompted Machiavelli's experiment with a citizen militia. Florence finally starved Pisa into surrender in 1509, but the Medici returned three years later.

Mieszko II, 1025-1034 (Poland, AD 1025–A.label: Mieszko II, 1025-1034
Mieszko II, 1025-1034 (Poland, AD 1025–A.prose:
[Poland , AD 1025–AD 1034] Mieszko II, 1025-1034. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Mieszko II, 1025-1034". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned after the death of his father Bolesław the Brave, Mieszko II faced invasion by the German emperor and Kievan Rus, rebellion by his brothers, and the loss of the royal title. He was driven into exile, returned only as a duke of a fragmented realm, and died leaving a state that soon collapsed into pagan revolt and Bohemian raids — the low point of the early Piast monarchy.

Ferdinand VII, 1813-1833 (Spain, AD 1813.label: Ferdinand VII, 1813-1833
Ferdinand VII, 1813-1833 (Spain, AD 1813.prose:
[Spain, AD 1813–AD 1833] Ferdinand VII, 1813-1833. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Ferdinand VII, 1813-1833". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Restored after Napoleon's defeat, he tore up the liberal Constitution of 1812 that had been written in his name and ruled as an absolutist, persecuting the liberals who had fought the French. A military revolt forced constitutional rule on him from 1820 to 1823 until a French army reinstalled his authority; meanwhile almost all of mainland Spanish America broke away. His decision to leave the throne to his infant daughter Isabel rather than his brother Carlos triggered the Carlist civil wars that convulsed Spain for the rest of the century.

French Domination, 1768-1794 (Corsica, A.label: French Domination, 1768-1794
French Domination, 1768-1794 (Corsica, A.prose:
[Corsica, AD 1768–AD 1794] French Domination, 1768-1794. Extracted from heading "Corsica--History--French Domination, 1768-1794". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.24 of LCSH 1987, and on p.18 of LCSH 1875. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Genoa sold its rebellious island to France, which crushed Pasquale Paoli's independent Corsican Republic at Ponte Novu the following year and absorbed the island as a province. Paoli's constitution, admired across Enlightenment Europe, was extinguished just months before the birth of Napoleon Bonaparte, who thus entered the world a French subject rather than a Corsican one.

Philip II, 1556-1598 (Spain, AD 1556–AD.label: Philip II, 1556-1598
Philip II, 1556-1598 (Spain, AD 1556–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 1556–AD 1598] Philip II, 1556-1598. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Philip II, 1556-1598". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruler of Spain, the Netherlands, Naples, and an American empire whose silver from Potosí funded endless war and repeated bankruptcies. He fought the Ottomans at Lepanto, annexed Portugal, faced the Dutch Revolt, and lost the Armada of 1588 against England. From the austere Escorial he tried to govern the world's first global empire by paperwork.

Conquest, 1522-1548 (Peru, AD 1522–AD 15.label: Conquest, 1522-1548
Conquest, 1522-1548 (Peru, AD 1522–AD 15.prose:
[Peru, AD 1522–AD 1548] Conquest, 1522-1548. Extracted from heading "Peru--History--Conquest, 1522-1548". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.90 of LCSH 1987, and p.76 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Pizarro's small force arrived as the Inca empire was tearing itself apart in civil war, seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca and ransomed then killed him. Cuzco fell, Manco Inca's great rebellion failed and retreated to Vilcabamba, and the conquerors then turned on each other in a decade of civil wars that killed nearly all of them. Spanish rule was only imposed properly once the crown sent viceroys to break the encomenderos.

Sino-Japanese War, 1894-1895 (Japan, AD.label: Sino-Japanese War, 1894-1895
Sino-Japanese War, 1894-1895 (Japan, AD.prose:
[Japan, Korea, China, AD 1894–AD 1895] Sino-Japanese War, 1894-1895. Spatial coverage: China, Japan. Extracted from heading "Sino-Japanese War, 1894-1895". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2006 and again in 2017. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rivalry over Korea brought Japan's modernised army and navy against the Qing empire, and Japan won decisively on land and at the Yalu. The Treaty of Shimonoseki gave Japan Taiwan, the Pescadores and a crushing indemnity, and ended Chinese suzerainty over Korea. The victory announced Japan as an imperial power, while the Triple Intervention that stripped it of the Liaodong Peninsula fed the resentment that led to war with Russia a decade later.

Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395 (Roman.node: Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395 (Roman Empire, AD 379–AD 395)
Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395 (Roman.label: Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395
Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395 (Roman.prose:
[Rome, AD 379–AD 395] Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Theodosius I, the Great, 379-395". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brought in to rebuild a Roman army shattered by the Goths at Adrianople, he settled them inside the empire as allied troops rather than defeating them - a bargain that changed how Rome dealt with barbarian peoples. He made Nicene Christianity the state religion, closed temples and banned sacrifice, and did public penance to Bishop Ambrose after massacring civilians at Thessalonica, a striking moment of a bishop disciplining an emperor. He was the last man to rule both halves of the empire, which he left divided between his two sons.

Revolution, 1899-1903 (Colombia, AD 1899.label: Revolution, 1899-1903
Revolution, 1899-1903 (Colombia, AD 1899.prose:
[Colombia, AD 1899–AD 1903] Revolution, 1899-1903. Extracted from heading "Colombia--History--Revolution, 1899-1903". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.23 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Thousand Days' War pitted Liberal armies against the Conservative government in a conflict that slid from set-piece battles into ruinous guerrilla warfare, killing perhaps 100,000 people and wrecking the coffee economy. With the country exhausted and the government unable to garrison its northern province, Panama seceded in 1903 with United States naval backing, and the canal was built on American terms. The war's memory shaped Colombian politics for decades.

Erik Menved, 1286-1319 (Denmark, AD 1286.label: Erik Menved, 1286-1319
Erik Menved, 1286-1319 (Denmark, AD 1286.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1286–AD 1319] Erik Menved, 1286-1319. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Erik Menved, 1286-1319". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Erik spent his reign pursuing an expensive ambition to dominate northern Germany, campaigning in Mecklenburg, Pomerania and Brandenburg. The wars were paid for by taxes so heavy that they provoked peasant risings in Jutland and forced him to mortgage great tracts of the kingdom to German counts. He left Denmark so indebted that his successor was briefly driven out and the realm effectively pawned.

Republic, 265-30 B.C (Roman Republic, 26.label: Republic, 265-30 B.C
Republic, 265-30 B.C (Roman Republic, 26.prose:
[Rome, 264 BC–29 BC] Republic, 265-30 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Republic, 265-30 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975.  This must be Middle/Late Republic in conventional chronology. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In this stretch Rome went from dominating Italy to ruling the Mediterranean: three wars with Carthage, the destruction of Corinth and Carthage in the same year, and the absorption of Greece, Spain, Asia Minor, Gaul and Egypt. Slave-worked estates, provincial tax farming and enormous booty transformed Roman society and destabilised its politics, producing the Gracchi, Marius and Sulla, Spartacus, and then the civil wars of Caesar, Pompey and Antony. It ends with Octavian's victory at Actium, after which republican forms survived only as the dress of one-man rule.

Northern War, 1700-1721 (Sweden, AD 1700.label: Northern War, 1700-1721
Northern War, 1700-1721 (Sweden, AD 1700.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1700–AD 1721] Northern War, 1700-1721. Extracted from heading "Northern War, 1700-1721". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A coalition of Denmark, Saxony-Poland and Russia attacked the Swedish empire; the young Charles XII beat them all in turn until his army was destroyed by Peter the Great at Poltava in 1709. The remaining years saw Sweden slowly stripped of its Baltic provinces, Charles killed in Norway in 1718, and the war closed by the Treaty of Nystad. Sweden ceased to be a great power and Russia took its place on the Baltic.

Civil War, 1960-1996 (Guatemala, AD 1960.label: Civil War, 1960-1996
Civil War, 1960-1996 (Guatemala, AD 1960.prose:
[Guatemala, AD 1960–AD 1996] Civil War, 1960-1996. Extracted from heading "Guatemala--History--Civil War, 1960-1996". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A junior officers' revolt grew into a thirty-six-year insurgency against a succession of military governments, fought most brutally in the Maya highlands. Army counter-insurgency campaigns of the early 1980s destroyed hundreds of villages; a later truth commission attributed the great majority of some 200,000 deaths to state forces and found acts of genocide against indigenous communities. UN-brokered peace accords in 1996 ended the fighting but left impunity largely intact.

Dutch Conquest, 1624-1654 (Brazil, AD 16.label: Dutch Conquest, 1624-1654
Dutch Conquest, 1624-1654 (Brazil, AD 16.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1624–AD 1654] Dutch Conquest, 1624-1654. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--Dutch Conquest, 1624-1654". Appears on p.10 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.12 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch West India Company struck at Portugal's Atlantic empire, taking Salvador da Bahia in 1624 only to lose it within a year, then seizing Pernambuco and its sugar mills in 1630. For two decades a Dutch Brazil stretched along the northeastern coast, tied to Company posts in West Africa that supplied enslaved labour. Portuguese and Luso-Brazilian planters revolted in 1645 and, after victories at Guararapes, forced the surrender of Recife.

Sepoy Rebellion, 1857-1858 (India, AD 18.label: Sepoy Rebellion, 1857-1858
Sepoy Rebellion, 1857-1858 (India, AD 18.prose:
[India, AD 1857–AD 1858] Sepoy Rebellion, 1857-1858. Extracted from heading "India--History--Sepoy Rebellion, 1857-1858". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A mutiny among Bengal Army sepoys over greased cartridges detonated a much wider revolt, drawing in dispossessed princes, landholders and townspeople across the north Indian plain. Delhi, Kanpur and Lucknow saw brutal fighting and reprisals on both sides. The aftermath abolished the East India Company and the Mughal throne alike, placing India under direct Crown rule and hardening racial divisions in the colonial state.

Philip IV, 1285-1314 (France, AD 1285–AD.label: Philip IV, 1285-1314
Philip IV, 1285-1314 (France, AD 1285–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1285–AD 1314] Philip IV, 1285-1314. Extracted from heading "France--History--Philip IV, 1285-1314". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An aggressive, legalistic king who taxed the clergy, humiliated Pope Boniface VIII, and helped move the papacy to Avignon. In 1307 he arrested the Knights Templar en masse to seize their wealth, and he summoned the first Estates General to back his policies. His debasement of the coinage earned him lasting hatred and his lawyer-bureaucrats set the pattern for the French state.

War with Spain, 1865-1866 (Chile, AD 186.label: War with Spain, 1865-1866
War with Spain, 1865-1866 (Chile, AD 186.prose:
[Chile, Peru, AD 1865–AD 1866] War with Spain, 1865-1866. Spatial coverage: Chile, Peru. Extracted from heading "Chile--History--War with Spain, 1865-1866". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spain, attempting to reassert itself in its former American colonies, seized Peru's guano-rich Chincha Islands; Chile sided with Peru and found itself at war. A Spanish squadron bombarded the undefended port of Valparaíso, then was repulsed at Callao and withdrew across the Pacific having gained nothing. The war stirred a wave of continental solidarity and pushed Chile to build the modern navy that would serve it in the War of the Pacific.

Song dynasty, 960-1279 (China, AD 960–AD.label: Song dynasty, 960-1279
Song dynasty, 960-1279 (China, AD 960–AD.prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 1279] Song dynasty, 960-1279. Extracted from heading "China--History--Song dynasty, 960-1279". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Sung dynasty, 960-1279" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987,. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Reunification after the fragmentation of the tenth century brought a state run by examination-trained civil officials rather than warrior aristocrats, with deliberate checks on generals' power. Woodblock printing spread books cheaply, seaborne trade linked ports to Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, and gunpowder first appears in military manuals. The court's weakness on land cost it the north in 1127 and eventually the whole empire to Kublai Khan.

Philip III, 1270-1285 (France, AD 1270–A.label: Philip III, 1270-1285
Philip III, 1270-1285 (France, AD 1270–A.prose:
[France, AD 1270–AD 1285] Philip III, 1270-1285. Extracted from heading "France--History--Philip III, 1270-1285". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Succeeding Louis IX, who died on crusade in Tunis, this king expanded royal territory by inheritance and pursued the disastrous Aragonese Crusade, dying on the retreat. His reign kept Capetian administration growing while French ambitions in the Mediterranean overreached. He is chiefly remembered as the link between his sainted father and his ruthless son.

İbrahim, 1640-1648 (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1.label: İbrahim, 1640-1648
İbrahim, 1640-1648 (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1640–AD 1648] İbrahim, 1640-1648. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--İbrahim, 1640-1648". Added to LCSH in 2016, revised in 2017. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ottoman rule under a sultan whose instability and reliance on palace favourites weakened central authority and drained the treasury. The invasion of Venetian Crete in 1645 began a war that would last a quarter of a century and repeatedly see Venetian fleets blockade the Dardanelles. His deposition and execution by the janissaries showed how far power had shifted from the sultan to the military and religious establishment.

Süleyman I, 1520-1566 (Turkey, AD 1520–A.label: Süleyman I, 1520-1566
Süleyman I, 1520-1566 (Turkey, AD 1520–A.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1520–AD 1566] Süleyman I, 1520-1566. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Süleyman I, 1520-1566". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Suleiman I, 1520-1566" appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ottoman Empire reached its widest reach and greatest confidence under a sultan the Europeans called the Magnificent and his own subjects the Lawgiver. He took Belgrade and Rhodes, crushed Hungary at Mohács, besieged Vienna, made the Mediterranean an Ottoman sea through his corsair admirals, and allied with France against the Habsburgs. At home he systematised the secular law codes and employed the architect Sinan, whose mosques still define the Istanbul skyline.

Louis I, 1342-1382 (Hungary, AD 1342–AD.label: Louis I, 1342-1382
Louis I, 1342-1382 (Hungary, AD 1342–AD.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1342–AD 1382] Louis I, 1342-1382. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Louis I, 1342-1382". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Angevin king who took Hungary to its greatest medieval extent, waging campaigns in Naples, Dalmatia and the Balkans and forcing Venice to surrender the Adriatic coast. He inherited Poland in 1370, briefly uniting the two crowns, and bought Polish noble support with the Privilege of Koszyce, a landmark in the growth of szlachta power. He also founded Hungary's first university at Pécs; having no son, he left a contested succession that unravelled his gains.

Liang dynasty, 502-557 (China, AD 502–AD.label: Liang dynasty, 502-557
Liang dynasty, 502-557 (China, AD 502–AD.prose:
[China, AD 502–AD 557] Liang dynasty, 502-557. Extracted from heading "China--History--Liang dynasty, 502-557". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The third of the Southern Dynasties, ruled for most of its existence by Emperor Wu, a devout Buddhist patron who several times entered a monastery and had to be ransomed back by his court. Jiankang flourished as a centre of Buddhist learning and letters, producing the Wen Xuan anthology and major literary criticism. The Hou Jing rebellion sacked the capital and shattered the southern aristocracy, leaving the dynasty to be swept away.

Northern Qi dynasty, 550-577 (China, AD.label: Northern Qi dynasty, 550-577
Northern Qi dynasty, 550-577 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 550–AD 577] Northern Qi dynasty, 550-577. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern Qi dynasty, 550-577". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the two rival successors to the Northern Wei, controlling the fertile eastern plains from its capital at Ye. Its brief span produced remarkable Buddhist statuary and painted tombs, and a court whose brutality became a byword in later Chinese histories. It fell to its western rival in 577, a step on the road to the Sui reunification.

Nicholas I, 1860-1918 (Montenegro, AD 18.label: Nicholas I, 1860-1918
Nicholas I, 1860-1918 (Montenegro, AD 18.prose:
[Montenegro, AD 1860–AD 1918] Nicholas I, 1860-1918. Extracted from heading "Montenegro--History--Nicholas I, 1860-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.79 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The long-lived ruler of Montenegro, prince and then from 1910 king, who won formal independence at the Congress of Berlin, roughly doubled his territory and married his daughters into the royal houses of Italy, Serbia and Russia. He gave the country its first constitution, roads and newspapers while keeping firm personal control. Defeat and occupation in the First World War ended his rule, and Montenegro was absorbed into the new Yugoslav kingdom.

Revolution, 1918-1919 (Hungary, AD 1918–.label: Revolution, 1918-1919
Revolution, 1918-1919 (Hungary, AD 1918–.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1918–AD 1919] Revolution, 1918-1919. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Revolution, 1918-1919". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Defeat broke Austria-Hungary apart, and Budapest passed in months from a liberal republic under Károlyi to Béla Kun's Soviet Republic, the first communist government outside Russia. It nationalised industry, fought Czechoslovak and Romanian armies over the country's shrinking borders, and collapsed after 133 days when Romanian troops entered Budapest. The White counter-terror and Horthy's regency followed, and the Treaty of Trianon left Hungary with a third of its former territory.

Leo X, 1513-1521 (Vatican City, AD 1513–.label: Leo X, 1513-1521
Leo X, 1513-1521 (Vatican City, AD 1513–.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1513–AD 1521] Leo X, 1513-1521. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Leo X, 1513-1521". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Medici pope turned Rome into Europe's most lavish artistic stage, employing Raphael and pouring money into the rebuilding of St Peter's. To fund it he pushed the sale of indulgences in Germany, which provoked Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses in 1517; Leo dismissed the affair as a monkish quarrel and excommunicated Luther in 1521, far too late to contain the Reformation. His spending left the papal finances wrecked.

Roger II, 1105-1154 (Sicily, AD 1105–AD.label: Roger II, 1105-1154
Roger II, 1105-1154 (Sicily, AD 1105–AD.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1105–AD 1154] Roger II, 1105-1154. Extracted from heading "Sicily (Italy)--History--Roger II, 1105-1154". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He welded the scattered Norman conquests of Sicily and southern Italy into a single kingdom, crowned at Palermo in 1130 over papal objections. His state was unusually centralised and unusually plural, staffed by Greeks, Arabs and Latins, minting in three scripts and producing the geographer al-Idrisi's world map for the king; the mosaics and muqarnas ceilings of the Cappella Palatina show the same fusion in stone and gold.

Maximilian I, 1493-1519 (Germany, AD 149.label: Maximilian I, 1493-1519
Maximilian I, 1493-1519 (Germany, AD 149.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1493–AD 1519] Maximilian I, 1493-1519. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Maximilian I, 1493-1519". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He gained the rich Burgundian Netherlands by marriage and then arranged his children's and grandchildren's marriages so shrewdly that his grandson Charles inherited Spain, the Low Countries, Austria and the Americas. At home he pushed through imperial reforms, an imperial court of justice and a common peace, though the Empire remained loosely governed and he was chronically short of money. He fought long and inconclusive wars in Italy, promoted the Landsknecht infantry, and used printed images and books to build his own legend.

Andronicus III Palaeologus, 1328-1341 (B.label: Andronicus III Palaeologus, 1328-1341
Andronicus III Palaeologus, 1328-1341 (B.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1328–AD 1341] Andronicus III Palaeologus, 1328-1341. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Andronicus III Palaeologus, 1328-1341". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Coming to the throne after years of civil war against his grandfather, Andronikos III overhauled the law courts, rebuilt a small navy, and brought Thessaly and Epirus back under Constantinople's control. He could not stop the Ottomans, who took Nicaea and Nicomedia on his watch. His early death left an infant heir and touched off a ruinous civil war that broke the empire's remaining strength.

First Seminole War, 1817-1818 (Florida,.label: First Seminole War, 1817-1818
First Seminole War, 1817-1818 (Florida,.prose:
[Florida , AD 1817–AD 1818] First Seminole War, 1817-1818. Extracted from heading "Seminole War, 1st, 1817-1818". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1990. Note that the alternate label includes the Second and Third Seminole Wars as well. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Andrew Jackson led American troops across the border into Spanish Florida, pursuing Seminoles and the free and escaped Black communities allied with them. He seized Spanish posts and executed two British traders, provoking an international incident. The campaign exposed Spain's inability to hold the colony and led directly to its cession to the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty.

Oscar I, 1844-1859 (Norway, AD 1844–AD 1.label: Oscar I, 1844-1859
Oscar I, 1844-1859 (Norway, AD 1844–AD 1.prose:
[Norway, AD 1844–AD 1859] Oscar I, 1844-1859. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Oscar I, 1844-1859". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruling Norway in personal union with Sweden, he was the first monarch to treat the Norwegians as partners rather than subordinates, permitting a separate Norwegian merchant flag and using the title king of Norway and Sweden when in Oslo. Reforms in law, trade, and communications accompanied a broader liberalising mood, while his sympathy for Scandinavian unity shaped his foreign policy.

Heian period, 794-1185 (Japan, AD 794–AD.label: Heian period, 794-1185
Heian period, 794-1185 (Japan, AD 794–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 794–AD 1185] Heian period, 794-1185. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Heian period, 794-1185". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Japan's classical age, centred on the new capital at Heian-kyō and a court aristocracy of a few thousand people whose diaries, poems and novels survive in extraordinary detail. Official missions to China ceased, and Japanese forms of writing, painting and Buddhism matured. Power drained to regents, retired emperors and finally to provincial warriors, ending with the Genpei War and the first shogunate.

Revolution, 1909-1910 (Nicaragua, AD 190.label: Revolution, 1909-1910
Revolution, 1909-1910 (Nicaragua, AD 190.prose:
[Nicaragua, AD 1909–AD 1910] Revolution, 1909-1910. Extracted from heading "Nicaragua--History--Revolution, 1909-1910". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Conservative revolt launched from Bluefields on the Caribbean coast, led by Juan Estrada with backing from American mining and commercial interests, overthrew the nationalist president Jose Santos Zelaya. The execution of two American mercenaries gave Washington its pretext to break relations and land marines. Zelaya's fall opened two decades of United States financial control and military occupation in Nicaragua, and the resistance to it eventually produced Sandino.

Maurice, 582-602 (Byzantine Empire, AD 5.label: Maurice, 582-602
Maurice, 582-602 (Byzantine Empire, AD 5.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 582–AD 602] Maurice, 582-602. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Maurice, 582-602". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A career soldier turned emperor, he ended the long Persian war on favourable terms by helping restore Khosrow II to his throne, then turned the army on the Avars and Slavs to push the Danube frontier back. His reorganisation of the western provinces into exarchates at Ravenna and Carthage shaped Byzantine administration for centuries, and the military manual known as the Strategikon is attributed to him. Cost-cutting mutinied his troops; his overthrow and murder by Phocas gave Persia a pretext for the catastrophic war that followed.
