Alekseĭ Mikhaĭlovich, 1645-1676 (Russia,.prose:
[Russia , AD 1645–AD 1676] Alekseĭ Mikhaĭlovich, 1645-1676. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Alekseĭ Mikhaĭlovich, 1645-1676". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alexis, 1645-1676" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The second Romanov tsar, whose law code of 1649 bound peasants to the land permanently and completed the making of Russian serfdom. His reign saw Patriarch Nikon's ritual reforms split the church and create the Old Believers, Stenka Razin's great Cossack and peasant revolt, and the absorption of left-bank Ukraine after war with Poland.

Warring States, 403-221 B.C. (China, 402.label: Warring States, 403-221 B.C.
Warring States, 403-221 B.C. (China, 402.prose:
[China, 402 BC–220 BC] Warring States, 403-221 B.C.. Extracted from heading "China--History--Warring States, 403-221 B.C.". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The formal partition of Jin into Han, Wei and Zhao is often taken as the starting point, leaving seven major powers in open competition. Diplomacy of alliances 'vertical' and 'horizontal' alternated with wars of annihilation such as Changping, where a defeated army was reportedly buried alive. Sunzi's and Sun Bin's military writings, the crossbow and cavalry all belong to this century of relentless competition, closed by Qin's unification.

Conquest, 1519-1540 (Mexico, AD 1519–AD.label: Conquest, 1519-1540
Conquest, 1519-1540 (Mexico, AD 1519–AD.prose:
[Mexico, AD 1519–AD 1540] Conquest, 1519-1540. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--Conquest, 1519-1540". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.76 of LCSH 1987, and p.62 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cortés landed on the Gulf coast, allied with Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Mexica, and by 1521 Tenochtitlan had fallen after siege and smallpox. Spanish and indigenous forces then pushed into Oaxaca, Michoacán, Guatemala and the north, while friars began mass conversions and dismantled temples. Epidemic disease killed a large share of the population within a generation, and colonial cities rose literally on the stones of the old ones.

Manuel II, 1908-1910 (Portugal, AD 1908–.label: Manuel II, 1908-1910
Manuel II, 1908-1910 (Portugal, AD 1908–.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1908–AD 1910] Manuel II, 1908-1910. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Manuel II, 1908-1910". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Portugal's last king, put on the throne as a teenager after his father and elder brother were shot dead in the streets of Lisbon. Two years of unstable governments ended when a republican rising drove him into exile in England, closing nearly eight centuries of Portuguese monarchy.

Ulrich, 1503-1550 (Germany, AD 1503–AD 1.label: Ulrich, 1503-1550
Ulrich, 1503-1550 (Germany, AD 1503–AD 1.prose:
[Württemberg (Germany), AD 1503–AD 1550] Ulrich, 1503-1550. Extracted from heading "Württemberg (Germany)--History--Ulrich, 1503-1550". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 131 of LCSH 1986 and p.109 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Duke Ulrich's rule over Württemberg was violent and interrupted: heavy taxation provoked the Poor Conrad rising, and after he seized the free city of Reutlingen the Swabian League drove him out in 1519, handing the duchy to the Habsburgs. Restored by force in 1534 with the backing of Philip of Hesse, he imposed the Reformation on Württemberg and dissolved its monasteries, turning the duchy into one of the strongest Lutheran states in southern Germany.

Fenian invasions, 1866-1870 (Canada, AD.label: Fenian invasions, 1866-1870
Fenian invasions, 1866-1870 (Canada, AD.prose:
[Canada, AD 1866–AD 1870] Fenian invasions, 1866-1870. Extracted from heading "Canada--History--Fenian invasions, 1866-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on .13 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Irish-American veterans of the US Civil War crossed the border in armed bands, hoping to seize British territory as a bargaining chip for Irish independence. The raids were beaten back, but the alarm they caused strengthened the case for uniting the British North American colonies and for a permanent Canadian militia.

James II, 1685-1688 (Ireland, AD 1685–AD.label: James II, 1685-1688
James II, 1685-1688 (Ireland, AD 1685–AD.prose:
[Ireland, AD 1685–AD 1688] James II, 1685-1688. Extracted from heading "Ireland--History--James II, 1685-1688". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry appears under heading "Great Britain--History--" with a distinct URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

England's last Catholic king inherited a broadly loyal country, crushed Monmouth's rebellion, then squandered support by packing the army and universities with Catholics and suspending the penal laws by prerogative. The birth of a Catholic son turned a temporary problem into a dynasty, and leading politicians invited William of Orange to intervene. James fled to France, and the Revolution settlement that followed made Parliament, not the crown, the final authority.

Carib War, 1795-1796 (Saint Vincent and.node: Carib War, 1795-1796 (Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, AD 1795–AD 1796)
Carib War, 1795-1796 (Saint Vincent and.label: Carib War, 1795-1796
Carib War, 1795-1796 (Saint Vincent and.prose:
[St Vincent, AD 1795–AD 1796] Carib War, 1795-1796. Extracted from heading "Saint Vincent--History--Carib War, 1795-1796". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Black Caribs of Saint Vincent, led by Chatoyer and encouraged by revolutionary France, rose against British planters who wanted their fertile windward lands. After more than a year of jungle fighting the British prevailed and deported some five thousand survivors, first to Balliceaux and then to the Bay Islands off Honduras. Those exiles became the Garifuna communities now spread along the Central American coast.

Soviet occupation, 1940-1941 (Lithuania,.label: Soviet occupation, 1940-1941
Soviet occupation, 1940-1941 (Lithuania,.prose:
[Lithuania, AD 1940–AD 1941] Soviet occupation, 1940-1941. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--Soviet occupation, 1940-1941". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under ultimatum, the country admitted Soviet troops, staged a rigged election and was incorporated into the USSR. Property was nationalised, the officer corps and political class arrested, and some 15,000 people deported eastward in a single June night in 1941. The German advance swept the Soviets out within days, leaving a legacy of trauma that fed both collaboration and later resistance.

Menalamba Rebellion, 1895-1899 (Madagasc.label: Menalamba Rebellion, 1895-1899
Menalamba Rebellion, 1895-1899 (Madagasc.prose:
[Madagascar, AD 1895–AD 1899] Menalamba Rebellion, 1895-1899. Extracted from heading "Madagascar--History--Menalamba Rebellion, 1895-1899". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.74 of LCSH 1987, and p.60 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After French troops took Antananarivo and turned the Merina monarchy into a protectorate, fighters wearing red-smeared shawls rose against foreign rule, Christian missions and the collaborating court elite. The revolt spread through the central highlands and drove France to depose and exile Queen Ranavalona III, ending the monarchy outright. General Gallieni crushed it with village burnings and executions, but the movement is remembered in Madagascar as an early assertion of national resistance.

Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C (E.node: Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C (Egypt, 1319 BC–1199 BC)
Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C (E.label: Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C
Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C (E.prose:
[Egypt, 1319 BC–1199 BC] Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Nineteenth dynasty, ca. 1320-1200 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ramesside age, when Seti I and Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a standstill at Kadesh and then signed the first surviving international peace treaty. Building on a colossal scale — Abu Simbel, the Karnak hypostyle hall, the Ramesseum and the new delta capital Pi-Ramesses — made this the most visible dynasty in Egyptian art. Merenptah's reign brought Libyan and 'Sea Peoples' raids and the earliest known mention of Israel, foreshadowing the empire's slow unravelling.

Romulus Augustulus, 475-476 (Roman Empir.label: Romulus Augustulus, 475-476
Romulus Augustulus, 475-476 (Roman Empir.prose:
[Rome, AD 475–AD 476] Romulus Augustulus, 475-476. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Romulus Augustulus, 475-476". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A teenage figurehead installed by his general father, he ruled little more than Italy before the commander Odoacer deposed him and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. Rather than appoint a new western emperor, Odoacer took the title of king, and no one replaced the office. Later historians made this brief reign the conventional end of the Roman Empire in the West, though for people at the time little changed overnight.

Battle of Athens, 1944-1945 (Greece, AD.label: Battle of Athens, 1944-1945
Battle of Athens, 1944-1945 (Greece, AD.prose:
[Greece, AD 1944–AD 1945] Battle of Athens, 1944-1945. Extracted from heading "Athens, Battle of, Athens, Greece, 1944-1945". Added to LCSH in 2015, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Weeks after the Germans withdrew, a demonstration in Syntagma Square was fired on and the capital erupted into six weeks of street fighting between the communist-led ELAS resistance and British troops backing the returning government. Churchill flew in at Christmas to broker terms; the Varkiza agreement disarmed the resistance but settled nothing. The fighting is generally seen as the opening act of the Greek Civil War and an early flashpoint of the Cold War.

Charles VII, 1742-1745 (Germany, AD 1742.label: Charles VII, 1742-1745
Charles VII, 1742-1745 (Germany, AD 1742.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1742–AD 1745] Charles VII, 1742-1745. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Charles VII, 1742-1745". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles Albert of Bavaria broke a three-century Habsburg monopoly on the imperial title, elected emperor while Maria Theresa's inheritance was being carved up by rival armies. It went badly: Austrian troops occupied his Bavarian homeland almost as soon as he was crowned, and he ruled largely as an emperor without lands. His death after three years let the title return to the Habsburg camp.

Charles V, 1506-1555 (Netherlands, AD 15.label: Charles V, 1506-1555
Charles V, 1506-1555 (Netherlands, AD 15.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1506–AD 1555] Charles V, 1506-1555. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--Charles V, 1506-1555". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born in Ghent and Burgundian by upbringing, he ruled the Low Countries as their natural prince while governing half of Europe from elsewhere, leaving regents — his aunt Margaret and sister Mary — in charge at Mechelen and Brussels. He completed the Seventeen Provinces by conquest and inheritance and bound them together by the Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 as a single indivisible unit. Antwerp became the commercial capital of the world in these decades, while his edicts against Protestants sowed the grievances that later exploded into the Dutch Revolt. He abdicated in the palace at Brussels in 1555.

James II, 1437-1460 (Scotland, AD 1437–A.label: James II, 1437-1460
James II, 1437-1460 (Scotland, AD 1437–A.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1437–AD 1460] James II, 1437-1460. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--James II, 1437-1460". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned at six after his father's murder, he grew up amid magnate rivalries and then destroyed the Douglas family that had dominated southern Scotland, killing the earl in person at Stirling. He exploited England's Wars of the Roses to press on the border. A keen artillerist, he died at Roxburgh when a bombard exploded at his side.

Charles X, 1824-1830 (France, AD 1824–AD.label: Charles X, 1824-1830
Charles X, 1824-1830 (France, AD 1824–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1824–AD 1830] Charles X, 1824-1830. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles X, 1824-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Bourbon to rule France tried to govern as if 1789 had never happened, compensating émigré nobles, favouring the clergy and finally suspending press freedom and the electoral law by decree. Paris answered in three days of barricades in July 1830, and he fled to exile in Britain. The "citizen king" Louis-Philippe replaced him, and the senior Bourbon line never reigned again.

Modern period, 640- (Egypt, AD 640–AD 20.label: Modern period, 640-
Modern period, 640- (Egypt, AD 640–AD 20.prose:
[Egypt, AD 640–AD 2015] Modern period, 640-. Extracted from heading "Egypt--Religion--640-". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1992. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Arab conquest ended a thousand years of Greek and Roman rule and began the long transformation of Egypt into an Arabic-speaking, largely Muslim country, with a new capital in the Nile-side garrison town that became Cairo. Fatimid, Ayyubid and Mamluk rulers made Cairo one of the great cities of the medieval world, its mosques, madrasas and markets still standing in the old city. Ottoman rule from 1517, Muhammad Ali's reforming dynasty, British occupation and the 1952 revolution brought Egypt to independence and to the Aswan High Dam and modern Cairo.

Eighty Years' War, 1568-1648 (Netherland.label: Eighty Years' War, 1568-1648
Eighty Years' War, 1568-1648 (Netherland.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1568–AD 1648] Eighty Years' War, 1568-1648. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--Eighty Years' War, 1568-1648". Added to LCSH in 1986. The alternate label "Wars of Independence, 1568-1648" appears on p.81 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

What began as a revolt of nobles and Calvinists against Philip II's taxes, centralising government and religious persecution turned into a long grinding war that split the Low Countries in two. The northern provinces held out behind their rivers and dykes, declared the Spanish king deposed and built a republic of merchants that became Europe's richest state, while the south stayed Catholic and Habsburg. Spain finally recognised Dutch independence at the Peace of Münster in 1648 - the same settlement that ended the Thirty Years' War.

Petŭr II, 1196-1197 (Bulgaria, AD 1196–A.label: Petŭr II, 1196-1197
Petŭr II, 1196-1197 (Bulgaria, AD 1196–A.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1196–AD 1197] Petŭr II, 1196-1197. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Petur II, 1196-1197". Appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987; added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He ruled briefly at Tarnovo after the murder of his brother Asen, during the violent early years of the revived Bulgarian state that had thrown off Byzantine rule. His own assassination within a year passed the throne to the third brother, Kaloyan, under whom the Second Bulgarian Empire became a serious rival to Constantinople.

Russian Conquest, 1808-1809 (Finland, AD.label: Russian Conquest, 1808-1809
Russian Conquest, 1808-1809 (Finland, AD.prose:
[Finland, AD 1808–AD 1809] Russian Conquest, 1808-1809. Extracted from heading "Finland--History--Russian Conquest, 1808-1809". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.34 of LCSH 1987, and p.26 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's pact with Alexander I set Russia loose on Sweden, and a swift campaign detached the eastern half of the Swedish realm. At Porvoo the tsar met the estates and confirmed Swedish law and Lutheran religion, creating an autonomous Grand Duchy with its own administration – the framework within which a separate Finnish national identity, and eventually independence, took shape.

Trần dynasty, 1225-1400 (Vietnam, AD 122.label: Trần dynasty, 1225-1400
Trần dynasty, 1225-1400 (Vietnam, AD 122.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1225–AD 1400] Trần dynasty, 1225-1400. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Trần dynasty, 1225-1400". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Trần took the Vietnamese throne by marriage and manoeuvre, then held it against three Mongol invasions, most famously when Trần Hưng Đạo destroyed a Yuan fleet on iron-tipped stakes in the Bạch Đằng river. Retired emperors ruled alongside their heirs, Zen Buddhism flourished under the Trúc Lâm school, and writing in the chữ Nôm script took hold. Later reigns weakened under Cham raids and land crises, ending in usurpation and Ming occupation.

John VIII Palaeologus, 1425-1448 (Byzant.label: John VIII Palaeologus, 1425-1448
John VIII Palaeologus, 1425-1448 (Byzant.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1425–AD 1448] John VIII Palaeologus, 1425-1448. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--John VIII Palaeologus, 1425-1448". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruling little more than Constantinople and scattered fragments, he gambled everything on Western help. He travelled to Italy and at the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1439 signed a union of the Greek and Latin churches, which most of his clergy and people angrily rejected. The crusade it produced was destroyed by the Ottomans at Varna in 1444; his death left the doomed city to his brother Constantine XI. Visitors to Renaissance Italy can still spot his distinctive hat in paintings by Pisanello and Piero della Francesca.

Famine, 1845-1852 (Ireland, AD 1845–AD 1.label: Famine, 1845-1852
Famine, 1845-1852 (Ireland, AD 1845–AD 1.prose:
[Ireland, AD 1845–AD 1852] Famine, 1845-1852. Extracted from heading "Ireland--History--Famine, 1845-1852". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Potato blight destroyed the crop that fed most of the rural poor, and about a million people died of starvation and disease while another million emigrated. Food continued to be exported under a government relief policy shaped by laissez-faire economics, a fact that poisoned Anglo-Irish politics for generations. The population never recovered its pre-famine level, and abandoned cabins, workhouses and mass graves remain across the landscape.

Hur Rebellion, 1942-1947 (Pakistan, AD 1.label: Hur Rebellion, 1942-1947
Hur Rebellion, 1942-1947 (Pakistan, AD 1.prose:
[Sindh (Pakistan), AD 1942–AD 1947] Hur Rebellion, 1942-1947. Extracted from heading "Sindh (Pakistan)--History--Hur Rebellion, 1942-1947". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An armed revolt in the Sindh desert by the Hurs, disciples of the Pir Pagaro, who attacked railways, telegraph lines and police posts while Britain was preoccupied with the Second World War. The colonial response was severe: martial law, special tribunals, internment camps for whole families, and the hanging of Pir Sibghatullah Shah II in 1943. The suppression left a lasting grievance in rural Sindh and made the Pir's followers a potent political force after Partition.

French occupation, 1798-1801 (Egypt, AD.label: French occupation, 1798-1801
French occupation, 1798-1801 (Egypt, AD.prose:
[Egypt, AD 1798–AD 1801] French occupation, 1798-1801. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--French occupation, 1798-1801". Added to LCSH 2004; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and on p.23 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's army defeated the Mamluks near the Pyramids but lost its fleet to Nelson at Aboukir Bay, leaving the expedition stranded and eventually forced out by Ottoman and British troops. Alongside the soldiers came a corps of scholars whose survey produced the monumental Description de l'Égypte and whose engineers unearthed the Rosetta Stone, the key to hieroglyphs. The invasion opened a century of European intervention in Egypt and effectively founded the discipline of Egyptology.

Ivan III, 1462-1505 (Russia, AD 1462–AD.label: Ivan III, 1462-1505
Ivan III, 1462-1505 (Russia, AD 1462–AD.prose:
[Russia , AD 1462–AD 1505] Ivan III, 1462-1505. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Ivan III, 1462-1505". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ivan the Great multiplied Muscovy's territory several times over, absorbing Novgorod and Tver, and stopped paying tribute to the Golden Horde after the bloodless standoff on the Ugra River. He married a Byzantine princess, adopted the double-headed eagle and the title of sovereign of all Rus, issued a new law code, and brought Italian architects to rebuild the Kremlin in brick. The state he assembled is the direct ancestor of the Russian empire.

War of Independence, 1820-1829 (Peru, AD.label: War of Independence, 1820-1829
War of Independence, 1820-1829 (Peru, AD.prose:
[Peru, AD 1820–AD 1829] War of Independence, 1820-1829. Extracted from heading "Peru--History--War of Independence, 1820-1829". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

San Martín landed on the coast from Chile and proclaimed independence in Lima, but the royalist armies held the highlands and the war stalled until Bolívar took command. Junín and then Ayacucho in 1824 destroyed the viceregal army and ended Spanish rule on the American mainland. The years that followed brought a war with Gran Colombia over borders and the beginning of Peru's long era of military caudillos.

Lê Văn Khôi's Rebellion, 1833-1835 (Viet.label: Lê Văn Khôi's Rebellion, 1833-1835
Lê Văn Khôi's Rebellion, 1833-1835 (Viet.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1833–AD 1835] Lê Văn Khôi's Rebellion, 1833-1835. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Lê Văn Khôi's Rebellion, 1833-1835". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An uprising in the south against Emperor Minh Mạng's centralising rule, launched by the adopted son of a former regional governor and seizing the citadel of Gia Định (Saigon). The rebels drew in Chinese settlers, Catholic converts and a Siamese intervention before the fortress fell after a long siege and its defenders were massacred. The involvement of Christians hardened imperial suspicion of the faith and triggered decades of persecution that European powers later cited to justify intervention in Vietnam.

Cambodian-Vietnamese Conflict, 1977-1991.label: Cambodian-Vietnamese Conflict, 1977-1991
Cambodian-Vietnamese Conflict, 1977-1991.prose:
[Vietnam, Cambodia, AD 1977–AD 1991] Cambodian-Vietnamese Conflict, 1977-1991. Spatial coverage: Cambodia, Vietnam. Extracted from heading "Cambodian-Vietnamese Conflict, 1977-1991". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Border raids by the Khmer Rouge escalated into a full Vietnamese invasion at the end of 1978, toppling Pol Pot's regime within weeks and installing a government in Phnom Penh under Hun Sen. China retaliated by attacking northern Vietnam in 1979, and Khmer Rouge and other resistance forces fought a long guerrilla war from camps on the Thai border while Vietnam faced international isolation and embargo. Vietnamese troops withdrew in 1989, and the fighting was formally ended by the Paris Peace Accords of 1991.

Eric III, 1400-1442 (Norway, AD 1400–AD.label: Eric III, 1400-1442
Eric III, 1400-1442 (Norway, AD 1400–AD.prose:
[Norway, AD 1400–AD 1442] Eric III, 1400-1442. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Eric III, 1400-1442". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Eric of Pomerania ruled Denmark, Norway and Sweden together as heir to Margaret I's Kalmar Union, and spent his reign trying to make that union work as a single power. His long wars with Holstein and the Hanseatic League drained the treasury, and his introduction of the Sound Dues — a toll on every ship passing Elsinore — became a mainstay of Danish revenue for four centuries. Deposed by rebellious nobles, he retreated to Gotland and lived for years as a Baltic pirate.

Han dynasty, 202 B.C.- 220 A.D. (China,.label: Han dynasty, 202 B.C.- 220 A.D.
Han dynasty, 202 B.C.- 220 A.D. (China,.prose:
[China, 201 BC–AD 220] Han dynasty, 202 B.C.- 220 A.D.. Extracted from heading "China--History--Han dynasty, 202 B.C.-220 A.D."  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The empire that gave Chinese civilisation its enduring shape, with a professional bureaucracy, an examined official class and a state ideology drawn from Confucius. Silk, lacquer and bronze mirrors travelled west along newly secured desert routes, while Buddhism first trickled east into China. Han tombs, packed with painted ceramics, jade suits and models of houses and farms, are the richest single source for daily life in early imperial China.

Classical period, 1500-1700 (Portugal, A.label: Classical period, 1500-1700
Classical period, 1500-1700 (Portugal, A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1500–AD 1700] Classical period, 1500-1700. Applies to literary periodization only. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Habsburg rule turned the newly unified kingdoms into the hub of the first global empire, funded by silver shipped from Potosí and Mexico through Seville. That wealth paid for wars in the Netherlands, Italy and against the Ottomans, and for the writers and painters of the Golden Age, from Cervantes to Velázquez. By the end of the period, inflation, plague, debt defaults and the loss of Portugal and the northern Netherlands had drained the treasury and moved economic power north.

Revolution, 1848-1849 (Germany, AD 1848–.label: Revolution, 1848-1849
Revolution, 1848-1849 (Germany, AD 1848–.prose:
[Germany , AD 1848–AD 1849] Revolution, 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Revolution, 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, 913-959.label: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, 913-959
Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, 913-959.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 913–AD 959] Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, 913-959. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, 913-959". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sidelined for over thirty years by a co-emperor who had married into the throne, he spent his time writing and commissioning books instead. The manuals he produced on court ceremonial, provincial administration and foreign peoples are among the richest sources we have for the medieval Balkans, the steppe and the Rus. His court's scholarship, art and ivory carving define what is often called the Macedonian renaissance.

Axis occupation, 1941-1945 (Slovenia, AD.label: Axis occupation, 1941-1945
Axis occupation, 1941-1945 (Slovenia, AD.prose:
[Yugoslavia, AD 1941–AD 1945] Axis occupation, 1941-1945. Spatial coverage: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro, Republic of Macedonia, Serbia, Slovenia. Extracted from heading "Yugoslavia--History--Axis occupation, 1941-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 130 of LCSH 1986 and p.109 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Slovenia was carved up three ways between Germany, Italy and Hungary, each occupier trying to erase it: German authorities banned the language and deported tens of thousands northwards, while Italy walled Ljubljana with barbed wire. The communist-led Liberation Front mounted one of Europe's most effective partisan movements, and a brutal civil war developed with the anti-communist Home Guard. Victory in 1945 brought both liberation and mass reprisal killings, and Slovenia entered communist Yugoslavia.

Pagan period, 849-1287 (Burma, AD 849–AD.label: Pagan period, 849-1287
Pagan period, 849-1287 (Burma, AD 849–AD.prose:
[Burma, AD 849–AD 1287] Pagan period, 849-1287. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Pagan period, 849-1287". Added to LCSH in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The kingdom centred on Bagan on the Irrawaddy unified much of the region for the first time and, under Anawrahta and his successors, made Theravada Buddhism the dominant faith of Burma. Merit-making by kings and wealthy donors filled the plain with thousands of brick temples and stupas, many still standing, and supported a monastic economy of tax-free land. Weakening under the strain of that endowment, the kingdom fragmented in the face of Mongol pressure in the late thirteenth century.

George II, 1727-1760 (United Kingdom, AD.label: George II, 1727-1760
George II, 1727-1760 (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1727–AD 1760] George II, 1727-1760. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Victoria, 1837-1901". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last British monarch to lead troops in battle, at Dettingen in 1743, he presided over an age of European wars that turned into a global contest with France. The Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart reached Derby in 1745 before being crushed at Culloden, and the Seven Years' War brought victories in Canada and Bengal that laid the foundations of empire.

Ferdinand I, 1556-1564 (Germany, AD 1556.label: Ferdinand I, 1556-1564
Ferdinand I, 1556-1564 (Germany, AD 1556.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1556–AD 1564] Ferdinand I, 1556-1564. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Ferdinand I, 1556-1564". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles V's younger brother took the imperial title after the abdication that split the Habsburg inheritance, leaving Spain and the Netherlands to Philip II and the Austrian lands, Bohemia and royal Hungary to the Vienna line. Ferdinand had already brokered the Peace of Augsburg, which let each German prince fix the religion of his own territory and froze the Reformation into a patchwork of Lutheran and Catholic states. His reign set the pattern of a Danubian Habsburg monarchy governing three very different realms while facing the Ottomans on the Hungarian frontier.

Bayezid I, 1389-1403 (Turkey, AD 1389–AD.label: Bayezid I, 1389-1403
Bayezid I, 1389-1403 (Turkey, AD 1389–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1389–AD 1403] Bayezid I, 1389-1403. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Bayezid I, 1389-1403". Added to LCSH in 1986. Nicknamed 'the Thunderbolt' for the speed of his campaigns, he absorbed the Anatolian emirates, pushed deep into the Balkans and crushed a western crusade at Nicopolis in 1396, then blockaded Constantinople for years. His empire came apart in a single afternoon at Ankara in 1402, when Timur defeated and captured him; he died in captivity and his sons fought an eleven-year civil war for the succession.

Maroon War, 1795-1796 (Jamaica, AD 1795–.label: Maroon War, 1795-1796
Maroon War, 1795-1796 (Jamaica, AD 1795–.prose:
[Jamaica, AD 1795–AD 1796] Maroon War, 1795-1796. Extracted from heading "Jamaica--History--Maroon War, 1795-1796". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Trelawny Town Maroons, descendants of escaped slaves living under treaty in the mountains, went to war with the colonial government after a dispute over the flogging of two of their number. British troops eventually brought in hunting dogs from Cuba and forced a surrender, then broke the terms and deported nearly six hundred Maroons to Nova Scotia and later to Sierra Leone. The war showed how fragile the plantation order was, at a moment when Britain was already fighting revolution in Saint-Domingue.

Stuarts, to the Union, 1371-1707 (Scotla.label: Stuarts, to the Union, 1371-1707
Stuarts, to the Union, 1371-1707 (Scotla.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1707] Stuarts, to the Union, 1371-1707. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Stuarts, to the Union, 1371-1707". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.101 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Stewart dynasty held Scotland for over three centuries, through a run of royal minorities, feuding magnates, and the long entanglement with England that ran from Flodden to Mary Queen of Scots. The Reformation of 1560 remade Scottish religion and education along Presbyterian lines, and in 1603 James VI inherited England, shifting the court south. The line ends with the parliamentary Union of 1707, which dissolved Scotland's separate legislature after the ruinous failure of the Darien colonial venture.

Vietnam War, 1961-1975 (United States, A.label: Vietnam War, 1961-1975
Vietnam War, 1961-1975 (United States, A.prose:
[United States, Vietnam, AD 1961–AD 1975] Vietnam War, 1961-1975. Spatial coverage: United States, Vietnam. Extracted from heading "Vietnam War, 1961-1975". Added to LCSH in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

American involvement escalated from advisers to more than half a million troops, sustained bombing and a war that could not be won on the terms it was fought. It killed some 58,000 Americans and millions of Vietnamese, Laotians and Cambodians, and at home it fractured public trust in government, fuelled a mass protest movement and ended the draft. Saigon fell in 1975, leaving a caution about foreign intervention that shaped US policy for decades.

Keichō Peasant Uprising, 1614-1615 (Japa.label: Keichō Peasant Uprising, 1614-1615
Keichō Peasant Uprising, 1614-1615 (Japa.prose: [Japan, AD 1614–AD 1615] Keichō Peasant Uprising, 1614-1615. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Keichō Peasant Uprising, 1614-1615". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry II, 1547-1559 (France, AD 1547–AD.label: Henry II, 1547-1559
Henry II, 1547-1559 (France, AD 1547–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1547–AD 1559] Henry II, 1547-1559. Extracted from heading "France--History--Henry II, 1547-1559". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He pressed on with the Valois struggle against the Habsburgs, taking Calais from the English and seizing the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun, before bankruptcy forced the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis and the abandonment of French claims in Italy. At home he created special court chambers to hunt down Protestants, hardening the divisions that would explode into the Wars of Religion. He died after a lance splinter pierced his eye in a tournament, leaving three short-lived sons and his widow Catherine de' Medici to manage the crisis.

Henry II, 1002-1024 (Germany, AD 1002–AD.label: Henry II, 1002-1024
Henry II, 1002-1024 (Germany, AD 1002–AD.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1002–AD 1024] Henry II, 1002-1024. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry II, 1002-1024". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Ottonians turned attention away from Italian adventures and towards consolidating royal power in Germany, using bishops and abbots as instruments of government and endowing his new see at Bamberg lavishly. He fought long wars against Bolesław the Brave of Poland, at times allying with pagan Slavs against a Christian rival. Canonised in 1146, he is the only German emperor to be venerated as a saint.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (South Carolina, AD.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (South Carolina, AD.prose:
[South Carolina, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "South Carolina--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.105 of LCSH 1987, and p.102 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Charles IX, 1604-1611 (Sweden, AD 1604–A.label: Charles IX, 1604-1611
Charles IX, 1604-1611 (Sweden, AD 1604–A.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1604–AD 1611] Charles IX, 1604-1611. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles IX, 1604-1611". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The youngest son of Gustav Vasa seized power from his Catholic nephew Sigismund of Poland, securing Sweden for Lutheranism after the Uppsala assembly and taking the crown himself. He pushed Sweden into the eastern Baltic, fighting Poland in Livonia and intervening in Russia's Time of Troubles, and left wars with Denmark, Poland and Russia to his son Gustavus Adolphus. He also promoted mining and founded towns, including Gothenburg's predecessor.

Boris Fyodorovich Godunov, 1598-1605 (Ru.label: Boris Fyodorovich Godunov, 1598-1605
Boris Fyodorovich Godunov, 1598-1605 (Ru.prose:
[Russia , AD 1598–AD 1605] Boris Fyodorovich Godunov, 1598-1605. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Boris Fyodorovich Godunov, 1598-1605". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A boyar who rose through the court of Ivan the Terrible and governed as regent before being elected tsar when the Rurikid line died out, he opened Russia further to foreign expertise and created the Moscow patriarchate. Catastrophic famine from 1601 killed perhaps a third of the population and destroyed his legitimacy; his sudden death amid the advance of a pretender claiming to be Ivan's dead son plunged Russia into the Time of Troubles.

Frederick William III, 1797-1840 (German.label: Frederick William III, 1797-1840
Frederick William III, 1797-1840 (German.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1797–AD 1840] Frederick William III, 1797-1840. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick William III, 1797-1840". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hesitant neutrality ended in catastrophe when Prussia was crushed at Jena and Auerstedt in 1806 and halved by Napoleon. The humiliation triggered the Stein–Hardenberg reforms — serfdom abolished, towns self-governing, the army remade, the University of Berlin founded — and in 1813 Prussia rose against the French and helped destroy the empire. Afterwards the king reneged on promises of a constitution, backed the repressive Carlsbad Decrees, and forced Lutherans and Calvinists into a single Prussian Union church, while the Zollverein quietly began knitting Germany together economically.

German occupation, 1914-1918 (Poland, AD.label: German occupation, 1914-1918
German occupation, 1914-1918 (Poland, AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1914–AD 1918] German occupation, 1914-1918. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--German occupation, 1914-1918". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.79 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ten northern departments, containing much of France's coal, iron and textile industry, spent the whole war behind German lines. Civilians faced requisitions, forced labour gangs, curfews and hostage-taking, while factories were stripped of machinery and orchards felled during the 1917 retreat to the Hindenburg Line. The devastated zone left behind shaped French demands for reparations and a decade of reconstruction.

Commonwealth and Protectorate, 1649-1660.label: Commonwealth and Protectorate, 1649-1660
Commonwealth and Protectorate, 1649-1660.prose:
[Great Britain, England, Scotland, Ireland, AD 1649–AD 1660] Commonwealth and Protectorate, 1649-1660. Spatial coverage: England, Ireland, Scotland. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Commonwealth and Protectorate, 1649-1660". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After executing Charles I, England was governed without a king, first by the Rump Parliament and then by Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector. Armies crushed resistance in Ireland and Scotland with lasting bitterness, the navy was rebuilt, and Jews were readmitted after centuries of exclusion. The regime rested on Cromwell personally and collapsed within two years of his death, bringing back the monarchy in 1660.

Dano-Swedish War, 1643-1645 (Denmark, AD.label: Dano-Swedish War, 1643-1645
Dano-Swedish War, 1643-1645 (Denmark, AD.prose:
[Denmark, Sweden, AD 1643–AD 1645] Dano-Swedish War, 1643-1645. Spatial coverage: Denmark, Sweden. Extracted from heading "Dano-Swedish War, 1643-1645". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sweden's field marshal Torstensson swung his army out of Germany and struck Jutland without a declaration of war, while Christian IV lost an eye fighting his own fleet at Kolberger Heide. The Peace of Bromsebro took Jamtland, Harjedalen, Gotland and Osel from Denmark and exempted Swedish ships from the Sound tolls, tipping the balance of the Baltic decisively toward Stockholm.

Elagabalus, 218-222 (Roman Empire, AD 21.label: Elagabalus, 218-222
Elagabalus, 218-222 (Roman Empire, AD 21.prose:
[Rome, AD 218–AD 222] Elagabalus, 218-222. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Elagabalus, 218-222". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A fourteen-year-old Syrian priest of the sun god Elagabal was hoisted onto the imperial throne by his grandmother and the eastern legions. He brought his black meteorite deity to Rome, installed it above Jupiter, married and discarded wives including a Vestal Virgin, and scandalised the senatorial elite so thoroughly that the ancient accounts of him are hard to separate from invective. The Praetorians murdered him and his mother at eighteen and replaced him with his cousin Severus Alexander.

Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (New Engl.label: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775
Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (New Engl.prose:
[New England , AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "New England--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.81 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C.node: Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C (Egypt, 1990 BC–1785 BC)
Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C.label: Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C
Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C.prose:
[Egypt, 1990 BC–1785 BC] Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Twelfth dynasty, 1991 B.C.-ca. 1786 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The high point of the Middle Kingdom: a line of kings named Amenemhat and Senwosret moved the capital north to Itjtawy, drained and farmed the Faiyum, and pushed the frontier deep into Nubia behind a chain of massive mudbrick fortresses. Their scribes produced the works later Egyptians treated as classics, including the Tale of Sinuhe, and the language they wrote became the standard 'Middle Egyptian' taught for centuries. The dynasty closed with Sobekneferu, one of the few women to rule Egypt as king.

George I, 1863-1913 (Greece, AD 1863–AD.label: George I, 1863-1913
George I, 1863-1913 (Greece, AD 1863–AD.prose:
[Greece, AD 1863–AD 1913] George I, 1863-1913. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--George I, 1863-1913". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975 under "Greece, Modern". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Danish prince installed by the great powers after the Greeks deposed their first king, he reigned for half a century and accepted a democratic constitution in 1864. Britain handed over the Ionian Islands as a welcome gift, Thessaly was gained in 1881, and after the humiliating defeat by the Ottomans in 1897 came the triumphs of the Balkan Wars, which nearly doubled the kingdom. He was shot dead in newly captured Thessaloniki.

Louis XVIII, 1814-1824 (France, AD 1814–.label: Louis XVIII, 1814-1824
Louis XVIII, 1814-1824 (France, AD 1814–.prose:
[France, AD 1814–AD 1824] Louis XVIII, 1814-1824. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XVIII, 1814-1824". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brought back to the throne on the baggage train of the allied armies that defeated Napoleon, the exiled brother of Louis XVI tried to graft monarchy onto revolutionary France. His Charter granted a parliament and kept the Napoleonic legal and administrative reforms, angering ultra-royalists who wanted the old order restored wholesale. The compromise held during his lifetime and collapsed under his successor.

Nero, 54-68 (Roman Empire, AD 54–AD 68).label: Nero, 54-68
Nero, 54-68 (Roman Empire, AD 54–AD 68).prose:
[Rome, AD 54–AD 68] Nero, 54-68. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Nero, 54-68". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Julio-Claudians, remembered for the great fire of Rome, the persecution of Christians, the murder of his mother, and a devotion to singing and chariot racing that scandalised the senatorial class. His reign saw Boudica's revolt in Britain and the outbreak of the Jewish War, and it ended in his suicide as the armies turned against him. His fall proved that emperors could be made outside Rome, and the civil war of the following year nearly tore the empire apart.

Korana War, 1st, 1868-1870 (South Africa.label: Korana War, 1st, 1868-1870
Korana War, 1st, 1868-1870 (South Africa.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1868–AD 1870] Korana War, 1st, 1868-1870. Extracted from heading "Korana War, 1st, 1868-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fighting along the middle Orange River between Korana Khoekhoe groups and colonial and Griqua forces, driven by cattle raiding, land loss and the pressure of settler expansion into the northern Cape frontier. Colonial commandos broke up the Korana strongholds, but the underlying grievances were unresolved and the conflict resumed a decade later.

Frederick I, 1523-1533 (Norway, AD 1523–.label: Frederick I, 1523-1533
Frederick I, 1523-1533 (Norway, AD 1523–.prose:
[Norway, AD 1523–AD 1533] Frederick I, 1523-1533. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Frederick I, 1523-1533". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He took the throne after the nobles deposed his nephew Christian II, promising to defend the Catholic Church and then quietly doing the opposite. At the Diet of Odense in 1527 he granted Lutheran preachers protection and let the reform movement spread through the towns. His death without a settled succession triggered the civil war known as the Count's Feud, out of which the Danish Reformation was imposed outright in 1536.

Philip V, 1316-1322 (France, AD 1316–AD.label: Philip V, 1316-1322
Philip V, 1316-1322 (France, AD 1316–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1316–AD 1322] Philip V, 1316-1322. Extracted from heading "France--History--Philip V, 1316-1322". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He took the throne by excluding his niece, establishing in practice the rule that women could not inherit the French crown, later dressed up as Salic law. He worked on standardising coinage and weights and tightening royal finance. His short reign, ending without a male heir, moved France closer to the succession crisis that opened the Hundred Years' War.

Frederick I, 1688-1713 (Germany, AD 1688.label: Frederick I, 1688-1713
Frederick I, 1688-1713 (Germany, AD 1688.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1688–AD 1713] Frederick I, 1688-1713. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick I, 1688-1713". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Elector of Brandenburg who talked his way into a crown: in 1701 he placed a royal diadem on his own head at Königsberg, becoming the first "King in Prussia" with the emperor's grudging consent. The substance of power changed little, but the title did, giving the Hohenzollern state a rank it would later grow into. His court spent lavishly on baroque building, porcelain and the new Academies of Arts and Sciences in Berlin, leaving debts his austere son would furiously reverse.

Attempted Mongol Invasions, 1274-1281 (J.label: Attempted Mongol Invasions, 1274-1281
Attempted Mongol Invasions, 1274-1281 (J.prose:
[Japan, AD 1274–AD 1281] Attempted Mongol Invasions, 1274-1281. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Attempted Mongol Invasions, 1274-1281". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kublai Khan sent two enormous fleets of Mongol, Chinese and Korean troops against Kyushu; both were mauled by Japanese defenders behind hastily built stone walls and then wrecked by typhoons, the kamikaze or 'divine winds'. Wrecks found off Takashima have yielded ships' timbers, ceramic bombs and armour. The victory drained the Kamakura shogunate, which could not reward its warriors with conquered land, and the myth of divine protection was still being invoked in the twentieth century.

John II, 1481-1495 (Portugal, AD 1481–AD.label: John II, 1481-1495
John II, 1481-1495 (Portugal, AD 1481–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1481–AD 1495] John II, 1481-1495. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John II, 1481-1495". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Perfect Prince broke the power of the great nobles by executing the Duke of Braganza and stabbing his own brother-in-law, then concentrated the crown's resources on the Atlantic. Under him Diogo Cão reached the Congo, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and spies were sent overland to India; he refused to back Columbus and then forced the Treaty of Tordesillas, which shifted the dividing line and gave Portugal Brazil.

House of Romanov, 1613-1917 (Russia, AD.label: House of Romanov, 1613-1917
House of Romanov, 1613-1917 (Russia, AD.prose:
[Russia , AD 1613–AD 1917] House of Romanov, 1613-1917. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--1613-1917". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in 1992. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A sixteen-year-old boy was elected tsar to end the Time of Troubles, and his descendants ruled for three centuries while the state expanded across Siberia to the Pacific and into the Black Sea steppe. Peter the Great forced Western technology, dress and a new capital on the country; Catherine II corresponded with philosophers while serfdom hardened around most of the population. Reform always lagged repression, and the dynasty ended with Nicholas II's abdication in 1917.

Sigismund, 1592-1599 (Sweden, AD 1592–AD.label: Sigismund, 1592-1599
Sigismund, 1592-1599 (Sweden, AD 1592–AD.prose:

Already king of Poland, the Catholic Sigismund inherited Lutheran Sweden and tried to rule it from abroad through regents. Swedish nobles and clergy rallied to his uncle Duke Charles, who beat him at Stångebro in 1598 and had him formally deposed the next year. The split turned Poland and Sweden into enemies and set off sixty years of Baltic warfare between the two branches of the Vasa family.

Leopold II, 1790-1792 (Austria, AD 1790–.label: Leopold II, 1790-1792
Leopold II, 1790-1792 (Austria, AD 1790–.prose:
[Austria, AD 1790–AD 1792] Leopold II, 1790-1792. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Leopold II, 1790-1792". Appears on p. 6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited a monarchy in turmoil from his brother Joseph II and quickly rolled back the most provocative reforms, calming rebellion in Hungary and the Austrian Netherlands. A capable and pragmatic ruler who had modernised Tuscany for decades beforehand, he tried to manage the French Revolution diplomatically, issuing the Declaration of Pillnitz with Prussia on behalf of his sister Marie Antoinette. He died suddenly, weeks before the war he had hoped to avoid broke out.

Justinian I, 527-565 (Byzantine Empire,.label: Justinian I, 527-565
Justinian I, 527-565 (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 527–AD 565] Justinian I, 527-565. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Justinian I, 527-565". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Justinian tried to put the Roman Empire back together, sending Belisarius and Narses to retake North Africa from the Vandals, Italy from the Ostrogoths and part of Spain, at enormous cost in money and lives. He had Roman law codified into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the foundation of most later European legal systems, and rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots burned the city centre. His reign ended under the shadow of the great plague of 541, which killed a vast share of the empire's population and left the reconquests impossible to hold.

Shōhei Revolt, 936-941 (Japan, AD 936–AD.label: Shōhei Revolt, 936-941
Shōhei Revolt, 936-941 (Japan, AD 936–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 936–AD 941] Shōhei Revolt, 936-941. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Shōhei Revolt, 936-941". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two simultaneous rebellions exposed how little the Kyoto court could control its provinces. In the east Taira no Masakado seized eight provinces and declared himself the New Emperor before being killed in battle; in the Inland Sea the former official Fujiwara no Sumitomo led pirate fleets that burned Dazaifu. The court had to rely on other provincial warriors to put both down, a lesson in who really held power that pointed toward the samurai age.

Charles XIV John, 1818-1844 (Sweden, AD.label: Charles XIV John, 1818-1844
Charles XIV John, 1818-1844 (Sweden, AD.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1818–AD 1844] Charles XIV John, 1818-1844. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles XIV John, 1818-1844". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born a lawyer's son in Gascony and made a marshal by Napoleon, he was elected heir to the Swedish throne by a foreign parliament and then led armies against his old emperor. He founded a dynasty that still reigns and set Sweden on the course of non-alignment and peace it has largely kept ever since. At home he grew increasingly conservative, resisting the liberal press and never fully mastering Swedish.

Irene, 797-802 (Byzantine Empire, AD 797.label: Irene, 797-802
Irene, 797-802 (Byzantine Empire, AD 797.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 797–AD 802] Irene, 797-802. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Irene, 797-802". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Irene had her son Constantine VI blinded and took the throne herself, styling herself basileus rather than empress and becoming the first woman to rule the Roman state in her own name. She had already reversed official iconoclasm at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, restoring the veneration of images. Western observers treated the imperial throne as vacant because a woman sat on it, one of the pretexts for crowning Charlemagne emperor in 800; Irene was deposed by her finance minister Nikephoros and died in exile on Lesbos.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Missouri, AD 1861–.label: Civil War, 1861-1865

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Russo-Turkish Wars, 1676-1878 (Turkey, A.prose:

Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A two-century sequence of wars in which Russia pushed south from the steppe to the Black Sea, the Crimea and eventually the approaches to Constantinople. Each round stripped territory from the Ottomans and gave Russia a claim to speak for their Orthodox subjects, feeding the independence movements of Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria. The final war ended at the gates of the Ottoman capital, and the European powers redrew its settlement at Berlin to keep Russia in check.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Romania, AD 1943.label: Bombardment, 1943-1944
Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Romania, AD 1943.prose:
[Muscel (Romania : Județ), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Muscel (Romania : Județ)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

Otto IV, 1208-1214 (Germany, AD 1208–AD.label: Otto IV, 1208-1214
Otto IV, 1208-1214 (Germany, AD 1208–AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1208–AD 1214] Otto IV, 1208-1214. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Otto IV, 1208-1214". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After his rival Philip of Swabia was murdered, Otto stood unchallenged as king and was crowned emperor in Rome. Breaking his promises to Innocent III, he attacked the papal-protected kingdom of Sicily and was excommunicated; his defeat at Bouvines by the French king destroyed his authority and handed the empire to Frederick II.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Alabama, AD 1861–A.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Alabama, AD 1861–A.prose:

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Irish Confederation, 1642-1648 (Ireland,.prose:

After the 1641 rising, Catholic landowners and clergy set up their own parliament and government at Kilkenny, controlling most of Ireland and fielding armies while professing loyalty to Charles I. The Confederation was split between those willing to settle for religious toleration under the king and a papal-nuncio party demanding the full restoration of the Catholic Church and its lands. Its factional collapse and eventual alliance with the royalists opened the way for Cromwell's brutal reconquest from 1649.

Revolution, 1896-1898 (Philippines, AD 1.label: Revolution, 1896-1898
Revolution, 1896-1898 (Philippines, AD 1.prose:
[Philippines, AD 1896–AD 1898] Revolution, 1896-1898. Extracted from heading "Philippines--History--Revolution, 1896-1898". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The secret Katipunan society under Andres Bonifacio rose against Spanish rule; after Jose Rizal's execution and Bonifacio's own killing by rivals, leadership passed to Emilio Aguinaldo, who returned from exile with American help in 1898 and declared independence at Kawit. Spain's defeat, however, ended with the islands sold to the United States at Paris. The unresolved claim to sovereignty led straight into the Philippine-American War, and 1896 remains the founding moment of Filipino nationhood.

Allied occupation, 1945-1948 (Korean Pen.label: Allied occupation, 1945-1948
Allied occupation, 1945-1948 (Korean Pen.prose:
[Korea, AD 1945–AD 1948] Allied occupation, 1945-1948. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Allied Occupation, 1945-1948". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Japan's surrender left Korea divided along the 38th parallel, Soviet forces to the north and American to the south, a line drawn hastily and meant to be temporary. Plans for trusteeship and reunification collapsed amid the widening Cold War, and each side built up a rival client government and army. Separate republics were proclaimed in 1948, setting up the war that broke out two years later.

Allied occupation, 1943-1947 (Italy, AD.label: Allied occupation, 1943-1947
Allied occupation, 1943-1947 (Italy, AD.prose:
[Italy, AD 1943–AD 1947] Allied occupation, 1943-1947. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Allied occupation, 1943-1947". Added in to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the landings in Sicily and the fall of Mussolini, Anglo-American military government took over liberated territory while the Germans held the north and a bitter partisan war raged behind their lines. Allied administrators controlled food, currency and the press, purged (unevenly) the Fascist apparatus, and gradually handed provinces back to Italian authorities. The occupation ended with a peace treaty, the loss of the colonies and Istria, and a republic voted in place of the monarchy.

Antoninus Pius, 138-161 (Roman Empire, A.label: Antoninus Pius, 138-161
Antoninus Pius, 138-161 (Roman Empire, A.prose:

Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign so uneventful in the sources that little narrative survives: no major wars in which the emperor took part, no travel outside Italy, and a treasury left in surplus. His main frontier act was advancing the British boundary to the Antonine Wall. He consolidated Hadrian's legal and administrative work and secured the smooth succession of Marcus Aurelius, whose accession the empire's later troubles would test.

New Plymouth, 1620-1691 (Massachusetts,.label: New Plymouth, 1620-1691
New Plymouth, 1620-1691 (Massachusetts,.prose:
[Massachusetts, AD 1620–AD 1691] New Plymouth, 1620-1691. Extracted from heading "Massachusetts--History--New Plymouth, 1620-1691". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.90 of LCSH 1987, and p.88 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A small band of Separatist exiles from England landed off course at Cape Cod, drew up the Mayflower Compact as a makeshift frame of self-government, and survived a first winter that killed half of them only with Wampanoag help. The colony stayed poor and thinly settled, overshadowed by Massachusetts Bay, and its alliance with the Wampanoag collapsed into the devastating King Philip's War. It was absorbed into the Massachusetts charter, but its founding story was later rebuilt into a national origin myth.

Toungoo dynasty, 1486-1752 (Burma, AD 14.label: Toungoo dynasty, 1486-1752
Toungoo dynasty, 1486-1752 (Burma, AD 14.prose:
[Burma, AD 1486–AD 1752] Toungoo dynasty, 1486-1752. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Toungoo dynasty, 1486-1752". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Burmese dynasty that rose from a small inland town to reunify the country, then under Bayinnaung built briefly the largest empire in the history of mainland Southeast Asia, swallowing the Mon kingdom of Pegu, the Shan states, Lan Na and Ayutthaya. Portuguese mercenaries, firearms and maritime trade fuelled its expansion; the later Toungoo kings retreated to a more compact, tightly administered realm around Ava before Mon rebels destroyed it in 1752.

Stuarts, 1603-1714 (United Kingdom, AD 1.label: Stuarts, 1603-1714
Stuarts, 1603-1714 (United Kingdom, AD 1.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1603–AD 1714] Stuarts, 1603-1714. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Stuarts, 1603-1714". Added to LCSH in 1986. James VI of Scotland's accession to the English throne joined the two crowns in one person, and the century that followed tested whether kings could rule without parliaments - the answer, arrived at through civil war, regicide, republic, restoration and the ejection of James II in 1688, was no. The 1707 Act of Union merged the English and Scottish parliaments into a single British state. Overseas trade, chartered companies and Atlantic colonies expanded rapidly, laying the commercial groundwork for later empire.

Puritan Revolution, 1642-1660 (England,.prose:

Civil war between King and Parliament tore England apart, ending with the trial and beheading of Charles I in 1649 - an unprecedented act that briefly abolished the monarchy. Under the Commonwealth and Oliver Cromwell's Protectorate, the country was governed by a general and an army, theatres were closed and Ireland and Scotland were subdued by force. The experiment collapsed after Cromwell's death, but the arguments it unleashed about religious liberty, popular sovereignty and the limits of royal power outlasted it.
