Count's War, 1534-1536 (Denmark, AD 1534.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1534–AD 1536] Count's War, 1534-1536. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Count's War, 1534-1536". Added to LCSH in 2005; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A civil war over the Danish succession that pitted burghers and peasants backed by Lübeck and Count Christopher of Oldenburg against the nobility's candidate, Christian III. His victory and the surrender of a starved Copenhagen settled more than a throne: the Catholic bishops were arrested, church property seized for the crown, and Denmark and Norway became Lutheran states.

Revolution, 1837-1838 (Brazil, AD 1837–A.label: Revolution, 1837-1838
Revolution, 1837-1838 (Brazil, AD 1837–A.prose:
[Bahia (Brazil), AD 1837–AD 1838] Revolution, 1837-1838. Extracted from heading "Bahia (Brazil : State)--History--Revolution, 1837-1838". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In Salvador, army officers and urban professionals led by the physician Francisco Sabino seized the city and proclaimed a Bahian republic, to last until the young Pedro II came of age. The rebels held Salvador for months before imperial troops besieged and stormed it, with heavy loss of life and mass arrests. The Sabinada, like other regency revolts, exposed how shallow imperial authority was in the provinces and hastened the 'majority' coup that put Pedro II on the throne in 1840.

Second Republic, 1848-1852 (France, AD 1.label: Second Republic, 1848-1852
Second Republic, 1848-1852 (France, AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1848–AD 1852] Second Republic, 1848-1852. Extracted from heading "France--History--Second Republic, 1848-1852". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.39 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born from the February barricades that toppled King Louis-Philippe, the republic introduced universal male suffrage overnight and abolished slavery in the French colonies, then turned on the Paris workers in the bloody June Days. Voters elected Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte president; he seized power by coup in December 1851 and crowned himself emperor a year later. The pattern of revolution, radical hope and authoritarian consolidation echoed across the Europe of 1848.

Revolution, 1830-1831 (Belarus, AD 1830–.label: Revolution, 1830-1831
Revolution, 1830-1831 (Belarus, AD 1830–.prose:
[Belarus, AD 1830–AD 1831] Revolution, 1830-1831. Extracted from heading "Belarus--History--Revolution, 1830-1831". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The November Uprising begun in Warsaw spread into the Belarusian provinces, where landowning gentry, students and some peasants formed partisan detachments against Russian garrisons. Poorly coordinated and lacking mass peasant support, the insurgent bands were defeated within months. Tsarist reprisals followed: estates confiscated, the Lithuanian Statute abolished, and the Greek Catholic Church dissolved into Orthodoxy, accelerating a long campaign of Russification.

Papal rule, 1815-1860 (Bologna, AD 1815–.label: Papal rule, 1815-1860
Papal rule, 1815-1860 (Bologna, AD 1815–.prose:
[Bologna (Italy), AD 1815–AD 1860] Papal rule, 1815-1860. Extracted from heading "Bologna (Italy)--History--Papal rule, 1815-1860". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Restored to the pope by the Congress of Vienna, the city chafed under clerical government, and its students and professionals made it a centre of conspiracy. Revolts in 1831 and 1848 were put down with Austrian troops garrisoned in the city for years afterwards, feeding the argument that the papacy could hold its territories only with foreign bayonets. In 1859 the legate left and a plebiscite the following year attached Bologna to the new Kingdom of Italy.

Abdul Aziz, 1861-1876 (Turkey, AD 1861–A.label: Abdul Aziz, 1861-1876
Abdul Aziz, 1861-1876 (Turkey, AD 1861–A.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1861–AD 1876] Abdul Aziz, 1861-1876. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Abdul Aziz, 1861-1876". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A sultan who built ironclad fleets and railways, toured European capitals, and borrowed heavily to pay for it, driving the Ottoman treasury into bankruptcy. Mounting debt and unrest in the Balkans led to his deposition by his own ministers and his death days later.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Virginia, AD 1775.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Virginia, AD 1775.prose:
[Virginia, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Virginia--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.129 of LCSH 1987, and p.127 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Delaware.label: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775
Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Delaware.prose:
[Delaware, AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "Delaware--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.26 of LCSH 1987, and p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Spanish rule, 1442-1707 (Naples, AD 1442.label: Spanish rule, 1442-1707
Spanish rule, 1442-1707 (Naples, AD 1442.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1442–AD 1707] Spanish rule, 1442-1707. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Spanish rule, 1442-1707". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.65 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alfonso of Aragon's capture of the city ended the Angevin kingdom and tied southern Italy to the Iberian crowns; from 1503 it was governed by viceroys answering to Madrid. Naples became one of the largest cities in Europe, taxed heavily to fund Spanish wars, and its resentments exploded in Masaniello's revolt of 1647. Austrian troops took the kingdom during the War of the Spanish Succession, ending more than two and a half centuries of Spanish control.

War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Latvia,.label: War of Independence, 1918-1920
War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Latvia,.prose:
[Latvia, AD 1918–AD 1920] War of Independence, 1918-1920. Extracted from heading "Latvia--History--War of Independence, 1918-1920". Added to LCSH in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Days after declaring independence, the new Estonian state had to fight off an invasion by Soviet Russia, and later German Baltic forces in the south, with help from Finnish volunteers and a British naval squadron. The Treaty of Tartu in 1920 saw Soviet Russia renounce all claims to Estonia — the first such recognition it granted anyone. Radical land reform, breaking up the Baltic German estates, followed as a reward to the soldiers who had fought.

Allied occupation, 1918-1930 (Germany, A.label: Allied occupation, 1918-1930
Allied occupation, 1918-1930 (Germany, A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1918–AD 1930] Allied occupation, 1918-1930. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Allied occupation, 1918-1930". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under the armistice and the Versailles treaty, French, British, Belgian and American troops held the German left bank of the Rhine and bridgeheads beyond it as a guarantee of reparations payments. Tension peaked when France and Belgium pushed into the Ruhr in 1923, triggering passive resistance and hyperinflation. Evacuation came early, in 1930, after the Locarno agreements and new reparations deals appeared to normalise relations.

Ordoño III, 951-956 (Spain, AD 951–AD 95.label: Ordoño III, 951-956
Ordoño III, 951-956 (Spain, AD 951–AD 95.prose:
[Leon , AD 951–AD 956] Ordoño III, 951-956. Extracted from heading "Leon (Kingdom)--History--Ordoño III, 951-956". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign in León spent holding a fractious kingdom together against his half-brother's claim and rebellious Castilian and Navarrese in-laws. He struck south with a celebrated raid that sacked Lisbon, then made peace with the Córdoban caliph before dying young, leaving the throne to the rival who had opposed him.

Mehmed II, 1451-1481 (Turkey, AD 1451–AD.label: Mehmed II, 1451-1481
Mehmed II, 1451-1481 (Turkey, AD 1451–AD.prose:

Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople in 1453 at the age of twenty-one, using enormous cast bronze cannon against walls that had held for a thousand years, and turned the city into his imperial capital. He built Topkapı Palace and the Grand Bazaar, converted Hagia Sophia to a mosque, and issued law codes that framed Ottoman administration for centuries. Further campaigns absorbed Serbia, the Morea, Trebizond and much of the Balkans, making a regional emirate into an empire straddling Europe and Asia.

Albert I, 1909-1934 (Belgium, AD 1909–AD.label: Albert I, 1909-1934
Albert I, 1909-1934 (Belgium, AD 1909–AD.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1909–AD 1934] Albert I, 1909-1934. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Albert I, 1909-1934". Appears on p.8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.9 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Refused to let German armies march through his neutral kingdom in 1914 and spent four years commanding the remnant of the Belgian army behind the flooded Yser, which made him an Allied symbol of small-nation defiance. Afterwards he oversaw reconstruction, universal male suffrage and the extension of Dutch-language rights, and died in a climbing fall on the Meuse cliffs.

Frederick II, 1544-1556 (Germany, AD 154.label: Frederick II, 1544-1556
Frederick II, 1544-1556 (Germany, AD 154.prose:

Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elector Palatine who came late to power after decades as an imperial soldier and diplomat, and who steered the Rhine Palatinate cautiously through the wars of the Reformation. In 1546 he permitted Protestant worship, and by the end of his reign the electorate had formally adopted Lutheranism, setting it on the path to becoming a leading Protestant power.

Augustus, 30 B.C.-14 A.D (Roman Empire,.label: Augustus, 30 B.C.-14 A.D
Augustus, 30 B.C.-14 A.D (Roman Empire,.prose:
[Rome, 29 BC–AD 14] Augustus, 30 B.C.-14 A.D. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Augustus, 30 B.C.-14 A.D". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Actium, Octavian kept the forms of the Republic while holding the substance of power, taking the name Augustus and ruling through accumulated offices rather than a crown. He reorganised the army, provinces and taxation, rebuilt Rome in marble, and sponsored Virgil, Horace and Livy in a literary golden age. The peace he imposed lasted two centuries, though the problem he never solved - how to hand power on - haunted every succession after him.

Christina, 1632-1654 (Sweden, AD 1632–AD.label: Christina, 1632-1654
Christina, 1632-1654 (Sweden, AD 1632–AD.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1632–AD 1654] Christina, 1632-1654. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Christina, 1632-1654". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Daughter of Gustavus Adolphus, she came to the throne as a child while Sweden fought in Germany, and her chancellor Oxenstierna steered the country to the triumphant Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Highly educated and impatient with the duties of queenship, she collected books and art, summoned Descartes to Stockholm — where he caught a fatal chill — and refused to marry. In 1654 she abdicated, converted to Catholicism and settled in Rome as a celebrated patron of music and the arts.

Herero Revolt, 1904-1907 (Namibia, AD 19.label: Herero Revolt, 1904-1907
Herero Revolt, 1904-1907 (Namibia, AD 19.prose:
[Namibia, AD 1904–AD 1907] Herero Revolt, 1904-1907. Extracted from heading "Namibia--History--Herero Revolt, 1904-1907". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.79 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Herero and later Nama communities rose against German settlers who were seizing their grazing land and cattle. After the battle at the Waterberg, General Lothar von Trotha issued an extermination order, driving survivors into the Omaheke desert and imprisoning the rest in labour camps; most of the Herero population died. It is widely regarded as the first genocide of the twentieth century, and its consequences still shape land ownership and politics in Namibia.

Interregnum, 1586-1587 (Poland, AD 1586–.label: Interregnum, 1586-1587
Interregnum, 1586-1587 (Poland, AD 1586–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1586–AD 1587] Interregnum, 1586-1587. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1586-1587". Added to LCSH in 2011, revised in 2012. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Stephen Báthory's sudden death split the nobility between the Habsburg archduke Maximilian and Sigismund Vasa of Sweden, and both were proclaimed king. The dispute was settled on the battlefield at Byczyna, where Maximilian was defeated and captured. Sigismund's victory tied Poland–Lithuania to the Swedish throne, a personal union that soon produced decades of war in the Baltic.

Charles VI, 1380-1422 (France, AD 1380–A.label: Charles VI, 1380-1422
Charles VI, 1380-1422 (France, AD 1380–A.prose:
[France, AD 1380–AD 1422] Charles VI, 1380-1422. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles VI, 1380-1422". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The king suffered recurring bouts of insanity from 1392, and in the vacuum his uncles and cousins fought for control, splitting France into Armagnac and Burgundian factions whose feud became open civil war in Paris. Henry V exploited the collapse, destroying the French nobility at Agincourt in 1415 and conquering Normandy. The Treaty of Troyes in 1420 disinherited the king's own son and made the English king his heir, a settlement the dauphin refused to accept.

Revolution, 1820-1823 (Spain, AD 1820–AD.label: Revolution, 1820-1823
Revolution, 1820-1823 (Spain, AD 1820–AD.prose:
[Spain, AD 1820–AD 1823] Revolution, 1820-1823. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Revolution, 1820-1823". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Colonel Rafael del Riego's mutiny among troops waiting to sail against the American colonies forced Ferdinand VII to swear to the liberal Constitution of 1812, opening three years of anticlerical reform, press freedom and bitter factional fighting known as the Trienio Liberal. Absolutist guerrillas and royalist juntas resisted from the start, and in 1823 a French army sent by the Congress of Verona restored the king, who executed Riego. The failure entrenched the split between liberals and absolutists that fed Spain's Carlist wars, and the distraction helped Spanish America secure independence.

Caste War, 1847-1855 (Mexico, AD 1847–AD.label: Caste War, 1847-1855
Caste War, 1847-1855 (Mexico, AD 1847–AD.prose:
[Yucatán (Mexico), AD 1847–AD 1855] Caste War, 1847-1855. Extracted from heading "Yucatán (Mexico : State)--History--Caste War, 1847-1855". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A rising of Maya villagers against the Spanish-speaking landowners and officials of Yucatán, sparked by land seizures for henequen and sugar, taxes and church fees. The rebels came close to driving the whites out of the peninsula entirely before being pushed back into the eastern forests, where they built an independent territory around the shrine of the Talking Cross at Chan Santa Cruz. Fighting and Maya autonomy in the east dragged on until Mexican troops took the shrine town in 1901.

Alexander II, 1855-1881 (Russia, AD 1855.label: Alexander II, 1855-1881
Alexander II, 1855-1881 (Russia, AD 1855.prose:
[Russia , AD 1855–AD 1881] Alexander II, 1855-1881. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Alexander II, 1855-1881". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The 'Tsar Liberator', who freed some twenty-three million serfs and followed it with new local assemblies, jury courts, universities and a reformed army, all intended to modernise Russia after defeat in the Crimea. Reform bred impatience rather than gratitude; after repeated attempts on his life he was blown apart by a bomb in Saint Petersburg on the day he approved a cautious step toward constitutional government.

Anglo-Dutch War, 1664-1667 (Netherlands,.label: Anglo-Dutch War, 1664-1667
Anglo-Dutch War, 1664-1667 (Netherlands,.prose:
[Netherlands, Great Britain, AD 1664–AD 1667] Anglo-Dutch War, 1664-1667. Spatial coverage: England, Netherlands. Extracted from heading "Anglo-Dutch War, 1664-1667". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fighting began with English seizures of Dutch trading posts in West Africa and North America — New Amsterdam became New York — and escalated into full naval war. After the Four Days' Battle and plague and fire in London, De Ruyter sailed into the Medway in 1667, burned English ships at anchor and towed away the flagship, one of the worst humiliations in Royal Navy history. The Treaty of Breda confirmed the swap of Manhattan for Suriname and eased the navigation laws.

Carl XVI Gustaf, 1973- (Sweden, AD 1973–.label: Carl XVI Gustaf, 1973-
Carl XVI Gustaf, 1973- (Sweden, AD 1973–.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1973–AD 2015] Carl XVI Gustaf, 1973-. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Carl XVI Gustaf, 1973-". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited the Swedish throne just as a new constitution stripped the monarch of all political functions, leaving a purely ceremonial head of state who does not even formally appoint governments. In 1980 Sweden adopted absolute primogeniture, making his eldest daughter Victoria heir ahead of her younger brother, a first among European monarchies.

Nicholas II, 1894-1917 (Russia, AD 1894–.label: Nicholas II, 1894-1917
Nicholas II, 1894-1917 (Russia, AD 1894–.prose:
[Russia , AD 1894–AD 1917] Nicholas II, 1894-1917. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Nicholas II, 1894-1917". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last tsar inherited an empire industrialising fast and governed by a man temperamentally unsuited to change. Defeat by Japan and the 1905 revolution forced him to concede an elected Duma he then undermined; the catastrophic cost of the First World War, and Rasputin's grip on the court, destroyed what credit the monarchy had left. He abdicated in February 1917 and was shot with his family in a cellar at Yekaterinburg the following year.

Revolution, 1789-1799 (France, AD 1789–A.label: Revolution, 1789-1799
Revolution, 1789-1799 (France, AD 1789–A.prose:
[France, AD 1789–AD 1799] Revolution, 1789-1799. Extracted from heading "France--History--Revolution, 1789-1799". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Multiple "Earlier Established Forms" indicate some disagreement about the date range of the historical event. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Financial crisis forced the calling of the Estates-General, and within months the Bastille had fallen, feudal privileges were abolished and the Declaration of the Rights of Man was proclaimed. War, the king's execution and the Terror followed, along with mass conscription, the metric system, a new calendar and the first modern experiment in a republic of citizens. It ended with Napoleon's coup, but it had already redrawn European politics and made monarchy everywhere provisional.

Balaiada Revolt, 1838-1841 (Brazil, AD 1.label: Balaiada Revolt, 1838-1841
Balaiada Revolt, 1838-1841 (Brazil, AD 1.prose:
[Maranhão (Brazil), AD 1838–AD 1841] Balaiada Revolt, 1838-1841. Extracted from heading "Maranhão (Brazil)--History--Balaiada Revolt, 1838-1841". Added to LCSH in 1993, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A rising of cowherds, artisans and runaway slaves in the backlands of Maranhão and Piauí, named for a maker of straw baskets who became one of its leaders. Sparked by conscription, abusive local officials and grinding poverty, the rebels took the town of Caxias and joined forces for a time with a quilombo of some three thousand escaped slaves. Its brutal suppression made the reputation of Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, the future Duke of Caxias, and helped convince Brazil's elite to end the Regency and crown the boy emperor Pedro II.

Henry II, 1002-1024 (Germany, AD 1002–AD.label: Henry II, 1002-1024
Henry II, 1002-1024 (Germany, AD 1002–AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1002–AD 1024] Henry II, 1002-1024. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry II, 1002-1024". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Ottonians turned attention away from Italian adventures and towards consolidating royal power in Germany, using bishops and abbots as instruments of government and endowing his new see at Bamberg lavishly. He fought long wars against Bolesław the Brave of Poland, at times allying with pagan Slavs against a Christian rival. Canonised in 1146, he is the only German emperor to be venerated as a saint.

An Lushan Rebellion, 755-763 (China, AD.label: An Lushan Rebellion, 755-763
An Lushan Rebellion, 755-763 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 755–AD 763] An Lushan Rebellion, 755-763. Extracted from heading "China--History--An Lushan Rebellion, 755-763". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A frontier general of Sogdian and Turkic descent turned his northeastern armies against the Tang court, seized Luoyang and Chang'an, and drove Emperor Xuanzong into flight. Eight years of war and the recruitment of Uighur and other allies to suppress it left the dynasty hollowed out: military governors became autonomous warlords, the census population collapsed on paper, and central control of land and taxation never recovered. Tang poetry, especially Du Fu's, is haunted by it.

Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD 1943–A.label: Bombardment, 1943-1945
Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD 1943–A.prose:
[Cuneo (Italy : Province), AD 1943–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1943-1945. Extracted from heading "Cuneo (Italy : Province)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1945". Added to LCSH in 2016. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A North Sea port and shipyard town on the Ems, it was attacked for its harbour and submarine construction and lost the overwhelming majority of its old buildings, with the centre effectively erased in a single raid in September 1944. Postwar reconstruction produced an almost entirely modern town on a medieval street plan.

Ferdinand I, 1887-1918 (Bulgaria, AD 188.label: Ferdinand I, 1887-1918
Ferdinand I, 1887-1918 (Bulgaria, AD 188.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1887–AD 1918] Ferdinand I, 1887-1918. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Ferdinand I, 1887-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Saxe-Coburg prince elected to a throne few European powers wanted to recognise, he turned a nominally Ottoman principality into a sovereign kingdom, declaring full independence in 1908 and taking the title of tsar. He led Bulgaria to victory over the Ottomans in the First Balkan War and then to disaster in the Second, and his choice to join the Central Powers in 1915 ended in defeat and his abdication in favour of his son. The pursuit of Macedonia through these wars left Bulgaria embittered and shaped its politics for decades.

Lancaster and York, 1399-1485 (England,.label: Lancaster and York, 1399-1485
Lancaster and York, 1399-1485 (England,.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1399–AD 1485] Lancaster and York, 1399-1485. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward I, 1272-1307". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry Bolingbroke's seizure of the throne from Richard II opened nearly a century in which rival branches of the Plantagenet family disputed the crown. It produced Henry V's spectacular victory at Agincourt and the loss of nearly all English lands in France, then the dynastic bloodletting later called the Wars of the Roses, fought by aristocratic retinues rather than national armies. Richard III's death at Bosworth handed the throne to the Tudors and closed the medieval English monarchy.

First Republic, 1792-1804 (France, AD 17.label: First Republic, 1792-1804
First Republic, 1792-1804 (France, AD 17.prose:
[France, AD 1792–AD 1804] First Republic, 1792-1804. Extracted from heading "France--History--First Republic, 1792-1804". Added to LCSH in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The monarchy was abolished, Louis XVI executed, and France governed successively by the Convention, the Terror, the Directory and Napoleon's Consulate. Mass conscription and revolutionary war put French armies across Europe, while the metric system, the republican calendar and the Civil Code remade daily life. It ended when the First Consul crowned himself emperor.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Kazakhstan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Kazakhstan, AD 19.prose:
[Kazakhstan, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Kazakhstan--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Christian VII, 1766-1808 (Norway, AD 176.label: Christian VII, 1766-1808
Christian VII, 1766-1808 (Norway, AD 176.prose:
[Norway, AD 1766–AD 1808] Christian VII, 1766-1808. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Christian VII, 1766-1808". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The king was mentally ill for most of his reign, so power lay with others — most spectacularly with the royal physician Struensee, who for sixteen months issued reforms abolishing censorship and torture before being executed in 1772. Later, under Crown Prince Frederik, serfdom was ended and the timber and grain trade made Norwegian merchants rich during Europe's wars. Neutrality collapsed in 1807 when the British bombarded Copenhagen and seized the fleet, cutting Norway off from Denmark by sea.

Henry III, 1216-1272 (England, AD 1216–A.label: Henry III, 1216-1272
Henry III, 1216-1272 (England, AD 1216–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1216–AD 1272] Henry III, 1216-1272. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry III, 1216-1272". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned at nine in the middle of a French invasion, he reigned for fifty-six years, pouring money into the rebuilding of Westminster Abbey and the cult of Edward the Confessor. Resentment at his foreign favourites, his failed Sicilian ambitions and his taxation drove the barons to impose the Provisions of Oxford and then to war under Simon de Montfort, who captured the king at Lewes and summoned a parliament including townsmen. Royal victory at Evesham restored Henry, but the habit of summoning parliaments stuck.

Gustav I Vasa, 1523-1560 (Sweden, AD 152.label: Gustav I Vasa, 1523-1560
Gustav I Vasa, 1523-1560 (Sweden, AD 152.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1523–AD 1560] Gustav I Vasa, 1523-1560. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav I Vasa, 1523-1560". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.112 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A nobleman turned rebel who broke Sweden out of the Danish-led Kalmar Union and made himself king, then made the crown hereditary in his family. He seized the wealth and lands of the Church to pay his debts and fund the state, steering Sweden into the Lutheran Reformation as much for revenue as for doctrine. The centralised, tax-collecting monarchy he built became the base for Sweden's rise as a great power in the following century.

Waziristan Campaign, 1919-1920 (India, A.label: Waziristan Campaign, 1919-1920
Waziristan Campaign, 1919-1920 (India, A.prose:
[India, AD 1919–AD 1920] Waziristan Campaign, 1919-1920. Extracted from heading "India--History--Waziristan Campaign, 1919-1920". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In the wake of the Third Anglo-Afghan War, British and Indian troops fought Mahsud and Wazir tribesmen in the mountains of the North-West Frontier, in some of the hardest fighting the Indian Army faced between the world wars. Convoys were ambushed on roads that had to be built as the army advanced, and aircraft and armoured cars were tried out against irregular fighters. The result was a permanent garrison and road network in tribal territory rather than a settled peace.

German occupation, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD.label: German occupation, 1943-1945
German occupation, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD.prose:
[Italy, AD 1943–AD 1945] German occupation, 1943-1945. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--German occupation, 1943-1945". Added in to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Italy signed an armistice with the Allies in September 1943, German forces disarmed the Italian army and seized the centre and north, installing Mussolini as head of the puppet Salò republic. The peninsula became a slow, brutal battlefield along the Gustav and Gothic Lines, with a growing partisan movement met by massacres such as Marzabotto and the Ardeatine Caves. The civil war that resulted shaped the politics of the postwar Italian Republic.

Aragonese and Spanish rule, 1297-1708 (S.label: Aragonese and Spanish rule, 1297-1708
Aragonese and Spanish rule, 1297-1708 (S.prose:
[Sardinia, AD 1297–AD 1708] Aragonese and Spanish rule, 1297-1708. Extracted from heading "Sardinia--History--Aragonese and Spanish rule, 1297-1708". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.101 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The pope handed the island to the king of Aragon on parchment in 1297; taking it in fact required decades of war against the Judicate of Arborea, whose resistance under Eleanor and her law code held out until 1420. Catalan-Aragonese feudal lords then reshaped landholding and settlement, and after the union of the Spanish crowns the island became a distant Habsburg viceroyalty, taxed and neglected in equal measure. Alghero still speaks a form of Catalan, a direct inheritance of the settlers planted there after the town's conquest.

Ava kingdom, ca. 1600-1752 (Burma, AD 16.label: Ava kingdom, ca. 1600-1752
Ava kingdom, ca. 1600-1752 (Burma, AD 16.prose:
[Burma, AD 1600–AD 1752] Ava kingdom, ca. 1600-1752. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Ava kingdom, ca. 1600-1752". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The restored Toungoo kings shifted their capital back to Ava and rebuilt the state on a smaller, more manageable core in the dry zone, with reformed tax rolls, a standing army and codified law. It was a long stretch of relative peace and administrative order, but the throne's grip on the Mon south and the Shan hills weakened. A Mon rebellion from Pegu captured Ava in 1752 and ended the dynasty, opening the way for Alaungpaya's Konbaung conquests.

Peasant Uprising, 1914-1915 (Albania, AD.label: Peasant Uprising, 1914-1915
Peasant Uprising, 1914-1915 (Albania, AD.prose:
[Albania, AD 1914–AD 1915] Peasant Uprising, 1914-1915. Extracted from heading "Albania--History--Peasant Uprising, 1914-1915". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Muslim peasants of central Albania, led by Haxhi Qamili, rose against the newly imported German prince Wilhelm of Wied and the landowning, Western-leaning government in Durrës, demanding the return of Ottoman authority. The rebels took much of the country and besieged the capital; Wied sailed away in September 1914 after barely six months on the throne. The collapse left Albania without a functioning state as the First World War began and foreign armies moved in from every direction.

Revolution, 1848-1849 (Germany, AD 1848–.label: Revolution, 1848-1849
Revolution, 1848-1849 (Germany, AD 1848–.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1848–AD 1849] Revolution, 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Prussia (Germany)--History--Revolution, 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

Frederick II, 1215-1250 (Germany, AD 121.label: Frederick II, 1215-1250
Frederick II, 1215-1250 (Germany, AD 121.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1215–AD 1250] Frederick II, 1215-1250. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Frederick II, 1215-1250". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Raised in Sicily and ruling an empire that stretched from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, this Hohenzollern-rival Hohenstaufen was called "the wonder of the world" for his multilingual, Arab-influenced court, his falconry treatise and his interest in natural science. He won Jerusalem by negotiation rather than battle while excommunicated, issued the Constitutions of Melfi as a model of centralised royal law, and fought the papacy so bitterly that he was deposed and denounced as Antichrist. His death left Germany to princely fragmentation and the Interregnum, and his dynasty was destroyed within a generation.

Russian occupation, 1713-1721 (Finland,.label: Russian occupation, 1713-1721
Russian occupation, 1713-1721 (Finland,.prose:
[Finland, AD 1713–AD 1721] Russian occupation, 1713-1721. Extracted from heading "Finland--History--Russian occupation, 1713-1721". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Remembered as the Great Wrath, the years when Peter the Great's armies overran the Finnish provinces during the Great Northern War. Requisitions, burnings and the seizure of people for forced labour emptied whole districts and drove the gentry and clergy across to Sweden. The Treaty of Nystad returned most of the territory but confirmed that Sweden's age as a great power was over.

Republic, 510-30 B.C (Roman Republic, 50.label: Republic, 510-30 B.C
Republic, 510-30 B.C (Roman Republic, 50.prose:
[Rome, 509 BC–29 BC] Republic, 510-30 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Republic, 510-30 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nearly five centuries of government without kings, run by elected consuls, a senate of ex-magistrates, and popular assemblies — a system later admired and copied by the framers of modern constitutions. Rome grew from one Italian city-state into an empire stretching from Spain to Syria, and the strains of that expansion (landless veterans, slave estates, generals with personal armies) tore the constitution apart. Civil war ended it, and Augustus replaced it with a monarchy that kept the republican vocabulary.

Constantines, 306-363 (Roman Empire, AD.label: Constantines, 306-363
Constantines, 306-363 (Roman Empire, AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 306–AD 363] Constantines, 306-363. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Constantines, 306-363". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The family that ruled the empire for two generations after Constantine seized power, through fratricidal civil wars between his sons and a long confrontation with Sasanian Persia. Christianity became entrenched at every level of the state, until the last of the line, Julian, tried and failed to reverse it and died on campaign in Mesopotamia.

Frederick III, 1440-1493 (Germany, AD 14.label: Frederick III, 1440-1493
Frederick III, 1440-1493 (Germany, AD 14.prose:
[Germany , AD 1440–AD 1493] Frederick III, 1440-1493. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Frederick III, 1440-1493". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The longest reign of any German king, and the last emperor to be crowned by a pope in Rome. Contemporaries mocked his slowness and his losses to Hungary, which drove him from Vienna, yet his patient dynastic manoeuvring paid off spectacularly when he married his son Maximilian to Mary of Burgundy, bringing the Low Countries into Habsburg hands. His mysterious motto AEIOU, read as "Austria will rule the whole world," proved less absurd than it looked.

Insurrection, 1831-1832 (India, AD 1831–.label: Insurrection, 1831-1832
Insurrection, 1831-1832 (India, AD 1831–.prose:
[Chota Nāgpur (India), AD 1831–AD 1832] Insurrection, 1831-1832. Extracted from heading "Chota Nāgpur (India)--History--Insurrection, 1831-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Kol peoples of the Chota Nagpur plateau rose against the outsiders — moneylenders, landlords and revenue farmers — brought in under East India Company rule, burning villages and killing hundreds before troops crushed the rising. It was one of the earliest of the tribal revolts that punctuated Company rule in eastern India, and it forced the administration to treat the highlands as a special case, eventually carving out separately governed tribal districts.

Franconian House, 1024-1125 (Germany, AD.label: Franconian House, 1024-1125
Franconian House, 1024-1125 (Germany, AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1024–AD 1125] Franconian House, 1024-1125. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Franconian House, 1024-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Also called the Salians, these four emperors pushed imperial authority to its height and then broke it against the reformed papacy. Henry IV's clash with Gregory VII over who appointed bishops produced the humiliation at Canossa in 1077 and decades of civil war, settled only by the Concordat of Worms in 1122. Their vast cathedral at Speyer, built as a dynastic burial church, remains the largest Romanesque building in Europe.

Israel-Arab War, 1948-1949 (Israel, AD 1.label: Israel-Arab War, 1948-1949
Israel-Arab War, 1948-1949 (Israel, AD 1.prose:
[Israel, Palestine, AD 1948–AD 1949] Israel-Arab War, 1948-1949. Spatial coverage: Israel, State of Palestine. Extracted from heading "Israel-Arab War, 1948-1949". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fighting that began between Jewish and Arab communities in Mandatory Palestine widened when neighbouring Arab states intervened after Israel declared independence. Israel survived and expanded beyond the UN partition lines; Egypt held Gaza and Jordan annexed the West Bank, leaving no Palestinian state. Around 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled — the Nakba — creating a refugee question that has shaped the region ever since, and the 1949 armistice lines became the de facto borders until 1967.

German occupation, 1914-1918 (Belgium, A.label: German occupation, 1914-1918
German occupation, 1914-1918 (Belgium, A.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1914–AD 1918] German occupation, 1914-1918. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--German occupation, 1914-1918". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ten northern departments, containing much of France's coal, iron and textile industry, spent the whole war behind German lines. Civilians faced requisitions, forced labour gangs, curfews and hostage-taking, while factories were stripped of machinery and orchards felled during the 1917 retreat to the Hindenburg Line. The devastated zone left behind shaped French demands for reparations and a decade of reconstruction.

Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962 (It.node: Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962 (Italy, AD 887–AD 962)
Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962 (It.label: Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962
Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962 (It.prose:
[Italy, AD 887–AD 962] Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Period of the Italian Kings, 887-962". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 63 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the Carolingian line in Italy extinguished, rival magnates – from Friuli, Spoleto, Provence and Ivrea – fought over the Iron Crown, several of them buying or seizing the imperial title in Rome for a few years at a time. Central authority dissolved into local lordships and fortified towns while Magyar and Saracen raiders roamed the peninsula. The scramble ended when Otto I of Germany came south, took the crown and tied Italy to the German monarchy for centuries.

Liao dynasty, 947-1125 (China, AD 947–AD.label: Liao dynasty, 947-1125
Liao dynasty, 947-1125 (China, AD 947–AD.prose:
[China, AD 947–AD 1125] Liao dynasty, 947-1125. Extracted from heading "China--History--Liao dynasty, 947-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Dated from the year the Khitan rulers formally adopted the Chinese dynastic name Liao after sacking the Later Jin capital, this was a steppe empire that governed nomads and Chinese farmers under two parallel administrations. Its pressure on the Song produced the treaty of Chanyuan in 1004, which bought a century of peace with annual tribute. Surviving timber pagodas and painted tombs show a distinctive fusion of Buddhist devotion, Chinese craftsmanship and steppe taste.

Edward VI, 1547-1553 (England, AD 1547–A.label: Edward VI, 1547-1553
Edward VI, 1547-1553 (England, AD 1547–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1547–AD 1553] Edward VI, 1547-1553. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward VI, 1547-1553". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A boy king ruled through protectors, Edward's short reign pushed England from Henry VIII's half-reformed church toward full Protestantism. Altars and images were stripped from parish churches and Cranmer's Books of Common Prayer imposed English-language worship. His early death at fifteen brought his Catholic half-sister Mary to the throne and a violent reversal.

Alexander III, 1249-1286 (Scotland, AD 1.label: Alexander III, 1249-1286
Alexander III, 1249-1286 (Scotland, AD 1.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1249–AD 1286] Alexander III, 1249-1286. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Alexander III, 1249-1286". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long reign remembered afterwards as a golden age of peace and prosperity. Alexander fought off Norwegian claims to the Western Isles at Largs and secured the Hebrides and Man by the Treaty of Perth in 1266, bringing the kingdom close to its modern shape. His sudden death riding along a cliff at Kinghorn left only an infant granddaughter as heir, and the succession crisis that followed opened the door to English intervention and the Wars of Independence.

Frontier Wars, 1811-1878 (South Africa,.label: Frontier Wars, 1811-1878
Frontier Wars, 1811-1878 (South Africa,.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1811–AD 1878] Frontier Wars, 1811-1878. Extracted from heading "Africa, South--History--Kafir Wars, 1811-1878". Added to the LCSH in 1986; appears on p.1 of LCSH 1975; revised in 2011. The current version of the LCSH uses "Frontier Wars" as the preferred variant, so we have changed this record to correspond to the online version. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long series of nine wars along the Cape's eastern frontier, in which Xhosa chiefdoms fought British troops and settlers over grazing land, cattle and sovereignty. Each round pushed the colonial boundary eastward, broke up Xhosa political independence and drew in mission stations, settler militias and imperial regiments. The cattle-killing of 1856-57, when prophecy led people to destroy their own herds, hastened the collapse; by the end the region was absorbed into the Cape Colony, setting the pattern of land dispossession that shaped modern South Africa.

War of 1689-1691 (Ireland, AD 1689–AD 16.label: War of 1689-1691
War of 1689-1691 (Ireland, AD 1689–AD 16.prose:
[Ireland, AD 1689–AD 1691] War of 1689-1691. Extracted from heading "Ireland--History--War of 1689-1691". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.61 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The deposed James II landed in Ireland with French support to reclaim his thrones, and Catholic Ireland became the battlefield of a European war. Apprentice boys shut the gates of Derry against him, William III beat him at the Boyne, and Jacobite hopes died at Aughrim before Limerick surrendered on terms that were swiftly broken. The Penal Laws and a Protestant landowning Ascendancy followed, and the sieges and battles are still commemorated on Ulster streets.

Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C. (.node: Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C. (China, 721 BC–480 BC)
Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C. (.label: Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C.
Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C. (.prose:
[China, 721 BC–480 BC] Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C.. Extracted from heading "China--History--Spring and Autumn period, 722-481 B.C.". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Named after the terse court chronicle of the state of Lu that covers exactly these years, this was an age of endless interstate diplomacy, oath-swearing conferences and wars fought under a nominal Zhou king. Ritual etiquette masked a brutal process of consolidation in which large states like Jin, Qi and Chu absorbed their neighbours. The chronicle's later commentaries became core texts of the Confucian canon.

South African Invasion, 1975-1976 (Angol.label: South African Invasion, 1975-1976
South African Invasion, 1975-1976 (Angol.prose:
[Angola, AD 1975–AD 1976] South African Invasion, 1975-1976. Extracted from heading "Angola--History--South African Invasion, 1975-1976". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As Portugal abandoned its colony, South African columns drove north toward Luanda in Operation Savannah to install the FNLA and UNITA before independence day. Cuban troops airlifted in by Havana halted the advance, the MPLA kept the capital, and Pretoria withdrew after its role became public and international opinion turned. The intervention internationalised Angola's civil war and locked Cuba into a decade and a half of commitment there.

Great Plague, London, England, 1664-1666.label: Great Plague, London, England, 1664-1666
Great Plague, London, England, 1664-1666.prose:
[London (England), AD 1664–AD 1666] Great Plague, London, England, 1664-1666. Extracted from heading "Great Plague, London, England, 1664-1666". Added to LCSH and revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last great bubonic epidemic in England killed perhaps a fifth of London's people, with parish clerks recording the weekly death tolls in the Bills of Mortality. The wealthy and the court fled to the country, infected households were shut up with a red cross on the door, and the dead went into mass pits outside the walls. The outbreak faded in the year the Great Fire cleared much of the old crowded city, and Defoe and Pepys made it one of the best-known disasters in English memory.

Taranaki War, 1860-1861 (New Zealand, AD.label: Taranaki War, 1860-1861
Taranaki War, 1860-1861 (New Zealand, AD.prose:
[New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1861] Taranaki War, 1860-1861. Extracted from heading "New Zealand--History--Taranaki War, 1860-1861". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fighting broke out when the colonial government pushed through a disputed purchase of Māori land at Waitara over the objections of the Te Āti Awa chief Wiremu Kīngi. British regulars found themselves bogged down against skilfully engineered Māori pā, and the war ended in an inconclusive truce. It shattered any pretence of peaceful settlement under the Treaty of Waitangi and led on to the far larger invasion of the Waikato and mass confiscation of Māori land.

Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C (E.node: Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C (Egypt, 2179 BC–1550 BC)
Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C (E.label: Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C
Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C (E.prose:

Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After a century of civil war and famine, Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt and his successors built a leaner, more bureaucratic state, moving the capital north to the Fayum region and draining land for agriculture. This was the classical age of Egyptian language and literature, producing the Tale of Sinuhe and the pessimistic wisdom texts still copied in schools a thousand years later, along with sober, watchful royal portrait sculpture. Royal power eventually frayed again, and rulers of Levantine origin, the Hyksos, took the Delta until Theban kings drove them out.

Civil War, 1955-1972 (Sudan, AD 1955–AD.label: Civil War, 1955-1972
Civil War, 1955-1972 (Sudan, AD 1955–AD.prose:
[Sudan, AD 1955–AD 1972] Civil War, 1955-1972. Extracted from heading "Sudan--History--Civil War, 1955-1972". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Southern soldiers mutinied on the eve of independence, fearing domination by the Arab and Muslim north, and the Anyanya insurgency fought on for seventeen years. Hundreds of thousands died and many more fled. The Addis Ababa Agreement granted the south regional autonomy — a settlement that held for barely a decade before war resumed.

Titus, 79-81 (Roman Empire, AD 79–AD 81).label: Titus, 79-81
Titus, 79-81 (Roman Empire, AD 79–AD 81).prose:
[Rome, AD 79–AD 81] Titus, 79-81. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Titus, 79-81". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign of barely two years crowded with disasters: Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum within weeks of his accession, then fire and plague struck Rome itself. Titus, popular for his relief efforts and his generosity, opened the Colosseum with a hundred days of games and completed the great baths beside it. He had made his name sacking Jerusalem a decade earlier, an event still advertised on the arch that bears his name.

Leo V, 813-820 (Byzantine Empire, AD 813.label: Leo V, 813-820
Leo V, 813-820 (Byzantine Empire, AD 813.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 813–AD 820] Leo V, 813-820. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Leo V, 813-820". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Armenian general who seized the throne after a crushing defeat by the Bulgars, he stabilised the northern frontier and defeated Khan Krum's successors. He revived iconoclasm in 815, arguing that the emperors who banned images had won victories while icon-venerating rulers lost them. He was murdered in the palace chapel on Christmas morning by supporters of his own former comrade, Michael the Amorian.

Henry VIII, 1509-1547 (England, AD 1509–.label: Henry VIII, 1509-1547
Henry VIII, 1509-1547 (England, AD 1509–.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1509–AD 1547] Henry VIII, 1509-1547. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry VIII, 1509-1547". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The quest for a male heir and an annulment from Catherine of Aragon led to the break with Rome, the Royal Supremacy, and the dissolution of the monasteries, which transferred perhaps a fifth of England's land to the crown and its allies. Six marriages, two executed queens and the fall of ministers from Wolsey to Cromwell made the court lethally unpredictable. He also built a permanent navy and coastal forts, leaving a realm religiously divided and financially strained.

Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989 (Iraq, AD 1986.label: Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989
Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989 (Iraq, AD 1986.prose:
[Iraq, AD 1986–AD 1989] Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989. Extracted from heading "Anfal Campaign, Iraq, 1986-1989". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A series of military operations by the Iraqi state against the Kurdish north, directed by Ali Hassan al-Majid, in which thousands of villages were bulldozed, their inhabitants deported to camps, and tens of thousands of men and boys shot in mass graves in the desert. Chemical weapons were used repeatedly, most notoriously on the town of Halabja in 1988. The campaign has been recognised as genocide by courts in Iraq and abroad, and it hardened Kurdish demands for autonomy that reshaped the country after 2003.

Theodosius II, 408-450 (Byzantine Empire.label: Theodosius II, 408-450
Theodosius II, 408-450 (Byzantine Empire.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 408–AD 450] Theodosius II, 408-450. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Theodosius II, 408-450". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Emperor from the age of seven, he reigned longer than any other Roman ruler while power lay largely with prefects, eunuchs and his formidable sister Pulcheria. His name is attached to the great land walls of Constantinople, which kept the city safe for a thousand years, and to the Theodosian Code of 438, the first official compilation of imperial law. His reign also saw the Council of Ephesus and the condemnation of Nestorius, and huge payments of gold to Attila to keep the Huns from the Danube frontier.

Frederick V, 1610-1623 (Germany, AD 1610.label: Frederick V, 1610-1623
Frederick V, 1610-1623 (Germany, AD 1610.prose:
[Palatinate (Germany), AD 1610–AD 1623] Frederick V, 1610-1623. Extracted from heading "Palatinate (Germany)--History--Frederick V, 1610-1623". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Source notes Palatinate is in modern Germany. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Calvinist Elector Palatine who accepted the crown of Bohemia offered by rebels against the Habsburgs, and lost it at the Battle of White Mountain little more than a year later, earning the nickname "the Winter King." His gamble helped ignite the Thirty Years' War; he was outlawed, stripped of the Palatinate and its electoral title, and spent his remaining years in exile in the Netherlands. His marriage to Elizabeth Stuart mattered enormously in the long run, since their descendants became the Hanoverian kings of Britain.

Weimar Republic, 1918-1933 (Germany, AD.label: Weimar Republic, 1918-1933
Weimar Republic, 1918-1933 (Germany, AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1918–AD 1933] Weimar Republic, 1918-1933. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--1918-1933". Added to LCSH in  1986, revised in 2003. Variant label used as primary, since it uses a name as well as a date range to define the period. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Germany's first democracy, born out of military defeat and revolution, with a constitution guaranteeing broad rights but a fragmented parliament and a president who could rule by decree. It survived hyperinflation, putsch attempts from left and right, and French occupation of the Ruhr, then enjoyed a few prosperous years of artistic and scientific brilliance — Bauhaus design, cabaret, expressionist film. The Depression destroyed its centre ground, and in 1933 Hitler was handed the chancellorship through the republic's own constitutional machinery.

Spanish colony, 1565-1763 (Florida, AD 1.label: Spanish colony, 1565-1763
Spanish colony, 1565-1763 (Florida, AD 1.prose:
[Florida , AD 1565–AD 1763] Spanish colony, 1565-1763. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--Spanish colony, 1565-1763". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.35 of LCSH 1987, and p.27 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded to guard the treasure fleets' route through the Bahama Channel and to expel French Protestants, St Augustine anchored a colony of soldiers, friars and mission Indians rather than planters. The Franciscan missions of Timucua and Apalachee collapsed under English and Creek raids in the early 1700s, leaving Spanish Florida a garrison huddled behind the stone walls of the Castillo de San Marcos. Spain traded the province to Britain for the return of Havana at the end of the Seven Years' War.

Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589.label: Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589
Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589.prose:
[China, AD 386–AD 589] Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two centuries of formal division, with Xianbei and other non-Han dynasties in the north and successive Chinese courts at Jiankang in the south. It was a formative age for Chinese Buddhism, for aristocratic clan politics, for poetry and calligraphy, and for the mixing of steppe and Chinese military and landholding practices. Reunification by the Sui in 589 inherited institutions worked out on both sides of the divide.

Albert I, 1298-1308 (Germany, AD 1298–AD.label: Albert I, 1298-1308
Albert I, 1298-1308 (Germany, AD 1298–AD.prose:
[Germany , AD 1298–AD 1308] Albert I, 1298-1308. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Albert I, 1298-1308". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Habsburg who seized the German throne by deposing and killing Adolf of Nassau in battle, then spent his reign clawing back crown lands and taxing the Rhine tolls, which set the electors and cities against him. He was murdered by his own nephew, and the crown passed out of Habsburg hands for a generation.

Frederick IV, 1699-1730 (Denmark, AD 169.label: Frederick IV, 1699-1730
Frederick IV, 1699-1730 (Denmark, AD 169.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1699–AD 1730] Frederick IV, 1699-1730. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick IV, 1699-1730". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spent much of his reign in the Great Northern War against Sweden, ending it with Denmark's hold on Schleswig confirmed but the old dream of recovering Scania gone. At home he abolished the last form of peasant bondage on Zealand, funded hundreds of village "cavalry schools" for rural children, and sent the first Danish missionaries to India. Copenhagen suffered plague and the catastrophic fire of 1728, while the king built Fredensborg and Frederiksberg palaces.

Ramiro II, 1134-1137 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: Ramiro II, 1134-1137
Ramiro II, 1134-1137 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1134–AD 1137] Ramiro II, 1134-1137. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Ramiro II, 1134-1137". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A monk pulled from the cloister to take the throne when his brother died childless and Aragon faced absorption by Navarre and Castile. He married, fathered a daughter, betrothed her to the count of Barcelona and promptly retired to religious life again, an arrangement that joined Aragon and Catalonia in the union that would dominate the western Mediterranean for centuries. Legend also credits him with the gruesome Bell of Huesca, beheading rebellious nobles and arranging their heads in a ring.

War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959 (Cy.node: War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959 (Cyprus, AD 1955–AD 1959)
War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959 (Cy.label: War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959
War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959 (Cy.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1955–AD 1959] War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

EOKA, led by Colonel Grivas with Archbishop Makarios as its political face, launched a guerrilla and bombing campaign to drive out the British and unite the island with Greece. The British responded with detentions, hangings and a huge garrison, while Turkish Cypriots organised against enosis and intercommunal violence took hold. The 1959 settlement gave Cyprus independence rather than union, with British bases retained and a constitution dividing power between the two communities — a compromise that satisfied neither side.

House of Austria, 1516-1700 (Spain, AD 1.label: House of Austria, 1516-1700
House of Austria, 1516-1700 (Spain, AD 1.prose:
[Spain, AD 1516–AD 1700] House of Austria, 1516-1700. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--House of Austria, 1516-1700". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Spanish Habsburgs, who inherited Castile, Aragon, the Netherlands and a growing American empire and for a time dominated Europe. American silver funded wars against the Ottomans, the Dutch rebels, France and England, but also fuelled inflation and repeated royal bankruptcies. The line ended with the childless, disabled Charles II, whose will triggered the War of the Spanish Succession and the partition of Spain's European possessions.

Despotate, 1204-1318 (Greece, AD 1204–AD.label: Despotate, 1204-1318
Despotate, 1204-1318 (Greece, AD 1204–AD.prose:
[Epirus, AD 1204–AD 1318] Despotate, 1204-1318. Spatial coverage: Albania, Greece. Extracted from heading "Epirus (Greece and Albania)--History--Despotate, 1204-1318". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Fourth Crusade shattered Byzantium, a branch of the Komnenos Doukas family carved out a Greek successor state in Epirus and western Greece, ruling from Arta and briefly holding Thessalonica and an imperial title. It was one of three rival claimants to the Byzantine legacy, fighting Latin crusader lords, Bulgarians and the emperors of Nicaea, and losing the contest to restore the empire. The line ended in 1318 with the murder of the last Komnenos Doukas ruler, after which Italian and Serbian powers moved in.

Tripolitan War, 1801-1805 (United States.label: Tripolitan War, 1801-1805
Tripolitan War, 1801-1805 (United States.prose:
[United States, AD 1801–AD 1805] Tripolitan War, 1801-1805. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Tripolitan War, 1801-1805". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 122 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The young United States refused further tribute to the Pasha of Tripoli and sent its new navy across the Atlantic instead. The war produced the burning of the captured frigate Philadelphia in Tripoli harbour and a march overland from Egypt by a handful of marines and mercenaries to take Derna — the "shores of Tripoli" of the Marine Hymn. It established the US Navy as a permanent force and set a precedent for American military action far from home.

Pastry War, 1838-1839 (Mexico, AD 1838–A.label: Pastry War, 1838-1839
Pastry War, 1838-1839 (Mexico, AD 1838–A.prose:
[Mexico, France, AD 1838–AD 1839] Pastry War, 1838-1839. Spatial coverage: France, Mexico. Extracted from heading "Pastry War, 1838-1839". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

France sent a fleet to blockade Veracruz and bombard the fortress of San Juan de Ulúa over unpaid claims by French residents, one of them a pastry cook whose shop had been ransacked. Mexico, broke and unstable, eventually agreed to pay 600,000 pesos; Antonio López de Santa Anna lost a leg driving the landing party back and used the wound to rebuild his political career. The affair set the pattern of European powers collecting debts by gunboat that culminated in the French invasion of 1862.

Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118 (Byzantine.label: Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118
Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118 (Byzantine.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1118] Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alexios took over an empire losing ground on every front and rebuilt it, beating back Norman invasions, destroying the Pechenegs and stabilising the currency with a reformed coinage. His appeal to the West for troops helped trigger the First Crusade, which he tried to steer by extracting oaths from the crusade leaders. Trading privileges granted to Venice in exchange for naval help became a long-term drain, and his daughter Anna's Alexiad remains one of the great medieval biographies.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Lithuania, AD 190.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Lithuania, AD 190.prose:
[Lithuania, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Revolution, 1830-1832 (Poland, AD 1830–A.label: Revolution, 1830-1832
Revolution, 1830-1832 (Poland, AD 1830–A.prose:
[Poland , AD 1830–AD 1832] Revolution, 1830-1832. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Revolution, 1830-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.79 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Insurrection against Russian rule spread from Warsaw into the former Grand Duchy, where noble-led detachments and peasant volunteers seized much of the countryside before regular Russian forces retook Vilnius and drove survivors into Prussia. The defeat brought sweeping punishment: Vilnius University was closed, estates were confiscated, and thousands went into exile, where Polish-Lithuanian emigre politics took root. The suppression pushed national feeling out of the manor houses and towards a new generation of writers and, eventually, peasant activists.

Tudors, 1485-1603 (England, AD 1485–AD 1.label: Tudors, 1485-1603
Tudors, 1485-1603 (England, AD 1485–AD 1.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1485–AD 1603] Tudors, 1485-1603. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Tudors, 1485-1603". Added to LCSH in 1986. Henry VII's victory at Bosworth ended the Wars of the Roses and began a dynasty that remade the English state: Henry VIII broke with Rome and dissolved the monasteries, Edward VI and Mary I pushed the country violently between Protestantism and Catholicism, and Elizabeth I settled a compromise church while fending off Spain. Royal administration, taxation and propaganda grew more centralised, and the crown began to look outward, chartering voyages that laid the groundwork for later empire. It is also the age of Shakespeare, Holbein portraits and the great brick prodigy houses.

Duchy, 1205-1458 (Greece, AD 1205–AD 145.label: Duchy, 1205-1458
Duchy, 1205-1458 (Greece, AD 1205–AD 145.prose:
[Athens, AD 1205–AD 1458] Duchy, 1205-1458. Extracted from heading "Athens (Greece)--History--Duchy, 1205-1458". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Carved out of Attica and Boeotia by crusader knights after the sack of Constantinople, the duchy centred on Athens with the Acropolis as its ducal palace and the Parthenon as its cathedral. It passed from Burgundian lords to the Catalan Company, who seized it by massacring the Frankish chivalry at the Battle of Halmyros, and later to Florentine bankers, the Acciaioli. Two and a half centuries of Latin rule left western towers and Gothic detail on classical monuments before the Ottomans took the city.

Venetian rule, 1474-1570 (Cyprus, AD 147.label: Venetian rule, 1474-1570
Venetian rule, 1474-1570 (Cyprus, AD 147.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1474–AD 1570] Venetian rule, 1474-1570. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--Venetian rule, 1474-1570". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Venice took control of Cyprus through the widowed queen Caterina Cornaro, who was persuaded to abdicate in 1489, turning the old Lusignan kingdom into a colony run for sugar, cotton and salt. Fearing Ottoman attack, the Republic threw vast bastioned walls around Nicosia and Famagusta, still the island's most striking monuments. They failed: the Ottoman invasion of 1570 and the brutal siege of Famagusta ended Venetian Cyprus and helped provoke the Holy League's victory at Lepanto.

King George's War, 1744-1748 (Rhode Isla.label: King George's War, 1744-1748
King George's War, 1744-1748 (Rhode Isla.prose:
[Rhode Island, AD 1744–AD 1748] King George's War, 1744-1748. Extracted from heading "Rhode Island--History--King George's War, 1744-1748". The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

Lothair II, 1125-1137 (Germany, AD 1125–.label: Lothair II, 1125-1137
Lothair II, 1125-1137 (Germany, AD 1125–.prose:
