Elected king over the hereditary Hohenstaufen claimant, a choice that ignited the long Welf-Hohenstaufen feud later exported to Italy as Guelphs and Ghibellines. He backed Pope Innocent II in a disputed papal election and was crowned emperor in Rome in return, and campaigned in southern Italy against the Norman kingdom. His death without a son left the succession open and the rivalry unresolved.

Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931 (Spain, AD 1886–.label: Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931
Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931 (Spain, AD 1886–.prose:
[Spain, AD 1886–AD 1931] Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

King from birth, he presided over the loss of Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines in 1898 and the national soul-searching that followed. Costly war in Morocco, culminating in the disaster at Annual, discredited the parliamentary system, and in 1923 he backed Primo de Rivera's dictatorship - a gamble that tied the crown to its failure. When republicans swept the 1931 municipal elections he left the country, and the Second Republic was proclaimed.

Pedro II, 1683-1706 (Portugal, AD 1683–A.label: Pedro II, 1683-1706
Pedro II, 1683-1706 (Portugal, AD 1683–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1683–AD 1706] Pedro II, 1683-1706. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Pedro II, 1683-1706". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had already governed for fifteen years as regent after deposing his brother, and had secured Spain's formal recognition of Portuguese independence in 1668, closing the long war of restoration. His reign brought the Methuen Treaty of 1703, trading English cloth for Portuguese wine and binding the two economies together, and Portugal's entry into the War of the Spanish Succession on the Allied side. Gold strikes in Minas Gerais in the 1690s began the Brazilian bonanza that would finance the extravagance of his successors.

Constantius II, 337-361 (Roman Empire, A.label: Constantius II, 337-361
Constantius II, 337-361 (Roman Empire, A.prose:
[Rome, AD 337–AD 361] Constantius II, 337-361. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Constantius II, 337-361". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Constantine's son secured his share of the empire in a bloody purge of relatives and spent his reign fighting rivals in the west and Persians in the east. A committed supporter of the Arian position, he used imperial power to force his theology on the church, exiling bishops who refused. Late in life he appointed his cousin Julian to defend Gaul, then died marching against him.

Ming dynasty, 1368-1644 (China, AD 1368–.label: Ming dynasty, 1368-1644
Ming dynasty, 1368-1644 (China, AD 1368–.prose:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1644] Ming dynasty, 1368-1644. Extracted from heading "China--History--Ming dynasty, 1368-1644". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Zhu Yuanzhang, a former monk and rebel commander, expelled the Mongols and founded a dynasty that made the examination-trained scholar-official the backbone of government. Cities grew, printing and vernacular fiction flourished, and merchants linked Chinese silk and porcelain to a world economy fuelled by New World silver. Peasant rebellion took Beijing in 1644, and the Manchus entered the passes to claim the throne.

Gustav V, 1907-1950 (Sweden, AD 1907–AD.label: Gustav V, 1907-1950
Gustav V, 1907-1950 (Sweden, AD 1907–AD.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1907–AD 1950] Gustav V, 1907-1950. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav V, 1907-1950". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sweden's longest-reigning king before Carl XVI Gustaf, whose 43 years spanned two world wars and the consolidation of parliamentary democracy. His 1914 Courtyard Speech, in which he defied the government over defence spending, was the last real attempt at personal rule and ended with the crown accepting that ministers, not the king, govern. He steered a careful neutrality in both wars, and in private life was a keen tennis player who competed internationally under the name 'Mr G'.

Civil War, 1975-1990 (Lebanon, AD 1975–A.label: Civil War, 1975-1990
Civil War, 1975-1990 (Lebanon, AD 1975–A.prose:
[Lebanon, AD 1975–AD 1990] Civil War, 1975-1990. Extracted from heading "Lebanon--History--Civil War, 1975-1990". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A sectarian power-sharing arrangement, strained by the presence of armed Palestinian factions and shifting demographics, collapsed into fifteen years of militia warfare. Syria and Israel both invaded and occupied territory, Beirut was split along a Green Line, and events such as the Sabra and Shatila massacre and the 1983 barracks bombings drew in outside powers. The Taif Agreement ended the fighting by adjusting the confessional formula that still governs Lebanese politics.

Boleslaus III, 1102-1138 (Poland, AD 110.label: Boleslaus III, 1102-1138
Boleslaus III, 1102-1138 (Poland, AD 110.prose:
[Poland , AD 1102–AD 1138] Boleslaus III, 1102-1138. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Boleslaus III, 1102-1138". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bolesław Wrymouth reunited Poland after a war with his half-brother, beat back a German invasion in 1109 and spent decades conquering and Christianising Pomerania, giving Poland access to the Baltic. His chaplain's chronicler, Gallus Anonymus, wrote the first history of the country at his court. His will, dividing the realm among his sons with seniority in Kraków, instead opened nearly two centuries of fragmentation.

Saxon House, 919-1024 (Germany, AD 919–A.label: Saxon House, 919-1024
Saxon House, 919-1024 (Germany, AD 919–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 919–AD 1024] Saxon House, 919-1024. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Henry the Fowler and his Ottonian successors turned the east Frankish kingdom into the dominant power of Latin Europe, breaking the Magyar raids at the Lechfeld in 955 and reviving the imperial title when Otto I was crowned in Rome in 962. Bishops and abbots were used as instruments of royal government, tying church and crown together in a bond that would explode into the Investiture Contest a century later. The dynasty's manuscripts, ivories and great churches mark a deliberate revival of Carolingian and Byzantine imperial style.

Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD 1943–A.label: Bombardment, 1943-1945
Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD 1943–A.prose:
[Vicenza (Italy : Province), AD 1943–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1943-1945. Extracted from heading "Vicenza (Italy : Province)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1945". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A North Sea port and shipyard town on the Ems, it was attacked for its harbour and submarine construction and lost the overwhelming majority of its old buildings, with the centre effectively erased in a single raid in September 1944. Postwar reconstruction produced an almost entirely modern town on a medieval street plan.

Later Three Years War, 1083-1087 (Japan,.label: Later Three Years War, 1083-1087
Later Three Years War, 1083-1087 (Japan,.prose:
[Japan, AD 1083–AD 1087] Later Three Years War, 1083-1087. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Later Three Years War, 1083-1087". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Minamoto no Yoshiie intervened in a succession quarrel among the Kiyowara of northern Honshu and won, but the court refused to call it an official campaign and paid nothing. He rewarded his warriors from his own pocket, an act that bound eastern fighting men to the Minamoto for generations and helped make them the leading samurai house. The victory also opened the north to the Northern Fujiwara, who built their golden temples at Hiraizumi.

British occupation, 1765-1947 (India, AD.label: British occupation, 1765-1947
British occupation, 1765-1947 (India, AD.prose:

The East India Company's acquisition of the revenues of Bengal turned a trading concern into a territorial power, and conquest spread across the subcontinent until the Crown took direct control after the 1857 rebellion. Railways, telegraphs, cash crops and English-language education reshaped Indian society while deindustrialisation and famine marked the cost. Nationalist mobilisation under the Congress and Gandhi ended in independence and the partition of 1947.

Danilo I, 1851-1860 (Montenegro, AD 1851.label: Danilo I, 1851-1860
Danilo I, 1851-1860 (Montenegro, AD 1851.prose:
[Montenegro, AD 1851–AD 1860] Danilo I, 1851-1860. Extracted from heading "Montenegro--History--Danilo I, 1851-1860". Added to LCSH in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Danilo refused ordination as prince-bishop and turned Montenegro into a secular principality, breaking a two-century tradition of clerical rule. He issued the country's first modern law code, taxed and disciplined the clans, and beat the Ottomans decisively at Grahovac in 1858, winning recognised borders; an exile shot him dead at Kotor two years later.

Revolution, 1895-1898 (Cuba, AD 1895–AD.label: Revolution, 1895-1898
Revolution, 1895-1898 (Cuba, AD 1895–AD.prose:

Jose Marti's organised exile movement launched the final war for Cuban independence, with Maximo Gomez and Antonio Maceo carrying the fight westward across the island. Spain's General Weyler answered by herding rural civilians into fortified towns, where perhaps 150,000 died of hunger and disease, a policy that horrified American opinion. The explosion of the USS Maine brought the United States in, ending Spanish rule but placing Cuba under American occupation and, later, the Platt Amendment.

Nama Revolt, 1904-1908 (Namibia, AD 1904.label: Nama Revolt, 1904-1908
Nama Revolt, 1904-1908 (Namibia, AD 1904.prose:
[Namibia, AD 1904–AD 1908] Nama Revolt, 1904-1908. Extracted from heading "Namibia--History--Nama Revolt, 1904-1908". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nama communities under Hendrik Witbooi and later the guerrilla leader Jakob Morenga rose against German colonial rule in the wake of the Herero war. German forces answered with extermination orders, mass deportation and camps such as Shark Island, where prisoners died in appalling numbers. Together with the Herero killings, the campaign is widely recognised as the first genocide of the twentieth century, and its consequences for land ownership in Namibia are still contested.

Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Barcelona, AD 19.label: Bombardment, 1937-1939
Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Barcelona, AD 19.prose:
[Barcelona (Spain), AD 1937–AD 1939] Bombardment, 1937-1939. Extracted from heading "Barcelona (Spain)--History--Bombardment, 1937-1939". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Republican-held port was hit again and again by Italian aircraft flying from Majorca and by warships offshore, aimed at the harbour, railway and the road link to Barcelona. Civilian districts were wrecked and much of the population fled; the raids ended only when Nationalist troops overran Catalonia.

Lý dynasty, 1010-1225 (Vietnam, AD 1010–.label: Lý dynasty, 1010-1225
Lý dynasty, 1010-1225 (Vietnam, AD 1010–.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1010–AD 1225] Lý dynasty, 1010-1225. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Lý dynasty, 1010-1225". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Lý Thái Tổ moved his capital to Thăng Long, the site of modern Hanoi, and built the first durable Vietnamese state after centuries of Chinese rule and short-lived native dynasties. Buddhism became the court religion while Confucian examinations and a Temple of Literature trained officials; armies fended off a Song invasion and pushed the frontier south against Champa. Much of what is thought of as classical Vietnamese culture — pagoda architecture, ceramics, the one-pillar pagoda, court ritual — takes shape here.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Ahmed III, 1703-1730 (Turkey, AD 1703–AD.label: Ahmed III, 1703-1730
Ahmed III, 1703-1730 (Turkey, AD 1703–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1703–AD 1730] Ahmed III, 1703-1730. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Ahmed III, 1703-1730". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign is remembered as the Tulip Era, when the Ottoman court cultivated gardens, pleasure palaces along the Golden Horn and a taste for French fashions, while embassies to Paris and Vienna brought back new ideas. Ibrahim Müteferrika's press, licensed in 1727, printed the first books in Turkish with movable type in the empire. Military defeat and economic strain fed resentment at courtly extravagance, and the Patrona Halil revolt of 1730 deposed the sultan and killed his grand vizier.

Justin II, 565-578 (Byzantine Empire, AD.label: Justin II, 565-578
Justin II, 565-578 (Byzantine Empire, AD.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 565–AD 578] Justin II, 565-578. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Justin II, 565-578". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Justinian's nephew inherited an exhausted, overstretched empire and made it worse by refusing the subsidies that had kept the Persians and the Avars quiet. Most of Italy was lost to the invading Lombards, and a renewed war with Persia went badly enough that Justin descended into mental collapse, leaving his wife Sophia and the general Tiberius to govern in his name.

Conference of Carnuntum, 308 (Austria, A.label: Conference of Carnuntum, 308
Conference of Carnuntum, 308 (Austria, A.prose:
[Rome, AD 308–AD 308] Conference of Carnuntum, 308. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Conference of Carnuntum, 308". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. With the tetrarchic system breaking down into rival claimants, the retired Diocletian was summoned back to a legionary fortress on the Danube to arbitrate. Licinius was made Augustus in the west, Maximian was ordered into retirement again, and Constantine was left with a subordinate rank he would not accept. The settlement lasted barely a moment and the empire slid on toward the wars that Constantine finally won.

Reconstruction, 1865-1877 (United States.label: Reconstruction, 1865-1877
Reconstruction, 1865-1877 (United States.prose:
[United States, AD 1865–AD 1877] Reconstruction, 1865-1877. Extracted from heading "Reconstruction (U.S. history, 1865-1877)". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Confederacy's defeat, four million freedpeople sought land, schooling, families reunited and the vote, and constitutional amendments abolished slavery and promised citizenship and equal protection. Black men were elected to state legislatures and Congress under governments backed by federal troops, while the Ku Klux Klan and other paramilitaries used terror to overthrow them. The bargain settling the 1876 election withdrew federal enforcement, leaving the South to segregation and disfranchisement, but the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments remained on the books as the legal foundation of the later civil rights movement.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Illinois, AD 1861–.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Illinois, AD 1861–.prose:
[Illinois, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Illinois--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.57 of LCSH 1987, and p.55 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572 (Poland.label: Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572
Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572 (Poland.prose:
[Poland , AD 1548–AD 1572] Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572". The last Jagiellonian king pushed through the Union of Lublin in 1569, merging Poland and Lithuania into a single Commonwealth with one elected monarch and one parliament. He kept religious peace at a moment when Protestantism was spreading fast among the nobility, and fought Russia for control of Livonia. He died childless, leaving a vast state whose kings would from then on be chosen by election.

William and Mary, 1689-1702 (England, AD.label: William and Mary, 1689-1702
William and Mary, 1689-1702 (England, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1689–AD 1702] William and Mary, 1689-1702. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--William and Mary, 1689-1702". Added to LCSH in 1986. The Dutch stadtholder and his English wife took the throne after James II fled, accepting it on terms set out in the Declaration of Rights, which barred Catholic monarchs, banned taxation and standing armies without parliament, and made regular parliaments unavoidable. The settlement was resisted in Ireland and Scotland, where it was decided by Jacobite war, and it dragged England into William's long struggle against Louis XIV. Financing that war produced the Bank of England and the national debt, the machinery of Britain's rise as a great power.

Domitian, 81-96 (Roman Empire, AD 81–AD.label: Domitian, 81-96
Domitian, 81-96 (Roman Empire, AD 81–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 81–AD 96] Domitian, 81-96. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Domitian, 81-96". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Flavian emperors ran an efficient, tightly controlled administration: he stabilised the coinage, pushed the frontier in Germany and Britain, and poured money into building in Rome. He also treated the Senate with open contempt, styled himself 'master and god', and executed enough aristocrats to earn lasting hatred from the writers who shaped his reputation. His assassination in the palace brought a smooth senatorial handover to Nerva and opened the era of the adoptive emperors.

Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648 (Pola.label: Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648
Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648 (Pola.prose:

A soldier-king who began by relieving the Russian siege of Smolensk and forcing a favourable peace, then largely kept the Commonwealth out of the Thirty Years' War raging around it. He was a lavish patron of Italian opera and painting, tolerant in religion, and repeatedly frustrated by a parliament unwilling to fund his plans for war against the Ottomans. He died just as the Cossack uprising under Khmelnytsky broke out, leaving his successor a catastrophe.

Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912 (China, A.label: Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912
Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912 (China, A.prose:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1912] Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Five and a half centuries in which China was governed by broadly similar institutions under two very different ruling houses: the Han Chinese Ming and the Manchu Qing who supplanted them in 1644. Population roughly quadrupled on New World crops, the empire expanded to its greatest extent across Central Asia and Tibet, and Chinese goods drew silver from Europe and the Americas. The era closes with the Opium Wars, the Taiping devastation, and the 1911 revolution that ended imperial rule altogether.

Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736 (Iran, AD 150.label: Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736
Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736 (Iran, AD 150.prose:

Shah Ismail's conquest gave Iran a single dynasty again and imposed Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion, a decision that still defines the country's religious map and its rivalry with the Sunni Ottomans. Under Shah Abbas I the capital moved to Isfahan, rebuilt around the great maidan with its tiled mosques, palaces and bazaar, while silk exports drew in European merchants and Armenian traders. Persian miniature painting, carpet weaving and metalwork reached a peak, before Afghan invasion collapsed the state in the 1720s.

Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D (Roman Empire, 2.label: Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D
Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D (Roman Empire, 2.prose:

Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From Augustus to the last western emperor, Rome governed the Mediterranean world as a single state, spreading cities, law, roads, coinage and Latin across three continents. Peace and trade in the first two centuries gave way to third-century military crisis, then to Diocletian's and Constantine's reorganisation and the rise of Christianity as the official religion. The western provinces fragmented into Germanic kingdoms in the fifth century, while the eastern half continued from Constantinople.

Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889 (Serbia, AD 1.label: Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889
Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889 (Serbia, AD 1.prose:
[Serbia, AD 1868–AD 1889] Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889. Extracted from heading "Serbia--History--Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Milan came to the throne as a boy and presided over Serbia's transformation from Ottoman vassal to sovereign state: independence recognised at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, a kingdom proclaimed in 1882, railways and a modern army built, and a disastrous war with Bulgaria in 1885. His autocratic style, scandalous marriage and quarrels with the Radicals wore down his support, and he abdicated in favour of his young son.

Đinh dynasty, 968-980 (Vietnam, AD 968–A.label: Đinh dynasty, 968-980
Đinh dynasty, 968-980 (Vietnam, AD 968–A.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980] Đinh dynasty, 968-980. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Đinh dynasty, 968-980". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Đinh Bộ Lĩnh defeated the twelve rival warlords, proclaimed the state of Đại Cồ Việt and set his capital in the limestone valley of Hoa Lư. It was the first durable Vietnamese monarchy after a thousand years of Chinese rule, with its own reign titles, court ranks and Buddhist clergy. The dynasty collapsed after Đinh Bộ Lĩnh's assassination, and his general Lê Hoàn took the throne in time to repel a Song invasion.

Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517 (Germ.label: Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517
Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517 (Germ.prose:
[Germany , AD 1493–AD 1517] Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517. Extracted from heading "Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A string of peasant conspiracies in the Upper Rhine and Black Forest that took as their emblem the Bundschuh, the laced peasant boot, raised on a banner against the knight's spur. Organisers such as Joss Fritz demanded the abolition of serfdom, an end to arbitrary dues and church courts, and the restoration of "godly law"; each plot was betrayed and its leaders broken on the wheel. They rehearsed the grievances and the symbolism that exploded in the German Peasants' War of 1525.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Ohio, AD 1775–AD.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Ohio, AD 1775–AD.prose:

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905 (Japan, AD.label: Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905
Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905 (Japan, AD.prose:
[Japan, Russia, AD 1904–AD 1905] Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905. Spatial coverage: Japan, Russia. Extracted from heading "Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A contest over Manchuria and Korea that opened with a surprise attack on Port Arthur and ended with the annihilation of the Russian Baltic Fleet at Tsushima. It was the first modern defeat of a European empire by an Asian state, electrifying nationalists from Turkey to India, and it triggered the 1905 revolution in Russia while confirming Japan's grip on Korea, annexed five years later.

Selim III, 1789-1807 (Turkey, AD 1789–AD.label: Selim III, 1789-1807
Selim III, 1789-1807 (Turkey, AD 1789–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1789–AD 1807] Selim III, 1789-1807. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Selim III, 1789-1807". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Watching European armies pull ahead, Selim built the Nizam-ı Cedid, a new infantry corps drilled and uniformed on Western lines, alongside new schools, embassies abroad and reformed taxes to pay for it. Napoleon's invasion of Egypt and provincial warlords stretched him thin, and the Janissaries, whose obsolescence the new army advertised, revolted and deposed him; he was murdered the following year. His programme became the template every later Ottoman reformer worked from.

Catherine I, 1725-1727 (Russia, AD 1725–.label: Catherine I, 1725-1727

A Livonian peasant woman taken captive in war who became Peter the Great's mistress, then his wife, then, on his death, the first woman to rule Russia in her own right. Real power lay with Menshikov and the Supreme Privy Council created during her short reign. Her accession, engineered by the guards regiments, set the pattern for the palace coups and female sovereigns that dominated eighteenth-century Russia.

Elizabeth, 1741-1762 (Russia, AD 1741–AD.label: Elizabeth, 1741-1762
Elizabeth, 1741-1762 (Russia, AD 1741–AD.prose:

Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peter the Great's daughter seized the throne in a guards' coup and ruled with a flair for spectacle, commissioning Rastrelli's Winter Palace and Smolny Cathedral and founding Moscow University and the Academy of Arts. She abolished the death penalty in practice, a striking gesture for the age. Her armies humbled Frederick the Great in the Seven Years' War and briefly occupied Berlin, only for her death to hand Prussia a reprieve when her admiring nephew Peter III made peace.

Carlist War, 1873-1876 (Spain, AD 1873–A.label: Carlist War, 1873-1876
Carlist War, 1873-1876 (Spain, AD 1873–A.prose:

The last great Carlist rising exploited the chaos of Spain's brief First Republic, and for a time Carlos VII ran a state of his own in Navarre and the Basque provinces, with its own mint, courts and university. The restored Bourbon monarchy defeated him and abolished the traditional Basque fueros in reprisal, an act that fed the growth of Basque nationalism.

Alfred, 871-899 (England, AD 871–AD 899).label: Alfred, 871-899
Alfred, 871-899 (England, AD 871–AD 899).prose:

Alfred ruled Wessex through the worst of the Viking onslaught, buying time after defeat, then breaking the Danish army at Edington and forcing its leader to accept baptism. He built a network of fortified burhs and a reorganised levy that made the kingdom hard to raid, issued a law code, and sponsored translations of Latin works into English so that his subjects could read them. His successors used that foundation to absorb the Danelaw and forge a single English kingdom.

New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872 (New Zealand.label: New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872
New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872 (New Zealand.prose:
[New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1872] New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872. Extracted from heading "New Zealand--History--New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

War resumed in Taranaki over a disputed land purchase and escalated into a full invasion of the Waikato aimed at breaking the Kīngitanga, the Māori King movement. Defeat was followed by mass confiscation of Māori land, which in turn fed guerrilla resistance under the prophets and leaders Te Ua Haumēne, Tītokowaru and Te Kooti. The fighting decided who controlled the North Island, and the confiscations remain the basis of Treaty settlement claims today.

Sancho II, 1223-1248 (Portugal, AD 1223–.label: Sancho II, 1223-1248
Sancho II, 1223-1248 (Portugal, AD 1223–.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1223–AD 1248] Sancho II, 1223-1248. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Sancho II, 1223-1248". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sancho II pushed the Portuguese frontier deep into the Alentejo and towards the Algarve, but lost control at home: clergy and nobles complained of lawlessness and appealed to Rome. In 1245 Pope Innocent IV declared him unfit to rule and authorised his brother Afonso to take over as regent, and after a short civil war Sancho died in exile in Toledo. It is one of medieval Europe's clearest cases of a pope deposing a reigning king.

Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699 (Austria,.label: Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699
Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699 (Austria,.prose:

The Ottoman grand vizier Kara Mustafa besieged Vienna in 1683 until a relief army led by Jan Sobieski of Poland broke the siege in a massive cavalry charge from the Kahlenberg. What followed was not a defensive war but a reconquest: Buda fell in 1686, Belgrade and Transylvania changed hands, and Eugene of Savoy shattered the Ottoman army at Zenta. The Treaty of Karlowitz gave Hungary to the Habsburgs and marked the first great Ottoman territorial retreat in Europe.

Wenzel, 1378-1400 (Germany, AD 1378–AD 1.label: Wenzel, 1378-1400
Wenzel, 1378-1400 (Germany, AD 1378–AD 1.prose:
[Germany , AD 1378–AD 1400] Wenzel, 1378-1400. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Wenzel, 1378-1400". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wenceslaus IV inherited Bohemia and the German kingship from his father Charles IV but proved unable to hold either together, quarrelling with the Bohemian nobility and the archbishop of Prague and leaving imperial affairs to drift during the Great Schism. The German electors deposed him as King of the Romans in 1400, though he kept the Bohemian crown for another decades of turmoil. His weak and indecisive rule helped open the space in which Jan Hus's reform movement grew.

Tanzimat, 1839-1876 (Turkey, AD 1839–AD.label: Tanzimat, 1839-1876
Tanzimat, 1839-1876 (Turkey, AD 1839–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1839–AD 1876] Tanzimat, 1839-1876. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Tanzimat, 1839-1876". Added to LCSH in 1989, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A programme of state remaking launched by imperial edict, promising security of life and property to all subjects regardless of religion and dismantling old privileges. New law codes, secular schools, provincial councils, conscription, banks and a telegraph network were introduced on European models, while the empire went into debt to pay for them. The reforms produced a new class of Western-educated officials who eventually demanded more than the sultan intended, culminating in the first Ottoman constitution.

Amid the chaos of the Year of the Four Emperors, the Batavian auxiliary commander Julius Civilis raised his people and neighbouring Germanic and Gallic tribes against Rome on the Rhine. Legions defected, forts burned, and a short-lived Gallic Empire was proclaimed before Vespasian's general Cerialis restored control. Rome afterwards reorganised its frontier armies to keep auxiliary units away from their homelands, and Tacitus made the episode a set piece on the limits of empire.

Alfonso VIII, 1158-1214 (Kingdom of Cast.prose:

His crushing defeat by the Almohads at Alarcos in 1195 was answered seventeen years later at Las Navas de Tolosa, where a coalition of Iberian kings broke Almohad power and opened Andalusia to conquest. He also founded the first Castilian university at Palencia and married Eleanor, daughter of Henry II of England, tying Castile into wider European politics.

Third Crusade, 1189-1192 (Anatolia, AD 1.label: Third Crusade, 1189-1192
Third Crusade, 1189-1192 (Anatolia, AD 1.prose:

Launched after Saladin destroyed the crusader army at Hattin and took Jerusalem, this campaign drew in three of Europe's greatest rulers. Frederick Barbarossa marched a vast German army overland across Anatolia, storming Konya before drowning in a Cilician river, after which his force largely dissolved; Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus came by sea. The crusaders retook Acre and the coast but never Jerusalem, settling for a truce that guaranteed Christian pilgrims access to the city.

The last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty came to the throne at sixteen, resettled populations wholesale, pushed hard against Bulgars and Arabs, and called the Quinisext Council to legislate on church discipline. He was the first ruler to put an image of Christ on his coins. Heavy taxation and the brutality of his officials provoked a revolt that ended with his nose slit and exile to the Crimea.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Azerbaijan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Azerbaijan, AD 19.prose:

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Otto IV, 1198-1215 (Germany, AD 1198–AD.label: Otto IV, 1198-1215
Otto IV, 1198-1215 (Germany, AD 1198–AD.prose:

The Welf candidate in the long double election against the Staufer Philip of Swabia, Otto won the crown only after Philip's murder and was made emperor by Pope Innocent III. He promptly turned on his papal patron by invading southern Italy, was excommunicated, and lost his cause at Bouvines, where his French and English coalition was broken by Philip Augustus. The young Frederick II took the empire, and Otto ended his life a deposed prince in Saxony.

Schism, 1837-1870 (United States, AD 183.label: Schism, 1837-1870
Schism, 1837-1870 (United States, AD 183.prose:

American Presbyterians split into Old School and New School factions over revivalism, doctrinal looseness and the churches' cooperation with interdenominational mission societies, with slavery straining every seam. Each faction later divided again along North-South lines as the Civil War approached, so that a single denomination became four. Reunion in the North came only in 1869-70, leaving a separate southern church that endured for over a century.

Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C (Greec.label: Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C
Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C (Greec.prose:
[Greece, 358 BC–322 BC] Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Philip II turned a peripheral northern kingdom into the dominant power in Greece, remodelling his army around the sarissa-armed phalanx and paying for it with Thracian gold mines. Victory at Chaeronea gave him control of the Greek city-states through the League of Corinth; his assassination handed the planned invasion of Persia to his son Alexander. Within thirteen years Macedonian armies had reached the Indus, and the independent Greek polis was finished as a political force.

British occupation, 1762-1763 (Cuba, AD.label: British occupation, 1762-1763
British occupation, 1762-1763 (Cuba, AD.prose:

A British expedition took Havana after a two-month siege in the Seven Years' War, seizing the treasure fleet and a third of the Spanish navy. Eleven months of free trade flooded the island with goods and enslaved Africans and gave Cuban planters a taste of open commerce. Britain handed Havana back in exchange for Florida, but the shock pushed Spain into reforming the colony's defences and economy.

Hova rule, 1810-1885 (Madagascar, AD 181.label: Hova rule, 1810-1885
Hova rule, 1810-1885 (Madagascar, AD 181.prose:

From the highland capital of Antananarivo, Radama I used muskets and British advisers to bring most of Madagascar under Merina control, while missionaries reduced Malagasy to writing. His successor Ranavalona I expelled the foreigners and persecuted Christian converts for three decades; later rulers reversed course, adopted Christianity as the court religion and abolished slavery. Growing French pressure ended the kingdom's independence in the 1880s.

Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D (Spain, 2.label: Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D
Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D (Spain, 2.prose:

Rome landed troops in Iberia to cut Carthage off from its Spanish silver and manpower, and stayed for six centuries. Conquest was slow and bloody – Numantia, the Lusitanian wars, the final Cantabrian campaigns – but the peninsula ended up among the most thoroughly Romanised provinces, exporting olive oil, garum and metals across the Mediterranean and sending Trajan, Hadrian and Seneca to Rome. Aqueducts, bridges and amphitheatres at Mérida, Segovia and Tarragona survive from it, and Latin here became Spanish and Portuguese.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (South Carolina, A.prose:

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Enthroned as a six-year-old after his father was strangled, he presided over decades in which real power lay with his mother and then with the Köprülü grand viziers, who restored the treasury and the army. Their campaigns took Crete from Venice and pushed into Poland and Ukraine, but the great gamble on Vienna in 1683 ended in catastrophe outside the city walls. Defeats to the Holy League followed, and the army deposed him.

Zhou dynasty, 1122-221 B.C. (China, 1121.label: Zhou dynasty, 1122-221 B.C.
Zhou dynasty, 1122-221 B.C. (China, 1121.prose:

Traditional dating for the dynasty that replaced the Shang and gave China the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven. Ritual bronzes, jades and inscribed vessels from its courts are among the finest ever cast, while its later centuries of warfare between rival states drove the rise of Confucianism, Daoism and Legalism. It ended when Qin conquered the last rivals and unified the empire.

Charles IV, 1859-1872 (Norway, AD 1859–A.label: Charles IV, 1859-1872
Charles IV, 1859-1872 (Norway, AD 1859–A.prose:
[Norway, AD 1859–AD 1872] Charles IV, 1859-1872. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Charles IV, 1859-1872". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ruling Norway in personal union with Sweden, where he reigned as Carl XV, he was a painter and poet, popular and inclined to constitutional compromise. His reign brought the end of Sweden's four-estate parliament and a new bicameral Riksdag, along with legal codification in Norway. His enthusiasm for Scandinavian unity ran ahead of his ministers, who blocked aid to Denmark in 1864 — a humiliation that killed political Scandinavianism.

Venetian Settlements, 1204-1715 (Greece,.label: Venetian Settlements, 1204-1715
Venetian Settlements, 1204-1715 (Greece,.prose:
[Peloponnesus, AD 1204–AD 1715] Venetian Settlements, 1204-1715. Extracted from heading "Peloponnesus (Greece : Peninsula)--History--Venetian Settlements, 1204-1715". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2012. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The partition of the Byzantine Empire after the Fourth Crusade let Venice pick out the harbours and islands it wanted: Crete, Negroponte, Modon and Coron, Corfu and the Ionian islands, and a scatter of Aegean lordships. These were commercial stepping-stones on the route to the Levant, garrisoned, fortified and run by governors sent from the lagoon. Piece by piece the Ottomans took them, and the bastions, loggias and winged lions left behind still mark the coastlines.

Mary Stuart, 1542-1567 (Scotland, AD 154.label: Mary Stuart, 1542-1567
Mary Stuart, 1542-1567 (Scotland, AD 154.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1542–AD 1567] Mary Stuart, 1542-1567. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Mary Stuart, 1542-1567". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned as an infant, raised at the French court and briefly queen of France, she came home to rule a Scotland newly won for Protestantism and never mastered its factions. A disastrous second marriage, the murder of her husband Darnley and her swift remarriage to the chief suspect brought armed rebellion and forced abdication in favour of her baby son. Her flight into England turned her into the focus of Catholic plotting against Elizabeth I and, eventually, into a martyr.

Edward I, 1272-1307 (England, AD 1272–AD.label: Edward I, 1272-1307
Edward I, 1272-1307 (England, AD 1272–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1272–AD 1307] Edward I, 1272-1307. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward I, 1272-1307". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward conquered Wales and ringed it with castles such as Caernarfon and Harlech, then intervened in the Scottish succession and began decades of war in the north. His reign systematised English law and made parliaments, including the summoning of knights and burgesses, a regular tool of royal taxation. He also expelled England's Jewish population in 1290, a ban that lasted centuries.

Mieszko I, 960-992 (Poland, AD 960–AD 99.label: Mieszko I, 960-992
Mieszko I, 960-992 (Poland, AD 960–AD 99.prose:
[Poland , AD 960–AD 992] Mieszko I, 960-992. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Mieszko I, 960-992". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Polish ruler known from written sources, Mieszko welded the Polans and neighbouring tribes into a single duchy and accepted Christian baptism in 966, marrying the Bohemian princess Doubravka. Conversion brought bishops, Latin literacy and a place in Latin Christendom, while his wars with the Germans and control of Pomerania set Poland's early frontiers. The document known as Dagome iudex placed his lands under papal protection.

Lothair II, 1125-1137 (Germany, AD 1125–.label: Lothair II, 1125-1137
Lothair II, 1125-1137 (Germany, AD 1125–.prose:
[Germany , AD 1125–AD 1137] Lothair II, 1125-1137. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Lothair II, 1125-1137". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Lothar II, 1125-1137" appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. In the online LCSH, the label is "Lothar III". Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected king over the hereditary Hohenstaufen claimant, a choice that ignited the long Welf-Hohenstaufen feud later exported to Italy as Guelphs and Ghibellines. He backed Pope Innocent II in a disputed papal election and was crowned emperor in Rome in return, and campaigned in southern Italy against the Norman kingdom. His death without a son left the succession open and the rivalry unresolved.

Julius II, 1503-1513 (Papal States, AD 1.label: Julius II, 1503-1513
Julius II, 1503-1513 (Papal States, AD 1.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1503–AD 1513] Julius II, 1503-1513. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Julius II, 1503-1513". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.75 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The "Warrior Pope" led armies in person to recover and expand papal territory in central Italy, drove the French out through the shifting alliances of the League of Cambrai and the Holy League, and founded the Swiss Guard. He also spent lavishly on art: he tore down the old St Peter's to begin Bramante's new basilica, set Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling and carve his tomb, and hired Raphael for the Vatican apartments. The fundraising for St Peter's, continued by his successor, helped provoke Luther's protest a few years later.

Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485 (England, A.label: Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485
Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485 (England, A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1455–AD 1485] Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485". Added to LCSH in 2003. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A drawn-out dynastic quarrel between the houses of Lancaster and York, fought by armed noble affinities across a country where the crown had lost both money and authority after defeat in France. Battles such as Towton and Tewkesbury killed off much of the old aristocracy and saw kings deposed, restored and murdered. Henry Tudor's victory at Bosworth ended the cycle and founded a dynasty that would rule for over a century, with a monarchy far less dependent on great magnates.

Self strengthening movement, 1861-1895 (.label: Self strengthening movement, 1861-1895
Self strengthening movement, 1861-1895 (.prose:
[China, AD 1861–AD 1895] Self strengthening movement, 1861-1895. Extracted from heading "China--History--Self strengthening movement, 1861-1895". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After defeats by Britain and France and the near-collapse of the Taiping years, Qing officials like Li Hongzhang and Zeng Guofan set out to buy and build Western military technology while leaving Confucian government intact. The result was arsenals, shipyards, telegraph lines, coal mines, steamship companies and the Beiyang Fleet — modern hardware bolted onto an unreformed state. Japan's crushing victory in 1894–95 exposed the limits of that bargain and pushed Chinese reformers toward changing the political system itself.

Huguenot colony, 1562-1565 (Florida, AD.label: Huguenot colony, 1562-1565
Huguenot colony, 1562-1565 (Florida, AD.prose:
[Florida , AD 1562–AD 1565] Huguenot colony, 1562-1565. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--Huguenot colony, 1562-1565". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.35 of LCSH 1987, and p.27 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

French Protestants under Jean Ribault and René de Laudonnière tried to plant a refuge and a privateering base on the Atlantic coast, building Fort Caroline near the St Johns River. Spain regarded it as heresy astride the treasure fleet route, and Pedro Menéndez de Avilés stormed the fort and executed the shipwrecked survivors at Matanzas. To hold the coast he founded St Augustine, the oldest continuously occupied European town in the United States.

Waldemar IV, 1340-1375 (Denmark, AD 1340.label: Waldemar IV, 1340-1375
Waldemar IV, 1340-1375 (Denmark, AD 1340.prose:
[Denmark , AD 1340–AD 1375] Waldemar IV, 1340-1375. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Waldemar IV, 1340-1375". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Waldemar Atterdag inherited a kingdom that had been mortgaged piece by piece to German creditors and spent his reign buying, bullying and fighting it back together. He sold Estonia to the Teutonic Order to fund the work, seized Scania and sacked Gotland's rich town of Visby, but his attack on Hanseatic trade provoked a league of merchant cities that beat him and imposed the Treaty of Stralsund, granting them privileges and a say in choosing Danish kings. His daughter Margaret would use the reassembled kingdom as the foundation of the Kalmar Union.

Tây Sơn dynasty, 1788-1802 (Vietnam, AD.label: Tây Sơn dynasty, 1788-1802
Tây Sơn dynasty, 1788-1802 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1788–AD 1802] Tây Sơn dynasty, 1788-1802. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Tây Sơn dynasty, 1788-1802". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A revolt led by three brothers from a Highland village swept away both the Nguyễn lords of the south and the Trịnh lords and Lê emperors of the north, ending two centuries of division. Nguyễn Huệ crushed a Qing invasion army at Thăng Long in the lunar new year of 1789, a victory still celebrated as a national epic. His early death left the regime weak, and Nguyễn Ánh reconquered the country in 1802 to found the Nguyễn dynasty and the unified state named Vietnam.

Modern, 1580- (Portugal, AD 1580–AD 2015.label: Modern, 1580-
Modern, 1580- (Portugal, AD 1580–AD 2015.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1580–AD 2015] Modern, 1580-. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Modern, 1580-". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Spanish Habsburgs took the Portuguese crown in 1580, and the sixty-year union drew Portugal into Spain's wars and cost it much of its Asian trading network to the Dutch. Independence was restored in 1640 under the Braganças, and Brazilian gold and diamonds funded a lavish court until the 1755 earthquake levelled Lisbon and prompted its rational rebuilding. Napoleonic invasion, the loss of Brazil, the republic of 1910, the long Salazar dictatorship and the 1974 Carnation Revolution and decolonisation follow.

Contestado Insurrection, 1912-1916 (Braz.label: Contestado Insurrection, 1912-1916
Contestado Insurrection, 1912-1916 (Braz.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1912–AD 1916] Contestado Insurrection, 1912-1916. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--Contestado Insurrection, 1912-1916". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A rebellion of backcountry settlers in the pine forests on the Santa Catarina-Paraná border, sparked by land seizures tied to a foreign-owned railway and timber concession. Followers of the wandering monk José Maria built fortified holy villages and fought under a messianic banner promising a restored monarchy; the Brazilian army eventually crushed them with thousands of troops, aircraft and scorched-earth tactics, killing perhaps 20,000 people.

Bảy Thưa Uprising, 1867-1873 (Vietnam, A.label: Bảy Thưa Uprising, 1867-1873
Bảy Thưa Uprising, 1867-1873 (Vietnam, A.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1867–AD 1873] Bảy Thưa Uprising, 1867-1873. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Bảy Thưa Uprising, 1867-1873". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An armed revolt in the Mekong Delta swamps led by Trần Văn Thành, a follower of the Bửu Sơn Kỳ Hương religious movement, after France annexed the western provinces of Cochinchina. His fortified base in the flooded Bảy Thưa forest held out for years before French troops overran it and he was killed. The rising shows how millenarian religious brotherhoods, not just the mandarin class, drove early southern resistance to colonial rule.

Valentinian III, 425-455 (Roman Empire,.label: Valentinian III, 425-455
Valentinian III, 425-455 (Roman Empire,.prose:
[Rome, AD 425–AD 455] Valentinian III, 425-455. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Valentinian III, 425-455". Added to LCSH in 2003, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A child emperor who never truly ruled, dominated first by his mother Galla Placidia and then by the general Aetius, whose armies held together what remained of the western provinces. During these decades North Africa was lost to the Vandals, Britain slipped away entirely, and Attila's Huns were fought to a standstill on the Catalaunian Plains. Valentinian murdered Aetius with his own hands in 454 and was assassinated in turn the next year, opening two decades of puppet emperors that ended the western empire.

Civil War, 1846-1847 (Portugal, AD 1846–.label: Civil War, 1846-1847
Civil War, 1846-1847 (Portugal, AD 1846–.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1846–AD 1847] Civil War, 1846-1847. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Civil War, 1846-1847". Added to LCSH in 1994, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Maria da Fonte rising, sparked by rural anger over taxes and new burial laws, toppled the government and slid into the wider Patuleia war between radicals based in Porto and the supporters of Queen Maria II. Neither side could win outright, and the conflict ended only when Britain and Spain intervened under the Quadruple Alliance, imposing the Convention of Gramido. The settlement ushered in the more stable era of Regeneration politics.

Soviet occupation, 1939-1941 (Estonia, A.label: Soviet occupation, 1939-1941
Soviet occupation, 1939-1941 (Estonia, A.prose:
[Baltic States, AD 1939–AD 1941] Soviet occupation, 1939-1941. Spatial coverage: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania. Extracted from heading "Baltic States--History--Soviet occupation, 1939-1941". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in 2010. Spatial coverage extent inferred from common use of term "Baltic States" as shorthand for Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Forced by the secret protocols of the Nazi-Soviet pact to accept Red Army bases, the republic was annexed outright in 1940 and its government, army and economy dismantled. Political leaders and thousands of ordinary families were arrested or deported to Siberia, culminating in the mass deportation of June 1941. German invasion ended the occupation weeks later, and the memory of that first Soviet year shaped Baltic politics for the rest of the century.

Spanish colony, 1784-1821 (Florida, AD 1.label: Spanish colony, 1784-1821
Spanish colony, 1784-1821 (Florida, AD 1.prose:
[Florida , AD 1784–AD 1821] Spanish colony, 1784-1821. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--Spanish colony, 1784-1821. Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.35 of LCSH 1987, and p.27 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spain regained Florida after the American Revolution but never repopulated or controlled it, tolerating British traders, Seminole towns and communities of escaped slaves. Repeated United States incursions, including Andrew Jackson's raids, made the province untenable. Spain ceded it under the Adams-Onís Treaty, completing the American acquisition of the Gulf coast.

Bombardment, 1944-1945 (Liège, AD 1944–A.label: Bombardment, 1944-1945
Bombardment, 1944-1945 (Liège, AD 1944–A.prose:
[Liège (Belgium), AD 1944–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1944-1945. Extracted from heading "Liège (Belgium)--History--Bombardment, 1944-1945". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From June 1944 the country was struck by pilotless V-1 flying bombs and then by V-2 rockets, which arrived without warning at supersonic speed and could not be intercepted. They killed thousands, triggered a second mass evacuation from London, and announced the age of the guided missile — the technology and many of the engineers passed straight into the Cold War rocket programmes.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Connecticut, AD 18.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Connecticut, AD 18.prose:
[Connecticut, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Connecticut--History--Civil War". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.24 of LCSH 1987, and p.20 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Bourbons, 1589-1789 (France, AD 1589–AD.label: Bourbons, 1589-1789
Bourbons, 1589-1789 (France, AD 1589–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1589–AD 1789] Bourbons, 1589-1789. Extracted from heading "France--History--Bourbons, 1589-1789". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry IV ended the Wars of Religion and founded a dynasty that turned France into Europe's dominant power, culminating in Louis XIV's centralised court at Versailles and near-continuous warfare. Royal absolutism was paid for by a tax system that spared the privileged, and by the 1780s the crown was bankrupt. The calling of the Estates-General in 1789 opened the revolution that swept the monarchy away.

Bombardment, 1863-1864 (Japan, AD 1863–A.label: Bombardment, 1863-1864
Bombardment, 1863-1864 (Japan, AD 1863–A.prose:
[Shimonoseki-shi (Japan), AD 1863–AD 1864] Bombardment, 1863-1864. Extracted from heading "Shimonoseki-shi (Japan)--History--Bombardment, 1863-1864". Added to LCSH in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British warships shelled Kagoshima in reprisal for the killing of an Englishman, and an allied fleet of British, French, Dutch and American ships smashed the Chōshū batteries commanding the Shimonoseki Strait. The samurai domains that had led the cry to 'expel the barbarians' learned first-hand how far Western firepower outclassed their own. Satsuma and Chōshū turned instead to buying ships and guns and to overthrowing the shogunate, the alliance that produced the Meiji Restoration.

Federalist Revolution, 1893-1895 (Brazil.label: Federalist Revolution, 1893-1895
Federalist Revolution, 1893-1895 (Brazil.prose:
[Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil), AD 1893–AD 1895] Federalist Revolution, 1893-1895. Extracted from heading "Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil : State)--History--Federalist Revolution, 1893-1895". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A savage civil war in southern Brazil between supporters of the positivist state government and federalist rebels, entangled with a naval revolt against the young republic in Rio. Prisoners were routinely executed by throat-cutting, and the government's victory consolidated the authoritarian style of politics in Rio Grande do Sul.

Alfonso XI, 1312-1350 (Kingdom of Castil.label: Alfonso XI, 1312-1350
Alfonso XI, 1312-1350 (Kingdom of Castil.prose:
[Castile, AD 1312–AD 1350] Alfonso XI, 1312-1350. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso XI, 1312-1350". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He broke the power of the great nobles who had run Castile during his long minority and, with the Ordenamiento de Alcalá, gave the kingdom a coherent legal hierarchy. His victory at the Río Salado in 1340 ended the last serious Moroccan invasion of Iberia. He died of plague while besieging Gibraltar, one of the few reigning monarchs killed by the Black Death.

Under Mediation act, 1803-1814 (Switzerl.label: Under Mediation act, 1803-1814
Under Mediation act, 1803-1814 (Switzerl.prose:
[Switzerland, AD 1803–AD 1814] Under Mediation act, 1803-1814. Extracted from heading "Switzerland--History--Under Mediation act, 1803-1814". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.114 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the centralised Helvetic Republic collapsed in disorder, Napoleon summoned Swiss delegates to Paris and imposed a settlement that restored the cantons as self-governing states within a loose confederation. Six new cantons, including Vaud, Aargau and Ticino, were created from former subject territories and admitted as equals, permanently ending the old system of ruling and ruled lands. The price was dependence on France and thousands of Swiss soldiers for its armies; the arrangement fell with Napoleon in 1814.

Revolution, 1902-1903 (Venezuela, AD 190.label: Revolution, 1902-1903
Revolution, 1902-1903 (Venezuela, AD 190.prose:
[Venezuela, AD 1902–AD 1903] Revolution, 1902-1903. Extracted from heading "Venezuela--History--Revolution, 1902-1903". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.106 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Liberating Revolution united regional caudillos and foreign-backed business interests under Manuel Antonio Matos in an attempt to unseat Cipriano Castro. It coincided with a British, German and Italian naval blockade of Venezuelan ports over unpaid debts, which rallied nationalist opinion behind Castro. His victory at Ciudad Bolivar broke the power of the old regional strongmen and centralised the state, while the debt crisis produced the Drago Doctrine and Theodore Roosevelt's corollary to the Monroe Doctrine.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Florida, AD 1775–.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Florida, AD 1775–.prose:
[Florida , AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.35 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Manuel I, 1495-1521 (Portugal, AD 1495–A.label: Manuel I, 1495-1521
Manuel I, 1495-1521 (Portugal, AD 1495–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1495–AD 1521] Manuel I, 1495-1521. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Manuel I, 1495-1521". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign in which Portugal's investment in exploration paid off spectacularly: Vasco da Gama reached India, Cabral touched Brazil, and Portuguese fleets seized Goa, Malacca and Hormuz to control the sea route in spices. The king took the title Lord of the Conquest, Navigation and Commerce of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia and India, and spent the profits on the exuberant maritime-themed Manueline architecture of Belém. He also forced the conversion or expulsion of Portugal's Jews, a decision that drove talent and capital abroad.

Mehmed VI, 1918-1922 (Turkey, AD 1918–AD.label: Mehmed VI, 1918-1922
Mehmed VI, 1918-1922 (Turkey, AD 1918–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1918–AD 1922] Mehmed VI, 1918-1922. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mehmed VI, 1918-1922". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Ottoman sultan inherited a defeated empire under Allied occupation, with foreign warships in the Bosphorus. His government signed the punitive Treaty of Sèvres and condemned the nationalist movement in Anatolia, which under Mustafa Kemal won the war of independence and abolished the sultanate. He left Istanbul aboard a British battleship, ending a dynasty of more than six hundred years.

Sigismund, 1411-1437 (Germany, AD 1411–A.label: Sigismund, 1411-1437
Sigismund, 1411-1437 (Germany, AD 1411–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1411–AD 1437] Sigismund, 1411-1437. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Sigismund, 1411-1437". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Luxembourg emperor summoned the Council of Constance, which ended the Great Schism of rival popes and restored a single papacy. The same council burned Jan Hus despite Sigismund's safe-conduct, igniting the Hussite wars that consumed Bohemia for a generation and repeatedly defeated imperial armies. He was crowned emperor only in 1433, and his death without a male heir passed the imperial title to the Habsburgs for good.

Civil War, 1462-1472 (Catalonia, AD 1462.label: Civil War, 1462-1472
Civil War, 1462-1472 (Catalonia, AD 1462.prose:
[Catalonia (Spain), AD 1462–AD 1472] Civil War, 1462-1472. Extracted from heading "Catalonia (Spain)--History--Civil War, 1462-1472". Added to LCSH in 2008, revised in 2012. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A ten-year struggle between John II of Aragon and the Catalan institutions - the Generalitat and the Barcelona oligarchy - which deposed him as count and offered the crown in turn to Castilian, Portuguese and Angevin princes. Peasant grievances over feudal dues and factional fighting inside Barcelona ran through the conflict. John's victory and the conciliatory Capitulation of Pedralbes ended Catalan political autonomy in practice and left the principality depopulated and impoverished, shifting the balance within Spain decisively toward Castile.

Bernese rule, 1536-1798 (Switzerland, AD.label: Bernese rule, 1536-1798
Bernese rule, 1536-1798 (Switzerland, AD.prose:
[Vaud (Switzerland), AD 1536–AD 1798] Bernese rule, 1536-1798. Extracted from heading "Vaud (Switzerland)--History--Bernese rule, 1536-1798". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bern seized the Vaud and other lands from Savoy, becoming the largest city-state north of the Alps and ruling its new subjects through appointed bailiffs from a patrician council. The Reformation was imposed at once, monasteries dissolved and their wealth turned to schools and poor relief, while the countryside was drained, surveyed and taxed. Resentment at rule by a closed Bernese elite fed the revolt that welcomed French troops in 1798 and swept the old order away.

War of 1912-1913 (Bulgaria, AD 1912–AD 1.label: War of 1912-1913
War of 1912-1913 (Bulgaria, AD 1912–AD 1.prose:
[Balkan Peninsula, AD 1912–AD 1913] War of 1912-1913. Spatial coverage: Bulgaria, Serbia, Turkey. Extracted from heading "Balkan Peninsula--History--War of 1912-1913". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Spatial coverage extracted from related subject headings. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bulgaria led the Balkan League that drove the Ottomans almost out of Europe, its armies bearing the heaviest fighting at Kirkkilise, Lule Burgas and the long siege of Adrianople. Victory turned to disaster when Bulgaria attacked its former allies over the division of Macedonia and was beaten by Serbia, Greece, Romania and the Ottomans together. The loss of most of the conquered land bred a bitterness that pushed Bulgaria into alliance with Germany in both world wars.

Julio-Claudians, 30 B.C.-68 A.D (Roman E.label: Julio-Claudians, 30 B.C.-68 A.D
Julio-Claudians, 30 B.C.-68 A.D (Roman E.prose:
[Rome, 29 BC–AD 68] Julio-Claudians, 30 B.C.-68 A.D. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Julio-Claudians, 30 B.C.-68 A.D". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975 as "The five Julii". Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Counted from Octavian's victory over Antony and Cleopatra, which left one man in control of the Roman world, to the suicide of Nero a century later. In between, the republic's institutions were kept as a facade over personal rule, the frontiers were pushed to the Danube, Rhine and into Britain, and provincial cities across the Mediterranean were remade in Roman form. The dynasty's collapse showed that emperors could be made by the armies, not only born to the purple.

Civil War, 1967-1970 (Nigeria, AD 1967–A.label: Civil War, 1967-1970
Civil War, 1967-1970 (Nigeria, AD 1967–A.prose:
[Nigeria, AD 1967–AD 1970] Civil War, 1967-1970. Extracted from heading "Nigeria--History--Civil War, 1967-1970". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.84 of LCSH 1987, and p.70 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The eastern region declared itself the Republic of Biafra after pogroms against Igbo civilians; the federal government responded with blockade and invasion. Mass starvation in the enclave was broadcast worldwide, giving rise to modern humanitarian campaigning and to Médecins Sans Frontières. Biafra surrendered in 1970 after perhaps a million or more deaths, most from hunger.

Edward III, 1327-1377 (England, AD 1327–.label: Edward III, 1327-1377
Edward III, 1327-1377 (England, AD 1327–.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1327–AD 1377] Edward III, 1327-1377. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward III, 1327-1377". Added to LCSH in 1986.
