Edward claimed the French crown and launched the Hundred Years War, winning famous victories at Crécy, Sluys and Poitiers and turning warfare into a source of national prestige. He cultivated chivalric display, founding the Order of the Garter, while parliament grew stronger as it funded his campaigns. The Black Death struck midway through the reign, killing perhaps a third of the population and reshaping labour, wages and law.

Tiberius, 14-37 (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD.label: Tiberius, 14-37
Tiberius, 14-37 (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 14–AD 37] Tiberius, 14-37. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Tiberius, 14-37". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Augustus's stepson inherited an office that had never before been handed on, and by taking it he proved the principate was a monarchy rather than a restored republic. An able commander and careful administrator who kept the frontiers quiet and the finances sound, he grew steadily more isolated, allowed the praetorian prefect Sejanus to terrorise the Senate through treason trials, and finally retired to Capri, ruling by letter amid rumours of cruelty and vice.

Frederick V, 1746-1766 (Norway, AD 1746–.label: Frederick V, 1746-1766
Frederick V, 1746-1766 (Norway, AD 1746–.prose:
[Norway, AD 1746–AD 1766] Frederick V, 1746-1766. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Frederick V, 1746-1766". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A charming, hard-drinking king who left government largely to able ministers, above all J. H. E. Bernstorff and A. G. Moltke, and Denmark enjoyed peace and profitable neutral trade while wars raged elsewhere. The reign built the Frederiksstaden district of Copenhagen with the Amalienborg palaces and the Marble Church, founded academies of art and sciences, and dispatched the celebrated scientific expedition to Arabia from which only Carsten Niebuhr returned.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Connecticut, AD 1.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Connecticut, AD 1.prose:
[Connecticut, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Connecticut--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.24 of LCSH 1987, and p.20 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

French Revolution, 1789-1793 (Corsica, A.label: French Revolution, 1789-1793
French Revolution, 1789-1793 (Corsica, A.prose:
[Corsica (France), AD 1789–AD 1794] French Revolution, 1789-1793. Extracted from heading "Corsica (France)--History--1789-1794". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Earlier established form used for primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Revolution made Corsica a full département of France and brought Paoli home from London exile to popular acclaim. Radicalisation in Paris soon split the island: Paoli, denounced by the Convention, broke with the Republic and turned to Britain, while the Bonaparte family fled to the mainland. The result was the short-lived Anglo-Corsican Kingdom and a permanent rupture in Corsican politics.

First Crusade, 1096-1099 (Anatolia, AD 1.label: First Crusade, 1096-1099
First Crusade, 1096-1099 (Anatolia, AD 1.prose:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1096–AD 1099] First Crusade, 1096-1099. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--First, 1096-1099". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Western armies crossed the Bosphorus, besieged and took Nicaea for the Byzantine emperor, and fought their way across the Anatolian plateau, beating the Seljuk Turks at Dorylaeum before the long, brutal siege of Antioch. The march restored western Anatolia to Byzantine control and opened the road to Jerusalem. It also created the first Crusader states and set the pattern of Latin involvement in the eastern Mediterranean for two centuries.

Otto I, 936-973 (Germany, AD 936–AD 973).label: Otto I, 936-973
Otto I, 936-973 (Germany, AD 936–AD 973).prose:
[Germany , AD 936–AD 973] Otto I, 936-973. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Otto I, 936-973". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned at Aachen on Charlemagne's throne, Otto subdued rebellious dukes, crushed the Magyars at the Lechfeld and ended their raids on the West, then took the imperial crown in Rome. He built his power on bishops and abbots appointed by the king, whose lands and troops served the crown but could not be inherited – a system that shaped German politics for centuries. His coronation is conventionally the founding of the Holy Roman Empire.

George IV, 1820-1830 (United Kingdom, AD.label: George IV, 1820-1830
George IV, 1820-1830 (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1820–AD 1830] George IV, 1820-1830. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George IV, 1820-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Extravagant, unpopular and heavily in debt, he had already governed as Prince Regent and left his mark chiefly on taste: Regency terraces, Nash's remodelling of London, and the fantastical Royal Pavilion at Brighton. His public attempt to divorce Queen Caroline turned into a national scandal, and Catholic Emancipation was forced through against his wishes in 1829.

Ferdinand II, 1619-1637 (Germany, AD 161.label: Ferdinand II, 1619-1637
Ferdinand II, 1619-1637 (Germany, AD 161.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1619–AD 1637] Ferdinand II, 1619-1637. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Ferdinand II, 1619-1637". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Austria--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Jesuit-educated hardliner whose determination to restore Catholicism to the Habsburg lands turned the Bohemian revolt into a European war. Victory at White Mountain let him execute or dispossess the Czech nobility and rebuild Bohemia as a Catholic, German-speaking crown land; his Edict of Restitution of 1629 then demanded the return of church property across the Empire and drove Protestant princes and Sweden into arms against him. He raised, and eventually murdered, the mercenary commander Wallenstein, whose private armies showed how war had become a business.

Civil War, 1992-1994 (Tajikistan, AD 199.label: Civil War, 1992-1994
Civil War, 1992-1994 (Tajikistan, AD 199.prose:
[Tajikistan, AD 1992–AD 1994] Civil War, 1992-1994. Extracted from heading "Tajikistan--History--Civil War, 1992-1994". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Independence from the Soviet Union was followed almost at once by fighting between the ex-communist government, supported by Russia and Uzbekistan, and an opposition alliance of Islamists and democrats, largely along regional lines. Tens of thousands were killed and much of the population displaced in the first year alone. A UN-brokered settlement in 1997 brought opposition figures into government, an unusual power-sharing outcome in post-Soviet Central Asia.

Alexander II, 1214-1249 (Scotland, AD 12.label: Alexander II, 1214-1249
Alexander II, 1214-1249 (Scotland, AD 12.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1214–AD 1249] Alexander II, 1214-1249. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Alexander II, 1214-1249". Added to LCSH in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Consolidated royal power in Scotland by suppressing revolts in Galloway and the north, and reached a lasting settlement with England at York that fixed the frontier and ended Scottish claims to the northern counties. He died on the island of Kerrera while pressing his campaign to buy or seize the Hebrides from Norway.

Revolution, 1926-1929 (Nicaragua, AD 192.label: Revolution, 1926-1929
Revolution, 1926-1929 (Nicaragua, AD 192.prose:
[Nicaragua, AD 1926–AD 1929] Revolution, 1926-1929. Extracted from heading "Nicaragua--History--Revolution, 1926-1929". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.84 of LCSH 1987, and p.70 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A constitutionalist revolt by Liberals against a Conservative government drew in the United States Marines, who imposed a peace settlement and supervised elections. Augusto César Sandino refused to disarm and took to the northern mountains, waging a guerrilla campaign that pinned down the Marines for years. His war made him a symbol of resistance to US intervention across Latin America and gave the Sandinistas of the 1970s their name.

German occupation, 1940-1945 (Norway, AD.label: German occupation, 1940-1945
German occupation, 1940-1945 (Norway, AD.prose:
[Norway, AD 1940–AD 1945] German occupation, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--German Occupation, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark was seized in a few hours and then governed with unusual lightness: the king stayed, parliament sat, and the country was presented as a model protectorate supplying food to Germany. Cooperation collapsed in August 1943 amid strikes and sabotage; when deportation of Denmark's Jews was ordered that October, the resistance and ordinary citizens ferried some 7,000 people to safety in Sweden.

Northern Seven Years' War, 1563-1570 (De.label: Northern Seven Years' War, 1563-1570
Northern Seven Years' War, 1563-1570 (De.prose:
[Denmark, Norway, Sweden, AD 1563–AD 1570] Northern Seven Years' War, 1563-1570. Spatial coverage: Denmark, Norway, Sweden. Extracted from heading "Three Crowns' War, 1563-1570". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark-Norway, with Lübeck and Poland, fought Sweden for control of Baltic trade and the Sound tolls in a war of sieges, naval battles and scorched-earth raiding across the border provinces. Neither side gained much: the Peace of Stettin restored the pre-war frontiers, and Sweden bought back the fortress of Älvsborg. The struggle set the pattern of Danish-Swedish rivalry that dominated Scandinavia for the next century and a half.

Xhosa Cattle-Killing, 1856-1857 (South A.label: Xhosa Cattle-Killing, 1856-1857
Xhosa Cattle-Killing, 1856-1857 (South A.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1856–AD 1857] Xhosa Cattle-Killing, 1856-1857. Extracted from heading "South Africa--History--Xhosa Cattle-Killing, 1856-1857". Added to LCSH in 1988. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Following the prophecies of the young seer Nongqawuse, Xhosa communities slaughtered their cattle and destroyed their grain in the belief that the ancestors would rise, drive out the British and restore the herds. Instead came famine: tens of thousands died and survivors streamed into the Cape Colony as labourers. The catastrophe shattered Xhosa independence on the eastern frontier and opened their land to white settlement.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (Massachusetts, AD.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (Massachusetts, AD.prose:

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

Ferdinand II, 1479-1516 (Kingdom of Arag.label: Ferdinand II, 1479-1516
Ferdinand II, 1479-1516 (Kingdom of Arag.prose:

His marriage to Isabella of Castile joined the two largest Iberian crowns while keeping their laws and institutions separate, creating a dynastic union rather than a single state. Under him Granada fell in 1492, Jews and later Muslims were expelled or forced to convert, Columbus sailed under Castilian patronage, and Spanish armies under Gonzalo de Córdoba won Naples from France. He annexed Navarre in 1512, leaving nearly all of Iberia except Portugal under one family.

German occupation, 1940-1945 (France, AD.prose:

Denmark was seized in a few hours and then governed with unusual lightness: the king stayed, parliament sat, and the country was presented as a model protectorate supplying food to Germany. Conspiracy of Catiline, 65-62 B.C (ancie.node: Conspiracy of Catiline, 65-62 B.C (ancient Rome, 64 BC–61 BC)
Conspiracy of Catiline, 65-62 B.C (ancie.label: Conspiracy of Catiline, 65-62 B.C
Conspiracy of Catiline, 65-62 B.C (ancie.prose:

Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A patrician bankrupted by failed election campaigns gathered indebted nobles, Sullan veterans and rural discontents in a plot to seize power in Rome. Cicero, as consul, exposed it in a famous series of speeches and had the captured conspirators executed without trial, a decision that later drove him into exile. Catiline died with his army in Etruria, and the affair became the standard example of how far the late Republic's politics had decayed.

Dano-Swedish Wars, 1657-1660 (Denmark, A.label: Dano-Swedish Wars, 1657-1660
Dano-Swedish Wars, 1657-1660 (Denmark, A.prose:
[Denmark, Sweden, AD 1657–AD 1660] Dano-Swedish Wars, 1657-1660. Spatial coverage: Denmark, Sweden. Extracted from heading "Dano-Swedish Wars, 1657-1660". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark's attempt to recover its losses collapsed when Karl X Gustav marched his army across the frozen Great and Little Belts to threaten Copenhagen; the Treaty of Roskilde stripped away Scania, Halland and Blekinge, fixing the modern Swedish-Danish border. The Swedes attacked again months later, but Copenhagen's citizens held the walls and a Dutch fleet broke the blockade. The humiliation discredited the nobility and led the king to impose hereditary absolute monarchy in 1660.

Frederick William, the Great Elector, 16.node: Frederick William, the Great Elector, 1640-1688 (Germany, AD 1640–AD 1688)
Frederick William, the Great Elector, 16.label: Frederick William, the Great Elector, 1640-1688
Frederick William, the Great Elector, 16.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1640–AD 1688] Frederick William, the Great Elector, 1640-1688. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick William, the Great Elector, 1640-1688". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inheriting a scattering of war-ruined territories from Brandenburg to the Rhine and East Prussia, Frederick William welded them together with a permanent standing army, a central war-tax administration and a cowed nobility that traded political rights for control over its serfs. He broke Polish overlordship in Prussia, drained marshes, dug canals and invited in Dutch settlers and some 20,000 Huguenot refugees after Louis XIV revoked their toleration. The machinery he built - army, bureaucracy, and a state geared to funding both - is the direct ancestor of the Prussian kingdom his son proclaimed.

Lam Sơn Uprising, 1418-1428 (Vietnam, AD.label: Lam Sơn Uprising, 1418-1428
Lam Sơn Uprising, 1418-1428 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1418–AD 1428] Lam Sơn Uprising, 1418-1428. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Lam Sơn Uprising, 1418-1428". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2012. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A ten-year guerrilla war led by Lê Lợi against the Ming occupation of Vietnam, beginning with a small band in the mountains of Thanh Hóa and ending with the siege and surrender of Ming garrisons in the Red River delta. Victory restored Vietnamese independence and founded the Later Lê dynasty, which ruled in some form for over three centuries. The strategist Nguyễn Trãi's proclamation of victory became a foundational text of Vietnamese national identity.

Michael VIII Palaeologus, 1261-1282 (Byz.label: Michael VIII Palaeologus, 1261-1282
Michael VIII Palaeologus, 1261-1282 (Byz.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1261–AD 1282] Michael VIII Palaeologus, 1261-1282. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Michael VIII Palaeologus, 1261-1282". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-regent who blinded the boy emperor he served, Michael seized Constantinople from its Latin occupiers in 1261 and restored the Byzantine Empire after fifty-seven years of exile. He spent the rest of his reign in relentless diplomacy, buying off Charles of Anjou, fomenting the Sicilian Vespers, and forcing an unpopular church union with Rome at Lyons to stave off a new crusade. The state he rebuilt was smaller and poorer than before, and his neglect of the Anatolian frontier left the door open to the Turkish emirates, among them the Ottomans.

Basil I, 867-886 (Byzantine Empire, AD 8.label: Basil I, 867-886
Basil I, 867-886 (Byzantine Empire, AD 8.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 867–AD 886] Basil I, 867-886. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Basil I, 867-886". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Macedonian peasant turned imperial groom who charmed his way to the throne and murdered his patron Michael III to take it, founding a dynasty that ruled Byzantium for nearly two centuries. He launched a sweeping revision of Roman law in Greek, later completed as the Basilika, rebuilt churches and pushed Byzantine power back into southern Italy and the Aegean.

Kenmu Restoration, 1333-1336 (Japan, AD.label: Kenmu Restoration, 1333-1336
Kenmu Restoration, 1333-1336 (Japan, AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 1333–AD 1336] Kenmu Restoration, 1333-1336. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Kenmu Restoration, 1333-1336". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Emperor Go-Daigo's attempt to abolish rule by warriors and restore government by the throne, made possible when Ashikaga Takauji and other commanders defected and burned Kamakura. The new regime handed offices and estates to courtiers and temples while the fighting men who had won the war went unrewarded; within three years Takauji turned on Go-Daigo, enthroned a rival emperor and founded the Ashikaga shogunate, leaving Go-Daigo to hold a court in exile in the mountains of Yoshino.

Nian Rebellion, 1853-1868 (China, AD 185.label: Nian Rebellion, 1853-1868
Nian Rebellion, 1853-1868 (China, AD 185.prose:
[China, AD 1853–AD 1868] Nian Rebellion, 1853-1868. Extracted from heading "China--History--Nian Rebellion, 1853-1868". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Nien Rebellion, 1853-1868" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bands of mounted raiders from the flood-ravaged Huai River plains fortified their earth-walled villages and struck at Qing tax collectors and grain convoys, moving too fast for imperial infantry to pin down. Running at the same time as the Taiping and Muslim revolts, the Nian stretched the dynasty to breaking point. They were finally crushed by Zeng Guofan's and Li Hongzhang's regional armies, whose success shifted real military power from the throne to provincial commanders.

House of York, 1461-1485 (England, AD 14.label: House of York, 1461-1485
House of York, 1461-1485 (England, AD 14.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1461–AD 1485] House of York, 1461-1485. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--House of York, 1461-1485". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward IV won the throne on the battlefield, lost it briefly to a Lancastrian restoration, and won it back at Barnet and Tewkesbury, presiding over a period of recovering trade and the arrival of Caxton's printing press. His early death left a twelve-year-old heir who vanished into the Tower with his brother while their uncle took the crown as Richard III. Two years later Richard died at Bosworth, the last English king killed in battle, and the Tudors took over.

War against the Peru-Bolivian Confederat.node: War against the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, 1837-1839 (Argentina, AD 1837–AD 1839)
War against the Peru-Bolivian Confederat.label: War against the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, 1837-1839
War against the Peru-Bolivian Confederat.prose:
[Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Peru, AD 1837–AD 1839] War against the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, 1837-1839. Spatial coverage: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Peru. Extracted from heading "Peru-Bolivian Confederation, War against the, 1837-1839". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Andrés de Santa Cruz's union of Peru and Bolivia alarmed its neighbours, and Rosas's Argentina joined Chile in trying to break it up. The Argentine northern campaign went badly and achieved little; it was the Chilean victory at Yungay that destroyed the Confederation. The episode fixed the borders and rivalries of the southern Andes for generations.

Probus, 276-282 (Roman Empire, AD 276–AD.label: Probus, 276-282
Probus, 276-282 (Roman Empire, AD 276–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 276–AD 282] Probus, 276-282. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Probus, 276-282". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A capable soldier-emperor who spent his short reign clearing Germanic invaders from Gaul and restoring the Rhine and Danube frontiers. He set legionaries to draining marshes and planting vineyards in the provinces, work that reportedly contributed to his murder by his own troops. His victories helped stabilise the empire just before Diocletian's sweeping reorganisation.

Seventh Crusade, 1248-1250 (Levant, AD 1.label: Seventh Crusade, 1248-1250
Seventh Crusade, 1248-1250 (Levant, AD 1.prose:
[Europe, Levant, AD 1248–AD 1250] Seventh Crusade, 1248-1250. Spatial coverage: Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Seventh, 1248-1250". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Louis IX of France sailed against Egypt, the seat of Ayyubid power, taking Damietta easily before his army was trapped and destroyed on the Nile at Mansurah. The king himself was captured and ransomed, and while in captivity the Mamluk regiments overthrew their Ayyubid masters, founding a sultanate that would eventually drive the crusaders from the mainland. Louis spent four more years in the Levant fortifying coastal towns, and his failure marked the end of large royal expeditions with any real chance of retaking Jerusalem.

Frederick William IV, 1840-1861 (Germany.label: Frederick William IV, 1840-1861
Frederick William IV, 1840-1861 (Germany.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1840–AD 1861] Frederick William IV, 1840-1861. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick William IV, 1840-1861". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A romantic, devout and artistically minded king who dreamed of a medieval Christian monarchy and pushed forward the completion of Cologne Cathedral. The revolution of 1848 forced him to concede a parliament and a constitution, but he refused the imperial crown offered by the Frankfurt Assembly because it came from the people rather than from princes, killing the liberal path to German unity. The 1850s brought conservative retrenchment and diplomatic humiliation by Austria; after a stroke in 1857 his brother ruled as regent.

Persian Wars, 500-449 B.C. (Greece, 499.label: Persian Wars, 500-449 B.C.
Persian Wars, 500-449 B.C. (Greece, 499.prose:
[Greece, 499 BC–448 BC] Persian Wars, 500-449 B.C.. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Persian Wars, 500-449 B.C.--Campaigns". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ionian cities' revolt drew Persian armies into Greece, and against the odds coalitions of Greek states won at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea. Victory left Athens with a powerful navy and the leadership of the Delian League, which soon hardened into an empire, and gave Greeks a durable sense of themselves as distinct from 'barbarians' – a confidence visible in the drama, history-writing and temple-building that followed.

Republic, 510-265 B.C (Roman Republic, 5.label: Republic, 510-265 B.C
Republic, 510-265 B.C (Roman Republic, 5.prose:
[Rome, 509 BC–264 BC] Republic, 510-265 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Republic, 510-265 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. This must be Early Republic in conventional chronology. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the expulsion of the kings, Rome was governed by annually elected magistrates and a senate, with plebeians slowly forcing their way into office through the long "Struggle of the Orders" — tribunes, the Twelve Tables, and eventually the consulship. Militarily it was a story of grinding local warfare: the Latin and Samnite wars, a Gallic sack of the city around 390 BC, and finally the defeat of Pyrrhus, which left Rome master of the Italian peninsula. The alliance system built in these centuries supplied the manpower that later beat Carthage.

Kings, 753-510 B.C (ancient Rome, 752 BC.label: Kings, 753-510 B.C
Kings, 753-510 B.C (ancient Rome, 752 BC.prose:
[Rome, 752 BC–509 BC] Kings, 753-510 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Kings, 753-510 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rome's legendary regal era, traditionally seven kings from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud, during which a cluster of hilltop villages became a walled city with a forum, temples, a senate and the beginnings of civic religion and law. Etruscan influence shows in its engineering and ritual. The expulsion of the last king established the Republic and left Romans with a lasting horror of monarchy.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Ukraine, AD 1917–.label: Revolution, 1917-1921
Revolution, 1917-1921 (Ukraine, AD 1917–.prose:
[Ukraine, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Ukraine--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Maine, AD 1861–AD.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Maine, AD 1861–AD.prose:
[Maine, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Maine--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 74 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Ararat Rebellion, 1927-1930 (Turkey, AD.label: Ararat Rebellion, 1927-1930
Ararat Rebellion, 1927-1930 (Turkey, AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1927–AD 1930] Ararat Rebellion, 1927-1930. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Ararat Rebellion, 1927-1930". Added to LCSH in 2007, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kurdish nationalists organised through the Xoybûn league declared a republic in the mountains around Mount Ararat and, under the former Ottoman officer Ihsan Nuri, held the highlands for three years. Ankara answered with aircraft, artillery and tens of thousands of troops, aided by a border agreement with Iran that closed off the rebels' refuge. The suppression was followed by deportations and resettlement laws aimed at breaking Kurdish regional autonomy for good.

Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660 (Finland, AD.label: Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660
Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660 (Finland, AD.prose:
[Finland, AD 1654–AD 1660] Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660. Extracted from heading "Finland--History--Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660". Added to LCSH 1986, revised in 2007. An identical entry exists under heading "Sweden--History" with a distinct URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-king who spent his entire short reign at war, most famously marching an army across the frozen Danish straits in a gamble that forced Denmark to surrender Scania and made Sweden's borders roughly what they are today. For Finland, then the realm's eastern half, it meant conscription, taxes and Russian raids along the Karelian frontier. His sudden death at 37 left an empire at its greatest extent and deepest exhaustion.

Albrecht von Mecklenburg, 1363-1388 (Swe.label: Albrecht von Mecklenburg, 1363-1388
Albrecht von Mecklenburg, 1363-1388 (Swe.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1363–AD 1388] Albrecht von Mecklenburg, 1363-1388. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Albrecht von Mecklenburg, 1363-1388". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A German prince brought in by Swedish magnates to replace Magnus Eriksson, whose reign filled the kingdom's castles with German nobles and merchants and drained royal power into aristocratic hands. His defeat and capture at Falköping handed Sweden to Margaret of Denmark and opened the way to the Kalmar Union.

Period of discoveries, 1385-1580 (Portug.label: Period of discoveries, 1385-1580
Period of discoveries, 1385-1580 (Portug.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1385–AD 1580] Period of discoveries, 1385-1580. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Period of discoveries, 1385-1580". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under the Aviz kings, a small Atlantic kingdom pushed down the African coast, settled Madeira and the Azores, rounded the Cape, and opened sea routes to India, Brazil, and eventually Japan. Spices, gold and enslaved Africans flowed through Lisbon, and fortified trading posts strung from Sofala to Macau made Portugal the first global maritime empire. The line ended with the young king Sebastião's death in Morocco and the crown's absorption by Spain.

Jagellons, 1386-1572 (Poland, AD 1386–AD.label: Jagellons, 1386-1572
Jagellons, 1386-1572 (Poland, AD 1386–AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1386–AD 1572] Jagellons, 1386-1572. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Jagellons, 1386-1572". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Lithuanian grand duke married Poland's queen, accepted baptism and founded a dynasty that ruled the largest state in Europe, at times adding the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary. Its armies broke the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410; its universities and courts carried the Renaissance into central Europe, and its relative religious tolerance sheltered Protestants and Jews. The line's last king pushed through the Union of Lublin, welding Poland and Lithuania into a single commonwealth just before he died childless.

Turkish Conquest, 1570-1571 (Cyprus, AD.label: Turkish Conquest, 1570-1571
Turkish Conquest, 1570-1571 (Cyprus, AD.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1570–AD 1571] Turkish Conquest, 1570-1571. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--Turkish Conquest, 1570-1571". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Ottoman expeditionary force landed and took Nicosia by storm, then besieged Famagusta for nearly a year; its Venetian commander Bragadin was flayed after the surrender. The loss of the island prompted the Holy League and the naval victory at Lepanto, which came too late to save Cyprus. Ottoman rule replaced the Latin elite and restored the Greek Orthodox hierarchy.

Mongol Invasion, 1241-1242 (Hungary, AD.label: Mongol Invasion, 1241-1242
Mongol Invasion, 1241-1242 (Hungary, AD.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1241–AD 1242] Mongol Invasion, 1241-1242. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Mongol Invasion, 1241-1242". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Mongol army annihilated the Hungarian host at Mohi within a year of crossing the Carpathians, and King Béla IV fled to the Adriatic coast while the countryside was burned and depopulated. The invaders withdrew abruptly in 1242, and Béla rebuilt the kingdom around stone castles, fortified towns and invited settlers - a defensive programme that reshaped Hungarian settlement patterns. The episode is remembered as the sharpest break in medieval Hungarian history.

Arab period, 640-885 (Armenia, AD 640–AD.label: Arab period, 640-885
Arab period, 640-885 (Armenia, AD 640–AD.prose:
[Armenia, AD 640–AD 885] Arab period, 640-885. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Arab period, 640-885". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.5 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Arab armies swept through the highlands in the 640s, and the Caliphate governed the country as the province of Arminiya from Dvin, ruling through a resident governor while leaving the great noble houses largely in place. Heavy taxation and periodic revolts — put down savagely — thinned the old aristocracy, but the Bagratuni and Artsruni families manoeuvred their way to dominance. The period closes with Ashot I crowned king in 885, restoring an Armenian monarchy with the Caliph's own blessing.

Rákóczi Uprising, 1703-1711 (Hungary, AD.label: Rákóczi Uprising, 1703-1711
Rákóczi Uprising, 1703-1711 (Hungary, AD.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1703–AD 1711] Rákóczi Uprising, 1703-1711. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Rákóczi Uprising, 1703-1711". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Francis II Rákóczi led peasants, serfs and nobles together against Habsburg rule, at one point controlling most of Hungary and Transylvania and being elected ruling prince. Lacking money, artillery and foreign backing, the movement was ground down; the Peace of Szatmar granted amnesty and confirmed noble privileges while leaving the Habsburgs in charge. Its songs and kuruc imagery became a lasting core of Hungarian patriotic memory.

Revolution, 1917-1920 (Armenia, AD 1917–.label: Revolution, 1917-1920
Revolution, 1917-1920 (Armenia, AD 1917–.prose:
[Armenia, AD 1917–AD 1920] Revolution, 1917-1920. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Revolution, 1917-1920". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As the Russian Empire disintegrated, Armenians on the Caucasus frontier found themselves defending survivors of the genocide with no state behind them. Victory at Sardarabad in 1918 made possible the first independent Armenian republic, a small, famine-stricken country crowded with refugees and squeezed between Turkey and Bolshevik Russia. It lasted barely two years before the Red Army entered Yerevan and Armenia became a Soviet republic.

Korean War, 1950-1953 (Korean Peninsula,.label: Korean War, 1950-1953
Korean War, 1950-1953 (Korean Peninsula,.prose:
[Korea, AD 1950–AD 1953] Korean War, 1950-1953. Extracted from heading "Korean War, 1950-1953". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

North Korean forces drove almost to the tip of the peninsula before a US-led United Nations counter-offensive pushed to the Chinese border, whereupon China entered the war and forced the front back to roughly where it began. Two more years of grinding attrition and mass bombing killed several million people and left both Koreas in ruins. The armistice of 1953 never became a peace treaty, so the demilitarised zone and the division of the peninsula remain in place.

Rum Rebellion, 1808-1809 (Australia, AD.label: Rum Rebellion, 1808-1809
Rum Rebellion, 1808-1809 (Australia, AD.prose:
[New South Wales, AD 1808–AD 1809] Rum Rebellion, 1808-1809. Extracted from heading "New South Wales--History--Rum Rebellion, 1808-1809". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Officers of the New South Wales Corps marched on Government House and arrested Governor William Bligh, ending his attempt to break their grip on trade – including the barter of spirits that gave the affair its later name. It remains the only successful armed takeover of government in Australian history, and the colony was run by the military for two years. London responded by recalling the Corps and sending Lachlan Macquarie with his own regiment, shifting the colony toward civil government.

Chosŏn dynasty, 1392-1910 (Korean Penins.label: Chosŏn dynasty, 1392-1910
Chosŏn dynasty, 1392-1910 (Korean Penins.prose:
[Korea, AD 1392–AD 1910] Chosŏn dynasty, 1392-1910. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Chosŏn dynasty, 1392-1910". Added to LCSH in 2003. The alternate label "Yi dynasty, 1392-1910" appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Five centuries of rule by the Yi house from Hanyang (Seoul), organised around Confucian ritual, a landed scholar-official elite and a hereditary status order. The court sponsored the invention of the Korean alphabet, astronomical instruments and vast documentary projects such as the Veritable Records, while yangban families dominated land and office. Japanese and Manchu invasions in the 1590s and 1630s left deep scars, and the dynasty's final decades of factional paralysis and foreign pressure ended with colonisation.

Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Malaysia.label: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945
Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Malaysia.prose:
[Malaya, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Malaya--History--Japanese occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.74 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch colonial regime collapsed in weeks, and Japan governed the archipelago as three separate military zones, extracting oil, rice and hundreds of thousands of romusha forced labourers. To mobilise support it released and promoted nationalists such as Sukarno and Hatta and trained Indonesian militias like PETA. When Japan surrendered, those leaders and those armed units declared independence, and the Dutch never regained control.

Medieval, 500-1500 (Europe, AD 500–AD 15.label: Medieval, 500-1500
Medieval, 500-1500 (Europe, AD 500–AD 15.prose:
[Europe, AD 500–AD 1500] Medieval, 500-1500. Extracted from heading "Social history--Medieval, 500-1500". Added to LCSH in 1986. Spatial coverage description inferred from usage of "Medieval" classifier in other subject headings. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A thousand years that began with Rome's western collapse and ended with printing presses, gunpowder and Atlantic voyages. Christianity became the organising framework of European life, monasteries preserved and copied texts, and lords traded land for military service in the arrangements later called feudalism. Towns, universities, cathedrals and long-distance trade fairs all revived from the eleventh century on, while plague in the 1340s killed perhaps a third of the population and reshaped labour, wages and landholding.

Charles IV, 1347-1378 (Germany, AD 1347–.label: Charles IV, 1347-1378
Charles IV, 1347-1378 (Germany, AD 1347–.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1347–AD 1378] Charles IV, 1347-1378. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Charles IV, 1347-1378". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry is present under "Germany--History", with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Luxembourg prince raised in Paris made Prague the capital of the Empire, founding its university in 1348, laying out the New Town and beginning the cathedral and the bridge that carries his name. His Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the imperial election in the hands of seven named princes, settling a question that had caused centuries of civil war and standing as constitutional law until 1806. He worked by diplomacy, marriage and purchase rather than campaigns, and left Bohemia the richest realm in central Europe.

Medici rule, 1557-1737 (Italy, AD 1557–A.label: Medici rule, 1557-1737
Medici rule, 1557-1737 (Italy, AD 1557–A.prose:
[Siena (Italy), AD 1557–AD 1737] Medici rule, 1557-1737. Extracted from heading "Siena (Italy)--History--Medici rule, 1557-1737". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After centuries as bankers and unofficial bosses of Florence, the Medici ruled Tuscany outright as grand dukes, absorbing Siena and building a centralised state with Livorno as its free port. Cosimo I and his successors commissioned the Uffizi, the Vasari Corridor and the Pitti apartments, and patronised Galileo, opera's first composers and the Accademia del Cimento. The dynasty ran out of heirs with Gian Gastone, and Tuscany passed to the house of Lorraine; the last Medici willed the family's art collections to the city in perpetuity.

Revolution, 1840-1841 (Colombia, AD 1840.label: Revolution, 1840-1841
Revolution, 1840-1841 (Colombia, AD 1840.prose:
[Antioquia (Colombia), AD 1840–AD 1841] Revolution, 1840-1841. Extracted from heading "Antioquia (Colombia : Department)--History--Revolution, 1840-1841". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The War of the Supremes began in Pasto over a law closing small convents and spread as regional caudillos, each styling himself 'supreme commander', rose against the government in Bogota. The scattered rebellions were defeated, but the fighting drew the country's politicians into two hostile camps that soon became the Liberal and Conservative parties. Colombia's long habit of civil war between those two blocs starts here.

Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713 (United Stat.label: Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713
Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713 (United Stat.prose:
[United States, AD 1702–AD 1713] Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Queen Anne's War, 1702-1713". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 121 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The North American front of the War of the Spanish Succession, fought between English colonists and New France with Native allies decisive on both sides. Frontier settlements bore the worst of it: the raid on Deerfield in 1704 left dozens dead and more than a hundred captives marched north to Canada. The peace at Utrecht handed Britain Acadia, Newfoundland and Hudson Bay, setting up the final struggle for the continent.

Ulrika Eleonora, 1718-1720 (Sweden, AD 1.label: Ulrika Eleonora, 1718-1720
Ulrika Eleonora, 1718-1720 (Sweden, AD 1.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1718–AD 1720] Ulrika Eleonora, 1718-1720. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Ulrika Eleonora, 1718-1720". Added to LCSH in 1990, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sister of Charles XII, she claimed the throne after he was shot at Fredriksten and could only keep it by accepting a constitution that stripped the crown of absolute power and handed authority to the Riksdag. Within two years she abdicated in favour of her husband, Frederick of Hesse. Her brief reign marks the end of Sweden's absolutist great-power era and the start of the parliamentary Age of Liberty.

Oscar II, 1872-1905 (Norway, AD 1872–AD.label: Oscar II, 1872-1905
Oscar II, 1872-1905 (Norway, AD 1872–AD.prose:
[Norway, AD 1872–AD 1905] Oscar II, 1872-1905. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Oscar II, 1872-1905". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His long reign over Norway ended with the union's collapse: Norwegian demands for their own consular service hardened into a parliamentary declaration that the king had ceased to function, confirmed by an overwhelming referendum. He refused the offer of a Bernadotte prince for the Norwegian throne, and the crown passed to a Danish prince as Haakon VII. The separation was achieved without war.

Civil War, 1975-2002 (Angola, AD 1975–AD.label: Civil War, 1975-2002
Civil War, 1975-2002 (Angola, AD 1975–AD.prose:
[Angola, AD 1975–AD 2002] Civil War, 1975-2002. Extracted from heading "Angola--History--Civil War, 1975-2002". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Portuguese withdrawal left three liberation movements fighting for the state, and the contest immediately became a Cold War proxy: Cuban troops and Soviet arms backed the MPLA government, while South Africa and the United States supported UNITA. After the superpowers withdrew, oil revenues and diamond smuggling funded another decade of war. Fighting ended only with the death in combat of UNITA's leader Jonas Savimbi, leaving the country mined and shattered.

Frederick VI, 1808-1814 (Norway, AD 1808.label: Frederick VI, 1808-1814
Frederick VI, 1808-1814 (Norway, AD 1808.prose:
[Norway, AD 1808–AD 1814] Frederick VI, 1808-1814. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Frederick VI, 1808-1814". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Danish king to rule Norway. His alliance with Napoleon dragged the joint monarchy into war with Britain, whose blockade cut Norway off from Danish grain and caused years of hunger. Defeat brought the Treaty of Kiel, by which Norway was handed to the king of Sweden — a transfer Norwegians resisted by writing their own constitution at Eidsvoll and briefly declaring independence.

Henry III, 1039-1056 (Germany, AD 1039–A.label: Henry III, 1039-1056
Henry III, 1039-1056 (Germany, AD 1039–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1039–AD 1056] Henry III, 1039-1056. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry III, 1039-1056". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Salian power reached its height under a ruler who marched into Italy, deposed three rival claimants to the papacy at the Synod of Sutri, and installed a series of German reforming popes. He made Bohemia and Hungary acknowledge his overlordship and promoted the Peace of God in the empire. Ironically, the reform movement he sponsored produced the papacy that would humiliate his son.

Korana War, 2nd, 1878-1879 (South Africa.label: Korana War, 2nd, 1878-1879
Korana War, 2nd, 1878-1879 (South Africa.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1878–AD 1879] Korana War, 2nd, 1878-1879. Extracted from heading "Korana War, 2nd, 1878-1879". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The final defeat of the Korana Khoekhoe of the Orange River, crushed by Cape colonial forces at a moment when the government was suppressing resistance across the northern and eastern frontier at once. Survivors were imprisoned or scattered as labourers, and Korana society as an independent force on the river ceased to exist.

Theophilus, 829-842 (Byzantine Empire, A.label: Theophilus, 829-842
Theophilus, 829-842 (Byzantine Empire, A.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 829–AD 842] Theophilus, 829-842. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Theophilus, 829-842". Added to LCSH in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last emperor to enforce iconoclasm, banning religious images and exiling or punishing their defenders; within a year of his death his widow Theodora restored icons for good. He fought hard campaigns against the Abbasids, losing Amorion, his dynasty's ancestral city, in a devastating raid of 838. He is also remembered for a lavish, Baghdad-influenced court - golden trees, mechanical lions and a roaring throne - and for a reputation as a stern dispenser of justice in the streets of Constantinople.

Catherine II, 1762-1796 (Russia, AD 1762.label: Catherine II, 1762-1796
Catherine II, 1762-1796 (Russia, AD 1762.prose:
[Russia , AD 1762–AD 1796] Catherine II, 1762-1796. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Catherine II, 1762-1796". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Catherine took the throne after guards officers deposed and killed her husband, and ruled for thirty-four years as the model of enlightened absolutism: she corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, convened a Legislative Commission, founded schools and hospitals, and built the art collection that became the Hermitage. Abroad she seized the Crimea and the northern Black Sea coast from the Ottomans and took the largest share in the three partitions that erased Poland from the map. At home, serfdom grew harsher and spread into the new lands, and Pugachev's massive Cossack and peasant revolt of 1773-75 was crushed with great brutality.

Victor Amadeus II, 1773-1796 (Sardinia,.label: Victor Amadeus II, 1773-1796
Victor Amadeus II, 1773-1796 (Sardinia,.prose:
[Sardinia, AD 1773–AD 1796] Victor Amadeus II, 1773-1796. Extracted from heading "Sardinia (Italy)--History--Victor Amadeus II, 1773-1796". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Savoyard state was drilled and fortified in these years, its army and its network of alpine strongholds among the best-regarded in Italy, while the court in Turin turned firmly against the ideas coming out of France. War with revolutionary France from 1792 exposed the limits of that strength: Bonaparte's Italian campaign broke the Piedmontese in weeks, and the Armistice of Cherasco surrendered Savoy and Nice.

Xi Xia dynasty, 1038-1227 (China, AD 103.label: Xi Xia dynasty, 1038-1227
Xi Xia dynasty, 1038-1227 (China, AD 103.prose:
[China, AD 1038–AD 1227] Xi Xia dynasty, 1038-1227. Extracted from heading "China--History--Xi Xia dynasty, 1038-1227". Added to LCSH in 2001. Alternate label "Hsi Hsia dynasty, 1038-1227" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Tangut rulers of the northwest declared their own empire, holding the Hexi Corridor and its Silk Road trade against both Song China and the Liao. They devised a complex script of their own and sponsored vast Buddhist printing and translation projects, leaving the cave temples and stupas of Ningxia and Gansu. Genghis Khan's Mongols destroyed the state in a campaign so thorough that Xia's language was forgotten until modern scholars decoded it.

Danish Settlements, 1659-1850 (Ghana, AD.label: Danish Settlements, 1659-1850
Danish Settlements, 1659-1850 (Ghana, AD.prose:
[Ghana, AD 1659–AD 1850] Danish Settlements, 1659-1850. Extracted from heading "Ghana--History--Danish Settlements, 1659-1850". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.46 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark held a string of forts on the eastern Gold Coast, chief among them Christiansborg at Osu, shipping enslaved Africans to the Danish West Indies and trading in gold and ivory. Denmark was the first European power to outlaw the Atlantic slave trade, in 1803, and afterwards tried plantation schemes inland before selling the forts to Britain; Christiansborg later became the seat of government in independent Ghana.

Opium War, 1840-1842 (China, AD 1840–AD.label: Opium War, 1840-1842
Opium War, 1840-1842 (China, AD 1840–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1840–AD 1842] Opium War, 1840-1842. Extracted from heading "China--History--Opium War, 1840-1842" Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain went to war after Chinese officials destroyed opium stocks at Canton, and steam gunboats and modern artillery overwhelmed Qing coastal defences. The Treaty of Nanking ceded Hong Kong, opened five treaty ports, and imposed a large indemnity. It began the era Chinese historians call the century of humiliation and set the pattern of unequal treaties with foreign powers.

Gallic Wars, 58-51 B.C (Gaul, 57 BC–50 B.label: Gallic Wars, 58-51 B.C
Gallic Wars, 58-51 B.C (Gaul, 57 BC–50 B.prose:
[Gaul, 57 BC–50 BC] Gallic Wars, 58-51 B.C. Extracted from heading "Gaul--History--Gallic Wars, 58-51 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.42 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Julius Caesar, as governor of a small border province, spent eight campaigning seasons conquering the whole of Gaul, bridging the Rhine and twice crossing to Britain. The war brought enormous plunder, a devoted veteran army and a political reputation built on his own bestselling account of it; for the Gauls it meant huge casualties, enslavement and the crushing of Vercingetorix's united revolt at Alesia. It made Caesar powerful enough to defy the Senate, and the civil war that destroyed the Republic followed immediately.

Spanish colony, 1540-1810 (Mexico, AD 15.label: Spanish colony, 1540-1810
Spanish colony, 1540-1810 (Mexico, AD 15.prose:
[Mexico, AD 1540–AD 1810] Spanish colony, 1540-1810. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--Spanish colony, 1540-1810". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.77 of LCSH 1987, and p.62 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

New Spain matured from a conquest society into the wealthiest and most populous of Spain's American possessions, run from Mexico City by viceroys, bishops and the merchant guild. Silver, cattle ranches and mission frontiers pushed north into what is now the United States, while creole elites grew resentful of peninsular privilege and Bourbon taxation. The colony ended when Napoleon's seizure of Spain shattered royal legitimacy and Father Hidalgo raised the banner of revolt.

Insurrection, 1771-1802 (Vietnam, AD 177.label: Insurrection, 1771-1802
Insurrection, 1771-1802 (Vietnam, AD 177.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1771–AD 1802] Insurrection, 1771-1802. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Insurrection, 1771-1802". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Tây Sơn brothers' peasant revolt toppled both the Nguyễn lords in the south and the Trịnh and the Lê emperors in the north, briefly unifying the country and repelling a Qing invasion. Their rule broke apart after the death of Nguyễn Huệ, and the surviving Nguyễn heir, aided by French adventurers, reconquered the country from the south. His victory founded the Nguyễn dynasty, established a capital at Huế, and gave France its first foothold of influence in Vietnam.

New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C (Egyp.node: New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC)
New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C (Egyp.label: New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C
New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C (Egyp.prose:
[Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC] New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--New Kingdom, ca. 1550-ca. 1070 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Reunified after the expulsion of the Hyksos, Egypt became a military power with holdings in Syria-Palestine and Nubia, and its kings poured captured wealth into the temples of Thebes. The period gave rise to the Valley of the Kings, the Amarna revolution, the treaty with the Hittites after Kadesh, and some of the finest surviving Egyptian painting and sculpture. Its decline brought foreign invasion, tomb robbery and a divided country.

Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Singapor.label: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945
Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Singapor.prose:
[Singapore, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Singapore--History--Japanese occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch colonial regime collapsed in weeks, and Japan governed the archipelago as three separate military zones, extracting oil, rice and hundreds of thousands of romusha forced labourers. To mobilise support it released and promoted nationalists such as Sukarno and Hatta and trained Indonesian militias like PETA. When Japan surrendered, those leaders and those armed units declared independence, and the Dutch never regained control.

Frederick IV, 1699-1730 (Norway, AD 1699.label: Frederick IV, 1699-1730
Frederick IV, 1699-1730 (Norway, AD 1699.prose:
[Norway, AD 1699–AD 1730] Frederick IV, 1699-1730. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Frederick IV, 1699-1730". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spent much of his reign in the Great Northern War against Sweden, ending it with Denmark's hold on Schleswig confirmed but the old dream of recovering Scania gone. At home he abolished the last form of peasant bondage on Zealand, funded hundreds of village "cavalry schools" for rural children, and sent the first Danish missionaries to India. Copenhagen suffered plague and the catastrophic fire of 1728, while the king built Fredensborg and Frederiksberg palaces.

Interregnum, 1034-1040 (Poland, AD 1034–.label: Interregnum, 1034-1040
Interregnum, 1034-1040 (Poland, AD 1034–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1034–AD 1040] Interregnum, 1034-1040. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1034-1040". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of Mieszko II left the young Piast state without an effective ruler and it came apart: a pagan reaction attacked churches and clergy, peasants turned on lords, and in 1038 the Bohemian duke Bretislav sacked Gniezno and carried off the relics of St Adalbert. Casimir the Restorer returned with German help to rebuild the monarchy, moving its centre from ruined Greater Poland to Kraków — a shift that lasted for centuries.

Malayan Emergency, 1948-1960 (Malaysia,.label: Malayan Emergency, 1948-1960
Malayan Emergency, 1948-1960 (Malaysia,.prose:
[Malaya, AD 1948–AD 1960] Malayan Emergency, 1948-1960. Extracted from heading "Malaya--History--Malayan Emergency, 1948-1960". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.74 of LCSH 1987, and p.60 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A twelve-year guerrilla war between British and Commonwealth forces and the largely Chinese communist insurgents of the Malayan National Liberation Army. Rather than relying on firepower alone, the British resettled half a million rural Chinese into guarded "New Villages", tightened food control and promised independence — a counter-insurgency model studied ever since. The insurgency withered, Malaya became independent in 1957, and the emergency was formally lifted three years later.

Japanese occupation, 1941-1944 (Guam, AD.label: Japanese occupation, 1941-1944
Japanese occupation, 1941-1944 (Guam, AD.prose:
[Guam, AD 1941–AD 1944] Japanese occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Guam--History--Japanese occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Guam fell within days of Pearl Harbor and was renamed Omiya Jima, its Chamorro population subjected to forced labour, compulsory Japanese schooling, and — as American forces approached — massacres and forced marches to camps. The US recaptured the island in a bloody campaign in July 1944. Guam then became a huge American air and naval base from which B-29s flew against Japan, and it has remained a major US military site ever since.

Mau Mau Emergency, 1952-1960 (Kenya, AD.label: Mau Mau Emergency, 1952-1960
Mau Mau Emergency, 1952-1960 (Kenya, AD.prose:
[Kenya, AD 1952–AD 1960] Mau Mau Emergency, 1952-1960. Extracted from heading "Kenya--History--Mau Mau Emergency, 1952-1960". Added to LCSH in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An armed revolt, largely by Kikuyu fighters driven off land taken for white settlement, met a declared state of emergency and one of the most severe counter-insurgency campaigns of the late British Empire. Over a million people were moved into guarded villages, tens of thousands were held in detention camps, and abuses there, exposed by the killing of detainees at Hola, damaged the case for continued colonial rule. Britain won militarily but conceded politically; Kenya was independent within three years of the emergency's end.

Civil War, 1983-2009 (Sri Lanka, AD 1983.label: Civil War, 1983-2009
Civil War, 1983-2009 (Sri Lanka, AD 1983.prose:
[Sri Lanka, AD 1983–AD 2009] Civil War, 1983-2009. Extracted from heading "Sri Lanka--History--Civil War, 1983-2009". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Anti-Tamil riots in Colombo triggered a war between the state and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, who sought a separate homeland in the north and east. The Tigers pioneered the systematic use of suicide bombers, assassinated a Sri Lankan president and an Indian prime minister, and ran a de facto state for years. A final government offensive crushed them in 2009 amid heavy civilian casualties that remain the subject of war crimes allegations.

Bombardment, 1917-1918 (London, AD 1917–.label: Bombardment, 1917-1918
Bombardment, 1917-1918 (London, AD 1917–.prose:
[London (England), AD 1917–AD 1918] Bombardment, 1917-1918. Extracted from heading "London (England)--History--Bombardment, 1917-1918". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

German Gotha and Giant bombers replaced the Zeppelin as the threat over the capital, striking in daylight and killing civilians in the streets below — including schoolchildren at Upper North Street School. The raids caused panic, mass sheltering in Tube stations and demands for reprisals, and drove the creation of a unified air defence system and, in 1918, the world's first independent air force.

War of Independence, 1810-1822 (Colombia.label: War of Independence, 1810-1822
War of Independence, 1810-1822 (Colombia.prose:
[Colombia, AD 1810–AD 1822] War of Independence, 1810-1822. Extracted from heading "Colombia--History--War of Independence, 1810-1822". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.23 of LCSH 1987, and on p.17 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Juntas in Bogotá, Cartagena and the provinces broke with Spain and then fell out with each other, a period of squabbling remembered as the Patria Boba that let Pablo Morillo's expedition reconquer New Granada with firing squads. Bolívar's audacious march across the flooded llanos and over the Andes ended in victory at Boyacá, and Carabobo and the storming of Cartagena finished the job. The liberated territories were bound together as Gran Colombia, a union that lasted only until 1830.

Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C (ancient.node: Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C (ancient Rome, 81 BC–71 BC)
Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C (ancient.label: Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C
Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C (ancient.prose:
[Rome, 81 BC–71 BC] Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Revolt of Sertorius, 82-72 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Marian officer Quintus Sertorius, driven from Italy by Sulla's victory, built a rival Roman state in Hispania backed by Lusitanian and Celtiberian allies, complete with its own senate and a school for the sons of Iberian nobles. His guerrilla campaigns humiliated a series of Roman commanders, including Pompey, for the better part of a decade. He was murdered by his own subordinate Perperna, and the resistance collapsed soon after.

Afonso II, 1211-1223 (Portugal, AD 1211–.label: Afonso II, 1211-1223
Afonso II, 1211-1223 (Portugal, AD 1211–.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1211–AD 1223] Afonso II, 1211-1223. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Afonso II, 1211-1223". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alfonso II, 1211-1223" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Portuguese king to concentrate on governing rather than conquering, issuing the kingdom's earliest written general laws and beginning inquiries into who legally held land. His attempts to tax and control the Church brought excommunication and a long quarrel with Rome. Portuguese knights nevertheless took Alcacer do Sal from the Almohads during his reign.

Athenian supremacy, 479-431 B.C (Greece,.label: Athenian supremacy, 479-431 B.C
Athenian supremacy, 479-431 B.C (Greece,.prose:
[Greece, 478 BC–430 BC] Athenian supremacy, 479-431 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Athenian supremacy, 479-431 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Persian defeat Athens turned the Delian League from an alliance into an empire, moving the treasury to the Acropolis and using allied tribute to fund the Parthenon and a fleet nobody could match. This is the age of Pericles, of tragedy performed at the Dionysia, of the sophists, Herodotus and the radical democracy of the assembly and the lot. Sparta's alarm at Athenian expansion led directly to the Peloponnesian War that ended it.

Emigration, 1731-1735 (Austria, AD 1731–.label: Emigration, 1731-1735
Emigration, 1731-1735 (Austria, AD 1731–.prose:
[Austria, AD 1731–AD 1735] Emigration, 1731-1735. Extracted from heading "Salzburgers--Emigration, 1731-1735". Added to LCSH in 1986. Spatial coverage description given as "Salzburgers", spatial coverage extent inferred from knowledge of the Salzburger Emigration. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Archbishop of Salzburg ordered the expulsion of some 20,000 Protestant subjects, who left in winter columns with what they could carry. Prussia's Frederick William I welcomed most of them to repopulate East Prussia, while smaller groups reached the Netherlands and the new colony of Georgia in America. The episode became a cause célèbre for Protestant Europe and one of the last mass religious expulsions in the West.

German occupation, 1941-1944 (Latvia, AD.label: German occupation, 1941-1944
German occupation, 1941-1944 (Latvia, AD.prose:
[Latvia, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Latvia--History--German occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

James IV, 1488-1513 (Scotland, AD 1488–A.label: James IV, 1488-1513
James IV, 1488-1513 (Scotland, AD 1488–A.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1488–AD 1513] James IV, 1488-1513. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--James IV, 1488-1513". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A confident Renaissance monarch who brought the Lordship of the Isles under crown control, patronised poets and scholars, licensed Scotland's first printing press, and built the huge warship Great Michael. His 1503 marriage to Margaret Tudor tied the Stewart line to the Tudors, the connection that later united the crowns. He died alongside much of his nobility at Flodden after invading England on France's behalf.

Vladislaus II Jagiello, 1386-1434 (Polan.label: Vladislaus II Jagiello, 1386-1434
Vladislaus II Jagiello, 1386-1434 (Polan.prose:
[Poland , AD 1386–AD 1434] Vladislaus II Jagiello, 1386-1434. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus II Jagiello, 1386-1434". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Lithuanian grand duke baptised as a Catholic, married to the young queen Jadwiga and crowned king of Poland, Jagiełło joined two very different states in a personal union that lasted, in various forms, four centuries. His reign brought the official Christianisation of Lithuania and the crushing defeat of the Teutonic Order at Grunwald in 1410, which broke the Knights' dominance of the Baltic. He also refounded the university at Kraków, giving the dynasty an intellectual centre to match its territorial reach.

American occupation, 1916-1924 (Dominica.label: American occupation, 1916-1924
American occupation, 1916-1924 (Dominica.prose:
[Dominican Republic , AD 1916–AD 1924] American occupation, 1916-1924. Extracted from heading "Dominican Republic--History--American occupation, 1916-1924". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and p.22 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

US Marines took over the country's government to secure customs revenues and end chronic political turmoil, ruling by military decree under a naval governor. They disarmed the population, built roads linking the regions for the first time, and fought a long guerrilla campaign against gavilleros in the eastern provinces. The constabulary they created became the power base from which Rafael Trujillo seized control in 1930.

Licchavi dynasty, ca. 400-600 (Nepal, AD.label: Licchavi dynasty, ca. 400-600
Licchavi dynasty, ca. 400-600 (Nepal, AD.prose:
[Nepal, AD 400–AD 600] Licchavi dynasty, ca. 400-600. Extracted from heading "Nepal--History--Licchavi dynasty, ca. 400-600". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rulers of the Kathmandu Valley who left Nepal's earliest dated documents, a series of Sanskrit stone inscriptions beginning with Manadeva's pillar at Changu Narayan in 464. Their patronage produced the first great flowering of Nepalese stone sculpture, Hindu and Buddhist alike, in a style closely related to Indian Gupta art. Trade and pilgrim routes through their valley linked India to Tibet, and later Nepalese kingdoms traced their legitimacy back to them.

William III, 1849-1890 (Netherlands, AD.label: William III, 1849-1890
William III, 1849-1890 (Netherlands, AD.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1849–AD 1890] William III, 1849-1890. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--William III, 1849-1890". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Willem III resented the constitution that had just stripped the crown of real power and spent forty years chafing against ministers he could not control. His reign saw slavery abolished in Suriname and the Antilles, canals and railways built, and the long, brutal Aceh war begun in the Indies. With no surviving sons, his death ended the male line: his daughter Wilhelmina inherited the Netherlands while Luxembourg passed to a different branch.

Henry VII, 1485-1509 (England, AD 1485–A.label: Henry VII, 1485-1509
Henry VII, 1485-1509 (England, AD 1485–A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1485–AD 1509] Henry VII, 1485-1509. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry VII, 1485-1509". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The victor at Bosworth Field took a crown with a thin hereditary claim and made it stick by marrying Elizabeth of York, crushing pretenders like Perkin Warbeck, and starving the great nobles of private armies. He ran the monarchy like a business, filling the treasury through bonds, recognisances and ruthless fiscal officials. The dynasty he founded would rule for over a century, and his marriage diplomacy tied England to Spain and Scotland.

Peter I, 1350-1369 (Kingdom of Castile,.label: Peter I, 1350-1369
Peter I, 1350-1369 (Kingdom of Castile,.prose:
[Castile, AD 1350–AD 1369] Peter I, 1350-1369. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Peter I, 1350-1369".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known to his enemies as Peter the Cruel and to his supporters as the Just, he ruled through a bitter civil war against his half-brother Henry of Trastámara, drawing English and French armies into Castile as an extension of the Hundred Years' War. His victory at Nájera with the Black Prince's help proved hollow; he was cornered at Montiel and stabbed to death by Henry, who founded a new dynasty. His reign left Castile's monarchy weakened and its nobility enormously strengthened.

Northern War, 1845-1846 (New Zealand, AD.label: Northern War, 1845-1846
Northern War, 1845-1846 (New Zealand, AD.prose:
[New Zealand, AD 1845–AD 1846] Northern War, 1845-1846. Earlier established form: Hone Heke's Rebellion, N.Z., 1844 -1846. Broader:. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Also called the Flagstaff War, this was the first of the New Zealand Wars, sparked when Hōne Heke repeatedly cut down the British flagstaff at Kororāreka in protest at the loss of Māori authority and customs revenue after the Treaty of Waitangi. Heke and Kawiti fought British troops in the Bay of Islands, and at Ohaeawai and Ruapekapeka built trench-and-bunker pā that absorbed artillery fire and inflicted heavy losses on the attackers. The fighting ended without conquest or confiscation, and Māori engineering lessons from it were used in later wars.

Ludwig IV, 1314-1347 (Germany, AD 1314–A.label: Ludwig IV, 1314-1347
Ludwig IV, 1314-1347 (Germany, AD 1314–A.prose:
