[Germany , AD 1314–AD 1347] Ludwig IV, 1314-1347. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Ludwig IV, 1314-1347". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected king of Germany in a disputed double election, Louis the Bavarian defeated his Habsburg rival in battle and then spent decades locked in conflict with the popes at Avignon, who refused to recognise him and placed his lands under interdict. He had himself crowned emperor in Rome by the citizens rather than the pope, a deliberate break with tradition. The polemicists he sheltered laid out early arguments for the separation of secular and church power.

Intifada, 1987-1993 (Gaza Strip, AD 1987.label: Intifada, 1987-1993
Intifada, 1987-1993 (Gaza Strip, AD 1987.prose:
[Gaza, West Bank, AD 1987–AD 1993] Intifada, 1987-1993. Spatial coverage: Gaza Strip, Israel, State of Palestine. Extracted from heading "Intifada, 1987-1993". Added to LCSH in 1989, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A traffic accident at the Erez crossing sparked a mass uprising of strikes, boycotts, barricades and stone-throwing youths that spread from Gaza's refugee camps through the occupied territories. Largely improvised and locally organised, it put images of children against tanks on the world's television screens, produced the Islamist movement Hamas, and shifted the initiative from the exiled PLO leadership to Palestinians under occupation. It ended with the mutual recognition of the Oslo Accords.

Francis I, 1745-1765 (Germany, AD 1745–A.label: Francis I, 1745-1765
Francis I, 1745-1765 (Germany, AD 1745–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1745–AD 1765] Francis I, 1745-1765. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Francis I, 1745-1765". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Duke of Lorraine turned Grand Duke of Tuscany, he was elected emperor mainly to give his wife Maria Theresa's Habsburg inheritance an imperial crown, since a woman could not wear it. Real authority stayed with her in Vienna while he pursued finance, mining and natural science, running profitable enterprises and building the collections that seeded Vienna's museums. Their marriage founded the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, which ruled until 1918.

Schism, 1130-1139 (Vatican City, AD 1130.label: Schism, 1130-1139
Schism, 1130-1139 (Vatican City, AD 1130.prose:
[Papacy, AD 1130–AD 1139] Schism, 1130-1139. Extracted from heading "Papacy--History--Schism, 1130-1139". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A disputed election produced two popes on the same day: Innocent II, backed by the reforming cardinals, and Anacletus II, who held Rome itself with Pierleoni family money and the support of Roger II of Sicily. Innocent won not in Italy but in the courts of northern Europe, where Bernard of Clairvaux campaigned tirelessly on his behalf, and the split ended with Anacletus's death and the Second Lateran Council. The episode showed how much papal legitimacy now depended on the monastic reform movement and on transalpine kings.

William I, 1861-1888 (Germany, AD 1861–A.label: William I, 1861-1888
William I, 1861-1888 (Germany, AD 1861–A.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1861–AD 1888] William I, 1861-1888. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--William I, 1861-1888". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wilhelm came to the Prussian throne determined to enlarge the army, and when parliament refused to pay for it he appointed Otto von Bismarck, who governed without a budget and won the wars against Denmark, Austria and France. Those victories left Prussia master of Germany and Wilhelm proclaimed emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. He was a conservative soldier who largely let his chancellor set the course, and survived two assassination attempts that Bismarck used as a pretext to outlaw the socialists.

Revolution, 1848-1849 (Brazil, AD 1848–A.label: Revolution, 1848-1849
Revolution, 1848-1849 (Brazil, AD 1848–A.prose:
[Pernambuco (Brazil), AD 1848–AD 1849] Revolution, 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Pernambuco (Brazil)--History--Revolution, 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

Tongzhi, 1861-1875 (China, AD 1861–AD 18.label: Tongzhi, 1861-1875
Tongzhi, 1861-1875 (China, AD 1861–AD 18.prose:
[China, AD 1861–AD 1875] Tongzhi, 1861-1875. Extracted from heading "China--History--Tongzhi, 1861-1875". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2001. Alternate identifier pulled from "Earlier Established Forms" due to its use of the older Wade-Giles transliteration method, as opposed to the Pinyin transliteration. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign that followed China's defeat in the Second Opium War and the vast destruction of the Taiping rebellion, run by regents around a child emperor. Officials like Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang rebuilt provincial armies, founded arsenals and steamship lines and opened a foreign affairs bureau, an experiment in limited modernisation whose objects - cannon, telescopes, translated textbooks - sit oddly beside the era's conservative Confucian rhetoric.

Sigismund, 1387-1437 (Hungary, AD 1387–A.label: Sigismund, 1387-1437
Sigismund, 1387-1437 (Hungary, AD 1387–A.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1387–AD 1437] Sigismund, 1387-1437. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Sigismund, 1387-1437". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sigismund of Luxembourg won the Hungarian crown by marriage and spent fifty years defending it, most disastrously at Nicopolis in 1396, where a crusading army was crushed by the Ottomans. He reorganised frontier defences against Turkish raids and founded the Order of the Dragon to bind nobles to the cause. His long reign tied Hungary tightly to imperial and Bohemian affairs, with consequences that outlived him.

Frederick William II, 1786-1797 (Germany.label: Frederick William II, 1786-1797
Frederick William II, 1786-1797 (Germany.prose:
[Prussia, AD 1789–AD 1797] Frederick William II, 1786-1797. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick William II, 1786-1797". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The nephew who followed Frederick the Great relaxed his uncle's austerity, patronised music and architecture — the Brandenburg Gate rose in his reign — and let favourites and mystics influence policy. Religious edicts imposed orthodoxy and tightened censorship, silencing critics including Kant. Prussia joined the war against revolutionary France, fought poorly and withdrew at the Peace of Basel in 1795, while gaining large Polish territories in the second and third partitions and leaving the state deep in debt.

Piast period, 960-1386 (Poland, AD 960–A.label: Piast period, 960-1386
Piast period, 960-1386 (Poland, AD 960–A.prose:
[Poland , AD 960–AD 1386] Piast period, 960-1386. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Piast period, 960-1386". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The dynasty that made Poland a state: Mieszko I's baptism in 966 tied the country to Latin Christendom, and Bolesław the Brave was crowned king in 1025. Two centuries of division among rival dukes followed, until reunification and the reforms of Casimir the Great, who founded Kraków's university and codified the law. The line ended in the male branch in 1370, and the crown passed by marriage to Lithuania's Jogaila in 1386.

Koryŏ period, 935-1392 (Korean Peninsula.label: Koryŏ period, 935-1392
Koryŏ period, 935-1392 (Korean Peninsula.prose:
[Korea, AD 935–AD 1392] Koryŏ period, 935-1392. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Koryŏ period, 935-1392". Added to LCSH in 2003; appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Buddhist kingdom governed by an aristocratic bureaucracy recruited through Chinese-style civil examinations, and the state that finally reunified the peninsula after the Later Three Kingdoms. Military officers seized power in 1170 and ruled as strongmen behind puppet kings, and from the 1230s the country endured repeated Mongol invasions and long submission to the Yuan. Its cultural legacy — celadon, the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, metal type printing — is among the most celebrated in Korean history.

Louis Philippe, 1830-1848 (France, AD 18.label: Louis Philippe, 1830-1848
Louis Philippe, 1830-1848 (France, AD 18.prose:
[France, AD 1830–AD 1848] Louis Philippe, 1830-1848. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis Philippe, 1830-1848". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.39 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Online version added in 2006 and revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Placed on the throne by the July Revolution as a deliberately modest 'King of the French', he ruled with a narrow electorate of property owners and the support of bankers and industrialists. Railways spread, industry grew and Algeria was conquered, but the regime resisted electoral reform and looked corrupt and complacent to workers and republicans alike. A banquet campaign for reform turned into the February Revolution of 1848, and he fled to England, ending monarchy in France for good after a brief Bonapartist interlude.

Oscar I, 1844-1857 (Sweden, AD 1844–AD 1.label: Oscar I, 1844-1857
Oscar I, 1844-1857 (Sweden, AD 1844–AD 1.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1844–AD 1857] Oscar I, 1844-1857. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Oscar I, 1844-1857". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cautiously liberal king who came to the throne with a reputation as a reformer, overhauling the criminal code, ending public flogging, granting women legal majority and equal inheritance, and easing guild restrictions and press controls. He encouraged Scandinavism, backing Denmark against Prussia, and expanded railways and free trade. Illness forced him to hand government to his son as regent.

Russian occupation, 1713-1721 (Finland,.label: Russian occupation, 1713-1721
Russian occupation, 1713-1721 (Finland,.prose:
[Finland, AD 1713–AD 1721] Russian occupation, 1713-1721. Extracted from heading "Finland--History--Russian occupation, 1713-1721". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Remembered as the Great Wrath, the years when Peter the Great's armies overran the Finnish provinces during the Great Northern War. Requisitions, burnings and the seizure of people for forced labour emptied whole districts and drove the gentry and clergy across to Sweden. The Treaty of Nystad returned most of the territory but confirmed that Sweden's age as a great power was over.

Sancho III, 1157-1158 (Kingdom of Castil.label: Sancho III, 1157-1158
Sancho III, 1157-1158 (Kingdom of Castil.prose:
[Castile, AD 1157–AD 1158] Sancho III, 1157-1158. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Sancho III, 1157-1158". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign of barely a year, but a consequential one. Sancho inherited Castile when his father Alfonso VII split his realms between two sons, undoing the union with León for the next seventy years, and in 1158 he granted the fortress of Calatrava to Cistercian monks, creating the first Iberian military order. His death left an infant heir, Alfonso VIII, and a long minority in which rival noble families fought for control.

Landgraviate, 1567-1806 (Germany, AD 156.label: Landgraviate, 1567-1806
Landgraviate, 1567-1806 (Germany, AD 156.prose:
[Hesse (Germany), AD 1567–AD 1806] Landgraviate, 1567-1806. Extracted from heading "Hesse (Germany)--History--1567-1806". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Philip the Magnanimous died his lands were split among his sons, and the Darmstadt line held its share as a landgraviate for over two centuries. It was a middling German principality of the sort that filled the Holy Roman Empire: Lutheran, dependent on careful diplomacy, badly mauled in the Thirty Years War and repeatedly fought over in the wars of Louis XIV and Napoleon. Alliance with France in 1806 brought its reward, as the last landgrave emerged from the Empire's collapse as a grand duke.

Sui dynasty, 581-618 (China, AD 581–AD 6.label: Sui dynasty, 581-618
Sui dynasty, 581-618 (China, AD 581–AD 6.prose:
[China, AD 581–AD 618] Sui dynasty, 581-618. Extracted from heading "China--History--Sui dynasty, 581-618". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and on p.16 of LCSH 19875. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Yang Jian seized power in the north and within a decade conquered the south, ending an age of rival dynasties. His government rebuilt the machinery of empire—census, granaries, canals, rebuilt capitals at Chang'an and Luoyang—at enormous human cost. When his son's Korean wars and building programmes exhausted the population, rebellion ended the house, but the Tang simply took over its blueprint.

German occupation, 1940-1945 (Netherland.label: German occupation, 1940-1945
German occupation, 1940-1945 (Netherland.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1940–AD 1945] German occupation, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--German occupation, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.81 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark was seized in a few hours and then governed with unusual lightness: the king stayed, parliament sat, and the country was presented as a model protectorate supplying food to Germany. Cooperation collapsed in August 1943 amid strikes and sabotage; when deportation of Denmark's Jews was ordered that October, the resistance and ordinary citizens ferried some 7,000 people to safety in Sweden.

Joseph Bonaparte, 1806-1808 (Naples, AD.label: Joseph Bonaparte, 1806-1808
Joseph Bonaparte, 1806-1808 (Naples, AD.prose:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1806–AD 1808] Joseph Bonaparte, 1806-1808. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Joseph Bonaparte, 1806-1808". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon drove the Bourbons out of the mainland kingdom and put his elder brother on the throne, backed by French bayonets while the exiled court held out in Sicily under British protection. In barely two years Joseph abolished feudal jurisdictions, suppressed monasteries, reorganised the tax system and imposed a French-style administration on a deeply conservative countryside. He was then moved to the Spanish throne, leaving Naples to Napoleon's cavalry marshal Joachim Murat.

Maria II, 1834-1853 (Portugal, AD 1834–A.label: Maria II, 1834-1853
Maria II, 1834-1853 (Portugal, AD 1834–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1834–AD 1853] Maria II, 1834-1853. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Maria II, 1834-1853". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

She came to the throne as a teenager after her uncle Miguel was defeated in a civil war between absolutists and liberals, and her reign was spent trying to hold a constitutional monarchy together through coups, revolts and rival liberal factions. Portugal in these years acquired parliamentary politics, a chartered constitution and chronic instability. She died at 34 giving birth to her eleventh child.

Charles III, 1759-1788 (Spain, AD 1759–A.label: Charles III, 1759-1788
Charles III, 1759-1788 (Spain, AD 1759–A.prose:
[Spain, AD 1759–AD 1788] Charles III, 1759-1788. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Charles III, 1759-1788". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Already an experienced king in Naples, he brought enlightened reform to Spain: ministers like Floridablanca and Campomanes overhauled taxes and trade, the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, and colonial administration in America was tightened to squeeze more revenue from it. Madrid was paved, lit and given the buildings that still define it, including the Prado. Reform from above provoked riots and resentment, and his backing of the American rebels against Britain won Menorca and Florida but drained the treasury.

Revolution, 1830-1839 (Belgium, AD 1830–.label: Revolution, 1830-1839
Revolution, 1830-1839 (Belgium, AD 1830–.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1830–AD 1839] Revolution, 1830-1839. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Revolution, 1830-1839". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Riots in Brussels sparked by an opera performance grew into a revolt against Dutch rule, and within weeks a provisional government declared independence and drafted one of Europe's most liberal constitutions. The Dutch king fought on and only accepted the outcome in 1839, when the Treaty of London fixed Belgium's borders and guaranteed its perpetual neutrality. That guarantee, the 'scrap of paper' violated by Germany in 1914, drew Britain into the First World War.

Interregnum, 1574-1575 (Poland, AD 1574–.label: Interregnum, 1574-1575
Interregnum, 1574-1575 (Poland, AD 1574–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1574–AD 1575] Interregnum, 1574-1575. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1574-1575". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry of Valois slipped out of Kraków by night after only months on the throne, riding for Paris to claim the French crown he had just inherited. The abandoned Commonwealth debated for over a year before the nobility rejected the Habsburg candidate and installed Stephen Báthory as king alongside Anna Jagiellon — a demonstration that the electorate, not dynastic right, decided who ruled.

Charles VII, 1422-1461 (France, AD 1422–.label: Charles VII, 1422-1461
Charles VII, 1422-1461 (France, AD 1422–.prose:
[France, AD 1422–AD 1461] Charles VII, 1422-1461. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles VII, 1422-1461". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited a kingdom split in two, mocked as the "King of Bourges" while the English and Burgundians held Paris. The arrival of Joan of Arc and his coronation at Reims turned the war, and by the end of his reign the English had been driven from all France but Calais. He also left France a permanent standing army paid by permanent taxation, and a church half-detached from Rome by the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges — foundations of royal power for centuries after.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Romania, AD 1943.label: Bombardment, 1943-1944
Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Romania, AD 1943.prose:
[Argeș (Romania : Județ), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Argeș (Romania : Județ)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

English Expedition, 1620-1621 (Algeria,.label: English Expedition, 1620-1621
English Expedition, 1620-1621 (Algeria,.prose:
[Algeria, AD 1620–AD 1621] English Expedition, 1620-1621. Extracted from heading "Algeria--History--English Expedition, 1620-1621". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An English fleet under Sir Robert Mansell was sent to Algiers to force an end to corsair raiding and to free Christian captives. A fireship attack in the harbour achieved little, and the squadron returned home having freed only a handful of prisoners; Algerine raiders were soon operating as far as the Channel and even Iceland. The failure exposed how limited European naval power still was against the Barbary regencies.

Uprising, 1848-1849 (Slovakia, AD 1848–A.label: Uprising, 1848-1849
Uprising, 1848-1849 (Slovakia, AD 1848–A.prose:
[Slovakia, AD 1848–AD 1849] Uprising, 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Slovakia--History--Uprising, 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Slovak volunteer corps took the field during the revolutions that shook the Habsburg Empire, demanding recognition of Slovak as a language of schools and administration and autonomy within Hungary. Led by Ľudovít Štúr and Jozef Hurban, they ended up fighting alongside imperial troops against the Hungarian revolutionaries. Vienna gave them almost nothing afterwards, but the campaign is remembered as the moment Slovak national demands were first backed by arms.

King George's War, 1744-1748 (Pennsylvan.label: King George's War, 1744-1748
King George's War, 1744-1748 (Pennsylvan.prose:
[Pennsylvania, AD 1744–AD 1748] King George's War, 1744-1748. Extracted from heading "Pennsylvania--History--King George's War, 1744-1748". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 90 of LCSH 1987, and p.88 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

Peter IV, 1336-1387 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: Peter IV, 1336-1387
Peter IV, 1336-1387 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon, AD 1336–AD 1387] Peter IV, 1336-1387. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--Peter IV, 1336-1387". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975; revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peter the Ceremonious spent fifty years fighting to hold his composite realm together — crushing the noble Unions of Aragon and Valencia, annexing Majorca, and waging exhausting campaigns against Genoa in Sardinia and against Castile in the War of the Two Peters. The Black Death struck midway through, killing perhaps a third of his subjects. A meticulous administrator and chronicler of his own reign, he left a strengthened royal bureaucracy but a treasury drained by war.

King William's War, 1689-1697 (United St.label: King William's War, 1689-1697
King William's War, 1689-1697 (United St.prose:
[United States, AD 1689–AD 1697] King William's War, 1689-1697. Extracted from heading "United States--History--King William's War, 1689-1697". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 121 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The American extension of Europe's war against Louis XIV was fought largely by raiding parties: French and Wabanaki forces struck Schenectady, Salmon Falls and Falmouth, while New England retaliated against Acadia. Sir William Phips took Port Royal but failed disastrously before Quebec in 1690. The peace restored the prewar borders and settled nothing, beginning a seventy-year contest for North America.

Rebellion, 1928-1930 (Ethiopia, AD 1928–.label: Rebellion, 1928-1930
Rebellion, 1928-1930 (Ethiopia, AD 1928–.prose:
[Ethiopia, AD 1928–AD 1930] Rebellion, 1928-1930. Extracted from heading "Ehtiopia--History--Rebellion, 1928-1930". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ras Gugsa Welle, governor of Begemder and estranged husband of Empress Zewditu, rose against the growing power of the regent Ras Tafari. He was defeated and killed at the battle of Anchem in March 1930, and Zewditu died days later. Tafari was crowned Haile Selassie I that November, completing the centralisation of imperial power in his hands.

Alfonso I, 1104-1134 (Kingdom of Aragon,.label: Alfonso I, 1104-1134
Alfonso I, 1104-1134 (Kingdom of Aragon,.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1104–AD 1134] Alfonso I, 1104-1134. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Alfonso I, 1104-1134". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as the Battler, he fought almost continuously against the Almoravids and captured Zaragoza in 1118, pushing the Aragonese frontier down to the Ebro and beyond. A raid deep into Andalusia brought back thousands of Mozarab Christians to settle the new lands. His marriage to Urraca of León-Castile ended in bitter war, and his childless will leaving the kingdom to the military orders was ignored, throwing the succession into crisis.

Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Hamburg, AD 1940.label: Bombardment, 1940-1945
Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Hamburg, AD 1940.prose:
[Hamburg (Germany), AD 1940–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Hamburg (Germany)--History--Bombardment, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British night raids and American daylight raids grew into a round-the-clock campaign that destroyed the centres of Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and dozens of other cities, killed several hundred thousand civilians and made millions homeless. It absorbed a vast share of German industry and manpower in air defence, and it left a moral argument about area bombing that has never been settled.

Philip VI, 1328-1350 (France, AD 1328–AD.label: Philip VI, 1328-1350
Philip VI, 1328-1350 (France, AD 1328–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1328–AD 1350] Philip VI, 1328-1350. Extracted from heading "France--History--Philip VI, 1328-1350". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Valois king, chosen over Edward III of England, whose rival claim to the French throne opened the Hundred Years' War. He suffered naval catastrophe at Sluys and a shattering defeat at Crécy in 1346, and lost Calais the following year. The Black Death struck in 1348, killing perhaps a third of his subjects.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Latvia, AD 1905–A.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Latvia, AD 1905–A.prose:
[Latvia, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Latvia--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Turkish occupation, 1526-1699 (Hungary,.label: Turkish occupation, 1526-1699
Turkish occupation, 1526-1699 (Hungary,.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1526–AD 1699] Turkish occupation, 1526-1699. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Turkish occupation, 1526-1699". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The catastrophe at Mohács in 1526 killed the king and split the country three ways: an Ottoman-governed centre based on Buda, Habsburg 'Royal Hungary' in the west and north, and a semi-independent Transylvania. Frontier warfare, castle sieges and depopulation shaped a landscape of garrisons and abandoned villages, while religious diversity, including a strong Protestant presence, took root under divided rule. The Habsburg reconquest after 1683 ended with the Treaty of Karlowitz.

Revolution, 1917-1918 (Finland, AD 1917–.label: Revolution, 1917-1918
Revolution, 1917-1918 (Finland, AD 1917–.prose:
[Finland, AD 1917–AD 1918] Revolution, 1917-1918. Extracted from heading "Finland--History--Revolution, 1917-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Russian authority let Finland declare independence, but the new state immediately split between socialist Reds in the industrial south and the Whites of the countryside. The civil war lasted barely four months and was savage out of proportion to its length, with executions and prison-camp deaths outnumbering battlefield casualties. German intervention decided it for the Whites, and the bitterness between the two sides shaped Finnish politics for generations.

German occupation, 1941-1944 (Estonia, A.label: German occupation, 1941-1944
German occupation, 1941-1944 (Estonia, A.prose:
[Estonia, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--German occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

Ploiești, Battles of, 1943-1944 (Ploieșt.label: Ploiești, Battles of, 1943-1944
Ploiești, Battles of, 1943-1944 (Ploieșt.prose:
[Ploiești (Romania), AD 1943–AD 1944] Ploiești, Battles of, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Ploiești, Battles of, Ploiești, Romania, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Romania's refineries supplied a large share of Germany's oil, making them one of the most heavily defended targets in Europe. The low-level American raid of 1 August 1943, Operation Tidal Wave, cost more than fifty bombers and produced five Medals of Honor for little lasting damage; sustained high-altitude bombing in 1944 finally crippled production. Romania's switch to the Allies that August handed the oilfields to the advancing Soviets.

Civil War, 1860-1862 (Colombia, AD 1860–.label: Civil War, 1860-1862
Civil War, 1860-1862 (Colombia, AD 1860–.prose:
[Colombia, AD 1860–AD 1862] Civil War, 1860-1862. Extracted from heading "Colombia--History--Civil War, 1860-1862". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.23 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera, governor of Cauca, rebelled against the centralising Conservative government of the Granadine Confederation and marched on Bogotá, capturing it in 1861. His victory installed a radical Liberal order that expropriated church property, expelled the Jesuits and rewrote the map, creating the loosely federal United States of Colombia under the 1863 Rionegro constitution. The state and church quarrel it opened shaped Colombian politics for decades.

George V, 1910-1936 (United Kingdom, AD.label: George V, 1910-1936
George V, 1910-1936 (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1910–AD 1936] George V, 1910-1936. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George V, 1910-1936". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.40 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He steered the monarchy through the First World War, the Irish partition and the first Labour government, and in 1917 renamed his dynasty Windsor to shed its German associations. His Christmas broadcasts, begun in 1932, made the sovereign a familiar voice in ordinary homes, and his 1935 Silver Jubilee revealed a monarchy more popular than the political system around it.

Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907.node: Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907-979 (China, AD 907–AD 979)
Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907.label: Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907-979
Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907.prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 979] Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907-979. Extracted from heading "China--History--Five dynasties and the Ten kingdoms, 907-979". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Half a century of political fragmentation between the Tang and the consolidated Song, with five military dynasties in the Yellow River basin and ten mostly southern regional kingdoms. The southern states were prosperous and culturally productive, sponsoring painting, celadon kilns and maritime trade. The period closes with the Song conquest of the last holdout, the Northern Han.

Commodus, 180-192 (Roman Empire, AD 180–.label: Commodus, 180-192
Commodus, 180-192 (Roman Empire, AD 180–.prose:
[Rome, AD 180–AD 192] Commodus, 180-192. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Commodus, 180-192". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The son of Marcus Aurelius abandoned his father's Danube campaigns and left government to a succession of favourites, ruling through the courts and the treasury. He styled himself a new Hercules and fought in the arena as a gladiator, scandalising the senatorial class who wrote the histories. His strangling by a wrestler on New Year's Eve 192 ended the Antonine line and touched off civil war.

Ivan Shishman, 1371-1393 (Bulgaria, AD 1.label: Ivan Shishman, 1371-1393
Ivan Shishman, 1371-1393 (Bulgaria, AD 1.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1371–AD 1393] Ivan Shishman, 1371-1393. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Ivan Shishman, 1371-1393". Added to LCSH in 1987; appears online. Revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited a Bulgarian realm already split among rival rulers and squeezed by the advancing Ottomans, and spent his reign as a tributary and reluctant ally of the sultan. Tarnovo, the capital, fell after a three-month siege, its churches converted and its clergy scattered; Bulgarian statehood ended for nearly five centuries. His name later became a fixture of folk legend, attached to ruins and fortresses across the country.

Ivan Alexander, 1331-1371 (Bulgaria, AD.label: Ivan Alexander, 1331-1371
Ivan Alexander, 1331-1371 (Bulgaria, AD.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1331–AD 1371] Ivan Alexander, 1331-1371. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Ivan Alexander, 1331-1371". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The long reign that Bulgarians remember as a cultural golden age: illuminated manuscripts like the Tetraevangelia produced at Tarnovo, church building, and a court modelled on Byzantium. Politically it was less golden — territory was lost to Serbia, Hungary and Byzantium, and Ivan Alexander divided the realm between his sons. Within two decades of his death the Ottomans had taken Tarnovo and Bulgaria ceased to exist as a state.

House of Hanover, 1714-1837 (United King.label: House of Hanover, 1714-1837
House of Hanover, 1714-1837 (United King.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1714–AD 1837] House of Hanover, 1714-1837. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--1714-1837". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Alternate label from LCSH used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A German elector was imported to keep the throne Protestant, and because George I and his son cared more for Hanover than Westminster, real power drifted to ministers and cabinet - Robert Walpole became the first recognisable prime minister. The same span saw the American colonies lost, India gained, Napoleon defeated, canals and steam engines remake the landscape, and the slave trade abolished. It closed with the Great Reform Act of 1832 already redrawing who could vote.

John I, 1387-1395 (Aragon, AD 1387–AD 13.label: John I, 1387-1395
John I, 1387-1395 (Aragon, AD 1387–AD 13.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1387–AD 1395] John I, 1387-1395. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--John I, 1387-1395". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as the Hunter and the Lover of Elegance, he preferred music, poetry and the chase to government, leaving much of it to his queen and courtiers. He founded the Consistori de la Gaia Ciència in Barcelona to stage troubadour poetry competitions in Catalan. Rebellion in Sardinia and pressure from Castile went largely unanswered before he died in a hunting accident without a male heir.

John I Tzimisces, 969-976 (Byzantine Emp.label: John I Tzimisces, 969-976
John I Tzimisces, 969-976 (Byzantine Emp.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 969–AD 976] John I Tzimisces, 969-976. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--John I Tzimisces, 969-976". Added to LCSH in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Armenian general who came to the throne by murdering his predecessor Nikephoros Phokas in his bedchamber, then spent his short reign proving himself in the field. He drove Sviatoslav's Rus army out of the Balkans after the siege of Dorostolon, annexed eastern Bulgaria outright, and led Byzantine armies deep into Syria and towards Palestine. His campaigns marked the high tide of Byzantine expansion before Basil II.

Ferdinand I, 1556-1564 (Germany, AD 1556.label: Ferdinand I, 1556-1564
Ferdinand I, 1556-1564 (Germany, AD 1556.prose:
[Germany , AD 1556–AD 1564] Ferdinand I, 1556-1564. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Ferdinand I, 1556-1564". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles V's younger brother took the imperial title after the abdication that split the Habsburg inheritance, leaving Spain and the Netherlands to Philip II and the Austrian lands, Bohemia and royal Hungary to the Vienna line. Ferdinand had already brokered the Peace of Augsburg, which let each German prince fix the religion of his own territory and froze the Reformation into a patchwork of Lutheran and Catholic states. His reign set the pattern of a Danubian Habsburg monarchy governing three very different realms while facing the Ottomans on the Hungarian frontier.

Magnus VII Eriksson, 1319-1343 (Norway,.label: Magnus VII Eriksson, 1319-1343
Magnus VII Eriksson, 1319-1343 (Norway,.prose:
[Norway, AD 1319–AD 1343] Magnus VII Eriksson, 1319-1343. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Magnus VII Eriksson, 1319-1343". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inherited Norway as a small child from his grandfather Haakon V and was elected king of Sweden in the same year, joining the two crowns under one ruler. Norwegian nobles resented an absentee king based largely in Sweden, and in 1343 the Norwegian throne was settled on his son Haakon VI. The episode set the pattern of dynastic unions that would culminate in the Kalmar Union.

Otto II, 973-983 (Germany, AD 973–AD 983.label: Otto II, 973-983
Otto II, 973-983 (Germany, AD 973–AD 983.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 973–AD 983] Otto II, 973-983. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Otto II, 973-983". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Otto I's son fought to hold his father's inheritance against Bavarian rebels and a French claim on Lorraine, and married the Byzantine princess Theophanu, bringing Greek culture to the German court. His attempt to take southern Italy ended in disaster at Cap Colonne against Muslim forces from Sicily; he died in Rome at twenty-eight, and the great Slav revolt of 983 wiped out imperial control east of the Elbe.

Turkish Wars, 17th century (Veneto, AD 1.label: Turkish Wars, 17th century
Turkish Wars, 17th century (Veneto, AD 1.prose:
[Venice (Italy), AD 1600–AD 1699] Turkish Wars, 17th century. Extracted from heading "Venice (Italy)--History--Turkish Wars, 17th century". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2015. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Venice fought two exhausting wars with the Ottomans: the twenty-four-year struggle for Crete, ending with the surrender of Candia in 1669, and the Morean War, which briefly won back the Peloponnese — and during which a Venetian shell blew up the Parthenon. The effort drained the Republic's finances and manpower without securing its empire. By the next century Venice had ceased to be a serious military power.

Revolution, 1964-1975 (Mozambique, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1964-1975
Revolution, 1964-1975 (Mozambique, AD 19.prose:
[Mozambique, AD 1964–AD 1975] Revolution, 1964-1975. Extracted from heading "Mozambique--History--Revolution, 1964-1975". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.79 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

FRELIMO began its campaign in the far north and slowly extended guerrilla control southwards against a Portuguese army relying on fortified villages and settler militias. Eduardo Mondlane's assassination in 1969 brought Samora Machel to the leadership and a sharper Marxist line. Independence in 1975 was followed by mass departure of Portuguese settlers, and within two years by a devastating civil war backed by Rhodesia and South Africa.

British rule, 1878-1960 (Cyprus, AD 1878.label: British rule, 1878-1960
British rule, 1878-1960 (Cyprus, AD 1878.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1878–AD 1960] British rule, 1878-1960. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--British rule, 1878-1960". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain leased the island from the Ottoman Empire as a base for protecting the approaches to the Suez Canal, then annexed it during the First World War. Colonial administration brought new courts, roads and taxes, and also hardened the political split between Greek Cypriot enosis campaigners and Turkish Cypriots. Armed struggle in the 1950s ended with independence in 1960 under a constitution that shared power between the two communities.

Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756.node: Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756 (Brazil, AD 1754–AD 1756)
Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756.label: Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756
Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756.prose:
[Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina, AD 1754–AD 1756] Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756. Spatial coverage: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay. Extracted from heading "Seven Reductions, War of the, 1754-1756". Added to LCSH in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Spain and Portugal redrew their South American border, seven Jesuit-run Guaraní mission towns east of the Uruguay River were ordered to abandon their fields, churches and herds and move. The Guaraní refused and fought a two-year war against a joint Spanish-Portuguese army, ending in slaughter at Caiboaté. The affair discredited the Jesuits in both courts and helped bring about their expulsion from the Portuguese and Spanish empires within a decade.

Spanish Conquest, 1476-1492 (Spain, AD 1.label: Spanish Conquest, 1476-1492
Spanish Conquest, 1476-1492 (Spain, AD 1.prose:
[Granada (Spain), AD 1476–AD 1492] Spanish Conquest, 1476-1492. Extracted from heading "Granada (Spain : Reino)--History--Spanish Conquest, 1476-1492". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The final campaigns of the Reconquista, waged by Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon against the emirate of Granada, ended with the surrender of the Alhambra. In the same year the monarchs expelled the Jews from their kingdoms and dispatched Columbus westward. A unified, crusading and newly confident Spain emerged, poised to become the dominant European power of the next century.

Revolution, 1879-1880 (Cuba, AD 1879–AD.label: Revolution, 1879-1880
Revolution, 1879-1880 (Cuba, AD 1879–AD.prose:
[Cuba, AD 1879–AD 1880] Revolution, 1879-1880. Extracted from heading "Cuba--History--Revolution, 1879-1880". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The 'Little War' was an attempt to reopen the independence struggle abandoned in the Pact of Zanjon, led by Calixto Garcia with strong support from Black and mixed-race veterans in the eastern provinces. Short of arms and money, and undermined by Spanish propaganda warning white Cubans of a race war, it collapsed within a year. Spain nonetheless moved to defuse discontent by beginning the abolition of slavery, and the exiled leaders regrouped for the far larger war of 1895.

Afonso IV, 1325-1357 (Portugal, AD 1325–.label: Afonso IV, 1325-1357
Afonso IV, 1325-1357 (Portugal, AD 1325–.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1325–AD 1357] Afonso IV, 1325-1357. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Afonso IV, 1325-1357". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alfonso IV, 1325-1357" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He led Portuguese troops alongside Castile to crush a Marinid invasion at the Rio Salado, one of the last great battles of the Reconquista. His reign was scarred by war with his own son and by the murder of Ines de Castro, ordered by the king and later turned into Portugal's most famous tragic legend. The Black Death struck near the end of his rule, killing a large share of the population.

Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C (ancient Rome,.node: Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C (ancient Rome, 134 BC–70 BC)
Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C (ancient Rome,.label: Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C
Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C (ancient Rome,.prose:
[Rome, 134 BC–70 BC] Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Servile Wars, 135-71 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975 (as "Servile War", later apparently subsumed under "Servile Wars"). Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three great slave uprisings shook Rome's expanding slave economy: two in Sicily, where rebels crowned their own kings and held large parts of the island, and the last led by the gladiator Spartacus, whose army roamed Italy for two years before Crassus crushed it and lined the Appian Way with crucifixions. The revolts exposed how completely conquest had remade Roman agriculture, filling the countryside with chained labour on vast estates. They left Rome with a lasting fear of servile rebellion and gave later ages one of its most enduring symbols of resistance.

Joseph II, 1765-1790 (Germany, AD 1765–A.label: Joseph II, 1765-1790
Joseph II, 1765-1790 (Germany, AD 1765–A.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1765–AD 1790] Joseph II, 1765-1790. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Joseph II, 1765-1790". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

On his father's death he became Holy Roman Emperor and co-regent of the Habsburg lands with his mother Maria Theresa, an uneasy partnership in which he pressed for radical reform and she restrained him. He spent these years travelling incognito through his territories and Europe, absorbing Enlightenment thinking and pushing for the partition of Poland and the acquisition of Bavaria, before gaining a free hand as sole ruler in 1780.

Leopold II, 1865-1909 (Belgium, AD 1865–.label: Leopold II, 1865-1909
Leopold II, 1865-1909 (Belgium, AD 1865–.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1865–AD 1909] Leopold II, 1865-1909. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Leopold II, 1865-1909". Appears on p.8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.9 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Frustrated by the smallness of Belgium, he acquired the Congo Free State as his personal property in 1885 and ran it as a private rubber and ivory concession enforced by mutilation, hostage-taking and forced labour, causing deaths counted in the millions. The campaign exposing it, led by E. D. Morel and Roger Casement, became one of the first modern international human rights movements and forced the Belgian state to annex the colony in 1908. At home he spent the profits on grand public buildings and boulevards.

Austrian rule, 1714-1796 (Lombardy, AD 1.label: Austrian rule, 1714-1796
Austrian rule, 1714-1796 (Lombardy, AD 1.prose:
[Lombardy, AD 1714–AD 1796] Austrian rule, 1714-1796. Source notes that Lombardy is in modern day Italy. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Milan passed from Spanish to Austrian Habsburg hands at the end of the War of the Spanish Succession, and under Maria Theresa and Joseph II became a laboratory of enlightened reform: a new land survey and tax cadastre, curbs on Church privilege, and reorganised schools. Milanese intellectuals such as Cesare Beccaria, whose attack on torture and the death penalty was read across Europe, and the Verri brothers flourished in this climate. Bonaparte's army ended the arrangement in 1796.

Paul I, 1796-1801 (Russia, AD 1796–AD 18.label: Paul I, 1796-1801
Paul I, 1796-1801 (Russia, AD 1796–AD 18.prose:
[Russia , AD 1796–AD 1801] Paul I, 1796-1801. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Paul I, 1796-1801". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Catherine the Great's resentful son spent his short reign undoing his mother's arrangements, imposing Prussian-style drill on the army and curbing noble privileges she had granted. His most durable act was a law of succession by male primogeniture that governed the Romanovs until 1917. Erratic foreign policy, sending Suvorov into Italy against France and then turning to alliance with Napoleon and threatening British India, helped convince a circle of officers to strangle him in his new castle in 1801.

Directory, 1795-1799 (France, AD 1795–AD.label: Directory, 1795-1799
Directory, 1795-1799 (France, AD 1795–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1795–AD 1799] Directory, 1795-1799. Extracted from heading "France--History--Directory, 1795-1799". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Robespierre's fall, France was governed by five directors and two elected chambers, a deliberately cautious regime meant to end both terror and monarchy. It presided over runaway inflation, corruption and repeated coups against election results it disliked, while its armies conquered Italy and the Rhineland and made generals into political players. That dependence on the army proved fatal: in Brumaire 1799 Napoleon Bonaparte overthrew the Directory with the help of directors themselves.

Ferdinand VI, 1746-1759 (Spain, AD 1746–.label: Ferdinand VI, 1746-1759
Ferdinand VI, 1746-1759 (Spain, AD 1746–.prose:
[Spain, AD 1746–AD 1759] Ferdinand VI, 1746-1759. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Ferdinand VI, 1746-1759". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A deliberately peaceful reign after decades of dynastic war: Spain stayed out of the Seven Years' War and used the respite for administrative and fiscal reform. Ministers such as Ensenada rebuilt the navy, surveyed Castile's wealth for a single tax, and founded scientific and naval institutions, while the 1753 Concordat gave the crown control over church appointments. The recovery of revenue and shipping laid the groundwork for the more ambitious reforms of his half-brother Charles III.

Padri War, 1803-1838 (Indonesia, AD 1803.label: Padri War, 1803-1838
Padri War, 1803-1838 (Indonesia, AD 1803.prose:
[Indonesia, AD 1803–AD 1838] Padri War, 1803-1838. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Padri War, 1803-1838". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A movement of Islamic reformers in the Minangkabau highlands of Sumatra, inspired by Wahhabi ideas brought back from Mecca, attacked local custom, gambling and the authority of traditional chiefs and royalty. The chiefs appealed to the Dutch, who intervened and turned a religious civil war into a long colonial campaign ending with the capture of Bonjol and its leader, Tuanku Imam Bonjol. The result was Dutch control of the Sumatran interior, and a lasting tension in Minangkabau society between Islamic law and matrilineal custom.

Frederick III, 1440-1493 (Germany, AD 14.label: Frederick III, 1440-1493
Frederick III, 1440-1493 (Germany, AD 14.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1440–AD 1493] Frederick III, 1440-1493. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Frederick III, 1440-1493". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The longest reign of any German king, and the last emperor to be crowned by a pope in Rome. Contemporaries mocked his slowness and his losses to Hungary, which drove him from Vienna, yet his patient dynastic manoeuvring paid off spectacularly when he married his son Maximilian to Mary of Burgundy, bringing the Low Countries into Habsburg hands. His mysterious motto AEIOU, read as "Austria will rule the whole world," proved less absurd than it looked.

Soviet occupation, 1939-1941 (Ukraine, A.label: Soviet occupation, 1939-1941
Soviet occupation, 1939-1941 (Ukraine, A.prose:
[Ukraine, AD 1931–AD 1941] Soviet occupation, 1939-1941. Extracted from heading "Ukraine, Western--History--Soviet occupation, 1939-1941". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Forced by the secret protocols of the Nazi-Soviet pact to accept Red Army bases, the republic was annexed outright in 1940 and its government, army and economy dismantled. Political leaders and thousands of ordinary families were arrested or deported to Siberia, culminating in the mass deportation of June 1941. German invasion ended the occupation weeks later, and the memory of that first Soviet year shaped Baltic politics for the rest of the century.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Berlin, AD 1943–.label: Bombardment, 1943-1944
Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Berlin, AD 1943–.prose:
[Berlin (Germany), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Berlin (Germany)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

Italo-Ethiopian War, 1895-1896 (Italy, A.label: Italo-Ethiopian War, 1895-1896
Italo-Ethiopian War, 1895-1896 (Italy, A.prose:
[Italy, Ethiopia, AD 1895–AD 1896] Italo-Ethiopian War, 1895-1896. Spatial coverage: Ethiopia, Italy. Extracted from heading "Italo-Ethiopian War, 1895-1896". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Italy's attempt to turn a protectorate treaty into outright conquest of Ethiopia ended at Adwa, where Menelik II's far larger and well-armed army destroyed the Italian force. It was the most decisive defeat of a European power by an African state in the colonial era, guaranteeing Ethiopian independence, toppling the Italian government, and turning Adwa into a touchstone for later anti-colonial and pan-African movements.

Insurrection, 1895-1896 (Crete, AD 1895–.label: Insurrection, 1895-1896
Insurrection, 1895-1896 (Crete, AD 1895–.prose:
[Crete (Greece), AD 1895–AD 1896] Insurrection, 1895-1896. Extracted from heading "Crete (Greece)--History--Insurrection, 1895-1896". Added to LCSH in 2015, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Renewed fighting between Cretan Christians and the Ottoman authorities drew in Greek volunteers and arms, and the great powers again intervened to impose reforms. The unrest spilled over into the Greco-Turkish war of 1897 and ended with Crete becoming an autonomous state under a European-backed high commissioner, a halfway house on the road to union with Greece in 1913.

Civil War, 1994- (Russia, AD 1994–AD 201.label: Civil War, 1994-
Civil War, 1994- (Russia, AD 1994–AD 201.prose:
[Chechni︠a︡ (Russia), AD 1994–AD 2015] Civil War, 1994-. Extracted from heading "Chechni︠a︡ (Russia)--History--Civil War, 1994-". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Russian federal forces invaded breakaway Chechnya, fought to a humiliating stalemate, then returned in 1999 to level Grozny in one of the most destructive urban campaigns since 1945. The conflict mutated from a nationalist independence struggle into a jihadist insurgency across the North Caucasus, marked by hostage sieges at a Moscow theatre and a school in Beslan. It shaped Vladimir Putin's rise and the hardening of the Russian state.

Dictatorship, 1923-1930 (Spain, AD 1923–.label: Dictatorship, 1923-1930
Dictatorship, 1923-1930 (Spain, AD 1923–.prose:
[Spain, AD 1923–AD 1930] Dictatorship, 1923-1930. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Dictatorship, 1923-1930". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

General Miguel Primo de Rivera seized power with the king's blessing, suspending the constitution and promising to clean up a discredited parliamentary system. He ended the disastrous Moroccan war with the Alhucemas landing, built roads, dams and state monopolies during a boom, and courted business and the socialist union while banning Catalan nationalism and censoring the press. When the economy soured the army withdrew its support, and by dragging the monarchy down with him he opened the way to the Republic of 1931.

Matthias I, 1458-1490 (Hungary, AD 1458–.label: Matthias I, 1458-1490
Matthias I, 1458-1490 (Hungary, AD 1458–.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1458–AD 1490] Matthias I, 1458-1490. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Matthias I, 1458-1490". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 56 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected king as a young man, he built a paid professional force, the Black Army, that made Hungary the strongest military power in central Europe, taking Moravia, Silesia and finally Vienna itself. He taxed heavily to pay for it and ruled around the great barons rather than through them. His Buda court was the first serious centre of Italian Renaissance culture north of the Alps, with a famous library, the Bibliotheca Corviniana; within decades of his death the kingdom was collapsing before the Ottomans.

Edo period, 1600-1868 (Japan, AD 1600–AD.label: Edo period, 1600-1868
Edo period, 1600-1868 (Japan, AD 1600–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 1600–AD 1868] Edo period, 1600-1868. Extracted from heading "Edo period, Japan, 1600-1868". Added to LCSH in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Dated from the Tokugawa victory at Sekigahara, this was the long peace that followed Japan's warring-states era. The shogunate froze social ranks, curbed the daimyo, expelled missionaries and limited trade, while castle towns and the vast city of Edo grew into centres of commerce and popular entertainment. Its collapse in 1868 opened the way to Japan's rapid modernisation.

Maximilian II, 1564-1576 (Germany, AD 15.label: Maximilian II, 1564-1576
Maximilian II, 1564-1576 (Germany, AD 15.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1564–AD 1576] Maximilian II, 1564-1576. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Maximilian II, 1564-1576". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Habsburg emperor of famously ambiguous religion, sympathetic to Lutheran ideas yet never breaking with Rome, he presided over an unusually tolerant interlude in the Empire and allowed Protestant nobles wide latitude in Austria. He kept the peace with the Ottomans at a price, paying tribute for Hungary, and cultivated humanists, botanists and collectors at his court. The confessional compromise he embodied collapsed under his more militantly Catholic successors.

Second Crusade, 1147-1149 (Anatolia, AD.label: Second Crusade, 1147-1149
Second Crusade, 1147-1149 (Anatolia, AD.prose:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1147–AD 1149] Second Crusade, 1147-1149. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Second, 1147-1149". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Summoned after the fall of Edessa, the armies of Conrad III and Louis VII marched overland and were shattered crossing Anatolia, ambushed by Seljuk cavalry near Dorylaeum and in the mountain passes above Laodicea. The survivors who reached Syria wasted their strength on a four-day failure before Damascus. The debacle poisoned relations between crusaders and Byzantium, discredited the idea of the great royal expedition, and left the Seljuks of Rum securely in control of the Anatolian plateau.

French occupation, 1918-1946 (Syria, AD.label: French occupation, 1918-1946
French occupation, 1918-1946 (Syria, AD.prose:
[Syria, AD 1918–AD 1946] French occupation, 1918-1946. Extracted from heading "Syria--History--French occupation, 1918-1946". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied victory over the Ottomans brought French troops to the coast and, under a League of Nations mandate, the creation of Greater Lebanon - the old autonomous mountain enlarged with Beirut, Tripoli, the Bekaa and the south, and with it a far more mixed population. A 1926 constitution introduced a republic whose offices were shared out by sect, the framework Lebanese politics still runs on. Independence was declared during the Second World War and confirmed when French troops finally withdrew.

Peter II, 1830-1851 (Montenegro, AD 1830.label: Peter II, 1830-1851
Peter II, 1830-1851 (Montenegro, AD 1830.prose:
[Montenegro, AD 1830–AD 1851] Peter II, 1830-1851. Extracted from heading "Montenegro--History--Peter II, 1830-1851". Added to LCSH in 2005. Alternate label "Petar II, 1830-1851" appears on p.79 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Petar II Petrović-Njegoš was both ruler and Montenegro's greatest poet, author of The Mountain Wreath, a verse drama still central to South Slav literature and still fiercely argued over. He set up a senate and a guard, imposed regular taxation, opened the first schools and printing press, and pressed the clans toward something resembling a state. Travellers described a warrior-bishop of extraordinary height who wrote Romantic philosophy between punitive expeditions.

Afonso V, 1438-1481 (Portugal, AD 1438–A.label: Afonso V, 1438-1481
Afonso V, 1438-1481 (Portugal, AD 1438–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1438–AD 1481] Afonso V, 1438-1481. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Afonso V, 1438-1481". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alfonso V, 1438-1481" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nicknamed 'the African' for his capture of Ksar es-Seghir, Arzila and Tangier, he pushed Portuguese power onto the Moroccan coast while Atlantic exploration continued under Prince Henry's successors. His claim to the Castilian throne through marriage to Joanna ended in defeat at Toro and the treaty that divided Atlantic spheres between Portugal and Castile. That settlement shaped how the two crowns would later carve up the wider world.

Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660 (Sweden, AD.label: Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660
Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660 (Sweden, AD.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1654–AD 1660] Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles X Gustav, 1654-1660". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.112 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-king who spent his entire short reign at war, most famously marching an army across the frozen Danish straits in a gamble that forced Denmark to surrender Scania and made Sweden's borders roughly what they are today. For Finland, then the realm's eastern half, it meant conscription, taxes and Russian raids along the Karelian frontier. His sudden death at 37 left an empire at its greatest extent and deepest exhaustion.

Louis VIII, 1223-1226 (France, AD 1223–A.label: Louis VIII, 1223-1226
Louis VIII, 1223-1226 (France, AD 1223–A.prose:
[France, AD 1223–AD 1226] Louis VIII, 1223-1226. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis VIII, 1223-1226". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Before becoming king he had invaded England at the barons' invitation and was briefly proclaimed there. As king for only three years he conquered Poitou and La Rochelle from the English and led the royal armies into Languedoc in the Albigensian Crusade, bringing the south under Capetian control. His will created great apanages for his younger sons, a practice that later produced dynasties like the dukes of Burgundy.

French occupation, 1792-1801 (Germany, A.label: French occupation, 1792-1801
French occupation, 1792-1801 (Germany, A.prose:
[Rhineland (Germany), AD 1792–AD 1801] French occupation, 1792-1801. Extracted from heading "Rhineland (Germany)--History--French occupation, 1792-1801". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Revolutionary armies swept across the Rhineland, and the left bank was annexed outright to France - the short-lived Mainz Republic was the first attempt at a German republic. Occupation abolished serfdom, seigneurial dues and guild privileges, introduced the metric system and civil registers, and stripped church lands. The Rhine frontier was confirmed by treaty, setting off the wholesale redrawing of German states that followed.

Kamakura period, 1185-1333 (Japan, AD 11.label: Kamakura period, 1185-1333
Kamakura period, 1185-1333 (Japan, AD 11.prose:
[Japan, AD 1185–AD 1333] Kamakura period, 1185-1333. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Kamakura period, 1185-1333". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The age of the first shogunate, when land-holding warriors displaced court aristocrats as the effective rulers of Japan. Art turned muscular and lifelike — the guardian figures of Unkei and Kaikei, vivid narrative handscrolls — and imported Chinese Zen brought new architecture, ink painting and tea. The dynasty of Hōjō regents fell in 1333 to a coalition rallying behind Emperor Go-Daigo.

Mexican War, 1846-1848 (Mexico, AD 1846–.label: Mexican War, 1846-1848
Mexican War, 1846-1848 (Mexico, AD 1846–.prose:
[Mexico, United States, AD 1846–AD 1848] Mexican War, 1846-1848. Spatial coverage: Mexico, United States. Extracted from heading "Mexican War, 1846-1848". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A border dispute over Texas escalated into a full American invasion that reached Mexico City itself. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred roughly half of Mexico's territory, California, Nevada, Utah and much of the Southwest, to the United States for $15 million. Gold was found in California within days of the signing, and the question of whether slavery would extend into the new territories pushed the United States towards civil war.

Bombardment, 1940-1943 (Palermo, AD 1940.label: Bombardment, 1940-1943
Bombardment, 1940-1943 (Palermo, AD 1940.prose:
[Palermo (Italy), AD 1940–AD 1943] Bombardment, 1940-1943. Extracted from heading "Palermo (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1940-1943". Added to LCSH in 2008, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the great ports of the Mediterranean and a supply hub for Axis forces in North Africa, the city was pounded by Allied aircraft, with the heaviest raids preceding the invasion of Sicily. Harbour, churches and dense old quarters were gutted, thousands were killed, and much of the historic centre still bore the scars for decades afterwards.

Stanislaus I Leszczynski, 1704-1709 (Pol.label: Stanislaus I Leszczynski, 1704-1709
Stanislaus I Leszczynski, 1704-1709 (Pol.prose:
[Poland , AD 1704–AD 1709] Stanislaus I Leszczynski, 1704-1709. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Stanislaus I Leszczynski, 1704-1709". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Polish noble installed on the throne by Charles XII of Sweden during the Great Northern War, and swept off it again after the Swedish defeat at Poltava. His brief reign showed how far the elective monarchy had fallen under the control of foreign armies. He later became father-in-law to Louis XV, and after a second failed bid for the crown was compensated with the duchy of Lorraine.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Georgia, AD 1861–A.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Georgia, AD 1861–A.prose:
[Georgia, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Georgia--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.42 of LCSH 1987, and p.40 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Japanese occupation, 1910-1945 (Korean P.label: Japanese occupation, 1910-1945
Japanese occupation, 1910-1945 (Korean P.prose:
[Korea, AD 1910–AD 1945] Japanese occupation, 1910-1945. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Japanese occupation, 1910-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Japan formally annexed Korea and governed it through a military governor-general, seizing land, restructuring the economy for Japanese benefit and suppressing dissent. The March First Movement of 1919 brought mass nonviolent protest and brutal reprisals; later policies tried to erase Korean language, names and religion, and wartime mobilisation conscripted labourers, soldiers and 'comfort women'. Liberation in 1945 came with division at the 38th parallel, and the grievances of these years still shape Japan–Korea relations.

War of 1880-1881 (South Africa, AD 1880–.label: War of 1880-1881
War of 1880-1881 (South Africa, AD 1880–.prose:
[Transvaal (South Africa), AD 1880–AD 1881] War of 1880-1881. Extracted from heading "Transvaal (South Africa)--History--War of 1880-1881". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.116 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Transvaal Boers rose against the British annexation of their republic, fighting in commandos of mounted marksmen against troops in red coats. A string of humiliating defeats culminating at Majuba Hill, where the British commander was shot dead on the summit, persuaded Gladstone to concede self-government rather than fight on. It was a rare Victorian reverse, and the unfinished quarrel over gold, sovereignty and the uitlanders led directly to the far bigger war of 1899.

Charles XV, 1859-1872 (Sweden, AD 1859–A.label: Charles XV, 1859-1872
Charles XV, 1859-1872 (Sweden, AD 1859–A.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1859–AD 1872] Charles XV, 1859-1872. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles XV, 1859-1872". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A painter and poet on the throne, he lent his name to a burst of modernisation: the four-estate Riksdag of nobles, clergy, burghers and peasants was finally scrapped in 1866 for a two-chamber parliament, and the criminal and commercial codes were overhauled. He was an enthusiast for Scandinavian unity, though Sweden stood aside when Denmark was crushed by Prussia in 1864, killing the movement's political hopes.

Colonial period, 1824-1948 (Burma, AD 18.label: Colonial period, 1824-1948
Colonial period, 1824-1948 (Burma, AD 18.prose:
[Burma, AD 1824–AD 1948] Colonial period, 1824-1948. Sources cited refer to Myanmar rather than Burma. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three Anglo-Burmese wars stripped the Konbaung kingdom of its territory piece by piece until the monarchy was abolished and Burma governed as a province of British India. The Irrawaddy delta was drained for rice on a huge scale, drawing in Indian labour and moneylenders and remaking the country's demography. Buddhist revival and student politics fed a nationalist movement that, after Japanese occupation and Aung San's assassination, produced independence in 1948.

Charles Emmanuel IV, 1796-1802 (Sardinia.label: Charles Emmanuel IV, 1796-1802
Charles Emmanuel IV, 1796-1802 (Sardinia.prose:
[Sardinia, AD 1796–AD 1802] Charles Emmanuel IV, 1796-1802. Extracted from heading "Sardinia (Italy)--History--Charles Emmanuel IV, 1796-1802". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign began as French revolutionary armies overran Piedmont; in 1798 he was forced to give up his mainland possessions and withdraw to the island of Sardinia, the last remnant of his kingdom. Grieving and childless, he abdicated in 1802 in favour of his brother and later joined the Jesuits.

Allied occupation, 1945-1955 (Germany, A.label: Allied occupation, 1945-1955
Allied occupation, 1945-1955 (Germany, A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1945–AD 1955] Allied occupation, 1945-1955. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--1945-1955". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.
