Austria was split into American, British, French and Soviet zones, with Vienna similarly quartered and patrolled by joint four-power teams. Treated as Hitler's first victim rather than an enemy state, the country kept its own government throughout and avoided the permanent partition that befell Germany. The State Treaty of 1955 withdrew all foreign troops in exchange for a pledge of permanent neutrality.

Reign of Terror, 1793-1794 (France, AD 1.label: Reign of Terror, 1793-1794
Reign of Terror, 1793-1794 (France, AD 1.prose:
[France, AD 1793–AD 1794] Reign of Terror, 1793-1794. Extracted from heading "France--History--Reign of Terror, 1793-1794". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With France at war abroad and in revolt at home, the Committee of Public Safety governed by emergency decree, and the guillotine became an instrument of policy: some 17,000 people were formally executed and many thousands more died in prison or in the crushing of the Vendée. Robespierre's regime also pushed price controls, mass conscription, dechristianisation and a new revolutionary calendar. It collapsed with his arrest in Thermidor, leaving Europe with an enduring vocabulary — "terror," "suspect," "revolutionary tribunal" — and a lasting argument about how revolutions consume themselves.

Hugh Capet, 987-996 (France, AD 987–AD 9.label: Hugh Capet, 987-996
Hugh Capet, 987-996 (France, AD 987–AD 9.prose:
[France, AD 987–AD 996] Hugh Capet, 987-996. Extracted from heading "France--History--Hugh Capet, 987-996". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected king of the Franks by the magnates after the Carolingian line faltered, Hugh controlled little more than the lands around Paris and Orléans, and had less real power than several of his own vassals. What he did secure was the succession: by crowning his son in his own lifetime he made the kingship hereditary in practice. The dynasty he founded held the French throne, in one branch or another, for over eight hundred years.

Papal Interdict, 1606-1607 (Veneto, AD 1.label: Papal Interdict, 1606-1607
Papal Interdict, 1606-1607 (Veneto, AD 1.prose:
[Venice, AD 1606–AD 1607] Papal Interdict, 1606-1607. Extracted from heading "Venice (Italy)--History--Papal Interdict, 1606-1607". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Paul V excommunicated the Venetian senate and placed the republic under interdict over its insistence on trying clergy in its own courts and limiting church property. Venice simply ordered its priests to keep saying mass, expelled the Jesuits, and let the theologian Paolo Sarpi argue in print that a state's civil authority came from God directly, not through Rome. French mediation ended the quarrel without Venice conceding anything, a public demonstration that papal spiritual weapons had lost their bite against a confident secular government.

Dhofar War, 1964-1976 (Oman, AD 1964–AD.label: Dhofar War, 1964-1976
Dhofar War, 1964-1976 (Oman, AD 1964–AD.prose:
[Oman , AD 1964–AD 1976] Dhofar War, 1964-1976. Extracted from heading "Oman--History--Dhofar War, 1964-1976". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.87 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A tribal revolt in Oman's southern mountains turned into a Marxist insurgency armed and sheltered by neighbouring South Yemen, and for a time the rebels held most of the Dhofar hinterland. The turning point came in 1970, when Sultan Said bin Taimur was deposed by his son Qaboos, who paired amnesties, wells, clinics and schools with a counter-insurgency campaign supported by British SAS teams and Iranian troops. Victory in 1976 secured the new sultan's rule and set the pattern for Oman's oil-funded modernisation.

Charles I, 1625-1649 (Scotland, AD 1625–.label: Charles I, 1625-1649
Charles I, 1625-1649 (Scotland, AD 1625–.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1625–AD 1649] Charles I, 1625-1649. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Charles I, 1625-1649". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king convinced of his divine right ruled eleven years without Parliament, raising money through ship money and other levies that many considered illegal, and pushed ceremonial reforms that Puritans read as creeping popery. Attempts to impose a prayer book on Scotland forced him to recall Parliament, and the quarrel escalated into civil war across the three kingdoms. Defeated twice, he was tried by his own subjects and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall — an event without precedent in Europe. His art collection, one of the finest ever assembled, was sold off by the victors.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Russia, AD 1905–A.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Russia, AD 1905–A.prose:
[Russia , AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Turco-Italian War, 1911-1912 (Italy, AD.label: Turco-Italian War, 1911-1912
Turco-Italian War, 1911-1912 (Italy, AD.prose:
[Italy, Turkey, Libya, Tripolitania, Cyrenaica, AD 1911–AD 1912] Turco-Italian War, 1911-1912. Spatial coverage: Italy, Libya, Turkey. Extracted from heading "Turco-Italian War, 1911-1912". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Italy seized Ottoman Libya and the Dodecanese islands, using aircraft for reconnaissance and bombing for the first time in warfare. The Ottomans, unable to reinforce North Africa, conceded at Lausanne, but the defeat exposed their weakness and encouraged the Balkan states to attack within weeks. The war is a direct link in the chain leading to the Balkan Wars and the First World War.

Louis IV, 936-954 (France, AD 936–AD 954.label: Louis IV, 936-954
Louis IV, 936-954 (France, AD 936–AD 954.prose:
[France, AD 936–AD 954] Louis IV, 936-954. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis IV, 936-954". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brought back from exile in England to take the West Frankish throne, hence his nickname 'd'Outremer', from overseas. His reign was a struggle against the overmighty Hugh the Great of the Robertian house, including a spell as a captive of the Normans, and he ruled little more than Laon and its surroundings. The episode shows how far Carolingian royal power in France had shrunk before the Capetians took over.

Axis occupation, 1941-1945 (Slovenia, AD.label: Axis occupation, 1941-1945
Axis occupation, 1941-1945 (Slovenia, AD.prose:
[Slovenia, AD 1941–AD 1945] Axis occupation, 1941-1945. Extracted from heading "Slovenia--History--Axis occupation, 1941-1945". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Slovenia was carved up three ways between Germany, Italy and Hungary, each occupier trying to erase it: German authorities banned the language and deported tens of thousands northwards, while Italy walled Ljubljana with barbed wire. The communist-led Liberation Front mounted one of Europe's most effective partisan movements, and a brutal civil war developed with the anti-communist Home Guard. Victory in 1945 brought both liberation and mass reprisal killings, and Slovenia entered communist Yugoslavia.

Osman II, 1618-1622 (Turkey, AD 1618–AD.label: Osman II, 1618-1622
Osman II, 1618-1622 (Turkey, AD 1618–AD.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1618–AD 1622] Osman II, 1618-1622. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Osman II, 1618-1622". Added to LCSH in 2017, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A teenage sultan who came to the throne amid war with Poland and blamed the failed Khotyn campaign on the Janissaries, whose privileges he set out to break by raising a new army from Anatolia and Syria. The corps mutinied, deposed him and had him strangled at Yedikule – the first killing of a reigning Ottoman sultan by his own soldiers, and a warning to every successor who contemplated military reform.

Gallienus, 260-268 (Roman Empire, AD 260.label: Gallienus, 260-268
Gallienus, 260-268 (Roman Empire, AD 260.prose:
[Rome, AD 260–AD 268] Gallienus, 260-268. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Gallienus, 260-268". Added to LCSH in 1990, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Gallienus ruled alone after his father Valerian was captured by the Persians, and presided over the empire's near-collapse: the Gallic provinces broke away under Postumus, Palmyra took the east, and plague, usurpers and raiding armies pressed the frontiers. He responded by building a mobile cavalry reserve and barring senators from legionary commands, changes that shaped the later Roman army, while the silver coinage sank to little more than washed bronze. Visitors often notice the contrast between the debased coins of these years and the elegant classicising portraits on them.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Texas, AD 1861–AD.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Texas, AD 1861–AD.prose:
[Texas, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Texas--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.91 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Turkish rule, 1669-1898 (Crete, AD 1669–.label: Turkish rule, 1669-1898
Turkish rule, 1669-1898 (Crete, AD 1669–.prose:
[Crete (Greece), AD 1669–AD 1898] Turkish rule, 1669-1898. Extracted from heading "Crete (Greece)--History--Turkish rule, 1669-1898". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The surrender of Candia after one of the longest sieges in history ended four centuries of Venetian control. Ottoman Crete saw substantial conversion to Islam among the local population, producing the Cretan Muslim community, alongside repeated and bloody insurrections through the nineteenth century. Great Power intervention forced the creation of an autonomous Cretan State, a step towards union with Greece.

Robert II, 1371-1390 (Scotland, AD 1371–.label: Robert II, 1371-1390
Robert II, 1371-1390 (Scotland, AD 1371–.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1390] Robert II, 1371-1390. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Robert II, 1371-1390". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Grandson of Robert the Bruce through his daughter, he came to the throne in late middle age as the first of the Stewart kings, a line that would hold Scotland until 1714 and later England as well. His reign saw renewed border warfare with England, culminating in the Scottish victory at Otterburn, while much of the day-to-day governing fell to his numerous and quarrelsome sons.

Margrethe II, 1972- (Denmark, AD 1972–AD.label: Margrethe II, 1972-
Margrethe II, 1972- (Denmark, AD 1972–AD.prose:
[Denmark , AD 1972–AD 2015] Margrethe II, 1972-. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Margrethe II, 1972-". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark's first queen regnant since the Middle Ages, made possible by a change to the succession law a few years before her accession. She combined the ceremonial role of a modern constitutional monarch with a working career as an artist, illustrator and stage designer, and her long reign spanned Denmark's deepening and often uneasy relationship with the European project.

Chimurenga War, 1896-1897 (Zimbabwe, AD.label: Chimurenga War, 1896-1897
Chimurenga War, 1896-1897 (Zimbabwe, AD.prose:
[Zimbabwe, AD 1896–AD 1897] Chimurenga War, 1896-1897. Extracted from heading "Zimbabwe--History--Chimurenga War, 1896-1897". Added to LCSH in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ndebele and Shona communities rose together against the British South Africa Company, whose settlers had seized land and cattle and imposed forced labour and a hut tax. Spirit mediums such as Nehanda and Kaguvi helped coordinate the revolt across chieftaincies, and their execution afterwards turned them into national martyrs. The rising was crushed by patrol columns and the destruction of grain stores, cementing settler rule, but it supplied the name and the memory that later nationalists claimed as their own.

Macrinus, 217-218 (Roman Empire, AD 217–.label: Macrinus, 217-218
Macrinus, 217-218 (Roman Empire, AD 217–.prose:
[Rome, AD 217–AD 218] Macrinus, 217-218. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Macrinus, 217-218". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The praetorian prefect who arranged Caracalla's murder and then took the purple himself — the first man to rule Rome without ever having sat in the Senate. He bought peace from the Parthians at heavy cost and tried to trim army pay, which cost him the loyalty of the eastern legions; within fourteen months they proclaimed the teenage Elagabalus instead, and Macrinus was hunted down and killed. His brief reign showed how completely emperors now depended on the soldiers rather than on Rome.

Casimir III, 1333-1370 (Poland, AD 1333–.label: Casimir III, 1333-1370
Casimir III, 1333-1370 (Poland, AD 1333–.prose:
[Poland , AD 1333–AD 1370] Casimir III, 1333-1370. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Casimir III, 1333-1370". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Piast king turned a fragmented, war-battered realm into a functioning kingdom: he codified law in separate statutes for Wielkopolska and Małopolska, built or rebuilt dozens of brick castles and town walls, founded the university at Kraków in 1364, and issued charters protecting Jewish settlers fleeing persecution further west. He traded claims on Silesia and Pomerania for expansion east into Halych-Volhynia, tilting Poland's future towards Ruthenia. Dying without a son, he left the crown to his Angevin nephew and ended the native dynasty.

Alfonso XII, 1875-1885 (Spain, AD 1875–A.label: Alfonso XII, 1875-1885
Alfonso XII, 1875-1885 (Spain, AD 1875–A.prose:
[Spain, AD 1875–AD 1885] Alfonso XII, 1875-1885. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Alfonso XII, 1875-1885". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His accession ended six years of republican turmoil and restored the Bourbons. The regime that followed brought the Third Carlist War to a close, produced the durable 1876 constitution and settled into the turno pacífico, an arrangement in which Liberals and Conservatives took turns in office through managed elections. Stability came at the price of an electoral system that excluded most Spaniards from real influence.

Armeno-Tatar Conflict, 1905-1907 (Russia.label: Armeno-Tatar Conflict, 1905-1907
Armeno-Tatar Conflict, 1905-1907 (Russia.prose:
[Russia , AD 1905–AD 1907] Armeno-Tatar Conflict, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Armeno-Tatar Conflict, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH and revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As imperial authority collapsed during the 1905 revolution, communal violence erupted between Armenians and the Muslim Turkic population of the Caucasus in Baku, Nakhichevan, Yerevan and Shusha. Thousands died, oilfields burned, and neighbourhoods were segregated by force. The bloodshed hardened national identities and prefigured the Armenian-Azerbaijani conflicts that followed the empire's fall.

Frederick I, 1152-1190 (Germany, AD 1152.label: Frederick I, 1152-1190
Frederick I, 1152-1190 (Germany, AD 1152.prose:

Barbarossa spent his reign trying to make imperial authority real in Italy, launching six expeditions south and destroying Milan, only to be beaten by the Lombard League at Legnano in 1176 and forced to recognise the cities' liberties. At home he broke his greatest rival, Henry the Lion, and redistributed his duchies, cementing the princes' power. He drowned in a river in Anatolia on the Third Crusade, and German legend later had him sleeping in a mountain, waiting to return.

A North Sea port and shipyard town on the Ems, it was attacked for its harbour and submarine construction and lost the overwhelming majority of its old buildings, with the centre effectively erased in a single raid in September 1944. Postwar reconstruction produced an almost entirely modern town on a medieval street plan.

Italian occupation, 1942-1943 (France, A.label: Italian occupation, 1942-1943

[France, AD 1942–AD 1943] Italian occupation, 1942-1943. Extracted from heading "France--History--Italian occupation, 1942-1943". After the Allied landings in North Africa, Italian troops moved into the southeast of France, taking Nice, Savoy and much of Provence up to the Rhône. Italian authorities repeatedly refused to hand over Jews to Vichy police or the Germans, and the zone became a refuge for thousands until Italy's armistice with the Allies, after which German forces took over and deportations began.

James I, 1213-1276 (Kingdom of Aragon, A.label: James I, 1213-1276
James I, 1213-1276 (Kingdom of Aragon, A.prose:
[Aragon, AD 1213–AD 1276] James I, 1213-1276. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--James I, 1213-1276". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975; revised 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

James the Conqueror came to the throne as a child and turned Aragon into a Mediterranean power, taking Mallorca and Ibiza from Muslim rulers and conquering the kingdom of Valencia. He fixed the frontier with Castile by treaty, effectively turning Aragonese expansion seaward rather than south. He left law codes, a chartered administration for his new territories, and an autobiography, the 'Llibre dels fets', one of the earliest royal memoirs in Europe.

A formidable soldier who beat back the Arabs and repeatedly crushed the Bulgars, and an uncompromising iconoclast who had a church council declare images heretical in 754 and persecuted the monks who defended them. His enemies later gave him the insulting nickname meaning 'dung-named' and did their best to blacken his record, but his campaigns and his reorganisation of the guard regiments left the empire far stronger than he found it.

Mustafa II, 1695-1703 (Turkey, AD 1695–A.label: Mustafa II, 1695-1703
Mustafa II, 1695-1703 (Turkey, AD 1695–A.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1695–AD 1703] Mustafa II, 1695-1703. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mustafa II, 1695-1703". Added to LCSH in 1987; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The sultan led Ottoman armies into the field in person against the Habsburgs, only to see his forces destroyed at Zenta in 1697. The Treaty of Karlowitz that followed handed Hungary and Transylvania to Austria and marked the first time the empire signed away large territories as a defeated power. His reliance on his old tutor as chief minister, and rising taxes, provoked a revolt of the Istanbul garrison that forced his abdication.

Renaissance, 1450-1600 (Europe, AD 1450–.prose:

Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Printing with movable type, the recovery of Greek and Latin texts, and the wealth of Italian and Flemish cities combined to produce a burst of new art and scholarship that spread north and west across Europe. Perspective painting, anatomical drawing, humanist education and the beginnings of a critical approach to sources all date from here, alongside Atlantic voyages that redrew the map and the Reformation that split the Church. Visitors meet the era through names like Leonardo, Dürer, Erasmus, Michelangelo and Shakespeare.

Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632 (Finland, AD.label: Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632
Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632 (Finland, AD.prose:
[Finland, AD 1611–AD 1632] Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632. Extracted from heading "Finland--History--Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632". Added to LCSH in 1986. Gustavus Adolphus turned a peripheral Baltic kingdom into a great power, overhauling the army with mobile field artillery, disciplined musket volleys and conscription, and reforming administration and taxation with his chancellor Axel Oxenstierna. His intervention in the Thirty Years' War rescued the Protestant cause in Germany and won stunning victories at Breitenfeld and the Lech, until he was killed leading a cavalry charge at Lützen. The blood-stained buff coat and horse relics of that battle became national relics, and his campaigns set the template for European warfare for a century.

Dutch rule, 1624-1661 (Taiwan, AD 1624–A.label: Dutch rule, 1624-1661
Dutch rule, 1624-1661 (Taiwan, AD 1624–A.prose:
[Taiwan, AD 1624–AD 1661] Dutch rule, 1624-1661. Extracted from heading "Taiwan--History--Dutch rule, 1624-1661". Added to LCSH in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch East India Company built Fort Zeelandia on a sandbar off the southwest coast as a base for trade with China and Japan, and gradually extended control over surrounding Indigenous villages through alliances, punitive campaigns and Reformed missionaries who wrote Austronesian languages in Latin script. The Company exported deerskins and sugar and encouraged Chinese migration from Fujian to farm and pay taxes, a decision that reshaped the island's population. Spanish rivals in the north were expelled in 1642; the colony itself fell to the Ming loyalist Koxinga after a long siege.

Clement VIII, 1592-1605 (Vatican City, A.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1592–AD 1605] Clement VIII, 1592-1605. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Clement VIII, 1592-1605". He reconciled Rome with Henry IV of France, absolving the converted Protestant king and loosening Spanish dominance over the papacy. His reign saw the Holy Year of 1600 draw huge pilgrim crowds, the Roman Inquisition burn Giordano Bruno, and long theological hearings on grace between Jesuits and Dominicans. He also annexed Ferrara to the Papal States and issued a revised Index of forbidden books.

Polish occupation, 1610-1612 (Russia, AD.label: Polish occupation, 1610-1612
Polish occupation, 1610-1612 (Russia, AD.prose:
[Moscow (Russia), AD 1610–AD 1612] Polish occupation, 1610-1612. Extracted from heading "Moscow (Russia)--History--Polish occupation, 1610-1612". Added to LCSH i 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

At the depth of the Time of Troubles, boyars deposed Vasily Shuisky and invited the Polish prince Władysław to the throne, and a Commonwealth garrison took control of the Moscow Kremlin. Sigismund III's refusal to let his son convert to Orthodoxy turned the arrangement into foreign occupation, and Patriarch Hermogenes' appeals helped spark national resistance. A volunteer army raised by the merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky retook Moscow in 1612, clearing the way for the election of Michael Romanov.

Carlist War, 1846-1849 (Spain, AD 1846–A.label: Carlist War, 1846-1849
Carlist War, 1846-1849 (Spain, AD 1846–A.prose:
[Spain, AD 1846–AD 1849] Carlist War, 1846-1849. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Carlist War, 1846-1849". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2002. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A smaller Carlist revolt centred on the Catalan hills, fought largely by guerrilla bands nicknamed matiners, or early risers. Sparked by the failure to marry Isabella II to the Carlist claimant, it drew in republicans and disaffected peasants before being ground down by government columns. It kept the Carlist cause alive in the countryside without ever threatening the state.

Frederick II, 1215-1250 (Germany, AD 121.label: Frederick II, 1215-1250
Frederick II, 1215-1250 (Germany, AD 121.prose:
[Germany , AD 1215–AD 1250] Frederick II, 1215-1250. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Frederick II, 1215-1250". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Raised in Sicily and ruling an empire that stretched from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, this Hohenzollern-rival Hohenstaufen was called "the wonder of the world" for his multilingual, Arab-influenced court, his falconry treatise and his interest in natural science. He won Jerusalem by negotiation rather than battle while excommunicated, issued the Constitutions of Melfi as a model of centralised royal law, and fought the papacy so bitterly that he was deposed and denounced as Antichrist. His death left Germany to princely fragmentation and the Interregnum, and his dynasty was destroyed within a generation.

Early modern and Elizabethan, 1500-1600.label: Early modern and Elizabethan, 1500-1600
Early modern and Elizabethan, 1500-1600.prose:

The break with Rome dissolved the monasteries and rewrote religious life, transferring vast estates into private hands and reshaping the landscape. Under Elizabeth I the country turned outward, with privateering voyages, the first American ventures and the defeat of the Spanish Armada, while London's theatres gave the age Marlowe and Shakespeare. Prices rose sharply, the gentry built new brick and glass country houses, and printed books spread ideas faster than ever before.

War of Independence, 1919-1921 (Republic.node: War of Independence, 1919-1921 (Republic of Ireland, AD 1919–AD 1921)
War of Independence, 1919-1921 (Republic.label: War of Independence, 1919-1921

Sinn Féin's elected MPs set up their own parliament in Dublin while IRA flying columns fought a guerrilla campaign of ambushes and assassinations against police and the auxiliary 'Black and Tans', who answered with reprisals and burnings. The truce and Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921 produced a self-governing Irish Free State but left six northern counties under British rule. Disagreement over that compromise split the independence movement into civil war within months.

Italo-Ethiopian War, 1935-1936 (Italy, A.label: Italo-Ethiopian War, 1935-1936

Mussolini avenged Adwa with aircraft, tanks and mustard gas, taking Addis Ababa and proclaiming an Italian empire. The League of Nations condemned the invasion and imposed sanctions that were too weak to bite, exposing the collective security system as hollow and encouraging Hitler. Haile Selassie's appeal to the League in Geneva became one of the defining speeches of the decade; he returned in 1941 with British help.

James I, 1406-1437 (Scotland, AD 1406–AD.label: James I, 1406-1437
James I, 1406-1437 (Scotland, AD 1406–AD.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1406–AD 1437] James I, 1406-1437. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--James I, 1406-1437". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Captured at sea as a boy and held in England for eighteen years, he returned to Scotland to impose royal authority with sudden force, destroying the Albany Stewarts and pursuing money and obedience from the nobility. He reformed the coinage, the courts and parliamentary procedure along English lines. Resentment ended in his assassination at Perth, and the crown passed again to a child.

A middling comital family from the western edge of the Empire won the imperial title and then acquired Bohemia, shifting the centre of gravity to Prague. Charles IV rebuilt that city with a new town, a stone bridge and central Europe's first university, and his Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the rules of imperial election for the next four centuries. His son Sigismund convened the Council of Constance, ending the papal schism and burning Jan Hus - which lit the Hussite wars that consumed Bohemia.

A boy king inherited a realm still reeling from plague and war taxes, and at fourteen rode out to face the rebels of the Peasants' Revolt. His adult rule turned on an exalted view of kingship, the crushing of the Lords Appellant who had curbed him, and confiscations that frightened the nobility into revolt; deposed by his cousin Henry Bolingbroke, he died in captivity, leaving a disputed succession that fed the Wars of the Roses. His court also patronised Chaucer and the Wilton Diptych, and gave England its first great flowering of courtly art.

Genroku period, 1688-1704 (Japan, AD 168.label: Genroku period, 1688-1704
Genroku period, 1688-1704 (Japan, AD 168.prose:
[Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704] Genroku period, 1688-1704. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Genroku period, 1688-1704". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peace and urban wealth produced Japan's first great popular culture: kabuki and bunraku theatre, the fiction of Ihara Saikaku, Bashō's haikai, and woodblock prints made for townspeople rather than lords. Merchants in Osaka and Edo grew rich while samurai stipends stagnated and the government debased its coins to pay its bills. The forty-seven rōnin vendetta of 1702 crystallised the era's tension between law and warrior honour.

Revolution, 1905-1907 (Uzbekistan, AD 19.label: Revolution, 1905-1907
Revolution, 1905-1907 (Uzbekistan, AD 19.prose:
[Uzbekistan, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Uzbekistan--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

Fourth Crusade, 1202-1204 (Anatolia, AD.prose:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1202–AD 1204] Fourth Crusade, 1202-1204. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Fourth, 1202-1204". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An expedition meant for Egypt that instead turned on the Christian capital of Constantinople, storming and sacking it in 1204 and carving the Byzantine Empire into Latin lordships. Greek successor states at Nicaea, Trebizond and Epirus kept the imperial idea alive, and Nicaea eventually retook the city in 1261 — but the empire never recovered its wealth or its hold on Anatolia. The looted bronze horses of Constantinople still stand at San Marco in Venice, whose doge helped steer the diversion.

Taika Reforms, 645-710 (Japan, AD 645–AD.prose:
[Japan, AD 645–AD 710] Taika Reforms, 645-710. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Taika Reforms, 645-710". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Following the coup that toppled the Soga, the Yamato court set about rebuilding itself as a Chinese-style centralised state, abolishing private control of land and labour, dividing the country into provinces and districts under appointed officials, and imposing uniform taxes and census registers. The process culminated in the Taihō legal codes and in the building of a permanent Chinese-style capital, ending the old custom of moving the court with each reign.

Ionian Revolt, 499-494 B.C (Greece, 498.label: Ionian Revolt, 499-494 B.C
Ionian Revolt, 499-494 B.C (Greece, 498.prose:
[Greece, 498 BC–493 BC] Ionian Revolt, 499-494 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Ionian Revolt, 499-494 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Greek cities of the Anatolian coast, led by Miletus, threw out their Persian-backed tyrants and burned Sardis with help from Athens and Eretria. Persia crushed the rebellion at the naval battle of Lade and sacked Miletus, deporting its people. Darius's determination to punish the mainland Greeks who had intervened set off the Persian Wars, making this local uprising the trigger for Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis.

He took the throne by blinding and deposing his own brother, then presided over a treasury emptied by bribes and tribute - at one point stripping imperial tombs to pay off the West. When the Fourth Crusade arrived to restore his nephew, he fled the capital with the crown jewels. The chaos he left behind ended in the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

Civil Disobedience, 1999-2001 (Puerto Ri.prose:

After a civilian guard was killed by an errant bomb on the US Navy's Vieques range, protesters occupied the bombing zone in camps and refused to leave, and hundreds were arrested over the following years. The campaign united Puerto Ricans across party lines and drew in church leaders, mainland politicians and celebrities, turning a local land dispute into a debate about the island's colonial relationship with Washington. The Navy finally abandoned Vieques in 2003, leaving behind contamination that is still being cleaned up.

Iraq-Kuwait Crisis, 1990-1991 (Iraq, AD.label: Iraq-Kuwait Crisis, 1990-1991
Iraq-Kuwait Crisis, 1990-1991 (Iraq, AD.prose:
[Iraq, Kuwait, AD 1990–AD 1991] Iraq-Kuwait Crisis, 1990-1991. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Extracted from heading "Iraq-Kuwait Crisis, 1990-1991". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait in August 1990, prompting a UN-authorised coalition of some three dozen states to assemble in Saudi Arabia. A five-week air campaign and a hundred-hour ground offensive drove Iraqi forces out, leaving burning oil wells and a crushed Shia and Kurdish uprising behind. The war left Iraq under punishing sanctions and no-fly zones, and put long-term American bases in the Gulf, with consequences that ran on into 2003 and beyond.

War of Reform, 1857-1861 (Mexico, AD 185.label: War of Reform, 1857-1861
War of Reform, 1857-1861 (Mexico, AD 185.prose:
[Mexico, AD 1857–AD 1861] War of Reform, 1857-1861. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--War of Reform, 1857-1861". Added to LCSH and revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Mexican liberals and conservatives fought a full civil war over the 1857 constitution and the Reform Laws, which stripped the Catholic Church and the army of their courts, privileges and vast landholdings. Benito Juárez's liberal government won and entered Mexico City in 1861, but the country was bankrupt — a suspension of foreign debt payments that immediately triggered French intervention and Maximilian's short-lived empire.

Palaeologi Dynasty, 1259-1448 (Byzantine.label: Palaeologi Dynasty, 1259-1448
Palaeologi Dynasty, 1259-1448 (Byzantine.prose:

Michael VIII seized the throne and recovered Constantinople from the Latins in 1261, but the restored Byzantine Empire was a diminished state hemmed in by Serbs, Venetians, Genoese and the rising Ottomans. Civil wars and the Black Death drained it further, until the emperors were paying tribute and touring Europe begging for aid, even accepting church union at Florence. Yet these decades produced the mosaics of the Chora church and a revival of classical scholarship whose exiles helped ignite the Italian Renaissance.

War of Independence, 1810-1811 (Paraguay.label: War of Independence, 1810-1811
War of Independence, 1810-1811 (Paraguay.prose:
[Paraguay, AD 1810–AD 1811] War of Independence, 1810-1811. Extracted from heading "Paraguay--History--War of Independence, 1810-1811". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Buenos Aires sent Manuel Belgrano to bring Paraguay into its revolution; Paraguayan militia defeated him at Paraguarí and Tacuarí, then promptly deposed the Spanish governor themselves. The result was independence from Spain and from Buenos Aires alike, a distinction Paraguay guarded fiercely. Dr José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia emerged from the new junta to rule as dictator, sealing the country off from its neighbours for decades.

The Conqueror's second surviving son took England while his brother Robert took Normandy, and much of his reign was spent fighting or buying that inheritance back. He was famous for extracting money from the Church, leaving bishoprics vacant to pocket their revenues, and for a bitter quarrel with Archbishop Anselm that drove him into exile. Rufus built Westminster Hall and campaigned in Wales and Scotland before dying from an arrow in the New Forest, an accident many contemporaries suspected was murder.

Revolution, 1917-1921 (Turkmenistan, AD.prose:

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

Reapers' War, 1640-1659 (Catalonia, AD 1.label: Reapers' War, 1640-1659
Reapers' War, 1640-1659 (Catalonia, AD 1.prose:
[Catalonia (Spain), AD 1640–AD 1659] Reapers' War, 1640-1659. Extracted from heading "Catalonia (Spain)--History--Reapers' War, 1640-1659". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Catalan peasants and townsmen rose against the billeting of Spanish troops and the tax demands of Olivares' war effort, killing the viceroy in Barcelona on the Corpus Christi that became known as the Bloody Body. Catalonia placed itself under the protection of the French king, turning a revolt into a front of the wider Franco-Spanish war. Barcelona fell back to Spain in 1652, and the final peace split the Catalan lands, handing Roussillon and part of Cerdanya to France, a border that survives today.

Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.89 of LCSH 1987, and p.75 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Asunción's colonists rose against the crown-appointed governor and the power of the Jesuit missions, invoking the old Castilian principle that the community's will outranked the king's officials. Led first by José de Antequera and later by Fernando Mompox, the comuneros held the province through years of intermittent fighting before Bruno Mauricio de Zabala suppressed them. The revolt is remembered in Paraguay as an early assertion of local self-government against Spanish authority.

[Europe, AD 1500–AD 1700] Early modern, 1500-1700. Spatial coverage: Europe, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Northern Ireland, Poland, Republic of Ireland, Switzerland. "Use as a chronological subdivision under individual languages and groups of languages, groups of literary authors, and individual literatures except drama.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two centuries that took the country from Reformation to revolution: the monasteries fell, the crowns of England and Scotland were united, a king was tried and executed, and a restored monarchy was finally bound by Parliament. Trade companies pushed into the Atlantic and Asia and the first lasting colonies were planted, while London grew into a metropolis and rebuilt itself after the Great Fire. New science, coffee houses and cheap print changed how knowledge circulated.

Mysore War, 1790-1792 (India, AD 1790–AD.label: Mysore War, 1790-1792
Mysore War, 1790-1792 (India, AD 1790–AD.prose:
[India, AD 1790–AD 1792] Mysore War, 1790-1792. Extracted from heading "India--History--Mysore War, 1790-1792". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.58 of LCSH 1987, and p.47 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Tipu Sultan of Mysore faced a coalition of the East India Company, the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad, with Cornwallis eventually taking the field himself and besieging Seringapatam. Tipu was forced to surrender half his kingdom and send two of his sons to the British as hostages for an enormous indemnity. The defeat broke the strongest indigenous check on Company power in southern India and set up its final conquest seven years later.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Chicago, AD 1861–A.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Chicago, AD 1861–A.prose:
[Chicago (Ill.), AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Chicago (Ill.)--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.23 of LCSH 1987, and p.20 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Famine, 1921-1922 (Russia, AD 1921–AD 19.label: Famine, 1921-1922
Famine, 1921-1922 (Russia, AD 1921–AD 19.prose:
[Soviet Union, AD 1921–AD 1922] Famine, 1921-1922. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Estonia, Georgia (country), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia. Extracted from heading "Soviet Union--History--Famine, 1921-1922". Added to LCSH in 2010, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Drought struck a countryside already stripped bare by grain requisitioning during the civil war, and famine spread through the Volga basin and Ukraine, killing perhaps five million people. The Bolsheviks abandoned War Communism for the New Economic Policy and accepted foreign aid, notably Herbert Hoover's American Relief Administration, which at its peak fed some ten million people daily. The government also used the crisis as grounds to confiscate church valuables.

Uprising, 1519-1522 (Valencian Community.label: Uprising, 1519-1522
Uprising, 1519-1522 (Valencian Community.prose:
[Valencia (Spain), AD 1519–AD 1522] Uprising, 1519-1522. Extracted from heading "Valencia (Spain : Region)--History--Uprising, 1519-1522". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Artisan guilds in Valencia, armed with royal permission to defend the coast against Barbary raids, turned their brotherhoods - the Germanies - against the nobility and the crown while Charles V was abroad. The revolt spread through the kingdom and to Mallorca, mixing demands for guild power in city government with attacks on aristocratic estates and forced baptisms of Muslim vassals. Royal and noble forces broke it by 1522, and its defeat helped consolidate seigneurial control over the Valencian countryside.

South African War, 1899-1902 (South Afri.label: South African War, 1899-1902
South African War, 1899-1902 (South Afri.prose:
[South Africa, AD 1899–AD 1902] South African War, 1899-1902. Extracted from heading "South African War, 1899-1902". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain's costly war against the Transvaal and Orange Free State, fought over gold, franchise rights for uitlanders and imperial supremacy. After early Boer victories and sieges, British numbers told, but the war dragged on through two years of guerrilla resistance answered with farm burning and concentration camps in which tens of thousands of Boer and African civilians died. The peace of Vereeniging brought the republics into the empire and set the terms for the whites-only Union of South Africa in 1910.

Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1941-1979 (Iran,.label: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1941-1979
Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1941-1979 (Iran,.prose:
[Iran, AD 1941–AD 1979] Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1941-1979. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1941-1979". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. REvised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The young shah was placed on the throne when Britain and the Soviet Union deposed his father and occupied Iran during the war. His authority was nearly ended by Mohammad Mossadegh's nationalisation of the oil industry, until a British- and American-backed coup in 1953 restored him; afterwards he pushed land reform and rapid modernisation, financed by soaring oil revenues and policed by the SAVAK secret service. Inequality, repression and cultural resentment culminated in the revolution of 1978-79 and the founding of the Islamic Republic.

Nara period, 710-794 (Japan, AD 710–AD 7.label: Nara period, 710-794
Nara period, 710-794 (Japan, AD 710–AD 7.prose:
[Japan, AD 710–AD 794] Nara period, 710-794. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Nara period, 710-794". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A permanent capital at Nara replaced the practice of moving the court at each reign, and with it came a Chinese-style bureaucracy, written histories and a national network of Buddhist temples. Smallpox epidemics and court intrigue strained the system, and monastic influence over the throne became a political danger. The move to Heian-kyō in 794 was in part an escape from Nara's monasteries.

Magnus I, 1035-1047 (Norway, AD 1035–AD.label: Magnus I, 1035-1047
Magnus I, 1035-1047 (Norway, AD 1035–AD.prose:
[Norway, AD 1035–AD 1047] Magnus I, 1035-1047. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Magnus I, 1035-1047". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Son of the martyred Olaf Haraldsson, brought back from exile in Rus' as a boy to reclaim his father's throne after Danish rule collapsed. He won Denmark as well, crushed a Wendish army at Lyrskov Heath, and issued one of Norway's earliest law compilations. His death left the kingdom to his uncle Harald Hardrada and locked Norway into a long rivalry with Denmark.

Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Clermont-Ferrand.label: Bombardment, 1943-1944
Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Clermont-Ferrand.prose:
[Clermont-Ferrand (France), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Clermont-Ferrand (France)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

Crimean War, 1853-1856 (France, AD 1853–.label: Crimean War, 1853-1856
Crimean War, 1853-1856 (France, AD 1853–.prose:
[France, Great Britain, Turkey, Russia, AD 1853–AD 1856] Crimean War, 1853-1856. Spatial coverage: France, Russia, Turkey, United Kingdom. Extracted from heading "Crimean War, 1853-1856". Added to LCSH in 1986. Explicit spatial coverage only includes Great Britain, France, and Turkey, but Russia can be inferred from "Russo-Turkish War" label. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain, France and the Ottomans fought Russia over influence in the declining Ottoman world, and the fighting settled into a grinding siege of Sevastopol that killed far more men through disease than combat. It was the first conflict reported by telegraph and recorded by war photographers and rifled artillery, and the scandal of the military hospitals launched Florence Nightingale and the reform of army nursing. Russia's defeat ended the post-Napoleonic balance in Europe and opened the way for Italian and German unification.

Henry IV, 1399-1413 (England, AD 1399–AD.label: Henry IV, 1399-1413
Henry IV, 1399-1413 (England, AD 1399–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1399–AD 1413] Henry IV, 1399-1413. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry IV, 1399-1413". Added to LCSH in 1986. The first Lancastrian king took the crown by deposing and probably starving his cousin Richard II, and spent his reign fighting to keep it. Owain Glyndŵr's rising kept Wales in revolt for years, the Percys of Northumberland turned on him at Shrewsbury, and money was always short. His shaky title left a claim that the House of York would revive fifty years later in the Wars of the Roses.

Hōgen and Heiji Insurrections, 1156-1159.label: Hōgen and Heiji Insurrections, 1156-1159
Hōgen and Heiji Insurrections, 1156-1159.prose:
[Japan, AD 1156–AD 1159] Hōgen and Heiji Insurrections, 1156-1159. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Hōgen and Heiji Insurrections, 1156-1159". Two short, brutal succession disputes in Kyoto in which rival emperors and Fujiwara nobles hired warrior clans to settle their quarrels. The samurai proved decisive, and Taira no Kiyomori emerged as the real power at court, the first warrior to dominate the imperial capital. The fighting set up the Taira–Minamoto rivalry that ended in the Genpei War and the shogunate, shifting Japanese politics permanently towards military rule.

Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Germany, AD 1576–A.label: Rudolf II, 1576-1612
Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Germany, AD 1576–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1576–AD 1612] Rudolf II, 1576-1612. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Rudolf II, 1576-1612". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Habsburg emperor moved his court to Prague and turned it into a magnet for astronomers, alchemists, painters and collectors – Tycho Brahe and Kepler worked under his patronage, and his cabinet of curiosities was the most famous in Europe. Politically he was indecisive and increasingly withdrawn, letting confessional tensions in the empire fester until his own family forced him to cede power. The Letter of Majesty he granted Bohemian Protestants in 1609, and its later breach, helped set up the revolt that began the Thirty Years' War.

Sixth Crusade, 1228-1229 (Anatolia, AD 1.label: Sixth Crusade, 1228-1229
Sixth Crusade, 1228-1229 (Anatolia, AD 1.prose:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1228–AD 1229] Sixth Crusade, 1228-1229. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Sixth, 1228-1229". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Frederick II sailed east while excommunicated and won Jerusalem not by battle but by treaty, negotiating a ten-year truce with the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil that returned the city to Christian rule with the Muslim holy places left in Muslim hands. He crowned himself in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, satisfying almost nobody: the pope condemned the deal and many Muslims were outraged. The arrangement showed that diplomacy could achieve what armies had not, but it collapsed within fifteen years.

Cantabrian War, 26-19 B.C (Spain, 25 BC–.label: Cantabrian War, 26-19 B.C
Cantabrian War, 26-19 B.C (Spain, 25 BC–.prose:
[Spain, 25 BC–18 BC] Cantabrian War, 26-19 B.C. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Cantabrian War, 26-19 B.C". Added to LCSH and revised in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Augustus committed several legions, and for a time his own presence, to crushing the Cantabri and Astures of the northern mountains, the last peoples of Iberia outside Roman control. Brutal campaigns of sieges, blockades and mass enslavement ended two centuries of piecemeal conquest that had begun with the Punic Wars. With the peninsula finally pacified, Rome reorganised it into provinces and opened its gold and silver mines on an industrial scale.

Capital Jurisdiction Question, 1857-1897.label: Capital Jurisdiction Question, 1857-1897
Capital Jurisdiction Question, 1857-1897.prose: [Minnesota, AD 1857–AD 1897] Capital Jurisdiction Question, 1857-1897. Republic, 1912-1949 (China, AD 1912–AD 1.prose:

Sun Yat-sen's revolution ended two millennia of imperial rule, but the republic that replaced it was fragmented almost at once between Yuan Shikai's ambitions and regional warlord armies. Nationalist reunification in 1928 brought a decade of state-building in Nanjing, cut short by full-scale war with Japan. Victory in 1945 gave way immediately to civil war and the establishment of the People's Republic.

Guangxu, 1875-1908 (China, AD 1875–AD 19.label: Guangxu, 1875-1908
Guangxu, 1875-1908 (China, AD 1875–AD 19.prose:

The reign of a boy emperor who spent most of his life under the control of the Empress Dowager Cixi, in decades when the Qing empire lost a war to Japan, ceded ports to European powers and faced the Boxer uprising. His backing of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898 ended with the reformers executed or exiled and the emperor confined to a palace island. He died a day before Cixi, of arsenic poisoning, leaving the dynasty three years from its end.

Tawfīq, 1879-1892 (Egypt, AD 1879–AD 189.label: Tawfīq, 1879-1892
Tawfīq, 1879-1892 (Egypt, AD 1879–AD 189.prose:
[Egypt, AD 1879–AD 1892] Tawfīq, 1879-1892. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Tawfīq, 1879-1892". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and on p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign of Khedive Tawfiq, installed after his father Ismail was deposed over Egypt's crushing debts to European creditors. Nationalist officers under Ahmad Urabi rose against foreign control, Britain answered by bombarding Alexandria and invading in 1882, and Tawfiq was left ruling under a British occupation that would outlast him by decades; meanwhile Egypt lost Sudan to the Mahdist revolt.

Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009 (Vietnam, AD.label: Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009
Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 980–AD 1009] Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The general Lê Hoàn seized the throne from the child heir of the Đinh and immediately faced a Song Chinese invasion, which he crushed in 981, confirming the independence of the young Vietnamese state. He also campaigned south against Champa, sacking its capital, and ruled from the fortified valley capital of Hoa Lư. The dynasty lasted only three reigns; its last, notoriously cruel ruler was replaced in 1009 by the founder of the long-lived Lý dynasty.

Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C (Greece.label: Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C
Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C (Greece.prose:
[Greece, 322 BC–280 BC] Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alexander's death set his generals against one another in forty years of war, while Greek cities such as Athens rebelled and were crushed, garrisoned and made to accept Macedonian-backed regimes. Antipater, Cassander, Demetrius the Besieger and others fought over Macedon and Greece until the battle of Corupedium settled the map into the three great Hellenistic kingdoms. Greece itself became a strategic prize rather than a maker of policy.

Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870 (Canada,.label: Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870
Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870 (Canada,.prose:
[Canada, AD 1869–AD 1870] Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870. Extracted from heading "Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Canada bought Rupert's Land from the Hudson's Bay Company without consulting the people living there, the Métis of the Red River Settlement seized Fort Garry and formed a provisional government under Louis Riel. Their List of Rights forced Ottawa to negotiate, and the result was the Manitoba Act, which brought a new province into Confederation with guarantees for French language and Catholic schools. The provisional government's execution of the Orangeman Thomas Scott poisoned relations between Ontario and Quebec, drove Riel into exile, and set the stage for the North-West Rebellion fifteen years later.

Zeno, 474-491 (Byzantine Empire, AD 474–.label: Zeno, 474-491
Zeno, 474-491 (Byzantine Empire, AD 474–.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 474–AD 491] Zeno, 474-491. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Zeno, 474-491". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Isaurian general who married into the imperial house and ruled the East through revolts, a usurpation that briefly drove him from Constantinople, and the final extinction of the Western Empire in 476. He acknowledged Odoacer's rule in Italy and then encouraged Theodoric and his Ostrogoths to go and take it, ridding the Balkans of them. His Henotikon, an attempt to paper over the split with the anti-Chalcedonians, instead caused a lasting schism with Rome.

Selim I, 1512-1520 (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1.label: Selim I, 1512-1520
Selim I, 1512-1520 (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1512–AD 1520] Selim I, 1512-1520. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Selim I, 1512-1520". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In eight years he roughly doubled the Ottoman Empire. He broke the Safavid army with gunpowder weapons at Chaldiran, then destroyed the Mamluk Sultanate, adding Syria, Egypt and the Hijaz with the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. From then on the Ottoman sultan was guardian of Islam's central shrines, and the empire's centre of gravity shifted decisively into the Arab world.

Java War, 1825-1830 (Indonesia, AD 1825–.label: Java War, 1825-1830
Java War, 1825-1830 (Indonesia, AD 1825–.prose:
[Indonesia, AD 1825–AD 1830] Java War, 1825-1830. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Java War, 1825-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta led a broad revolt against Dutch encroachment on land, custom and courtly authority, blending Javanese kingship with Islamic messianic appeal. Five years of guerrilla fighting cost around 200,000 Javanese lives and drained the Dutch treasury; Diponegoro was finally seized while under a flag of truce during negotiations. To recoup the cost the Dutch imposed the Cultivation System, forcing peasants to grow export crops.

Revolutionary period, 1868-1875 (Spain,.label: Revolutionary period, 1868-1875
Revolutionary period, 1868-1875 (Spain,.prose:
[Spain, AD 1868–AD 1875] Revolutionary period, 1868-1875. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Revolutionary period, 1868-1875". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Generals and liberals drove Isabella II from the throne in the "Glorious Revolution", then spent six years failing to agree on what should replace her. An imported Italian king, Amadeo of Savoy, abdicated in disgust; the First Republic that followed had four presidents in eleven months while Carlist war raged in the north and cantonalist risings split the south. Exhaustion brought a military coup and the restoration of the Bourbons under Alfonso XII, which set up the long, managed two-party system of the Restoration.

Confederation, 1783-1789 (United States,.label: Confederation, 1783-1789
Confederation, 1783-1789 (United States,.prose:
[United States, AD 1783–AD 1789] Confederation, 1783-1789. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Confederation, 1783-1789". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Independence won, the thirteen states governed themselves through a Congress with no power to tax or regulate trade, and the war debt went unpaid. The Northwest Ordinance set the rules by which new territories would become equal states and barred slavery north of the Ohio, one of the era's lasting achievements. Debt riots in Massachusetts convinced enough leaders that the framework was failing to force a constitutional convention.

Uprising, 1652-1653 (France, AD 1652–AD.label: Uprising, 1652-1653
Uprising, 1652-1653 (France, AD 1652–AD.prose:
[Bordeaux (Aquitaine, France), AD 1652–AD 1653] Uprising, 1652-1653. Extracted from heading "Bordeaux (Aquitaine, France)--History--Uprising, 1652-1653". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The final, bloodiest phase of the Fronde, when the Prince de Condé turned his army against the crown, fought in the streets of Paris and then took Spanish pay against his own king. The revolt collapsed, Mazarin returned in triumph, and the boy Louis XIV emerged with a lifelong distrust of Paris and of the great nobility. His answer was Versailles: a court that kept aristocrats close, ornamental and harmless.

Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735 (S.label: Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735
Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735 (S.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1700–AD 1735] Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735. Extracted from heading "Sicily (Italy)--History--Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The end of the Spanish Habsburg line turned Sicily into a bargaining chip among Europe's powers. The Treaty of Utrecht handed the island and its crown to Victor Amadeus II of Savoy in 1713; seven years later a further diplomatic swap transferred it to the Austrian Habsburgs, who governed from Vienna until a Spanish Bourbon army under the future Charles III took it by force. Two decades of absentee rulers left little affection and few reforms, but the conquest of 1734-35 created the independent Bourbon kingdom of Naples and Sicily that lasted until Italian unification.

Christian VII, 1766-1808 (Denmark, AD 17.label: Christian VII, 1766-1808
Christian VII, 1766-1808 (Denmark, AD 17.prose:
[Denmark, AD 1766–AD 1808] Christian VII, 1766-1808. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian VII, 1766-1808". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The king was mentally ill for most of his reign, so power lay with others — most spectacularly with the royal physician Struensee, who for sixteen months issued reforms abolishing censorship and torture before being executed in 1772. Later, under Crown Prince Frederik, serfdom was ended and the timber and grain trade made Norwegian merchants rich during Europe's wars. Neutrality collapsed in 1807 when the British bombarded Copenhagen and seized the fleet, cutting Norway off from Denmark by sea.

Civil War, 68-69 (Roman Empire, AD 68–AD.label: Civil War, 68-69
Civil War, 68-69 (Roman Empire, AD 68–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 68–AD 69] Civil War, 68-69. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Civil War, 68-69". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nero's suicide ended the Julio-Claudian line and four men claimed the throne in quick succession: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and finally Vespasian. Legions from Spain, the Rhine and the East marched on Italy, and Rome itself saw street fighting and the burning of the Capitol. The episode exposed what Tacitus called the secret of empire - that an emperor could be made away from Rome - and installed the Flavian dynasty.

Civil War, 49-45 B.C (ancient Rome, 48 B.node: Civil War, 49-45 B.C (ancient Rome, 48 BC–44 BC)
Civil War, 49-45 B.C (ancient Rome, 48 B.label: Civil War, 49-45 B.C
Civil War, 49-45 B.C (ancient Rome, 48 B.prose:
