Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Caesar crossed the Rubicon with a single legion rather than surrender his command, and the Republic split between his supporters and those of Pompey and the Senate. Campaigns ranged across Italy, Spain, Greece, Egypt and North Africa, ending with victories at Pharsalus, Thapsus and Munda. Caesar emerged as dictator with no rival left standing - a concentration of power that provoked his murder and the wars that followed.

Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328 (By.label: Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328
Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328 (By.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1282–AD 1328] Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long, financially strapped reign in which the emperor scrapped the fleet to save money and hired the Catalan Company as mercenaries, who promptly ravaged the empire's own provinces. Meanwhile Byzantine Anatolia slipped away to Turkish emirates, among them the small principality of Osman. Yet these same decades produced the mosaics and frescoes of the Chora church and a brilliant revival of classical scholarship, and they ended with the old emperor deposed by his own grandson.

Theodosians, 379-455 (Roman Empire, AD 3.label: Theodosians, 379-455
Theodosians, 379-455 (Roman Empire, AD 3.prose:
[Rome, AD 379–AD 455] Theodosians, 379-455. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Theodosians, 379-455". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dynasty that began with a general summoned to salvage the Balkans after Adrianople and ended with the murder of Valentinian III. Under its rule Nicene Christianity became the empire's official faith, pagan sacrifice was outlawed, and the administrative division of 395 between Constantinople and Ravenna hardened into a permanent split. The western half meanwhile lost Britain, Africa and much of Gaul and Spain to Germanic kingdoms, and Rome itself was sacked in 410, while the east stabilised behind new walls and a codified body of law.

Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945 (Vietnam, AD.label: Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945
Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945 (Vietnam, AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945] Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Vietnam's last imperial house, founded when Gia Long crushed the Tây Sơn and ruled the whole country from a new citadel at Huế. Its Confucian, China-facing court resisted Western contact and persecuted Catholic converts, which France used to justify conquest, reducing later emperors to salaried figureheads of a protectorate. Bảo Đại's abdication in 1945 closed a thousand years of Vietnamese monarchy.

Revolution, 1917-1918 (Estonia, AD 1917–.label: Revolution, 1917-1918
Revolution, 1917-1918 (Estonia, AD 1917–.prose:
[Estonia, AD 1917–AD 1918] Revolution, 1917-1918. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--Revolution, 1917-1918". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987, and p.25 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Russian authority let Finland declare independence, but the new state immediately split between socialist Reds in the industrial south and the Whites of the countryside. The civil war lasted barely four months and was savage out of proportion to its length, with executions and prison-camp deaths outnumbering battlefield casualties. German intervention decided it for the Whites, and the bitterness between the two sides shaped Finnish politics for generations.

Alfonso II, 1162-1196 (Kingdom of Aragon.label: Alfonso II, 1162-1196
Alfonso II, 1162-1196 (Kingdom of Aragon.prose:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1162–AD 1196] Alfonso II, 1162-1196. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Alfonso II, 1162-1196". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first ruler to hold both the kingdom of Aragon and the county of Barcelona, creating the composite state known as the Crown of Aragon. He divided future conquest zones with Castile by the Treaty of Cazorla, tying Aragonese expansion to Valencia, and built up holdings north of the Pyrenees. A poet himself, he made his court a centre of troubadour culture.

Ferdinand I, 1521-1564 (Austria, AD 1521.label: Ferdinand I, 1521-1564
Ferdinand I, 1521-1564 (Austria, AD 1521.prose:
[Austria, AD 1521–AD 1564] Ferdinand I, 1521-1564. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Ferdinand I, 1521-1564". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles V's younger brother took the Austrian duchies and then, after the Hungarian king's death at Mohács, claimed the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary, forming the Danubian monarchy that lasted until 1918. He defended Vienna from Suleiman's siege, negotiated the Peace of Augsburg that let German princes choose Lutheranism or Catholicism, and succeeded his abdicating brother as emperor.

Albert II, 1993- (Belgium, AD 1993–AD 20.label: Albert II, 1993-
Albert II, 1993- (Belgium, AD 1993–AD 20.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1993–AD 2015] Albert II, 1993-. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Albert II, 1993-". Added to LCSH and revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Took the Belgian throne unexpectedly on his brother's death and reigned through the country's sharpest strains: the Dutroux scandal, the steady federalisation of the state, and a record-breaking 541 days without a government. He abdicated in favour of his son Philippe, the first Belgian king to step down voluntarily.

Justinian II, 705-711 (Byzantine Empire,.label: Justinian II, 705-711
Justinian II, 705-711 (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 705–AD 711] Justinian II, 705-711. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Justinian II, 705-711". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Mutilated and exiled, Justinian escaped, married a Khazar princess, then took Constantinople back with a Bulgar army and spent his second reign hunting down those who had deposed him. The vendetta politics and a disastrous punitive expedition against Cherson turned the army against him; his execution ended the Heraclian line and left the empire in two decades of instability.

Uprising, 1918-1919 (Poland, AD 1918–AD.label: Uprising, 1918-1919
Uprising, 1918-1919 (Poland, AD 1918–AD.prose:
[Wielkopolska (Poland), AD 1918–AD 1919] Uprising, 1918-1919. Extracted from heading "Wielkopolska (Poland)--History--Uprising, 1918-1919". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As the German Empire collapsed, Poles in the Poznań region rose against German rule and, unusually among Polish insurrections, won. Well-organised local militias took most of Greater Poland within weeks and held it until the Treaty of Versailles confirmed the territory for the reborn Polish state. The victory gave interwar Poland its most prosperous province and a trained officer cadre.

Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960 (China, AD.label: Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960
Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960 (China, AD.prose:
[China, AD 618–AD 960] Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A single label for the Tang empire and the fractured half-century that followed its fall, when five short-lived regimes succeeded one another in the north and ten kingdoms shared the south. Despite the political chaos, the interval saw printing spread, tea culture and porcelain industries flourish, and southern China grow into the empire's economic centre. It closed with the Song reunification, which deliberately built a civilian state to prevent any repeat of warlord rule.

Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254 (Germany, AD 113.label: Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254
Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254 (Germany, AD 113.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1138–AD 1254] Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under Frederick Barbarossa, Henry VI and Frederick II the Staufen ruled Germany, imperial Italy and eventually Sicily, and pursued a vision of universal empire that brought them into repeated, ruinous conflict with the papacy and the Lombard cities. Their courts fostered chivalric culture, Minnesang, and in Frederick II's Palermo a famously cosmopolitan mix of Latin, Greek and Arabic learning. The dynasty's extinction left Germany without an effective king and its princes and towns permanently stronger.

SLORC period, 1988-1997 (Burma, AD 1988–.label: SLORC period, 1988-1997
SLORC period, 1988-1997 (Burma, AD 1988–.prose:
[Burma, AD 1988–AD 1997] SLORC period, 1988-1997. Extracted from variant for header "Burma--History--1988-". Added to LCSH in 2009. The same header includes a second period, "Burma--History--SPDC period, 1997-", which we have not included here. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The State Law and Order Restoration Council took power after crushing the 1988 uprising, renamed the country Myanmar, and then annulled the 1990 election won overwhelmingly by Aung San Suu Kyi's party. It opened the economy to border trade and foreign investment while keeping political life closed, fighting or buying off ethnic insurgencies and holding Suu Kyi under house arrest. Renamed the SPDC in 1997, the same generals ran the country for another decade.

Rebellion, 1837-1838 (Canada, AD 1837–AD.label: Rebellion, 1837-1838
Rebellion, 1837-1838 (Canada, AD 1837–AD.prose:
[Canada, AD 1837–AD 1838] Rebellion, 1837-1838. Extracted from heading "Canada--History--Rebellion, 1837-1838". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Reformers in Lower Canada under Louis-Joseph Papineau and in Upper Canada under William Lyon Mackenzie took up arms against colonial oligarchies, the Château Clique and the Family Compact, that controlled patronage and blocked elected assemblies. Both risings were quickly defeated, with hangings and transportations to follow. London's response, Lord Durham's report, produced the union of the Canadas and eventually responsible government, a step on the road to Confederation.

Otto III, 983-1002 (Germany, AD 983–AD 1.label: Otto III, 983-1002
Otto III, 983-1002 (Germany, AD 983–AD 1.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 983–AD 1002] Otto III, 983-1002. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Otto III, 983-1002". Added to LCSH in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Made king as a three-year-old, he grew up under the regency of his Byzantine mother Theophanu and his grandmother Adelaide, and as an adult pursued a visionary programme of renewing the Roman Empire from Rome itself. He installed his tutor Gerbert of Aurillac as Pope Sylvester II, recognised new Christian kingdoms in Poland and Hungary at Gniezno, and dreamed of a Christian empire uniting Latin and Greek traditions. His death at twenty-one left the plan unfinished and Italy in revolt.

Jin dynasty, 265-419 (China, AD 265–AD 4.label: Jin dynasty, 265-419
Jin dynasty, 265-419 (China, AD 265–AD 4.prose:
[China, AD 265–AD 419] Jin dynasty, 265-419. Extracted from heading "China--History--Jin dynasty, 265-419".  Added to LCSH in 2000. Revised in 2000. Alternate label "Chin dynasty, 265-419" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born when the Sima family usurped the throne of Wei, the Jin briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, then tore itself apart in the War of the Eight Princes. Nomadic groups seized the north, and the court fled south to Jiankang, leaving a divided China for the next 270 years. The refugee aristocracy in the south nurtured a golden age of calligraphy, landscape poetry and the spread of Buddhism, and produced figures such as Wang Xizhi and Tao Yuanming.

Revolution, 1923-1924 (Mexico, AD 1923–A.label: Revolution, 1923-1924
Revolution, 1923-1924 (Mexico, AD 1923–A.prose:
[Mexico, AD 1923–AD 1924] Revolution, 1923-1924. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--Revolution, 1923-1924". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Adolfo de la Huerta and much of the federal army rebelled when Obregón chose Calles as his successor rather than allowing an open contest. Peasant militias and, importantly, US arms and recognition kept Obregón in power, and the rebellion was crushed within months. Its defeat broke the army's ability to make presidents and helped shift power to the civilian party machine that would become the PRI.

Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355 (Italy, AD 1.label: Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355
Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355 (Italy, AD 1.prose:
[Siena (Italy), AD 1287–AD 1355] Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355. Extracted from heading "Siena (Italy)--History--Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Siena was governed by a rotating council of nine merchants and bankers drawn from the middle ranks of the city, deliberately excluding the great noble families. Their regime paid for the Campo, the Palazzo Pubblico and much of the cathedral, and commissioned Lorenzetti's Allegory of Good and Bad Government as a portrait of their own ideals. Plague, banking failures and popular anger brought the government down in 1355, and Siena never recovered its former standing.

Bayezid II, 1481-1512 (Turkey, AD 1481–A.label: Bayezid II, 1481-1512
Bayezid II, 1481-1512 (Turkey, AD 1481–A.prose:
[Turkey , AD 1481–AD 1512] Bayezid II, 1481-1512. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Bayezid II, 1481-1512". Added to LCSH in 1988 revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cautious consolidator after his father's conquests, he spent years neutralised by his brother Cem, a rival claimant held hostage in Europe. He rebuilt the treasury and legal administration, expanded the navy that would dominate the eastern Mediterranean, and sent ships to carry Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 to Ottoman territory, where they settled in Salonica and Istanbul. Ageing and challenged by rebellion, he was forced to abdicate by his son Selim.

Isaurian dynasty, 717-811 (Byzantine Emp.label: Isaurian dynasty, 717-811
Isaurian dynasty, 717-811 (Byzantine Emp.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 811] Isaurian dynasty, 717-811. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Isaurian dynasty, 717-811". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Leo III seized power just as an Arab army and fleet closed on Constantinople; the siege broke, and with it the momentum of Umayyad expansion into Anatolia. The dynasty reorganised the provinces and army, issued the concise Ecloga law code, and — most divisively — banned religious images, launching a century of iconoclasm that pitted emperors against monks and popes and helped push the papacy towards the Franks. Surviving art from these years is largely crosses and ornament rather than saints' faces.

John II Casimir, 1648-1668 (Poland, AD 1.label: John II Casimir, 1648-1668
John II Casimir, 1648-1668 (Poland, AD 1.prose:
[Poland , AD 1648–AD 1668] John II Casimir, 1648-1668. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--John II Casimir, 1648-1668". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A former Jesuit cardinal who inherited a crown as the Khmelnytsky Cossack uprising exploded in Ukraine, followed by the Swedish invasion remembered as the Deluge, which overran most of the country. The wars gutted Poland-Lithuania's population and wealth, and the Truce of Andrusovo ceded Kyiv and left-bank Ukraine to Moscow. The liberum veto was first used to break a Sejm in his reign; worn out and thwarted in his reform plans, he abdicated and retired to France.

Time of Troubles, 1598-1613 (Russia, AD.label: Time of Troubles, 1598-1613
Time of Troubles, 1598-1613 (Russia, AD.prose:
[Russia , AD 1598–AD 1613] Time of Troubles, 1598-1613. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Time of Troubles, 1598-1613". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Epoch of confusion, 1605-1613" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of the last Rurikid tsar left Russia without an accepted ruler, and famine, civil war and a succession of pretenders claiming to be the murdered prince Dmitry tore the state apart. Polish and Swedish armies intervened, Moscow was occupied, and perhaps a third of the population died. A militia raised in Nizhny Novgorod retook the capital and an assembly elected Michael Romanov, founding the dynasty that ruled until 1917.

Elective monarchy, 1572-1763 (Poland, AD.label: Elective monarchy, 1572-1763
Elective monarchy, 1572-1763 (Poland, AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1572–AD 1763] Elective monarchy, 1572-1763. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Elective monarchy, 1572-1763". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Jagiellonian line died out, the Polish-Lithuanian nobility chose each new king by open vote on a field outside Warsaw, extracting binding concessions before the crown was handed over. The system made the szlachta the most powerful gentry in Europe and produced a genuinely mixed constitution, but it also invited foreign bribery and let a single deputy's veto paralyse the parliament. The resulting weakness left the vast Commonwealth unable to resist its neighbours, setting up the partitions that erased it from the map.

Ancient Chinese, 600-1200 (China, AD 600.label: Ancient Chinese, 600-1200
Ancient Chinese, 600-1200 (China, AD 600.prose: [China, AD 600–AD 1200] Ancient Chinese, 600-1200. Extracted from heading "Chinese language--Ancient Chinese, 600-1200". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Civil War, 1997- (Democratic Republic of.node: Civil War, 1997- (Democratic Republic of the Congo, AD 1997–AD 2015)
Civil War, 1997- (Democratic Republic of.label: Civil War, 1997-
Civil War, 1997- (Democratic Republic of.prose:
[Democratic Republic of the Congo, AD 1997–AD 2015] Civil War, 1997-. Extracted from heading "Congo (Democratic Republic)--History--1997-". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in 2012. Alternate identifier used to supply PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rebellion in Zaire toppled Mobutu, and the new government's break with its Rwandan and Ugandan backers triggered a second, far larger war that drew in nine African states - often called Africa's World War. Millions died, mostly from disease and hunger rather than combat, and armed groups financed themselves through coltan, gold and diamonds. Even after formal peace and elections, militias continued to fight over the mineral-rich eastern provinces.

Ferdinand III, 1637-1657 (Germany, AD 16.label: Ferdinand III, 1637-1657
Ferdinand III, 1637-1657 (Germany, AD 16.prose:
[Germany , AD 1637–AD 1657] Ferdinand III, 1637-1657. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Ferdinand III, 1637-1657". Added to LCSH in 2008, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited the Thirty Years' War in its worst phase and, unlike his father, accepted that it could not be won, negotiating the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. The settlement recognised Calvinism, confirmed the near-sovereignty of the German princes and the independence of the Dutch and Swiss, and ended the emperor's hope of ruling Germany as a real monarch. Habsburg energies turned instead to consolidating the hereditary lands and Hungary.

Plantagenets, 1154-1399 (England, AD 115.label: Plantagenets, 1154-1399
Plantagenets, 1154-1399 (England, AD 115.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1154–AD 1399] Plantagenets, 1154-1399. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Plantagenets, 1154-1399". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry II's accession joined England to a sprawl of French territories and brought reforms that became the common law, though his quarrel with Thomas Becket ended in murder. Baronial resistance produced Magna Carta and a permanent parliament, while later kings conquered Wales, fought Scotland and launched the Hundred Years War. The Black Death, the Peasants' Revolt and finally the deposition of Richard II closed the line and opened the way to dynastic civil war.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (California, AD 186.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (California, AD 186.prose:
[California, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "California--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and p.17 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Republic, 1873-1875 (Spain, AD 1873–AD 1.label: Republic, 1873-1875
Republic, 1873-1875 (Spain, AD 1873–AD 1.prose:
[Spain, AD 1873–AD 1875] Republic, 1873-1875. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Republic, 1873-1875". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spain's First Republic lasted under two years and burned through four presidents, declared after Amadeo of Savoy gave up the throne in despair. It faced the Third Carlist War, a Cuban insurgency, and the cantonalist revolt in which cities like Cartagena declared themselves independent. A military coup restored the Bourbons under Alfonso XII, beginning the long Restoration settlement.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (Louisiana, AD 1861.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (Louisiana, AD 1861.prose:
[Louisiana, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Louisiana--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 73 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Restoration, 1814-1830 (France, AD 1814–.label: Restoration, 1814-1830
Restoration, 1814-1830 (France, AD 1814–.prose:
[France, AD 1814–AD 1830] Restoration, 1814-1830. Extracted from heading "France--History--Restoration, 1814-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.39 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Bourbons returned after Napoleon's fall, with Louis XVIII accepting a Charter that preserved much of the Revolution's legal and administrative settlement while restoring the monarchy and a privileged Catholic Church. Ultra-royalists pressed for a fuller reversal, and under Charles X the attempt to muzzle the press and rig the electorate provoked the July Revolution. The regime's collapse showed that no French government could simply undo 1789.

Second Seminole War, 1835-1842 (Florida,.label: Second Seminole War, 1835-1842
Second Seminole War, 1835-1842 (Florida,.prose:
[Florida , AD 1835–AD 1842] Second Seminole War, 1835-1842. Extracted from heading "Seminole War, 2nd, 1835-1842". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1990. Note that alternate label "Seminole Wars" includes the First and Third Seminole Wars as well. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The costliest Indian war in United States history began when Seminoles resisted forced removal west, fighting a guerrilla campaign in the swamps and hammocks under leaders such as Osceola, who was seized under a flag of truce. Thousands of US troops died, mostly of disease, and the war drained the treasury before most Seminoles were deported to Indian Territory. A few hundred stayed hidden in the Everglades, ancestors of today's Florida Seminole and Miccosukee communities.

Famine, 1932-1933 (Ukraine, AD 1932–AD 1.label: Famine, 1932-1933
Famine, 1932-1933 (Ukraine, AD 1932–AD 1.prose:
[Ukraine, AD 1932–AD 1933] Famine, 1932-1933. Extracted from heading "Ukraine--History--Famine, 1932-1933". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Impossible grain quotas, forced collectivisation and the blacklisting of villages that failed to deliver produced mass starvation in the Ukrainian countryside, killing roughly four million people. Peasants were barred from leaving to search for food, and the regime denied the famine while continuing to export grain. Known as the Holodomor, it is recognised by many states as a genocide and remains central to Ukrainian national memory.

George III, 1760-1820 (United Kingdom, A.label: George III, 1760-1820
George III, 1760-1820 (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1760–AD 1820] George III, 1760-1820. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George III, 1760-1820". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His long reign spanned the loss of the American colonies, the wars against revolutionary and Napoleonic France, and the union with Ireland in 1801. It was also the age of canals, steam engines, cotton mills and enclosure, when Britain became the first industrial nation. Recurrent bouts of madness left him incapacitated from 1810, and his son ruled as Prince Regent for the last decade.

Leopold II, 1790-1792 (Hungary, AD 1790–.label: Leopold II, 1790-1792
Leopold II, 1790-1792 (Hungary, AD 1790–.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1790–AD 1792] Leopold II, 1790-1792. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Leopold II, 1790-1792". Appears on p. 46 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.56 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited a monarchy in turmoil from his brother Joseph II and quickly rolled back the most provocative reforms, calming rebellion in Hungary and the Austrian Netherlands. A capable and pragmatic ruler who had modernised Tuscany for decades beforehand, he tried to manage the French Revolution diplomatically, issuing the Declaration of Pillnitz with Prussia on behalf of his sister Marie Antoinette. He died suddenly, weeks before the war he had hoped to avoid broke out.
