Don Cossacks under Kondraty Bulavin rose against Peter the Great's punitive expeditions to drag runaway serfs back from the steppe frontier. The revolt spread along the Don and Volga while Russia was fighting Sweden, but government troops crushed it, Bulavin died in 1708, and whole Cossack towns were burned. Its defeat ended the Don's traditional autonomy — the Cossack host was absorbed into the imperial state, and the followers of Ignat Nekrasov fled to Ottoman lands rather than submit.

American occupation, 1847-1848 (Mexico C.label: American occupation, 1847-1848
American occupation, 1847-1848 (Mexico C.prose:
[Mexico City (Mexico), AD 1847–AD 1848] American occupation, 1847-1848. Extracted from heading "Mexico City (Mexico)--History--American occupation, 1847-1848". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Winfield Scott's army fought its way inland from Veracruz, stormed Chapultepec and entered the Mexican capital in September 1847, holding it for nine months. Occupation troops policed a hostile city while diplomats negotiated. The resulting Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred roughly half of Mexico's territory to the United States, reshaping the map of North America and igniting the American quarrel over slavery in the new lands.

Henry II, 1154-1189 (England, AD 1154–AD.label: Henry II, 1154-1189
Henry II, 1154-1189 (England, AD 1154–AD.prose:
[Great Britain, AD 1154–AD 1189] Henry II, 1154-1189. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry II, 1154-1189". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Plantagenet ended England's civil war and ruled an assemblage of lands stretching from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, held together by ceaseless travel. His legal reforms — itinerant royal justices, standardised writs, juries of presentment — laid the foundations of the English common law, while his attempt to bring clergy under royal courts led to the murder of Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. His last years were consumed by rebellions raised by his own sons and his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine.

Alexander III, 1881-1894 (Russia, AD 188.label: Alexander III, 1881-1894
Alexander III, 1881-1894 (Russia, AD 188.prose:
[Russia , AD 1881–AD 1894] Alexander III, 1881-1894. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Alexander III, 1881-1894". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Coming to the throne after his father was blown apart by revolutionaries, Alexander abandoned reform for repression: political trials, censorship, tightened control over universities and peasants, aggressive Russification of minorities and legal restrictions that helped drive Jewish emigration. At the same time the state pushed industrialisation and began the Trans-Siberian Railway, and turned diplomatically towards France. His reign avoided major war but stored up the grievances his son Nicholas II inherited.

Revolution, 1961-1975 (Angola, AD 1961–A.label: Revolution, 1961-1975
Revolution, 1961-1975 (Angola, AD 1961–A.prose:
[Angola, AD 1961–AD 1975] Revolution, 1961-1975. Extracted from heading "Angola--History--Revolution, 1961-1975". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Revolts in the cotton districts and coffee plantations grew into a guerrilla war against Portuguese rule, fought by three rival movements with different regional and ethnic bases and different foreign backers. Portugal held the cities but bled in the bush until its own army overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon in 1974. Independence the next year came without a settlement between the movements, and the war simply continued as a Cold War proxy conflict lasting to 2002.

Henry III, 1039-1056 (Germany, AD 1039–A.label: Henry III, 1039-1056
Henry III, 1039-1056 (Germany, AD 1039–A.prose:
[Germany , AD 1039–AD 1056] Henry III, 1039-1056. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry III, 1039-1056". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Salian power reached its height under a ruler who marched into Italy, deposed three rival claimants to the papacy at the Synod of Sutri, and installed a series of German reforming popes. He made Bohemia and Hungary acknowledge his overlordship and promoted the Peace of God in the empire. Ironically, the reform movement he sponsored produced the papacy that would humiliate his son.

Innocent X, 1644-1655 (Papal States, AD.label: Innocent X, 1644-1655
Innocent X, 1644-1655 (Papal States, AD.prose:
[Papal States, AD 1644–AD 1655] Innocent X, 1644-1655. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Innocent X, 1644-1655". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.89 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Giambattista Pamphilj's pontificate opened with an assault on the wealth of his Barberini predecessors and was dominated by the influence of his formidable sister-in-law, Olimpia Maidalchini. He denounced the Peace of Westphalia for conceding too much to Protestants, but Europe's rulers ignored him, a sign of the papacy's shrinking political weight. He rebuilt Piazza Navona as a family showpiece, commissioning Bernini's Four Rivers fountain, and sat for Velázquez's famously unflattering portrait.

Maximilian I, 1597-1651 (Germany, AD 159.label: Maximilian I, 1597-1651
Maximilian I, 1597-1651 (Germany, AD 159.prose:
[Bavaria, AD 1597–AD 1651] Maximilian I, 1597-1651. Extracting from heading "Bavaria--History--Maximilian I, 1597-1651". Appears on p.8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.8 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1994. Source notes Bavaria is in modern Germany. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Maximilian of Bavaria turned a middling duchy into a major Catholic power: he reorganised its finances and army, led the Catholic League to victory at White Mountain in 1620, and was rewarded with the Upper Palatinate and the electoral dignity stripped from his Protestant cousin. His long reign spans almost the whole Thirty Years' War, including the Swedish invasion that reached Munich itself, and ends with the Peace of Westphalia confirming Bavaria as an electorate. His patronage left Munich much of its early Baroque face.

John V, 1706-1750 (Portugal, AD 1706–AD.label: John V, 1706-1750
John V, 1706-1750 (Portugal, AD 1706–AD.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1706–AD 1750] John V, 1706-1750. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John V, 1706-1750". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brazilian gold and diamonds poured into Lisbon and were spent on absolutist magnificence: the colossal palace-convent of Mafra, the Águas Livres aqueduct, the library at Coimbra, and lavish bribes to secure Lisbon's elevation to a patriarchate. He never summoned the Cortes, ruling in imitation of Louis XIV. The spending left the treasury exhausted and Portugal's economy dependent on colonial bullion and English manufactures.

Vespasian, 69-79 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD.label: Vespasian, 69-79
Vespasian, 69-79 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD.prose:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 79] Vespasian, 69-79. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Vespasian, 69-79". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A commander of modest Italian family, Vespasian won the civil wars of 69 and founded the Flavian dynasty, restoring order and, above all, solvency to a state emptied by Nero. His son Titus stormed Jerusalem in 70 and destroyed the Temple; the spoils helped pay for the Colosseum, built on the site of Nero's private lake as a deliberate gift back to the Roman people. He was remembered for blunt humour, heavy taxation and for dying with a joke about becoming a god.

Henrique, 1578-1580 (Portugal, AD 1578–A.label: Henrique, 1578-1580
Henrique, 1578-1580 (Portugal, AD 1578–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1578–AD 1580] Henrique, 1578-1580. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Henrique, 1578-1580". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Henry I, 1578-1580" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cardinal in his sixties took the throne after his young great-nephew Sebastian vanished with the Portuguese army at Alcácer Quibir in Morocco. Childless and celibate, he spent his short reign vainly seeking a dispensation to marry and an heir, while the treasury drained paying ransoms for captured nobles. His death opened a succession crisis that Philip II of Spain settled by invasion, beginning sixty years of Habsburg rule over Portugal.

British Intervention, 1838-1842 (Afghani.label: British Intervention, 1838-1842
British Intervention, 1838-1842 (Afghani.prose:
[Afghanistan, AD 1838–AD 1842] British Intervention, 1838-1842. Extracted from heading "Afghanistan--History--British Intervention, 1838-1842". Added to LCSH in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fearing Russian influence, Britain invaded to replace Dost Mohammad Khan with a compliant former ruler, Shah Shuja. The occupation of Kabul collapsed in a general uprising, and the winter retreat of 1842 destroyed an army of some 16,000 soldiers and camp followers. A punitive expedition burned Kabul's bazaar and withdrew, leaving Dost Mohammad back on the throne and Afghanistan with a reputation as a graveyard of empires.

Israeli intervention, 1982-1985 (Lebanon.label: Israeli intervention, 1982-1985
Israeli intervention, 1982-1985 (Lebanon.prose:
[Lebanon, AD 1982–AD 1985] Israeli intervention, 1982-1985. Earlier established form: Lebanon--History--Israeli intervention, 1982-1984. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Israel invaded to drive the PLO out of Lebanon, besieged Beirut, and saw its Phalangist allies massacre civilians at Sabra and Shatila. The PLO leadership was evacuated to Tunis, but the occupation of the south bogged down against a newly mobilised Shia population and helped bring Hezbollah into being. Israeli forces withdrew to a 'security zone' along the border, which they held for another fifteen years.

Operation Moses, 1984-1985 (Ethiopia, AD.label: Operation Moses, 1984-1985
Operation Moses, 1984-1985 (Ethiopia, AD.prose:
[Ethiopia, AD 1984–AD 1985] Operation Moses, 1984-1985. Extracted from heading "Operation Moses, 1984-1985". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A covert airlift carried roughly eight thousand Ethiopian Jews, the Beta Israel, out of famine-stricken refugee camps in Sudan to Israel on chartered flights. Thousands had walked hundreds of miles to reach the camps and many died on the way. When the operation leaked to the press, Arab pressure forced Sudan to halt it, stranding families for years until later rescues reunited them.

German occupation, 1940-1945 (Belgium, A.label: German occupation, 1940-1945
German occupation, 1940-1945 (Belgium, A.prose:
[Belgium, AD 1940–AD 1945] German occupation, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--German occupation, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Denmark was seized in a few hours and then governed with unusual lightness: the king stayed, parliament sat, and the country was presented as a model protectorate supplying food to Germany. Cooperation collapsed in August 1943 amid strikes and sabotage; when deportation of Denmark's Jews was ordered that October, the resistance and ordinary citizens ferried some 7,000 people to safety in Sweden.

Restoration, 1853-1870 (Japan, AD 1853–A.label: Restoration, 1853-1870
Restoration, 1853-1870 (Japan, AD 1853–A.prose:
[Japan, AD 1853–AD 1870] Restoration, 1853-1870. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Restoration, 1853-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Commodore Perry's warships forced Japan open after two centuries of restricted contact, and the resulting crisis destroyed the Tokugawa shogunate. Domains such as Satsuma and Chōshū rallied around the slogan of honouring the emperor and expelling the barbarians, then seized power themselves and returned formal rule to the young Meiji emperor. Within a few years the samurai class, the domains and the old capital were all swept away in favour of a centralised state bent on industrial and military modernisation.

War of Independence, 1810-1824 (Chile, A.label: War of Independence, 1810-1824
War of Independence, 1810-1824 (Chile, A.prose:
[Chile, AD 1810–AD 1824] War of Independence, 1810-1824. Extracted from heading "Chile--History--War of Independence, 1810-1824". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.18 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A creole junta in Santiago began as self-government under a captive king and hardened into revolution, until royalist armies from Peru crushed the Patria Vieja at Rancagua and drove the patriots over the Andes. They came back with San Martín's Army of the Andes, winning at Chacabuco and decisively at Maipú, after which O'Higgins governed the new republic and helped launch the naval expedition that carried the war to Peru. The southern frontier and Chiloé held out for royalism until 1826.

Period of civil wars, 1480-1603 (Japan,.label: Period of civil wars, 1480-1603
Period of civil wars, 1480-1603 (Japan,.prose:
[Japan, AD 1480–AD 1603] Period of civil wars, 1480-1603. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Period of civil wars, 1480-1603". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Sengoku age, when the shogunate's authority collapsed and provincial warlords fought for territory with mass armies of pikemen and, after 1543, Portuguese-style firearms. Castles, castle-towns and new commercial networks grew out of the fighting, and Christian missionaries arrived alongside European traders. Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and finally Tokugawa Ieyasu reunified the country, ending in a shogunate that would keep the peace for 250 years.

Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C (Greece,.label: Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C
Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C (Greece,.prose:
[Greece, 278 BC–277 BC] Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Celtic war bands swept south through Macedonia and Thessaly, killed the Macedonian king and pushed into central Greece before being turned back near Delphi, a repulse the Greeks credited to Apollo himself and commemorated for centuries. Part of the horde crossed into Asia Minor at the invitation of a Bithynian king and settled in the highlands around Ankara, becoming the Galatians. Their defeat became a favourite theme of Hellenistic art and propaganda, most famously in the Pergamene statues of dying Gauls.

Alexander, 1501-1506 (Poland, AD 1501–AD.label: Alexander, 1501-1506
Alexander, 1501-1506 (Poland, AD 1501–AD.prose:
[Poland , AD 1501–AD 1506] Alexander, 1501-1506. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Alexander, 1501-1506". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign dominated by war with Muscovy and the Tatars and by the ruler's chronic shortage of money. In 1505 he accepted the Nihil novi statute, which barred the king from making laws without the consent of the Sejm - a decisive shift of power to the nobility that shaped Polish politics for the next three centuries.

Romanus II, 959-963 (Byzantine Empire, A.label: Romanus II, 959-963
Romanus II, 959-963 (Byzantine Empire, A.prose: [Byzantine Empire, AD 959–AD 963] Romanus II, 959-963. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Romanus II, 959-963". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Joseph II, 1780-1790 (Hungary, AD 1780–A.label: Joseph II, 1780-1790
Joseph II, 1780-1790 (Hungary, AD 1780–A.prose:
[Hungary, AD 1780–AD 1790] Joseph II, 1780-1790. Extracted from heading "Austria--history--Joseph II, 1780-1790". Added to LCSH in 1986;  on p.46 of LCSH 1975, and on p.56 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The most impatient of the enlightened despots issued some six thousand decrees in ten years: serfdom abolished, religious toleration extended to Protestants and Jews, contemplative monasteries dissolved, censorship relaxed, torture ended, and German imposed as the language of administration everywhere. The pace and the disregard for local privilege provoked open revolt in the Austrian Netherlands and near-rebellion in Hungary, and he died revoking much of his own work - a warning about reform from above that Europe noted just as the French Revolution began.

Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871 (France,.label: Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871
Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871 (France,.prose:
[France, Germany, AD 1870–AD 1871] Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871. Spatial coverage: France, Germany. Extracted from heading "Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bismarck manoeuvred Napoleon III into declaring war and the German states, fighting together, destroyed the French armies in weeks; the emperor himself surrendered at Sedan. Paris held out through a winter siege and then exploded into the Commune, while in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles the German Empire was proclaimed. The annexation of Alsace and much of Lorraine left a grievance that shaped European politics until 1918.

Medieval and modern Iran, 640- (Iran, AD.label: Medieval and modern Iran, 640-
Medieval and modern Iran, 640- (Iran, AD.prose:
[Iran, AD 640–AD 2015] Medieval and modern Iran, 640-. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--640-". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Earlier established form used as primary label. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Arab conquest ended the Sasanian empire and brought Islam, but Persian language and administrative tradition survived and shaped the caliphate; later came Seljuk and Mongol invasions, the brilliance of Timurid Herat and Samarkand, and the Safavids, who made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion and built Isfahan into one of the world's great cities. Qajar rule saw Iran squeezed between Russia and Britain, then the constitutional revolution of 1906 and the Pahlavi drive to modernise on oil revenues. The 1979 revolution replaced the monarchy with an Islamic republic.

Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Norway, AD 164.label: Frederick III, 1648-1670
Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Norway, AD 164.prose:
[Norway, AD 1648–AD 1670] Frederick III, 1648-1670. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Frederick III, 1648-1670". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign began with a disastrous war against Sweden that cost Denmark Scania and the provinces east of the Sound, permanently fixing the modern Scandinavian border. But when Copenhagen's citizens helped hold the city under siege, he used the crisis to break the nobility: in 1660-61 the elective monarchy was abolished and the King's Law of 1665 made him one of the most absolute rulers in Europe, on paper at least. He was also a passionate collector, founding the royal library and Kunstkammer.

Interregnum, 1886-1887 (Bulgaria, AD 188.label: Interregnum, 1886-1887
Interregnum, 1886-1887 (Bulgaria, AD 188.prose:
[Bulgaria, AD 1886–AD 1887] Interregnum, 1886-1887. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Interregnum, 1886-1887". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Prince Alexander of Battenberg was kidnapped by pro-Russian officers and, though briefly restored, abdicated under pressure from St Petersburg, leaving the young principality without a ruler. A regency dominated by Stefan Stambolov defied Russian attempts to control the succession and eventually found a candidate in Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. The episode marked Bulgaria's break from Russian tutelage and the start of Stambolov's hard-handed rule.

Rupert, 1400-1410 (Germany, AD 1400–AD 1.label: Rupert, 1400-1410
Rupert, 1400-1410 (Germany, AD 1400–AD 1.prose:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1400–AD 1410] Rupert, 1400-1410. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Rupert, 1400-1410". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rupert of the Palatinate was raised to the German throne by electors who had just deposed Wenceslaus IV, but he never controlled more than his own Rhineland lands. His expedition to Italy to be crowned emperor collapsed in failure, and his short reign shows how far the monarchy had shrunk against the princes; the crown passed afterwards to the Luxembourg Sigismund.

Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180 (Byzantine.label: Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180
Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180 (Byzantine.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1143–AD 1180] Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An emperor who spent lavishly to restore Byzantine dominance, intervening in Italy, Hungary and the Crusader states and courting Western knights and customs at his court. His army's destruction in the pass of Myriokephalon in 1176 ended hopes of driving the Turks from Anatolia, and the debts and resentments he left behind helped unravel the empire within a generation.

Third Republic, 1870-1940 (France, AD 18.label: Third Republic, 1870-1940
Third Republic, 1870-1940 (France, AD 18.prose:
[France, AD 1870–AD 1940] Third Republic, 1870-1940. Extracted from heading "France--History--Third Republic, 1870-1940". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born from the collapse of Napoleon III's empire and the bloody suppression of the Paris Commune, this republic became the longest-lasting French regime since 1789. It built free secular schooling, separated church and state, expanded a vast colonial empire, and tore itself apart over the Dreyfus Affair. It produced the Paris of Haussmann's boulevards, the Eiffel Tower and Impressionism, and ended with the German invasion of 1940.

Civil War, 1959-1962 (Rwanda, AD 1959–AD.label: Civil War, 1959-1962
Civil War, 1959-1962 (Rwanda, AD 1959–AD.prose:
[Ruanda-Urundi, AD 1959–AD 1962] Civil War, 1959-1962. Extracted from heading "Ruanda-Urundi--History--Civil War, 1959-1962". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The "Hutu Revolution" overturned the Tutsi monarchy that Belgian colonial rule had propped up, replacing it with a Hutu-led republic at independence. Thousands of Tutsi were killed and hundreds of thousands fled to Uganda, Burundi and Congo. Those refugee communities produced the rebel movement that invaded in 1990, linking this upheaval directly to the genocide of 1994.

Empire, 1822-1889 (Brazil, AD 1822–AD 18.label: Empire, 1822-1889
Empire, 1822-1889 (Brazil, AD 1822–AD 18.prose:
[Brazil, AD 1822–AD 1889] Empire, 1822-1889. Extracted from "Brazil--History--Empire, 1822-1889". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brazil broke from Portugal without a long war of independence, keeping a monarchy under Pedro I and then the long, stabilising reign of Pedro II. It remained a single vast state while Spanish America fragmented, built railways and a coffee export boom, and fought the devastating Paraguayan War. Its economy rested on slavery until abolition in 1888; a year later the army deposed the emperor and proclaimed a republic.

German occupation, 1941-1944 (Russia, AD.label: German occupation, 1941-1944
German occupation, 1941-1944 (Russia, AD.prose:
[Soviet Union, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Estonia, Georgia (country), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia. Extracted from heading "Soviet Union--History--German Occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.108 of LCSH 1987, and on p.87 of LCSH 1975 (source uses term "Russia"). Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

Civil War, 1983-2005 (Sudan, AD 1983–AD.label: Civil War, 1983-2005
Civil War, 1983-2005 (Sudan, AD 1983–AD.prose:
[Sudan, AD 1983–AD 2005] Civil War, 1983-2005. Extracted from heading "Sudan--History--Civil War, 1983-2005". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

War resumed when the Khartoum government scrapped southern autonomy and extended sharia law, with John Garang's SPLA leading resistance in the south. Around two million people died, largely from famine and displacement, and oil discovered in the south raised the stakes. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement promised a referendum on secession, which in 2011 created the independent state of South Sudan.

Gustav IV Adolf, 1792-1809 (Sweden, AD 1.label: Gustav IV Adolf, 1792-1809
Gustav IV Adolf, 1792-1809 (Sweden, AD 1.prose:
[Sweden, AD 1792–AD 1809] Gustav IV Adolf, 1792-1809. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav IV Adolf, 1792-1809". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.112 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A rigid, deeply pious king whose loathing of Napoleon dragged Sweden into coalition wars it could not afford. Defeat by Russia cost Sweden Finland, held for six centuries, and the resulting anger led officers to depose him in a coup; he died in exile under an assumed name. His overthrow produced the 1809 constitution and the invitation to the French marshal Bernadotte that founded the present royal house.

Colonial Period, ca. 1600-1775 (North Ca.label: Colonial Period, ca. 1600-1775
Colonial Period, ca. 1600-1775 (North Ca.prose:
[North Carolina, AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial Period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "North Carolina--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

English settlement spread inland from the Albemarle Sound and the Cape Fear, joined by Highland Scots, Germans and Scots-Irish moving down the Great Wagon Road. Tobacco, naval stores from the pine forests, and enslaved labour shaped the coastal economy, while Tuscarora and Cherokee lands were pushed back by war and treaty. Backcountry resentment of coastal elites boiled over in the Regulator movement, foreshadowing the split with Britain.

Civil War, 1861-1865 (North Carolina, AD.label: Civil War, 1861-1865
Civil War, 1861-1865 (North Carolina, AD.prose:
[North Carolina, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "North Carolina--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

Regulator Insurrection (North Carolina,.label: Regulator Insurrection
Regulator Insurrection (North Carolina,.prose:
[North Carolina, AD 1766–AD 1771] Regulator Insurrection. Extracted from heading "North Carolina--History--Regulator Insurrection, 1766-1771--Campaigns". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Farmers in the North Carolina backcountry organised against sheriffs and court officials who overcharged fees, rigged taxes and seized land for debt, at first through petitions and then by shutting down courts by force. Governor Tryon marched the eastern militia west and broke them at Alamance, hanging several leaders. The grievances — corrupt local government and an unresponsive assembly dominated by the coastal elite — carried straight into the divisions of the Revolution a few years later.

Revolution, 1775-1783 (North Carolina, A.label: Revolution, 1775-1783
Revolution, 1775-1783 (North Carolina, A.prose:
[North Carolina, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "North Carolina--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-14.node: War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-1479 (Spain, AD 1475–AD 1479)
War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-14.label: War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-1479
War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-14.prose:
[Spain, Portugal, AD 1475–AD 1479] War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-1479. Spatial coverage: Portugal, Spain. Extracted from "War of the Castilian Succession, 1475-1479"; added to LCSH in 2009, revised in 2010. Spatial coverage inferred from connection of term to broader subject headings for both Spain and Portugal. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Isabella's claim to Castile was contested by her niece Juana, backed by her husband Afonso V of Portugal, making the succession dispute an international war. Isabella's victory secured the throne and with it the dynastic union of Castile and Aragon that became Spain. The Treaty of Alcáçovas that ended it also carved up the Atlantic: Portugal kept the African coast and islands, Castile kept the Canaries — the first European treaty dividing overseas spheres.

Restoration, 1814-1830 (France, AD 1814–.label: Restoration, 1814-1830
Restoration, 1814-1830 (France, AD 1814–.prose:
[Paris (France), AD 1814–AD 1830] Restoration, 1814-1830. Extracted from heading "Paris (France)--History--Restoration, 1814-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; differentiated from the period "Restoration" of the same dates applied to France as a whole. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Bourbons returned after Napoleon's fall, with Louis XVIII accepting a Charter that preserved much of the Revolution's legal and administrative settlement while restoring the monarchy and a privileged Catholic Church. Ultra-royalists pressed for a fuller reversal, and under Charles X the attempt to muzzle the press and rig the electorate provoked the July Revolution. The regime's collapse showed that no French government could simply undo 1789.

William I, 1154-1166 (Sicily, AD 1154–AD.label: William I, 1154-1166
William I, 1154-1166 (Sicily, AD 1154–AD.prose:
[Sicily, AD 1154–AD 1166] William I, 1154-1166. Extracted from heading "Sicily (Italy)--History--William I, 1154-1166". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Called 'the Bad' by hostile chroniclers, the second Norman king of Sicily inherited his father Roger II's multicultural kingdom of Latins, Greeks, Arabs and Jews and faced immediate baronial revolt. He crushed the rebels and secured papal recognition at the Treaty of Benevento in 1156, but lost the Norman foothold in North Africa to the Almohads. His court at Palermo kept up its Arab-Norman splendour, and he built the pleasure palace of the Zisa.

William I, 1816-1864 (Germany, AD 1816–A.label: William I, 1816-1864
William I, 1816-1864 (Germany, AD 1816–A.prose:
[Württemberg (Germany), AD 1816–AD 1864] William I, 1816-1864. Extracted from heading "Württemberg (Germany)--History--William I, 1816-1864". Added to LCSH in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wilhelm's long reign over Württemberg began in the famine year that followed Napoleon's fall, and he responded with agricultural reform, a state agricultural school at Hohenheim, and a constitution agreed with the estates in 1819. He pushed railway building and joined the customs union that knit the German states into a single market, while riding out the revolution of 1848 with concessions he later withdrew. His kingdom was a middling power trying to keep its independence between Austria and a rising Prussia.

Revolutionary period, 1775-1783 (United.label: Revolutionary period, 1775-1783
Revolutionary period, 1775-1783 (United.prose:
[United States, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolutionary period, 1775-1783. Extracted from "American literature--Revolutionary period, 1775-1783", added to LCSH in 1986. The temporal term is only used as a descriptor for creative fields (literature, drama, poetry) in the US; the "History--" subject for the same period is organized by state. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

What began as a colonial tax dispute became a war for independence after Lexington and Concord, and the Declaration of Independence turned rebellion into a claim about natural rights. French intervention after Saratoga made it a global war, and the surrender at Yorktown effectively ended British hopes of reconquest. The result was a new republic without a monarchy or hereditary nobility, an example that fed directly into the revolutionary politics of Europe and Latin America.

Restoration, 1660-1700 (England, AD 1660.label: Restoration, 1660-1700
Restoration, 1660-1700 (England, AD 1660.prose:
[England, AD 1660–AD 1700] Restoration, 1660-1700. Extracted from heading "English drama--Restoration, 1660-1700". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1990. This definition appears to apply specifically to literature, and differs in its end date from the historical period of the same name listed under Great Britain--History. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Taken broadly to the end of the century, this span runs from the return of the Stuarts through the Glorious Revolution to the settled Protestant monarchy of William and Mary. Parliament emerged with the power to make and unmake kings, guaranteed by the Bill of Rights and regular taxation, and the Bank of England was founded to fund war against France. Science, commerce and empire all accelerated, and English public life acquired coffee houses, newspapers and party politics.

Period of Iconoclasm (Turkey, AD 726–AD.label: Period of Iconoclasm
Period of Iconoclasm (Turkey, AD 726–AD.prose:
[Turkey, AD 726–AD 843] Period of Iconoclasm. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Israel, Russia, Turkey, Ukraine. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 235. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

For over a century Byzantine emperors banned and destroyed religious images, purging monasteries, exiling defenders of icons and stripping churches of their mosaics. The conflict was as much about imperial authority over the church as about theology, and it widened the rift with Rome. Its end, celebrated as the Triumph of Orthodoxy in 843, fixed the place of icons in Eastern Christian worship and released a flowering of new religious art.

Proto-Geometric Period (Greece, 1049 BC–.label: Proto-Geometric Period
Proto-Geometric Period (Greece, 1049 BC–.prose:
[Greece, 1049 BC–899 BC] Proto-Geometric Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, Greek potters began decorating vases with compass-drawn circles and clean horizontal bands, the first sign of a new artistic order. Iron working spread, cremation burial became common, and settlers crossed the Aegean to the coast of Asia Minor. Small communities like Lefkandi, with its enormous hero's building and rich burials, show that trade and wealth had not disappeared entirely.

Roman Empire (Italy, 26 BC–AD 395).label: Roman Empire
Roman Empire (Italy, 26 BC–AD 395).prose:
[Italy, 26 BC–AD 395] Roman Empire. Spatial coverage: Egypt, France, Greece, Israel, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Tunisia. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 171. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Augustus replaced the wrecked Republic with rule by one man dressed in republican language, beginning three centuries of imperial government. Italy sat at the centre of a Mediterranean-wide economy of grain fleets, roads, aqueducts and mass-produced pottery, and the city of Rome grew to perhaps a million people. Citizenship was extended to nearly all free provincials in AD 212, and Christianity moved from persecuted sect to state religion. Civil war, plague and pressure on the frontiers reshaped the state, and by the end of the fourth century power had shifted east.

Late Minoan (Greece, 1449 BC–1099 BC).label: Late Minoan
Late Minoan (Greece, 1449 BC–1099 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1449 BC–1099 BC] Late Minoan. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Crete's palace civilisation reached its most brilliant phase — frescoed halls, marine-style pottery, bronze work and trade reaching Egypt and the Levant — before a run of disasters. The eruption of Thera, then island-wide destructions, left Knossos alone in charge, now under Greek-speaking Mycenaean rulers who kept their accounts in Linear B. The palace system finally failed altogether, and Cretans retreated to defensible hilltop villages as the wider Bronze Age world collapsed.

Kushan and Later Andhra Periods (India,.node: Kushan and Later Andhra Periods (India, 29 BC–AD 433)
Kushan and Later Andhra Periods (India,.label: Kushan and Later Andhra Periods
Kushan and Later Andhra Periods (India,.prose:
[South Asia, 29 BC–AD 433] Kushan and Later Andhra Periods. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Northern India and Central Asia were bound together by the Kushan empire, while the Satavahanas of the Deccan controlled the routes between the two coasts. Roman gold flowed in through the ports in exchange for pepper, gems and textiles, and the wealth paid for Buddhist stupas at Amaravati and the rock-cut halls of the western Ghats. Gandharan workshops produced some of the earliest sculpted images of the Buddha, blending Hellenistic drapery with Indian iconography.

Orientalizing Period (Greece, 699 BC–599.label: Orientalizing Period
Orientalizing Period (Greece, 699 BC–599.prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–599 BC] Orientalizing Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Greek artists absorbed the visual language of the Near East, filling vases and bronzes with lions, sphinxes, and floral ornament borrowed from Phoenician and Syrian models. Trading posts and colonies carried the exchange in both directions, and Corinth grew rich exporting the resulting painted pottery. Alongside the imagery came the alphabet and Eastern myths that resurface in Hesiod and Homer.

Carolingian Empire (France, AD 768–AD 88.label: Carolingian Empire
Carolingian Empire (France, AD 768–AD 88.prose:
[France, AD 768–AD 887] Carolingian Empire. Spatial coverage: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 235 and pages 450-1. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Under Charlemagne and his heirs the Frankish realm expanded across most of western Europe and was crowned an empire in Rome on Christmas Day 800, reviving an imperial title in the west. Missionary bishops, county administration and a deliberate revival of learning produced the clear script and the copied classical manuscripts on which much of our knowledge of antiquity depends. Division among Charlemagne's descendants, sealed at Verdun in 843, marked out the future France and Germany.

Minoan New Palace period (Greece, 1699 B.node: Minoan New Palace period (Greece, 1699 BC–1449 BC)
Minoan New Palace period (Greece, 1699 B.label: Minoan New Palace period
Minoan New Palace period (Greece, 1699 B.prose:
[Crete, 1699 BC–1449 BC] Minoan New Palace period. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After earthquakes levelled the first palaces, Crete rebuilt them on a grander scale, and this was the height of Minoan civilisation. Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros stood at the centre of a world of frescoed halls, bull-leaping, Linear A archives and gold and ivory craftsmanship, with Minoan goods and styles spreading across the Aegean and to Egypt. The eruption of Thera and a wave of destructions ended it, leaving Knossos in Mycenaean Greek hands.

Middle Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 843–.label: Middle Byzantine Period
Middle Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 843–.prose:
[Turkey, AD 843–AD 1204] Middle Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Israel, Russia, Turkey, Ukraine. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 235. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Byzantine forces retook the island from its Arab emirate in 961, and a wave of church building, monastic foundation and resettlement followed. Fresco-painted small churches survive in the hundreds from these centuries, and noble families were transplanted from Constantinople to secure the island. Venetian rule replaced Byzantine after the Fourth Crusade.

Helladic period (Greece, 2999 BC–999 BC).label: Helladic period
Helladic period (Greece, 2999 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Mycenae, Crete, Greece, 2999 BC–999 BC] Helladic period. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The Bronze Age of mainland Greece, running from the first metal-using farming villages to the fall of the Mycenaean palaces. Over these two millennia settlements grew into fortified centres, writing appeared in the form of Linear B, and Greek-speaking rulers built the citadels of Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos before the whole system collapsed around 1200 BC.

Etruscan Supremacy (Italy, 699 BC–508 BC.label: Etruscan Supremacy
Etruscan Supremacy (Italy, 699 BC–508 BC.prose:
[Italian peninsula, Etruria, 699 BC–508 BC] Etruscan Supremacy. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

At their height the Etruscan city-states controlled a swathe of Italy from the Po valley to Campania, growing rich on Tuscan iron and copper and trading with Greeks, Phoenicians and Celts. Their painted chamber tombs, bronze work and gold jewellery are among the finest art of early Italy, and their cities passed on urban planning, engineering and religious ritual to Rome. Naval defeat, Greek and Samnite pressure and the rise of the Roman Republic ended their ascendancy.

Minoan Old Palace period (Greece, 1899 B.node: Minoan Old Palace period (Greece, 1899 BC–1699 BC)
Minoan Old Palace period (Greece, 1899 B.label: Minoan Old Palace period
Minoan Old Palace period (Greece, 1899 B.prose:
[Crete, 1899 BC–1699 BC] Minoan Old Palace period. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The first great palace complexes rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia: sprawling courtyard buildings with vast storage magazines, workshops and administrative archives, marking the shift from village society to centralised states. Cretan hieroglyphic writing appeared, potters produced the eggshell-thin polychrome Kamares ware prized in Egypt, and Cretan ships worked the eastern Mediterranean. A violent destruction, probably by earthquake, closed the period and cleared the ground for the more famous later palaces.

Late Empire (Italy, AD 192–AD 476).label: Late Empire
Late Empire (Italy, AD 192–AD 476).prose:
[Italy, AD 192–AD 476] Late Empire. Spatial coverage: Egypt, France, Greece, Israel, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Tunisia. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 171. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Rome passed from the assassination of Commodus into a century of civil war, plague and currency collapse, then was rebuilt by Diocletian and Constantine as a more bureaucratic, militarised state with new capitals and a Christian emperor. Italy itself lost its privileged position — the court moved to Milan and then Ravenna — and Rome was sacked by the Goths in 410. Visitors see the shift in art too, from naturalistic portraiture to the frontal, hieratic style that leads into Byzantine imagery.

Periods of the Shungas and Early Andhras.node: Periods of the Shungas and Early Andhras (India, 184 BC–AD 50)
Periods of the Shungas and Early Andhras.label: Periods of the Shungas and Early Andhras
Periods of the Shungas and Early Andhras.prose:
[South Asia, 184 BC–AD 50] Periods of the Shungas and Early Andhras. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After a general murdered the last Maurya, the Shungas held the Ganges heartland while Satavahana kings rose in the Deccan and Indo-Greek, Shaka and Kushan rulers pressed in from the northwest. Political fragmentation went with a boom in stone Buddhist art – the carved railings and gateways of Bharhut and Sanchi, and the earliest rock-cut chaitya halls of the Western Ghats – paid for largely by merchants and guilds along thriving trade routes.

High Classical Period (Greece, 449 BC–39.label: High Classical Period
High Classical Period (Greece, 449 BC–39.prose:
[Greece, 449 BC–399 BC] High Classical Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Athens at its wealthiest and most confident: the Parthenon and the Propylaia rising on the Acropolis, tragedy and comedy performed to citizen audiences, Pheidias and Polykleitos defining an ideal of proportioned human form. Democratic politics and imperial tribute were two sides of the same system. The period ends in defeat by Sparta and the execution of Socrates.

Geometric Period (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Geometric Period
Geometric Period (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

In the southwest Peloponnese this is a thinly settled landscape of small villages, a long way from the palace society that had ruled from Pylos in the Bronze Age. Sanctuaries and cemeteries show local communities reforming and Corinthian and Argive pottery arriving through trade. By the period's end Sparta was pressing across the Taygetos mountains, and Messenia's conquest and centuries of helot servitude lay just ahead.

Gupta Period (India, AD 320–AD 486).label: Gupta Period
Gupta Period (India, AD 320–AD 486).prose:
[South Asia, AD 320–AD 486] Gupta Period. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

An empire built out of northern India by a line of rulers who preferred alliances and tribute to direct rule, presiding over a court culture that later Indians looked back on as a golden age. Sanskrit literature and drama flourished, Hindu temple architecture took recognisable form, and mathematicians and astronomers set out the decimal place-value system and calculations of the earth's rotation. Its wealth also funded the great Buddhist university at Nalanda and the cave paintings at Ajanta.

Persian Empire (Iran, 558 BC–330 BC).label: Persian Empire
Persian Empire (Iran, 558 BC–330 BC).prose:
[Persia, Syria, Phoenicia, Asia Minor, 558 BC–330 BC] Persian Empire. Spatial coverage: Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Cyrus and his successors built the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Indus to the Aegean and Egypt, governed through satrapies, tribute, a royal road system and a multilingual bureaucracy. Persepolis, Susa and the rock-cut royal tombs advertised a kingship that ruled many peoples while tolerating their gods and customs. It fell to Alexander's invasion, but its administrative model shaped every later empire in the region.

Roman Republic (Italy, 508 BC–26 BC) [p0.label: Roman Republic
Roman Republic (Italy, 508 BC–26 BC) [p0.prose:
[Italy, 508 BC–26 BC] Roman Republic. Spatial coverage: France, Italy, Spain, Tunisia. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 171. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After expelling its kings, Rome developed a government of elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and citizen assemblies, and an army of property-owning citizens. It absorbed Italy, destroyed Carthage and took the Greek east, becoming the dominant Mediterranean power within two centuries. The wealth and slaves that flooded in wrecked the old order, producing land crises, political violence and the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Caesar. Its institutions and its collapse became the standard reference point for later republics.

Archaic Period (Greece, 599 BC–479 BC).label: Archaic Period
Archaic Period (Greece, 599 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Greece, 599 BC–479 BC] Archaic Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The island's many small city-states — Knossos, Gortyn, Dreros, Lyktos — produced the earliest surviving Greek law inscribed on stone, and a strong tradition of hammered bronze work and Daedalic sculpture that influenced sculptors on the mainland. Votive deposits in the Idaean Cave and the temples of Dreros and Prinias show a distinctive local blend of Greek and Near Eastern forms. Crete then turned inward, staying out of the Persian Wars and playing little part in the classical politics that followed.

High Empire (Italy, AD 96–AD 192).label: High Empire
High Empire (Italy, AD 96–AD 192).prose:
[Italy, AD 96–AD 192] High Empire. Spatial coverage: Egypt, France, Greece, Israel, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Tunisia. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 171. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

From Nerva to Commodus, the empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan and then settled into consolidation behind fixed frontiers like Hadrian's Wall. Cities across the provinces filled with baths, aqueducts and forums, provincials rose to the throne, and law and citizenship spread widely. The Antonine plague and Commodus's murder in 192 exposed how much depended on a single life, ushering in civil war.

Ottonian Empire (France, AD 919–AD 1024).label: Ottonian Empire
Ottonian Empire (France, AD 919–AD 1024).prose:
[France, AD 919–AD 1024] Ottonian Empire. Spatial coverage: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 235 and pages 450-1. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The Saxon kings Henry I and the three Ottos rebuilt royal authority in East Francia, defeated the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955 and revived the western imperial title when Otto I was crowned in Rome in 962. Bishops and abbeys were used as pillars of government, and the court sponsored a burst of manuscript painting, ivory carving and church building that art historians call the Ottonian renaissance. The empire they made became the medieval German Reich and set the pattern of conflict and cooperation between emperors and popes.

Late Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 1261–A.label: Late Byzantine Period
Late Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 1261–A.prose:
[Turkey, AD 1261–AD 1453] Late Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Israel, Russia, Turkey, Ukraine. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 235. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After the Byzantines retook Constantinople, the southwest Peloponnese stayed a patchwork: Frankish barons of the Principality of Achaea held castles like Methoni and Koroni ports fell to Venice, while the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, ruled from Mystras, pushed steadily westward. The result is a landscape of fortified towns, Latin and Greek churches side by side, and Venetian harbours built for the trade in oil, silk and currants. Ottoman raids and the Venetian-Ottoman wars closed the era, leaving the region's castles to be reused for centuries.

Imperial Christian (Lebanon, AD 313–AD 4.label: Imperial Christian
Imperial Christian (Lebanon, AD 313–AD 4.prose:
[Canaan, Judaea, AD 313–AD 476] Imperial Christian. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, Syria. Map on page 235: "The eastern Mediterranean lands of Canaan and Judaea were centers of Jewish settlement.". Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After Constantine legalised Christianity, the coastal cities of the Levant filled with basilicas, martyr shrines and pilgrim traffic, while older temples were closed, stripped or rebuilt as churches. Berytus (Beirut) ran the most famous law school in the empire, training the jurists whose work fed into the Justinianic codes. Mosaic floors from village churches of these centuries are among the most abundant archaeological finds of the region.

Late Classical Period (Greece, 399 BC–32.label: Late Classical Period
Late Classical Period (Greece, 399 BC–32.prose:
[Greece, 399 BC–322 BC] Late Classical Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The century between the fall of Athens and the death of Alexander, when Sparta, Thebes and a revived Athens exhausted each other and Macedon under Philip II took control of Greece. Alexander's campaigns then carried Greek arms and language to Egypt, Persia and the Indus, remaking the eastern Mediterranean. It was also the age of Plato and Aristotle, of Praxiteles and Skopas softening the severe classical body, and of Demosthenes' losing argument for Athenian independence.

Aegean Bronze Age (Greece, 2999 BC–1999.label: Aegean Bronze Age
Aegean Bronze Age (Greece, 2999 BC–1999.prose:
[Greece, 2999 BC–1999 BC] Aegean Bronze Age. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The Early Bronze Age of the Aegean, when copper and tin alloys, longboats and the potter's wheel transformed island and mainland life. Cycladic craftsmen carved the spare white marble figurines that still look startlingly modern, while fortified settlements and metal hoards point to growing wealth and competition. Disruptions at the end of the period gave way to the palace societies of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.

Maurya Period (India, 321 BC–184 BC).label: Maurya Period
Maurya Period (India, 321 BC–184 BC).prose:
[South Asia, 321 BC–184 BC] Maurya Period. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Chandragupta seized Magadha and, in the wake of Alexander's withdrawal, built the first empire to cover most of the Indian subcontinent, run through a taxed countryside, spies and a large standing army from the capital at Pataliputra. His grandson Ashoka conquered Kalinga, recoiled at the slaughter and had edicts on moral rule carved on rocks and polished stone pillars across the empire, sponsoring Buddhist missions as far as Sri Lanka. Those inscriptions are the earliest deciphered writing in India and the first Indian ruler's own words we can read.

Vedic Period (India, 1749 BC–321 BC).label: Vedic Period
Vedic Period (India, 1749 BC–321 BC).prose:
[South Asia, 1749 BC–321 BC] Vedic Period. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The centuries in which the Sanskrit hymns of the Rig Veda and the later ritual texts were composed and transmitted orally by priestly families. Cattle-keeping Indo-Aryan communities moved from the Punjab into the Ganges plain, adopted iron, and grew into the janapadas and kingdoms that later texts remember. Out of it came the sacrificial religion, the four-varna social order and the language and literature underpinning later Hinduism.

Romanesque period (England, AD 1056–AD 1.label: Romanesque period
Romanesque period (England, AD 1056–AD 1.prose:
[England, AD 1056–AD 1189] Romanesque period. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Italy, Switzerland. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 475. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

After 1066 the Normans rebuilt almost every English cathedral and major abbey in a heavy new style of round arches and cylindrical piers, and studded the country with castles from timber mottes to the stone White Tower. Durham's rib-vaulted nave was among the most technically advanced buildings in Europe. The building boom was a statement of conquest as much as of faith.

Early Classical Period (Greece, 479 BC–4.label: Early Classical Period
Early Classical Period (Greece, 479 BC–4.prose:
[Greece, 479 BC–449 BC] Early Classical Period. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The decades between the repulse of Persia and the peace that ended the wars, when Athens converted a defensive alliance into a maritime empire. Sculptors broke with archaic convention, giving figures real balance and inward expression in what is called the Severe Style, seen in the temple of Zeus at Olympia.

Early Empire (Italy, 26 BC–AD 96).prose:

From Augustus's settlement of the state to the death of Domitian, one man held permanent control of army, treasury and law while the Republic's institutions were kept as scenery. Peace across the Mediterranean fuelled trade, urban building and a boom in monumental architecture — the Colosseum, aqueducts, the rebuilt Forum — and the frontier armies pushed into Britain and along the Rhine and Danube. It is also the period preserved in freeze-frame at Pompeii and Herculaneum.

Crete began this stretch as a rich, densely settled Christian province of grain estates and mosaic-floored basilicas centred on Gortyn, and ended it in upheaval. Earthquakes, plague and the collapse of Mediterranean security shrank its cities, and in the 820s Arab settlers took the island and founded the Emirate of Crete. Byzantine rule was only restored in 961.

The islanders of the central Aegean carved slender marble figurines with folded arms and blank faces - abstract to modern eyes and hugely influential on twentieth-century sculpture. They were skilled seafarers and metalworkers whose obsidian and silver moved across the Aegean, and their fortified settlements and long-boat imagery show a maritime world that flourished before Minoan Crete and Mycenae came to dominate it.

German forces occupied Denmark on 9 April 1940 after only hours of fighting, and for three years the Danish government pursued a policy of cooperation that kept parliament, police and monarchy in place. Strikes and sabotage forced the collapse of that policy in August 1943; the Germans imposed martial law, the navy scuttled its fleet, and in October almost all of Denmark's Jews were ferried to safety in Sweden. Resistance groups, an underground press and Allied air support grew through 1944-45 until the German surrender in Denmark took effect on 5 May 1945. Bunkers, coastal batteries and Atlantic Wall works from the occupation still dot the Jutland coast.

The 1920 plebiscites returned North Schleswig to Denmark, an outcome celebrated as Reunification but preceded by a constitutional crisis when the king dismissed the government. Social Democratic and Radical governments under Thorvald Stauning built the foundations of the Danish welfare state, above all in the Kanslergade Agreement of 1933, which combined social reform with support for depressed farmers. Unemployment, currency crises and a strong agricultural export trade dominated the economy, while functionalist architecture and modern design took hold in the towns.

Denmark's early Bronze Age was extraordinarily wealthy: amber and cattle went south, and bronze came back to be cast into distinctive Nordic swords, axes, lurs and spiral-decorated jewellery. Chiefs and their families were buried in thousands of turf barrows, and in some the airtight mound conditions preserved oak coffins with woollen clothing, hair and skin — the Egtved girl and the Borum Eshøj family among them. The Trundholm sun chariot and the era's rock art point to a religion centred on the sun's daily journey.

Beginning with the Lutheran Reformation and the crown's seizure of church property, this era saw the Danish king rule alongside a powerful noble council. Royal wealth funded Renaissance castles, new towns and Christian IV's ambitious building schemes, while disastrous wars with Sweden stripped away territory. It closed with the collapse of noble power and the introduction of hereditary absolute monarchy.

The Danish church took shape around new dioceses and the archbishopric of Lund, and villages across the country replaced wooden chapels with Romanesque stone churches. Decades of dynastic civil war ended with Valdemar I, whose ally Bishop Absalon fortified a fishing harbour that became Copenhagen. Royal power was now grounded in landed estates, taxes and an alliance with the church rather than in the loyalty of a warrior fleet alone.

Wealth shifted from bog offerings of weapons to gold hoards and hall-based aristocracies, then to towns, coinage and long-distance raiding and trade; it closes with a Christian kingdom of Denmark ruled from Jelling and Roskilde.

What follows is a kingdom of stone churches and royal towns, medieval castles and market places, the Reformation and the loss and reshaping of territory, down to the industrial and modern eras. Finds are dated by documents, coins and imported ceramics as much as by typology.

Plague and agrarian crisis emptied villages, while Margrete I bound Denmark, Norway and Sweden together in the Kalmar Union of 1397. Brick castles, market towns and Hanseatic trade shaped the landscape, and the era ends in the civil war known as the Count's Feud and the Lutheran Reformation.

Contacts with Central Europe brought in the first Nordic-style axes and neck ornaments, and the tradition of raising turf barrows over single inhumations took hold. Everything that follows in the Danish Bronze Age grows out of these tentative beginnings.

They overlapped with the Funnel Beaker farmers around them but kept separate economies and burial customs. Their existence shows that the shift to agriculture in southern Scandinavia was reversible and uneven.

As the ice retreated and the sea flooded the land bridges, Denmark's hunter-gatherers passed through the Maglemose, Kongemose and Ertebølle traditions, moving from inland lake and bog camps to a rich life on the coast. Waterlogged sites preserve an extraordinary record: dugout canoes, leister prongs, bows, fish weirs, and huge shell middens of oyster and cockle. Ertebølle communities were settled enough to build cemeteries and make pottery while still living entirely by hunting and fishing, and they traded with farming neighbours for generations before taking up farming around 4000 BC.

A blanket Danish term for everything before the medieval period, from the first reindeer hunters following the retreating ice to the Viking kings. It takes in the Stone Age farmers who built megalithic tombs, the Bronze Age chiefs buried in oak coffins with lurs and sun-discs, the Iron Age bog bodies and weapon sacrifices, and finally the seafarers who raided and settled across the North Sea. Denmark's peat bogs preserved wood, cloth and human remains from these millennia in exceptional condition.

At Jelling, Harald Bluetooth's rune-stone claims he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian. Under Cnut the Great the kingdom briefly ruled England and Norway together.

Its emblem is the chieftain's burial at Hoby on Lolland, furnished with a pair of Roman silver cups showing scenes from Homer — diplomatic gifts or plunder that ended up in a Danish grave. Ordinary people were still cremated with little more than a brooch or a pot.

Coastal foragers of the last Danish Mesolithic settled at fjord mouths and river outlets, piling up the shell middens that gave archaeology the word 'kitchen midden'. They fished with weirs and leisters, hunted seals and boar, travelled in dugout canoes, and buried their dead in cemeteries — signs of a settled, territorial way of life without farming. Their descendants would take up cattle and cereals only around 4000 BC, making these centuries the long final chapter of hunting-and-gathering Scandinavia.

Contact with the Roman Empire brought coins, glass and weapons north, while great weapon deposits in bogs and preserved bog bodies record war and ritual. The later centuries brought kings, towns and ships, ending with the Viking expansion and Denmark's conversion to Christianity.

Bog finds from these millennia — flint axes, amber beads, pottery and sacrificed bodies — are among the best-preserved prehistoric material anywhere.

Danish kings fortified the Danevirke across the neck of Jutland and fostered the trading towns of Ribe and Hedeby, where silver, glass and furs changed hands with Frisia and the Frankish empire. Improved sailing ships turned coastal raiding into long-distance expeditions to England and the Continent, and the first Christian missions arrived under Ansgar. Pagan burial with weapons, horses and boats was still the norm, and runic memorials record the warriors and traders who paid for it.

The Law of Jutland, promulgated in 1241, opened with the words 'with law shall the land be built' and became a foundation of Danish legal tradition. Brick building spread from churches to castles and town halls, and market towns won charters as trade with the Hanseatic ports grew.

The countryside was surveyed and reshaped, and in the late 1700s the great agrarian reforms broke up village open fields and moved farms out onto their own land – a change still legible in the map today.

Individuals were buried singly under low round barrows, men with polished stone battle-axes and beakers, in a sharp break from the collective megalithic tombs of earlier farmers. Ancient DNA links this change to incoming steppe-derived populations who reshaped the genetic and linguistic map of northern Europe.

Pottery grew more elaborate, with deep-cut ornament on beakers and flasks, and enormous quantities of flint were mined and traded. The shift is really a social one — from scattered pioneer farmsteads to groups who marked their claim on the land with permanent monuments.

Animal-style ornament and Nordic mythological imagery took shape here, weapon sacrifices in bogs continued, and long-distance contacts reached the Roman and Byzantine worlds. The elite halls, ships and seafaring skills of this period led directly into the Viking Age.

Settlement spread onto the light sandy soils of central and western Jutland, with more emphasis on cattle and pastoralism. Ancient DNA links this change to migration from the Pontic steppe, and it is central to arguments about how Indo-European languages reached Scandinavia.

Denmark lost its fleet, went bankrupt, and gave up Norway, then lost Schleswig and Holstein in 1864 – and turned inward, reclaiming heathland and remaking its economy. Steam power, railways, harbours and Copenhagen's factories drew people off the land, while farmers organised cooperative dairies and bacon factories that made Denmark an export food producer. Absolutism ended with the constitution of 1849, and mass politics, trade unions and emigration followed.

The Kalmar Union held together, uneasily, under kings who leaned on German advisers and quarrelled endlessly with Swedish nobles. Wealth flowed from herring fisheries and the Sound tolls, paying for brick churches whose vaults were covered in the vivid, often comic wall paintings visitors still come to see. The Oldenburg dynasty took the throne in 1448 and would hold it for four centuries; Copenhagen gained a university in 1479.

Wealth came from copper, timber for warships and grain, and the island's sanctuaries - above all that of Aphrodite at Palaipaphos - drew pilgrims from across the Greek world. Archaic-Hellenistic (Cyprus, 749 BC–99 B.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Ottoman (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1877).label: Ottoman
Ottoman (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1877).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1877] Ottoman. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.
Ottoman (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1877).source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Ceramic Age (Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 2008).label: Ceramic Age
Ceramic Age (Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 2008).prose:
[Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 2008] Ceramic Age. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A broad umbrella label covering everything on Cyprus from the point when pottery was in general use onward, lumping the Chalcolithic, Bronze Age and later historical eras into a single container. It is a convenience of archaeological record-keeping rather than a real cultural unit, and is worth reading as "pottery-bearing" rather than as a coherent phase.
Ceramic Age (Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 2008).source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 473 BC–311 BC).label: Cypro-Classical
Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 473 BC–311 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 473 BC–311 BC] Cypro-Classical. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Under Persian suzerainty the island's kings played Greek and Persian interests against each other, most famously Evagoras I of Salamis, who fought a long war for independence and promoted Greek language and art. Cypriot syllabic writing survived alongside the Greek alphabet and Phoenician, and royal tombs at Salamis were furnished with chariots, horses and Homeric-looking grave goods. The kingdoms ended when Ptolemy I abolished them and absorbed Cyprus into his empire.
Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 473 BC–311 BC).source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Medieval-Modern (Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 2008.label: Medieval-Modern
Medieval-Modern (Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 2008.prose:
[Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 2008] Medieval-Modern. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Wrested from its Byzantine governor by Richard the Lionheart and sold on, the island passed through Lusignan kings, Venetian fortress-builders, three centuries of Ottoman rule, and British administration from 1878. Each layer left visible marks: Gothic cathedrals converted to mosques, massive Venetian walls at Nicosia and Famagusta, and colonial-era infrastructure. Independence in 1960 was followed by intercommunal conflict and the division of the island in 1974.
Medieval-Modern (Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 2008.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Protogeometric-Hellenistic (Cyprus, 1049.label: Protogeometric-Hellenistic
Protogeometric-Hellenistic (Cyprus, 1049.prose:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–99 BC] Protogeometric-Hellenistic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A single long sweep covering the whole Cypriot Iron Age and its aftermath, when the island was divided among rival city-kingdoms such as Salamis, Kition and Paphos. Phoenician settlers, Assyrian, Egyptian and then Persian overlords all left their mark while local dynasts grew rich on copper and kept writing in the Cypriot syllabary. The kingdoms were abolished under the successors of Alexander, and Cyprus became a Ptolemaic possession governed from Alexandria.
Protogeometric-Hellenistic (Cyprus, 1049.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1449 BC–1199 BC.label: Late Cypriot II
Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1449 BC–1199 BC.prose:
[Cyprus, 1449 BC–1199 BC] Late Cypriot II. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

The peak of Bronze Age Cyprus. Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke functioned as cosmopolitan port towns handling copper, and the island — almost certainly the 'Alashiya' whose kings corresponded with the pharaoh in the Amarna letters — dealt with Egypt and the Hittites as a power in its own right. Tombs yield Mycenaean pictorial kraters, ivory, faience and gold, and clay tablets carry the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script.
Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1449 BC–1199 BC.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Post-Prehistoric (Cyprus, 998 BC–AD 2008.label: Post-Prehistoric
Post-Prehistoric (Cyprus, 998 BC–AD 2008.prose:
[Cyprus, 998 BC–AD 2008] Post-Prehistoric. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

An umbrella label covering everything from the Iron Age onward, when Cyprus stopped being a self-contained archaeological sequence and became a documented crossroads. Phoenician settlers and independent city-kingdoms gave way in turn to Assyrian, Egyptian, Persian, Hellenistic and Roman overlords, then Byzantine, Lusignan, Venetian, Ottoman and British rule. Copper, timber and a position between Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt kept the island valuable to every one of them.
Post-Prehistoric (Cyprus, 998 BC–AD 2008.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

Hellenistic (Cyprus, 310 BC–99 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Cyprus, 310 BC–99 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 310 BC–99 BC] Hellenistic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.
Hellenistic (Cyprus, 310 BC–99 BC).source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

The Old Empire (Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC).label: The Old Empire
The Old Empire (Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC).prose:
[on the banks of the Nile, 2699 BC–2079 BC] The Old Empire. "The Old Empire (2700-2080 B. C.)" page 15
"..the civilization which grew up on the banks of the Nile..." page 15, and map on page 16.
