The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour and administration needed to raise the monuments at Giza and Saqqara and were regarded as gods on earth. A literate bureaucracy of scribes, standardised art conventions and the first monumental stone architecture were all established here and set the pattern for three thousand years. Its end came as provincial governors grew independent and royal power dissolved, plunging Egypt into a period of competing local rulers.
The Old Empire (Egypt, 2699 BC–2079 BC).source: Barnes general history. : a brief history of ancient, mediaeval, and modern peoples, with some account of their monuments, institutions, arts, manners, and customs

The Middle Empire (Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 B.label: The Middle Empire
The Middle Empire (Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 B.prose:
[on the banks of the Nile, 2079 BC–1524 BC] The Middle Empire. "The Middle Empire (2080-1525 B.C.)" page 16.
"..the civilization which grew up on the banks of the Nile..." page 15, and map on page 16. Period definition from Barnes general history. : a brief history of ancient, mediaeval, and modern peoples, with some account of their monuments, institutions, arts, manners, and customs — Joel Dorman Steele, 1883.

After the collapse of centralised rule, the Theban kings reunified Egypt and governed from a new capital near the Faiyum, pushing fortresses deep into Nubia and mining the Sinai. Pyramids were built again, though of mudbrick cores that have since slumped into mounds, while sculpture turned to careworn, watchful royal faces unlike the serene masks of earlier ages. Later Egyptians treated its literature — the Tale of Sinuhe, the Eloquent Peasant — as classic, and its language became the standard for formal writing.
The Middle Empire (Egypt, 2079 BC–1524 B.source: Barnes general history. : a brief history of ancient, mediaeval, and modern peoples, with some account of their monuments, institutions, arts, manners, and customs

The New Empire (Egypt, 1524 BC–526 BC).label: The New Empire
The New Empire (Egypt, 1524 BC–526 BC).prose:
[on the banks of the Nile, 1524 BC–526 BC] The New Empire. "The New Empire (1525-527 B.C.)" page 17.
"..the civilization which grew up on the banks of the Nile..." page 15, and map on page 16. Period definition from Barnes general history. : a brief history of ancient, mediaeval, and modern peoples, with some account of their monuments, institutions, arts, manners, and customs — Joel Dorman Steele, 1883.

Egypt at its most expansive: warrior pharaohs campaigned into Syria and Nubia, tribute and gold flowed in, and rulers were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings rather than under pyramids. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Akhenaten's short-lived solar heresy, Tutankhamun, and Ramesses II's colossal building programme at Karnak and Abu Simbel. The long aftermath saw central authority fragment, Libyan and Kushite dynasties take the throne, and Assyrian and Persian armies eventually march into the Nile valley.
The New Empire (Egypt, 1524 BC–526 BC).source: Barnes general history. : a brief history of ancient, mediaeval, and modern peoples, with some account of their monuments, institutions, arts, manners, and customs

Later Babylonian Empire (Syria, 624 BC–5.prose:
[Babylonia, 624 BC–537 BC] Later Babylonian Empire. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. "Later Babylonian Empire (625-538)... in 625 B.C., their combined forces captured Nineveh...captured by Cyrus the Great (538 B.C.)." page 50.

Nabopolassar broke free of Assyria and, with Median allies, destroyed Nineveh; his son Nebuchadnezzar II then took the Levant from Egypt. Syrian and Palestinian cities were absorbed or destroyed, Jerusalem was sacked and its population deported, and tribute funded the rebuilding of Babylon with its Ishtar Gate and processional way. The empire lasted barely ninety years before Cyrus the Persian took Babylon without a fight.
Later Babylonian Empire (Syria, 624 BC–5.source: Barnes general history. : a brief history of ancient, mediaeval, and modern peoples, with some account of their monuments, institutions, arts, manners, and customs

Egypt moves from Nile-side farming villages and the Naqada chiefdoms to a unified kingdom with writing, a divine monarchy and monumental stone building. The Old Kingdom produced the great pyramids at Giza and a centralised bureaucracy, then fragmented into competing provincial dynasties before Theban rulers reunified the country and opened the Middle Kingdom. Almost every enduring feature of pharaonic culture - hieroglyphs, mummification, the royal ideology - was fixed in this span.
Ancient History, Period I (Egypt, 4003 B.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Ancient History, Period V (Egypt, 751 BC.node: Ancient History, Period V (Egypt, 751 BC–322 BC)

Kushite pharaohs from Nubia reunited Egypt and revived archaic art and building, only to be driven out by Assyrian invasions. The Saite kings that followed presided on a deliberate cultural renaissance, opened the country to Greek traders and mercenaries, and fell to the Persians in 525 BC. After spells of rebellion and brief independence, Alexander the Great took Egypt in 332 BC and was welcomed as a liberator.

Dominated by the Thirty Years' War, which began with a revolt in Bohemia and drew in Denmark, Sweden, Spain and France until much of the Holy Roman Empire had been fought over, plundered and depopulated - some regions losing a third or more of their people. The Peace of Westphalia ended it by recognising the confessional and territorial autonomy of the German states, weakening the emperor and confirming the Dutch Republic and Switzerland as independent. It is the conflict usually credited with establishing the European order of sovereign states.

Modern History, Period II (Spain, AD 155.label: Modern History, Period II
Modern History, Period II (Spain, AD 155.prose:

Spain at the height of its power under Philip II, financed by American silver and committed to defending Catholicism across a monarchy that briefly included Portugal and its empire. The Dutch revolt, the Armada's failure against England and repeated state bankruptcies exposed the limits of that ambition, and the expulsion of the Moriscos stripped whole regions of their farmers. The same decades produced Cervantes, El Greco and the beginnings of Spain's literary Golden Age.
Modern History, Period II (Spain, AD 155.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Modern History, Period IX (Brazil, AD 18.label: Modern History, Period IX
Modern History, Period IX (Brazil, AD 18.prose:
[Brazil and Portugal, Spanish America, Greece, France, Russia, Prussia, Austria, Poland, Belgium, Great Britain, United States of America, AD 1815–AD 1835] Modern History, Period IX. Brazil separated from Portugal without a war of independence, becoming an empire under Pedro I in 1822 while keeping slavery, the plantation economy and a monarchy at a time when its Spanish-American neighbours turned republican. Pedro's abdication in 1831 left a child heir and a decade of regency, during which regional revolts flared from Pará to Rio Grande do Sul and the country's unity looked genuinely fragile. Coffee was beginning its rise in the southeast, shifting wealth and power away from the sugar northeast.

Britain's contest with France went global in the Seven Years' War, winning Canada, dominance in India and command of the seas, and leaving a victorious state with debts it tried to recover by taxing its American colonies. Those taxes provoked the resistance that ends the period with the Declaration of Independence. At home, enclosure, canal building, improved iron smelting and Watt's steam engine were laying the groundwork of industrialisation.

Roman authority in Gaul dissolved and was replaced by Frankish, Burgundian and Visigothic kingdoms; Clovis's conversion to Catholic Christianity tied the new Merovingian monarchy to the bishops and the surviving Gallo-Roman elite. Towns shrank, villa estates were abandoned or reoccupied, and burial with weapons and jewellery became the fashion. The map of medieval France was drawn in these centuries.

Britain lost its thirteen American colonies, fighting a war that became a four-power struggle with France, Spain and the Dutch, then turned its imperial attention to India, the Pacific and a new penal colony at Botany Bay. The French Revolution split British politics, brought years of repression at home and a long war abroad, and its aftershocks produced rebellion in Ireland and the Act of Union of 1801. Cotton mills, canals and the first factory towns were transforming the north; the brief Peace of Amiens closes the period.

Ancient History, Period IV (Egypt, 979 B.node: Ancient History, Period IV (Egypt, 979 BC–751 BC)

Egypt was ruled in parallel by Delta dynasties of Libyan descent and by the god's wives and priests of Amun at Thebes, with power resting on family networks rather than a single throne. Kings such as Shoshenq I could still campaign into Palestine, but authority steadily fragmented into rival principalities. The weakness invited the Kushite kings of Napata to intervene from the south.

Christian kingdoms pushed steadily south against Almoravid and Almohad rule, decisively so after the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa; by the mid-thirteenth century only Granada remained Muslim. Conquest brought resettlement, new cathedrals over mosques, and centuries of uneasy coexistence between Christians, Muslims and Jews. The union of Castile and Aragon and the fall of Granada in 1492 ended the era and launched Spain outward across the Atlantic.
Middle History, Period V (Spain, AD 1100.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

The decades after Utrecht, when Britain settled into Hanoverian rule and Robert Walpole, effectively its first prime minister, kept the country out of expensive wars while the national debt, the Bank of England and a stock market matured into an unmatched machine for financing the state. Overseas trade, slaving voyages and the East India Company's factories expanded steadily, and the last Jacobite rising in 1745 marched to Derby before collapsing. The War of the Austrian Succession pulled Britain back into continental fighting and ended inconclusively at Aix-la-Chapelle.
Modern History, Period V (England, AD 17.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Thirteen years of near-continuous war with Napoleonic France, decided at sea by Trafalgar and on land by the Peninsular campaign and finally Waterloo, with Britain paying subsidies that kept coalition after coalition in the field. Blockade and the Continental System reshaped world trade in Britain's favour, the slave trade was abolished in 1807, and wartime taxation and industrial demand accelerated the factory economy. Victory left Britain the dominant naval and colonial power for the century that followed.

The age of Louis XIV, who ruled without a chief minister, built Versailles as a machine for controlling the nobility, and made French the language of European courts. Colbert's economic management and a huge standing army funded wars that pushed France's frontiers outward but ended in exhaustion, while the revocation of the Edict of Nantes drove Huguenot craftsmen into exile across Protestant Europe. The Treaty of Utrecht closed the period by checking French ambitions and dividing the Spanish inheritance.

The age of empire: pharaohs campaigned from the Euphrates to the fourth cataract, filled Karnak and the Valley of the Kings, and exchanged letters with the great kings of the Near East. It contains Akhenaten's brief solar revolution and its erasure, the reign of Ramesses II, and the battles against the Sea Peoples. Tomb robbery, strikes at Deir el-Medina and the growing power of the Amun priesthood mark the slide into division between Delta kings and Theban high priests.

Ancient History, Period II (Egypt, 1920.node: Ancient History, Period II (Egypt, 1920 BC–1490 BC)

[Assyria, Babylonia, Egypt, 1920 BC–1490 BC] Ancient History, Period II. Period definition from A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps — Emma Willard, 1835.

The confident Middle Kingdom state of forts, irrigation works and classic literature gave way to fragmentation and the rule of Hyksos kings from the Levant in the Delta. Their chariots, composite bows and bronze technology were turned against them when Theban princes expelled them and founded the New Kingdom. Egypt emerged militarised and expansionist, pushing armies into Nubia and Syria for the first time.

Syria passed from Byzantine to Muslim rule within a decade and then became the political centre of the Islamic world when the Umayyads made Damascus their capital. Arabic replaced Greek in administration, coinage was reformed, and desert palaces and the Great Mosque of Damascus fused Byzantine craftsmanship with new religious purpose. The Abbasid revolution moved the caliphate to Iraq, leaving Syria a wealthy province rather than a seat of empire.
Middle History, Period III (Syria, AD 62.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Ancient History, Period VI (Egypt, 322 B.label: Ancient History, Period VI
Ancient History, Period VI (Egypt, 322 B.prose:
[Egypt, Syria, Macedonia, Thrace, Asia Minor, Greece, Rome, Carthage, Numidia, Parthia, Armenia, Gaul, Britain, Spain, 322 BC–AD 1] Ancient History, Period VI. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Armenia, Bulgaria, Egypt, England, France, Greece, Iran. The year is not noted on this first page, but it is on the page for the Middle History Period I, page 103. Period definition from A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps — Emma Willard, 1835.

Under the Ptolemies, a Macedonian dynasty ruled Egypt from Alexandria, a Greek city with a lighthouse, Museum and Library that became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean, while temples in the traditional style still rose at Edfu and Dendera. Greek administration and coinage sat over a Egyptian countryside taxed for grain. Cleopatra VII's defeat at Actium ended the line, and Egypt became the personal province that fed Rome.
Ancient History, Period VI (Egypt, 322 B.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Middle History, Period IV (Spain, AD 800.label: Middle History, Period IV
Middle History, Period IV (Spain, AD 800.prose:
[Germany, Italy, France, England, Scotland, Spain, Russia, Greek Empire, Empire of the Caliphs, Turkey, AD 800–AD 1100] Middle History, Period IV. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Greece, Iran, Iraq, Russia, Scotland. Period definition from A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps — Emma Willard, 1835.

Muslim al-Andalus reached its height under the Córdoban Umayyads, whose caliphate made Córdoba one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe, while small Christian kingdoms consolidated in the north. The caliphate's collapse after 1031 splintered the south into taifa states that paid tribute to Christian rulers and invited Almoravid intervention from Morocco. The fall of Toledo in 1085 marked the turning of the balance.
Middle History, Period IV (Spain, AD 800.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Modern History, Period I (England, AD 14.label: Modern History, Period I
Modern History, Period I (England, AD 14.prose:
[England, Scotland, Spain, France, Germany, Portugal, Switzerland, Italy, Russia, Sweden, Denmark, Poland, Ottoman Empire, Cuba, Hispaniola, Orinoco River, Brazil, AD 1492–AD 1559] Modern History, Period I. Spatial coverage: Brazil, Cuba, Denmark, Dominican Republic, England, France, Germany, Haiti. The generation in which Europe's horizons split open: Atlantic voyages, Luther's challenge to Rome, and the printing press turning argument into mass politics. In England the Tudors broke with the papacy, dissolved the monasteries and redistributed a huge share of the country's land, then swung through Protestant and Catholic reigns before Elizabeth's accession. The era closes with the Habsburg-Valois wars settled at Cateau-Cambrésis and Europe divided along confessional lines it would fight over for a century.
Modern History, Period I (England, AD 14.source: A system of universal history, in perspective : accompanied by an atlas exhibiting chronology in a picture of nations and progressive geography in a series of maps

Age du bronze ancien et moyen (second mi.label: Age du bronze ancien et moyen (second millénaire)
Age du bronze ancien et moyen (second mi.prose:
[Chypre, 1999 BC–999 BC] Age du bronze ancien et moyen (second millénaire). Period definition from Corpus Vasorum Antiquorum, France. Fascicule 5, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 4. — Edmond Pottier, 1926.

Cypriot villages grew rich on the island's copper, which was smelted and cast in quantity and traded outward to the Levant and Anatolia; the distinctive Red Polished pottery and the crowded chamber tombs of sites like Vounous and Lapithos come from these centuries. Over time small farming communities gave way to fortified towns and coastal harbours, and Cyprus entered the international correspondence of the eastern Mediterranean as the copper-supplying land of Alashiya. Visitors can trace the arc from modest household metalworking to an island economy geared to export.
Age du bronze ancien et moyen (second mi.source: Corpus Vasorum Antiquorum, France. Fascicule 5, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 4.

Style attique à figures noires (Cyprus,.node: Style attique à figures noires (Cyprus, 599 BC–499 BC)

[Chypre, 599 BC–499 BC] Style attique à figures noires. Period definition from Corpus Vasorum Antiquorum, France. Fascicule 5, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 4. — Edmond Pottier, 1926.

Athenian black-figure pottery, with dark silhouetted figures and incised detail on orange clay, reached Cyprus through Aegean trade and turns up in sanctuaries and graves across the island. Its presence tracks the growing pull of Greek fashion on Cypriot elites who were simultaneously under Persian overlordship and long exposed to Phoenician and Levantine goods. For archaeologists the vases are a portable dating tool, tying Cypriot deposits to a well-studied Athenian sequence.
Style attique à figures noires (Cyprus,.source: Corpus Vasorum Antiquorum, France. Fascicule 5, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 4.

[Troade (Hissarlik), 1999 BC–999 BC] Age du bronze (second millénaire av. J.-C.). Period definition from Corpus Vasorum Antiquorum, France. Fascicule 5, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 4. — Edmond Pottier, 1926.

Anatolia's second millennium opened with Assyrian merchants running donkey caravans of tin and textiles to trading colonies at Kanesh, leaving thousands of clay tablets that record their business and family quarrels. Out of the competing local kingdoms rose the Hittites, who built the fortified capital of Hattusa, fought Egypt at Kadesh and left the earliest documents in an Indo-European language. The whole system collapsed around 1200 BC amid destructions that ended the Bronze Age across the eastern Mediterranean.

High Empire (Italy, AD 96–AD 180).label: High Empire
High Empire (Italy, AD 96–AD 180).prose:
[Rome, AD 96–AD 180] High Empire. Period definition from Rome : an Oxford archaeological guide to Rome — Claridge, Amanda., 1998.

From Nerva to Commodus, the empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan and then settled into consolidation behind fixed frontiers like Hadrian's Wall. Cities across the provinces filled with baths, aqueducts and forums, provincials rose to the throne, and law and citizenship spread widely. The Antonine plague and Commodus's murder in 192 exposed how much depended on a single life, ushering in civil war.
High Empire (Italy, AD 96–AD 180).source: Rome : an Oxford archaeological guide to Rome

The Severans (Italy, AD 193–AD 238).label: The Severans
The Severans (Italy, AD 193–AD 238).prose:
[Rome, AD 193–AD 238] The Severans. Period definition from Rome : an Oxford archaeological guide to Rome — Claridge, Amanda., 1998.

Septimius Severus, a North African general, seized power after another round of civil war and openly based his rule on the loyalty of the army, raising soldiers' pay and their status. His dynasty extended Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire in AD 212 and left grand monuments in Rome and at Lepcis Magna. Its violent end — a run of murdered emperors — opened the way to fifty years of near-collapse.
The Severans (Italy, AD 193–AD 238).source: Rome : an Oxford archaeological guide to Rome

The Flavians (Italy, AD 69–AD 96).label: The Flavians
The Flavians (Italy, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 96] The Flavians. Period definition from Rome : an Oxford archaeological guide to Rome — Claridge, Amanda., 1998.

After the chaos of the civil wars of AD 69, Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian founded a new dynasty drawn from Italian municipal gentry rather than the old Roman aristocracy. They stabilised the finances, rebuilt a burnt city, and put up the Colosseum on the drained site of Nero's private lake — a deliberate gift of imperial luxury back to the people. Their reigns also saw the destruction of Jerusalem's Temple and the eruption that buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.
The Flavians (Italy, AD 69–AD 96).source: Rome : an Oxford archaeological guide to Rome

Saka (Kazakhstan, 699 BC–99 BC).label: Saka
Saka (Kazakhstan, 699 BC–99 BC).prose:
[South eastern Kazakhstan, 699 BC–99 BC] Saka. In A. Rosen, C. Chang, and F. Grigoriev, 2000, "Palaeoenvironments and economy of Iron Age Saka-Wusun agro-pastoralists in southeastern Kazakhstan", Antiquity 74:611-623, the Wusun period in this region is defined as "c. 300 BC-AD 200" and the Saka period as "c. 750-300 BC" (p. 611). Period definition from Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan — Perry A. Tourtellotte, 2003-06.

Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the Central Asian steppe, known to the Persians as Saka and to the Greeks as Scythians of the east. They buried their elite under great kurgan mounds with horses, weapons and gold worked in the animal style, most spectacularly the armoured "Golden Man" of Issyk near Almaty. They fought and sometimes served the Achaemenid Persians, and their mobile, mounted way of life set the pattern for steppe empires for the next thousand years.
Saka (Kazakhstan, 699 BC–99 BC).source: Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan

Mongol (Kazakhstan, AD 1210–AD 1500).label: Mongol
Mongol (Kazakhstan, AD 1210–AD 1500).prose:
[South eastern Kazakhstan, AD 1210–AD 1500] Mongol. Period definition from Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan — Perry A. Tourtellotte, 2003-06.

Chinggis Khan's armies swept through the steppe and the Silk Road cities of the south, folding the region into the Mongol empire and then into the Golden Horde and Chagatai realms. Nomadic pastoral life continued much as before, but trade routes, tribute systems and ruling dynasties were reorganised, and Islam spread among the steppe elite. Out of the later fragmentation came the Kazakh Khanate, the direct ancestor of the modern nation.
Mongol (Kazakhstan, AD 1210–AD 1500).source: Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan

Historic Kazakh (Kazakhstan, AD 1500–AD.label: Historic Kazakh
Historic Kazakh (Kazakhstan, AD 1500–AD.prose:
[South eastern Kazakhstan, AD 1500–AD 2003] Historic Kazakh. "Present" in date range interpreted as date of publication. Period definition from Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan — Perry A. Tourtellotte, 2003-06.

Spans the Kazakh Khanate and its successor states, from a nomadic society organised into three great hordes to the modern republic. Long wars with the Dzungars in the eighteenth century pushed the khans toward Russian protection, which became outright annexation, then Soviet rule, forced settlement and the famine of the early 1930s. Steppe burial grounds, mausolea, winter camps and later Soviet-era towns all fall within the period, ending with independence in 1991.
Historic Kazakh (Kazakhstan, AD 1500–AD.source: Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan

A confederation of horse-riding pastoralists in the Ili valley and Tianshan foothills, known mainly from Chinese histories that record their vast herds and their kings' marriages to Han princesses. Positioned between the Han empire and the Xiongnu, they were courted as allies by both and helped keep the Silk Road routes north of the Tarim Basin open. Their kurgan burials, with gold ornaments and horse gear, are among the richest steppe finds in the region.
Wusun (Kazakhstan, 199 BC–AD 500).source: Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan

Turkic (Kazakhstan, AD 600–AD 900).label: Turkic
Turkic (Kazakhstan, AD 600–AD 900).prose:
[South eastern Kazakhstan, AD 600–AD 900] Turkic. Period definition from Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan — Perry A. Tourtellotte, 2003-06.

Nomadic confederations speaking Turkic languages dominated the steppe and the settled oases, first under the Türk khaganates and then the Türgesh and Karluks. They controlled the caravan roads that carried silk, silver and religions across Inner Asia, and left runic inscriptions, elite burials with horses, and stone figures marking graves. This is the era in which Turkic peoples became the lasting demographic and political fact of Central Asia.
Turkic (Kazakhstan, AD 600–AD 900).source: Iron Age society and chronology in South-east Kazakhstan

The era of Chaco Canyon, when massive multi-storey great houses, great kivas and a network of engineered roads linked communities across tens of thousands of square miles. Small farmsteads spread over almost every arable pocket of the Colorado Plateau, tied to regional centres by shared architecture and ritual. Trade brought turquoise, macaws and copper bells from as far as Mesoamerica.

Farming families across the Colorado Plateau moved out of scattered pithouses into rows of aboveground rooms built of jacal and stone, clustered into the first true villages. Populations grew fast, some settlements reaching hundreds of people, and pottery, turkey-keeping and bean cultivation spread. Many of these villages were short-lived, breaking up and reforming elsewhere - a pattern of movement that would define Puebloan history.

Migrants and existing populations coalesced into very large adobe and stone pueblos with enclosed plazas, along the Rio Grande and in the Hopi and Zuni country. Plaza-centred settlements went with new religious practices, including the katsina ceremonialism recorded in vivid kiva murals at Awatovi and Pottery Mound. These are the towns the Spanish would encounter, and the ancestors of today's Pueblo communities.

Pueblo III (United States, AD 1145–AD 12.prose:
[Utah, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, AD 1145–AD 1285] Pueblo III. Period definition from Exploration and exploitation in the macrohistory of the pre-Hispanic Pueblo Southwest — K. W. Kintigh, 2016-04-01.

After Chaco's decline people drew together into large, tightly packed towns, many of them tucked into canyon alcoves - the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde and Canyon de Chelly belong to this time. Defensive placement, towers and reservoirs suggest competition for land and water. By about 1300 the Four Corners country was emptied entirely, its inhabitants moving south and east in one of the great migrations of North American history.

Basketmaker III (United States, AD 500–A.prose:
[Utah, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, AD 500–AD 700] Basketmaker III. Period definition from Exploration and exploitation in the macrohistory of the pre-Hispanic Pueblo Southwest — K. W. Kintigh, 2016-04-01.

Pottery arrives in quantity, the bow and arrow replaces the atlatl, and beans join maize in the diet, allowing bigger and more permanent settlements. People lived in deep pithouses clustered into hamlets, often with an oversized structure for communal use that foreshadows the later kiva. These villages are the direct foundation of the Pueblo world that followed.

Byzantine (United Kingdom, AD 491–AD 145.label: Byzantine
Byzantine (United Kingdom, AD 491–AD 145.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 491–AD 1453] Byzantine. This period does not appear in the EH timeline. When this broad period is used, the database will automatically map it onto either Iron Age (for the earlier coins) or Roman (for the later coins) depending on the precise years entered. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.

Middle Bronze (United Kingdom, 1599 BC–1.label: Middle Bronze
Middle Bronze (United Kingdom, 1599 BC–1.prose:
[United Kingdom, 1599 BC–1000 BC] Middle Bronze. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Canaan revived after a long rural interlude, with substantial cities ringed by massive earthen ramparts and glacis, and a material culture of fine wheel-made pottery, bronze weapons and scarab seals. Trade linked the coast to Egypt, Cyprus and Syria, and Canaanite settlers in the Nile Delta eventually gave rise to Hyksos rule in Egypt. Many of the biblical cities - Hazor, Megiddo, Jericho, Shechem - reached their greatest size in these centuries.

Early Neolithic (United Kingdom, 3999 BC.label: Early Neolithic
Early Neolithic (United Kingdom, 3999 BC.prose:
[United Kingdom, 3999 BC–3500 BC] Early Neolithic. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Farming, pottery and domesticated animals arrived in Britain, and within a few generations people were building monuments: earthen long barrows over the bones of the dead, ditched causewayed enclosures for gatherings and feasts, and deep flint mines. Woodland was cleared for cereals and pasture, beginning the long transformation of the British landscape. These communities laid the groundwork for the great henge and stone circle building that followed.

Mesolithic (United Kingdom, 9999 BC–4000.label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (United Kingdom, 9999 BC–4000.prose:
[United Kingdom, 9999 BC–4000 BC] Mesolithic. Can be split into Early and Late. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Middle Iron Age (United Kingdom, 399 BC–.node: Middle Iron Age (United Kingdom, 399 BC–100 BC)
Middle Iron Age (United Kingdom, 399 BC–.label: Middle Iron Age
Middle Iron Age (United Kingdom, 399 BC–.prose:
[United Kingdom, 399 BC–100 BC] Middle Iron Age. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Hillforts, enclosed farmsteads and grain storage pits dominated the landscape, and roundhouse communities produced increasingly regionalised pottery and fine metalwork in flowing La Tène style. Many hillforts were abandoned or slimmed down to fewer, larger centres, hinting at the consolidation of the tribal groupings Roman writers would later name. Bodies and objects placed deliberately in disused pits offer a glimpse of ritual life.

Bronze Age (United Kingdom, 2349 BC–800.label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (United Kingdom, 2349 BC–800.prose:
[United Kingdom, 2349 BC–800 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Modern (United Kingdom, AD 1901–AD 2050).label: Modern
Modern (United Kingdom, AD 1901–AD 2050).prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 1901–AD 2050] Modern. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 1066–AD 153.prose: [United Kingdom, AD 1066–AD 1539] Medieval. English Heritage do not specify the boundaries of any sub-periods within the Medieval period. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Late Iron Age (United Kingdom, 99 BC–AD.prose:
[United Kingdom, 99 BC–AD 42] Late Iron Age. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Late Neolithic (United Kingdom, 2699 BC–.label: Late Neolithic
Late Neolithic (United Kingdom, 2699 BC–.prose:
[United Kingdom, 2699 BC–2350 BC] Late Neolithic. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.

Neolithic (United Kingdom, 3999 BC–2350.label: Neolithic
Neolithic (United Kingdom, 3999 BC–2350.prose:
[United Kingdom, 3999 BC–2350 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Early Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–4.node: Early Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–400 BC)
Early Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–4.label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–4.prose:
[United Kingdom, 799 BC–400 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 42).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 42).prose:
[United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 42] Iron Age. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410) [p0.label: Roman
Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410) [p0.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410] Roman. Can be split into Early and Late. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Late Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD.label: Late Early Medieval
Late Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 851–AD 1066] Late Early Medieval. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Viking armies overran most of the English kingdoms until Alfred of Wessex held out, and his successors then conquered the Danelaw to forge a single kingdom of England with shires, burhs and a silver coinage. Danish kings including Cnut later ruled it as part of a North Sea empire. The period ends abruptly at Hastings.

Middle Early Medieval (United Kingdom, A.label: Middle Early Medieval
Middle Early Medieval (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 701–AD 850] Middle Early Medieval. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The age of Mercian supremacy in England, when Offa built his dyke against the Welsh, issued a reformed silver penny and dealt with Charlemagne as an equal. Monasteries such as Jarrow and Lindisfarne turned out scholars, illuminated gospel books and the works of Bede, and English missionaries preached across the Continent. It closes with Viking fleets moving from raiding to overwintering, a shock that would remake the English kingdoms.

Middle Neolithic (United Kingdom, 3499 B.label: Middle Neolithic
Middle Neolithic (United Kingdom, 3499 B.prose:
[United Kingdom, 3499 BC–2700 BC] Middle Neolithic. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Communal long barrows and causewayed enclosures fell out of use, and people began building cursus monuments – enormous parallel-ditched avenues running for miles across the landscape – along with the first great henges. Pottery grew heavier and more elaborately decorated, and forest clearance and herding reshaped the countryside. The earthwork phase of Stonehenge belongs to the end of this stretch of time.

Early Bronze (United Kingdom, 2349 BC–16.label: Early Bronze
Early Bronze (United Kingdom, 2349 BC–16.prose:
[United Kingdom, 2349 BC–1600 BC] Early Bronze. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The southern Levant saw its first experiment with urban life: villages grew into walled towns with temples, palaces, granaries and planned streets at places like Arad, Megiddo and Bet Yerah. Olive oil and wine were produced for export, and trade with Egypt was intense enough that Egyptian rulers' names appear on jars in Canaan. Around 2500–2300 BC the towns were abandoned and people returned to villages and pastoralism, a collapse still debated by archaeologists.

Late Bronze (United Kingdom, 999 BC–800.label: Late Bronze
Late Bronze (United Kingdom, 999 BC–800.prose:
[United Kingdom, 999 BC–800 BC] Late Bronze. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Canaan was an Egyptian province of walled city-states, each with its ruler answering to a pharaoh's garrison and paying tribute. The Amarna letters capture their rivalries and pleas for help, while Cypriot, Mycenaean and Egyptian goods in the tombs show how deeply the region was tied into eastern Mediterranean trade. Widespread destructions and the appearance of new groups, including the earliest mention of Israel, close the age.

Greek and Roman Provincial (United Kingd.node: Greek and Roman Provincial (United Kingdom, 699 BC–AD 297)
Greek and Roman Provincial (United Kingd.label: Greek and Roman Provincial
Greek and Roman Provincial (United Kingd.prose: [United Kingdom, 699 BC–AD 297] Greek and Roman Provincial. This period does not appear in the EH timeline. When this broad period is used, the database will automatically map it onto either Iron Age (for the earlier coins) or Roman (for the later coins) depending on the precise years entered. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Late Roman (United Kingdom, AD 201–AD 41.label: Late Roman
Late Roman (United Kingdom, AD 201–AD 41.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 201–AD 410] Late Roman. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

Late Mesolithic (United Kingdom, 6999 BC.label: Late Mesolithic
Late Mesolithic (United Kingdom, 6999 BC.prose:
[United Kingdom, 6999 BC–4000 BC] Late Mesolithic. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Hunter-gatherers in dense post-glacial woodland made tiny geometric microliths set into composite arrows and worked the coasts, rivers and clearings with fire to draw in game. Rising seas finally drowned Doggerland during this period, cutting Britain off from the Continent and leaving its foragers on an island. Their world ended with the arrival of farming, and the debate over how much they contributed to what came next is still unresolved.

Early Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD.label: Early Early Medieval
Early Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 410–AD 700] Early Early Medieval. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

After Roman administration ended, towns emptied, coinage stopped circulating and villa estates were abandoned, while incoming Germanic-speaking groups reshaped eastern and southern Britain. Cremation and furnished inhumation cemeteries, brooches and weapon burials mark new identities and small competing kingdoms; the Sutton Hoo ship burial is the spectacular end of the process. Christian missions from Rome and Ireland arrived in the seventh century, bringing literacy, monasteries and a new political order.

Post-Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 1500–A.label: Post-Medieval
Post-Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 1500–A.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 1500–AD 1900] Post-Medieval. Early post-medieval is generally used for the 16th century and sometimes for the 17th century. The term 'middle post-medieval' is not used, and there is debate as to what constitutes the late post-medieval period. For the 18th century, it is best to stick simply to 'post-medieval' and qualify it using calendar dates. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The centuries after 1500 brought the Reformation, overseas empire, and the shift from an agrarian to an industrial society, all leaving dense archaeological traces. Sites of this age are full of dateable mass-produced material - clay pipes, glass bottles, glazed and printed pottery - which makes them unusually precise chronological anchors. Field boundaries, mills, docks, mines and workers' housing from this span still form the framework of the modern landscape.

Early Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 20.label: Early Roman
Early Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 20.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 200] Early Roman. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The Claudian invasion turned southern Britain into a province: legions pushed north and west, client kings were absorbed, and the revolt of Boudica was crushed. Towns with forums, baths and grid streets appeared where none had existed, roads linked new civitas capitals, and villas began to dot the countryside. By the end of the period the frontier had settled at Hadrian's Wall.

Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 410–A.label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 410–A.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 410–AD 1066] Early Medieval. This period is diverse and must be qualified wherever possible with Early, Middle or Late. The currently accepted chronology (spring 2013) is given below, but this is likely to change in the near future. English Heritage do not specify the boundaries of these sub-periods. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

La première époque (Italy, 699 BC–449 BC.label: La première époque
La première époque (Italy, 699 BC–449 BC.prose:
[Italy, 699 BC–449 BC] La première époque. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy. "On sait l'extrème difficulté qu'il y a de fixer l'époque des monumens anciens avec quelque dégré de précision, soit en les considérant d'après le style de l'Art, soit d'après les principes de la paléographie, lorsqu'ils présentent des caractères. Mais en combinant ce qu'ont rapporté les auteurs anciens avec les monumens de toute espèce, surtout les médailles et les inscriptions, il semble qu'on peut établir trois époques principales." (Millingen 1813, viii)

cf. Millingen 1813, n. 6: "V. Planches XX à XXII, XXXI, XXXII". Period definition from Peintures antiques et inédites de vases grecs, tirées de diverses collections, avec des explications — James V. Millingen, 1813.
La première époque (Italy, 699 BC–449 BC.source: Peintures antiques et inédites de vases grecs, tirées de diverses collections, avec des explications

Tufa Period (Pompeii, 199 BC–79 BC).label: Tufa Period
Tufa Period (Pompeii, 199 BC–79 BC).prose:
[Pompeii, 199 BC–79 BC] Tufa Period. Period definition from Pompeii : an architectural history — Richardson, Lawrence, Jr., 1920-2013., 1988.

Named for the grey Nocera tufa that became the standard building stone, this was Pompeii's Samnite heyday, when the town filled with Hellenistic-style architecture: the colonnaded Forum, the Temple of Jupiter, the Stabian Baths and grand atrium houses like the House of the Faun with its Alexander mosaic. Wealth from Campanian agriculture and trade paid for a townscape modelled on the Greek east. Much of what visitors see at Pompeii today was already standing before the Roman colony was planted in 80 BC.

Early Roman Colony (Pompeii, 79 BC–29 BC.label: Early Roman Colony
Early Roman Colony (Pompeii, 79 BC–29 BC.prose:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–29 BC] Early Roman Colony. Period definition from Pompeii : an architectural history — Richardson, Lawrence, Jr., 1920-2013., 1988.

Sulla planted a colony of army veterans in the town after besieging it, and Pompeii was refounded under Roman law with new settlers taking land and office. Latin displaced Oscan in public inscriptions, and the newcomers built the stone amphitheatre and the small covered theatre — the earliest surviving permanent amphitheatre anywhere. Older Pompeian families and the incoming veterans coexisted uneasily in a rapidly Romanised town.

Julio-Claudian (Pompeii, 29 BC–AD 62).label: Julio-Claudian
Julio-Claudian (Pompeii, 29 BC–AD 62).prose:
[Pompeii, 29 BC–AD 62] Julio-Claudian. Period definition from Pompeii : an architectural history — Richardson, Lawrence, Jr., 1920-2013., 1988.

The line of emperors descended from or adopted into the families of Augustus and Livia, spanning Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. Under them the improvised rule of one man hardened into a permanent monarchy with a court, a praetorian guard and an imperial bureaucracy; Britain was invaded, Egypt's grain fed Rome, and the succession repeatedly turned on poisonings, adoptions and palace intrigue. The line ended with Nero's suicide and a year of civil war.

Siglos XVI y XVII (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1.label: Siglos XVI y XVII
Siglos XVI y XVII (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1500–AD 1700] Siglos XVI y XVII. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia under the Habsburgs was a kingdom without a king in residence, governed by a royal captain-general and represented by the Junta of the Kingdom, whose seven cities voted taxes and troops. Its Atlantic coast made it a front line: Drake sacked Vigo and besieged A Coruña, and shipyards and coastal forts multiplied. Inland, monasteries and the pilgrimage to Santiago remained the great landowners and the great draw, while Baroque granite facades reshaped the cities.

Primera Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC.node: Primera Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–400 BC)
Primera Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC.label: Primera Edad del Hierro
Primera Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 800 BC–400 BC] Primera Edad del Hierro. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Phoenician traders settled the southern coasts, bringing iron, the potter's wheel, the alphabet and wine, and the wealth of the mines fed the legend of Tartessos. Inland, urnfield communities in the northeast absorbed influences from beyond the Pyrenees while Greek merchants founded Emporion. Out of this mix emerged the Iberian and Celtiberian cultures that Carthage and Rome would later fight over.

Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–50 BC).label: Edad del Hierro
Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–50 BC).prose: [Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 800 BC–50 BC] Edad del Hierro. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Edad Contemporánea (Galicia, AD 1900–AD.label: Edad Contemporánea
Edad Contemporánea (Galicia, AD 1900–AD.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1900–AD 2100] Edad Contemporánea. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia's twentieth century: mass emigration to Argentina, Cuba and later Europe emptied villages, while agrarian unions, the Rexurdimento's literary legacy and the Statute of Autonomy of 1936 fed a Galician national movement that Franco's dictatorship suppressed. Coastal industry, fishing fleets and canneries grew around Vigo and A Coruña, and after 1978 the region gained an autonomous government and official status for the Galician language.

Indígena-Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200).label: Indígena-Romano
Indígena-Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 50 BC–AD 200] Indígena-Romano. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. The Indigenous-Roman and Early Roman subdivisions of Roman Period have identical dates, but they refer to very different cultural contexts. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

After Augustus finished the conquest of the northwest, the hillfort communities of the castros kept living behind their walls in round stone houses, but began using Roman pottery, coins and Latin names. Rome reorganised the region for gold: enormous hydraulic mines, roads and administrative districts reshaped the landscape. The result is a distinctly hybrid material culture, with native warrior statues and torcs alongside Roman altars and imported tableware.

Edad del Bronce Media (Galicia, 1700 BC–.node: Edad del Bronce Media (Galicia, 1700 BC–1200 BC)
Edad del Bronce Media (Galicia, 1700 BC–.label: Edad del Bronce Media
Edad del Bronce Media (Galicia, 1700 BC–.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 1700 BC–1200 BC] Edad del Bronce Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

In southeastern Spain the El Argar world reached its height and then collapsed around 1550 BC, ending the fortified towns and their sharply hierarchical jar burials. Across the interior and the Atlantic side, herding communities used mould-cast bronze weapons and buried their dead in cists, and new alloys and forms circulated along routes that reached the Mediterranean and northwestern Europe. The period sets up the far-reaching metal trade of the Late Bronze Age.

Neolítico (Galicia, 4500 BC–2300 BC).label: Neolítico
Neolítico (Galicia, 4500 BC–2300 BC).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 4500 BC–2300 BC] Neolítico. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. The Neolithic category is split between Early Prehistory and Late Prehistory. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The first farmers in the peninsula grew cereals and pulses and kept sheep, goats and cattle, spreading along the Mediterranean coast with distinctive shell-impressed Cardial pottery and inland through cave and open-air settlements. Burial in caves and, increasingly, in megalithic tombs marks a new concern with ancestors and place. Rock art and the earliest large communal monuments belong to these centuries.

Alto Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200).label: Alto Romano
Alto Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 50 BC–AD 200] Alto Romano. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

With the Cantabrian wars finished, Hispania settled into provincial life under the Empire: new towns with forums and theatres, roads and bridges, the aqueducts of Segovia and Mérida, and vast exports of olive oil, wine, garum and silver to Rome. Latin, Roman law and urban citizenship spread widely, and the peninsula gave the empire Seneca, Martial, Trajan and Hadrian.

Edad del Bronce Inicial (Galicia, 2300 B.node: Edad del Bronce Inicial (Galicia, 2300 BC–1700 BC)
Edad del Bronce Inicial (Galicia, 2300 B.label: Edad del Bronce Inicial
Edad del Bronce Inicial (Galicia, 2300 B.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2300 BC–1700 BC] Edad del Bronce Inicial. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galician communities took up bronze metallurgy, and the great age of megalithic tomb-building gave way to individual burials in cists and to settlement in small, dispersed farmsteads. Local smiths produced flat axes, halberds and daggers, and gold lunulae and torcs signal an emerging elite with links along the Atlantic seaways. Rock carvings of weapons, deer and cup-marks across the region belong to this world.

Siglos XVIII y XIX (Galicia, AD 1700–AD.label: Siglos XVIII y XIX
Siglos XVIII y XIX (Galicia, AD 1700–AD.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1700–AD 1900] Siglos XVIII y XIX. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Maritime trade, Catalan-run sardine salting and the naval arsenal at Ferrol brought new money to the coast, while the interior stayed locked in smallholdings and rents. Napoleonic armies invaded in 1809 and were driven out by local risings within months. The century closed with two lasting transformations: mass emigration to Cuba, Argentina and Uruguay, and the Rexurdimento, the literary revival that made Galician a written language again through writers such as Rosalía de Castro.

Prehistoria Reciente (Galicia, 2700 BC–8.label: Prehistoria Reciente
Prehistoria Reciente (Galicia, 2700 BC–8.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2700 BC–800 BC] Prehistoria Reciente. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia's landscape filled with monuments: megalithic tombs under earthen mounds, then, in the Bronze Age, thousands of open-air rock carvings of deer, weapons and cup-marks on granite outcrops. Metalworkers produced flat axes, halberds and remarkable gold ornaments, some deposited in hoards or bogs. By the end of the period people were gathering into fortified hilltop settlements, the seeds of the castro culture.

Edad Media central (Galicia, AD 700–AD 1.label: Edad Media central
Edad Media central (Galicia, AD 700–AD 1.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 700–AD 1200] Edad Media central. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The centuries of al-Andalus at its height and of the Christian counter-advance: the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba flourished and then shattered into taifa kingdoms, inviting Almoravid and Almohad intervention from North Africa. Northern kingdoms — León, Castile, Navarre, Aragon, Portugal — pushed south, repopulating conquered land with charters and towns, while the pilgrimage road to Santiago de Compostela drew people and Romanesque architecture across the Pyrenees. The decisive Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 opened Andalusia to conquest.

Prehistoria Temprana (Galicia, 2500000 B.label: Prehistoria Temprana
Prehistoria Temprana (Galicia, 2500000 B.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2500000 BC–2700 BC] Prehistoria Temprana. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The long span from the first stone tools to the arrival of farming, represented in Galicia by quartzite handaxes and river-terrace scatters, coastal shell middens left by foragers, and finally the earliest Neolithic communities. Their most visible legacy is the mámoas — mounded chambered tombs raised on hilltops and passes, which fixed communal memory into the landscape for millennia.

Neolítico Antiguo (Galicia, 4500 BC–2700.label: Neolítico Antiguo
Neolítico Antiguo (Galicia, 4500 BC–2700.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 4500 BC–2700 BC] Neolítico Antiguo. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Farming arrived in the Atlantic northwest slowly, and the most visible legacy is the mámoa — the earthen mound covering a stone burial chamber — which spread in thousands across the Galician uplands from the mid-fifth millennium. These tombs staked out grazing land and routes as much as they housed the dead. Settlement traces are slight by comparison, so the monuments and their engraved and painted stones carry most of the story.

Edad del Bronce Final (Galicia, 1200 BC–.node: Edad del Bronce Final (Galicia, 1200 BC–800 BC)
Edad del Bronce Final (Galicia, 1200 BC–.label: Edad del Bronce Final
Edad del Bronce Final (Galicia, 1200 BC–.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 1200 BC–800 BC] Edad del Bronce Final. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Long-distance Atlantic exchange peaked, moving bronze weapons, cauldrons and gold ornaments between Iberia, Brittany, Britain and Ireland, while carved warrior stelae in the southwest depict shields, swords and mirrors as symbols of rank. In the south, contacts with the eastern Mediterranean prepared the ground for Phoenician colonies and the emergence of Tartessos. Hoards of scrap and finished metal from these centuries are among the richest in western Europe.

Neolítico Final (Galicia, 2700 BC–2300 B.label: Neolítico Final
Neolítico Final (Galicia, 2700 BC–2300 B.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2700 BC–2300 BC] Neolítico Final. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The closing phase of the Neolithic, when settlements grew larger, ditched and walled enclosures appeared, and copper metallurgy began to be practised alongside older stone technologies. Collective burial in megalithic tombs and artificial caves reached its peak, with rich grave goods hinting at emerging differences in status. Within a few generations these communities would build the fortified Chalcolithic towns of the south.

Epipaleolítico (Galicia, 7000 BC–4500 BC.label: Epipaleolítico
Epipaleolítico (Galicia, 7000 BC–4500 BC.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 7000 BC–4500 BC] Epipaleolítico. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

After the ice sheets retreated, hunter-gatherers adapted to warmer forests and rising seas, hunting deer and rabbit, gathering shellfish in huge quantities and making tiny geometric flint blades to arm composite tools. Their shell middens and cemeteries show settled, territorial communities living in the same coasts and river valleys that farmers would occupy a few centuries later.

Edad del Bronce (Galicia, 2300 BC–800 BC.label: Edad del Bronce
Edad del Bronce (Galicia, 2300 BC–800 BC.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2300 BC–800 BC] Edad del Bronce. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Metalworking in copper and tin spread across the peninsula, and in the southeast the El Argar culture built fortified hilltop towns with rectangular houses, buried its dead in jars beneath house floors, and marked out sharp differences of wealth in silver and bronze grave goods. Elsewhere communities raised cairns and stelae, worked gold, and traded along Atlantic and Mediterranean routes. It was the first period in Iberia with clearly stratified societies controlling metal and land.

Edad Moderna (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1900).label: Edad Moderna
Edad Moderna (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1900).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1500–AD 1900] Edad Moderna. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia entered the era as a kingdom without its own parliament, governed from Castile and dominated by monasteries and a landholding gentry; peasants worked under the foro leasehold system that shaped rural life for centuries. Maize and potatoes from America transformed farming and allowed the population to grow, while the ports lived off fishing, and A Coruña and Ferrol became naval and Atlantic trade centres. Compostela remained a pilgrimage capital, rebuilt in exuberant Baroque granite.

Alta Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 700).label: Alta Edad Media
Alta Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 700).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 400–AD 700] Alta Edad Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Roman authority in Hispania gave way to Germanic kingdoms, above all the Visigoths, who ruled from Toledo, absorbed the Suevi and eventually converted from Arianism to Catholicism. Cities shrank, coinage and trade contracted, and the church became the chief institution of learning, producing figures such as Isidore of Seville. The period closed with the Muslim invasion of 711, which swept the Visigothic state away in a few campaigns.

Segunda Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 400 BC.node: Segunda Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 400 BC–50 BC)
Segunda Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 400 BC.label: Segunda Edad del Hierro
Segunda Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 400 BC.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 400 BC–50 BC] Segunda Edad del Hierro. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Iberian communities along the Mediterranean coast built walled hilltop towns, wrote in their own scripts, minted coins and carved stone sculpture such as the Dama de Elche, while Celtiberian peoples of the interior fielded the warriors Rome found so hard to beat. Greek and Punic contact fed the trade in wine, oil and fine pottery. The period ends with the long Roman conquest, from the Second Punic War through the sieges of Numantia and the final campaigns in the north.

Siglos XX y XXI (Galicia, AD 1900–AD 210.label: Siglos XX y XXI
Siglos XX y XXI (Galicia, AD 1900–AD 210.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1900–AD 2100] Siglos XX y XXI. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Emigration continued on a huge scale, first to the Americas and later to Germany and Switzerland, hollowing out villages and funding the schools and quays the emigrants sent money home to build. Statutes of autonomy were drafted in the Republic, suppressed under Franco, and finally achieved in 1981, with Galician recognised as a co-official language. Fishing remained the region's signature industry, and the Prestige tanker disaster of 2002 brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets.

Bajo Romano (Galicia, AD 200–AD 400).label: Bajo Romano
Bajo Romano (Galicia, AD 200–AD 400).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 200–AD 400] Bajo Romano. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Hispania passed through third-century insecurity into the reorganised empire of Diocletian and Constantine, split into new provinces under a vicarius and taxed more heavily. Cities shrank behind walls while enormous rural villas with mosaic floors — Carranque, La Olmeda, Centcelles — became the centres of aristocratic power and wealth. Christianity spread fast, producing bishops, the council of Elvira and the Priscillianist controversy, and the landowning elite that emerged here survived to serve the Visigothic kings.

Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 1500).label: Edad Media
Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 1500).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 400–AD 1500] Edad Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Visigothic kingdoms gave way in 711 to the Muslim conquest, and for centuries the peninsula was divided between al-Andalus — with Córdoba among the largest and most learned cities in Europe — and the Christian kingdoms of the north. Warfare, frontier settlement and dynastic marriage steadily pushed the border south until only Granada remained, while Jews, Muslims and Christians lived in an uneasy and often violent proximity that also transmitted Greek and Arabic learning to the rest of Europe. Castile and Aragon were united by Ferdinand and Isabella, who took Granada in 1492.

Baja Edad Media (Galicia, AD 1200–AD 150.label: Baja Edad Media
Baja Edad Media (Galicia, AD 1200–AD 150.prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1200–AD 1500] Baja Edad Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The great southward conquests after Las Navas de Tolosa left Castile and the Crown of Aragon holding almost all Iberia, with Muslim rule reduced to Granada paying tribute. Aragon turned seaward to Sicily, Sardinia and Naples while Castile developed wool exports, Cortes assemblies and violent noble factionalism; plague, pogroms against Jewish communities and civil wars punctuated the era. It closes with the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella, the fall of Granada and the voyages that carried Iberian power across the Atlantic.

Época Romana (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 400).label: Época Romana
Época Romana (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 400).prose:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 50 BC–AD 400] Época Romana. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. The Indigenous-Roman and Early Roman subdivisions of Roman Period have identical dates, but they refer to very different cultural contexts. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Rome's conquest of the northwest completed the subjugation of Iberia and turned the region into the province of Gallaecia, exploited above all for gold — the vast hydraulic workings of Las Médulas being the most spectacular result. New cities such as Lucus Augusti and Bracara Augusta anchored a road network, while many hillfort communities carried on in Roman-influenced form for generations. Latin, Roman law and eventually Christianity took root here and shaped the region's later identity.

Archaic (Libya, 649 BC–499 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Libya, 649 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Lepcis Magna, 649 BC–499 BC] Archaic. Derived from Leptis Magna Forum Vetus excavations, "level 4"; absolute dates determined from Greek material (term. post quem: Late Proto-Corinthian). On Liby-phoenicians, see Birley (1988), Lancel (1995). Period definition from Western Phoenicians at Lepcis Magna — Theresa Howard Carter, 1965.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

Early Iron Age (Spain, 749 BC–449 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Spain, 749 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Spain, 749 BC–449 BC] Early Iron Age. Contemporary with Hallstatt B-D (S. Germany). Overlaps LBA III/ Tartessian period, 750-600 B.C. (- cf. M. Diaz-Andreu & S. Keay, 1997. The Archaeology of Iberia.); includes Iberian I (600-500 B.C.) and II (500-450 B.C.) (ibid.). See also T. Chapa & M. Belen, 1997. La Edad del Hierro. Period definition from Iron Age Archaeology of the Northwest Iberian Peninsula — César Parcero Oubiña, 2005.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.
Early Iron Age (Spain, 749 BC–449 BC).source: Iron Age Archaeology of the Northwest Iberian Peninsula

Lerna III (Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC).label: Lerna III
Lerna III (Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC] Lerna III. Applies to Lerna; equivalent to Lerna III. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 1: Jelyne Jesusa and Kevin Sartin. Period definition from C-14 Dates for Sites in the Mediterranean Area — Ellen L. Kohler, 1961.

The Early Bronze Age settlement in the Argolid dominated by the House of the Tiles, a large two-storey corridor building with a fired roof that burned down and was sealed under a tumulus. Its clay sealings imply centralised storage and administration, evidence of unusual social complexity in mainland Greece well before the Mycenaeans. The destruction of the building is a key marker in debates about upheaval at the end of Early Helladic II.
Lerna III (Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC).source: C-14 Dates for Sites in the Mediterranean Area

I. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1520–AD 1566).label: I. Süleyman
I. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1520–AD 1566).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1520–AD 1566] I. Süleyman. wikipedia: 17 shawwal 926 - 20 or 21 safar 974. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The empire's longest-reigning sultan took Belgrade and Rhodes, destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, besieged Vienna, and made the Ottoman navy dominant in the Mediterranean under Barbarossa. At home he was 'the Lawgiver', systematising secular law alongside religious law, while Mimar Sinan built the mosques that still define Istanbul's skyline and poetry and miniature painting flourished. His marriage to Hürrem Sultan and the executions of his own sons opened a new era of harem politics.
I. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1520–AD 1566).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

III. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730).label: III. Ahmed
III. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1703–AD 1730] III. Ahmed. wikipedia: 9 r2 1115 - 18/19 r1 1143. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Ahmed III's long reign is remembered as the Tulip Era, a period of French-influenced garden palaces, poetry, tulip mania among the elite and the first Ottoman-run printing press in Turkish, set up by İbrahim Müteferrika. He sheltered Charles XII of Sweden after Poltava, recovered the Morea from Venice, but lost Belgrade and Serbia at Passarowitz in 1718. The lavishness ended in 1730 when the Patrona Halil revolt of janissaries and artisans burned the pleasure pavilions and forced him from the throne.
III. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Murat (Turkey, AD 1360–AD 1389).label: I. Murat
I. Murat (Turkey, AD 1360–AD 1389).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1360–AD 1389] I. Murat. wikipedia: 9 j2 791. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He took Adrianople (Edirne) and made it his capital, turning the Ottoman beylik into a European power that reduced Serbian and Bulgarian princes to tributaries. The standing janissary corps and the timar system of cavalry fiefs took shape under him, along with the practice of levying Christian boys for state service. He was killed at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, a defeat for the Balkan coalition that became a founding memory of Serbian national identity.
I. Murat (Turkey, AD 1360–AD 1389).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754).label: I. Mahmud
I. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1730–AD 1754] I. Mahmud. wikipedia: 19 r1 1143 - 27 safar 1168. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Raised to the throne by the Patrona Halil janissary revolt that ended the Tulip Era, he later crushed the rebels and ruled through a long round of frontier wars. Victory over Austria and Russia brought the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739, recovering Belgrade and northern Serbia, the last major Ottoman territorial gain. He employed the French convert Humbaracı Ahmed Pasha (Comte de Bonneval) to reorganise the bombardier corps, an early experiment in European-style military reform.
I. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

VI. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1922).label: VI. Mehmed
VI. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1922).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1918–AD 1922] VI. Mehmed. wikipedia: 25 ramadan 1336 - 11 r1 1341. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Vahdettin took the throne as the empire collapsed, signing the Armistice of Mudros and presiding over an Istanbul occupied by Allied troops. His government accepted the punitive Treaty of Sèvres, which pushed Turkish nationalists in Anatolia to rally behind Mustafa Kemal and fight their own war of independence. When the nationalists won, the Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate; Mehmed left aboard a British warship, ending more than six centuries of Ottoman rule.
VI. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1922).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1617–AD 1618).label: I. Mustafa
I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1617–AD 1618).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1617–AD 1618] I. Mustafa. first reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

A brother of Ahmed I who had spent his life confined in the palace and was widely regarded as mentally unfit, he was enthroned by court factions in place of a direct heir.
