His accession broke the rule of father-to-son succession and established succession by seniority within the dynasty. Deposed after a few months, he was briefly restored in 1622 before being set aside for good.
I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1617–AD 1618).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1622–AD 1623).label: I. Mustafa
I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1622–AD 1623).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1622–AD 1623] I. Mustafa. second reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

A brother of Ahmed I who had spent his life confined in the palace and was widely regarded as mentally unfit, he was enthroned by court factions in place of a direct heir. His accession broke the rule of father-to-son succession and established succession by seniority within the dynasty. Deposed after a few months, he was briefly restored in 1622 before being set aside for good.
I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1622–AD 1623).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789).label: I. Abdülhamid
I. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1774–AD 1789] I. Abdülhamid. wikipedia: 8 dh-q 1187 - 10 racab 1203. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He came to the throne days before the humiliating Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca gave Russia influence over Ottoman Orthodox subjects and opened the Black Sea. Russia annexed the Crimea in 1783, and his attempt to reverse the losses led to another disastrous war in 1787. He backed cautious modernisation of the navy, artillery and engineering schools, laying groundwork for the later reform programmes.
I. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

Abdülaziz (Turkey, AD 1861–AD 1876).label: Abdülaziz
Abdülaziz (Turkey, AD 1861–AD 1876).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1861–AD 1876] Abdülaziz. wikipedia: 16 d-h 1277 - 6 j1 1293. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Naval expansion, railways and a state visit to Paris and London marked an outward-looking reign, funded by European loans that ended in default. Financial collapse and Balkan revolts brought his overthrow by reforming ministers.
Abdülaziz (Turkey, AD 1861–AD 1876).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

IV. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1807–AD 1808).label: IV. Mustafa
IV. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1807–AD 1808).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1807–AD 1808] IV. Mustafa. wikipedia: 21 r1 1222 - 4 j2 1223. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mustafa IV owed his brief reign to a janissary revolt that overthrew his cousin Selim III and destroyed the New Order army Selim had built. When reformist troops marched on Istanbul to restore Selim, Mustafa had him killed, but was deposed anyway; the survivor of the purge, Mahmud II, took the throne and later executed him.
IV. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1807–AD 1808).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691).label: II. Süleyman
II. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1687–AD 1691] II. Süleyman. wikipedia: 2 m 1099 - 25 ramadan 1102. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Süleyman II was pulled out of decades of confinement in the palace to replace his deposed brother at the low point of the war against the Holy League. Belgrade had fallen, mutinous troops filled the capital, and the treasury was empty; his grand vizier Fazıl Mustafa Pasha restored discipline, reformed taxation and retook Belgrade in 1690. The sultan died the following year with the war still unresolved.
II. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

IV. Murad (Turkey, AD 1623–AD 1640).label: IV. Murad
IV. Murad (Turkey, AD 1623–AD 1640).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1623–AD 1640] IV. Murad. wikipedia: 15 dh-q 1032 - 15/16 shawwal 1049. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad IV seized real power in his twenties and used terror to restore it, executing officials, banning tobacco, coffee and alcohol, and reportedly prowling Istanbul in disguise to catch offenders. He led campaigns in person, retaking Baghdad from Safavid Persia in 1638. The Treaty of Zuhab that followed fixed an Ottoman-Persian border that has largely survived as the Iraq-Iran frontier.
IV. Murad (Turkey, AD 1623–AD 1640).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1444–AD 1446).label: II. Mehmed
II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1444–AD 1446).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1444–AD 1446] II. Mehmed. first reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed II's first reign began as a boy of twelve, when his father abdicated in his favour. A crusading army under the king of Poland-Hungary promptly invaded, and although it was crushed at Varna in 1444, factional strife and a Janissary mutiny in the capital forced the child sultan aside and brought Murad II back. The humiliation shaped Mehmed's later determination to rule absolutely — and to take Constantinople.
II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1444–AD 1446).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

V. Murad (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1876).label: V. Murad
V. Murad (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1876).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1876–AD 1876] V. Murad. wikipedia: 6 j1 1293 - 10 sha'ban 1293. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

One of the shortest reigns in Ottoman history: installed by reformist ministers who had deposed his uncle Abdülaziz, Murad suffered a mental breakdown within weeks and was removed after 93 days. His fall brought Abdülhamid II to the throne, whose long autocracy shaped the empire's final decades. Murad spent the rest of his life confined in the Çırağan Palace, a focus of plots that never came to anything.
V. Murad (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1876).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

III. Murad (Turkey, AD 1574–AD 1595).label: III. Murad
III. Murad (Turkey, AD 1574–AD 1595).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1574–AD 1595] III. Murad. wikipedia: 8 ramadan 982 - 5 j1 1003. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad III ruled from the palace, never leaving Istanbul, while his mother Nurbanu, his wife Safiye and a shifting cast of viziers competed for influence — the period later Ottomans called the 'sultanate of women'. A long, expensive war with Safavid Iran gained Caucasian territory that was soon lost, and in 1593 the Long War with Austria began. Currency debasement, inflation and the sale of offices strained the empire's finances, though the court also produced some of the finest Ottoman illustrated manuscripts.
III. Murad (Turkey, AD 1574–AD 1595).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1389–AD 1402).label: I. Bayezid
I. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1389–AD 1402).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1389–AD 1402] I. Bayezid. wikipedia: 19 j2 791 - 19 dh 804. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Nicknamed 'the Thunderbolt' for the speed of his campaigns, he absorbed the Anatolian beyliks, pressed deep into the Balkans and blockaded Constantinople, crushing a Western crusade at Nicopolis in 1396. His dispossession of the Turkish emirs drove them to Timur, who destroyed his army at Ankara in 1402 and took him prisoner. His death in captivity plunged the empire into an eleven-year civil war among his sons.
I. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1389–AD 1402).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1691–AD 1695).label: II. Ahmed
II. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1691–AD 1695).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1691–AD 1695] II. Ahmed. wikipedia: 25 ramadan 1102 - 21 j2 1106. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Ahmed II inherited the Ottoman half of the Great Turkish War against the Habsburg-led Holy League and lost ground almost throughout. His ablest minister, the grand vizier Fazıl Mustafa Pasha, was killed at the battle of Slankamen in 1691, and the empire slid toward the defeats that ended in the Treaty of Karlowitz. A short, unlucky reign in which the Ottoman state was clearly on the defensive in Europe for the first time.
II. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1691–AD 1695).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1603–AD 1617).label: I. Ahmed
I. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1603–AD 1617).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1603–AD 1617] I. Ahmed. wikipedia: 17 racab 1012 - 23 dh-q 1026. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He signed the Treaty of Zsitvatorok, which for the first time acknowledged the Habsburg ruler as an equal rather than a tributary, and struggled with Celali revolts across Anatolia and renewed war with Safavid Iran. He abandoned the custom of executing royal brothers, replacing it with confinement and eventual succession by seniority, a change that reshaped Ottoman dynastic politics. His great monument is the Sultan Ahmed (Blue) Mosque facing Hagia Sophia.
I. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1603–AD 1617).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1446–AD 1451).label: II. Murad
II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1446–AD 1451).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1446–AD 1451] II. Murad. second reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad II returned to the throne to steady an empire shaken by crusade and by the failure of his boy-successor. He beat John Hunyadi at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448, secured the Balkan frontier and left his son a consolidated state, a disciplined army and a treasury capable of the siege that followed. He was also a notable patron of Turkish letters and of the mosques of Edirne and Bursa.
II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1446–AD 1451).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

İbrahim (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1648).label: İbrahim
İbrahim (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1648).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1640–AD 1648] İbrahim. wikipedia: 16 shawwal 1049 - 18 racab 1058. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

A sultan who came to the throne as the last surviving male of the Ottoman line, having spent his youth confined in the palace. His reign is remembered for extravagance, erratic favouritism and the grip of court factions, and for launching the long war against Venice over Crete in 1645. Janissaries and jurists deposed and strangled him in 1648, putting his six-year-old son Mehmed IV on the throne.
İbrahim (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1648).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

III. Osman (Turkey, AD 1754–AD 1757).label: III. Osman
III. Osman (Turkey, AD 1754–AD 1757).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1754–AD 1757] III. Osman. wikipedia: 27 safar 1168 - 15/16 safar 1171. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Osman III reached the throne after fifty years shut up in the palace's kafes, and the isolation showed: contemporaries described an irritable, eccentric ruler who disliked music and women's presence and changed his grand viziers constantly. His brief reign is remembered mainly for repeated great fires in Istanbul and for the completion of the baroque Nuruosmaniye Mosque begun by his brother.
III. Osman (Turkey, AD 1754–AD 1757).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Orhan (Turkey, AD 1324–AD 1360).label: I. Orhan
I. Orhan (Turkey, AD 1324–AD 1360).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1324–AD 1360] I. Orhan. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Under him the small frontier principality became a state: Bursa fell and became a capital, Nicaea and Nicomedia followed, and the first Ottoman silver coins and organised standing troops appeared. His alliance and marriage with the Byzantine claimant John VI Kantakouzenos brought Ottoman soldiers into Europe, and by 1354 they held Gallipoli. That foothold in Thrace opened the Balkans to permanent Ottoman conquest.
I. Orhan (Turkey, AD 1324–AD 1360).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1695–AD 1703).label: II. Mustafa
II. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1695–AD 1703).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1695–AD 1703] II. Mustafa. wikipedia: 21 j2 1106 - 9 r2 1115. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mustafa II revived the old practice of leading armies in person, with disastrous results: the Habsburg commander Prince Eugene destroyed his army at Zenta in 1697. The resulting Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 handed Hungary and Transylvania to Austria — the first time the Ottomans ceded large territories by negotiation, and a turning point in their relations with Europe. He withdrew to Edirne, left government to his old tutor the şeyhülislam, and was deposed by a revolt of soldiers and clerics in 1703.
II. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1695–AD 1703).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Osman (Turkey, AD 1281–AD 1324).label: I. Osman
I. Osman (Turkey, AD 1281–AD 1324).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1281–AD 1324] I. Osman. 680-724 Hijri. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The warrior chief whose small band in the Byzantine borderlands of northwest Anatolia gave its name to the Ottoman dynasty. His defeat of a Byzantine force at Bapheus in 1302 drew ghazi fighters and nomads to his banner and began the slow strangulation of Bursa. From these obscure beginnings grew an empire that would last six centuries; later chroniclers wrapped his career in the legend of a prophetic dream.
I. Osman (Turkey, AD 1281–AD 1324).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1808–AD 1839).label: II. Mahmud
II. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1808–AD 1839).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1808–AD 1839] II. Mahmud. wikipedia: 4 j2 1223 - 18 r2 1255. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mahmud II broke the Janissary corps in 1826 in the bloody purge known as the Auspicious Incident, removing the obstacle that had destroyed earlier reformers, and rebuilt the army, bureaucracy and taxation on European lines. He also introduced the fez and frock coat, opened the first Ottoman newspaper and sent students abroad. His reign nonetheless lost Greece, saw Algeria taken by France, and nearly ended in defeat by his own governor of Egypt, Mehmed Ali; the centralising groundwork he laid produced the Tanzimat reforms announced months after his death.
II. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1808–AD 1839).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Selim (Turkey, AD 1566–AD 1574).label: II. Selim
II. Selim (Turkey, AD 1566–AD 1574).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1566–AD 1574] II. Selim. wikipedia: 14 r1 974 - 7 ramadan 982. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Selim II left the running of the empire largely to his grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, and the machine of state worked well enough without him. His reign brought the conquest of Cyprus and the crushing naval defeat at Lepanto in 1571 — after which the Ottoman fleet was rebuilt within a year — and the Selimiye Mosque at Edirne, which the architect Sinan regarded as his masterpiece. He is remembered by the unkind nickname 'the Sot' and as the first sultan who neither campaigned nor governed personally.
II. Selim (Turkey, AD 1566–AD 1574).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Selim (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1520).label: I. Selim
I. Selim (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1520).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1512–AD 1520] I. Selim. wikipedia: 8 safar 918 - 8 shawwal 926. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

In eight years he doubled the size of the empire, crushing the Safavid Shah Ismail's cavalry with firearms at Chaldiran and then overthrowing the Mamluk sultanate to take Syria, Egypt and the Hejaz. Custody of Mecca and Medina gave the Ottoman sultans leadership of the Sunni world and control of the Red Sea and eastern trade routes. Known as 'the Grim' for his purges, he left his son Süleyman the wealthiest state in the region.
I. Selim (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1520).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1451–AD 1481).label: II. Mehmed
II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1451–AD 1481).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1451–AD 1481] II. Mehmed. second reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed II's first reign began as a boy of twelve, when his father abdicated in his favour. A crusading army under the king of Poland-Hungary promptly invaded, and although it was crushed at Varna in 1444, factional strife and a Janissary mutiny in the capital forced the child sultan aside and brought Murad II back. The humiliation shaped Mehmed's later determination to rule absolutely — and to take Constantinople.
II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1451–AD 1481).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

III. Selim (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807).label: III. Selim
III. Selim (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1789–AD 1807] III. Selim. wikipedia: 11 racab 1203 - 21 r1 1222. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Selim III created the Nizam-ı Cedid, the 'New Order' — a European-style trained and uniformed army with its own tax fund — alongside new military schools, permanent embassies in European capitals and reforms of the fleet. His reign coincided with the French Revolution's shockwaves, Napoleon's invasion of Egypt and Serbian revolt. In 1807 a rebellion of auxiliary troops and Janissaries overthrew him; he was murdered the following year, but his programme was resumed by his cousin Mahmud II.
III. Selim (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

IV. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687).label: IV. Mehmed
IV. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1648–AD 1687] IV. Mehmed. wikipedia: 18 racab 1058 - 2 m 1099. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Enthroned as a child during a palace crisis, Mehmed IV left government largely to the Köprülü grand viziers, who restored discipline and finances and made this a last age of Ottoman expansion — Crete taken from Venice, gains in Ukraine and Hungary. His own passion was hunting, which earned him the nickname Avcı. The catastrophic failure before Vienna in 1683 and the losses that followed cost him his throne in 1687.
IV. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1839–AD 1861).label: Abdülmecid
Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1839–AD 1861).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1839–AD 1861] Abdülmecid. wikipedia: 18 r2 1255 - 16 dh 1277. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The Tanzimat era of decrees promising legal equality, a reformed bureaucracy and a modern conscript army. The Crimean War drew the empire into the European alliance system, while Dolmabahçe Palace and new ministries in Istanbul showed the westward turn in taste and government.
Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1839–AD 1861).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

I. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1403–AD 1421).label: I. Mehmed
I. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1403–AD 1421).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1403–AD 1421] I. Mehmed. at first in Anatolia only, after 816/1413 in Rumeli also. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He won the civil war that followed his father's capture by Timur, defeating his brothers to reunite the shattered Ottoman state from Edirne and Bursa. He rebuilt the army and administration, put down the radical religious revolt of Şeyh Bedreddin, and kept the peace with Byzantium and Venice while consolidating Anatolia. Contemporaries called him the second founder of the empire; his tiled Green Mosque and tomb at Bursa date from his reign.
I. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1403–AD 1421).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

V. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1909–AD 1918).label: V. Mehmed
V. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1909–AD 1918).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1909–AD 1918] V. Mehmed. wikipedia: 6 r2 1327 - 24 ramadan 1336. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed Reşad came to the throne after the Young Turks deposed his brother Abdülhamid II, and reigned as a constitutional figurehead while the Committee of Union and Progress ran the state. Under him the empire lost Libya and nearly all its Balkan territory, then entered the First World War alongside Germany; his proclamation of jihad in 1914 largely failed to rouse Muslims under Allied rule. The Armenian genocide and the defence of Gallipoli both fell within his reign. He died months before the armistice that dismantled the empire.
V. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1909–AD 1918).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Osman (Turkey, AD 1618–AD 1622).label: II. Osman
II. Osman (Turkey, AD 1618–AD 1622).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1618–AD 1622] II. Osman. wikipedia: 21 r1 1027 - 8 racab 1031. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Known as Genç Osman, the Young Osman, he took the throne as a teenager and returned from an inconclusive campaign against Poland at Khotyn convinced that the Janissaries were useless and corrupt. His plan to raise a new army in Anatolia and, allegedly, to move the capital leaked out; the Janissaries rose, imprisoned him in the Yedikule fortress and strangled him. It was the first killing of a reigning Ottoman sultan by his own soldiers, and it made the corps a standing threat to every reformer for the next two centuries.
II. Osman (Turkey, AD 1618–AD 1622).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512).label: II. Bayezid
II. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1481–AD 1512] II. Bayezid. wikipedia: 20 r1 886 - 8 safar 918. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Bayezid II spent his early years fighting off his brother Cem, whose flight to Christian Europe made him a hostage-pawn of popes and kings. He consolidated his father's conquests rather than expanding, rebuilt Istanbul after the 1509 earthquake, invested heavily in the navy, and sent ships to carry Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 to Ottoman lands. He was forced to abdicate by his son Selim I, backed by the Janissaries, and died shortly afterwards.
II. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

III. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603).label: III. Mehmed
III. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1595–AD 1603] III. Mehmed. wikipedia: 16 j1 1003 - 16 or 17 rajab 1012. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed III began his reign by having nineteen of his brothers executed, the largest and last of the great Ottoman fratricides. He was the final sultan to command an army in the field, winning at Mezőkeresztes in 1596 during the long, grinding war with the Habsburgs. Behind the front, Anatolia was convulsed by the Celali rebellions of unpaid soldiers and displaced peasants, and real power at court passed to his mother, the valide sultan Safiye.
III. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1922–AD 1924).label: Abdülmecid
Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1922–AD 1924).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1922–AD 1924] Abdülmecid. as Caliph only. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The Tanzimat era of decrees promising legal equality, a reformed bureaucracy and a modern conscript army. The Crimean War drew the empire into the European alliance system, while Dolmabahçe Palace and new ministries in Istanbul showed the westward turn in taste and government.
Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1922–AD 1924).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1909).label: II. Abdülhamid
II. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1909).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1876–AD 1909] II. Abdülhamid. wikipedia: 10 sha'ban 1293 - 6 r2 1327. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Abdülhamid II came to the throne amid bankruptcy and revolt, allowed a constitution and parliament for barely a year, then shelved both and ruled for three decades through a palace bureaucracy, an extensive spy network and strict press censorship. He also modernised aggressively — telegraph lines, schools, the Hejaz Railway — and cultivated his role as caliph to appeal to Muslims beyond his borders. His reign saw the loss of the Balkans and Cyprus, the massacres of Armenians in the 1890s, and finally the Young Turk revolution of 1908, which restored the constitution and deposed him the next year.
II. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1909).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

III. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1757–AD 1774).label: III. Mustafa
III. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1757–AD 1774).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1757–AD 1774] III. Mustafa. wikipedia: 16 safar 1171 - 8 dh-q 1187. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mustafa III tried to rebuild Ottoman finances and modernise the artillery and navy with European advisers such as the Hungarian-French Baron de Tott, founding schools of mathematics and gunnery. He also rebuilt Istanbul after the earthquake of 1766 and raised the Laleli Mosque. Against his own better judgement he was pushed into war with Catherine the Great's Russia in 1768; the war went catastrophically, and he died before the punishing peace of Küçük Kaynarca.
III. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1757–AD 1774).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1421–AD 1444).label: II. Murad
II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1421–AD 1444).prose:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1421–AD 1444] II. Murad. first reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad II returned to the throne to steady an empire shaken by crusade and by the failure of his boy-successor. He beat John Hunyadi at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448, secured the Balkan frontier and left his son a consolidated state, a disciplined army and a treasury capable of the siege that followed. He was also a notable patron of Turkish letters and of the mosques of Edirne and Bursa.
II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1421–AD 1444).source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

Fase III (Sicily, 499 BC–399 BC).label: Fase III
Fase III (Sicily, 499 BC–399 BC).prose: [Sicily, 499 BC–399 BC] Fase III. This period only applies to the indigenous necropolis of Monte Casasia in Sicily. The end date is provided by the assumption that the site was destroyed by the Carthaginians in 405 B.C. Period definition from Monte Casasia (Ragusa) : campagne di scavo 1966, 1972-73 nella necropoli indigena — Frasca, Massimo., 1996.
Fase III (Sicily, 499 BC–399 BC).source: Monte Casasia (Ragusa) : campagne di scavo 1966, 1972-73 nella necropoli indigena

Period of the American and French Revolu.node: Period of the American and French Revolutions (United States, AD 1718–AD 1815)
Period of the American and French Revolu.label: Period of the American and French Revolutions
Period of the American and French Revolu.prose:
[America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1718–AD 1815] Period of the American and French Revolutions. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Portugal, Spain, United States. "From the Death of Charles XII of Sweden to the Battle of Waterloo, A.D. 1718-1815."
"America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. The World, Elsewhere" pages 134-145. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

An age when the idea that governments derive authority from the governed moved from pamphlets to practice: British colonies in North America broke away and wrote a federal constitution, and France destroyed its monarchy and aristocratic order. Slave rebellion in Haiti produced the first independent Black republic, and Napoleon's wars carried the new legal and administrative models across Europe. The same decades saw steam engines, factories and the first stirrings of industrial society.
Period of the American and French Revolu.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Period of the New Western Empire (France.node: Period of the New Western Empire (France, AD 800–AD 1066)
Period of the New Western Empire (France.label: Period of the New Western Empire
Period of the New Western Empire (France.prose:
[New Western Empire/France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England/ England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere, AD 800–AD 1066] Period of the New Western Empire. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Scotland, Spain. "From the Crowning of Charlemagne at Rome to the Battle of Hastings, A.D. 800-1066" page 47
"New Western Empire/France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England/ England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere" pages 74-77. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Charlemagne's coronation in Rome revived the idea of a Western emperor and briefly united most of Latin Christendom under Frankish rule, with a court-driven revival of learning, script and church reform. The empire was divided among his heirs at Verdun and then battered by Viking, Magyar and Saracen raids, and defence devolved onto local counts and castles – the roots of feudal France. By the close of the period the Capetians held a shrunken royal title and Normandy's dukes were strong enough to conquer England.
Period of the New Western Empire (France.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss.node: Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss (France, AD 1299–AD 1453)
Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss.label: Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss
Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss.prose:
[France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1299–AD 1453] Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Scotland, Spain. "From the Founding of the Turkish Empire to the Taking of Constantinople, A.D. 1299-1453." page 47
"France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere" pages 102-111. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

An older textbook label for the late Middle Ages: plague and the Hundred Years' War tore through France and England, the papacy split between rival claimants, and reformers like Wyclif and Hus attacked church wealth and doctrine a century before Luther. In the east Timur's armies shattered empires from Delhi to Anatolia, and the age closed with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople and the first printing with movable type.
Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Persian Period (Italy, 587 BC–329 BC).label: Persian Period
Persian Period (Italy, 587 BC–329 BC).prose:
[Asia. Africa. Greece. Rome, Etc/Rome and Italy, 587 BC–329 BC] Persian Period. "From Captivity, to Alexander the Great, B.C. 588-330.....258 years.....The Persian Period." page 2.
"Asia. Africa. Greece. Rome, Etc.", pages 20-23. "Asia. Africa. Greece. Rome and Italy.", pages 18-19, 24-25. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.
Persian Period (Italy, 587 BC–329 BC).source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Period of the Reformation; Discoveries a.node: Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions (Spain, AD 1453–AD 1598)
Period of the Reformation; Discoveries a.label: Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions
Period of the Reformation; Discoveries a.prose:
[England. Scotland. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1453–AD 1598] Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions. Spatial coverage: Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain. "From the Taking of Constantinople to the Edict of Nantes, A.D. 1453-1598} Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions." page 47
"England. Scotland. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere" pages 112-121. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Printing, ocean navigation and gunpowder reshaped Europe just as Spain became its dominant power: Granada fell, Columbus crossed the Atlantic, and American silver funded Habsburg armies from Italy to the Netherlands. Luther's challenge split Western Christianity, and Spain answered with the Council of Trent, the Inquisition and the Armada. Visitors can trace how conquest, bullion and religious war together made and then overstretched a global empire.
Period of the Reformation; Discoveries a.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Period of the English Commonwealth and W.node: Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV (Spain, AD 1598–AD 1718)
Period of the English Commonwealth and W.label: Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV
Period of the English Commonwealth and W.prose:
[America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1598–AD 1718] Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV. Spatial coverage: Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain. "From the Edict of Nantes to the Death of Charles XII of Sweden, A.D. 1598-1718." page 47
"America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere" pages 122-133. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Spain slid from superpower to junior partner. The later Habsburg kings, propped up by American silver and ruinous credit, lost the northern Netherlands and Portugal, saw Catalonia revolt, and watched French armies take the initiative under Louis XIV. When Charles II died childless, the resulting War of the Spanish Succession installed a Bourbon dynasty and stripped away the Italian and Netherlandish possessions, leaving a smaller, more centrally governed Spain.
Period of the English Commonwealth and W.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Period of The Crusades (France, AD 1066–.label: Period of The Crusades
Period of The Crusades (France, AD 1066–.prose:
[France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1066–AD 1299] Period of The Crusades. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Scotland, Spain. "From the Battle of Hastings to the Founding of the Turkish Empire, A.D. 1066-1299." page 47.
"France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere" pages 78-101. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Two centuries in which Latin Christendom went on the offensive - into Syria and Palestine, into Muslim Spain, into the Baltic - and came home with new tastes, texts and banking arrangements. The same centuries saw the Norman Conquest of England, the growth of towns and universities, Gothic cathedral building, and the rise of strong monarchies in France and England. By the end the crusader states were gone but Europe was far richer and better connected than before.
Period of The Crusades (France, AD 1066–.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC).label: Middle Kingdom
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC] Middle Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Troy III-V (Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC).label: Troy III-V
Troy III-V (Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC).prose:
[Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC] Troy III-V. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Three modest phases in which Troy was a small, ordinary Anatolian town rather than a rich stronghold. Houses were cramped, imports scarce and the architecture unambitious, yet occupation was continuous and the pottery shows unbroken local tradition. These quiet centuries separate the treasure-filled Early Bronze Age citadel from the grand walled city that followed.
Troy III-V (Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Old Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1574 BC–139.label: Old Hittite Kingdom
Old Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1574 BC–139.prose:
[Anatolia, 1574 BC–1399 BC] Old Hittite Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The earliest phase of Hittite power, when kings ruling from Hattusa welded central Anatolian towns into a single state and raided as far as Aleppo and Babylon. Their surviving laws, land grants and royal proclamations, written in cuneiform on clay, record an Indo-European language and a court perpetually troubled by assassination and disputed succession. The kingdom contracted sharply afterwards before re-emerging as the empire that would fight Egypt at Kadesh.
Old Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1574 BC–139.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Predynastic (Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC).label: Predynastic
Predynastic (Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC] Predynastic. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Farming villages along the Nile grew into competing chiefdoms with cemeteries, craft workshops and long-distance trade in lapis, cedar and gold. Naqada-culture potters, flint-knappers and stone-vase makers reached extraordinary technical heights, and the imagery on their palettes and painted jars — kings smiting enemies, sacred boats, animal standards — is already the visual language of pharaonic Egypt. It ends with the unification of the Nile Valley under a single ruler.
Predynastic (Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Neolithic (Syria, 8549 BC–4999 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Syria, 8549 BC–4999 BC).prose:
[Near East, 8549 BC–4999 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, West Bank. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.
Neolithic (Syria, 8549 BC–4999 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Achaemenids (Iran, 549 BC–329 BC).label: Achaemenids
Achaemenids (Iran, 549 BC–329 BC).prose:
[Persia, 549 BC–329 BC] Achaemenids. Gates discusses only the Achaemenids in Persia proper in this chapter. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The dynasty founded by Cyrus the Great that ruled from the Aegean to the Indus, tolerating local gods and customs while extracting tribute through satraps. Its kings left carved cliff reliefs at Bisitun and Naqsh-e Rostam and vast terraced palaces at Persepolis, whose burnt ruins mark Alexander's conquest. Greek writers such as Herodotus defined 'Persia' for the West through their wars with these rulers.
Achaemenids (Iran, 549 BC–329 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Middle Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1399 BC–.label: Middle Hittite Kingdom
Middle Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1399 BC–.prose:
[Anatolia, 1399 BC–1349 BC] Middle Hittite Kingdom. Spatial coverage: Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

A period of crisis in which enemies closed in from every direction — Kaska tribes burned Hattusa itself — and the kingdom nearly disappeared. Tudhaliya III rebuilt from a temporary capital and passed a restored army to his son Suppiluliuma I, who turned survival into conquest. The near-collapse and the recovery that followed are documented in unusually vivid royal annals and prayers.
Middle Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1399 BC–.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Late Period (Egypt, 759 BC–331 BC).label: Late Period
Late Period (Egypt, 759 BC–331 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 759 BC–331 BC] Late Period. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

Late Classical (Greece, 399 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Greece, 399 BC–322 BC] Late Classical. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. The chapter associated with this term covers sites in both Greece and Turkey, although map of conquests of Alexander also covers the Levant, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan, and parts of India and Pakistan. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

In the Greek cities of the south, this was the era of grand Apulian and Lucanian red-figure vases, tomb painting, and lavish burials, even as Oscan and Lucanian peoples took over cities like Poseidonia. Central Italy saw Etruscan power ebb and Rome fight its way through the Latin and Samnite wars, absorbing neighbours and building the first roads and aqueducts. By the end of the century the peninsula's future belonged to Rome rather than to the Greek or Etruscan cities.

Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1474 BC–1224 BC.label: Late Cypriot II
Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1474 BC–1224 BC.prose:
[Cyprus, 1474 BC–1224 BC] Late Cypriot II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The peak of Bronze Age Cyprus. Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke functioned as cosmopolitan port towns handling copper, and the island — almost certainly the 'Alashiya' whose kings corresponded with the pharaoh in the Amarna letters — dealt with Egypt and the Hittites as a power in its own right. Tombs yield Mycenaean pictorial kraters, ivory, faience and gold, and clay tablets carry the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script.

Roman Republic (Lazio, 508 BC–26 BC).label: Roman Republic
Roman Republic (Lazio, 508 BC–26 BC).prose:
[Rome, 508 BC–26 BC] Roman Republic. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After expelling its kings, Rome developed a government of elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and citizen assemblies, and an army of property-owning citizens. It absorbed Italy, destroyed Carthage and took the Greek east, becoming the dominant Mediterranean power within two centuries. The wealth and slaves that flooded in wrecked the old order, producing land crises, political violence and the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Caesar. Its institutions and its collapse became the standard reference point for later republics.
Roman Republic (Lazio, 508 BC–26 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

[Troy, 1259 BC–1189 BC] Troy VIIb 1. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Survivors rebuilt among the burnt ruins, reusing walls and keeping the old pottery styles, so life on the mound continued rather than stopping. Alongside the familiar wares appear crude handmade pots of a type foreign to Anatolia, hinting at newcomers arriving in the unsettled years after the Bronze Age collapse.

Post-Palatial (Crete, 1424 BC–1049 BC).label: Post-Palatial
Post-Palatial (Crete, 1424 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1424 BC–1049 BC] Post-Palatial. "(= Late Minoan IIIA, B, and C)". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the destruction of Knossos, the palace system that had administered Crete for centuries was gone, and with it the centralised storage, seal-based bureaucracy and Linear B records. Settlement shifted toward smaller centres and, increasingly, to defensible upland sites such as Karfi, while burial customs, dress and pottery drew closer to mainland Mycenaean styles. Trade continued but on a reduced scale, and the period slides into the Aegean's early Iron Age.

Hittite Empire (Turkey, 1349 BC–1199 BC).label: Hittite Empire
Hittite Empire (Turkey, 1349 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Anatolia, 1349 BC–1199 BC] Hittite Empire. Spatial coverage: Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

At its height the Hittite kingdom fought Egypt and Assyria for control of Syria, sacked and absorbed the kingdom of Mitanni, and clashed with Ramesses II at Kadesh before signing the earliest surviving peace treaty between great powers. Vassal kings across Anatolia and the Levant were bound by written oaths, and the capital Hattusa was rebuilt on a monumental scale. The whole structure collapsed around 1200 BC, the city burned and abandoned, leaving only small successor states in the southeast.
Hittite Empire (Turkey, 1349 BC–1199 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Early Classical (Greece, 479 BC–449 BC).label: Early Classical
Early Classical (Greece, 479 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Greece, 479 BC–449 BC] Early Classical. Gates concentrates on Athens, so Greece is most appropriate coverage. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The generation after the defeat of Persia at Plataea and Mycale, when Athens built the Delian League and turned it toward empire. In art it is the 'Severe Style': figures like the Delphi Charioteer and the Riace bronzes abandoned the archaic smile for calm, weighted naturalism. The confidence and tribute money of these decades made the Parthenon and the high classical age possible.
Early Classical (Greece, 479 BC–449 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Old Palace (Protopalatial) (Crete, 1929.prose:
[Crete, 1929 BC–1699 BC] Old Palace (Protopalatial). "(= Middle Minoan IB)". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first great palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia rose as centres of storage, craft production and ritual, surrounded by growing towns. Cretan scribes began keeping records in Cretan Hieroglyphic and Linear A, and potters produced eggshell-thin Kamares ware painted in white, red and orange. Earthquakes or conflict levelled these palaces, but they were promptly rebuilt on a grander scale.

Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Greece, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates notes "to the Battle of Actium". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Troy I (Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC).label: Troy I
Troy I (Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC).prose:
[Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC] Troy I. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first fortified settlement on the mound of Hisarlık: a small walled citadel of long, narrow megaron houses overlooking the entrance to the Dardanelles. Its people used handmade dark burnished pottery and worked copper, living off farming, fishing and the traffic passing through the straits. Ten building phases show the place was rebuilt again and again on the same spot, beginning the deep layer-cake of ruins Schliemann later dug through.
Troy I (Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Classical (Greece, 478 BC–322 BC).label: Classical
Classical (Greece, 478 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Greece, 478 BC–322 BC] Classical. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates notes "to the death of Alexander the Great". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.
Classical (Greece, 478 BC–322 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

[Troy, 1189 BC–1099 BC] Troy VIIb 2. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

A distinctive knobbed pottery, Buckelkeramik, with parallels in the Balkans, becomes common, suggesting a new population settling on the old citadel. The town was poor and provincial, its great walls now sheltering modest houses, and after its end the site was largely deserted for centuries before Greek settlers returned.

Halaf and Ubaid (Syria, 4999 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Near East, 4999 BC–3499 BC] Halaf and Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, West Bank. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The distinctive painted Halaf wares gave way to plainer, mass-produced Ubaid pottery spreading north from southern Mesopotamia, a sign of village societies being drawn into a much wider cultural orbit. Settlements grew larger, some with tripartite houses and small temples rebuilt on the same spot for generations, and irrigation and ploughing supported bigger surpluses. These centuries set the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.

Harappan, or Mature (Pakistan, 2599 BC–1.label: Harappan, or Mature
Harappan, or Mature (Pakistan, 2599 BC–1.prose:
[Indus Valley, 2599 BC–1899 BC] Harappan, or Mature. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. Indus Valley is defined as "a region now situated in modern Pakistan and north-west India". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The high point of the Indus civilisation, when planned cities of baked brick with drains, granaries and citadels spread from the Arabian Sea to the foothills of the Himalaya. Craftsmen produced carnelian beads, bronze figurines and steatite seals inscribed with a script no one can read; standardised weights and bricks imply strong shared conventions rather than visible kings. Trade reached Mesopotamia by sea before the cities were gradually abandoned.

Akkadian (Iraq, 2349 BC–2149 BC).label: Akkadian
Akkadian (Iraq, 2349 BC–2149 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2349 BC–2149 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.
Akkadian (Iraq, 2349 BC–2149 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Geometric
Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates discusses Greek cities that are now in the territory of Turkey, although he does not refer to Anatolia specifically. Greece emerging from the post-Mycenaean dark age, its pottery covered in meanders, zigzags and banded panels, later giving way to silhouetted horses, chariots and mourners on the huge Dipylon grave markers of Athens. Communities coalesced into the first city-states, sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filled with dedications, the Phoenician alphabet was adapted to Greek, and settlers began sailing west to Italy and Sicily. The oral traditions that became the Iliad and Odyssey took shape in these years.
Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Protoliterate (Uruk) (Iraq, 3499 BC–2899.label: Protoliterate (Uruk)
Protoliterate (Uruk) (Iraq, 3499 BC–2899.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–2899 BC] Protoliterate (Uruk). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Uruk swelled into the world's first true city, with monumental temple platforms, mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls and an administration that used cylinder seals and clay tokens to track goods. To keep the accounts, scribes pressed signs into clay — the proto-cuneiform tablets that are the earliest writing known. Uruk-style material spread far up the Euphrates and into Iran, marking the first great expansion of an urban economy.

Gutian (Iraq, 2149 BC–1999 BC).label: Gutian
Gutian (Iraq, 2149 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2149 BC–1999 BC] Gutian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. According to Gates, Gutian domination of Mesopotamia was ended by Ur-Nammu, the first ruler of the Third dynasty of Ur (2100 B.C.-2000 B.C.), which contradicts the end date of 2000 BC (p. 55). Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the Akkadian empire collapsed, groups from the Zagros mountains known as the Gutians took control of parts of Babylonia, and later Mesopotamian scribes blamed them for ruin, famine and the fall of civilised order. Their actual rule is thinly documented, and southern cities such as Lagash appear to have flourished during it, which makes the 'Gutian dark age' a case study in how history is written by later winners. Their expulsion by Utu-hegal of Uruk was celebrated as a liberation and opened the way for the Third Dynasty of Ur.
Gutian (Iraq, 2149 BC–1999 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

New Palace (Neopalatial) (Crete, 1699 BC.label: New Palace (Neopalatial)
New Palace (Neopalatial) (Crete, 1699 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1699 BC–1449 BC] New Palace (Neopalatial). "(= Middle Minoan III, Late Minoan IA and B)". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Minoan Crete at its height: the palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros were rebuilt on a grand scale after earthquake destruction, surrounded by towns, villas and harbours. Frescoes of bull-leapers, dolphins and processions, fine pottery, and Linear A archives belong to these centuries, as does Cretan influence across the Aegean. The eruption of Thera and later destructions ended it, with power passing to Mycenaean Greeks at Knossos.

Troy II (Troy, 2399 BC–2099 BC).label: Troy II
Troy II (Troy, 2399 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Troy, 2399 BC–2099 BC] Troy II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The citadel grew richer, with a monumental gateway, a ramp still visible today and larger megara inside sloping stone-and-mudbrick walls. Potters adopted the fast wheel, and gold, silver and lapis jewellery was buried here — the hoard Schliemann seized and named "Priam's Treasure", though it is a thousand years older than any Homeric war. The settlement ended in a great fire, which Schliemann mistook for the sack of Homer's Troy.

Severans (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235).label: Severans
Severans (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235] Severans. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Septimius Severus won power in civil war and openly based his rule on the army, raising soldiers' pay and telling his sons to enrich the troops and ignore everyone else. His son Caracalla extended Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire in 212, a sweeping change to what it meant to be Roman. The dynasty brought African and Syrian families to the centre of imperial politics, and its collapse in 235 opened fifty years of civil war and invasion.

The height of Mycenaean expansion, with palaces functioning, chamber-tomb cemeteries filling, and standardised stirrup jars and kylikes shipped to Egypt, the Levant and Italy. Hittite records of a kingdom called Ahhiyawa probably refer to these Greeks, dealing as equals with the great powers of the Near East.

High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193).label: High Empire
High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193] High Empire. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

From Nerva to Commodus, the empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan and then settled into consolidation behind fixed frontiers like Hadrian's Wall. Cities across the provinces filled with baths, aqueducts and forums, provincials rose to the throne, and law and citizenship spread widely. The Antonine plague and Commodus's murder in 192 exposed how much depended on a single life, ushering in civil war.

Flavians (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96).label: Flavians
Flavians (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96] Flavians. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Vespasian emerged from the civil wars of 69 as the first emperor from an ordinary Italian family, restoring stability and imperial finances. His reign saw the crushing of the Jewish revolt and the sack of Jerusalem, funding the Colosseum built on the site of Nero's private lake. Titus faced the eruption of Vesuvius, and Domitian's autocratic rule ended in assassination, opening the way to the adoptive emperors.
Flavians (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

The palaces reached their fullest form, with the Lion Gate and the huge walls of Tiryns raised and Linear B scribes tallying grain, textiles, chariots and rowers. Late in the phase came fire, abandonment and hurried defensive works, ending in the destruction of every mainland palace and the loss of writing.

Second Intermediate (Egypt, 1794 BC–1549.label: Second Intermediate
Second Intermediate (Egypt, 1794 BC–1549.prose:
[Egypt, 1794 BC–1549 BC] Second Intermediate. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Central authority fragmented as a rapid succession of kings at Memphis and then Thebes lost control of the Delta, where rulers of Levantine origin - the Hyksos - established a kingdom at Avaris. Nubian Kerma took the south, so Egypt was divided three ways. The invaders' legacy was technological as much as political: the horse and chariot, composite bow and new bronze-working entered Egypt in these years and equipped the armies that later built an empire.

Troy VI (Troy, 1799 BC–1299 BC).label: Troy VI
Troy VI (Troy, 1799 BC–1299 BC).prose:
[Troy, 1799 BC–1299 BC] Troy VI. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Troy was rebuilt on a grand scale, with sloping ashlar walls, watchtowers and great gates enclosing terraced mansions — the most impressive city ever built on the mound. Mycenaean pottery, horse bones and links to the Hittite world place it in the wider Late Bronze Age network, and Hittite texts probably name it Wilusa. A geological survey found the outer town, defended by a rock-cut ditch, making the city far larger than Schliemann realised; it fell to what excavators read as an earthquake.

Etruscan rule (Lazio, 599 BC–508 BC).label: Etruscan rule
Etruscan rule (Lazio, 599 BC–508 BC).prose:
[Rome, 599 BC–508 BC] Etruscan rule. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Rome and much of Latium fell under the sway of Etruscan dynasts, a period credited with the city's first monumental building: the Cloaca Maxima, the Circus Maximus and the Capitoline temple. Latin towns absorbed Etruscan religious ritual, insignia of office and the alphabet that would become Latin script. The overthrow of the last king in 509 BC is the traditional birth date of the Roman Republic.
Etruscan rule (Lazio, 599 BC–508 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Julio-Claudians (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD.label: Julio-Claudians
Julio-Claudians (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD.prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 69] Julio-Claudians. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Rome's first imperial dynasty, ruling from Augustus's death to Nero's fall. Their reigns settled the awkward question of what an emperor actually was: a first citizen in theory, an autocrat in practice, with the army and the treasury in his hands. Conquests in Britain and along the Rhine and Danube, monumental building in the capital, and a spectacular record of family murder have kept them the most notorious rulers in Roman history.

Early Dynastic (Archaic) (Egypt, 3049 BC.prose:
[Egypt, 3049 BC–2674 BC] Early Dynastic (Archaic). Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first two dynasties, when the Nile valley was consolidated into a single kingdom governed from Memphis. Kings such as Narmer, Djer and Khasekhemwy left palace-facade tombs, ivory labels bearing the earliest Egyptian writing, and grand ceremonial palettes. The administrative and religious system built in these centuries made the pyramid age possible.

Destructions and abandonments hit the coastal towns, and the island is resettled and rebuilt in a noticeably Aegean idiom: locally made Mycenaean-style pottery, megaron-plan buildings, new sanctuaries at Kition and Enkomi. Greek-speaking newcomers appear to have arrived and stayed, laying the basis for the later Greek city-kingdoms, while Cypriot smiths became early masters of iron.

Third Intermediate (Egypt, 1069 BC–714 B.prose:
[Egypt, 1069 BC–714 BC] Third Intermediate. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the New Kingdom collapsed, Egypt split between kings ruling from the Delta and the high priests of Amun controlling Thebes. Libyan dynasties from settled military families took the throne, royal burials moved into temple precincts at Tanis, and the country fractured further into competing local rulers. Egypt's weakness invited outside powers, and the era ends with Kushite kings from Nubia asserting control over the south.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

[Greece, 1184 BC–1049 BC] Late Helladic IIIC. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Life after the palaces: no kings, no scribes, no frescoes, but surviving communities at Tiryns, Lefkandi, Perati and in the islands, some prospering briefly. Painters produced lively pictorial vases of ships and warriors, and refugees and traders kept Aegean contacts alive. A final decline led into the Protogeometric period and the Iron Age.

[Greece, 1499 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Chieftains stopped digging shaft graves and began building tholoi, great stone beehive chambers approached by long passages, a display of labour and permanence. Mycenaean goods spread through the Aegean and mainlanders took control of Knossos, where Linear B was adapted to write Greek.

Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1759 BC).label: Isin-Larsa
Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1759 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1759 BC] Isin-Larsa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Named for the two Mesopotamian cities that fought over the legacy of the fallen Ur III empire, this horizon in the east coincides with the rise of the Sukkalmah rulers of Elam, who traded, intermarried and intrigued with the kings of southern Iraq. Cuneiform contracts, cylinder seals and standardised pottery show how closely the Iranian lowlands were tied into Babylonian economic life. It ends with Hammurabi's conquests reshaping the region.

Archaic (Greece, 599 BC–478 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Greece, 599 BC–478 BC).prose:
[Greece, 599 BC–478 BC] Archaic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates notes "to the end of the Persian Wars". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Greece, 599 BC–478 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Kassite (Iraq, 1529 BC–1149 BC).label: Kassite
Kassite (Iraq, 1529 BC–1149 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1529 BC–1149 BC] Kassite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the Hittite raid that toppled Hammurabi's dynasty, Kassite kings—outsiders of uncertain origin—ruled Babylonia for close to four centuries, the longest single dynasty in Mesopotamian history. They stabilised the south, corresponded as equals with Egypt's pharaohs in the Amarna letters, built the new capital of Dur-Kurigalzu, and left the carved kudurru stones that recorded royal land grants.
Kassite (Iraq, 1529 BC–1149 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Neo-Babylonian Empire (Iraq, 611 BC–538.label: Neo-Babylonian Empire
Neo-Babylonian Empire (Iraq, 611 BC–538.prose:
[Mesopotamia, the Levant, 611 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian Empire. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

For roughly seventy years Babylon replaced Nineveh as the centre of the Near East, ruling Mesopotamia and the Levant and rebuilding its capital on a monumental scale with glazed-brick gates, ziggurat and walls that Greek visitors later listed among the world's wonders. Temple archives from Sippar, Uruk and Babylon document a busy economy of land, silver and dependent labour. Cyrus the Great entered the city in 539 BC and the empire passed intact into Persian hands.
Neo-Babylonian Empire (Iraq, 611 BC–538.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Neo-Assyrian Empire (Iraq, 999 BC–611 BC.label: Neo-Assyrian Empire
Neo-Assyrian Empire (Iraq, 999 BC–611 BC.prose:
[northern Mesopotamia or Assyria (= today's north Iraq and north-east Syria), 999 BC–611 BC] Neo-Assyrian Empire. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Assyria rebuilt itself into the largest empire the Near East had yet seen, ruling from Iran to Egypt through a machine of provinces, governors, standing armies and mass deportations of conquered populations. Its kings built colossal palaces at Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh, lined with carved stone reliefs of war, hunt and ritual, and assembled the great library of Ashurbanipal. When the empire collapsed under Median and Babylonian attack its administrative and military template passed to its successors.
