High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC).label: High Classical
High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC).prose:
[Greece, 449 BC–399 BC] High Classical. Gates concentrates on Athens, so Greece is most appropriate coverage. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The decades after the Persian wars when Athens, funded by its maritime empire, rebuilt the Acropolis and put up the Parthenon under Pheidias's direction. Sophocles and Euripides were writing for the theatre, Socrates was arguing in the agora, and sculptors worked out an idealised human figure that European art would copy for two thousand years. The same era brought the Peloponnesian War, plague, and the collapse of Athenian power in 404.
High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Troy VIIa (Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC).label: Troy VIIa
Troy VIIa (Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC).prose:
[Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC] Troy VIIa. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The earthquake-damaged city was patched up and packed with small houses, their floors sunk with huge storage jars as though a population had crowded inside the walls expecting trouble. It ended in fire, with unburied bodies and sling stones in the ruins. This is the layer most archaeologists nominate as the historical basis for Homer's Trojan War.
Troy VIIa (Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Ur III (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999 BC).label: Ur III
Ur III (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC] Ur III. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The Third Dynasty of Ur built a tightly administered state that reached across the Iranian lowlands, holding Susa and planting garrisons and governors in the Zagros foothills. Its scribes produced tens of thousands of accounting tablets recording livestock, labour and grain in obsessive detail, the densest bureaucratic archive of the ancient world. The empire fell when Elamite forces sacked Ur, an event lamented in Sumerian poetry for centuries afterwards.
Ur III (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC).label: Late Cypriot I
Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC] Late Cypriot I. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Cyprus enters the Late Bronze Age as coastal towns like Enkomi grow rich on copper, smelted inland and shipped abroad in oxhide ingots. Distinctive Base Ring and White Slip pottery begins turning up across Egypt and the Levant, evidence of an island trading network reaching far beyond its shores. Fortified sites and warrior burials suggest the wealth also brought competition and insecurity.
Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC).label: Late Minoan II
Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC] Late Minoan II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Knossos alone functioned as a palace, and its rulers were Greek-speaking Mycenaeans who kept inventories on clay tablets in Linear B — the earliest readable Greek. Burials changed too, with 'warrior graves' containing swords, helmets and boar's-tusk gear appearing around the city. Pottery turned formal and imposing in the Palace Style, adapting old Minoan motifs to a stiffer, more heraldic taste.
Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Ubaid (Iraq, 4999 BC–3499 BC).label: Ubaid
Ubaid (Iraq, 4999 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 4999 BC–3499 BC] Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first widespread village culture of southern Mesopotamia, marked by pale greenish painted pottery, mudbrick houses of tripartite plan and small temples rebuilt again and again on the same spot, most famously at Eridu. Irrigation let farmers work the dry alluvium, herds and fishing filled out the diet, and communities grew large enough to support differences in status visible in burials and buildings. Ubaid pottery and styles spread north into Syria and Anatolia and down the Gulf, setting the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.
Ubaid (Iraq, 4999 BC–3499 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

First Intermediate (Egypt, 2189 BC–2059.label: First Intermediate
First Intermediate (Egypt, 2189 BC–2059.prose:
[Egypt, 2189 BC–2059 BC] First Intermediate. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Central authority at Memphis broke down after the long reign of Pepi II, and provincial governors ruled their nomes as effectively independent lords, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Tomb art becomes rougher and more regional, but funerary texts and coffins once reserved for kings now appear for ordinary officials. Theban victory under Mentuhotep II ended the split and began the Middle Kingdom.

Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC).label: Old Kingdom
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC] Old Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC] Late Bronze Age (= Late Cypriot). Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Cyprus turned its copper into international power, exporting oxhide ingots across the eastern Mediterranean and appearing in Egyptian and Hittite records as the kingdom of Alashiya. Coastal towns like Enkomi and Kition grew into planned cities with ashlar sanctuaries, harbours and workshops, while the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script came into use. Destructions and the arrival of Aegean settlers around 1200 BC reshaped the island's language and culture.

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p0.prose:
[Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2124 BC–1999 BC).label: Neo-Sumerian
Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2124 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2124 BC–1999 BC] Neo-Sumerian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The Third Dynasty of Ur reunited southern Mesopotamia after the Akkadian collapse and ran it through an extraordinarily detailed bureaucracy that has left tens of thousands of accounting tablets. Ur-Nammu and Shulgi built the great stepped ziggurats, issued one of the earliest law collections and promoted Sumerian as a language of high culture even as Akkadian took over daily speech. The state fell to famine, Amorite pressure and an Elamite attack, but its scribal schools shaped Mesopotamian literature for a thousand years.
Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2124 BC–1999 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1529 BC).label: Old Babylonian
Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1529 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1529 BC] Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.
Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1529 BC).source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

Eastern motifs and craft techniques transformed Greek art as trade with the Levant intensified, replacing the tidy geometry of earlier pottery with animal friezes, floral scrolls, and monsters. Corinthian workshops mass-produced small scented-oil vessels for export, and metalworkers took up hammered bronze and granulation. The alphabet arrived by the same routes, making written Greek possible.

Protogeometric (Greece, 999 BC–899 BC).label: Protogeometric
Protogeometric (Greece, 999 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Greece, 999 BC–899 BC] Protogeometric. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates discusses Greek cities that are now in the territory of Turkey, although he does not refer to Anatolia specifically. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

In the aftermath of the Mycenaean collapse, potters in Athens imposed a new discipline on their work: compass-drawn concentric circles and semicircles, crisp horizontal bands, and dark glaze over the vessel's shoulders. It is the first sign of confidence returning after the palaces fell, and it coincides with the spread of iron tools and weapons. The style travelled with Aegean settlers to the coast of Asia Minor and set the pattern for Geometric art that followed.

Classical (Cypro-Classical) I (Cyprus, 4.label: Classical (Cypro-Classical) I
Classical (Cypro-Classical) I (Cyprus, 4.prose:
[Cyprus, 474 BC–399 BC] Classical (Cypro-Classical) I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cyprus remained a patchwork of city-kingdoms under Persian overlordship, torn between loyalty to the Great King and the pull of the Greek world. Evagoras of Salamis pushed Hellenizing culture and the Greek alphabet, minted fine coinage and led a long revolt against Persia before being forced back into submission. Sculpture and architecture on the island blend Greek, Levantine and Egyptian models.

Iron Age (Cyprus, 1049 BC–AD 250).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Cyprus, 1049 BC–AD 250).prose:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–AD 250] Iron Age. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Bronze Age (Cyprus, 2499 BC–1049 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Cyprus, 2499 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 2499 BC–1049 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) II (C.prose:
[Cyprus, 1799 BC–1724 BC] Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Copper production intensified and Cypriot goods began appearing more regularly in Levantine and Egyptian contexts, drawing the island into eastern Mediterranean trade. New pottery styles, notably White Painted wares, spread across regional workshops. Settlement was still village-scale, but the wealth differences visible in tomb goods hint at emerging elites.

[Cyprus, 2074 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cemeteries such as Vounous and Lapithos on the north coast fill with elaborate Red Polished vessels and modelled clay scenes of ploughing, cattle and ritual gatherings — some of the earliest pictures of everyday Cypriot life. The quantity of copper goods buried with the dead shows communities growing wealthy on metal, with differences in status becoming visible in the grave. Visitors are usually struck by the exuberance of the pottery, tubular, horned and encrusted with white-filled incision.

Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) II (Cyprus, 599.label: Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) II
Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) II (Cyprus, 599.prose:
[Cyprus, 599 BC–474 BC] Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Egyptian and then Persian overlords replaced the Assyrians, but the city-kingdoms kept minting their own coins and pursuing their own quarrels. Sculpture in soft local limestone flourished, mixing Egyptian stance with Greek drapery and Cypriot beards, and the free-field pottery style produced its famous birds and fish. The period ends in violence: most of the kingdoms joined the Ionian Revolt against Persia and were crushed at the battle of Salamis on Cyprus in 498 BC.

Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) III (Cy.node: Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) III (Cyprus, 1999 BC–1899 BC)
Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) III (Cy.label: Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) III
Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) III (Cy.prose:
[Cyprus, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) III. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Settlement pushed inland and southward, closer to the copper sources and to the ports that faced the Levant and Egypt. Cypriot copper begins to appear abroad, and imported goods appear on the island, setting up the export trade that would later make Alashiya a name known to Egyptian and Hittite kings. The period runs straight into the Middle Cypriot centuries, when fortified sites and sharper social divisions emerge.

Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) II (Cyprus,.label: Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) II
Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) II (Cyprus,.prose:
[Cyprus, 949 BC–849 BC] Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

A quieter, more prosperous stretch when Cypriot towns rebuilt trade links across the eastern Mediterranean and Phoenicians from Tyre established themselves at Kition, rebuilding its great temple. Cypriot copper again moved abroad, and Bichrome pottery with its concentric circles and friezes reached the Levant and the Aegean. The island's separate kingdoms were beginning to take the shape they would hold for centuries.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IA (Cypru.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IA (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1574 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IA (Cypru.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IA
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IA (Cypru.prose:
[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1574 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IA. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The inward-looking village world of the Middle Bronze Age gave way to new coastal settlements positioned for overseas trade, above all Enkomi near the copper routes of the east. Distinctive White Slip 'milk bowls' and Base Ring juglets began the ceramic tradition that would soon be found from Egypt to Anatolia. Copper production intensified and the island's export economy took shape.

Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) I (Cypr.node: Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) I (Cyprus, 2499 BC–2074 BC)
Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) I (Cypr.label: Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) I
Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) I (Cypr.prose:
[Cyprus, 2499 BC–2074 BC] Early Bronze Age (Early Cypriot) I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cyprus turned decisively towards its copper ores, and a distinctive island culture took shape: Red Polished pottery, cattle and the plough, and new village sites clustered near the mineral-rich foothills. Much of what survives comes from cemeteries outside the settlements, where the dead were laid in rock-cut chamber tombs with pots, jewellery and copper tools. The metal that would make Cyprus famous across the eastern Mediterranean was already being smelted here.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIB (Cyp.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIB (Cyprus, 1189 BC–1149 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIB (Cyp.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIB
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIB (Cyp.prose:
[Cyprus, 1189 BC–1149 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIB. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

A period of rebuilding and reorientation, when the great Bronze Age harbour towns were finally abandoned or shrank and new centres such as Salamis began to take their place. Potters produced Proto-White Painted ware, the direct ancestor of Iron Age Cypriot pottery, and burial customs shifted, marking the point where the island's population began to look and sound increasingly Greek.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IB (Cypru.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IB (Cyprus, 1574 BC–1474 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IB (Cypru.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IB
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IB (Cypru.prose:
[Cyprus, 1574 BC–1474 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IB. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cypriot pottery spread widely through the Levant and Egypt, and imports flowed back, marking the island's arrival as a serious trading partner. Fortified sites and rich tomb groups indicate competition among emerging elites, and copper smelting expanded around the Troodos foothills. The framework of Cypriot international trade for the next three centuries was set here.

Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) I (Cyprus, 1.label: Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) I
Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) I (Cyprus, 1.prose:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–949 BC] Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cyprus reorganised itself after the collapse of the Bronze Age palace world: many old towns were abandoned and new centres such as Salamis and Kition took their place. Greek-speaking settlers were absorbed into the island's population, chamber tombs replaced older burial forms, and iron working became routine for tools and weapons. White Painted and Bichrome wares decorated with compass-drawn circles and bands define the pottery of these generations.

Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) III (.node: Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) III (Cyprus, 1724 BC–1649 BC)
Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) III (.label: Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) III
Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) III (.prose:
[Cyprus, 1724 BC–1649 BC] Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) III. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Fortified sites appear across the island, including strongholds inland and on the northern coast, suggesting insecurity or competition over the copper trade. Coastal towns such as Enkomi began to take shape as gateways to overseas markets. This unsettled phase leads directly into the prosperous, cosmopolitan Late Cypriot period when Alashiya's copper was famous from Egypt to Anatolia.

Hellenistic II (Cyprus, 149 BC–49 BC).label: Hellenistic II
Hellenistic II (Cyprus, 149 BC–49 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 149 BC–49 BC] Hellenistic II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Ptolemaic rule continued but weakened as Egypt itself fell into dynastic crisis and Roman interference. Rome annexed the island in 58 BC, briefly restored it to Cleopatra, and finally absorbed it for good - a shift from Alexandrian to Roman orbit that reoriented Cypriot trade and administration westward.

Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) I (Cy.node: Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) I (Cyprus, 1899 BC–1799 BC)
Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) I (Cy.label: Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) I
Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) I (Cy.prose:
[Cyprus, 1899 BC–1799 BC] Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Island communities continued the village-based pattern of the Early Bronze Age, burying their dead in rock-cut chamber tombs stocked with distinctive Red Polished pottery. Copper working expanded, laying the groundwork for the island's later fame as a metal exporter. Change came slowly, and the material culture is largely a continuation of what came before.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIC (Cyp.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIC (Cyprus, 1149 BC–1049 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIC (Cyp.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIC
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIC (Cyp.prose:
[Cyprus, 1149 BC–1049 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIC. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The last stretch of the Bronze Age tradition on Cyprus, blending into the Cypro-Geometric Iron Age. Iron tools and weapons became ordinary rather than exotic, settlement clustered around the coastal sites that would grow into the island's classical kingdoms, and the Greek-speaking element in Cypriot culture became firmly established.

Roman I (Cyprus, 49 BC–AD 150).label: Roman I
Roman I (Cyprus, 49 BC–AD 150).prose:
[Cyprus, 49 BC–AD 150] Roman I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cyprus, annexed from the Ptolemies, settled into life as a quiet senatorial province exporting copper, timber, grain and wine. Cities such as Paphos, Salamis and Kourion were rebuilt in Roman style with theatres, gymnasia and aqueducts, often after devastating earthquakes. This is also the island of the earliest Christian mission recorded in Acts, when Paul and Barnabas preached to the Roman governor.

Hellenistic I (Cyprus, 324 BC–149 BC).label: Hellenistic I
Hellenistic I (Cyprus, 324 BC–149 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 324 BC–149 BC] Hellenistic I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The island's ancient city-kingdoms were abolished and Cyprus became a Ptolemaic possession governed from Egypt, valued for its copper, timber and shipbuilding. Nea Paphos replaced Salamis as the administrative capital, and Alexandrian styles in sculpture, mosaics and burial architecture reshaped island culture. Greek language and Ptolemaic coinage displaced the old Cypro-syllabic script and local dynasties.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIB (Cypr.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIB (Cyprus, 1399 BC–1324 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIB (Cypr.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIB
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIB (Cypr.prose:
[Cyprus, 1399 BC–1324 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIB. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The king of Alashiya corresponded with the pharaoh as an equal in the Amarna letters, shipping hundreds of talents of copper in exchange for silver, ivory and luxury goods. Mycenaean pictorial kraters imported in bulk filled Cypriot tombs, and urban centres at Enkomi and Kition consolidated. Wealth from metal underpinned an increasingly stratified society.

Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) I (Cyprus, 749 B.label: Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) I
Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) I (Cyprus, 749 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–599 BC] Archaic (Cypro-Archaic) I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The island's independent city-kingdoms — Salamis, Kition, Paphos and their rivals — flourished under a light Assyrian overlordship, paying tribute while running their own affairs. Rich chamber tombs at Salamis contain chariots, horse burials and bronze cauldrons that read like scenes from Homer, and sanctuaries filled with thousands of terracotta votive figures, as at Ayia Irini. Cypriot craftsmen worked Phoenician, Egyptian and Greek motifs into a distinctive local style, and the syllabic Cypriot script remained in use alongside Phoenician.

Roman II (Cyprus, AD 150–AD 250).label: Roman II
Roman II (Cyprus, AD 150–AD 250).prose:
[Cyprus, AD 150–AD 250] Roman II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cypriot cities reached their most lavish phase, with grand houses whose mosaic floors set out mythological scenes still visible at Paphos. The island's Jewish community was destroyed in the revolt of AD 116, and Christian congregations grew steadily thereafter. Prosperity rested on copper, agriculture and a position on the shipping routes between Syria, Egypt and the Aegean.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIC (Cypr.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIC (Cyprus, 1324 BC–1224 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIC (Cypr.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIC
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIC (Cypr.prose:
[Cyprus, 1324 BC–1224 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIC. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cypriot urbanism reached its height: gridded towns, monumental ashlar sanctuaries and copper workshops at Enkomi, Kition and Palaepaphos, with fortified coastal outposts guarding the sea lanes. Cypro-Minoan inscriptions, imported Aegean and Levantine goods and mass metal production all peak. The period ends in destructions amid the wider collapse of the Bronze Age world, followed by an influx of Aegean settlers.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIA (Cypr.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIA (Cyprus, 1474 BC–1399 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIA (Cypr.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIA
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIA (Cypr.prose:
[Cyprus, 1474 BC–1399 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIA. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Towns grew and organised themselves around copper production and export, with the standard oxhide ingot becoming a recognised unit of Mediterranean metal trade. Mycenaean and Levantine imports accumulated in Cypriot tombs, and administrative use of the Cypro-Minoan script increased. This is when the island's rulers begin to look like the kings of Alashiya known from foreign archives.

Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III (Cyprus,.label: Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III
Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III (Cyprus,.prose:
[Cyprus, 849 BC–749 BC] Geometric (Cypro-Geometric) III. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Wealth returned in force: rich tombs, imported Levantine and Egyptian luxuries, and orientalising motifs appearing on Cypriot pots alongside the old geometric designs. Phoenician Kition flourished and the island's kingdoms grew powerful enough that, soon after, ten of their kings would submit to the Assyrian empire. The period ends as Cypro-Archaic art takes over, full of figures, animals and floral ornament.

Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIA (Cyp.node: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIA (Cyprus, 1224 BC–1189 BC)
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIA (Cyp.label: Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIA
Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIA (Cyp.prose:
[Cyprus, 1224 BC–1189 BC] Late Bronze Age (Late Cypriot) IIIA. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The old order on Cyprus broke apart: several thriving harbour towns burned, populations shifted, and newcomers using Aegean-style Mycenaean IIIC pottery settled at Enkomi, Kition and Maa-Palaeokastro. Yet copper working continued on a grand scale, with ashlar-built sanctuaries set beside metallurgical workshops, showing that the island's smiths adapted rather than vanished when the eastern Mediterranean palace economies collapsed.

Classical (Cypro-Classical) II (Cyprus,.label: Classical (Cypro-Classical) II
Classical (Cypro-Classical) II (Cyprus,.prose:
[Cyprus, 399 BC–324 BC] Classical (Cypro-Classical) II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The island's kings continued to balance Persian tribute against Greek cultural and commercial ties, supplying ships and timber to whichever power was ascendant. Cypriot rulers backed Alexander at the siege of Tyre, and after his death the island became a prize in the wars of his successors. The Ptolemies eventually abolished the city-kingdoms, ending a political system that had lasted for centuries.

Early Bronze Age (Ras Shamra, 2999 BC–21.node: Early Bronze Age (Ras Shamra, 2999 BC–2199 BC)
Early Bronze Age (Ras Shamra, 2999 BC–21.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Ras Shamra, 2999 BC–21.prose:
[Ras Shamra, 2999 BC–2199 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The city of Ugarit at Tell Ras Shamra — Yon, Marguerite., 2006.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Ras Shamra, 2999 BC–21.source: The city of Ugarit at Tell Ras Shamra

Roman period (Ras Shamra, 99 BC–AD 1).label: Roman period
Roman period (Ras Shamra, 99 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Ras Shamra, 99 BC–AD 1] Roman period. Period definition from The city of Ugarit at Tell Ras Shamra — Yon, Marguerite., 2006.

The northern Syrian coast, long after the Bronze Age city of Ugarit had been abandoned, was drawn into Roman Syria following Pompey's annexation. Activity in the area centred on the nearby harbour and rural settlement rather than the old tell, which saw only scattered later use.
Roman period (Ras Shamra, 99 BC–AD 1).source: The city of Ugarit at Tell Ras Shamra

Geometric (Sardinia, 849 BC–729 BC).label: Geometric
Geometric (Sardinia, 849 BC–729 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 849 BC–729 BC] Geometric. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Greece emerging from the post-Mycenaean dark age, its pottery covered in meanders, zigzags and banded panels, later giving way to silhouetted horses, chariots and mourners on the huge Dipylon grave markers of Athens. Communities coalesced into the first city-states, sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filled with dedications, the Phoenician alphabet was adapted to Greek, and settlers began sailing west to Italy and Sicily. The oral traditions that became the Iliad and Odyssey took shape in these years.
Geometric (Sardinia, 849 BC–729 BC).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Middle Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1899 BC–129.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1899 BC–129.prose:
[Sardinia, 1899 BC–1299 BC] Middle Bronze Age. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1899 BC–129.source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Phoenician (Sardinia, 849 BC–509 BC).label: Phoenician
Phoenician (Sardinia, 849 BC–509 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 849 BC–509 BC] Phoenician. Also known as Nuragic IV (cf. Sardinian). Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Traders from Tyre and Sidon planted settlements at Nora, Sulcis, Tharros and Bithia, drawn by Sardinia's metals and its position on routes to Spain. Their sanctuaries, or tophets, with urns of cremated infants and carved stelae, are among the most-discussed finds on the island. Contact and conflict with the indigenous Nuragic communities reshaped Sardinian society before Carthage took control.
Phoenician (Sardinia, 849 BC–509 BC).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Bronze Age (Sardinia, 2199 BC–849 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Sardinia, 2199 BC–849 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 2199 BC–849 BC] Bronze Age. See also G. Lilliu, 2003. La civiltÃ dei Sardi dal paleolitico all'etÃ dei nuraghi; G.S. Webster, 1996. A Prehistory of Sardinia 2300-500BC. Also known as Nuragic III (following Nuragic I = Early Bronze Age, 1800-1500 B.C.; & Nuragic II = Middle Bronze Age, 1500-1200 B.C.). Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Sardinia, 2199 BC–849 BC).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Republican (Sardinia, 237 BC–AD 1).label: Republican
Republican (Sardinia, 237 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Sardinia, 237 BC–AD 1] Republican. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.
Republican (Sardinia, 237 BC–AD 1).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Late Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1299 BC–1149.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1299 BC–1149.prose:
[Sardinia, 1299 BC–1149 BC] Late Bronze Age. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1299 BC–1149.source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Final Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1149 BC–849.label: Final Bronze Age
Final Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1149 BC–849.prose:
[Sardinia, 1149 BC–849 BC] Final Bronze Age. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Sardinia's nuragic communities stopped raising new tower-fortresses and instead expanded the villages clustered around the older nuraghi, with round huts, meeting rooms and sacred wells. Metalworkers turned copper ingots from Cyprus and Aegean contacts into tools and the first of the small bronze figurines of warriors, archers and worshippers that are the island's most distinctive art. It is the phase in which nuragic society shifted from building monuments to trading across the Mediterranean, setting the stage for the Iron Age encounters with Phoenicians.
Final Bronze Age (Sardinia, 1149 BC–849.source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Late Iron Age (Sardinia, 509 BC–237 BC).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (Sardinia, 509 BC–237 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 509 BC–237 BC] Late Iron Age. Also known as Nuragic V, or final Nuragic (cf. Late Iron Age & Iron Age Sardinian) = period of Carthaginian hegemony, ending in Roman annexation of Sardinia, 238 B.C. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.
Late Iron Age (Sardinia, 509 BC–237 BC).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Orientalizing (Sardinia, 729 BC–579 BC).label: Orientalizing
Orientalizing (Sardinia, 729 BC–579 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 729 BC–579 BC] Orientalizing. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Rich hillforts and enormous burial mounds in the Dolenjska region mark a wealthy Hallstatt-era elite trading with Italy and the eastern Alps. Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. The imagery borrows from Etruscan and Near Eastern art but tells local stories.
Orientalizing (Sardinia, 729 BC–579 BC).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Eneolithic (Copper Age) (Sardinia, 3199.label: Eneolithic (Copper Age)
Eneolithic (Copper Age) (Sardinia, 3199.prose:
[Sardinia, 3199 BC–2199 BC] Eneolithic (Copper Age). added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Sardinian communities took up copper metallurgy while building some of the island's most striking monuments: thousands of rock-cut chamber tombs known as domus de janas, and the stepped stone platform of Monte d'Accoddi, unique in the Mediterranean. Successive cultural groups (Filigosa, Abealzu, Monte Claro, and later Bell Beaker) left distinctive pottery and the first standing-stone statues. These traditions set the stage for the Bronze Age nuraghi.
Eneolithic (Copper Age) (Sardinia, 3199.source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Archaic (Sardinia, 579 BC–509 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Sardinia, 579 BC–509 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 579 BC–509 BC] Archaic. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Sardinia, 579 BC–509 BC).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Imperial (Sardinia, AD 1–AD 476).label: Imperial
Imperial (Sardinia, AD 1–AD 476).prose:
[Sardinia, AD 1–AD 476] Imperial. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

Augustus kept the forms of the Republic while holding its powers alone, and the arrangement lasted five centuries. Roads, aqueducts, standard coinage and Roman law knit together territory from Britain to the Euphrates, mass-produced goods travelled the length of the Mediterranean, and Latin and Greek became the vehicles of law, literature and eventually Christianity. Civil war, plague, currency collapse and pressure on the frontiers reshaped the state repeatedly before the western half dissolved into Germanic kingdoms.
Imperial (Sardinia, AD 1–AD 476).source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Early Bronze Age (Sardinia, 2199 BC–1899.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Sardinia, 2199 BC–1899.prose:
[Sardinia, 2199 BC–1899 BC] Early Bronze Age. added. Period definition from Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors — Dyson, Stephen L., 2007.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Sardinia, 2199 BC–1899.source: Archaeology and history in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages : shepherds, sailors, and conquerors

Florid Style (Italy, 318 BC–271 BC).label: Florid Style
Florid Style (Italy, 318 BC–271 BC).prose:
[Italy, 318 BC–271 BC] Florid Style. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy. p. 288-290: "It is by no means necessary to suppose that one style of fabric ceased immediately on the introduction of another and improved one; on the contrary, it probably continued till so entirely superseded that the fabric became obsolete. Hence the transition from the 'fine' style of the earlier vases to a subsequent one, which may be termed florid--analogous to the state of art in the time of Pyrrhus.". Period definition from History of ancient pottery. — Samuel Birch, 1858.

The last flourish of South Italian red-figure vase painting, when Apulian workshops covered huge funerary vases with tiers of figures, added white and yellow overpainting, and framed scenes in dense floral scrollwork. The pots were made for tomb display rather than the table, and their mythological and underworld scenes are a major source for lost Greek tragedy. Within a generation the tradition died out as Rome absorbed the region.

Decadence (Italy, 403 BC–199 BC).label: Decadence
Decadence (Italy, 403 BC–199 BC).prose:
[Italy, 403 BC–199 BC] Decadence. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy. p. 296: "The vases of this style at its best period are later than the introduction of the double letters in the Archonship of Euclid, Olympiad XCIV, B.C. 404, and come down to nearly B.C. 200. [see note 4]"

p.296, n. 4: "Thiersch., s. 81-2". Period definition from History of ancient pottery. — Samuel Birch, 1858.

Tidig medeltid (Sweden, AD 1100–AD 1250).label: Tidig medeltid
Tidig medeltid (Sweden, AD 1100–AD 1250).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1100–AD 1250] Tidig medeltid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Sweden became Christian in these generations: bishoprics were established, the last pagan cult centre at Uppsala gave way to a cathedral, and wooden churches were replaced by stone ones whose fonts and portals survive across the countryside. Rune stones fell out of fashion as parchment charters and Latin literacy arrived with monks and canons. Rival royal houses, the Sverkers and the Eriks, fought for a crown that was still elective, while Sigtuna, Skara and Visby grew into real towns.

Yngre mesolitikum (Sweden, 5499 BC–3999.label: Yngre mesolitikum
Yngre mesolitikum (Sweden, 5499 BC–3999.prose:
[Sweden, 5499 BC–3999 BC] Yngre mesolitikum. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Hunter-fisher-gatherers along the coasts and lakes used slotted bone points, microliths and dugout canoes, and increasingly stayed put where seals, fish and hazelnuts were reliable. Shell middens, fish weirs and cemeteries such as Skateholm show communities settled enough to bury their dead in marked graves, sometimes with dogs. Contact with farming groups to the south brought new ideas long before crops and cattle themselves took hold.

Bronsålder period i (Sweden, 1699 BC–149.label: Bronsålder period i
Bronsålder period i (Sweden, 1699 BC–149.prose:
[Sweden, 1699 BC–1499 BC] Bronsålder period i. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

The first true bronze-working phase in the north, when imported flanged axes and daggers began to displace the fine flint daggers that Scandinavian knappers had perfected. Metal was rare and concentrated in the hands of a few, buried in barrows in the Danish and Scanian farmland. Montelius built his six-period scheme on exactly these shifts in ornament and weapon form, and it still frames Nordic Bronze Age chronology.

Stenålder (Sweden, 11999 BC–1699 BC).label: Stenålder
Stenålder (Sweden, 11999 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Sweden, 11999 BC–1699 BC] Stenålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

The Swedish Stone Age begins with hunters following the retreating ice sheet north along a coastline that was still rising out of the sea. Later came Funnel Beaker farmers with their megalithic tombs, the seal-hunting Pitted Ware people of the Baltic islands, and the Battle Axe groups whose corded pottery and stone axes link Sweden to a wider northern European world.

Senneolitikum (Sweden, 2299 BC–1699 BC).label: Senneolitikum
Senneolitikum (Sweden, 2299 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Sweden, 2299 BC–1699 BC] Senneolitikum. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Farming communities across the south adopted the flint dagger, skilfully pressure-flaked in imitation of imported metal blades and produced almost industrially at the Scanian mine sites. Large gallery graves held collective burials, longhouses grew substantial, and the first copper and bronze objects trickled in through wide exchange networks. These contacts set up the metal-rich Bronze Age that followed.

Yngre stenålder (Sweden, 3999 BC–1699 BC.label: Yngre stenålder
Yngre stenålder (Sweden, 3999 BC–1699 BC.prose:
[Sweden, 3999 BC–1699 BC] Yngre stenålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Farming, pottery and polished flint axes arrived, and with them a new way of marking the land: dolmens, passage graves and causewayed enclosures built by communities of the Funnel Beaker tradition. Along the eastern coasts, Pitted Ware groups kept hunting seals for centuries, so herders and hunters lived side by side. Later came Battle Axe burials with corded pottery, and finally the superbly flaked flint daggers copied from imported bronze weapons.

Äldre järnålder (Sweden, 499 BC–AD 400).label: Äldre järnålder
Äldre järnålder (Sweden, 499 BC–AD 400).prose:

Iron smelted from bog ore replaced imported bronze, putting metal within reach of ordinary farmers and changing tools, weapons and land clearance. Villages of longhouses with stone-walled field systems spread across Öland, Gotland and the mainland; hillforts multiplied, and Roman glass, bronze and coins reached the north through trade and mercenary service. Weapon-rich graves and the earliest runic inscriptions signal an emerging warrior aristocracy.

Bronsålder period iv (Sweden, 1099 BC–89.label: Bronsålder period iv
Bronsålder period iv (Sweden, 1099 BC–89.prose:
[Sweden, 1099 BC–899 BC] Bronsålder period iv. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Cremation became universal, and the dead were now placed in urns in flat cemeteries or inserted into older mounds rather than given new monuments of their own. Contacts shifted as urnfield practices spread from central Europe, and new object types appeared, including the earliest of the great bronze lurs. Ship-shaped stone settings began to be built as grave markers.

Senmedeltid (Sweden, AD 1350–AD 1500).label: Senmedeltid
Senmedeltid (Sweden, AD 1350–AD 1500).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1350–AD 1500] Senmedeltid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

The centuries after the Black Death saw depopulated farms, a shift toward livestock, and Hanseatic merchants dominating the copper and iron trade through Stockholm and Visby. Politically it was the age of the Kalmar Union with Denmark and Norway, punctuated by revolts, the Stockholm Bloodbath, and finally Gustav Vasa's breakaway. Brick churches with vivid painted vaults, still standing across the countryside, are its most visible legacy.

Vikingatid (Sweden, AD 800–AD 1100).label: Vikingatid
Vikingatid (Sweden, AD 800–AD 1100).prose:
[Sweden, AD 800–AD 1100] Vikingatid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Swedish Vikings looked east, following the rivers of Russia to Novgorod, Kiev, the Caspian and Byzantium, and bringing back the Arab silver dirhams found by the tens of thousands in Gotland hoards. Birka and later Sigtuna grew as trading towns, and hundreds of rune-stones were raised across the Mälaren region, many commemorating men who died on eastern voyages. The period closes with the slow arrival of Christianity and the consolidation of a Swedish kingdom.

Vendeltid (Sweden, AD 550–AD 800) [p0vn2.label: Vendeltid
Vendeltid (Sweden, AD 550–AD 800) [p0vn2.prose:
[Sweden, AD 550–AD 800] Vendeltid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

The generations before the Viking Age, named after the boat graves at Vendel where chieftains were buried with horses, weapons and ornate helmets of gilded bronze and garnet inlay. Aristocratic halls, great mounds at Old Uppsala and animal-style metalwork show a society of warrior retinues and long-distance contacts reaching Britain and the Continent. The seamanship, wealth and craft of these elites are what the Viking expeditions were built on.

Äldre stenålder (Sweden, 11999 BC–3999 B.label: Äldre stenålder
Äldre stenålder (Sweden, 11999 BC–3999 B.prose:
[Sweden, 11999 BC–3999 BC] Äldre stenålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

As the ice sheet melted back, hunter-gatherer-fishers followed the retreating shoreline into what became Sweden, living on seal, fish, elk and wild plants and moving between coastal and inland camps. Their toolkits of flint blades, microliths, bone points and dugout canoes link them to the Maglemose, Kongemose and Ertebølle traditions of the southern Baltic. Rapid land uplift and sea-level change means many of their settlements now lie far inland or beneath the sea, which is why coastal sites are so prized by archaeologists.

Yngre bronsålder (Sweden, 1099 BC–499 BC.label: Yngre bronsålder
Yngre bronsålder (Sweden, 1099 BC–499 BC.prose:
[Sweden, 1099 BC–499 BC] Yngre bronsålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Cremation and urn burial replaced mound inhumation, and bronze was worked into thin ornamental sheet metal, hanging vessels and lur trumpets, much of it deliberately deposited in bogs and lakes. This is the period of the great rock-carving sites of Bohuslän and Östergötland, with their ships, sun discs and processions, and of far-reaching trade that carried southern metal deep into Scandinavia.

Högmedeltid (Sweden, AD 1250–AD 1350).label: Högmedeltid
Högmedeltid (Sweden, AD 1250–AD 1350).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1250–AD 1350] Högmedeltid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Sweden became a settled kingdom in these years: stone castles and cathedrals went up, provincial laws were written down, and Stockholm and other towns grew on Hanseatic trade in iron, copper and butter. The Church, royal administration and a tax-exempt noble cavalry class took recognisable shape, and Magnus Eriksson's national law code drew the provinces together. Visitors will see brick and granite buildings, church wall paintings and imported German goods that mark the shift from a rural chiefly society to a European monarchy.

Äldre bronsålder (Sweden, 1699 BC–1099 B.label: Äldre bronsålder
Äldre bronsålder (Sweden, 1699 BC–1099 B.prose:
[Sweden, 1699 BC–1099 BC] Äldre bronsålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Bronze arrived in Scandinavia through exchange networks reaching to Central Europe and the British Isles — Sweden had no copper or tin of its own, so metal was wealth. Chiefly families were buried in stone cairns and earth barrows placed prominently on ridges and coasts, accompanied by swords, razors, and spiral-ornamented ornaments, while rock carvings of ships, sun discs and axe-bearing figures cover the granite of Bohuslän and Östergötland. Farming settlements with longhouses and the beginnings of a sun-centred religion define the era.

Tidigneolitikum (Sweden, 3999 BC–3299 BC.label: Tidigneolitikum
Tidigneolitikum (Sweden, 3999 BC–3299 BC.prose:
[Sweden, 3999 BC–3299 BC] Tidigneolitikum. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Farming reached southern Scandinavia: people began keeping cattle, sheep and pigs, sowing barley and wheat in clearings burned out of the forest, and making the flared funnel-necked pots that give the culture its name. They also began building for the dead, raising the first dolmens and passage graves out of massive stones — the oldest monuments in Sweden and often the most visible prehistoric feature in the landscape today. Flint mining, polished axes and long-distance exchange networks came with the new way of life.

Järnålder (Sweden, 499 BC–AD 1100).label: Järnålder
Järnålder (Sweden, 499 BC–AD 1100).prose:
[Sweden, 499 BC–AD 1100] Järnålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Sweden's long Iron Age runs from the first bog-iron smelting through the Roman trade contacts that brought glass, bronze vessels and gold to Scandinavian graves, then the boat burials and helmets of the Vendel elite, and finally the Viking centuries of raiding, silver hoards and trade routes to Byzantium and the Caliphate. It is the period of runic writing, of hillforts and great hall complexes like Uppåkra and Gamla Uppsala. It closes as Christian kingship takes hold and Sweden enters the written record of medieval Europe.

Bronsålder period ii (Sweden, 1499 BC–12.label: Bronsålder period ii
Bronsålder period ii (Sweden, 1499 BC–12.prose:
[Sweden, 1499 BC–1299 BC] Bronsålder period ii. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

The classic age of Nordic barrow burials: oak coffins and stone cists under high mounds, holding men with swords and razors and women with belt discs, tutuli and corded skirts. Spiral ornament reached its peak, and the sheer quantity of bronze suggests well-organised long-distance exchange with the Carpathian and Alpine metal sources. The Trundholm sun chariot belongs to this world.

Medeltid (Sweden, AD 1100–AD 1500).label: Medeltid
Medeltid (Sweden, AD 1100–AD 1500).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1100–AD 1500] Medeltid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Sweden took shape as a Christian kingdom in these centuries: stone churches and cathedrals replaced pagan cult sites, towns like Stockholm and Visby grew rich on Baltic trade with the Hanseatic League, and provincial laws were gradually welded into a national code. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish crowns were joined in the Kalmar Union from 1397, an arrangement Swedish nobles resented and repeatedly rebelled against. The Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 ended it, opening the way to Gustav Vasa and the Reformation.

Förromersk järnålder (Sweden, 499 BC–AD.prose:

Iron, smelted from local bog ore, replaced imported bronze and put tools and weapons within reach of ordinary farmers. Settlements became small, dispersed farmsteads with byre-and-dwelling longhouses, grave goods grew sparse, and burials shifted to modest cremations. Contacts with the Celtic world to the south brought new forms and ideas well before Roman goods began arriving.

Mellanneolitikum (Sweden, 3299 BC–2299 B.label: Mellanneolitikum
Mellanneolitikum (Sweden, 3299 BC–2299 B.prose:
[Sweden, 3299 BC–2299 BC] Mellanneolitikum. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Farming societies split into strikingly different traditions: megalith-building Funnel Beaker communities, the seal-hunting and fish-eating Pitted Ware people of the eastern coasts, and finally the Battle Axe groups with their single graves and corded pottery. Long stone chambers and passage graves were filled with generations of bones and offerings, while amber, flint axes and elaborately decorated pots moved along wide exchange networks. It is the period when Sweden's ancestry and culture were reshaped by newcomers from the Continental steppe world.

Nyare tid (Sweden, AD 1500–AD 2100).label: Nyare tid
Nyare tid (Sweden, AD 1500–AD 2100).prose:
[Sweden, AD 1500–AD 2100] Nyare tid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Sweden broke with the Danish-led union and with Rome, built a centralised Lutheran state, and for a century fought its way to control of the Baltic before losing it again. Later came agrarian reform, mass emigration to America, industry built on iron and timber, and the making of the welfare state. It is the stretch in which Sweden turns from a thinly populated northern kingdom into a modern industrial society.

Bronsålder (Sweden, 1699 BC–499 BC).label: Bronsålder
Bronsålder (Sweden, 1699 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Sweden, 1699 BC–499 BC] Bronsålder. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Southern Scandinavia had no copper or tin of its own, yet became one of the richest bronze-using regions in Europe by trading amber, furs and hides southwards along routes to central Europe and the Mediterranean. The wealth shows in mound burials with swords and folding stools, in the great bronze lurs, and in tens of thousands of rock carvings of ships, sun discs and warriors along the Bohuslän coast. It is also the period when the sun-and-ship imagery that underlies later Norse cosmology first appears.

Bronsålder period vi (Sweden, 699 BC–499.label: Bronsålder period vi
Bronsålder period vi (Sweden, 699 BC–499.prose:
[Sweden, 699 BC–499 BC] Bronsålder period vi. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Bronze supplies faltered as the central European exchange networks that fed the north broke down, and objects grew thinner, plainer and smaller. Iron began to appear in the region, and burial in simple urns under low cairns became the norm. Within a century or two the lavish material world of the Nordic Bronze Age had given way to the sparse archaeology of the pre-Roman Iron Age.

Romersk järnålder (Sweden, AD 1–AD 400).label: Romersk järnålder
Romersk järnålder (Sweden, AD 1–AD 400).prose:

Roman glass, bronze vessels, coins and weapons reached Sweden through trade and mercenary service, concentrating in the hands of emerging elites on Öland, Gotland and in the Mälar valley. Farms grew into more permanent settlements with stone-walled field systems, and burials became sharply unequal in wealth. The first runic inscriptions appear, and weapon deposits and hillforts point to organised warfare between competing chiefdoms.

Yngre järnålder (Sweden, AD 400–AD 1100).label: Yngre järnålder

Spanning the Migration, Vendel and Viking periods, these centuries saw hoarded gold and gold-foil figures, boat burials at Vendel and Valsgärde, and the rise of central places such as Old Uppsala, Helgö and later Birka. Traders and raiders pushed east along the Russian rivers and west across the Atlantic, and by its close runestones record the arrival of Christianity and the making of a Swedish kingdom.

Bronsålder period v (Sweden, 899 BC–699.label: Bronsålder period v
Bronsålder period v (Sweden, 899 BC–699.prose:
[Sweden, 899 BC–699 BC] Bronsålder period v. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

One of the most productive phases of Scandinavian bronze casting, giving the huge decorated shields, hanging vessels, neck rings and paired lurs that fill museum cases today. Enormous quantities of metal were deliberately deposited in bogs and lakes, an offering practice on a scale seen nowhere else in Europe. Ship settings and cairns dominate the coastal burial landscape.

Folkvandringstid (Sweden, AD 400–AD 550).label: Folkvandringstid
Folkvandringstid (Sweden, AD 400–AD 550).prose:
[Sweden, AD 400–AD 550] Folkvandringstid. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

The Migration Period in Scandinavia, when contact with a collapsing Roman world brought floods of gold into the North: bracteates, neck-rings and hoards buried in bogs and fields. Chieftains built hillforts and ring-forts such as Eketorp on Öland, and abandoned farms across the region hint at the crisis following the dust-veil and cold years of the 530s. Out of this upheaval came the wealthy warrior aristocracy of the Vendel age.

Bronsålder period iii (Sweden, 1299 BC–1.label: Bronsålder period iii
Bronsålder period iii (Sweden, 1299 BC–1.prose:
[Sweden, 1299 BC–1099 BC] Bronsålder period iii. Period definition from Sök i samlingarna (beta) — Historiska museet, 2011.

Wealthy mound burials continued, but cremation began to take over, with burnt bones placed in stone cists or pots inside the barrows. Bronze-working reached technical maturity in cast hanging vessels, swords and elaborate female ornaments. Rock carving along the west coast flourished, filling granite slabs with ships, ploughing scenes and armed figures.

Bronze Age (Poland, 1800 BC–400 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Poland, 1800 BC–400 BC).prose:
[Poland, 1800 BC–400 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Greek (Romania, 650 BC–30 BC).prose:

Greek colonists from Miletus and Heraclea Pontica planted cities on the western Black Sea coast, among them Histria, Tomis and Callatis. They traded wine, oil and fine pottery inland for grain, honey, hides and slaves from the Getic and Dacian populations, introducing coinage, stone architecture and writing to the region. These ports remained the main channel between the Mediterranean world and the lower Danube until Rome absorbed them.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

Beginning with the dissolution of the monasteries and the Reformation's stripping of parish churches, these centuries carried England through civil war, the growth of an Atlantic empire, enclosure of open fields, and industrialisation. Excavations of the period yield mass-produced goods - tin-glazed and transfer-printed pottery, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes, machine-made nails - that let sites be dated to within a decade or two. Landscapes changed as thoroughly as objects: hedged fields, canals, railways, mines and terraced workers' housing all belong to this span.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 1066–AD 154.prose: [United Kingdom, AD 1066–AD 1540] Medieval. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Iron Age (Romania, 1200 BC–AD 106).prose:
[Romania, 1200 BC–AD 106] Iron Age. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Bronze Age (Romania, 3200 BC–1200 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Romania, 3200 BC–1200 BC).prose:
[Romania, 3200 BC–1200 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Bronze Age (United Kingdom, 2500 BC–700.label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (United Kingdom, 2500 BC–700.prose:
[United Kingdom, 2500 BC–700 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Mesolithic (Denmark, 9000 BC–3900 BC).label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (Denmark, 9000 BC–3900 BC).prose:
[Denmark, 9000 BC–3900 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Iron Age (United Kingdom, 800 BC–AD 43).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (United Kingdom, 800 BC–AD 43).prose:
[United Kingdom, 800 BC–AD 43] Iron Age. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Neolithic (Poland, 4500 BC–1800 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Poland, 4500 BC–1800 BC).prose:
[Poland, 4500 BC–1800 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Post Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 1540–A.label: Post Medieval
Post Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 1540–A.prose:
[United Kingdom, AD 1540–AD 1901] Post Medieval. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Beginning with the dissolution of the monasteries and the Reformation's stripping of parish churches, these centuries carried England through civil war, the growth of an Atlantic empire, enclosure of open fields, and industrialisation. Excavations of the period yield mass-produced goods - tin-glazed and transfer-printed pottery, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes, machine-made nails - that let sites be dated to within a decade or two. Landscapes changed as thoroughly as objects: hedged fields, canals, railways, mines and terraced workers' housing all belong to this span.

Early Medieval (Romania, AD 353–AD 900).label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (Romania, AD 353–AD 900).prose:
[Romania, AD 353–AD 900] Early Medieval. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Mesolithic (United Kingdom, 10000 BC–400.label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (United Kingdom, 10000 BC–400.prose:
[United Kingdom, 10000 BC–4000 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Medieval (Iceland, AD 1100–AD 1600).label: Medieval
Medieval (Iceland, AD 1100–AD 1600).prose: [Iceland, AD 1100–AD 1600] Medieval. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Medieval (Romania, AD 900–AD 1821).label: Medieval
Medieval (Romania, AD 900–AD 1821).prose: [Romania, AD 900–AD 1821] Medieval. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.

Early Medieval (Poland, AD 375–AD 600).label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (Poland, AD 375–AD 600).prose:
[Poland, AD 375–AD 600] Early Medieval. Period definition from ARENA - The ARENA Portal — ADS, 2004.
