Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Sixteen Kingdoms Period (China, AD 304–A.label: Sixteen Kingdoms Period
Sixteen Kingdoms Period (China, AD 304–A.prose:
[China, AD 304–AD 439] Sixteen Kingdoms Period. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

After nomadic and frontier peoples overthrew the Western Jin and sacked Luoyang and Chang'an, northern China broke into a churn of short-lived states founded by Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Qiang and Jie rulers. Massive migration pushed Chinese elites south of the Yangtze, while northern courts blended steppe military power with Chinese bureaucracy. The chaos ended when the Xianbei Northern Wei conquered the north, laying the groundwork for the eventual reunification of China.

Zhou Period (China, 1046 BC–256 BC).label: Zhou Period
Zhou Period (China, 1046 BC–256 BC).prose:
[China, 1046 BC–256 BC] Zhou Period. First capital: 镐京 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The longest-lasting Chinese dynasty began when the Zhou overthrew the Shang and justified it with the Mandate of Heaven, an idea that would legitimise - and threaten - every later dynasty. Power devolved to a patchwork of feudal states that grew independent and then predatory, producing the Spring and Autumn and Warring States eras of near-constant warfare, iron tools, mass infantry armies and vast irrigation works. Out of that turmoil came Confucius, Laozi, Mozi and the Legalists, the intellectual foundation of Chinese civilisation. Ritual bronzes with long cast inscriptions are the period's most striking material legacy.

Tang Dynasty (China, AD 618–AD 907).label: Tang Dynasty
Tang Dynasty (China, AD 618–AD 907).prose:
[China, AD 618–AD 907] Tang Dynasty. First capital: 长安 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

A cosmopolitan empire at its height ruled from Chang'an, then the largest city on earth, where Sogdian merchants, Japanese students, Nestorian Christians and Buddhist pilgrims mixed. Tang armies pushed control deep into Central Asia along the Silk Road, while the examination system, printing and a golden age of poetry took shape at home. The An Lushan rebellion of 755 gutted central authority, and the dynasty's long decline ended in warlord partition.

Northern and Southern Dynasties Period (.node: Northern and Southern Dynasties Period (China, AD 420–AD 577)
Northern and Southern Dynasties Period (.label: Northern and Southern Dynasties Period
Northern and Southern Dynasties Period (.prose:
[China, AD 420–AD 577] Northern and Southern Dynasties Period. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

China was split between steppe-founded regimes in the north and a series of short-lived Chinese courts in the south, each claiming legitimate succession. Buddhism spread rapidly on both sides, sustained by cave temples and monasteries in the north and philosophical debate and aristocratic patronage in the south, while migration filled the Yangtze basin with northern refugees. The division ended when the north reunified and swept south.

Southern Jing Kingdom (China, AD 925–AD.label: Southern Jing Kingdom
Southern Jing Kingdom (China, AD 925–AD.prose:
[China, AD 925–AD 963] Southern Jing Kingdom. First capital: 南京, latitude: 32.05, longitude: 118.76. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The smallest of the Ten Kingdoms, better known as Jingnan or Nanping, a sliver of territory around Jiangling on the middle Yangtze. Its rulers survived by acknowledging every neighbouring power as overlord at once and by seizing tribute caravans passing through, earning their prince a mocking nickname. It was absorbed by the Song on the way to the conquest of the south.

Later Han Dynasty (China, AD 947–AD 950).label: Later Han Dynasty
Later Han Dynasty (China, AD 947–AD 950).prose:
[China, AD 947–AD 950] Later Han Dynasty. First capital: 开封, latitude: 34.78, longitude: 114.34. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

One of the short-lived northern regimes of the Five Dynasties, founded by the Shatuo general Liu Zhiyuan after the Khitan withdrew from the Central Plains. It lasted under four years and two rulers before a purge of senior officers provoked a mutiny and the founding of the Later Zhou. A branch of the family held out in Shanxi as the Northern Han, the last state to be swallowed by the reunifying Song.

Wu Yue Kingdom (China, AD 907–AD 978).label: Wu Yue Kingdom
Wu Yue Kingdom (China, AD 907–AD 978).prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 978] Wu Yue Kingdom. First capital: 錢塘 (杭州), latitude: 30.29, longitude: 120.16. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

One of the southern states of the Ten Kingdoms era, centred on Hangzhou, which grew rich on rice, silk and maritime trade with Japan and Korea while northern China fractured. Its rulers avoided major wars, invested in seawalls, irrigation and Buddhist temples and pagodas, and cultivated Chan Buddhism. In 978 the last king surrendered his territory to the Song without a fight, sparing the region devastation and leaving Hangzhou positioned to become the greatest city of the later Song.

Northern Wei Dynasty (China, AD 386–AD 5.label: Northern Wei Dynasty
Northern Wei Dynasty (China, AD 386–AD 5.prose:
[China, AD 386–AD 534] Northern Wei Dynasty. First capital: 盛樂 (呼和浩特), latitude: 40.81, longitude: 111.65. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Tuoba clan of the Xianbei conquered the rival kingdoms of northern China and held the region for a century and a half, the longest-lasting of the northern regimes. Their patronage created the colossal Buddhist cave shrines at Yungang and Longmen, and Emperor Xiaowen's move to Luoyang in 494 came with orders to adopt Chinese dress, language and surnames. The equal-field system of land allocation begun here shaped Chinese agrarian policy for four hundred years.

Later Liang Dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 92.label: Later Liang Dynasty
Later Liang Dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 92.prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 923] Later Liang Dynasty. First capital: 西都 (河南洛阳), latitude: 34.68, longitude: 112.45. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Zhu Wen, a former rebel general who had murdered the last Tang emperor, declared his own dynasty and began the fractured era known as the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. His regime controlled little more than the Yellow River heartland and spent its short life fighting the Shatuo Turkish warlords of Shanxi, who eventually destroyed it. The collapse of centralised power let regional courts in the south grow rich and culturally distinct.

Xia Dynasty (China, 2070 BC–1600 BC).label: Xia Dynasty
Xia Dynasty (China, 2070 BC–1600 BC).prose:
[China, 2070 BC–1600 BC] Xia Dynasty. First capital: 安邑 (山西夏县) - 阳翟 (河南禹县), latitude: 35.06, longitude: 111.04. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Chinese tradition names Xia as the first dynasty, founded by Yu the Great after he tamed the floods, and casts its last king as a tyrant overthrown by Shang. No writing from it has been found, so its historicity is debated, but archaeologists link it to the Erlitou culture of the Yellow River valley, with its palace foundations and cast-bronze ritual vessels. Whether legend or memory, the Xia story set the pattern of dynastic rise and fall that Chinese historians used ever after.

Xin Wang Mang Dynasty (China, AD 23–AD 2.label: Xin Wang Mang Dynasty
Xin Wang Mang Dynasty (China, AD 23–AD 2.prose:
[China, AD 23–AD 25] Xin Wang Mang Dynasty. First capital: 长安 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The collapse of Wang Mang's regime: rebel armies took Chang'an and killed him, and the Gengshi Emperor of the Han house was installed, only to be overwhelmed by the Red Eyebrows peasant armies. Out of the chaos Liu Xiu emerged to found the Eastern Han at Luoyang.

Western Wei Dynasty (China, AD 535–AD 55.label: Western Wei Dynasty
Western Wei Dynasty (China, AD 535–AD 55.prose:
[China, AD 535–AD 556] Western Wei Dynasty. First capital: 长安 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

One half of the Northern Wei after that empire tore in two, ruled from Chang'an by puppet emperors while the general Yuwen Tai held actual power. Poorer and smaller than its eastern rival, it compensated by reorganising its army into the fubing system of self-supporting soldier-farmers and by binding Chinese and Xianbei elites into a single military aristocracy. That Guanlong elite went on to found the Northern Zhou, Sui and Tang dynasties.

Xixia Dynasty (China, AD 1032–AD 1227).label: Xixia Dynasty
Xixia Dynasty (China, AD 1032–AD 1227).prose:
[China, AD 1032–AD 1227] Xixia Dynasty. First capital: 興慶府 (宁夏银川), latitude: 38.5, longitude: 106.2. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The state of the Tangut people, wedged between Song China, the Liao and later the Jin, controlling the Gansu corridor and the caravan trade to Central Asia. Its rulers invented a complex script of their own, printed Buddhist scriptures in Tangut, and played their powerful neighbours off against one another for two centuries. Genghis Khan's armies destroyed it in 1227, and the Mongols left it out of the official dynastic histories, so much of what is known comes from excavated libraries such as Khara-Khoto.

Warring States Period (China, 475 BC–221.label: Warring States Period
Warring States Period (China, 475 BC–221.prose:
[China, 475 BC–221 BC] Warring States Period. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Seven great kingdoms fought for supremacy with mass conscript infantry, iron weapons and the crossbow, replacing the chariot duels and ritual restraint of earlier Zhou warfare. Rulers hired scholars and administrators wherever they could find them, producing the Confucian, Daoist, Mohist and Legalist writings of the 'Hundred Schools'. Qin, reorganised on ruthless Legalist lines, swallowed its rivals one by one and made the first Chinese empire.

Wu Kingdom (China, AD 222–AD 280).label: Wu Kingdom
Wu Kingdom (China, AD 222–AD 280).prose:
[China, AD 222–AD 280] Wu Kingdom. First capital: 建业 (江苏南京), latitude: 32.06, longitude: 118.77. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The southeastern of the Three Kingdoms, ruled by the Sun family from Jianye, the site of modern Nanjing. Its strength lay in river fleets and the Yangtze, which held off northern invasions for decades, and its rulers pushed Chinese settlement and administration deep into the south, sending ships as far as Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Its conquest by the Jin in 280 briefly reunified China.

Republic of China (China, AD 1912–AD 194.label: Republic of China
Republic of China (China, AD 1912–AD 194.prose:
[China, AD 1912–AD 1949] Republic of China. First capital: 北京, latitude: 39.92, longitude: 116.38. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded on the collapse of imperial rule, the new state struggled to make a republic function: Yuan Shikai's attempted monarchy, a decade of warlord conflict, then Chiang Kai-shek's Nanjing government. It was also a period of intense cultural change — written vernacular Chinese, mass journalism, new schools and student politics. Japanese invasion from 1937 and the ensuing civil war exhausted the regime, which withdrew to Taiwan in 1949.

Jin Dynasty (China, AD 1115–AD 1234).label: Jin Dynasty
Jin Dynasty (China, AD 1115–AD 1234).prose:
[China, AD 1115–AD 1234] Jin Dynasty. First capital: 上京会宁府 (黑龙江哈尔滨市阿城区南白城), latitude: 45.52, longitude: 126.97. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded by the Jurchen chieftain Aguda in the forests of Manchuria, this state destroyed the Khitan Liao and then the Northern Song, capturing two emperors and taking all of China north of the Huai River. Its rulers governed a mixed population through a dual system, adopted Chinese bureaucracy and script, and made Beijing a capital for the first time. Mongol invasions ground it down over two decades until its last emperor died in 1234.

Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period (.node: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period (China, AD 907–AD 1279)
Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period (.label: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period
Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period (.prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 1279] Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Tang empire fragmented into a rapid succession of northern dynasties and a patchwork of southern kingdoms, several of them wealthy trading states in Sichuan, the lower Yangtze and coastal Fujian. Economic weight shifted decisively southward, ceramic and printing industries flourished under regional courts, and the northern frontier was lost to the Khitan. Reunification under the Song produced a civil-service state that dominated Chinese governance thereafter.

Eastern Jin Dynasty (China, AD 317–AD 42.label: Eastern Jin Dynasty
Eastern Jin Dynasty (China, AD 317–AD 42.prose:
[China, AD 317–AD 420] Eastern Jin Dynasty. First capital: 建康 (江苏南京), latitude: 32.06, longitude: 118.77. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

After nomadic armies overran the north and sacked Luoyang and Chang'an, the Jin court fled south and re-established itself at Jiankang (modern Nanjing), ruling only the Yangtze basin. Great émigré families dominated a weak throne, while the south was drained, diked and settled on a new scale, shifting China's economic centre of gravity toward the rice lands of the lower Yangtze. It was a brilliant age for Buddhism, landscape poetry and calligraphy — Wang Xizhi and the poet Tao Yuanming belong to it — and repeated northern expeditions never recovered the lost heartland.

Later Jin Dynasty (China, AD 936–AD 946).label: Later Jin Dynasty
Later Jin Dynasty (China, AD 936–AD 946).prose:
[China, AD 936–AD 946] Later Jin Dynasty. First capital: 开封, latitude: 34.78, longitude: 114.34. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Shi Jingtang won his throne with the help of Khitan cavalry and paid for it by ceding the Sixteen Prefectures, the strategic frontier belt including the site of modern Beijing. That loss left the North China Plain without its mountain defences and haunted Chinese strategy for four centuries. When his successor tried to defy the Liao, Khitan armies sacked the capital and carried the emperor into captivity.

Three Kingdoms Period (China, AD 220–AD.label: Three Kingdoms Period
Three Kingdoms Period (China, AD 220–AD.prose:
[China, AD 220–AD 280] Three Kingdoms Period. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Warlords carved the fallen Han empire into three states, and the resulting wars pushed millions of migrants south, opening the Yangtze basin to Chinese settlement and agriculture. Crossbow armies, naval warfare and huge military colonies defined the age, while Confucian state orthodoxy loosened and Daoist and Buddhist ideas spread. Reunification under the Jin proved brief, beginning centuries of division.

Yuan Dynasty (China, AD 1206–AD 1388).label: Yuan Dynasty
Yuan Dynasty (China, AD 1206–AD 1388).prose:
[China, AD 1206–AD 1388] Yuan Dynasty. First capital: 大都  (北京), latitude: 39.92, longitude: 116.38. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Dated from the proclamation of Genghis Khan as ruler of the Mongols, this span covers the whole arc of Mongol power in East Asia, from steppe conquest to the collapse of rule in China and retreat north. Chinese cities, Persian astronomers, Tibetan lamas and Italian merchants were drawn into a single empire linked by post roads and paper money. Its fall left the Ming in control of China and the Mongol courts in exile on the steppe.

Spring and Autumn Period (China, 770 BC–.node: Spring and Autumn Period (China, 770 BC–476 BC)
Spring and Autumn Period (China, 770 BC–.label: Spring and Autumn Period
Spring and Autumn Period (China, 770 BC–.prose:
[China, 770 BC–476 BC] Spring and Autumn Period. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Zhou kings kept their ritual prestige but lost real power, and dozens of contending states fought, allied and swallowed one another under a succession of hegemons. Iron tools, ox-drawn ploughs and coined money spread, cities grew, and hereditary aristocracies began giving way to appointed officials. It is also the age credited with Confucius and the first great debates about how a ruler should govern.

Shu Kingdom (China, AD 221–AD 263).label: Shu Kingdom
Shu Kingdom (China, AD 221–AD 263).prose:
[China, AD 221–AD 263] Shu Kingdom. First capital: 成都 (四川成都), latitude: 30.66, longitude: 104.06. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Liu Bei's state in the Sichuan basin, one of the three rivals that carved up the Han empire, defended by mountain passes and sustained by the fertile Chengdu plain. Its chancellor Zhuge Liang and general Guan Yu became the most famous figures of the era, later worshipped as gods of wisdom and loyalty. Militarily the weakest of the three, it was overrun by Wei in 263.

Later Tang Dynasty (China, AD 923–AD 936.label: Later Tang Dynasty
Later Tang Dynasty (China, AD 923–AD 936.prose:
[China, AD 923–AD 936] Later Tang Dynasty. First capital: 洛阳 (河南洛阳), latitude: 34.68, longitude: 112.45. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Shatuo Turkish Li family, who had taken the Tang imperial surname, overthrew the Later Liang and claimed to be restoring the great dynasty. They ruled from Luoyang over the largest territory any of the Five Dynasties held, but succession disputes among adopted sons and generals kept the court unstable. A rebellious son-in-law with Khitan backing brought it down in little over a decade.

People’s Republic of China (China, AD 19.label: People’s Republic of China
People’s Republic of China (China, AD 19.prose:
[China, AD 1949–AD 2016] People’s Republic of China. First capital: 北京, latitude: 39.92, longitude: 116.38. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded after the Communist victory in the civil war, the new state pushed through land reform and mass literacy, then the catastrophic Great Leap Forward famine and the upheaval of the Cultural Revolution. From 1978 market reforms and opening to foreign trade produced the fastest large-scale industrialisation in history, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty and turning a rural society into an urban one within two generations.

Qin Dynasty (China, 221 BC–206 BC).label: Qin Dynasty
Qin Dynasty (China, 221 BC–206 BC).prose:
[China, 221 BC–206 BC] Qin Dynasty. First capital: 咸阳 (陕西咸阳), latitude: 34.33, longitude: 108.71. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The First Emperor's conquest of the remaining warring states created a single Chinese empire governed not by hereditary lords but by appointed officials in commanderies and counties. Script, coinage, weights, measures and even cart axle widths were standardised, frontier walls linked, and dissenting scholarship suppressed. The dynasty collapsed within a few years of the emperor's death, but its administrative template underpinned two millennia of Chinese government, and its ruler left behind the terracotta army.

Southern Liang Dynasty (China, AD 502–AD.label: Southern Liang Dynasty
Southern Liang Dynasty (China, AD 502–AD.prose:
[China, AD 502–AD 557] Southern Liang Dynasty. First capital: 建康 (江苏南京), latitude: 32.06, longitude: 118.77. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The longest-lived of the southern regimes, dominated by Emperor Wu, whose nearly fifty-year reign made Jiankang a centre of Buddhist devotion, learning and literary compilation; he took monastic vows repeatedly and had to be ransomed back by his court. The dynasty ended in catastrophe when the defector Hou Jing rebelled and sacked the capital, starving the emperor in his own palace. The southern aristocracy never recovered, and the weakened Chen succeeded it.

Chen Dynasty (China, AD 557–AD 589).label: Chen Dynasty
Chen Dynasty (China, AD 557–AD 589).prose:
[China, AD 557–AD 589] Chen Dynasty. First capital: 建康 (江苏南京), latitude: 32.06, longitude: 118.77. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The last and weakest of the Southern Dynasties, founded by a general who seized a court already wrecked by rebellion and holding little more than the lower Yangtze. Its cultured, poetry-writing final ruler was captured when Sui armies crossed the river, ending nearly three centuries of division between north and south.

Shang Dynasty (China, 1600 BC–1046 BC).label: Shang Dynasty
Shang Dynasty (China, 1600 BC–1046 BC).prose:
[China, 1600 BC–1046 BC] Shang Dynasty. First capital: 亳 (河南商丘) - 殷 (河南安阳), latitude: 34.44, longitude: 115.65. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The first Chinese dynasty confirmed by its own written records, ruling the Yellow River plain from a series of capitals, the last and greatest at Anyang. Its kings consulted ancestors and gods by heating ox bones and turtle shells and reading the cracks, and the inscriptions scratched on them are the ancestors of the Chinese script still used today. Shang workshops cast ritual bronzes of a technical brilliance unmatched anywhere in the ancient world, and royal tombs held chariots, jade and hundreds of sacrificed retainers. The Zhou overthrew the last king at Muye and justified it with the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven.

Liao Dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 1214).label: Liao Dynasty
Liao Dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 1214).prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 1214] Liao Dynasty. First capital: 上京 (内蒙赤峰市巴林左旗), latitude: 44.2, longitude: 119.25. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Khitan, a horse-riding people from the steppe fringe of Manchuria, built an empire that ruled northern China, Mongolia and much of Manchuria from five mobile capitals, taxing settled farmers and nomads under separate systems of law. They forced the Song to pay annual tribute for peace, and their name travelled west as 'Cathay', the word by which Europeans knew China. Even after the Jurchen overthrew them, a Khitan remnant founded the Qara Khitai state in Central Asia, carrying the dynasty's memory far beyond China.

Western Zhou Period (China, 1046 BC–771.label: Western Zhou Period
Western Zhou Period (China, 1046 BC–771.prose:
[China, 1046 BC–771 BC] Western Zhou Period. First capital: 洛邑 (河南洛阳), latitude: 34.68, longitude: 112.45. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

After overthrowing the Shang, the Zhou kings justified their conquest with the Mandate of Heaven — the idea that rule is granted by Heaven and forfeited by misgovernment, an argument used in Chinese politics for the next three thousand years. Land was parcelled out to relatives and allies as hereditary domains, and inscribed ritual bronzes recording grants and campaigns are the richest documents of the age. When nomadic Quanrong attackers sacked the western capital in 771, the court fled east and royal authority became largely ceremonial.

Later Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 951–AD 960.label: Later Zhou Dynasty
Later Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 951–AD 960.prose:
[China, AD 951–AD 960] Later Zhou Dynasty. First capital: 汴京 (开封), latitude: 34.78, longitude: 114.34. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The last of the Five Dynasties, and the one that laid the groundwork for reunification. Emperor Shizong reformed the army, curbed monastic landholding and melted down bronze Buddhas for coin, then campaigned successfully against the Southern Tang and the Khitan. His death left a child on the throne, and his general Zhao Kuangyin took power to found the Song.

Southern Qi Dynasty (China, AD 479–AD 50.label: Southern Qi Dynasty
Southern Qi Dynasty (China, AD 479–AD 50.prose:
[China, AD 479–AD 502] Southern Qi Dynasty. First capital: 建康 (江苏南京), latitude: 32.06, longitude: 118.77. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The second of the Southern Dynasties, founded when Xiao Daocheng seized the throne from the Liu Song. It lasted barely two decades, torn apart by purges within the imperial clan and by a run of short, violent reigns, before a cousin of the ruling house declared the Liang dynasty. Despite the political chaos, its court at Jiankang patronised Buddhist art and refined literary criticism, and its tomb sculpture and celadon wares are among the finest of the age.

Southern Song (China, AD 1127–AD 1279).label: Southern Song
Southern Song (China, AD 1127–AD 1279).prose:
[China, AD 1127–AD 1279] Southern Song. First capital: 临安 (杭州), latitude: 30.29, longitude: 120.16. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

After Jurchen armies sacked Kaifeng and carried off two emperors, the Song court fled south and rebuilt itself at Lin'an (Hangzhou), abandoning the northern heartland for good. The truncated empire became the richest and most commercialised society on earth, with paper money, ocean-going junks, printed books, gunpowder weapons and cities of a million people. Neo-Confucian philosophy took its classic shape here, and landscape painting reached a spare, misty perfection, until Mongol armies ended it at the sea battle of Yamen.

Eastern Zhou Period (China, 770 BC–256 B.label: Eastern Zhou Period
Eastern Zhou Period (China, 770 BC–256 B.prose:
[China, 770 BC–256 BC] Eastern Zhou Period. First capital: 咸阳 (陕西咸阳), latitude: 34.33, longitude: 108.71. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

With the Zhou kings reduced to ceremonial figures after fleeing east to Luoyang, real power passed to competing states that fought, allied and swallowed one another for five centuries. Iron tools, mass infantry armies, coined money and written law codes replaced the old chariot aristocracy, and the crisis of the old order produced Confucius, Laozi, Mozi and the other 'hundred schools' of thought. The contest ended with Qin's conquest of all rivals and the first unified empire.

Min Kingdom (China, AD 909–AD 945).label: Min Kingdom
Min Kingdom (China, AD 909–AD 945).prose:
[China, AD 909–AD 945] Min Kingdom. First capital: 北京, latitude: 39.92, longitude: 116.38. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

One of the Ten Kingdoms that fragmented China after the Tang collapse, Min controlled the coast of Fujian from its capital at Fuzhou. Its rulers fortified Quanzhou and Fuzhou as ports, encouraging maritime trade, tea cultivation and ceramics exports, and Chinese settlement pushed deeper into the region's hills. Family feuds and civil war tore the kingdom apart, and it was divided between Southern Tang and Wuyue.

Liu Song Dynasty (China, AD 420–AD 479).label: Liu Song Dynasty
Liu Song Dynasty (China, AD 420–AD 479).prose:
[China, AD 420–AD 479] Liu Song Dynasty. First capital: 建康 (江苏南京), latitude: 32.06, longitude: 118.77. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded when the general Liu Yu deposed the last Jin emperor, this was the first and strongest of the Southern Dynasties that ruled from Jiankang while the north lay under non-Chinese regimes. Its early decades brought settled government, land registration and prosperity in the Yangtze region, though the court soon tore itself apart in murderous succession struggles. Southern poetry, landscape painting and Buddhist scholarship flourished under its patronage.

Han Dynasties (China, 206 BC–AD 220).label: Han Dynasties
Han Dynasties (China, 206 BC–AD 220).prose:
[China, 206 BC–AD 220] Han Dynasties. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Four centuries of imperial rule that set the pattern for the Chinese state: a centralised bureaucracy staffed by men trained in the Confucian classics, state monopolies on salt and iron, and a standing frontier army. Armies pushed into Central Asia, Korea and the south, opening the Silk Road caravan routes that carried Chinese silk toward Rome. Paper, the seismoscope, the wheelbarrow and the first great dynastic history all belong to this era, and the majority Chinese ethnic group still calls itself 'Han'.

Northern Qi Dynasty (China, AD 550–AD 57.label: Northern Qi Dynasty
Northern Qi Dynasty (China, AD 550–AD 57.prose:
[China, AD 550–AD 577] Northern Qi Dynasty. First capital: 鄴 (河北省临漳县), latitude: 36.34, longitude: 114.6. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Gao family took over the eastern half of the divided Wei realm, ruling from Ye on the North China Plain over the richest and most populous territory of the north. The court was notorious for murderous palace intrigue, yet its workshops produced some of the finest Buddhist sculpture ever made in China, the serene columnar figures in white marble and limestone from Qingzhou and Xiangtangshan. Its armies were broken by the Northern Zhou in 577.

Wei Kingdom (China, AD 220–AD 265).label: Wei Kingdom
Wei Kingdom (China, AD 220–AD 265).prose:
[China, AD 220–AD 265] Wei Kingdom. First capital: 洛阳 (河南洛阳), latitude: 34.68, longitude: 112.45. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The northernmost and strongest of the three states that divided China after the Han collapse, founded when Cao Cao's son deposed the last Han emperor. Wei controlled the Yellow River heartland, revived agriculture through military farming colonies, and introduced the nine-rank system for choosing officials that entrenched great families for centuries. Real power slipped to the Sima clan, who overthrew Wei and founded the Jin dynasty that briefly reunified China.

Ming Dynasty (China, AD 1368–AD 1644).label: Ming Dynasty
Ming Dynasty (China, AD 1368–AD 1644).prose:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1644] Ming Dynasty. First capital: 應天府  (江苏南京), latitude: 32.05, longitude: 118.76. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded by a peasant rebel who drove out the Mongol Yuan, the Ming restored Han Chinese rule and rebuilt the empire around a rigorous Confucian bureaucracy and the civil service examinations. The capital moved to Beijing, where the Forbidden City was raised; the Great Wall took its familiar brick form; and Zheng He's treasure fleets reached East Africa before the court abandoned such voyages. Ming blue-and-white porcelain became the first truly global luxury commodity, traded from Manila to Amsterdam.

Western Jin Dynasty (China, AD 265–AD 31.label: Western Jin Dynasty
Western Jin Dynasty (China, AD 265–AD 31.prose:
[China, AD 265–AD 316] Western Jin Dynasty. First capital: 洛阳 (河南洛阳), latitude: 34.68, longitude: 112.45. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Sima Yan seized power from the Wei state and in 280 finally reunited China after generations of Three Kingdoms warfare — a reunification that lasted barely a decade before collapsing. The ruinous War of the Eight Princes turned imperial relatives against each other and drew in nomadic auxiliaries who soon fought for themselves. The sack of Luoyang in 311 and the capture of two emperors sent the elite fleeing south, beginning nearly three centuries of division.

Sui Dynasty (China, AD 581–AD 618).label: Sui Dynasty
Sui Dynasty (China, AD 581–AD 618).prose:
[China, AD 581–AD 618] Sui Dynasty. First capital: 大兴 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Two emperors reunified China after nearly four centuries of division, rebuilding a centralised bureaucracy, standardising law and coinage, and driving vast conscript labour projects—above all the Grand Canal linking the rice-growing south to the northern capitals. Ruinous campaigns against Korea and relentless corvée demands broke the regime within a generation. The Tang inherited its institutions and its canal, and built three centuries of prosperity on them.

Song (China, AD 960–AD 1279).label: Song
Song (China, AD 960–AD 1279).prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 1279] Song. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

An age when China's wealth and technology outran its armies. Printing, paper money, gunpowder weapons, the magnetic compass and vast commercial cities made this one of the most inventive societies of the medieval world, while examination-recruited scholar-officials replaced the old aristocracy and neo-Confucian philosophy took shape. Militarily the dynasty was on the defensive throughout, paying tribute to northern neighbours, losing the north to the Jurchen in 1127, and finally falling to the Mongols.

Northern Song (China, AD 960–AD 1127).label: Northern Song
Northern Song (China, AD 960–AD 1127).prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 1127] Northern Song. First capital: 汴梁 (开封), latitude: 34.78, longitude: 114.34. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

China reunified under a civilian bureaucracy recruited by written examination rather than birth, with its capital at the commercial city of Kaifeng. It was a period of extraordinary invention and prosperity — printed books, paper money, gunpowder weapons, coal-fired ironworks, monumental landscape painting — coupled with chronic military weakness against the Liao and Xi Xia. Jurchen armies sacked Kaifeng in 1127 and carried off the emperor, driving the court south.

Eastern Wei Dynasty (China, AD 534–AD 55.label: Eastern Wei Dynasty
Eastern Wei Dynasty (China, AD 534–AD 55.prose:
[China, AD 534–AD 550] Eastern Wei Dynasty. First capital: 鄴 (河北省临漳县), latitude: 36.34, longitude: 114.6. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

A short-lived rump state created when the Northern Wei split in two, with a puppet Tuoba emperor at Ye and real power held by the warlord Gao Huan and his Xianbei army. Its constant warfare with the rival Western Wei defined the balance of northern China until Gao's son deposed the emperor and founded the Northern Qi. The period left magnificent Buddhist sculpture in the Hebei style and cave temples at Xiangtangshan.

Eastern Han Dynasty (China, AD 25–AD 220.label: Eastern Han Dynasty
Eastern Han Dynasty (China, AD 25–AD 220.prose:
[China, AD 25–AD 220] Eastern Han Dynasty. First capital: 洛阳 (河南洛阳), latitude: 34.68, longitude: 112.45. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

After a usurpation and civil war, the Han were restored with a new capital at Luoyang, further east than the old seat at Chang'an. Paper-making, the seismoscope and advances in ironworking date from these years, and Buddhism first reached China along the Silk Road caravan routes. Power drifted from the throne to court eunuchs, consort clans and great landholding families, and after the Yellow Turban rebellion the empire broke apart into the Three Kingdoms.

Jin Dynasty (China, AD 265–AD 420).label: Jin Dynasty
Jin Dynasty (China, AD 265–AD 420).prose:
[China, AD 265–AD 420] Jin Dynasty. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded by the Jurchen chieftain Aguda in the forests of Manchuria, this state destroyed the Khitan Liao and then the Northern Song, capturing two emperors and taking all of China north of the Huai River. Its rulers governed a mixed population through a dual system, adopted Chinese bureaucracy and script, and made Beijing a capital for the first time. Mongol invasions ground it down over two decades until its last emperor died in 1234.

Northern Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 557–AD.label: Northern Zhou Dynasty
Northern Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 557–AD.prose:
[China, AD 557–AD 581] Northern Zhou Dynasty. First capital: 长安 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

The Yuwen clan ruled the poorer western half of the north, compensating with the fubing system of self-supporting soldier-farmers and a tightly bound Guanlong aristocracy. Emperor Wu suppressed Buddhism and Daoism in 574 to seize monastic wealth and manpower, then conquered the Northern Qi in 577 to unify the north. His son's regent, Yang Jian, took the throne in 581 and founded the Sui.

Western Han Dynasty (China, 206 BC–AD 23.label: Western Han Dynasty
Western Han Dynasty (China, 206 BC–AD 23.prose:
[China, 206 BC–AD 23] Western Han Dynasty. First capital: 长安 (陕西西安), latitude: 34.3, longitude: 109.02. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

Founded by a village official turned rebel, Liu Bang, this was the dynasty that made the Qin experiment in unified empire permanent. From the capital at Chang'an, Emperor Wu pushed armies deep into Central Asia and Korea, made Confucian learning the basis of official recruitment, and nationalised salt and iron; Zhang Qian's embassies west opened the routes later called the Silk Road. Sima Qian wrote the first great Chinese history under this dynasty, and paper, the seismoscope and sophisticated iron casting all belong to the Han world.

Qing Dynasty (China, AD 1644–AD 1911).label: Qing Dynasty
Qing Dynasty (China, AD 1644–AD 1911).prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1911] Qing Dynasty. First capital: 京师顺天府 (北京), latitude: 39.92, longitude: 116.38. Period definition from CHGIS: Major Chinese Periods Chronology — Merrick Lex Berman, 2015.

China's last imperial dynasty, established by the Manchus, who ruled a multi-ethnic empire encompassing Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang and forced Chinese men to wear the queue as a sign of submission. The eighteenth century brought unprecedented prosperity, population growth and territorial expansion; the nineteenth brought the Opium Wars, unequal treaties, the catastrophic Taiping rebellion and foreign concessions. The court's failure to reform fast enough ended in the 1911 revolution and the abdication of a child emperor.

Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sé.node: Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sévère) (Greece, 499 BC–449 BC)
Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sé.label: Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sévère)
Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sé.prose:
[Attique (Grèce), 499 BC–449 BC] Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sévère). Period definition from Corpus vasorum antiquorum, France. Fascicule 1, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 1 — 1923.

The technique inverted: the background was painted black and the figures left in reserved clay, so anatomy and drapery could be drawn with a flexible brushline instead of scratched in. In the decades around the Persian Wars, painters exploited this to attempt foreshortening, three-quarter faces and convincing weight-bearing bodies - the same restrained naturalism seen in contemporary sculpture such as the Kritios Boy. The result is the closest surviving evidence for the lost wall-paintings of classical Athens.
Style Attique à Figures Rouges (Style Sé.source: Corpus vasorum antiquorum, France. Fascicule 1, Musée du Louvre. Fascicule 1

IJzertijd midden (Netherlands, 499 BC–24.label: IJzertijd midden
IJzertijd midden (Netherlands, 499 BC–24.prose:
[Netherlands, 499 BC–249 BC] IJzertijd midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming communities lived in scattered wooden byre-houses shared with their cattle, moving the farmstead every generation or so as the buildings decayed. Rectangular Celtic fields with low earth banks covered large stretches of the sandy soils, while in the northern clay districts people built up artificial mounds to keep dry. Burials are modest, and iron working became routine.

Nieuwe tijd A (Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 1.label: Nieuwe tijd A
Nieuwe tijd A (Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 1.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 1650] Nieuwe tijd A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The century and a half in which the northern Netherlands broke from Habsburg Spain, turned Calvinist, and built a trading empire run by chartered companies. Amsterdam swelled behind its new ring of canals, and finds from this phase — majolica, early Chinese export porcelain, pipe bowls, whaling gear — track a society suddenly plugged into Asia and the Atlantic. Urban archaeology of the period is unusually rich because rubbish went into brick-lined cesspits that sealed and preserved it.

Middeleeuwen vroeg D (Netherlands, AD 90.label: Middeleeuwen vroeg D
Middeleeuwen vroeg D (Netherlands, AD 90.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 900–AD 1050] Middeleeuwen vroeg D. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Viking pressure eased and local rulers filled the political gap: counts in Holland and Gelre, and the bishops of Utrecht, built up territorial lordships. New trading centres such as Tiel and Deventer took over Dorestad's role, and the first dikes and drainage ditches appeared on the coastal peat. Ringforts, mottes and early stone churches mark the emergence of a settled feudal order.

Romeinse tijd midden B (Netherlands, AD.label: Romeinse tijd midden B
Romeinse tijd midden B (Netherlands, AD.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 150–AD 270] Romeinse tijd midden B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The frontier zone reached its greatest prosperity – dense rural settlement, brick and tile industries, busy river shipping – before conditions turned in the third century. Raids from across the Rhine, political instability and the breakaway Gallic Empire disrupted supply and administration, and villas and forts were damaged or deserted. By around 270 much of the limes had been given up, closing the classic Roman era in the delta.

Neolithicum midden A (Netherlands, 4199.label: Neolithicum midden A
Neolithicum midden A (Netherlands, 4199.prose:
[Netherlands, 4199 BC–3399 BC] Neolithicum midden A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Communities in the delta and river wetlands of the Swifterbant tradition kept cattle and pigs and grew a little grain while still relying heavily on fish, fowl and wild plants - a drawn-out, part-time route into farming. Their settlements on river dunes and levees, sealed under later peat and clay, preserve house plans, fish traps and even ard-marked fields, giving an unusually detailed picture of daily life.

Nieuwe tijd (Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 205.label: Nieuwe tijd
Nieuwe tijd (Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 205.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 2050] Nieuwe tijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The Dutch archaeological catch-all for the modern era, running from the Reformation and the revolt against Spain through the Republic, the Kingdom, industrialisation and the present. Material culture becomes mass-produced and datable to the decade: tin-glazed earthenware, clay pipes, brick housing, then factory ceramics and machine-made glass. Excavations of this period often deal with urban cesspits, harbour fills, polders and shipwrecks, where documents and dug evidence can be checked against each other.

Romeinse tijd vroeg (Netherlands, 11 BC–.label: Romeinse tijd vroeg
Romeinse tijd vroeg (Netherlands, 11 BC–.prose:
[Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 70] Romeinse tijd vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Roman forces campaigned across the Rhine and built supply bases and camps in the delta, treating the region first as a springboard for conquering Germania and then, after that project failed, as the frontier itself. Local tribes were reorganised into Roman-recognised groups, above all the Batavians, who paid tribute in soldiers rather than grain. Native farmsteads changed slowly, but imported pottery, coins and army demand for food began reshaping the rural economy.

IJzertijd laat (Netherlands, 249 BC–11 B.label: IJzertijd laat
IJzertijd laat (Netherlands, 249 BC–11 B.prose:
[Netherlands, 249 BC–11 BC] IJzertijd laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Contact with the Celtic world to the south intensified: imported goods, the first coinage, and larger, more organised settlements. Tribal names enter history through Roman writers, among them the Batavi, Frisii and Eburones. Caesar's campaigns and the Augustan advance to the Rhine ended local independence in the south and made the river a frontier.

Neolithicum laat B (Netherlands, 2449 BC.label: Neolithicum laat B
Neolithicum laat B (Netherlands, 2449 BC.prose:
[Netherlands, 2449 BC–1999 BC] Neolithicum laat B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Bell Beaker communities dominate, burying their dead under barrows with finely decorated beakers, archers' wristguards, flint daggers and the occasional copper or gold ornament. Later Veluwe and Barbed Wire beaker styles carry the tradition through to the start of the Bronze Age, and metalworking becomes a regular, if still rare, part of life.

Middeleeuwen laat B (Netherlands, AD 125.label: Middeleeuwen laat B
Middeleeuwen laat B (Netherlands, AD 125.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1250–AD 1500] Middeleeuwen laat B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Towns came into their own, with Dordrecht, Utrecht, Deventer and Kampen trading grain, cloth and beer across the Hanseatic and North Sea networks. Sinking reclaimed peat and storm surges reshaped the coast, drowning villages and enlarging the Zuiderzee, while communities organised water boards to fight back. Political fragmentation gave way to Burgundian control, setting up the later Netherlands as a single state.

Nieuwe tijd C (Netherlands, AD 1850–AD 2.label: Nieuwe tijd C
Nieuwe tijd C (Netherlands, AD 1850–AD 2.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1850–AD 2050] Nieuwe tijd C. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Railways, steam pumping, the great reclamation schemes and explosive urban growth transformed the Dutch landscape, followed by two world wars and post-war reconstruction. Archaeology here includes factory sites, defence lines, bunkers, crash sites and the drained Zuiderzee polders, where the seabed gave up hundreds of wrecks. It is the period where excavation shades into living memory and industrial heritage.

Neolithicum laat (Netherlands, 2849 BC–1.label: Neolithicum laat
Neolithicum laat (Netherlands, 2849 BC–1.prose:
[Netherlands, 2849 BC–1999 BC] Neolithicum laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The dead were now buried singly under round barrows with a beaker, a battle axe or a dagger, first in the Corded Ware or Single Grave tradition and then in the Bell Beaker style. Copper and gold objects appear, along with flint daggers imitating metal ones, and wheeled transport and wool-bearing sheep reshaped the rural economy. This is the period in which the barrow landscapes of the sandy soils took their lasting form.

Romeinse tijd laat A (Netherlands, AD 27.label: Romeinse tijd laat A
Romeinse tijd laat A (Netherlands, AD 27.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 270–AD 350] Romeinse tijd laat A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

After the crisis of the 250s–260s the Rhine frontier was rebuilt on a smaller scale, with fewer, stronger fortifications and a heavier reliance on soldiers recruited from beyond the river. Large parts of the countryside emptied out, and villa estates in the south fell out of use. Coin hoards and burnt farmsteads from these decades mark an unsettled landscape of raids and reorganisation.

Neolithicum vroeg (Netherlands, 5299 BC–.label: Neolithicum vroeg
Neolithicum vroeg (Netherlands, 5299 BC–.prose:
[Netherlands, 5299 BC–4199 BC] Neolithicum vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming entered the Low Countries, first as an intrusive settlement of loess-soil villages in the far south and then as a slow blurring of frontiers with the hunter-fisher communities of the wet north. Longhouses, cereal fields and cattle appear alongside people who still lived largely from the marshes and rivers. It is one of Europe's clearest examples of an agricultural frontier that stalled for centuries before advancing.

Middeleeuwen vroeg C (Netherlands, AD 72.label: Middeleeuwen vroeg C
Middeleeuwen vroeg C (Netherlands, AD 72.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 725–AD 900] Middeleeuwen vroeg C. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The Frankish takeover of Frisia and the Carolingian empire's expansion brought churches, tithes and royal estates to the region. Dorestad reached its peak as an emporium, its wooden quays stretching along the Rhine and its workshops handling Rhineland pottery, glass and coin. From the 830s Viking fleets raided repeatedly, and the trading town declined.

Mesolithicum (Netherlands, 8799 BC–4899.label: Mesolithicum
Mesolithicum (Netherlands, 8799 BC–4899.prose:
[Netherlands, 8799 BC–4899 BC] Mesolithicum. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Postglacial forests of birch, pine and oak filled the sandy soils and river valleys, and small mobile bands hunted, fished and gathered hazelnuts along the streams and lakeshores. Their toolkit shrank to microliths hafted into arrows and knives; dugout canoes and paddles from Dutch bogs show how much travel went by water. Meanwhile the North Sea rose steadily, drowning the vast hunting grounds of Doggerland and reshaping the coast into something recognisable.

Bronstijd vroeg (Netherlands, 1999 BC–17.label: Bronstijd vroeg
Bronstijd vroeg (Netherlands, 1999 BC–17.prose:
[Netherlands, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Bronstijd vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Metal arrived only in a trickle, and much daily equipment was still flint and stone; the crude "barbed wire" decorated beakers of this phase carry on Bell Beaker potting habits. Communities were small and mobile, burying a few individuals under earthen mounds that reused and extended older Neolithic barrow groups. The real transformation came later, when permanent longhouse farms took hold.

Bronstijd midden (Netherlands, 1799 BC–1.label: Bronstijd midden
Bronstijd midden (Netherlands, 1799 BC–1.prose:
[Netherlands, 1799 BC–1099 BC] Bronstijd midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farmsteads with long byre houses sheltering people and cattle under one roof became the standard settlement form, surrounded by fields and cattle enclosures. Communities of the Hilversum tradition in the south and the Elp group in the north raised round barrows, often in rows along tracks, before cremation and urnfields took over. All bronze had to be imported, arriving through exchange networks reaching to Britain, central Germany and beyond.

Neolithicum vroeg B (Netherlands, 4899 B.label: Neolithicum vroeg B
Neolithicum vroeg B (Netherlands, 4899 B.prose:
[Netherlands, 4899 BC–4199 BC] Neolithicum vroeg B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

After the Bandkeramik villages were abandoned, the loess belt was occupied by successor groups while, in the wetlands to the north, Swifterbant communities began making pottery and keeping a few animals without giving up hunting and fishing. Excavated riverbank and dune sites preserve fishtraps, canoes and food remains in waterlogged detail. The result is an unusually clear record of foragers adopting farming on their own terms.

Middeleeuwen laat (Netherlands, AD 1050–.label: Middeleeuwen laat
Middeleeuwen laat (Netherlands, AD 1050–.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1500] Middeleeuwen laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The centuries of systematic reclamation, when peat bogs were drained on a huge scale, dikes closed off the coast, and windmills and water boards were invented to keep the new land dry. The drained peat shrank and sank, causing floods that formed the Zuiderzee and forced ever more engineering. Trading towns multiplied and grew rich, and by the close of the period the counties and duchies had been gathered under Burgundian rule.

Neolithicum midden B (Netherlands, 3399.label: Neolithicum midden B
Neolithicum midden B (Netherlands, 3399.prose:
[Netherlands, 3399 BC–2849 BC] Neolithicum midden B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The centuries when farming communities north of the great rivers built the hunebedden — the boulder-slab megalithic tombs of Drenthe — as part of the Funnel Beaker (TRB) world. To the west, in the delta wetlands, Vlaardingen and related groups mixed cereal growing and stock keeping with fishing and fowling, showing that the Dutch "Neolithic" arrived piecemeal rather than all at once. Pottery, polished flint axes and the first substantial burial monuments make this the period when the landscape began to be permanently marked.

Middeleeuwen vroeg A (Netherlands, AD 45.label: Middeleeuwen vroeg A
Middeleeuwen vroeg A (Netherlands, AD 45.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 450–AD 525] Middeleeuwen vroeg A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The generations immediately after Roman authority vanished, when towns, villas and roads in the river area fell out of use and the population thinned dramatically. Terp mounds in the north stayed occupied, while newcomers from across the Rhine filtered into the emptied landscape. Coins and pottery become scarce, making this one of the least visible periods in Dutch archaeology.

Nieuwe tijd B (Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1.label: Nieuwe tijd B
Nieuwe tijd B (Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1850] Nieuwe tijd B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The long stretch from the height of the Republic through its decline, French annexation, and the founding of the Kingdom. Land reclamation, peat cutting and windmill drainage reshaped the countryside, while towns filled with Delftware, refined white clay pipes and imported tea and tobacco wares. Datable pipe stems and pottery marks from this phase let archaeologists pin deposits to within a few decades.

Romeinse tijd laat B (Netherlands, AD 35.label: Romeinse tijd laat B
Romeinse tijd laat B (Netherlands, AD 35.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 350–AD 450] Romeinse tijd laat B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Roman authority faded from the Rhine delta in stages, with garrisons withdrawn or absorbed into Frankish forces and imperial coin drying up. Newcomers from the north and east settled the emptied river landscape, producing handmade pottery and burying their dead with weapons and brooches in a style already recognisably early medieval. What survived of Roman infrastructure – roads, ruined forts, church-linked memories at Maastricht – became raw material for the Frankish kingdoms.

IJzertijd (Netherlands, 799 BC–11 BC).label: IJzertijd
IJzertijd (Netherlands, 799 BC–11 BC).prose:
[Netherlands, 799 BC–11 BC] IJzertijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Iron, smelted locally from bog ore, replaced imported bronze and put decent tools in far more hands. People lived on small family farms with byre-houses, laid out rectangular Celtic field systems, and in the northern salt marshes began raising dwelling mounds above the tides. The period closes with Roman armies on the Rhine and the Low Countries divided between an occupied south and a free north.

Romeinse tijd midden (Netherlands, AD 70.label: Romeinse tijd midden
Romeinse tijd midden (Netherlands, AD 70.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 70–AD 270] Romeinse tijd midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

With the Batavian revolt crushed, the Rhine frontier settled into two centuries of relative stability: forts rebuilt in stone, a military road along the river, and the towns of Ulpia Noviomagus and Forum Hadriani granted urban status. Rural families adopted Roman goods and building styles while keeping much of their older farming life, and villa estates spread across the loess soils of the south. The period ends with raids, frontier disruption and the abandonment of much of the limes.

Neolithicum vroeg A (Netherlands, 5299 B.label: Neolithicum vroeg A
Neolithicum vroeg A (Netherlands, 5299 B.prose:
[Netherlands, 5299 BC–4899 BC] Neolithicum vroeg A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Bandkeramik farmers settled the fertile loess of southern Limburg, building timber longhouses in small hamlets and bringing wheat, barley, cattle and pottery from central Europe. Their villages sat at the northwestern edge of the whole continental farming expansion, with foragers still occupying the sandy and marshy lands just beyond. Sites such as Elsloo and Sittard give a remarkably detailed picture of house plans, cemeteries and imported stone.

Romeinse tijd vroeg A (Netherlands, 11 B.label: Romeinse tijd vroeg A
Romeinse tijd vroeg A (Netherlands, 11 B.prose:
[Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 25] Romeinse tijd vroeg A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Drusus and his successors used the Rhine delta as a launching point for campaigns into Germania, digging canals and planting military bases such as those at Nijmegen and Velsen. The loss of Varus's legions in AD 9 ended ambitions of a province beyond the river and forced Rome to think of the Rhine as a limit. For local communities the main change was the sudden arrival of an army that had to be fed, housed and supplied.

Romeinse tijd laat (Netherlands, AD 270–.label: Romeinse tijd laat
Romeinse tijd laat (Netherlands, AD 270–.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 270–AD 450] Romeinse tijd laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Frontier defence contracted sharply: many limes forts were abandoned or replaced by heavily walled strongpoints, rural settlement thinned dramatically, and coin supply became erratic. Franks and other groups from beyond the Rhine settled inside the old province, sometimes as raiders, sometimes as Roman-sponsored soldiers and farmers. By the end of the period Roman government had effectively evaporated, leaving Frankish-led communities as the successors.

Bronstijd laat (Netherlands, 1099 BC–799.label: Bronstijd laat
Bronstijd laat (Netherlands, 1099 BC–799.prose:
[Netherlands, 1099 BC–799 BC] Bronstijd laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Burial practice shifted decisively to cremation in urns set within large, densely used urnfields, a custom shared across much of northwest Europe. Settlements of byre houses moved every generation or two across the sandy landscape, and bronze objects circulated in growing numbers alongside deliberate deposits in wet places. The first iron objects appear towards the end of the period.

Middeleeuwen vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 52.label: Middeleeuwen vroeg B
Middeleeuwen vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 52.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 525–AD 725] Middeleeuwen vroeg B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Merovingian times, known largely from row-grave cemeteries where the dead were buried with swords, brooches and glass vessels. Frisian traders worked the coast and rivers while Frankish kings pushed north, and settlements of timber longhouses spread again across the sandy soils. Dorestad and Domburg began their careers as trading places, and the first missionaries arrived.

IJzertijd vroeg (Netherlands, 799 BC–499.label: IJzertijd vroeg
IJzertijd vroeg (Netherlands, 799 BC–499.prose:
[Netherlands, 799 BC–499 BC] IJzertijd vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Iron working arrived while urnfield burial customs were still in use, and a handful of exceptionally rich graves — the Chieftain's Grave at Oss with its bent sword in a bronze situla is the famous one — show contacts with the Hallstatt elites of central Europe. Most people, though, lived in modest farmsteads and fields on the sandy uplands. Bog iron made metal locally available for the first time, without the long-distance networks bronze had required.

Romeinse tijd vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 2.label: Romeinse tijd vroeg B
Romeinse tijd vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 2.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 25–AD 70] Romeinse tijd vroeg B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The Rhine hardened into a defended border, with a line of forts, Corbulo's canal linking the rivers, and Claudius abandoning further conquest to the north. Batavian and Cananefate auxiliaries became a mainstay of the imperial army, and the emperors' German bodyguard was recruited here. The period ends violently with the Batavian revolt of AD 69–70, when Julius Civilis exploited Rome's civil war to besiege and burn frontier forts.

Bronstijd midden B (Netherlands, 1499 BC.label: Bronstijd midden B
Bronstijd midden B (Netherlands, 1499 BC.prose:
[Netherlands, 1499 BC–1099 BC] Bronstijd midden B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farmsteads with byre-houses spread widely across the sandy soils, and in the north the Elp culture built settlements that shifted every generation or two across a landscape of small fields and barrow cemeteries. Burial practice changed decisively as cremation replaced inhumation, laying the groundwork for the great urnfields of the following centuries. Bronze circulated more freely now, with local smiths casting socketed axes, sickles and ornaments.

Neolithicum laat A (Netherlands, 2849 BC.label: Neolithicum laat A
Neolithicum laat A (Netherlands, 2849 BC.prose:
[Netherlands, 2849 BC–2449 BC] Neolithicum laat A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Dominated by the Single Grave or Corded Ware culture, in which individuals were buried in a crouched position under a round barrow, men with a stone battle axe and a corded beaker. The custom spread rapidly across the sandy soils of the north and east, replacing the collective megalithic burials of the preceding centuries and reflecting new populations and ideas moving in from the east.

Romeinse tijd (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 450.label: Romeinse tijd
Romeinse tijd (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 450.prose:
[Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 450] Romeinse tijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Roman armies pushed to the Rhine and turned it into the empire's northern frontier, leaving the Netherlands split between provincial territory in the south and free Germanic lands in the north. Forts, roads, harbours and the towns of Nijmegen and Voorburg brought coined money, wheel-thrown pottery, wine and writing to farming communities that had lived in timber longhouses for centuries. Local groups such as the Batavians supplied auxiliary soldiers to Rome in extraordinary numbers, and one of them, the revolt of AD 69, nearly broke Roman control of the region. Waterlogged sites along the limes preserve leather, wooden writing tablets and whole river barges.

Bronstijd midden A (Netherlands, 1799 BC.label: Bronstijd midden A
Bronstijd midden A (Netherlands, 1799 BC.prose:
[Netherlands, 1799 BC–1499 BC] Bronstijd midden A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming communities in the low countries settled into long timber houses that sheltered people and cattle under one roof, while their dead were buried under round barrows ringed by posts. Bronze itself remained scarce and had to be imported as ingots or finished axes from Britain, central Europe and the Alps, so metal objects were prized and often deposited in rivers and bogs. Pottery of the Hilversum tradition in the south shows links across the North Sea to southern England.

Romeinse tijd midden A (Netherlands, AD.label: Romeinse tijd midden A
Romeinse tijd midden A (Netherlands, AD.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 70–AD 150] Romeinse tijd midden A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Rebuilding after the Batavian revolt fixed the shape of the frontier: a chain of auxiliary forts along the Rhine linked by a paved military road, with legionary and civilian centres at Nijmegen. Trade in Gaulish samian ware, wine and metalwork reached deep into the countryside, and local men served across the empire in Batavian and Cananefatian units. Hadrian's reign brought town charters and monumental building to the two main urban settlements.

Mesolithicum laat (Netherlands, 6449 BC–.label: Mesolithicum laat
Mesolithicum laat (Netherlands, 6449 BC–.prose:
[Netherlands, 6449 BC–4899 BC] Mesolithicum laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

In the final Mesolithic centuries the flint industry shifted to broad trapezoidal points and regular blades, and settlements clustered along wetland margins and stream valleys. Communities here were in contact with the first farmers of the loess belt to the south, exchanging goods and ideas long before adopting farming themselves. The Swifterbant sites show the result: fisher-hunters who gradually added pottery, cattle and small-scale cereal growing to an older way of life.

Middeleeuwen vroeg (Netherlands, AD 450–.label: Middeleeuwen vroeg
Middeleeuwen vroeg (Netherlands, AD 450–.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1050] Middeleeuwen vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

After the Roman frontier collapsed, much of the river country was abandoned before being resettled by Frisian, Frankish and Saxon groups living in timber farmsteads and burying their dead with weapons and jewellery. Frankish conquest and missionaries such as Willibrord and Boniface brought Christianity and Carolingian administration, and Dorestad grew into one of northwest Europe's greatest trading places. Viking raids and settlement disrupted the region before local counts and bishops began to consolidate power.

Middeleeuwen laat A (Netherlands, AD 105.label: Middeleeuwen laat A
Middeleeuwen laat A (Netherlands, AD 105.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1250] Middeleeuwen laat A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Landlords and monasteries organised the draining of the great peat bogs, laying out the long ribbon-shaped farm plots still visible in the Dutch landscape. Local lords built mottes and then stone keeps, brick came into use for churches, and the first city rights were granted. Counts of Holland, dukes of Brabant and bishops of Utrecht emerged as the region's dominant powers.

Middeleeuwen (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 150.label: Middeleeuwen
Middeleeuwen (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 150.prose:
[Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1500] Middeleeuwen. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The thousand years between Roman withdrawal and the Habsburg era, during which the Low Countries were settled by Frisians, Franks and Saxons, Christianised, and drawn into the Carolingian world. Rising sea levels and human drainage made water management the central fact of life, producing dikes, dams and polders. By the end, the region held some of Europe's densest concentrations of towns, living on cloth, shipping and trade.

Bronstijd (Netherlands, 1999 BC–799 BC).label: Bronstijd
Bronstijd (Netherlands, 1999 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Netherlands, 1999 BC–799 BC] Bronstijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Metal reached the low countries in quantity, mostly as imported bronze axes, swords and ornaments, since the region has neither copper nor tin. Farming communities lived in long timber byre houses on sandy soils, raising cattle and burying their dead first under round barrows and later in cremation urnfields. Bogs and rivers received deliberate deposits of weapons and ornaments, some of the most striking finds in Dutch archaeology.

Neolithicum midden (Netherlands, 4199 BC.label: Neolithicum midden
Neolithicum midden (Netherlands, 4199 BC.prose:
[Netherlands, 4199 BC–2849 BC] Neolithicum midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

In the wetlands and river country, Swifterbant and Hazendonk communities combined fishing, fowling and hunting with small-scale cattle keeping and cereal growing, leaving exceptionally well preserved sites in the peat and clay. On the northern sandy soils the Funnel Beaker culture raised the hunebedden, chambered tombs of glacial boulders used for collective burial with quantities of decorated pottery. Together they mark the point at which farming finally took hold across the whole country.

Neolithicum (Netherlands, 5299 BC–1999 B.label: Neolithicum
Neolithicum (Netherlands, 5299 BC–1999 B.prose:
[Netherlands, 5299 BC–1999 BC] Neolithicum. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming reached the Netherlands in two very different ways: Linear Pottery farmers settled the fertile loess of southern Limburg in longhouse villages, while in the wetlands to the north hunter-fisher communities of the Swifterbant tradition adopted cattle and cereals slowly, over centuries. Later came the Funnel Beaker builders of the hunebedden, the great boulder tombs of Drenthe, and finally Corded Ware and Bell Beaker groups burying individuals under round barrows. Waterlogged sites preserve wooden trackways, dugout canoes and even ploughed field surfaces.

Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC.node: Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC) (Syria, 1200 BC–700 BC)
Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC.label: Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC)
Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC.prose:
[Northern Levant, 1200 BC–700 BC] Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC). Syro-Hittite Northern Levant. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

After the fall of the Bronze Age empires, a patchwork of Syro-Hittite and Aramaean city-states filled northern Syria, ruling from citadels at Carchemish, Aleppo, Tell Halaf and Zincirli. They carved monumental basalt reliefs and inscribed monuments in Luwian hieroglyphs and alphabetic Aramaic, an art that fed directly into Assyrian palace sculpture. Their independence ended with the Assyrian conquests of the eighth century.
Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC.source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (160.node: Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (1600-1000 BC) (Iran, 1600 BC–1000 BC)
Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (160.label: Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (1600-1000 BC)
Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (160.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1600 BC–1000 BC] Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (1600-1000 BC). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Middle Assyrian/Middle Babylonian/Kassite Mesopotamia, LBA-Early Iron Age Mesopotamia, incl. Sea Peoples. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

After the fall of Hammurabi's dynasty, power in the region was shared between Kassite Babylon, the rising Middle Assyrian kingdom and the Middle Elamite state on the Iranian side. It was an age of literate diplomacy, with kings exchanging letters and gifts across the Near East, and of monumental building such as the great ziggurat at Chogha Zanbil. Elamite armies eventually sacked Babylon and carried off trophies including the stele of Hammurabi, before the whole system unravelled around 1100 BC.
