Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-.label: Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-1258)
Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-.prose:
[Middle East, AD 1037–AD 1258] Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-1258). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Turkic dynasties ruled the Iranian world in these centuries: first the Seljuqs, then the Khwarazmshahs, who inherited much of their territory and pushed into Afghanistan against the Ghurids. Persian remained the language of administration and poetry, and the period produced great brick minarets, madrasas and lustre ceramics. It ended catastrophically with the Mongol invasions, which shattered the Khwarazmian state and destroyed cities across the region.
Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-.source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720.node: Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720-540 BC) (Egypt, 720 BC–540 BC)
Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720.label: Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720-540 BC)
Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720.prose:
[Middle East, 720 BC–540 BC] Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720-540 BC). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Two successive Mesopotamian empires dominated the region: Assyria, which invaded Egypt in the 670s and sacked Thebes, and then Babylon, which inherited the western provinces after Nineveh fell. For Egypt this meant foreign armies in the Nile Delta, the end of Kushite rule and the rise of the Saite dynasty as a client-turned-rival power. The whole eastern Mediterranean was drawn into a single imperial arena, a pattern the Persians would simply take over.
Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720.source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

Colonial-Modern Middle East (AD 1800-200.label: Colonial-Modern Middle East (AD 1800-2000)
Colonial-Modern Middle East (AD 1800-200.prose:
[Middle East, AD 1800–AD 2000] Colonial-Modern Middle East (AD 1800-2000). Spatial coverage: Djibouti, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Yemen. Late Ottoman-Colonial-Mandate Modern Middle east. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

France took the Gulf of Tadjoura coast in the 1880s, and Djibouti city grew as the port terminus of the railway to Addis Ababa, making it Ethiopia's outlet to the sea. Colonial rule set Afar and Issa communities against one another in a competition for political weight that outlasted independence in 1977. The port's strategic position at the mouth of the Red Sea has kept foreign fleets and garrisons there ever since.
Colonial-Modern Middle East (AD 1800-200.source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC).node: Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC) (Turkey, 2000 BC–1750 BC)
Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC).label: Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC)
Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC).prose:
[Anatolia, 2000 BC–1750 BC] Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC). Karum Anatolia. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Merchants from Assur established trading colonies in central Anatolia, above all the karum at Kanesh (Kültepe), exchanging tin and textiles for Anatolian silver and gold. Their thousands of clay tablets in Old Assyrian cuneiform are the first written records from Anatolia, naming local kings, their households and even family quarrels and debts. Out of the small competing kingdoms they describe came the Hittite state that would dominate the region.
Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC).source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

Middle Byzantine (AD 850-1200) (Albania,.label: Middle Byzantine (AD 850-1200)
Middle Byzantine (AD 850-1200) (Albania,.prose:
[Albania, AD 850–AD 1200] Middle Byzantine (AD 850-1200). Spatial coverage: Albania, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Iraq, Italy, Kenya, Lebanon. Middle Byzantine period in areas where such designations are appropriate. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Byzantine rule was reimposed over much of the region through new themes and fortified towns, competing with Bulgarian expansion under Samuel and, later, Norman raids from across the Adriatic. Churches with brick-and-stone masonry and fresco decoration went up in towns such as Berat and along the Via Egnatia. It was a frontier zone where Latin and Greek Christianity met and where control changed hands repeatedly.

This is the Umm an-Nar era, when southeastern Arabia was the land the Mesopotamians called Magan and supplied them with copper and diorite by sea. Communities built round stone towers with wells at their heart, irrigated date gardens, and buried their dead collectively in monumental circular tombs faced with dressed white stone. Imported Indus and Mesopotamian goods in these tombs show Oman sitting at the hinge of Gulf trade.

Mesopotamian kings from Sargon onward campaigned into these lands, naming Elam, Marhashi and Anshan among their rivals and trading partners. Proto-Elamite writing had faded, but Elam's kingdoms consolidated in the southwest around Susa and Anshan, setting up the long rivalry with Sumer and Akkad.

A long, austere stretch between the disruptions of the Early Bronze Age and the rise of Mycenae. People lived in small unwalled villages, made grey and yellow Minyan pottery and matt-painted jars, and buried their dead in cist graves inside or beside the settlement. Contact with Minoan Crete grew through the period, and by its close the spectacular shaft graves at Mycenae announce a new and far more hierarchical mainland society.

From their fortified capital at Hattusa, the first Hittite kings pushed out across the Anatolian plateau and into Syria, and one of them, Mursili I, marched all the way to Babylon and destroyed it. Royal succession was violent and contested, prompting edicts like that of Telipinu that tried to fix the rules of inheritance. The state archives preserve treaties, laws and annals in cuneiform, giving an unusually candid view of how an early empire justified itself.

The Hittite kingdom, ruled from the fortified mountain capital of Hattusa, grew into an empire that fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and produced the earliest surviving international peace treaty. The great palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros were at their peak, with light wells, frescoes, storage magazines and workshops supporting an export trade in oil, wine and fine pottery. The Thera eruption and a later wave of burnings ended most of it; Knossos carried on under Mycenaean administrators writing Greek in Linear B. By the close, palaces were gone, cremation and new burial customs had appeared, and survivors were living in refuge sites high in the mountains.

A wealthy Canaanite port kingdom on the Syrian coast, trading between Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean and the Hittite empire whose vassal it became. Its scribes used a 30-sign cuneiform alphabet to write their own language, preserving the Baal Cycle and other myths that transformed understanding of Canaanite religion and of the background to the Hebrew Bible. The city was burned around 1190 BC in the wave of destructions that ended the Bronze Age, and was never reoccupied, leaving its archives where they fell.

Grey burnished pottery, iron weapons and rich warrior graves mark the era, and sites like Hasanlu preserve a fortified citadel destroyed and burned around 800 BC with its inhabitants still inside. Out of this fragmented world of local chiefdoms came the Medes and, soon after, the Persians.

Madagascar was still, so far as the firm evidence goes, essentially empty of people — one of the last large habitable landmasses on Earth to be settled. Giant lemurs, elephant birds and pygmy hippos lived on an island shaped only by fire, cyclone and forest. Scattered claims of much earlier human butchery marks on bones remain contested, and the debate over when the first arrivals came is one of the liveliest in Indian Ocean archaeology.

After Jerusalem's destruction the southern Levant became a chain of imperial provinces, first Babylonian and then Persian, governed through local elites and temple institutions rather than annexed kingdoms. Under Persian rule exiles returned, the Jerusalem temple was rebuilt, and coinage, Aramaic administration and Greek trade goods spread through the region. It is the setting for the emergence of Second Temple Judaism and for Ezra and Nehemiah, and it closed with Alexander's arrival.

Claudius's invasion turned the tribal societies of southern Britain into a Roman province, with legionary fortresses, straight roads, planned towns like London, Colchester and York, and villas farming for a market economy. The north was never fully absorbed, and Hadrian's Wall fixed a garrisoned frontier across the island. Visitors can still see mosaics, bathhouses, curse tablets and writing tablets that record ordinary life in Latin. When the army and administration were withdrawn in the early fifth century, towns and coinage collapsed within a generation.

[Caucasus, AD 1200–AD 1500] Late Medieval Caucasus (AD 1200–1500). Spatial coverage: Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Syria, Turkey. Turco-Mongol, Seljuq-Georgian-Ilkhanate-Turkmen Caucasus [[1200,1500]]. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Georgia entered this era at its height, a unified kingdom with wealth from trade and a burst of church building and manuscript painting, and left it in pieces. Mongol armies arrived in the 1220s and imposed tribute, Timur's campaigns devastated the countryside repeatedly, and by the end the crown had split into the rival kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti with semi-independent princes between them. The fall of Constantinople cut the old trade and religious links westward, leaving Georgia isolated between Ottoman and Persian power.
Late Medieval Caucasus (AD 1200–1500) (G.source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

Assyrian Imperial (Turkey, 929 BC–609 BC.label: Assyrian Imperial
Assyrian Imperial (Turkey, 929 BC–609 BC.prose:
[North Syria, 929 BC–609 BC] Assyrian Imperial. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean — Hodos, Tamar., 2006.

The Neo-Assyrian kings turned Anatolia's southeastern kingdoms into provinces or tribute-payers, and their campaigns brought down the Neo-Hittite city-states and pressed against Urartu in the highlands. Royal inscriptions and palace reliefs record the machinery of it all: siege engines, mass deportations, standing armies and a road and messenger system that held a vast territory together. Assyrian collapse in 612–609 BC left a vacuum that Medes, Babylonians and later Lydians moved to fill.
Assyrian Imperial (Turkey, 929 BC–609 BC.source: Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean

Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 109.node: Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 1099 BC–899 BC)
Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 109.label: Iron Age I (Early Iron Age)
Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 109.prose:
[North Syria, 1099 BC–899 BC] Iron Age I (Early Iron Age). Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean — Hodos, Tamar., 2006.

The centuries immediately after the fall of Hattusa, when centralised palace administration and cuneiform record-keeping vanished from Anatolia. Handmade and painted wares replace standardised Hittite pottery, settlements are smaller and more defensive, and written evidence is scarce. Continuity survived mainly in the south and south-east, where local dynasts kept Hittite royal titles and hieroglyphic script alive.
Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 109.source: Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean

Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 8.node: Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 899 BC–599 BC)
Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 8.label: Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age)
Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 8.prose:
[North Syria, 899 BC–599 BC] Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age). Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. This period is used to designate the moment of Phoenician colonization in the West before the development of a distinctive Punic identity. Period definition from Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean — Hodos, Tamar., 2006.

Anatolia was divided among successor kingdoms: Neo-Hittite city-states in the southeast carrying on Bronze Age Hittite art and hieroglyphic writing, Urartu in the eastern highlands with its fortresses and canals, and Phrygia in the centre with its rock-cut monuments and tumulus burials at Gordion. Assyrian armies pressed westward for metal, horses and timber, absorbing one kingdom after another. The period's monumental reliefs and bilingual inscriptions are among the richest sources for how small states survived between empires.
Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 8.source: Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean

Roman (Israel, 62 BC–AD 325).label: Roman
Roman (Israel, 62 BC–AD 325).prose:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 62 BC–AD 325] Roman. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Iron I-II (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC).label: Iron I-II
Iron I-II (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron I-II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

The full sweep of the Iron Age here, from the collapse of Late Bronze Age Canaan through the rise of Israel, Judah, Philistia, Ammon, Moab and Edom, to their absorption by Assyria and Babylon. Over these six centuries alphabetic writing spread, olive oil and wine were produced for export, and cities grew walls, water systems and royal quarters. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem.

Byzantine (Israel, AD 325–AD 636).label: Byzantine
Byzantine (Israel, AD 325–AD 636).prose:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, AD 325–AD 636] Byzantine. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.

Persian (Israel, 538 BC–331 BC) [p0qwcp6.label: Persian
Persian (Israel, 538 BC–331 BC) [p0qwcp6.prose:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 538 BC–331 BC] Persian. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. see also Mazar, 1992. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and Judah became Yehud, a small tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire. Under governors and an increasingly powerful priesthood, much of the Hebrew Bible took shape and Aramaic became the everyday language. Coins, imported Greek pottery and administrative seal impressions show a province tied into imperial and Mediterranean networks.

Hellenistic (Israel, 321 BC–61 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Israel, 321 BC–61 BC).prose:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 321 BC–61 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

MB I-II (Israel, 1999 BC–1649 BC).label: MB I-II
MB I-II (Israel, 1999 BC–1649 BC).prose:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 1999 BC–1649 BC] MB I-II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Town life returned to the southern Levant after the collapse and rural interlude of the preceding centuries. Fortified city-states with massive earthen ramparts and multiple-entry gates dominated the plains and valleys, supported by grain, olive oil and wine and by brisk trade with Egypt, Cyprus and Syria. This is the Canaanite world at its height, and the archaeological setting for the Middle Kingdom Egyptian texts that name its rulers.

Classical Iberian Period (Spain, 399 BC–.label: Classical Iberian Period
Classical Iberian Period (Spain, 399 BC–.prose:
[Catalan area, 399 BC–199 BC] Classical Iberian Period. Equivalent to Iberian III (450-350 B.C.) and IV (350-200 B.C.) - cf. M. Diaz-Andreu & S. Keay, 1997. The Archaeology of Iberia; Dominguez in C. Sanchez & G.R. Tsetskhladze, 2001. Greek Pottery from the Iberian Peninsula. Period definition from Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).  — Belarte, M.C..

Iberian communities in eastern and southern Spain lived in dense hilltop towns, wrote in their own scripts, struck coinage and produced sharply painted pottery and stone sculpture for elite sanctuaries and tombs. Trade with Greeks, Phoenicians and Carthaginians brought wine, luxury goods and new ideas, while warrior aristocracies fought and hired themselves out as mercenaries. The Second Punic War brought Roman armies into the peninsula and began the long conquest that absorbed these societies.
Classical Iberian Period (Spain, 399 BC–.source: Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).

Early Iberian Period (Spain, 524 BC–399.label: Early Iberian Period
Early Iberian Period (Spain, 524 BC–399.prose:
[Catalan area, 524 BC–399 BC] Early Iberian Period. Period definition from Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).  — Belarte, M.C..

Native communities of eastern and southern Spain, enriched by centuries of contact with Phoenician and Greek traders, developed into the Iberian culture: fortified hilltop towns, wheel-made painted pottery, an alphabet of their own, and stone sculpture of warriors, beasts and veiled ladies. Coastal trade brought wine, oil and luxury goods inland in exchange for metals and grain. These were the peoples Carthage and then Rome would encounter and absorb.
Early Iberian Period (Spain, 524 BC–399.source: Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).

Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 43).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 43).prose:
[Roman Britain, 799 BC–AD 43] Iron Age. May be an inference, not statement / assertion. Period definition from The Oxford illustrated history of Roman Britain — Salway, Peter., 1993.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 43).source: The Oxford illustrated history of Roman Britain

Sasanian (Iraq, AD 224–AD 651).label: Sasanian
Sasanian (Iraq, AD 224–AD 651).prose:
[ancient Near East, AD 224–AD 651] Sasanian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Sasanian Iran, 224- 651 CE : portrait of a late antique empire — Daryaee, Touraj, 1967-, 2008.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.
Sasanian (Iraq, AD 224–AD 651).source: Sasanian Iran, 224- 651 CE : portrait of a late antique empire

Archaic (Spain, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Spain, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Spain, 899 BC–699 BC] Archaic. See also van Dommelen et al. (2008). Period definition from Colonial encounters in ancient Iberia Phoenician, Greek, and indigenous relations — 2009.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Spain, 899 BC–699 BC).source: Colonial encounters in ancient Iberia Phoenician, Greek, and indigenous relations

Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1739 BC).label: Isin-Larsa
Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1739 BC).prose:
[Ur, Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1739 BC] Isin-Larsa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Robins' chronology is being used in preference to Freeman's, since it seems to represent the general textbook situation more accurately. Period definition from Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1982.

Named for the two Mesopotamian cities that fought over the legacy of the fallen Ur III empire, this horizon in the east coincides with the rise of the Sukkalmah rulers of Elam, who traded, intermarried and intrigued with the kings of southern Iraq. Cuneiform contracts, cylinder seals and standardised pottery show how closely the Iranian lowlands were tied into Babylonian economic life. It ends with Hammurabi's conquests reshaping the region.
Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1739 BC).source: Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur

Early Dynastic IIIa (Iraq, 2649 BC–2549.label: Early Dynastic IIIa
Early Dynastic IIIa (Iraq, 2649 BC–2549.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2649 BC–2549 BC] Early Dynastic IIIa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Removed due to inferences in GeoDia: al-'Ubaid (5500-4000 B.C.), Uruk (4000-3250 B.C.), Jamdat Nasr periods (3250-3000 B.C.), and Ur of the Chaldees (1150-800 B.C.). Note this quote p.15: "At an archaeological congress of excavators held at Baghdad in 1929 it was agreed that the early stages of human settlement in south Mesopotamia could be classified n successive phases which should be called, after the places where the evidence for each was first discovered, the al-'Ubaid period, the Uruk period, the Jamdat Nasr period, and then the Early Dynastic period, towards the end of which (in IIIb) comes the First Dynasty of Ur." p.16: "Archaeological excavation ... does not of itself offer an absolute chronology in years B.C./A.D.". Period definition from Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1982.

The phase of the great archives from Shuruppak (Fara) and Abu Salabikh, where cuneiform tablets first carry proverbs, word lists and literary texts rather than just accounts. The spectacular graves of the Royal Cemetery at Ur, with their sacrificed attendants and imported lapis lazuli and carnelian, belong here, showing how far Sumerian trade reached into Iran and beyond.
Early Dynastic IIIa (Iraq, 2649 BC–2549.source: Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur

Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2153 BC).label: Akkadian
Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2153 BC).prose:
[Ur, Mesopotamia, 2333 BC–2153 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Removed due to inferences in GeoDia: al-'Ubaid (5500-4000 B.C.), Uruk (4000-3250 B.C.), Jamdat Nasr periods (3250-3000 B.C.), and Ur of the Chaldees (1150-800 B.C.). Note this quote p.15: "At an archaeological congress of excavators held at Baghdad in 1929 it was agreed that the early stages of human settlement in south Mesopotamia could be classified n successive phases which should be called, after the places where the evidence for each was first discovered, the al-'Ubaid period, the Uruk period, the Jamdat Nasr period, and then the Early Dynastic period, towards the end of which (in IIIb) comes the First Dynasty of Ur." p.16: "Archaeological excavation ... does not of itself offer an absolute chronology in years B.C./A.D.". Period definition from Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1982.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.
Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2153 BC).source: Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur

The Tetrarchs (Italy, AD 284–AD 312).label: The Tetrarchs
The Tetrarchs (Italy, AD 284–AD 312).prose:
[Italy, AD 284–AD 312] The Tetrarchs. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy, Turkey. Period definition from Roman art : Romulus to Constantine — Ramage, Nancy H., 1942-, 2001.

Diocletian concluded that the empire was too large for one ruler and divided authority among four — two senior emperors and two juniors — each with his own army, court and regional capital. Sweeping reforms multiplied provinces and officials, fixed prices, reorganised taxation and made the emperor a remote, ceremonial figure; the last great persecution of Christians also belongs here. The system depended on cooperation among men who mostly wanted supreme power, and it dissolved in the wars that carried Constantine to the throne.

The Soldier Emperors (Italy, AD 235–AD 2.label: The Soldier Emperors
The Soldier Emperors (Italy, AD 235–AD 2.prose:
[Italy, AD 235–AD 284] The Soldier Emperors. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy, Turkey. Period definition from Roman art : Romulus to Constantine — Ramage, Nancy H., 1942-, 2001.

For half a century emperors were made and unmade by their troops, most reigning only months before being killed; meanwhile Gothic and Persian invasions broke through the frontiers and plague and debased coinage wrecked the economy. Britain, Gaul and Palmyra broke away as separate regimes before being clawed back. Cities across the empire built walls for the first time in generations, a physical sign of how insecure life had become.

Constantine (Italy, AD 307–AD 337).label: Constantine
Constantine (Italy, AD 307–AD 337).prose:
[Italy, AD 307–AD 337] Constantine. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy, Turkey. Period definition from Roman art : Romulus to Constantine — Ramage, Nancy H., 1942-, 2001.

Sole ruler after defeating Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge and Licinius in the east, he ended the tetrarchy and refounded the empire around a new capital on the Bosphorus. His patronage transformed Christianity from a persecuted sect into the favoured religion of the state, and the Council of Nicaea in 325 set the creed still recited today. His reforms of coinage, army and administration shaped the later Roman world.

Late Phrygian (Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC).label: Late Phrygian
Late Phrygian (Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC] Late Phrygian. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

Under Persian rule the old Phrygian heartland around Gordion became part of a satrapy, its Anatolian traditions continuing alongside imported Achaemenid tastes in metalwork, seals and tumulus burial. Phrygian remained in use in inscriptions, and the cult of the mother goddess Matar (later Cybele) spread far beyond the region. Alexander's passage through Gordion in 333 BC – the setting of the Gordian knot story – brought the era to a close.
Late Phrygian (Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC).source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Middle Bronze Age (Gordion, 1999 BC–1499.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Gordion, 1999 BC–1499.prose:
[Gordion, 1999 BC–1499 BC] Middle Bronze Age. added post-GeoDia. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Gordion, 1999 BC–1499.source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Initial Early Phrygian (Turkey, 949 BC–8.label: Initial Early Phrygian
Initial Early Phrygian (Turkey, 949 BC–8.prose:
[Turkey, 949 BC–899 BC] Initial Early Phrygian. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

The earliest layers of Phrygian occupation at Gordion, when the settlement on the Sangarios began to take on the plan of a citadel with megaron-style halls. Buildings and pottery from these levels underlie the more famous city of the Midas era and the great burial mounds that surround it. For archaeologists, the phase matters mainly for dating: it anchors the start of Phrygian material culture in central Anatolia after the collapse of Hittite power.
Initial Early Phrygian (Turkey, 949 BC–8.source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Early Phrygian (Gordion, 899 BC–799 BC).label: Early Phrygian
Early Phrygian (Gordion, 899 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Gordion, 899 BC–799 BC] Early Phrygian. added post-GeoDia. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

The citadel at Gordion took shape as the seat of Phrygian power in central Anatolia, with a monumental stone gate, ranks of megaron halls and a terrace of industrial buildings where women wove and ground grain on a near-industrial scale. Grey burnished and geometric painted pottery, bronze fibulae and the earliest Phrygian inscriptions belong to this horizon. A catastrophic fire ended the phase, sealing whole rooms of furniture, textiles and vessels and giving archaeologists an unusually complete snapshot of Iron Age life.
Early Phrygian (Gordion, 899 BC–799 BC).source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 2499 BC–1999 B.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 2499 BC–1999 B.prose:
[Turkey, 2499 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 2499 BC–1999 B.source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Early Iron Age (Turkey, 1179 BC–949 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Turkey, 1179 BC–949 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 1179 BC–949 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.
Early Iron Age (Turkey, 1179 BC–949 BC).source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Middle Phrygian (Turkey, 799 BC–539 BC).label: Middle Phrygian
Middle Phrygian (Turkey, 799 BC–539 BC).prose:
[Turkey, 799 BC–539 BC] Middle Phrygian. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

After the fire that destroyed the citadel of Gordion, the Phrygian kingdom rebuilt on a grand scale – the era Greeks remembered through the legendary Midas. Phrygian craftsmen produced fine inlaid furniture, bronze vessels and bold geometric wall painting, and wrote their language in an alphabet borrowed from the Levant. Cimmerian raids and then Lydian expansion ended Phrygian independence, and the region passed to Persia in the 540s BC.
Middle Phrygian (Turkey, 799 BC–539 BC).source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

Early Phrygian Destruction (Gordion, 799.label: Early Phrygian Destruction
Early Phrygian Destruction (Gordion, 799.prose:
[Gordion, 799 BC–799 BC] Early Phrygian Destruction. added post-GeoDia. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

A catastrophic fire swept the citadel of Gordion, collapsing the great megaron halls and sealing their contents — furniture, textiles, pottery and tools — under debris that preserved them in extraordinary detail. Long blamed on a Cimmerian raid in the days of King Midas, the layer was pushed back roughly a century by tree-ring and radiocarbon dating, and is now usually read as an accident that the Phrygians rebuilt over on a massive new platform. It remains one of the richest single deposits of Iron Age Anatolian material anywhere.
Early Phrygian Destruction (Gordion, 799.source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

modern (Europe, AD 1600–AD 1918).label: modern
modern (Europe, AD 1600–AD 1918).prose:
[the world, AD 1600–AD 1918] modern. "After 1600 [the ideals] of the modern stage have clearly outlined themselves" (p. 64). Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

Europe in these centuries built centralised states and overseas empires, argued its way through the Reformation's aftermath, the Enlightenment and revolution, and then industrialised. Steam, railways, factories and mass literacy transformed daily life faster than at any earlier time, while nationalism redrew the map. The era ends in the wreckage of the First World War and the collapse of the continent's old dynastic empires.

Century of Enlightenment (Europe, AD 170.label: Century of Enlightenment
Century of Enlightenment (Europe, AD 170.prose:
[the world, AD 1701–AD 1800] Century of Enlightenment. "The sixteenth is the Century of Reformation; the eighteenth is the Century of Enlightenment" page 67. Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

Educated Europeans took reason, observation and criticism as their tools for judging religion, law and government, arguing their case in coffee houses, salons, learned academies and above all in print. Diderot's Encyclopédie, Adam Smith on markets, Beccaria on punishment and Rousseau on the social contract circulated far beyond scholars, while rulers from Vienna to St Petersburg adopted the vocabulary of reform. The century closed with those ideas turned into constitutions in America and revolution in France.

Century of Reformation (Europe, AD 1501–.label: Century of Reformation
Century of Reformation (Europe, AD 1501–.prose:
[the world, AD 1501–AD 1600] Century of Reformation. "The sixteenth is the Century of Reformation; the eighteenth is the Century of Enlightenment" page 67. Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

Luther's protest of 1517 was carried across Europe by the printing press and split western Christendom permanently, followed by Zwingli, Calvin, the radical Anabaptists and Henry VIII's break with Rome. Church lands changed hands on a huge scale, literacy and vernacular Bibles spread, and rulers gained control over religion in their territories. Rome answered with the Council of Trent and the Jesuits, and the confessional divide fed decades of civil and international war.

First European Transition (Europe, AD 40.label: First European Transition
First European Transition (Europe, AD 40.prose:
[Europe, AD 400–AD 800] First European Transition. "To save the meaning of "mediaeval" and at the same time to give greater clearness and validity to both "ancient" and "modern", it is worth while to carry on our process of division a stage further and to create for our use two additional periods, one preceding, one following that of the Middle Ages proper. If we think of this purely mediaeval section as beginning with Karl the Great about the year 800 and ending with Dante about 1300 these two new periods will then define themselves chronologically as covering respectively the years from about 400 to 800 and from about 1300 to 1600" (pp. 63-64); "At first thought these two added periods seem to be lacking in our first essential requirement, a distinctive character; but this difficulty grows less upon reflection. Superficially they seem to be characterized only by a greater degree of confusion than the others but, as we try to penetrate this apparent confusion, we see that it is better described as "transition"..." (p. 64); "And what has been said of the First European Transition is equally true of the second" (p. 65). Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

The Roman order in the West dissolved into kingdoms ruled by Franks, Goths, Lombards and others, while the eastern empire survived at Constantinople. Cities shrank, coinage and long-distance trade contracted, and bishops and monasteries took over much of the administration and learning that the state had once provided. Out of this reshuffling came the political map and the Christian institutional framework of medieval Europe.

Middle Ages (Europe, AD 800–AD 1300).label: Middle Ages
Middle Ages (Europe, AD 800–AD 1300).prose:
[the world, AD 800–AD 1300] Middle Ages. "If we think of this purely mediæval section as beginning with Karl the Great about the year 800 and ending with Dante about 1300..." page 64. Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman rule in the west and the Renaissance saw Latin Christendom take shape: monasteries preserved and reworked classical learning, kingdoms hardened into states, and lords, peasants and towns settled into new legal relationships. Population and cultivated land grew steadily until plague and famine reversed it in the fourteenth century. Cathedrals, universities, guilds, parliaments and the vernacular literatures of Europe all date from this span.

Second European Transition (Europe, AD 1.label: Second European Transition
Second European Transition (Europe, AD 1.prose:
[Europe, AD 1300–AD 1600] Second European Transition. "To save the meaning of "mediaeval" and at the same time to give greater clearness and validity to both "ancient" and "modern", it is worth while to carry on our process of division a stage further and to create for our use two additional periods, one preceding, one following that of the Middle Ages proper. If we think of this purely mediaeval section as beginning with Karl the Great about the year 800 and ending with Dante about 1300 these two new periods will then define themselves chronologically as covering respectively the years from about 400 to 800 and from about 1300 to 1600" (pp. 63-64); "At first thought these two added periods seem to be lacking in our first essential requirement, a distinctive character; but this difficulty grows less upon reflection. Superficially they seem to be characterized only by a greater degree of confusion than the others but, as we try to penetrate this apparent confusion, we see that it is better described as "transition"..." (p. 64); "And what has been said of the First European Transition is equally true of the second" (p. 65); "Small wonder that this period was until lately neglected by the general student of history or that it has been claimed alternately by the historians of the Middle Ages and by those of modern Europe. It becomes interesting and illuminating when it is treated by itself as the Second European Transition... These two added periods, then, have a character of their own, the character of transition" (p. 65). Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

The centuries in which medieval Europe was remade: plague cut the population by a third and loosened serfdom, printing spread ideas at unprecedented speed, and the Reformation broke the unity of Latin Christendom. Atlantic voyages linked Europe to the Americas and Asian sea routes, pouring silver and new crops into its economies. By the end, compact territorial states with standing armies and taxation had largely replaced the patchwork of lordships.

ancient (Europe, 910 BC–AD 400).label: ancient
ancient (Europe, 910 BC–AD 400).prose:
[the world, 910 BC–AD 400] ancient. Spatial coverage: Europe, Middle East, North Africa. "What we ordinarily call "ancient history" has a certain character of its own. It presents to our view a majestic succession of great empires, Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, Greek and Roman; and these, with all their obvious differences, have certain common features. The theory of sovereignty is in each case the same. Each believes itself called upon in its own time to dominate as much of the earth's surface as it can reach with its arms or, in the case of Greece, with the even more penetrating weapon of its civilization. There is room in the world for only one sovereignty at a time, and the price it has to pay for its domination is the destruction of the world sovereignty that has preceded it" (p. 59); "Before the
year 400 the ideals of antiquity still dominate the world" (p. 64). Period definition from The periodization of history. — Ephraim Emerton, 1918.

La Tène (Northern Europe, 449 BC–AD 43).label: La Tène
La Tène (Northern Europe, 449 BC–AD 43).prose:
[Northern and Western Europe, 449 BC–AD 43] La Tène. Spatial coverage: Northern Europe, Western Europe. Western Europe: 450BC-43AD.  The term La Tène is used to describe the material culture of the latter half of the Iron Age across much of northern and western Europe, from 450BC to the Roman conquest. The name is derived from a site on Lake Neuchâtel, Switzerland, where the first 'La Tène' type objects were excavated in the late 19thC.  In addition to describing a broad chronological timeframe, the term La Tène is also used to refer to certain types of object characteristic of this period, for example a La Tène sword or brooch. La Tène can be subdivided into La Tène I, II and III, or La Tène A, B, C and D. Using these subdivisions well established typologies of La Tène objects have been created. For example, the attachment of the foot to the bow on La Tène brooches follows a pattern which is consistent over time and across much of Europe. For example, the foot of a La Tène I brooch is not attached to the bow. If a brooch of this type is discovered it is an important piece of dating evidence for other types of object. Period definition from British Museum.

Named after a votive deposit of weapons in a Swiss lake, this culture spread across Gaul with a new elite of horse-riding warriors buried with chariots, swords and imported wine services. Its curvilinear art, all tendrils, palmettes and hidden faces, is the most recognisable Celtic style. By the final century large fortified towns, coinage and mass production were emerging, and it all ended with the Roman conquest.

Ninpyo Era (Japan, AD 1151–AD 1154).label: Ninpyo Era
Ninpyo Era (Japan, AD 1151–AD 1154).prose:
[Japan, AD 1151–AD 1154] Ninpyo Era. 1151-1154. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era late in the Heian period, under the boy emperor Konoe, when retired sovereigns and rival Fujiwara factions manoeuvred for control of the court. The disputes over succession and clan leadership taking shape in these years erupted shortly afterwards in the Hōgen Rebellion, which drew warrior houses into capital politics for good.

Tang dynasty (China, AD 618–AD 906).label: Tang dynasty
Tang dynasty (China, AD 618–AD 906).prose:
[China, AD 618–AD 906] Tang dynasty. 618-906. Period definition from British Museum.

China's most outward-looking imperial age, when Chang'an drew traders, monks and envoys from across Asia and Chinese silk, porcelain and paper travelled west. Buddhism reached its greatest influence, woodblock printing appeared, and poets such as Li Bai and Du Fu wrote verse that later ages treated as unsurpassable. Rebellion after 755 broke the state's grip on its provinces, and regional military governors eventually carved the empire up.

Tumaco-La Tolita (Colombia, 699 BC–AD 40.label: Tumaco-La Tolita
Tumaco-La Tolita (Colombia, 699 BC–AD 40.prose:
[Colombia, 699 BC–AD 400] Tumaco-La Tolita. The term refers to a period of the Tumaco cultural tradition of Colombia in the south of the Pacific coast from 700 BC to 400 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

A single cultural tradition straddling the modern Colombia–Ecuador border, centred on the mound site of La Tolita. Its craftspeople produced mould-made and modelled ceramic figures of remarkable realism and gold-platinum alloy ornaments, including the famous sun mask. Artificial mounds served as platforms for houses and burials in a landscape of mangrove and flood-prone river mouths.

Three Kingdoms China (China, AD 221–AD 2.label: Three Kingdoms China
Three Kingdoms China (China, AD 221–AD 2.prose:
[China, AD 221–AD 280] Three Kingdoms China. 221-280. Period definition from British Museum.

The Han empire's collapse left three rival states, Wei in the north, Shu in the west and Wu in the south, each claiming legitimate succession. Decades of shifting alliances, river campaigns and famous stratagems, including the fire attack at Red Cliffs, followed before Wei's successors conquered Wu and briefly reunited the realm. The era's warlords and advisers became China's most enduring literary subject through the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Enkyo Era (Japan, AD 1744–AD 1748).label: Enkyo Era
Enkyo Era (Japan, AD 1744–AD 1748).prose:
[Japan, AD 1744–AD 1748] Enkyo Era. 1744-1748. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief Edo-period era name spanning the end of Tokugawa Yoshimune's rule and the succession of his son Ieshige as shogun. Yoshimune's Kyoho reforms — austerity, rice-price management and legal codification — had just run their course, and the far less capable Ieshige left government largely to his officials.

Late Minoan IIIA2 (Crete, 1374 BC–1299 B.label: Late Minoan IIIA2
Late Minoan IIIA2 (Crete, 1374 BC–1299 B.prose:
[Crete, 1374 BC–1299 BC] Late Minoan IIIA2. 1375BC-1300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of Cretan participation in eastern Mediterranean trade, when Cretan stirrup jars carrying oil and wine reached Egypt, Cyprus and Sardinia and Aegean names appear in Egyptian inscriptions. Settlements such as Chania and Kommos flourished as ports while Knossos declined. Chamber tombs with painted larnakes spread across the island, marking a broad, prosperous elite rather than a single royal centre.

Bunkyu Era (Japan, AD 1861–AD 1864).label: Bunkyu Era
Bunkyu Era (Japan, AD 1861–AD 1864).prose:
[Japan, AD 1861–AD 1864] Bunkyu Era. 1861-1864. Period definition from British Museum.

Three turbulent years of the bakumatsu crisis. The shogunate accepted reforms that relaxed the alternate attendance system and brought court and daimyo into national politics, while radical loyalists preaching "revere the emperor, expel the barbarians" filled Kyoto with assassinations. The killing of an English merchant at Namamugi brought a British squadron to bombard Kagoshima, and Chōshū's attacks on foreign shipping ended in the shelling of Shimonoseki — object lessons that convinced Satsuma and Chōshū that expulsion was impossible and the shogunate had to go.

Zangid dynasty (Iraq, AD 1127–AD 1251).label: Zangid dynasty
Zangid dynasty (Iraq, AD 1127–AD 1251).prose:
[Jazira and Syria, AD 1127–AD 1251] Zangid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. 1127-1251 (AH 521-AH 649). Jazira and Syria, originally Seljuq goverors, began Muslim counter-attack against Crusader states. The end of the Zangids came with the rise of power of Badr al-Din Lu'lu who ruled in Mosul until the arrival of the Mongols under Hulegu. Period definition from British Museum.

Turkish atabegs, beginning with Zengi, built a state from Mosul and Aleppo that turned the fragmented Muslim response to the crusader states into a coordinated campaign. Zengi's capture of Edessa in 1144 destroyed the first crusader county and provoked the Second Crusade; his son Nur al-Din united Syria and sent the expedition to Egypt that brought Saladin to power. Saladin then supplanted them, though Zangid branches lingered in northern Iraq.

Karyaku Era (Japan, AD 1326–AD 1329).label: Karyaku Era
Karyaku Era (Japan, AD 1326–AD 1329).prose:
[Japan, AD 1326–AD 1329] Karyaku Era. 1326-1329. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Kamakura, with the ambitious Emperor Go-Daigo on the throne and the regent Hōjō Takatoki more interested in dogs and dancers than government. Disputes over imperial succession between the two rival branches of the family festered, and within a few years Go-Daigo's open revolt would bring the shogunate down.

Meiji Era (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).label: Meiji Era
Meiji Era (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).prose:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912] Meiji Era. 1868-1912. Period definition from British Museum.

Samurai rule ended and a teenage emperor became the symbol of a state determined to catch up with the West. In a few decades Japan built railways, telegraphs, conscript armies, a modern navy, universal schooling and a constitution, abolished the samurai class and its stipends, and moved the capital to Tokyo. Victories over China in 1895 and Russia in 1905 made it the first Asian power to defeat a European empire, and set it on the road to colonial expansion in Korea and Taiwan.

Jianyan (China, AD 113–AD 1127).label: Jianyan
Jianyan (China, AD 113–AD 1127).prose:
[China, AD 113–AD 1127] Jianyan. 1127-1131 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era proclaimed by Emperor Gaozong after Jurchen armies sacked Kaifeng and carried off two emperors, ending the Northern Song. The new court had no capital, fleeing south by land and sea while generals such as Yue Fei fought rearguard campaigns. Out of this flight came the Southern Song, based on the Yangtze and the port cities, prosperous in commerce but permanently cut off from the north.

Bakun (Iran, 4999 BC–3999 BC).label: Bakun
Bakun (Iran, 4999 BC–3999 BC).prose:
[Fars, 4999 BC–3999 BC] Bakun. Fars, 5000BC-4000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Chalcolithic villages on the Marvdasht plain of Fars, best known from Tall-i Bakun near the later site of Persepolis, produced some of prehistoric Iran's finest painted pottery: thin buff wares with bold black geometric animals and abstract designs. Excavated houses contain kilns, copper working and storage rooms, and large numbers of stamp seals and clay sealings show goods being counted and controlled. That administrative record-keeping, centuries before writing, points towards the bureaucratic societies of the later Iranian plateau.

Bunsei Era (Japan, AD 1818–AD 1830).label: Bunsei Era
Bunsei Era (Japan, AD 1818–AD 1830).prose:
[Japan, AD 1818–AD 1830] Bunsei Era. 1818-1830. Period definition from British Museum.

The height of late-Edo urban culture under the long, extravagant rule of shogun Tokugawa Ienari, when Osaka and Edo townspeople supported kabuki, comic fiction and colour woodblock printing on a scale never seen before. The shogunate paid for it by repeatedly debasing the coinage, storing up inflation and rural distress. It was also a time of hardening attitudes to the outside world: foreign ships were ordered driven off on sight, and the German physician Siebold was expelled for carrying maps out of the country.

Tianxi (China, AD 1017–AD 1021).label: Tianxi
Tianxi (China, AD 1017–AD 1021).prose:
[China, AD 1017–AD 1021] Tianxi. 1017-1021 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Zhenzong's later years were dominated by an elaborate programme of Daoist theatre: 'heavenly texts' that conveniently fell from the sky, colossal sacrifices at Mount Tai and vast new temples, all staged to restore prestige after buying peace with the Liao. The spending drained the treasury and drew criticism from officials, and as the emperor's health failed his consort, the future Empress Dowager Liu, took increasing control of government.

Seljuq dynasty (Iran, AD 1040–AD 1194).label: Seljuq dynasty
Seljuq dynasty (Iran, AD 1040–AD 1194).prose:
[Persia, Iraq and Syria, AD 1040–AD 1194] Seljuq dynasty. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. 1040-1194 (AH 431-AH 590). Turkic dynasty ruling in Persia, Iraq and Syria that  reunited central 'Abbasid lands. The Seljuqs had originally their home in the steppes north of the Caspian and Aral Seas. They converted to Islam at the end of the 10th century. Under Toghril I Beg they seized Nishapur, the capital of the Ghaznavids in 1038 (AH 429). He entered Baghdad in 1055 (AH 447) and had his title of sultan confirmed by the caliph. The sultanate of the Great Seljuqs was based on a hierarchically organised state in the Perso-Islamic monarchic system, with the supreme sultan supported by a Perian and Arab beaurocracy and a multi-national army directed by Turkish slave commanders. Under Alp Arslan and his son Malik Shah the Great Seljuq empire reached its zenith and Isfahan was the capital. The Seljuqs founded various orthodox Sunni madrasas or religious colleges in Irag and the Persian lands and encouraged a synthesis of traditional theological and legal studies with the spirit of Sufism. Period definition from British Museum.

Turkmen horsemen from the Central Asian steppe took Iran from the Ghaznavids and Buyids and entered Baghdad in 1055, leaving the Abbasid caliph as a figurehead while the sultan ruled. Under Alp Arslan and Malik Shah, with the administrator Nizam al-Mulk, they built madrasas, caravanserais and a Persian-style bureaucracy, and their victory at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement. The empire fragmented among rival princes and atabegs, a splintering that helped shape the world the Crusaders walked into.

Shotai Era (Japan, AD 898–AD 901).label: Shotai Era
Shotai Era (Japan, AD 898–AD 901).prose:
[Japan, AD 898–AD 901] Shotai Era. 898-901. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Daigo's reign began with an unusual experiment: the scholar-official Sugawara no Michizane, a man of modest birth, was raised to the top of government as a counterweight to the Fujiwara. In 901 the Fujiwara struck back, and Michizane was exiled to Kyushu, where he died in disgrace. A run of plagues, lightning strikes and deaths at court was blamed on his angry spirit, and he was eventually deified as Tenjin, the god of learning, worshipped at shrines across Japan.

Late Minoan IIIC (Crete, 1199 BC–1059 BC.label: Late Minoan IIIC
Late Minoan IIIC (Crete, 1199 BC–1059 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1199 BC–1059 BC] Late Minoan IIIC. 1200BC-1060BC.  Late Minoan IIIC and Late Helladic IIIC pottery is normally divided into Early, Middle and Late. Where these classifications are used, the following dates are accepted: Early: 1200BC-1130BC.  Middle: 1130BC-1090BC.  Late: 1090BC-1060BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The refuge era: Cretans moved to steep, defensible inland sites such as Karphi, Vrokastro and Kavousi Kastro, leaving the great coastal centres empty. Writing and centralised administration vanished, but potters produced lively new octopus and pictorial styles, and iron began to appear alongside bronze. Out of these small upland communities came the settlement pattern and cults of Early Iron Age Crete.

Kyuju Era (Japan, AD 1154–AD 1156).label: Kyuju Era
Kyuju Era (Japan, AD 1154–AD 1156).prose:
[Japan, AD 1154–AD 1156] Kyuju Era. 1154-1156. Period definition from British Museum.

The last calm before the storm: the boy emperor Konoe died in 1155 and the disputed succession that followed set the retired emperor Sutoku against the new emperor Go-Shirakawa. The quarrel erupted in 1156 as the Hōgen Rebellion, fought in the streets of Kyoto by Taira and Minamoto warriors on both sides. From that point the court could no longer settle its own disputes without soldiers, and warrior rule was only a generation away.

Terminal Christian Period (Egypt, AD 140.label: Terminal Christian Period
Terminal Christian Period (Egypt, AD 140.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 1400–AD 1500] Terminal Christian Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1400-1500. Period definition from British Museum.

The last phase of Nubian Christianity along the Middle Nile, as the kingdoms of Makuria and Alwa fragmented under Arab migration and Mamluk pressure. Churches fell out of use or were converted, Arabic and Islam spread among the riverine population, and a Christian tradition roughly 800 years old finally dissolved.

Eicho Era (Japan, AD 1096–AD 1097).label: Eicho Era
Eicho Era (Japan, AD 1096–AD 1097).prose:
[Japan, AD 1096–AD 1097] Eicho Era. 1096-1097. Period definition from British Museum.

A short late-Heian era under Emperor Horikawa, when real power lay with the retired emperor Shirakawa and his cloistered government. It is remembered for a sudden craze for dengaku dancing that swept through Kyoto in 1096, with nobles and commoners alike caught up in the frenzy, taken by some at court as an omen of disorder.

Cauca (Colombia, AD 1000–AD 1600).label: Cauca
Cauca (Colombia, AD 1000–AD 1600).prose: [Colombia, AD 1000–AD 1600] Cauca. The term refers to a region and a style of Colombia in the Popayan valley and the Central Range in the Cauca department from 1000 to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Tumaco (Colombia, 699 BC–AD 1600).label: Tumaco
Tumaco (Colombia, 699 BC–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, 699 BC–AD 1600] Tumaco. The term refers to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the south of the Pacific coast from 700 BC to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

A society of the mangrove coast and river deltas of the Pacific lowlands, best known for astonishingly lifelike ceramic figurines: portrait heads, dancers, mothers with children, and depictions of illness and deformity. Its metalworkers were among the first anywhere to work platinum, sintering it with gold. Villages were built on artificial earth mounds raised above the tidal wetlands.

Jin dynasty (China, AD 1115–AD 1234).label: Jin dynasty
Jin dynasty (China, AD 1115–AD 1234).prose:
[China, AD 1115–AD 1234] Jin dynasty. 1115-1234. Period definition from British Museum.

A Jurchen empire that rose fast: within a decade of rebelling against the Liao it had conquered its former overlords, and within two it had driven the Song court south of the Yangtze. It ruled tens of millions of Chinese subjects with a hybrid administration, minted paper money and held civil service examinations. Squeezed between a hostile Song and the rising Mongols, it fell to Ögedei's armies.

Shocho Era (Japan, AD 1428–AD 1429).label: Shocho Era
Shocho Era (Japan, AD 1428–AD 1429).prose:
[Japan, AD 1428–AD 1429] Shocho Era. 1428-1429. Period definition from British Museum.

The shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi died without naming an heir and his successor was chosen by drawing lots at a shrine. In the same year, carters and villagers around Kyoto rose in the first great tokusei ikki, storming pawnshops and moneylenders to destroy debt records and force a cancellation of debts — the opening of a century of peasant leagues that would repeatedly bring the capital to a standstill.

Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Helladic
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Helladic. 2000BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Mainland Greece at its poorest and plainest: modest villages of mudbrick houses, burials in simple cist graves and tumuli, and the grey wheel-made pottery known as Minyan ware. Messenia's communities were small and dispersed, with little sign of the wealth or hierarchy to come. Towards its end, richer graves and imported Cretan goods signal the emergence of the warrior elites who would build the Mycenaean palace at Pylos.

Meireki Era (Japan, AD 1655–AD 1658).label: Meireki Era
Meireki Era (Japan, AD 1655–AD 1658).prose:
[Japan, AD 1655–AD 1658] Meireki Era. 1655-1658. Period definition from British Museum.

Remembered almost entirely for the fire of 1657, which burned for three days, destroyed the greater part of Edo including the keep of the shogun's castle, and killed tens of thousands. The rebuilding reshaped the city, with firebreaks, wider streets and temples and warrior residences pushed out to the suburbs. The castle tower was never replaced.

Kaitai (Japan, AD 1012–AD 1019).label: Kaitai
Kaitai (Japan, AD 1012–AD 1019).prose: [Japan, AD 1012–AD 1019] Kaitai. 1012-1019 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Restored Le dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1533–AD.label: Restored Le dynasty
Restored Le dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1533–AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1533–AD 1788] Restored Le dynasty. Vietnamese dynasty, 1533-1788.  state name: Dai Viet. Period definition from British Museum.

The Lê emperors were put back on the throne after the Mạc usurpation, but they reigned rather than ruled: real power lay with the Trịnh lords in the north and the Nguyễn lords in the south. Their rivalry split Vietnam along the Gianh River for over a century, walled off and fought over, while the Nguyễn pushed the southern frontier into the Mekong Delta at the expense of Champa and Cambodia. The whole arrangement collapsed in the Tây Sơn uprising.

Indus Civilisation (Pakistan, 2499 BC–19.label: Indus Civilisation
Indus Civilisation (Pakistan, 2499 BC–19.prose:
[Pakistan and western India, 2499 BC–1999 BC] Indus Civilisation. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. Urban civilisation based in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent, today in Pakistan and western India.  Developing out of earlier prehistoric cultures, it flourished over a very wide area between approximately 2,500 and 2,000 BC.  Script was known but is undeciphered today, not least as surviving inscriptions (mostly on seals) are no more than about a dozen characters.  Major settlements, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, were laid out on a grid pattern with drainage and were clearly organised by a central power.  The earliest fragments of woven cotton from the subcontinent come from these sites.  Trade with sites in the Persian Gulf, as well as with settlements on the Oxus, has been substantiated. Period definition from British Museum.

At its height, cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa held tens of thousands of people in gridded streets with brick drains, wells and public baths, supplied by farming villages across the Indus plain and beyond. Standardised weights, fired bricks and carved seals travelled as far as Mesopotamia, yet no palaces or royal tombs have been found, and the script remains unread. Within a few centuries the great cities were largely emptied, their populations dispersing eastward into smaller settlements.

Shoryaku Era (Japan, AD 990–AD 995).label: Shoryaku Era
Shoryaku Era (Japan, AD 990–AD 995).prose:
[Japan, AD 990–AD 995] Shoryaku Era. 990-995. Period definition from British Museum.

The high tide of Fujiwara dominance at the Heian court, when the regent Michitaka installed his daughter as empress and packed the offices of state with his own sons. Court life of these years is the world recorded in the diaries and poetry of the imperial salons. Michitaka's death soon after, followed by an epidemic that killed much of the senior nobility, cleared the way for his brother Michinaga to take power.

Greco-Bactrian (Afghanistan, 249 BC–144.label: Greco-Bactrian
Greco-Bactrian (Afghanistan, 249 BC–144.prose:
[Afghanistan north of the Hindu Kush, Central Asian Amu Darya region of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, 249 BC–144 BC] Greco-Bactrian. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. The term refers to a Greek kingdom (c. 250-145 BC) in Bactria (Afghanistan north of the Hindu Kush) and Sogdiana (the Central Asian Amu Darya region of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan). The region was originally part of the Seleucid empire, but the Bactrian governor Diodotus gained independence in c. 250 BC. Sogdiana broke away in turn from Bactria c. 200 BC; the rest of the region was lost to nomadic tribes of the Indo-Scythians and Yuezhi by c. 145 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Diodotus, the Seleucid governor of Bactria, broke away to found a Greek kingdom on the Oxus, the easternmost heir of Alexander's conquests. Its cities, above all Ai Khanoum with its gymnasium, theatre and Greek inscriptions, sat astride the routes between the Mediterranean, India and China, and its kings struck some of the finest portrait coins of antiquity. Nomadic invasions swept the kingdom away, though its Greek rulers survived south of the Hindu Kush as the Indo-Greeks.

Hotoku Era (Japan, AD 1449–AD 1452).label: Hotoku Era
Hotoku Era (Japan, AD 1449–AD 1452).prose:
[Japan, AD 1449–AD 1452] Hotoku Era. 1449-1452. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era at the start of Ashikaga Yoshimasa's shogunate, when the boy ruler was installed under the control of his mother and the powerful shogunal deputies. Real authority lay with great warrior houses whose rivalries were already hardening, and peasant debt-cancellation uprisings pressed on Kyoto. The disputes taking shape here led on to the Onin War and the collapse of central authority.

Kanna Era (Japan, AD 985–AD 987).label: Kanna Era
Kanna Era (Japan, AD 985–AD 987).prose:
[Japan, AD 985–AD 987] Kanna Era. 985-987. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief span at the height of Fujiwara power, ended when Emperor Kazan was tricked into taking Buddhist vows in 986 and the boy Ichijō was placed on the throne with Fujiwara no Kaneie as regent. It also saw the monk Genshin complete the Ōjōyōshū, whose vivid descriptions of hell and the Pure Land shaped Japanese religious imagination for centuries.

Enkyu Era (Japan, AD 1069–AD 1074).label: Enkyu Era
Enkyu Era (Japan, AD 1069–AD 1074).prose:
[Japan, AD 1069–AD 1074] Enkyu Era. 1069-1074. Period definition from British Museum.

Go-Sanjō ruled without a Fujiwara regent behind him, and used the moment to issue the Enkyū land-records ordinance, which forced estate holders to prove their titles and cancelled manors created without proper documents. It was the first serious imperial attempt in generations to claw back land and revenue from the great noble houses and temples, and it prepared the ground for the later system of rule by retired emperors.

Eastern Mediterranean (Levant, 1399 BC–1.label: Eastern Mediterranean
Eastern Mediterranean (Levant, 1399 BC–1.prose:
[along the Mediterranean coastline from the Aegean to Egypt, 1399 BC–1199 BC] Eastern Mediterranean. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Levant. The term is used by the Greek and Roman Department for objects with multiple centres of production along the Mediterranean coastline from the Aegean to Egypt. It reflects the broad cultural connections between regions at certain periods, particularly the 'International Style' c. 1400 BC-1200 BC. For this reason it is usually for objects from Bronze Age Cypriot sites: after this period, centres of production are better defined. The term is not used for Hellenistic (q.v.) or Roman (q.v.) objects. See also the Place term 'Mediterranean' with Comment 'East Mediterranean' for objects described as 'East Mediterranean' in the records for the Prehistory and Europe Department.  See also the term 'Cypriot' and its Narrow Terms. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of Late Bronze Age internationalism: Egyptian garrisons held Canaanite city-states as vassals, Hittite armies pressed down from Anatolia, and Mycenaean, Cypriot and Ugaritic ships carried copper, tin, ivory and oil between palace economies. Kings corresponded in Akkadian on clay tablets, as the Amarna letters show, and the Uluburun shipwreck preserves a single cargo drawn from a dozen lands. The system collapsed at the end of the period amid destructions, famine and the movements known as the Sea Peoples, clearing the ground for Israelites, Philistines and Phoenicians.

Kyuan Era (Japan, AD 1145–AD 1151).label: Kyuan Era
Kyuan Era (Japan, AD 1145–AD 1151).prose:
[Japan, AD 1145–AD 1151] Kyuan Era. 1145-1151. Period definition from British Museum.

A late Heian reign name during the cloistered rule of the retired emperor Toba, when court politics turned on rivalries within the imperial family itself. The Taira and Minamoto warrior houses, hired as guards and enforcers, were steadily becoming indispensable to the aristocrats who employed them. Within a few years those tensions broke into open fighting in the capital.

Zhenghe (China, AD 1111–AD 1118).label: Zhenghe
Zhenghe (China, AD 1111–AD 1118).prose:
[China, AD 1111–AD 1118] Zhenghe. 1111-1118 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The height of Emperor Huizong's aesthetic court, when the Song throne poured money into painting academies, antiquarian catalogues of bronzes, Ru ware ceramics and an enormous artificial garden-mountain in the capital. The emperor promoted Daoism to near state religion and gave himself Daoist titles. The extravagance and the tax exactions behind it fed rebellion and left the dynasty unprepared for the Jurchen invasion that would sack Kaifeng within a decade.

Joryaku Era (Japan, AD 1077–AD 1081).label: Joryaku Era
Joryaku Era (Japan, AD 1077–AD 1081).prose:
[Japan, AD 1077–AD 1081] Joryaku Era. 1077-1081. Period definition from British Museum.

A quiet stretch of Emperor Shirakawa's reign, remembered above all for the dedication of Hosshoji, the vast temple he raised in the eastern hills of the capital with a nine-storey pagoda visible across Kyoto. Such imperial temple-building projects were as much political statements as religious ones, asserting the throne's wealth against the Fujiwara nobility.

Dadi (China, AD 222–AD 252).label: Dadi
Dadi (China, AD 222–AD 252).prose:
[China, AD 222–AD 252] Dadi. 222-252 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Sun Quan, who ruled the southeast from Jianye (modern Nanjing) and in 229 proclaimed himself emperor of Wu, making the Three Kingdoms division formal. His long rule pushed Chinese settlement and shipbuilding south of the Yangtze, sent maritime expeditions as far as Taiwan and Vietnam, and ended in bitter court feuding over the succession.

Qianning (China, AD 894–AD 898).label: Qianning
Qianning (China, AD 894–AD 898).prose:
[China, AD 894–AD 898] Qianning. 894-898 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign era of the Tang emperor Zhaozong, when the dynasty survived only as a name. Regional warlords fought openly around the capital, the emperor was seized and moved at their convenience, and within a decade the Tang would be extinguished by one of them.

Hallstatt B (Europe, 1124 BC–799 BC).label: Hallstatt B
Hallstatt B (Europe, 1124 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Europe, 1124 BC–799 BC] Hallstatt B. Europe; 1125-800 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The later Urnfield phase, still bronze-using, with cremation cemeteries, hoards of scrap and finished metalwork, and hilltop enclosures. Iron begins to appear in small quantities as an exotic material, and salt mining at Hallstatt itself gets under way, setting up the wealth of the centuries to come.

Dazhong Xiangfu (China, AD 1008–AD 1016).label: Dazhong Xiangfu
Dazhong Xiangfu (China, AD 1008–AD 1016).prose:
[China, AD 1008–AD 1016] Dazhong Xiangfu. 1008-1016 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Following the Chanyuan treaty that bought peace with the Liao, Song Zhenzong staged an elaborate campaign of religious legitimation: heaven-sent texts miraculously appeared, and the emperor performed the ancient feng and shan sacrifices at Mount Tai amid enormous expense. Temples and Daoist establishments multiplied across the empire. The spectacle papered over the humiliation of paying tribute to a northern rival, and later officials remembered it as a costly fraud.

Koryo Dynasty (Japan, AD 918–AD 1392).label: Koryo Dynasty
Koryo Dynasty (Japan, AD 918–AD 1392).prose:
[Japan, AD 918–AD 1392] Koryo Dynasty. 918 - 1392. Period definition from British Museum.

The Korean dynasty founded by Wang Kŏn, which reunited the peninsula in 936 and gave the country the name by which the West still knows it. Its court produced jade-green celadon ware of unmatched quality, the world's first movable metal type, and the Tripitaka Koreana, over 80,000 woodblocks carved as a Buddhist plea for deliverance from Mongol invasion. Decades of Mongol domination and a military dictatorship at home eventually exhausted the dynasty, which fell to the general who founded Chosŏn.

Late Kaftari (Iran, 1799 BC–1599 BC).label: Late Kaftari
Late Kaftari (Iran, 1799 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Fars, 1799 BC–1599 BC] Late Kaftari. Fars, 1800BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Distinctive buff pottery painted with bands, birds and geometric motifs identifies this phase in the highland plain around Anshan, a major Elamite centre. The city shrank from its earlier extent even as it remained tied by trade and politics to lowland Susa and Mesopotamia under the sukkalmah rulers. Its end is followed by a marked contraction of settlement in the region.

Kenkyu Era (Japan, AD 1190–AD 1199).label: Kenkyu Era
Kenkyu Era (Japan, AD 1190–AD 1199).prose:
[Japan, AD 1190–AD 1199] Kenkyu Era. 1190-1199. Period definition from British Museum.

The decade in which Minamoto no Yoritomo made his warrior government permanent: he took the title of shogun in 1192 and presided over the rededication of the rebuilt Great Buddha hall at Tōdai-ji, a public display that the man in Kamakura, not the court in Kyoto, now held the country together. His death in 1199 left the shogunate to his sons and, in practice, to his widow's Hōjō kin.

Jian Era (China, AD 1021–AD 1024).label: Jian Era
Jian Era (China, AD 1021–AD 1024).prose: [China, AD 1021–AD 1024] Jian Era. 1021-1024. Period definition from British Museum.

Qatabanian (Yemen, 499 BC–AD 1).label: Qatabanian
Qatabanian (Yemen, 499 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Qataban kingdom, ancient Yemen, 499 BC–AD 1] Qatabanian. Refers to the kingdom of Qataban (capital at Timna?) based in the Wadi Beihan region that controlled large parts of ancient Yemen during the second half of the first millennium BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Qataban was one of the caravan kingdoms of South Arabia, its capital Timna sitting astride the incense road that carried frankincense and myrrh north to the Mediterranean. Its rulers taxed the trade, built dams and irrigation works in the Wadi Bayhan, and left thousands of monumental inscriptions in the Qatabanic script, along with alabaster funerary heads that stare out of museum cases today. Squeezed between Saba and Hadramawt, the kingdom was eventually absorbed by its neighbours as sea routes undercut the overland incense traffic.

Majiayao culture (China, 3799 BC–1999 BC.label: Majiayao culture
Majiayao culture (China, 3799 BC–1999 BC.prose:
[China, 3799 BC–1999 BC] Majiayao culture. Neolithic culture c BC 3800 - BC 2000. Period definition from British Museum.

A late Neolithic tradition of the upper Yellow River in Gansu and Qinghai, descended from Yangshao and famous for boldly painted spiral-decorated pottery. Its people farmed millet in loess valleys and produced some of the earliest bronze objects yet found in China, including a small cast knife. Through its later Banshan and Machang stages it links the painted-pottery world of the northwest to the metal-using cultures that followed.

Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1399 BC–1059.label: Late Cycladic III
Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1399 BC–1059.prose:
[Greece, 1399 BC–1059 BC] Late Cycladic III. 1400BC-1060BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The islands under mainland Mycenaean culture, with megaron-plan buildings and a sanctuary at Phylakopi holding clay idols, and fortification walls going up as conditions worsened. Around 1200 BC the palatial system collapsed and many sites were burned, abandoned or reduced to villages. Scattered communities carried on into the early Iron Age, with new cemeteries and the first signs of the later island city-states.

Kansei Era (Japan, AD 1789–AD 1801).label: Kansei Era
Kansei Era (Japan, AD 1789–AD 1801).prose:
[Japan, AD 1789–AD 1801] Kansei Era. 1789-1801. Period definition from British Museum.
