Matsudaira Sadanobu drove through austerity measures after the devastating Tenmei famine: samurai debts cancelled, rice stockpiled, peasants pushed back to the land, and the Kansei Edict restricting the shogunal academy to orthodox Zhu Xi Confucianism. These were also the years when Russian ships began appearing off Ezo asking to trade, opening the long argument about foreign contact that would end the shogunate.

Late Helladic IIIB1 (Greece, 1299 BC–124.label: Late Helladic IIIB1
Late Helladic IIIB1 (Greece, 1299 BC–124.prose:
[Greece, 1299 BC–1249 BC] Late Helladic IIIB1. 1300BC-1250BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Fortifications were enlarged and the palaces at their most elaborate, decorated with processional frescoes and served by workshops of specialised craftsmen. Pottery is plain and mass-produced, the signature of a centrally organised economy.

Kowa Era 1099-1104 (Japan, AD 1099–AD 11.label: Kowa Era 1099-1104
Kowa Era 1099-1104 (Japan, AD 1099–AD 11.prose:
[Japan, AD 1099–AD 1104] Kowa Era 1099-1104. 1099-1104. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Heian reign name adopted, as often happened, in the hope of shaking off earthquakes, epidemics and bad omens. Real power lay not with the young emperor but with the retired sovereign Shirakawa, whose cloistered government had begun to sideline the Fujiwara regents. Provincial warrior houses and armed monks from the great temples were meanwhile becoming forces the court could neither ignore nor control.

Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1279–AD 1368).label: Yuan dynasty
Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1279–AD 1368).prose:
[China, AD 1279–AD 1368] Yuan dynasty. 1279-1368. Period definition from British Museum.

With the drowning of the last Song claimant, Mongol rulers held all of China for the first time, governing from Dadu (Beijing) through a ranked system that placed Mongols and Central Asians above northern and southern Chinese. Overland and maritime trade flourished, drama and vernacular fiction thrived while the old examination elite was sidelined, and foreign travellers such as Marco Polo described the wealth of the capital. Inflation, floods on the Yellow River and rebel movements broke the regime, and the court fled back to the steppe.

Dakang (China, AD 1075–AD 1084).label: Dakang
Dakang (China, AD 1075–AD 1084).prose:
[China, AD 1075–AD 1084] Dakang. 1075-1084 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign era of Daozong of the Liao, the Khitan empire ruling the steppe and northern China. Court intrigue defined it: the empress was forced to death and the heir apparent killed on the strength of forged accusations by the minister Yelu Yixin, purges that hollowed out the dynasty a generation before the Jurchen destroyed it.

Gangyo Era (Japan, AD 877–AD 885).label: Gangyo Era
Gangyo Era (Japan, AD 877–AD 885).prose:
[Japan, AD 877–AD 885] Gangyo Era. 877-885. Period definition from British Museum.

A Heian era dominated by Fujiwara no Mototsune, who deposed the erratic young Emperor Yōzei in 884 and installed the elderly Kōkō in his place. The episode showed how completely the Fujiwara regents now controlled the throne, and Mototsune's position soon hardened into the office of kampaku, the civil dictatorship that ran the court for generations.

Xianping (China, AD 998–AD 1004).label: Xianping
Xianping (China, AD 998–AD 1004).prose:
[China, AD 998–AD 1004] Xianping. 998-1004 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The opening era of Emperor Zhenzong's reign, a period of consolidation after the Song's failed attempts to retake the northern frontier from the Liao. Administration settled into civil-official hands and the examination system expanded, while raids across the border continued until the two courts made peace soon after.

Recent Bronze Age (Italy, 1349 BC–1199 B.label: Recent Bronze Age
Recent Bronze Age (Italy, 1349 BC–1199 B.prose:
[Italy, 1349 BC–1199 BC] Recent Bronze Age. Italy: c. 1350 BC - 1200 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The Bronzo Recente saw the terramare villages of the Po plain reach their peak of population and organisation before collapsing abruptly, while in the south Subapennine communities traded with Mycenaean sailors for painted pottery and metals. Bronze metallurgy became standardised across the peninsula, with hoards of tools and weapons buried in large numbers. The upheaval at the end of this phase reshaped Italian settlement patterns and led into the proto-Villanovan world of the Final Bronze Age.

Former Shu Kingdom (China, AD 25–AD 907).label: Former Shu Kingdom
Former Shu Kingdom (China, AD 25–AD 907).prose:
[China, AD 25–AD 907] Former Shu Kingdom. 907-25. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the states that broke away as the Tang empire collapsed, founded by the warlord Wang Jian with its capital at Chengdu. Sheltered by Sichuan's mountains, it was prosperous and comparatively peaceful, attracting poets, painters and refugee officials; the earliest anthology of Chinese lyric ci poetry was compiled at its court. It fell to the armies of the Later Tang after less than two decades.

Khans of Ganja (Iran, AD 1747–AD 1805).label: Khans of Ganja
Khans of Ganja (Iran, AD 1747–AD 1805).prose:
[Iran , AD 1747–AD 1805] Khans of Ganja. Also known as the Ganja khanate, under the dominion of Iran in 1747-1805 (AH 1160-AH 1220). Period definition from British Museum.

After Nader Shah's assassination shattered central authority, Ganja became one of a patchwork of semi-independent khanates ruling the South Caucasus, its Ziyadoglu khans manoeuvring between Iranian, Georgian and Ottoman pressure. Russian expansion ended it: Tsitsianov stormed the citadel in 1804, killed the last khan, and renamed the city Elisavetpol. The conquest helped trigger the Russo-Persian war that transferred the region to St Petersburg.

Ming dynasty (China, AD 1368–AD 1644).label: Ming dynasty
Ming dynasty (China, AD 1368–AD 1644).prose:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1644] Ming dynasty. 1368-1644. Period definition from British Museum.

A native Chinese dynasty that followed the Mongol Yuan, ruling from Nanjing and then Beijing for nearly three centuries. It produced the Forbidden City, the stone-and-brick Great Wall, vast encyclopedic compilations, and the porcelain kilns of Jingdezhen whose wares reached every continent. American silver flooding in through Manila transformed the economy, while a combination of famine, rebellion and Manchu pressure brought the dynasty down in 1644.

Kowa Era 1381-1384 (Japan, AD 1381–AD 13.label: Kowa Era 1381-1384
Kowa Era 1381-1384 (Japan, AD 1381–AD 13.prose:
[Japan, AD 1381–AD 1384] Kowa Era 1381-1384. 1381-1384. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the reign names used by the Southern Court during the split between rival imperial lines. By this point the southern claimants were a shrinking movement in the mountains of Yoshino, while the Ashikaga shoguns and their northern emperor held Kyoto and most of the country. Within a decade the two courts would be reunited on the shogun's terms.

Jiading (China, AD 1208–AD 1225).label: Jiading
Jiading (China, AD 1208–AD 1225).prose:
[China, AD 1208–AD 1225] Jiading. 1208-1225 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A Southern Song reign era that opened with a humiliating peace: after a failed northern offensive, the Song court sent the head of its own war minister to the Jin and agreed to higher annual tribute. The following years were relatively quiet but financially strained, with paper currency inflating and the chief councillor Shi Miyuan dominating government. Far to the north, Mongol armies were beginning to tear the Jin state apart.

Bahmani Dynasty (India, AD 1347–AD 1538).label: Bahmani Dynasty
Bahmani Dynasty (India, AD 1347–AD 1538).prose:
[north Deccan, AD 1347–AD 1538] Bahmani Dynasty. 1347-1538 (AH 748-944): Muslim state in the north Deccan (territory now divided between Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka), ruled by the Bahmani dynasty. The founder, 'Ala al-Din Bahman Shah (1347-1359), governor of Gulbarga for the Delhi Sultanate, declared independence in 1347. Period definition from British Museum.

A revolt by nobles against Delhi's overstretched rule created the first lasting Muslim kingdom in the Deccan, ruled from Gulbarga and later Bidar. Its sultans fought Vijayanagara across the Raichur Doab for generations, recruited Persian and Turkish officers whose rivalry with Indian-born nobles eventually tore the state apart, and under the minister Mahmud Gawan built madrasas, forts and a strong revenue system. Its breakup produced the five Deccan sultanates whose art, Persianate court culture and Golconda diamonds shaped southern India until the Mughals absorbed them.

Dogra dynasty (India, AD 1819–AD 1979).label: Dogra dynasty
Dogra dynasty (India, AD 1819–AD 1979).prose:
[Kashmir, AD 1819–AD 1979] Dogra dynasty. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. Local rulers of Kashmir under Sikh suzerainty (1819-46); then rulers of the Indian Princely State of Kashmir (1846-1979). From 1846 under the British, the following rulers issued anonymous coins dated in the Vikrama era: Gulab Singh 1846-1856 (VS 1903-1913); Ranbir Singh 1857-1885 (VS 1914-1942); Pertab Singh 1885-1925 (VS 1942-1979). Period definition from British Museum.

Gulab Singh, a Dogra Rajput chief in Jammu who rose in Sikh service, bought the Vale of Kashmir from the British after their 1846 victory and welded Jammu, Kashmir, Ladakh and Gilgit into the largest princely state in India. His Hindu dynasty ruled a mostly Muslim population, and resentment of its taxation and land system fed Kashmiri political awakening. In 1947 the last maharaja, Hari Singh, hesitated over accession, then signed with India as tribal fighters crossed the border — the origin of the Kashmir dispute.

Tularosa (Arizona, AD 1050–AD 1550).label: Tularosa
Tularosa (Arizona, AD 1050–AD 1550).prose:
[Arizona, AD 1050–AD 1550] Tularosa. Spatial coverage: Arizona, New Mexico. 1050–1550. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase of Mogollon village life in the mountain country of the Southwest, when scattered pithouse hamlets gave way to masonry pueblos of many rooms clustered around plazas. Its marker is Tularosa Black-on-white pottery, with tight interlocking hatched and solid designs. The concentration of people into fewer, larger settlements was followed by the general depopulation of the region, part of the broad reshuffling of Southwestern communities before the Spanish arrived.

Gallo-Visigothic (France, AD 414–AD 507).label: Gallo-Visigothic
Gallo-Visigothic (France, AD 414–AD 507).prose:
[Southern France, AD 414–AD 507] Gallo-Visigothic. The term refers to the period of the Visigoths in Southern France from the time of the establishment of the Kingdom of Toulouse in AD 414 until the expulsion of the Visigoths by Clovis in  AD 507. Period definition from British Museum.

After sacking Rome, the Visigoths moved into southern Gaul and in 418 were settled as federates around Toulouse, where they built the first durable barbarian kingdom on Roman soil. Their kings governed a Roman provincial population through Roman officials, issued written law such as the Code of Euric and the Breviary of Alaric, and fought alongside Aetius against Attila. Frankish victory at Vouillé in 507 drove them south of the Pyrenees, leaving Gaul to Clovis and his heirs.

Enryaku Era (Japan, AD 782–AD 806).label: Enryaku Era
Enryaku Era (Japan, AD 782–AD 806).prose:
[Japan, AD 782–AD 806] Enryaku Era. 782-806. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Kanmu moved his court away from the temple-dominated capital at Nara, first to Nagaoka and then, in 794, to Heian-kyō, the city that would be Japan's capital for the next thousand years. His armies pushed north against the Emishi of Honshū under the general Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, and the monk Saichō established the Tendai school on Mount Hiei, whose great monastery Enryaku-ji still carries the era's name.

Gaozong (China, AD 1127–AD 1162).label: Gaozong
Gaozong (China, AD 1127–AD 1162).prose:
[China, AD 1127–AD 1162] Gaozong. 1127-1162 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Gaozong escaped the Jurchen sack of Kaifeng and refounded the Song dynasty in the south, eventually fixing his court at Lin'an (Hangzhou). He chose accommodation over reconquest, accepting the 1141 treaty that ceded the north and paid tribute to the Jin, and had the popular general Yue Fei killed for opposing it. The truncated Southern Song that resulted became one of the richest, most commercial and most artistically refined states in the world.

Meio Era (Japan, AD 1492–AD 1501).label: Meio Era
Meio Era (Japan, AD 1492–AD 1501).prose:
[Japan, AD 1492–AD 1501] Meio Era. 1492-1501. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign-era at the opening of Japan's long civil-war century. In 1493 the deputy shogun Hosokawa Masamoto deposed the sitting shogun in a palace coup, exposing how little authority the Ashikaga still held. Five years later an enormous earthquake and tsunami struck the Pacific coast, sweeping away the hall that had sheltered the Great Buddha at Kamakura, which has stood in the open ever since.

Umayyads of Spain (Spain, AD 756–AD 1031.label: Umayyads of Spain
Umayyads of Spain (Spain, AD 756–AD 1031.prose:
[Spain, AD 756–AD 1031] Umayyads of Spain. 756-1031 (AH 138-422). Revival in Spain of Umayyad rule. In 756 (AH 138) 'Abd al-Rahman I, later called al-Dakhil (the Incomer), who had escaped slaughter in the Abbasid Revolution, appeared in Spain and created the Umayyad state there. Period definition from British Museum.

A survivor of the Abbasid massacre of his family fled to Iberia and founded an independent Umayyad emirate at Cordoba, which Abd al-Rahman III raised to a caliphate in 929. At its height Cordoba was among the largest cities in the world, with paved streets, libraries and the endlessly extended Great Mosque, and its scholars transmitted Greek philosophy, mathematics and medicine to Latin Europe. The state fractured in civil war after 1009 and collapsed into the small taifa kingdoms, opening the way for Christian expansion southward.

Tongzhi (China, AD 1862–AD 1874).label: Tongzhi
Tongzhi (China, AD 1862–AD 1874).prose:
[China, AD 1862–AD 1874] Tongzhi. 1862-1874 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The boy emperor's reign was in practice the government of the Empress Dowager Cixi and a group of reforming officials, coming immediately after the Taiping and Nian rebellions and the burning of the Summer Palace. Their "restoration" combined Confucian moral revival with arsenals, shipyards, a foreign-language college and China's first modern diplomatic office, the Zongli Yamen - the beginning of self-strengthening, and of the argument about how much of the West China needed to absorb.

Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC–1449.label: Haftavan Period VIB
Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC–1449.prose:
[Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 1899 BC–1449 BC] Haftavan Period VIB. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.1900BC-1450BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The classic Middle Bronze Age horizon at this mound in Iranian Azerbaijan, defined by the boldly painted 'Urmia ware' pottery that links the Lake Urmia basin with Transcaucasia and eastern Anatolia. Excavations here produced the reference sequence archaeologists still use to date the period across the region.

Chunxi (China, AD 1174–AD 1190).label: Chunxi
Chunxi (China, AD 1174–AD 1190).prose:
[China, AD 1174–AD 1190] Chunxi. 1174-1190 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The longest era of Emperor Xiaozong's reign, a stretch of peace with the Jin in the north that let the Southern Song economy, cities and maritime trade flourish. Frugal government and careful finances made it a byword for good rule in later Chinese writing. It was also the height of Neo-Confucian debate, when Zhu Xi was assembling the commentaries that would shape Chinese thought and examinations for the next 700 years.

Dinh dynasty (Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980).label: Dinh dynasty
Dinh dynasty (Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980] Dinh dynasty. Vietnamese dynasty, 968-980.  state name: Dai Co Viet. Period definition from British Museum.

Đinh Bộ Lĩnh defeated the twelve warlords who had fragmented the country after the collapse of Chinese control, declared himself emperor and named his realm Đại Cồ Việt. He built a fortified capital at Hoa Lư among limestone hills, organised an army and ranks of officials, and secured recognition from the Song court. His assassination in 979 left a child on the throne, and the general Lê Hoàn took the crown to face a Song invasion — but the principle of an independent Vietnamese monarchy had been established.

Classical World (Mediterranean Basin, 99.label: Classical World
Classical World (Mediterranean Basin, 99.prose:
[ancient Mediterranean, 999 BC–AD 400] Classical World. Classical World is a broad term referring to the civilisations of the ancient Mediterranean from around 1000 BC to 400 AD, centred on the idea of a continuous development of literature, ideas and material culture originating in Aegean Greece and its overseas settlements and later adapted and modified by the Roman state from the time of the late Republic and early Empire. The term was originally defined after the Renaissance by the literary and artistic inheritance of Greece in the fifth and fourth centuries BC and Rome between the first century BC and fourth century AD, but later took on a broader meaning including history, material culture, settlement and economy within much wider chronological and geographical parameters. The term also includes cultures in close proximity to or in contact with Greeks and Romans, such as Cyprus, the non-Greek peoples of Anatolia such as Lycians and Carians, and the Villanovan, Etruscan and Italic communities of Italy. Other cultures, such as Phoenicians and Carthaginians, local peoples of Spain and North Africa (including Dynastic Egypt), Phrygians, Thracians, Scythians, Celts and the Germanic tribes tend to be included under other Top Terms in the thesaurus (Prehistoric, Levantine and Middle Eastern periods and cultures, and Historic European Periods and cultures). Chronologically, the term sometimes is extended to the earlier periods of Greek history before 1000 BC, including the Bronze Age Minoan and Mycenaean civilisations based on the idea of cultural ancestry. Period definition from British Museum.

The Mediterranean became a single connected arena, first through Phoenician and Greek colonies scattered around its shores, then through the empires of Athens, Alexander's successors, and finally Rome, which turned the sea into an internal lake. Coined money, alphabetic literacy, monumental stone architecture and codified law spread along the same shipping lanes as grain, wine and slaves. The philosophy, drama, sculpture and political vocabulary produced in these centuries were repeatedly rediscovered by later Europeans, and the Roman road and city network shaped where people still live today.

Ayyubid dynasty (Syria, AD 1169–AD 1260).label: Ayyubid dynasty
Ayyubid dynasty (Syria, AD 1169–AD 1260).prose:
[Syria, Egypt, AD 1169–AD 1260] Ayyubid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Syria. 1169-1260 (AH 564-AH 658). Dynasty of Kurdish origin whose most famous ruler was Saladin I, the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty in Damascus. He conquered Fatimid Egypt and replaced Isma'ili Shi'ism with strong orthodox Sunni religious and educational policy. The Ayyubids were continuing the policy of the Zangids in Syria and the earlier Great Seljuqs. After the death of the Ayyubid al-Kamil Nasir al-Din Muhammad in 1238 (AH 635) internal quarrels turned the Ayyubid empire into a confederation of principalities. The Mongol invasion put an end to Ayyubid rule. Period definition from British Museum.

Saladin's family ruled Syria from Damascus and Aleppo as a network of related princes rather than a single centralised realm, fighting the crusader states, each other, and eventually the Mongols. Their legacy in the Syrian landscape is architectural: rebuilt citadels, city walls, and a wave of madrasas and hospitals that made Damascus a centre of Sunni learning. The Mongol sack of 1260 and the Mamluk victory that followed ended Ayyubid power.

Xingzong (China, AD 1031–AD 1055).label: Xingzong
Xingzong (China, AD 1031–AD 1055).prose:
[China, AD 1031–AD 1055] Xingzong. 1031-1055 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Liao emperor Xingzong used the Song's troubles with the Tanguts to demand higher annual tribute, extracting more silk and silver by threat alone. His own campaigns against Western Xia went badly, and the court's heavy patronage of Buddhism strained finances. Liao power still looked formidable, but the internal fractures that the Jurchens would exploit were forming.

Hoei Era (Japan, AD 1704–AD 1711).label: Hoei Era
Hoei Era (Japan, AD 1704–AD 1711).prose:
[Japan, AD 1704–AD 1711] Hoei Era. 1704-1711. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era remembered for catastrophe: a huge earthquake and tsunami struck the Pacific coast in 1707, and seven weeks later Mount Fuji erupted, dusting Edo with ash and ruining farmland for years. The Tokugawa government, already strained after the extravagance of the Genroku years, debased the coinage and levied special taxes to pay for relief. It closed with the death of the shogun Tsunayoshi and a reform-minded change of regime.

Proto-Etruscan (Italy, 999 BC–779 BC).label: Proto-Etruscan
Proto-Etruscan (Italy, 999 BC–779 BC).prose:
[Italy, 999 BC–779 BC] Proto-Etruscan. 1000BC-780BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Villanovan communities in Etruria cremated their dead in distinctive biconical urns and clustered into large settlements on the volcanic plateaus that would become Tarquinia, Cerveteri and Vulci. Access to copper and iron ore made these villages rich, and imported Greek and Levantine goods began arriving. Within a few generations they had grown into the walled cities of Etruscan civilisation.

Shunzhi (China, AD 1644–AD 1661).label: Shunzhi
Shunzhi (China, AD 1644–AD 1661).prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1661] Shunzhi. 1644-1661 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The first Qing reign from Beijing, after Manchu forces entered the capital in 1644 in the wake of the rebel sack that ended the Ming. Real power belonged to the regent Dorgon, who ordered Chinese men to shave their foreheads and wear the queue on pain of death, while Qing armies fought Ming loyalist regimes south through the Yangzi valley. Much Ming administration was kept intact, staffed by Chinese officials under Manchu supervision, a formula that held the empire together for two and a half centuries.

Byzantine (Greece, AD 330–AD 1453).label: Byzantine
Byzantine (Greece, AD 330–AD 1453).prose:
[eastern Mediterranean, AD 330–AD 1453] Byzantine. Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Greece, Turkey. The term refers to the successor state to the Roman empire in the eastern Mediterranean, from the foundation  of Constantinople by Constantine the Great in AD 330 until its fall to the Ottoman Turks in AD 1453. The Byzantine period is often divided into three phases: the early Byzantine period from the early 4thC to the 7thC (see also the term Late Antique) which saw the losses of the key provinces of Syria and Egypt to the Arabs; the Middle Byzantine period from the 8thC to the early 13thC covering Iconoclasm and ending with the sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204; the Late Byzantine period from the early 13thC to the mid-15thC, a period of geographical and political decline, but also of a flowering of the arts under the Palaeologan dynasty.  See also the terms Late Roman and Medieval and its Narrow Terms. Period definition from British Museum.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.

Daiji Era (Japan, AD 1126–AD 1131).label: Daiji Era
Daiji Era (Japan, AD 1126–AD 1131).prose:
[Japan, AD 1126–AD 1131] Daiji Era. 1126-1131. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Heian years in which the young Emperor Sutoku sat on the throne while the retired Emperor Toba directed affairs from his cloister, the pattern of "rule by retired sovereigns" that had displaced Fujiwara regents. Provincial warrior houses, the Taira and Minamoto among them, were meanwhile being drawn into the capital as the armed clients of court factions.

Burid dynasty (Syria, AD 1104–AD 1154).label: Burid dynasty
Burid dynasty (Syria, AD 1104–AD 1154).prose:
[Damascus and southern Syria, AD 1104–AD 1154] Burid dynasty. 1104-1154 (AH 497-549). Damascus and southern Syria.  Dynasty derived from Tughtigin, Atabeg of the Seljuq Amie of Damascus (Buri is the son of Tughtigin). They maintained their power through skilful diplomacy with the Fatamids and the Frankish Crusaders but these balancing policies were not popular with the 'Abbasid Caliphs. Period definition from British Museum.

A line of Turkish atabegs who made Damascus an independent power, founded by Toghtekin out of the wreckage of the Seljuk empire. Squeezed between the Crusader states and rival Muslim rulers, the Burids alternately fought and allied with the Franks, and repelled the Second Crusade's siege of the city in 1148. Their independence ended when Nur al-Din of Aleppo took Damascus, uniting Muslim Syria against the Crusaders.

Keio Era (Japan, AD 1865–AD 1868).label: Keio Era
Keio Era (Japan, AD 1865–AD 1868).prose:
[Japan, AD 1865–AD 1868] Keio Era. 1865-1868. Period definition from British Museum.

The last era of the Tokugawa order, opening with a failed shogunal campaign against Chōshū and the secret Satsuma–Chōshū alliance brokered against the regime. The shogun Iemochi and Emperor Kōmei both died; Tokugawa Yoshinobu returned power to the throne in 1867, and the Boshin War began the fighting that would carry the young Meiji emperor to Edo.

Cypro-Classical I (Cyprus, 479 BC–399 BC.label: Cypro-Classical I
Cypro-Classical I (Cyprus, 479 BC–399 BC.prose:
[Cyprus, 479 BC–399 BC] Cypro-Classical I. 480 BC-400 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Persian control was reasserted after the failed Ionian Revolt, but the city-kingdoms kept their thrones, mints and distinctive syllabic script. Evagoras I of Salamis dominated the era, extending his rule over much of the island and courting Athens before Persia forced him back into submission. Greek styles increasingly shaped Cypriot sculpture and coin design, while Phoenician Kition remained a rival power.

Genbun Era (Japan, AD 1736–AD 1741).label: Genbun Era
Genbun Era (Japan, AD 1736–AD 1741).prose:
[Japan, AD 1736–AD 1741] Genbun Era. 1736-1741. Period definition from British Museum.

Best remembered for the recoinage of 1736, when the shogunate deliberately reduced the gold and silver content of its currency and issued it in greater quantity. After decades of Yoshimune's austerity and falling prices, the move eased the deflation and brought a period of relative stability to the Tokugawa economy, and Genbun coins remained in circulation for the rest of the century.

Haftavan Period V (Iran, 1449 BC–1099 BC.label: Haftavan Period V
Haftavan Period V (Iran, 1449 BC–1099 BC.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 1449 BC–1099 BC] Haftavan Period V. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.1450BC-1100BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Kyotoku Era (Japan, AD 1452–AD 1455).label: Kyotoku Era
Kyotoku Era (Japan, AD 1452–AD 1455).prose:
[Japan, AD 1452–AD 1455] Kyotoku Era. 1452-1455. Period definition from British Museum.

The murder of the Uesugi deputy by the Kamakura kubō in 1454 set off the Kyōtoku Incident, a war that tore the Kantō apart for nearly thirty years. It was the first of the great conflicts in which shogunal arbitration simply failed, and eastern Japan effectively went its own way. Historians often treat it, rather than the Ōnin War, as the true beginning of the Warring States age.

Commagenian (Turkey, 162 BC–AD 72).label: Commagenian
Commagenian (Turkey, 162 BC–AD 72).prose:
[southern Turkey, 162 BC–AD 72] Commagenian. Commagene was a small kingdom in southern Turkey, which began life as a tributary state of the Seleucid Empire c. 163 BC and later became an independent kingdom, before eventually being annexed by the Roman Empire in  AD 72. Period definition from British Museum.

A small kingdom on the upper Euphrates that broke away from the Seleucids and survived by playing Rome against Parthia. Its rulers claimed descent from both Persian and Macedonian royalty, a mix made spectacular at Antiochos I's mountaintop sanctuary on Nemrut Dağ, where colossal seated gods carry blended Greek and Iranian names. Rome finally annexed the territory under Vespasian.

Qiandao (China, AD 1165–AD 1174).label: Qiandao
Qiandao (China, AD 1165–AD 1174).prose:
[China, AD 1165–AD 1174] Qiandao. 1165-1174 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign era of the Southern Song emperor Xiaozong, following the peace settlement with the Jin that fixed the border along the Huai River. With the northern campaigns abandoned, the court concentrated on fiscal reform, canal and coastal trade, and the flourishing printing and porcelain industries of the Jiangnan south.

Kakwayhid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1008–AD 10.label: Kakwayhid dynasty
Kakwayhid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1008–AD 10.prose:
[Zagros region, AD 1008–AD 1051] Kakwayhid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. 1008-1051 (AH 398-AH 443). Petty Kurdish and Daylami dynasty of the Zagros region when the power of the Buyids (q.v.) began to fade. With the rise of the Seljuqs in Persia the Kakwayhid's lost their independence and were reduced to vasaledge. Muhammad known as Ibn Kakuya, who was the son of Dushmanziyar, was the governor of Isfahan in 1008 (AH 398). He soon expanded his power to Hamadan and Kurdistan and his court circle included the philosopher and physian Ibn Sina (Avicenna) who functioned as his vizier. Period definition from British Museum.

A Daylamite line that seized Isfahan and Hamadan as Buyid power crumbled, holding out against Ghaznavid and then Seljuk armies before surviving as Seljuk vassals in Yazd. Its most famous ruler, Ala al-Dawla Muhammad, employed the philosopher-physician Avicenna as his minister and companion, and several of Avicenna's major works were written at his court.

Calima (Colombia, 1499 BC–AD 1600).label: Calima
Calima (Colombia, 1499 BC–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, 1499 BC–AD 1600] Calima. The term refers to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the Western Range of the Valle del Cauca department from 1500 BC to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

A sequence of societies in the mountainous Calima region of the Cauca Valley, running from the early Ilama and Yotoco periods to the later Sonso. They are best known for goldwork of astonishing quality, hammered masks, diadems and pectorals, and for expressive ceramic figures, alongside enormous terraced fields and drainage ditches cut into the hillsides. The gold was buried with the dead in shaft tombs, which made the region a target of looting long before archaeologists arrived.

Chunyou (China, AD 1241–AD 1253).label: Chunyou
Chunyou (China, AD 1241–AD 1253).prose:
[China, AD 1241–AD 1253] Chunyou. 1241-1253 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era of the Southern Song emperor Lizong, when the court in Hangzhou watched the Mongols destroy the Jin and turn south. It was a time of hard defensive war along the Yangtze and Sichuan frontiers paid for by inflated paper money, and also of cultural consolidation: Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian synthesis was made state orthodoxy, fixing the intellectual framework of Chinese officialdom for the next six centuries. The famous Suzhou stone star chart, engraved with a map of the heavens and one of China, dates from these years.

Canh Hung reign period (Vietnam, AD 1740.label: Canh Hung reign period
Canh Hung reign period (Vietnam, AD 1740.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1740–AD 1786] Canh Hung reign period. Canh Hung reign period (1740-1786). Period definition from British Museum.

The long era-name of Lê Hiển Tông, a monarch who reigned while the Trịnh lords ran the government from Thăng Long and the Nguyễn ruled the south. Peasant revolts, famine and factional violence gnawed at Trịnh authority, and in 1771 the Tây Sơn brothers rose in revolt, sweeping away both lordly houses within two decades. The nominal Lê court outlived the reign by only a few years.

Kansho Era (Japan, AD 1460–AD 1466).label: Kansho Era
Kansho Era (Japan, AD 1460–AD 1466).prose:
[Japan, AD 1460–AD 1466] Kansho Era. 1460-1466. Period definition from British Museum.

Under the aesthete shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, drought and flood produced the Kanshō famine, which filled the streets of Kyoto with tens of thousands of refugees and corpses while relief was left largely to priests. Shogunal authority visibly failed, and within a year of the era's end the Ōnin War broke out and burned the capital.

Western Wei dynasty (China, AD 535–AD 55.label: Western Wei dynasty
Western Wei dynasty (China, AD 535–AD 55.prose:
[China, AD 535–AD 557] Western Wei dynasty. 535-557. Period definition from British Museum.

A rump state carved from the collapsing Northern Wei, based at Chang'an and dominated by Yuwen Tai rather than its nominal emperors. Its innovations in military organisation and in fusing Xianbei and Chinese aristocratic families proved far more important than its short life. The dynasty was formally replaced by the Northern Zhou, whose ruling house came from the same power base.

Luluid dynasty (Iraq, AD 1234–AD 1262).label: Luluid dynasty
Luluid dynasty (Iraq, AD 1234–AD 1262).prose:
[Mosul; Ayyubid territory in the Jazira, AD 1234–AD 1262] Luluid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. 1234-1262 (AH 631-AH 660). Probably of Armenian origin. Badr al-Din Lulu was recognised by the Abbasid caliph as the ruler of the city of Mosul in 1234 (AH 631). He extended his authority into Ayyubid territory in the Jazira. His son's brief rule came to an end with the invasion of the region under Il-Khanid ruler Hulegu in 1260 (AH 658). Lu'lu's sons fled to the Mamluks in Egypt. Period definition from British Museum.

Badr al-Din Lu'lu', a freed slave who had served the Zengid rulers of Mosul, took the city for himself and governed it through the turbulent decades before the Mongol conquest, surviving by shifting allegiance from the Ayyubids to Hulagu. Mosul under him was a centre of fine metalwork, and inlaid brasses made for his court survive in museums worldwide. His sons lost the city when they turned against the Mongols.

Kofun Period (Japan, AD 250–AD 552).label: Kofun Period
Kofun Period (Japan, AD 250–AD 552).prose: [Japan, AD 250–AD 552] Kofun Period. 250-552 - Tumulus. Period definition from British Museum.

Lambayeque (Peru, AD 900–AD 1250).label: Lambayeque
Lambayeque (Peru, AD 900–AD 1250).prose:
[ancient Peru , AD 900–AD 1250] Lambayeque. The date range covered is AD 900-AD 1250.  Christopher Donnan, 'Ceramics of Ancient Peru', Fowler Museum of Cultural History, University of California, Los Angeles, 1992. Period definition from British Museum.

Also known as Sicán, this north-coast culture rose in the irrigated valleys after the Moche collapse, building great adobe pyramid complexes at Batán Grande and Túcume. Its metalsmiths were among the finest in the Americas, mass-producing arsenical bronze and burying lords with hoards of hammered gold masks and ceremonial tumi knives whose almond-eyed face became an emblem of ancient Peru. Drought and fire ended the Batán Grande phase, and the Chimú of Chan Chan eventually absorbed the region.

Zhaowu (China, AD 1674–AD 1678).label: Zhaowu
Zhaowu (China, AD 1674–AD 1678).prose:
[China, AD 1674–AD 1678] Zhaowu. 1674-1678 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The era name proclaimed by Wu Sangui, the general who had opened the passes to the Manchus and then turned on them, during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. He declared himself emperor of a new Zhou dynasty in the south and cast his own coins, which survive in quantity today. His death and the collapse of the revolt let the young Kangxi emperor consolidate Qing control over all of China.

Eastern Jin dynasty (China, AD 317–AD 41.label: Eastern Jin dynasty
Eastern Jin dynasty (China, AD 317–AD 41.prose:
[China, AD 317–AD 419] Eastern Jin dynasty. 317-419. Period definition from British Museum.

The Jin house, driven out of the north by steppe conquerors, ruled from Jiankang over the Yangtze valley while rival non-Chinese kingdoms fought over the plains above. Powerful aristocratic clans and warlord generals dominated the emperors, and the great southward migration of northern elites transformed the south into China's cultural and agricultural core. The era produced Tao Yuanming's poetry, Wang Xizhi's calligraphy and the first great flowering of Chinese Buddhist scholarship.

Qiantong (China, AD 1101–AD 1109).label: Qiantong
Qiantong (China, AD 1101–AD 1109).prose:
[China, AD 1101–AD 1109] Qiantong. 1101-1109 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The opening era of the reign of Tianzuo, last emperor of the Liao. The Khitan state still ruled a broad band of Mongolia and north China, but hunting-obsessed and inattentive rule alienated its Jurchen subjects in the northeast, who rose within a few years and destroyed the dynasty.

Middle Minoan IA (Crete, 1999 BC–1949 BC.label: Middle Minoan IA
Middle Minoan IA (Crete, 1999 BC–1949 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1999 BC–1949 BC] Middle Minoan IA. 2000BC-1950BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The last phase before the palaces, when Cretan communities were growing fast and burying their dead in collective tombs, while mountaintop peak sanctuaries filled with clay votive offerings. Potters experimented with light-on-dark polychrome painting, the direct ancestor of the famous Kamares ware.

Genchu Era (Japan, AD 1384–AD 1390).label: Genchu Era
Genchu Era (Japan, AD 1384–AD 1390).prose:
[Japan, AD 1384–AD 1390] Genchu Era. 1384-1390. Period definition from British Museum.

The final era name used by the Southern Court during the long schism between two rival imperial lines. By now the southern cause was nearly spent, its court holding out in the mountains of Yoshino while the Ashikaga shoguns backed the northern emperors in Kyoto; within a few years the two lines were formally reunited on northern terms.

Inca (Peru, AD 1530–AD 1660).label: Inca
Inca (Peru, AD 1530–AD 1660).prose:
[Peru, AD 1530–AD 1660] Inca. Spatial coverage: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, Peru. 1530-1660. Period definition from British Museum.

Tawantinsuyu was the largest state the Americas ever produced, run without money or writing through labour tribute, storehouses, knotted-cord khipu records and thousands of kilometres of paved road. Pizarro's capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca broke the imperial centre, and Spanish rule, epidemic disease and resettlement into reducciones transformed Andean life within a couple of generations - though the neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba held out for decades and Inca stonework still underpins Cusco.

Jingo'keiun Era (China, AD 767–AD 770).label: Jingo'keiun Era
Jingo'keiun Era (China, AD 767–AD 770).prose:
[China, AD 767–AD 770] Jingo'keiun Era. 767-770. Period definition from British Museum.

The closing years of Empress Shōtoku's reign in Nara Japan, dominated by the monk Dōkyō, whose extraordinary influence at court nearly won him the throne before an oracle from Usa Hachiman blocked him. His fall after the empress's death soured relations between the throne and the great monasteries and helped push the capital away from Nara.

Otoku Era (Japan, AD 1084–AD 1087).label: Otoku Era
Otoku Era (Japan, AD 1084–AD 1087).prose:
[Japan, AD 1084–AD 1087] Otoku Era. 1084-1087. Period definition from British Museum.

A short late-Heian era name spanning the final years of Emperor Shirakawa's personal reign, which ended when he abdicated in favour of his infant son and continued to govern as a retired sovereign. That move inaugurated the cloistered-rule system that sidelined the Fujiwara regents and dominated court politics for the next century. In the north, the fighting that became the Later Three-Year War was drawing the Minamoto deeper into provincial warrior affairs.

Taiping Xingguo (China, AD 976–AD 983).label: Taiping Xingguo
Taiping Xingguo (China, AD 976–AD 983).prose:
[China, AD 976–AD 983] Taiping Xingguo. 976-983 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The opening years of Emperor Taizong's reign, when the Song completed the reunification of China by annexing Wuyue and destroying the Northern Han. Emboldened, Taizong pushed north to recover the Sixteen Prefectures from the Liao and was routed at the Gaoliang River, a defeat that fixed the Song on a defensive northern posture for generations.

Shoan Era (Japan, AD 1299–AD 1302).label: Shoan Era
Shoan Era (Japan, AD 1299–AD 1302).prose:
[Japan, AD 1299–AD 1302] Shoan Era. 1299-1302. Period definition from British Museum.

A quiet stretch of the Kamakura period, with the shogunate run by the Hōjō regents at Kamakura and the throne passing between the two rival imperial lines under a compromise that had them alternate the succession. Court and warrior government were still absorbing the strains left by the Mongol invasions, whose defenders had been rewarded with little more than prayers and promises.

Thai Duc (Vietnam, AD 1776–AD 1793).label: Thai Duc
Thai Duc (Vietnam, AD 1776–AD 1793).prose: [Vietnam, AD 1776–AD 1793] Thai Duc. Vietnamese reign period 1776-1793. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Minoan IIIB1 (Crete, 1299 BC–1249 B.label: Late Minoan IIIB1
Late Minoan IIIB1 (Crete, 1299 BC–1249 B.prose:
[Crete, 1299 BC–1249 BC] Late Minoan IIIB1. 1300BC-1250BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cretan communities continued much as before, with regional workshops turning out uniform stirrup jars and deep bowls and Chania acting as the island's busiest port. Shrines with wheel-made clay goddess figures raising their arms became a common form of worship. Beneath the surface stability, trade routes to the east were beginning to falter.

Southern Han Kingdom (China, AD 905–AD 9.label: Southern Han Kingdom
Southern Han Kingdom (China, AD 905–AD 9.prose:
[China, AD 905–AD 971] Southern Han Kingdom. 905-971. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the Ten Kingdoms of the post-Tang fragmentation, ruled by the Liu family from Guangzhou. Its prosperity came from maritime trade with Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, and its court became notorious for luxury, cruelty and reliance on eunuch officials. Song armies annexed it, bringing the southern coast and its ports under the new empire.

Wei Kingdom (China, AD 220–AD 265) [p08m.label: Wei Kingdom
Wei Kingdom (China, AD 220–AD 265) [p08m.prose:
[China, AD 220–AD 265] Wei Kingdom. 220-265. Period definition from British Museum.

The northernmost and strongest of the three states that divided China after the Han collapse, founded when Cao Cao's son deposed the last Han emperor. Wei controlled the Yellow River heartland, revived agriculture through military farming colonies, and introduced the nine-rank system for choosing officials that entrenched great families for centuries. Real power slipped to the Sima clan, who overthrew Wei and founded the Jin dynasty that briefly reunified China.

Qaleh (Iran, 1599 BC–1349 BC).label: Qaleh
Qaleh (Iran, 1599 BC–1349 BC).prose:
[Fars, 1599 BC–1349 BC] Qaleh. Fars, 1600BC-1350BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase in the Kur River Basin of Fars, defined by its distinctive painted Qaleh ware and following the more prosperous Kaftari period. Settlement in the plain appears thinner and more dispersed, while lowland Elam under the Middle Elamite kings was at its height, raising long-running questions about how the highland valleys related to the lowland states.

Mon Kings (Thailand, AD 550–AD 1030).label: Mon Kings
Mon Kings (Thailand, AD 550–AD 1030).prose:
[Dvaravati kingdom, AD 550–AD 1030] Mon Kings. The Mon kings are associated with the kingdom of Dvaravati (AD 550-1030) in what is now Thailand. Period definition from British Museum.

Mon-speaking communities of the Chao Phraya basin, known to archaeologists as Dvaravati, built moated towns surrounded by rice fields and were among the first in mainland Southeast Asia to adopt Theravada Buddhism from India. Their stone dharma wheels, stucco reliefs and serene Buddha images are the earliest major Buddhist art of the region, and sites such as Nakhon Pathom and U Thong preserve substantial monastic remains. Related Mon polities spread north to Haripunchai at Lamphun before Khmer expansion and the arrival of Tai-speaking groups absorbed them.

Dali Kingdom (China, AD 937–AD 1253).label: Dali Kingdom
Dali Kingdom (China, AD 937–AD 1253).prose:
[China, AD 937–AD 1253] Dali Kingdom. 937-1253. Period definition from British Museum.

A Buddhist state centred on the lakeside city of Dali in Yunnan, founded by Duan Siping on the ruins of Nanzhao and ruled by his family for three centuries. It traded horses to the Song, produced remarkable gilt-bronze images and the painted Zhang Shengwen scroll, and several of its kings abdicated to become monks. Kublai Khan's armies destroyed it in 1253, bringing Yunnan permanently into the Chinese empire.

Choji Era (Japan, AD 1104–AD 1106).label: Choji Era
Choji Era (Japan, AD 1104–AD 1106).prose:
[Japan, AD 1104–AD 1106] Choji Era. 1104-1106. Period definition from British Museum.

Government ran through the retired emperor Shirakawa, whose cloistered rule bypassed the reigning boy emperor and the Fujiwara regents. Provincial warrior houses, the Taira and Minamoto among them, were drawn to the retired emperor's household as guards and enforcers, a habit that gradually armed the politics of the capital.

Shochu Era (Japan, AD 1324–AD 1326).label: Shochu Era
Shochu Era (Japan, AD 1324–AD 1326).prose:
[Japan, AD 1324–AD 1326] Shochu Era. 1324-1326. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Go-Daigo's first conspiracy against the Kamakura shogunate was betrayed and crushed by the Rokuhara deputies in 1324, and his courtiers were arrested and exiled while the emperor himself denied all knowledge. The plot failed, but it announced Go-Daigo's intention to rule as well as reign, and led within a decade to the shogunate's destruction and the split of the imperial house into rival courts.

Manju Era (Japan, AD 1024–AD 1028).label: Manju Era
Manju Era (Japan, AD 1024–AD 1028).prose:
[Japan, AD 1024–AD 1028] Manju Era. 1024-1028. Period definition from British Museum.

The closing years of Fujiwara no Michinaga's dominance at the Heian court, when the regents' family stood at the height of its power and Michinaga's great Hōjōji temple embodied its aristocratic Buddhism. His death in 1027 was followed almost at once by Taira no Tadatsune's revolt in the eastern provinces, an early sign that the court's grip on the countryside was slipping toward the warrior houses.

Old Bering Sea Culture (Alaska, 499 BC–A.label: Old Bering Sea Culture
Old Bering Sea Culture (Alaska, 499 BC–A.prose:
[Bering Strait, 499 BC–AD 500] Old Bering Sea Culture. 500 BC-500 - Bering Strait. Period definition from British Museum.

Sea-mammal hunters on both sides of the Bering Strait developed toggling harpoons, skin boats and the techniques for taking walrus and whale from the ice edge. They are best known for engraved ivory harpoon heads and winged objects covered in swirling curvilinear designs, some of the finest carving in the Arctic. Their descendants carried this maritime way of life across northern Alaska, laying the basis for later Thule and Inuit whaling societies.

Western Han dynasty (China, 205 BC–AD 9).label: Western Han dynasty
Western Han dynasty (China, 205 BC–AD 9).prose:
[China, 205 BC–AD 9] Western Han dynasty. 206 BC-9 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The first enduring Chinese empire, ruled from Chang'an by the house of Liu, which softened Qin legalism into a Confucian bureaucratic order staffed by examined officials. Expansion under Emperor Wu opened trans-Eurasian trade and pushed the Xiongnu steppe confederation back beyond the Gobi. It ended not in conquest but in a palace coup, when the regent Wang Mang declared his own short-lived dynasty.

Tay Son dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1777–AD 180.label: Tay Son dynasty
Tay Son dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1777–AD 180.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1777–AD 1802] Tay Son dynasty. Vietnamese reign period 1777-1802. Period definition from British Museum.

Three brothers from a village in the central highlands led a peasant revolt that toppled both the Nguyen lords in the south and the Trinh lords and Le emperors in the north, briefly reuniting Vietnam. Their greatest moment was Nguyen Hue's rout of an invading Qing army at Dong Da in 1789; after his early death the regime weakened and fell to Nguyen Anh, who founded the Nguyen dynasty.

Liangzhu culture (China, 3299 BC–2249 BC.label: Liangzhu culture
Liangzhu culture (China, 3299 BC–2249 BC.prose:
[China, 3299 BC–2249 BC] Liangzhu culture. Neolithic culture circa 3300 BC-2250 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A rice-farming society of the Yangtze delta that built a walled city of some 300 hectares at Liangzhu, ringed by an enormous system of dams and levees - among the earliest large-scale water engineering anywhere. Its elite were buried with hundreds of finely worked jades, especially the tubular cong and disc-shaped bi, cut with abrasive sand to a precision that still puzzles specialists. The jade forms and the ritual ideas behind them echoed through later Chinese civilisation long after the culture itself vanished, probably amid flooding.

Ningzong (China, AD 1195–AD 1224).label: Ningzong
Ningzong (China, AD 1195–AD 1224).prose:
[China, AD 1195–AD 1224] Ningzong. 1195-1224 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A long Southern Song reign dominated by ministers rather than the emperor: first Han Tuozhou, who banned Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian teaching as false learning and then launched a disastrous war to retake the north from the Jin, losing his head to buy peace. His successor Shi Miyuan reversed course and made Zhu Xi's commentaries orthodox, a decision that shaped Chinese education for the next seven centuries. Meanwhile Hangzhou flourished as a commercial capital, and Mongol power was rising beyond the Jin frontier.

Tiancong (China, AD 1627–AD 1643).label: Tiancong
Tiancong (China, AD 1627–AD 1643).prose:
[China, AD 1627–AD 1643] Tiancong. 1627-1643 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Hong Taiji's years at the head of the Jurchen state turned his father's tribal confederation into a bureaucratic empire capable of taking China. He absorbed the Chahar Mongols and the Korean kingdom of Joseon, recruited Han Chinese officials and artillery, created Mongol and Chinese banner armies, and renamed his people the Manchus and his dynasty the Qing. When he died, Ming defences in the northeast were already hollowed out; his son entered Beijing within a year.

Cypro-Archaic II (Cyprus, 599 BC–449 BC).label: Cypro-Archaic II
Cypro-Archaic II (Cyprus, 599 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 599 BC–449 BC] Cypro-Archaic II. 600 BC-450 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The city-kingdoms passed from Assyrian to Egyptian and then Persian overlordship, each keeping its own king, coinage and script. Cypriot sculptors blended Egyptian wigs and kilts with Greek dress and the archaic smile, producing limestone statues that belong to no single tradition. The period closes with the Ionian Revolt, when most Cypriot kings joined the rebellion against Persia and were crushed.

Late Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–2999 BC).label: Late Uruk
Late Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–2999 BC] Late Uruk. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia dating to between 3500-3000 BC. During this period the Uruk culture spread to western Iran, Syria and southeast Anatolia. Period definition from British Museum.

The world's first cities took shape in the Mesopotamian lowlands, and their institutions, goods and administrators reached deep into the Iranian plateau and Khuzestan. Mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and the earliest clay tablets with proto-cuneiform signs mark the birth of bureaucratic record-keeping. When the Uruk network contracted, Susa and its neighbours went their own way, developing the Proto-Elamite script and state.

Qin dynasty (China, 220 BC–206 BC).label: Qin dynasty
Qin dynasty (China, 220 BC–206 BC).prose:
[China, 220 BC–206 BC] Qin dynasty. 221 BC-207 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

China's first unified empire, imposed by conquest and run on Legalist principles: uniform law, standardised script and measures, mass conscript labour for roads, canals and frontier walls. Aristocratic states were replaced by a bureaucracy of appointed governors, a system every later dynasty inherited. Harsh taxation and corvée provoked rebellion almost as soon as the First Emperor died, and the regime fell after barely fifteen years.

Lagash II (Iraq, 2189 BC–2099 BC).label: Lagash II
Lagash II (Iraq, 2189 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Lagash in southern Mesopotamia, 2189 BC–2099 BC] Lagash II. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia. A term used for a dynasty of rulers of the city-state of Lagash in southern Mesopotamia who expanded their authority following the collapse of the Akkadian empire around 2190 BC. Lagash was eventually absorbed into the kingdom of the Third Dynasty of Ur after 2100 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

After the collapse of the Akkadian empire, the city-state of Lagash flourished independently under rulers who rebuilt temples and traded for stone, timber and metals from Magan and the Levant. Its most famous ruler, Gudea, left dozens of hard diorite statues and inscribed clay cylinders describing the building of the god Ningirsu's temple — among the finest Sumerian sculpture and literature to survive. The city was soon absorbed into the Third Dynasty of Ur.

Guangtian (China, AD 918–AD 918).label: Guangtian
Guangtian (China, AD 918–AD 918).prose:
[China, AD 918–AD 918] Guangtian. 918. Period definition from British Museum.

A reign era lasting less than a year in the kingdom of Former Shu, one of the short-lived states carved out of the collapse of the Tang. Era names changed rapidly in this period as rulers tried to mark new beginnings; this one is remembered mainly as a dating label on coins, inscriptions and documents.

Karoku Era (Japan, AD 1225–AD 1227).label: Karoku Era
Karoku Era (Japan, AD 1225–AD 1227).prose:
[Japan, AD 1225–AD 1227] Karoku Era. 1225-1227. Period definition from British Museum.

With Hōjō Masako and the veteran administrator Ōe no Hiromoto both dead, the regent Hōjō Yasutoki reorganised the Kamakura government around a council of senior vassals and a co-signer, replacing personal rule with collective bureaucracy. The infant courtier Kujō Yoritsune was installed as shogun, a figurehead beneath the Hōjō, and Kyoto monks attacked the followers of the Pure Land teacher Hōnen.

Tenpyo-jingo Era (Japan, AD 765–AD 767).label: Tenpyo-jingo Era
Tenpyo-jingo Era (Japan, AD 765–AD 767).prose:
[Japan, AD 765–AD 767] Tenpyo-jingo Era. 765-767. Period definition from British Museum.

Empress Shōtoku raised the monk Dōkyō to unprecedented rank and lavished state resources on Buddhism, including the great temple of Saidai-ji. Her programme of a million miniature wooden pagodas, each holding a printed charm, produced some of the oldest surviving printed texts in the world.

Konin Era (Japan, AD 810–AD 824).label: Konin Era
Konin Era (Japan, AD 810–AD 824).prose:
[Japan, AD 810–AD 824] Konin Era. 810-824. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Saga survived an armed challenge from his retired brother in 810 and answered it by creating the kurōdodokoro, a private secretariat that let the throne bypass the regular bureaucracy. His court prized Chinese learning and calligraphy, and it patronised Kūkai and Saichō as they established the Shingon and Tendai schools that would shape Japanese Buddhism ever after.

Momoyama Period (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603).label: Momoyama Period
Momoyama Period (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603).prose:
[Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603] Momoyama Period. 1573-1603. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief, spectacular interval in which Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi broke the power of the warring provincial lords and reunified Japan, disarming the peasantry and surveying the land for taxation. Newly rich warlords built vast stone-based castles with soaring keeps and filled them with gold-leaf screen paintings, while the tea ceremony was refined by Sen no Rikyū and Portuguese traders and missionaries brought guns and new tastes. Hideyoshi's failed invasions of Korea drained the regime, and Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara led to the shogunate established in 1603.

Namazga V (Turkmenistan, 2499 BC–2199 BC.label: Namazga V
Namazga V (Turkmenistan, 2499 BC–2199 BC.prose: [Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, 2499 BC–2199 BC] Namazga V. Term derived from Soviet excavations at the type-site of Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, dating to ca 2500-2200 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Roman Period (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 641).label: Roman Period
Roman Period (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 641).prose:
[Egypt, 29 BC–AD 641] Roman Period. This term refers to the start of the Roman rule of Egypt in 30 BC to the Islamic Conquest in AD 641.  Researchers seeking Byzantine material from Egypt should search under Roman Period as well as Coptic. Period definition from British Museum.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

Hakuho Era (Japan, AD 672–AD 686).label: Hakuho Era
Hakuho Era (Japan, AD 672–AD 686).prose:
[Japan, AD 672–AD 686] Hakuho Era. 672-686. Period definition from British Museum.

An unofficial era label attached to the reign of Emperor Tenmu, who seized power in the Jinshin War and ruled without a chancellor, concentrating authority in the throne itself. He ordered the compiling of national histories and law codes, promoted Buddhism as a state cult, and began the planned capital at Fujiwara.

Qingning (China, AD 1055–AD 1064).label: Qingning
Qingning (China, AD 1055–AD 1064).prose:
[China, AD 1055–AD 1064] Qingning. 1055-1064 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

An era name of the Liao empire under Emperor Daozong, when the Khitan rulers held northern China and the steppe and drew heavily on Chinese administrative style alongside their own tribal traditions. Court politics in these years were poisoned by factional intrigue that would later cost the empress her life, weakening the dynasty from within.

Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3199 BC–2999 BC).label: Proto-Elamite
Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3199 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[region later known as Elam, 3199 BC–2999 BC] Proto-Elamite. circa 3200 BC-3000BC. Term usually used to describe script rather than a culture within the region that was later known as Elam. Period definition from British Museum.

Cities on the Iranian plateau adopted urban administration and produced their own still-undeciphered script, written on clay tablets recording livestock, grain and workers. Susa, Tepe Yahya and Shahr-i Sokhta shared this bureaucratic culture, evidence of an interaction network stretching from Mesopotamia to the edge of the Indus. Its cylinder seals, showing animals acting as humans, are among the most inventive images of early Iran.

Eikyu Era (Japan, AD 1113–AD 1118).label: Eikyu Era
Eikyu Era (Japan, AD 1113–AD 1118).prose:
[Japan, AD 1113–AD 1118] Eikyu Era. 1113-1118. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era under the cloistered rule of retired emperor Shirakawa, whose informal court overshadowed the reigning sovereign. It saw further armed clashes between the warrior-monks of the great Nara and Hiei monasteries, whose descents on the capital the retired emperor famously counted among the few things he could not control.

Ocho Era (Japan, AD 1311–AD 1312).label: Ocho Era
Ocho Era (Japan, AD 1311–AD 1312).prose:
[Japan, AD 1311–AD 1312] Ocho Era. 1311-1312. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief Japanese era name of barely a year, proclaimed during the reign of Emperor Hanazono while real power lay with the Hōjō regents in Kamakura. Such short reign-names were often declared to break a run of epidemics, fires or ill omens, and this one came amid the political drift of the shogunate's final decades.

Sui dynasty (China, AD 589–AD 618).label: Sui dynasty
Sui dynasty (China, AD 589–AD 618).prose:
[China, AD 589–AD 618] Sui dynasty. 589-618. Period definition from British Museum.

The short-lived regime that put China back together after centuries of north–south division, imposing a uniform legal code, a reformed tax and land system, and the beginnings of examination-based recruitment. Its greatest legacy, the Grand Canal, permanently tied the southern rice economy to the northern capitals. Overreach in Korea and mass forced labour triggered revolts that swept the dynasty away.

Banshan Period (China, 2599 BC–2299 BC).label: Banshan Period
Banshan Period (China, 2599 BC–2299 BC).prose:
[China, 2599 BC–2299 BC] Banshan Period. circa 2600 BC-2300 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase of the Majiayao painted-pottery tradition in Gansu and Qinghai, celebrated for large funerary urns covered in bold black-and-red spirals bordered with sawtooth bands. The vessels were made for burial, placed with the dead in cemeteries on the loess terraces, and show a pottery craft of remarkable technical control before the wheel. Millet farming, pig and sheep keeping and the earliest copper and bronze objects in the region belong to the same communities, marking the corridor along which metallurgy reached China.

Kenpo Era (Japan, AD 1213–AD 1219).label: Kenpo Era
Kenpo Era (Japan, AD 1213–AD 1219).prose:
[Japan, AD 1213–AD 1219] Kenpo Era. 1213-1219. Period definition from British Museum.

The Hōjō regents crushed the last great rival among the Kamakura warrior houses when Wada Yoshimori's revolt was destroyed in the streets of the city in 1213, leaving Hōjō Yoshitoki in unchallenged control. The era closed with the shogun Sanetomo — poet as much as soldier, whose verse collection survives — cut down by his own nephew on the steps of the Tsurugaoka shrine, extinguishing Yoritomo's male line.

Late Minoan IIIB2 (Crete, 1249 BC–1199 B.label: Late Minoan IIIB2
Late Minoan IIIB2 (Crete, 1249 BC–1199 B.prose:
[Crete, 1249 BC–1199 BC] Late Minoan IIIB2. 1250BC-1200BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The last decades of the old order on Crete, as destructions and abandonments struck settlements across the Aegean and imports dried up. Pottery became plainer and more local in style. Some communities were already shifting to higher, more defensible ground in anticipation of the disruption to come.

Haftavan Period VII (Iran, 2599 BC–2199.label: Haftavan Period VII
Haftavan Period VII (Iran, 2599 BC–2199.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 2599 BC–2199 BC] Haftavan Period VII. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.2600BC-2200BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Gennin Era (Japan, AD 1224–AD 1225).label: Gennin Era
Gennin Era (Japan, AD 1224–AD 1225).prose:
[Japan, AD 1224–AD 1225] Gennin Era. 1224-1225. Period definition from British Museum.

Hōjō Yoshitoki died and his son Yasutoki took over as regent, steering the shogunate away from one-man rule toward government by council of senior warriors. That shift laid the groundwork for the Goseibai Shikimoku, the warrior law code issued a few years later, which shaped samurai legal practice for centuries.

Kenmu Era (Japan, AD 1334–AD 1336).label: Kenmu Era
Kenmu Era (Japan, AD 1334–AD 1336).prose:
[Japan, AD 1334–AD 1336] Kenmu Era. 1334-1336. Period definition from British Museum.

The brief window in which Emperor Go-Daigo tried to rule Japan directly from Kyoto after the destruction of the Kamakura shogunate, issuing land judgements and rewards from a hastily improvised bureaucracy. Warriors who felt cheated of their due rallied to Ashikaga Takauji, who drove Go-Daigo out and set up a rival emperor, opening sixty years of civil war between two imperial courts.

Ghurid dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 1000–AD.label: Ghurid dynasty
Ghurid dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 1000–AD.prose:
[Khurasan, Afghanistan, Northern India, AD 1000–AD 1215] Ghurid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, India, Iran, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. Ruled circa 1000-1215 in Khurasan, Afghanistan and Northern India. Period definition from British Museum.

A dynasty from the mountainous heart of Ghor that grew from local chieftains into an empire, burning Ghazni and displacing the Ghaznavids before pushing east into the Punjab and Ganges plain. Muhammad of Ghor's victories at Tarain opened northern India to Muslim rule, and his Turkic slave commanders founded the Delhi Sultanate after his death. The dynasty's own end came quickly, swallowed by the Khwarazmshahs; its finest monument, the soaring brick Minaret of Jam, still stands in a remote river valley.

Tairona Period (Colombia, AD 900–AD 1600.label: Tairona Period
Tairona Period (Colombia, AD 900–AD 1600.prose:
[Colombia, AD 900–AD 1600] Tairona Period. The term refers to a period in the Tairona cultural tradition of Colombia in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and the Caribbean Coast in the Magdalena department from 900 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The climax of settlement in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, when populations concentrated in large stone-built towns of terraces, retaining walls and paved paths, supported by intensive terraced farming and by trade running from the coast to the high mountains. Elaborate goldwork, carved stone and painted ceramics accompanied a priestly class. Spanish campaigns from the 1520s onwards eventually shattered these towns, driving survivors up into the highlands.

Mamluk dynasty (Egypt, AD 1250–AD 1517).label: Mamluk dynasty
Mamluk dynasty (Egypt, AD 1250–AD 1517).prose:
[Egypt and Damascus, Syria, AD 1250–AD 1517] Mamluk dynasty. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Syria. 1250-1517 (AH 648-AH 923). The Mamluks (meaning 'one possessed, slave') arose from the Turkic troops of Ayyubids of Egypt and Damascus. Two lines of Mamluk sultans are distinguished: the Bahri Mamluks and the Burji Mamluks. The Bahris were ethnically Turkic from the southern Russian steppes with a mixture of other races including Kurds and also Mongols. The Burjis were Circassians from the Christian areas of the northern Caucasus. The Mamluks continued the strongly Sunni policy of the Ayyubids with the sultans, governors and amirs founding numerous mosques, madrasas and other religious and charitable institutions in Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo and elsewhere. They saw their role as defenders of Islam against the infidel Mongols, Frankish crusaders and heterodox Muslims in the mountains of western Syria. Egypt and Syria enjoyed considerable prosperity under the Mamluks until the 15th century. Period definition from British Museum.

Slave-soldiers of Turkic and later Circassian origin seized power in Cairo and turned a military caste into a ruling elite, where sultans were raised from the barracks rather than born to the throne. They halted the Mongol advance at Ayn Jalut in 1260, finished off the Crusader states, and made Egypt the hinge of the spice and slave trades between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean. Their wealth paid for the mosques, madrasas and mausolea that still crowd Cairo's old city. Portuguese ships rounding Africa and Ottoman guns at Marj Dabiq ended the regime.

Six Dynasties (China, AD 220–AD 589).label: Six Dynasties
Six Dynasties (China, AD 220–AD 589).prose:
[capital at Jiankang, AD 220–AD 589] Six Dynasties. The Six Dynasties with legitimate lineage (220-589) includes those kingdoms considered the legitimate successors of the Han Dynasty.  The Six Dynasties with the capital at Jiankang (222-589) include the Wu Kingdom but not the Wei Kingdom. Period definition from British Museum.

Between the collapse of the Han and the Sui reunification, China split into rival north and south, with a line of short-lived southern dynasties ruling from Jiankang (modern Nanjing). Aristocratic clans dominated politics, Buddhism and Daoism spread deeply into elite life, and refugees from the north carried Chinese settlement into the Yangtze basin and beyond. It was an extraordinarily creative age for poetry, calligraphy and landscape painting — Wang Xizhi's brushwork and the recluse poets set standards that later dynasties treated as classics.

Ninnan Era (Japan, AD 1166–AD 1169).label: Ninnan Era
Ninnan Era (Japan, AD 1166–AD 1169).prose:
[Japan, AD 1166–AD 1169] Ninnan Era. 1166-1169. Period definition from British Museum.

A short late-Heian era in which Taira no Kiyomori was appointed Grand Minister of State, the first warrior to reach the summit of the civil aristocracy. The Taira clan's grip on the court, built on Inland Sea trade and military force, made the old nobility dependent on samurai power. Within two decades that dominance would trigger the Genpei War and the birth of shogunal rule.

Tianzan (China, AD 926–AD 926).label: Tianzan
Tianzan (China, AD 926–AD 926).prose:
[China, AD 926–AD 926] Tianzan. 926 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

In these years Abaoji, the first Khitan emperor, campaigned west against the Tanguts and Uighurs and then east against Balhae, the long-established kingdom in Manchuria, which fell after a swift winter campaign. The victory gave the Liao control of the northeast and the ports and trade routes toward Korea. Abaoji died shortly after, at the height of his power.

Lydian (Turkey, 1299 BC–545 BC).label: Lydian
Lydian (Turkey, 1299 BC–545 BC).prose:
[western Turkey, 1299 BC–545 BC] Lydian. An Iron Age culture of western Turkey named after the kingdom of Lydia (c1300-546 BC). At its greatest extent the kingdom covered all of western Turkey and its capital was the city of Sardis. Coins were invented in Lydia around  660 BC. In 546 BC king Cyrus II captured Sardis and Lydia became part of the Achaemenid empire. The region never regained independence and was subsequently ruled by Alexander the Great and then the Seleucid dynasty. Period definition from British Museum.

The kingdom of Lydia, ruled from Sardis, grew rich on the gold-bearing silt of the Pactolus river and, around 600 BC, produced the world's first coins of standardised weight and stamp - an invention that reshaped commerce everywhere it spread. Lydian kings dominated the Greek cities of the Anatolian coast and absorbed much of their culture. The proverbially wealthy Croesus lost the kingdom to Cyrus the Great, and Lydia became a Persian satrapy.

Kaixi (China, AD 1205–AD 1208).label: Kaixi
Kaixi (China, AD 1205–AD 1208).prose:
[China, AD 1205–AD 1208] Kaixi. 1205-1208 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The era of the Southern Song's disastrous northern expedition, launched by the chief councillor Han Tuozhou to reclaim the lands lost to the Jin. The offensive collapsed, and to get peace the court had Han assassinated and sent his head to the Jin, agreeing to higher tribute in the settlement that followed.

Taizong Liao dynasty (China, AD 926–AD 9.label: Taizong Liao dynasty
Taizong Liao dynasty (China, AD 926–AD 9.prose:
[China, AD 926–AD 947] Taizong Liao dynasty. 926-947 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Yelü Deguang consolidated his father's Khitan empire and turned it southward: in 938 he took the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing as payment for backing a Chinese usurper, giving the steppe rulers a permanent foothold inside the Great Wall. He adopted the dynastic name Liao and ran a dual administration, governing nomads and Chinese farmers under separate systems. His sack of Kaifeng in 947 destroyed the Later Jin but ended in a hasty retreat, and he died on the road home.

Late Helladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.label: Late Helladic I
Late Helladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Helladic I. 1600BC-1500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The moment mainland Greece grew rich: the Mycenae shaft graves were cut, filled with gold death masks, inlaid daggers, amber and ostrich eggs, evidence of warrior chiefs with long-distance connections. Fine matt-painted and lustrous decorated pottery shows Minoan Crete's influence being absorbed and reworked into something distinctly mainland.

Salghurid dynasty (Iran, AD 1148–AD 1282.label: Salghurid dynasty
Salghurid dynasty (Iran, AD 1148–AD 1282.prose:
[Fars, southern Iran; Persia, AD 1148–AD 1282] Salghurid dynasty. 1148-1282 (AH 543-AH 681). Ruled in Fars, southern Iran, as vassals of the Seljuqs and then in the 13th century as vassals of the Khwarazm Shahs and Mongols. They were of Turkmen origin. Sunqur was the founder of the Salghurids of Fars who consolidated his position in Persia when the power of the Great Seljuqs declined. Period definition from British Museum.

A line of Turkmen atabegs who ruled Fars from Shiraz, holding the province through the century when the Mongols destroyed most of the Iranian dynasties around them. They survived by submitting early and paying tribute, which spared Shiraz the massacres suffered elsewhere and let it flourish as a refuge for scholars and poets, including Sa'di, who dedicated works to Salghurid rulers. The line ended when Fars passed directly into Ilkhanid hands.

Cypro-Geometric II (Cyprus, 949 BC–899 B.label: Cypro-Geometric II
Cypro-Geometric II (Cyprus, 949 BC–899 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 949 BC–899 BC] Cypro-Geometric II. ca. 950 BC-900 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A short phase of consolidation in which the coastal towns grew and Cyprus resumed contact with the Levant. Phoenician settlers took root at Kition, rebuilding its great temple, and imported and locally made Black-on-Red flasks began circulating widely across the eastern Mediterranean.

Hoen Era (Japan, AD 1135–AD 1141).label: Hoen Era
Hoen Era (Japan, AD 1135–AD 1141).prose:
[Japan, AD 1135–AD 1141] Hoen Era. 1135-1141. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign-era in the last decades of Heian rule, when retired emperors governed through their private household offices and the Fujiwara regents' grip had loosened. Temple armies and provincial warrior clans, above all the Taira and Minamoto, were becoming forces the court could neither control nor do without.

Late Helladic IIIA2 (Greece, 1374 BC–129.label: Late Helladic IIIA2
Late Helladic IIIA2 (Greece, 1374 BC–129.prose:
[Greece, 1374 BC–1299 BC] Late Helladic IIIA2. 1375BC-1300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Mycenaean exports peaked, with mainland pots found from Sardinia to Syria and in the rubbish of Akhenaten's city. At home the great citadels took shape and rulers commissioned frescoes, roads and drainage on a scale never before attempted in Greece.

Shaoxi (China, AD 1190–AD 1194).label: Shaoxi
Shaoxi (China, AD 1190–AD 1194).prose:
[China, AD 1190–AD 1194] Shaoxi. 1190-1194 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of the mentally unstable Emperor Guangzong, who refused even to visit his retired father and left ritual and government in disarray while his domineering empress dominated the palace. The crisis ended in a bloodless coup: ministers and the empress dowager forced his abdication in favour of his son, and the men who engineered it, Han Tuozhou and Zhao Ruyu, then turned on each other.

Shi Le (China, AD 319–AD 333).label: Shi Le
Shi Le (China, AD 319–AD 333).prose:
[China, AD 319–AD 333] Shi Le. 319-333 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Born a Jie tribesman and sold as a slave in a famine year, Shi Le rose through the chaos of northern China to found the Later Zhao and rule most of the north from Xiangguo. He destroyed the rival Former Zhao in 329, patronised the Buddhist monk Fotudeng and set up schools for his sons in the Chinese classics — an early and telling example of a steppe conqueror governing through Chinese institutions during the Sixteen Kingdoms.

Choson Dynasty (Korean Peninsula, AD 139.label: Choson Dynasty
Choson Dynasty (Korean Peninsula, AD 139.prose:
[Korean Peninsula, AD 1392–AD 1910] Choson Dynasty. 1392-1910. Period definition from British Museum.

Founded when General Yi Songgye overthrew Koryo, this state made Neo-Confucianism the framework of law, education and family life, demoted Buddhism, and governed through an examination-recruited scholar bureaucracy. It produced the hangul alphabet, rain gauges and metal-type printing, survived devastating Japanese and Manchu invasions, then spent centuries in careful seclusion under Chinese suzerainty. Its slow forced opening in the late 1800s ended in annexation by Japan, and its institutions and social hierarchies still shape both Koreas.

Liang dynasty (China, AD 502–AD 557).label: Liang dynasty
Liang dynasty (China, AD 502–AD 557).prose:
[China, AD 502–AD 557] Liang dynasty. 502-557. Period definition from British Museum.

The third of the Southern Dynasties, ruled for most of its existence by Emperor Wu, a devout Buddhist who several times gave himself to a monastery and had to be ransomed back by his court. Jiankang became a centre of Buddhist scholarship and literary refinement, producing the Wen Xuan anthology and important works of criticism. The dynasty collapsed after the defector Hou Jing rebelled and sacked the capital, devastating the southern aristocracy.

Anyang (China, 1299 BC–1049 BC).label: Anyang
Anyang (China, 1299 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[China, 1299 BC–1049 BC] Anyang. circa 1300 BC-circa 1050 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The final capital of the Shang dynasty, where royal ritual and administration are documented in tens of thousands of inscribed oracle bones — the earliest substantial body of Chinese writing. Excavations revealed vast royal tombs, chariot burials, human sacrifice, bronze foundries and the undisturbed tomb of the warrior-queen Fu Hao. The site anchors the transition from legendary to documented Chinese history.

Kyowa Era (Japan, AD 1801–AD 1804).label: Kyowa Era
Kyowa Era (Japan, AD 1801–AD 1804).prose:
[Japan, AD 1801–AD 1804] Kyowa Era. 1801-1804. Period definition from British Museum.

A quiet three-year reign name in the long, extravagant rule of the shogun Tokugawa Ienari, after the austerity of the Kansei Reforms had faded. Urban culture in Edo and Osaka was flourishing, with a booming trade in popular fiction, woodblock prints and kabuki. Beyond the closed coasts, Russian and British ships were probing Japanese waters with growing persistence.
