Chenghua (China, AD 1465–AD 1487).label: Chenghua
Chenghua (China, AD 1465–AD 1487).prose:
[China, AD 1465–AD 1487] Chenghua. 1465-1487 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign dominated by the emperor's much older consort Lady Wan and by palace eunuchs, who ran a secret police bureau, the Western Depot, that terrified officials. Its lasting fame is on the shelf rather than in the archives: the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen produced small, exquisite doucai porcelains, including the "chicken cups" that are among the most expensive objects ever sold at auction.

Wuzong (China, AD 840–AD 846).label: Wuzong
Wuzong (China, AD 840–AD 846).prose:
[China, AD 840–AD 846] Wuzong. 840-846 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A Tang emperor remembered above all for the Huichang persecution of 845, when tens of thousands of Buddhist monasteries and shrines were destroyed and hundreds of thousands of monks and nuns were returned to lay life. The motives were partly fiscal, seizing tax-exempt land, metal and labour for a strained treasury, and partly a Daoist-leaning court's hostility to a foreign faith. Chinese Buddhism never fully recovered its institutional wealth, and the schools that survived best were the ones least dependent on great monasteries.

Post-Medieval (England, AD 1500–AD 2015).label: Post-Medieval
Post-Medieval (England, AD 1500–AD 2015).prose:
[England , AD 1500–AD 2015] Post-Medieval. This is a catch-all term used for post-1500 objects mainly from England. Period definition from British Museum.

The centuries after 1500 brought the Reformation, overseas empire, and the shift from an agrarian to an industrial society, all leaving dense archaeological traces. Sites of this age are full of dateable mass-produced material - clay pipes, glass bottles, glazed and printed pottery - which makes them unusually precise chronological anchors. Field boundaries, mills, docks, mines and workers' housing from this span still form the framework of the modern landscape.

Dong Khanh (Vietnam, AD 1886–AD 1888).label: Dong Khanh
Dong Khanh (Vietnam, AD 1886–AD 1888).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1886–AD 1888] Dong Khanh. (1886-1888) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

Placed on the Nguyen throne by the French after the court fled Hue and the Can Vuong resistance broke out, he ruled as a cooperative figurehead while French officials took over real administration. His short reign confirmed the pattern that would hold until 1945: an emperor with ceremonial dignity at Hue and colonial power behind him. Loyalist rebels in the countryside refused to recognise him at all.

Seljuqs of Rum (Turkey, AD 1081–AD 1307).label: Seljuqs of Rum
Seljuqs of Rum (Turkey, AD 1081–AD 1307).prose:
[most of Anatolia, AD 1081–AD 1307] Seljuqs of Rum. 1081-1307 (AH 473-AH 707). Turkic dynasty which originated in west-central Anatolia with capital at Konya but later spread over most of Anatolia except the western fringes. The Seljuqs of Rum were an offshoot of the Great Seljuqs. After Alp Arslan's victory over the Byzantines, one of the descendants of one of the sons established a local Seljuq sultanate in Anatolia. The Latin conquest of Constantinople in 1204 (AH 600) gave the Seljuqs and oppurtunity to reestablish their power and extend their influence to the Mediterranean. With this and control over northern coastlands a flourishing transit trade developed between Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean across Anatolia to the Black Sea, the Crimea and the lands of the Mongol Golden Hoard. After circa 1225 commercial relations began with Italian trading cities. Period definition from British Museum.

A branch of the Seljuq family carved out a sultanate in the Anatolian interior in the wake of Manzikert, making Konya its capital and turning a Byzantine province into a Turkish and Muslim land. Its thirteenth-century peak brought Mediterranean and Black Sea ports, a boom in caravan trade and the stone caravanserais, mosques and tiled tombs that still dot Anatolia. Defeat by the Mongols in 1243 reduced it to a vassal, and as it dissolved the small emirates that succeeded it included that of the Ottomans.

Jianwen (China, AD 1399–AD 1402).label: Jianwen
Jianwen (China, AD 1399–AD 1402).prose:
[China, AD 1399–AD 1402] Jianwen. 1399-1402 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The short reign of the Hongwu emperor's grandson, who tried to curb the power of his warlike uncles by stripping princes of their commands. One uncle, the Prince of Yan, revolted and after three years of civil war took Nanjing; the palace burned and the young emperor vanished, fuelling centuries of rumour that he escaped as a monk. The victor ruled as the Yongle emperor and had his predecessor's reign expunged from the record.

Eastern Ganga Dynasty (India, AD 1078–AD.label: Eastern Ganga Dynasty
Eastern Ganga Dynasty (India, AD 1078–AD.prose:
[parts of Orissa and West Bengal, AD 1078–AD 1434] Eastern Ganga Dynasty. The Eastern Ganga Dynasty (c. 1078-1434) ruled parts of Orissa and West Bengal. Period definition from British Museum.

Rulers based in Kalinga, on the eastern seaboard, united coastal Odisha and stood off repeated invasions from the north while trading by sea with Southeast Asia. Their patronage produced some of India's greatest temple architecture: the Jagannath temple at Puri and the colossal stone chariot of the Sun Temple at Konark. Their court also fixed the Jagannath cult at the centre of Odia religious and political identity, where it remains.

Zand dynasty (Iran, AD 1751–AD 1794).label: Zand dynasty
Zand dynasty (Iran, AD 1751–AD 1794).prose:
[Persia, AD 1751–AD 1794] Zand dynasty. The Zand dynasty ruled Persia (except Khurasan) from 1751-1794 (AH 1164-AH 1209), the first ruler Karim Khan reigned as regent (vakil) for Ismail III of the Safavids. Period definition from British Museum.

Karim Khan Zand took power in the disorder after Nader Shah's assassination and ruled most of Iran from Shiraz, refusing the title of shah and calling himself merely the people's deputy. His reign brought tax relief, rebuilt bazaars, gardens and the great mosque of Shiraz, and revived trade with the Gulf. The dynasty tore itself apart in succession fights after his death and was crushed by the rising Qajars.

Zhiping (China, AD 1064–AD 1067).label: Zhiping
Zhiping (China, AD 1064–AD 1067).prose:
[China, AD 1064–AD 1067] Zhiping. 1064-1067 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The brief reign of Emperor Yingzong, an adopted heir whose accession triggered a long, bitter court dispute over what ritual titles his biological father should receive - a quarrel that revealed the depth of factional feeling among Song officials. He backed Sima Guang's work on the great historical survey that became the Comprehensive Mirror. His early death brought to the throne the emperor who would launch Wang Anshi's reforms.

Qajar dynasty (Iran, AD 924–AD 1779).label: Qajar dynasty
Qajar dynasty (Iran, AD 924–AD 1779).prose:
[Persia, AD 924–AD 1779] Qajar dynasty. The Qajars ruled from 1779 to 1924. Dynasty from Astarabad, south-east of the Caspian Sea. Under the Qajars the capital of Persia was moved to Tehran. Period definition from British Museum.

The Qajars, a Turkmen tribal dynasty, took Tehran as their capital and ruled Iran through a century of pressure from Russia and Britain, losing the Caucasus by treaty and conceding trade and tobacco monopolies to foreign concessionaires. Their court sponsored a distinctive art of huge oil portraits, lacquerwork and, later, some of the earliest photography in the Middle East. Resentment at royal weakness and foreign privilege produced the Constitutional Revolution and Iran's first parliament, and eventually the dynasty's fall.

Xuandi (China, AD 569–AD 582).label: Xuandi
Xuandi (China, AD 569–AD 582).prose:
[China, AD 569–AD 582] Xuandi. 569-582 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Emperor Xuan of the southern Chen dynasty, the last of the Southern Dynasties. He briefly pushed north of the Yangtze to seize the Huai river lands, then lost them again to the Northern Zhou, leaving Chen exposed. Within seven years of his death the reunified Sui swept south and ended three centuries of division.

Middle Kaftari (Iran, 1899 BC–1799 BC).label: Middle Kaftari
Middle Kaftari (Iran, 1899 BC–1799 BC).prose:
[Fars, 1899 BC–1799 BC] Middle Kaftari. Fars, 1900BC-1800BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of the Kaftari ceramic tradition at Anshan, in the Elamite highlands of Fars, marked by distinctive buff pottery with painted bands and a large walled urban centre. The city was tied politically to lowland Susa under the sukkalmah rulers, who traded and quarrelled with the Mesopotamian kingdoms of Larsa and Babylon. Finds here anchor the chronology of highland Elam in the earlier second millennium.

Early Dynastic Middle East (Iraq, 2899 B.node: Early Dynastic Middle East (Iraq, 2899 BC–2349 BC)
Early Dynastic Middle East (Iraq, 2899 B.label: Early Dynastic Middle East
Early Dynastic Middle East (Iraq, 2899 B.prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2349 BC] Early Dynastic Middle East. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia in the period approximately 2900 BC-2350 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Southern Mesopotamia's first era of competing city-states, when kingship, monumental temple platforms and standing armies took shape. Craft workshops produced the shell-inlaid Standard of Ur, copper statuary and cylinder seals showing banquets and combat, supplied by trade routes running to Iran, the Gulf and Anatolia. It ended with the Akkadian conquest, which turned a patchwork of rival cities into an empire.

Tentoku Era (Japan, AD 957–AD 961).label: Tentoku Era
Tentoku Era (Japan, AD 957–AD 961).prose: [Japan, AD 957–AD 961] Tentoku Era. 957-961. Period definition from British Museum.

Thien Hung reign period (Vietnam, AD 145.label: Thien Hung reign period
Thien Hung reign period (Vietnam, AD 145.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1459–AD 1460] Thien Hung reign period. Thien Hung reign period (1459-1460). Period definition from British Museum.

The brief era name of Le Nghi Dan, who took the Vietnamese throne by scaling the palace walls at night and killing his half-brother the reigning emperor. His rule lasted barely eight months before court officials overthrew and executed him. The coup opened the way for Le Thanh Tong, whose long reign became the high point of the Le dynasty.

Late Bronze Age/Early Iron Age (England,.node: Late Bronze Age/Early Iron Age (England, 999 BC–599 BC)
Late Bronze Age/Early Iron Age (England,.label: Late Bronze Age/Early Iron Age
Late Bronze Age/Early Iron Age (England,.prose:
[Britain, 999 BC–599 BC] Late Bronze Age/Early Iron Age. The transition period covering the end of the Bronze Age and the beginning of the Iron Age is not always clearly defined in material culture terms.  This mainly applies to British material, for the period spanning 1000BC to 600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Britain's bronze economy reached its height and then unravelled: enormous quantities of metalwork were buried in hoards or thrown into rivers and bogs, and vast field systems and ringwork enclosures reshaped the landscape. As iron came into use bronze lost its value as stored wealth, hoarding stopped, and communities began building the hillforts that would dominate later prehistory.

Tenji Era (Japan, AD 1124–AD 1126).label: Tenji Era
Tenji Era (Japan, AD 1124–AD 1126).prose:
[Japan, AD 1124–AD 1126] Tenji Era. 1124-1126. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Kiyohira completed the Konjikidō, the gold-leafed hall of Chūson-ji at Hiraizumi, the surviving showpiece of the wealthy Northern Fujiwara who ruled the far north almost as an independent state. At court, Emperor Sutoku sat on the throne while his grandfather Shirakawa and then his father Toba held real power as retired sovereigns.

Ottoman dynasty (Anatolia, AD 1281–AD 19.label: Ottoman dynasty
Ottoman dynasty (Anatolia, AD 1281–AD 19.prose:
[Middle Eastern and European empire, AD 1281–AD 1924] Ottoman dynasty. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Balkans, Egypt, Gaza Strip, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon. 1281-1924; Middle Eastern and European empire, centred from 1453 on Constantinople.  For the period of the Bosnian garrison at Qasr Ibrim use Ottoman dynasty and a date range 1550-1811 unless a more specific date is known. Period definition from British Museum.

One family, descended from Osman, ruled continuously for more than six centuries, longer than almost any dynasty in world history. Succession was fought over between sons, and for a time settled by fratricide, before princes were confined to the palace; from 1517 the sultans also claimed the caliphate and guardianship of Mecca and Medina. The sultanate was abolished in 1922 and the caliphate in 1924, sending the family into exile.

Kangi Era (Japan, AD 1229–AD 1232).label: Kangi Era
Kangi Era (Japan, AD 1229–AD 1232).prose:
[Japan, AD 1229–AD 1232] Kangi Era. 1229-1232. Period definition from British Museum.

Dominated by one of medieval Japan's worst subsistence crises: cold summers and failed harvests brought the Kangi famine, with mass starvation, epidemic disease and abandoned fields across the country. The shogunate suspended debts and rice loans, and the disaster fed the popular appeal of the new Buddhist preachers who promised salvation to the desperate.

Late Quimbaya (Colombia, AD 800–AD 1600).label: Late Quimbaya
Late Quimbaya (Colombia, AD 800–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, AD 800–AD 1600] Late Quimbaya. The term refers to a cultural period and a style of the Quimbaya region of Colombia in the Middle Cauca valley and the Central Range in the Antioquia, Caldas, Risaralda and Quindio departments from 800 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Populations in the middle Cauca valley grew and dispersed across the slopes, leaving cemeteries with distinctive incised and painted ceramics quite unlike the earlier tradition, along with shaft tombs and terraced hillsides. Goldworking continued but in simpler, more standardised forms than the celebrated earlier pieces. These were the communities Spanish expeditions met and shattered in the sixteenth century.

Rimac (Peru, AD 900–AD 1430).label: Rimac
Rimac (Peru, AD 900–AD 1430).prose:
[Central Coast, AD 900–AD 1430] Rimac. 900-1430, Central Coast. Period definition from British Museum.

On Peru's central coast, valley polities built and rebuilt great adobe compounds with ramped pyramids, farming irrigated cotton and maize and trading up and down the shoreline. The pilgrimage centre at Pachacamac drew worshippers from far beyond the region, and its oracle kept its prestige even after the Inca annexed the coast in the fifteenth century and grafted their own temples onto it.

Yongchang (China, AD 1644–AD 1645).label: Yongchang
Yongchang (China, AD 1644–AD 1645).prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1645] Yongchang. 1644-1645. Period definition from British Museum.

The era name proclaimed by Li Zicheng, the rebel leader whose Shun forces took Beijing in 1644 and drove the last Ming emperor to hang himself on Coal Hill. Within weeks Li was beaten at Shanhai Pass by Ming general Wu Sangui allied with the Manchus, who occupied the capital and kept it. His brief regime marks the hinge between the Ming and Qing.

Neo-Babylonian Dynasty (Babylonia, 625 B.label: Neo-Babylonian Dynasty
Neo-Babylonian Dynasty (Babylonia, 625 B.prose:
[Babylonian empire, Jerusalem, 625 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian Dynasty. Spatial coverage: Babylonia, Old City of Jerusalem and its Walls. Having previously been under the domination of their northerly neighbours, the Assyrians, native rule returned to Babylon in 626 BC, when Nabopolassar seized the throne. He was part of the coalition that would later destroy the Assyrian empire, and set the stage for the rise of the Babylonian empire. Perhaps the most famous king of the dynasty is his son Nebuchadnezzar, who in 598 BC captured Jerusalem and deported some of the population -- an event immortalised in the Bible. After a long and illustrious reign Nebuchadnezzar II died in 562 BC, to be followed by a series of kings with very short reigns. The empire fell in 539 BC when king Cyrus II of Persia overthrew Nabonidus, the last native ruler of Babylon. Period definition from British Museum.

Founded by the Chaldean Nabopolassar, who broke Assyrian power, and brought to its height by Nebuchadnezzar II, this dynasty made Babylon the richest city on earth, with the Ishtar Gate, vast temple complexes and processional ways paid for by tribute and conquest. Its kings destroyed Jerusalem, fought Egypt for the Levant, and sponsored astronomers whose systematic sky records underpin later Greek astronomy. The line ended with Nabonidus, whose religious eccentricities and long absence at Tayma left the city ready to fall to Cyrus.
places: Old City of Jerusalem and its Walls

Tianshun (China, AD 1457–AD 1464).label: Tianshun
Tianshun (China, AD 1457–AD 1464).prose:
[China, AD 1457–AD 1464] Tianshun. 1457-1464 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Yingzong returned to the throne in a palace coup after years first as a Mongol captive and then under house arrest while his brother ruled. The general Yu Qian, who had saved Beijing from the Mongols, was executed on trumped-up charges by the men who restored the old emperor. Yingzong's one lasting humane act was to abolish the practice of forcing imperial concubines to follow a dead emperor into the grave.

Shizu (China, AD 1260–AD 1294).label: Shizu
Shizu (China, AD 1260–AD 1294).prose:
[China, AD 1260–AD 1294] Shizu. 1260-1294 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Kublai Khan's reign, in which the Mongol ruler moved his capital to Dadu (modern Beijing), proclaimed the Yuan dynasty and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279 — the first time all of China was ruled by a foreign house. He ranked his subjects by ethnicity, employed Muslims, Tibetans and Europeans in his service, and hosted Marco Polo; his two invasion fleets sent against Japan were wrecked by storms.

Renzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1311–AD.label: Renzong Yuan dynasty
Renzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1311–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1311–AD 1320] Renzong Yuan dynasty. 1311-1320 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan was the Mongol emperor most at home in Chinese learning, and in 1315 he restored the civil service examinations that had lapsed for decades, fixing Zhu Xi's commentaries as the basis of the curriculum for the next six centuries. He sponsored translations of Chinese classics into Mongolian and tried to rein in the great appanage households. Quotas still favoured Mongols and Central Asians, so the reform reopened Chinese elite careers only partly.

Urartian (Turkey, 859 BC–584 BC).label: Urartian
Urartian (Turkey, 859 BC–584 BC).prose:
[Urartu kingdom, eastern Turkey, 859 BC–584 BC] Urartian. An Iron Age culture of eastern Turkey named after the kingdom of Urartu (c 860-585 BC) centred around Lake Van. At its height, the Urartian kingdom extended north into modern Armenia and southern Georgia; west to the sources of the River Euphrates in Turkey; east to modern Lake Urmia and south to the sources of the River Tigris. Urartu passed into the hands of the Orontid kingdom of Armenia after invasions by Scythians and Medes from the areas of modern Ukraine, Russia, Kazakhstan and Iran around 612 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The kingdom of Urartu, ruled from the citadel of Tushpa on Lake Van, was Assyria's great northern rival. Its kings cut cuneiform inscriptions into cliff faces, built massive stone fortresses on volcanic outcrops, and engineered canals and vineyards across a harsh highland landscape. Urartian bronze cauldrons and belts travelled as far as Etruscan Italy, and the kingdom's collapse under Assyrian and steppe pressure left the region open to the Armenians who followed.

Late Helladic IIIA1 (Greece, 1399 BC–137.label: Late Helladic IIIA1
Late Helladic IIIA1 (Greece, 1399 BC–137.prose:
[Greece, 1399 BC–1374 BC] Late Helladic IIIA1. 1400BC-1375BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Mycenaean pottery became remarkably uniform across the mainland and islands, suggesting tightly organised production. Palace building was underway, and Aegean goods reached Amarna in Egypt in quantity.

Haftavan Period VIII (Iran, 2599 BC–2599.label: Haftavan Period VIII
Haftavan Period VIII (Iran, 2599 BC–2599.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 2599 BC–2599 BC] Haftavan Period VIII. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.2600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Dashun Ming-Qing (China, AD 1644–AD 1647.label: Dashun Ming-Qing
Dashun Ming-Qing (China, AD 1644–AD 1647.prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1647] Dashun Ming-Qing. 1644-1647 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Li Zicheng, a former postal courier turned rebel leader, proclaimed the Dashun dynasty and took Beijing, driving the last Ming emperor to hang himself on Coal Hill. His triumph lasted weeks: the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the passes to the Manchus, who seized the capital and founded Qing rule over China. The rump of Li's forces and the southern Ming loyalists fought on for years, making this one of the bloodiest dynastic transitions in Chinese history.

Encho Era (Japan, AD 923–AD 931).label: Encho Era
Encho Era (Japan, AD 923–AD 931).prose:
[Japan, AD 923–AD 931] Encho Era. 923-931. Period definition from British Museum.

The closing years of Emperor Daigo's reign, remembered in later tradition for disaster: in 930 lightning struck the Seiryoden of the imperial palace, killing courtiers, and the strike was read as the vengeance of the exiled scholar Sugawara no Michizane. Daigo abdicated and died within months, and the cult of Michizane as the thunder deity Tenjin grew out of the episode.

Late Helladic IIB (Greece, 1449 BC–1399.label: Late Helladic IIB
Late Helladic IIB (Greece, 1449 BC–1399.prose:
[Greece, 1449 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic IIB. 1450BC-1400BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Pottery decoration grew more restrained and standardised, a sign of workshops producing for a wider market. Mycenaean influence over Crete tightened, and mainland centres were on the verge of building the palaces that would define the following century.

Arab-Sasanian (Iran, AD 651–AD 794).label: Arab-Sasanian
Arab-Sasanian (Iran, AD 651–AD 794).prose:
[Sasanian eastern provinces, AD 651–AD 794] Arab-Sasanian. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia (country), Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Tajikistan. The term Arab-Sasanian covers the period circa 651-794 (AH 31-AH 178) and  is used for early Islamic coins with Pahlavi and/or Arabic legends which were struck in the Sasanian fashion with the conventional Sasanian portrait on the obverse and on the reverse with a Zoroastrian fire-altar and two attendants. These coins were issued by the Arabs and Muslim authorities who governed the Sasanian provinces after the overthrow of the Sasanian empire. This coin type persisted in the eastern provinces of the caliphate for almost 200 years.  The Yazdgird Era, commonly abbreviated as YE, is the first era inscribed on Tabaristan coins and on some Arab-Sasanian coins. YE1 (ie. year 1 of the Yazdgird Era) corresponds to AD 632/633, the first regnal year of the last Sasanian ruler Yazdgird III (632/3-651). Period definition from British Museum.

After the fall of the Sasanian empire, the new Muslim governors of Iran kept the old administration running almost unchanged — including its coinage. Silver drachms continued to show a Persian king's bust and a fire altar with Pahlavi legends, now with a short Arabic phrase such as bismillah squeezed into the margin, and were dated by Yazdgird's or the Hijra era. These hybrid coins map the slow substitution of one imperial culture for another, until Abd al-Malik's reforms replaced images entirely with Arabic script.

Uruk (Iraq, 3999 BC–2999 BC).label: Uruk
Uruk (Iraq, 3999 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[Uruk, southern Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–2999 BC] Uruk. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia represented by objects excavated at the site of Uruk that date to approximately 4000 BC-3000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities in this period, with Uruk itself swelling to a size no settlement had reached before. Monumental temple platforms, mass-produced bevel-rim bowls for rationed labour, cylinder seals for accounting and finally the earliest writing all appear together, the machinery of a society organised around institutions rather than kin. Uruk-style material spread up the Euphrates into Syria and Anatolia, whether by colony, trade or imitation.

Showa Era (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).label: Showa Era
Showa Era (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).prose:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989] Showa Era. 昭和 1926-1989. Period definition from British Museum.

The longest reign in Japanese history, and the most violently divided. It opened with financial crisis and army officers assassinating politicians, ran through the invasion of China, Pearl Harbor, firebombed cities, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and defeat and American occupation, then turned into the decades of extraordinary growth that made Japan the world's second-largest economy. Hirohito's own responsibility for the war, and his transformation from living god to constitutional symbol, remain contested.

Late Minoan IB (Crete, 1499 BC–1449 BC).label: Late Minoan IB
Late Minoan IB (Crete, 1499 BC–1449 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1499 BC–1449 BC] Late Minoan IB. 1500BC-1450BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Potters produced the celebrated Marine Style, with octopuses and nautili wrapped around jars and flasks, and stone vases and seals reached a technical peak. Then almost every settlement, villa and palace on the island except Knossos was burned or abandoned in a single horizon of destruction. Whether the cause was earthquake, revolt, invasion or the long aftermath of the Thera eruption is still argued.

Old Elamite (Iran, 2599 BC–1499 BC).label: Old Elamite
Old Elamite (Iran, 2599 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Elam, 2599 BC–1499 BC] Old Elamite. Term used to describe period from circa 2600 BC-1500 BC in Elam. Includes the dynasty of Shimashki (c.2100 BC) and Sukkalmah period (c.1900 BC-1600 BC). Period definition from British Museum.

In the highlands and plains of southwestern Iran, the rulers of Awan, Simashki and later the Sukkalmah dynasty of Susa alternated between war and marriage alliances with the Mesopotamian kingdoms next door. Elamite armies sacked Ur and carried off its last king, and later hauled Babylonian monuments home as trophies. The period produced a distinctive script and language unrelated to any neighbours, and a religious tradition centred on Inshushinak and Napirisha.

Shucho Era (Japan, AD 686–AD 701).label: Shucho Era
Shucho Era (Japan, AD 686–AD 701).prose:
[Japan, AD 686–AD 701] Shucho Era. 686-701. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for the final year of Emperor Tenmu, who had seized the throne in civil war and built a centralised state on Chinese lines. After his death his widow ruled as Empress Jitō, no further era names were declared for fifteen years, and the court pushed through law codes, a household registration system and the building of Fujiwara-kyō, Japan's first true planned capital. The work culminated in the Taihō Code of 701, which gave Japan its imperial bureaucracy.

Ptolemaic (Egypt, 331 BC–30 BC).label: Ptolemaic
Ptolemaic (Egypt, 331 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 331 BC–30 BC] Ptolemaic. This period begins from the conquest of Egypt by Alexander in 332 BC down to the Battle of Actium in 31 BC.  The term Ptolemaic is frequently used by G&R for Hellenistic terracottas made in Egypt. Period definition from British Museum.

Alexander's general Ptolemy seized Egypt after his death and founded a Greek-speaking dynasty that ruled from Alexandria for nearly three centuries. The city became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean, with its Library, Museum and lighthouse, while the countryside kept its temples and priesthoods - pharaonic architecture built by kings with Macedonian names. The line ended with Cleopatra VII, whose defeat alongside Mark Antony delivered Egypt to Rome.

Late Helladic IIA (Greece, 1499 BC–1449.label: Late Helladic IIA
Late Helladic IIA (Greece, 1499 BC–1449.prose:
[Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC] Late Helladic IIA. 1500BC-1450BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Palatial-style jars and elegant Ephyraean goblets show mainland potters mastering and transforming Minoan design. Wealth concentrated in a few centres whose rulers were buried in early tholos tombs, and Mycenaean exports began appearing regularly in the eastern Mediterranean.

Dading (China, AD 1161–AD 1170).label: Dading
Dading (China, AD 1161–AD 1170).prose:
[China, AD 1161–AD 1170] Dading. 1161-1170 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era of Shizong of the Jurchen Jin, who took power amid the collapse of his predecessor's invasion of the Song and then made peace, cut taxes and restored the treasury. Later writers called him the "Little Yao and Shun" for these decades of prosperity, though he worried openly that his Jurchen elite were losing their language and martial habits to Chinese ways.

Taizu Liao dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 926.label: Taizu Liao dynasty
Taizu Liao dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 926.prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 926] Taizu Liao dynasty. 907-926 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Yelü Abaoji welded the eight Khitan tribes into a single hereditary monarchy, breaking with the steppe custom of electing chiefs every few years. He built walled cities for captured Chinese farmers and artisans, commissioned a Khitan script, and in 926 destroyed the kingdom of Balhae in Manchuria. The empire he left behind dominated the northern frontier for two centuries and gave Europe and Central Asia their name for China: Khitai, or Cathay.

Abbasid dynasty (Iraq, AD 749–AD 1258).label: Abbasid dynasty
Abbasid dynasty (Iraq, AD 749–AD 1258).prose:
[Iraq, AD 749–AD 1258] Abbasid dynasty. 749-1258 (AH 132-AH 923). Dynasty ruling the Muslim world as caliphs with Iraq at it's centre and Baghdad it's capital. The Abbasids derived from the family of the Prophet Muhammad's uncle al-'Abbas and the Meccan clan of Hashim. The Abbasids were influenced by older Persian traditions of divine rulership. The Abbasid revolution, while in origin an Arab movement, began on Persian soil and took advantage of discontent in the Persian lands. The shifting of the capital from Damascus under the Umayyads to Baghdad in Iraq symbolised a new eastward orientation of the caliphate with increasingly evident Persian material and cultural practives of the next centuries. The Abbasid caliphs adopted honorific titles expressing divine support for their rule. The first three centuries of Abbasid rule saw the full flowering of medieval Islamic civilisation and influences coming in from Persia and the Hellenistic and Byzantine cultures. The Abbasid ruler best known in the West is Harun al-Rashid (786-809 AH 170-193), who is associated with the stories of 1001 Nights. Period definition from British Museum.

Five centuries of caliphs based first at Baghdad, whose round city became the largest urban centre west of China and home to the translation movement that preserved and extended Greek science. Political control fragmented early, with Buyid and then Seljuk warlords holding real power while the caliph kept religious prestige. The line ended when Mongol armies sacked Baghdad in 1258.

Tughluqid dynasty (India, AD 1320–AD 141.label: Tughluqid dynasty
Tughluqid dynasty (India, AD 1320–AD 141.prose:
[India, AD 1320–AD 1414] Tughluqid dynasty. Spatial coverage: India, Nepal, Pakistan. Rulers of the Delhi Sultanate 1320-1414 (AH 720-817). Period definition from British Museum.

The third great dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, at its height ruling almost the entire subcontinent. Muhammad bin Tughluq is remembered for spectacular experiments that failed — moving the capital to Daulatabad, issuing token bronze coinage — while his successor Firuz Shah turned to canals, colleges and new towns. The Deccan and Bengal broke away, and Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left the dynasty a shadow, opening the way for the Sayyids and eventually the Mughals.

Tennin Era (Japan, AD 1108–AD 1110).label: Tennin Era
Tennin Era (Japan, AD 1108–AD 1110).prose:
[Japan, AD 1108–AD 1110] Tennin Era. 1108-1110. Period definition from British Museum.

Mount Asama erupted violently in 1108, burying farmland across the Kantō and leaving a deposit that geologists still use as a dating layer. In the same year Taira no Masamori crushed the rebel Minamoto no Yoshichika, a victory that launched the Ise Taira on their climb to national power.

Shaoxing (China, AD 1131–AD 1162).label: Shaoxing
Shaoxing (China, AD 1131–AD 1162).prose:
[China, AD 1131–AD 1162] Shaoxing. 1131-1162 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Gaozong's long era in exile after the Jurchen sack of Kaifeng, when the Song court settled at Hangzhou and rebuilt a wealthy southern state on maritime trade and paddy rice. The 1141 peace accord with the Jin fixed the frontier at the Huai River and required tribute in silver and silk; to seal it, the general Yue Fei, who wanted to fight on, was executed in prison — a betrayal Chinese memory has never forgiven.

Middle Minoan I (Crete, 1999 BC–1849 BC).label: Middle Minoan I
Middle Minoan I (Crete, 1999 BC–1849 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1999 BC–1849 BC] Middle Minoan I. 2000BC-1850BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The transition out of the scattered village world of the Early Bronze Age: settlements grew, hilltop peak sanctuaries filled with clay votive figurines, and by the end of the phase the first palaces were going up at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia. Communal circular tombs on the Mesara plain were still in use, and the potter's wheel and new polychrome decoration were beginning to change Cretan ceramics.

Moche (Peru, 99 BC–AD 700).label: Moche
Moche (Peru, 99 BC–AD 700).prose:
[ancient Peru, 99 BC–AD 700] Moche. The term refers to a culture and style, named after the place.  The date range covered is 100 BC- AD 700.  Christopher Donnan, 'Ceramics of Ancient Peru', Fowler Museum of Cultural History, University of California, Los Angeles, 1992. Period definition from British Museum.

Along the desert river valleys of Peru's north coast, Moche lords built vast adobe pyramids such as the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, sustained by irrigation canals that turned sand into farmland. Their potters made astonishingly lifelike portrait vessels and scenes of warfare, ritual and sex, and their metalsmiths worked gold, silver and copper with techniques rediscovered only in the intact tombs of Sipán, whose occupants matched figures painted on the pots. Drought and flooding linked to El Niño helped unsettle the polity, but its art and statecraft shaped everything that came after on the coast.

Huangqing (China, AD 1312–AD 1313).label: Huangqing
Huangqing (China, AD 1312–AD 1313).prose:
[China, AD 1312–AD 1313] Huangqing. 1312-1313 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign era of the Yuan emperor Renzong, remembered for his effort to govern in Confucian rather than purely Mongol fashion. His decree of 1313 restored the civil service examinations, abolished for decades under Mongol rule, with quotas splitting places between Mongols, Central Asians and Chinese - reopening a path into government for the Chinese scholarly class.

Zhizhi (China, AD 1321–AD 1323).label: Zhizhi
Zhizhi (China, AD 1321–AD 1323).prose:
[China, AD 1321–AD 1323] Zhizhi. 1321-1323 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A short-lived attempt at reform in the Yuan, as the young Emperor Yingzong and his chancellor Baiju promoted Confucian administration, a new law code and cuts to the privileges of the Mongol aristocracy. Conservative princes and officials responded by murdering both emperor and chancellor at a summer camp. The coup opened a period of rapid, contested successions that badly weakened the dynasty.

Tianming (China, AD 1616–AD 1626).label: Tianming
Tianming (China, AD 1616–AD 1626).prose:
[China, AD 1616–AD 1626] Tianming. 1616-1626 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Nurhaci united the Jurchen tribes, declared the Later Jin state and issued the Seven Grievances as a manifesto for war against the Ming. He organised his followers into the banner system that would structure Manchu society for three centuries, commissioned a written script for the Manchu language, and overran the Ming province of Liaodong. His defeat and mortal wounding at Ningyuan checked but did not reverse the advance.

Pahlavi dynasty (Iran, AD 1925–AD 1979).label: Pahlavi dynasty
Pahlavi dynasty (Iran, AD 1925–AD 1979).prose:
[Iran , AD 1925–AD 1979] Pahlavi dynasty. 1925-1979 (SH 1304-SH 1358). Iranian dynasty succeeding the Qajar dynasty. The Pahlavis under Muhammad Reza Shah gave up the throne during the Islamic Revolution of 1979. Iran became an Islamic Republic with Ayatollah Khomeini as the Head of State. Period definition from British Museum.

Reza Khan, a Cossack Brigade officer, took the throne and pushed through rapid state-building: conscription, railways, a secular legal code, western dress and a ban on the veil. His son Mohammad Reza ruled through the nationalisation crisis over oil, the 1953 coup that removed Mosaddegh, and the land reforms and oil boom of the White Revolution. Repression, inequality and clerical opposition brought the monarchy down in the revolution of 1979.

Tenjo Era (Japan, AD 1131–AD 1132).label: Tenjo Era
Tenjo Era (Japan, AD 1131–AD 1132).prose:
[Japan, AD 1131–AD 1132] Tenjo Era. 1131-1132. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era under Emperor Sutoku in which Taira no Tadamori was rewarded for endowing a temple for the retired emperor with the rare privilege of entering the imperial palace hall. That admission of a provincial warrior chief into the inner court marked the Ise Taira's arrival among the ruling elite, the platform for his son Kiyomori's later dominance.

Larsa Dynasty (Iraq, 1899 BC–1749 BC).label: Larsa Dynasty
Larsa Dynasty (Iraq, 1899 BC–1749 BC).prose:
[Larsa, 1899 BC–1749 BC] Larsa Dynasty. A term used to describe the dynasty of kings ruling the city of Larsa in the period approximately 1900 BC-1750 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

An Amorite dynasty ruling a southern Mesopotamian city that fought Isin for control of the old Sumerian heartland and its canals, eventually winning it. Under Rim-Sin I, its longest-reigning king, Larsa dominated the far south for six decades and left a rich record of law, temple building and business archives. Hammurabi's defeat of Rim-Sin brought the whole region under Babylon.

Late Classic (Mexico, AD 700–AD 900).label: Late Classic
Late Classic (Mexico, AD 700–AD 900).prose:
[Mexico, AD 700–AD 900] Late Classic. Spatial coverage: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico. Period covering 700-900 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The height of Classic Maya civilisation, when dozens of rival city-states — Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán, Yaxchilán — raised temple-pyramids and carved stelae recording dynastic history in hieroglyphs, the richest written record of the ancient Americas. With Teotihuacan's collapse, central Mexico fragmented and centres like Cholula, Xochicalco and El Tajín rose in its place, while Monte Albán was abandoned. In the ninth century the southern lowland cities stopped building and recording dates and were largely emptied, one of archaeology's most debated collapses.

Copper Age (Italy, 3799 BC–2199 BC).label: Copper Age
Copper Age (Italy, 3799 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[Italy, 3799 BC–2199 BC] Copper Age. Term used to define transitional period between Neolithic and Bronze Age.  See also Chalcolithic (literally "Copper Stone Age") in the Middle East.  Soviet literature uses Aeneolithic.  Copper Age is not a term used in Britain, Ireland or Scandinavia.  For Italy:  3800BC-2200BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Metal working spread through the Italian peninsula and with it a new social order: single graves with daggers, arrowheads and drinking cups instead of communal tombs, and regional groups such as Remedello, Rinaldone and Gaudo. Carved stone stelae in the Alpine valleys show armed male figures, and the frozen body of the Iceman, found with his copper axe in the Ötztal Alps, comes from the beginning of this period.

Eastern Zhou dynasty (China, 769 BC–220.label: Eastern Zhou dynasty
Eastern Zhou dynasty (China, 769 BC–220.prose:
[China, 769 BC–220 BC] Eastern Zhou dynasty. 770 BC-221 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The Zhou royal house survived at Luoyang as a shadow authority while its former vassal states became independent kingdoms, first jostling for hegemony in the Spring and Autumn era, then fighting wars of annihilation in the Warring States. Iron ploughs, irrigation works, bureaucratic taxation and conscript armies remade society, and rival rulers hired the philosophers and strategists whose texts became the classics of Chinese thought. Qin's victory in 221 BC closed the age and imposed a single empire.

Xiaozhuangdi (China, AD 528–AD 530).label: Xiaozhuangdi
Xiaozhuangdi (China, AD 528–AD 530).prose:
[China, AD 528–AD 530] Xiaozhuangdi. 528-530 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Placed on the Northern Wei throne by the warlord Erzhu Rong after he drowned the empress dowager and butchered the court at Heyin, this emperor ruled as a figurehead. He turned on his patron and had him killed in the palace, only to be seized and executed by Erzhu kinsmen months later. The struggle broke the Wei into rival eastern and western halves.

Hakuho Period (Japan, AD 646–AD 710).label: Hakuho Period
Hakuho Period (Japan, AD 646–AD 710).prose:
[Japan, AD 646–AD 710] Hakuho Period. 646-710. Period definition from British Museum.

The art-historical bridge between Asuka and Nara, when Japanese Buddhist sculpture and architecture absorbed fresh Tang Chinese and Korean models: rounder, softer bronze figures, and temples like Yakushi-ji and the Hōryū-ji rebuilding. The same decades saw the Taika reforms mature into the Taihō law codes, a Chinese-style bureaucracy, and Japan's first grid-planned capitals. Visitors often notice the gentle, almost childlike faces of Hakuhō Buddhas, quite unlike the archaic smiles of earlier Asuka work.

Late Roman (Italy, AD 293–AD 476).label: Late Roman
Late Roman (Italy, AD 293–AD 476).prose:
[Western Roman Empire, AD 293–AD 476] Late Roman. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, England, France, Germany. The term is used for the material culture of the Western Roman Empire during the period from AD 293 (reforms by Diocletian) to AD 476 (the deposition of the last official western Roman emperor).  For the eastern Roman empire from about the early 4thC AD see 'Late Antique' and 'Byzantine'. Period definition from British Museum.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

Xuanwu (China, AD 500–AD 515).label: Xuanwu
Xuanwu (China, AD 500–AD 515).prose:
[China, AD 500–AD 515] Xuanwu. 500-515 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of the Northern Wei emperor Xuanwu, ruling from the newly established capital at Luoyang. Sponsorship of Buddhism reached an extraordinary pitch, with the Binyang caves at Longmen cut on imperial orders and monasteries multiplying in the city. Campaigns against the southern Liang won territory, but the sinicised court grew increasingly estranged from the frontier garrisons that would later destroy the dynasty.

Guangzong (China, AD 1189–AD 1194).label: Guangzong
Guangzong (China, AD 1189–AD 1194).prose:
[China, AD 1189–AD 1194] Guangzong. 1189-1194 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief and troubled reign in the Southern Song, when the emperor's mental illness and his feud with his own retired father paralysed the court. Ministers eventually forced his abdication in favour of his son. The episode exposed how much Southern Song politics turned on the personalities and rivalries of the imperial family.

Shundi (China, AD 1333–AD 1370).label: Shundi
Shundi (China, AD 1333–AD 1370).prose:
[China, AD 1333–AD 1370] Shundi. 1333-1370 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Toghon Temür, last Mongol emperor to rule China. Factional murder at court, hyperinflation of the paper currency, floods of the Yellow River and forced labour on its dykes fed the Red Turban risings, which the Yuan armies could not suppress. In 1368 he abandoned Dadu to Zhu Yuanzhang's forces and fled to the steppe, where he died; his successors kept the dynasty alive in Mongolia while the Ming took China.

An'ei Era (Japan, AD 1772–AD 1781).label: An'ei Era
An'ei Era (Japan, AD 1772–AD 1781).prose:
[Japan, AD 1772–AD 1781] An'ei Era. 1772-1781. Period definition from British Museum.

A Tokugawa reign-name spanning the height of Tanuma Okitsugu's influence, when the shogunate leaned on merchant capital, licensed monopolies and currency manipulation to shore up its finances. Dutch learning flourished, with the anatomical translation Kaitai shinsho appearing in 1774. Crop failures and urban fires in these years fed the criticism that would later bring Tanuma down.

Qianheng (China, AD 917–AD 924).label: Qianheng
Qianheng (China, AD 917–AD 924).prose:
[China, AD 917–AD 924] Qianheng. 917-924 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The era in which Liu Yan proclaimed himself emperor at Guangzhou, founding the southern kingdom later known as the Southern Han. Its wealth came from the sea: Guangzhou remained the great port for Arab, Persian and Southeast Asian shipping, and customs revenue funded a lavish and notoriously cruel court.

Samanid dynasty (Iran, AD 819–AD 1005).label: Samanid dynasty
Samanid dynasty (Iran, AD 819–AD 1005).prose:
[Khurasan and Transoxania, AD 819–AD 1005] Samanid dynasty. 819-1005 (AH 204-AH 395). Dynasty of local land owners in Khurasan and Transoxania who claimed descent from pre-Islamic Sasanian emperors of Iran. New Persian language and literature flourished under Samanid rule. In the middle of the 10th century a series of revolts resulted in decentralisation and enabled the Qarakhanids and Ghaznavids to cease control over Samanid territories in 1005 (AH 395). Period definition from British Museum.

Under the Samanids, Persian written in Arabic script became a court and literary language again for the first time since the Arab conquest, producing Rudaki's poetry and the prose and verse traditions Ferdowsi drew on for the Shahnameh. Their capital Bukhara was a centre of learning where the young Ibn Sina read his way through the royal library. Their power rested on the Central Asian trade in silver, textiles and slaves, and dissolved when Turkic Qarakhanids and Ghaznavids divided their territory.

Middle Cypriot (Cyprus, 1899 BC–1649 BC).label: Middle Cypriot
Middle Cypriot (Cyprus, 1899 BC–1649 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 1899 BC–1649 BC] Middle Cypriot. ca. 1900 BC-1650 BC. The second division of the Cypriot Bronze Age, marking an expansion in the range of pottery types (including White Painted wares which appeared at the end of the EC period), the spread of settlements all over the island (including fortified sites) and the first signs of significant overseas contacts in the form of numerous ceramic exports to surrounding regions. Many artefacts types, including metal goods, are similar to those from the EC and continue in use into the LC. The last phase of Middle Cypriot, MCIII, witnesses a major increase in the economic and cultural dynamism of the island, including the establishment of new coastal settlements. Period definition from British Museum.

A restless phase on Cyprus when settlement spread inland and eastward, fortress-like structures appeared in the north, and White Painted pottery joined the older Red Polished wares. Copper from the Troodos foothills was increasingly worked for export, drawing the island into Levantine and Egyptian trade networks and building the wealth that would produce the great coastal towns of the Late Bronze Age.

Safavid dynasty (Iran, AD 1501–AD 1722).label: Safavid dynasty
Safavid dynasty (Iran, AD 1501–AD 1722).prose:
[Iran; Persia, AD 1501–AD 1722] Safavid dynasty. 1501-1722 (AH 907-AH 1135). The family traced its ancestry to Shaykh Safi al-Din who died in 1334 and is buried at the shrine in Adabil in north-western Iran. In 1501 (AH 905) Isma'il defeated the Aq Qoyunlu, seized Azarbaijan and took control of the whole of Persia. He declared Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion of Iran. The Safavids traced their lineage through the seventh Imam, Musa al-Kazim to ‘Ali, the Prophet Muhammad's son in law and his family. In 1514 (AH 920) Isma'il I and his army of Turkmen Qizilbash ('red heads' because of their red caps) suffered a humiliating defeat by the Ottoman Sultan Selim I at the battle of Chaldiran in north-western Iran. His son and successor Tahmasp I was either defending his western and eastern borders or controlling the Qizilbash. The most outstanding ruler of this dynasty was Shah ‘Abbas who drove the Ottomans out of the Azabarjian and established Persian control over the Caucasus and the Persian Gulf. Isfahan became the capital of Safavid Iran. Safavid rule collapsed with the invasion of the country  by the Afghan Ghilzays in 1722 (AH 1135). Period definition from British Museum.

Shah Ismail imposed Twelver Shi'ism on Iran by force, creating the religious divide with the Sunni Ottomans that still shapes the region. Under Abbas I the state was rebuilt around a standing army of slave soldiers and a rebuilt capital at Isfahan, whose vast maidan, blue-tiled mosques and bridges drew astonished European visitors. Safavid silk, carpets and painting reached Europe through Armenian merchants and the Dutch and English trading companies.

Dashun Zhaozong (China, AD 890–AD 892).label: Dashun Zhaozong
Dashun Zhaozong (China, AD 890–AD 892).prose: [China, AD 890–AD 892] Dashun Zhaozong. 890-892 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Wanli (China, AD 1573–AD 1620).label: Wanli
Wanli (China, AD 1573–AD 1620).prose:
[China, AD 1573–AD 1620] Wanli. 1573-1620 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The longest reign of the Ming dynasty began with a decade of vigorous fiscal reform under the grand secretary Zhang Juzheng, then curdled after the emperor withdrew from public business, refusing for years to meet ministers or fill vacant offices. Costly campaigns, above all the defence of Korea against Hideyoshi's invasions, drained the treasury just as silver from the Americas and Japan was reshaping the economy. Government by eunuchs and factional feuding took hold, and historians have long dated the Ming collapse to the rot that set in here.

Timurid dynasty (Uzbekistan, AD 1370–AD.label: Timurid dynasty
Timurid dynasty (Uzbekistan, AD 1370–AD.prose:
[Samarkand (modern Uzbekistan); Transoxiana; Khurasan; Persia, AD 1370–AD 1507] Timurid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. 1370-1507  (AH 7721-AH 913). Dynasty named after Timur Lang (Tamerlain) who came from the Barlas clan of Turkicised Mongols. Timur acquired the title guregen/kureken, Mongolian for 'royal son-in-law' because of his marriage to a Chingizid princess. Timur was interested in settled lands of ancient Islamic or Indian culture and eventually built his capital at Samarkand (modern Uzbekistan). His rise to power began in Transoxiana. The later Timurids were mere local rulers in Khurasan and Transoxiana. The Timurid period was one of the most glorious periods in Medieval Islamic art in Transoxiana and Persia. Period definition from British Museum.

Timur made Samarkand the showpiece of his empire, filling it with tiled mausolea, the vast Bibi Khanum mosque and gardens fed by tribute and deported craftsmen from conquered cities. His grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory whose star catalogue was the most accurate before the telescope, and the Herat court produced the finest Persian painting and manuscript art of the age. Uzbek armies ended the dynasty's rule, but its architecture still defines the skylines of Samarkand and Bukhara.

Ten Kingdoms (China, AD 907–AD 960).label: Ten Kingdoms
Ten Kingdoms (China, AD 907–AD 960).prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 960] Ten Kingdoms. 907-960. Period definition from British Museum.

While short-lived dynasties fought over the north, a patchwork of regional states ruled southern and western China, some of them wealthy and stable. Freed from northern warfare, they promoted trade, seaborne commerce, printing and painting, and the demographic and economic centre of China shifted decisively south before the Song reunified the country.

Hongwu (China, AD 1368–AD 1398).label: Hongwu
Hongwu (China, AD 1368–AD 1398).prose:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1398] Hongwu. 1368-1398 (reign).   Emperor Taizu (Zhu Yuanzhang). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan turned rebel general who drove out the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming dynasty. He rebuilt a war-shattered country through mass resettlement, land registers and hereditary military colonies, while purging tens of thousands of officials and abolishing the chancellorship to concentrate power in the throne. The autocratic, inward-looking state he designed shaped Chinese government for the next five centuries.

Ninna Era (Japan, AD 885–AD 889).label: Ninna Era
Ninna Era (Japan, AD 885–AD 889).prose:
[Japan, AD 885–AD 889] Ninna Era. 885-889. Period definition from British Museum.

The era of Emperor Kōkō, during which Fujiwara no Mototsune held power so completely that he was made kampaku — chief civil regent for an adult sovereign — a title that fixed Fujiwara dominance over the throne for the next two centuries. It also gave its name to Ninna-ji, the great Kyoto temple founded at its close and long headed by imperial princes. The transition from direct imperial rule to regency government is the era's lasting legacy.

Bun'ei Era (Japan, AD 1264–AD 1275).label: Bun'ei Era
Bun'ei Era (Japan, AD 1264–AD 1275).prose:
[Japan, AD 1264–AD 1275] Bun'ei Era. 1264-1275. Period definition from British Museum.

The years in which Kublai Khan's envoys demanded Japan's submission and were refused. In 1274 a Mongol and Korean fleet stormed Tsushima and Iki and landed at Hakata Bay, where massed formations, gunpowder bombs and coordinated archery shocked the samurai before the fleet withdrew and was scattered at sea. The Kamakura shogunate spent the following years building a stone defensive wall and mobilising warriors for the second attack it knew was coming.

Tengyo Era (Japan, AD 938–AD 947).label: Tengyo Era
Tengyo Era (Japan, AD 938–AD 947).prose:
[Japan, AD 938–AD 947] Tengyo Era. 938-947. Period definition from British Museum.

Two simultaneous provincial revolts — Taira no Masakado's in the eastern plain and Fujiwara no Sumitomo's piracy in the Inland Sea — shook confidence that the court could police its own provinces. Both were crushed by other warriors rather than by imperial armies, a lesson in where power now lay.

Einin Era (Japan, AD 1293–AD 1299).label: Einin Era
Einin Era (Japan, AD 1293–AD 1299).prose:
[Japan, AD 1293–AD 1299] Einin Era. 1293-1299. Period definition from British Museum.

A troubled stretch of the Kamakura period. A devastating earthquake and tsunami struck Kamakura in 1293, and the shogunate's warrior vassals, impoverished by the costs of defending against the Mongol invasions, fell deep into debt. The regime responded in 1297 with the Einin debt-cancellation edict, wiping out their obligations - a measure that wrecked lenders' confidence and did little to halt the shogunate's decline.

Kassite (Iraq, 1599 BC–1154 BC).label: Kassite
Kassite (Iraq, 1599 BC–1154 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–1154 BC] Kassite. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia. With the collapse of strong control at Babylon around 1600 BC, a dynasty of Kassite kings, whose original homeland may have been in the mountains to the east, was able to claim the throne and eventually united the cities of southern Mesopotamia into a single country, Babylonia. The last Kassite king was defeated by the Elamites of southwest Iran in 1155 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

After the Hittite raid that toppled Hammurabi's dynasty, Kassite kings—outsiders of uncertain origin—ruled Babylonia for close to four centuries, the longest single dynasty in Mesopotamian history. They stabilised the south, corresponded as equals with Egypt's pharaohs in the Amarna letters, built the new capital of Dur-Kurigalzu, and left the carved kudurru stones that recorded royal land grants.

Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Cycladic
Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Cyclades, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Cycladic. The Middle Cycladic period (2000BC – 1600BC) refers to material produced in the Cyclades during the Aegean Middle Bronze Age. As with the Middle Minoan and Middle Helladic periods, it is further divided into I, II and III. Period definition from British Museum.

After the fragmented villages of the earlier islands, Cycladic life concentrated into a few substantial, sometimes walled towns — Phylakopi on Melos, Ayia Irini on Kea, Akrotiri on Thera — living off obsidian, trade and the sea. Potters produced matt-painted jars and beaked jugs decorated with birds and spirals, and Cretan goods and habits arrived in growing quantity. The Minoan connection deepened until the islands became cultural satellites of Crete, setting the stage for the frescoed town buried by the Thera eruption.

Bunnan Era (Japan, AD 1444–AD 1449).label: Bunnan Era
Bunnan Era (Japan, AD 1444–AD 1449).prose: [Japan, AD 1444–AD 1449] Bunnan Era. 1444-1449. Period definition from British Museum.

Indo-Scythian (Afghanistan, 74 BC–AD 64).label: Indo-Scythian
Indo-Scythian (Afghanistan, 74 BC–AD 64).prose:
[south-east Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan, 74 BC–AD 64] Indo-Scythian. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Pakistan. Dynasty of Central Asian nomadic origin, who ruled in south-east Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan circa 75 BC-AD 64. Period definition from British Museum.

Saka horsemen pushed out of Central Asia took over Bactria, Gandhara and much of the Indus plain, ruling through kings such as Maues and Azes and their satraps. Their coinage borrowed Greek portraits and legends alongside Kharoshthi script, and their courts mixed steppe, Hellenistic, Iranian and Indian traditions. Objects from this world sit behind the rise of Gandharan Buddhist art, and inscriptions from their era give some of the earliest firm dates for Buddhist patronage in the northwest.

Early Medieval (England, AD 400–AD 1050).label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (England, AD 400–AD 1050).prose:
[British Isles, AD 400–AD 1050] Early Medieval. For the British Isles, the term refers to the period from about AD 400 to about AD 1050. The term 'Celtic' is used to refer generally to Early Medieval objects from Ireland, Scotland, Wales and Cornwall, ie. the non-Anglo-Saxon areas.   For Continental Europe, for the western territories of the former Roman Empire (Italy, France, Spain, etc.) the Early Medieval period is generally accepted to begin in around AD 400. For the eastern Roman Empire, the term Byzantine is used.   N.B.   For all European coins, the term 'Medieval' (rather than the Narrow Terms 'Early Medieval' and 'Late Medieval') is used as a general term for the period c. 400 to c. 1500. Other term can also be entered, such as 'Burgundian'. Period definition from British Museum.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Tolima (Colombia, AD 1–AD 1600).label: Tolima
Tolima (Colombia, AD 1–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, AD 1–AD 1600] Tolima. The term refers to a region of Colombia in the Magdalena valley in the Tolima and Huila departments from 1 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The middle Magdalena valley gave its name to one of Colombia's most striking goldworking styles: flat, sharply geometric anthropomorphic pectorals with outstretched limbs, hammered from gold-copper alloy. Communities here farmed the river valleys and traded gold, salt and cotton, and their descendants, the Pijao and Panche, resisted Spanish conquest fiercely into the seventeenth century.

Kao Era (Japan, AD 1169–AD 1171).label: Kao Era
Kao Era (Japan, AD 1169–AD 1171).prose:
[Japan, AD 1169–AD 1171] Kao Era. 1169-1171. Period definition from British Museum.

The retired emperor Go-Shirakawa took Buddhist vows and ruled as a cloistered sovereign, while Taira no Kiyomori and his kinsmen filled court posts and controlled the trade with Song China. The uneasy partnership between the cloister and the Taira set up the collapse into civil war a decade later.

Tingyou (China, AD 1314–AD 1320).label: Tingyou
Tingyou (China, AD 1314–AD 1320).prose:
[China, AD 1314–AD 1320] Tingyou. 1314-1320 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign era of the Yuan dynasty under Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan, who leaned on Confucian advisers and in 1315 revived the civil service examinations that the Mongols had suspended for decades. Chinese classics were translated into Mongolian and administrative reform was attempted, though hostility from the Mongol nobility limited how far it went.

Maritime Archaic (Maine, 6999 BC–AD 2000.label: Maritime Archaic
Maritime Archaic (Maine, 6999 BC–AD 2000.prose:
[Northern Atlantic coast between Newfoundland and Maine, 6999 BC–AD 2000] Maritime Archaic. Spatial coverage: Canada, Maine. 7000 BC - modern times.  Northern Atlantic coast between Newfoundland and Maine. Sea mammal hunting culture, winters were spent inland hunting caribou, elk etc. Period definition from British Museum.

Coastal hunters of the far Northeast who took swordfish, seals and walrus from open boats and worked ground slate into long lances and knives. They are best known for elaborate cemeteries in which the dead were laid out with tools, ornaments and heaps of red ochre, which led nineteenth-century antiquarians to call them the Red Paint People. Their long-distance trade in Ramah chert and native copper shows coastal communities in contact along thousands of kilometres of shoreline.

Ostrogothic (Italy, AD 493–AD 493).label: Ostrogothic
Ostrogothic (Italy, AD 493–AD 493).prose:
[Italy, AD 493–AD 493] Ostrogothic. The term refers to the period of domination of Italy by the Ostrogoths, a Gothic barbarian people originally from Sweden, from AD 493-AD 553 (but including several years of warfare either side of these dates). See also the terms Byzantine and Late Antique.  In Spain, the Ostrogothic short lived domination began after the Battle of Vouillé in AD 507. Period definition from British Museum.

Theodoric's defeat and murder of Odoacer gave Italy a Gothic king who governed through Roman law, Roman officials and the Senate, keeping the machinery of the western empire running under barbarian arms. Ravenna became a capital of mosaics and palaces, Cassiodorus and Boethius wrote at court, and Arian Goths and Catholic Romans lived side by side in an uneasy settlement. Justinian's reconquest destroyed it within two generations, leaving Italy devastated and open to the Lombards.

Choroku Era (Japan, AD 1457–AD 1460).label: Choroku Era
Choroku Era (Japan, AD 1457–AD 1460).prose:
[Japan, AD 1457–AD 1460] Choroku Era. 1457-1460. Period definition from British Museum.

In the north, Ainu resistance to Japanese trading posts exploded in Koshamain's revolt, which destroyed most of the fortified settlements on the Oshima peninsula before being put down, setting the pattern of frontier conflict in Ezo. Far to the east, the retainer Ōta Dōkan raised a fort on the marshy bay that would eventually become Edo, and later Tokyo.

Adil Shahi dynasty (India, AD 1490–AD 16.label: Adil Shahi dynasty
Adil Shahi dynasty (India, AD 1490–AD 16.prose:
[western part of the Bahmanid Sultanate at Bijapur, AD 1490–AD 1686] Adil Shahi dynasty. 1490-1686 (AH 895-AH 1097). Dynasty ruling in the western part of the Bahmanid Sultanate at Bijapur. The founder of the dynasty was Yusuf Khan, previously a commander and provisional governor for the Bahmanids. He proclaimed his independence in 1489 (AH 895).  The capital Bijapur became a centre for learning and the arts, where Persian literature became part of the Persianisation process in the region. Bijapur was captured by the Mogul emperor Aurangzib Alamgir in 1686 (AH 1097). Period definition from British Museum.

One of the Deccan sultanates that emerged from the break-up of the Bahmani kingdom, ruling from Bijapur over a wealthy, cosmopolitan court of Persian, Turkish, Maratha and African officers. Its rulers joined the alliance that destroyed Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565 and left behind spectacular architecture, above all the vast dome of the Gol Gumbaz. Aurangzeb's armies finally swallowed the kingdom in 1686, extending Mughal rule deep into southern India.

Shaosheng (China, AD 1094–AD 1097).label: Shaosheng
Shaosheng (China, AD 1094–AD 1097).prose:
[China, AD 1094–AD 1097] Shaosheng. 1094-1097 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The young Emperor Zhezong of Song took personal control from his conservative grandmother's regents and swung the court back to Wang Anshi's reform programme — the era name itself announced a 'continuation' of his father Shenzong's policies. Reformists under Zhang Dun purged their rivals, driving figures such as Su Shi into distant exile and hardening the factional split that would poison Song politics until the dynasty's northern collapse.

Five Dynasties (China, AD 907–AD 960).label: Five Dynasties
Five Dynasties (China, AD 907–AD 960).prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 960] Five Dynasties. 907-960. Period definition from British Museum.

After the Tang collapse, five short-lived military regimes succeeded one another in the north, most founded by generals and several with Turkic roots. Frontier control slipped, the Sixteen Prefectures were ceded to the Khitan Liao, and the old aristocratic families were broken for good. Printing of the Confucian classics began in these decades, and the Song reunification that followed built a state deliberately designed to keep generals in check.

Western Xia dynasty (China, AD 1038–AD 1.label: Western Xia dynasty
Western Xia dynasty (China, AD 1038–AD 1.prose:
[western China, AD 1038–AD 1227] Western Xia dynasty. A kingdom in western China from 1038-1227. Period definition from British Museum.

The Tangut state of the northwest, straddling the Hexi Corridor and the Silk Road trade that ran through it, which forced Song China to buy peace with annual payments. Its rulers commissioned a distinctive logographic script of nearly 6,000 characters and printed vast quantities of Buddhist scripture; the buried library at Khara-Khoto later yielded thousands of these texts. Genghis Khan destroyed the kingdom in 1227, and he died during that final campaign.

Bunryaku Era (Japan, AD 1234–AD 1235).label: Bunryaku Era
Bunryaku Era (Japan, AD 1234–AD 1235).prose:
[Japan, AD 1234–AD 1235] Bunryaku Era. 1234-1235. Period definition from British Museum.

A two-year regnal name in the Kamakura age, proclaimed under the boy-emperor Shijō while real power lay with the Hōjō regents in Kamakura. Era names like this were often changed after fires, epidemics or famine in the hope of breaking a run of bad fortune, which is why the calendar of medieval Japan is crowded with such brief labels.

Western Zhou dynasty (China, 1049 BC–770.label: Western Zhou dynasty
Western Zhou dynasty (China, 1049 BC–770.prose:
[China, 1049 BC–770 BC] Western Zhou dynasty. 1050 BC-771 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The conquest of Shang by the Zhou brought a new political theology of Heaven's mandate and a network of kin-based domains radiating from the Wei valley. Long bronze inscriptions, ancestral ritual and a reformed vessel repertoire define the period archaeologically, while its idealised institutions became the model Confucius looked back to. The move of the capital eastward marks the end of effective royal power and the start of contests among the regional states.

Phylakopi I Culture (Greece, 2299 BC–199.label: Phylakopi I Culture
Phylakopi I Culture (Greece, 2299 BC–199.prose:
[Cyclades, 2299 BC–1999 BC] Phylakopi I Culture. The latest of the three cultural groups into which the Early Cycladic (q.v.) period is divided, based on consistently recurring types of pottery, bronze and marble objects. The name refers to the type site used by Colin Renfrew to define the culture, although the term applies to material from the Cyclades as a whole. There are not always clear boundaries between cultural groups, but an approximate date range is 2300BC – 2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for the earliest settlement at Phylakopi on Melos, this phase follows the disruptions that ended the earlier Cycladic Bronze Age. Islanders regrouped into fewer, larger coastal settlements, and Melos continued to export obsidian across the Aegean while pottery styles shifted toward painted dark-on-light decoration. The pattern of nucleated, outward-looking island towns set the stage for the Minoan-influenced Cycladic centres of later centuries.

Daozong (China, AD 1055–AD 1101).label: Daozong
Daozong (China, AD 1055–AD 1101).prose:
[China, AD 1055–AD 1101] Daozong. 1055-1101 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A long Liao reign in which the dynasty's Khitan rulers poured resources into Buddhism — temple building, colossal pagodas and the printing of a vast Buddhist canon — while political control decayed. Court intrigue reached its peak when the emperor was persuaded to have his own empress and heir killed, weakening the succession. The Jurchen tribes who would destroy the Liao a generation later were already growing restive on the northeastern frontier.

Ubaid (Fertile Crescent, 5899 BC–3999 BC.label: Ubaid
Ubaid (Fertile Crescent, 5899 BC–3999 BC.prose:
[southern Iraq and much of the Fertile Crescent, 5899 BC–3999 BC] Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Fertile Crescent, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria. The Ubaid period falls within the Pottery Neolithic and Early Chalcolithic periods (c.5900-4000 BC). Ubaid culture began in southern Iraq and spread northwards to cover much of the Fertile Crescent around 4500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The first widespread village culture of southern Mesopotamia, marked by pale greenish painted pottery, mudbrick houses of tripartite plan and small temples rebuilt again and again on the same spot, most famously at Eridu. Irrigation let farmers work the dry alluvium, herds and fishing filled out the diet, and communities grew large enough to support differences in status visible in burials and buildings. Ubaid pottery and styles spread north into Syria and Anatolia and down the Gulf, setting the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.

Haftavan Period III (Iran, 799 BC–699 BC.label: Haftavan Period III
Haftavan Period III (Iran, 799 BC–699 BC.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 799 BC–699 BC] Haftavan Period III. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.800BC-700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Ham Nghi (Vietnam, AD 1885–AD 1885).label: Ham Nghi
Ham Nghi (Vietnam, AD 1885–AD 1885).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1885–AD 1885] Ham Nghi. (1885) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

The boy emperor's advisers launched a night attack on the French garrison at Huế; it failed, and he fled the capital into the mountains. From there his court issued the Cần Vương edict summoning loyal scholars and officials to expel the French, igniting a decade of guerrilla resistance across central and northern Vietnam. Captured in 1888 and exiled to Algeria, he became a lasting symbol of anticolonial defiance.

Lichhavi (Nepal, AD 576–AD 750).label: Lichhavi
Lichhavi (Nepal, AD 576–AD 750).prose:
[Nepal, AD 576–AD 750] Lichhavi. Ruling Dynasty of Nepal c.576-750 AD.  This culture was based on the Kathmandu valley and was influenced by the Gupta culture of lowland India to the south. Period definition from British Museum.

The later phase of the dynasty that ruled the Kathmandu Valley, when Nepal was drawn into wider Himalayan politics — a Licchavi princess was said to have married the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo, and Chinese envoys crossed the valley on their way to India. Inscriptions record land grants, water conduits and temple endowments, and the period's serene stone images set the pattern for Nepalese sculpture for centuries afterwards.

Gurkha dynasty (Nepal, AD 1749–AD 1815).label: Gurkha dynasty
Gurkha dynasty (Nepal, AD 1749–AD 1815).prose:
[hills of Nepal, north-west of Kathmandu, AD 1749–AD 1815] Gurkha dynasty. Kingdom in the hills of Nepal, north-west of Kathmandu, which first minted coins in AD 1749 under the ruler Prithvi Narayan Shah (1742-1775). He conquered the Kathmandu valley in 1768, moved his capital to Kathmandu and established the Shah dynasty. He attacked Sikkim in 1789, then Tibet in 1790. Further territorial expansion southwards brought the kingdom into conflict with the British. Following the treaty of Sagauli in 1815, a British Resident was installed in Kathmandu. Men from this region are still recruited into the elite Gorkha regiment of the British army. Period definition from British Museum.

The Shah kings of the small hill state of Gorkha conquered the Kathmandu Valley and pushed outward until they had forged a single Nepali kingdom stretching along the Himalaya. Expansion west and south brought them into collision with the British East India Company; the war that followed cost Nepal a third of its territory but won its soldiers a lasting military reputation and its state a lasting independence.

Chokan Era (Japan, AD 1163–AD 1165).label: Chokan Era
Chokan Era (Japan, AD 1163–AD 1165).prose:
[Japan, AD 1163–AD 1165] Chokan Era. 1163-1165. Period definition from British Museum.

A tangle of rival retired emperors and a sickly young sovereign left real power contested between the cloistered Go-Shirakawa and the court around Emperor Nijō. Taira no Kiyomori, rewarded for his part in the recent civil disturbances, used the confusion to climb through the official ranks toward a position no warrior had held before.

Oei Era (Japan, AD 1394–AD 1428).label: Oei Era
Oei Era (Japan, AD 1394–AD 1428).prose:
[Japan, AD 1394–AD 1428] Oei Era. 1394-1428. Period definition from British Museum.

The longest era of the Muromachi period, covering the height of Ashikaga power after the northern and southern courts were reunited. Yoshimitsu's Kitayama culture produced the Golden Pavilion and patronised the new Noh theatre, while official tribute trade with Ming China brought copper coins and silk into Japan. It also saw the Ōei Invasion of 1419, when a Korean fleet attacked the pirate bases of Tsushima.

Eikyo Era (Japan, AD 1429–AD 1441).label: Eikyo Era
Eikyo Era (Japan, AD 1429–AD 1441).prose:
[Japan, AD 1429–AD 1441] Eikyo Era. 1429-1441. Period definition from British Museum.

The shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori tried to restore central authority by force, crushing the rebellious Kanto deputy Ashikaga Mochiuji in the Eikyo Rebellion and bullying rival warlords and monasteries into line. His methods earned him enemies, and the era ended when a vassal murdered him at a banquet - a killing that exposed the shogunate's weakness and helped open the road to the Sengoku wars.

Hoki Era (Japan, AD 770–AD 781).label: Hoki Era
Hoki Era (Japan, AD 770–AD 781).prose:
[Japan, AD 770–AD 781] Hoki Era. 770-781. Period definition from British Museum.

Following the death of Empress Shōtoku and the fall of the monk Dōkyō, the throne passed to the elderly Kōnin and the succession returned to a different imperial line. His government cut costs, curbed the political power the great Nara temples had gained, and tried to restore the strained provincial tax system. His son Kanmu succeeded him and soon moved the capital away from Nara altogether.

Qiande (China, AD 919–AD 924).label: Qiande
Qiande (China, AD 919–AD 924).prose:
[China, AD 919–AD 924] Qiande. 919-924. Period definition from British Museum.

A reign era of the Former Shu, the wealthy kingdom based on Chengdu that broke away during the collapse of the Tang. Sheltered by the mountains from the wars of the north China plain, its court supported poets, painters and printers, but weak rule under its second ruler soon invited conquest from the Later Tang.

Early Minoan IIA (Crete, 2899 BC–2499 BC.label: Early Minoan IIA
Early Minoan IIA (Crete, 2899 BC–2499 BC.prose:
[Crete, 2899 BC–2499 BC] Early Minoan IIA. 2900BC-2500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cretan communities grew into substantial villages like Myrtos Fournou Korifi and Vasiliki, with sophisticated potting—the mottled red-and-black Vasiliki ware—and imported gold, ivory and Cycladic marble figurines showing the island plugged into wider Aegean exchange. Collective burial in circular tholos tombs on the Mesara plain and house tombs in the east reached its height. Much of what would define palatial Crete—craft specialisation, seal use, seaborne trade—was already taking shape.

Kan'en Era (Japan, AD 1748–AD 1751).label: Kan'en Era
Kan'en Era (Japan, AD 1748–AD 1751).prose:
[Japan, AD 1748–AD 1751] Kan'en Era. 1748-1751. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief mid-Edo era chiefly remembered in theatre history: the puppet play Kanadehon Chūshingura, the definitive dramatisation of the forty-seven rōnin vendetta, premiered in Osaka in 1748 and was almost immediately adapted for kabuki. It became the most performed and most illustrated story in Japanese popular culture.

Qianlong (China, AD 1736–AD 1795).label: Qianlong
Qianlong (China, AD 1736–AD 1795).prose:
[China, AD 1736–AD 1795] Qianlong. 1736-1795 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The long reign of the Qianlong emperor was the Qing at its greatest extent, with campaigns in Xinjiang, Tibet and the southwest doubling the empire's territory, and a population that surged past three hundred million. He was a compulsive collector and cataloguer, assembling the imperial art collection and commissioning the vast Siku Quanshu library while censoring the books that displeased him.
