Trade at Canton boomed, the Macartney embassy was politely rebuffed, and behind the splendour corruption and fiscal strain were already setting up the crises of the next century.

Kerma Classique (Egypt, 1749 BC–1449 BC).label: Kerma Classique
Kerma Classique (Egypt, 1749 BC–1449 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1749 BC–1449 BC] Kerma Classique. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. c. 1750 BC-1450 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The peak of the Nubian kingdom of Kush, ruled from a city dominated by the Deffufa, a colossal mud-brick temple tower still standing today. Its kings were buried under enormous tumuli up to ninety metres across, accompanied by hundreds of sacrificed retainers, imported Egyptian statuary and bronze daggers; they controlled Lower Nubia, garrisoned captured Egyptian forts, and allied with the Hyksos against Thebes. Their kingdom was finally smashed by the reunified Egyptian army under Thutmose I.

Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2189 BC).label: Akkadian
Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2189 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2333 BC–2189 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Mesopotamia, Syria, Turkey. The first king of the Akkadian Dynasty (Sargon I) united the whole of Mesopotamia under one ruler. Sargon and his descendants ruled from 2334 BC until around 2190 BC when the empire collapsed owing to invasion and rebellion.   Akkadian is also a language spoken from around 2600 BC until the 1st and 2nd centuries AD. Within that period texts written between 2600 BC-2000 BC use the Old Akkadian language. The language then developed into Babylonian (2000 BC onwards) and Assyrian (2000 BC-600 BC) forms. Period definition from British Museum.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.

Jingde (China, AD 1004–AD 1007).label: Jingde
Jingde (China, AD 1004–AD 1007).prose:
[China, AD 1004–AD 1007] Jingde. 1004-1007 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The opening years of Emperor Zhenzong's reign, marked by the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005, which ended war with the Khitan Liao by paying them annual silver and silk in exchange for a century of peace. The imperial kilns at Changnan were renamed Jingdezhen after this era, and the name still stands on porcelain made there today.

Kohei Era (Japan, AD 1058–AD 1065).label: Kohei Era
Kohei Era (Japan, AD 1058–AD 1065).prose:
[Japan, AD 1058–AD 1065] Kohei Era. 1058-1065. Period definition from British Museum.

These years fall inside the long campaign in the northeast that Japanese tradition calls the Former Nine Years War, ending in 1062 when Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and his son Yoshiie destroyed the Abe clan of Mutsu. The victory made the Minamoto the pre-eminent warrior house of eastern Japan and gave later samurai their founding heroic legends.

Hongguang (China, AD 1644–AD 1645).label: Hongguang
Hongguang (China, AD 1644–AD 1645).prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1645] Hongguang. 1644-1645 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

After Beijing fell to rebels and then to the Qing, Ming loyalists proclaimed the Prince of Fu emperor at Nanjing, hoping to hold the Yangzi and rule the south as the Song had once done. The court dissolved into factional quarrels and drunken misrule while its generals defected, and Qing armies took Nanjing within a year. Its collapse opened four decades of scattered Southern Ming resistance, from Fujian to Yunnan.

Tianxian Taizu (China, AD 926–AD 926).label: Tianxian Taizu
Tianxian Taizu (China, AD 926–AD 926).prose:
[China, AD 926–AD 926] Tianxian Taizu. 926 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Abaoji, founder of the Khitan Liao state, adopted this era name after destroying the kingdom of Balhae in Manchuria and reorganising it as a puppet realm for his heir. He died on the return march, leaving an empire that combined a steppe tribal army with Chinese-style administration, a new Khitan script and a capital city. The succession passed instead to his second son, backed by his formidable widow Empress Shulü.

Yuanfeng (China, AD 1078–AD 1085).label: Yuanfeng
Yuanfeng (China, AD 1078–AD 1085).prose:
[China, AD 1078–AD 1085] Yuanfeng. 1078-1085 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The later years of Emperor Shenzong of Song, when Wang Anshi had withdrawn from court but his New Policies were kept running by the emperor himself. A sweeping reorganisation of the central bureaucracy, known by this reign name, tidied up overlapping offices and set the shape of later Song government. Ambitions against the Tangut Xia ended in heavy defeat, draining the treasury the reforms had been meant to fill.

Zhidao (China, AD 995–AD 997).label: Zhidao
Zhidao (China, AD 995–AD 997).prose:
[China, AD 995–AD 997] Zhidao. 995-997 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The closing years of Emperor Taizong, the second Song ruler, who had abandoned hopes of retaking the northern territories from the Khitan and turned to consolidating civil administration. The era's coins are prized by collectors because the inscriptions were written in the emperor's own hand in several scripts. His death brought a peaceful succession, still rare in Chinese dynastic history.

Liu Song dynasty (China, AD 420–AD 479).label: Liu Song dynasty
Liu Song dynasty (China, AD 420–AD 479).prose:
[China, AD 420–AD 479] Liu Song dynasty. 420-479. Period definition from British Museum.

Founded when the general Liu Yu deposed the last Jin emperor, this was the first and strongest of the Southern Dynasties that ruled from Jiankang while non-Chinese regimes held the north. Its early decades brought orderly government and prosperity in the Yangtze lands, before palace coups and fratricide wrecked the ruling house. The southern gentry culture of poetry, calligraphy and Buddhist learning it sheltered shaped Chinese literature for generations.

Taihe Northern Wei dynasty (China, AD 47.label: Taihe Northern Wei dynasty
Taihe Northern Wei dynasty (China, AD 47.prose:
[China, AD 477–AD 499] Taihe Northern Wei dynasty. 477-499 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The great reforming era of Emperor Xiaowen and the dowager who ruled before him, when the Xianbei rulers of north China remade their state on Chinese lines: the equal-field land system, salaried officials, a new law code, and the move of the capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang. Xianbei dress, language and surnames were banned at court in favour of Chinese ones. The Buddhist cave temples at Yungang and the first work at Longmen date from these decades.

BMAC (Afghanistan, 2199 BC–1699 BC).label: BMAC
BMAC (Afghanistan, 2199 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Central Asia, 2199 BC–1699 BC] BMAC. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. Bronze Age culture of Central Asia, dated circa 2200BC-1700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Also called the Oxus civilisation, this was a network of fortified mudbrick towns on the oases of the Amu Darya, with monumental walled compounds at sites like Gonur Tepe in Margiana and Sapallitepa in Bactria. Its people irrigated the desert margins, worked gold, silver, lapis and tin bronze, and made distinctive compartmented seals and stone 'handbag' weights that turn up in Mesopotamia, Elam and the Indus valley. Its collapse and its possible links to early Indo-Iranian speakers moving south remain much argued over.

Kokoku Era (Japan, AD 1340–AD 1346).label: Kokoku Era
Kokoku Era (Japan, AD 1340–AD 1346).prose:
[Japan, AD 1340–AD 1346] Kokoku Era. 1340-1346. Period definition from British Museum.

A reign-name used by the Southern Court of Go-Murakami during the schism between two rival imperial lines, and therefore not recognised in Kyoto, where the Ashikaga-backed Northern Court dated documents differently. The Southern cause was weakening: its great commanders were dead and Kitabatake Chikafusa was reduced to defending its legitimacy in writing rather than in the field.

Late Cypriot IB (Cyprus, 1599 BC–1449 BC.label: Late Cypriot IB
Late Cypriot IB (Cyprus, 1599 BC–1449 BC.prose:
[Cyprus, 1599 BC–1449 BC] Late Cypriot IB. 1600 BC-1450 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cypriot exports hit their stride: White Slip 'milk bowls' and Base Ring juglets travel to Egypt, Syria and the Aegean in quantity, some of the juglets probably carrying opium. At home, urban settlements on the east and south coasts expand around the business of copper smelting and export.

Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1349 BC–1049 BC).label: Middle Assyrian
Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1349 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[the Euphrates in the west and parts of Babylonia in the south, 1349 BC–1049 BC] Middle Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Babylonia, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. From around 135O BC, the Assyrians expanded their territories and eventually established an empire reaching to the Euphrates in the west and parts of Babylonia in the south. By 1050 BC the territories had been reduced by attacks and rebellions to the Assyrian homeland around the cities of Ashur and Nineveh. Period definition from British Museum.

Assyria emerged from vassalage to Mitanni to become a great power, its kings conquering northern Mesopotamia and, under Tukulti-Ninurta I, briefly capturing Babylon itself. An efficient provincial administration, meticulous royal archives and the Middle Assyrian Laws - unusually harsh, especially toward women - date from this era. Weakened by Aramaean pressure after 1100 BC, the kingdom nevertheless kept the institutions that its Neo-Assyrian successors used to build an empire.

Joho Era (Japan, AD 1074–AD 1077).label: Joho Era
Joho Era (Japan, AD 1074–AD 1077).prose:
[Japan, AD 1074–AD 1077] Joho Era. 1074-1077. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign-name at the start of Emperor Shirakawa's rule, when the young sovereign was consolidating his position after the death of his reformist father Go-Sanjo. The court was still dominated by Fujiwara regents, but Shirakawa would go on to invent the system of 'cloistered rule', abdicating while continuing to govern as retired emperor - a device that shaped Japanese politics for the next century.

Jianzhong Qingguo (China, AD 1101–AD 110.label: Jianzhong Qingguo
Jianzhong Qingguo (China, AD 1101–AD 110.prose:
[China, AD 1101–AD 1101] Jianzhong Qingguo. 1101 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The single year that opened Emperor Huizong's reign, its name meaning to establish balance and settle the state, a signal that the new ruler would reconcile the warring reformist and conservative parties. The compromise collapsed almost at once; the following year Huizong took the reformists' side wholesale under a new era name, and opponents were blacklisted by the hundred.

Aq Qoyunlu (Iran, AD 1378–AD 1508).label: Aq Qoyunlu
Aq Qoyunlu (Iran, AD 1378–AD 1508).prose:
[Diyar Bakr (center) to Khurasan, Iraq and the Persian Gulf, AD 1378–AD 1508] Aq Qoyunlu. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. The Aq Qoyunlu '[those with] white sheep' were a nomadic Turkmen confederation centred on Diyar Bakr 1378-1508 (AH 780-908), who established power through marital alliances with the Byzantines in the later 14th century. They submitted to Timur (q.v.) and were rewarded with the grant of Diyar Bakr. Under Uzun Hasan (1457-1478), they extended their rule as far as Khurasan, Iraq and the Persian Gulf, but were overthrown by the Ottomans (q.v.) and Safavids (q.v.). Period definition from British Museum.

The 'White Sheep' Turkoman confederation rose from eastern Anatolia to overthrow its Qara Qoyunlu rivals and, under Uzun Hasan, to rule Iran, Iraq and much of Anatolia from Tabriz. Uzun Hasan courted Venice against the Ottomans but was crushed by their firearms at Otlukbeli in 1473. Internal succession wars then let the Safavid Shah Ismail sweep the dynasty away and impose Shi'ism on Iran.

Tianhan (China, AD 917–AD 917).label: Tianhan
Tianhan (China, AD 917–AD 917).prose:
[China, AD 917–AD 917] Tianhan. 917. Period definition from British Museum.

Wang Jian, the old warlord who had carved the kingdom of Former Shu out of Sichuan after the Tang collapse, briefly renamed his state Han and adopted a new era name to match. The change did not stick and the name Shu was restored the following year. It is a small illustration of how the Five Dynasties rulers used titles and era names to stake grand claims from modest territories.

Middle Minoan IIA (Crete, 1849 BC–1799 B.label: Middle Minoan IIA
Middle Minoan IIA (Crete, 1849 BC–1799 B.prose:
[Crete, 1849 BC–1799 BC] Middle Minoan IIA. 1850BC-1800BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Crete's first palaces were fully operating, concentrating storage, craft workshops and ritual in complexes around a central court. Administrators used stamped clay sealings and the Cretan Hieroglyphic script, and potters produced the earliest fine Kamares wares.

Haftavan Period VIC (Iran, 2199 BC–1999.label: Haftavan Period VIC
Haftavan Period VIC (Iran, 2199 BC–1999.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Haftavan Period VIC. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.2200BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Shizong Jin Dynasty (China, AD 1161–AD 1.label: Shizong Jin Dynasty
Shizong Jin Dynasty (China, AD 1161–AD 1.prose:
[China, AD 1161–AD 1189] Shizong Jin Dynasty. 1161-1189 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Remembered as the 'Little Yao and Shun', the Jurchen emperor Wanyan Yong came to power amid the collapse of his predecessor's invasion of the south, made peace with the Song on softened terms and gave north China nearly thirty years of good harvests and light government. He also worried that his people were dissolving into the Chinese majority, and pushed the Jurchen language, script and hunting traditions in a deliberate campaign of cultural revival.

Middle Archaic (United States, 5999 BC–3.label: Middle Archaic
Middle Archaic (United States, 5999 BC–3.prose:
[United States, 5999 BC–3999 BC] Middle Archaic. Spatial coverage: Canada, United States. 6000 BC-4000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

Chokyu Era (Japan, AD 1040–AD 1044).label: Chokyu Era
Chokyu Era (Japan, AD 1040–AD 1044).prose:
[Japan, AD 1040–AD 1044] Chokyu Era. 1040-1044. Period definition from British Museum.

A quiet stretch in the reign of Emperor Go-Suzaku, with Fujiwara no Yorimichi as regent and the Fujiwara house still monopolising court office. Beneath the calm, the court's control of the provinces was thinning as tax-exempt private estates multiplied and armed monks and local landholders grew bolder.

Woodland Period (United States, 999 BC–A.label: Woodland Period
Woodland Period (United States, 999 BC–A.prose:
[North America, 999 BC–AD 1000] Woodland Period. Spatial coverage: Canada, United States. The term refers to a period covering 1000 BC to 1000 AD in North America. Period definition from British Museum.

Across eastern North America this is the time of the first widespread pottery, of mound building and earthwork ceremonial centres, and of long-distance exchange in copper, mica and marine shell. Communities domesticated a suite of native seed crops before maize became important, and populations grew as settlements became more permanent. Adena and Hopewell burial mounds, still visible on the landscape, belong to its earlier and middle centuries.

Christian Period (Sudan, AD 550–AD 1504).label: Christian Period
Christian Period (Sudan, AD 550–AD 1504).prose:
[Nubia; Sudan, AD 550–AD 1504] Christian Period. The term Christian period is used specifically for Nubia and Sudan to refer to the period from 6thC AD (550) - 1504 AD.  For Egypt, the term Coptic is used to refer to Christian artefacts from 4thC to the present day. Period definition from British Museum.

After missionaries arrived from Byzantine Egypt, the Nubian kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alwa adopted Christianity and built stone churches decorated with brilliant wall paintings, best known from Faras. A treaty with the Muslim rulers of Egypt, the baqt, regulated trade and kept Nubia independent for centuries, with Old Nubian written in a Greek-derived alphabet. Arab migration and internal decline eroded the kingdoms from the 14th century, and the fall of Soba around 1504 ended Christian rule on the middle Nile.

Xianfeng (China, AD 1851–AD 1861).label: Xianfeng
Xianfeng (China, AD 1851–AD 1861).prose:
[China, AD 1851–AD 1861] Xianfeng. 1851-1861 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign consumed by crisis: the Taiping rebels seized the Yangzi valley and held Nanjing, while Britain and France fought the Second Opium War, occupied Beijing and burned the Summer Palace. The emperor fled to Rehe and died there, and the treaties signed in his name opened the interior to foreign trade, missionaries and diplomats. His death left a small child on the throne and brought the Empress Dowager Cixi to power.

Haftavan Period IV (Iran, 1099 BC–799 BC.label: Haftavan Period IV
Haftavan Period IV (Iran, 1099 BC–799 BC.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 1099 BC–799 BC] Haftavan Period IV. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.1100BC-800BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Genji Era (Japan, AD 1864–AD 1865).label: Genji Era
Genji Era (Japan, AD 1864–AD 1865).prose:
[Japan, AD 1864–AD 1865] Genji Era. 1864-1865. Period definition from British Museum.

A single turbulent year of the late Tokugawa crisis. Chōshū samurai attacked the imperial palace in Kyoto and were beaten back at the Hamaguri Gate, a Western fleet bombarded Shimonoseki in retaliation for attacks on foreign shipping, and the shogunate launched a punitive expedition against Chōshū. The failure of these efforts to restore order pushed Japan towards the fall of the shogunate four years later.

Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1199.label: Late Helladic IIIB
Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1299 BC–1199.prose:
[Greece, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Late Helladic IIIB. 1300BC-1200BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The palaces reached their fullest form, with the Lion Gate and the huge walls of Tiryns raised and Linear B scribes tallying grain, textiles, chariots and rowers. Late in the phase came fire, abandonment and hurried defensive works, ending in the destruction of every mainland palace and the loss of writing.

Huichang (China, AD 841–AD 846).label: Huichang
Huichang (China, AD 841–AD 846).prose:
[China, AD 841–AD 846] Huichang. 841-846 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era of Tang Wuzong, dominated by the greatest persecution of Buddhism in Chinese history. Tens of thousands of monasteries and shrines were destroyed, some 260,000 monks and nuns forced back into lay life, and their bronze bells and statues melted into coin - driven as much by the state's need for taxpayers and metal as by doctrine. Manichaeans, Nestorian Christians and Zoroastrians were swept up too, and Chinese Buddhism never fully regained its institutional wealth.

Artuqid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1101–AD 1409.label: Artuqid dynasty
Artuqid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1101–AD 1409.prose:
[Diyar Bakr, Khartpert, Mardin and Mayyafariqin, AD 1101–AD 1409] Artuqid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. c.1101-1409 (c.AH 494-AH 812). Turkic dynasty ruling in Diyar Bakr, Khartpert, Mardin and Mayyafariqin, an area strongly settled by Turkmens. The rise of the Zangids halted their expansion and in the thirteenth century they became for a while vassals of the Seljuks of Rum. They submitted to the Mongol Hulegu and the dynasty came to an end with the Timurid invasion. Period definition from British Museum.

A Turkmen dynasty ruling from Diyarbakır, Mardin and Hasankeyf, the Artuqids held their ground amid the Crusades, Zengids, Ayyubids and finally the Mongols. They are remembered above all for building: fortified bridges, mosques and the mechanical marvels described by their court engineer al-Jazari, whose treatise on ingenious devices catalogued water clocks, automata and pumps. Their copper coins, oddly, carried classical and Byzantine portrait imagery long after Islamic convention had turned to script.

Proto-Urban Period (West Bank, 3499 BC–2.label: Proto-Urban Period
Proto-Urban Period (West Bank, 3499 BC–2.prose:
[Palestine, 3499 BC–2999 BC] Proto-Urban Period. Spatial coverage: Gaza Strip, State of Palestine, West Bank. Term used in Palestinian archaeology, sub-divided into three phases, "Proto-Urban A" etc, dating between ca 3500-3000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Kathleen Kenyon coined this label at Jericho for the stretch between the farming villages of the Chalcolithic and the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age. Settlements grew larger and denser, distinctive painted and burnished pottery was buried with the dead in rock-cut shaft tombs, and communities began investing in fortification and communal building. Within a few centuries the region's first true towns, ringed by mudbrick walls, would emerge from these foundations.

Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.label: Late Cycladic I
Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Cycladic I. 1600BC-1500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The moment captured at Akrotiri on Thera: a prosperous multi-storey town with paved streets, plumbing and walls painted with boxing boys, saffron gatherers and a fleet of ships. Cretan weights, script and pottery shapes show how deeply the islands were tied into the Minoan world, without being ruled by it. A volcanic eruption buried the town under metres of pumice, preserving it and ending the phase abruptly.

Bunsho Era (Japan, AD 1466–AD 1467).label: Bunsho Era
Bunsho Era (Japan, AD 1466–AD 1467).prose:
[Japan, AD 1466–AD 1467] Bunsho Era. 1466-1467. Period definition from British Museum.

A single year at the end of the Muromachi peace, notable mainly for what came immediately after: the succession dispute in the Ashikaga house boiled over and Kyoto's rival armies began the Ōnin War, burning much of the capital. The era name was abandoned as the fighting started, and Japan slid into a century of warlord conflict.

Early Helladic II (Greece, 2899 BC–2299.label: Early Helladic II
Early Helladic II (Greece, 2899 BC–2299.prose:
[Greece, 2899 BC–2299 BC] Early Helladic II. 2900BC-2300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The most prosperous stage of the early mainland Bronze Age in Messenia, marked by larger settlements, standardised wheel-influenced pottery and active exchange around the Aegean. Elsewhere in the Peloponnese this is the age of monumental corridor houses and sealing systems, and Messenian sites participate in the same expanding economy. Its end came with disruption and abandonment at many sites.

Danishmandid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1104–AD.label: Danishmandid dynasty
Danishmandid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1104–AD.prose:
[north-central Anatolia and Cappadocia, AD 1104–AD 1178] Danishmandid dynasty. 1104-1178 (AH 497-AH 573). Turkman dynasty originally from north-central Anatolia and Cappadocia who controlled the northerly route of Turkmen access into Asia Minor. The name comes from Persian Danishmand meaning wise, learned man, scholar. In 1174 the line in Sivas was conquered by the Seljuqs of Rum, the line in Malatya and Elbistan fell to the Seljuqs of Rum in 1178. Period definition from British Museum.

A Turkmen dynasty ruling central and eastern Anatolia from Sivas, Malatya and Kayseri in the generations after Manzikert. Its founder's successors defeated crusader armies, captured Bohemond of Antioch, and for a time overshadowed the Seljuks of Rum, until the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan II absorbed their lands and left Rum master of Anatolia.

Engen Era (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1349).label: Engen Era
Engen Era (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1349).prose:
[Japan, AD 1336–AD 1349] Engen Era. 1336-1340. Period definition from British Museum.

An era name proclaimed by the Southern Court after Go-Daigo fled Kyoto for the mountains of Yoshino, leaving the Ashikaga shogunate to install a rival emperor in the capital. For decades Japan had two imperial lines and two competing calendars, and which era name a document uses reveals which side its writer served.

Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1059 BC).label: Late Cycladic
Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1059 BC).prose:
[Cyclades, 1599 BC–1059 BC] Late Cycladic. The Late Cycladic period (1600BC – 1060BC) refers to material produced in the Cyclades during the Aegean Late Bronze Age. As with the Late Minoan and Late Helladic periods, it is further divided into I, II and III. Period definition from British Museum.

The Bronze Age islands at their most connected, when Cretan influence in architecture, script, fresco and fashion gave way after about 1450 BC to Mycenaean control from the mainland. Towns like Akrotiri on Thera, Phylakopi on Melos and Ayia Irini on Keos were substantial harbour settlements with shrines, drainage and painted rooms. The eruption of Thera, the rise of Mycenaean palatial trade and the upheavals around 1200 BC all fall within this span.

Chengdi (China, 31 BC–6 BC).label: Chengdi
Chengdi (China, 31 BC–6 BC).prose:
[China, 31 BC–6 BC] Chengdi. 32-7BC (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Real power drifted from the emperor to the family of his mother, the empress dowager, whose brothers and nephews monopolised the great offices of state — among them a young Wang Mang, who would later take the throne outright. The court is remembered for the emperor's obsession with the dancer Zhao Feiyan and her sister, and for disastrous Yellow River flooding that the treasury struggled to repair.

Shoka Era (Japan, AD 1257–AD 1259).label: Shoka Era
Shoka Era (Japan, AD 1257–AD 1259).prose:
[Japan, AD 1257–AD 1259] Shoka Era. 1257-1259. Period definition from British Museum.

Two years remembered in Japan for disaster: a violent earthquake wrecked Kamakura, and storms, floods and crop failure brought a famine so severe that it entered the record as the Shōka famine, with corpses in the streets of the capital. The catastrophes fed a mood of religious crisis, and shortly afterwards the monk Nichiren pointed to them as proof that the country's rulers had embraced false teaching. Ideas of the age of the Latter Dharma spread widely among ordinary people as a result.

Tianli (China, AD 1328–AD 1330).label: Tianli
Tianli (China, AD 1328–AD 1330).prose:
[China, AD 1328–AD 1330] Tianli. 1328-1330 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Tugh Temür took the Yuan throne after the War of the Two Capitals, a civil war between rival Mongol factions in Dadu and Shangdu that showed how unstable the succession had become. A cultivated ruler who wrote Chinese poetry and calligraphy, he founded the Pavilion of the Star of Literature as an academy and sponsored a huge compendium of Yuan institutions. Behind the cultural display, real power lay with the warlord El Temür.

Choho Era (Japan, AD 999–AD 1004).label: Choho Era
Choho Era (Japan, AD 999–AD 1004).prose:
[Japan, AD 999–AD 1004] Choho Era. 999-1004. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Michinaga tightened his grip on the court of Emperor Ichijō, installing his daughter Shōshi as a second empress alongside Teishi and making marriage politics the engine of government. The rival salons of these two consorts drew in Sei Shōnagon and Murasaki Shikibu, so the court intrigues of these years lie directly behind the golden age of Heian women's literature.

Longshan culture (China, 2999 BC–1699 BC.label: Longshan culture
Longshan culture (China, 2999 BC–1699 BC.prose:
[China, 2999 BC–1699 BC] Longshan culture. Neolithic culture circa 3000 BC-1700 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Neolithic communities across the Yellow River basin built rammed-earth town walls, buried some dead with lavish grave goods and others with none, and turned out wheel-thrown black pottery so thin it is called eggshell ware. The scale of building and the gap between rich and poor graves point to chiefs, warfare and craft specialists. Out of this world of competing walled towns came the first Chinese states of the Bronze Age.

Wu Di (China, AD 561–AD 578).label: Wu Di
Wu Di (China, AD 561–AD 578).prose:
[China, AD 561–AD 578] Wu Di. 561-578 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, Yuwen Yong, spent years as a figurehead under a domineering regent before seizing real power and having him killed. He then suppressed Buddhism and Daoism, confiscating monastic wealth and forcing monks back into lay life to boost the tax base and army, and in 577 conquered the rival Northern Qi to unite the north. His early death left the throne to weak successors, and his general's family founded the Sui, which finished the reunification of China.

Early Helladic (Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Helladic
Early Helladic (Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic. 3200BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The mainland Greek Bronze Age begins: bronze tools and weapons, donkeys and sailing craft, and settlements engaged in Aegean-wide exchange. Its most striking buildings are the 'corridor houses' such as the House of the Tiles at Lerna — large, tiled, administratively organised structures, sealed storerooms and all — which suggest emerging central authority. Widespread destructions and abandonments end the period, and the mainland enters the poorer Middle Helladic era.

Ryakunin Era (Japan, AD 1238–AD 1239).label: Ryakunin Era
Ryakunin Era (Japan, AD 1238–AD 1239).prose:
[Japan, AD 1238–AD 1239] Ryakunin Era. 1238-1239. Period definition from British Museum.

A reign-era of barely a year in the Kamakura age, proclaimed under the boy-emperor Shijō while real authority rested with the Hōjō regents in the east. Such short eras were routinely declared and then abandoned, often after a fire, epidemic or unlucky omen prompted a fresh start.

Narino (Colombia, AD 600–AD 600).label: Narino
Narino (Colombia, AD 600–AD 600).prose: [Colombia, AD 600–AD 600] Narino. The term refers to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the highlands of the Nariño department from 600 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Wado Era (Japan, AD 708–AD 715).label: Wado Era
Wado Era (Japan, AD 708–AD 715).prose:
[Japan, AD 708–AD 715] Wado Era. 708-715. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief but consequential Japanese era named for a find of native copper in Musashi province, which prompted the state to strike the Wadōkaichin coins in an attempt to create a money economy. The court moved to a new permanent capital at Heijō-kyō, modelled on Chinese Chang'an, and commissioned the provincial gazetteers and the Kojiki that followed soon after.

Daiho Era (Japan, AD 701–AD 704).label: Daiho Era
Daiho Era (Japan, AD 701–AD 704).prose:
[Japan, AD 701–AD 704] Daiho Era. 701-704. Period definition from British Museum.

The Taiho Code was promulgated at the start of these years, a comprehensive body of administrative and penal law modelled on Tang China that defined ministries, provinces, land allotment and taxation. It set the framework of the ritsuryo state that governed Japan for centuries, and the era itself marks the point from which Japanese year-names run without a break.

Duanping (China, AD 1234–AD 1236).label: Duanping
Duanping (China, AD 1234–AD 1236).prose:
[China, AD 1234–AD 1236] Duanping. 1234-1236 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign era of Emperor Lizong of the Southern Song, opening with the destruction of the Jin dynasty by a joint Song-Mongol campaign. Song forces then marched north to reclaim Kaifeng and Luoyang, found the cities ruined and undefendable, and were routed — the so-called Duanping incursion. It gave the Mongols their pretext for war, beginning the forty-year struggle that would end the Song.

Eiho Era (Japan, AD 1081–AD 1084).label: Eiho Era
Eiho Era (Japan, AD 1081–AD 1084).prose:
[Japan, AD 1081–AD 1084] Eiho Era. 1081-1084. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign-period late in the Heian age, remembered chiefly for violence at both ends of the country. Armed monks of the great Buddhist monasteries fought each other and intimidated the capital, while in the far northeast the Later Three-Year War broke out, drawing Minamoto no Yoshiie into the campaigns that made his family's military reputation in the provinces.

Enpo Era (Japan, AD 1673–AD 1681).label: Enpo Era
Enpo Era (Japan, AD 1673–AD 1681).prose:
[Japan, AD 1673–AD 1681] Enpo Era. 1673-1681. Period definition from British Museum.

The middle years of the fourth Tokugawa shogun, Ietsuna, when the peace imposed after the civil wars had settled into routine and Edo, Osaka and Kyoto were filling with merchants, publishers and theatre-goers. The era closed with Ietsuna's death and the accession of Tsunayoshi, whose sterner and more eccentric rule would follow.

Suzong (China, AD 756–AD 762).label: Suzong
Suzong (China, AD 756–AD 762).prose:
[China, AD 756–AD 762] Suzong. 756-762 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

He was proclaimed emperor in the northwest while his father fled the rebel armies that had taken both Tang capitals, and spent his reign fighting to recover them. Recapturing Chang'an and Luoyang required Uyghur cavalry and huge concessions to regional generals, decisions that left provincial warlords permanently entrenched. The Tang survived the An Lushan rebellion, but never again controlled its own frontiers as before.

Yuantong (China, AD 1333–AD 1335).label: Yuantong
Yuantong (China, AD 1333–AD 1335).prose:
[China, AD 1333–AD 1335] Yuantong. 1333-1335 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign period at the start of the rule of Toghon Temür, the last Yuan emperor, who came to the throne as a teenager after a rapid succession of short-lived rulers. Real power lay with the chancellor Bayan and rival Mongol factions at court. The instability of these years foreshadowed the rebellions that would end Mongol rule in China.

Jiayou (China, AD 1056–AD 1064).label: Jiayou
Jiayou (China, AD 1056–AD 1064).prose:
[China, AD 1056–AD 1064] Jiayou. 1056-1064 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The closing years of Emperor Renzong's long, mild reign, remembered as a golden age of civil government. The examinations of 1057, presided over by Ouyang Xiu, passed Su Shi, Su Zhe and Zeng Gong in a single cohort and turned literary style away from ornate parallel prose. Renzong died without a son, and the succession question opened the way to the bitter reform politics of the next generation.

Cypro-Archaic I (Cyprus, 749 BC–599 BC).label: Cypro-Archaic I
Cypro-Archaic I (Cyprus, 749 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–599 BC] Cypro-Archaic I. ca. 750 BC-600 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cyprus was divided among a set of rival city-kingdoms - Salamis, Paphos, Kition, Amathus and others - that paid tribute to Assyria while trading freely with Phoenicia, Egypt and the Aegean. Potters turned out bold Bichrome wares painted with birds, fish and stylised lotus, and sanctuaries filled with thousands of terracotta votive figures, like the crowded ranks of worshippers found at Ayia Irini. Phoenician settlers at Kition rebuilt its temples and made the island a hinge between the Levant and the Greek world.

Jahangir reign (India, AD 1605–AD 1627).label: Jahangir reign
Jahangir reign (India, AD 1605–AD 1627).prose:
[India, AD 1605–AD 1627] Jahangir reign. Ruled 1605-1627. Period definition from British Museum.

Akbar's son inherited a settled empire and spent it on connoisseurship: the finest era of Mughal painting, with meticulous studies of birds, animals and courtiers, and gardens laid out in Kashmir and Lahore. Real power drifted to his wife Nur Jahan, who issued coins in her own name and led a court faction. English envoy Thomas Roe secured trading rights here, the small opening through which the East India Company entered India.

Kanbun Era (Japan, AD 1661–AD 1673).label: Kanbun Era
Kanbun Era (Japan, AD 1661–AD 1673).prose:
[Japan, AD 1661–AD 1673] Kanbun Era. 1661-1673. Period definition from British Museum.

The years when Edo was rebuilt after the catastrophic Meireki fire and the shogunate, under Tokugawa Ietsuna, turned from conquest to administration — banning the practice of retainers following their lord in death and easing rules on daimyo succession. In the arts it gives its name to the elegant standing beauties of early ukiyo-e painting and print design.

Thieu Binh reign period (Vietnam, AD 143.label: Thieu Binh reign period
Thieu Binh reign period (Vietnam, AD 143.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1434–AD 1440] Thieu Binh reign period. Thieu Binh reign period (1434-1440). Period definition from British Museum.

The opening years of Le Thai Tong, who came to the throne as a boy after the death of Le Loi, the founder of the Le dynasty. Real power lay with the regent Le Sat and the veteran commanders of the war against Ming China, until the young emperor removed and executed him. The court intrigues of these years led on to the notorious case of the scholar Nguyen Trai, condemned after the emperor's sudden death.

Early Uruk (Iraq, 3999 BC–3499 BC).label: Early Uruk
Early Uruk (Iraq, 3999 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Early Uruk. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia dating to between 4000-3500 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Southwestern Iran was drawn into the orbit of the emerging urban world of lowland Mesopotamia, adopting its mass-produced, undecorated pottery, its architecture and its systems of accounting with clay tokens and seals. Susa and its neighbours on the Susiana plain grew into centres with monumental buildings and clear differences in wealth. The exchange of highland metal, stone and timber for lowland goods set up a relationship that shaped Elamite civilisation for millennia.

Longwu (China, AD 1645–AD 1646).label: Longwu
Longwu (China, AD 1645–AD 1646).prose:
[China, AD 1645–AD 1646] Longwu. 1645-1646 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A Southern Ming court proclaimed in Fujian after the Qing took Nanjing, headed by the Prince of Tang and propped up by the maritime warlord Zheng Zhilong. Rival Ming claimants refused to cooperate, and when Zheng defected to the Qing the regime collapsed within a year and the emperor was captured and killed. Its chief legacy was Zheng Zhilong's son, Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga), who carried on the loyalist resistance at sea and later seized Taiwan from the Dutch.

Archaic Period North America (United Sta.node: Archaic Period North America (United States, 7999 BC–999 BC)
Archaic Period North America (United Sta.label: Archaic Period North America
Archaic Period North America (United Sta.prose:
[North America, 7999 BC–999 BC] Archaic Period North America. Spatial coverage: Canada, United States. The term refers to a period ranging from approximately 8000 BC to 1000 BC.in North America. Period definition from British Museum.

After the last Ice Age megafauna disappeared, people across the continent settled into intimate knowledge of particular landscapes - fishing rivers, gathering nuts and shellfish, hunting deer with spearthrowers. Ground and polished stone tools, cemeteries, long-distance trade in copper and marine shell, and the first cultivation of native seed plants all appear in these millennia. By its end, communities at places like Poverty Point were raising huge earthworks, showing that monumental building did not require farming.

Shohei Era (Japan, AD 1346–AD 1370).label: Shohei Era
Shohei Era (Japan, AD 1346–AD 1370).prose:
[Japan, AD 1346–AD 1370] Shohei Era. 1346-1370. Period definition from British Museum.

The era name used by the Southern Court of Emperor Go-Murakami during the war of the two courts, when Japan had rival emperors, rival calendars and shifting allegiances among warrior families. Its length reflects Southern resilience: exploiting the Kannō feud that tore the Ashikaga house apart, Southern forces briefly reoccupied Kyoto more than once, though they were always driven back into the mountains of Yoshino.

Early Dynastic II (Iraq, 2699 BC–2599 BC.label: Early Dynastic II
Early Dynastic II (Iraq, 2699 BC–2599 BC.prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 2699 BC–2599 BC] Early Dynastic II. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. A term used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia between approximately 2700-2600 BC; it has been questioned whether Early Dynastic II material culture can really be distinguished from that of the preceding Early Dynastic I. Period definition from British Museum.

A middle phase in which independent city-states hardened into rivals, each with its patron deity, temple estate and palace. Later Mesopotamian tradition placed its legendary kings, including Gilgamesh of Uruk, in roughly this era. Temple sculpture of wide-eyed worshippers in fringed skirts, made to stand in perpetual prayer on behalf of the donor, belongs to this world.

Hung Tri reign period (Vietnam, AD 1588–.label: Hung Tri reign period
Hung Tri reign period (Vietnam, AD 1588–.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1588–AD 1591] Hung Tri reign period. The Hung Tri reign period (1588-1591) of the ruler Mac Mau Hop of the Mac Dynasty (1527-1592) of Vietnam. Period definition from British Museum.

An era name of Mạc Mậu Hợp, the last effective ruler of the Mạc dynasty in Đông Kinh (Hanoi). By these years the Mạc were losing ground to the Lê restoration armies commanded by the Trịnh, who took the capital in 1592 and drove the surviving Mạc into the northern hills of Cao Bằng. The reign marks the closing phase of Vietnam's long north–south dynastic war and the start of centuries of Trịnh dominance behind puppet Lê emperors.

Late Minoan III (Crete, 1399 BC–1059 BC).label: Late Minoan III
Late Minoan III (Crete, 1399 BC–1059 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1399 BC–1059 BC] Late Minoan III. 1400BC-1060BC. Period definition from British Museum.

After the fall of Knossos, Crete became a landscape of towns and villages rather than palaces, with Mycenaean-style chamber tombs and painted clay coffins (larnakes) showing hunts, octopuses and mourners. Pottery grew standardised and was traded widely, but the old centralised bureaucracy was gone. When the eastern Mediterranean system collapsed around 1200 BC, Cretans moved to defensible mountain refuges such as Karphi, carrying older cults with them into the Iron Age.

Genki Era (Japan, AD 1570–AD 1573).label: Genki Era
Genki Era (Japan, AD 1570–AD 1573).prose:
[Japan, AD 1570–AD 1573] Genki Era. 1570-1573. Period definition from British Museum.

Oda Nobunaga's most dangerous years, spent fighting an encirclement of rival warlords, warrior monks and militant Buddhist leagues. He won at Anegawa, burned the great monastery complex of Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei in 1571, and survived defeat by Takeda Shingen at Mikatagahara. The era closed with Nobunaga expelling the last Ashikaga shogun from Kyoto, ending the Muromachi shogunate and opening the way to the reunification of Japan.

Inju dynasty (Iran, AD 1336–AD 1356).label: Inju dynasty
Inju dynasty (Iran, AD 1336–AD 1356).prose:
[Shiraz, AD 1336–AD 1356] Inju dynasty. Dynasty ruling Shiraz from c. 1336-1356. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the successor states carved out of Iran as Mongol Ilkhanid authority collapsed, the Injuids ruled Fars from Shiraz. Their most famous ruler, Abu Ishaq, presided over a wine-and-poetry court celebrated by Hafez, who lived through the dynasty's fall. Rival Muzaffarids took Shiraz and executed him, and the region passed into the harsher rule that Timur would later interrupt.

Oho Era (Japan, AD 1161–AD 1163).label: Oho Era
Oho Era (Japan, AD 1161–AD 1163).prose:
[Japan, AD 1161–AD 1163] Oho Era. 1161-1163. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era in the closing decades of the Heian period, following the Hōgen and Heiji disturbances that had drawn warrior families into court politics. Real influence was passing to Taira no Kiyomori, whose rise would soon give a samurai clan control of the imperial capital.

Yingzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1321–AD.label: Yingzong Yuan dynasty
Yingzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1321–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1321–AD 1323] Yingzong Yuan dynasty. 1321-1323 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Gegeen Khan (Yingzong) came to the Mongol throne as a teenager and, with his chancellor Baiju, pushed Confucian-style reforms, trimmed the bloated court and issued a comprehensive law code for the empire. The measures alienated the old Mongol aristocracy, and he was murdered by conspirators while travelling back from the summer capital, one of the palace coups that made the later Yuan increasingly unstable.

Southern Tang Kingdom (China, AD 75–AD 9.label: Southern Tang Kingdom
Southern Tang Kingdom (China, AD 75–AD 9.prose:
[China, AD 75–AD 937] Southern Tang Kingdom. 937-75. Period definition from British Museum.

The largest and wealthiest of the Ten Kingdoms that divided China after the Tang collapse, ruling the lower Yangzi from Jinling (Nanjing). Its court became a refuge for painters, poets and scholars fleeing the wars of the north, and its last ruler Li Yu is remembered as one of China's greatest lyric poets rather than as a king. Song armies absorbed the kingdom, and much of its cultural inheritance passed into the new empire.

Late Minoan IIIB (Crete, 1299 BC–1199 BC.label: Late Minoan IIIB
Late Minoan IIIB (Crete, 1299 BC–1199 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Late Minoan IIIB. 1300BC-1200BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A period of steady output and shrinking horizons: pottery workshops kept producing the standard Aegean repertoire, but decoration grew formulaic and long-distance contacts thinned. Chania emerged as the island's leading centre, exporting inscribed stirrup jars whose Linear B labels record oil shipments. The phase ends amid the wider destructions that brought down the Mycenaean palaces on the mainland.

Xuantong (China, AD 1908–AD 1911).label: Xuantong
Xuantong (China, AD 1908–AD 1911).prose:
[China, AD 1908–AD 1911] Xuantong. 1908-1911 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign title of Puyi, who came to the throne as a toddler and was the last emperor of the Qing. Provincial revolts after the Wuchang uprising of 1911 unravelled dynastic rule with startling speed. Two millennia of imperial government ended in an abdication edict negotiated by Yuan Shikai.

Southern Song dynasty (China, AD 1127–AD.label: Southern Song dynasty
Southern Song dynasty (China, AD 1127–AD.prose:
[China, AD 1127–AD 1279] Southern Song dynasty. 1127-1279. Period definition from British Museum.

A refugee dynasty that turned loss into prosperity: cut off from the north by the Jin, it made the Yangzi delta and the southeast coast the economic centre of China. Maritime trade, rice double-cropping and urban markets funded a state that paid tribute to keep peace, while scholars like Zhu Xi reshaped Confucianism into an orthodoxy that lasted 700 years. Its ceramics, silks and paintings were exported across Asia; its conquest by Kublai Khan brought all of China under foreign rule for the first time.

Northern Wei dynasty (China, AD 386–AD 5.label: Northern Wei dynasty
Northern Wei dynasty (China, AD 386–AD 5.prose:
[China, AD 386–AD 534] Northern Wei dynasty. 386-534. Period definition from British Museum.

Steppe rulers of Xianbei origin unified the north in 439 and governed it through a hybrid of tribal and Chinese institutions. Buddhism became a state cult on a monumental scale, and the sinicising reforms of Emperor Xiaowen provoked resentment among frontier garrisons that eventually erupted in the revolts tearing the state apart. Its collapse left the rival Eastern and Western Wei successor states.

Sikh (India, AD 1469–AD 1849).label: Sikh
Sikh (India, AD 1469–AD 1849).prose:
[Punjab, AD 1469–AD 1849] Sikh. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. Adherent of Sikhism, a religion based on the teachings of Guru Nanak (1469-1539) and nine successive gurus. Under Ranjit Singh (reg. 1799-1839), the Sikhs created an independent kingdom in the Punjab (1799-1849). Period definition from British Museum.

Beginning with Guru Nanak's teaching of one God and rejection of caste ritual, the Sikh community grew through nine successor Gurus, acquired scripture in the Guru Granth Sahib and a martial identity in the Khalsa founded in 1699. Persecution under the Mughals and later Afghan invasions hardened it into a military power organised in misls. Ranjit Singh welded these into an empire ruling Punjab, Kashmir and Peshawar from Lahore, until British annexation ended Sikh sovereignty in 1849.

Early Cypriot II (Cyprus, 2149 BC–2099 B.label: Early Cypriot II
Early Cypriot II (Cyprus, 2149 BC–2099 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 2149 BC–2099 BC] Early Cypriot II. ca. 2150-2100 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase within the island's early Bronze Age, defined chiefly by changes in red polished pottery styles and tomb assemblages in the cemeteries of the north coast, notably Vounous and Lapithos.

La Tène I (Europe, 449 BC–319 BC).label: La Tène I
La Tène I (Europe, 449 BC–319 BC).prose:
[Europe, 449 BC–319 BC] La Tène I. Europe; 450-320 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The first phase of the Celtic Iron Age, when a new curvilinear art style — tendrils, palmettes and stylised faces borrowed from Greek and Etruscan models — appeared on brooches, scabbards and drinking gear. Rich chariot burials in the Marne and Moselle regions replaced the older princely tombs, and warrior equipment became a standard part of graves. This is the era of the great Celtic migrations that carried raiders into Italy and the Balkans.

Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 742 BC–645 BC).label: Neo-Elamite II
Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 742 BC–645 BC).prose:
[Iran, 742 BC–645 BC] Neo-Elamite II. circa 743 BC-646 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Elam's final decades, following the Assyrian sack of Susa, when fragmented kingdoms and princes ruled the lowlands while Persian groups established themselves in Anshan and the highlands. Elamite scribal and administrative traditions passed directly to these newcomers, and within a lifetime Cyrus the Great had absorbed the whole region into Persia.

Nasca (Peru, 99 BC–AD 600).label: Nasca
Nasca (Peru, 99 BC–AD 600).prose:
[ancient Peru, 99 BC–AD 600] Nasca. The term refers to a culture and style, named after the place Nazca, and covering the period 100 BC-AD 600 (dates according to Christopher Donnan, 'Ceramics of Ancient Peru', Fowler Museum of Cultural History, University of California, Los Angeles, 1992).Moche:. Period definition from British Museum.

On the arid south coast of Peru, communities produced some of the ancient Americas' finest polychrome pottery and textiles, painted with hummingbirds, killer whales and trophy-head-carrying deities. They scraped the desert floor into the vast lines and animal figures of the Nazca pampa, and dug underground filtration galleries, some still watering fields today. The ceremonial centre of Cahuachi, with its adobe mounds, drew pilgrims rather than a settled population.

Chongzhen (China, AD 1628–AD 1644).label: Chongzhen
Chongzhen (China, AD 1628–AD 1644).prose:
[China, AD 1628–AD 1644] Chongzhen. 1628-1644 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The last Ming emperor inherited a treasury drained by war in the northeast, a bureaucracy hollowed out by eunuch politics, and a run of catastrophic droughts, famines and epidemics. Peasant armies under Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong overran the interior while Manchu forces pressed the Great Wall frontier; when rebels entered Beijing the emperor hanged himself on the hill behind the palace. Ming loyalists fought on in the south, but the Qing took the capital within weeks and held China for the next 268 years.

Late Christian Period II (Sudan, AD 1300.label: Late Christian Period II
Late Christian Period II (Sudan, AD 1300.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 1300–AD 1400] Late Christian Period II. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1300-1400. Period definition from British Museum.

The final Christian phase on the middle Nile, after the throne hall at Old Dongola had been turned into a mosque and Mamluk-backed claimants were installed on the Nubian throne. Communities shrank, some retreated to fortified villages, and the successor kingdom of Dotawo survived in the north around Qasr Ibrim, its last documents written in Old Nubian. Arab settlement and intermarriage steadily transformed the population, ending a thousand years of Nubian Christianity.

Chojo Era (Japan, AD 1132–AD 1135).label: Chojo Era
Chojo Era (Japan, AD 1132–AD 1135).prose:
[Japan, AD 1132–AD 1135] Chojo Era. 1132-1135. Period definition from British Museum.

Under the cloistered emperor Toba, the warrior Taira no Tadamori won unusual favour at court, building a temple for the retired emperor and being granted access to the palace, to the disgust of established nobles. Commissions to suppress pirates in the Inland Sea gave his family naval power and wealth from western sea routes, the foundation of his son Kiyomori's later dominance.

Asuka Period (Japan, AD 552–AD 646).label: Asuka Period
Asuka Period (Japan, AD 552–AD 646).prose: [Japan, AD 552–AD 646] Asuka Period. 552-646. Period definition from British Museum.

Namazga III (Turkmenistan, 3499 BC–2999.label: Namazga III
Namazga III (Turkmenistan, 3499 BC–2999.prose: [Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, 3499 BC–2999 BC] Namazga III. Term derived from Soviet excavations at the type-site of Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, and dating to ca 3500-3000 BC.  Within Soviet archaeological literature, this period term is also referred as late eneolithic period. Period definition from British Museum.

Engi Era (Japan, AD 901–AD 923).label: Engi Era
Engi Era (Japan, AD 901–AD 923).prose:
[Japan, AD 901–AD 923] Engi Era. 901-923. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign years of Emperor Daigo, remembered by later Japanese writers as a lost golden age when emperors still governed in person rather than through Fujiwara regents. It produced the Kokin Wakashū, the first imperially commissioned anthology of Japanese verse, and the compilation of the Engi-shiki, a vast codification of court ceremony and administrative law that remains a key source on early Shinto ritual. The idealisation was partly nostalgia: aristocratic control of land and office was already eroding the old imperial state.

Kushano-Sasanian (Afghanistan, AD 233–AD.label: Kushano-Sasanian
Kushano-Sasanian (Afghanistan, AD 233–AD.prose:
[Afghanistan, AD 233–AD 370] Kushano-Sasanian. c.233-370. Sasanian-appointed governors of Afghanistan who retained the title 'Kushahshah' from their predecessors, the Kushans. Period definition from British Museum.

After Sasanian armies broke Kushan power, Persian princes governed Bactria and Gandhara as kushanshahs, striking their own coinage that mixed Iranian titles with Kushan designs. The result was a hybrid frontier culture where Zoroastrian fire altars, Buddhist monasteries and Greek-derived script coexisted. Their rule ended when the Kidarite and later Hephthalite horsemen swept down from the steppe.

Heiji Era (Japan, AD 1159–AD 1160).label: Heiji Era
Heiji Era (Japan, AD 1159–AD 1160).prose:
[Japan, AD 1159–AD 1160] Heiji Era. 1159-1160. Period definition from British Museum.

A two-year era named for the Heiji Disturbance, a palace coup in the capital in which Minamoto no Yoshitomo and Fujiwara no Nobuyori seized the retired emperor and were then crushed by Taira no Kiyomori. The defeat broke Minamoto power for a generation and made the Taira the dominant force at court — and spared the young Minamoto no Yoritomo, who would later destroy them.

Wendi (China, AD 424–AD 453).label: Wendi
Wendi (China, AD 424–AD 453).prose:
[China, AD 424–AD 453] Wendi. 424-453 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Emperor Wen of the Liu Song, remembered as the Yuanjia era of good government — lower taxes, restored schools, careful officials and a prosperous lower Yangtze. His repeated attempts to reconquer the north from the Northern Wei ended in disaster, with enemy cavalry reaching the Yangtze. He was murdered by his own heir, and the southern dynasty never recovered its earlier strength.

Kaya Kingdom (Japan, AD 42–AD 562).label: Kaya Kingdom
Kaya Kingdom (Japan, AD 42–AD 562).prose:
[Japan, AD 42–AD 562] Kaya Kingdom. 42-562. Period definition from British Museum.

A loose confederation of small states along the Nakdong River in southern Korea, famous for rich iron ore and skilled ironworking that supplied armour and ingots across the region. Kaya traded and intermarried intensively with the emerging Yamato court, which is why its history is so entangled with Japan's; squeezed between Baekje and Silla, it was finally annexed by Silla in 562.

Jokyo Era (Japan, AD 1684–AD 1688).label: Jokyo Era
Jokyo Era (Japan, AD 1684–AD 1688).prose:
[Japan, AD 1684–AD 1688] Jokyo Era. 1684-1688. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for the Jokyo calendar, the first calendar system devised in Japan itself, worked out by the astronomer Shibukawa Shunkai to correct errors that had accumulated over eight centuries of using an imported Chinese reckoning. It marked a new confidence in native scholarship under the shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, in a peaceful era of expanding cities, publishing and commercial wealth.

Troy II (Troy, 2499 BC–1999 BC).label: Troy II
Troy II (Troy, 2499 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Troy, 2499 BC–1999 BC] Troy II. circa 2500BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The citadel grew richer, with a monumental gateway, a ramp still visible today and larger megara inside sloping stone-and-mudbrick walls. Potters adopted the fast wheel, and gold, silver and lapis jewellery was buried here — the hoard Schliemann seized and named "Priam's Treasure", though it is a thousand years older than any Homeric war. The settlement ended in a great fire, which Schliemann mistook for the sack of Homer's Troy.

Kangen Era (Japan, AD 1243–AD 1247).label: Kangen Era
Kangen Era (Japan, AD 1243–AD 1247).prose:
[Japan, AD 1243–AD 1247] Kangen Era. 1243-1247. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era under Hōjō regency rule at Kamakura, when the aristocratic shogun Kujō Yoritsune was pushed aside in favour of his young son and real authority stayed firmly with the Hōjō. Court and warrior government coexisted uneasily, with Kyoto supervised by the shogunate's deputies.

Cypro-Classical II (Cyprus, 399 BC–309 B.label: Cypro-Classical II
Cypro-Classical II (Cyprus, 399 BC–309 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 399 BC–309 BC] Cypro-Classical II. 400 BC- 310 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The kings of Cyprus manoeuvred between Persia and the rising Macedonian power, and most sided with Alexander after Issos, supplying the fleet that took Tyre. In the wars of his successors the island became a prize contested by Ptolemy and Antigonos. Ptolemy's victory brought the abolition of the ancient city-kingdoms and the start of three centuries of rule from Alexandria.

Xiaowudi (China, AD 454–AD 464).label: Xiaowudi
Xiaowudi (China, AD 454–AD 464).prose: [China, AD 454–AD 464] Xiaowudi. 454-464 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Majiayao Period (China, 3099 BC–2699 BC).label: Majiayao Period
Majiayao Period (China, 3099 BC–2699 BC).prose:
[China, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Majiayao Period. 3100BC-2700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The classic phase of painted pottery in the upper Yellow River, when potters covered globular jars and basins with swirling black spirals, waves and dancing figures. Villages grew millet, kept pigs, and buried their dead with striking ceramic assemblages that rank among the finest painted wares of Neolithic China.

Baoqing (China, AD 1225–AD 1227).label: Baoqing
Baoqing (China, AD 1225–AD 1227).prose: [China, AD 1225–AD 1227] Baoqing. 1225-1227 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Nuzi (Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–1349 BC).label: Nuzi
Nuzi (Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–1349 BC).prose:
[Nuzi, northern Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–1349 BC] Nuzi. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of northern Mesopotamia as represented by objects excavated at the site of Nuzi that date to approximately 1600 BC-1350 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A Hurrian town in the kingdom of Arrapha, east of the Tigris, under the shadow of Mitanni. Excavation of its houses and palace produced thousands of cuneiform tablets recording ordinary business – adoptions used as a dodge to transfer land, marriage contracts, loans, lawsuits – giving one of the fullest pictures anywhere of family and property law in the ancient Near East. Its distinctive painted "Nuzi ware" pottery, with white designs on a dark ground, spread across northern Mesopotamia and Syria.

Sub-Minoan (Crete, 1059 BC–999 BC).label: Sub-Minoan
Sub-Minoan (Crete, 1059 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1059 BC–999 BC] Sub-Minoan. 1060BC-1000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The last phase of Cretan Bronze Age culture, after the palaces had gone: pottery still recognisably Minoan in shape but coarser and looser in decoration, made by communities that had largely withdrawn to defensible upland refuges such as Karphi. Metal is scarcer, settlements smaller, writing gone. Out of this thinned-out world came the Cretan communities of the Early Iron Age.

Troy III (Troy, 2249 BC–2099 BC).label: Troy III
Troy III (Troy, 2249 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Troy, 2249 BC–2099 BC] Troy III. circa 2250BC-2100BC. Period definition from British Museum.

After the burning of the previous citadel the site was rebuilt smaller and more crowded, with cramped houses packed along narrow lanes inside the old walls. Wealth and long-distance contacts fell away sharply, though the community survived and kept the same Anatolian traditions of building and pottery.

Lizong (China, AD 1225–AD 1260).label: Lizong
Lizong (China, AD 1225–AD 1260).prose:
[China, AD 1225–AD 1260] Lizong. 1225-1260 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A Song emperor who reigned for four decades while the empire's fate was decided elsewhere: his armies joined the Mongols to destroy the Jin in 1234, then failed disastrously when he tried to seize the old northern capitals, opening a long war with the Mongols. At court he made the Neo-Confucian teachings of Zhu Xi state orthodoxy, fixing the philosophical curriculum of imperial China until the twentieth century.

Neo-Elamite (Iran, 999 BC–538 BC).label: Neo-Elamite
Neo-Elamite (Iran, 999 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Iran, 999 BC–538 BC] Neo-Elamite. circa 1000 BC-539 BC. Divided into three phases Neo-Elamite I c.1000 BC-744 BC; Neo-Elamite II 743 BC-646 BC; Neo-Elamite III 646 BC-539 BC. Period ends with the conquest by Cyrus the Great. Period definition from British Museum.

Elam re-emerged in southwestern Iran after a long dark age, its kings ruling from Susa and the Zagros valleys and playing a dangerous game of alliance with Babylon against Assyria. Assyrian armies sacked Susa in 646 BC, but Elamite scribes, art and administrative practice survived to be absorbed by the Persians, who took over Elamite script and bureaucracy at Persepolis. The period is the bridge between ancient Elam and the Achaemenid Empire.

Hongshan culture (China, 4499 BC–2999 BC.label: Hongshan culture
Hongshan culture (China, 4499 BC–2999 BC.prose:
[China, 4499 BC–2999 BC] Hongshan culture. Neolithic culture, circa 4500 BC-3000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A Neolithic society of the Liao river valleys known for finely carved jade pig-dragons, cloud-shaped plaques and hooked "C" dragons, some of the earliest sophisticated jade working anywhere. At Niuheliang its people built a hilltop complex of stone platform tombs, altars and a temple containing a life-size clay female head with jade-inlaid eyes. The scale of that ceremonial landscape, far from the Yellow River heartland, forced archaeologists to rethink where Chinese civilisation began.

Northern Qi dynasty (China, AD 550–AD 57.label: Northern Qi dynasty
Northern Qi dynasty (China, AD 550–AD 57.prose:
[China, AD 550–AD 577] Northern Qi dynasty. 550-577. Period definition from British Museum.

Ruling the eastern half of northern China from Ye, the Gao emperors presided over a violent, faction-ridden court and a strongly Xianbei military elite that resisted assimilation. Their sculptors and tomb painters left extraordinary work — the Qingzhou Buddhas and the Loyang-style processional murals of Xu Xianxiu's tomb among them. Conquest by the Northern Zhou in 577 cleared the way for the reunification of China.

Kerma Ancien (Egypt, 2499 BC–2049 BC).label: Kerma Ancien
Kerma Ancien (Egypt, 2499 BC–2049 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2499 BC–2049 BC] Kerma Ancien. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. c. 2500 BC-2050 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The first phase of the Nubian town at Kerma above the third cataract, where cattle-herding communities settled into a permanent urban centre with mud-brick buildings and round tumulus graves furnished with fine black-topped burnished pottery. Egyptian expeditions came south for gold, ivory and cattle, but Kerma was building an independent society of its own — the beginnings of the state the Egyptians would call Kush.

Ten'ei Era (Japan, AD 1110–AD 1113).label: Ten'ei Era
Ten'ei Era (Japan, AD 1110–AD 1113).prose:
[Japan, AD 1110–AD 1113] Ten'ei Era. 1110-1113. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign-era of the late Heian court under the boy emperor Toba, when actual power was held by the cloistered ex-emperor Shirakawa and government ran through the retired emperor's household rather than the throne. Court life continued in the polished style of the age even as provincial warrior families grew steadily stronger.

Cypro-Geometric I (Cyprus, 1049 BC–949 B.label: Cypro-Geometric I
Cypro-Geometric I (Cyprus, 1049 BC–949 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–949 BC] Cypro-Geometric I. ca. 1050 BC-950 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The generations after the fall of the Bronze Age towns saw settlement shift and shrink, with cremation and chamber tombs marking new burial habits. Iron working became routine - Cyprus produced some of the earliest iron knives in the Mediterranean - and White Painted pottery with simple concentric circles and bands replaced Mycenaean-derived styles.

Late Christian Period (Sudan, AD 1100–AD.label: Late Christian Period
Late Christian Period (Sudan, AD 1100–AD.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 1100–AD 1400] Late Christian Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1100-1400. It is subdivided into and earlier and later phase designated Late Christian Period I (AD 1100-1300) and Late Christian Period II (AD 1300-1400) respectively. Period definition from British Museum.

The long twilight of Christian Nubia, when the kingdom of Makuria — and Alwa to the south — faced Ayyubid and Mamluk pressure from Egypt and growing Arab tribal settlement along the Nile. Churches were rebuilt on a smaller scale and painted with dark-robed saints and royal figures, and the pilgrimage complex at Banganarti flourished; Old Dongola's throne hall was converted to a mosque in 1317. By the end of the period Christian kingship survived only in fragments, and Nubia was on its way to becoming Muslim and Arabic-speaking.

Grotta-Pelos Culture (Greece, 3199 BC–27.label: Grotta-Pelos Culture
Grotta-Pelos Culture (Greece, 3199 BC–27.prose:
[Cyclades, 3199 BC–2799 BC] Grotta-Pelos Culture. The earliest of the three cultural groups into which the Early Cycladic (q.v.) period is divided, based on consistently recurring types of pottery, bronze and marble objects. The name refers to the type sites used by Colin Renfrew to define the culture, although the term applies to material from the Cyclades as a whole. There are not always clear boundaries between cultural groups, but an approximate date range is 3200BC – 2800BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The opening phase of the Cycladic Bronze Age, named after two island cemeteries of small stone-lined graves. Alongside the dead were placed marble bowls and the earliest of the schematic 'violin-shaped' figurines that would develop into the famous folded-arm idols. Small island communities were already working marble, obsidian and the first metals, laying the groundwork for the Aegean trading world.

Entoku Era (Japan, AD 1489–AD 1492).label: Entoku Era
Entoku Era (Japan, AD 1489–AD 1492).prose:
[Japan, AD 1489–AD 1492] Entoku Era. 1489-1492. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief span in the disordered decades after the Ōnin War, when the Ashikaga shogunate governed little beyond Kyoto and provincial warlords ruled as they pleased. The young shogun Yoshihisa died on campaign, and the retired Yoshimasa, who had turned his back on politics for tea, gardens and the Silver Pavilion, died soon after.

Early Iron Age early (Italy, 999 BC–879.node: Early Iron Age early (Italy, 999 BC–879 BC)
Early Iron Age early (Italy, 999 BC–879.label: Early Iron Age early
Early Iron Age early (Italy, 999 BC–879.prose:
[Italy, 999 BC–879 BC] Early Iron Age early. For Italy: Early Iron Age early c. 1000 BC to 880 BC.  Early Iron Age late c. 900 BC to 780 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The Villanovan culture took shape across Etruria and the Po valley, its people cremating their dead and burying the ashes in distinctive biconical urns under hut-shaped or helmet lids. Scattered Bronze Age villages coalesced into large plateau settlements at places like Veii, Tarquinia and Bologna, laying the ground plans of the later Etruscan cities. Iron working spread rapidly, and cemeteries begin to show clear differences of wealth between graves.

Shoo Era (Japan, AD 1288–AD 1293).label: Shoo Era
Shoo Era (Japan, AD 1288–AD 1293).prose:
[Japan, AD 1288–AD 1293] Shoo Era. 1288-1293. Period definition from British Museum.

A generation after the repulse of the Mongol invasions, the Kamakura regime was still bankrupted by rewarding the warriors who had fought and by keeping coastal defences manned. The era ended in 1293, when a massive earthquake and tsunami devastated Kamakura, killing thousands, and the Hōjō regent used the chaos to destroy his powerful deputy Taira no Yoritsuna and his followers.

Chunhua (China, AD 990–AD 995).label: Chunhua
Chunhua (China, AD 990–AD 995).prose:
[China, AD 990–AD 995] Chunhua. 990-995 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

An era of the second Song emperor, remembered above all for the Chunhua Ge Tie of 992, an imperially sponsored set of engraved model calligraphy that fixed the canon of Chinese brushwork for centuries afterwards. It was also a time of strain in the provinces: heavy taxation and the state monopoly on tea and silk helped set off Wang Xiaobo and Li Shun's peasant rising in Sichuan.

Middle Minoan IIIB (Crete, 1649 BC–1599.label: Middle Minoan IIIB
Middle Minoan IIIB (Crete, 1649 BC–1599.prose:
[Crete, 1649 BC–1599 BC] Middle Minoan IIIB. 1650BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The immediate prelude to Crete's Neopalatial peak, with palaces and grand town houses at Knossos, Malia, Phaistos and Zakros in full working order, frescoes on the walls and Linear A tablets in the archives. Cretan pottery, weights and building techniques circulate widely across the southern Aegean.

Vuppadeva (Kashmir, AD 1172–AD 1213).label: Vuppadeva
Vuppadeva (Kashmir, AD 1172–AD 1213).prose: [Kashmir, AD 1172–AD 1213] Vuppadeva. Spatial coverage: India, Kashmir, Pakistan. Dynasty ruling in Kashmir c. AD 1172-1213. Period definition from British Museum.

Kencho Era (Japan, AD 1249–AD 1256).label: Kencho Era
Kencho Era (Japan, AD 1249–AD 1256).prose:
[Japan, AD 1249–AD 1256] Kencho Era. 1249-1256. Period definition from British Museum.

The regent Hōjō Tokiyori tightened the shogunate's grip, expanding the judicial panels that settled the endless disputes between warriors over land. In 1253 the Chinese Chan master Lanxi Daolong founded Kenchō-ji at Kamakura, the first fully Chinese-style Zen monastery in Japan and the seed of the warrior class's long attachment to Zen discipline, ink painting and tea.

Muromachi Period (Japan, AD 1333–AD 1573.label: Muromachi Period
Muromachi Period (Japan, AD 1333–AD 1573.prose:
[Japan, AD 1333–AD 1573] Muromachi Period. 1333-1573. Period definition from British Museum.

The Ashikaga shoguns ruled from Kyoto in uneasy partnership with the imperial court and powerful provincial lords, and their weakness eventually broke the country apart in the Ōnin War and the century of civil war that followed. Yet it was a brilliant cultural age: Zen temple gardens, the tea ceremony, ink painting, Noh drama, and the Golden and Silver Pavilions. Trade with Ming China and the arrival of Portuguese ships with firearms near its close set the stage for Japan's reunification.

Shu Han Kingdom (China, AD 221–AD 263).label: Shu Han Kingdom
Shu Han Kingdom (China, AD 221–AD 263).prose:
[China, AD 221–AD 263] Shu Han Kingdom. 221-263. Period definition from British Museum.

The smallest of the Three Kingdoms, founded in the mountains of Sichuan by Liu Bei, who claimed to be restoring the fallen Han dynasty. Its chancellor Zhuge Liang launched repeated northern campaigns against Wei from a base that could never match its rival's manpower, and became the archetype of the brilliant, loyal strategist in Chinese culture. Wei armies crossed the mountains and forced its surrender in 263; the wars of these decades supplied the plot of the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Qingyuan (China, AD 1195–AD 1201).label: Qingyuan
Qingyuan (China, AD 1195–AD 1201).prose:
[China, AD 1195–AD 1201] Qingyuan. 1195-1201 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign era of the Southern Song under Emperor Ningzong, remembered above all for the ban on "false learning" that outlawed Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian teaching and purged its followers from office. The proscription failed in the long run: within a few decades Zhu Xi's synthesis became the orthodox basis of the civil service examinations for the next six centuries.

Kengen Era (Japan, AD 1302–AD 1303).label: Kengen Era
Kengen Era (Japan, AD 1302–AD 1303).prose:
[Japan, AD 1302–AD 1303] Kengen Era. 1302-1303. Period definition from British Museum.

A single-year era under Emperor Go-Nijō, at a time when the throne itself was passed back and forth between two rival branches of the imperial family under arrangements dictated from Kamakura. The compromise kept the peace for a generation but bred the resentments that would explode a few decades later in Go-Daigo's revolt.

Onin Era (Japan, AD 1467–AD 1469).label: Onin Era
Onin Era (Japan, AD 1467–AD 1469).prose:
[Japan, AD 1467–AD 1469] Onin Era. 1467-1469. Period definition from British Museum.

The Ōnin War broke out over a disputed shogunal succession and two rival warlord coalitions fighting it out in the streets of Kyoto. The capital burned for years, temples and palaces were destroyed, and the Ashikaga shogunate never recovered real authority. Power drained to provincial warlords, opening the century of civil war known as the Sengoku period.

Xiaoming (China, AD 516–AD 527).label: Xiaoming
Xiaoming (China, AD 516–AD 527).prose:
[China, AD 516–AD 527] Xiaoming. 516-527 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A child emperor of the Northern Wei whose mother, the Empress Dowager Hu, ruled in his name and poured resources into Buddhist building, including Luoyang's colossal Yongning pagoda. Frontier garrisons revolted in the Six Garrisons rebellion, and when the emperor died the warlord Erzhu Rong marched on the capital and massacred the court at Heyin. The dynasty never recovered and split apart within a decade.

Early Christian Period II (Sudan, AD 700.label: Early Christian Period II
Early Christian Period II (Sudan, AD 700.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 700–AD 850] Early Christian Period II. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 700-850. Period definition from British Museum.

Nubian Christianity settled into a mature local form as Makuria absorbed Nobadia and negotiated a long truce with Muslim Egypt. Church architecture standardised, a distinctive painted pottery industry flourished at Faras and elsewhere, and Old Nubian began to be written.

Shaybanid dynasty (Uzbekistan, AD 1500–A.label: Shaybanid dynasty
Shaybanid dynasty (Uzbekistan, AD 1500–A.prose:
[Transoxiana; Uzbek Republic, AD 1500–AD 1599] Shaybanid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. 1500-1599 (AH 906-AH 1007). Dynasty of Mongol origin who came to be known as the Shaybanids or Shibanids. They moved into Transoxiana where the members of the clan acquired the name of Ozbeg (or Uzbeg) thus becoming the greater part of the inhabitant of the present day Uzbek Republic. Period definition from British Museum.

Uzbek warriors under Muhammad Shaybani swept out of the steppe to break the last Timurid princes in Transoxiana, chasing Babur south towards India and his eventual founding of the Mughal Empire. As militant Sunnis facing Shi‘a Safavid Iran, they turned Bukhara and Samarkand into a rival centre of Islamic learning and architecture while the wars along the Amu Darya cut the old caravan links westward.

Late Chalcolithic (Syria, 4499 BC–3499 B.label: Late Chalcolithic
Late Chalcolithic (Syria, 4499 BC–3499 B.prose:
[north-western Mesopotamia, 4499 BC–3499 BC] Late Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Syria, Turkey. In the Middle East, the term chalcolithic is used to describe the broad period between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age (c. 5000-3000 BC). The Late Chalcolithic is a specific term used in north-western Mesopotamia to describe the period spanning the end of the Ubaid and the start of the Uruk (c.4500-3500 BC). Period definition from British Museum.

The final stage of Cyprus's distinctive Chalcolithic villages, best seen at Kissonerga-Mosphilia and Lemba, where people lived in circular mudbrick and stone houses, carved picrolite ornaments and used the island's first copper in small quantities. Settlements grew larger and some buildings stand out in size and contents, hinting at emerging differences in status. The tradition ended as the Philia culture introduced cattle, the plough, extramural cemeteries and serious copper metallurgy, launching the Cypriot Bronze Age.

Early Minoan III (Crete, 2299 BC–1999 BC.label: Early Minoan III
Early Minoan III (Crete, 2299 BC–1999 BC.prose:
[Crete, 2299 BC–1999 BC] Early Minoan III. 2300BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A quieter, poorly understood stretch between the collapses of the Early Bronze Age and the sudden appearance of the palaces.
