Potters adopted white-painted decoration on dark burnished surfaces, hieroglyphic-style seals began to circulate, and settlement concentrated at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia—the very sites where monumental courts would soon rise.

Neolithic/Bronze Age (United Kingdom, 39.label: Neolithic/Bronze Age
Neolithic/Bronze Age (United Kingdom, 39.prose:
[United Kingdom, 3999 BC–799 BC] Neolithic/Bronze Age. This period spans 4000BC to 800BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Taken as one long stretch, this covers the arrival of farming, the great age of tomb and henge building, and the coming of metal. Communal long barrows gave way to individual burials under round barrows with beakers, daggers and gold ornaments; Stonehenge was rebuilt in sarsen; bronze tools and weapons became standard. By its close the landscape was divided by field systems and boundary ditches, farmed by settled communities rather than shaped mainly by monuments.

Chengzong (China, AD 1294–AD 1307).label: Chengzong
Chengzong (China, AD 1294–AD 1307).prose:
[China, AD 1294–AD 1307] Chengzong. 1294-1307 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Kublai Khan's grandson inherited a Yuan empire that had stopped expanding, and largely kept it that way — abandoning further invasions of Japan and Southeast Asia and repairing relations with the other Mongol khanates, which briefly acknowledged him as senior ruler. He cut taxes and tried to curb corruption, but overspending on gifts to the Mongol aristocracy drained the treasury and left his successors weaker.

Namazga II (Turkmenistan, 3999 BC–3499 B.label: Namazga II
Namazga II (Turkmenistan, 3999 BC–3499 B.prose: [Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Namazga II. Term derived from Soviet excavations at the type-site of Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, and dating to ca 4000-3500 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Haftavan Period II (Iran, 538 BC–330 BC).label: Haftavan Period II
Haftavan Period II (Iran, 538 BC–330 BC).prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 538 BC–330 BC] Haftavan Period II. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.539BC-331BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Keicho Era (Japan, AD 1596–AD 1615).label: Keicho Era
Keicho Era (Japan, AD 1596–AD 1615).prose:
[Japan, AD 1596–AD 1615] Keicho Era. 1596-1615. Period definition from British Museum.

A generation of upheaval packed into twenty years: Hideyoshi's second invasion of Korea and his death, the battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu's appointment as shogun in 1603, and the winter and summer sieges of Osaka that destroyed the Toyotomi. Massive earthquakes and tsunami struck as well, and it was in these years that the foundations of 250 years of Tokugawa peace were laid.

Xiantong (China, AD 860–AD 873).label: Xiantong
Xiantong (China, AD 860–AD 873).prose:
[China, AD 860–AD 873] Xiantong. 860-873 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The long reign-era of the Tang emperor Yizong, marked by lavish court Buddhism, including the spectacular procession of the Buddha's finger relic from Famen Temple, and by mutiny and rebellion in the south under Pang Xun. It also gives the date on the Dunhuang Diamond Sutra of 868, the world's earliest surviving printed book bearing a date. The strains visible here ran on into the rebellions that brought the Tang down.

Late Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1549 BC–.node: Late Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1549 BC–1449 BC)
Late Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1549 BC–.label: Late Haftavan Period VIB
Late Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1549 BC–.prose: [Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 1549 BC–1449 BC] Late Haftavan Period VIB. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.1550BC-1450BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Dorset (Canada, 999 BC–AD 1000).label: Dorset
Dorset (Canada, 999 BC–AD 1000).prose:
[North coast of Canada to Greenland, 999 BC–AD 1000] Dorset. Spatial coverage: Canada, Greenland. 1000 BC-1000 - North coast of Canada to Greenland. Period definition from British Museum.

Arctic hunters who spread across the Canadian North and Greenland, taking seal and walrus at breathing holes and ice edges with harpoons but, unusually, without dogsleds or bows for much of their history. They left behind some of the finest miniature art of the ancient Arctic: ivory and antler carvings of bears, birds and human faces, often linked to shamanic practice. They vanished within a few centuries of the arrival of Thule whale-hunters from Alaska, leaving no descendants among today's Inuit.

Yongli (China, AD 1646–AD 1659).label: Yongli
Yongli (China, AD 1646–AD 1659).prose:
[China, AD 1646–AD 1659] Yongli. 1646-1659 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The era of Zhu Youlang, last serious claimant of the Southern Ming, whose court retreated across the southwestern provinces as Qing armies advanced. He relied on former rebel commanders and even appealed to the Pope for help, while parts of his entourage converted to Christianity. Driven into Burma, he was handed over and executed, ending organised Ming resistance on the mainland.

Chokyo Era (Japan, AD 1487–AD 1489).label: Chokyo Era
Chokyo Era (Japan, AD 1487–AD 1489).prose:
[Japan, AD 1487–AD 1489] Chokyo Era. 1487-1489. Period definition from British Museum.

Shogun Ashikaga Yoshihisa personally led an army into Ōmi against the defiant Rokkaku family, an attempt to prove that the shogunate still counted after the devastation of the Ōnin War; he died in camp without winning. In the same span, the Ikkō-ikki leagues of peasants and True Pure Land believers drove out the governor of Kaga and began governing the province themselves, a startling instance of commoners holding a domain.

Late Minoan IIIA (Crete, 1399 BC–1299 BC.label: Late Minoan IIIA
Late Minoan IIIA (Crete, 1399 BC–1299 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1399 BC–1299 BC] Late Minoan IIIA. 1400BC-1300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The stage when Knossos, whether still functioning or newly ruined, no longer commanded Crete, and power was spread among regional centres such as Chania and Ayia Triada. Cretan potters turned out mass-produced stirrup jars and kylikes matching mainland Mycenaean shapes, and the island's exports travelled to Egypt and the Levant. Painted limestone and clay larnakes, decorated with octopuses, chariots and mourners, are the era's most vivid survivals.

Tiansheng (China, AD 1023–AD 1031).label: Tiansheng
Tiansheng (China, AD 1023–AD 1031).prose:
[China, AD 1023–AD 1031] Tiansheng. 1023-1031 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Song Renzong came to the throne as a child, and real authority rested with his adoptive mother, Empress Dowager Liu, who governed from behind a screen for over a decade — the most powerful woman of the Song. During these years the Sichuan merchant notes known as jiaozi were taken over by the state, producing the world's first government-issued paper currency.

Tenpyo Era (Japan, AD 729–AD 749).label: Tenpyo Era
Tenpyo Era (Japan, AD 729–AD 749).prose:
[Japan, AD 729–AD 749] Tenpyo Era. 729-749. Period definition from British Museum.

The height of Nara court culture, remembered for Buddhist sculpture, temple building and the treasures later stored in the Shōsōin. A smallpox epidemic in the 730s killed perhaps a third of the population and wiped out the ruling Fujiwara brothers, after which Emperor Shōmu moved his capital repeatedly and vowed to build the colossal bronze Buddha of Tōdai-ji.

Jingyou (China, AD 1034–AD 1038).label: Jingyou
Jingyou (China, AD 1034–AD 1038).prose: [China, AD 1034–AD 1038] Jingyou. 1034-1038 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Man'en Era (Japan, AD 1860–AD 1861).label: Man'en Era
Man'en Era (Japan, AD 1860–AD 1861).prose:
[Japan, AD 1860–AD 1861] Man'en Era. 1860-1861. Period definition from British Museum.

A single turbulent year and a half in which the shogunate's chief minister Ii Naosuke was cut down outside Edo Castle by anti-foreign samurai, shattering the government's authority. The same months saw the first Japanese embassy cross the Pacific to the United States to ratify the commercial treaty, a delegation whose members returned with firsthand knowledge of the West.

Chongning (China, AD 1102–AD 1106).label: Chongning
Chongning (China, AD 1102–AD 1106).prose:
[China, AD 1102–AD 1106] Chongning. 1102-1106 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Huizong's chancellor Cai Jing revived the reform programme with state schools, granaries and welfare institutions, while purging opponents: the names of hundreds of 'Yuanyou faction' officials, Su Shi among them, were cut into stone tablets and their writings banned. The court also poured money into art, ritual and imperial collecting, and the factional bitterness of these years left the Northern Song badly placed to meet the Jurchen invasion two decades later.

Graeco-Roman (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 400).label: Graeco-Roman
Graeco-Roman (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 400).prose:
[Hellenistic and Roman Egypt, 331 BC–AD 400] Graeco-Roman. This term is only used by the Department of Ancient Egypt and Sudan to include both Hellenistic Egypt from 332 BC to 30 BC and Roman Egypt from 30 BC to around AD 400 (later Roman material in Egypt down to AD 641 usually being placed under Roman Period or Coptic). It is an imprecise term for material from Ptolemaic or Roman Egypt which has not yet been ascribed more accurately to one or the other. See also the terms 'Greek' and 'Roman'. Period definition from British Museum.

Egypt after Alexander was ruled first by the Macedonian Ptolemies from their new capital at Alexandria, then, after Cleopatra's defeat, as the personal grain-basket of the Roman emperors. Greek became the language of administration while Egyptian temples were still built and decorated in pharaonic style, and the two worlds met in things like the painted mummy portraits from the Fayum. The papyri preserved in the dry sand make this one of the best-documented societies of the ancient world.

Taizu Guangshun (China, AD 951–AD 954).label: Taizu Guangshun
Taizu Guangshun (China, AD 951–AD 954).prose:
[China, AD 951–AD 954] Taizu Guangshun. 951-954 (reign); Emperor Taizu. Period definition from British Museum.

Guo Wei, a general who seized power from the collapsing Later Han, founded the Later Zhou and used his brief reign to cut punitive taxes, curb corruption and rein in the plundering of the imperial armies. Childless, he passed the throne to his adopted son rather than a kinsman. The competent, reforming state he began was the direct springboard for the Song reunification a decade later.

Halaf (Syria, 5999 BC–4999 BC).label: Halaf
Halaf (Syria, 5999 BC–4999 BC).prose:
[Syria, 5999 BC–4999 BC] Halaf. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. c.6000BC-5000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Farming villages across northern Syria, Iraq and southeastern Turkey shared one of the ancient world's most beautiful ceramic traditions: thin, kiln-fired bowls painted in red, black and white with geometric bands, bulls' heads and dancing figures. People lived in clusters of circular domed mud-brick buildings called tholoi, kept cattle and sheep, and traded obsidian hundreds of kilometres from Anatolian sources. Stamp seals and standardised pottery hint at growing ideas of ownership and identity, without any sign yet of kings or cities.

Yangdi (China, AD 605–AD 618).label: Yangdi
Yangdi (China, AD 605–AD 618).prose:
[China, AD 605–AD 618] Yangdi. 605-618 reign. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of the second Sui emperor, whose ambitions were enormous and whose timing was disastrous. He completed the Grand Canal linking the Yangtze rice lands to the northern capitals, rebuilt Luoyang on a lavish scale and rebuilt stretches of the Great Wall, all on conscripted labour. Three failed invasions of Koguryo broke the dynasty; he was strangled by his own guards and the Tang took over.

Shang dynasty (China, 1499 BC–1049 BC).label: Shang dynasty
Shang dynasty (China, 1499 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[China, 1499 BC–1049 BC] Shang dynasty. circa.1500 BC-circa 1050 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Bronze-casting kings ruled the north China plain from walled capitals, mustering armies of chariots and divining the future on inscribed oracle bones. Their ritual vessels, script and ancestor cult set the pattern for Chinese elite culture for the next three thousand years. Excavations at Anyang, with its royal tombs and workshop quarters, turned a semi-legendary dynasty into documented history.

Heisei Era (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2015).label: Heisei Era
Heisei Era (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2015).prose:
[Japan, AD 1989–AD 2015] Heisei Era. 1989-onwards. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Emperor Akihito, opening just as the asset bubble burst and settling into decades of slow growth, deflation and an ageing, shrinking population. It was punctuated by shocks — the Kobe earthquake, the Aum sarin attack, the 2011 tsunami and Fukushima meltdown — and by Japan's global cultural reach through anime, games and design.

Muisca (Colombia, AD 600–AD 1600).label: Muisca
Muisca (Colombia, AD 600–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, AD 600–AD 1600] Muisca. The term refers to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the highlands of the Eastern Range in the Cundinamarca and Boyaca departments from 600 Ad to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

In the high basins around Bogotá and Tunja, farming communities growing maize and potatoes and mining salt and emeralds coalesced into chiefdoms led by the zipa and zaque. Their goldsmiths made the tunjo offering figures and the famous raft depicting an initiation rite on Lake Guatavita, the ceremony behind the El Dorado legend. Densely populated and wealthy, the highlands drew Spanish conquistadors in the 1530s, whose settlement grid still underlies Colombian cities.

Jotoku Era (Japan, AD 1097–AD 1099).label: Jotoku Era
Jotoku Era (Japan, AD 1097–AD 1099).prose: [Japan, AD 1097–AD 1099] Jotoku Era. 1097-1099. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Helladic III (Greece, 1399 BC–1059.label: Late Helladic III
Late Helladic III (Greece, 1399 BC–1059.prose:
[Greece, 1399 BC–1059 BC] Late Helladic III. 1400BC-1060BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The palace centuries and their collapse. Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes ran redistributive economies recorded on clay tablets, walled themselves in cyclopean masonry, and exported uniform pottery all over the Mediterranean; then, around 1200 BC, the palaces burned and were never rebuilt. Population fell sharply, writing was lost, and Greece slid into the centuries before the Iron Age recovery.

Daiei Era (Japan, AD 1521–AD 1528).label: Daiei Era
Daiei Era (Japan, AD 1521–AD 1528).prose:
[Japan, AD 1521–AD 1528] Daiei Era. 1521-1528. Period definition from British Museum.

Years in the Warring States age when the Ashikaga shoguns were figureheads shuttled in and out of Kyoto by the Hosokawa house, and real authority lay with provincial warlords building their own domains and law codes. The imperial court was so poor that enthronement ceremonies were delayed for want of funds.

Tenpyo-shoho Era (Japan, AD 749–AD 757).label: Tenpyo-shoho Era
Tenpyo-shoho Era (Japan, AD 749–AD 757).prose:
[Japan, AD 749–AD 757] Tenpyo-shoho Era. 749-757. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Empress Kōken, when the court poured its resources into Buddhism: the colossal bronze Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji was dedicated in 752 in a ceremony attended by monks from India and Vietnam, and the eye-opening brush was wielded by an Indian priest. The treasures presented at the temple were sealed into the Shōsōin storehouse, which still preserves glassware, textiles and instruments carried along the Silk Road. Casting the statue consumed much of Japan's copper and left the state deep in debt.

Ei'en Era (Japan, AD 987–AD 989).label: Ei'en Era
Ei'en Era (Japan, AD 987–AD 989).prose:
[Japan, AD 987–AD 989] Ei'en Era. 987-989. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign-era in the Heian court, when the child emperor Ichijo sat on the throne and real authority rested with the Fujiwara regents. Court life revolved around ritual, poetry and marriage politics rather than administration of the provinces.

Gen'ei Era (Japan, AD 1118–AD 1120).label: Gen'ei Era
Gen'ei Era (Japan, AD 1118–AD 1120).prose:
[Japan, AD 1118–AD 1120] Gen'ei Era. 1118-1120. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era name in the late Heian court, when the retired emperor Shirakawa still governed from behind the throne as cloistered sovereign and the reigning Toba was largely a figurehead. Taira no Kiyomori, who would later make his family the dominant power in Japan, was born in these years.

Shenzong (China, AD 1068–AD 1085).label: Shenzong
Shenzong (China, AD 1068–AD 1085).prose:
[China, AD 1068–AD 1085] Shenzong. 1068-1085 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The emperor who backed Wang Anshi's New Policies, an ambitious attempt to remake the Song state: government loans to farmers, a tax on labour service, state trading offices, militia registration and a reformed examination curriculum. The programme raised revenue and infuriated the scholar-official establishment, splitting the bureaucracy into reformist and conservative camps whose feud outlasted both men and shaped the rest of the dynasty.

Wenzong (China, AD 1328–AD 1332).label: Wenzong
Wenzong (China, AD 1328–AD 1332).prose:
[China, AD 1328–AD 1332] Wenzong. 1328-1329 and 1329-1332 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Tugh Temür came to the Yuan throne through the civil war known as the War of the Two Capitals, and his brief reign was shadowed by the suspicious death of his elder brother, whom he had briefly ceded the throne to. A committed patron of Chinese letters despite ruling a Mongol empire, he founded the Academy of the Pavilion of the Star of Literature and sponsored the vast institutional compendium Jingshi dadian. Real power lay with the Merkid strongman El Temür, a pattern of overmighty ministers that helped unravel Yuan rule.

Achaemenid Dynasty (Iran, 549 BC–330 BC).label: Achaemenid Dynasty
Achaemenid Dynasty (Iran, 549 BC–330 BC).prose:
[India to Egypt, 549 BC–330 BC] Achaemenid Dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Iranian dynasty owing its origins to Teispes, son of Achaemenes. Originally kings of a territory called Anshan, subject to Median control, Persian independence was attained around 550 BC by Cyrus II (“The Great”). Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The empire grew to control a vast territory extending from India to Egypt. The Achaemenids were brought to an end in 331 BC, following the victory of Alexander of Macedon over Darius III’s troops at the Battle of Gaugamela. Period definition from British Museum.

From Cyrus's conquest of Media and Babylon to Darius III's defeat, the Persian kings ruled an empire stretching from the Aegean to the Indus. They ran it through provincial satraps, a relay post system, and a policy of tolerating local religions and customs, famously allowing the Judaeans to return and rebuild their temple. Their wars with the Greek city-states shaped how the West remembered them.

Bunchu Era (Japan, AD 1372–AD 1375).label: Bunchu Era
Bunchu Era (Japan, AD 1372–AD 1375).prose:
[Japan, AD 1372–AD 1375] Bunchu Era. 1372-1375. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the era names used only by the exiled Southern Court during Japan's dynastic schism, when two rival imperial lines each kept their own calendar. By these years the southern cause was fading, its armies pushed back in Kyushu and its court reduced to mountain strongholds, while the Ashikaga shoguns consolidated control from Kyoto.

Meiwa Era (Japan, AD 1764–AD 1772).label: Meiwa Era
Meiwa Era (Japan, AD 1764–AD 1772).prose:
[Japan, AD 1764–AD 1772] Meiwa Era. 1764-1772. Period definition from British Museum.

A period of relative stability in Edo Japan as Tanuma Okitsugu rose to dominate the shogunal government with policies favouring commerce, monopolies and coinage reform. Ukiyo-e printing advanced sharply, with Suzuki Harunobu's full-colour brocade prints appearing in the 1760s. The era closed badly: a huge tsunami devastated the Yaeyama Islands in 1771, and a great fire swept Edo the following year.

Teotihuacan (Mexico, 99 BC–AD 750).label: Teotihuacan
Teotihuacan (Mexico, 99 BC–AD 750).prose:
[Teotihuacan, 99 BC–AD 750] Teotihuacan. The term applies to objects made in the style of, and under the sphere of influence of, the city of Teotihuacan, dated c. 100 BC - AD 750. Period definition from British Museum.

At its height this was the largest city in the Americas, home to perhaps 100,000 people living in hundreds of walled apartment compounds laid out on a rigid grid along the Avenue of the Dead. Its Pyramid of the Sun, obsidian workshops and green-glaze pottery reached across Mesoamerica, and Teotihuacan warlords installed a new dynasty at Maya Tikal in 378. The city centre was deliberately burned in the mid-first millennium, but its ruins so awed the later Aztecs that they made it the birthplace of the sun in their myths.

Kaftari (Iran, 2199 BC–1599 BC).label: Kaftari
Kaftari (Iran, 2199 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Fars, 2199 BC–1599 BC] Kaftari. Fars, 2200BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A Bronze Age culture of the Fars highlands, best known from Tal-e Malyan — ancient Anshan, one of the two capitals of Elam. Its buff pottery with simple painted bands turns up across southern Iran, marking a period of urban revival and wide contact with Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf.

Genkyo Era (Japan, AD 1321–AD 1324).label: Genkyo Era
Genkyo Era (Japan, AD 1321–AD 1324).prose:
[Japan, AD 1321–AD 1324] Genkyo Era. 1321-1324. Period definition from British Museum.

Go-Daigo took over the running of government from the retired emperor Go-Uda, ending cloistered rule and beginning his push to make the throne a real centre of power again. He reformed court offices, markets and taxation in Kyoto, all of which set him on a collision course with the Hōjō regents in Kamakura. The plotting that followed would erupt within a decade.

Nasrid dynasty (Spain, AD 1230–AD 1492).label: Nasrid dynasty
Nasrid dynasty (Spain, AD 1230–AD 1492).prose:
[Granada, Spain, AD 1230–AD 1492] Nasrid dynasty. 1230-1492 (AH 629-AH 897). Dynasty in Granada, last Muslim state of Spain. Period definition from British Museum.

Ruling from Granada, the Nasrids were the last Muslim dynasty in Iberia, surviving for over two centuries by paying tribute to Castile and playing Christian and North African powers against each other. Their court built the Alhambra, with its stucco muqarnas, courtyards and inscriptions, the high point of western Islamic architecture. The fall of Granada in 1492 ended al-Andalus and freed Castile to fund an Atlantic voyage.

Fatimid dynasty (Morocco, AD 909–AD 1171.label: Fatimid dynasty
Fatimid dynasty (Morocco, AD 909–AD 1171.prose:
[North Africa; Egypt; southern Syria, AD 909–AD 1171] Fatimid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Syria, Tunisia. 909-1171 (AH 297-AH 555). Rulers of North Africa, then Egypt and southern Syria who claimed title of caliph. They claimed descent from Fatima the daughter of the Prophet Mohammad and wife of the fourth Caliph 'Ali. In 909 (AH 297) the Mahdi was proclaimed caliph in rivalry to the 'Abbasids of Baghdad. From Egypt the Fatimids extended into Palestine and Syria and reached the zenith of their power in the 11th century. Period definition from British Museum.

Beginning as a revolutionary Isma'ili movement among the Berbers of Ifriqiya, the dynasty proclaimed a rival caliphate, conquered Egypt and built Cairo. For two and a half centuries it contested religious authority with Baghdad and Córdoba and controlled the trade of the Red Sea, until Saladin ended it and restored Sunni rule.

Susa II (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC).label: Susa II
Susa II (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[Khuzestan, 3499 BC–3099 BC] Susa II. Khuzestan, ca 3500BC-3100BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Susa was drawn tightly into the Uruk world of southern Mesopotamia: bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals, wheel-made pottery and, crucially, numerical clay tablets and bullae for tracking goods. This is the moment when accounting technology arrives on the Susiana plain, laying the groundwork for writing. The city functioned as a major node between lowland Mesopotamia and the Iranian highlands.

Southern Dynasties (China, AD 420–AD 589.label: Southern Dynasties
Southern Dynasties (China, AD 420–AD 589.prose:
[China, AD 420–AD 589] Southern Dynasties. 420-589. Period definition from British Museum.

Four short-lived regimes - Song, Qi, Liang and Chen - ruled the Yangtze valley from Jiankang while non-Chinese dynasties held the north. Aristocratic emigre families from the north dominated court life, Buddhism won imperial patronage and vast monastic wealth, and poetry, calligraphy and literary criticism flourished amid frequent coups. The south's population and economy grew rapidly, laying groundwork for later Chinese prosperity before the Sui reunified the country.

Han dynasty (China, 205 BC–AD 220).label: Han dynasty
Han dynasty (China, 205 BC–AD 220).prose:
[China, 205 BC–AD 220] Han dynasty. 206 BC-220 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Rising from the wreckage of the short-lived Qin, the Han kept the unified empire but softened its harshness, making the Confucian classics the basis of official learning and recruitment. Expansion into the Tarim Basin secured the Silk Road; paper, water-powered bellows and the seismoscope were invented; Sima Qian wrote the first comprehensive history of China. Court intrigue, land concentration and peasant revolts finally splintered the empire into the Three Kingdoms.

Ghilzay Afghan dynasty (Iran, AD 1722–AD.label: Ghilzay Afghan dynasty
Ghilzay Afghan dynasty (Iran, AD 1722–AD.prose:
[Persia, AD 1722–AD 1729] Ghilzay Afghan dynasty. 1722-1729 (AH 1135-AH 1142). Persia. Period definition from British Museum.

Pashtun tribesmen from Kandahar under Mahmud Hotak invaded Persia, besieged Isfahan into starvation and forced the Safavid shah to abdicate in 1722, ending two centuries of Safavid power. Their hold on the country was violent and shallow, resisted in the provinces and squeezed by Ottoman and Russian seizures of territory, and Nader Qoli, the future Nader Shah, drove them out within a few years.

Classical Greek (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).label: Classical Greek
Classical Greek (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Greece, 479 BC–322 BC] Classical Greek. 480 BC - 323 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The century and a half between the defeat of Persia and the death of Alexander produced the temples, sculpture, tragedy, history and philosophy that later ages took as a standard. It was also a period of near-constant warfare between city-states, with hegemony passing from Athens to Sparta to Thebes and finally to Macedon. Philip and Alexander ended the independence of the polis and carried Greek culture to Egypt and India.

Yowa Era (Japan, AD 1181–AD 1182).label: Yowa Era
Yowa Era (Japan, AD 1181–AD 1182).prose:
[Japan, AD 1181–AD 1182] Yowa Era. 1181-1182. Period definition from British Museum.

A two-year reign name that falls in the middle of the Genpei War, as the Taira clan fought Minamoto armies for control of Japan. It is remembered above all for a catastrophic famine, worsened by drought and epidemic, that filled the streets of Kyoto with corpses and was described unforgettably in Kamo no Chōmei's later essay Hōjōki. The chaos helped destroy Taira power and opened the way to the warrior government founded at Kamakura.

Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 449 BC–299 BC).label: Cypro-Classical
Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 449 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 449 BC–299 BC] Cypro-Classical. 450 BC-300 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Under Persian suzerainty the island's kings played Greek and Persian interests against each other, most famously Evagoras I of Salamis, who fought a long war for independence and promoted Greek language and art. Cypriot syllabic writing survived alongside the Greek alphabet and Phoenician, and royal tombs at Salamis were furnished with chariots, horses and Homeric-looking grave goods. The kingdoms ended when Ptolemy I abolished them and absorbed Cyprus into his empire.

Muzaffarid dynasty (Iran, AD 1314–AD 139.label: Muzaffarid dynasty
Muzaffarid dynasty (Iran, AD 1314–AD 139.prose:
[Kirman, Fars, and western Iran, AD 1314–AD 1393] Muzaffarid dynasty. 1314-1393 (AH 713-795). The Muzaffarids, distantly of Khurasanian Arab origin, came to power in Kirman, Fars and western Iran as the Il-Khanid empire declined. Period definition from British Museum.

A family of provincial governors who carved out an independent state in Fars and Kerman as Mongol Ilkhanid rule disintegrated. Their court at Shiraz was the setting for the poetry of Hafez, who wrote for and about these rulers even as they fought one another savagely for the throne. Timur ended the dynasty by conquest, having most of its surviving princes executed.

Daguan (China, AD 1107–AD 1111).label: Daguan
Daguan (China, AD 1107–AD 1111).prose:
[China, AD 1107–AD 1111] Daguan. 1107-1111 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

One of the reign eras of Huizong, the Song emperor who governed as an aesthete while his chief councillor Cai Jing ran the state. The court academy of painting, the imperial collections of bronzes and calligraphy, and the emperor's own treatise on tea date from these years; the fiscal strain and factional purges behind the splendour helped bring on the loss of the north two decades later.

Kennin Era (Japan, AD 1201–AD 1204).label: Kennin Era
Kennin Era (Japan, AD 1201–AD 1204).prose:
[Japan, AD 1201–AD 1204] Kennin Era. 1201-1204. Period definition from British Museum.

The monk Eisai, back from study in Song China, founded Kennin-ji in Kyoto in 1202, establishing Rinzai Zen — and the tea drinking he promoted with it — at the heart of the capital. The same years saw the shogun Yoriie deposed and murdered and his brother Sanetomo installed as a figurehead, with Hōjō Tokimasa taking the office of regent that his family would hold for over a century.

Eisho Era (Japan, AD 1504–AD 1521).label: Eisho Era
Eisho Era (Japan, AD 1504–AD 1521).prose:
[Japan, AD 1504–AD 1521] Eisho Era. 1504-1521. Period definition from British Museum.

A long era of chaos in the disintegrating Muromachi order. The assassination of the shogunal strongman Hosokawa Masamoto plunged his house into civil war, rival Ashikaga claimants were installed and expelled by whichever warlord held Kyoto, and real authority drained away to provincial lords who owed the capital nothing. It is one of the eras in which the Sengoku pattern of endemic regional warfare hardened into place.

Tensho Era (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1592).label: Tensho Era
Tensho Era (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1592).prose:
[Japan, AD 1573–AD 1592] Tensho Era. 1573-1592. Period definition from British Museum.

Oda Nobunaga toppled the last Ashikaga shogun and smashed his rivals, and after his murder at Honnō-ji in 1582 Toyotomi Hideyoshi finished the work, bringing nearly all Japan under one command. Hideyoshi ordered land surveys and the great sword hunt that disarmed the peasantry and froze the social classes. Christian daimyo sent an embassy to Rome, and the first European printing press reached Japan.

Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1199 BC–1059.label: Late Helladic IIIC
Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1199 BC–1059.prose:
[Greece, 1199 BC–1059 BC] Late Helladic IIIC. 1200BC-1060BC.  Late Helladic IIIC and Late Minoan IIIC pottery is normally divided into Early, Middle and Late. Where these classifications are used, the following dates are accepted: Early: 1200BC-1130BC.  Middle: 1130BC-1090BC.  Late: 1090BC-1060BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Life after the palaces: no kings, no scribes, no frescoes, but surviving communities at Tiryns, Lefkandi, Perati and in the islands, some prospering briefly. Painters produced lively pictorial vases of ships and warriors, and refugees and traders kept Aegean contacts alive. A final decline led into the Protogeometric period and the Iron Age.

Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.label: Middle Cycladic III
Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.prose:
[Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Cycladic III. 1700BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cretan influence becomes overwhelming: Minoan pottery, weights, loomweights and even Linear A writing appear in island towns, and local products imitate palatial styles. The transformation carries directly into the frescoed, richly furnished Akrotiri destroyed by the eruption of Thera in the following period.

Xining (China, AD 1068–AD 1078).label: Xining
Xining (China, AD 1068–AD 1078).prose:
[China, AD 1068–AD 1078] Xining. 1068-1078 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The era in which Emperor Shenzong backed Wang Anshi's New Policies: state loans to farmers, a hired-labour tax replacing forced service, government price regulation and militia and horse-breeding schemes, all meant to fund the army and curb great landowners. The programme split the bureaucracy into reform and conservative factions, with Sima Guang and Su Shi in opposition, and the feud dominated Song politics for the next half century.

Jianxing (China, AD 223–AD 237).label: Jianxing
Jianxing (China, AD 223–AD 237).prose:
[China, AD 223–AD 237] Jianxing. 223-237 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The era of Liu Shan's accession in the kingdom of Shu, following the death of his father Liu Bei. Real power lay with the chancellor Zhuge Liang, who restored the alliance with Wu, pacified the southern tribes and launched repeated invasions of Wei across the mountains. His death in the field in 234 ended Shu's best hope of reuniting China.

Yoro Era (Japan, AD 717–AD 724).label: Yoro Era
Yoro Era (Japan, AD 717–AD 724).prose:
[Japan, AD 717–AD 724] Yoro Era. 717-724. Period definition from British Museum.

A Nara-period era under Empress Genshō, remembered for the compilation of the Yōrō Code, the legal framework that would govern the imperial state for centuries once it was finally enacted. The Nihon Shoki, Japan's first official chronicle, was presented to the court in 720. Provincial administration, tax registers and road networks were being built out on the Chinese model.

Chimu (Peru, AD 900–AD 1470).label: Chimu
Chimu (Peru, AD 900–AD 1470).prose:
[Peru, AD 900–AD 1470] Chimu. The date range covered is AD 900-AD 1470.  Christopher Donnan, 'Ceramics of Ancient Peru', Fowler Museum of Cultural History, University of California, Los Angeles, 1992. Period definition from British Museum.

The Chimú built the largest state on the Peruvian coast before the Inca, ruling the desert valleys from Chan Chan, a city of vast adobe compounds whose walls still stand near Trujillo. Their engineers moved water across dozens of kilometres of sand to irrigate cotton and maize, and their smiths produced sheet-gold and silver work and glossy blackware pottery in enormous quantities. The Inca conquered them around 1470 and carried their goldsmiths off to Cuzco.

Early Dynastic I (Iraq, 2899 BC–2699 BC).label: Early Dynastic I
Early Dynastic I (Iraq, 2899 BC–2699 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2699 BC] Early Dynastic I. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. A term used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia between approximately 2900-2700 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The opening phase of the southern Mesopotamian sequence that follows the Jemdet Nasr period, felt across the Susiana plain as well. Cities pulled inward behind massive fortification walls — Uruk's is the most famous — as competing centres emerged from the earlier Uruk world. Seal designs shift to dense, repetitive 'brocade' patterns, and cuneiform writing is still largely a tool of accountants rather than storytellers.

Dai Hoa reign period (Vietnam, AD 1443–A.label: Dai Hoa reign period
Dai Hoa reign period (Vietnam, AD 1443–A.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1443–AD 1453] Dai Hoa reign period. Dai Hoa reign period (1443-1453). Period definition from British Museum.

The boy-emperor Le Nhan Tong's era, when Vietnam was governed by his mother as regent in the aftermath of his father's sudden death and the mass execution of the scholar Nguyen Trai's family. The Le court fought Champa in the south while regents and generals manoeuvred at home, a rivalry that ended in the young emperor's murder and the accession of Le Thanh Tong.

Jingtai (China, AD 1450–AD 1456).label: Jingtai
Jingtai (China, AD 1450–AD 1456).prose:
[China, AD 1450–AD 1456] Jingtai. 1450-1456 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of the Ming emperor placed on the throne after his brother was captured by the Mongols at Tumu in 1449. He steadied the dynasty and let Beijing's defences hold, but was deposed when the returned former emperor seized power back in 1457. Cloisonné enamel of the period became so admired that Chinese still call the ware jingtai lan, 'Jingtai blue'.

Khalji dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 1296–AD.label: Khalji dynasty
Khalji dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 1296–AD.prose:
[Afghanistan, AD 1296–AD 1320] Khalji dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, India, Pakistan. Rulers of the Delhi Sultanate 1296-1320. Period definition from British Museum.

Under Alauddin Khalji the Delhi Sultanate became the dominant power in India: he beat back repeated Mongol invasions from the northwest, stormed the great Rajput fortresses of Ranthambore and Chittor, and sent his general Malik Kafur raiding as far as the southern tip of the peninsula. At home he imposed strict market price controls and a heavy land tax to pay for a huge standing army, an experiment in state economic management unlike anything before it in the subcontinent. The dynasty collapsed in palace intrigue within a decade of his death.

Bunmei Era (Japan, AD 1469–AD 1487).label: Bunmei Era
Bunmei Era (Japan, AD 1469–AD 1487).prose:
[Japan, AD 1469–AD 1487] Bunmei Era. 1469-1487. Period definition from British Museum.

The Ōnin War ground to its exhausted end in these years, leaving Kyoto burnt out and the Ashikaga shogunate a shadow with no power over the provinces. Warlords, village leagues and militant Buddhist congregations filled the vacuum, opening the century of Sengoku warfare. Meanwhile the retired shogun Yoshimasa began building his villa at Higashiyama, the setting for the tea ceremony, ink painting and garden aesthetics that became a lasting Japanese ideal.

Tahirid dynasty (Iraq, AD 821–AD 875).label: Tahirid dynasty
Tahirid dynasty (Iraq, AD 821–AD 875).prose:
[Khurasan; Baghdad; Iraq, AD 821–AD 875] Tahirid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Iraq, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. 821-875 (AH 205-AH 261). Governors of Khurasan, and in Baghdad and Iraq. The family receives its name from Tahir ibn al-Husain who was probably of Persian origin. He rose to favour under the caliph al-Ma'mun and after the fall of Baghdad became the governor that city and Jazira. He as then appointed Governor of the East. The Tahirid's had great wealth and estates in Baghdad and were renownd as patrons of Arabic culture. Period definition from British Museum.

A family of Persian generals rewarded with the governorship of Khurasan by the caliph al-Ma'mun, who ruled the east in the caliph's name while keeping the peace and the tax revenue flowing, and simultaneously held the security command of Baghdad itself. Though formally loyal, their hereditary and largely autonomous rule from Nishapur is usually counted as the first step in the political fragmentation of the Abbasid empire and the revival of Iranian regional power.

Qing dynasty (China, AD 1644–AD 1911).label: Qing dynasty
Qing dynasty (China, AD 1644–AD 1911).prose:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1911] Qing dynasty. 1644-1911. Period definition from British Museum.

Manchu conquerors from beyond the Great Wall took Beijing in 1644 and built the largest and most populous empire China had known, governing Han Chinese through familiar institutions while keeping a separate banner military and Inner Asian identity. Porcelain, tea and silk flowed out through Canton; opium, gunboats and missionaries came back in. Defeat by Britain, Japan and internal rebellion hollowed out the state, and the dynasty's collapse ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule.

Longqing (China, AD 1567–AD 1572).label: Longqing
Longqing (China, AD 1567–AD 1572).prose:
[China, AD 1567–AD 1572] Longqing. 1567-1572 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A short Ming reign that quietly repaired two of the empire's worst problems. The court lifted the ban on private overseas trade, letting Chinese merchants sail legally from Fujian and drawing a flood of New World silver into the economy, and it made peace with the Mongol leader Altan Khan by opening frontier horse markets, ending decades of raiding. The emperor himself left the work to able ministers and died after six years.

Tenna Era (Japan, AD 1681–AD 1684).label: Tenna Era
Tenna Era (Japan, AD 1681–AD 1684).prose:
[Japan, AD 1681–AD 1684] Tenna Era. 1681-1684. Period definition from British Museum.

The opening years of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi's rule, when he purged lax officials and pressed a Confucian moral order on the samurai class. Edo burned in the great fire of 1683, an event fixed in popular memory through the tale of the greengrocer's daughter Oshichi.

Northern Song dynasty (China, AD 960–AD.label: Northern Song dynasty
Northern Song dynasty (China, AD 960–AD.prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 1126] Northern Song dynasty. 960-1126. Period definition from British Museum.

After half a century of fragmentation the Song reunited most of China under a government of examination-trained scholar-officials based at Kaifeng. Cities grew, coinage and paper money circulated in vast quantities, printing spread learning widely, and painters produced the great monochrome landscapes still regarded as the summit of Chinese art. Wang Anshi's sweeping reforms split the bureaucracy, and the dynasty ended when the Jurchen took the capital.

Kannin Era (Japan, AD 1017–AD 1021).label: Kannin Era
Kannin Era (Japan, AD 1017–AD 1021).prose:
[Japan, AD 1017–AD 1021] Kannin Era. 1017-1021. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Michinaga stood at the summit of court power, handing the regency to his son Yorimichi and beginning the great temple Hōjō-ji, while three of his daughters served as imperial consorts. The calm was broken in 1019 when Jurchen raiders from the mainland attacked Tsushima, Iki and northern Kyushu, exposing how little military force the court could muster.

Koji Era 1142-1144 (Japan, AD 1142–AD 11.label: Koji Era 1142-1144
Koji Era 1142-1144 (Japan, AD 1142–AD 11.prose:
[Japan, AD 1142–AD 1144] Koji Era 1142-1144. 1142-1144. Period definition from British Museum.

The retired emperor Toba ruled as cloistered sovereign while a child sat on the throne, the classic arrangement of Japan's insei system, in which real authority lay with a monastic ex-emperor and his private household. Rivalries among imperial princes and the Fujiwara nurtured during these quiet years erupted a decade later in the Hōgen Disturbance, which brought warrior families into court politics for good.

Hakuchi Era (Japan, AD 650–AD 672).label: Hakuchi Era
Hakuchi Era (Japan, AD 650–AD 672).prose:
[Japan, AD 650–AD 672] Hakuchi Era. 650-672. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for a white pheasant presented to the court as an auspicious omen, this reign-name covered the years when the Taika reforms were being pressed forward: land and tax registers, provincial governors, and a Chinese-style bureaucracy grafted onto clan-based rule. It was one of Japan's first experiments with dated eras, after which the practice lapsed for decades. Embassies to Tang China returned with models for law, writing, and Buddhist institutions.

Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (Sudan, AD 1899–AD.label: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (Sudan, AD 1899–AD.prose:
[Sudan, AD 1899–AD 1955] Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. The term refers to the date range 1899 to 1955. Period definition from British Museum.

After Kitchener's army destroyed the Mahdist state at Omdurman, Sudan was governed as a condominium — nominally shared between Britain and Egypt, in practice run by British officials. They built railways and the vast Gezira cotton scheme, and administered the largely non-Muslim south separately from the Arabic-speaking north, restricting movement between them. That division left a fractured state at independence in 1956 and helped set off decades of civil war.

Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.label: Late Helladic II
Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.prose:
[Greece, 1499 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic II. 1500BC-1400BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Chieftains stopped digging shaft graves and began building tholoi, great stone beehive chambers approached by long passages, a display of labour and permanence. Mycenaean goods spread through the Aegean and mainlanders took control of Knossos, where Linear B was adapted to write Greek.

Shengui (China, AD 517–AD 519).label: Shengui
Shengui (China, AD 517–AD 519).prose:
[China, AD 517–AD 519] Shengui. 517-519 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Northern Wei was governed by the formidable Empress Dowager Hu on behalf of her child emperor, and she poured the treasury into Buddhism — above all the colossal wooden pagoda of the Yongning Temple in Luoyang, said to be visible from miles across the plain. Monks were dispatched to India for scriptures, and the cave shrines at Longmen were extended, even as the ruinous expense and neglect of the northern garrisons stored up the revolts that would tear the dynasty apart.

Koan Era (Japan, AD 1278–AD 1288).label: Koan Era
Koan Era (Japan, AD 1278–AD 1288).prose:
[Japan, AD 1278–AD 1288] Koan Era. 1278-1288. Period definition from British Museum.

The Kamakura shogunate's great test: in 1281 a second Mongol armada, far larger than the first, landed in Kyushu and was held off by defensive stone walls and warrior levies before a typhoon wrecked the fleet. Victory brought no plunder, so the Hōjō regents could not reward the samurai who had fought, breeding resentment that gnawed at the regime for decades. Coastal defence duties became a permanent, ruinous burden on western warrior houses.

Kenji Era (Japan, AD 1275–AD 1278).label: Kenji Era
Kenji Era (Japan, AD 1275–AD 1278).prose:
[Japan, AD 1275–AD 1278] Kenji Era. 1275-1278. Period definition from British Museum.

The uneasy interval between the two Mongol invasions of Japan. Having beaten off the first attack and executed Kublai Khan's envoys, the shogunate mobilised the warriors of Kyushu to build a long stone wall around Hakata Bay and mount coastal watches — defences that would help break the far larger fleet that arrived in 1281.

Karts of Herat (Afghanistan, AD 1245–AD.label: Karts of Herat
Karts of Herat (Afghanistan, AD 1245–AD.prose:
[eastern Khurasan and northern Afghanistan, AD 1245–AD 1277] Karts of Herat. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran. The Karts or Kurts of eastern Khurasan and northern Afghanistan were an indiginous dynasty who claimed to be heirs of the Ghurids. The Mongols allowed Shams al-Din I Muhammad (1245-1277, AH 643-676) to rule as a vassal prince in Herat and the mountains of Ghur. They remained loyal allies of the Il-Khans of Persia. Period definition from British Museum.

The Kart (Kartid) dynasty took over Herat and much of what is now western Afghanistan as vassals of the Mongol Ilkhans, holding their position by careful submission and military service. They rebuilt a city that Chinggis Khan's armies had left in ruins, restoring its walls, bazaars and irrigation and reviving it as a centre of trade and learning.

Ken'ei Era (Japan, AD 1206–AD 1207).label: Ken'ei Era
Ken'ei Era (Japan, AD 1206–AD 1207).prose:
[Japan, AD 1206–AD 1207] Ken'ei Era. 1206-1207. Period definition from British Museum.

A two-year name-change early in the Kamakura shogunate, when real power in Japan had passed from the imperial court to the warrior government in the east — and, within that government, from the Minamoto line to the Hōjō family acting as regents for the young shogun Sanetomo. The same years saw the court in Kyoto growing hostile to the new Pure Land preaching of Hōnen and his followers, whose message that salvation came through calling the Buddha's name alone was spreading rapidly among ordinary people.

Eiroku Era (Japan, AD 1558–AD 1570).label: Eiroku Era
Eiroku Era (Japan, AD 1558–AD 1570).prose:
[Japan, AD 1558–AD 1570] Eiroku Era. 1558-1570. Period definition from British Museum.

The Warring States period at full boil. Oda Nobunaga destroyed Imagawa Yoshimoto at Okehazama in 1560 and vaulted from minor lord to national contender; the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiteru was murdered in his own residence in 1565; and in 1568 Nobunaga marched into Kyoto with a puppet shogun in tow, beginning the reunification of Japan. Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries were meanwhile spreading firearms and Christianity through the western provinces.

Shoji Era (Japan, AD 1199–AD 1201).label: Shoji Era
Shoji Era (Japan, AD 1199–AD 1201).prose:
[Japan, AD 1199–AD 1201] Shoji Era. 1199-1201. Period definition from British Museum.

The era opened with the death of Minamoto no Yoritomo, founder of the Kamakura shogunate, and the immediate unravelling of his personal authority. Power slid toward a council of senior warriors and, above all, toward Yoritomo's in-laws the Hōjō, who would rule as regents for the shoguns for over a century. Yoritomo's heir Yoriie proved unable to hold the warrior houses together, and the coup and killings that followed set the pattern of Kamakura politics.

Xiankang (China, AD 925–AD 925).label: Xiankang
Xiankang (China, AD 925–AD 925).prose: [China, AD 925–AD 925] Xiankang. 925. Period definition from British Museum.

Nguyen dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945.label: Nguyen dynasty
Nguyen dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945] Nguyen dynasty. Vietnamese dynasty, 1802-1945. Period definition from British Museum.

Gia Long defeated the Tây Sơn and ruled a Vietnam united from the Chinese border to the Mekong delta for the first time, governing from a new walled capital and citadel at Huế modelled on Beijing. His successors doubled down on Confucian orthodoxy and persecuted Christian missionaries, giving France a pretext for invasion; by the 1880s the emperors were figureheads in a French protectorate. The line ended when Bảo Đại abdicated to the Việt Minh in 1945.

Togau (Pakistan, 4299 BC–3799 BC).label: Togau
Togau (Pakistan, 4299 BC–3799 BC).prose:
[Pakistan, 4299 BC–3799 BC] Togau. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. 4300BC-3800BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase of the Balochistan uplands known for its distinctive painted pottery: fine buff wares carried friezes of stylised ibex or caprid heads, reduced over time to little more than repeated hooks. The ware turns up across a wide swathe of the region, evidence that farming villages there were already linked by shared craft traditions and exchange. These communities, with their mud-brick houses, herds and irrigated plots, lie on the road that leads to the Indus cities.

Keiun Era (Japan, AD 704–AD 708).label: Keiun Era
Keiun Era (Japan, AD 704–AD 708).prose:
[Japan, AD 704–AD 708] Keiun Era. 704-708. Period definition from British Museum.

The first decades of rule under the Taihō Code, when Japan was being rebuilt as a Chinese-style state of provinces, ministries and written law. Emperor Monmu died in 707 and was succeeded by his mother Genmei, who soon exploited a new copper strike to mint the Wadō coinage and to move the capital to Heijō-kyō at Nara.

Sabaean (Yemen, 999 BC–500 BC).label: Sabaean
Sabaean (Yemen, 999 BC–500 BC).prose:
[Saba? kingdom, ancient Yemen, 999 BC–500 BC] Sabaean. Refers to the kingdom of Saba? (capital at Marib) based in the Wadi Adhana region that controlled large parts of ancient Yemen during the first half of the first millennium BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Saba was the dominant power of ancient South Arabia, ruling from Marib, where an immense earthen dam channelled seasonal floodwater across irrigated fields and supported a dense oasis population. Its wealth came from frankincense and myrrh carried north by camel caravan to the Mediterranean world, and its rulers left thousands of monumental inscriptions in the Sabaic script on temples such as Awwam. Assyrian records mention its kings; later Hebrew tradition remembered it as Sheba.

Ziyarid dynasty (Iran, AD 931–AD 1090).label: Ziyarid dynasty
Ziyarid dynasty (Iran, AD 931–AD 1090).prose:
[Daylam, AD 931–AD 1090] Ziyarid dynasty. 931-c.1090 (AH 319-AH 413). Local dynasty in the remote highland region of Daylam at the south-west corner of the Caspian Sea. The Ziyarids descended from Mardawij ibn Ziyar of the royal clan of Gilan. His power extended as far south as Isfahan and Hamadan but he was murdered in 935 (AH 323) by his own Turkish slave troops. The Ziyarids lost their power but Mardawij's brother, Wushmgir, retained a foot hold in the eastern Caspian provinces by acknowledging as his overlords the Samanids. In the 11th century the Ziyarids has to recognise the overlordship of the Ghnazvids and survived as vassals of the Seljuqs in the highland region. Period definition from British Museum.

A dynasty of Iranian soldiers from the Caspian highlands who carved out a kingdom in Tabaristan and Gurgan as Abbasid authority collapsed, later surviving as vassals of the Ghaznavids and Seljuks. Their most famous monuments are cultural: the soaring brick tomb tower of Qabus, one of the masterpieces of Iranian architecture, and the Qabus-nama, a witty book of advice on life written by a Ziyarid prince for his son.

Kanji Era (Japan, AD 1087–AD 1094).label: Kanji Era
Kanji Era (Japan, AD 1087–AD 1094).prose:
[Japan, AD 1087–AD 1094] Kanji Era. 1087-1094. Period definition from British Museum.

The era opened with the end of the Later Three-Year War in the northeast, where Minamoto no Yoshiie's victory built the reputation that made his family the pre-eminent warrior house. In Kyoto the retired emperor Shirakawa was consolidating rule from outside the throne, the cloistered-emperor system that would sideline the Fujiwara regents and the reigning sovereign alike.

Zenu (Colombia, 149 BC–AD 1600).label: Zenu
Zenu (Colombia, 149 BC–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, 149 BC–AD 1600] Zenu. The term refers to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the Caribbean lowlands from 150 BC to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Peoples of the Caribbean lowlands of northern Colombia reshaped the flood plains of the San Jorge and Sinú rivers with thousands of kilometres of drainage canals and raised fields, controlling seasonal flooding to farm and fish on a large scale. They are best known for gold and tumbaga work, especially filigree ear ornaments cast in intricate openwork. Their communities were still there, much reduced, when Spanish expeditions arrived to loot the burial mounds.

Anglo-Viking (England, AD 875–AD 954).label: Anglo-Viking
Anglo-Viking (England, AD 875–AD 954).prose:
[England, AD 875–AD 954] Anglo-Viking. Anglo-Viking is used in the context of numismatics only.  It is defined as the period from c. AD 875-954 in which there were settlements within England under the authority of Scandinavian rulers.  In this way, it applies to coins issued by Viking East Anglia (c. 880-910), Viking Northumbria (c. 895-954) and at unspecified sites within the Danelaw (c. 875-c. 930). It is not used with reference to Scandinavian imitations of Anglo-Saxon coins, or to coins of Cnut and his sons in the 11thC, since that period of Danish rule did not fundamentally affect the basic 'Anglo-Saxon' character of either culture or coinage. Period definition from British Museum.

Scandinavian armies that had come to raid stayed to settle, carving out a Viking kingdom centred on York and a swathe of eastern and northern England later called the Danelaw. Norse landholding, law and speech soaked into the region, leaving place-names in -by and -thorpe and hundreds of everyday words in English, while York grew into a busy trading town linked to Dublin and the Baltic. Wessex kings pushed back generation by generation, and the killing of Erik Bloodaxe brought the last independent Norse kingdom in England under a single English crown.

Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1799 BC).label: Isin-Larsa
Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1799 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Isin-Larsa. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the period approximately 2000 BC-1800 BC when southern Mesopotamia was dominated by the cities Isin and Larsa. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for the two Mesopotamian cities that fought over the legacy of the fallen Ur III empire, this horizon in the east coincides with the rise of the Sukkalmah rulers of Elam, who traded, intermarried and intrigued with the kings of southern Iraq. Cuneiform contracts, cylinder seals and standardised pottery show how closely the Iranian lowlands were tied into Babylonian economic life. It ends with Hammurabi's conquests reshaping the region.

Zhengde (China, AD 1506–AD 1521).label: Zhengde
Zhengde (China, AD 1506–AD 1521).prose:
[China, AD 1506–AD 1521] Zhengde. 1506-1521.  Emperor Wuzong. Period definition from British Museum.

A young, restless Ming emperor who preferred military play-acting, exotic entertainments and his private Leopard Quarter to the routines of court, leaving vast influence to the eunuch Liu Jin and later to favoured generals. His reign saw a princely rebellion crushed by the philosopher-official Wang Yangming and the first Portuguese ships reaching the south China coast. Officials remembered him as the model of a wayward ruler; collectors remember his reign for its distinctive blue-and-white porcelain, some of it bearing Arabic inscriptions.

Gentoku Era (Japan, AD 1329–AD 1331).label: Gentoku Era
Gentoku Era (Japan, AD 1329–AD 1331).prose:
[Japan, AD 1329–AD 1331] Gentoku Era. 1329-1331. Period definition from British Museum.

Go-Daigo, outwardly performing ritual and prayer, was quietly recruiting warrior monks and provincial allies against the Kamakura shogunate. The conspiracy was exposed in 1331 and the emperor fled the capital, tipping Japan into the war that would destroy Hōjō rule.

Warring States period (China, 480 BC–220.label: Warring States period
Warring States period (China, 480 BC–220.prose:
[China, 480 BC–220 BC] Warring States period. 481BC-221BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The last Zhou kings were figureheads while rival states annexed one another outright, building walled frontiers, canals and bureaucracies to feed armies of hundreds of thousands. Coinage spread, iron farming tools raised yields, and philosophers from Mencius to Han Fei argued over how a state should be run. It ended when Qin conquered the rest and imposed a single administration, script and law on the whole.

Shoho Era (Japan, AD 1644–AD 1648).label: Shoho Era
Shoho Era (Japan, AD 1644–AD 1648).prose:
[Japan, AD 1644–AD 1648] Shoho Era. 1644-1648. Period definition from British Museum.

News reached Japan that the Ming dynasty had fallen to rebels and Manchus, and Ming loyalists sent repeated appeals to Edo for troops; the shogunate declined every one, holding to its policy of seclusion. At home the government ordered every domain to submit detailed provincial maps and land surveys, producing the Shōhō country maps — among the first systematic cartographic pictures of the whole country.

Eastern Wei dynasty (China, AD 534–AD 55.label: Eastern Wei dynasty
Eastern Wei dynasty (China, AD 534–AD 55.prose:
[China, AD 534–AD 550] Eastern Wei dynasty. 534-550. Period definition from British Museum.

One half of the fractured Northern Wei realm, ruled from Ye in the North China Plain by a puppet emperor under the general Gao Huan. Its wars with the Western Wei in the Guanzhong basin set the pattern of north Chinese politics for a generation, and its Xianbei military elite resisted the earlier drive toward Chinese customs. The dynasty ended when Gao's family took the throne outright as the Northern Qi.

Kaiqing (China, AD 1259–AD 1260).label: Kaiqing
Kaiqing (China, AD 1259–AD 1260).prose:
[China, AD 1259–AD 1260] Kaiqing. 1259-1260 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A one-year era of the Southern Song under Emperor Lizong, during the great Mongol offensive in which Möngke Khan died besieging Diaoyu Fortress in Sichuan. His death forced Kublai to break off his own campaign and return north to fight for the succession, buying the Song two more decades.

Mughal dynasty (India, AD 1526–AD 1805).label: Mughal dynasty
Mughal dynasty (India, AD 1526–AD 1805).prose:
[India, AD 1526–AD 1805] Mughal dynasty. 1526-1805; India. Period definition from British Museum.

Babur's victory at Panipat founded an empire that, under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, governed most of the subcontinent through a salaried military aristocracy and a cash revenue system assessed on measured land. Its courts fused Persian, Central Asian and Indian traditions into the architecture of Fatehpur Sikri and the Taj Mahal, miniature painting, and the Urdu language. After Aurangzeb's costly southern wars the empire fragmented, and later emperors ruled in name only under Maratha and then British protection.

Late Cypriot (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC) [.label: Late Cypriot
Late Cypriot (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC) [.prose:
[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC] Late Cypriot. 1650 BC-1050 BC.  The third major division of the Cypriot Bronze Age is marked by the appearance of new pottery types, such as White Slip, Base Ring and Monochrome in the North West of the island, which gradually replace older fabrics which continue in use from the Middle Bronze Age. Other important fabrics included Bichrome Wheelmade, Red Lustrous Wheelmade and various Plain and Painted Wheelmade wares; the latter are heavily influenced by imports from the Mycenaean world in particular (but also the Levant) which gradually displace the older hand-made wares by the 12th century.  The period is characterised by a thriving copper extraction industry, intense commercial interchange with surrounding regions – with imports visible from all around the Eastern Mediterranean - , and the emergence of more complex forms of social organisation, which can be called towns by LCIIC and LCIIIA. Literacy is attested in the form of documents written in a script called Cypro-Minoan, which has some links with Bronze Age Crete.  The last phase of the LC period, LCIII is a transitional period marked by major changes in the settlement pattern, burial practices, economy and material culture (including pottery types); the development of Proto-White Painted and Proto-Bichrome wares signal the beginning of the Iron Age in ceramic terms. The development of iron-making technology, in which Cypriot metallurgists played a leading role, develops apace at this time. Period definition from British Museum.

Cyprus's boom as the Mediterranean's copper supplier, exporting oxhide ingots from harbour towns such as Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke and appearing in Egyptian and Hittite records as Alashiya. Ashlar buildings, imported Mycenaean and Levantine pottery, ivories and the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script mark an urban, cosmopolitan society. After 1200 BC, when the surrounding Bronze Age states collapsed, Aegean settlers arrived, new sanctuaries and iron-working appeared, and the foundations of the Iron Age Cypriot kingdoms were laid.

Liu Shan (China, AD 223–AD 263).label: Liu Shan
Liu Shan (China, AD 223–AD 263).prose:
[China, AD 223–AD 263] Liu Shan. 223-263 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The son of Liu Bei and second and last emperor of Shu Han, who inherited a small mountain kingdom in Sichuan at sixteen and left its government largely to Zhuge Liang and his successors. When Wei armies broke through in 263 he surrendered without a final fight and was resettled in comfort at the enemy capital, allegedly saying he did not miss home at all. His reign ends one of the three kingdoms whose wars became China's most retold historical drama.

Johei Era (Japan, AD 931–AD 938).label: Johei Era
Johei Era (Japan, AD 931–AD 938).prose:
[Japan, AD 931–AD 938] Johei Era. 931-938. Period definition from British Museum.

The years when Taira no Masakado's feuds in eastern Japan escalated into open rebellion against the court, while Fujiwara no Sumitomo turned to piracy in the Inland Sea. Together these revolts exposed how little real power the Kyoto government held in the provinces, and how much it depended on other warriors to suppress them.

Dien Ninh reign period (Vietnam, AD 1454.label: Dien Ninh reign period
Dien Ninh reign period (Vietnam, AD 1454.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1454–AD 1459] Dien Ninh reign period. Dien Ninh reign period (1454-1459). Period definition from British Museum.

The era name of the boy-emperor Lê Nhân Tông's personal rule, after his mother's long regency ended. Court politics remained tense between rival factions of the Lê aristocracy, and the reign closed violently when the emperor and his mother were killed in a palace coup by his elder brother. The usurper lasted less than a year before officials overthrew him and installed Lê Thánh Tông, whose reign became the dynasty's golden age.

Gaudo (Campania, 2999 BC–1999 BC).label: Gaudo
Gaudo (Campania, 2999 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Campania, 2999 BC–1999 BC] Gaudo. 3000BC-2000BC.  Used with Campania as production place. Period definition from British Museum.

Known above all from its cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs near Paestum, where the dead were laid in groups in artificial caves reached by shafts. The pottery is unmistakable: sharply carinated flasks, asymmetric bowls and double vessels in a dark burnished ware, buried alongside copper daggers and flint arrowheads. It marks the arrival of metal-using communities in southern Italy and a new emphasis on the warrior in burial display.

Zhenzong (China, AD 998–AD 1022).label: Zhenzong
Zhenzong (China, AD 998–AD 1022).prose:
[China, AD 998–AD 1022] Zhenzong. 998-1022 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

After a costly stalemate with the Khitan Liao, the Song court bought peace with the Treaty of Chanyuan, paying annual silver and silk in exchange for a stable northern border that held for over a century. The emperor then staged elaborate and expensive Heaven-sent-text ceremonies and imperial sacrifices to shore up his prestige. Peace underwrote a boom in trade, printing and the examination-trained bureaucracy that defined Song government.

Sonso (Colombia, AD 700–AD 1600).label: Sonso
Sonso (Colombia, AD 700–AD 1600).prose:
[Calima region of Colombia in the Western Range of the Valle del Cauca department, AD 700–AD 1600] Sonso. The term refers to a period and a culture of the Calima region of Colombia in the Western Range of the Valle del Cauca department from 700 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The last prehispanic phase of the Calima region in Colombia's western cordillera, following the goldworking heyday of Yotoco. Communities lived in dispersed hamlets on artificial house terraces cut into the slopes, farming maize on ridged fields, and buried their dead in deep shaft-and-chamber tombs. Its pottery and simpler gold ornaments were still in use when Spanish forces entered the valley.

Northern Zhou dynasty (China, AD 557–AD.label: Northern Zhou dynasty
Northern Zhou dynasty (China, AD 557–AD.prose:
[China, AD 557–AD 581] Northern Zhou dynasty. 557-581. Period definition from British Museum.

Successor to the Western Wei in the Wei valley, this regime turned a weaker resource base into military advantage through the fubing militia and an aristocratic elite fusing Xianbei and Chinese families. It absorbed its eastern rival in 577 and briefly ruled all of northern China. Its usurpation by Yang Jian led directly to the Sui reunification of the empire.

Enkei Era (Japan, AD 1308–AD 1311).label: Enkei Era
Enkei Era (Japan, AD 1308–AD 1311).prose:
[Japan, AD 1308–AD 1311] Enkei Era. 1308-1311. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Kamakura-period era name, beginning with the accession of Emperor Hanazono after the death of Go-Nijo. It falls within the awkward arrangement, brokered by the Hojo regents in Kamakura, under which the throne alternated between two rival imperial lines — a compromise that would eventually fracture into the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts.

Genryaku Era (Japan, AD 1184–AD 1185).label: Genryaku Era
Genryaku Era (Japan, AD 1184–AD 1185).prose:
[Japan, AD 1184–AD 1185] Genryaku Era. 1184-1185. Period definition from British Museum.

The closing act of the Genpei War: Minamoto no Yoshitsune's victories at Ichi-no-Tani and Yashima drove the Taira to sea, and at Dan-no-ura their fleet was destroyed and the child emperor Antoku drowned with the imperial sword. With the Taira annihilated, Minamoto no Yoritomo began installing stewards and constables across the provinces — the skeleton of Japan's first warrior government.

Tianshou (China, AD 1038–AD 1048).label: Tianshou
Tianshou (China, AD 1038–AD 1048).prose:
[China, AD 1038–AD 1048] Tianshou. 1038-1048. Period definition from British Museum.

Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Xia, converting the Tangut border state into a rival empire that refused to accept Song overlordship. He promoted a distinctive Tangut script, court dress and rituals, and fought the Song to a standstill in a series of battles that ended with Kaifeng paying annual silver, silk and tea in exchange for nominal submission. His murder by his own son plunged the new state into a long regency.

Jokyu Era (Japan, AD 1219–AD 1222).label: Jokyu Era
Jokyu Era (Japan, AD 1219–AD 1222).prose:
[Japan, AD 1219–AD 1222] Jokyu Era. 1219-1222. Period definition from British Museum.

Dominated by the Jokyu War of 1221, when the retired emperor Go-Toba raised troops to overthrow the Hojo regents who controlled the Kamakura shogunate. The imperial forces were crushed in weeks; Go-Toba was exiled to the Oki Islands, court estates were confiscated and handed to warrior loyalists, and the shogunate installed governors in Kyoto to watch the throne. Military government had definitively become the real power in Japan.

Jogan Era (Japan, AD 859–AD 877).label: Jogan Era
Jogan Era (Japan, AD 859–AD 877).prose:
[Japan, AD 859–AD 877] Jogan Era. 859-877. Period definition from British Museum.

A formative stretch of early Heian Japan in which the Fujiwara secured the regency for the first time under Yoshifusa, and esoteric Tendai and Shingon Buddhism reshaped religious art. Art historians still use 'Jōgan style' for the heavy, brooding wooden sculpture of these decades. The era also saw the great Sanriku earthquake and tsunami of 869, whose deposits were studied again after 2011.

Eiryaku Era (Japan, AD 1160–AD 1161).label: Eiryaku Era
Eiryaku Era (Japan, AD 1160–AD 1161).prose:
[Japan, AD 1160–AD 1161] Eiryaku Era. 1160-1161. Period definition from British Museum.

The short era immediately after the Heiji Disturbance, in which Taira no Kiyomori destroyed his Minamoto rivals and made himself the dominant figure at court. The defeated Minamoto no Yoshitomo was killed and his young son Yoritomo exiled to Izu - a mercy that would cost the Taira everything twenty years later.

San Agustin Regional Classic (Colombia,.label: San Agustin Regional Classic
San Agustin Regional Classic (Colombia,.prose:
[Colombia, AD 1–AD 900] San Agustin Regional Classic. The terms refer to a period of the San Agustin cultural tradition of Colombia in the upper Magdalena valley in the Huila department from 1 AD to 900 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The peak of monument building in the upper Magdalena, when the great stone sculptures were carved and installed inside mound-covered burial chambers made of massive slabs, some painted red, black and yellow. The scale of the tombs implies chiefs able to command a great deal of labour, while the imagery of jaguar mouths, twinned figures and staff-bearing guardians suggests a shamanic religion. Nothing comparable in stone was produced anywhere else in Colombia.

Meitoku Era (Japan, AD 1390–AD 1394).label: Meitoku Era
Meitoku Era (Japan, AD 1390–AD 1394).prose:
[Japan, AD 1390–AD 1394] Meitoku Era. 1390-1394. Period definition from British Museum.

The Yamana clan's revolt against the shogun was crushed in 1391, breaking the power of a family said to control a sixth of Japan's provinces. The following year Ashikaga Yoshimitsu negotiated the return of the southern emperor's regalia, ending the sixty-year split between rival imperial courts. It marks the high point of Ashikaga authority.

Yongzheng (China, AD 1723–AD 1735).label: Yongzheng
Yongzheng (China, AD 1723–AD 1735).prose:
[China, AD 1723–AD 1735] Yongzheng. 1723-1735 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A famously hard-working and suspicious emperor who tightened Qing control: he created the Grand Council, merged the poll tax into the land tax, attacked corruption through secret palace memorials, and hid his chosen heir's name behind a palace tablet. Imperial kilns at Jingdezhen reached a technical peak under his eye, producing the delicate famille rose and monochrome wares collectors prize. His short reign paid for his son Qianlong's expansive one.

Kogen Era (Japan, AD 1256–AD 1257).label: Kogen Era
Kogen Era (Japan, AD 1256–AD 1257).prose:
[Japan, AD 1256–AD 1257] Kogen Era. 1256-1257. Period definition from British Museum.

Marked by epidemic disease and by the retirement of the shogunal regent Hōjō Tokiyori, who took Buddhist vows but continued to steer policy from behind the scenes. The episode showed how real power in Japan had detached itself from formal office — an emperor who did not rule, a shogun who did not command, and a retired regent who did both.

Gia Long (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1819).label: Gia Long
Gia Long (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1819).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1819] Gia Long. (1802-1819) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

Nguyen Anh's defeat of the Tay Son ended decades of civil war and, for the first time, brought the whole length of the country from the Red River delta to the Mekong under one ruler. He took the reign name Gia Long, made Hue his capital and built a vast citadel there, adopted the name Vietnam for the realm, and issued a legal code closely modelled on Qing China. The dynasty he founded lasted until 1945.

Daido Era (Japan, AD 806–AD 810).label: Daido Era
Daido Era (Japan, AD 806–AD 810).prose:
[Japan, AD 806–AD 810] Daido Era. 806-810. Period definition from British Museum.

The short reign of Emperor Heizei and the first year of his brother Saga, at the beginning of the Heian age. It closed with the Kusuko Incident of 810, in which the retired Heizei tried to seize back power and move the capital to Nara; his defeat confirmed Kyoto as the seat of government and gave the Fujiwara family a further foothold at court.

Northern Dynasties (China, AD 386–AD 581.label: Northern Dynasties
Northern Dynasties (China, AD 386–AD 581.prose:
[China, AD 386–AD 581] Northern Dynasties. 386-581. Period definition from British Museum.

A succession of regimes founded largely by Xianbei and other steppe elites ruled northern China while rival Chinese dynasties held the south. Their rulers adopted Chinese administration, promoted Buddhism on a huge scale — the cave temples at Yungang and Longmen date from this time — and devised the equal-field land system and fubing militia that later empires inherited. Intermarriage between steppe and Chinese aristocratic families produced the northwestern elite from which the Sui and Tang ruling houses emerged.

Later Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 951–AD 960.label: Later Zhou Dynasty
Later Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 951–AD 960.prose:
[China, AD 951–AD 960] Later Zhou Dynasty. 951-960. Period definition from British Museum.

The last of the Five Dynasties, and the one that laid the groundwork for reunification. Emperor Shizong reformed the army, curbed monastic landholding and melted down bronze Buddhas for coin, then campaigned successfully against the Southern Tang and the Khitan. His death left a child on the throne, and his general Zhao Kuangyin took power to found the Song.

Tongzheng (China, AD 916–AD 916).label: Tongzheng
Tongzheng (China, AD 916–AD 916).prose:
[China, AD 916–AD 916] Tongzheng. 916. Period definition from British Museum.

A single-year reign title used by Wang Jian, the former bandit and general who had carved the rich Sichuan basin out of the collapsing Tang empire and ruled it as the Former Shu kingdom. His frequent changing of era names near the end of his life reflects the restless legitimacy-seeking of the Five Dynasties warlord states, each claiming imperial dignity over a fragment of the old empire.

Daoguang (China, AD 1821–AD 1850).label: Daoguang
Daoguang (China, AD 1821–AD 1850).prose:
[China, AD 1821–AD 1850] Daoguang. 1821-1850 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Qing emperor who confronted the opium crisis, sending Lin Zexu to destroy the drug stocks at Canton and provoking the First Opium War. Defeat brought the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842: Hong Kong ceded, five ports opened, an indemnity paid, and the tributary system of foreign relations broken. Silver drained abroad, the Yellow River and Grand Canal fell into disrepair, and the rural distress that produced the Taiping rebellion was already building.

Jogen Era 976-978 (Japan, AD 976–AD 978).label: Jogen Era 976-978
Jogen Era 976-978 (Japan, AD 976–AD 978).prose: [Japan, AD 976–AD 978] Jogen Era 976-978. 976-978. Period definition from British Museum.

Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–999 BC).label: Middle Elamite
Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Iran, 1499 BC–999 BC] Middle Elamite. circa 1500 BC-1000 BC. Period normally divided into three phases; Middle Elamite I c.1500 BC-1400 BC, Middle Elamite II c.1400 BC-1200 BC, Middle Elamite III c.1200 BC-1100 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Elam's most powerful era, when kings ruling from Susa and Anshan wrote in Elamite rather than Akkadian and built on a monumental scale. Untash-Napirisha founded the sacred city of Chogha Zanbil with its huge stepped ziggurat, still the best-preserved in the world, and later Shutrukid rulers sacked Babylon and carried off the stele of Hammurabi's laws and the victory monument of Naram-Sin as trophies for Susa. Assyrian and Babylonian counterattacks eventually broke the dynasty.

Ninevite 5 (Iraq, 2999 BC–2499 BC).label: Ninevite 5
Ninevite 5 (Iraq, 2999 BC–2499 BC).prose:
[northern Mesopotamia, 2999 BC–2499 BC] Ninevite 5. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Syria, Turkey. Period within sequence excavated by Campbell-Thompson at Nineveh. Divided into incised and painted for pottery, but can be used as general chronological description c.3000-2500 B.C. for northern Mesopotamia. Period definition from British Museum.

The culture of northern Mesopotamia in the centuries after the Uruk expansion collapsed, when the region returned to smaller farming villages and modest towns while southern Sumer built cities. It is defined by its distinctive fine pottery — first painted, later carved and incised — found from the Tigris to the Khabur.
