By its end, sites like Tell Brak and Tell Leilan were growing into walled cities again, setting the stage for the Akkadian conquest of the north.

Early Iron Age late (Italy, 899 BC–779 B.node: Early Iron Age late (Italy, 899 BC–779 BC)
Early Iron Age late (Italy, 899 BC–779 B.label: Early Iron Age late
Early Iron Age late (Italy, 899 BC–779 B.prose:
[Italy, 899 BC–779 BC] Early Iron Age late. For Italy: Early Iron Age early c. 1000 BC to 880 BC. Early Iron Age late c. 900 BC to 780 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Villanovan settlements grew into genuine proto-urban centres of hundreds of hectares, with organised cemeteries ringing them. Graves become sharply unequal: some hold weapons, horse gear and imported bronzes, signalling the emergence of an aristocracy. The first Greek and Levantine pottery arrives on the Tyrrhenian coast, the beginning of contacts that would transform Italian art, writing and trade.

Tenpyo-hoji Era (Japan, AD 757–AD 765).label: Tenpyo-hoji Era
Tenpyo-hoji Era (Japan, AD 757–AD 765).prose:
[Japan, AD 757–AD 765] Tenpyo-hoji Era. 757-765. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Nakamaro reached unmatched power, installing his own candidate as Emperor Junnin and remodelling the government on Chinese lines. His rebellion against the retired Empress Kōken failed in 764 and he was killed; she retook the throne as Empress Shōtoku with the monk Dōkyō at her side.

Tenmei Era (Japan, AD 1781–AD 1789).label: Tenmei Era
Tenmei Era (Japan, AD 1781–AD 1789).prose:
[Japan, AD 1781–AD 1789] Tenmei Era. 1781-1789. Period definition from British Museum.

The Tenmei famine killed hundreds of thousands, worsened by the catastrophic 1783 eruption of Mount Asama, and triggered rice riots that tore through Edo and Osaka. The crisis brought down the powerful senior councillor Tanuma Okitsugu and ushered in Matsudaira Sadanobu's austere Kansei reforms.

Early Helladic III (Greece, 2299 BC–1999.label: Early Helladic III
Early Helladic III (Greece, 2299 BC–1999.prose:
[Greece, 2299 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic III. 2300BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

After the destructions, Messenian settlements were smaller and simpler, with apsidal houses and new dark-on-light painted pottery of the Tiryns type. Population and long-distance contacts contracted sharply. The pottery and building traditions of this phase carry directly into the Middle Helladic period.

Western Ganga Dynasty (India, AD 350–AD.label: Western Ganga Dynasty
Western Ganga Dynasty (India, AD 350–AD.prose:
[parts of Karnataka in the Deccan, AD 350–AD 1000] Western Ganga Dynasty. The Western Ganga Dynasty (c. 350-1000) ruled parts of Karnataka in the Deccan. Period definition from British Museum.

A long-lived dynasty of southern Karnataka, ruling from Kolar and later Talakad, usually as the junior partner of larger neighbours such as the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas. They were exceptional patrons of Jainism, and under them Kannada emerged as a literary language. Their most famous legacy is the 17-metre monolithic statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, carved around 983 for the Ganga minister Chavundaraya and still bathed in milk and saffron at festivals today.

Bunka Era (Japan, AD 1804–AD 1818).label: Bunka Era
Bunka Era (Japan, AD 1804–AD 1818).prose:
[Japan, AD 1804–AD 1818] Bunka Era. 1804-1818. Period definition from British Museum.

A high point of late Edo townsman culture, when Hokusai was at work, kabuki and comic fiction flourished, and the pleasure districts set the fashions of the age. Beyond the closed coast, foreign pressure was mounting: a Russian mission was rebuffed at Nagasaki, a British warship forced the harbour there, and Japanese surveyors began mapping the northern islands. Prosperity in the cities sat alongside rural distress and a shogunate increasingly unsure of how to answer the outside world.

Dawenkou culture (China, 4299 BC–2399 BC.label: Dawenkou culture
Dawenkou culture (China, 4299 BC–2399 BC.prose:
[China, 4299 BC–2399 BC] Dawenkou culture. Neolithic culture, circa 4300 BC-2400 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Farming communities in Shandong and the lower Yellow River who grew millet, kept pigs, and buried their dead with striking differences in wealth — some graves crammed with fine pottery, jade and ivory, others nearly bare. Distinctive customs included the deliberate extraction of upper teeth and the shaping of skulls. Their elegant wheel-thrown vessels and incised pottery marks anticipate the Longshan culture that followed, and the whole sequence feeds into the emergence of early Chinese states.

Eiso Era (Japan, AD 989–AD 990).label: Eiso Era
Eiso Era (Japan, AD 989–AD 990).prose:
[Japan, AD 989–AD 990] Eiso Era. 989-990. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era at the Heian court marked by the death of the regent Fujiwara no Kaneie and the passing of his offices to his son Michitaka, part of the fierce competition within the Fujiwara house to control the boy emperor Ichijo through marriage. The court culture of these decades produced the great writing of Sei Shonagon and Murasaki Shikibu.

Yarmukian (Levant, 5599 BC–4999 BC).label: Yarmukian
Yarmukian (Levant, 5599 BC–4999 BC).prose:
[Levant, 5599 BC–4999 BC] Yarmukian. The Yarmukian Culture (5600-5000 BC) was first recognised at the site of  Shaar Hagolan (Central Jordan Valley) and was named after the nearby Yarmuk River. In this period the Levant region was characterized by regional cultures and sites are distinguished by distinct forms of material culture (pottery, flint etc). Period definition from British Museum.

One of the first pottery-making cultures of the Levant, following the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic villages. At sites like Sha'ar HaGolan people lived in substantial courtyard houses along planned streets and made pottery decorated with incised herringbone bands. They also left hundreds of pebble and clay figurines with slit 'coffee-bean' eyes, among the earliest large bodies of figurative art in the region.

Early Cycladic (Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Cycladic
Early Cycladic (Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Cyclades, 3199 BC–1999 BC] Early Cycladic. The Early Cycladic period (3200BC – 2000BC) refers to material produced in the Cyclades during the Aegean Early Bronze Age. Although it is part of the tripartite scheme (Early, Middle and Late) into which the Aegean Bronze Age is conventionally divided, it is difficult to apply the same subdivisions (I,II,III) as for Early Minoan or Early Helladic. For this reason it is divided into partly overlapping cultural groups, initially defined by Colin Renfrew. The three main groups used to subdivide the period are Grotta-Pelos (q.v.), Keros-Syros (q.v.) and Phylakopi I (q.v.). Period definition from British Museum.

The islands of the Aegean supported small farming and fishing communities that became skilled sailors and metalworkers, moving obsidian, copper and marble around the sea. They are best known for the marble folded-arm figurines placed in graves, pared down to abstract simplicity and much admired by modern artists. Their trading networks laid the groundwork for the later Minoan and Mycenaean maritime world.

Tianqi (China, AD 1621–AD 1627).label: Tianqi
Tianqi (China, AD 1621–AD 1627).prose:
[China, AD 1621–AD 1627] Tianqi. 1621-1627 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The teenage Zhu Youjiao preferred carpentry to government, leaving affairs to his old wet nurse and the eunuch Wei Zhongxian, who built a secret police apparatus and had temples raised to himself while still alive. The reformist Donglin scholars who opposed him were purged, imprisoned and tortured to death, poisoning court politics for a generation. Famine, revolt and Manchu pressure on the frontier all deepened while the factions fought.

Yongle (China, AD 1403–AD 1424).label: Yongle
Yongle (China, AD 1403–AD 1424).prose:
[China, AD 1403–AD 1424] Yongle. 1403-1424 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Yongle Emperor seized the throne from his nephew and then spent two decades making the usurpation look like destiny: he moved the capital north, built the Forbidden City, reopened the Grand Canal and commissioned the vast Yongle Encyclopedia. Zheng He's treasure fleets sailed as far as East Africa, and armies pushed into Mongolia and Vietnam. The costs were enormous, and his successors pulled back from the sea.

Republic (China, AD 1912–AD 1949).label: Republic
Republic (China, AD 1912–AD 1949).prose:
[China, AD 1912–AD 1949] Republic. 1912-1949. Period definition from British Museum.

The Qing abdication left a republic on paper and warlords in practice: parliamentary government collapsed within years, and provincial militarists fought over the north while the Nationalists built a base in the south. Beneath the fighting came the May Fourth movement, vernacular literature, new universities, and the founding of both the Nationalist and Communist parties. Nanjing government, Japanese invasion and civil war followed, ending with the Communist victory and the Nationalist retreat to Taiwan.

Tu Duc (Vietnam, AD 1848–AD 1883).label: Tu Duc
Tu Duc (Vietnam, AD 1848–AD 1883).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1848–AD 1883] Tu Duc. (1848-1883) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

Tự Đức ruled as French warships arrived, and lost the southern provinces piece by piece until Cochinchina became a French colony and Tonkin fell in his last years. A conservative Confucian scholar-emperor, he persecuted Catholic missionaries and converts, giving France its pretext, and rejected the modernising proposals of reformers like Nguyễn Trường Tộ. He died childless as the court accepted a protectorate, and Vietnam's independence ended with him.

Late Christian Period I (Sudan, AD 1100–.label: Late Christian Period I
Late Christian Period I (Sudan, AD 1100–.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 1100–AD 1300] Late Christian Period I. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1100-1300. Period definition from British Museum.

Makuria's last confident centuries, when Nubian kings still ruled from Old Dongola but faced repeated Egyptian raids and mounting tribute demands. Church building continued on a reduced scale, wall paintings took on a heavier, more schematic style, and pilgrimage centres such as Banganarti drew visitors from across the middle Nile. Handmade pottery replaced much of the fine wheelmade tradition, a sign of contracting workshops and trade.

Zhenglong (China, AD 1156–AD 1161).label: Zhenglong
Zhenglong (China, AD 1156–AD 1161).prose:
[China, AD 1156–AD 1161] Zhenglong. 1156-1161 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The last era of Wanyan Liang, the Jin ruler who murdered his way to the throne, moved the capital south and razed the old Jurchen homeland centre. He launched a massive invasion of Southern Song, only for his fleet to be shattered at Caishi; his own officers then assassinated him in camp. The failure fixed the Huai River frontier between Jin and Song for decades.

Hoan Era (Japan, AD 1120–AD 1124).label: Hoan Era
Hoan Era (Japan, AD 1120–AD 1124).prose:
[Japan, AD 1120–AD 1124] Hoan Era. 1120-1124. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign-era of the late Heian court, when real power lay not with the reigning emperor but with a retired sovereign ruling from his cloistered household, and with the Fujiwara regents at the palace. Provincial warrior houses were meanwhile accumulating land and armed followings that would soon dominate the country.

Taisho Era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).label: Taisho Era
Taisho Era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).prose:
[Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926] Taisho Era. 1912-1926. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign, under an emperor too ill to govern, in which power drifted from the old oligarchs to political parties and the Diet. Cities boomed, mass newspapers and cinema spread, women entered offices and factories, and the era's liberal mood gave Japan its first genuine party cabinets and universal male suffrage. The great Kantō earthquake of 1923 levelled Tokyo and Yokohama and hardened the state's repressive instincts.

Joei Era (Japan, AD 1232–AD 1233).label: Joei Era
Joei Era (Japan, AD 1232–AD 1233).prose:
[Japan, AD 1232–AD 1233] Joei Era. 1232-1233. Period definition from British Museum.

In 1232 the Kamakura regent Hōjō Yasutoki issued the Goseibai Shikimoku, a plain-spoken code of fifty-one articles governing land disputes, inheritance and the duties of warriors. It was the first legal system written by and for the samurai rather than the imperial court, and it shaped Japanese law for centuries.

Guangxu (China, AD 1875–AD 1908).label: Guangxu
Guangxu (China, AD 1875–AD 1908).prose:
[China, AD 1875–AD 1908] Guangxu. 1875-1908 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of a boy emperor who spent most of his life under the thumb of the Empress Dowager Cixi, in decades when the Qing empire lost a war to Japan, ceded ports to European powers and faced the Boxer uprising. His backing of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898 ended with the reformers executed or exiled and the emperor confined to a palace island. He died a day before Cixi, of arsenic poisoning, leaving the dynasty three years from its end.

Early Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC.node: Early Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC–1549 BC)
Early Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC.label: Early Haftavan Period VIB
Early Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC.prose:
[Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 1899 BC–1549 BC] Early Haftavan Period VIB. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.1900BC-1550BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A Middle Bronze Age phase in the Lake Urmia basin, named from the levels at Haftavan Tepe. Its signature is the handsome painted 'Urmia ware' — dark burnished vessels with geometric designs — which links the region to painted pottery traditions running through eastern Anatolia and the Caucasus, and to the mobile, pastorally inclined societies that succeeded the Kura-Araxes world.

Later Zhao (China, AD 319–AD 351).label: Later Zhao
Later Zhao (China, AD 319–AD 351).prose:
[China, AD 319–AD 351] Later Zhao. 319-351. Period definition from British Museum.

A state founded by Shi Le, a man sold into slavery as a youth who rose to command armies and rule much of northern China during the chaos after the fall of Western Jin. His court patronised the Central Asian Buddhist monk Fotudeng, an early foothold for Buddhism among northern rulers. The dynasty ended in massacre and civil war after the tyrannical reign of Shi Hu.

Ten'yo Era (Japan, AD 1144–AD 1145).label: Ten'yo Era
Ten'yo Era (Japan, AD 1144–AD 1145).prose:
[Japan, AD 1144–AD 1145] Ten'yo Era. 1144-1145. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era in the reign of the boy-emperor Konoe, when real authority lay with the retired emperor Toba, who governed as a cloistered sovereign from outside the formal court. The rivalries among Toba's sons and consorts nursed during these years erupted a decade later in the Hōgen Disturbance, opening the door to warrior rule.

Kyoroku Era (Japan, AD 1528–AD 1532).label: Kyoroku Era
Kyoroku Era (Japan, AD 1528–AD 1532).prose:
[Japan, AD 1528–AD 1532] Kyoroku Era. 1528-1532. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign name in the middle of the Sengoku wars, when the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiharu was repeatedly driven out of Kyoto and depended on rival Hosokawa and Miyoshi warlords for protection. Real authority had passed to provincial daimyo who fought over the capital as a prize. The court continued to issue era names it had no power to enforce.

Bunpo Era (Japan, AD 1317–AD 1319).label: Bunpo Era
Bunpo Era (Japan, AD 1317–AD 1319).prose:
[Japan, AD 1317–AD 1319] Bunpo Era. 1317-1319. Period definition from British Museum.

The era of the Bunpō Compromise, a brokered agreement by which the Kamakura shogunate tried to settle the quarrel between the two branches of the imperial house by having them alternate on the throne. It brought Go-Daigo to power — the emperor who would reject the arrangement, overthrow the shogunate, and plunge Japan into the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts.

Cypro-Geometric III (Cyprus, 899 BC–749.label: Cypro-Geometric III
Cypro-Geometric III (Cyprus, 899 BC–749.prose:
[Cyprus, 899 BC–749 BC] Cypro-Geometric III. 900 BC-750 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cypriot trade expanded sharply: Black-on-Red juglets, probably carrying perfumed oil, reached Greece, Crete, the Levant and the west, while Levantine and Aegean goods flowed back. Rich tombs and the rebuilding of sanctuaries show emerging royal families, the ancestors of the historical city-kingdoms that would soon submit to Assyria.

Xiaozong (China, AD 1163–AD 1190).label: Xiaozong
Xiaozong (China, AD 1163–AD 1190).prose:
[China, AD 1163–AD 1190] Xiaozong. 1163-1190 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Usually reckoned the ablest Southern Song emperor: he cleared the name of the executed general Yue Fei, tried one campaign against the Jin, then settled for a treaty on better terms that held for decades. The peace paid for a flourishing of trade, printing and Neo-Confucian scholarship, with Zhu Xi active at court and in the academies. He ended by abdicating to his son, as his own predecessor had done.

Wuzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1308–AD 1.label: Wuzong Yuan dynasty
Wuzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1308–AD 1.prose:
[China, AD 1308–AD 1311] Wuzong Yuan dynasty. 1308-1311 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief Yuan reign that came out of a contested succession settled by military backing, and spent freely on rewards to supporters, temple building and Buddhist patronage. To pay for it the court issued a new paper currency, which quickly lost value and worsened the fiscal disorder that dogged the dynasty. His death after three years reopened the succession struggles that steadily weakened Mongol rule in China.

Zhaodi (China, 85 BC–72 BC).label: Zhaodi
Zhaodi (China, 85 BC–72 BC).prose:
[China, 85 BC–72 BC] Zhaodi. 86-73BC (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A child emperor of the Han ruled in name while the general Huo Guang held actual power, steering the empire away from the ruinously expensive wars and expansion of Emperor Wu. Taxes and labour levies were eased and frontier campaigning scaled back. The famous court debate on the state monopolies of salt and iron, later written up as the Discourses on Salt and Iron, pitted Legalist-minded officials against Confucian critics of state enterprise.

Kanpyo Era (Japan, AD 889–AD 898).label: Kanpyo Era
Kanpyo Era (Japan, AD 889–AD 898).prose:
[Japan, AD 889–AD 898] Kanpyo Era. 889-898. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Uda governed without a Fujiwara regent after Mototsune's death, raising the scholar Sugawara no Michizane to counterbalance the great house—a short-lived experiment later remembered as good government. In 894 the court cancelled the embassy to Tang China, ending two and a half centuries of official missions and turning the aristocracy inward toward a distinctly Japanese court culture.

Early Helladic I (Greece, 3199 BC–2899 B.label: Early Helladic I
Early Helladic I (Greece, 3199 BC–2899 B.prose:
[Greece, 3199 BC–2899 BC] Early Helladic I. 3200BC-2900BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Small farming hamlets in the southwest Peloponnese take up metal and new pottery shapes, the first mainland stage of the Bronze Age. Settlements were modest and scattered, with burials in simple pits and cists rather than monumental tombs. It provides the baseline against which the wealthier, more centralised communities of the following centuries stand out.

Thieu Tri (Vietnam, AD 1841–AD 1847).label: Thieu Tri
Thieu Tri (Vietnam, AD 1841–AD 1847).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1841–AD 1847] Thieu Tri. (1841-1847) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of a Nguyen emperor who inherited his father Minh Mang's centralised, Confucian state and his hostility to Christian missionaries. Persecution of Catholics continued and gave France a pretext for intervention: in 1847 French warships destroyed the Vietnamese fleet at Da Nang, an early step toward colonial conquest. He died soon after, leaving the crisis to his son Tu Duc.

Bosnian (Egypt, AD 1550–AD 1811).label: Bosnian
Bosnian (Egypt, AD 1550–AD 1811).prose: [fortress of Qasr Ibrim, AD 1550–AD 1811] Bosnian. The term Bosnian as a narrower term of Ottoman dynasty refers to a specific cultural period on the fortress of  Qasr Ibrim between 1550-1811 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Genroku Era (Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704).label: Genroku Era
Genroku Era (Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704).prose:
[Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704] Genroku Era. 1688-1704. Period definition from British Museum.

A boom time for the merchant cities, when Osaka and Edo money paid for kabuki, the puppet theatre of Chikamatsu, the novels of Ihara Saikaku, Bashō's poetry and the first great wave of ukiyo-e prints. The shogunate under Tsunayoshi debased the coinage to cover its spending and issued the notorious edicts protecting dogs and other animals. The revenge of the forty-seven rōnin in 1702 gave the age its most enduring story.

Zhiyuan Shundi (China, AD 1335–AD 1340).label: Zhiyuan Shundi
Zhiyuan Shundi (China, AD 1335–AD 1340).prose:
[China, AD 1335–AD 1340] Zhiyuan Shundi. 1335-1340 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The early years of Toghon Temür, the last Yuan emperor, when real power lay with the chancellor Bayan, who abolished the civil service examinations and pushed harshly anti-Chinese measures that alienated the literati the dynasty needed. Bayan's own nephew overthrew him and reversed course. The reprieve came too late to steady a regime already sliding toward rebellion.

Middle Minoan II (Crete, 1849 BC–1699 BC.label: Middle Minoan II
Middle Minoan II (Crete, 1849 BC–1699 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1849 BC–1699 BC] Middle Minoan II. 1850BC-1700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of the first palaces, when Phaistos and Knossos ran centralised storage and craft production and kept records with seals and Cretan Hieroglyphic script. Kamares ware reached its technical peak, thin as an eggshell and painted with swirling white, red and orange designs, and it turns up in Egypt and along the Levantine coast as evidence of Cretan trade. The phase closed with widespread destruction, probably by earthquake.

Middle Minoan (Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC).label: Middle Minoan
Middle Minoan (Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Minoan. 2000BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Crete's first palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, huge multi-storey complexes built around a central court, packed with storage magazines for oil and grain and workshops for craft production. Administrators kept accounts on clay in Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A, potters threw eggshell-thin Kamares ware painted in white and red on black, and Cretan goods travelled to Egypt and the Levant. Earthquakes levelled the palaces around 1700 BC; they were rebuilt grander still.

Zhongxi (China, AD 1032–AD 1054).label: Zhongxi
Zhongxi (China, AD 1032–AD 1054).prose:
[China, AD 1032–AD 1054] Zhongxi. 1032-1054 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The long Chongxi era of Emperor Xingzong of the Khitan Liao, a settled period of dual Khitan-Chinese administration, Buddhist temple building and the casting of Chongxi coinage. Taking advantage of Song troubles with the Tanguts, the Liao court extracted an increase in the annual payments agreed at Chanyuan without going to war. Repeated Liao campaigns against Western Xia, however, went badly.

Yuanzhen (China, AD 1295–AD 1297).label: Yuanzhen
Yuanzhen (China, AD 1295–AD 1297).prose:
[China, AD 1295–AD 1297] Yuanzhen. 1295-1297 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The first reign period of Temür Öljeytü, who succeeded his grandfather Kublai and inherited an empire that had stopped expanding. He ended the costly campaigns against Vietnam and Japan, patched up relations with rival Mongol khanates and tried to curb corruption and runaway spending. It was a short, comparatively peaceful interlude before the succession struggles that destabilised the later Yuan court.

Early Historic (India, 499 BC–AD 500).label: Early Historic
Early Historic (India, 499 BC–AD 500).prose:
[India, 499 BC–AD 500] Early Historic. The term is used to broadly define the period in India between about 500 BC - AD 500 and follows the Iron Age. It includes the periods of the Mauryan empire and the Guptas. Period definition from British Museum.

Cities returned to the subcontinent on a large scale, with fortified capitals, punch-marked coins, writing in Brahmi and Kharoshthi, and organised craft and trade guilds. Buddhism and Jainism took shape and then spread under Mauryan patronage, leaving Ashoka's rock edicts, stupas and rock-cut monasteries. Ports on both coasts traded with Rome and Southeast Asia, and the era's texts, sculpture and inscriptions form the foundation of Indian history proper.

Susa III (Iran, 3099 BC–2699 BC).label: Susa III
Susa III (Iran, 3099 BC–2699 BC).prose:
[Khuzestan, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Susa III. Khuzestan, ca 3100BC-2700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The Proto-Elamite horizon, when Susa and sites across the Iranian plateau used a still-undeciphered script of their own on thousands of accounting tablets. Distinctive glyptic art depicts animals acting as humans—lions enthroned, bulls holding vessels. The network collapsed after a few centuries, leaving Susa oriented once more toward Mesopotamia.

Cypro-Geometric (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC).label: Cypro-Geometric
Cypro-Geometric (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC] Cypro-Geometric. 1050 BC-750 BC.  The Cypro-Geometric period, some three hundred years in duration, is the first division of the Cypriot Iron Age. Settlements founded during the transitional LCIII period become the urban centres of the city-kingdoms into which the island is divided in historic times. Economic and cultural contacts with the Levantine world with are re-established (or become archaeologically visible) after a short period of isolation; contacts with the Aegean become apparent again somewhat later in this horizon. Important ceramic types include White Painted and Bichrome wares, which are decorated with geometric motifs and often occur in inventive shapes; slightly later, the distinctive Black-on-Red wares are developed on Cyprus, partly as a result of contact with the Levantine world; fine metalworking in bronze abounds, particularly in burials. Inscriptions point to the existence of Greek and Phoenician speakers on the island living alongside the local Cypriot population. Period definition from British Museum.

After the collapse of the Late Bronze Age palaces, Cyprus rebuilt around new coastal centres such as Salamis, Kition and Palaepaphos, with iron replacing bronze for tools and weapons. Greek-speaking settlers left their mark in dialect and burial customs, and a Cypriot syllabary continued to be written. Phoenicians established themselves at Kition, and by the end of the period the island's kingdoms were wealthy enough to attract Assyrian attention.

Quimbaya (Colombia, 499 BC–AD 1600).label: Quimbaya
Quimbaya (Colombia, 499 BC–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, 499 BC–AD 1600] Quimbaya. The term refers to a region of Colombia in the Middle Cauca valley and the Central Range in the Antioquia, Caldas, Risaralda and Quindio departments from 500 BC to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Goldsmiths of the middle Cauca valley whose work is among the finest ever produced in the Americas: hollow-cast flasks and lime containers of astonishing smoothness, made in a gold-copper alloy called tumbaga and finished by chemically etching the copper from the surface. Their serene, rounded human figures and the famous Quimbaya Treasure made the name famous worldwide. Spanish arrival brought conquest, disease and the looting of tombs that still continues.

Yuanyou (China, AD 1086–AD 1093).label: Yuanyou
Yuanyou (China, AD 1086–AD 1093).prose:
[China, AD 1086–AD 1093] Yuanyou. 1086-1093 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

With the young Emperor Zhezong on the throne, his grandmother Empress Dowager Gao ruled as regent and recalled Sima Guang and the conservatives, who dismantled most of Wang Anshi's New Policies within months. The reversal was itself reversed when Zhezong took power, and those who had served in these years were blacklisted as the "Yuanyou faction", their names carved on stone tablets of proscription. The bitter factionalism weakened the Song state on the eve of the Jurchen invasions.

Xuanhe (China, AD 1119–AD 1125).label: Xuanhe
Xuanhe (China, AD 1119–AD 1125).prose:
[China, AD 1119–AD 1125] Xuanhe. 1119-1125 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The final era of the Song emperor Huizong, an aesthete who catalogued the imperial painting and bronze collections, founded an academy of court artists and beggared the treasury shipping exotic rocks for his garden. Peasant and bandit uprisings spread while the court allied with the Jurchen Jin to destroy the Liao. The Jin turned on Song immediately after, and by 1127 Huizong and his son were prisoners in the north.

Hailingwang (China, AD 1149–AD 1161).label: Hailingwang
Hailingwang (China, AD 1149–AD 1161).prose:
[China, AD 1149–AD 1161] Hailingwang. 1149-1161 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Wanyan Liang, the Jin ruler stripped of imperial title after his death and demoted to "Prince of Hailing." He purged rival princes, moved the Jurchen capital south to Yanjing (modern Beijing) to govern his Chinese subjects more directly, and pushed sinicising reforms on the court. His huge invasion of the Southern Song collapsed at the Yangtze, and his own officers murdered him in camp, leaving the Song–Jin border much as it had been.

Jinki Era (China, AD 724–AD 729).label: Jinki Era
Jinki Era (China, AD 724–AD 729).prose:
[China, AD 724–AD 729] Jinki Era. 724-729. Period definition from British Museum.

The years around the accession of Emperor Shōmu, the ruler whose devotion to Buddhism would later produce the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji. The Nara court was consolidating its Chinese-style law codes, land registers and provincial administration, and the Fujiwara family was tightening its grip on the throne through marriage.

Mongol (People's Republic of China, AD 1.label: Mongol
Mongol (People's Republic of China, AD 1.prose:
[Mongolia; China; 'Abbasid empire; south Russian steppes; central Europe, AD 1206–AD 1370] Mongol. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Eastern Europe, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Kazakhstan. 1206-1370 (AH 602-AH 771). Rulers of Mongolia who conquered China, the 'Abbasid empire, the south Russian steppes and central Europe. The Mongol expansion took place under Genghis Khan in 1209 (AH 606). He took Beijing in 1215 (AH 612) thus controlling numerous commercial routes across central Asia to China. In 1220 (AH 616) Genghis Khan captured Bukhara and soon the whole of Transoxiana was part of the Mongol empire. In 1258 (AH 656) the Mongols sacked Baghdad under Hulegu grandson of Ghengis Khan and founder of the Il-Khanid dynasty (q.v.). Period definition from British Museum.

Chinggis Khan's armies swept through the steppe and the Silk Road cities of the south, folding the region into the Mongol empire and then into the Golden Horde and Chagatai realms. Nomadic pastoral life continued much as before, but trade routes, tribute systems and ruling dynasties were reorganised, and Islam spread among the steppe elite. Out of the later fragmentation came the Kazakh Khanate, the direct ancestor of the modern nation.

Hissar III (Iran, 2499 BC–1699 BC).label: Hissar III
Hissar III (Iran, 2499 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[north-east Iran, 2499 BC–1699 BC] Hissar III. Period based on the excavated sequence at this site in north-east Iran and corresponding to an approximate date of c. 2500-1700 BC, or the Middle Bronze Age in this region. Period definition from British Museum.

The final and richest phase at Tepe Hisar on the northern Iranian plateau, marked by mass-produced burnished grey pottery and burials stocked with gold, silver, lapis and alabaster. The town sat on the route linking Central Asia to Mesopotamia, and its metalwork shows close ties to the Oxus civilisation and to Turkmenistan. A destruction level and eventual abandonment closed the site, part of a wider collapse of plateau towns at the end of the third millennium.

Shengzong (China, AD 982–AD 1031).label: Shengzong
Shengzong (China, AD 982–AD 1031).prose:
[China, AD 982–AD 1031] Shengzong. 982-1031 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The longest reign of the Liao dynasty, when the Khitan state was at its height and its Chinese-style administration matured alongside the tribal one. In 1005 his armies drove deep into Song territory and extracted the Treaty of Chanyuan, under which the Song paid annual silver and silk to a northern neighbour it had to recognise as an equal — buying a century of peace along a frontier that had been at war for decades.

Chowa Era (Japan, AD 1012–AD 1017).label: Chowa Era
Chowa Era (Japan, AD 1012–AD 1017).prose:
[Japan, AD 1012–AD 1017] Chowa Era. 1012-1017. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Sanjō, an adult sovereign who resisted Fujiwara no Michinaga's direction, was worn down by palace fires, failing eyesight and relentless pressure until he abdicated in favour of Michinaga's grandson. Michinaga then took the regency himself before handing it to his son Yorimichi, completing the family's total command of the throne.

Sub-Mycenaean (Greece, 1059 BC–999 BC).label: Sub-Mycenaean
Sub-Mycenaean (Greece, 1059 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1059 BC–999 BC] Sub-Mycenaean. 1060BC-1000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The bleak aftermath of the palatial collapse, known mainly from small cemeteries of simple cist graves around Athens, Salamis and Argos, with clumsy undecorated pots and modest bronze pins and fibulae. Population, settlement size and long-distance contact all shrank sharply, and Linear B writing disappeared entirely. It is the trough between the Mycenaean world and the Protogeometric recovery, and a key exhibit in debates about how societies lose complexity.

La Tène A (Europe, 449 BC–399 BC).label: La Tène A
La Tène A (Europe, 449 BC–399 BC).prose:
[Europe, 449 BC–399 BC] La Tène A. "La Tène I: The term is used in reference to material culture from Europe dating from 450 BC-320 BC. It corresponds, broadly speaking, to the alternative classifications La Tène A (450 BC-400 BC) and part of La Tène B (400 BC-275 BC).". Period definition from British Museum.

The opening phase of the La Tène Iron Age, when a wealthy elite in the Rhine, Moselle and Marne regions buried its dead with two-wheeled chariots, gold neck-rings and imported Etruscan and Greek wine service. Out of contact with those Mediterranean imports came the Early Style of Celtic art, which took palmettes, lotus buds and lion masks and reworked them into the swirling, ambiguous designs seen on the Glauberg and Reinheim finds. The old Hallstatt hillfort centres further west collapsed at about this time, and power shifted north.

Mac dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592).label: Mac dynasty
Mac dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592] Mac dynasty. Vietnamese dynasty, 1527-1592. Period definition from British Museum.

Mạc Đăng Dung, a court official and former palace guard, deposed the Lê emperor and seized the throne, holding the northern Red River delta from Đông Kinh. Loyalists led by the Nguyễn and Trịnh families restored a rival Lê court in the south, and decades of civil war followed until the Mạc lost the capital and retreated to a rump domain at Cao Bằng. The split began the long division of Vietnam between competing warlord houses.

Classic Christian Period (Sudan, AD 850–.label: Classic Christian Period
Classic Christian Period (Sudan, AD 850–.prose:
[Nubia; Sudan, AD 850–AD 1100] Classic Christian Period. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 850-1100. It is subdivided into an earlier and a later phase designated Classic Christian Period I (AD 850-1000) and Classic Christian Period II (AD 1000-1100) respectively. Period definition from British Museum.

The Nubian kingdoms, above all Makuria with its capital at Old Dongola, reached their height as Christian states holding their own against Muslim Egypt under the terms of the baqt treaty. Builders raised red-brick churches and monasteries, and painters covered their walls with royal and saintly portraits, most famously at Faras. Nubian, Greek and Coptic were all written, and the period represents the fullest flowering of Christian culture on the middle Nile.

Shogen Era (Japan, AD 1259–AD 1260).label: Shogen Era
Shogen Era (Japan, AD 1259–AD 1260).prose: [Japan, AD 1259–AD 1260] Shogen Era. 1259-1260. Period definition from British Museum.

Renzong (China, AD 1022–AD 1063).label: Renzong
Renzong (China, AD 1022–AD 1063).prose:
[China, AD 1022–AD 1063] Renzong. 1022-1063 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The longest reign of the Northern Song, and the period people later looked back on as the dynasty's golden age: a densely bureaucratic state run by examination-trained scholar-officials, a booming money economy with the first government paper currency, and the world's first movable-type printing described by Bi Sheng. Costly stalemate with the Tangut Xia state prompted Fan Zhongyan's short-lived Qingli reforms, a rehearsal for the bigger reform battles to come. Su Shi, Ouyang Xiu and Sima Guang all began their careers under him.

Katei Era (Japan, AD 1235–AD 1238).label: Katei Era
Katei Era (Japan, AD 1235–AD 1238).prose:
[Japan, AD 1235–AD 1238] Katei Era. 1235-1238. Period definition from British Museum.

The Kamakura shogunate under the regent Hōjō Yasutoki was applying the new Goseibai Shikimoku law code, the first legal system written by and for the warrior class rather than the court. Kyoto meanwhile struggled with famine and with armed monks from the great temples pressing their demands on the government.

Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1849.label: Middle Helladic I
Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1849.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1849 BC] Middle Helladic I. 2000BC-1850BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The opening of a subdued era on the Greek mainland, following widespread destruction and abandonment at the end of the Early Bronze Age. Settlements are small and simply built, grave goods are few, and the characteristic burnished grey Minyan pottery becomes standard — a material culture that gives little hint of the Mycenaean wealth to come.

Yangshao culture (China, 4999 BC–2999 BC.label: Yangshao culture
Yangshao culture (China, 4999 BC–2999 BC.prose:
[China, 4999 BC–2999 BC] Yangshao culture. Neolithic culture circa 5000 BC-3000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Farming villages along the middle Yellow River, growing foxtail millet, keeping pigs and living in semi-subterranean houses clustered around larger communal buildings, as at Banpo. They are best known for handsome red pottery painted in black with fish, frogs, birds and swirling geometric bands. This long Neolithic tradition laid the demographic and agricultural foundations of later Chinese civilisation.

Kanpo Era (Japan, AD 1741–AD 1744).label: Kanpo Era
Kanpo Era (Japan, AD 1741–AD 1744).prose:
[Japan, AD 1741–AD 1744] Kanpo Era. 1741-1744. Period definition from British Museum.

The closing years of Tokugawa Yoshimune's rule, when the shogunate consolidated decades of Kyōhō reform into a compiled body of law and pushed on with astronomical and calendrical work in Edo. In 1741 a collapse of the Oshima-Ōshima volcano sent tsunami waves along the Japan Sea coast, drowning well over a thousand people.

Huizong (China, AD 1101–AD 1125).label: Huizong
Huizong (China, AD 1101–AD 1125).prose:
[China, AD 1101–AD 1125] Huizong. 1101-1125 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

An emperor who would rather have been an artist: he painted birds and flowers, invented the elegant 'slender gold' calligraphic style, ran an imperial painting academy, and bankrupted the treasury shipping exotic rocks to his garden in Kaifeng. His government's Daoist extravagance and factional politics coincided with a disastrous alliance with the Jurchen Jin against the Liao. The Jin turned on him, and he died a prisoner in Manchuria - the end of the Northern Song.

Romano-British (England, AD 43–AD 410).label: Romano-British
Romano-British (England, AD 43–AD 410).prose:
[Britain, AD 43–AD 410] Romano-British. The term is used for material culture which can be assigned to Britain during the period of Roman administration, AD 43 to circa AD 410. Period definition from British Museum.

The hybrid culture that formed when British communities lived under Roman rule – people who wore brooches in native styles, worshipped gods with paired Celtic and Roman names, and lived in towns and villas from Silchester to Fishbourne. Wealth was uneven: the villa-rich south looked very different from the militarised north. The label ends with the collapse of Roman administration in the early fifth century.

Tenpyo-kampo Era (Japan, AD 749–AD 749).label: Tenpyo-kampo Era
Tenpyo-kampo Era (Japan, AD 749–AD 749).prose:
[Japan, AD 749–AD 749] Tenpyo-kampo Era. 749. Period definition from British Museum.

A single year, created and then swiftly replaced because of an auspicious event: the discovery of gold in the province of Mutsu, the first found in Japan. The gold gilded the newly cast Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji, and Emperor Shōmu, treating it as heaven's approval, abdicated in favour of his daughter Kōken.

Ansei Era (Japan, AD 1854–AD 1860).label: Ansei Era
Ansei Era (Japan, AD 1854–AD 1860).prose:
[Japan, AD 1854–AD 1860] Ansei Era. 1854-1860. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era crowded with disasters and decisions that undid the shogunate: catastrophic earthquakes, a cholera epidemic carried in by foreign ships, and the treaties that ended two centuries of restricted contact with the outside world. The commercial treaties opened ports to American and European traders on terms Japan could not control, wrecking the currency and inflaming samurai opinion. Out of the anger came the slogan "revere the emperor, expel the barbarians" and the political violence that led to the Meiji Restoration.

Taiding (China, AD 1323–AD 1328).label: Taiding
Taiding (China, AD 1323–AD 1328).prose:
[China, AD 1323–AD 1328] Taiding. 1323-1328 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era of Yesün Temür, a Mongol prince raised on the steppe who took the Yuan throne after the assassination of his predecessor. His court leaned on Mongol and Central Asian officials rather than Chinese literati, and his death at Shangdu triggered a violent succession war between rival capitals that further weakened the dynasty.

Kien Phuc (Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1884).label: Kien Phuc
Kien Phuc (Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1884).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1884] Kien Phuc. (1884) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

A boy emperor installed by the regents Ton That Thuyet and Nguyen Van Tuong during the chaos that followed the French seizure of Hue, he reigned only months before dying at fifteen. His short rule bracketed the Treaty of Hue that made Annam and Tonkin French protectorates. His death brought the young Ham Nghi to the throne and, soon after, the anti-French Can Vuong uprising.

Phrygian (Turkey, 899 BC–545 BC).label: Phrygian
Phrygian (Turkey, 899 BC–545 BC).prose:
[west central Turkey, 899 BC–545 BC] Phrygian. An Iron Age culture of west central Turkey named after the kingdom of Phrygia (c900-700 BC) with a capital at Gordion. Invasions by Cimmerians, nomads from the Ukraine and Russia, around 700BC culminated in the capture of Gordion in 696 BC, but Phrygian art and culture continued to flourish. Lydians then took over the territory in the 620s BC until the capture of Sardis by king Cyrus II in 546 BC when Lydia became part of the Achaemenid empire. Period definition from British Museum.

A kingdom centred on Gordion in the Anatolian highlands, remembered through the legends of Midas and the Gordian knot, and known archaeologically for monumental rock-cut façades, huge burial mounds and fine inlaid wooden furniture. Phrygians adapted an alphabet related to the Greek one, leaving some of the earliest inscriptions in inner Anatolia. Cimmerian raids in the seventh century broke royal power, and the region eventually fell under Lydian and then Persian rule.

Eikan Era (Japan, AD 983–AD 985).label: Eikan Era
Eikan Era (Japan, AD 983–AD 985).prose:
[Japan, AD 983–AD 985] Eikan Era. 983-985. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era in the middle Heian court, notable for the monk Genshin's completion of the Ojoyoshu, a vivid account of the Buddhist hells and of rebirth in Amida's Pure Land. The book shaped Japanese religious imagination and art for centuries and helped set the devotional currents that later produced the Pure Land schools.

Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC) [.label: Old Babylonian
Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC) [.prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia between approximately 2000 BC-1600 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.

Middle Minoan IB (Crete, 1949 BC–1849 BC.label: Middle Minoan IB
Middle Minoan IB (Crete, 1949 BC–1849 BC.prose:
[Crete, 1949 BC–1849 BC] Middle Minoan IB. 1950BC-1850BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The first palaces were built at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, each a large complex of storerooms, workshops and shrines wrapped around a rectangular central court. Administration begins to leave traces in clay sealings and early Cretan Hieroglyphic signs, and fine polychrome Kamares pottery comes into its own.

Middle Babylonian (Iraq, 1599 BC–999 BC).label: Middle Babylonian
Middle Babylonian (Iraq, 1599 BC–999 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–999 BC] Middle Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. The term is used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia between approximately 1600 BC-1000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Under the Kassite dynasty Babylonia enjoyed unusual stability, its kings corresponding as equals with the pharaohs and the Hittites and rebuilding the great temples of Nippur and Babylon. Land grants were recorded on kudurru boundary stones carved with divine symbols, and scribes fixed the classic versions of Babylonian literature, including Gilgamesh. Elamite invaders sacked Babylon and carried off the statue of Marduk; Nebuchadnezzar I later won it back.

Eiman Era (Japan, AD 1165–AD 1166).label: Eiman Era
Eiman Era (Japan, AD 1165–AD 1166).prose:
[Japan, AD 1165–AD 1166] Eiman Era. 1165-1166. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era of rapid succession at court: the young emperor Nijo died and the throne passed to an infant, leaving real power in the hands of retired emperors and, increasingly, of Taira no Kiyomori. Within a few years the Taira would dominate the government outright, the first warrior house to do so.

Shahi (Pakistan, AD 750–AD 850).label: Shahi
Shahi (Pakistan, AD 750–AD 850).prose:
[Kabul to Punjab and Kashmir; Pakistan, AD 750–AD 850] Shahi. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, India, Pakistan. Dynasty known as Turki Shahi, ruling from Kabul and established as far as Punjab and Kashmir, circa 750 - 850 AD. Became known as Hindu Shahi after they moved capital to Ohind on Indus river in the North-West Froniter (Pakistan) following the capture of Kabul by Arab general Ya'qub b. Layth in 871 AD. On coins they used the titles Spalapati Deva, Samanta Deva and Vakka Deva. Overthrown by Mahmud of Ghazna [q.v.] in a series of campaigns between 1018 and 1026. Period definition from British Museum.

Turkic rulers based at Kabul and Gandhara held the mountain passes against Arab armies pushing east from Sistan, keeping the Indus borderlands outside the caliphate for generations. Their coinage, Buddhist and Hindu shrines and hilltop fortresses reflect a frontier culture blending Iranian, Turkic and Indian traditions. Their line was eventually supplanted by the Hindu Shahis, who fought the same ground against Mahmud of Ghazni.

Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC).label: Late Minoan II
Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC] Late Minoan II. 1450BC-1400BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Knossos alone functioned as a palace, and its rulers were Greek-speaking Mycenaeans who kept inventories on clay tablets in Linear B — the earliest readable Greek. Burials changed too, with 'warrior graves' containing swords, helmets and boar's-tusk gear appearing around the city. Pottery turned formal and imposing in the Palace Style, adapting old Minoan motifs to a stiffer, more heraldic taste.

Choryaku Era (Japan, AD 1037–AD 1040).label: Choryaku Era
Choryaku Era (Japan, AD 1037–AD 1040).prose:
[Japan, AD 1037–AD 1040] Choryaku Era. 1037-1040. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Go-Suzaku reigned with Fujiwara no Yorimichi as regent, at the height of the Fujiwara house's control of the throne through marriage. Armed monks from Enryaku-ji and other great temples repeatedly descended on the capital to press their demands, exposing how little coercive force the civil government actually commanded.

Bunji Era (Japan, AD 1185–AD 1190).label: Bunji Era
Bunji Era (Japan, AD 1185–AD 1190).prose:
[Japan, AD 1185–AD 1190] Bunji Era. 1185-1190. Period definition from British Museum.

The years in which Minamoto no Yoritomo turned military victory into a system of government. With the Taira destroyed, he obtained imperial sanction to appoint provincial constables and estate stewards across Japan, planting warrior authority inside the old court order. His brother Yoshitsune was hunted down and the Northern Fujiwara of Hiraizumi annihilated, leaving Yoritomo unchallenged on the eve of the Kamakura shogunate's formal founding.

Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.label: Late Cycladic II
Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 B.prose:
[Greece, 1499 BC–1399 BC] Late Cycladic II. 1500BC-1400BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The generations after the Theran eruption, when island settlements rebuilt on a smaller scale and Minoan influence gave way to Mycenaean. Pottery, burial customs and imports increasingly point towards the mainland palaces rather than Crete. Phylakopi and Ayia Irini remained the main harbours, now nodes in a Mycenaean-run trade network.

Shizong (China, AD 947–AD 951).label: Shizong
Shizong (China, AD 947–AD 951).prose:
[China, AD 947–AD 951] Shizong. 947-951 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Yelü Ruan was acclaimed emperor of the Liao by the army as it withdrew from its brief, disastrous occupation of the Chinese capital at Kaifeng, and he spent his short reign fighting off Khitan rivals who disputed the succession. He was murdered at a hunting camp in 951 while preparing another campaign against the Chinese south — one of several violent successions that dogged the Khitan state before it settled into stability.

Liao dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 1125).label: Liao dynasty
Liao dynasty (China, AD 907–AD 1125).prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 1125] Liao dynasty. 907-1125. Period definition from British Museum.

The Khitan founded a dual empire, governing Chinese farmers through a Chinese-style bureaucracy and their own tribal followers by steppe custom, with a court that moved seasonally between five capitals. Their armies extracted humiliating annual payments of silk and silver from the Song, and their name gave Europe the word 'Cathay'. Liao tombs have yielded gilt-silver funerary masks, wire body suits and vivid wall paintings of hunting and feasting; the Jurchen destroyed the dynasty in 1125.

Duptala (India, AD 855–AD 939).label: Duptala
Duptala (India, AD 855–AD 939).prose: [Kashmir , AD 855–AD 939] Duptala. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. Dynasty ruling in Kashmir c. AD 855-939. Period definition from British Museum.

Genkyu Era (Japan, AD 1204–AD 1206).label: Genkyu Era
Genkyu Era (Japan, AD 1204–AD 1206).prose:
[Japan, AD 1204–AD 1206] Genkyu Era. 1204-1206. Period definition from British Museum.

The Kamakura shogunate was still settling its internal quarrels: the young shogun Sanetomo held office while the Hōjō family fought off rivals and tightened its grip on the regency. In the same span the court completed the Shin Kokin Wakashū, the great imperial poetry anthology of the age, showing that Kyoto's cultural authority survived the loss of its political power.

Namazga IV (Turkmenistan, 2999 BC–2499 B.label: Namazga IV
Namazga IV (Turkmenistan, 2999 BC–2499 B.prose: [Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, 2999 BC–2499 BC] Namazga IV. Term derived from Soviet excavations at the type-site of Namazga-depe in south-west Turkmenistan, and dating to ca 3000-2500 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Kamakura Period (Japan, AD 1185–AD 1333).label: Kamakura Period
Kamakura Period (Japan, AD 1185–AD 1333).prose:
[Japan, AD 1185–AD 1333] Kamakura Period. 1185-1333. Period definition from British Museum.

Power shifted from the imperial court in Kyoto to a warrior government at Kamakura, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo and soon controlled by the Hōjō regents. Samurai law, land stewardship and vassalage were formalised, while new Buddhist movements — Pure Land, Nichiren and Zen — brought salvation within reach of ordinary people. Two Mongol invasion fleets were beaten back with the help of storms, but the cost of defence left the regime unable to reward its warriors and hastened its fall.

Tonghe (China, AD 983–AD 1011).label: Tonghe
Tonghe (China, AD 983–AD 1011).prose:
[China, AD 983–AD 1011] Tonghe. 983-1011 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The long reign-era of the Liao emperor Shengzong, dominated in its early years by the formidable regent Empress Dowager Xiao Chuo, who overhauled the law codes, taxation and the dual Khitan-Chinese administration. It culminated in the invasion of Song China and the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005, which bought a century of peace in exchange for annual Song payments of silver and silk and fixed the northern frontier as a diplomatic rather than a military problem.

Late Medieval (Europe, AD 1050–AD 1500).label: Late Medieval
Late Medieval (Europe, AD 1050–AD 1500).prose:
[Europe, AD 1050–AD 1500] Late Medieval. The term is used for the period from about 1050 to about 1500.  N.B. For pottery of this period, the term 'Medieval' rather than 'Late Medieval' is used.  For all European coins, the term 'Medieval' (rather than the Narrow terms 'Early Medieval' and 'Late Medieval') is used to cover the period c. 400 - c. 1500.  For all European coins, the term 'Medieval' (rather than the Narrow Terms 'Early Medieval' and 'Late Medieval') is used as a general term for the period c. 400 to c. 1500. Other term can also be entered, such as 'Burgundian'. Period definition from British Museum.

Bulgaria spent much of this stretch inside the Byzantine Empire after the fall of the First Bulgarian state, then broke free in 1185 to build a Second Empire ruled from Tarnovo, whose churches, painted tombs and silver coinage mark a confident revival. Ivan Asen II briefly made it the dominant power in the Balkans before Mongol raids, noble feuding and territorial splintering wore it down. Ottoman armies took Tarnovo and then Vidin, ending Bulgarian independence for nearly five centuries.

Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1849 BC–1699.label: Middle Helladic II
Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1849 BC–1699.prose:
[Greece, 1849 BC–1699 BC] Middle Helladic II. 1850BC-1700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Mainland Greek villages of small mudbrick houses, cist-grave cemeteries and plain, wheel-made grey 'Minyan' pottery, materially far poorer than Minoan Crete across the sea. Communities like Lerna, Asine and Kolonna on Aegina were farming settlements with modest hierarchies, though Aegina's fortified town shows some were already trading widely. The apparent simplicity is deceptive: this is the society out of which Mycenaean Greece grew.

Late Minoan IA (Crete, 1599 BC–1499 BC).label: Late Minoan IA
Late Minoan IA (Crete, 1599 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Minoan IA. 1600BC-1500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Palaces and villas across Crete were richly decorated with frescoes, and potters favoured flowing floral designs on light grounds. Minoan style dominated the southern Aegean, visible in the wall paintings of Akrotiri on Thera, which was buried by the volcano's eruption in this phase. Debate over the eruption's date and its consequences for Crete remains one of the sharpest arguments in Aegean archaeology.

Taihe Jin dynasty (China, AD 1201–AD 120.label: Taihe Jin dynasty
Taihe Jin dynasty (China, AD 1201–AD 120.prose:
[China, AD 1201–AD 1208] Taihe Jin dynasty. 1201-1208 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The mature years of Jurchen rule in north China under Emperor Zhangzong, marked by the promulgation of the Taihe legal code, a flourishing of Chinese-style scholarship and painting at the Jin court, and mounting problems with Yellow River flooding and currency. It closed with the Song invasion of 1206, which the Jin repelled decisively, and with the first stirrings of Mongol power on the northern frontier.

Jiaqing (China, AD 1796–AD 1820).label: Jiaqing
Jiaqing (China, AD 1796–AD 1820).prose:
[China, AD 1796–AD 1820] Jiaqing. 1796-1820 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Qing emperor who inherited an empire that looked magnificent and was quietly breaking down. He began by forcing his father's corrupt favourite Heshen to commit suicide, then spent years and vast sums crushing the White Lotus rebellion and clearing pirate fleets from the south coast. Population pressure, official corruption and the first serious opium prohibitions all date from these decades.

Kan'ei Era (Japan, AD 1624–AD 1644).label: Kan'ei Era
Kan'ei Era (Japan, AD 1624–AD 1644).prose:
[Japan, AD 1624–AD 1644] Kan'ei Era. 1624-1644. Period definition from British Museum.

The Tokugawa order hardened into its lasting shape: alternate attendance was made compulsory for daimyo, Christianity was crushed after the Shimabara Rebellion, and foreign contact was reduced to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. A standard copper coinage, the Kan'ei tsūhō, was issued and stayed in circulation for two centuries. Famine at the era's end pushed the government into new controls on peasant land and crops.

Almohad dynasty (Morocco, AD 1130–AD 126.label: Almohad dynasty
Almohad dynasty (Morocco, AD 1130–AD 126.prose:
[North Africa and Spain, AD 1130–AD 1269] Almohad dynasty. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Gibraltar, Morocco, Portugal, Spain. The Almohad dynasty ruled in North Africa and Spain from AD 1130-1269. Period definition from British Museum.

A Berber reform movement from the High Atlas, preaching a rigorous doctrine of God's unity, overthrew the Almoravids and built the largest state the Maghreb has ever known, stretching from Marrakesh to Tripoli and across into al-Andalus. Its court patronised Ibn Rushd and Ibn Tufayl and raised the Kutubiyya and Giralda minarets, whose austere geometry set the style of western Islamic architecture. Defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 broke its hold on Spain, and the empire fragmented into the successor sultanates of Morocco, Tlemcen and Tunis.

Sulayhid dynasty (Yemen, AD 1047–AD 1138.label: Sulayhid dynasty
Sulayhid dynasty (Yemen, AD 1047–AD 1138.prose:
[Yemen, AD 1047–AD 1138] Sulayhid dynasty. 1047-1138 (AH 439-AH 532). Ima'ili dynasty in the Yemen and vassals of the Fatimids of Egypt who defeated the Abasyian slave dynasty of the Najahids of Tihama and by 1063 (AH 455 had captured San'a from the Zaydi Imams. Period definition from British Museum.

An Isma'ili Shi'i dynasty that ruled much of Yemen as allies of the Fatimid caliphs in Cairo, controlling Sana'a, Aden and the pilgrim routes. Its most famous figure is Queen Arwa, who governed for decades from Jibla, built mosques and roads, and was recognised as a religious authority—an unusually powerful woman in the medieval Islamic world. The dynasty's missionary networks helped seed Isma'ili communities in western India.

Early Quimbaya (Colombia, 499 BC–AD 600).label: Early Quimbaya
Early Quimbaya (Colombia, 499 BC–AD 600).prose:
[Colombia, 499 BC–AD 600] Early Quimbaya. The term refers to a cultural period and style of the Quimbaya region of Colombia in the Middle Cauca valley and the Central Range in the Antioquia, Caldas, Risaralda and Quindio departments from 500 BC to 600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

In the middle Cauca valley, goldsmiths produced some of the most technically accomplished metalwork in the Americas — cast lime flasks, helmets and serene seated figures in a high-karat gold-copper alloy, made by lost-wax casting and depletion gilding. The objects come mostly from shaft tombs and accompanied elite burials in scattered chiefdoms rather than a single state. Spanish looting and later collecting scattered the finest pieces across European museums.

Tianzuo (China, AD 1101–AD 1125).label: Tianzuo
Tianzuo (China, AD 1101–AD 1125).prose:
[China, AD 1101–AD 1125] Tianzuo. 1101-1125 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The last Liao emperor was a keen hunter with little appetite for government, and when a Jurchen chieftain named Aguda refused to dance at his fishing feast the resulting revolt destroyed the empire. Jurchen armies took the Liao capitals one after another, the Song joined in hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures and got the Jin invasion instead, and Tianzuo was hunted down and captured in the desert. Khitan survivors fled west and founded the Qara Khitai in Central Asia.

Jiryaku Era (China, AD 1065–AD 1069).label: Jiryaku Era
Jiryaku Era (China, AD 1065–AD 1069).prose: [China, AD 1065–AD 1069] Jiryaku Era. 1065-1069. Period definition from British Museum.

Kyoho Era (Japan, AD 1716–AD 1736).label: Kyoho Era
Kyoho Era (Japan, AD 1716–AD 1736).prose:
[Japan, AD 1716–AD 1736] Kyoho Era. 1716-1736. Period definition from British Museum.

The shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune launched a sweeping programme of reform: austerity at court, a fixed land tax, legal codification, a petition box for commoners' complaints, and the cautious lifting of the ban on Western books. He also encouraged new crops and land reclamation to steady the rice economy on which samurai stipends depended. The great famine of 1732 in western Japan showed the limits of the effort, but the reforms became the model every later Tokugawa administration measured itself against.

Tenju Era (Japan, AD 1375–AD 1381).label: Tenju Era
Tenju Era (Japan, AD 1375–AD 1381).prose:
[Japan, AD 1375–AD 1381] Tenju Era. 1375-1381. Period definition from British Museum.

An era proclaimed by the Southern Court under Emperor Chōkei during the long dynastic split, ignored by the rival Northern Court in Kyoto, which counted the same years by different names. By this stage the Southern loyalists were a shrinking mountain force in Yoshino and Kyushu, and the Ashikaga shogunate held the capital.

Mycenaean (Greece, 1599 BC–1059 BC).label: Mycenaean
Mycenaean (Greece, 1599 BC–1059 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1599 BC–1059 BC] Mycenaean. The term ‘Mycenaean' was originally used to describe Greek Bronze Age material of the period 1600BC-1060BC , following the discoveries made at the site of Mycenae by Heinrich Schliemann in the 19th century. Subsequently the term Helladic was introduced for material produced on mainland Greece during the Bronze Age, as a counterpart to Minoan and Cycladic. However, ‘Mycenaean’ continues to be used to describe Late Bronze Age Greek material culture, particularly that relating to the palatial era, when sites such as Mycenae flourished.  The term 'Mycenaean' is used in preference to ‘Late Helladic’. Where a specific 'Late Helladic' sub-division term (such as 'Late Helladic I') can be defined, particularly in the case of pottery, the specific sub-division term should be used instead of 'Mycenaean'. Period definition from British Museum.

Mainland Greece moved from farming villages to fortified palace centres at Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns, ruled by warrior elites buried with gold masks, weapons and imported luxuries. Their scribes kept accounts in Linear B, the earliest written Greek, recording rations, livestock and offerings to gods later worshipped in the classical world. The palaces burned around 1200 BC and writing vanished with them, but memories of these citadels survived to become the world of Homer's epics.

Chimu-Inca (Peru, AD 1470–AD 1660).label: Chimu-Inca
Chimu-Inca (Peru, AD 1470–AD 1660).prose:
[Peru, AD 1470–AD 1660] Chimu-Inca. 1470-1660. This refers to the fusion of the Chimu and Inca cultures after the conquest of the Chimu by the Inca. Period definition from British Museum.

After the Inca conquest of the north coast, local potters and metalworkers kept their old shapes and black burnished finish but adopted Inca forms such as the aryballos jar — a hybrid style archaeologists use to date sites to the imperial and early colonial decades. The blending shows how the Inca ruled through existing craft traditions and elites rather than replacing them, and the style outlived the empire itself under Spanish rule.

Ten'o Era (Japan, AD 781–AD 782).label: Ten'o Era
Ten'o Era (Japan, AD 781–AD 782).prose:
[Japan, AD 781–AD 782] Ten'o Era. 781-782. Period definition from British Museum.

A one-year era that saw the aged Emperor Kōnin abdicate to his son Kanmu, one of the most consequential successions in early Japanese history. Kanmu would go on to break with the entrenched temples and aristocracy of Nara by moving the capital, ultimately founding Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794.

Early Dynastic III (Iraq, 2599 BC–2299 B.label: Early Dynastic III
Early Dynastic III (Iraq, 2599 BC–2299 B.prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 2599 BC–2299 BC] Early Dynastic III. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. A term used to describe the culture of southern Mesopotamia between approximately 2600 BC and the establishment of the Akkadian empire around 2300 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The richest phase of the early city-state era, ending with conquest by Sargon of Akkad. Royal inscriptions become genuinely historical — border disputes between Lagash and Umma are recorded in detail — and cuneiform is used for literature, hymns and law. The Royal Cemetery of Ur, with its lyres, gold headdresses and mass retainer burials, dates to these centuries.

Rasulid dynasty (Yemen, AD 1229–AD 1454).label: Rasulid dynasty
Rasulid dynasty (Yemen, AD 1229–AD 1454).prose:
[Yemen, AD 1229–AD 1454] Rasulid dynasty. 1229-1454 (AH 626-AH 858). Dynasty in Yemen descended from Rasul, a Turkman of Oghuz origin, employed as an envoy (rasul) by the 'Abbasid caliphs. Period definition from British Museum.

Rulers of Yemen from Ta'izz and Zabid who presided on the country's most prosperous medieval era, controlling Aden at the hinge of the Indian Ocean trade in spices, textiles and horses. The sultans were themselves scholars, writing on medicine, astronomy, agriculture, horse-breeding and genealogy, and they endowed madrasas whose ornate brickwork and carved stucco still stand. Their fall left Yemen fragmented among rival tribal and imam-led powers.

Bunroku Era (Japan, AD 1592–AD 1596).label: Bunroku Era
Bunroku Era (Japan, AD 1592–AD 1596).prose:
[Japan, AD 1592–AD 1596] Bunroku Era. 1592-1596. Period definition from British Museum.

Hideyoshi, master of a newly unified Japan, launched a vast invasion of Korea aimed ultimately at Ming China. Japanese armies took Seoul and Pyongyang within months, then were bled by Korean guerrillas, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle-ship fleet cutting their supply lines, and a Chinese relief army. The campaign settled into stalemate and fruitless peace talks, devastating Korea and draining the resources of Hideyoshi's regime.

Kaho Era (Japan, AD 1094–AD 1096).label: Kaho Era
Kaho Era (Japan, AD 1094–AD 1096).prose:
[Japan, AD 1094–AD 1096] Kaho Era. 1094-1096. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief Heian era in the reign of the young Emperor Horikawa, when actual authority rested with his father Shirakawa, ruling as a retired "cloistered emperor" — the arrangement that sidelined the Fujiwara regents and shaped court politics for the next century.

Third Dynasty of Ur (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999.node: Third Dynasty of Ur (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999 BC)
Third Dynasty of Ur (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999.label: Third Dynasty of Ur
Third Dynasty of Ur (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999.prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC] Third Dynasty of Ur. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Mesopotamia. With his capital at Ur, Ur-Nammu established his control over southern Mesopotamia around 2100 BC. Ur-Nammu and his descendants ruled until approximately 2000 BC when the kingdom collapsed owing to invasion and rebellion. Period definition from British Museum.

A short-lived empire that reunited southern Mesopotamia under Ur-Nammu and his son Shulgi, remembered for the great stepped ziggurat at Ur and the oldest surviving law code. Its administration was obsessively documented: tens of thousands of clay tablets record livestock, rations, labour and taxes, giving an unmatched view of how an ancient bureaucratic state actually worked. Sumerian was cultivated as a literary language even as Amorite pressure and an Elamite attack brought the dynasty down.

Jingming (China, AD 500–AD 503).label: Jingming
Jingming (China, AD 500–AD 503).prose: [China, AD 500–AD 503] Jingming. 500-503 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Jingzong (China, AD 969–AD 982).label: Jingzong
Jingzong (China, AD 969–AD 982).prose:
[China, AD 969–AD 982] Jingzong. 969-982 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Khitan Liao emperor who restored stability after a period of murderous palace politics, leaning heavily on Chinese-style administration and on his formidable consort Xiao Yanyan. She ruled as regent after his death and led the campaigns that forced the Song to terms in 1005.

Traikutaka dynasty (India, AD 388–AD 480.label: Traikutaka dynasty
Traikutaka dynasty (India, AD 388–AD 480.prose:
[Gujarat, AD 388–AD 480] Traikutaka dynasty. Successors to the Western Satraps in part of Gujarat. The dynasty is only known from coins and a few dated inscriptions ranging between AD 388 to AD 480. Period definition from British Museum.

A modest but well-documented dynasty ruling the northern Konkan coast and parts of Gujarat and the Nashik region between the fall of the Satavahanas and the rise of the Kalachuris. They are known mainly from copperplate land grants and from silver coins imitating Western Kshatrapa types, and the era they used, beginning in AD 249, was carried on for centuries afterwards as the Kalachuri-Chedi era.

Final Bronze Age (Italy, 1199 BC–974 BC).label: Final Bronze Age
Final Bronze Age (Italy, 1199 BC–974 BC).prose:
[Italy, 1199 BC–974 BC] Final Bronze Age. Italy: c. 1200 BC - 975 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Sardinia's nuragic communities stopped raising new tower-fortresses and instead expanded the villages clustered around the older nuraghi, with round huts, meeting rooms and sacred wells. Metalworkers turned copper ingots from Cyprus and Aegean contacts into tools and the first of the small bronze figurines of warriors, archers and worshippers that are the island's most distinctive art. It is the phase in which nuragic society shifted from building monuments to trading across the Mediterranean, setting the stage for the Iron Age encounters with Phoenicians.

Kakitsu Era (Japan, AD 1441–AD 1444).label: Kakitsu Era
Kakitsu Era (Japan, AD 1441–AD 1444).prose:
[Japan, AD 1441–AD 1444] Kakitsu Era. 1441-1444. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era remembered for a shock to the warrior order: in 1441 the shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori was murdered at a banquet by the vassal lord Akamatsu Mitsusuke, and the Ashikaga house never fully recovered its authority. In the confusion that followed, armed peasant leagues around Kyoto pressed the government into debt-cancellation decrees. The episode is often read as an early crack in the structure that would break open in the Ōnin War a generation later.

Hallstatt D (Europe, 599 BC–449 BC).label: Hallstatt D
Hallstatt D (Europe, 599 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Europe, 599 BC–449 BC] Hallstatt D. Europe; 600-450 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The climax and collapse of Hallstatt society. Fortified "princely seats" like the Heuneburg, with its Mediterranean-style mudbrick wall, controlled trade in Greek wine, bronze vessels and coral, while nearby mounds held spectacular burials such as the woman of Vix with her huge Greek bronze krater. Long swords gave way to short daggers, and by the end of the phase the centres were abandoned and the La Tène style was taking shape.

Middle Minoan III (Crete, 1699 BC–1599 B.label: Middle Minoan III
Middle Minoan III (Crete, 1699 BC–1599 B.prose:
[Crete, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Minoan III. 1700BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The palaces were rebuilt after destruction, larger and more architecturally sophisticated, with light-wells, gypsum-faced walls and the first true frescoes. Linear A replaced hieroglyphic writing for administration, and Cretan influence spread through the Aegean islands. This is the threshold of the Neopalatial heyday, and the town of Akrotiri on Thera was flourishing under strong Cretan influence.

Early Tolima (Colombia, AD 1–AD 900).label: Early Tolima
Early Tolima (Colombia, AD 1–AD 900).prose:
[Colombia, AD 1–AD 900] Early Tolima. The term refers to a cultural period and a style in the Tolima region of Colombia in the Magdalena valley in the Tolima and Huila departments from 1 AD to 900 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Communities in the upper Magdalena valley produced the flat, sharply geometric gold pectorals — stylised human figures with outstretched bat-like arms and crescent heads — that give the Tolima style its name. The pieces were hammered and cast in gold-copper alloy and placed in tombs, alongside pottery and stone work from the region's dispersed chiefdoms. Later Spanish accounts of the Pijao describe descendants of these societies resisting conquest fiercely.

Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.label: Middle Helladic III
Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.prose:
[Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Helladic III. 1700BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The moment mainland Greece began to pull ahead. Warrior burials filled with bronze weapons, gold and imported Cretan goods — above all Grave Circle B at Mycenae — reveal families accumulating wealth and advertising it in death for the first time. Within a couple of generations these lineages would build the shaft-grave dynasties and palatial citadels of the Mycenaean world.

Minaean (Yemen, 499 BC–AD 1).label: Minaean
Minaean (Yemen, 499 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Wadi Jawf, 499 BC–AD 1] Minaean. Refers to the small trading kingdom of Ma?in (capital at Qarnaw) based in the Wadi Jawf that was of economic importance during the second half of the first millennium BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The kingdom of Ma'in controlled a stretch of the incense road through the Yemeni highlands, and its merchants ran trading colonies as far north as Dedan in the Hijaz. Frankincense and myrrh moving toward the Mediterranean paid for stone temples, city walls at Qarnawu and Yathill, and thousands of inscriptions in the Minaic script. It was a merchant state rather than a conquering one, and was eventually eclipsed by Saba and the rising power of Himyar.

Late Minoan IIIA1 (Crete, 1399 BC–1374 B.label: Late Minoan IIIA1
Late Minoan IIIA1 (Crete, 1399 BC–1374 B.prose:
[Crete, 1399 BC–1374 BC] Late Minoan IIIA1. 1400BC-1375BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A short phase in which Mycenaean administrative habits were fully embedded on Crete, with Greek-language Linear B accounting and warrior burials with bronze weapons. Pottery grew more uniform and less inventive than the marine and floral styles of earlier generations. Scholars still argue over whether the palace at Knossos was destroyed at the start of this phase or survived into the next.

Ghaznavid dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 977–A.label: Ghaznavid dynasty
Ghaznavid dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 977–A.prose:
[Khurasan, Afghanistan, northern India, AD 977–AD 1186] Ghaznavid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, India, Iran, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. 977-1186 (AH 366-AH 582). Khurasan, Afghanistan, northern India. Rulers played main part in expansion of Islam into India. With the adoption of Persian administrative and cultural ways the Ghaznavid abandoned their original Turkish steppe background and became largely integrated with the Perso-Islamic tradition. Under Mas'ud I, the son of Mahmud I, the Ghaznavid empire could not be maintained in the west against the Seljuqs, and Khwarazm, Khurasan and northern Persia were lost. The rise of the Ghurids reduced the power of the Ghaznavids and the dynasty was extinguished in 1186 (AH 582). Period definition from British Museum.

Founded by Turkic slave-soldiers who broke away from the Samanids, the Ghaznavids built an empire from their capital at Ghazni across eastern Iran, Central Asia and the Punjab. Mahmud of Ghazni's repeated raids into India, including the sack of the temple at Somnath, brought back enormous plunder and opened the way to lasting Muslim rule in northern India. Their court sponsored Persian literature, most famously Firdawsi's Shahnameh, spreading Persian culture eastward before the Seljuks and then the Ghurids cut the dynasty down.

Minh Mang (Vietnam, AD 1820–AD 1840).label: Minh Mang
Minh Mang (Vietnam, AD 1820–AD 1840).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1820–AD 1840] Minh Mang. (1820-1840) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

The second Nguyen emperor pushed Vietnam toward a tightly centralised Confucian state modelled on China, replacing regional viceroys with provinces staffed by examination graduates and codifying law and ritual. He extended Vietnamese control over Cambodia and the Lao uplands, imposed Vietnamese customs on minority peoples, and met the resulting revolts with force. His persecution of Catholic missionaries and refusal of European trade overtures gave France the pretexts it later used to invade.

Orientalising Period (Greece, 699 BC–599.label: Orientalising Period
Orientalising Period (Greece, 699 BC–599.prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–599 BC] Orientalising Period. The term covers the date range: about 700BC-600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Contact with Phoenicia, Syria, and Assyria flooded Greek workshops with new images: griffins, sphinxes, lions, palmettes, and rosettes crowding onto painted pottery, ivories, and bronzes.
