Corinth led the way with its miniature perfume flasks traded across the Mediterranean. The same contacts brought the alphabet, adapted from Phoenician script, and with it the recording of poetry and law.

Late Minoan I (Crete, 1599 BC–1449 BC).label: Late Minoan I
Late Minoan I (Crete, 1599 BC–1449 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1599 BC–1449 BC] Late Minoan I. 1600BC-1450BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of Minoan Crete: multi-storey palaces and elegant country villas, bull-leaping frescoes, stone rhyta and pottery painted with octopuses, lilies and reeds. Minoan styles and craftsmen turn up across the Aegean and in Egyptian tomb paintings. The Thera eruption buried Akrotiri during this phase, and it ended with fires and abandonments at sites all over the island.

Kocho Era (Japan, AD 1261–AD 1264).label: Kocho Era
Kocho Era (Japan, AD 1261–AD 1264).prose:
[Japan, AD 1261–AD 1264] Kocho Era. 1261-1264. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign-name in the middle Kamakura years, when the Hōjō regents governed from Kamakura and the emperor in Kyoto reigned largely as a ceremonial figure. It falls in the years when the monk Nichiren was persecuted and exiled for his attacks on rival Buddhist schools, and when reports of Mongol power were beginning to reach Japan.

San Agustin (Colombia, 999 BC–AD 1600).label: San Agustin
San Agustin (Colombia, 999 BC–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, 999 BC–AD 1600] San Agustin. The terms refer to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the upper Magdalena valley in the Huila department from 1000 BC to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

In the headwaters of the Magdalena River, communities of farmers spent centuries carving volcanic rock into hundreds of monumental statues — fanged human-jaguar figures, warriors, birds of prey — and setting them to guard stone-lined tombs beneath earthen mounds. There was no city and no state, but a scattered landscape of ceremonial precincts, terraces and carved rock channels along the streams. The tradition faded before the Spanish arrived, leaving the statues to be found standing in the forest.

Tenpuku Era (Japan, AD 1233–AD 1234).label: Tenpuku Era
Tenpuku Era (Japan, AD 1233–AD 1234).prose:
[Japan, AD 1233–AD 1234] Tenpuku Era. 1233-1234. Period definition from British Museum.

A one-year era under the child emperor Shijō, when the country was governed from Kamakura by the Hōjō regents. Yasutoki had recently issued the Goseibai Shikimoku, the warrior law code that became the basis of samurai justice for centuries.

Showa Era 1312-1317 (Japan, AD 1312–AD 1.label: Showa Era 1312-1317
Showa Era 1312-1317 (Japan, AD 1312–AD 1.prose:
[Japan, AD 1312–AD 1317] Showa Era 1312-1317. 正和 1312-1317. Period definition from British Museum.

A quiet-looking stretch of the late Kamakura period in which real power lay with the Hōjō regents and their household officers rather than the shogun or the emperor. The teenage Hōjō Takatoki, remembered by later chroniclers for his dog-fights and dancing, took over as regent at the end of it. Meanwhile the imperial house was splitting into two rival lines, a quarrel that would soon tear the country apart.

Shouchang (China, AD 1092–AD 1100).label: Shouchang
Shouchang (China, AD 1092–AD 1100).prose: [China, AD 1092–AD 1100] Shouchang. 1092-1100 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Kaei Era (Japan, AD 1848–AD 1854).label: Kaei Era
Kaei Era (Japan, AD 1848–AD 1854).prose:
[Japan, AD 1848–AD 1854] Kaei Era. 1848-1854. Period definition from British Museum.

The years when the long isolation of Tokugawa Japan broke: Commodore Perry's black ships appeared in Edo Bay in 1853 and returned in 1854 to force the Convention of Kanagawa, opening ports to American ships. Famine, coastal defence panic and the shogunate's visible weakness in the face of foreign demands set off the political crisis that would topple it within fifteen years.

Western Jin dynasty (China, AD 265–AD 31.label: Western Jin dynasty
Western Jin dynasty (China, AD 265–AD 31.prose:
[China, AD 265–AD 313] Western Jin dynasty. 265-313. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief moment of unity between the Three Kingdoms and the long north–south split, achieved when the Sima clan absorbed the last rival state in 280. Court luxury, weak emperors and a bloody succession war among princes hollowed the regime out from within. Its collapse before Xiongnu and other steppe armies triggered one of the great population movements of Chinese history, as northern aristocrats resettled the Yangtze valley.

Zhou dynasty (China, 1049 BC–220 BC).label: Zhou dynasty
Zhou dynasty (China, 1049 BC–220 BC).prose:
[China, 1049 BC–220 BC] Zhou dynasty. circa 1050 BC-221 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The longest-lasting of China's dynasties, founded when the Zhou overthrew the Shang and justified it with the "Mandate of Heaven" — the idea that rulers hold power only while they govern justly, an argument invoked in Chinese politics for the next three thousand years. Real Zhou control faded early, leaving hundreds of rival states to fight it out through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States eras. That upheaval produced Confucius, Laozi, the Legalists and the other thinkers of the "Hundred Schools," along with iron tools, crossbows, coinage and mass infantry armies.

Duy Tan (Vietnam, AD 1907–AD 1916).label: Duy Tan
Duy Tan (Vietnam, AD 1907–AD 1916).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1907–AD 1916] Duy Tan. (1907-1916) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

Placed on the throne as a boy of seven after the French deposed his father, this Nguyen emperor grew into an unexpected opponent of the protectorate. In 1916 he slipped out of the Hue citadel to lead a rising planned with the scholars Tran Cao Van and Thai Phien, timed to exploit France's distraction by the First World War. The plot was betrayed within days, its leaders executed, and the young emperor exiled to Reunion, where he became a symbol for later nationalists.

Xiaowen (China, AD 471–AD 499).label: Xiaowen
Xiaowen (China, AD 471–AD 499).prose:
[China, AD 471–AD 499] Xiaowen. 471-499 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Xiaowen drove the most thorough sinicisation of any northern conquest dynasty: he moved the capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang, banned Xianbei dress and speech at court, ordered Chinese surnames for the ruling clans and encouraged intermarriage with Han aristocrats. His equal-field land system, distributing land to households in return for tax and service, was copied by later dynasties down to the Tang. The Longmen cave temples outside Luoyang were begun in his reign.

Hogen Era (Japan, AD 1156–AD 1159).label: Hogen Era
Hogen Era (Japan, AD 1156–AD 1159).prose:
[Japan, AD 1156–AD 1159] Hogen Era. 1156-1159. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for the brief but decisive Hōgen Disturbance of 1156, when a quarrel over the imperial succession split the court and both sides hired warriors from the Taira and Minamoto to settle it in the streets of Kyoto. The victory of Taira no Kiyomori's faction showed that provincial fighting men, not courtiers, now decided who ruled. Within thirty years the country was in full civil war and the age of the samurai had begun.

Middle Minoan IIIA (Crete, 1699 BC–1649.label: Middle Minoan IIIA
Middle Minoan IIIA (Crete, 1699 BC–1649.prose:
[Crete, 1699 BC–1649 BC] Middle Minoan IIIA. 1700BC-1650BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The rebuilding phase after the first palaces fell: new complexes with light-wells, ashlar masonry and the earliest painted plaster decoration, and a shift to Linear A for record-keeping. Some settlements were damaged again by earthquake during the phase, prompting further repair and remodelling.

Almoravid dynasty (Morocco, AD 1056–AD 1.label: Almoravid dynasty
Almoravid dynasty (Morocco, AD 1056–AD 1.prose:
[Morocco; Spain, AD 1056–AD 1147] Almoravid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Morocco, Spain. 1056-1147; Morocco; Spain. Originating in religious movement among Berber nomads. Almoravid is the Spanish form of 'murabitun', meaning those dwelling in a hermitage or frontier fortress. This term was used for these warriors who wore veils over their faces against the sand and wind hence they were also known as 'al-mutalaththimun' meaning the veiled ones. The Almoravid recognised the Abbasid Caliphs as spiritual heads of Islam. Period definition from British Museum.

Sanhaja Berber nomads from the Sahara, welded together by a puritanical religious teaching, swept north to found Marrakesh and unify Morocco and western Algeria, while their control of the gold routes to Ghana enriched the state. Invited into Spain by the taifa kings, they crushed the Castilians at Sagrajas and then annexed al-Andalus outright, halting the Christian advance for two generations. Their rule was overthrown by the Almohads, who denounced them as religiously lax.

Serrania de San Jacinto (Colombia, AD 90.label: Serrania de San Jacinto
Serrania de San Jacinto (Colombia, AD 90.prose: [Colombia, AD 900–AD 1600] Serrania de San Jacinto. The term refers to a region, a style and a period of Colombia in the Serrania de San Jacinto in the Zenu area in the Caribbean lowlands from 900 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Anterior Le dynasty (Vietnam, AD 980–AD.label: Anterior Le dynasty
Anterior Le dynasty (Vietnam, AD 980–AD.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 980–AD 1009] Anterior Le dynasty. Vietnamese dynasty, 980-1009.  state name: Dai Co Viet. Period definition from British Museum.

Lê Hoàn, a general who took the throne from an infant Đinh heir, beat back a Song Chinese invasion and campaigned against Champa to the south, securing the young independent Vietnamese state. His court built up a royal capital at Hoa Lư, patronised Buddhist monks as advisers and traded with Song China as a tributary. The dynasty lasted only three reigns, collapsing amid the cruelty of its last king and giving way to the long-lived Lý dynasty.

Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1799 BC).label: Old Assyrian
Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1799 BC).prose:
[Assyria, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Old Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. The term is used to describe the culture of Assyria between approximately 2000 BC-1800 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Merchants from Assur ran a long-distance trade network carrying tin and woollen textiles by donkey caravan into Anatolia, exchanging them for silver and gold. Their archives at the Kanesh trading colony preserve thousands of clay letters, contracts and lawsuits, including those of women managing textile production at home. Shamshi-Adad I briefly welded northern Mesopotamia into a kingdom before Hammurabi's Babylon overshadowed it.

Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1849.label: Middle Cycladic I
Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1849.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1849 BC] Middle Cycladic I. 2000BC-1850BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The islands settle into fewer, larger communities as the scattered hamlets of the Early Bronze Age are abandoned. Local potters develop matt-painted wares with dark geometric designs on pale slip, while imports show contact with Crete and the Greek mainland is still modest.

Longxing (China, AD 1163–AD 1164).label: Longxing
Longxing (China, AD 1163–AD 1164).prose:
[China, AD 1163–AD 1164] Longxing. 1163-1164 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The opening reign era of Emperor Xiaozong of the Southern Song, who came to the throne determined to recover the north from the Jurchen Jin and rehabilitated the executed general Yue Fei. His northern expedition was defeated at Fuli within months, forcing a negotiated settlement that lowered the Song from vassal to junior kin of the Jin and reduced the annual tribute. The compromise held for four decades of relative peace and prosperity.

Chotoku Era (Japan, AD 995–AD 999).label: Chotoku Era
Chotoku Era (Japan, AD 995–AD 999).prose:
[Japan, AD 995–AD 999] Chotoku Era. 995-999. Period definition from British Museum.

An epidemic swept the capital and killed most of the senior ministers in a single season, clearing the path for Fujiwara no Michinaga, who then engineered the exile of his nephews Korechika and Takaie after a scandal involving a stray arrow shot at a retired emperor. With rivals removed, Michinaga began the four decades of dominance that mark the peak of Fujiwara regency government and of Heian court culture.

Prehistoric (Korean Peninsula, 5999 BC–1.label: Prehistoric
Prehistoric (Korean Peninsula, 5999 BC–1.prose:
[Korea, 5999 BC–1999 BC] Prehistoric. Korea: C6000 BC - 2000 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Chalcolithic communities on the Iranian plateau and in Khuzestan used mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, copper metallurgy and clay tokens and seals to track goods. Susa emerged as a major centre in close contact with Mesopotamian Uruk, and the accounting systems developed here fed directly into the invention of writing.

Yotoco (Colombia, 199 BC–AD 1200).label: Yotoco
Yotoco (Colombia, 199 BC–AD 1200).prose:
[Colombia, 199 BC–AD 1200] Yotoco. The term refers to a period and a culture of the Calima region of Colombia in the Western Range of the Valle del Cauca department from 200 BC to 1200 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase of the Calima region in the Cauca valley known above all for its goldwork: hammered masks, diadems, nose ornaments and pins of remarkable scale, made by communities living in dispersed settlements on terraced hillsides. Their painted and modelled ceramics and elaborate shaft tombs point to ranked societies with specialist craftsmen. Much of what survives came out of the ground through looting, which is why context matters so much to archaeologists here.

Ninevite 5 Incised (Iraq, 2749 BC–2499 B.label: Ninevite 5 Incised
Ninevite 5 Incised (Iraq, 2749 BC–2499 B.prose:
[Iraq, 2749 BC–2499 BC] Ninevite 5 Incised. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. c.2750-2500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The later half of the Ninevite 5 sequence in northern Mesopotamia, when painted decoration gave way to pots carved, incised and excised with grooved and hatched patterns on grey and buff fabrics. It coincides with renewed urban growth at Tell Brak, Tell Leilan and other mounds, and with the appearance of seals, administrative sealings and larger public buildings — the local build-up to the region's absorption by southern powers.

Persian Period (Lachish, 538 BC–330 BC).label: Persian Period
Persian Period (Lachish, 538 BC–330 BC).prose:
[Lachish, 538 BC–330 BC] Persian Period. This term is used in the Lachish Collection as a chronological term covering the period 539 B.C. to 331 B.C.  For cuneiform tablets belonging to the same period, use the term 'Achaemenid Dynasty'. Period definition from British Museum.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.

Manji Era (Japan, AD 1658–AD 1661).label: Manji Era
Manji Era (Japan, AD 1658–AD 1661).prose:
[Japan, AD 1658–AD 1661] Manji Era. 1658-1661. Period definition from British Museum.

The years immediately following the Meireki fire that had destroyed most of Edo, spent rebuilding the city on a safer plan with firebreaks, relocated temples and a castle keep that was never replaced. The disaster and its aftermath reshaped the shogunal capital into the sprawling wooden metropolis of the later Tokugawa period.

Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 2999 BC–2899 BC).label: Jemdet Nasr
Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 2999 BC–2899 BC).prose:
[Jemdet Nasr, 2999 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr. Jemdet Nasr is the name of a site located in modern Iraq to the south of Baghdad. The name is applied to a culture based on excavations at the site that have produced a distinct assemblage of objects (c.3000BC-2900BC). The assemblage is restricted to the neighbouring region. Period definition from British Museum.

Named for a mound in central Iraq, this phase sits between Uruk and the Early Dynastic city-states. Distinctive polychrome painted jars in red and black appear alongside the earliest archives of proto-cuneiform tablets, which record grain, livestock and labour rather than stories. Settlements across southern Mesopotamia show a shared culture of seals, accounting and temple economies, the administrative machinery that would soon underpin Sumerian kingship.

Jidle III (Syria, 1699 BC–1599 BC).label: Jidle III
Jidle III (Syria, 1699 BC–1599 BC).prose: [Tell Jidle, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Jidle III. Term referring to material from level III at Tell Jidle as excavated by M.E.L. Mallowan, and dating to ca 1700-1600 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Koji Era 1555-1558 (Japan, AD 1555–AD 15.label: Koji Era 1555-1558
Koji Era 1555-1558 (Japan, AD 1555–AD 15.prose:
[Japan, AD 1555–AD 1558] Koji Era 1555-1558. 1555-1558. Period definition from British Museum.

Deep in the Warring States era, when the imperial court was so poor it struggled to pay for ceremonies and provincial warlords made their own law. Mōri Motonari's surprise attack at Miyajima in 1555 won him western Honshu, while Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin fought another round of their long duel at Kawanakajima.

Banijurid dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 848–A.label: Banijurid dynasty
Banijurid dynasty (Afghanistan, AD 848–A.prose:
[Tukharistan; Hindu Kush, AD 848–AD 908] Banijurid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Turkmenistan. c.848-c.908 (c.AH 233-c.AH 295). The Banijurids, who were probably of Iranian origin, were local rulers at Balkh and Andaraba in the region of Tukharistan to the south of the middle Oxus, and also at Panjhir in the Hindu Kush. They were vassals of the Samanids. Period definition from British Museum.

A local Iranian ruling house of Khuttal and the Balkh region in the upper Oxus lands, holding power as tributaries under Saffarid and then Samanid overlordship. They struck their own coinage and controlled a district famous for horses and mountain trade before being absorbed into the Samanid state.

Bao Dai (Vietnam, AD 1926–AD 1945).label: Bao Dai
Bao Dai (Vietnam, AD 1926–AD 1945).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1926–AD 1945] Bao Dai. (1926-1945) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of the thirteenth and last Nguyễn emperor, who inherited a throne emptied of power by the French protectorate and spent much of his youth in France. He attempted administrative reform, then ruled nominally under Japanese occupation, declaring independence in March 1945 before abdicating that August and handing the imperial seal and sword to the Việt Minh. His departure ended more than a thousand years of Vietnamese monarchy, though the French later brought him back as a figurehead head of state.

Koka Era (Japan, AD 1844–AD 1848).label: Koka Era
Koka Era (Japan, AD 1844–AD 1848).prose:
[Japan, AD 1844–AD 1848] Koka Era. 1844-1848. Period definition from British Museum.

The Tokugawa shogunate's Tenpō reforms had just collapsed, leaving a government short of money and increasingly rattled by foreign ships. A letter from the Dutch king urging Japan to open its ports was refused, and American and British vessels probing the coast were turned away — pressure that would prove irresistible when Perry arrived a few years later.

Kanko Era (Japan, AD 1004–AD 1012).label: Kanko Era
Kanko Era (Japan, AD 1004–AD 1012).prose:
[Japan, AD 1004–AD 1012] Kanko Era. 1004-1012. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of Fujiwara no Michinaga's dominance, when he governed through daughters married into the imperial line and the court's wealth and confidence were at their peak. These are the years in which Murasaki Shikibu served in the empress's household and was writing The Tale of Genji, and in which the polished aesthetic culture of the Heian court reached its fullest expression.

Reiki Era (Japan, AD 715–AD 717).label: Reiki Era
Reiki Era (Japan, AD 715–AD 717).prose:
[Japan, AD 715–AD 717] Reiki Era. 715-717. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Nara-period era name adopted when Empress Genshō came to the throne, taken from the omen of an auspicious tortoise presented to the court. Government ran from the new grid-planned capital at Heijō-kyō under the Chinese-style law codes, with provincial land registers and tax rolls being pushed out across the country.

Lapui (Iran, 3899 BC–3399 BC).label: Lapui
Lapui (Iran, 3899 BC–3399 BC).prose:
[Fars, 3899 BC–3399 BC] Lapui. Fars, 3900BC-3400BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A phase in the Kur River basin of Fars marked by plain red burnished pottery, replacing the elaborately painted wares of the preceding Bakun period. Settlement shifted towards smaller sites and a more mobile, herding-oriented way of life, and the valley's population appears to have thinned. What followed was the Banesh period and the rise of Anshan at Tal-e Malyan, one of the great early urban centres of the Iranian plateau.

Tennan Era (Japan, AD 857–AD 859).label: Tennan Era
Tennan Era (Japan, AD 857–AD 859).prose:
[Japan, AD 857–AD 859] Tennan Era. 857-859. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Yoshifusa became chancellor and then, on the accession of his infant grandson Seiwa, effectively ruled as regent — the first time a man outside the imperial family held that role. This established the pattern of Fujiwara regency government that shaped the court for the next three centuries.

Tairona (Colombia, AD 200–AD 1600).label: Tairona
Tairona (Colombia, AD 200–AD 1600).prose:
[Colombia, AD 200–AD 1600] Tairona. The term refers to a region and a cultural tradition of Colombia in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and the Caribbean Coast in the Magdalena department from 200 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

In the foothills and slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, chiefdoms built stone-paved terraces, staircases and ring-shaped house platforms linked by paved roads, of which Ciudad Perdida is the largest survivor. Their goldsmiths produced some of the finest cast tumbaga ornaments in the Americas. They resisted Spanish conquest fiercely for decades; the surviving Kogi and Wiwa peoples are their descendants.

Heian Period (Japan, AD 794–AD 1185).label: Heian Period
Heian Period (Japan, AD 794–AD 1185).prose:
[Japan, AD 794–AD 1185] Heian Period. 794-1185. Period definition from British Museum.

Court society at its most refined and most inward-looking: an aristocracy dominated by the Fujiwara regents, who married their daughters to emperors and ruled through them. The kana syllabary made possible a literature written largely by court women, including 'The Tale of Genji' and 'The Pillow Book', while Japanese Buddhism developed its own Tendai and Shingon schools. Provincial administration slipped into the hands of private estates and armed clans, and the era ended when the Taira and Minamoto fought their way to power.

Da'an (China, AD 1083–AD 1091).label: Da'an
Da'an (China, AD 1083–AD 1091).prose: [China, AD 1083–AD 1091] Da'an. 1083-1091 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Yingzong (China, AD 1063–AD 1067).label: Yingzong
Yingzong (China, AD 1063–AD 1067).prose:
[China, AD 1063–AD 1067] Yingzong. 1063-1067 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A short and mostly ineffectual reign in the Northern Song, dominated by the emperor's ill health and by a bitter court dispute over how to honour his birth father, since he had been adopted as heir by the previous emperor. That quarrel hardened the factional divisions that would explode over Wang Anshi's reforms a few years later. He did commission Sima Guang to begin the vast chronicle that became the Zizhi Tongjian.

Genko Era (Japan, AD 1331–AD 1334).label: Genko Era
Genko Era (Japan, AD 1331–AD 1334).prose:
[Japan, AD 1331–AD 1334] Genko Era. 1331-1334. Period definition from British Museum.

Named amid open war between Emperor Go-Daigo and the Kamakura shogunate, this short era saw the emperor's flight to Kasagi, his capture and exile to the Oki Islands, and then the collapse of Hōjō power in 1333. The court and the shogunate even used rival era names, a sign of how completely authority had split. It closes with Go-Daigo back on the throne attempting to rule directly.

Kantoku Era (Japan, AD 1044–AD 1046).label: Kantoku Era
Kantoku Era (Japan, AD 1044–AD 1046).prose:
[Japan, AD 1044–AD 1046] Kantoku Era. 1044-1046. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era spanning the death of Emperor Go-Suzaku and the accession of Go-Reizei, with Fujiwara no Yorimichi continuing his father Michinaga's grip on the court. An edict on estate holdings attempted to rein in the tax-free provincial manors that were steadily draining the imperial treasury.

Susa IV (Iran, 2699 BC–2099 BC).label: Susa IV
Susa IV (Iran, 2699 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Khuzestan, 2699 BC–2099 BC] Susa IV. Khuzestan ca 2700BC-2100BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Susa moved firmly into the Mesopotamian orbit, using Sumerian and then Akkadian in its records and falling under the rule of Sargon's dynasty and later Ur, while indigenous Elamite dynasties such as Awan asserted themselves in between. Treaty texts, royal inscriptions and imported styles document the constant push and pull between lowland Susiana and the highland kingdom of Anshan that would eventually fuse into the Elamite state.

Neo-Assyrian (Neo-Assyrian Empire, 929 B.label: Neo-Assyrian
Neo-Assyrian (Neo-Assyrian Empire, 929 B.prose:
[as far as Egypt, 929 BC–611 BC] Neo-Assyrian. Around 930 BC the Assyrians expanded their territories eventually forming an empire that reached as far as Egypt. This collapsed in 612 BC with the fall of the capital at Nineveh to the armies of the Babylonians and the Medes. Period definition from British Museum.

Assyrian armies pushed repeatedly into the Zagros in these centuries, campaigning for horses, tribute and control of the trade routes across the Iranian plateau, and leaving royal inscriptions and reliefs that give the first written glimpses of the Medes and Persians. Local fortified centres and elite burials, such as those at Hasanlu and Ziwiye, reflect both Assyrian pressure and the wealth it drew in. The eventual Median coalition that helped destroy Assyria grew out of this long confrontation.

Hispano-Visigothic (Spain, AD 507–AD 711.label: Hispano-Visigothic
Hispano-Visigothic (Spain, AD 507–AD 711.prose:
[Iberia, AD 507–AD 711] Hispano-Visigothic. The term refers to the period of the settlement of the Visigoths in Iberia from AD 507, following their expulsion from most of Gaul. The Kindom of Toledo, which they formed, lasted until the Islamic conquest in  AD 711. Period definition from British Museum.

After losing most of Gaul to the Franks, the Visigothic kings refounded their realm around Toledo and ruled a largely Hispano-Roman population. The conversion of King Reccared from Arian to Catholic Christianity in 589 fused the two elites, and church councils at Toledo produced a body of law and learning — above all the encyclopaedic writings of Isidore of Seville — that shaped medieval Europe. Elective kingship and civil war left the kingdom brittle, and it collapsed within a few years of the Muslim landing in 711, though later Christian kings claimed its legacy.

Chagatayid dynasty (Turkmenistan, AD 122.label: Chagatayid dynasty
Chagatayid dynasty (Turkmenistan, AD 122.prose:
[Transoxiana, Mogholistan and eastern Turkistan, AD 1227–AD 1363] Chagatayid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. 1227-1363 (?) (AH 624-764). Transoxiana, Mogholistan and eastern Turkistan. Named after Chagatay, son of Chengiz. The founder of the Chagatayid khanate (dynasty) was Chagatay's grandson Alughu who seized Khwarazm, western Turkestan and Afghanstan. These territories became the nucleus of the khanate. The unity of the Chagatayids began to disintegrate with the rise of Timurlang in Transoxiana. Period definition from British Museum.

The Central Asian share of the Mongol empire, granted to Genghis Khan's second son and his heirs. Its rulers gradually adopted Islam and Turkic speech while quarrelling over whether to remain steppe nomads or govern the rich oasis cities they controlled; the khanate split in two, and from the wreckage of its western half Timur built his own empire.

Tenryaku Era (Japan, AD 947–AD 957).label: Tenryaku Era
Tenryaku Era (Japan, AD 947–AD 957).prose:
[Japan, AD 947–AD 957] Tenryaku Era. 947-957. Period definition from British Museum.

Later writers looked back on the personal rule of Emperor Murakami as a golden age of imperial government, when no Fujiwara regent held office and the throne itself set policy. Court poetry flourished, and the era became a byword for good governance invoked by reformers for centuries afterwards.

Roman Republican (ancient Rome, 509 BC–2.label: Roman Republican
Roman Republican (ancient Rome, 509 BC–2.prose:
[ancient Rome, 509 BC–26 BC] Roman Republican. Spatial coverage: Roman Republic, ancient Rome. The Roman Republic is traditionally said to date from the expulsion of the last King of Rome in 510 BC. The end of the Republic can be dated to the battle of Actium in 31 BC or the date when Octavian took the title of Augustus in 27 BC. The former date is generally used for coins. For material issued in areas of Italy outside Roman rule during this period see 'Italic'. Period definition from British Museum.

Rome pushed north-east from the colony at Aquileia into the world of the Iron Age Alpine and Adriatic peoples, trading before it conquered. Local hillforts and cemeteries fill with Italic wine vessels, coinage and weapons, showing communities drawn into Mediterranean commerce well before annexation. By the time of Augustus the region had been incorporated outright, and the town of Emona was founded to hold the route into Italy.

Hittite (Turkey, 1399 BC–1199 BC).label: Hittite
Hittite (Turkey, 1399 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[central Turkey, north western Syria, and Upper Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–1199 BC] Hittite. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Between 1400 and 1200 BC the Hittites established one of the great empires of the ancient Middle East. At its height, the empire (also called the New Kingdom) encompassed central Turkey, north western Syria, and Upper Mesopotamia (north eastern Syria and northern Iraq). By 1300 the Hittite Empire bordered on Egypt and both powers vied for control of wealthy cities on the Mediterranean coast. This led to the Battle of Kadesh with Rameses II (1274 BC). Period definition from British Museum.

An Indo-European-speaking people built a state around Hattusa on the Anatolian plateau, first known from the tablets of Assyrian merchants and then from their own cuneiform archives. They fielded light chariots, wrote some of the earliest surviving law codes and international treaties, and preserved older Hattian and Hurrian gods alongside their own. Their capital's rock-cut sanctuaries and lion gates, and a royal archive of tens of thousands of clay tablets, make them one of the best-documented Bronze Age powers.

Taika Era (Japan, AD 645–AD 650).label: Taika Era
Taika Era (Japan, AD 645–AD 650).prose:
[Japan, AD 645–AD 650] Taika Era. 645-650. Period definition from British Museum.

Japan's first official reign era, proclaimed after a palace coup destroyed the dominant Soga family. Its name, meaning "Great Change," announced a programme of reform on the Chinese model: land and people declared to belong to the throne, provinces placed under appointed governors, and a census and tax system begun.

Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1299.label: Late Helladic IIIA
Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1299.prose:
[Greece, 1399 BC–1299 BC] Late Helladic IIIA. 1400BC-1300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The height of Mycenaean expansion, with palaces functioning, chamber-tomb cemeteries filling, and standardised stirrup jars and kylikes shipped to Egypt, the Levant and Italy. Hittite records of a kingdom called Ahhiyawa probably refer to these Greeks, dealing as equals with the great powers of the Near East.

Dezong (China, AD 780–AD 805).label: Dezong
Dezong (China, AD 780–AD 805).prose:
[China, AD 780–AD 805] Dezong. 780-805 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Dezong came to the Tang throne determined to break the autonomous military governors of the provinces, but his campaigns collapsed into mutiny and he was driven from his own capital in 783. The lasting achievement of his reign was fiscal: the twice-yearly tax of 780 abandoned the old system of levies on individuals in favour of assessments on land and property, an arrangement that outlasted the dynasty. He spent his later years distrustful of ministers, relying on eunuchs and building up the palace treasury.

Manteño (Ecuador, AD 800–AD 1530).label: Manteño
Manteño (Ecuador, AD 800–AD 1530).prose:
[Ecuador, AD 800–AD 1530] Manteño. The term refers to a period in Ecuador, from circa 800 to circa 1530. Period definition from British Museum.

Seafaring communities along the Ecuadorian coast whose balsa sailing rafts carried Spondylus shell, textiles and metalwork north to Mexico and south toward Peru, making them the great maritime traders of the pre-Columbian Pacific. Their towns were built of stone-footed houses, and they left distinctive U-shaped stone seats supported by crouching human and animal figures. It was a Manteño raft, met at sea, that first showed Spanish explorers the wealth of the Andean world.

Dali (China, AD 766–AD 779).label: Dali
Dali (China, AD 766–AD 779).prose:
[China, AD 766–AD 779] Dali. 766-779 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The later part of Daizong's Tang reign, spent managing an empire in which regional military governors were effectively autonomous and Tibetan raids reached deep into the northwest. Revenue now depended heavily on the salt monopoly and on the rice-growing south, a fiscal shift that shaped the rest of the dynasty.

Keian Era (Japan, AD 1648–AD 1652).label: Keian Era
Keian Era (Japan, AD 1648–AD 1652).prose:
[Japan, AD 1648–AD 1652] Keian Era. 1648-1652. Period definition from British Museum.

The stern third shogun Iemitsu died and was succeeded by his ten-year-old son Ietsuna, prompting a rash of anxious edicts on peasant conduct. In 1651 the military scholar Yui Shōsetsu plotted to seize Edo and Sunpu with masterless samurai displaced by the shogunate's confiscation of domains; the plot failed but forced the government to soften the rules that were creating rōnin.

Tenpo Era (Japan, AD 1830–AD 1844).label: Tenpo Era
Tenpo Era (Japan, AD 1830–AD 1844).prose:
[Japan, AD 1830–AD 1844] Tenpo Era. 1830-1844. Period definition from British Museum.

Repeated harvest failures produced the Tenpō famine and, in 1837, Ōshio Heihachirō's armed uprising in Osaka — a shogunal official turning on his own government. Foreign ships pressing at the coast added to the alarm, prompting Mizuno Tadakuni's sweeping and unpopular Tenpō Reforms and exposing how brittle Tokugawa rule had become.

Kagen Era (Japan, AD 1303–AD 1306).label: Kagen Era
Kagen Era (Japan, AD 1303–AD 1306).prose:
[Japan, AD 1303–AD 1306] Kagen Era. 1303-1306. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Japanese era name of the Kamakura period, in the reign of Emperor Go-Nijō, when real power lay with the Hōjō regents in Kamakura and the imperial house was split between the rival Daikakuji and Jimyōin lines that alternated on the throne.

Xiping (China, AD 516–AD 517).label: Xiping
Xiping (China, AD 516–AD 517).prose:
[China, AD 516–AD 517] Xiping. 516-517 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign-era of the Northern Wei, when the child emperor Xiaoming sat on the throne and his mother, Empress Dowager Hu, held real power. Court wealth poured into Buddhism: the colossal Yongning Temple pagoda rose at Luoyang, and cave-shrine carving continued at Longmen. Behind the splendour the dynasty's finances and frontier garrisons were fraying, and rebellion followed within a decade.

Saiko Era (Japan, AD 854–AD 857).label: Saiko Era
Saiko Era (Japan, AD 854–AD 857).prose:
[Japan, AD 854–AD 857] Saiko Era. 854-857. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Japanese reign era of the early Heian court, spanning the last years of Emperor Montoku's reign, when real power was consolidating in the hands of the Fujiwara regental house. Era names like this were proclaimed and changed in response to auspicious omens, disasters or accessions, and they remain the standard framework for dating Japanese documents and objects.

Early Minoan I (Crete, 3199 BC–2899 BC).label: Early Minoan I
Early Minoan I (Crete, 3199 BC–2899 BC).prose:
[Crete, 3199 BC–2899 BC] Early Minoan I. 3200BC-2900BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The opening phase of the Cretan Bronze Age, when new burial customs appeared: circular stone tholos tombs in the south and burial caves elsewhere, used by whole communities over generations. Dark burnished Pyrgos ware and red-on-buff Agios Onouphrios pottery mark the period, alongside the first regular use of copper. Change came gradually from the preceding Neolithic, with some sites showing signs of newcomers arriving on the island.

Early Christian Period (Sudan, AD 550–AD.label: Early Christian Period
Early Christian Period (Sudan, AD 550–AD.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 550–AD 850] Early Christian Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 550-850. It is subdivided into an earlier and a later phase designated Early Christian Period I (AD 550-700) and Early Christian Period II (AD 700-850) respectively. Period definition from British Museum.

The Nubian kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alwa adopted Christianity in the sixth century, sending missions from Byzantium and reorienting the middle Nile toward the Mediterranean church. Mud-brick and stone churches went up across Nubia, often reusing temple blocks, and burials shifted to simple Christian graves. The period established a literate, Greek- and Coptic-using Christian civilisation that endured for some eight hundred years.

Khwarazm Shahs (Turkmenistan, AD 995–AD.label: Khwarazm Shahs
Khwarazm Shahs (Turkmenistan, AD 995–AD.prose:
[classical Chorasmia on the lower Oxus, AD 995–AD 1231] Khwarazm Shahs. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. 995-1231 (AH 385-AH 628). Khwarazm is the classical Chorasmia, the rich and well irrigated region on the lower Oxus. In later times it was known as the Khanate of Khiva. It may have been an early home of the Iranians. Khwarazm was under Samanid rule until it was added to the Ghaznavid empire under Mahmud in 1017 (AH 408). After the middle of the 11th century Khwarazm was under Seljuq rule. Since the time of Malik Shah the hereditary governors of Khwarazm received the title of Khwarazm Shah. After the conquest of Transoxiana by Genghis Khan in 1220 (AH 617) Khwarazm came first under the rule of Mongols and then Turkish Central Asian steppe peoples. Period definition from British Museum.

Governors of the oasis of Khwarazm on the lower Amu Darya turned themselves into independent rulers and then into the dominant power of the eastern Islamic world, absorbing Iran and much of Central Asia. Their capital Gurganj rivalled Bukhara and Samarkand for wealth and scholarship. The dynasty's fall was spectacular: the shah's execution of Mongol merchants and envoys brought Genghis Khan's armies west in 1219, and within a decade the cities were in ruins.

Geometric Greek (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Geometric Greek
Geometric Greek (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric Greek. About 900-700 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The centuries when Greek art was built from ruler and compass — meanders, checkerboards and concentric circles covering vases, and later stiff silhouette figures in funeral and battle scenes. Behind the pottery lies real change: population growth, the first temples, the reintroduction of writing through the Phoenician alphabet, and colonies planted overseas. Out of this world came the polis and the Homeric epics.

Honghua (China, AD 1678–AD 1681).label: Honghua
Honghua (China, AD 1678–AD 1681).prose:
[China, AD 1678–AD 1681] Honghua. 1678-1681 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The era name used by Wu Shifan, who inherited his grandfather Wu Sangui's rebel throne in the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. Based in Yunnan and Guizhou, his shrinking regime was worn down by Kangxi's armies until he took his own life at Kunming. His defeat ended the last serious military challenge to Qing control of southern China and abolished the semi-independent feudatories.

Early Minoan (Crete, 3199 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Minoan
Early Minoan (Crete, 3199 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Crete, 3199 BC–1999 BC] Early Minoan. 3200BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Bronze Age Crete before the palaces: farming communities grew in size and wealth, buried their dead collectively in circular tholos tombs and rock shelters, and began working copper, bronze, gold and fine stone. Distinctive mottled Vasiliki ware, elaborate stone vases and engraved seals appear, along with imports showing contact with Egypt, the Levant and the Cyclades. The accumulating wealth and administrative habits of these centuries made the first Cretan palaces possible.

Baoyuan (China, AD 1038–AD 1040).label: Baoyuan
Baoyuan (China, AD 1038–AD 1040).prose:
[China, AD 1038–AD 1040] Baoyuan. 1038-1040 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A short Northern Song era name whose years were dominated by events on the northwestern frontier: Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of the Western Xia in 1038, and the Song court's refusal to accept him opened a costly war. The fighting exposed the weaknesses of Song military organisation and finance and fed the reform debates of Emperor Renzong's later reign.

Late Minoan (Crete, 1599 BC–1159 BC).label: Late Minoan
Late Minoan (Crete, 1599 BC–1159 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1599 BC–1159 BC] Late Minoan. 1600BC-1160BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Crete's palace civilisation reached its most brilliant phase — frescoed halls, marine-style pottery, bronze work and trade reaching Egypt and the Levant — before a run of disasters. The eruption of Thera, then island-wide destructions, left Knossos alone in charge, now under Greek-speaking Mycenaean rulers who kept their accounts in Linear B. The palace system finally failed altogether, and Cretans retreated to defensible hilltop villages as the wider Bronze Age world collapsed.

Jowa Era (Japan, AD 834–AD 848).label: Jowa Era
Jowa Era (Japan, AD 834–AD 848).prose:
[Japan, AD 834–AD 848] Jowa Era. 834-848. Period definition from British Museum.

Under Emperor Ninmyo the Fujiwara tightened their hold on the throne: the Jowa Incident of 842 saw the crown prince deposed and rival courtiers exiled, clearing the way for Fujiwara Yoshifusa's descendants to monopolise the regency for centuries. The last official Japanese embassy to Tang China also sailed in this era, carrying the monk Ennin, whose diary of nine years' travel is one of the great eyewitness accounts of medieval China.

Dulafid dynasty (Iran, AD 840–AD 897).label: Dulafid dynasty
Dulafid dynasty (Iran, AD 840–AD 897).prose:
[Jibal (ancient Media) in central and western Iran, AD 840–AD 897] Dulafid dynasty. 840-897 (AH 225-AH 284). Arab governors appointed by the 'Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid to rule the Jibal (ancient Media) in central and western Iran. The centre of power was at Karaj. Period definition from British Museum.

An Arab family from the Banu Ijl who governed the Jibal region of western Iran from Karaj, initially as Abbasid appointees and increasingly as autonomous rulers during the caliphate's ninth-century weakness. They minted their own coinage, patronised poets, and controlled the strategic road between Baghdad and Khurasan. Caliph al-Mu'tadid finally broke them, and their lands passed to the rising Saffarids and Samanids.

Jin dynasties (China, AD 265–AD 420).label: Jin dynasties
Jin dynasties (China, AD 265–AD 420).prose:
[China, AD 265–AD 420] Jin dynasties. 265-420. Period definition from British Museum.

Founded when the Sima family usurped the throne of Wei, this dynasty briefly reunited China in 280 before collapsing into a bloody civil war among imperial princes. Nomadic armies then overran the north, and the court fled south of the Yangtze to rule a diminished realm from Jiankang. The exodus of northern elites reshaped the south, spread Buddhism widely, and produced the calligraphy of Wang Xizhi and the poetry of Tao Yuanming.

Tengi Era (Japan, AD 1053–AD 1058).label: Tengi Era
Tengi Era (Japan, AD 1053–AD 1058).prose:
[Japan, AD 1053–AD 1058] Tengi Era. 1053-1058. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Yorimichi converted his villa at Uji into the Byōdō-in and raised the Phoenix Hall, still one of the most admired buildings in Japan, as a vision of Amida's Western Paradise on earth. In the far north, meanwhile, the long campaign against the Abe family known as the Former Nine Years War ground on, building the reputation of the Minamoto warriors who fought it.

Eiji Era (Japan, AD 1141–AD 1142).label: Eiji Era
Eiji Era (Japan, AD 1141–AD 1142).prose:
[Japan, AD 1141–AD 1142] Eiji Era. 1141-1142. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era at the heart of the intrigue that would tear the court apart. Emperor Sutoku was pressured into abdicating in favour of the infant Konoe by the retired emperor Toba, who ruled from behind the throne; the resentment this bred erupted fifteen years later in the Hogen Disturbance, the conflict that first brought samurai armies into the streets of the capital.

Later Han Dynasty (China, AD 948–AD 951).label: Later Han Dynasty
Later Han Dynasty (China, AD 948–AD 951).prose:
[China, AD 948–AD 951] Later Han Dynasty. 948-951. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the short-lived northern regimes of the Five Dynasties, founded by the Shatuo general Liu Zhiyuan after the Khitan withdrew from the Central Plains. It lasted under four years and two rulers before a purge of senior officers provoked a mutiny and the founding of the Later Zhou. A branch of the family held out in Shanxi as the Northern Han, the last state to be swallowed by the reunifying Song.

Le Dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1788).label: Le Dynasty
Le Dynasty (Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1788).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1788] Le Dynasty. Dynasty ruling Vietnam from 1428-1788. Period definition from British Museum.

Lê Lợi expelled the occupying Ming armies and founded a dynasty that gave Vietnam a Confucian civil service, the Hồng Đức law code and a great southward expansion at the expense of Champa. Later emperors were figureheads while the Trịnh and Nguyễn lords ruled north and south from rival capitals. The Tây Sơn uprising finally swept the dynasty away.

Vinca (Balkans, 4999 BC–3999 BC).label: Vinca
Vinca (Balkans, 4999 BC–3999 BC).prose:
[central Balkans, 4999 BC–3999 BC] Vinca. The Vinca culture developed throughout the central Balkans during the middle-late Neolithic (c. 5000-4000 BC). Vinca sites are the first tells of the central Balkans, therefore they are characterised by multi-phase sequences. During the later phases simple tools and ornaments hammered from copper were made. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the most substantial Neolithic societies of prehistoric Europe, centred on the middle Danube, where tells of mudbrick houses grew into settlements of thousands of people. Its potters made dark, highly burnished vessels and thousands of stylised clay figurines with angular, mask-like faces; incised marks on some objects have been argued, controversially, to be an early sign system. Sites such as Belovode and Rudna Glava contain some of the world's earliest evidence for copper smelting and deep-shaft mining.

Romanesque (Europe, AD 1050–AD 1200).label: Romanesque
Romanesque (Europe, AD 1050–AD 1200).prose:
[Europe, AD 1050–AD 1200] Romanesque. The term refers to a style from about 1050 to about 1200. Period definition from British Museum.

Stone building returned to Europe on a scale unseen since antiquity: round arches, massive walls, barrel vaults and carved doorways teeming with monsters and Last Judgements. Monastic reform, the pilgrimage roads to Santiago and the wealth of a growing population paid for it, and abbeys such as Cluny set the fashion. Its structural limits – thick walls, small windows, dim interiors – are exactly what Gothic builders set out to overcome.

Zhengtong (China, AD 1436–AD 1449).label: Zhengtong
Zhengtong (China, AD 1436–AD 1449).prose:
[China, AD 1436–AD 1449] Zhengtong. 1436-1449 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The first reign of the boy emperor Yingzong, run at first by senior ministers and then by the eunuch Wang Zhen. It ended in the Tumu Crisis, when a badly led Ming army was destroyed by Oirat Mongols and the emperor himself was taken prisoner. The court enthroned his brother and defended Beijing successfully, but the shock pushed the Ming onto the defensive and toward the great wall-building of later reigns.

Gen'o Era (Japan, AD 1319–AD 1321).label: Gen'o Era
Gen'o Era (Japan, AD 1319–AD 1321).prose:
[Japan, AD 1319–AD 1321] Gen'o Era. 1319-1321. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era at the close of the Kamakura period, opening soon after Go-Daigo took the throne with ambitions to rule in fact as well as in name. The Hōjō regents in Kamakura still held real power, but their grip was loosening, and within little more than a decade Go-Daigo's revolt would bring their government down.

Middle Minoan IIB (Crete, 1799 BC–1699 B.label: Middle Minoan IIB
Middle Minoan IIB (Crete, 1799 BC–1699 B.prose:
[Crete, 1799 BC–1699 BC] Middle Minoan IIB. 1800BC-1700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The last and richest phase of the first palaces, with eggshell-thin polychrome Kamares pottery, elaborate seal engraving, and Cretan exports reaching Egypt and the Syrian coast. It ended in destructions at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, usually blamed on earthquake, which cleared the way for the grander second palaces.

Shu Kingdom (China, AD 907–AD 925).label: Shu Kingdom
Shu Kingdom (China, AD 907–AD 925).prose:
[China, AD 907–AD 925] Shu Kingdom. 907-925. Period definition from British Museum.

Liu Bei's state in the Sichuan basin, one of the three rivals that carved up the Han empire, defended by mountain passes and sustained by the fertile Chengdu plain. Its chancellor Zhuge Liang and general Guan Yu became the most famous figures of the era, later worshipped as gods of wisdom and loyalty. Militarily the weakest of the three, it was overrun by Wei in 263.

Kentoku Era (Japan, AD 1370–AD 1372).label: Kentoku Era
Kentoku Era (Japan, AD 1370–AD 1372).prose:
[Japan, AD 1370–AD 1372] Kentoku Era. 1370-1372. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the year-names used by the Southern Court of Emperor Go-Daigo's heirs at Yoshino, still refusing to recognise the Ashikaga-backed emperors in Kyoto. By these years the southern cause was fading everywhere except Kyushu, and the shogunate was despatching commanders to finish it off.

Hellenistic (Egypt, 322 BC–30 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Egypt, 322 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic. 323 BC-31 BC.   Do not use for cuneiform tablets (instead use Macedonian Dynasty, Seleucid or Late Babylonian for anything without a specific date).   Ptolemaic is frequently used by G&R for Hellenistic terracottas made in Egypt. Period definition from British Museum.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1849 BC–1699.label: Middle Cycladic II
Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1849 BC–1699.prose:
[Greece, 1849 BC–1699 BC] Middle Cycladic II. 1850BC-1700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The mature phase of island town life, when Phylakopi, Ayia Irini and Akrotiri were compact, densely built settlements with organised streets and defences. Painted pottery, including jugs decorated with birds and flowers, shows Cycladic workshops absorbing Cretan taste while keeping their own style, and Melian obsidian and trade in metals kept the islands prosperous.

Chogen Era (Japan, AD 1028–AD 1037).label: Chogen Era
Chogen Era (Japan, AD 1028–AD 1037).prose:
[Japan, AD 1028–AD 1037] Chogen Era. 1028-1037. Period definition from British Museum.

The rebellion of Taira no Tadatsune tore through the Bōsō peninsula in eastern Japan, ruining provinces for years before the court finally turned to Minamoto no Yorinobu, who ended it without a battle. His success planted Minamoto prestige and clientage in the eastern provinces, the base from which the family would later dominate the country.

Eastern Han dynasty (China, AD 23–AD 220.label: Eastern Han dynasty
Eastern Han dynasty (China, AD 23–AD 220.prose:
[China, AD 23–AD 220] Eastern Han dynasty. 23-220.  In some sources, 25-220. Period definition from British Museum.

Restored by Emperor Guangwu after the collapse of Wang Mang's regime, the dynasty ruled from Luoyang and reasserted control over the Silk Road oases. It was an age of technical invention - paper, water-powered bellows, the seismoscope - and of the first Buddhist communities in China. Factional struggle between eunuchs, empresses' families and scholar-officials hollowed out the court until warlords divided the empire between them.

Zhizheng (China, AD 1341–AD 1368).label: Zhizheng
Zhizheng (China, AD 1341–AD 1368).prose:
[China, AD 1341–AD 1368] Zhizheng. 1341-1368 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The long final era of the Yuan, when famine, hyperinflated paper money and a disastrous Yellow River flood-control levy sparked the Red Turban risings and a decade of civil war among rebel warlords. Zhu Yuanzhang emerged the winner, drove the Mongol court back to the steppe and founded the Ming. The era also gives its name to the finest early blue-and-white porcelain, including the dated David Vases of 1351.

Koho Era (Japan, AD 964–AD 968).label: Koho Era
Koho Era (Japan, AD 964–AD 968).prose:
[Japan, AD 964–AD 968] Koho Era. 964-968. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Murakami died in 967, closing a reign later remembered as a golden age of court poetry and personal rule by the sovereign. His sickly successor could not govern, and the Fujiwara resumed the regency for good — the arrangement that would dominate the Heian court for the next century and a half.

Muzong (China, AD 951–AD 969).label: Muzong
Muzong (China, AD 951–AD 969).prose:
[China, AD 951–AD 969] Muzong. 951-969 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The fourth Liao emperor, remembered in Chinese sources as the "Sleeping Emperor" for drinking through the night and ignoring government for days. His indifference to expansion gave the newly founded Song state breathing space in the south, while his cruelty towards servants and attendants provoked repeated plots. He was murdered by his own cooks and grooms on a hunting trip.

Hallstatt C (Europe, 799 BC–599 BC).label: Hallstatt C
Hallstatt C (Europe, 799 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Europe, 799 BC–599 BC] Hallstatt C. Europe; 800-600 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Iron becomes the ordinary metal for weapons and tools, and a new warrior display emerges: long iron slashing swords, and burials under mounds containing four-wheeled wagons and horse gear. Salt extraction at Hallstatt reached its height, and the goods buried in its miners' graves show trade reaching to the Mediterranean and the Baltic.

Joan Era (Japan, AD 1171–AD 1175).label: Joan Era
Joan Era (Japan, AD 1171–AD 1175).prose:
[Japan, AD 1171–AD 1175] Joan Era. 1171-1175. Period definition from British Museum.

Late Heian years in which Taira no Kiyomori's clan reached the height of its power, packing the court with kinsmen and marrying into the imperial line. In 1175 the monk Hōnen began preaching that simple recitation of Amida's name could save anyone, launching the Pure Land movement that became the largest strand of Japanese Buddhism.

Zhengshi (China, AD 504–AD 508).label: Zhengshi
Zhengshi (China, AD 504–AD 508).prose:
[China, AD 504–AD 508] Zhengshi. 504-508 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

An era of Emperor Xuanwu of the Northern Wei, when the Tuoba dynasty ruled north China from Luoyang and pressed on with the sinicizing reforms of the previous reign. Buddhism enjoyed lavish imperial patronage, with work continuing on the cave temples at Longmen. Wei armies pushed south against the Liang, but court factionalism was already eating at the regime that would fracture within thirty years.

Taizu (China, AD 960–AD 976).label: Taizu
Taizu (China, AD 960–AD 976).prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 976] Taizu. 960-976 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Zhao Kuangyin, a palace guard commander, was raised to the throne by his own troops and founded the Song, ending half a century of short-lived military regimes. He famously persuaded his generals to trade their commands for wealth and retirement, then rebuilt the army under central civilian control and began picking off the southern kingdoms one by one. The result was a state where scholars outranked soldiers, an arrangement that made Song China prosperous and cultured but chronically vulnerable on its northern frontier.

Jiajing (China, AD 1522–AD 1566).label: Jiajing
Jiajing (China, AD 1522–AD 1566).prose:
[China, AD 1522–AD 1566] Jiajing. 1522-1566 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A Ming emperor who spent decades pursuing Daoist immortality elixirs and refused to meet his ministers, leaving grand secretaries to run the state and factions to devour one another. His reign saw Mongol horsemen reach the walls of Beijing in 1550 and Japanese-linked pirates ravage the southeast coast. Its blue-and-white porcelain, made in huge imperial commissions, is prized by collectors today.

Dade (China, AD 1297–AD 1307).label: Dade
Dade (China, AD 1297–AD 1307).prose:
[China, AD 1297–AD 1307] Dade. 1297-1307 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The later years of Temür Khan's rule over the Yuan empire, when the grandson of Kublai held together the Mongol realm his predecessor had built, curbed the ruinous military expeditions abroad and tried to rein in fiscal corruption at home. His death without an heir at the era's close opened decades of contested successions among Mongol princes that steadily weakened the dynasty.

Hallstatt A (Europe, 1199 BC–1124 BC).label: Hallstatt A
Hallstatt A (Europe, 1199 BC–1124 BC).prose:
[Europe, 1199 BC–1124 BC] Hallstatt A. Europe; 1200-1125 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Despite the name, these are Late Bronze Age generations in Reinecke's scheme: the Urnfield world, where the dead were cremated and their ashes buried in pots in vast flat cemeteries. Bronzesmiths worked sheet metal into helmets, cuirasses and buckets, and fortified hilltop settlements multiplied across southern Germany.

Sumerian (Iraq, 2999 BC–2349 BC).label: Sumerian
Sumerian (Iraq, 2999 BC–2349 BC).prose:
[southern Mesopotamia, ancient region of Sumer, 2999 BC–2349 BC] Sumerian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia. Sumerian is not used as a period culture term but as a language (see inscription field), instead see narrower terms. The period from circa 3000 BC-2350 BC in southern Mesopotamia is sub-divided into three main phases known as Early Dynastic I, II & III. Part of this region at this period corresponds to the ancient region of Sumer hence the assumption that all of the material culture is Sumerian. Period definition from British Museum.

The world's first cities matured here into rival city-states—Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish—each centred on a temple and its god, ruled by kings who fought over land and water. Cuneiform writing developed from accounting tallies into a tool for literature, law and letters, while craftsmen produced the gold, lapis and shell work found in the royal graves at Ur. Sumerian language, myth and administrative practice shaped Mesopotamian civilisation long after Sumerians ceased to be a political power.

Daye (China, AD 605–AD 618).label: Daye
Daye (China, AD 605–AD 618).prose:
[China, AD 605–AD 618] Daye. 605-618. reign period. Period definition from British Museum.

The era name covering the ambitious and ruinous later years of Sui Yangdi. He completed the Grand Canal linking the Yangtze to the north, rebuilt Luoyang as a second capital, and mobilised millions for construction and for three catastrophic invasions of Koguryo. The human cost triggered mass revolts; the emperor was strangled by his own guards and the Tang seized the empire, inheriting the infrastructure his exactions had built.

Hongzhi (China, AD 1488–AD 1505).label: Hongzhi
Hongzhi (China, AD 1488–AD 1505).prose:
[China, AD 1488–AD 1505] Hongzhi. 1488-1505 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A reign remembered by later Chinese historians as a rare stretch of clean, conscientious government in the Ming: the emperor listened to his ministers, curbed eunuch influence and revised the dynastic legal code. He kept only one consort and no harem, an unheard-of arrangement for a Chinese emperor. The calm ended abruptly with his son Zhengde, whose antics undid much of the recovery.

Begtiginid dynasty (Iraq, AD 1145–AD 123.label: Begtiginid dynasty
Begtiginid dynasty (Iraq, AD 1145–AD 123.prose:
[north-eastern Iraq and Kurdistan; northern Syria, AD 1145–AD 1233] Begtiginid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. 1145-1233 (AH 529-AH 630). Turkish rulers controlling north-eastern Iraq and Kurdistan with a centre at Irbil, also in control of Harran in northern Syria.They arose out of the Turkish military entourage of the Zangids (q.v.). Period definition from British Museum.

A Kurdish dynasty that governed Irbil (Erbil) and its hinterland, first as officers of the Zengids and then as semi-independent lords allied to Saladin. Its best-known ruler, Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri, fought at Saladin's side, endowed hospitals and hospices, and made Erbil's public celebration of the Prophet's birthday famous throughout the Islamic world. When he died without an heir the city passed to the Abbasid caliph, and within a decade the Mongols were at the gates.

Khai Dinh (Vietnam, AD 1916–AD 1925).label: Khai Dinh
Khai Dinh (Vietnam, AD 1916–AD 1925).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1916–AD 1925] Khai Dinh. (1916-1925) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

A Nguyễn emperor who ruled Vietnam with almost no power, the French Résident Supérieur making the real decisions while the court at Huế kept its ceremonies. His fondness for European dress, his heavy taxation and his 1922 tour of France made him a target for nationalists — the young Nguyễn Ái Quốc, later Hồ Chí Minh, mocked him in a Paris satire. He left behind a spectacular hillside tomb of blackened concrete inlaid with porcelain and glass, and a son, Bảo Đại, who would be Vietnam's last emperor.

Kerma Moyen (Egypt, 2049 BC–1749 BC).label: Kerma Moyen
Kerma Moyen (Egypt, 2049 BC–1749 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2049 BC–1749 BC] Kerma Moyen. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. c. 2050 BC-1750 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Kerma grew into a walled city with a large cemetery of increasingly rich tumulus burials, at exactly the time Egypt's Middle Kingdom pharaohs were building their chain of massive fortresses through Lower Nubia to control the river trade. The scale of those Egyptian defences is the best measure of how formidable the Nubian kingdom upstream had become.

Xin dynasty (China, AD 9–AD 23).label: Xin dynasty
Xin dynasty (China, AD 9–AD 23).prose:
[China, AD 9–AD 23] Xin dynasty. 9-23.  In some sources: 9-25. Period definition from British Museum.

Wang Mang, regent for a line of infant Han emperors, took the throne himself and set out to remake the empire on the model of the ancient classics, nationalising land, abolishing private slave trading and repeatedly recoining the currency. The reforms failed, and when the Yellow River changed course and famine spread, the Red Eyebrows and other rebel armies rose. Wang Mang was killed in his palace and the Han were restored, leaving him the classic villain of Chinese official history.

Shotoku Era (Japan, AD 1711–AD 1716).label: Shotoku Era
Shotoku Era (Japan, AD 1711–AD 1716).prose:
[Japan, AD 1711–AD 1716] Shotoku Era. 1711-1716. Period definition from British Museum.

Under two short-lived shoguns, the Confucian scholar Arai Hakuseki effectively ran Tokugawa policy, trying to undo the debasement of the coinage and restore the currency's silver content. He also cut the number of Chinese and Dutch ships allowed into Nagasaki each year, to stem the outflow of precious metals, and trimmed the extravagant ceremonial of the shogun's court. The reforms ended abruptly when Yoshimune became shogun and dismissed him.

Zhaozong (China, AD 888–AD 904).label: Zhaozong
Zhaozong (China, AD 888–AD 904).prose:
[China, AD 888–AD 904] Zhaozong. 888-904 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The next-to-last Tang emperor was a hostage of his own generals, shuttled between warlord camps as the imperial court's authority shrank to little more than ceremony. His attempts to break the power of the palace eunuchs and the provincial military governors ended in massacre and his own murder by the warlord Zhu Wen. Three years later Zhu deposed the last Tang ruler and founded his own dynasty, opening the fragmented Five Dynasties era.

Owa Era (Japan, AD 961–AD 964).label: Owa Era
Owa Era (Japan, AD 961–AD 964).prose: [Japan, AD 961–AD 964] Owa Era. 961-964. Period definition from British Museum.

Shamsabad (Iran, 4799 BC–4499 BC).label: Shamsabad
Shamsabad (Iran, 4799 BC–4499 BC).prose: [Fars, 4799 BC–4499 BC] Shamsabad. Fars, 4800BC-4500BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Tenroku Era (Japan, AD 970–AD 973).label: Tenroku Era
Tenroku Era (Japan, AD 970–AD 973).prose:
[Japan, AD 970–AD 973] Tenroku Era. 970-973. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief span in the mid-Heian court, remembered chiefly through the Fujiwara regents' tightening grip on the boy-emperor's government and the diaries and poetry anthologies produced by the aristocracy.

Nara Period (Japan, AD 710–AD 794).label: Nara Period
Nara Period (Japan, AD 710–AD 794).prose:
[Japan, AD 710–AD 794] Nara Period. 710-794. Period definition from British Museum.

For most of the eighth century Japan was governed from Heijō-kyō, a grid-planned capital modelled on Chinese Chang'an, under Chinese-style law codes, land allotment and taxation. The court sponsored Buddhism on a colossal scale, above all the bronze Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, and commissioned the Kojiki, Nihon shoki and the poetry anthology Man'yōshū. Aristocratic and monastic power at the capital grew so heavy that the court eventually moved away to Heian-kyō.

Mangujakid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1118–AD 1.label: Mangujakid dynasty
Mangujakid dynasty (Turkey, AD 1118–AD 1.prose:
[northern Anatolia, AD 1118–AD 1242] Mangujakid dynasty. 1118-1242 (AH 512-AH 640). Dynasty in northern Anatolia with centres at Erzincan, Kemakh and Divrigi. The Mangujakid's clashed with the Seljiqs of Rum and sought allies with the Byzantines. Period definition from British Museum.

One of the small Turkmen principalities carved out of eastern Anatolia after the Seljuk victory at Manzikert, ruling from Erzincan and Divriği. Their most lasting act was the building of the Great Mosque and hospital at Divriği, whose extravagantly carved stone portals are unlike anything else in Islamic architecture and are now a World Heritage Site. The line was absorbed by the Seljuks of Rum.

Vicus (Peru, 999 BC–AD 300).label: Vicus
Vicus (Peru, 999 BC–AD 300).prose:
[Peru, 999 BC–AD 300] Vicus. The term refers to a culture (c. 1000 BC-300 AD); also a style. Period definition from British Museum.

A culture of the far north coast of Peru, in the Piura valley, best known from the deep shaft tombs of Cerro Vicús, which were largely emptied by looters before archaeologists reached them. Its metalworkers were among the most accomplished in the ancient Andes, producing gilded copper, silver and gold ornaments using techniques later associated with the Moche. Its modelled ceramics, including double-spout-and-bridge vessels, show contacts stretching north into Ecuador and south to the Moche heartland.

Horeki Era (Japan, AD 1751–AD 1764).label: Horeki Era
Horeki Era (Japan, AD 1751–AD 1764).prose:
[Japan, AD 1751–AD 1764] Horeki Era. 1751-1764. Period definition from British Museum.

A mid-Edo era under the shogun Tokugawa Ieshige, in which the long-outdated Chinese-derived calendar was replaced by a new Japanese reckoning informed by Western astronomy. The shogunate also forced the Satsuma domain to pay for vast flood-control works on the Kiso rivers, ruining its finances and driving its chief engineer to suicide. In Kyoto, courtiers who studied loyalist doctrines under Takenouchi Shikibu were punished, an early stirring of the imperial revival that would matter a century later.

Tianqing (China, AD 1110–AD 1118).label: Tianqing
Tianqing (China, AD 1110–AD 1118).prose: [China, AD 1110–AD 1118] Tianqing. 1110-1118 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Thuan Thien reign period (Vietnam, AD 14.label: Thuan Thien reign period
Thuan Thien reign period (Vietnam, AD 14.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1433] Thuan Thien reign period. Thuan Thien reign period (1428-1433). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era of Lê Lợi, who had just driven the Ming occupation out of Vietnam after a decade of insurgency and founded the Lê dynasty. He redistributed land to soldiers and villages, restored the civil examinations and reasserted Vietnamese independence while sending tribute to Beijing. The legend of the returned magic sword at Hoan Kiem Lake in Hanoi belongs to this moment.

Tenmon Era (Japan, AD 1532–AD 1555).label: Tenmon Era
Tenmon Era (Japan, AD 1532–AD 1555).prose:
[Japan, AD 1532–AD 1555] Tenmon Era. 1532-1555. Period definition from British Museum.

Warlord politics at its most fragmented, when the shogunate barely controlled Kyoto and armed Buddhist leagues fought pitched battles in the streets. Portuguese traders reached Tanegashima with matchlock guns in 1543, and Francis Xavier landed in 1549 to begin the Christian mission — two imports that reshaped Japanese warfare and culture within a generation.

Qianyuan (China, AD 758–AD 759).label: Qianyuan
Qianyuan (China, AD 758–AD 759).prose:
[China, AD 758–AD 759] Qianyuan. 758-759 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era in the middle of the An Lushan rebellion, when Tang armies had retaken Chang'an and Luoyang but the war ground on inconclusively. To pay for it the court issued the grossly overvalued Qianyuan Zhongbao coins, triggering inflation and counterfeiting; the fiscal and military improvisations of these years permanently shifted power towards regional commanders.

En'o Era (Japan, AD 1239–AD 1240).label: En'o Era
En'o Era (Japan, AD 1239–AD 1240).prose: [Japan, AD 1239–AD 1240] En'o Era. 1239-1240. Period definition from British Museum.

Xuande (China, AD 1426–AD 1435).label: Xuande
Xuande (China, AD 1426–AD 1435).prose:
[China, AD 1426–AD 1435] Xuande. 1426-1435 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of the Ming emperor Xuanzong, remembered as a settled, prosperous interval after decades of expansion. Zheng He's treasure fleet made its last voyage and the costly occupation of Vietnam was abandoned, while the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen produced blue-and-white porcelain that later collectors treated as the summit of the craft. The emperor himself painted and kept a famous menagerie of cricket-fighting champions.

Susa I (Iran, 4199 BC–3699 BC).label: Susa I
Susa I (Iran, 4199 BC–3699 BC).prose:
[Khuzestan, 4199 BC–3699 BC] Susa I. Khuzestan, ca 4200BC-3700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The first great occupation of Susa opened with the raising of a huge platform on the Acropole and a cemetery holding well over a thousand burials. The dead were accompanied by tall, thin-walled beakers painted with astonishing economy—ibexes reduced to a pair of sweeping horns, running dogs, wading birds—among the finest ceramic art of prehistoric Iran. Copper axes and stamp seals in the same graves show a community already ranked and administratively organised.

Ilkhanid dynasty (Iran, AD 1256–AD 1353).label: Ilkhanid dynasty
Ilkhanid dynasty (Iran, AD 1256–AD 1353).prose:
[regions of Persia, Iraq, Transcaucasia and Anatolia, AD 1256–AD 1353] Ilkhanid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Anatolia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Pakistan. 1256-1353 (AH 654-AH 754). The Mongol Il-Khanids were rulers of the regions of Persia, Iraq, Transcaucasia and Anatolia. Hulegu (Huluku), son of Toluy, adopted the title of Il-Khan meaning territorial Khan and subordinate to the Great Khan. The capitals of the Il-Khanid's of Persia were Tabriz and Maragha in the north-west, and later at Sultaniyya near Qazwin. Period definition from British Museum.

Hulagu's Mongol armies swept away the Abbasid caliphate and left a branch of Chinggis Khan's house ruling Iran from Tabriz and Sultaniyya. The khans converted to Islam within two generations and poured tribute into a spectacular fusion culture: Chinese-influenced painting in illustrated manuscripts of the Shahnama, blue-and-white ceramics, huge brick domes, and Rashid al-Din's world history, arguably the first attempt to write the history of all Eurasia. Succession quarrels broke the state into rival principalities and left the way open for Timur.

Early Minoan II (Crete, 2899 BC–2299 BC).label: Early Minoan II
Early Minoan II (Crete, 2899 BC–2299 BC).prose:
[Crete, 2899 BC–2299 BC] Early Minoan II. 2900BC-2300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The most prosperous stretch of prepalatial Crete, when craftsmen produced mottled orange-and-black Vasiliki ware, translucent stone vases and fine gold ornaments. Excavated settlements such as Myrtos Fournou Korifi and the House on the Hill at Vasiliki show planned, agglomerated buildings with storage and workshop space. Seals came into common use for marking goods, an early hint of the record-keeping that would underpin the palaces.

Idrisid dynasty (Morocco, AD 789–AD 926).label: Idrisid dynasty
Idrisid dynasty (Morocco, AD 789–AD 926).prose:
[region of Morocco, AD 789–AD 926] Idrisid dynasty. 789-926 (AH 172-AH 375). The first dynasty to introduce the doctrines of Shi'ism into the region of Morocco. Idris I was a great-grandson of Imam Hasan and therefore a direct descendant of the Prophet Mohammad and his son-in-law 'Ali ibn 'Ali Talib. Period definition from British Museum.

Founded by Idris ibn Abd Allah, a great-great-grandson of Ali who fled the Abbasids and was welcomed by Berber tribes, this was the first Muslim dynasty to rule an independent Morocco. Its lasting monument is Fez, which filled with refugees from Kairouan and Islamic Spain and became a centre of learning and trade. The dynasty's fragmentation among heirs left it prey to the Fatimids and the Umayyads of Córdoba, but its founder remains Morocco's patron saint.

Ninju Era (Japan, AD 851–AD 854).label: Ninju Era
Ninju Era (Japan, AD 851–AD 854).prose:
[Japan, AD 851–AD 854] Ninju Era. 851-854. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief early Heian era under Emperor Montoku, when real influence at court was passing to the Fujiwara through marriage to the imperial line. The capital at Heian-kyō was consolidating as the centre of an aristocratic culture modelled on, but steadily diverging from, Chinese precedent. Such short reign eras are chiefly useful now as fine-grained dating labels in chronicles and inscriptions.

Mahdiya (Sudan, AD 1881–AD 1898).label: Mahdiya
Mahdiya (Sudan, AD 1881–AD 1898).prose:
[Sudan, AD 1881–AD 1898] Mahdiya. The term refers to the period between 1881 and 1898 of the Sudanese nationalist movement led by Mohamed Ahmed al-Mahdi (the Mahdi) against the Turkiya which led to the capture of  Khartoum in 1885. After his death in 1885, Mohamed Ahmed is succeeded by Abdullahi ibn Mohamed (the Khalifa) who ruled until his defeat at the battle of Omdurman by General Kitchener in 1898. Period definition from British Museum.

Muhammad Ahmad proclaimed himself the Mahdi and led a religious revolt that swept away Turco-Egyptian rule, annihilating an Egyptian army and taking Khartoum in 1885, where General Gordon was killed. After the Mahdi's death his successor, the Khalifa Abdallahi, ran a centralised Islamic state from Omdurman for over a decade. It ended under British machine guns at Omdurman in 1898 — one of the few African states to defeat and then be destroyed by a European power.

Bun'o Era (Japan, AD 1260–AD 1261).label: Bun'o Era
Bun'o Era (Japan, AD 1260–AD 1261).prose:
[Japan, AD 1260–AD 1261] Bun'o Era. 1260-1261. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era remembered for a document: the monk Nichiren presented his "Treatise on Establishing the Correct Teaching for the Peace of the Land" to the Kamakura authorities, blaming earthquakes, famine and epidemic on false Buddhist schools and warning of foreign invasion. The regime's response was persecution and exile, but the prophecy gained enormous authority when the Mongols arrived a decade later.

Elamite (Iran, 2999 BC–538 BC).label: Elamite
Elamite (Iran, 2999 BC–538 BC).prose:
[land of Elam, 2999 BC–538 BC] Elamite. Term not used in its own right, instead see narrower terms.  Term used to describe the period and material culture of south-western Iran between circa 3000-539 BC which was referred to as the land of Elam in ancient Mesopotamian sources. Elamite is also an ancient language spoken in this region at that time. Period definition from British Museum.

The great rival civilisation to Mesopotamia, centred on Susa in the lowlands and Anshan in the Zagros highlands, writing first in an undeciphered proto-Elamite script and later in cuneiform. Elamite armies sacked Ur and carried off Babylonian treasures - including Hammurabi's law stele, found at Susa - and Elamite kings built the towering ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil. Weakened by Assyrian devastation in the seventh century, Elam was absorbed by the rising Persians, who kept its language for their imperial accounts at Persepolis.

Kangxi (Japan, AD 1662–AD 1722).label: Kangxi
Kangxi (Japan, AD 1662–AD 1722).prose:
[Japan, AD 1662–AD 1722] Kangxi. 1662-1722 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The 61-year reign of the second Qing emperor to rule from Beijing, who crushed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, annexed Taiwan, fixed the northern border with Russia by treaty at Nerchinsk, and campaigned against the Zunghars. He sponsored huge scholarly projects including the dictionary that bears his name, welcomed Jesuit astronomers and mathematicians, and presided over a revival of imperial porcelain prized by collectors ever since.

Sixteen kingdoms (China, AD 304–AD 439).label: Sixteen kingdoms
