Sixteen kingdoms (China, AD 304–AD 439).prose:
[China, AD 304–AD 439] Sixteen kingdoms. 304-439. Period definition from British Museum.

Northern China dissolved into a rapid succession of rival regimes founded mostly by peoples from the steppe frontier, each claiming imperial legitimacy and few lasting a generation. Warfare and famine drove waves of refugees south, while rulers such as Fu Jian of the Former Qin briefly came close to reuniting the whole country before disastrous defeat. The period closed with the Northern Wei conquest, which fused steppe rule and Chinese administration.

Thien Phuc reign period (Vietnam, AD 980.label: Thien Phuc reign period
Thien Phuc reign period (Vietnam, AD 980.prose:
[Vietnam, AD 980–AD 988] Thien Phuc reign period. Thien Phuc reign period (980-988). Period definition from British Museum.

The first era of Le Hoan, a general who took the throne from a child emperor and founded the Early Le dynasty. In 981 he defeated a Song Chinese invasion by land and river, securing the independence of the young Vietnamese state, and the following year he sacked the Cham capital to the south. His reign set the pattern of a Vietnamese ruler acknowledging Chinese suzerainty on paper while fighting off Chinese armies in practice.

Early Minoan IIB (Crete, 2499 BC–2299 BC.label: Early Minoan IIB
Early Minoan IIB (Crete, 2499 BC–2299 BC.prose:
[Crete, 2499 BC–2299 BC] Early Minoan IIB. 2500BC-2300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A prosperous phase that ended badly: Vasiliki, Myrtos and other settlements burned or were abandoned, and the pattern of Cretan habitation shifted. Before that, potters produced elegant spouted jugs and teapots, and seal-carving in ivory and bone spread as a way of marking property. The disruptions cleared the ground for the reorganisation that led to the first palaces.

Kajo Era 848-851 (Japan, AD 848–AD 851).label: Kajo Era 848-851
Kajo Era 848-851 (Japan, AD 848–AD 851).prose:
[Japan, AD 848–AD 851] Kajo Era 848-851. 848-851. Period definition from British Museum.

An early Heian era that saw the death of Emperor Ninmyō and the accession of Montoku in 850, a succession engineered by Fujiwara no Yoshifusa, whose sister was the new emperor's mother. It marks a decisive step in the Fujiwara family's capture of the throne through marriage politics.

Xianyong (China, AD 1066–AD 1073).label: Xianyong
Xianyong (China, AD 1066–AD 1073).prose: [China, AD 1066–AD 1073] Xianyong. 1066-1073 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Chen dynasty (China, AD 557–AD 589).label: Chen dynasty
Chen dynasty (China, AD 557–AD 589).prose:
[China, AD 557–AD 589] Chen dynasty. 557-589. Period definition from British Museum.

Founded by Chen Baxian after decades of civil war had gutted the southern state, it ruled a shrunken territory around the Yangtze delta with its capital at Jiankang, modern Nanjing. Its fall to the Sui reunified China under a single throne for the first time since the Han, and the southern aristocratic culture it preserved was absorbed into the empire that followed.

Cheng Wang (China, 1114 BC–1076 BC).label: Cheng Wang
Cheng Wang (China, 1114 BC–1076 BC).prose:
[China, 1114 BC–1076 BC] Cheng Wang. 1115BC-1077BC (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The second Zhou king came to the throne as a child, with his uncle the Duke of Zhou governing in his name — an arrangement that provoked a major rebellion by other royal kinsmen and their Shang allies. Its suppression secured Zhou control of the eastern plain, and a new administrative capital was built at Chengzhou near modern Luoyang. Later Confucians treated the regency and the young king's eventual assumption of power as the model of virtuous government.

Kajo Era 1106-1108 (Japan, AD 1106–AD 11.label: Kajo Era 1106-1108
Kajo Era 1106-1108 (Japan, AD 1106–AD 11.prose:
[Japan, AD 1106–AD 1108] Kajo Era 1106-1108. 1106-1108. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Heian era spanning the death of Emperor Horikawa in 1107 and the accession of his four-year-old son Toba, which left the retired emperor Shirakawa firmly in control of the court as cloistered ruler.

Early Christian Period I (Sudan, AD 550–.label: Early Christian Period I
Early Christian Period I (Sudan, AD 550–.prose:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 550–AD 700] Early Christian Period I. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 550-700. Period definition from British Museum.

The first generations after the conversion of the Nubian kingdoms, when churches were built in almost every settlement and older temples were reconsecrated or dismantled. Pottery and burial customs changed sharply as pagan tumulus burial with grave goods gave way to plain Christian interment.

Tianxian Taizong (China, AD 927–AD 938).label: Tianxian Taizong
Tianxian Taizong (China, AD 927–AD 938).prose:
[China, AD 927–AD 938] Tianxian Taizong. 927-938 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The Khitan ruler Abaoji died just after conquering Balhae, and after a contested succession his second son Deguang took the throne as Emperor Taizong. His great coup came when he backed a Chinese rebel's bid for the throne in return for the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing and Datong — the first time a steppe power held rich agricultural land and walled cities south of the frontier. Those prefectures became the central grievance of Chinese politics for the next four hundred years.

Wudi (China, 86 BC–AD 140).label: Wudi
Wudi (China, 86 BC–AD 140).prose: [China, 86 BC–AD 140] Wudi. 140-87BC (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Juei Era (Japan, AD 1182–AD 1184).label: Juei Era
Juei Era (Japan, AD 1182–AD 1184).prose:
[Japan, AD 1182–AD 1184] Juei Era. 1182-1184. Period definition from British Museum.

The middle years of the Genpei War, when Minamoto no Yoshinaka drove the Taira out of the capital and they fled west with the child emperor and the imperial regalia. In the confusion the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa issued an edict recognising Minamoto no Yoritomo's authority over the eastern provinces - the first formal step towards an independent warrior government based at Kamakura.

Zhiyuan (China, AD 1264–AD 1294).label: Zhiyuan
Zhiyuan (China, AD 1264–AD 1294).prose:
[China, AD 1264–AD 1294] Zhiyuan. 1264-1294 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Kublai Khan's long era, in which a Mongol khan remade himself as a Chinese emperor: he proclaimed the Yuan dynasty, built the capital of Dadu on the site of modern Beijing, and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279 - the first time all of China was ruled from the steppe. Grand Canal extensions, paper money and Muslim and European officials and travellers, Marco Polo among them, knitted China into a Eurasian network. Two seaborne invasions of Japan failed disastrously, and expeditions into Vietnam and Java achieved little.

Indo-Greek (Afghanistan, 179 BC–AD 10).label: Indo-Greek
Indo-Greek (Afghanistan, 179 BC–AD 10).prose:
[Afghanistan and north-western Pakistan, 179 BC–AD 10] Indo-Greek. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Pakistan. The term refers to a specific independent Greek kingdom (c.180 BC-AD 10), ruling in Afghanistan south of the Hindu Kush mountains and north-western Pakistan up to the Indus and Sutlej rivers (i.e. including the Punjab).  The Indo-Greeks lost Afghanistan and most of Pakistan to Indo-Scythians c. 70 BC, but survived in the Punjab until c. AD 10. They are the successors to the Greco-Bactrians, who broke away from the Seleucid empire c. 250 BC to form an independent Greek kingdom in Bactria (Afghanistan north of the Hindu Kush) and Sogdiana (modern Tajikistan), which was lost to nomadic tribes of the Indo-Scythians and Yuezhi by c. 100 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Greek-speaking rulers descended from Bactrian settlers held kingdoms across eastern Afghanistan and the Punjab, striking bilingual coins in Greek and Kharoshthi with some of the finest portraiture of the ancient world. Menander appears in Buddhist tradition as King Milinda, debating doctrine with the monk Nagasena, and Greek artistic conventions fed into the Buddha images later produced in Gandhara. Scythian and Kushan incomers gradually squeezed the last of these kingdoms out of existence.

Eijo Era (Japan, AD 1046–AD 1053).label: Eijo Era
Eijo Era (Japan, AD 1046–AD 1053).prose:
[Japan, AD 1046–AD 1053] Eijo Era. 1046-1053. Period definition from British Museum.

The high noon of Fujiwara power, when the regent Yorimichi governed on behalf of his imperial nephews and was converting his villa at Uji into the Byodo-in, whose Phoenix Hall still stands as the age's supreme image of the Pure Land paradise. At the same time fighting broke out in the northeast that grew into the Former Nine Years War, the long campaign in which provincial warrior clans learned their trade.

Song dynasty (China, AD 960–AD 1279).label: Song dynasty
Song dynasty (China, AD 960–AD 1279).prose:
[China, AD 960–AD 1279] Song dynasty. 960-1279. Period definition from British Museum.

China's commercial revolution: rice surpluses from the south fed cities of a million people, iron output soared, merchants used printed paper money, and the civil service examinations opened high office to a literate gentry. Painters, poets and neo-Confucian philosophers of these centuries set standards later dynasties measured themselves against. All of it sat behind fragile frontiers, and the dynasty ended under Mongol conquest.

Proto-Corinthian (Greece, 699 BC–639 BC).label: Proto-Corinthian
Proto-Corinthian (Greece, 699 BC–639 BC).prose:
[Corinth, 699 BC–639 BC] Proto-Corinthian. 700BC-640BC.  Used with Corinth as Production place.  The term only applies to pottery. Period definition from British Museum.

Corinthian potters invented a miniature style painted with rows of lions, sphinxes and warriors, incised in silhouette in the manner learned from Near Eastern metalwork. Tiny perfume flasks carried Corinthian scent and Corinthian art to Italy, Sicily and the Levant, making the city the dominant exporter of fine pottery in the Greek world. The black-figure technique developed here was later taken up and perfected in Athens.

Jogen Era 1207-1211 (Japan, AD 1207–AD 1.label: Jogen Era 1207-1211
Jogen Era 1207-1211 (Japan, AD 1207–AD 1.prose:
[Japan, AD 1207–AD 1211] Jogen Era 1207-1211. 1207-1211. Period definition from British Museum.

The years of the Jōgen persecution, when the court banned Hōnen's Pure Land preaching, executed several of his followers and exiled the master himself along with his disciple Shinran. The exile scattered the movement across the provinces, spreading it far more widely than it had reached in the capital.

Edo Period (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868).label: Edo Period
Edo Period (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868).prose:
[Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868] Edo Period. 1603-1868.  N.B. The Edo period is routinely said to start in 1600, 1603 or 1615, depending on its definition, but the date used here is 1603. Period definition from British Museum.

Under the Tokugawa shoguns, Japan was united after a century of civil war and locked into a rigid order of samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, with regional lords held in check by compulsory attendance at the shogun's capital. Foreign contact was cut to a trickle through Nagasaki, and Christianity was suppressed. Two and a half centuries of peace produced booming cities, mass literacy, kabuki theatre and woodblock prints, before American warships and internal pressure brought the system down.

Yong'an (China, AD 528–AD 530).label: Yong'an
Yong'an (China, AD 528–AD 530).prose:
[China, AD 528–AD 530] Yong'an. 528-530 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign era of the puppet emperor Xiaozhuang, installed by the warlord Erzhu Rong after his troops drowned the dowager empress and slaughtered the Northern Wei court at Heyin. Xiaozhuang had Erzhu Rong assassinated in the palace and was strangled in revenge months later. The dynasty never recovered, splitting within a few years into Eastern and Western Wei.

Keros-Syros Culture (Greece, 2799 BC–229.label: Keros-Syros Culture
Keros-Syros Culture (Greece, 2799 BC–229.prose:
[Cyclades, 2799 BC–2299 BC] Keros-Syros Culture. The second of the three cultural groups into which the Early Cycladic (q.v.) period is divided, based on consistently recurring types of pottery, bronze and marble objects. The name refers to the islands used by Colin Renfrew to define the culture, although the term applies to material from the Cyclades as a whole. There are not always clear boundaries between cultural groups, but an approximate date range is 2800BC – 2300BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of Early Bronze Age culture in the Cyclades, producing the spare white marble figurines with folded arms that later fascinated modern sculptors, along with incised 'frying pan' vessels showing longboats with dozens of oars. Those boats carried obsidian, metal and marble around the Aegean, and on the islet of Dhaskalio beside Keros islanders gathered from across the archipelago to deposit thousands of deliberately broken figurines and bowls — the earliest known maritime sanctuary in the Aegean.

Tokuji Era (Japan, AD 1306–AD 1308).label: Tokuji Era
Tokuji Era (Japan, AD 1306–AD 1308).prose:
[Japan, AD 1306–AD 1308] Tokuji Era. 1306-1308. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era name in the late Kamakura period, spanning the last years of Emperor Go-Nijo's reign. His death brought Hanazono to the throne under the awkward arrangement by which two rival imperial lines alternated, a dispute that would eventually split the court into northern and southern factions. Real power lay with the Hojo regents in Kamakura, still recovering from the strain of the Mongol invasions.

Genna Era (Japan, AD 1615–AD 1624).label: Genna Era
Genna Era (Japan, AD 1615–AD 1624).prose:
[Japan, AD 1615–AD 1624] Genna Era. 1615-1624. Period definition from British Museum.

The name marks the end of fighting after Tokugawa forces destroyed the Toyotomi at Osaka Castle, and contemporaries spoke of "laying down arms" for good. The shogunate used the peace to impose lasting controls: one castle per province, codes of conduct for warrior houses and the imperial court, and tightening restrictions on Christianity and foreign trade. It is the moment the Tokugawa settlement hardened into a system that would last two and a half centuries.

Saffarid dynasty (Iran, AD 861–AD 1003).label: Saffarid dynasty
Saffarid dynasty (Iran, AD 861–AD 1003).prose:
[Eastern Persia to India, AD 861–AD 1003] Saffarid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan. 861-1003 (AH 247-AH 393). Dynasty in Eastern Persia. Ya'qub and his brother 'Amr derived their name from their founders trade of coppersmith (Saffar). The province of Sistan became the centre of a vast empire which covered almost all of Persia, except for the north-west and the Caspian region. The empire stretched to the frontiers of India. The Saffarids openly proclaimed their contempt for the 'Abbasids and effectively demolished the 'caliphal fiction'. Period definition from British Museum.

Ya'qub ibn Layth, a coppersmith turned warlord from Sistan, built an army out of frontier volunteers and swept up Khurasan, toppling the Tahirids and marching on Baghdad itself before being turned back. The Saffarids were the first substantial dynasty to rule eastern Iran in open defiance of the Abbasid caliphs, and tradition holds that Ya'qub demanded poetry in Persian rather than Arabic, an early moment in the revival of New Persian literature.

Hoji Era (Japan, AD 1247–AD 1249).label: Hoji Era
Hoji Era (Japan, AD 1247–AD 1249).prose:
[Japan, AD 1247–AD 1249] Hoji Era. 1247-1249. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era dominated by the Hōji Disturbance of 1247, in which the regent Hōjō Tokiyori destroyed the powerful Miura family in Kamakura. With the last serious rival warrior house gone, the Hōjō regency held unchallenged control of the shogunate for the rest of the century.

Ten'en Era (Japan, AD 973–AD 976).label: Ten'en Era
Ten'en Era (Japan, AD 973–AD 976).prose:
[Japan, AD 973–AD 976] Ten'en Era. 973-976. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Heian reign-era under Emperor En'yu, with the Fujiwara regents controlling appointments and court politics. It ended amid disaster — earthquake and fire damaging the imperial palace — which prompted the court to change the era name in hope of better fortune.

Thai Binh reign period (Vietnam, AD 970–.label: Thai Binh reign period
Thai Binh reign period (Vietnam, AD 970–.prose: [Vietnam, AD 970–AD 980] Thai Binh reign period. Thai Binh reign period (970-979; 979-980). Period definition from British Museum.

Nasca-Huari (Peru, AD 650–AD 850).label: Nasca-Huari
Nasca-Huari (Peru, AD 650–AD 850).prose:
[Peru, AD 650–AD 850] Nasca-Huari. 650-850.  Transitional phase between Nasca and Huari cultures. Period definition from British Museum.

The expanding Wari state from the Ayacucho highlands drew the Nazca valleys into a much larger political and religious world, introducing new administrative sites, iconography and ceramic styles. Local traditions blended with imperial ones, and the old ceremonial landscape lost its central role. It is a key episode in the Middle Horizon spread of Andean statecraft.

Kenryaku Era (Japan, AD 1211–AD 1213).label: Kenryaku Era
Kenryaku Era (Japan, AD 1211–AD 1213).prose:
[Japan, AD 1211–AD 1213] Kenryaku Era. 1211-1213. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era remembered chiefly for a book: Kamo no Chōmei, a courtier turned hermit, wrote the Hōjōki in 1212, describing the fires, famine, earthquake and whirlwind that had wrecked Kyoto and the ten-foot hut in which he had withdrawn from the world. It became one of the classic statements of Japanese ideas about impermanence.

La Tène B (Europe, 399 BC–274 BC).label: La Tène B
La Tène B (Europe, 399 BC–274 BC).prose:
[Europe, 399 BC–274 BC] La Tène B. "La Tène I: The term is used in reference to material culture from Europe dating from 450 BC-320 BC. It corresponds, broadly speaking, to the alternative classifications La Tène A (450 BC-400 BC) and part of La Tène B (400 BC-275 BC).". Period definition from British Museum.

The phase of the great Celtic migrations, when war bands from the north moved into the Po valley, the middle Danube and the Balkans; the sack of Rome and the raid on Delphi belong to these generations. Large flat cemeteries of inhumations replace the earlier princely tumuli, with men buried with sword, spear and shield and women with brooches and rings. Metalworkers developed the Waldalgesheim or Vegetal Style, a flowing tendril ornament that spread across Europe with astonishing uniformity.

Taizong (China, AD 976–AD 997).label: Taizong
Taizong (China, AD 976–AD 997).prose:
[China, AD 976–AD 997] Taizong. 976-997 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Zhao Kuangyi succeeded his brother as Song emperor and finished the job of reunification, absorbing the last independent southern states and Northern Han in 979. His attempts to retake the Sixteen Prefectures from the Khitan Liao ended in costly defeats, fixing the Song as a state that bought peace rather than conquered. At home he vastly expanded the civil service examinations, filling the bureaucracy with degree-holders and setting the pattern of scholar-official government that lasted a thousand years.

Chincha-Atacama (Chile, AD 1100–AD 1350).label: Chincha-Atacama
Chincha-Atacama (Chile, AD 1100–AD 1350).prose: [northern Chile, AD 1100–AD 1350] Chincha-Atacama. The term refers to a style form 1100 to 1350 in northern Chile. Period definition from British Museum.

Gaozu (China, AD 917–AD 925).label: Gaozu
Gaozu (China, AD 917–AD 925).prose: [China, AD 917–AD 925] Gaozu. 917-925 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Quang Trung (Vietnam, AD 1788–AD 1792).label: Quang Trung
Quang Trung (Vietnam, AD 1788–AD 1792).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1788–AD 1792] Quang Trung. Vietnamese reign period 1788-1792. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Nguyen Hue, the ablest of the three Tay Son brothers, who overturned the old order after decades of peasant rebellion and civil war. In a lightning campaign timed for the Lunar New Year he destroyed a large Qing invasion army outside Thang Long, a victory still celebrated as one of Vietnam's greatest. He promoted the vernacular Nom script over classical Chinese and planned sweeping reforms, but died at forty, and his fragile state soon fell to the Nguyen.

Yayoi Period (Japan, 199 BC–AD 250).label: Yayoi Period
Yayoi Period (Japan, 199 BC–AD 250).prose:
[Japan, 199 BC–AD 250] Yayoi Period. 200 BC - 250 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Wet-rice paddy farming, bronze and iron working and the potter's techniques arrived in Japan from the Korean peninsula, transforming a long-established foraging society. Villages grew, some ringed with ditches and palisades, and surplus rice supported chiefs buried with bronze mirrors, weapons and bell-shaped dotaku. Chinese histories record envoys from these emerging polities, including the queen Himiko of Yamatai, marking Japan's entry into the written record.

Ninji Era (Japan, AD 1240–AD 1243).label: Ninji Era
Ninji Era (Japan, AD 1240–AD 1243).prose:
[Japan, AD 1240–AD 1243] Ninji Era. 1240-1243. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Kamakura-period era name, falling in the years when the Hōjō regents governed in the shogun's name and the court at Kyoto had largely ceremonial power. Hōjō Yasutoki, architect of the warrior law code, died during it. Japanese eras like this were declared and changed for political or auspicious reasons and are still used to date documents, artworks and temple records.

Jijo Era (China, AD 1177–AD 1181).label: Jijo Era
Jijo Era (China, AD 1177–AD 1181).prose: [China, AD 1177–AD 1181] Jijo Era. 1177-1181. Period definition from British Museum.

Jianzhong (China, AD 780–AD 783).label: Jianzhong
Jianzhong (China, AD 780–AD 783).prose:
[China, AD 780–AD 783] Jianzhong. 780-783 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Dezong's opening years, when the court tried to reassert control over the semi-independent military governors who had run the provinces since the An Lushan rebellion. The reform that lasted was fiscal: the twice-a-year tax, which taxed land and wealth instead of individuals and became the basis of Chinese taxation for centuries. The political attempt failed, and mutinying troops drove the emperor from his capital.

Bunki Era (Japan, AD 1501–AD 1504).label: Bunki Era
Bunki Era (Japan, AD 1501–AD 1504).prose:
[Japan, AD 1501–AD 1504] Bunki Era. 1501-1504. Period definition from British Museum.

A short era in the opening decades of the Sengoku wars, when the Ashikaga shoguns had become the creatures of rival deputies and real power lay with provincial warlords and armed religious leagues. Kyoto's authority barely reached beyond the capital's neighbouring provinces.

Nuraghic (Sardinia, 1599 BC–499 BC).label: Nuraghic
Nuraghic (Sardinia, 1599 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Sardinia, 1599 BC–499 BC] Nuraghic. 1600BC-500BC.  Used with Sardinia as Production place. Period definition from British Museum.

Sardinia filled with nuraghi – conical drystone towers, some rising three storeys, of which several thousand still stand. Communities built them as strongholds and gathering places, buried their dead in collective "giants' tombs", and cast small bronze figurines of warriors, archers and chieftains that give a rare glimpse of how islanders saw themselves. Copper and Aegean and Cypriot imports show the island plugged into long-distance Bronze Age trade before Phoenician and Carthaginian settlement reshaped it.

Zhangzong (China, AD 1190–AD 1208).label: Zhangzong
Zhangzong (China, AD 1190–AD 1208).prose:
[China, AD 1190–AD 1208] Zhangzong. 1190-1208 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Jurchen Jin dynasty under Emperor Zhangzong reached its cultural high point, with a sinicized court, flourishing scholarship and law codes, and a capital at Zhongdu (modern Beijing) that rivalled Song cities. Behind the polish, disaster was accumulating: catastrophic Yellow River flooding, fiscal strain from paper money, and Mongol raids on the northern frontier. A Song attempt to reconquer the north in 1206 was beaten off, but within two decades of the emperor's death the Mongols would tear the Jin state apart.

Valdivia (Ecuador, 3499 BC–1499 BC).label: Valdivia
Valdivia (Ecuador, 3499 BC–1499 BC).prose: [coastal Ecuador, 3499 BC–1499 BC] Valdivia. The term refers to a culture (c. 3500 BC-1500 BC); also a style named after the type site on coastal Ecuador. Period definition from British Museum.

Kosho Era (Japan, AD 1455–AD 1457).label: Kosho Era
Kosho Era (Japan, AD 1455–AD 1457).prose:
[Japan, AD 1455–AD 1457] Kosho Era. 1455-1457. Period definition from British Museum.

A two-year reign name in the late Muromachi years, dominated by the war that had erupted in the Kantō between the Kamakura kubō Ashikaga Shigeuji and the Uesugi deputies. Driven from Kamakura, Shigeuji set himself up at Koga, splitting eastern Japan into rival camps that would fight for decades. The shogunate in Kyoto could do little but take sides, an early sign of the collapse of central authority that culminated in the Ōnin War.

Thanh Thai (Vietnam, AD 1889–AD 1907).label: Thanh Thai
Thanh Thai (Vietnam, AD 1889–AD 1907).prose:
[Vietnam, AD 1889–AD 1907] Thanh Thai. (1889-1907) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

A young emperor placed on the Nguyễn throne by French administrators who had reduced the Vietnamese court to a ceremonial shell. He encouraged modern schooling and showed increasing sympathy for anti-colonial sentiment, and the French deposed him in 1907 and eventually exiled him to Réunion, as they would his son Duy Tân.

Ninevite 5 Painted (Iraq, 2999 BC–2749 B.label: Ninevite 5 Painted
Ninevite 5 Painted (Iraq, 2999 BC–2749 B.prose:
[Iraq, 2999 BC–2749 BC] Ninevite 5 Painted. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. c.3000-2750BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The earlier phase of the Ninevite 5 sequence, marked by delicate cups and jars painted with geometric bands, animals and stylised figures. Settlements were mostly small villages, a striking contrast with the emerging city-states of southern Mesopotamia at the same moment. The style is one of the clearest markers archaeologists have for dating the early third millennium in the north.

Archaic Greek (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).label: Archaic Greek
Archaic Greek (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–479 BC] Archaic Greek. The term covers the date range: about 700BC-480BC. Period definition from British Museum.

This is the age of the kouros and the kore, of black-figure vases signed by their painters, and of the first stone temples with their columns worked out by trial and error. Trade and colonisation spread Greek settlements across the Mediterranean and brought eastern art and ideas home, while lyric poets like Sappho and the first natural philosophers in Ionia began writing about the world in new ways. Political experiment ran from law codes to tyranny to citizen assemblies, and the whole period closes with the Persian Wars.

Tengen Era (Japan, AD 978–AD 983).label: Tengen Era
Tengen Era (Japan, AD 978–AD 983).prose:
[Japan, AD 978–AD 983] Tengen Era. 978-983. Period definition from British Museum.

Years in the reign of Emperor En'yū, when the Fujiwara house dominated court appointments and competing branches of the family manoeuvred for the regency. Fire and storm repeatedly struck the capital in this period, damaging the palace compound and the great Rashōmon gate at the city's southern entrance.

Late Helladic IIIB2 (Greece, 1249 BC–119.label: Late Helladic IIIB2
Late Helladic IIIB2 (Greece, 1249 BC–119.prose:
[Greece, 1249 BC–1199 BC] Late Helladic IIIB2. 1250BC-1200BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The last palace generation. Walls were thickened, water supplies secured with hidden underground cisterns, and Linear B tablets at Pylos mention watchers posted on the coast; then every major centre was destroyed by fire, and the tablets survive only because the flames baked them.

Southern Qi dynasty (China, AD 479–AD 50.label: Southern Qi dynasty
Southern Qi dynasty (China, AD 479–AD 50.prose:
[China, AD 479–AD 502] Southern Qi dynasty. 479-502. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief southern regime ruled by the Xiao clan from Jiankang (modern Nanjing), sandwiched between the Liu Song and Liang dynasties. Fratricidal struggles among princes destroyed it in a generation, yet its aristocratic court produced influential poetry and the earliest systematic Chinese writing on tonal prosody. Its rulers' spirit-road stone lions and winged beasts still stand outside Nanjing.

Zhezong (China, AD 1086–AD 1101).label: Zhezong
Zhezong (China, AD 1086–AD 1101).prose:
[China, AD 1086–AD 1101] Zhezong. 1086-1101 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign opened with a regency that swept away Wang Anshi's New Policies and recalled conservatives like Sima Guang, then reversed course when the young emperor took charge and restored the reforms under Zhang Dun. Officials were purged and exiled with each swing, including the poet Su Shi. This vicious factional see-sawing hollowed out the Song civil service and set the tone for the crisis-prone reign that followed.

Daizong (China, AD 762–AD 779).label: Daizong
Daizong (China, AD 762–AD 779).prose:
[China, AD 762–AD 779] Daizong. 762-779 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Tang emperor who finally ended the An Lushan rebellion, but at the cost of buying Uighur help and leaving the northeastern provinces in the hands of former rebel commanders who paid no taxes and named their own successors. Tibetan armies sacked Chang'an in 763, court eunuchs took control of the palace armies, and the centralised empire of the early Tang never recovered.

Cypro-Archaic (Cyprus, 749 BC–449 BC).label: Cypro-Archaic
Cypro-Archaic (Cyprus, 749 BC–449 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–449 BC] Cypro-Archaic. 750 BC-450 BC.  The economic and commercial trends of the Cypro-Geometric period (q.v) culminated in a flowering of cultural activity in the Cypro-Archaic period. The numerous city-kingdoms, whose wealth and power are visible in tombs and increasingly monumental architecture (including urban fortifications), appear as vassals in the historical records of the Assyrian Empire. Pictorial art on vases develops considerably, while three-dimensional representation, in the form of stone and terracotta statues deposited in large numbers in tombs, reaches impressive levels. Period definition from British Museum.

Cyprus was carved into competing city-kingdoms that submitted in turn to Assyria, Egypt and Persia while growing rich on copper and trade. Its sanctuaries and tombs produced some of the ancient Mediterranean's most striking hybrid art, mixing Greek, Egyptian and Near Eastern styles in limestone statues and terracotta votives left by the thousand.

Jingdi (China, AD 579–AD 581).label: Jingdi
Jingdi (China, AD 579–AD 581).prose:
[China, AD 579–AD 581] Jingdi. 579-581 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of a child emperor of the Northern Zhou, wholly controlled by his regent Yang Jian. In 581 Yang forced the boy's abdication and founded the Sui dynasty, which within a decade reunified China after nearly three centuries of division.

Kaibao (China, AD 968–AD 976).label: Kaibao
Kaibao (China, AD 968–AD 976).prose:
[China, AD 968–AD 976] Kaibao. 968-976 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The final era of Song Taizu, in which the new dynasty swallowed its southern rivals: the Southern Han fell in 971 and the Southern Tang capital at Nanjing in 975, largely completing the reunification of China after the Five Dynasties. Taizu also ordered the first printed edition of the Buddhist canon, the Kaibao Tripitaka, a landmark in the history of printing.

Afsharid dynasty (Iran, AD 1736–AD 1796).label: Afsharid dynasty
Afsharid dynasty (Iran, AD 1736–AD 1796).prose:
[Iran, AD 1736–AD 1796] Afsharid dynasty. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia (country), Iran. 1736-1796 (AH 1148-AH 1210). Dynasty led by chieftain Nadir who was crowned Nadir Shah in 1736 (AH 1148). Period definition from British Museum.

Founded by Nader Shah, a Turkmen warlord who drove the Afghans out of Iran, restored its frontiers and made himself king. His invasion of India in 1739 sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor, briefly making him the most feared ruler in Asia. Heavy taxation and his own growing paranoia ended in his assassination, after which the empire fragmented within a generation.

Zhida (China, AD 1308–AD 1311).label: Zhida
Zhida (China, AD 1308–AD 1311).prose:
[China, AD 1308–AD 1311] Zhida. 1308-1311 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

A short Yuan reign marked by financial improvisation: a new issue of paper currency and the casting of copper coins, an unusual step for a dynasty that had relied on notes. Lavish grants to Mongol princes and Buddhist establishments drained the treasury. The emperor's successors promptly cancelled much of what he had done, a pattern of policy reversal that weakened Yuan government.

The Middle Ages (United Kingdom, AD 700–.label: The Middle Ages
The Middle Ages (United Kingdom, AD 700–.prose:
[British Isles, AD 700–AD 1485] The Middle Ages. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. The medieval period in English literature extends for more than 800 years, from Cædmon’s Hymn at the end of the 7th century to Everyman at the end of the 15th. (p. 1). Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

From the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and Viking incursions through the Norman Conquest to the end of the Wars of the Roses, this long stretch produced English common law, Parliament, the universities and the great cathedrals. Written English disappeared as an elite language after 1066 and re-emerged transformed, giving us Chaucer and Langland. Plague in the fourteenth century killed perhaps a third of the population and reshaped labour, landholding and the power of ordinary people.
The Middle Ages (United Kingdom, AD 700–.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Sixteenth Century (United Kingdom, A.label: The Sixteenth Century
The Sixteenth Century (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1485–AD 1603] The Sixteenth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

Tudor rule brought a break with Rome, the dissolution of the monasteries and repeated swings between Protestant and Catholic settlements that touched every parish in the country. A growing population, rising prices and enclosure reshaped the countryside, while London swelled into a major European city. Under Elizabeth I came the defeat of the Armada, the first English ventures across the Atlantic, and the theatre of Marlowe and Shakespeare.
The Sixteenth Century (United Kingdom, A.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Seventeenth Century (United Kingdom,.label: The Seventeenth Century
The Seventeenth Century (United Kingdom,.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1603–AD 1660] The Seventeenth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

Under the early Stuarts, arguments over money, prerogative and church ceremony hardened into armed conflict across England, Scotland and Ireland, ending with a king tried and beheaded by his own subjects. The republic and Protectorate that followed left a lasting sense that royal power had limits. In print and pulpit it was an extraordinarily fertile time: the King James Bible, metaphysical poetry, Hobbes's Leviathan and the first stirrings of the scientific revolution.
The Seventeenth Century (United Kingdom,.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Restoration and the Eighteenth Centu.node: The Restoration and the Eighteenth Century (United Kingdom, AD 1660–AD 1798)
The Restoration and the Eighteenth Centu.label: The Restoration and the Eighteenth Century
The Restoration and the Eighteenth Centu.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1660–AD 1798] The Restoration and the Eighteenth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

Charles II's return ended the republican experiment and ushered in a period of licensed theatre, scientific societies and a commercial print culture that made writers into public figures. Constitutional monarchy, party politics and a powerful fiscal-military state took shape, funding wars that won Britain an empire in India and North America. By the end of the century, steam, canals and factory production were remaking the landscape of the north.
The Restoration and the Eighteenth Centu.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Romantic Period (United Kingdom, AD.label: The Romantic Period
The Romantic Period (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1798–AD 1832] The Romantic Period. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Following the common usage of historians of English literature, we will denote by the “Romantic period” the span between the year 1798, in which Wordsworth and Coleridge published their Lyrical Ballads, and 1832, when Sir Walter Scott died, when other major writers of the earlier century were either dead or no longer productive, and when the passage of the first Reform Bill, after more than three decades of political stagnation and repression, inaugurated the Victorian era of cautious readjustment of political power to conform to the economic and social realities of a new industrial age (Volume 2, page 1). Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

Poets and radicals responded to the French Revolution and the industrial transformation of Britain by turning to nature, imagination and the individual voice — Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads, then Byron, Shelley and Keats. It was also an era of repression and unrest at home, from Peterloo to machine-breaking, with the long war against Napoleon dominating national life. It closes with the Reform Act, the first serious widening of the franchise.
The Romantic Period (United Kingdom, AD.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Victorian Age (United Kingdom, AD 18.label: The Victorian Age
The Victorian Age (United Kingdom, AD 18.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1832–AD 1901] The Victorian Age. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

Railways, factories and cities grew at a pace no society had experienced before, making Britain the workshop of the world and its empire the largest in history. The same decades produced sanitary reform, mass literacy, the extension of the vote and a self-critical literature — Dickens, Eliot, the Brontës — obsessed with poverty and social change. Darwin's work, geology and biblical criticism unsettled religious certainty and provoked debates still running today.
The Victorian Age (United Kingdom, AD 18.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Twentieth Century (United Kingdom, A.label: The Twentieth Century
The Twentieth Century (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1890–AD 1960] The Twentieth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Stop is inferred from latest work (Ted Hughes: Relic) in this volume (p. 1954). Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature : revised — 1968.

Two world wars, the loss of an empire and the building of the welfare state remade British society within a lifetime, while women won the vote and mass democracy arrived. Modernist writing broke with Victorian forms in the hands of Woolf, Joyce, Eliot and Lawrence, and cinema and broadcasting created a shared national culture. Postwar immigration from the Caribbean and South Asia began to reshape who counted as British.
The Twentieth Century (United Kingdom, A.source: The Norton anthology of English literature : revised

The Victorian Age (United Kingdom, AD 18.label: The Victorian Age
The Victorian Age (United Kingdom, AD 18.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1830–AD 1901] The Victorian Age. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature — 2013.

Railways, factories and cities grew at a pace no society had experienced before, making Britain the workshop of the world and its empire the largest in history. The same decades produced sanitary reform, mass literacy, the extension of the vote and a self-critical literature — Dickens, Eliot, the Brontës — obsessed with poverty and social change. Darwin's work, geology and biblical criticism unsettled religious certainty and provoked debates still running today.
The Victorian Age (United Kingdom, AD 18.source: The Norton anthology of English literature

The Early Seventeenth Century (United Ki.node: The Early Seventeenth Century (United Kingdom, AD 1603–AD 1660)
The Early Seventeenth Century (United Ki.label: The Early Seventeenth Century
The Early Seventeenth Century (United Ki.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1603–AD 1660] The Early Seventeenth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature — 2013.

The Stuart accession joined the English and Scottish crowns, and disputes over royal prerogative, taxation and religion escalated into civil war, the execution of Charles I and a decade of republican rule. It was the age of the King James Bible, Donne and Herbert, Milton's political prose, and an explosion of cheap print and radical pamphleteering once censorship collapsed. English settlement in North America and the Caribbean began in earnest at the same time.
The Early Seventeenth Century (United Ki.source: The Norton anthology of English literature

The Romantic Period (United Kingdom, AD.label: The Romantic Period
The Romantic Period (United Kingdom, AD.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1785–AD 1832] The Romantic Period. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. The Romantic period … is, tellingly, demarcated differently than any of the other eras that literary historians and anthologists include in their timelines. By convention, the boundaries delimiting those other epochs are either set by the regions of monarchs … or conceptualized as coinciding with the openings and closings of centuries … The date usually serving as the terminus of the Romantic age, 1832, represents a contrast to this pattern, strongly associated as it is with a signal political event, the first major reform of the British Parliament. A diverse range of dates have been identified as marking off the beginning of the Romantic period, but, almost always, each of these, too is associated with an event of tremendous political and social impact. (Volume 2, pages 3–4). Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature — 2013.

Poets and radicals responded to the French Revolution and the industrial transformation of Britain by turning to nature, imagination and the individual voice — Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads, then Byron, Shelley and Keats. It was also an era of repression and unrest at home, from Peterloo to machine-breaking, with the long war against Napoleon dominating national life. It closes with the Reform Act, the first serious widening of the franchise.
The Romantic Period (United Kingdom, AD.source: The Norton anthology of English literature

The Restoration and The Eighteenth Centu.node: The Restoration and The Eighteenth Century (United Kingdom, AD 1660–AD 1785)
The Restoration and The Eighteenth Centu.label: The Restoration and The Eighteenth Century
The Restoration and The Eighteenth Centu.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1660–AD 1785] The Restoration and The Eighteenth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature — 2013.

The return of the monarchy reopened the theatres and brought a worldly, satirical literary culture — Dryden, Pope, Swift — alongside the rise of newspapers, coffee houses and the novel. Parliamentary supremacy was settled after 1688, the Bank of England and a national debt financed global war, and union with Scotland created Great Britain. Empire, slavery and Atlantic trade generated the capital and the raw materials on which early industrialisation was built.
The Restoration and The Eighteenth Centu.source: The Norton anthology of English literature

The Sixteenth Century (United Kingdom, A.label: The Sixteenth Century
The Sixteenth Century (United Kingdom, A.prose:
[British Isles, AD 1485–AD 1603] The Sixteenth Century. Spatial coverage: Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom. Period definition from The Norton anthology of English literature — 2013.

Tudor rule brought a break with Rome, the dissolution of the monasteries and repeated swings between Protestant and Catholic settlements that touched every parish in the country. A growing population, rising prices and enclosure reshaped the countryside, while London swelled into a major European city. Under Elizabeth I came the defeat of the Armada, the first English ventures across the Atlantic, and the theatre of Marlowe and Shakespeare.

The earlier half of Greece's Late Neolithic, marked by the spread of black-burnished and matt-painted wares and by settlements such as Arapi and Otzaki in Thessaly. Communities remained village-based farmers of wheat, barley, sheep and goats, but exchange networks in obsidian and shell reached far beyond the Aegean. Population and site numbers rose sharply compared with earlier centuries.

On the tells of eastern Macedonia — Sitagroi, Dikili Tash and their neighbours — the long Neolithic and Chalcolithic occupation gives way to a new phase with different pottery, more metal and closer links to north-western Anatolia and the Troad. These deep mounds, dug in the twentieth century, provide one of the key stratified sequences for dating prehistoric south-eastern Europe.

The upper Bronze Age levels of the Drama plain tells, including Sitagroi's well-preserved 'Burnt House' with its stored grain and standing pots, give a rare snapshot of an ordinary household destroyed by fire. Pottery and metalwork of these levels show northern Greece firmly tied into an Aegean and Anatolian world of exchange.

A late facies of the earliest mainland Bronze Age, recognised through the Talioti pottery group of the Argolid and later levels at Eutresis. It bridges the modest village world of the earlier phase and the far more prosperous, hierarchically organised settlements that followed.

The final Bronze Age occupation of the Sitagroi mound, with pottery and metal types linking the Drama plain to Troy and the northern Aegean. After this the great tell was largely abandoned, ending a settlement sequence that had run for some three thousand years.

Fortified towns in the southern Levant reached their peak, with thick town walls, temples, palaces and the huge circular storage structure at Beth Yerah. Distinctive burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, related to northern traditions, spreads through the region. By the close of the period nearly all these towns had been abandoned, and urban life vanished for centuries.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.

Farming communities spread out from the old tell villages of the plains into caves, hilltops and small coastal sites, and herding became a bigger part of the economy. Copper and silver objects appear alongside new pottery styles such as the Attica-Kephala group, and contacts across the Aegean intensified. These centuries laid the groundwork for the metal-using, seafaring societies of the Early Bronze Age.

Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3299 BC–2899 B.prose:

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

The opening ceramic stage of the mainland Bronze Age, defined by dark burnished and red-slipped wares from the stratified sequences at Eutresis in Boeotia and Perachora. Communities were small, agricultural and relatively undifferentiated, but copper and bronze objects and contacts across the Aegean were beginning to appear.

Cretan villages continued to expand and bury their dead collectively in tholoi and house tombs, while contacts with the Cyclades and the Near East brought in metal and ideas. Pottery diversified into scored and dark-burnished wares, and the first substantial multi-room houses appear. The island was moving from scattered farming hamlets toward the denser, craft-rich communities of the later Early Bronze Age.

Cyprus at its most distinctive before metals took hold: villages of round, mud-and-timber houses at Erimi, Lemba and Kissonerga, with wells, storage pits and cemeteries set apart from the living. Craftworkers carved blue-green picrolite into cruciform figurines with outstretched arms, worn as pendants and buried with the dead, and modelled clay figures of women giving birth. The island stayed largely self-contained, developing its own idiom while the mainland moved into the Bronze Age.

The first farmers in Europe established themselves on the plains of Thessaly and Macedonia, growing wheat, barley and pulses and keeping sheep, goats, cattle and pigs brought from Anatolia. Their mud-brick villages were rebuilt on the same spot for centuries, piling up the artificial mounds known as magoules or tells. Fine burnished and painted pottery and small clay figurines of women and animals are the signature finds.

The opening of the Cretan Bronze Age, when new burial customs appear—the round tholos tombs of the Mesara and rock-shelter ossuaries—along with distinctive Pyrgos chalices and Aghios Onouphrios painted jugs. Copper working begins in earnest and settlements spread into previously empty parts of the island. The communal tombs, reused for centuries, suggest kin groups asserting claims to land.

Early Cycladic I Late (Kampos Group) (Gr.node: Early Cycladic I Late (Kampos Group) (Greece, 2899 BC–2699 BC)
Early Cycladic I Late (Kampos Group) (Gr.label: Early Cycladic I Late (Kampos Group)
Early Cycladic I Late (Kampos Group) (Gr.prose:
[Peloponnese, Central Greece, Epirus-Northwestern Greece, Ionian Islands, Western Greece, Cyclades, 2899 BC–2699 BC] Early Cycladic I Late (Kampos Group). Derived from:
Reingruber, A., Die Argissa-Magula II. Die Frühbronzezeit in Griechenland mit Ausnahme von Kreta. Period definition from Digitizing Early Farming Cultures (DEFC) — Institut für Orientalische und Europäische Archäologie (OREA), 2017.

A transitional horizon between the earliest island cultures and the flowering of Early Cycladic II, named after a cemetery on Paros. Its hallmarks are frying-pan vessels incised with spirals and longboats, and the first fully modelled figurines, evidence of increasing seafaring and contact with Crete and the mainland.

Early Helladic I (Greece, 3299 BC–2899 B.label: Early Helladic I
Early Helladic I (Greece, 3299 BC–2899 B.prose:
[Peloponnese, Central Greece, Epirus-Northwestern Greece, Ionian Islands, Western Greece, Cyclades, 3299 BC–2899 BC] Early Helladic I. Derived from: 
Reingruber, A., Die Argissa-Magula II.
