Die Frühbronzezeit in Griechenland mit Ausnahme von Kreta. Period definition from Digitizing Early Farming Cultures (DEFC) — Institut für Orientalische und Europäische Archäologie (OREA), 2017.

Small farming hamlets in the southwest Peloponnese take up metal and new pottery shapes, the first mainland stage of the Bronze Age. Settlements were modest and scattered, with burials in simple pits and cists rather than monumental tombs. It provides the baseline against which the wealthier, more centralised communities of the following centuries stand out.

Chalkolithikum (Turkey, 3499 BC–2999 BC).label: Chalkolithikum
Chalkolithikum (Turkey, 3499 BC–2999 BC).prose: [Turkey and Eastern Aegean, 3499 BC–2999 BC] Chalkolithikum. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Period definition from Das anatolische Chalkolithikum. Eine chronologische Untersuchung zur vorbronzezeitlichen Kultursequenz im nördlichen Zentralanatolien und den angrenzenden Gebieten — U.-D. Schoop, 2005.
Chalkolithikum (Turkey, 3499 BC–2999 BC).source: Das anatolische Chalkolithikum. Eine chronologische Untersuchung zur vorbronzezeitlichen Kultursequenz im nördlichen Zentralanatolien und den angrenzenden Gebieten

Late Islamic Period (Jordan, AD 1516–AD.label: Late Islamic Period
Late Islamic Period (Jordan, AD 1516–AD.prose:
[Udhruh (Southern Jordan), AD 1516–AD 1918] Late Islamic Period. "By the first half of the 16th century, the entire region of Greater Syria and Egypt came under the Ottoman rule. In 1516 Jordan was taken over following the defeat of Mamluk governor of Aleppo." (page 229)

"For the rest four [sic] centuries (until 1918), the country remained under the Ottoman political and administrative systems." (page 229). Period definition from Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods — Fawzi Abudanh, 2006.

Ottoman rule brought tax registers, garrisons and, above all, responsibility for the Damascus pilgrimage caravan, whose forts and cisterns strung across the desert are the era's most visible monuments. Settled agriculture contracted for centuries before reviving in the 1800s with new land laws and immigrant Circassian and Chechen villages. The Hejaz Railway and the Arab Revolt that tore it up mark the period's dramatic close.
Late Islamic Period (Jordan, AD 1516–AD.source: Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods

Byzantine period (Jordan, AD 324–AD 636).label: Byzantine period
Byzantine period (Jordan, AD 324–AD 636).prose:
[Udhruh (Southern Jordan), AD 324–AD 636] Byzantine period. "The end of this period in the East, particularly in the Levant, is
well established and commonly dated to the year AD 636 when the Muslim army
defeated a Byzantine force near the River Yarmuk in northwest Jordan." (page 215). Period definition from Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods — Fawzi Abudanh, 2006.

Jordan's most densely settled ancient centuries, when Christianity brought a boom in church building and pilgrimage traffic to sites linked to Moses and John the Baptist. Towns such as Madaba, Jerash and Umm al-Rasas paved their churches with mosaics of astonishing quality, including the Madaba map, the oldest surviving cartographic depiction of the Holy Land. Byzantine rule ended with the Muslim victory at the Yarmuk river, though the villages and their mosaicists carried on working for generations afterwards.
Byzantine period (Jordan, AD 324–AD 636).source: Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods

Iron Age (Jordan, 1199 BC–538 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Jordan, 1199 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Udhruh (Southern Jordan), 1199 BC–538 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods — Fawzi Abudanh, 2006.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Jordan, 1199 BC–538 BC).source: Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods

Persian Period (Jordan, 538 BC–331 BC).label: Persian Period
Persian Period (Jordan, 538 BC–331 BC).prose:
[Udhruh (Southern Jordan), 538 BC–331 BC] Persian Period. Period definition from Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods — Fawzi Abudanh, 2006.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.
Persian Period (Jordan, 538 BC–331 BC).source: Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods

Roman period: Provincia Arabia (Jordan,.label: Roman period: Provincia Arabia
Roman period: Provincia Arabia (Jordan,.prose:
[Udhruh (Southern Jordan), AD 106–AD 324] Roman period: Provincia Arabia. The Roman period encompasses the period "Third century and the Tetrarch period." The 324 C.E. end date is the beginning of the Byzantine period. Period definition from Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods — Fawzi Abudanh, 2006.

Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom in AD 106 and turned Petra's desert trading realm into a garrisoned province governed from Bostra. Legionary engineers drove the Via Nova Traiana from the Red Sea to Syria, and caravan wealth from incense and spice routes paid for colonnaded streets, theatres and temples at Petra, Gerasa and Philadelphia. The province guarded Rome's eastern desert flank until the empire's reorganisation under Constantine.
Roman period: Provincia Arabia (Jordan,.source: Settlement patterns and military organisation in the region of Udhruh (Southern Jordan) in the Roman and Byzantine periods

Chalcolithic (State of Palestine, 3999 B.label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (State of Palestine, 3999 B.prose:
[Palestine, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. "What we have just summarized pertains to the latter part of the period, which came to an end probably ca. 3500 B.C., a CRD terminus based on radiocarbon dates (I-353, I-285, I-1341) from Nahal Mishmar and the initial phase of EB I, which was contemporary with the Early Gerzean, or Naqada II, of Egypt." (page 27)
"How much before ca. 4000 B.C. early Chalcolithic culture begins, its origin, and its relationship, if any, to the terminal Neolithic must remain unanswered questions." (page 27). Period definition from Chronologies in old world archaeology — 1992.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Early Bronze I (State of Palestine, 3499.node: Early Bronze I (State of Palestine, 3499 BC–3099 BC)
Early Bronze I (State of Palestine, 3499.label: Early Bronze I
Early Bronze I (State of Palestine, 3499.prose:
[Palestine, 3499 BC–3099 BC] Early Bronze I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. "this preurban period of EB I has been shrouded in confusing terminology, which reflects chronological uncertainty; this, in turn, has led to muddled periodization." (page 28). Period definition from Chronologies in old world archaeology — 1992.

Farming villages coalesced into large unwalled settlements, and olive and vine cultivation, donkey caravans and copper from the Arabah began to knit the region into wider trade. Egyptian traders and settlers established themselves in the southern coastal plain, leaving pottery and serekhs of the earliest pharaohs, including Narmer. Out of this came the region's first true towns.

Early Bronze III (State of Palestine, 26.node: Early Bronze III (State of Palestine, 2649 BC–2249 BC)
Early Bronze III (State of Palestine, 26.label: Early Bronze III
Early Bronze III (State of Palestine, 26.prose:
[Palestine, 2649 BC–2249 BC] Early Bronze III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Alternate label "Phase III" comes from "The Periodization of International Trade" and corresponds with Dynasties IV-VI in Egypt. (page 41). Period definition from Chronologies in old world archaeology — 1992.

The high point of the region's first urban age, with heavily walled towns, planned temple precincts and large public granaries. Distinctive red-and-black burnished Khirbet Kerak pottery, of northern origin, appears alongside local mass-produced wares, and trade in oil and wine continued with Egypt. Towards its end the towns were abandoned in a wave that left the landscape without cities for centuries.

EB IV/MB I (State of Palestine, 2249 BC–.node: EB IV/MB I (State of Palestine, 2249 BC–1999 BC)
EB IV/MB I (State of Palestine, 2249 BC–.label: EB IV/MB I
EB IV/MB I (State of Palestine, 2249 BC–.prose:
[Palestine, 2249 BC–1999 BC] EB IV/MB I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Alternate label "Phase IV" comes from "The Periodization of International Trade" and corresponds with the First Intermediate period in Egypt. (page 41). Period definition from Chronologies in old world archaeology — 1992.

Cities gave way to villages, camps and cemeteries as people shifted towards herding and seasonal movement — a rare reversal of urban life that lasted around 250 years. The dead were buried in shaft tombs with distinctive copper weapons, and the pottery breaks sharply with earlier traditions. Urban Canaan revived afterwards on a different footing, in the Middle Bronze Age.

Middle Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1999 BC–1.node: Middle Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1999 BC–1749 BC)
Middle Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1999 BC–1.label: Middle Bronze Age IIA
Middle Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1999 BC–1.prose:
[Holy Land, 1999 BC–1749 BC] Middle Bronze Age IIA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Urban life re-emerged along the coastal plain and in the valleys, with new towns, wheel-made pottery in fine forms and revived bronze metallurgy. Strong maritime and overland contacts with Byblos and coastal Syria brought in luxury goods and new ideas. The city-state landscape established now dominated the region for centuries.
Middle Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1999 BC–1.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 2999 BC–269.node: Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 2999 BC–2699 BC)
Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 2999 BC–269.label: Early Bronze Age II
Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 2999 BC–269.prose:
[Holy Land, 2999 BC–2699 BC] Early Bronze Age II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.
Early Bronze Age II (Israel, 2999 BC–269.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Byzantine period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).label: Byzantine period
Byzantine period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).prose:
[Holy Land, AD 324–AD 638] Byzantine period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Jordan's most densely settled ancient centuries, when Christianity brought a boom in church building and pilgrimage traffic to sites linked to Moses and John the Baptist. Towns such as Madaba, Jerash and Umm al-Rasas paved their churches with mosaics of astonishing quality, including the Madaba map, the oldest surviving cartographic depiction of the Holy Land. Byzantine rule ended with the Muslim victory at the Yarmuk river, though the villages and their mosaicists carried on working for generations afterwards.
Byzantine period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Iron Age IIC (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).label: Iron Age IIC
Iron Age IIC (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 699 BC–585 BC] Iron Age IIC. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Judah alone remained, prospering under Assyrian overlordship as an exporter of oil and wine before the empire crumbled. Attempts at independence brought Babylonian retaliation, and Jerusalem was burned and its population exiled. The exile that followed reshaped Judaean religion and produced much of the biblical literature that survives.
Iron Age IIC (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.node: Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel, 585 BC–331 BC)
Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.label: Babylonian and Persian Periods
Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.prose:
[Holy Land, 585 BC–331 BC] Babylonian and Persian Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Babylonian period and Persian period are grouped together without differentiated dates in chronological table (page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Judah began this stretch as a wrecked Babylonian province, Jerusalem burned and its elite deported, and ended it as Yehud, a small temple-centred district of the Achaemenid Empire. Exiles returning under Persian permission rebuilt the Temple and, with Ezra and Nehemiah, reshaped Judaism around law, scripture and priesthood rather than monarchy. Aramaic spread as the everyday language, coinage and imperial administration arrived, and the Hebrew Bible took much of the shape it still has.
Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Crusader period (Israel, AD 1099–AD 1291.label: Crusader period
Crusader period (Israel, AD 1099–AD 1291.prose:
[Holy Land, AD 1099–AD 1291] Crusader period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Two centuries of Latin rule based first on Jerusalem and later on Acre, visible archaeologically in castles such as Belvoir and Montfort, in vaulted church architecture, and in sugar mills and harbours serving Mediterranean trade. Frankish settlers were a thin layer over a mixed Muslim, Jewish and Eastern Christian countryside, and the balance of power shifted with each Ayyubid and Mamluk campaign. The fall of Acre closed the episode and reshaped the coast for centuries.
Crusader period (Israel, AD 1099–AD 1291.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Iron Age IIB (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Iron Age IIB
Iron Age IIB (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 899 BC–699 BC] Iron Age IIB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The kingdoms of Israel and Judah flourished side by side, leaving palaces at Samaria, water systems at Megiddo and Hezekiah's tunnel in Jerusalem, along with the earliest substantial Hebrew inscriptions. Assyrian conquest ended the north in 722 BC, scattering its people; Judah endured as a tribute-paying vassal after Sennacherib's assault on Lachish, a siege carved in stone for a Nineveh palace wall.
Iron Age IIB (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.node: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–2199 BC)
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.label: Early Bronze Age III
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.prose:
[Holy Land, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Early Bronze Age III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Fortified towns in the southern Levant reached their peak, with thick town walls, temples, palaces and the huge circular storage structure at Beth Yerah. Distinctive burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, related to northern traditions, spreads through the region. By the close of the period nearly all these towns had been abandoned, and urban life vanished for centuries.
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–129.node: Late Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–1299 BC)
Late Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–129.label: Late Bronze Age IIA
Late Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–129.prose:
[Holy Land, 1399 BC–1299 BC] Late Bronze Age IIA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The Amarna age in Canaan, known from hundreds of cuneiform letters in which petty kings flatter and accuse one another before the Egyptian pharaoh. Mycenaean and Cypriot imports flooded local markets, and rich temple deposits and burials show a small ruling class living well off trade and Egyptian patronage.
Late Bronze Age IIA (Israel, 1399 BC–129.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Iron Age IB (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).label: Iron Age IB
Iron Age IB (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 1149 BC–999 BC] Iron Age IB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Philistine bichrome ware, urban planning and Aegean-derived customs mark the coastal cities, while highland settlement expands rapidly with terraces, cisterns and pillared houses. Canaanite traditions persist in the valleys alongside Phoenician revival to the north. The competition and consolidation of this phase set the stage for the emergence of territorial monarchies around 1000 BC.
Iron Age IB (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Herodian period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70).label: Herodian period
Herodian period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70).prose:
[Holy Land, 36 BC–AD 70] Herodian period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Herodian period is encompassed by Early Roman period. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Herod the Great, installed by Rome as king of the Jews, remade Judaea with enormous building projects: the enlarged Temple Mount, the artificial harbour at Caesarea Maritima, the fortress-palaces of Masada and Herodium. His family ruled as Roman clients over a society deeply divided over how far to accommodate Rome. The period closes with the First Jewish Revolt and the destruction of the Second Temple.
Herodian period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–119.node: Late Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–1199 BC)
Late Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–119.label: Late Bronze Age IIB
Late Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–119.prose:
[Holy Land, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age IIB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Egypt tightened its grip on Canaan under the Ramesside pharaohs, planting garrison towns and administrative residences among the local city-states. Then the system failed: cities burned, Egyptian control evaporated, and by the end of the period new settlements were spreading in the highlands and Philistine communities were forming on the coast.
Late Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1299 BC–119.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Bronze Age (Israel, 3299 BC–1199 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Israel, 3299 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 3299 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Israel, 3299 BC–1199 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Middle Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1749 BC–1.node: Middle Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1749 BC–1549 BC)
Middle Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1749 BC–1.label: Middle Bronze Age IIB
Middle Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1749 BC–1.prose:
[Holy Land, 1749 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age IIB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Canaanite cities reached maximum size and were defended by enormous earthen ramparts and monumental gates. Rich tomb assemblages, scarabs and Egyptian imports reveal prosperous elites in close contact with the Nile Delta, where Hyksos rulers of Levantine descent had taken control. Widespread destructions at the end of the period coincide with Egyptian campaigns into Canaan.
Middle Bronze Age IIB (Israel, 1749 BC–1.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Nabatean kingdom (Israel, 167 BC–AD 106).label: Nabatean kingdom
Nabatean kingdom (Israel, 167 BC–AD 106).prose:
[Holy Land, 167 BC–AD 106] Nabatean kingdom. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. "Aretas I, the first known Nabatean ruler, is mentioned in 2 Maccabees 5:8. He is the Arabian prince from whom the deposed High Priest Jason requested asylum in 168 BCE. He may be the Aretas, king of the Arabs, mentioned in a Nabatean inscription from Elusa. The Nabatean royal dynasty at Petra may have been founded by Erotimus (Justin, Historiarum Philippicarum, XXXIX, 5, 5-6), probably the Greek name of Aretas II, who reigned at about the end of the second century BCE. Most of the Nabatean kings who reigned in Petra from that date until the abolishment of the Nabatean kingdom in 106 CE are known." (page 1181). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

An Arab trading state whose merchants handled the incense and spice traffic between Arabia and the Mediterranean, with outposts and caravan stations reaching across the Negev to the port of Gaza. Their kings minted coins, built temples and cultivated the desert using runoff irrigation. The kingdom ended when Rome annexed it in AD 106.
Nabatean kingdom (Israel, 167 BC–AD 106).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 109.label: Early Arab Period
Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 109.prose:
[Holy Land, AD 638–AD 1099] Early Arab Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Early Arab period (Umayyad and Abbasid) (page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Muslim armies took Palestine from Byzantium in the 630s, and the region was governed successively from Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo. The Umayyads built the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem and founded Ramla as a new provincial capital, while Christians and Jews continued to live under the protected-subject system. Earthquakes, Bedouin unrest and Fatimid–Seljuk conflict weakened the area before the Crusaders stormed Jerusalem in 1099.
Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 109.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC.label: Hellenistic Period
Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC.prose:
[Holy Land, 331 BC–36 BC] Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.
Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0dkm.label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0dkm.prose:
[Holy Land, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0dkm.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Iron Age IA (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).label: Iron Age IA
Iron Age IA (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 1199 BC–1149 BC] Iron Age IA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The immediate aftermath of the Bronze Age collapse in Canaan: destructions and abandonments at major cities, the end of Egyptian garrisons, and the arrival of newcomers on the southern coast using locally produced Aegean-style pottery. Inland, small unfortified farming settlements appear in previously empty hill country. Material culture is simpler and more local than in the palace-dominated age before it.
Iron Age IA (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Bronze Age IA-B (Israel, 3299 BC–2.node: Early Bronze Age IA-B (Israel, 3299 BC–2999 BC)
Early Bronze Age IA-B (Israel, 3299 BC–2.label: Early Bronze Age IA-B
Early Bronze Age IA-B (Israel, 3299 BC–2.prose:
[Holy Land, 3299 BC–2999 BC] Early Bronze Age IA-B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Across the southern Levant, farming villages grew into sprawling unwalled settlements, olive and vine products were produced for export, and copper metallurgy expanded. Egyptian pottery, seals and administration appear in the south, marking a period of intense contact just before the first city walls went up.
Early Bronze Age IA-B (Israel, 3299 BC–2.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Nabatean Period (Jordan, 331 BC–36.label: Early Nabatean Period
Early Nabatean Period (Jordan, 331 BC–36.prose:
[Petra, 331 BC–36 BC] Early Nabatean Period. "Aretas I, the first known Nabatean ruler, is mentioned in 2 Maccabess 5:8. He is the Arabian prince from who the deposed High Priest Jason requested asylym in 168 BCE....Most of the Nabatean kings who reigned in Petra from that date until the abolishment of the Nabatean kingdom in 106 CE are known." (page 1181). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The Nabataeans emerge in the historical record as nomadic traders controlling the incense and spice routes from Arabia to the Mediterranean—first described when a Hellenistic army failed to subdue them. Over these centuries they settled, mastered desert water catchment, and began carving the tombs and cult places at Petra. Their wealth came from taxing caravans rather than farming, and their kingdom grew rich enough to strike its own coinage.
Early Nabatean Period (Jordan, 331 BC–36.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3299 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3299 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 4499 BC–3299 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Corresponding cultural periods are Early phase and Ghassulian phase (derived from chronological table on page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.
Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3299 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Ottoman period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).label: Ottoman period
Ottoman period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).prose:
[Holy Land, AD 1516–AD 1917] Ottoman period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Selim I's defeat of the Mamluks brought Palestine under Ottoman rule, and Suleiman the Magnificent rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem that still stand today. For most of four centuries the region was a quiet cluster of districts governed from Damascus and Sidon, its towns supported by pilgrimage, soap and grain, though the nineteenth century brought European consuls, missionary institutions, new farming colonies and the first Zionist settlements. British forces took the country in 1917.
Ottoman period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Bronze Age (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC.prose:
[Holy Land, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Roman period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.label: Late Roman period
Late Roman period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.prose:
[Holy Land, AD 132–AD 324] Late Roman period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

After the crushing of the Bar Kokhba revolt, Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina, Jerusalem was rebuilt as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from the city. Jewish life regrouped in Galilee, where the Mishnah and later the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled and monumental stone synagogues began to appear. Cities like Caesarea and Beth Shean flourished on Roman roads and aqueducts, while a small Christian community grew that would soon, under Constantine, transform the whole country.
Late Roman period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Arab period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 151.label: Late Arab period
Late Arab period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 151.prose:
[Holy Land, AD 1291–AD 1516] Late Arab period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. The Late Arab period encompasses the Fatimid and Mameluke, which are not differentiated chronologically here. (page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Mamluk rule from Cairo replaced the Crusader states, and administration shifted decisively inland. Jerusalem gained a dense fabric of religious colleges and fountains around the Haram, caravanserais and bridges served the Cairo–Damascus post road, and the demolished harbours of the coast stayed empty. Ottoman conquest ended the era.
Late Arab period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 151.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–199.node: Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–1999 BC)
Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–199.label: Middle Bronze Age I
Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–199.prose:
[Holy Land, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Middle Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Towns and cities were re-established across the southern Levant after centuries of largely village and pastoral life, with fortifications, wheel-made pottery and true bronze metallurgy returning. Coastal sites looked north to Byblos and the Syrian world for trade and inspiration. This revival set the framework of Canaanite city-states that Egyptian and biblical sources would later describe.
Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–199.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Roman period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132.label: Early Roman period
Early Roman period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132.prose:
[Holy Land, 36 BC–AD 132] Early Roman period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Encompasses the Herodian period, 37 BCE-70 CE (page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Herod the Great, ruling as Rome's client king, rebuilt the Jerusalem Temple on a vast scale and founded Caesarea Maritima, Masada and other showpiece projects. Direct Roman rule and heavy taxation followed, along with the ferment of sects and messianic movements from which Christianity and rabbinic Judaism both emerged. Two catastrophic revolts frame the era's end: the destruction of the Temple in AD 70 and the crushing of Bar Kokhba's rising.
Early Roman period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Hellenistic period (Israel, 166 BC–.label: Late Hellenistic period
Late Hellenistic period (Israel, 166 BC–.prose:
[Holy Land, 166 BC–36 BC] Late Hellenistic period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The Maccabean revolt against Seleucid rule produced an independent Jewish state under the Hasmoneans, which expanded aggressively into Galilee, Idumaea and the coastal plain. Fortified palaces, ritual baths and the first distinctly Jewish coinage appear in the archaeological record, alongside Greek imports and architectural styles the Hasmoneans happily borrowed. Roman intervention and dynastic infighting ended the kingdom, clearing the way for Herod.
Late Hellenistic period (Israel, 166 BC–.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Early Hellenistic period (Israel, 331 BC.label: Early Hellenistic period
Early Hellenistic period (Israel, 331 BC.prose:
[Holy Land, 331 BC–166 BC] Early Hellenistic period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Alexander's conquest ended two centuries of Persian rule and pulled the southern Levant into the contest between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek cities, gymnasia, coinage and language spread along the coast and into Jerusalem's elite, provoking tensions over Judaean religious practice. The period closes with Antiochus IV's decrees and the Maccabean revolt.
Early Hellenistic period (Israel, 331 BC.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.node: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.label: Late Bronze Age I
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.prose:
[Holy Land, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Late Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Canaan's towns recovered slowly from the upheavals that ended the Middle Bronze Age, now under Egyptian overlordship after repeated pharaonic campaigns. Settlements were smaller and rarely walled, and the wealth that remained came from trade: painted bichrome jugs, Cypriot base-ring flasks and Aegean vessels found their way into local tombs and temples.
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Pottery Neolithic (Israel, 5499 BC–4499.label: Pottery Neolithic
Pottery Neolithic (Israel, 5499 BC–4499.prose:
[Holy Land, 5499 BC–4499 BC] Pottery Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Based on chronological table on page 1529, this period coincides with part of the post-glacial period of the Ice Age in Europe and the Holocene geological epoch. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

After the great stone-built farming towns of the pre-pottery era broke up, people settled in smaller, looser villages of pit dwellings and courtyard houses, herding sheep and goats alongside their crops. Fired clay vessels came into everyday use for cooking and storage, decorated with incised herringbone bands and red paint, and small clay figurines appear in numbers. It is a period of apparent decline in scale that in fact laid the technical groundwork for the Chalcolithic villages that followed.
Pottery Neolithic (Israel, 5499 BC–4499.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Iron Age IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).label: Iron Age IIA
Iron Age IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Holy Land, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron Age IIA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Villages grew into fortified towns with gates, palaces and storehouses, and the first real state institutions appear in the southern Levant. Scholars argue bitterly over whether these remains belong to a Solomonic kingdom or to the later Omride dynasty, and radiocarbon dating has become central to the fight. Distinctive red-slipped, burnished pottery marks the horizon at sites from Megiddo to Beersheba.
Iron Age IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

Late Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800).label: Late Islamic 2
Late Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800] Late Islamic 2. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Ottoman authority over the region was mostly exercised through subsidies to tribal leaders and control of the Hajj route rather than direct administration. Settlement was sparse and largely pastoral, with seasonal camps, small fortified farms and pilgrimage forts making up most of the built record. Coffee and tobacco consumption spread, leaving distinctive clay pipe bowls at almost every site.
Late Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516).label: Mamluk
Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516] Mamluk. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Under the Cairo sultanate this region became a well-run frontier province, its roads carrying the barid postal relay that linked Egypt to Damascus and its valleys filled with irrigated sugar plantations and refineries. Karak and other castles were rebuilt as administrative centres, and villages grew around the pilgrimage and trade routes. The whole system passed to the Ottomans in 1516.
Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Late Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600).label: Late Islamic 1
Late Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600] Late Islamic 1. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Late Mamluk sugar estates and villages contracted, and after 1516 the region passed to the Ottomans, who surveyed it for taxation and reorganised the annual Hajj caravan route through it. Fortified way-stations, cisterns and khans were built or refurbished along that road. Many settled sites were abandoned as tribal groups took control of the land.
Late Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Middle Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1200–AD 140.label: Middle Islamic 2
Middle Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1200–AD 140.prose:
[Jordan, AD 1200–AD 1400] Middle Islamic 2. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Mamluk rule brought administrative reorganisation, a functioning postal and road system, and investment in sugar production, mills and market towns. Karak served as a provincial capital and place of exile for rival princes, and the pilgrimage route south was maintained with forts and cisterns. Prosperity faded in the later fourteenth century with plague, Bedouin unrest and economic decline.
Middle Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1200–AD 140.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

modern (Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918).label: modern
modern (Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918] modern. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Europe in these centuries built centralised states and overseas empires, argued its way through the Reformation's aftermath, the Enlightenment and revolution, and then industrialised. Steam, railways, factories and mass literacy transformed daily life faster than at any earlier time, while nationalism redrew the map. The era ends in the wreckage of the First World War and the collapse of the continent's old dynastic empires.
modern (Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171).label: Fatimid
Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171).prose:
[Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171] Fatimid. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Cairo's Shi'i caliphs held the Jordanian lands as a frontier zone of their Syrian province, valuable for the pilgrimage and caravan routes running down the desert edge. Bedouin power and Seljuk pressure eroded that control, and the arrival of the Crusaders left the region divided between Frankish castles and Muslim rulers.
Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Umayyad (Jordan, AD 630–AD 750).label: Umayyad
Umayyad (Jordan, AD 630–AD 750).prose:
[Jordan, AD 630–AD 750] Umayyad. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Under the caliphs at Damascus, the lands east of the Jordan sat close to the centre of an empire reaching from Spain to Central Asia, rather than on its margins. Umayyad princes built the so-called desert castles here, among them Qusayr Amra with its startling frescoes of bathers, hunters and kings, and Qasr al-Kharana and Qasr al-Mshatta. Towns like Jerash and Pella continued to thrive with new markets and mosques until the earthquake of 749, and the dynasty fell to the Abbasid revolution the following year.
Umayyad (Jordan, AD 630–AD 750).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Middle Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 120.label: Middle Islamic 1
Middle Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 120.prose:
[Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1200] Middle Islamic 1. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Fatimid and then Crusader and Ayyubid power contested the region, and the great fortresses of Karak and Shobak were raised on the plateau to control the caravan and pilgrim roads. Saladin's victories brought the territory under Ayyubid rule and stimulated the sugar plantations of the Jordan Valley. Villages of this era are recognised by distinctive handmade painted pottery.
Middle Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 120.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Early Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000).label: Early Islamic 2
Early Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000).prose:
[Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000] Early Islamic 2. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

With the caliphate's centre shifted east to Baghdad, the region lost its patrons; many Umayyad estates were abandoned and settlement contracted. Abbasid and later Fatimid authority was exercised at a distance through provincial towns, while the countryside grew poorer and thinner on the ground. Pottery and glass of this era show the region plugged into wider Islamic trade networks even as its own towns shrank.
Early Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 600).label: late Byzantine
late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 600).prose:
[Jordan, AD 491–AD 600] late Byzantine. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Christian building reached its peak: town after town rebuilt with basilicas paved in mosaic, including the famous map of the Holy Land at Madaba. Pilgrim traffic, olive oil and wine production and imperial patronage under Justinian supported dense settlement even at the desert margins. Plague, earthquakes and Persian invasion would shortly break this prosperity, and within a generation the region passed to Muslim rule.
late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 600).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Caliphal (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969).label: Caliphal
Caliphal (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969).prose:
[Jordan, AD 630–AD 969] Caliphal. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. The Caliphal period encompasses the Umayyad and Abbasid periods. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Arab-Muslim armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and Jordan became part of the province of Bilad al-Sham, close to the Umayyad heartland at Damascus. The countryside is dotted with the results: the so-called desert castles such as Qusayr Amra and Qasr al-Kharana, with their bathhouses and painted walls, and towns where churches, mosques and mosaic floors sit side by side. When the Abbasids moved the centre of the caliphate to Iraq after 750, the area slipped to the margins, and its towns shrank.
Caliphal (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263).label: Ayyubid
Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263] Ayyubid. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Saladin's Kurdish dynasty ruled Egypt, Syria and the lands east of the Jordan, and his defeat of the crusaders at Hattin in 1187 brought Jerusalem back under Muslim rule. In Transjordan the period left striking military architecture, above all the castle of Ajlun, built to watch the crusader lords and guard the iron mines and communications with Damascus. Family infighting weakened the realm until Mamluk soldiers seized Egypt and the Mongols swept through Syria.
Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

High Islam (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918).label: High Islam
High Islam (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918] High Islam. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. Encompasses the Fatimid/Crusader, Ayyubid, and Mamluk periods.  (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Four centuries of Ottoman rule, when the region was governed from Damascus as a frontier of settled administration facing the desert tribes. Its central institution was the pilgrimage road to Mecca, guarded by a chain of forts and cisterns and later paralleled by the Hejaz Railway. Ottoman authority ended with the Arab Revolt and the First World War.
High Islam (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Early Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 600–AD 800).label: Early Islamic 1
Early Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 600–AD 800).prose:
[Jordan, AD 600–AD 800] Early Islamic 1. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

The Byzantine defeat at the Yarmuk in AD 636 handed the region to the new Muslim state, but the change on the ground was gradual: the same villages, farms and craft traditions continued, and Christian communities kept building and paving churches with mosaics. Under the Umayyads, ruling from nearby Damascus, elites built rural estates and pleasure palaces along the steppe fringe. Arabic gradually replaced Greek in administration, and coinage and inscriptions took on a new Islamic idiom.
Early Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 600–AD 800).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Abbasid (Jordan, AD 750–AD 969).label: Abbasid
Abbasid (Jordan, AD 750–AD 969).prose:
[Jordan, AD 750–AD 969] Abbasid. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Under Abbasid rule the Levant became a province rather than a heartland, as the capital moved from Damascus to Baghdad and Syrian elites lost their privileged position. Desert palaces were abandoned or repurposed, while pilgrimage roads to Mecca and the ports of the coast kept trade alive. Glazed pottery and glass from Iraq spread widely, marking sites of the period.
Abbasid (Jordan, AD 750–AD 969).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 630).label: late Byzantine
late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 630).prose:
[Jordan, AD 491–AD 630] late Byzantine. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Christian building reached its peak: town after town rebuilt with basilicas paved in mosaic, including the famous map of the Holy Land at Madaba. Pilgrim traffic, olive oil and wine production and imperial patronage under Justinian supported dense settlement even at the desert margins. Plague, earthquakes and Persian invasion would shortly break this prosperity, and within a generation the region passed to Muslim rule.
late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 630).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918).label: Ottoman
Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918).prose:
[Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918] Ottoman. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.
Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918).source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

Early Nabataean (Egypt, 167 BC–84 BC).label: Early Nabataean
Early Nabataean (Egypt, 167 BC–84 BC).prose: [Central Negev, 167 BC–84 BC] Early Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.
Early Nabataean (Egypt, 167 BC–84 BC).source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

Middle Nabataean (Egypt, 84 BC–AD 70).label: Middle Nabataean
Middle Nabataean (Egypt, 84 BC–AD 70).prose:
[Central Negev, 84 BC–AD 70] Middle Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

The Nabataean kingdom at its height, when its rulers grew rich taxing incense and spice caravans moving from Arabia to the Mediterranean and pushed their commercial reach into Sinai and the Egyptian frontier. Petra's rock-cut facades, sophisticated water engineering and distinctive eggshell-thin painted pottery date largely from these generations. Nabataean fortunes shifted as Rome absorbed the surrounding region, and the kingdom survived as a client until its annexation in AD 106.
Middle Nabataean (Egypt, 84 BC–AD 70).source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

Late Nabataean (Egypt, AD 70–AD 106).label: Late Nabataean
Late Nabataean (Egypt, AD 70–AD 106).prose:
[Central Negev, AD 70–AD 106] Late Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

The last generation of independent Nabataean rule, under Rabbel II, when the kingdom's centre of gravity shifted north toward Bostra and its caravan wealth faced growing Roman competition. Potters were still producing the astonishingly thin, painted 'eggshell' bowls that are the culture's signature. It ended in 106 when Trajan absorbed the kingdom as the province of Arabia.
Late Nabataean (Egypt, AD 70–AD 106).source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

Roman Period (Egypt, AD 106–AD 295).label: Roman Period
Roman Period (Egypt, AD 106–AD 295).prose:
[Central Negev, AD 106–AD 295] Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.
Roman Period (Egypt, AD 106–AD 295).source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 295–AD 635).label: Byzantine Period
Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 295–AD 635).prose:
[Central Negev, AD 295–AD 635] Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.
Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 295–AD 635).source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–11.node: Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–1199 BC)
Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–11.label: Late Bronze Age II B
Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–11.prose:
[The Levant, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age II B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The Ramesside phase of Egyptian control in Canaan, marked by Egyptian-style administrative buildings at Beth Shean and elsewhere, hieratic inscriptions and anthropoid clay coffins. It ends with the unravelling of Egyptian power, the burning of major cities, and the first mention of Israel on the Merneptah stele.
Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–11.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Early Roman Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132.label: Early Roman Period
Early Roman Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132.prose:
[The Levant, 36 BC–AD 132] Early Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.
Early Roman Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).node: Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC)
Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).label: Iron Age I A
Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).prose:
[The Levant, 1199 BC–1149 BC] Iron Age I A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The opening decades after the Late Bronze Age collapse, marked by the burning or abandonment of Canaanite centres and the final withdrawal of Egyptian authority. Locally made Aegean-style Mycenaean IIIC pottery appears at Ashdod, Ekron and Ashkelon, the archaeological signature of Philistine settlement. Meanwhile small new villages begin to dot the central highlands.
Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land
