Early Bronze Age II (State of Palestine,.prose:
[The Levant, 2999 BC–2699 BC] Early Bronze Age II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.
Early Bronze Age II (State of Palestine,.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC.label: Hellenistic Period
Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC.prose:
[The Levant, 331 BC–36 BC] Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.
Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).node: Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC)
Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Iron Age II B
Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[The Levant, 899 BC–699 BC] Iron Age II B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Two rival kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south, reached their fullest development, with royal capitals at Samaria and Jerusalem, ivory-inlaid furniture, olive oil industries and administrative ostraca. Assyrian pressure grew until Samaria fell in 722 BC and the northern kingdom's population was deported. Judah absorbed refugees, expanded rapidly, and survived Sennacherib's devastating campaign of 701 BC as an Assyrian vassal.
Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).node: Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC)
Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).label: Iron Age II C
Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).prose:
[The Levant, 699 BC–585 BC] Iron Age II C. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Judah lived on as a client of Assyria and then Babylon, its countryside dotted with olive-oil and textile towns and its bureaucracy leaving thousands of stamped jar handles and inscribed seals. When Assyrian power collapsed, Judah gambled on revolt; Nebuchadnezzar's armies answered by razing Jerusalem and its temple and deporting the elite. The destruction layers of this moment are among the most vividly excavated in the region.
Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0hsq.label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0hsq.prose:
[The Levant, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0hsq.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–.node: Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–2999 BC)
Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–.label: Early Bronze Age I A-B
Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–.prose:
[The Levant, 3499 BC–2999 BC] Early Bronze Age I A-B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Farming villages in the southern Levant expanded into large unwalled settlements, with growing craft specialisation in copper and pottery. Contact with Egypt intensified until Egyptian-style pottery, seal impressions and even Egyptian residents appear in the southern coastal plain. Within a few generations these communities would build the region's first fortified towns.
Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC.label: Early Hellenistic Period
Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC.prose:
[The Levant, 331 BC–166 BC] Early Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Alexander's conquest ended two centuries of Persian rule and pulled the southern Levant into the contest between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek cities, gymnasia, coinage and language spread along the coast and into Jerusalem's elite, provoking tensions over Judaean religious practice. The period closes with Antiochus IV's decrees and the Maccabean revolt.
Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Crusader and Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD.label: Crusader and Ayyubid Periods
Crusader and Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD.prose:
[The Levant, AD 1099–AD 1291] Crusader and Ayyubid Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The First Crusade's capture of Jerusalem installed a Latin ruling class that built castles, churches and fortified towns across the country, while Muslim and Eastern Christian villagers continued to work the land. Saladin's Ayyubids destroyed the field army at Hattin in 1187 and reduced the kingdom to a coastal strip governed from Acre, sustained by Italian merchant colonies and the military orders. The Mamluk capture of Acre in 1291 ended the Latin presence and left much of the coast deliberately ruined.
Crusader and Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).label: Byzantine Period
Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).prose:
[The Levant, AD 324–AD 638] Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.
Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Roman and Byzantine Periods (Israel, 36.label: Roman and Byzantine Periods
Roman and Byzantine Periods (Israel, 36.prose:
[The Levant, 36 BC–AD 638] Roman and Byzantine Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

From Herod's reign to the Arab conquest, this long stretch covers the destruction of the Second Temple, the rise of rabbinic Judaism, and the birth and eventual triumph of Christianity. Under Byzantine rule the region became a landscape of churches, monasteries and pilgrim routes, with mosaic-floored basilicas in almost every town. Population and agriculture reached a peak, with terraces and wine presses pushed far into the Negev, before Persian invasion and then Muslim armies ended imperial control.
Roman and Byzantine Periods (Israel, 36.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Herodian Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70).label: Herodian Period
Herodian Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70).prose:
[The Levant, 36 BC–AD 70] Herodian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from  Encompassed by Early Roman Period (37 BCE - 132 CE) (page xvi). Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Herod the Great, installed by Rome as king of the Jews, spent his reign building on a spectacular scale: the vastly enlarged Temple Mount platform, the harbour city of Caesarea Maritima, the desert palaces at Masada and Herodium. Under him and his heirs Judaea was a client kingdom balanced uneasily between Roman power and Jewish religious life, the setting for the events of the Gospels. It ended with revolt against Rome and the burning of the Temple in AD 70.
Herodian Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.node: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC) [p0hsq83tspw]
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.label: Late Bronze Age I
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.prose:
[The Levant, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Late Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Canaan's towns recovered slowly from the upheavals that ended the Middle Bronze Age, now under Egyptian overlordship after repeated pharaonic campaigns. Settlements were smaller and rarely walled, and the wealth that remained came from trade: painted bichrome jugs, Cypriot base-ring flasks and Aegean vessels found their way into local tombs and temples.
Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1.node: Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1999 BC)
Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1.label: Middle Bronze Age I A
Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1.prose:
[The Levant, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Middle Bronze Age I A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

A transitional, largely rural phase between the collapse of the Early Bronze Age towns and the urban revival that followed, known mostly from cemeteries of shaft graves and small seasonal camps rather than settlements. Pastoralism and mobility dominated, and copper daggers and simple pottery are the characteristic finds. Scholars have long argued over whether this reflects newcomers from the north or local people adapting to hard times.
Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.node: Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel, 585 BC–331 BC) [p0hsq83g9mg]
Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.label: Babylonian and Persian Periods
Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.prose:
[The Levant, 585 BC–331 BC] Babylonian and Persian Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Judah began this stretch as a wrecked Babylonian province, Jerusalem burned and its elite deported, and ended it as Yehud, a small temple-centred district of the Achaemenid Empire. Exiles returning under Persian permission rebuilt the Temple and, with Ezra and Nehemiah, reshaped Judaism around law, scripture and priesthood rather than monarchy. Aramaic spread as the everyday language, coinage and imperial administration arrived, and the Hebrew Bible took much of the shape it still has.
Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel,.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).label: Ottoman Period
Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).prose:
[The Levant, AD 1516–AD 1917] Ottoman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.
Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.label: Late Roman Period
Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.prose:
[The Levant, AD 132–AD 324] Late Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.
Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Late Arab Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 151.label: Late Arab Period
Late Arab Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 151.prose:
[The Levant, AD 1291–AD 1516] Late Arab Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

With the fall of Acre in 1291 the last Crusader foothold was gone and the region was governed from Cairo by the Mamluk sultans. Coastal towns were deliberately left ruined to deter a European return, while inland Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed prospered, filling with madrasas, markets and pilgrim hostels built in banded Mamluk stonework. The period closes with the Ottoman victory that absorbed the whole area into a new empire.
Late Arab Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 151.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 166 BC–.label: Late Hellenistic Period
Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 166 BC–.prose:
[The Levant, 166 BC–36 BC] Late Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Seleucid power collapsed into dynastic civil war, and the old Phoenician harbour cities — Tyre, Sidon, Berytus — bought or seized autonomy, minting their own coins and trading across the Mediterranean. Greek civic institutions and temple architecture were grafted onto older Canaanite religious traditions, producing the hybrid sanctuaries later rebuilt on a colossal scale at Baalbek. Pompey's arrival ended the experiment, folding the coast into the Roman province of Syria.
Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 166 BC–.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.node: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–2199 BC) [p0hsq83knpb]
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.label: Early Bronze Age III
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.prose:
[The Levant, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Early Bronze Age III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Fortified towns in the southern Levant reached their peak, with thick town walls, temples, palaces and the huge circular storage structure at Beth Yerah. Distinctive burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, related to northern traditions, spreads through the region. By the close of the period nearly all these towns had been abandoned, and urban life vanished for centuries.
Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–21.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).node: Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC)
Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).label: Iron Age II A
Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).prose:
[The Levant, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron Age II A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Small highland villages consolidated into towns with public architecture, casemate walls and six-chambered gates at sites such as Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer. This is the horizon traditionally linked to the biblical united monarchy of David and Solomon, and the dating of its pottery and buildings remains one of the fiercest debates in Levantine archaeology. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature find.
Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).node: Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC)
Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).label: Iron Age I B
Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).prose:
[The Levant, 1149 BC–999 BC] Iron Age I B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Distinctive Philistine bichrome pottery and planned coastal towns mark the consolidation of the Philistine pentapolis, while the highland villages multiply and grow, with terraced fields, storage pits and four-room houses. Egyptian and Canaanite power in the lowlands fades for good. By the end of the phase, larger political units are forming that will become the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 109.label: Early Arab Period
Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 109.prose:
[The Levant, AD 638–AD 1099] Early Arab Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Muslim armies took Palestine from Byzantium in the 630s, and the region was governed successively from Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo. The Umayyads built the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem and founded Ramla as a new provincial capital, while Christians and Jews continued to live under the protected-subject system. Earthquakes, Bedouin unrest and Fatimid–Seljuk conflict weakened the area before the Crusaders stormed Jerusalem in 1099.
Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 109.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Bronze Age (Israel, 3499 BC–1199 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Israel, 3499 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[The Levant, 3499 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Israel, 3499 BC–1199 BC).source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–.node: Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–1549 BC)
Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–.label: Middle Bronze Age II B
Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–.prose:
[The Levant, 1749 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age II B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Fortified Canaanite cities were at their peak, with rampart defences, palace complexes and cemeteries containing weapons, jewellery and imported goods. Levantine populations settled in the eastern Nile Delta and Hyksos rulers of Semitic origin took power in northern Egypt. The period ends amid destructions as Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty pushed back into Asia.
Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

The Seleucid Era (Syria, 310 BC–63 BC).label: The Seleucid Era
The Seleucid Era (Syria, 310 BC–63 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 310 BC–63 BC] The Seleucid Era. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Inferred from the following discussions: page 30 states that Seleucus I declared the official Year 1 of the Seleucid Era to be 311 BCE; Figure 1 on page 6 indicates the final Seleucid king, Philip II Barypous, ended his reign in 64 BCE; and page 234 explicitly states the dissolution of the Seleukid kingdom by Pompey in 64 BCE. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Seleucus I took the eastern share of Alexander's empire and built a Greek-ruled state stretching from the Aegean towards India, anchored on new foundations like Antioch and Seleucia on the Tigris. Greek settlers, coinage and city institutions were grafted onto Babylonian, Persian and Syrian populations, producing genuinely hybrid cultures. Continual wars with the Ptolemies, the loss of the east to the Parthians and the Maccabean revolt in Judaea whittled the kingdom down until Pompey annexed what was left as the Roman province of Syria.
The Seleucid Era (Syria, 310 BC–63 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (I.node: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (Iraq, 322 BC–315 BC)
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (I.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (I.prose:
[Babylonia, 322 BC–315 BC] Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1. Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 1: From the death of Alexander the great in 323 BCE to Antigonus Monophthalmus' expulsion of Seleucus Nicator from Babylon in 316 BCE, records were dated by the years of king Philip III Arrhidaeus and then, after his posthumous eighth year, by the years of king Alexander IV;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Babylonian scribes dated legal tablets and astronomical diaries by the regnal years of the reigning king, and after Alexander's death those formulae named his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus, a figurehead ruling under the generals. The dating clauses are therefore a running record of who was recognised as sovereign in Babylonia during the wars of the successors. Cuneiform bookkeeping outlasted the Persian empire and the Macedonian conquest with little change.
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (I.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Philip I Philadelphus (Syria, 93 BC–82 B.label: Philip I Philadelphus
Philip I Philadelphus (Syria, 93 BC–82 B.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 93 BC–82 BC] Philip I Philadelphus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

One of the last Seleucid kings, ruling a rump state around Antioch while fighting his own brothers for scraps of a once-vast empire. Cities effectively governed themselves, and Armenian and then Roman power filled the vacuum. His abundant tetradrachms kept circulating long after the dynasty fell, copied even under Roman rule.
Philip I Philadelphus (Syria, 93 BC–82 B.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (I.node: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (Iraq, 315 BC–310 BC)
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (I.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (I.prose:
[Babylonia, 315 BC–310 BC] Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2. Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 2: From late 316 to 311 BCE, the preiod of Antigonus Monophthalmus's undisputed dominance in Babylonia and Seleucus's exile in Ptolemy's Egypt, records were no longer dated by the reigning monarch, Alexander IV, who was absent in Macedonia. Instead, scribes introduced a year count of Antigonus in his official capacity as lúrab uqu, the Akkadian term for the Greek title stratêgos (general) of Asia....The beginning of this count, in an important precedent for the Seleucid Era, was retrojected to 317/316 BCE;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

After Philip Arrhidaeus was killed, Babylonian tablets began counting the regnal years of Alexander's posthumous son, Alexander IV, still a child in the custody of the Macedonian generals. The shift in the dating clause marks a change of recognised authority rather than any real change of ruler. These formulae are one of the sharpest tools chronologists have for pinning down the chaotic politics of the successor wars.
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (I.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus XIII Asiaticus (Syria, 68 BC–6.label: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus
Antiochus XIII Asiaticus (Syria, 68 BC–6.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 68 BC–66 BC] Antiochus XIII Asiaticus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The last Seleucid to be recognised as king, installed in Antioch by the Roman general Lucullus after Tigranes of Armenia's occupation collapsed. His authority never extended much past the capital, and Pompey deposed him and annexed Syria as a Roman province; he was killed soon after by an Arab dynast. With him ended the line founded by Alexander's general Seleucus more than 240 years earlier.
Antiochus XIII Asiaticus (Syria, 68 BC–6.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Alexander II Zabinas (Syria, 127 BC–122.label: Alexander II Zabinas
Alexander II Zabinas (Syria, 127 BC–122.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 127 BC–122 BC] Alexander II Zabinas. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A usurper set up by Ptolemy VIII of Egypt, who passed him off as an adopted heir of Antiochus VII; his nickname means roughly 'the bought one'. He beat and killed Demetrius II, ruled much of Syria briefly, then lost Egyptian support and was destroyed by Antiochus VIII, another turn in the fratricidal collapse of the Seleucid kingdom.
Alexander II Zabinas (Syria, 127 BC–122.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus Hierax (Syria, 241 BC–226 BC).label: Antiochus Hierax
Antiochus Hierax (Syria, 241 BC–226 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 241 BC–226 BC] Antiochus Hierax. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

"The Hawk", younger brother of Seleucus II, was set up to govern Asia Minor and promptly made war on him, hiring Galatian mercenaries and splitting the empire in two. The fraternal war exhausted Seleucid authority in Anatolia and gave Attalus I of Pergamon the opening to defeat both Galatians and Hierax and build an independent kingdom. Hierax died a fugitive, but the damage let Parthia and Bactria consolidate their breakaway in the east.
Antiochus Hierax (Syria, 241 BC–226 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus VI Dionysus (Syria, 143 BC–140.label: Antiochus VI Dionysus
Antiochus VI Dionysus (Syria, 143 BC–140.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 143 BC–140 BC] Antiochus VI Dionysus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A child raised to the throne as a figurehead by the general Diodotus Tryphon, who used him to fight Demetrius II and issued coins in his name. Tryphon eventually murdered him and ruled outright, an act of usurpation that split the kingdom between rival courts. The chaos let Jonathan and Simon of the Hasmonean house play both sides and win effective independence for Judaea.
Antiochus VI Dionysus (Syria, 143 BC–140.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign) (Syri.label: Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign)
Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign) (Syri.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 144 BC–AD 139] Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Derived from Figure 1 ("The House of Seleucus, simplified") on page 6, which lays out the genealogy of the Seleucid kings. Demetrius II Nicator reigned twice, with other claimants forcing him out of power in between. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The son of Demetrius I ousted the usurper Alexander Balas with Ptolemaic help, then lost ground to rivals and to mercenary troops who turned the population of Antioch against him. To keep Judaean support he conceded tax exemptions to Jonathan Maccabeus, effectively recognising Jewish autonomy. His eastern campaign against the Parthians ended in disaster: he was captured and held for years at the Arsacid court.
Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign) (Syri.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus II Theos (Syria, 260 BC–245 BC.label: Antiochus II Theos
Antiochus II Theos (Syria, 260 BC–245 BC.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 260 BC–245 BC] Antiochus II Theos. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

He won back territory from Ptolemaic Egypt in the Second Syrian War and courted the Greek cities of Asia Minor with grants of freedom, earning the title "God" from grateful Miletus. To seal peace he set aside his wife Laodice and married the Ptolemaic princess Berenice; his death left two rival queens and two heirs, and the resulting bloodshed dragged Egypt into a fresh invasion of Syria. In these same years Parthia and Bactria slipped out of Seleucid control, a loss the dynasty never reversed.
Antiochus II Theos (Syria, 260 BC–245 BC.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus VII Sidetes (Syria, 137 BC–128.label: Antiochus VII Sidetes
Antiochus VII Sidetes (Syria, 137 BC–128.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 137 BC–128 BC] Antiochus VII Sidetes. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The last Seleucid king to command real power destroyed the usurper Tryphon, forced John Hyrcanus to submit after besieging Jerusalem, and reasserted royal authority across Syria. He then led a great campaign east against the Parthians, winning battles and briefly recovering Babylonia and Media before his scattered winter quarters were attacked and he was killed. With him died Seleucid rule beyond the Euphrates; what remained shrank into a patchwork of feuding claimants absorbed by Rome within two generations.
Antiochus VII Sidetes (Syria, 137 BC–128.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign) (Syr.node: Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign) (Syria, 128 BC–124 BC)
Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign) (Syr.label: Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign)
Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign) (Syr.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 128 BC–124 BC] Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Derived from Figure 1 ("The House of Seleucus, simplified") on page 6, which lays out the genealogy of the Seleucid kings. Demetrius II Nicator reigned twice, with other claimants forcing him out of power in between. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Released by the Parthians as a weapon against his own brother, he returned to a shrunken and exhausted Seleucid realm. An attempt to intervene in Egypt backfired when Ptolemy VIII sponsored the pretender Alexander Zabinas, who defeated him in battle. Abandoned by his wife Cleopatra Thea and the city of Ptolemais, he was hunted down and killed at Tyre.
Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign) (Syr.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

High Seleucid Empire (Syria, 299 BC–149.label: High Seleucid Empire
High Seleucid Empire (Syria, 299 BC–149.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 299 BC–149 BC] High Seleucid Empire. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Derived from the discussion on page 189: "It may be helpful to distinguish...the high Seleucid empire from the third to the middle of the second century BCE....". Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The eastern bulk of Alexander's conquests, held together by Seleucus and his heirs from new Greek-style capitals like Antioch and Seleucia-on-the-Tigris. Greek colonists, coinage and city planning were grafted onto Babylonian, Iranian and Syrian populations, producing one of antiquity's most thoroughly mixed cultures. The empire steadily shed its edges — Bactria and Parthia broke away in the east, and defeat by Rome at Magnesia in 190 BC ended its ambitions in Asia Minor — leaving a shrinking Syrian core.
High Seleucid Empire (Syria, 299 BC–149.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Seleucus III Ceraunus (Syria, 225 BC–222.label: Seleucus III Ceraunus
Seleucus III Ceraunus (Syria, 225 BC–222.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 225 BC–222 BC] Seleucus III Ceraunus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A brief reign spent trying to recover Seleucid territory in Anatolia lost to Attalus I of Pergamon. He was assassinated by officers of his own army while campaigning across the Taurus, and the throne passed to his younger brother Antiochus III, who would restore the dynasty's fortunes.
Seleucus III Ceraunus (Syria, 225 BC–222.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Seleucus II Callinicus (Syria, 245 BC–22.label: Seleucus II Callinicus
Seleucus II Callinicus (Syria, 245 BC–22.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 245 BC–225 BC] Seleucus II Callinicus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

He inherited a war with Ptolemy III that cost him Seleucia in Pieria and much of Syria, then had to share power with his rebellious brother Antiochus Hierax in a ruinous fraternal conflict. During his reign Parthia and Bactria broke away in the east, permanently detaching the Iranian plateau's eastern provinces. His reign marks the point at which Seleucid overstretch became visible.
Seleucus II Callinicus (Syria, 245 BC–22.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Demetrius I Soter (Syria, 161 BC–149 BC).label: Demetrius I Soter
Demetrius I Soter (Syria, 161 BC–149 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 161 BC–149 BC] Demetrius I Soter. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Held as a hostage in Rome, he escaped, sailed to Syria and seized the Seleucid throne from his young cousin. His generals fought the Maccabean rebels in Judaea, killing Judas Maccabeus in battle, while his heavy-handedness alienated neighbouring kings and the Roman senate. They backed a pretender, Alexander Balas, who defeated and killed him — opening the long cycle of rival claimants that consumed the dynasty.
Demetrius I Soter (Syria, 161 BC–149 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus XI Epiphanes (Syria, 93 BC–92.label: Antiochus XI Epiphanes
Antiochus XI Epiphanes (Syria, 93 BC–92.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 93 BC–92 BC] Antiochus XI Epiphanes. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

One of the five sons of Antiochus VIII who fought each other for the shrinking Seleucid throne, he seized Antioch after avenging his twin brother Seleucus VI, only to be driven out within months by his cousin Antiochus X and drowned in the Orontes while fleeing. His reign is a snapshot of the dynasty's terminal phase, when rival kings issued coins from a handful of cities and controlled little beyond them. The civil wars left Syria open to Armenian, Nabataean and finally Roman intervention.
Antiochus XI Epiphanes (Syria, 93 BC–92.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus V Eupator (Syria, 163 BC–161 B.label: Antiochus V Eupator
Antiochus V Eupator (Syria, 163 BC–161 B.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 163 BC–161 BC] Antiochus V Eupator. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A boy king ruling in the shadow of the regent Lysias, in whose name the army marched into Judaea and defeated the Maccabees at Beth-Zechariah. Unable to finish the war because of a rival at court, the regime conceded the Jews' religious freedom, a turning point in the revolt. Both boy and regent were killed when Demetrius I, escaping from hostage-life in Rome, landed and seized the throne.
Antiochus V Eupator (Syria, 163 BC–161 B.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Philip II Barypous (Syria, 66 BC–64 BC).label: Philip II Barypous
Philip II Barypous (Syria, 66 BC–64 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 66 BC–64 BC] Philip II Barypous. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A brief, contested Seleucid claimant in the final collapse of the dynasty, backed at times by Arab chiefs and rejected by Rome. Pompey ended the line by annexing Syria as a Roman province in 64 BC. His coinage is scarce and marks the literal last gasp of Alexander's successors in Asia.
Philip II Barypous (Syria, 66 BC–64 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3 (I.node: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3 (Iraq, 310 BC–304 BC)
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3 (I.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3 (I.prose:
[Babylonia, 310 BC–304 BC] Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3. Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 3: Following Seleucus Nicator's return to Babylon in 311 BCE, the interrupted regnal count of Alexander IV was restored. Thus, year 7 of general Antigonus was renamed year 6 of Alexander IV. The count was continued even after the young king's murder in 310 BCE. Seleucus's name and the title lúrab uqu, previously used for Antigonus, were added to the regnal year date of Alexander IV, thereby combining features of the stage 1 and stage 2 formulae;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Alexander IV was murdered around 310, yet Babylonian scribes went on counting his years for some time, because no successor had yet claimed the royal title. When Seleucus assumed kingship the count was recalculated back to his return to Babylon in 311, creating the Seleucid Era, the first continuous year-count in history that ran on without resetting at each new reign.
Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3 (I.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Alexander I Balas (Syria, 149 BC–144 BC).label: Alexander I Balas
Alexander I Balas (Syria, 149 BC–144 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 149 BC–144 BC] Alexander I Balas. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A pretender of obscure birth who claimed to be a son of Antiochus IV and, with Roman, Pergamene and Egyptian backing, toppled Demetrius I to take the Seleucid throne. To hold it he courted the Maccabees, making Jonathan high priest, but his father-in-law Ptolemy VI turned against him and he was killed in flight, deepening the dynastic civil wars that hollowed out Seleucid Syria.
Alexander I Balas (Syria, 149 BC–144 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Seleucus V (Syria, 124 BC–124 BC).label: Seleucus V
Seleucus V (Syria, 124 BC–124 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 124 BC–124 BC] Seleucus V. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

He claimed the Seleucid throne after his father Demetrius II was killed, and lasted only months. His own mother, Cleopatra Thea, is said to have had him killed for taking the diadem without her consent — a compact illustration of how far the dynasty had decayed into family bloodletting while Parthia ate its eastern provinces.
Seleucus V (Syria, 124 BC–124 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus IV Epiphanes (Syria, 174 BC–16.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
Antiochus IV Epiphanes (Syria, 174 BC–16.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 174 BC–163 BC] Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

He nearly conquered Ptolemaic Egypt before a single Roman envoy drew a line in the sand and ordered him home, a humiliation that showed where power in the Mediterranean now lay. In Jerusalem he backed Hellenizing high priests, plundered the Temple and banned Jewish religious practice, provoking the Maccabean revolt that eventually created an independent Jewish state. His flamboyant self-presentation as a god manifest, and his lavish festivals and building at Antioch, made him one of the most talked-about kings of his age.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes (Syria, 174 BC–16.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus I Soter (Syria, 280 BC–260 BC).label: Antiochus I Soter
Antiochus I Soter (Syria, 280 BC–260 BC).prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 280 BC–260 BC] Antiochus I Soter. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Inheriting Seleucus I's sprawling empire from the Aegean to Central Asia, he spent his reign holding it together, founding and refounding cities and ruling Babylonia as a traditional Mesopotamian king who restored its temples. His epithet "Saviour" came from crushing invading Galatians in a battle in which his war elephants panicked their cavalry. Against Ptolemaic Egypt he fared worse, losing ground in the coastal provinces during the First Syrian War.
Antiochus I Soter (Syria, 280 BC–260 BC).source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Seleucus IV Philopator (Syria, 186 BC–17.label: Seleucus IV Philopator
Seleucus IV Philopator (Syria, 186 BC–17.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 186 BC–174 BC] Seleucus IV Philopator. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Ruling a Seleucid empire stripped of Asia Minor and saddled with a crushing war indemnity owed to Rome, he spent his reign scraping together money and keeping quiet, his brother Antiochus held hostage in Rome as a guarantee of good behaviour. The hunt for cash produced the famous episode of his minister Heliodorus being sent to seize the treasure of the Temple in Jerusalem. Heliodorus later murdered him, opening the way for Antiochus IV and the crisis that led to the Maccabean revolt.
Seleucus IV Philopator (Syria, 186 BC–17.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Antiochus III Megas (Syria, 222 BC–186 B.label: Antiochus III Megas
Antiochus III Megas (Syria, 222 BC–186 B.prose:
[Seleucid Empire, 222 BC–186 BC] Antiochus III Megas. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The most energetic Seleucid king marched from Asia Minor to India, bringing rebellious satraps and eastern kingdoms back into allegiance and taking Coele-Syria and Judaea from Egypt after his victory at Panium. Overreach followed: invited into Greece by the Aetolians, he collided with Rome and was beaten at Thermopylae and then decisively at Magnesia. The Treaty of Apamea stripped him of Asia Minor and imposed a crushing indemnity, and he died looting a temple to help pay it, leaving Rome the arbiter of the Greek East.
Antiochus III Megas (Syria, 222 BC–186 B.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

Bronze Age (Austria, 2699 BC–799 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Austria, 2699 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Austria, 2699 BC–799 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Younger Hallstatt culture/period (Ha D1).node: Younger Hallstatt culture/period (Ha D1) (Austria, 599 BC–549 BC)
Younger Hallstatt culture/period (Ha D1).label: Younger Hallstatt culture/period (Ha D1)
Younger Hallstatt culture/period (Ha D1).prose:
[Austria, 599 BC–549 BC] Younger Hallstatt culture/period (Ha D1). Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

Iron-using elites in the eastern Alpine region buried their dead under mounds with wagons, weapons and imported bronze vessels, while the salt mines that gave Hallstatt its name kept generating wealth. Fortified hilltop centres controlled routes and trade with the Mediterranean world. Distinctive arched fibulae and figured bronze situlae showing feasts, boxing matches and processions date to this horizon.

Serpentine fibula-horizon (Slovenia, 579.label: Serpentine fibula-horizon
Serpentine fibula-horizon (Slovenia, 579.prose: [Slovenia, 579 BC–549 BC] Serpentine fibula-horizon. Based on. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

Lusitanian culture (Ha A2) (Slovakia, 10.label: Lusitanian culture (Ha A2)
Lusitanian culture (Ha A2) (Slovakia, 10.prose:
[SW-Slovakia, 1099 BC–1049 BC] Lusitanian culture (Ha A2). Based on. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

A late Bronze Age phase of the Lusatian culture, marked by continued urnfield burial and increasingly elaborate bronze metalwork. Fortified hilltop settlements with ramparts of timber and earth appear more often, hinting at rising competition for land and metal routes.

Hallstatt culture/period (Hungary, 799 B.label: Hallstatt culture/period
Hallstatt culture/period (Hungary, 799 B.prose:
[Hungary, 799 BC–499 BC] Hallstatt culture/period. Based on. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

The first fully iron-using culture of central Europe, named after a salt-mining village in the Austrian Alps whose cemetery yielded thousands of richly furnished graves. Wealth built on salt, copper and control of trade routes produced a warrior aristocracy buried under mounds with four-wheeled wagons, bronze feasting gear and imported Mediterranean luxuries. In the Carpathian Basin these communities lived in fortified hilltop settlements and later absorbed waves of horse-riding steppe newcomers; their descendants form the background to the historically attested Celts.

Lusitanian culture (Ha A1) (Slovakia, 11.label: Lusitanian culture (Ha A1)
Lusitanian culture (Ha A1) (Slovakia, 11.prose:
[SW-Slovakia, 1199 BC–1099 BC] Lusitanian culture (Ha A1). Based on. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

Lusatian communities in this phase lived in dense village clusters and produced quantities of bronze work, with hoards of tools, ornaments and weapons deposited in ground and water. Cremation cemeteries could hold thousands of urn burials, suggesting stable and long-lived settlements.

Podzemelj 1-2 (Slovenia, 799 BC–699 BC).label: Podzemelj 1-2
Podzemelj 1-2 (Slovenia, 799 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Slovenia, 799 BC–699 BC] Podzemelj 1-2. Based on. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

The opening phase of the Early Iron Age in southeastern Slovenia, named after the cemetery at Podzemelj in Bela krajina. Communities began raising barrow cemeteries beside fortified hilltop settlements, and iron tools and weapons spread alongside imported bronze vessels and ornaments. It marks the start of the wealthy Hallstatt-period culture whose later centres, such as Stična and Novo mesto, produced the region's famous decorated bronze buckets.

Podzemelj 1-2 (Slovenia, 799 BC–719 BC).label: Podzemelj 1-2
Podzemelj 1-2 (Slovenia, 799 BC–719 BC).prose:
[Styria, Lower Carniola (Slovenia), 799 BC–719 BC] Podzemelj 1-2. Derived from. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

The opening phase of the Early Iron Age in southeastern Slovenia, named after the cemetery at Podzemelj in Bela krajina. Communities began raising barrow cemeteries beside fortified hilltop settlements, and iron tools and weapons spread alongside imported bronze vessels and ornaments. It marks the start of the wealthy Hallstatt-period culture whose later centres, such as Stična and Novo mesto, produced the region's famous decorated bronze buckets.

Middle Urnfield culture/period (Ha A2) (.node: Middle Urnfield culture/period (Ha A2) (Austria, 1099 BC–1049 BC)
Middle Urnfield culture/period (Ha A2) (.label: Middle Urnfield culture/period (Ha A2)
Middle Urnfield culture/period (Ha A2) (.prose:
[Austria, 1099 BC–1049 BC] Middle Urnfield culture/period (Ha A2). Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

Cremation had become the near-universal rite, with ashes placed in urns and buried in large, orderly cemeteries that give the culture its name. Bronzeworkers mastered sheet-metal techniques, hammering out vessels, helmets and armour, while fortified hilltop settlements spread across the Alpine foreland. These communities laid the economic and social groundwork for the Hallstatt world that followed.

Stična 1 (Slovenia, 719 BC–669 BC).label: Stična 1
Stična 1 (Slovenia, 719 BC–669 BC).prose:
[Styria, Lower Carniola (Slovenia), 719 BC–669 BC] Stična 1. Derived from. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

Named for the great hillfort and its surrounding field of burial mounds in southeastern Slovenia, this is the opening stage of the Early Iron Age in the region. Massive ramparts enclosed the settlement while chieftains were buried under barrows with bronze vessels, weapons and imported goods, evidence of a wealthy elite plugged into trade routes running from Italy to the eastern Alps.

Frög 1 (Austria, 849 BC–799 BC).label: Frög 1
Frög 1 (Austria, 849 BC–799 BC).prose:

Named after the great barrow cemetery in Carinthia, where hundreds of burial mounds cluster around a settlement at the head of Alpine trade routes. The graves are rich in early Hallstatt metalwork, including small cast lead figurines of riders, horses and wagons that are unlike anything else in Europe. The community's wealth came from controlling iron and copper sources and the traffic passing between Italy and the Alpine north.

Communities began raising barrow cemeteries beside fortified hilltop settlements, and iron tools and weapons spread alongside imported bronze vessels and ornaments. It marks the start of the wealthy Hallstatt-period culture whose later centres, such as Stična and Novo mesto, produced the region's famous decorated bronze buckets.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Late Bronze Age communities abandoned inhumation for cremation, placing the ashes in pottery urns buried in large flat cemeteries, sometimes with hundreds of graves. In the eastern Alps and Slovenian lowlands these communities lie directly behind the Hallstatt Iron Age societies that followed.

Hallstatt culture/period (Croatia, 799 B.prose:
[Croatia, 799 BC–449 BC] Hallstatt culture/period. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

The first fully iron-using culture of central Europe, named after a salt-mining village in the Austrian Alps whose cemetery yielded thousands of richly furnished graves. Wealth built on salt, copper and control of trade routes produced a warrior aristocracy buried under mounds with four-wheeled wagons, bronze feasting gear and imported Mediterranean luxuries. In the Carpathian Basin these communities lived in fortified hilltop settlements and later absorbed waves of horse-riding steppe newcomers; their descendants form the background to the historically attested Celts.

Late Bronze Age communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in pottery urns in large flat cemeteries, a rite that spread across much of central Europe and reached the Sava and Drava valleys. Metalworkers turned out sheet-bronze vessels, helmets and sword types traded over long distances, and huge hoards of scrap and finished bronzes were buried in the ground. Fortified hilltop settlements multiplied, hinting at competition and insecurity in the centuries before iron came into common use.

It belongs to the wider Hallstatt world of the eastern Alps, whose workshops produced the famous embossed bronze situlae showing feasts, processions and boxing matches.

The transition from bronze to iron in the northern Balkans and the eastern Alpine fringe, when local Urnfield communities adopted iron weapons and new burial display. Chieftains were buried under mounds with long slashing swords, horse gear and sometimes wagons, and hillforts became centres controlling metal and salt routes. It sets up the wealthy princely societies of the later Hallstatt Iron Age.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

Fortified hilltop centres controlled routes and trade with the Mediterranean world. Distinctive arched fibulae and figured bronze situlae showing feasts, boxing matches and processions date to this horizon.

Settlements shifted to defensible hilltops, and cremation gave ground to inhumation in the wealthiest graves. The regional groups formed here set the pattern for the princely centres of the following centuries.

A late phase of the Iron Age in the northern Balkans and eastern Alps, when fortified hillforts and their mound cemeteries reached their height and Greek and Etruscan imports reached inland elites. Situla art, decorated bronze belt plates and richly furnished warrior and women's graves belong to this horizon. Contact with the Mediterranean and with steppe horsemen from the east both left marks on local metalwork.

The first fully iron-using culture of central Europe, named after a salt-mining village in the Austrian Alps whose cemetery yielded thousands of richly furnished graves. Wealth built on salt, copper and control of trade routes produced a warrior aristocracy buried under mounds with four-wheeled wagons, bronze feasting gear and imported Mediterranean luxuries. In the Carpathian Basin these communities lived in fortified hilltop settlements and later absorbed waves of horse-riding steppe newcomers; their descendants form the background to the historically attested Celts.

In the Carpathian Basin this was a period of fortified hilltop settlements and richly furnished mound burials containing weapons, horse harness and wagon fittings. Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons while bronze remained the medium for display vessels and ornaments. Contacts stretched south to the Adriatic and east to the steppe, from which mounted warrior groups would soon arrive.

Communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large flat cemeteries, a rite that spread across much of central Europe. Bronze working reached a peak of output and skill, with sheet-metal vessels, swords and ornaments deposited in hoards and rivers, and hilltop settlements were fortified. Within a century iron working and the richer, more hierarchical burials of the Hallstatt Iron Age took over.

Cremation had become the near-universal rite, with ashes placed in urns and buried in large, orderly cemeteries that give the culture its name. Bronzeworkers mastered sheet-metal techniques, hammering out vessels, helmets and armour, while fortified hilltop settlements spread across the Alpine foreland. These communities laid the economic and social groundwork for the Hallstatt world that followed.

Iron Age IIa (Jordan, 999 BC–899 BC).prose:

Villages and tribal groupings east of the Jordan hardened into the territorial kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom, each with a capital, a national god and its own script. Fortified towers and border sites spread across the plateau, and the trade routes carrying incense and copper north became the region's economic backbone.
Iron Age IIa (Jordan, 999 BC–899 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Babylonian/Persian (Jordan, 538 BC–299 B.label: Babylonian/Persian
Babylonian/Persian (Jordan, 538 BC–299 B.prose:
[Petra, 538 BC–299 BC] Babylonian/Persian. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After Babylonian campaigns broke the small kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom, the lands east of the Jordan became thinly settled districts of empire, first Babylonian and then Achaemenid. Urban life contracted, pastoral and tribal groups became more prominent, and Arab traders — the ancestors of the Nabataean power at Petra — took control of the incense routes. Aramaic administration, Persian-style imports and Greek pottery show a region tied loosely but firmly into a wider imperial economy.
Babylonian/Persian (Jordan, 538 BC–299 B.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

[Petra, 49 BC–AD 450] Roman. After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.
Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 450).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Iron Age III (Jordan, 585 BC–538 BC).label: Iron Age III
Iron Age III (Jordan, 585 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Petra, 585 BC–538 BC] Iron Age III. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Lydia rose to dominate western Anatolia from Sardis, striking some of the world's first coins and drawing wealth from the Pactolus river, while Phrygia declined after Cimmerian raids. In the east, Urartu was worn down and the Assyrian empire fell, leaving Medes and Babylonians to divide the spoils. The era closed abruptly when Cyrus the Great took Sardis and made Anatolia Persian.
Iron Age III (Jordan, 585 BC–538 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Iron Age I (Jordan, 1199 BC–999 BC).label: Iron Age I
Iron Age I (Jordan, 1199 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Petra, 1199 BC–999 BC] Iron Age I. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The Hittite empire disappeared and Anatolia fragmented into small, often illiterate societies, with monumental hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions kept alive only by the Neo-Hittite successor states of the south-east. Phrygians moved into the central plateau and settlement clustered on defensible mounds, while in the east the tribal groups later unified as Urartu began to coalesce. From this fractured landscape came the kingdoms - Phrygia, Urartu, Lydia and the Syro-Hittite city-states - that dominated the following centuries.
Iron Age I (Jordan, 1199 BC–999 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Chalcolithic (Jordan, 5499 BC–4299 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Jordan, 5499 BC–4299 BC).prose:
[Petra, 5499 BC–4299 BC] Chalcolithic. (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.
Chalcolithic (Jordan, 5499 BC–4299 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Kingdom of Edom (Jordan, 999 BC–538 BC).label: Kingdom of Edom
Kingdom of Edom (Jordan, 999 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Petra, 999 BC–538 BC] Kingdom of Edom. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

A kingdom of herders, traders and copper workers in the arid highlands and Wadi Arabah south of the Dead Sea, with its centre at Bozrah and huge smelting operations at Khirbat en-Nahas and Faynan. It controlled caravan routes to Arabia and fought repeatedly with Judah, which the Hebrew Bible remembers bitterly. Assyrian tribute lists record its kings; after Babylon crushed Judah, Edomites moved west into the Negev, the region that became Idumaea.
Kingdom of Edom (Jordan, 999 BC–538 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

late prehistory (Jordan, 6349 BC–2499 BC.prose:
[Petra, 6349 BC–2499 BC] late prehistory. (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After the collapse of the great early farming villages, people spread into smaller hamlets, adopted pottery, and turned increasingly to sheep, goats and orchard crops. Copper working began in earnest, with the extraordinary metalwork and painted shrines of the Chalcolithic at sites like Teleilat Ghassul. By the end of the span, walled towns with public buildings had appeared, the first urban experiment in the region.
late prehistory (Jordan, 6349 BC–2499 BC.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Late Bronze Age (Jordan, 1549 BC–1199 BC.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Jordan, 1549 BC–1199 BC.prose:
[Petra, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Jordan, 1549 BC–1199 BC.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Under the Cairo sultanate this region became a well-run frontier province, its roads carrying the barid postal relay that linked Egypt to Damascus and its valleys filled with irrigated sugar plantations and refineries. Karak and other castles were rebuilt as administrative centres, and villages grew around the pilgrimage and trade routes. The whole system passed to the Ottomans in 1516.
Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516) [p072r4.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.
Hellenistic (Jordan, 299 BC–49 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1800).label: Islamic
Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1800).prose:
[Petra, AD 650–AD 1800] Islamic. Arab armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and over the following centuries its towns were reshaped by mosques, congregational plans and new trade routes running to Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo. Umayyad rulers built desert palaces and bath-houses here decorated with startling frescoes and mosaics; later the land passed through Crusader castles, Mamluk garrisons and finally Ottoman provincial administration and the pilgrimage road to Mecca. Village and nomadic life continued beneath these changes of regime, visible archaeologically in pottery, sugar mills and irrigation works.
Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1800).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Nabatean Kingdom (Jordan, 167 BC–AD 106).label: Nabatean Kingdom
Nabatean Kingdom (Jordan, 167 BC–AD 106).prose:
[Petra, 167 BC–AD 106] Nabatean Kingdom. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

From Petra, hidden in the sandstone canyons of southern Jordan, a dynasty of Arab traders controlled the incense route north from Arabia. They mastered desert hydrology, cutting cisterns and channels that let cities flourish where rainfall could not support them, and carved monumental facades blending Hellenistic columns with local design. Trajan annexed the kingdom peacefully as the province of Arabia Petraea.
Nabatean Kingdom (Jordan, 167 BC–AD 106).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918) [p072r.label: Ottoman
Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918) [p072r.prose:
[Petra, AD 1516–AD 1918] Ottoman. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.
Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918) [p072r.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Umayyad-Abbasid (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969).label: Umayyad-Abbasid
Umayyad-Abbasid (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969).prose:
[Petra, AD 630–AD 969] Umayyad-Abbasid. Arab-Muslim armies took the region from Byzantium after the battle of Yarmuk, and under the Umayyads of Damascus it sat at the heart of the caliphate rather than on its edge - the era of the desert palaces at Qusayr Amra and Qasr al-Mshatta, with their frescoes and carved stone facades. Arabic replaced Greek in administration and the gold dinar replaced Byzantine coin. When the Abbasids moved the capital to Iraq in 750, the area became a provincial backwater, and a series of earthquakes finished off several of its Roman-era cities.
Umayyad-Abbasid (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Following Alexander's conquest, the region fell under Ptolemaic and then Seleucid rule, with Greek-style cities, coinage and administration layered over older Transjordanian communities. The Nabataeans of Petra were meanwhile building wealth from the incense trade. Greek architectural forms, imported amphorae and new fortified estates mark the change on the ground.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171) [p072r4.prose:

Cairo's Shi'i caliphs held the Jordanian lands as a frontier zone of their Syrian province, valuable for the pilgrimage and caravan routes running down the desert edge. Bedouin power and Seljuk pressure eroded that control, and the arrival of the Crusaders left the region divided between Frankish castles and Muslim rulers.
Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171) [p072r4.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Early Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1000).label: Early Islamic
Early Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1000).prose:
[Petra, AD 650–AD 1000] Early Islamic. Arab armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and under the Umayyads it lay close to the heart of the new empire, dotted with the rural palaces and bath-houses known as the desert castles. Village life, churches and mosaic workshops carried on with surprising continuity, though the devastating earthquake of AD 749 wrecked many towns. When the Abbasids moved the capital to Iraq, the area slipped from imperial centre to provincial backwater.
Early Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1000).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Middle Islamic (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1400).label: Middle Islamic
Middle Islamic (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1400).prose:
[Petra, AD 1000–AD 1400] Middle Islamic. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Jordan sat between Crusader lordships, Ayyubid armies and finally the Mamluk sultanate, whose castles, sugar mills and postal routes reshaped the countryside. Karak and Shobak changed hands amid the wars of Saladin and his successors, and villages prospered on sugar cane, pottery and the pilgrimage road to Mecca. Handmade geometric-painted wares are the characteristic find of the period.
Middle Islamic (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1400).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Late Roman (Jordan, AD 250–AD 450).label: Late Roman
Late Roman (Jordan, AD 250–AD 450).prose:
[Petra, AD 250–AD 450] Late Roman. Derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is unclear.
