"Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.
Late Roman (Jordan, AD 250–AD 450).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Iron Age IIb-c (Jordan, 899 BC–585 BC).label: Iron Age IIb-c
Iron Age IIb-c (Jordan, 899 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Petra, 899 BC–585 BC] Iron Age IIb-c. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Ammon, Moab and Edom reached their peak as Assyrian vassals, paying tribute in exchange for a share of the caravan trade in incense and spices; their kings appear by name on Assyrian monuments. Ammonite palaces, distinctive stone statuary and inscribed seals date from these centuries. Babylonian campaigns after Assyria's fall brought the kingdoms to an end.
Iron Age IIb-c (Jordan, 899 BC–585 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Early Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–2499 B.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–2499 B.prose:
[Petra, 4299 BC–2499 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–2499 B.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Middle Bronze Age (Jordan, 2499 BC–1549.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Jordan, 2499 BC–1549.prose:
[Petra, 2499 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Jordan, 2499 BC–1549.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Byzantine (Jordan, AD 450–AD 650).label: Byzantine
Byzantine (Jordan, AD 450–AD 650).prose:
[Petra, AD 450–AD 650] Byzantine. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.
Byzantine (Jordan, AD 450–AD 650).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–1199 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[Petra, 4299 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Start date is derived from that of the Early Bronze Age, which is in turn derived from  page xvi with "slight adaptations to reflect the specific situation in southern Jordan" (page 627). End date is derived from that of the Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–1199 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Middle Roman (Jordan, AD 100–AD 250).label: Middle Roman
Middle Roman (Jordan, AD 100–AD 250).prose:
[Petra, AD 100–AD 250] Middle Roman. Derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is unclear.

"Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Following Rome's annexation of the Nabataean kingdom, the new province of Arabia was tied together by the Via Nova Traiana running from the Red Sea to Syria. Cities such as Gerasa, Philadelphia and Bostra rebuilt themselves with colonnaded streets, theatres and temples, and garrisons secured the desert edge. It was the most prosperous and heavily built-up phase in the region's ancient history.
Middle Roman (Jordan, AD 100–AD 250).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Early Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 100).label: Early Roman
Early Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 100).prose:
[Petra, 49 BC–AD 100] Early Roman. Derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is unclear.

"Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The Claudian invasion turned southern Britain into a province: legions pushed north and west, client kings were absorbed, and the revolt of Boudica was crushed. Towns with forums, baths and grid streets appeared where none had existed, roads linked new civitas capitals, and villas began to dot the countryside. By the end of the period the frontier had settled at Hadrian's Wall.
Early Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 100).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Late Hellenistic (Jordan, 199 BC–49 BC).label: Late Hellenistic
Late Hellenistic (Jordan, 199 BC–49 BC).prose:
[Petra, 199 BC–49 BC] Late Hellenistic. Derived from Erickson-Gini 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Seleucid armies took the region from the Ptolemies at the start of this stretch, but imperial control soon frayed: Hasmonean rulers pushed east of the Jordan, the Greek-styled cities that would become the Decapolis asserted themselves, and the Nabataeans of Petra grew rich taxing incense and spice caravans. Greek language, coinage and civic architecture spread widely while local Semitic culture persisted underneath. The period closes as Rome moves into Syria and begins rearranging the whole region.
Late Hellenistic (Jordan, 199 BC–49 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Late Islamic (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1800).label: Late Islamic
Late Islamic (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1800).prose:
[Petra, AD 1400–AD 1800] Late Islamic. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Mamluk administration gave way to Ottoman rule, and much of the countryside shifted from villages to a more mobile, tribally organised way of life based on herding and seasonal cultivation. State attention concentrated on the pilgrimage road to Mecca, guarded by a chain of forts with cisterns where caravans watered. Handmade painted pottery and clay tobacco pipes are the period's most common archaeological markers.
Late Islamic (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1800).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263) [p072r.label: Ayyubid
Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263) [p072r.prose:
[Petra, AD 1171–AD 1263] Ayyubid. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Saladin's Kurdish dynasty ruled Egypt, Syria and the lands east of the Jordan, and his defeat of the crusaders at Hattin in 1187 brought Jerusalem back under Muslim rule. In Transjordan the period left striking military architecture, above all the castle of Ajlun, built to watch the crusader lords and guard the iron mines and communications with Damascus. Family infighting weakened the realm until Mamluk soldiers seized Egypt and the Mongols swept through Syria.
Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263) [p072r.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Iron Age II (Jordan, 999 BC–499 BC).label: Iron Age II
Iron Age II (Jordan, 999 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Petra, 999 BC–499 BC] Iron Age II. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Greek settlers pushed out from Syracuse and Naxos to found a chain of colonies around the coast, while Phoenicians held the western tip at Motya and Panormus. The indigenous Sikels, Sikanians and Elymians adopted Greek pottery, building styles and writing even as they lost land, and Sikel resistance culminated in Ducetius' short-lived confederation. Sicily's grain, its tyrants and its rivalry with Carthage made the island a major player in the wider Mediterranean world.
Iron Age II (Jordan, 999 BC–499 BC).source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

Incrustation Style (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC).label: Incrustation Style
Incrustation Style (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC).prose:
[Pompeii, 199 BC–89 BC] Incrustation Style. "The Tufa Period coincides throughout with the time of the first style of decoration." (page 41). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

The first of the Pompeian wall-painting styles, in which plaster was moulded and painted to imitate blocks of coloured marble veneer - a cheap way of giving an ordinary house the look of a Hellenistic palace. It marks the point at which Greek luxury tastes reached Italian domestic architecture on a large scale. Later styles abandoned the illusion of masonry for painted architecture and figured scenes.
Incrustation Style (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

Architectural Style (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC).label: Architectural Style
Architectural Style (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC).prose:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–26 BC] Architectural Style. "The wall decoration of the fourth period is of the second Pompeian style, which came into vogue just after the founding of the colony, and which we shall call the Architectural Style." (page 42)

"The Architectural Style, already mentioned, remained in vogue to the time of Augustus." (page 43). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

Roman wall painters stopped imitating masonry and began dissolving walls altogether, framing rooms with painted columns, coffered ceilings, shrines and vistas onto imaginary buildings and gardens. This 'Second Style', best seen at Pompeii, Boscoreale and the Villa of Livia, is the first sustained European experiment in illusionistic perspective. Wealthy Romans used it to turn modest rooms into stage sets of aristocratic Hellenistic luxury.
Architectural Style (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

Intricate Style (Italy, AD 50–AD 79).label: Intricate Style
Intricate Style (Italy, AD 50–AD 79).prose:
[Pompeii, AD 50–AD 79] Intricate Style. "The fourth or Intricate Style came in about the year 50 A.D." (page 43). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

The last of the four Pompeian wall-painting styles, buried mid-development by the eruption of Vesuvius. Painters abandoned the sober architectural illusionism of earlier decades for crowded fantasy: impossible slender colonnades, theatrical stage-fronts, delicate ornamental panels and framed mythological pictures set like hung paintings. Its ornate, layered compositions survive in the House of the Vettii and the rebuilt houses of the post-earthquake years, giving an unusually precise snapshot of Roman taste in a single generation.
Intricate Style (Italy, AD 50–AD 79).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

The third period (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC).label: The third period
The third period (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC).prose: [Pompeii, 199 BC–89 BC] The third period. "Certain Oscan inscriptions, an early Latin monumental inscription, and a few words, dating from 78 B.C., scratched upon the plaster of the Basilica, oblige us to place the Tufa Period before the time of the Roman colony; yet not long before, for the next oldest buildings date from the first years of the colony. The time of peace that furnished the background for the period can only have been that between the Second Punic War and the Social War, about 200 to 90 B.C.; the Tufa Period was approximately the second century before Christ." (page 40). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.
The third period (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

The sixth period (Italy, AD 63–AD 79).label: The sixth period
The sixth period (Italy, AD 63–AD 79).prose: [Pompeii, AD 63–AD 79] The sixth period. "The sixteen years between the earthquake of 63 A.D. and the destruction of the city form the sixth period in the architectural history of Pompeii." (page 44). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.
The sixth period (Italy, AD 63–AD 79).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

Ornate Style (Italy, 26 BC–AD 50).label: Ornate Style
Ornate Style (Italy, 26 BC–AD 50).prose:
[Pompeii, 26 BC–AD 50] Ornate Style. "The Architectural Style, already mentioned, remained in vogue to the time of Augustus; it then gave place to the third or Ornate Style." (page 43). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

Roman wall painters abandoned illusionistic architecture for flat panels of deep red, black, and gold, framed by impossibly slender columns and candelabra, with tiny landscapes or mythological scenes floating at the centre. Egyptian motifs and delicate ornament reflect Augustan taste and the recent conquest of Egypt. Villas around the Bay of Naples preserve the best surviving examples.
Ornate Style (Italy, 26 BC–AD 50).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

The fourth period (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC).label: The fourth period
The fourth period (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC).prose: [Pompeii, 79 BC–26 BC] The fourth period. "The fourth period covers the earlier decades of the Roman colony, from 80 B.C. to near the end of the Republic." (page 41). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.
The fourth period (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC).source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

Plague of Provence (France, AD 1720–AD 1.label: Plague of Provence
Plague of Provence (France, AD 1720–AD 1.prose:
[Continental Europe, AD 1720–AD 1722] Plague of Provence. Period definition from Putting Africa on the Black Death map: Narratives from genetics and history — Monica H. Green, 2018-12-24.

Plague came ashore at Marseille in 1720 aboard a merchant ship from the Levant whose quarantine was cut short for commercial reasons, and it killed roughly half the city's people before spreading through Provence. Authorities sealed off the region with troops and a drystone barrier, the mur de la peste, parts of which still stand. It was the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in western Europe and a landmark case in the history of quarantine.
Plague of Provence (France, AD 1720–AD 1.source: Putting Africa on the Black Death map: Narratives from genetics and history

Great Plague of Marseille (France, AD 17.label: Great Plague of Marseille
Great Plague of Marseille (France, AD 17.prose:
[Provence (France), AD 1720–AD 1722] Great Plague of Marseille. Source describes period as "one of the last well-documented European epidemics, the Great Plague of Marseille (1720–1722), that occurred in the Provence region of France at the end of the second pandemic.". Period definition from Eighteenth century Yersinia pestis genomes reveal the long-term persistence of an historical plague focus — Stephen A Forrest, 2016-01-21.

Plague came ashore with the merchant ship Grand-Saint-Antoine from the Levant, and quarantine rules bent for the sake of a valuable cargo of silk and cotton. Around half the city's population died, and the epidemic spread through Provence despite a stone plague wall built across the countryside to contain it. It was the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in western Europe, and it hardened maritime quarantine practice for the next century.
Great Plague of Marseille (France, AD 17.source: Eighteenth century Yersinia pestis genomes reveal the long-term persistence of an historical plague focus

Fifth Syrian War (Syria, 201 BC–199 BC).label: Fifth Syrian War
Fifth Syrian War (Syria, 201 BC–199 BC).prose:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 201 BC–199 BC] Fifth Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus III of the Seleucids exploited the accession of the child king Ptolemy V to attack Egypt's possessions in Palestine and Phoenicia. His victory at Panium near the sources of the Jordan broke the Ptolemaic field army and transferred Coele-Syria and Judaea to Seleucid rule for the first time. Jerusalem's new masters granted the Temple privileges, but the shift set up the tensions that erupted a generation later in the Maccabean revolt.
Fifth Syrian War (Syria, 201 BC–199 BC).source: The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire

Fourth Syrian War (Syria, 218 BC–216 BC).label: Fourth Syrian War
Fourth Syrian War (Syria, 218 BC–216 BC).prose:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 218 BC–216 BC] Fourth Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus III of the Seleucids drove south to seize Coele-Syria and Phoenicia from Ptolemaic Egypt, and was stopped at Raphia in 217 BC by an Egyptian army stiffened with tens of thousands of native Egyptian troops. The victory saved Ptolemaic Syria for a generation, but arming and training Egyptians fed decades of revolt in the Nile valley. Antiochus returned twenty years later and took the province for good.
Fourth Syrian War (Syria, 218 BC–216 BC).source: The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire

Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era (Yemen, 310 B.label: Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era
Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era (Yemen, 310 B.prose:
[Yemen, 310 BC–AD 2015] Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era. Derived from discussion on page 101: "To this day the Yemeni Jewish community dates its documents and activities according to Seleucus I's return to Babylon after the battle of Gaza [311 BCE, 1 SE]....". Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

The Seleucid year-count, known to Jews as the 'era of contracts', began with Seleucus I's seizure of Babylon and became the standard dating system across the Near East. Most Jewish communities abandoned it in the Middle Ages for the count from Creation, but the Jews of Yemen kept using it in deeds, marriage contracts and colophons into the twentieth century. It is the longest continuously used era in recorded history.
Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era (Yemen, 310 B.source: The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire

Third Syrian War (Syria, 245 BC–240 BC).label: Third Syrian War
Third Syrian War (Syria, 245 BC–240 BC).prose:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 245 BC–240 BC] Third Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Ptolemy III of Egypt invaded Seleucid territory after his sister, married to the Seleucid king, was murdered along with her infant son in a succession struggle. Egyptian forces marched deep into Mesopotamia and briefly took Antioch and Seleucia, and Ptolemy returned with plunder that included cult statues carried off from Persia centuries earlier. Egypt kept the port of Seleucia Pieria and coastal gains, leaving the Seleucid realm weakened on its western flank.
Third Syrian War (Syria, 245 BC–240 BC).source: The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire

Sixth Syrian War (Syria, 169 BC–167 BC).label: Sixth Syrian War
Sixth Syrian War (Syria, 169 BC–167 BC).prose:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 169 BC–167 BC] Sixth Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus IV of Syria invaded Ptolemaic Egypt, captured the young king Ptolemy VI and stood at the gates of Alexandria before a single Roman envoy, Popillius Laenas, drew a circle in the sand and ordered him to withdraw. He did — a humiliation that marked Rome as the real arbiter of the eastern Mediterranean. Antiochus turned his energies on Judaea instead, and his measures against the Jerusalem Temple touched off the Maccabean revolt.
Sixth Syrian War (Syria, 169 BC–167 BC).source: The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire

Second Syrian War (Syria, 259 BC–252 BC).label: Second Syrian War
Second Syrian War (Syria, 259 BC–252 BC).prose:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 259 BC–252 BC] Second Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus II and Ptolemy II fought over the coast of Syria, Asia Minor and the Aegean islands, with cities changing hands and Rhodes and Macedon drawn in. It ended in a diplomatic bargain: Antiochus set aside his wife Laodice to marry Ptolemy's daughter Berenice, a match whose collapse would trigger the next war. The struggle shows how the Hellenistic kingdoms treated dynastic marriage as an instrument of war.
Second Syrian War (Syria, 259 BC–252 BC).source: The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire

III Fase (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79).label: III Fase
III Fase (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79).prose:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–AD 79] III Fase. "III Fase - Età romana dalla fondazione della colonia sillana (80 a.C.) alla distruzione della città (79 d.C.)" (page 88)
"Per primo il Fiorelli comprese la necessità di una divisione storica della edilizia pompeiana, e propose questa prima classificazione." (page 88). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.
III Fase (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79).source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

5° periodo (Italy, 26 BC–AD 63).label: 5° periodo
5° periodo (Italy, 26 BC–AD 63).prose:
[Pompeii, 26 BC–AD 63] 5° periodo. "...più completo il Mau che suddivise l'edilizia pompeiana in fasi principali." (pages 88-89) "Dal 27 a.C. al terremoto del 63 d.C. Caratteristica la tecnica del reticolato. È il periodo coevo del II e III e dell'inizio del IV stile della pittura parietale." (page 89). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The Augustan and Julio-Claudian phase at Pompeii, when imperial patronage reshaped the town: a new aqueduct brought running water to street fountains and private houses, the forum was rebuilt in marble, and a temple to the imperial cult appeared. Painted decoration shifted to the delicate 'Third Style', and bakeries, fulleries and shops spread into once-grand houses.
5° periodo (Italy, 26 BC–AD 63).source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

Periodo sannitico secondo (Italy, 299 BC.label: Periodo sannitico secondo
Periodo sannitico secondo (Italy, 299 BC.prose:
[Pompeii, 299 BC–179 BC] Periodo sannitico secondo. "Periodo sannitico secondo" translates to "Second Samnite Period." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Maiuri does not explain the gap between this period and the Third Samnite Period. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The wealthiest phase of Campania's Oscan towns, when trade after Rome's victory over Carthage paid for grand tufa-built houses with atria and peristyles, painted plaster in the 'First Style', temples, theatres and baths. Greek and Hellenistic taste is everywhere in the plans and decoration, even though public inscriptions remained in Oscan.
Periodo sannitico secondo (Italy, 299 BC.source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

Periodo sannitico primo (Italy, 399 BC–2.label: Periodo sannitico primo
Periodo sannitico primo (Italy, 399 BC–2.prose:
[Pompeii, 399 BC–299 BC] Periodo sannitico primo. "Periodo sannitico primo" translates to "First Samnite Period." "Periodo paleosannitica" translates to "Paleo-Samnite Period." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

Oscan-speaking Samnite communities dominated inland and coastal Campania, and towns such as Pompeii took on their first real urban shape – a defensive circuit, a street grid and the earliest public buildings in local limestone. It was also the era of the Samnite wars with Rome, which slowly drew these cities into the Roman alliance system.
Periodo sannitico primo (Italy, 399 BC–2.source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

Periodo sannitico terzo (Italy, 119 BC–8.prose:

The last decades of Oscan self-government, ending in the Social War when the allied Italian cities rose against Rome and Sulla besieged and stormed Pompeii. Defeat brought Roman citizenship, a colony of veterans, and the rapid replacement of Oscan by Latin in public life.
Periodo sannitico terzo (Italy, 119 BC–8.source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

Epoca romana (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79).label: Epoca romana
Epoca romana (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79).prose:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–AD 79] Epoca romana. "Epoca romana" translates to "Roman era." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

A century that carried Italy from the wreckage of Sulla's dictatorship through the civil wars of Caesar, Pompey, Antony and Octavian into the peace and monumental building of the early emperors. Rome became a city of marble, concrete vaults and a million inhabitants, fed by grain fleets and supplied by aqueducts. The period ends with the eruption of Vesuvius, which buried Pompeii and Herculaneum and preserved for us the ordinary streets, shops and painted rooms of Roman life.
Epoca romana (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79).source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

6° periodo (Italy, AD 63–AD 79).prose:
[Pompeii, AD 63–AD 79] 6° periodo. "...più completo il Mau che suddivise l'edilizia pompeiana in fasi principali." (pages 88-89) 
"Sono gli ultimi 16 anni della città compresi fra due disastri, quello tellurico del 63 e la tremenda eruzione vesuviana del 79: ultime fase del IV stile." (page 90). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The last sixteen years of Pompeii, between the earthquake that wrecked the town in AD 62/63 and the eruption that buried it. Much of the city was a building site — temples propped up, houses subdivided, the water system still broken — which is why so many rooms preserve fresh 'Fourth Style' paintings, stacked materials and unfinished repairs at the moment of destruction.
6° periodo (Italy, AD 63–AD 79).source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

Pompeii's late Republican phase, after Sulla planted a colony of Roman veterans on a town that had backed the losing side. Latin replaced Oscan in public inscriptions, the amphitheatre and covered theatre went up, and wealthy incomers built the large atrium houses whose walls carry the illusionistic 'Second Style' frescoes.
4° periodo (Italy, 79 BC–27 BC).source: Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49

Talmudic Period (Egypt, AD 70–AD 640).label: Talmudic Period
Talmudic Period (Egypt, AD 70–AD 640).prose:
[Egypt, Libya, Judea, Palestine, several other places, AD 70–AD 640] Talmudic Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Libya, State of Palestine. “This article presents a narrative history of the Jews between the destruction of the Second Temple (70 ce) and the Arab conquest of Palestine (c.640 CE). After the destruction, Palestine was made into a standard Roman province in a way which at least curtailed the Jews' traditional autonomy. Nevertheless, the Jews rebelled again, with disastrous results. The Diaspora Revolt (115–17 CE) seems to have ended in the decimation or destruction of the Jewish settlements in Egypt, Libya, and several other places, while the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132–5) brought an end to the Jews' hopes for the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple and, more tangibly, to Jewish settlement in the district of Judaea. The historiography of the past sixty years on the Jews in the ‘Talmud period’ can be divided into two very broad tendencies, which may be designated Israeli and non-Israeli" (Abstract). Period definition from Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE) — Seth Schwartz, 2004.

Framed by the destruction of the Second Temple and the Arab conquest, these centuries saw Judaism reinvent itself around rabbis, synagogues and study rather than sacrifice, producing the Mishnah and then the Talmuds. Egypt's once-vast Jewish community, centred on Alexandria, had been shattered by the revolt of 115-117 and rebuilt slowly under Roman and Byzantine rule. The same span covers the rise of Egyptian Christianity and the flight of a religious minority to the margins of an increasingly Christian empire.
Talmudic Period (Egypt, AD 70–AD 640).source: Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE)

Diaspora Revolt (Egypt, AD 115–AD 117).label: Diaspora Revolt
Diaspora Revolt (Egypt, AD 115–AD 117).prose:
[Egypt, Libya, Judea, Palestine, several other places, AD 115–AD 117] Diaspora Revolt. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Libya, State of Palestine. “This article presents a narrative history of the Jews between the destruction of the Second Temple (70 ce) and the Arab conquest of Palestine (c.640 CE). After the destruction, Palestine was made into a standard Roman province in a way which at least curtailed the Jews' traditional autonomy. Nevertheless, the Jews rebelled again, with disastrous results. The Diaspora Revolt (115–17 CE) seems to have ended in the decimation or destruction of the Jewish settlements in Egypt, Libya, and several other places, while the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132–5) brought an end to the Jews' hopes for the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple and, more tangibly, to Jewish settlement in the district of Judaea. The historiography of the past sixty years on the Jews in the ‘Talmud period’ can be divided into two very broad tendencies, which may be designated Israeli and non-Israeli" (Abstract). Period definition from Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE) — Seth Schwartz, 2004.

While Trajan campaigned against Parthia, Jewish communities rose in Cyrenaica, Cyprus, Mesopotamia and Egypt in a bitter war marked by massacres on both sides. Fighting reached the Egyptian countryside and Alexandria, where the great Jewish population that had produced Philo and the Greek Bible was effectively destroyed. Papyri record ruined estates and a commemorative 'day of victory' still observed decades later; Egyptian Jewry did not recover for centuries.
Diaspora Revolt (Egypt, AD 115–AD 117).source: Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE)

The northern Syrian coast, long after the Bronze Age city of Ugarit had been abandoned, was drawn into Roman Syria following Pompey's annexation. Activity in the area centred on the nearby harbour and rural settlement rather than the old tell, which saw only scattered later use.

Nabatean period (Jordan, 311 BC–AD 106).label: Nabatean period
Nabatean period (Jordan, 311 BC–AD 106).prose:
[Petra, 311 BC–AD 106] Nabatean period. "The Nabatean period extends from the earliest reference to the Nabateans in 312 B.C. by Diodorus Siculus to the Roman annexation in A.D. 106." (page 16). Period definition from Petra Great Temple. Volume III, Brown University excavations 1993-2008 : architecture and material culture — 2017.

Beginning as nomadic herders and caravaneers who repelled a Greek attack on their desert stronghold, the Nabataeans became settled city-builders with Petra at their centre. Their engineers dammed flash floods and piped water for miles; their masons cut temple facades directly into cliff faces. Wealth from the incense trade sustained them until Roman annexation folded the kingdom into the empire.
Nabatean period (Jordan, 311 BC–AD 106).source: Petra Great Temple. Volume III, Brown University excavations 1993-2008 : architecture and material culture

Geometrische Zeit (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC.label: Geometrische Zeit
Geometrische Zeit (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC.prose:
[Griechenland, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometrische Zeit. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The period when Greek craftsmen filled their vases with ruled bands, meanders and compass circles, later adding stick-like figures in funeral processions and sea battles. Populations grew, iron replaced bronze for tools, communal sanctuaries appeared, and writing returned with an alphabet adapted from Phoenician. By its end Greeks were founding cities overseas and the city-state had taken shape.

frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).label: frühgeometrisch
frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 899 BC–849 BC] frühgeometrisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Athenian potters imposed a strict new order on their vases — bands of meanders, concentric circles and zigzags covering black-glazed surfaces — in the first coherent Greek art style after the collapse of the Mycenaean world. Populations were growing again, iron working was routine, and cremation burials with modest metal goods hint at families asserting rank. The Lefkandi hero-burial shows how much wealth and long-distance contact could still be commanded.

mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC.label: mittelgeometrisch
mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC.prose:
[Griechenland, 849 BC–759 BC] mittelgeometrisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Athenian potters tightened the geometric repertoire inherited from the previous century, filling vases with meanders, zigzags and the first tentative silhouette animals. Behind the pottery lies a society climbing out of the post-Mycenaean slump: population growing, metalwork and burial goods richer, contacts with Cyprus and the Levant resuming. The stage is being set for the huge grave-marker amphorae and figured scenes of the Late Geometric, and for the eighth-century surge of colonisation and writing.

spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).label: spätgeometrisch
spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 759 BC–699 BC] spätgeometrisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Painters filled Athenian grave vases with meanders, chariot processions and rows of mourners – the first narrative scenes in Greek art after centuries of abstraction. Population and settlement grew sharply, sanctuaries filled with dedications, the alphabet was adopted from Phoenician traders, and Greeks began founding colonies in Italy and Sicily as the polis took shape.

früharchaisch (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC).label: früharchaisch
früharchaisch (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 699 BC–619 BC] früharchaisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Greek communities emerged from centuries of isolation to trade and settle across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, absorbing Near Eastern art, myth and technology in the process. The alphabet was put to work on Homer and on the first written laws; the first monumental stone temples and life-size statues appeared; and the citizen militia of massed hoplites began to reshape who held power in the polis.

mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).label: mittelarchaisch
mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 619 BC–559 BC] mittelarchaisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Athens and Corinth turned out black-figure vases traded across the Mediterranean, sculptors carved the first life-size marble kouroi and korai, and cities replaced timber shrines with stone temples. Tyrants seized power in many poleis, while Solon's reforms reshaped Athenian law and citizenship. Colonies planted from the Black Sea to Spain spread Greek language, coinage and the alphabet.

Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC).label: Hochklassik
Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 449 BC–429 BC] Hochklassik. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The high point of Athenian art and confidence, funded by tribute from the Delian League under Pericles: the Parthenon and the Propylaia rose on the Acropolis, Phidias made his colossal cult statues, and Polykleitos worked out the canon of ideal bodily proportion. Sculpture achieved the balanced, idealised naturalism that later ages took as the definition of classical beauty. It ended with the outbreak of war with Sparta and the plague that killed Pericles himself.

Reicher Stil (Greece, 429 BC–399 BC).label: Reicher Stil
Reicher Stil (Greece, 429 BC–399 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 429 BC–399 BC] Reicher Stil. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The 'Rich Style' of late fifth-century Greek sculpture, in which drapery becomes an end in itself — clinging, transparent, breaking into deep swirling folds that reveal the body beneath. The Nike balustrade on the Athenian Acropolis is its showpiece, along with a wave of elegant grave stelai and small-scale reliefs. Emerging as Athens fought and lost the Peloponnesian War, it turns away from the calm authority of the Parthenon towards elaborate surface and emotional grace.

hochhellenistisch (Greece, 229 BC–149 BC.label: hochhellenistisch
hochhellenistisch (Greece, 229 BC–149 BC.prose:
[Griechenland, 229 BC–149 BC] hochhellenistisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The mature phase of the Hellenistic world, when the Antigonid, Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms and the Achaean and Aetolian leagues fought each other into exhaustion while Rome, drawn in as an ally, steadily became the arbiter of Greek affairs. Sculpture and architecture reached their most theatrical, emotionally charged form, seen in works like the Great Altar of Pergamon. The sequence of Macedonian wars ended with the sack of Corinth and the reduction of Greece to Roman control.

späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC).label: späthellenistisch
späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC).prose:
[Griechenland, 149 BC–29 BC] späthellenistisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Roman power closed over the Greek world: Corinth was destroyed in 146 BC, Athens was sacked by Sulla, and Mithridates' wars ravaged Asia Minor and the Aegean. Kings and cities became clients or provinces, artists and philosophers migrated to Rome, and the last independent Hellenistic kingdom ended with Cleopatra's defeat at Actium.

Früheisenzeit (Rome, 999 BC–619 BC).label: Früheisenzeit
Früheisenzeit (Rome, 999 BC–619 BC).prose:
[Rom, 999 BC–619 BC] Früheisenzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Iron working spread through the Italian peninsula while communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in hut-shaped urns. Villanovan villages in Etruria and Latial hut settlements on the hills above the Tiber grew, merged and hardened into towns, and imported Greek and Phoenician goods appear in increasingly rich graves. Out of this came the Etruscan city-states and the small settlement that Romans later remembered as the founding of their city.

Archaische Zeit (Rome, 619 BC–508 BC).label: Archaische Zeit
Archaische Zeit (Rome, 619 BC–508 BC).prose: [Rom, 619 BC–508 BC] Archaische Zeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Republikanische Zeit (Rome, 508 BC–30 BC.label: Republikanische Zeit
Republikanische Zeit (Rome, 508 BC–30 BC.prose:
[Rom, 508 BC–30 BC] Republikanische Zeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

After the expulsion of the kings, Rome was governed by annually elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and assemblies of citizens, a system built as much on custom as on law. In under five centuries the city went from one player among many in central Italy to master of the Mediterranean, absorbing Carthage, Greece and much of Gaul and the Near East. The wealth and armies that conquest produced eventually broke the system itself, in a century of civil war that ended with Augustus.

frührepublikanisch (Rome, 508 BC–366 BC).label: frührepublikanisch
frührepublikanisch (Rome, 508 BC–366 BC).prose:
[Rom, 508 BC–366 BC] frührepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

After driving out its kings, Rome spent a century and a half as one middling Latin city among many, fighting neighbours in the hills while plebeians wrung concessions from the patrician aristocracy. The Twelve Tables put law in public writing, the Gauls sacked the city around 390 BC, and the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 finally opened the consulship to plebeians. The institutions improvised in these struggles — consuls, tribunes, the Senate's authority — became the machinery of Mediterranean empire.

mittelrepublikanisch (Rome, 366 BC–201 B.label: mittelrepublikanisch
mittelrepublikanisch (Rome, 366 BC–201 B.prose:
[Rom, 366 BC–201 BC] mittelrepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Rome moved from being one central Italian power among many to master of the western Mediterranean, absorbing the Samnites, Etruscans and Greek cities of the south, then surviving Hannibal. Plebeians won access to the consulship and the senatorial governing class took its classic shape. Conquest brought slaves, silver and provinces, remaking Roman society as thoroughly as it remade the map.

spätrepublikanisch (Rome, 201 BC–30 BC).label: spätrepublikanisch
spätrepublikanisch (Rome, 201 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Rom, 201 BC–30 BC] spätrepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Victory over Carthage and the eastern kingdoms brought Rome enormous wealth, slaves and provinces – and a political system unable to manage them. Land struggles, the murders of the Gracchi, civil wars between Marius and Sulla, and generals with private armies culminated in Caesar's dictatorship and assassination, ending with Octavian's supremacy and the birth of the empire.

Frühe Kaiserzeit (Rome, 30 BC–AD 68).label: Frühe Kaiserzeit
Frühe Kaiserzeit (Rome, 30 BC–AD 68).prose:
[Rom, 30 BC–AD 68] Frühe Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Augustus turned the wreckage of the civil wars into a monarchy dressed as a restored republic, and his successors made the arrangement permanent. Provinces were reorganised, a standing army and professional bureaucracy took shape, and the Mediterranean enjoyed unusually uninterrupted peace and trade. It was also the age of Virgil, Ovid and Livy, of the imperial cult, and of the dynastic scandals under Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero that ended when the last Julio-Claudian killed himself.

Mittlere Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 69–AD 192).label: Mittlere Kaiserzeit
Mittlere Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 69–AD 192).prose:
[Rom, AD 69–AD 192] Mittlere Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Rome's high imperial century and a bit more, running from the chaos of the four emperors of AD 69 through the Flavian dynasty and the so-called Five Good Emperors to the murder of Commodus. The empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan, hardened its frontiers under Hadrian, and spread a shared urban culture of baths, amphitheatres and aqueducts from Britain to Syria - the Colosseum, Pantheon and Trajan's Column all belong here. Citizenship and imperial office opened to provincials, so that emperors themselves came from Spain and North Africa, while trade goods and coinage circulated across an unprecedented single market.

Späte Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 193–AD 306).label: Späte Kaiserzeit
Späte Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 193–AD 306).prose:
[Rom, AD 193–AD 306] Späte Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

From the Severan dynasty to the tetrarchy, the empire lurched through soldier-emperors, currency debasement, plague and simultaneous invasions on the Rhine, Danube and Persian frontiers. Provinces broke away as the Gallic and Palmyrene empires before being reconquered. Diocletian's reforms — a divided command, a swollen bureaucracy and a fixed tax system — rebuilt the state on far more authoritarian lines.

Spätantike (Rome, AD 306–AD 395).label: Spätantike
Spätantike (Rome, AD 306–AD 395).prose:
[Rom, AD 306–AD 395] Spätantike. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. No end date for this period provided in the chronological chart, probably because Hölscher does not provide an explicit end date in his chronological chart. We have provided a value of 0395, following Hölscher, so that the temporal coverage can be visualized. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Constantine's rise ended the tetrarchic experiment, legalised Christianity and founded a new capital on the Bosphorus; by the reign of Theodosius, Christianity was the state religion and the empire was permanently administered as eastern and western halves. Art, coinage and government all took on the hierarchical, ceremonial character we call late Roman, and bishops became figures of political weight.

Gumelnița Culture (Romania, 4199 BC–3699.label: Gumelnița Culture
Gumelnița Culture (Romania, 4199 BC–3699.prose:
[Dobruja, 4199 BC–3699 BC] Gumelnița Culture. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Copper Age farmers who lived on tells built up by generations of rebuilt mud-brick houses, some ringed by ditches and palisades. They made graphite-painted pottery and clay figurines, and their smiths worked copper and gold on a scale unmatched anywhere at the time, linked to the goldwork of the Varna cemetery. Their tells were abandoned in a widespread collapse that ended settled life in the region for centuries.

Hamangia Culture (Romania, 5199 BC–4599.label: Hamangia Culture
Hamangia Culture (Romania, 5199 BC–4599.prose:
[Dobruja, 5199 BC–4599 BC] Hamangia Culture. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Neolithic villages along the western Black Sea coast, sustained by cereals, cattle, fishing and shellfish, and remarkable for their art. Their extensive inhumation cemeteries and their strikingly modern-looking clay figurines, above all the seated Thinker of Cernavodă, are among the best-known finds of Old Europe. The culture eventually merged into the copper-using Gumelnița world that followed.

Boian Culture (Romania, 4499 BC–3999 BC).label: Boian Culture
Boian Culture (Romania, 4499 BC–3999 BC).prose:
[Dobruja, 4499 BC–3999 BC] Boian Culture. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Farming communities of the lower Danube plain and southeastern Romania, living in villages of rectangular houses and burying their dead in flat cemeteries beside the settlements. They are recognised by dark burnished pots incised with meanders and spirals filled with white paste, and by an economy of cereals, cattle and pigs. Their late phases feed directly into the Gumelnița culture, which took copper and gold working much further.

Middle Archaic (Romania, 619 BC–559 BC).label: Middle Archaic
Middle Archaic (Romania, 619 BC–559 BC).prose:
[Dobruja, 619 BC–559 BC] Middle Archaic. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

High Classical (Romania, 449 BC–399 BC).label: High Classical
High Classical (Romania, 449 BC–399 BC).prose:
[Dobruja, 449 BC–399 BC] High Classical. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

The decades after the Persian wars when Athens, funded by its maritime empire, rebuilt the Acropolis and put up the Parthenon under Pheidias's direction. Sophocles and Euripides were writing for the theatre, Socrates was arguing in the agora, and sculptors worked out an idealised human figure that European art would copy for two thousand years. The same era brought the Peloponnesian War, plague, and the collapse of Athenian power in 404.

Late Classical (Romania, 399 BC–322 BC).label: Late Classical
Late Classical (Romania, 399 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Dobruja, 399 BC–322 BC] Late Classical. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

In the Greek cities of the south, this was the era of grand Apulian and Lucanian red-figure vases, tomb painting, and lavish burials, even as Oscan and Lucanian peoples took over cities like Poseidonia. Central Italy saw Etruscan power ebb and Rome fight its way through the Latin and Samnite wars, absorbing neighbours and building the first roads and aqueducts. By the end of the century the peninsula's future belonged to Rome rather than to the Greek or Etruscan cities.

Middle Hellenistic II (Romania, 199 BC–9.label: Middle Hellenistic II
Middle Hellenistic II (Romania, 199 BC–9.prose: [Dobruja, 199 BC–99 BC] Middle Hellenistic II. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Late Roman (Romania, AD 330–AD 641).label: Late Roman
Late Roman (Romania, AD 330–AD 641).prose:
[Dobruja, AD 330–AD 641] Late Roman. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

Ottoman (Romania, AD 1420–AD 1878).label: Ottoman
Ottoman (Romania, AD 1420–AD 1878).prose:
[Dobruja, AD 1420–AD 1878] Ottoman. closeMatch with. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

World War I (Romania, AD 1916–AD 1918).label: World War I
World War I (Romania, AD 1916–AD 1918).prose:
[Dobruja, AD 1916–AD 1918] World War I. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Romania stayed neutral for two years before joining the Allies in August 1916, hoping to win Transylvania from Austria-Hungary. The offensive collapsed within months; German and Bulgarian armies took Bucharest and the government fled to Iasi, holding a rump of Moldavia until Russia's collapse forced a punitive peace in 1918. Romania re-entered the war days before the armistice and emerged doubled in size, gaining Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina to form Greater Romania.

Interwar (Romania, AD 1918–AD 1941).label: Interwar
Interwar (Romania, AD 1918–AD 1941).prose:
[Dobruja, AD 1918–AD 1941] Interwar. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Britain emerged from the Great War victorious, indebted and short of a generation of young men, and spent the following two decades wrestling with mass unemployment, the General Strike, the slump and the slow retreat from the gold standard. It was also the age of the wireless and the cinema, suburban semis and arterial roads, votes for all women in 1928, and the abdication crisis. Rearmament and the failure of appeasement brought it to a close.

World War II (Romania, AD 1941–AD 1945).label: World War II
World War II (Romania, AD 1941–AD 1945).prose:
[Dobruja, AD 1941–AD 1945] World War II. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Romania joined the Axis under Marshal Ion Antonescu and sent large armies east alongside Germany in 1941, recovering Bessarabia and occupying territory beyond the Dniester. Romanian and German forces carried out mass killings of Jews and Roma in Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transnistria, one of the war's largest national contributions to the Holocaust outside Germany itself. After catastrophic losses at Stalingrad and with the Red Army on the frontier, King Michael arrested Antonescu in August 1944 and switched sides, opening the way to Soviet occupation and a communist state.

Post-Communist (Romania, AD 1989–AD 2020.label: Post-Communist
Post-Communist (Romania, AD 1989–AD 2020.prose:
[Dobruja, AD 1989–AD 2020] Post-Communist. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

The violent overthrow and execution of Nicolae Ceaușescu in December 1989 ended one of the harshest regimes in the Eastern bloc and opened a rough transition: privatisation, mass emigration, hyperinflation and the closing of the huge state factories built by communist industrial policy. Institutions were rebuilt to meet Western criteria, bringing NATO membership in 2004 and European Union accession in 2007. Communist-era housing blocks, unfinished megaprojects and the Palace of the Parliament remain the most visible legacy in Romanian cities.

Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III (Greece,.node: Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC)
Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III (Greece,.label: Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III
Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III (Greece,.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 3199 BC–2099 BC] Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from the title of the chronological table on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Farming villages around the Aegean began working bronze, sailing longer routes and accumulating wealth in metal. This is the age of the Cycladic marble figurines, of fortified coastal settlements and of the first monumental buildings in mainland Greece, such as the House of the Tiles at Lerna. Widespread destructions and disruption at the end of the period cleared the way for the palace societies of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.

Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 20.label: Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit
Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 20.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 2099 BC–1699 BC] Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

On Crete the first great palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia - sprawling complexes of storerooms, workshops and courts that ran regional economies and used the still-undeciphered Linear A script. Cretan pottery, frescoes and seafaring reached across the Aegean to Thera and the Cyclades, while the Greek mainland remained comparatively modest until the spectacular shaft graves of Mycenae appear at the period's close. The wealth, bureaucracy and long-distance trade built up here became the foundation of Mycenaean civilisation.

MM / MH I-II (Greece, 2099 BC–1799 BC).label: MM / MH I-II
MM / MH I-II (Greece, 2099 BC–1799 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 2099 BC–1799 BC] MM / MH I-II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Alte Paläste, Kreta. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

On Crete the first great palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, with central courts, vast storage magazines, the Kamares polychrome pottery style and the earliest Cretan writing. The Greek mainland was poorer and simpler, its villages producing grey Minyan ware and burying their dead in modest cist graves. The contrast between palatial Crete and rustic mainland Greece defines the age.

MM / MH III (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 BC).label: MM / MH III
MM / MH III (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1799 BC–1699 BC] MM / MH III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Neue Paläste, Kreta. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The first Cretan palaces were destroyed and immediately rebuilt on a grander scale, opening the brilliant Neopalatial era of frescoes, seal-stones and Linear A administration. On the mainland the first shaft graves at Mycenae appear, packed with gold, weapons and imported goods — the earliest sign of the warrior elites who would later dominate the Aegean.

Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 1699.label: Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit
Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 1699.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1699 BC–1049 BC] Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The age of the Cretan palaces at their height and then of the Mycenaean citadels — Linear B archives, shaft graves, tholos tombs and warrior kings who traded with Egypt and the Levant. Thera's eruption and the fall of Knossos shifted power to the Greek mainland. Around 1200 BC the palace system collapsed everywhere, taking writing and monumental building with it.

SM I A / SH I (Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC).node: SM I A / SH I (Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC)
SM I A / SH I (Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC).label: SM I A / SH I
SM I A / SH I (Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1699 BC–1599 BC] SM I A / SH I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Schachtgräber Mykene, Eruption Thera. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The height of Minoan Crete: rebuilt palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, elegant frescoed towns, and pottery painted with dark spiralling plants on light clay. The eruption of Thera, which buried the town of Akrotiri, falls within these years. On the mainland the first Mycenaean elites announce themselves in the shaft graves of Mycenae, heaped with gold masks, weapons and imported goods.

SM I B / SH II A (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 B.node: SM I B / SH II A (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC)
SM I B / SH II A (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 B.label: SM I B / SH II A
SM I B / SH II A (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 B.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1599 BC–1499 BC] SM I B / SH II A. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Zerstörung der Neuen Paläste". Date range noted as "außer Knossos". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The moment of the Marine Style, with octopuses and argonauts sprawling across Cretan jars, and of intense Aegean contact with Egypt, where Keftiu envoys appear in Theban tomb paintings. It closes with widespread burning and abandonment of Cretan country houses and towns, while on the mainland the Mycenaeans begin building monumental tholos tombs.

SM II / SH II B (Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC.node: SM II / SH II B (Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC)
SM II / SH II B (Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC.label: SM II / SH II B
SM II / SH II B (Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1499 BC–1449 BC] SM II / SH II B. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Knossos alone remains a functioning palace, now run by a mainland-linked elite: Linear B tablets record Greek, warrior graves are furnished with swords and boar's-tusk helmets, and stiff, formal Palace Style jars replace the earlier fluid decoration. The balance of Aegean power has swung from Crete to the mainland.

SM III A1 / SH III A1 (Greece, 1449 BC–1.node: SM III A1 / SH III A1 (Greece, 1449 BC–1399 BC)
SM III A1 / SH III A1 (Greece, 1449 BC–1.label: SM III A1 / SH III A1
SM III A1 / SH III A1 (Greece, 1449 BC–1.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1449 BC–1399 BC] SM III A1 / SH III A1. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Mycenaean Greece consolidates into palace states, with the great citadels and their bureaucracies taking shape and Mycenaean pottery turning up in quantity in Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt. Crete is administered from Knossos in its final palatial phase, and standardised Mycenaean styles spread so widely that regional differences blur across the Aegean.

SM III A2 / SH III A2 (Greece, 1399 BC–1.node: SM III A2 / SH III A2 (Greece, 1399 BC–1349 BC)
SM III A2 / SH III A2 (Greece, 1399 BC–1.label: SM III A2 / SH III A2
SM III A2 / SH III A2 (Greece, 1399 BC–1.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1399 BC–1349 BC] SM III A2 / SH III A2. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Zerstörung u. Wiederaufbau von Knossos. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The high point of Mycenaean power on the mainland, when palace centres like Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns were rebuilt on a grand scale and Knossos on Crete lay under mainland-style control. Standardised Mycenaean pottery was exported the length of the Mediterranean, turning up in Egypt at Amarna, along the Levantine coast and in Italy, and this uniform tableware is what lets archaeologists date sites hundreds of miles apart to the same generation.

SM III B / SH III B (Greece, 1349 BC–119.node: SM III B / SH III B (Greece, 1349 BC–1199 BC)
SM III B / SH III B (Greece, 1349 BC–119.label: SM III B / SH III B
SM III B / SH III B (Greece, 1349 BC–119.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1349 BC–1199 BC] SM III B / SH III B. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "myken. Burgen um 1200 zerstört". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The palace system reached its most bureaucratic form: Linear B tablets recording rations, textiles, chariot wheels and offerings, roads, dams and drained basins, and the massive Cyclopean walls thrown up around the citadels of Mycenae and Tiryns. Those fortifications, and hoarded valuables, hint at rising insecurity. Around 1200 BC nearly every mainland palace burned within a few decades, ending centralised record-keeping in Greece for some four hundred years.

SM III C / SH III C (Greece, 1199 BC–104.node: SM III C / SH III C (Greece, 1199 BC–1049 BC)
SM III C / SH III C (Greece, 1199 BC–104.label: SM III C / SH III C
SM III C / SH III C (Greece, 1199 BC–104.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1199 BC–1049 BC] SM III C / SH III C. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Ende der myken. Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Life after the palaces: no more tablets, no more frescoed throne rooms, but people carried on in smaller, scattered settlements, some perched in defensible spots like Lefkandi, Perati and the Cretan mountain refuges. Potters produced some of the liveliest Mycenaean painting yet, including ships, warriors and the famous octopus jars, while population fell sharply and long-distance trade thinned. The period ends with the shift to Protogeometric styles and the beginning of the Greek Iron Age.

Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche (Greece,.label: Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche
Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche (Greece,.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 1049 BC–999 BC] Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Dark Ages" provided as gloss in English for this period in chart. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The last flicker of Bronze Age Aegean traditions after the palaces at Knossos and on the mainland had fallen: potters still worked in degenerate Minoan and Mycenaean shapes, but writing, monumental building and centralised administration were gone. Communities were small, burial customs shifted toward single graves and cremation, and iron began to appear alongside bronze. Out of this impoverished interval grew the Protogeometric style and the reorganised Greece of the early Iron Age.

Protogeometrische Epoche (Greece, 999 BC.label: Protogeometrische Epoche
Protogeometrische Epoche (Greece, 999 BC.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 999 BC–899 BC] Protogeometrische Epoche. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athenian workshops reinvented vase decoration after the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, using a compass and multiple brush to lay out precise concentric circles and banded zones. Cremation burial became standard in Attica and iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons. The style spread across the Aegean and to the new Greek settlements on the Anatolian coast.

Geometrische Epoche (Greece, 899 BC–699.label: Geometrische Epoche
Geometrische Epoche (Greece, 899 BC–699.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometrische Epoche. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Greek communities rebuilt after the fall of the Mycenaean world, and their pottery — meanders, zigzags, concentric circles, then silhouetted mourners and horses on monumental grave vases — gives the age its name. Sanctuaries at Olympia and Delphi began receiving dedications, the alphabet was borrowed from the Phoenicians, and the first western colonies were founded. The polis and the Homeric epics emerged from this world.

frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).label: frühgeometrisch
frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 899 BC–849 BC] frühgeometrisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athenian potters imposed a strict new order on their vases — bands of meanders, concentric circles and zigzags covering black-glazed surfaces — in the first coherent Greek art style after the collapse of the Mycenaean world. Populations were growing again, iron working was routine, and cremation burials with modest metal goods hint at families asserting rank. The Lefkandi hero-burial shows how much wealth and long-distance contact could still be commanded.

mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC.label: mittelgeometrisch
mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 849 BC–759 BC] mittelgeometrisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athenian potters tightened the geometric repertoire inherited from the previous century, filling vases with meanders, zigzags and the first tentative silhouette animals. Behind the pottery lies a society climbing out of the post-Mycenaean slump: population growing, metalwork and burial goods richer, contacts with Cyprus and the Levant resuming. The stage is being set for the huge grave-marker amphorae and figured scenes of the Late Geometric, and for the eighth-century surge of colonisation and writing.

spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).label: spätgeometrisch
spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 759 BC–699 BC] spätgeometrisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Entstehung der Polis-Kultur, Erste Gründungen von 'Kolonie'-Städten". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Painters filled Athenian grave vases with meanders, chariot processions and rows of mourners – the first narrative scenes in Greek art after centuries of abstraction. Population and settlement grew sharply, sanctuaries filled with dedications, the alphabet was adopted from Phoenician traders, and Greeks began founding colonies in Italy and Sicily as the polis took shape.
