früharchaisch (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC) [p.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 699 BC–619 BC] früharchaisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Greek communities emerged from centuries of isolation to trade and settle across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, absorbing Near Eastern art, myth and technology in the process. The alphabet was put to work on Homer and on the first written laws; the first monumental stone temples and life-size statues appeared; and the citizen militia of massed hoplites began to reshape who held power in the polis.

mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).label: mittelarchaisch
mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 619 BC–559 BC] mittelarchaisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athens and Corinth turned out black-figure vases traded across the Mediterranean, sculptors carved the first life-size marble kouroi and korai, and cities replaced timber shrines with stone temples. Tyrants seized power in many poleis, while Solon's reforms reshaped Athenian law and citizenship. Colonies planted from the Black Sea to Spain spread Greek language, coinage and the alphabet.

Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC) [p0w.label: Hochklassik
Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC) [p0w.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 449 BC–429 BC] Hochklassik. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Kimon, Perikles". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The high point of Athenian art and confidence, funded by tribute from the Delian League under Pericles: the Parthenon and the Propylaia rose on the Acropolis, Phidias made his colossal cult statues, and Polykleitos worked out the canon of ideal bodily proportion. Sculpture achieved the balanced, idealised naturalism that later ages took as the definition of classical beauty. It ended with the outbreak of war with Sparta and the plague that killed Pericles himself.

Reicher Stil (Greece, 429 BC–399 BC) [p0.label: Reicher Stil
Reicher Stil (Greece, 429 BC–399 BC) [p0.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 429 BC–399 BC] Reicher Stil. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "431-404 Peloponnes. Krieg". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The 'Rich Style' of late fifth-century Greek sculpture, in which drapery becomes an end in itself — clinging, transparent, breaking into deep swirling folds that reveal the body beneath. The Nike balustrade on the Athenian Acropolis is its showpiece, along with a wave of elegant grave stelai and small-scale reliefs. Emerging as Athens fought and lost the Peloponnesian War, it turns away from the calm authority of the Parthenon towards elaborate surface and emotional grace.

hochhellenistisch (Greece, 229 BC–149 BC.label: hochhellenistisch
hochhellenistisch (Greece, 229 BC–149 BC.prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 229 BC–149 BC] hochhellenistisch. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Syria, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur", together with the areas defined by the note on kingdoms. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The mature phase of the Hellenistic world, when the Antigonid, Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms and the Achaean and Aetolian leagues fought each other into exhaustion while Rome, drawn in as an ally, steadily became the arbiter of Greek affairs. Sculpture and architecture reached their most theatrical, emotionally charged form, seen in works like the Great Altar of Pergamon. The sequence of Macedonian wars ended with the sack of Corinth and the reduction of Greece to Roman control.

späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC).label: späthellenistisch
späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC).prose:
[Griechische Kultur, 149 BC–29 BC] späthellenistisch. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Syria, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur", together with the areas defined by the note on kingdoms. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Roman power closed over the Greek world: Corinth was destroyed in 146 BC, Athens was sacked by Sulla, and Mithridates' wars ravaged Asia Minor and the Aegean. Kings and cities became clients or provinces, artists and philosophers migrated to Rome, and the last independent Hellenistic kingdom ended with Cleopatra's defeat at Actium.

Früheisenzeit (Italy, 999 BC–619 BC).label: Früheisenzeit
Früheisenzeit (Italy, 999 BC–619 BC).prose:
[Römische Kultur, 999 BC–619 BC] Früheisenzeit. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Iron working spread through the Italian peninsula while communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in hut-shaped urns. Villanovan villages in Etruria and Latial hut settlements on the hills above the Tiber grew, merged and hardened into towns, and imported Greek and Phoenician goods appear in increasingly rich graves. Out of this came the Etruscan city-states and the small settlement that Romans later remembered as the founding of their city.

Archaische Zeit (Italy, 619 BC–508 BC).label: Archaische Zeit
Archaische Zeit (Italy, 619 BC–508 BC).prose: [Römische Kultur, 619 BC–508 BC] Archaische Zeit. "Etruskische Könige in Rom". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Republikanische Zeit (Italy, 508 BC–30 B.label: Republikanische Zeit
Republikanische Zeit (Italy, 508 BC–30 B.prose:
[Römische Kultur, 508 BC–30 BC] Republikanische Zeit. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

After the expulsion of the kings, Rome was governed by annually elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and assemblies of citizens, a system built as much on custom as on law. In under five centuries the city went from one player among many in central Italy to master of the Mediterranean, absorbing Carthage, Greece and much of Gaul and the Near East. The wealth and armies that conquest produced eventually broke the system itself, in a century of civil war that ended with Augustus.

frührepublikanisch (Italy, 508 BC–366 BC.label: frührepublikanisch
frührepublikanisch (Italy, 508 BC–366 BC.prose:
[Römische Kultur, 508 BC–366 BC] frührepublikanisch. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

After driving out its kings, Rome spent a century and a half as one middling Latin city among many, fighting neighbours in the hills while plebeians wrung concessions from the patrician aristocracy. The Twelve Tables put law in public writing, the Gauls sacked the city around 390 BC, and the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 finally opened the consulship to plebeians. The institutions improvised in these struggles — consuls, tribunes, the Senate's authority — became the machinery of Mediterranean empire.

mittelrepublikanisch (Italy, 366 BC–201.label: mittelrepublikanisch
mittelrepublikanisch (Italy, 366 BC–201.prose:
[Römische Kultur, 366 BC–201 BC] mittelrepublikanisch. "264-241 1. punischer Krieg"; "218-201 2. punischer Krieg". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Rome moved from being one central Italian power among many to master of the western Mediterranean, absorbing the Samnites, Etruscans and Greek cities of the south, then surviving Hannibal. Plebeians won access to the consulship and the senatorial governing class took its classic shape. Conquest brought slaves, silver and provinces, remaking Roman society as thoroughly as it remade the map.

spätrepublikanisch (Italy, 201 BC–30 BC).label: spätrepublikanisch
spätrepublikanisch (Italy, 201 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Römische Kultur, 201 BC–30 BC] spätrepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: France, Greece, Italy, Roman Republic, Spain, Tunisia, Turkey. "149-146 3. punischer Krieg"; "146 Eroberung Korinths"; "133 'Schenkung' von Pergamon an Rom"; "Marius, Sulla; Pompeius, Caesar". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Victory over Carthage and the eastern kingdoms brought Rome enormous wealth, slaves and provinces – and a political system unable to manage them. Land struggles, the murders of the Gracchi, civil wars between Marius and Sulla, and generals with private armies culminated in Caesar's dictatorship and assassination, ending with Octavian's supremacy and the birth of the empire.

Frühe Kaiserzeit (Italy, 30 BC–AD 68).label: Frühe Kaiserzeit
Frühe Kaiserzeit (Italy, 30 BC–AD 68).prose:
[Römische Kultur, 30 BC–AD 68] Frühe Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt, France, Greece. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Augustus turned the wreckage of the civil wars into a monarchy dressed as a restored republic, and his successors made the arrangement permanent. Provinces were reorganised, a standing army and professional bureaucracy took shape, and the Mediterranean enjoyed unusually uninterrupted peace and trade. It was also the age of Virgil, Ovid and Livy, of the imperial cult, and of the dynastic scandals under Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero that ended when the last Julio-Claudian killed himself.

Iulisch-claudisch (Italy, 30 BC–AD 68).label: Iulisch-claudisch
Iulisch-claudisch (Italy, 30 BC–AD 68).prose:
[Römische Kultur, 30 BC–AD 68] Iulisch-claudisch. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt, France, Greece. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The first Roman imperial dynasty, from Augustus's settlement of the state through Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. The republican façade concealed a monarchy, provinces were reorganised and Britain annexed, and Rome was rebuilt in marble; imperial portraiture, Arretine ware and the mass production of the early empire spread a common material culture across the Mediterranean. Nero's suicide ended the family and brought the civil war of 69.

Vierkaiserjahr (Italy, AD 68–AD 69).label: Vierkaiserjahr
Vierkaiserjahr (Italy, AD 68–AD 69).prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 68–AD 69] Vierkaiserjahr. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt, France, Greece, Italy. This is included as a subperiod under "Frühe Kaiserzeit" even though the parent period is described as ending in 68 CE. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Nero's suicide left no heir and no rule for choosing one, and in eighteen months four men wore the purple: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian. Legions from Spain, the Rhine and the East marched on Italy, Rome saw street fighting and the Capitol burned. The lesson, as Tacitus put it, was that an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome — a discovery that shaped every later succession crisis.

Mittlere Kaiserzeit (Italy, AD 69–AD 192.label: Mittlere Kaiserzeit
Mittlere Kaiserzeit (Italy, AD 69–AD 192.prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 69–AD 192] Mittlere Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt, France. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Rome's high imperial century and a bit more, running from the chaos of the four emperors of AD 69 through the Flavian dynasty and the so-called Five Good Emperors to the murder of Commodus. The empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan, hardened its frontiers under Hadrian, and spread a shared urban culture of baths, amphitheatres and aqueducts from Britain to Syria - the Colosseum, Pantheon and Trajan's Column all belong here. Citizenship and imperial office opened to provincials, so that emperors themselves came from Spain and North Africa, while trade goods and coinage circulated across an unprecedented single market.

Flavische Dynastie (Italy, AD 69–AD 96).label: Flavische Dynastie
Flavische Dynastie (Italy, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 69–AD 96] Flavische Dynastie. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian restored order after the civil wars of 69, replacing the Julio-Claudian aristocracy with a family of modest Italian origin. They rebuilt Rome after the fires and the Jewish War, financing the Colosseum with spoils from Jerusalem, and tightened imperial control over finances and the provinces. Domitian's assassination ended the line and opened the way to the adoptive emperors of the second century.

'Adoptivkaiser' (Italy, AD 96–AD 192).label: 'Adoptivkaiser'
'Adoptivkaiser' (Italy, AD 96–AD 192).prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 96–AD 192] 'Adoptivkaiser'. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Rome's rulers from Nerva through Marcus Aurelius came to power by adoption rather than birth, a run of relatively stable successions that later writers looked back on as the empire's golden age. Trajan pushed the frontiers to their greatest extent in Dacia and Mesopotamia; Hadrian pulled back and walled them, and building projects from the Pantheon to provincial cities reshaped the Roman world. The sequence broke when Marcus Aurelius left the throne to his own son, Commodus, whose murder in 192 opened a civil war.

Severer (Italy, AD 193–AD 235).label: Severer
Severer (Italy, AD 193–AD 235).prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 193–AD 235] Severer. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt. Pertinax is listed separately in 193 CE in the chronological chart. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Imperial rule passed to a family from Roman Africa, backed by the army and by influential women of a Syrian priestly dynasty. In Italy the era left the Baths of Caracalla, the Arch of Septimius Severus and a legal literature of lasting importance, written by jurists such as Ulpian and Papinian. Its violent end in 235 ushered in decades of instability.

Soldatenkaiser (Italy, AD 235–AD 284).label: Soldatenkaiser
Soldatenkaiser (Italy, AD 235–AD 284).prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 235–AD 284] Soldatenkaiser. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Austria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Egypt. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Fifty years in which the empire was made and unmade by its armies: more than twenty men were raised to the purple by legions or praetorians, and almost all died violently. Plague, debased silver coinage, Persian and Germanic invasions, and breakaway regimes in Gaul and Palmyra came close to tearing the state apart. Recovery under Aurelian and then Diocletian left a more militarised, bureaucratic empire, with power drifting away from Rome and the Senate toward frontier commanders and their camps.

Spätantike (Italy, AD 306–AD 395).label: Spätantike
Spätantike (Italy, AD 306–AD 395).prose:
[Römische Kultur, AD 306–AD 395] Spätantike. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Egypt, France. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Latest date in the chronological chart is the end of the reign of Theodosius in 395 CE, so this has been taken as the end date of this period according to this authority. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Constantine's rise ended the tetrarchic experiment, legalised Christianity and founded a new capital on the Bosphorus; by the reign of Theodosius, Christianity was the state religion and the empire was permanently administered as eastern and western halves. Art, coinage and government all took on the hierarchical, ceremonial character we call late Roman, and bishops became figures of political weight.

Âge du Bronze (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC).label: Âge du Bronze
Âge du Bronze (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC] Âge du Bronze. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

In the Aegean this is the age of Europe's first literate, palace-based societies: Minoan Crete with its labyrinthine complexes, frescoes and Linear A script; the marble-figurine cultures of the Cyclades; and the Mycenaean citadels of the mainland with their shaft graves, gold masks and Linear B archives. Long-distance trade carried Aegean pottery and metalwork across the Mediterranean and brought in copper, tin and ivory. The collapse of the palaces around 1200 BC ended writing and centralised rule for centuries, but left the legends that Homer later drew on.
Âge du Bronze (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique (Greece, 3099 BC–1049 BC).label: Helladique
Helladique (Greece, 3099 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–1049 BC] Helladique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The mainland Greek Bronze Age, divided into Early, Middle and Late phases. It traces the path from small agricultural communities using copper and bronze, through a long, materially modest middle stretch, to the warrior elites of the shaft graves and the palace bureaucracies of the Mycenaeans.
Helladique (Greece, 3099 BC–1049 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Minoen (Crete, 3099 BC–1049 BC).label: Minoen
Minoen (Crete, 3099 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Crete, 3099 BC–1049 BC] Minoen. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The Bronze Age civilisation of Crete, named by Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos. It runs from farming villages and communal tholos tombs, through the building of the great palaces with their storerooms, frescoes and undeciphered Linear A script, to the arrival of Mycenaean Greeks and the final abandonment of the palatial centres. Its seafaring reach across the Aegean and Egypt made it Europe's earliest complex state society.
Minoen (Crete, 3099 BC–1049 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Âge du Fer (Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC).label: Âge du Fer
Âge du Fer (Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC] Âge du Fer. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

After the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, Greece rebuilt from small, scattered communities — the era once called the Dark Age. Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons, cremation burials and Protogeometric then Geometric pottery mark a new visual language, and by its end the alphabet had been adapted from Phoenician, the first monumental temples were rising, and the polis was taking shape. Population growth pushed Greeks overseas as colonists and traders, setting the stage for the Archaic world.
Âge du Fer (Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Antiquité (Greece, 799 BC–AD 324).label: Antiquité
Antiquité (Greece, 799 BC–AD 324).prose:
[Greece, 799 BC–AD 324] Antiquité. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The long stretch in which Gaul moved from Iron Age chiefdoms trading with Mediterranean merchants to a fully Roman province and then to a Christianised, increasingly fragmented late-imperial society. It covers Greek colonial contact on the southern coast, Caesar's conquest, the Gallo-Roman towns with their forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, and the arrival of Frankish and Visigothic settlers. Most of France's monumental ancient remains, from Nîmes to Vienne, belong to it.
Antiquité (Greece, 799 BC–AD 324).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Période byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 145.label: Période byzantine
Période byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 145.prose:
[Greece, AD 324–AD 1453] Période byzantine. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

With Constantinople founded as a new imperial capital, the Greek lands became the heartland of a Christian, Greek-speaking Roman empire. Ancient temples were rebuilt as churches, cities contracted into fortified hilltop kastra under waves of Slav, Arab and Norman attack, and mosaic and icon painting reached extraordinary heights at Thessaloniki, Mystras and the monasteries of Athos. It ends with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453.
Période byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 145.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Période médiévale/franque (Greece, AD 32.label: Période médiévale/franque
Période médiévale/franque (Greece, AD 32.prose:
[Greece, AD 323–AD 1453] Période médiévale/franque. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

After the Fourth Crusade shattered Byzantine rule in 1204, western knights carved Greece into crusader lordships - the Principality of Achaea, the Duchy of Athens - while Venice took the ports and islands. Frankish castles like Chlemoutsi and Mistra's fortress still dominate the landscape, and Latin and Greek elites intermarried and competed for two centuries. Byzantine rulers clawed back parts of the Peloponnese before Ottoman armies absorbed the whole region.
Période médiévale/franque (Greece, AD 32.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Période moderne (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821.label: Période moderne
Période moderne (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821.prose:
[Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821] Période moderne. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

France emerged from the Italian Wars with a taste for Renaissance art and architecture - the châteaux of the Loire, Leonardo at Amboise - then tore itself apart in decades of Catholic-Protestant conflict resolved by the Edict of Nantes. The Bourbon monarchy afterwards built the most centralised state in Europe, culminating in Louis XIV at Versailles, with a global empire in Canada, the Caribbean and India. Enlightenment writing, fiscal crisis and social resentment brought the whole edifice down in 1789.
Période moderne (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Final (Greece, 4499 BC–2999.label: Néolithique Final
Néolithique Final (Greece, 4499 BC–2999.prose:
[Greece, 4499 BC–2999 BC] Néolithique Final. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Farming villages spread out of the Thessalian plains onto the islands, the coasts and previously thinly settled uplands, and the Aegean became a connected world of small boats and exchanged goods. Copper and silver working began, pottery grew more varied and less painted, and the first fortified or ditched sites appear. These are the communities out of which the Early Bronze Age societies of the Cyclades and mainland Greece grew.
Néolithique Final (Greece, 4499 BC–2999.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Moyen (Greece, 5799 BC–4749.label: Néolithique Moyen
Néolithique Moyen (Greece, 5799 BC–4749.prose:
[Greece, 5799 BC–4749 BC] Néolithique Moyen. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The tell villages of Thessaly reached their fullest form, with mudbrick houses rebuilt on the same spots for generations until the mounds stood metres above the plain. Sesklo and its neighbours produced fine red-on-white painted pottery, clay figurines of women and animals, and the earliest substantial planned settlements in Europe. The accumulated debris of these places is why the Greek plains are dotted with artificial hills.
Néolithique Moyen (Greece, 5799 BC–4749.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Récent (Greece, 5299 BC–4499.label: Néolithique Récent
Néolithique Récent (Greece, 5299 BC–4499.prose:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Néolithique Récent. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Settlement expanded beyond the old farming heartlands into northern Greece, the caves of the south and the islands, and villages were increasingly enclosed by ditches or walls. Painted wares gave way in many places to burnished dark and grey pottery, spindle whorls and loom weights point to textile production, and obsidian and other goods travelled further. It is also when the first copper objects appear in the Aegean.
Néolithique Récent (Greece, 5299 BC–4499.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Récent (Crete, 5299 BC–4499.label: Néolithique Récent
Néolithique Récent (Crete, 5299 BC–4499.prose:
[Crete, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Néolithique Récent. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Painted wares gave way in many places to burnished dark and grey pottery, spindle whorls and loom weights point to textile production, and obsidian and other goods travelled further. It is also when the first copper objects appear in the Aegean.

Antiquité (Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 324).label: Antiquité
Antiquité (Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 324).prose:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 324] Antiquité. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The long stretch in which Gaul moved from Iron Age chiefdoms trading with Mediterranean merchants to a fully Roman province and then to a Christianised, increasingly fragmented late-imperial society. It covers Greek colonial contact on the southern coast, Caesar's conquest, the Gallo-Roman towns with their forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, and the arrival of Frankish and Visigothic settlers. Most of France's monumental ancient remains, from Nîmes to Vienne, belong to it.
Antiquité (Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 324).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Récent I (Greece, 5299 BC–47.label: Néolithique Récent I
Néolithique Récent I (Greece, 5299 BC–47.prose:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4799 BC] Néolithique Récent I. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The early part of the Greek Late Neolithic, when villages spread into new regions and pottery styles diversified sharply from one district to another, with burnished dark wares joining and replacing older painted traditions. Exchange in obsidian, fine pottery and ornaments tied distant communities together across the mainland and the islands.
Néolithique Récent I (Greece, 5299 BC–47.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Récent II (Greece, 4799 BC–4.label: Néolithique Récent II
Néolithique Récent II (Greece, 4799 BC–4.prose:
[Greece, 4799 BC–4499 BC] Néolithique Récent II. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The later Greek Late Neolithic, associated with sites such as Dimini in Thessaly with its concentric enclosure walls and central courtyard building. Communities invested more in defining and defending their settlements, and the first copper objects and metalworking debris appear in the Aegean.
Néolithique Récent II (Greece, 4799 BC–4.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Bronze Ancien (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC).label: Bronze Ancien
Bronze Ancien (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC] Bronze Ancien. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Metalworking, longboats and sail-borne trade knitted the Aegean islands, Crete and the Greek mainland together for the first time. Substantial buildings like the House of the Tiles at Lerna and the Cycladic marble figurines belong here, along with the potter's wheel and the first fortified coastal settlements. Widespread destructions and abandonments toward the end of the period reshaped the map before the palaces appeared.
Bronze Ancien (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Bronze Moyen (Greece, 2099 BC–1549 BC).label: Bronze Moyen
Bronze Moyen (Greece, 2099 BC–1549 BC).prose:
[Greece, 2099 BC–1549 BC] Bronze Moyen. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

On Crete the first palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, with storage magazines, Kamares ware and the earliest Aegean writing in Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A. The mainland was poorer and more rural until its final generations, when the Mycenaean shaft graves at Mycenae were filled with gold masks, weapons and imported goods. That sudden concentration of wealth marks the beginning of mainland dominance in the Aegean.
Bronze Moyen (Greece, 2099 BC–1549 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Ancien (Greece, 3099 BC–1999.label: Helladique Ancien
Helladique Ancien (Greece, 3099 BC–1999.prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Helladique Ancien. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The first phase of the mainland Bronze Age, when villages of mudbrick houses spread across the Peloponnese and central Greece, bronze metallurgy took hold, and the vine and olive joined grain in the farming economy. Its middle stage produced remarkable communal buildings such as the House of Tiles at Lerna, along with clay sealings implying record-keeping — an early experiment in centralised authority that was destroyed and not immediately repeated.
Helladique Ancien (Greece, 3099 BC–1999.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Moyen (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 B.label: Helladique Moyen
Helladique Moyen (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 B.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Helladique Moyen. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

A long, materially austere stretch of the mainland Bronze Age: modest villages, apsidal houses, and the grey and yellow 'Minyan' wares turned on the wheel. Little suggests great wealth or hierarchy until its final generations, when the shaft graves at Mycenae suddenly fill with gold masks, weapons and imported goods — the prelude to the Mycenaean palace states.
Helladique Moyen (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 B.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Ancien I (Greece, 3099 BC–269.label: Helladique Ancien I
Helladique Ancien I (Greece, 3099 BC–269.prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Helladique Ancien I. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The opening of the mainland Bronze Age, with small unwalled villages, handmade dark burnished pottery and only limited use of copper and bronze. Life differed little from the preceding Neolithic, but the settlement pattern shifted toward coasts and fertile plains, and contacts with the Cyclades and Anatolia began to bring in new metal and pottery forms.
Helladique Ancien I (Greece, 3099 BC–269.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Néolithique Récent (Greece, 5499 BC–3249.label: Néolithique Récent
Néolithique Récent (Greece, 5499 BC–3249.prose:
[Northern Greece, 5499 BC–3249 BC] Néolithique Récent. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Settlement expanded beyond the old farming heartlands into northern Greece, the caves of the south and the islands, and villages were increasingly enclosed by ditches or walls. Painted wares gave way in many places to burnished dark and grey pottery, spindle whorls and loom weights point to textile production, and obsidian and other goods travelled further. It is also when the first copper objects appear in the Aegean.
Néolithique Récent (Greece, 5499 BC–3249.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Ancien II (Greece, 2699 BC–21.label: Helladique Ancien II
Helladique Ancien II (Greece, 2699 BC–21.prose:
[Greece, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Helladique Ancien II. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The high point of the early mainland Bronze Age, when sites such as Lerna, Tiryns and Kolonna grew into substantial centres. Monumental 'corridor houses' with tiled roofs, clay sealings used to control stored goods, and fine sauceboats and tankards suggest emerging elites and organised administration. The phase ended in widespread destructions whose cause is still debated.
Helladique Ancien II (Greece, 2699 BC–21.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Ancien III (Greece, 2199 BC–1.label: Helladique Ancien III
Helladique Ancien III (Greece, 2199 BC–1.prose:
[Greece, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Helladique Ancien III. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

A markedly poorer, more scattered period following the destruction of the corridor-house centres. New material traits appear — apsidal houses, wheelmade grey wares and patterned Tiryns-style pottery — which some archaeologists have linked to the arrival of new populations, possibly early Greek speakers, though continuity is equally arguable.
Helladique Ancien III (Greece, 2199 BC–1.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Moyen I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.label: Helladique Moyen I
Helladique Moyen I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Helladique Moyen I. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Mainland Greece settled into a quieter, poorer rhythm after the collapse of Early Helladic settlements: small villages of apsidal and long-room houses, burials in simple cist graves set among the dwellings, and the spread of the grey burnished wheel-made pottery known as Minyan ware. There is little sign of the monumental building or long-distance display that Crete was then enjoying, and most communities lived off grain, sheep and the sea. It is the flat stretch of the story from which Mycenaean Greece would suddenly rise.
Helladique Moyen I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Moyen II (Greece, 1899 BC–169.label: Helladique Moyen II
Helladique Moyen II (Greece, 1899 BC–169.prose:
[Greece, 1899 BC–1699 BC] Helladique Moyen II. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Villages grew steadily and pottery styles standardised, with grey and yellow Minyan wares and matt-painted jars in use across the mainland. Contact with Minoan Crete and the Cycladic islands increased, bringing new shapes, metals and ideas into what had been an inward-looking farming world. Burials began to show differences in wealth, the first hints of the ranked society that followed.
Helladique Moyen II (Greece, 1899 BC–169.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Helladique Moyen III (A-B) (Greece, 1699.label: Helladique Moyen III (A-B)
Helladique Moyen III (A-B) (Greece, 1699.prose:
[Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Helladique Moyen III (A-B). Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Within a few generations some mainland communities became conspicuously rich: at Mycenae the shaft graves of Grave Circle B were filled with bronze weapons, gold ornaments and imported Cretan goods. Warrior burials, larger settlements and heavy borrowing from Minoan craft and art mark the emergence of a mainland elite. This is the threshold of Mycenaean civilisation, the world later remembered in Homeric epic.
Helladique Moyen III (A-B) (Greece, 1699.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Archaïque (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).label: Archaïque
Archaïque (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–479 BC] Archaïque. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The Greek world emerged from its dark age with an explosion of energy: the alphabet was adopted, cities sent out colonies from Spain to the Black Sea, coinage spread, and the polis became the basic unit of political life. Monumental stone temples, life-size kouros statues and the poetry of Sappho and Homer's written text all belong here, as do the first tyrants and the first experiments in citizen government at Athens. It ends with the Persian invasions, which the Greeks improbably survived.
Archaïque (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Classique (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).label: Classique
Classique (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Greece, 479 BC–322 BC] Classique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Between the defeat of the Persian invasion and the death of Demosthenes, the Greek city-states reached their political and artistic peak and then exhausted themselves. Athens built the Parthenon, staged the great tragedies and experimented with direct democracy while fighting Sparta in the Peloponnesian War; Plato and Aristotle founded schools that shaped philosophy for two thousand years. Macedonian victory at Chaeronea ended the independence of the city-states and opened the Hellenistic age.
Classique (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Hellénistique (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).label: Hellénistique
Hellénistique (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Greece, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellénistique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Alexander's successors divided his conquests into large monarchies, and Greek culture, language and city planning spread far beyond the Aegean. Old Greek city-states kept their institutions but lost real independence, while new capitals in Egypt and Asia became the centres of scholarship, sculpture and royal patronage. Rome's piecemeal conquest of the Mediterranean brought the era to a close.
Hellénistique (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Romain (Greece, 26 BC–AD 324).label: Romain
Romain (Greece, 26 BC–AD 324).prose:
[Greece, 26 BC–AD 324] Romain. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Greece under Roman rule was a province of prestige rather than power: Athens and Sparta traded on their past, wealthy Romans sent their sons to study philosophy there, and emperors from Augustus to Hadrian paid for temples, aqueducts and festivals. Corinth was refounded as a colony, old sanctuaries kept working, and the Greek language and learning spread through the empire even as political initiative moved elsewhere.
Romain (Greece, 26 BC–AD 324).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Chypro-archaïque (Cyprus, 749 BC–479 BC).label: Chypro-archaïque
Chypro-archaïque (Cyprus, 749 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–479 BC] Chypro-archaïque. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The age of the Cypriot city-kingdoms, which paid tribute in turn to Assyria, Egypt and Persia while keeping their own kings, scripts and sanctuaries. Greek- and Phoenician-speaking communities lived side by side, and craftsmen produced the island's most exuberant art: bichrome jugs painted with birds and fish in open fields, and sanctuaries crowded with thousands of terracotta worshippers. Rich chamber tombs at Salamis, furnished with chariots, horses and Near Eastern bronzes, show rulers burying their dead in a style that recalls Homer.
Chypro-archaïque (Cyprus, 749 BC–479 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Fer ancien/Submycénien (Greece, 1099 BC–.label: Fer ancien/Submycénien
Fer ancien/Submycénien (Greece, 1099 BC–.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–1049 BC] Fer ancien/Submycénien. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The generation or two after the Mycenaean palaces finally failed, when populations were small, settlements shrank and the old wall paintings, archives and prestige workshops were gone. Burial shifted to single cist graves, pottery became plain and simple, and the first iron objects appear, pointing towards the Protogeometric recovery.
Fer ancien/Submycénien (Greece, 1099 BC–.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Chypro-Classique (Cyprus, 479 BC–309 BC).label: Chypro-Classique
Chypro-Classique (Cyprus, 479 BC–309 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 479 BC–309 BC] Chypro-Classique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Cyprus's ten city-kingdoms lived under nominal Persian overlordship while their courts, coinage and tombs grew steadily more Greek. Evagoras of Salamis briefly defied the Great King and made his city a centre of Hellenic art and diplomacy; the island's syllabic script gradually gave way to the Greek alphabet. The period closes with Alexander's conquest and the wars of his successors, after which Ptolemaic Egypt abolished the kingdoms and ruled Cyprus directly.
Chypro-Classique (Cyprus, 479 BC–309 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Protogéométrique (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC.label: Protogéométrique
Protogéométrique (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Protogéométrique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The first distinctly post-Mycenaean art, in which potters used compasses and a fast wheel to produce clean concentric circles, tight bands and elegantly proportioned amphorae. It accompanies the spread of ironworking and of cremation cemeteries in Attica and Euboea, and the beginnings of Greek movement eastward across the Aegean. Out of it grew the fully Geometric style with its friezes of meanders and figures.
Protogéométrique (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Géométrique (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).label: Géométrique
Géométrique (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Géométrique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The Greek world's recovery after the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, named for the crisp bands of meanders, zigzags and triangles that cover its pottery. Iron working spread, trade with the Levant resumed, the alphabet was adapted from Phoenician script, and by the end of the period human figures reappear in art on huge Athenian grave vases showing funerals and battles. This is the world in which the Homeric poems took shape and the polis began to form.
Géométrique (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Chypro-géométrique (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749.label: Chypro-géométrique
Chypro-géométrique (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749.prose:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC] Chypro-géométrique. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

After the collapse of the Bronze Age cities, Cyprus reorganised around new coastal centres such as Salamis, Kition and Paphos, and iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons far earlier here than in much of the Mediterranean. Greek-speaking settlers took root, and Phoenicians from Tyre established a colony at Kition with a great temple to Astarte. Out of these centuries came the territorial kingdoms that would dominate the island for the next 700 years.
Chypro-géométrique (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Chypro-archaïque I (Cyprus, 749 BC–599 B.label: Chypro-archaïque I
Chypro-archaïque I (Cyprus, 749 BC–599 B.prose:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–599 BC] Chypro-archaïque I. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Cypriot kings first appear in outside records now: Sargon II's stele set up at Kition names seven rulers who submitted to Assyria, and later lists give ten kingdoms. Wealth from copper and trade filled the royal tombs at Salamis with chariot burials, ivory furniture and imported bronzes, while potters developed the lively 'free-field' style of birds and fish on bichrome jugs.
Chypro-archaïque I (Cyprus, 749 BC–599 B.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Chypro-archaïque II (Cyprus, 599 BC–479.label: Chypro-archaïque II
Chypro-archaïque II (Cyprus, 599 BC–479.prose:
[Cyprus, 599 BC–479 BC] Chypro-archaïque II. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Assyrian influence faded and Cyprus passed to Egypt under Amasis and then to Persia. The island's kings joined the Ionian Revolt in 499 BC and were crushed; the huge Persian siege ramp piled against the walls of Palaipaphos, packed with statues looted from a nearby sanctuary, survives as one of the best-preserved siege works of the ancient world. Sanctuaries filled with limestone and terracotta votives blend Egyptian, Greek and Near Eastern styles.
Chypro-archaïque II (Cyprus, 599 BC–479.source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Protobyzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).label: Protobyzantine
Protobyzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).prose:
[Greece, AD 324–AD 610] Protobyzantine. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The eastern Roman world became Christian and Greek-speaking, with Constantinople as its capital and vast new basilicas replacing temples as the focus of civic life. Justinian's reign brought Hagia Sophia, a codified body of Roman law and a brief reconquest of the west, followed by plague and exhaustion. Slav and Avar incursions and the loss of the Balkan countryside close the era and mark the shift to a smaller, more embattled Byzantium.
Protobyzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Médiobyzantine (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204).label: Médiobyzantine
Médiobyzantine (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204).prose:
[Greece, AD 610–AD 1204] Médiobyzantine. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Stripped of Egypt and Syria by the Arab conquests, the empire reorganised itself around Greek language, provincial army districts and a fortified Constantinople that repeatedly held off siege. Iconoclasm tore at religious life for over a century before images were restored; missionaries then carried Orthodox Christianity to the Slavs. Greece itself was resettled and re-Hellenised, monasteries and domed churches multiplied, and the era ended abruptly when the Fourth Crusade sacked the capital.
Médiobyzantine (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Tardobyzantine (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453).label: Tardobyzantine
Tardobyzantine (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453).prose:
[Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453] Tardobyzantine. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204 split the empire into Latin principalities and Greek successor states; the Nicaean rulers recovered the capital in 1261 but never the old power. The Palaiologan centuries were ones of shrinking territory, civil war and Venetian and Genoese commercial dominance, yet also of brilliant art, mosaics and scholarship at Mystras and Constantinople. Ottoman advance narrowed the empire to little more than its capital, which fell in 1453.
Tardobyzantine (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Vénitienne (Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650).label: Vénitienne
Vénitienne (Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650).prose:
[Greece, Crete , AD 1200–AD 1650] Vénitienne. Spatial coverage: Crete, Greece. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Venice took control of Crete, the Ionian islands and other Aegean ports after the Fourth Crusade, ruling a maritime empire built on grain, wine and the galley route to the Levant. Venetian fortifications, harbours and town houses reshaped Greek cities, while Orthodox and Catholic populations lived under an uneasy colonial administration. Cretan painters trained in this mixed world, El Greco among them, before Ottoman conquest ended Venetian rule.
Vénitienne (Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Ottomane (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).label: Ottomane
Ottomane (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).prose:
[Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821] Ottomane. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

After the fall of Constantinople the Greek lands passed under Ottoman administration, with Orthodox bishops made responsible for their communities and Venetian holdings in the Aegean and Peloponnese picked off one by one. Village life continued around church and taxation, while Greek merchants prospered in the empire's ports and abroad, and mountain klephts kept up a tradition of armed defiance. Ideas from the diaspora and from revolutionary Europe fed the uprising of 1821.
Ottomane (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Contemporain (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).label: Contemporain
Contemporain (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).prose:
[Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000] Contemporain. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Begins with the revolt against Ottoman rule that produced an independent Greek kingdom, a state built as much by European powers as by Greeks themselves. The following century and a half brought territorial expansion, the catastrophic 1922 defeat in Anatolia and the exchange of populations that emptied Greek Asia Minor, then occupation, civil war, dictatorship and eventual entry into the European Community.
Contemporain (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Minoen Ancien I (Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC).label: Minoen Ancien I
Minoen Ancien I (Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC] Minoen Ancien I. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

The opening phase of the Cretan Bronze Age, when small farming communities began using copper and burying their dead collectively in circular tholos tombs on the Mesara plain and rock shelters elsewhere. Distinctive burnished Pyrgos ware and painted Aghios Onouphrios pottery appear, along with the first stone vases. There are no palaces yet, but the burial grounds show communities investing heavily in ancestors and group identity.
Minoen Ancien I (Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC).source: La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online

Minoen Ancien II (Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC.label: Minoen Ancien II
Minoen Ancien II (Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC.prose:
[Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC] Minoen Ancien II. Period definition from La Chronique des fouilles en ligne / Archaeology in Greece Online — École française d'Athènes, 2019.

Cretan settlements grew denser and wealthier, with substantial multi-room houses at sites such as Myrtos and Vasiliki, whose mottled red-and-black pottery is the period's signature. Bronze tools and weapons, imported obsidian and Cycladic goods, and the first seal-stones point to expanding trade and to individuals marking property and status. These are the foundations from which the palace societies emerged a few centuries later.

The mid-Holocene, when hunter-gatherer bands across the Andean highlands, the Pampas and Patagonia lived without pottery, hunting guanaco and vicuña with dart and spearthrower and grinding wild plant foods. Rockshelters occupied over and over again preserve the record: stone points, grinding slabs, and in places painted and stencilled art on the walls.

The last stretch of life before pottery, when highland groups in the northwest began keeping llamas and growing quinoa, maize and squash alongside continued hunting. Camps grow larger and more permanent, storage appears, and the foundations are laid for the settled farming villages that follow.

Colonial temprano (Argentina, AD 1601–AD.label: Colonial temprano
Colonial temprano (Argentina, AD 1601–AD.prose:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), AD 1601–AD 1700] Colonial temprano. Period definition from Arqueología Histórica (Colonial Temprana hasta la actualidad) en el Predio del Colegio de Escribanos de Córdoba — Berberián  E.E, 2008.

Spanish towns in the northwest and the interior became the framework of colonial life, tied to the silver economy of Potosí by mule trains and wagon roads. Jesuit missions gathered Guaraní communities in the northeast, while the Calchaquí wars ended only with the forced removal of whole populations. Buenos Aires remained a small, contraband-fed port on the empire's edge.
Colonial temprano (Argentina, AD 1601–AD.source: Arqueología Histórica (Colonial Temprana hasta la actualidad) en el Predio del Colegio de Escribanos de Córdoba

eldre steinalder (Norway, 9499 BC–3999 B.label: eldre steinalder
eldre steinalder (Norway, 9499 BC–3999 B.prose:
[Norway, 9499 BC–3999 BC] eldre steinalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

As the ice sheet withdrew, hunter-fisher-gatherers followed the coast north, living off seals, fish and seabirds and leaving their camps on beaches now raised far above sea level. Their flint and quartzite toolkits — the Fosna and Komsa assemblages among them — represent the earliest human presence in Norway. Boats and open-sea skills were fundamental from the outset, as the settled sites are almost all shoreline sites.

yngre steinalder (Norway, 3999 BC–1699 B.label: yngre steinalder
yngre steinalder (Norway, 3999 BC–1699 B.prose:
[Norway, 3999 BC–1699 BC] yngre steinalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Farming reached southern Norway during this long stretch, with cereal cultivation, cattle and sheep taking hold alongside — never fully replacing — hunting, fishing and sealing, which remained the mainstay along the coast and in the north. Polished flint and slate tools, ground stone axes and, later, Corded Ware-style battle axes and beaker pottery show contacts running south into Denmark and east into Sweden. Rock art shifts over time from wild game towards boats and human figures, hinting at changing beliefs.

tidlig metalltid (Norway, 1999 BC–299 BC.label: tidlig metalltid
tidlig metalltid (Norway, 1999 BC–299 BC.prose:
[Norway, 1999 BC–299 BC] tidlig metalltid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

In northern Norway the neat Bronze Age/Iron Age sequence of the south does not fit, so archaeologists speak simply of an Early Metal Age. Copper and bronze objects arrived through exchange with the east and south, but stone and slate tools stayed in use and communities kept hunting, fishing and sealing. Asbestos-tempered pottery and rich coastal settlement sites are its most recognisable traces.

mellomneolitikum (Norway, 2799 BC–2399 B.label: mellomneolitikum
mellomneolitikum (Norway, 2799 BC–2399 B.prose:
[Norway, 2799 BC–2399 BC] mellomneolitikum. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Along the coast, hunters and fishers of the Pitted Ware tradition kept to the sea, harpooning seals and making distinctive pit-decorated pots, while inland the Battle Axe or Corded Ware people arrived with stone shaft-hole axes, single graves and stock-keeping. The two ways of life overlapped for centuries. Genetic and material evidence links the newcomers to migrations sweeping across northern Europe from the steppe.

romertid (Norway, AD 1–AD 400).label: romertid
romertid (Norway, AD 1–AD 400).prose:
[Norway, AD 1–AD 400] romertid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Norwegian farming communities never saw a Roman soldier, but Roman glass, bronze vessels, coins and swords travelled north through Danish and Germanic middlemen into the graves of local chieftains. Farms grew more permanent, iron production expanded, and the first runic inscriptions in the elder futhark appear on weapons and stones – the earliest writing in Scandinavia.

nyere tid (Norway, AD 1500–AD 2050).label: nyere tid
nyere tid (Norway, AD 1500–AD 2050).prose:
[Norway, AD 1500–AD 2050] nyere tid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. A numeric end year of 2050 has been entered as the data supplied had an end year of "present". Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Norway passed from the Reformation and Danish rule through union with Sweden to full independence in 1905, while timber, fisheries, mining and later hydroelectric power and oil transformed the economy. Farmsteads, sawmills, mining towns like Røros and coastal fishing stations dominate the archaeological record, along with wartime remains from the German occupation. It is the period in which most of the present Norwegian landscape of roads, farms and towns took shape.

senneolitikum (Norway, 2399 BC–1699 BC).label: senneolitikum
senneolitikum (Norway, 2399 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Norway, 2399 BC–1699 BC] senneolitikum. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Farming finally took hold across southern Norway, with cereal fields, cattle and pigs, and two-aisled timber longhouses replacing older settlement patterns. Finely pressure-flaked flint daggers, imported from Denmark and copied locally, became the prestige object of the age, and burial in stone cists signalled new ideas about family and property.

jernalder (Norway, 499 BC–AD 1050).label: jernalder
jernalder (Norway, 499 BC–AD 1050).prose:
[Norway, 499 BC–AD 1050] jernalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Iron worked from local bog ore ended Norway's reliance on imported bronze and put tools and weapons within reach of ordinary farms, opening up new land for settlement. Over these fifteen centuries came contact with the Roman world, runic writing, boat graves and chieftains' halls, and finally the Viking expansion overseas. It ends with the consolidation of a Christian kingdom.

eldre bronsealder (Norway, 1699 BC–1099.label: eldre bronsealder
eldre bronsealder (Norway, 1699 BC–1099.prose:
[Norway, 1699 BC–1099 BC] eldre bronsealder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Bronze arrived through southern Scandinavian networks, reaching Norway as prestige weapons, razors and neck rings acquired by farming elites along the coast. The dead were buried under large stone cairns set on prominent headlands, and rock surfaces were carved with ships, sun symbols and figures. Long timber houses and cleared grazing land show farming taking firm hold in the coastal south and west.

merovingertid (Norway, AD 550–AD 750).label: merovingertid
merovingertid (Norway, AD 550–AD 750).prose:
[Norway, AD 550–AD 750] merovingertid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Grave goods become fewer and settlements harder to find, suggesting a population contraction possibly linked to the climate downturn after AD 536. Yet craft skill was high: gilded animal-ornament brooches, pattern-welded swords and the first sailing rigs on Nordic ships. The technology and elite networks assembled here made the Viking expansion that followed possible.

yngre jernalder (Norway, AD 550–AD 1050).label: yngre jernalder
yngre jernalder (Norway, AD 550–AD 1050).prose:
[Norway, AD 550–AD 1050] yngre jernalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Half a millennium in which chieftain-led societies grew into kingdoms: animal-style ornament and fine weaponry mark the Merovingian centuries, followed by the outward explosion of the Viking Age. Boathouses, ship burials, farms and market sites show a society organised around seafaring, land and lordship. It ends with a unified Christian Norway and the beginning of written records.

eldre jernalder (Norway, 499 BC–AD 550).label: eldre jernalder
eldre jernalder (Norway, 499 BC–AD 550).prose:
[Norway, 499 BC–AD 550] eldre jernalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Iron smelted from local bog ore made tools and weapons widely available, and permanent farms with names still in use today spread across the arable districts. Roman trade brought glass, bronze vessels and the alphabet that became the runic script, first cut on objects in the early centuries AD. By its end, boat graves, hillforts and the great weapon deposits point to increasingly militarised chiefdoms.

førromersk jernalder (Norway, 499 BC–AD.label: førromersk jernalder
førromersk jernalder (Norway, 499 BC–AD.prose:
[Norway, 499 BC–AD 1] førromersk jernalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Bronze, which had always been imported, gave way to iron that could be smelted from local bog ore, putting tools and weapons within reach of ordinary farmsteads. Burials become simple and finds scarce, and a cooling, wetter climate pushed settlement towards more sheltered land, so the archaeological record is thin compared with the Bronze Age. The long, three-aisled longhouse and the farming pattern it served took shape here and lasted for a millennium.

senmiddelalder (Norway, AD 1350–AD 1500).label: senmiddelalder
senmiddelalder (Norway, AD 1350–AD 1500).prose:
[Norway, AD 1350–AD 1500] senmiddelalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

The plague of 1349 killed perhaps half the population, farms were abandoned across whole districts, and rents and royal revenues collapsed. A weakened kingdom slid into dynastic union with Denmark and Sweden, while German Hanseatic merchants took firm control of the Bergen stockfish trade – leaving Norway politically subordinate for centuries to come.

bronsealder (Norway, 1699 BC–499 BC).label: bronsealder
bronsealder (Norway, 1699 BC–499 BC).prose:
[Norway, 1699 BC–499 BC] bronsealder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Metal reached the far north through long trade chains that ran all the way to central Europe, and Scandinavian chiefs paid for it with furs, amber and hides. Bronze here is bound up with sun symbolism — lurs, razors and rock carvings showing ships, sun discs and processions — and with the great burial mounds and cairns raised along the coast. Farming settlements grew more permanent, and the ship became the enduring image of northern life and the afterlife.

eldre romertid (Norway, AD 1–AD 200).label: eldre romertid
eldre romertid (Norway, AD 1–AD 200).prose:
[Norway, AD 1–AD 200] eldre romertid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Contact with the Roman Empire, via Denmark and the German provinces, brought bronze cauldrons, glass beakers and silver into Norwegian graves. Wealthy burials with weapon sets and imported drinking gear mark the emergence of a chiefly class controlling trade and warfare. The oldest runic inscriptions in Scandinavia belong to this time, written in the elder futhark.

vikingtid (Norway, AD 750–AD 1050).label: vikingtid
vikingtid (Norway, AD 750–AD 1050).prose:
[Norway, AD 750–AD 1050] vikingtid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Norwegian ships carried raiders, traders and settlers to Britain, Ireland, the Atlantic islands, Iceland and Greenland, and eastward along the Russian rivers. Silver flowed home in hoards, chieftains were buried in ships such as those at Oseberg and Gokstad, and towns and markets began to form. By its end the many petty kingdoms had been welded into one realm and Christianity had displaced the old gods.

tidligneolitikum (Norway, 3999 BC–2799 B.label: tidligneolitikum
tidligneolitikum (Norway, 3999 BC–2799 B.prose:
[Norway, 3999 BC–2799 BC] tidligneolitikum. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Farming reached southern Norway at the margins of the Funnel Beaker world, bringing pottery, polished flint axes and the first small plots of grain and grazing. Adoption was patchy and slow; most communities went on hunting elk, fishing and sealing much as before, so the change is visible more in objects and burial customs than in diet. Coastal Norway remained a place where farming was one option among several.

yngre bronsealder (Norway, 1099 BC–499 B.label: yngre bronsealder
yngre bronsealder (Norway, 1099 BC–499 B.prose:
[Norway, 1099 BC–499 BC] yngre bronsealder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Cremation became the standard rite, with burnt bone placed in small cairns and urns rather than the great mounds of earlier centuries. Imported bronze grew scarcer while local production and recycling continued, and hoards were deposited in bogs and waters as offerings. Much of Norway's rock art, with its ships, sun symbols and human figures, belongs to these centuries.

steinalder (Norway, 9499 BC–1699 BC).label: steinalder
steinalder (Norway, 9499 BC–1699 BC).prose:
[Norway, 9499 BC–1699 BC] steinalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

After the ice retreated, hunters followed the coastline north, living on seals, fish, whales and reindeer; their settlement sites cluster on old raised beaches now stranded far above the sea. Rock carvings and paintings at places like Alta record elk, reindeer, boats and bears in astonishing detail. Farming arrived only late and patchily in the south, so for most of this immensely long span Norway was a land of skilled maritime foragers rather than farmers.

tidligmiddelalder (Norway, AD 1050–AD 11.label: tidligmiddelalder
tidligmiddelalder (Norway, AD 1050–AD 11.prose:
[Norway, AD 1050–AD 1130] tidligmiddelalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

The generation after Norway's conversion, when the church took root as an institution: bishoprics, the first stone churches, tithes and burial in consecrated ground. Kings minted coins and backed the growth of Bergen, Nidaros and Oslo as real towns with wharves and workshops. The peace ended with the disputed succession of 1130, which opened a century of civil war.

yngre romertid (Norway, AD 200–AD 400).label: yngre romertid
yngre romertid (Norway, AD 200–AD 400).prose:
[Norway, AD 200–AD 400] yngre romertid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Norway's Late Roman Iron Age brought a flood of imported goods north — glass beakers, bronze vessels, silver and Roman coins — that ended up in unusually rich graves, marking the rise of chieftains who controlled trade and warrior followings. Farms grew larger and more permanent, and the first runic inscriptions in the older futhark appear on weapons, brooches and stones. These local power centres laid the groundwork for the petty kingdoms of the later Iron Age and the Viking Age.

folkevandringstid (Norway, AD 400–AD 550.label: folkevandringstid
folkevandringstid (Norway, AD 400–AD 550.prose:
[Norway, AD 400–AD 550] folkevandringstid. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

With the western Roman Empire unravelling, Norwegian chieftains built hilltop forts and buried their dead with gold bracteates, imported glass and weapons, while a distinctive animal-ornament style spread across the North Sea world. Large halls and boat-graves show power concentrating in the hands of warrior elites. The period ends in crisis: the volcanic dust-veil of 536 brought failed harvests, and large numbers of farms across the country were simply abandoned.

middelalder (Norway, AD 1050–AD 1500).label: middelalder
middelalder (Norway, AD 1050–AD 1500).prose:
[Norway, AD 1050–AD 1500] middelalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Christianity became fully institutionalised, with an archbishopric at Nidaros, stone cathedrals and hundreds of stave churches, while Bergen, Oslo and Trondheim grew into real towns trading dried cod for grain. Royal power consolidated after a century of civil wars, and Norway briefly ruled an Atlantic realm including Iceland and Greenland. The Black Death of 1349 killed perhaps half the population and led to union with Denmark.

senmesolitikum (Norway, 5999 BC–3999 BC).label: senmesolitikum
senmesolitikum (Norway, 5999 BC–3999 BC).prose:
[Norway, 5999 BC–3999 BC] senmesolitikum. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Hunter-fisher groups worked the coastline from open-air sites near the shifting shoreline, taking seals, fish and seabirds from boats and leaving behind ground stone axes and quantities of debitage. Sea levels and land uplift constantly reshaped their world, and by the end of the period contacts with farming societies to the south were introducing new tools and ideas.

høymiddelalder (Norway, AD 1050–AD 1350).label: høymiddelalder
høymiddelalder (Norway, AD 1050–AD 1350).prose:
[Norway, AD 1050–AD 1350] høymiddelalder. Norwegian archaeological periods provided by University of Oslo for ARIADNEplus project. Period definition from Norsk arkeologisk leksikon — 2005.

Norway settled into a single kingdom with a working church, coinage, towns like Bergen and Nidaros, and law codes that applied across the realm. Wealth from stockfish and timber paid for hundreds of stave churches and stone cathedrals, and royal authority reached out to Iceland, Greenland and the Isles. The era closed abruptly with the Black Death, which killed perhaps half the population and gutted the kingdom's finances.

Ongamirense (Argentina, 3000 BC–AD 1573).label: Ongamirense
Ongamirense (Argentina, 3000 BC–AD 1573).prose:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), 3000 BC–AD 1573] Ongamirense. Period definition from Excavaciones arqueológicas en el yacimiento de Ongamira, Córdoba (Rep. Arg.) : nota preliminar — Oswald Menghin, 1954.

A stone-tool tradition named for the rockshelters at Ongamira in the Sierras de Córdoba, where hunter-gatherers returned over thousands of years, leaving hearths, grinding stones, and burials in the caves. The sequence became a reference point for early Argentine archaeology and for arguments about how highland foragers lived before European arrival.

Archaic Stage (Texas, 6549 BC–AD 700).label: Archaic Stage
Archaic Stage (Texas, 6549 BC–AD 700).prose:
[Central Texas, 6549 BC–AD 700] Archaic Stage. Date range of general period inferred from start date of earliest phase and end date of latest stage; 8500 BP to 1250 BP also specified in chronological chart on p. 75. Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

For thousands of years Texas peoples lived as mobile hunters and gatherers, tuned to the very different worlds of the coastal plain, the Hill Country and the Chihuahuan Desert. They left burned rock middens where sotol and agave were baked in earth ovens, deep dry-cave deposits with sandals and basketry, and the great painted rock-shelter murals of the lower Pecos. The way of life proved so durable that it persisted here long after farming villages had taken hold elsewhere in North America.

Neoarchaic Stage (Texas, AD 700–AD 1750).label: Neoarchaic Stage
Neoarchaic Stage (Texas, AD 700–AD 1750).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 700–AD 1750] Neoarchaic Stage. Date range of broader stage inferred from start and end dates of its earliest and latest stages; range of 1250 B.P. to 200 B.P. also provided in chart on p. 75. Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

A term for the final pre-contact centuries in parts of Texas, when foraging populations adopted arrow points and, in places, pottery, but continued the mobile hunting and gathering economy of earlier millennia. Bison hunting intensified and long-distance exchange linked these groups to Puebloan and Caddoan farmers. Spanish entradas and European diseases brought the pattern to an end.

San Geronimo Phase (Texas, 5049 BC–4049.label: San Geronimo Phase
San Geronimo Phase (Texas, 5049 BC–4049.prose:
[Central Texas, 5049 BC–4049 BC] San Geronimo Phase. Cited: "Weir, 1976". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

The Early Archaic in central Texas, when the last Ice Age megafauna were long gone and people had settled into hunting deer and small game and grinding wild plant foods. Populations were thin and highly mobile, leaving scattered small hearths and camps rather than the massive cooking middens of later millennia. Split-stem and Martindale-style dart points are the signature artefacts.

Jarrell Phase (Texas, 4049 BC–3049 BC).label: Jarrell Phase
Jarrell Phase (Texas, 4049 BC–3049 BC).prose: [Central Texas, 4049 BC–3049 BC] Jarrell Phase. Cited: "new name; Sorrow et al., 1967". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

Oakalla Phase (Texas, 3049 BC–2649 BC).label: Oakalla Phase
Oakalla Phase (Texas, 3049 BC–2649 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 3049 BC–2649 BC] Oakalla Phase. Cited: "new name; Sorrow et al., 1967". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

One of the named divisions of the central Texas Archaic hunter-gatherer sequence, recognised from dart point styles and the burned-rock cooking features that build up at repeatedly used camps. Plant baking in earth ovens and hunting of deer and small game supported a mobile way of life along the region's rivers and springs.

Clear Fork Phase (Texas, 2649 BC–2049 BC.prose: [Central Texas, 2649 BC–2049 BC] Clear Fork Phase. Cited: "Weir, 1976". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.
