Marshall Ford Phase (Texas, 2049 BC–1449.prose: [Central Texas, 2049 BC–1449 BC] Marshall Ford Phase. Cited: "new name; Weir, 1976". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

Round Rock Phase (Texas, 1449 BC–649 BC).label: Round Rock Phase
Round Rock Phase (Texas, 1449 BC–649 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 1449 BC–649 BC] Round Rock Phase. Cited: "Weir, 1976". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

Defined within the central Texas Archaic sequence by Pedernales dart points and heavy use of burned rock middens for oven-baking plant foods. Repeated returns to the same hearth mounds imply predictable seasonal rounds and increasing reliance on gathered resources beside hunting. The resulting rock mounds, sometimes metres across, are the region's most visible Archaic monuments.

San Marcos Phase (Texas, 649 BC–299 BC).label: San Marcos Phase
San Marcos Phase (Texas, 649 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 649 BC–299 BC] San Marcos Phase. Cited: "Weir, 1976". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

A Late Archaic phase in central Texas marked by the return of bison to the region and a corresponding shift toward big-game hunting alongside plant baking. Broad-bladed Marcos, Montell and Castroville dart points appear in quantity, and burned-rock middens grow into mounds metres across. Cemeteries from these centuries suggest groups were laying claim to particular stretches of land.

Driftwood Phase (Texas, AD 550–AD 700).prose: [Central Texas, AD 550–AD 700] Driftwood Phase. Cited: "new name; Weir, 1976". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

Austin Phase (Texas, AD 700–AD 1300).label: Austin Phase
Austin Phase (Texas, AD 700–AD 1300).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 700–AD 1300] Austin Phase. Cited: "Jelks, 1962". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

Central Texas hunter-gatherers took up the bow and arrow, and the small Scallorn and Edwards points they left behind are the signature find of these centuries. Burials in cemeteries along the river valleys sometimes hold skeletons with arrow points lodged in bone, hinting at competition over territory. The phase gives way to the bison-hunting Toyah culture, whose people used different tools and pottery.

Toyah Phase (Texas, AD 1300–AD 1750).label: Toyah Phase
Toyah Phase (Texas, AD 1300–AD 1750).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 1300–AD 1750] Toyah Phase. Cited: "Jelks, 1962". Period definition from Cultural chronology in Central Texas — Elton Prewitt, 1981.

Late prehistoric hunters across central and southern Texas who followed bison herds returning to the southern plains, leaving a distinctive toolkit of small Perdiz arrow points, thin beveled knives, end scrapers and bone-tempered pottery. The kit is essentially a mobile bison-processing outfit, and it appears suddenly over a huge area, prompting long debate over whether it marks migrating peoples or local groups adopting a new way of life - a way of life still going when the first Spanish expeditions arrived.

Archaic (Texas, 6550 BC–AD 700).label: Archaic
Archaic (Texas, 6550 BC–AD 700).prose:
[Central Texas, 6550 BC–AD 700] Archaic. Start date parsed from general chart in figure 1, with end date provided by chart in figure 2. Period definition from From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology — Elton Prewitt, 1983.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Texas, 6550 BC–AD 700).source: From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology

Early Archaic (Texas, 6550 BC–2650 BC).label: Early Archaic
Early Archaic (Texas, 6550 BC–2650 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 6550 BC–2650 BC] Early Archaic. Parsed from chart on p. 215. Period definition from From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology — Elton Prewitt, 1983.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.
Early Archaic (Texas, 6550 BC–2650 BC).source: From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology

Middle Archaic (Texas, 2650 BC–300 BC).label: Middle Archaic
Middle Archaic (Texas, 2650 BC–300 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 2650 BC–300 BC] Middle Archaic. Dates from chart on p. 215. Period definition from From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology — Elton Prewitt, 1983.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.
Middle Archaic (Texas, 2650 BC–300 BC).source: From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology

Late Archaic (Texas, 300 BC–AD 700).label: Late Archaic
Late Archaic (Texas, 300 BC–AD 700).prose:
[Central Texas, 300 BC–AD 700] Late Archaic. Dates from chart on p. 215. Period definition from From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology — Elton Prewitt, 1983.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.
Late Archaic (Texas, 300 BC–AD 700).source: From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology

Neoarchaic (Texas, AD 700–AD 1750).label: Neoarchaic
Neoarchaic (Texas, AD 700–AD 1750).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 700–AD 1750] Neoarchaic. Dates from chart on p. 215. Period definition from From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology — Elton Prewitt, 1983.

A label used for the late prehistoric hunter-gatherers of the Texas borderlands, who kept a broadly Archaic way of life long after farming villages had appeared to the north and west. The bow and arrow replaced the atlatl, pottery appeared in some areas, and bison returned to the southern plains, drawing mobile groups into new hunting and trading patterns. It ends with the arrival of Spanish colonists, horses and epidemic disease.
Neoarchaic (Texas, AD 700–AD 1750).source: From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology

Historic (Texas, AD 1750–AD 1950).label: Historic
Historic (Texas, AD 1750–AD 1950).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 1750–AD 1950] Historic. Dates from chart on p. 215. Period definition from From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology — Elton Prewitt, 1983.

Opens with the first European descent of the Mississippi and covers French lead mining and river villages, Spanish administration, and then American statehood, steamboats and railroads. Sites from these centuries include trading posts, farmsteads, Civil War fortifications and industrial works, and are studied with documents and maps alongside the ground itself. Native communities persisted and were pushed out during the same span, so the archaeology records both settlement and dispossession.
Historic (Texas, AD 1750–AD 1950).source: From Circleville to Toyah: comments on Central Texas chronology

A phase in the central Texas Archaic sequence, when small mobile bands hunted deer and bison and gathered plant foods across the Edwards Plateau margins. Their most visible traces are accumulations of fire-cracked rock from repeated earth-oven cooking, together with dart points and grinding stones.

Round Rock (Texas, 1550 BC–650 BC).prose:

A phase of the central Texas Archaic identified by Pedernales dart points and the growth of large burned rock middens – accumulations of fire-cracked stone from repeatedly baking plant foods such as sotol and prickly pear bulbs. The pattern suggests hunter-gatherer bands returning again and again to the same cooking places, spending more effort on processing plants alongside deer hunting. These middens are among the most conspicuous archaeological features on the Edwards Plateau.

Late Prehistoric (Texas, AD 630–AD 1700).label: Late Prehistoric
Late Prehistoric (Texas, AD 630–AD 1700).prose:
[Lower Pecos River Region, AD 630–AD 1700] Late Prehistoric. This period does not appear at all in the chart on p. 11, but is clearly defined with two subperiods in the text on pp. 35-36. Period definition from The radiocarbon chronology of the Lower Pecos River Region — Solveig A. Turpin, 1991.

Maize farming, fortified riverside towns and platform mounds spread across the region, with communities organised into chiefdoms whose leaders were buried with shell, copper and finely made pottery. Bows replaced spearthrowers, and shell-tempered pots and triangular arrow points are the typical finds. These were the societies encountered and severely disrupted by the De Soto expedition and the diseases that followed.
Late Prehistoric (Texas, AD 630–AD 1700).source: The radiocarbon chronology of the Lower Pecos River Region

San Felipe Period (Texas, 2150 BC–1250 B.prose:

A Middle Archaic interval in the arid canyonlands and hill country of southern Texas, when small bands of foragers relied heavily on baked desert plants such as sotol and lechuguilla. The huge burned-rock middens and earth-oven pits from these centuries are the accumulated debris of the same cooking spots being reused for generations, a sign that groups were moving in predictable rounds through familiar territory rather than wandering. Distinctive stemmed dart points thrown with the atlatl are the main tool marker.

Infierno Phase (Texas, AD 1500–AD 1700).label: Infierno Phase
Infierno Phase (Texas, AD 1500–AD 1700).prose:
[Lower Pecos River Region, AD 1500–AD 1700] Infierno Phase. "Story's Period VII, Collins' Period J, Dibble's Infierno Phase, Shafer's Comstock Interval" (p. 36); "The Infierno phase is here subsumed under the Late Prehistoric or Flecha period because although 15 radiocarbon dates fall within its estimated span... only one is at all relevant to the cultural phenomena that define this period" (p. 36). In this case, the construction of regional chronologies has helped keep the two distinct" (p. 37). Period definition from The radiocarbon chronology of the Lower Pecos River Region — Solveig A. Turpin, 1991.

The final prehistoric phase of the Lower Pecos canyonlands, when small mobile groups hunted bison and deer with small arrow points and left campsites in rockshelters that earlier peoples had painted. Bows had fully replaced the older dart-and-atlatl toolkit, and pottery and trade goods hint at contacts with peoples further out on the plains and in the Rio Grande valley. These were the communities that Spanish expeditions would meet at the edge of the Chihuahuan Desert.
Infierno Phase (Texas, AD 1500–AD 1700).source: The radiocarbon chronology of the Lower Pecos River Region

Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 1995 BC–1813 BC).label: Middle Kingdom
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 1995 BC–1813 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1995 BC–1813 BC] Middle Kingdom. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt. Period definition from Tell el-Daba Chronology — Manfred Bietak, 2020.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1813.label: Second Intermediate Period
Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1813.prose:
[Egypt, 1813 BC–1530 BC] Second Intermediate Period. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt. Period definition from Tell el-Daba Chronology — Manfred Bietak, 2020.

A divided Egypt, with the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the Delta from Avaris, a rump Theban kingdom in the south, and the Kushite kings of Kerma pressing the frontier. Trade with the Levant and the Aegean flourished at Avaris even as pharaonic art and building shrank. The Theban wars of liberation under Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and finally Ahmose reunified the country and launched the New Kingdom.

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1530 BC–1071 BC).label: New Kingdom
New Kingdom (Egypt, 1530 BC–1071 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1530 BC–1071 BC] New Kingdom. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt. Period definition from Tell el-Daba Chronology — Manfred Bietak, 2020.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1071 B.label: Third Intermediate Period
Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1071 B.prose:
[Egypt, 1071 BC–663 BC] Third Intermediate Period. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt. Period definition from Tell el-Daba Chronology — Manfred Bietak, 2020.

A long stretch of divided rule in which no single king controlled the whole Nile valley. Pharaohs of Libyan descent ruled the Delta while Thebes answered to a priestly dynasty of Amun, and royal tombs were tucked into the temple enclosure at Tanis - one of the few Egyptian royal burials found nearly intact. Kushite kings from Nubia later reunified the country, only for Assyrian invasion to end the period and usher in the Saite revival.

Post-Glacial Period (Texas, 8050 BC–AD 1.label: Post-Glacial Period
Post-Glacial Period (Texas, 8050 BC–AD 1.prose:
[Texas, 8050 BC–AD 1950] Post-Glacial Period. "Present" understood in traditional B.P. dating context as 1950. Period definition from A Late-Quaternary Paleoenvironmental Record of Texas — Vaughn Bryant, 1985.

As the last glaciation ended, Texas warmed and dried, mammoth and other big game vanished, and grasslands, deserts and woodlands shifted into roughly their present arrangement. Foragers adapted with a huge variety of dart points, ground-stone tools and earth ovens for cooking desert plants, leaving the burned-rock middens found across the Hill Country. Farming villages appeared in some regions, but much of the state remained hunter-gatherer country until Europeans arrived.
Post-Glacial Period (Texas, 8050 BC–AD 1.source: A Late-Quaternary Paleoenvironmental Record of Texas

Historic Period (Texas, AD 1690–AD 1950).label: Historic Period
Historic Period (Texas, AD 1690–AD 1950).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 1690–AD 1950] Historic Period. "I consider three subperiods in the Historic period of central Texas—early, middle, and late. In the first two, vestiges of both indigenous and European peoples and cultures are represented; in the third, the indigenous peoples have virtually disappeared" (p 123). "The early Historic subperiod in central Texas begins in the late seventeenth century with the first documented arrival of Europeans... The late Historic subperiod, extending into the twentieth century, encompasses minor numbers of mission Indians, farflung nomadic native groups (primarily the Comanches) until the late nineteenth century, and a rich archeological record of the European-derived cultural presence (D. Fox 1983)" (pp. 123-124). Period definition from Archeology in Central Texas — Michael B. Collins, 2004.

Begins with the first Spanish missions among the Caddo of East Texas and runs through Spanish, Mexican, Republic, and United States rule. Presidios, missions, ranchos, cattle trails, frontier forts and oil-boom towns all fall inside it, alongside Native sites now full of European goods. Few places in North America changed hands and changed character so often in so short a span.

Early Archaic (Texas, 6850 BC–4050 BC).label: Early Archaic
Early Archaic (Texas, 6850 BC–4050 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 6850 BC–4050 BC] Early Archaic. "The early part of the Archaic, from ca. 8800 to 6000 B.P., is here subdivided into the three projectile point style intervals: Angostura (see Fig. 3.13b), early split-stem (see Fig. 3.13e, f ), and Martindale- Uvalde (see Fig. 3.13g–k) (see also Fig. 3.9a)" (p. 119). Period definition from Archeology in Central Texas — Michael B. Collins, 2004.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.

Middle Archaic (Texas, 4050 BC–2050 BC).label: Middle Archaic
Middle Archaic (Texas, 4050 BC–2050 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 4050 BC–2050 BC] Middle Archaic. "The middle subperiod of the Archaic, from ca. 6000 to 4000 B.P., too, is further subdivided into three style intervals: Bell-Andice-Calf Creek, Taylor, and Nolan-Travis (see Figs. 3.9a and 3.14b–g)" (p. 120). Period definition from Archeology in Central Texas — Michael B. Collins, 2004.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

Middle Historic (Texas, AD 1730–AD 1800).label: Middle Historic
Middle Historic (Texas, AD 1730–AD 1800).prose:
[Central Texas, AD 1730–AD 1800] Middle Historic. "The middle Historic subperiod, when much of the record on aboriginal peoples is in reference to remnants of native groups living in the Spanish missions, began in about 1730 and ended in about 1800 as the mission system was failing (Hester 1989a, 1989b)" (p. 124). Period definition from Archeology in Central Texas — Michael B. Collins, 2004.

Spanish missions, presidios and ranches pushed into Texas, while Apache and — increasingly — Comanche horsemen dominated the plains and dictated the terms of trade and war. Native groups adopted horses, guns and metal goods but largely resisted mission life, and epidemics thinned older village societies. Sites from these decades mix European ceramics, glass beads and gunflints with traditional stone tools.

Early Archaic Period (Texas, 6499 BC–359.label: Early Archaic Period
Early Archaic Period (Texas, 6499 BC–359.prose:
[Central Texas, 6499 BC–3599 BC] Early Archaic Period. End date for period taken from chart on p. 5 and from start date of following period. Period definition from A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau — LeRoy Johnson, 1994.

As the Ice Age megafauna vanished and the climate turned warmer and drier, Texas foragers shifted to smaller game, plant foods and a much wider range of dart point styles than their Paleoindian predecessors. Groups became more tied to particular river valleys and springs, and the first earth ovens and burned rock cooking features appear, used to bake bulbs and roots over many hours. Cemeteries at a few sites suggest people were returning to the same places generation after generation.
Early Archaic Period (Texas, 6499 BC–359.source: A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau

Middle Archaic Period (Texas, 3599 BC–22.label: Middle Archaic Period
Middle Archaic Period (Texas, 3599 BC–22.prose:
[Central Texas, 3599 BC–2299 BC] Middle Archaic Period. "The short Middle Archaic period of some 1300 years commences around 3600 B.C. and can best be taken as a transitional epoch" (p. 24). Period definition from A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau — LeRoy Johnson, 1994.

Hunter-gatherer bands adapted to a drier, warmer climate, ranging between water sources and relying more heavily on plant foods, deer and small game than on the big-game hunting of earlier millennia. Burned rock middens - accumulations from earth-oven cooking of plants like sotol and agave - become a characteristic site type. Cemeteries and repeatedly used camps suggest groups were tied to particular stretches of land.
Middle Archaic Period (Texas, 3599 BC–22.source: A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau

Late Archaic I (Texas, 2299 BC–599 BC).label: Late Archaic I
Late Archaic I (Texas, 2299 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Central Texas, 2299 BC–599 BC] Late Archaic I. "However dry the climate of the Edwards Interval, Part I of the Late Archaic period (2300 B.C. to 600 B.C.) witnessed no hardships for the aborigines, who apparently came to thrive on upland semi-succulents" (p. 34). Period definition from A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau — LeRoy Johnson, 1994.

Hunter-gatherers ranged widely over the plains, hills and coast, without pottery or farming but with increasingly regular seasonal rounds. Burned rock middens used for baking plant foods accumulated into large mounds, and formal cemeteries suggest groups were claiming territory. Dart points thrown with the atlatl remained the standard weapon.
Late Archaic I (Texas, 2299 BC–599 BC).source: A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau

Late Archaic II (Texas, 599 BC–AD 600).label: Late Archaic II
Late Archaic II (Texas, 599 BC–AD 600).prose:
[Central Texas, 599 BC–AD 600] Late Archaic II. "In the Late Archaic II subperiod (largely corresponding to the Middle Woodland in eastern North America), which lasted from 600 B.C. to A.D. 600, fairly mesic conditions had returned to all but the western and southwestern parts of the Edwards Plateau" (p. 36). Period definition from A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau — LeRoy Johnson, 1994.

Foraging life continued along familiar routes, but cemeteries, trade goods and regional point styles point to more defined territories and contacts reaching to the Southwest and the Gulf. Burned rock middens went on being used for large-scale plant cooking. The period ends as the bow and arrow, and in some areas pottery, arrive.
Late Archaic II (Texas, 599 BC–AD 600).source: A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau

Middle Byzantine (Byzantine Empire, AD 8.label: Middle Byzantine
Middle Byzantine (Byzantine Empire, AD 8.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 843–AD 1204] Middle Byzantine. "The resolution of the Iconoclastic controversy in favor of the use of icons
ushered in a second flowering of the empire, the Middle Byzantine period (843–1204).". Period definition from The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453) — Sarah Brooks, 2001-2009.

After the disruptions of the early medieval centuries, imperial administration and the church reasserted control over the southwest Peloponnese, and new bishoprics, monasteries and small cross-in-square churches were built. Settlement and agriculture expanded, and Slavic-speaking populations in the interior were gradually Christianised and absorbed. The period ends with the Fourth Crusade, after which Frankish lords carved up the Morea.
Middle Byzantine (Byzantine Empire, AD 8.source: The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453)

Latin Occupation (Byzantine Empire, AD 1.label: Latin Occupation
Latin Occupation (Byzantine Empire, AD 1.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1261] Latin Occupation. "In 1204, armies of the Fourth Crusade invaded from western Europe, conquering the ancient Byzantine imperial capital and founding the “Latin Empire of Constantinople,” while other imperial territories also fell to Crusader rule. The Crusader state in Constantinople was one of several in the thirteenth-century Levant, all under the spiritual authority of the pope as head of the Latin Church of Western Europe... This Crusader state lasted from 1204 until 1261, when Byzantine rule was reestablished in Constantinople and limited portions of the former Byzantine empire were also retaken. The Latin Occupation of 1204–61 had a profound effect on the empire and the Byzantine peoples, causing major political fragmentation as well as the dislocation of Byzantine populations, especially the empire’s nobility and ruling classes.". Period definition from The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453) — Sarah Brooks, 2001-2009.

The Fourth Crusade turned on Constantinople, sacked it in 1204, and installed a Latin emperor while Venice took the harbours and islands it wanted. The Byzantine world fragmented into rival successor states at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond, and the looted relics and bronzes of the city ended up in western churches. Nicaea eventually retook the capital in 1261, but the empire never recovered its wealth or reach.
Latin Occupation (Byzantine Empire, AD 1.source: The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453)

Byzantium (Byzantine Empire, AD 330–AD 1.label: Byzantium
Byzantium (Byzantine Empire, AD 330–AD 1.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 330–AD 1453] Byzantium. Period term derived from the heading of the essay on Byzantine culture and chronology. Period definition from The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453) — Sarah Brooks, 2001-2009.

The eastern half of the Roman empire, refounded on the Bosphorus at Constantinople and outliving the west by a thousand years while gradually becoming Greek-speaking and wholly Christian. Justinian's reconquests, the loss of Egypt and Syria to the Arabs, the icon controversies, the missions that gave the Slavs their alphabet and their Orthodoxy, and the catastrophe of the Fourth Crusade all belong to its story. Its scholars preserved the classical texts that fed the Renaissance, and its end came when Ottoman cannon breached the walls of Constantinople.
Byzantium (Byzantine Empire, AD 330–AD 1.source: The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453)

13th century (Earth, AD 1200–AD 1299).label: 13th century
13th century (Earth, AD 1200–AD 1299).prose:
[World, AD 1200–AD 1299] 13th century. Broad designation derived from pottery chronology and from the stratigraphic history of the site (final period of occupation), independent of historical/art-historical periodization (hence the start at 1200 rather than with the Fourth Crusade and the capture of Constantinople in 1204). Used for the final phase of occupation in the South Region, which seems to have been destroyed before the end of the 13th century and largely abandoned. Period definition from Chersonesos South Region Periodization — Adam Rabinowitz, 2020.

The Mongol conquests linked China, Central Asia, Persia and Russia under one political system for the first time, opening trade and travel routes across Eurasia and carrying goods, ideas and eventually disease along them. In Europe universities, friars and Gothic cathedrals took shape, while Islamic Baghdad fell in 1258. It was a century of unusually wide contact between distant societies.

14th century (Earth, AD 1300–AD 1399).label: 14th century
14th century (Earth, AD 1300–AD 1399).prose:
[World, AD 1300–AD 1399] 14th century. Period definition from Chersonesos South Region Periodization — Adam Rabinowitz, 2020.

Plague spread from Central Asia across the Middle East, North Africa and Europe, killing tens of millions and reshaping labour, land and religion wherever it struck. The Mongol order broke apart: the Yuan fell to the Ming in China, the Ilkhanate collapsed in Persia, and Timur began carving out a new empire. Meanwhile the Ottoman Turks crossed into Europe and West African gold from Mali flowed into Mediterranean markets.

pravěk (Czech Republic, 1000000 BC–AD 58.label: pravěk
pravěk (Czech Republic, 1000000 BC–AD 58.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1000000 BC–AD 580] pravěk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The whole span from the first stone tools left by early humans in the Bohemian Massif to the eve of written history, taking in Neanderthal and mammoth-hunter camps, the arrival of farming villages, the copper and bronze metalworkers of the Únětice world, Celtic oppida with coinage and ironworking, and finally Germanic groups trading across the Roman frontier. Almost everything known about these millennia comes from excavation rather than texts, which is why the label covers so vast a stretch of time. Its close marks the point where the first Slavic settlers and, soon after, written sources begin to define the region.

zemědělský pravěk (Czech Republic, 5600.label: zemědělský pravěk
zemědělský pravěk (Czech Republic, 5600.prose:
[Czech Republic, 5600 BC–AD 580] zemědělský pravěk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

An umbrella term for the whole span of Czech prehistory in which people lived by farming, from the arrival of the first Neolithic villages with their longhouses and linear-decorated pottery to the end of the Migration Period. It covers the introduction of copper and then bronze metallurgy, the plough and the wheel, fortified hilltop settlements, Celtic oppida and coinage, Germanic kingdoms, and finally Roman frontier contact. The thread running through it is the reshaping of the Bohemian and Moravian landscape by cleared fields, permanent settlements and burial grounds.

neolit–eneolit (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–.label: neolit–eneolit
neolit–eneolit (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–.prose:
[Czech Republic, 5600 BC–2301 BC] neolit–eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A single span covering the whole arc from the first farmers to the eve of the Bronze Age. It begins with Linear Pottery longhouses and the ceremonial rondel enclosures, and ends with copper metallurgy, wagons, hilltop strongholds and the individual warrior burials of the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker groups. Between those poles lie the arrival of farming, the plough and wheel, and a major turnover in the region's population.

neolit (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4201 BC).label: neolit
neolit (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4201 BC).prose:
[Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4201 BC] neolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Farming arrived in the Czech lands with the Linear Pottery culture: long timber houses grouped in villages on loess soils, polished stone axes, querns and the first pottery. Later Stroked Pottery and Lengyel communities dug the great circular ditched enclosures - rondels - whose purpose, ceremonial or astronomical, is still debated. The shift from foraging to farming fixed the settlement pattern of the fertile lowlands for millennia.

starší neolit (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4.label: starší neolit
starší neolit (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4.prose:
[Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4701 BC] starší neolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Linear Pottery culture brought agriculture to Bohemia and Moravia, with longhouses of oak posts clustered in villages on fertile loess soils. Farmers grew emmer and einkorn, kept cattle and made distinctive incised pottery, and they raised great circular ditched enclosures - rondels - whose purpose was probably ceremonial. The famous ceramic head from Brno and figurines from the region come from this first farming world.

kultura s lineární keramikou (Czech Repu.node: kultura s lineární keramikou (Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4901 BC)
kultura s lineární keramikou (Czech Repu.label: kultura s lineární keramikou
kultura s lineární keramikou (Czech Repu.prose:
[Czech Republic, 5600 BC–4901 BC] kultura s lineární keramikou. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The first farmers of central Europe, whose arrival brought cereals, cattle, polished stone tools and permanent villages of massive timber longhouses to Bohemia and Moravia. Their pottery, incised with running spirals and meanders, is remarkably uniform from the Rhine to the Danube bend, evidence of fast expansion and close-knit exchange. The end of the period saw ditched enclosures, fortified sites and, at places such as Talheim and Asparn, the earliest clear traces of massacre in the region.

šárecký typ (Czech Republic, 5000 BC–490.label: šárecký typ
šárecký typ (Czech Republic, 5000 BC–490.prose:
[Czech Republic, 5000 BC–4901 BC] šárecký typ. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The final phase of the Linear Pottery culture in Bohemia, named after the Šárka valley near Prague. Vessel decoration became crowded and elaborate, with dense incised bands and knobs, as the long-established longhouse villages of the first farmers reached the end of their run. Within a few generations the region's pottery and settlement patterns changed completely.

želiezovská skupina (Czech Republic, 500.label: želiezovská skupina
želiezovská skupina (Czech Republic, 500.prose:
[Czech Republic, 5000 BC–4701 BC] želiezovská skupina. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late regional branch of the Linear Pottery culture across southern Slovakia, Moravia and into Bohemia and Hungary. Its potters filled the usual incised bands with painted or notched infill, producing an unusually decorative style that archaeologists use to trace contacts across the middle Danube. It represents the last generations of the first farming communities before the Copper Age transformation.

oberlauterbašská skupina (Czech Republic.label: oberlauterbašská skupina
oberlauterbašská skupina (Czech Republic.prose: [Czech Republic, 5000 BC–4601 BC] oberlauterbašská skupina. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

střední–mladší neolit (Czech Republic, 4.label: střední–mladší neolit
střední–mladší neolit (Czech Republic, 4.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4700 BC–4201 BC] střední–mladší neolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Stroked Pottery culture succeeded the earliest farmers, keeping longhouse villages but changing pottery styles and building ever more elaborate circular rondel enclosures with concentric ditches and precisely aligned gateways. Towards the end of the phase the painted wares of the Lengyel tradition spread in from the southeast. These enclosures are among the oldest monumental architecture anywhere in Europe.

kultura s vypíchanou keramikou (Czech Re.node: kultura s vypíchanou keramikou (Czech Republic, 4900 BC–4401 BC)
kultura s vypíchanou keramikou (Czech Re.label: kultura s vypíchanou keramikou
kultura s vypíchanou keramikou (Czech Re.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4900 BC–4401 BC] kultura s vypíchanou keramikou. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The successor to Linear Pottery in Bohemia and central Germany, distinguished by decoration made with a stabbing, rocking tool that produced bands of stitch-like punctures. Longhouses grew trapezoidal, and the first circular ditched enclosures - the roundels - appear, among the oldest monumental architecture in Europe. Communities became more regionally distinct as the uniform world of the first farmers broke up.

kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou.node: kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou 1 (Czech Republic, 4700 BC–4501 BC)
kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou.label: kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou 1
kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4700 BC–4501 BC] kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou 1. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Moravian branch of the Lengyel world at its height, producing thin-walled bowls and pedestalled vessels painted in red, yellow and white. This phase is famous for the roundels - circular ditched enclosures with precisely aligned entrances - built across Moravia and Lower Austria and interpreted as gathering places or calendrical monuments. Fired clay figurines, including the celebrated 'Venus' from Střelice, come from these settlements.

lengyelská kultura (Czech Republic, 4600.label: lengyelská kultura
lengyelská kultura (Czech Republic, 4600.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4600 BC–4201 BC] lengyelská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Farmers of this period made fine painted pottery and, most strikingly, dug the great circular ditch-and-palisade enclosures known as rondels, some over a hundred metres across, with entrances aligned on solar events. These are among the oldest monumental structures in Europe, built for gatherings or ritual rather than defence. Longhouse settlements, copper ornaments and figurines round out a picture of increasingly organised village life.

kultura münchshöfenská (Czech Republic,.label: kultura münchshöfenská
kultura münchshöfenská (Czech Republic,.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4500 BC–4201 BC] kultura münchshöfenská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A Middle Neolithic culture of Bavaria that reached into southwestern Bohemia, following on from the painted-ware traditions of the Danube. Its farmers lived in dispersed settlements and made plain, dark, well-burnished pottery, including distinctive footed bowls and drum-shaped vessels. The period saw copper objects and salt exchange spreading up the Danube corridor.

eneolit (Czech Republic, 4500 BC–2301 BC.label: eneolit
eneolit (Czech Republic, 4500 BC–2301 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4500 BC–2301 BC] eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Copper metallurgy, the ard, wheeled vehicles and draught cattle transformed farming and travel, while society grew more visibly hierarchical and male-centred. A rapid succession of cultures — Funnel Beaker, Baden, then the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker groups with their single graves and standardised drinking vessels — reflects both local change and incoming steppe ancestry. Hilltop enclosures and the first defended settlements appear across Bohemia and Moravia.

časný eneolit (Czech Republic, 4500 BC–3.label: časný eneolit
časný eneolit (Czech Republic, 4500 BC–3.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4500 BC–3801 BC] časný eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The centuries when copper began to matter in Bohemia. Farming changed with the ard plough, ox traction and greater reliance on cattle and dairy, settlement shifted towards higher and more defensible ground, and copper axes and ornaments circulated as marks of status. It is the point at which Neolithic village society gives way to a more mobile, more hierarchical world.

kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou.node: kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou 2 (Czech Republic, 4500 BC–4101 BC)
kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou.label: kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou 2
kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4500 BC–4101 BC] kultura s moravskou malovanou keramikou 2. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The later Lengyel phase in Moravia, when painted decoration faded and pottery became plainer and more angular. Roundel building ceased, settlements shifted and copper began to circulate more widely, foreshadowing the Eneolithic. It closes the long era of Danubian painted-ware farming in the region.

jordanovská kultura (Czech Republic, 420.label: jordanovská kultura
jordanovská kultura (Czech Republic, 420.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4200 BC–4001 BC] jordanovská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Named after Jordanów in Silesia, this culture grew out of the late Lengyel tradition in Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia as painted pottery gave way to plain, finely finished wares. Copper ornaments and small tools appear more regularly in its graves, marking the shift from the Neolithic into the Copper Age. Burials in flat cemeteries with grave goods graded by wealth hint at growing social distinctions.

schusseriedská kultura (Czech Republic,.label: schusseriedská kultura
schusseriedská kultura (Czech Republic,.prose: [Czech Republic, 4200 BC–3801 BC] schusseriedská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

michelsberská kultura (Czech Republic, 4.label: michelsberská kultura
michelsberská kultura (Czech Republic, 4.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4000 BC–3801 BC] michelsberská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Communities of this horizon built causewayed enclosures ringed by interrupted ditches, used simple undecorated tulip beakers and clay 'baking plates', and mined and traded flint over long distances. In Bohemia their material appears at the western edge of the culture's range, marking contact with the Rhineland and central Germany. The enclosures served as meeting places, refuges and settings for ritual deposits of bone and pottery.

starší eneolit (Czech Republic, 3900 BC–.label: starší eneolit
starší eneolit (Czech Republic, 3900 BC–.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3900 BC–3351 BC] starší eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Copper metallurgy took hold and society changed with it: the plough, wheeled vehicles and greater use of cattle transformed farming, while the old large Neolithic villages gave way to smaller, more dispersed settlements. The Funnel Beaker culture spread across Bohemia and Moravia, building the first megalithic-style long barrows in the region. Rising conflict is suggested by new hilltop enclosures and by the appearance of copper and stone axes as symbols of male status.

kultura Retz-Bajč-Křepice (Czech Republi.label: kultura Retz-Bajč-Křepice
kultura Retz-Bajč-Křepice (Czech Republi.prose:
[Czech Republic, 4000 BC–3501 BC] kultura Retz-Bajč-Křepice. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

An Early Eneolithic group spanning Lower Austria, Moravia and southwestern Slovakia, recognised above all by its Furchenstich pottery - vessels decorated with dragged, stabbed lines often filled with white paste. It belongs to the unsettled centuries after the collapse of the great Lengyel roundel-building communities, when populations dispersed and older painted-ware traditions disappeared.

kultura nálevkovitých pohárů (Czech Repu.node: kultura nálevkovitých pohárů (Czech Republic, 3900 BC–3301 BC)
kultura nálevkovitých pohárů (Czech Repu.label: kultura nálevkovitých pohárů
kultura nálevkovitých pohárů (Czech Repu.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3900 BC–3301 BC] kultura nálevkovitých pohárů. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Farming communities across Bohemia and Moravia who took their name from the funnel-necked beaker, part of a vast network stretching from the Netherlands to Ukraine. They brought the plough, wheeled vehicles and heavier reliance on cattle, and in some regions built long earthen barrows and fortified hilltop sites. Their landscape clearance and monument-building mark the point when Neolithic farmers began reshaping the countryside on a large scale.

ohrozimský typ (Czech Republic, 3500 BC–.label: ohrozimský typ
ohrozimský typ (Czech Republic, 3500 BC–.prose: [Czech Republic, 3500 BC–3301 BC] ohrozimský typ. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

střední eneolit (Czech Republic, 3350 BC.label: střední eneolit
střední eneolit (Czech Republic, 3350 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3350 BC–2801 BC] střední eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Baden culture and its relatives spread from the middle Danube, bringing distinctive channelled pottery, wagon models and evidence of ox traction. Settlement shifted towards higher, defensible ground, and burial customs diversified, including occasional cattle burials. It is a phase of mobility and contact stretching from the Carpathian Basin deep into central Europe.

badenská kultura (Czech Republic, 3400 B.label: badenská kultura
badenská kultura (Czech Republic, 3400 B.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3400 BC–2901 BC] badenská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Copper Age culture spread across the Danube basin, known for dark burnished pottery with channelled decoration, hilltop and lakeside settlements, and unusually rich evidence for a new economy built on cattle. Clay models of four-wheeled wagons and paired ox burials from Baden sites are among the earliest proof of wheeled transport in Europe. Cremation appears alongside inhumation, and its wide, loosely shared style hints at long-distance contacts running from the Alps to the Balkans.

chamská kultura (Czech Republic, 3100 BC.label: chamská kultura
chamská kultura (Czech Republic, 3100 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3100 BC–2801 BC] chamská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Copper Age culture of the upper Danube region and neighbouring uplands, marked by fortified hilltop settlements with ditches and palisades and by coarse, sparsely decorated pottery. The defended sites suggest a more unsettled, competitive landscape, and it stands at the threshold of the Bell Beaker and Corded Ware world that followed.

řivnáčská kultura (Czech Republic, 3100.label: řivnáčská kultura
řivnáčská kultura (Czech Republic, 3100.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3100 BC–2801 BC] řivnáčská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Late Copper Age communities of central Bohemia, known from fortified hilltop settlements such as Řivnáč itself and from pottery with distinctive handled jugs and amphorae. They lived alongside and after the Baden and Globular Amphora groups, in an era of small, defensible sites, herding and copper exchange, just before the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker horizons reshaped the region.

kultura kulovitých amfor (Czech Republic.node: kultura kulovitých amfor (Czech Republic, 3100 BC–2801 BC)
kultura kulovitých amfor (Czech Republic.label: kultura kulovitých amfor
kultura kulovitých amfor (Czech Republic.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3100 BC–2801 BC] kultura kulovitých amfor. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Herders of the north European plain who pushed into Bohemia and Moravia, named for their round-bodied amphorae with short necks and cord- or stab-decorated shoulders. They are best known for burials in stone cists and for ritual deposits of cattle, sometimes whole teams, interred with as much care as people. Their mobile, stock-raising way of life anticipates the Corded Ware world that followed.

mladší eneolit (Czech Republic, 3100 BC–.label: mladší eneolit
mladší eneolit (Czech Republic, 3100 BC–.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3100 BC–2301 BC] mladší eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Copper-using farming communities of the Baden and Rivnac type built fortified hilltop settlements and used ox-drawn wagons and the plough, changes that reshaped how land was farmed and who controlled it. Burials shift towards individual graves with weapons and drinking vessels rather than communal rites. The period closes as Corded Ware groups spread across the region with their battle-axes and crouched single burials.

jevišovická kultura (Czech Republic, 310.label: jevišovická kultura
jevišovická kultura (Czech Republic, 310.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3100 BC–2801 BC] jevišovická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Copper Age culture of Moravia and neighbouring Lower Austria, named after the stratified hilltop site at Jevišovice, whose layered deposits helped establish the region's prehistoric sequence. Its people favoured fortified positions on high ground and made dark, burnished pottery with incised and channelled decoration. It belongs to the post-Baden world that preceded the Corded Ware horizon.

bošácká skupina (Czech Republic, 3000 BC.label: bošácká skupina
bošácká skupina (Czech Republic, 3000 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 3000 BC–2601 BC] bošácká skupina. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Copper Age group of the middle Danube region, generally seen as a post-Baden development, recognised chiefly from its distinctive pottery in cave and open settlements and in cremation burials.

mladší/pozdní eneolit (Czech Republic, 2.label: mladší/pozdní eneolit
mladší/pozdní eneolit (Czech Republic, 2.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2900 BC–2201 BC] mladší/pozdní eneolit. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Dominated by Corded Ware and then Bell Beaker communities, whose single graves - men and women laid on opposite sides, facing a set direction, with axes, daggers and beakers - replaced older collective burial customs. Copper and the first gold ornaments circulate, along with archery gear and wrist-guards. Genetic and archaeological work now links these groups to large-scale movement of people from the steppe, a turning point in European ancestry.

kultura se šňůrovou keramikou (Czech Rep.node: kultura se šňůrovou keramikou (Czech Republic, 2900 BC–2501 BC)
kultura se šňůrovou keramikou (Czech Rep.label: kultura se šňůrovou keramikou
kultura se šňůrovou keramikou (Czech Rep.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2900 BC–2501 BC] kultura se šňůrovou keramikou. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A sweeping change in burial and belief: individual graves under barrows, men laid on their right side and women on their left, accompanied by stone battle-axes and cord-impressed beakers. Ancient DNA shows these communities carried steppe ancestry from the Pontic region, part of a migration that reshaped the genetic make-up of Europe and is tied to the spread of Indo-European languages. Settlement traces are scarce, suggesting a mobile, pastoral way of life.

kultura Kosihy-Čaka (Czech Republic, 280.label: kultura Kosihy-Čaka
kultura Kosihy-Čaka (Czech Republic, 280.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2800 BC–2301 BC] kultura Kosihy-Čaka. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Eneolithic to earliest Bronze Age horizon of southern Moravia and southern Slovakia, closely tied to the Makó group of the Carpathian Basin. Settlement was dispersed and shallow, with simple coarse pottery bearing knobs and brushed surfaces, and cremation appears alongside inhumation. It marks the point at which the Carpathian Basin began the shift toward the tell-building, bronze-working world of the Early Bronze Age.

kultura zvoncovitých pohárů (Czech Repub.node: kultura zvoncovitých pohárů (Czech Republic, 2500 BC–2201 BC)
kultura zvoncovitých pohárů (Czech Repub.label: kultura zvoncovitých pohárů
kultura zvoncovitých pohárů (Czech Repub.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2500 BC–2201 BC] kultura zvoncovitých pohárů. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The last Eneolithic phenomenon before the Bronze Age, marked by bell-shaped beakers with zoned stamped decoration, archers' wristguards, tanged copper daggers and gold ornaments. It spread from Iberia to the Carpathians as a shared package of prestige objects and burial customs rather than a single people, though migration and intermarriage clearly played a part. In Bohemia and Moravia its graves show the arrival of skilled metalworking and long-distance contacts that the Early Bronze Age would build on.

kultura Chlopice-Veselé (Czech Republic,.label: kultura Chlopice-Veselé
kultura Chlopice-Veselé (Czech Republic,.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2400 BC–2101 BC] kultura Chlopice-Veselé. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Corded Ware offshoot of the eastern Moravian, west Slovak and south Polish uplands, known mainly from crouched burials with cord-impressed and incised cups. It sits on the hinge between the Eneolithic and the Early Bronze Age, and its communities fed directly into the Nitra culture and the metal-using societies that followed. The grave goods show stone battle-axes and flint giving ground to the first regular copper ornaments.

doba bronzová–halštatská (Czech Republic.label: doba bronzová–halštatská
doba bronzová–halštatská (Czech Republic.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2300 BC–481 BC] doba bronzová–halštatská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A broad bracket used for finds that can only be placed somewhere between the first flourishing of bronze metallurgy and the early Iron Age. It covers the shift from Únětice hoards through the Urnfield cremation cemeteries to the wealthy chiefly burials of the Hallstatt world. Objects dated this loosely usually come from disturbed contexts or surface collections.

doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 2300 BC–7.label: doba bronzová
doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 2300 BC–7.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2300 BC–751 BC] doba bronzová. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Metal moved from novelty to necessity: Únětice communities buried hoards of bronze axes and ingot rings, and later Tumulus and Urnfield populations reorganised settlement, burial and warfare across Bohemia and Moravia. Long-distance exchange linked the region to Baltic amber and Carpathian copper, and cremation in urnfields replaced older inhumation rites. The fortified hilltop sites and metalwork hoards of this era are among the richest prehistoric finds in the Czech lands.

starší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 23.node: starší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 2300 BC–1551 BC)
starší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 23.label: starší doba bronzová
starší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 23.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2300 BC–1551 BC] starší doba bronzová. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Únětice culture dominated Bohemia and Moravia, with tightly organised cemeteries of crouched burials and a metal industry that turned out ingot torcs, daggers and pins on an almost industrial scale. Control of copper and tin routes and the amber trade made local elites rich, and spectacular hoards were buried in the ground. This was the moment when central Europe first developed a genuine bronze economy with standardised, widely traded products.

protoúnětická kultura (Czech Republic, 2.label: protoúnětická kultura
protoúnětická kultura (Czech Republic, 2.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2300 BC–2001 BC] protoúnětická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The bridge between the Bell Beaker world and the full Early Bronze Age in Bohemia and Moravia, when small farming communities began burying their dead in crouched position in flat cemeteries with modest copper ornaments and pins. Pottery forms and metalworking habits developed here grew directly into those of the Únětice culture, whose bronze hoards and wealthy graves would dominate central Europe for the next five centuries.

únětická kultura (Czech Republic, 2300 B.label: únětická kultura
únětická kultura (Czech Republic, 2300 B.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2300 BC–1651 BC] únětická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Central Europe's first fully metal-using society, built on tin bronze rather than copper alone. Flat cemeteries of crouched burials, standardised axes, daggers and pins, and spectacular hoards of ingot-rings show craft specialisation and long-distance trade in tin, amber and gold. Wealth concentrated in a few princely graves and fortified sites, marking the beginnings of hereditary rank in the region.

nitranská kultura (Czech Republic, 2100.label: nitranská kultura
nitranská kultura (Czech Republic, 2100.prose:
[Czech Republic, 2100 BC–1801 BC] nitranská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

An Early Bronze Age community known almost entirely from its cemeteries: rows of crouched inhumations, men often with flint arrowheads and copper daggers, women with spiral hair-rings and bone or shell ornaments. The graves show clear differences in wealth and weaponry, one of the earliest signs of ranked warrior society in the middle Danube region. It stands at the threshold of the Únětice world that would dominate Central Europe's bronze trade.

hatvanská kultura (Czech Republic, 1800.label: hatvanská kultura
hatvanská kultura (Czech Republic, 1800.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1800 BC–1601 BC] hatvanská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A Bronze Age population of the northern Carpathian Basin whose villages were rebuilt on the same spot for generations, piling up tell mounds behind ditches and ramparts. Their fortified settlements and standardised, textile-impressed pottery point to organised communities controlling routes towards the copper and gold of the Slovak ore mountains, and they were eventually absorbed into the Otomani and Füzesabony world.

věteřovská kultura (Czech Republic, 1700.label: věteřovská kultura
věteřovská kultura (Czech Republic, 1700.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1700 BC–1501 BC] věteřovská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The successor to Únětice in Moravia, marked by a shift to strongly fortified hilltop settlements with ditches and ramparts. Metalwork and pottery show close ties to the tell-building cultures of the Carpathian Basin, suggesting competition over trade routes carrying copper, tin and amber. The defensive turn hints at a more unsettled, hierarchical world at the close of the Early Bronze Age.

střední doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 1.node: střední doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 1700 BC–1251 BC)
střední doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 1.label: střední doba bronzová
střední doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 1.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1700 BC–1251 BC] střední doba bronzová. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Burial under mounds became the norm, giving the Tumulus culture its name, and the tight order of Únětice cemeteries dissolved into a more dispersed pattern of settlement. Bronze became abundant, with new sword types, sheet-metal ornaments and body armour reflecting a warrior ethos. Hoards deposited in wet places and on hilltops suggest ritual as much as safekeeping.

středodunajská mohylová kultura (Czech R.node: středodunajská mohylová kultura (Czech Republic, 1650 BC–1251 BC)
středodunajská mohylová kultura (Czech R.label: středodunajská mohylová kultura
středodunajská mohylová kultura (Czech R.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1650 BC–1251 BC] středodunajská mohylová kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A Middle Danube branch of the tumulus tradition, centred on Moravia and the neighbouring Danube lands, whose people buried their dead under earth mounds with bronze pins, arm rings and sword daggers. Settlement was dispersed, with a strong reliance on stock-keeping and seasonal movement in upland areas. Its pottery and metalwork show close ties to Bavaria, Austria and the Carpathian Basin, and its communities fed directly into the later Urnfield world.

českofalcká mohylová kultura (Czech Repu.node: českofalcká mohylová kultura (Czech Republic, 1650 BC–1251 BC)
českofalcká mohylová kultura (Czech Repu.label: českofalcká mohylová kultura
českofalcká mohylová kultura (Czech Repu.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1650 BC–1251 BC] českofalcká mohylová kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Middle Bronze Age communities of western Bohemia and the Upper Palatinate who buried their dead under earthen mounds, often with bronze pins, spiral ornaments, daggers and swords. The barrow cemeteries, still visible in woodland today, replaced the flat graves of earlier centuries and suggest kin groups marking their claim to the landscape. Their metalwork links them to a broad Tumulus culture stretching across central Europe.

období popelnicových polí (Czech Republi.node: období popelnicových polí (Czech Republic, 1300 BC–801 BC)
období popelnicových polí (Czech Republi.label: období popelnicových polí
období popelnicových polí (Czech Republi.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1300 BC–801 BC] období popelnicových polí. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Communities across Bohemia and Moravia abandoned burial mounds for vast cemeteries of cremated dead placed in pottery urns, giving the period its name. Bronze production reached industrial scale, with sheet-metal vessels, swords and ornaments buried in hoards, and fortified hilltop settlements appeared across the landscape. These populations laid the demographic and technological foundations for the Iron Age Hallstatt world.

mladší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 12.node: mladší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 1250 BC–1001 BC)
mladší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 12.label: mladší doba bronzová
mladší doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 12.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1250 BC–1001 BC] mladší doba bronzová. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Urnfield communities dominated Bohemia and Moravia: the dead were cremated and buried in urns in large flat cemeteries, and villages clustered near fertile lowlands with hillforts above them. Bronze became genuinely abundant, and hoards of sickles, axes, swords and ornaments were buried in the ground in numbers never seen before. The Knovíz and Lusatian groups of this time set the settlement pattern that carried on into the Iron Age.

lužická kultura (Czech Republic, 1300 BC.label: lužická kultura
lužická kultura (Czech Republic, 1300 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1300 BC–1026 BC] lužická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Cremation replaced inhumation, and the dead were buried in urns in cemeteries that could hold thousands of graves, giving the wider Urnfield tradition its name. Communities built hilltop strongholds with ramparts and produced sheet-bronze vessels, sickles and pins in quantity. The pattern of fortified sites and mass-produced metalwork points to a crowded, competitive Late Bronze Age landscape.

velatická kultura (Czech Republic, 1300.label: velatická kultura
velatická kultura (Czech Republic, 1300.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1300 BC–1001 BC] velatická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A Moravian branch of the great Urnfield world, whose people cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large flat cemeteries. Bronze was produced and consumed on an unprecedented scale, and hoards of axes, sickles, swords and sheet-bronze vessels are found across the region. Fortified hilltop settlements point to organised communities linked into long-distance trade along the Danube and Morava.

milavečská kultura (Czech Republic, 1250.label: milavečská kultura
milavečská kultura (Czech Republic, 1250.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1250 BC–976 BC] milavečská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

This west Bohemian group buried its dead cremated beneath barrows, a bridge between the older tumulus tradition and the urnfields to come. Its best-known find is the bronze four-wheeled cart carrying a cauldron from the Milavče barrow, a ceremonial vehicle probably tied to sun symbolism found across Bronze Age Europe. Rich bronze hoards from the region show skilled local casting and wide trade contacts.

knovízská kultura (Czech Republic, 1250.label: knovízská kultura
knovízská kultura (Czech Republic, 1250.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1250 BC–951 BC] knovízská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The dominant Late Bronze Age culture of central and western Bohemia, part of the wider Urnfield world, whose people cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large communal cemeteries. Settlements are known mainly from clusters of deep storage pits, some containing scattered and cut human bones that have fuelled long debate about ritual killing or cannibalism. Bronze production and hoarding reached a peak, and hilltop sites were fortified.

chebská kultura (Czech Republic, 1200 BC.label: chebská kultura
chebská kultura (Czech Republic, 1200 BC.prose: [Czech Republic, 1200 BC–1001 BC] chebská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

saská lužická kultura (Czech Republic, 1.node: saská lužická kultura (Czech Republic, 1300 BC–751 BC)
saská lužická kultura (Czech Republic, 1.label: saská lužická kultura
saská lužická kultura (Czech Republic, 1.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1300 BC–751 BC] saská lužická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A regional branch of the wider Lusatian urnfield world in the north-west, where the dead were cremated and their ashes placed in urns in large flat cemeteries. Bronze casting was prolific – pins, sickles, razors and vessels – and communities gathered around fortified hilltop sites that controlled routes across the mountains into Saxony.

pozdní doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 10.node: pozdní doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 1000 BC–751 BC)
pozdní doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 10.label: pozdní doba bronzová
pozdní doba bronzová (Czech Republic, 10.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1000 BC–751 BC] pozdní doba bronzová. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Urnfield societies reached their height: the dead were cremated and buried in cemeteries of hundreds of urns, while metalworkers turned out sheet-bronze vessels, sickles, swords and ornaments in quantities never seen before. Enormous hoards were buried across the landscape, and fortified hilltop settlements controlled routes and metal supplies. Iron begins to appear at the very end, opening the way to the Hallstatt period.

slezskoplatěnická kultura (Czech Republi.label: slezskoplatěnická kultura
slezskoplatěnická kultura (Czech Republi.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1100 BC–451 BC] slezskoplatěnická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The eastern Bohemian branch of the Lusatian urnfield tradition, named after two type sites, which cremated its dead and buried them with elaborate pottery services. Over its long life it shifted from bronze to iron, absorbed Hallstatt fashions in metalwork and horse gear, and produced painted and graphite-decorated vessels among the finest of prehistoric central Europe.

slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaB) (Czech R.label: slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaB)
slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaB) (Czech R.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1100 BC–801 BC] slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaB). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The earlier, Silesian-style phase of the eastern Bohemian urnfields, still firmly a bronze-using world. Cemeteries hold hundreds of cremations in urns accompanied by richly profiled and grooved pottery, and hoards of bronze ornaments and tools point to busy local workshops and long-distance exchange.

podolská kultura (Czech Republic, 1025 B.label: podolská kultura
podolská kultura (Czech Republic, 1025 B.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1025 BC–751 BC] podolská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The last phase of the urnfield world in Moravia, following on from the Velatice culture. Communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large flat cemeteries, produced fine burnished pottery, and deposited large hoards of bronze tools, weapons and ornaments in the ground. Its settlements and metalwork traditions carried directly into the Hallstatt Iron Age.

štítarská kultura (Czech Republic, 1025.label: štítarská kultura
štítarská kultura (Czech Republic, 1025.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1025 BC–751 BC] štítarská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The final stage of the Knovíz tradition in Bohemia, at the close of the Bronze Age. People cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urn cemeteries, lived in open lowland settlements with deep storage pits, and produced fine dark burnished pottery. Their world dissolved into the earliest Hallstatt phase, when iron began to displace bronze.

slezská kultura (Czech Republic, 1000 BC.label: slezská kultura
slezská kultura (Czech Republic, 1000 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 1000 BC–801 BC] slezská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Bronze Age urnfield group of the north-east, cremating its dead and placing the ashes in tall, sharply profiled urns within extensive flat cemeteries. Bronze remained the metal of choice for ornaments, weapons and vessels, and the culture forms the direct ancestor of the later Silesian–Platěnice tradition.

nynická kultura (Czech Republic, 975 BC–.label: nynická kultura
nynická kultura (Czech Republic, 975 BC–.prose:
[Czech Republic, 975 BC–751 BC] nynická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Urnfield community of western Bohemia, known from cremation cemeteries where ashes were placed in urns alongside distinctive fine, often graphite-burnished pottery. Its metalwork and hoards mark the transition from the Bronze Age into the earliest Iron Age in the region. The group's territory sat between the Bavarian and central Bohemian worlds and shows influences from both.

billendorfská kultura (Czech Republic, 9.label: billendorfská kultura
billendorfská kultura (Czech Republic, 9.prose:
[Czech Republic, 950 BC–451 BC] billendorfská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late offshoot of the Lusatian urnfield tradition in Lusatia and the neighbouring borderlands, carrying cremation burial in large urnfields into the Hallstatt Iron Age. Its graves show iron slowly displacing bronze while the older Urnfield burial rite continued largely unchanged.

doba halštatská–laténská (Czech Republic.label: doba halštatská–laténská
doba halštatská–laténská (Czech Republic.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–31 BC] doba halštatská–laténská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A combined span covering the whole Iron Age, from the wagon-grave aristocracies of the early period to the Celtic oppida and coinage of the later one. It is used when material — a scatter of iron slag, a settlement pit, a plain sherd — cannot be pinned to either half. The transition itself saw art styles, weaponry and social organisation transformed by contact with the Mediterranean world.

doba halštatská (Czech Republic, 800 BC–.label: doba halštatská
doba halštatská (Czech Republic, 800 BC–.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–371 BC] doba halštatská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Iron replaced bronze for everyday tools while elites displayed their status in wagon burials under great mounds, furnished with imported bronze vessels and horse gear. Bohemian and Moravian communities sat at the northern edge of a network reaching to the Alpine salt mines and to Mediterranean traders. Painted pottery, fortified hilltop residences and richly equipped graves make this one of the most visible prehistoric periods in the landscape.

starší doba halštatská (HaC–D1) (Czech R.node: starší doba halštatská (HaC–D1) (Czech Republic, 800 BC–541 BC)
starší doba halštatská (HaC–D1) (Czech R.label: starší doba halštatská (HaC–D1)
starší doba halštatská (HaC–D1) (Czech R.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–541 BC] starší doba halštatská (HaC–D1). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons, and society became sharply hierarchical: chieftains were buried in timber chambers under mounds with four-wheeled wagons, horse harness and imported goods. Bylany-culture communities in eastern Bohemia and the Horákov culture in Moravia mark the region's western and eastern faces. Trade contacts reached the Alps and, further off, the Mediterranean, bringing bronze vessels and new tastes in feasting.

billendorfská kultura (HaC) (Czech Repub.label: billendorfská kultura (HaC)
billendorfská kultura (HaC) (Czech Repub.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–626 BC] billendorfská kultura (HaC). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The earlier Iron Age stage of this late Lusatian group, when iron objects begin appearing in cremation graves alongside traditional bronze ornaments and urn burial continued in the old Urnfield manner.

bylanská kultura (Czech Republic, 800 BC.label: bylanská kultura
bylanská kultura (Czech Republic, 800 BC.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–531 BC] bylanská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The early Iron Age elite culture of central Bohemia, best known for its chamber graves under mounds containing dismantled four-wheeled wagons, horse harness, bronze vessels and imported goods. These burials mark the emergence of a warrior aristocracy that controlled trade routes to the Hallstatt world further south, laying the ground for the Celtic societies that followed.

halštatská mohylová kultura (Czech Repub.node: halštatská mohylová kultura (Czech Republic, 800 BC–531 BC)
halštatská mohylová kultura (Czech Repub.label: halštatská mohylová kultura
halštatská mohylová kultura (Czech Repub.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–531 BC] halštatská mohylová kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

West and south Bohemian communities returned to burying their dead under earthen mounds, some containing four-wheeled wagons, horse gear and imported bronze vessels — the graves of a warrior aristocracy enriched by control of trade and metal. Iron replaced bronze for weapons and tools, and hilltop seats of power appeared. These are the societies from which the Celtic princely centres of the following century grew.

horákovská kultura (Czech Republic, 800.label: horákovská kultura
horákovská kultura (Czech Republic, 800.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–461 BC] horákovská kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Moravia's version of the Hallstatt world, sitting at the western edge of the eastern Hallstatt sphere and named after a cemetery near Brno. Elite families were buried under large mounds in timber chambers, sometimes with four-wheeled wagons, bronze vessels and finely made painted and graphite pottery. The tradition faded as La Tène Celtic culture spread through the region.

platěnická kultura (Czech Republic, 800.label: platěnická kultura
platěnická kultura (Czech Republic, 800.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–401 BC] platěnická kultura. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The final stage of the Lusatian urnfield tradition in the eastern Czech lands, when cremation burial continued but grave goods grew richer and more varied under influences from the Hallstatt world to the west. Cemeteries yield elegant black burnished pottery with graphite decoration, iron tools alongside bronze, and occasional horse gear and wagon fittings marking out leading families. It represents the last generations of urnfield society before Celtic La Tène culture reshaped the region.
