slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaC–D) (Czech.label: slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaC–D)
slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaC–D) (Czech.prose:
[Czech Republic, 800 BC–371 BC] slezskoplatěnická kultura (HaC–D). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Platěnice phase, when iron tools and weapons became common and Hallstatt influences arrived from the west and south. Potters produced graphite-coated and painted vessels in large sets, some burials contain horse harness and wagon fittings, and the culture faded as Celtic La Tène groups moved into the region.

turnovský typ (Czech Republic, 410 BC–32.label: turnovský typ
turnovský typ (Czech Republic, 410 BC–32.prose: [Czech Republic, 410 BC–321 BC] turnovský typ. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

HaD–LtA (Czech Republic, 625 BC–371 BC).label: HaD–LtA
HaD–LtA (Czech Republic, 625 BC–371 BC).prose:
[Czech Republic, 625 BC–371 BC] HaD–LtA. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The late Hallstatt into early La Tène transition, when Central European elites were buried under great mounds with wagons, gold neck-rings and imported Mediterranean drinking vessels, and hilltop centres controlled trade routes to the Greek and Etruscan south. Around the end of the period the new La Tène art style emerged, with sinuous plant and animal motifs that would define Celtic craftsmanship for centuries.

mladší doba halštatská (HaD2–3) (Czech R.node: mladší doba halštatská (HaD2–3) (Czech Republic, 540 BC–461 BC)
mladší doba halštatská (HaD2–3) (Czech R.label: mladší doba halštatská (HaD2–3)
mladší doba halštatská (HaD2–3) (Czech R.prose:
[Czech Republic, 540 BC–461 BC] mladší doba halštatská (HaD2–3). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Late Hallstatt society in Bohemia was topped by an elite buried under barrows with wagons, weapons and imported bronze vessels, drinking wine that had travelled north from Greek and Etruscan workshops. Fortified seats controlled the trade in salt, amber and metals. Within a generation or two the ornament on their metalwork twists into the new curvilinear style that marks the start of the La Tene world.

doba laténská–římská (Czech Republic, 45.label: doba laténská–římská
doba laténská–římská (Czech Republic, 45.prose:
[Czech Republic, 450 BC–AD 400] doba laténská–římská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A wide bracket spanning the Celtic Iron Age and the following centuries when Germanic groups such as the Marcomanni dominated the region and Roman goods flowed north across the frontier. Finds dated this way typically come from long-used settlements or from contexts too poor to separate La Tène from Roman-period material. Between the two lies one of the sharpest cultural breaks in Czech prehistory.

doba laténská (Czech Republic, 450 BC–31.label: doba laténská
doba laténská (Czech Republic, 450 BC–31.prose:
[Czech Republic, 450 BC–31 BC] doba laténská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Celtic centuries in Bohemia and Moravia: flat cemeteries with warrior graves, curvilinear La Tène ornament, the potter's wheel, iron-working on an industrial scale and the first coins struck north of the Alps. Late in the period, large fortified oppida such as Závist and Staré Hradisko functioned as manufacturing and trading towns. The Boii, who gave their name to Bohemia, are the first inhabitants of the region known to history by name.

časná doba laténská (LtA) (Czech Republi.node: časná doba laténská (LtA) (Czech Republic, 480 BC–381 BC)
časná doba laténská (LtA) (Czech Republi.label: časná doba laténská (LtA)
časná doba laténská (LtA) (Czech Republi.prose:
[Czech Republic, 480 BC–381 BC] časná doba laténská (LtA). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The first phase of Celtic La Tène culture, when a new curvilinear art style appeared on weapons, brooches and gold neck-rings. Rich graves contain imported Etruscan and Greek wine flagons and drinking gear, showing chieftains adopting Mediterranean feasting habits and reworking their motifs into something wholly their own. These communities were the ancestors of the Celts who raided Italy and Greece in the following century.

podmokelská skupina (Czech Republic, 400.label: podmokelská skupina
podmokelská skupina (Czech Republic, 400.prose: [Czech Republic, 400 BC–131 BC] podmokelská skupina. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

střední doba laténská (LtB–C1) (Czech Re.node: střední doba laténská (LtB–C1) (Czech Republic, 370 BC–171 BC)
střední doba laténská (LtB–C1) (Czech Re.label: střední doba laténská (LtB–C1)
střední doba laténská (LtB–C1) (Czech Re.prose:
[Czech Republic, 370 BC–171 BC] střední doba laténská (LtB–C1). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Celtic communities of the La Tène world flourished in Bohemia and Moravia, cremating and inurning their dead, farming with iron tools and producing curvilinear art on brooches, scabbards and torcs. Some populations left in the great Celtic migrations that struck Italy, the Balkans and Delphi, and returned with plunder and new ideas. Coinage in gold and silver began to circulate, a first for the region.

mladší–pozdní doba laténská (LtC2–D) (Cz.node: mladší–pozdní doba laténská (LtC2–D) (Czech Republic, 170 BC–31 BC)
mladší–pozdní doba laténská (LtC2–D) (Cz.label: mladší–pozdní doba laténská (LtC2–D)
mladší–pozdní doba laténská (LtC2–D) (Cz.prose:
[Czech Republic, 170 BC–31 BC] mladší–pozdní doba laténská (LtC2–D). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Celtic Boii built fortified towns - oppida such as Zavist, Stradonice and Trisov - with gates, streets, workshops and coin minting, the first genuinely urban places north of the Alps. Iron tools, potter's-wheel ceramics, glass bracelets and Mediterranean wine amphorae show a connected, specialised economy. The oppida were abandoned around the mid first century BC, and Germanic groups moved into the vacated landscape.

kultura púchovská (Czech Republic, 480 B.label: kultura púchovská
kultura púchovská (Czech Republic, 480 B.prose:
[Czech Republic, 480 BC–AD 180] kultura púchovská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A hillfort culture of the northwestern Carpathians, blending Celtic, Dacian and local traditions, and generally associated with the Cotini known to Roman writers. Its fortified upland sites, such as Havránok, controlled routes across the mountains and the trade in iron and amber. Roman coins and imported goods show how deeply these highland communities were drawn into Mediterranean commerce before their settlements were abandoned in the second century AD.

kultura przeworská (Czech Republic, 200.label: kultura przeworská
kultura przeworská (Czech Republic, 200.prose:
[Czech Republic, 200 BC–AD 400] kultura przeworská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

An Iron Age culture of the upper Vistula and Oder that extended into Czech Silesia and northeastern Moravia, usually linked with the Lugii and later the Vandals. Its people cremated their dead and buried warriors with deliberately bent or broken swords, shield bosses and spearheads. Large-scale iron smelting and lively trade with the Roman provinces - wine vessels, brooches, coins - made it a key player in the barbarian world beyond the Danube frontier.

pozdní doba laténská (LtD) (Czech Republ.node: pozdní doba laténská (LtD) (Czech Republic, 130 BC–31 BC)
pozdní doba laténská (LtD) (Czech Republ.label: pozdní doba laténská (LtD)
pozdní doba laténská (LtD) (Czech Republ.prose:
[Czech Republic, 130 BC–31 BC] pozdní doba laténská (LtD). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The age of the oppida — vast fortified towns such as Závist, Stradonice and Staré Hradisko, with planned streets, workshops, imported wine and locally struck gold and silver coins. This was the closest the region came to urban life before the Middle Ages, sustained by mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, iron tools and long-distance trade with the Mediterranean. Within a few decades the oppida were abandoned and Germanic groups took over the lowlands.

kobylská skupina (Czech Republic, 110 BC.label: kobylská skupina
kobylská skupina (Czech Republic, 110 BC.prose: [Czech Republic, 110 BC–91 BC] kobylská skupina. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

doba římská–stěhování národů (Czech Repu.label: doba římská–stěhování národů
doba římská–stěhování národů (Czech Repu.prose:
[Czech Republic, 30 BC–AD 580] doba římská–stěhování národů. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A combined span running from the Germanic kingdoms facing the Roman frontier through to the arrival of the Slavs. It brackets the long decline of Roman trade contacts and the upheavals that emptied and reshaped the settled landscape. The label is applied to sites and finds that cannot be assigned firmly to one side of that transition.

doba římská (Czech Republic, 30 BC–AD 40.label: doba římská
doba římská (Czech Republic, 30 BC–AD 40.prose:
[Czech Republic, 30 BC–AD 400] doba římská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Germanic peoples — the Marcomanni under Maroboduus, later the Quadi — occupied the region just beyond the Danube frontier, close enough to trade intensively with the Empire and to fight it during the Marcomannic Wars. Roman coins, bronze vessels, glass and terra sigillata reached local farms and graves, and a Roman military post was briefly maintained at Mušov in south Moravia. The period offers the first written descriptions of the area's inhabitants, by Tacitus and others.

starší doba římská (Czech Republic, 30 B.label: starší doba římská
starší doba římská (Czech Republic, 30 B.prose:
[Czech Republic, 30 BC–AD 180] starší doba římská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Beyond the imperial frontier, Germanic peoples - the Marcomanni under Marobodus and later the Quadi - built up powerful kingdoms in Bohemia and Moravia that Rome alternately courted and fought. Roman coins, bronze vessels, glass and fine terra sigillata flowed north in exchange for slaves, cattle and amber, and are found in graves and settlements far from any Roman road. The Marcomannic Wars at the end of this span brought Roman legions themselves into Moravia, leaving marching camps and an inscription at Trenčín nearby.

plaňanský typ (Czech Republic, 30 BC–6 B.label: plaňanský typ
plaňanský typ (Czech Republic, 30 BC–6 B.prose:
[Czech Republic, 30 BC–6 BC] plaňanský typ. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A short-lived pottery horizon in Bohemia named after finds at Plaňany, falling in the last decades of Celtic oppida life. Its wheel-made vessels mark the very end of the La Tène sequence, at the point where the great hillfort towns were abandoned and Germanic-speaking newcomers began settling the lowlands. The horizon is a key chronological hinge between the Celtic and Germanic periods in the region.

mladší doba římská (Czech Republic, AD 1.label: mladší doba římská
mladší doba římská (Czech Republic, AD 1.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 181–AD 400] mladší doba římská. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Germanic communities beyond the Danube frontier - Marcomanni, Quadi and their neighbours - lived through the aftermath of the Marcomannic Wars and kept trading with the empire for coins, glass, bronze vessels and terra sigillata. Rich weapon burials and imported drinking sets mark out a warrior aristocracy tied to Roman patronage. As imperial power weakened in the fourth century these networks unravelled, pushing the region towards the upheavals of the Migration Period.

doba stěhování národů (Czech Republic, A.label: doba stěhování národů
doba stěhování národů (Czech Republic, A.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 381–AD 580] doba stěhování národů. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Germanic kingdoms rose and collapsed as Huns, Lombards and others moved across central Europe, and the settled landscape of the Roman-period farms thinned dramatically. Rich furnished graves with polychrome garnet jewellery and gold sheet fibulae mark a mobile warrior elite. By the end of the period the first Slavic settlers were establishing themselves in Bohemia and Moravia, setting the region's linguistic future.

starší doba stěhování národů (Czech Repu.node: starší doba stěhování národů (Czech Republic, AD 381–AD 480)
starší doba stěhování národů (Czech Repu.label: starší doba stěhování národů
starší doba stěhování národů (Czech Repu.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 381–AD 480] starší doba stěhování národů. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

As Roman power collapsed on the Danube, Germanic groups moved through and settled the Bohemian and Moravian basins, leaving richly furnished graves with Roman-style gold and garnet jewellery, weapons and imported vessels. Old settlement patterns broke down and populations shifted repeatedly, with Hunnic influence felt in dress and in artificially shaped skulls found in some burials. It is a period known mainly from cemeteries rather than villages, a sign of how unsettled life had become.

dobrodzieńská skupina (Czech Republic, A.label: dobrodzieńská skupina
dobrodzieńská skupina (Czech Republic, A.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 381–AD 480] dobrodzieńská skupina. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A late Roman and early Migration-period grouping in Upper Silesia and the adjoining Czech borderlands, developing out of the Przeworsk cultural tradition. It is recognised chiefly from cremation cemeteries and from large-scale production of wheel-thrown grey pottery, made in specialised kiln centres. The group marks the last phase of settled Germanic occupation in the region before the landscape was largely abandoned.

mladší doba stěhování národů (Czech Repu.node: mladší doba stěhování národů (Czech Republic, AD 481–AD 580)
mladší doba stěhování národů (Czech Repu.label: mladší doba stěhování národů
mladší doba stěhování národů (Czech Repu.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 481–AD 580] mladší doba stěhování národů. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

After the Roman frontier collapsed, the Czech lands passed through Lombard hands before Slavic-speaking groups settled the river valleys in small farming hamlets with sunken-floored huts and plain hand-made pottery. Grave goods thin out, cremation returns, and the archaeological record becomes far poorer than in Roman times. This is the moment the region's later population and language take root.

středověk–novověk (Czech Republic, AD 58.label: středověk–novověk
středověk–novověk (Czech Republic, AD 58.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 581–AD 1800] středověk–novověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A catch-all bracket used when finds can only be placed somewhere between the early Slavic centuries and the eve of industrialisation. Within it Bohemia and Moravia went from tribal hillforts to a Přemyslid kingdom, from Gothic town foundations and silver booms to Hussite upheaval, Habsburg rule and Baroque estates. Material assigned here is usually pottery or building rubble too long-lived to date more tightly.

středověk (Czech Republic, AD 581–AD 150.label: středověk
středověk (Czech Republic, AD 581–AD 150.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 581–AD 1500] středověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Slavic settlement gave rise to Great Moravia, whose rulers received the missionaries Cyril and Methodius and the Slavonic liturgy, and then to the Přemyslid duchy and kingdom of Bohemia. Prague grew into a European capital under Charles IV, with its cathedral, stone bridge and the first university north of the Alps. The Hussite revolution in the fifteenth century shattered the religious unity of the kingdom and anticipated the Reformation by a century.

raný středověk (Czech Republic, AD 581–A.label: raný středověk
raný středověk (Czech Republic, AD 581–A.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 581–AD 1200] raný středověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Six centuries during which Slavic-speaking farmers settled the Bohemian basin, built the first hillforts, and were drawn into the orbit of the Frankish empire. Great Moravia gave the region its first substantial state and, with the mission of Cyril and Methodius, its first Slavonic literacy; after its fall the Přemyslids of Prague built a lasting duchy, secured a bishopric in 973, and turned the country into a Christian kingdom of the Empire. The material record runs from simple sunken huts and hand-made pots to stone churches, coins and stone castles.

raný středověk 1 (Czech Republic, AD 581.label: raný středověk 1
raný středověk 1 (Czech Republic, AD 581.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 581–AD 650] raný středověk 1. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The earliest Slavic-speaking settlers appear in the Bohemian basin, living in small clusters of sunken-floored huts with corner ovens and using plain hand-made Prague-type pots. To the south and east the Avar Khaganate dominated the middle Danube, and it was against Avar pressure that the merchant Samo is said to have led a short-lived tribal alliance, the first political grouping in the region named in a written source.

raný středověk 2–4 (Czech Republic, AD 6.label: raný středověk 2–4
raný středověk 2–4 (Czech Republic, AD 6.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 651–AD 1150] raný středověk 2–4. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Five centuries that carried the Bohemian lands from scattered farming hamlets to a Christian principality. Hillforts multiplied, Great Moravia rose and fell, the Přemyslids made Prague the centre of a duchy with its own bishopric, coinage and stone churches, and by the end towns and castles were beginning to reshape the landscape.

raný středověk 2 (Czech Republic, AD 651.label: raný středověk 2
raný středověk 2 (Czech Republic, AD 651.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 651–AD 800] raný středověk 2. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

After Samo's alliance dissolved, settlement spread and thickened along the river valleys, and the first fortified centres were raised, marking the emergence of chieftains able to command labour. The destruction of the Avar Khaganate by Charlemagne's armies at the end of the eighth century removed the dominant power of the middle Danube and opened the region to Frankish influence.

raný středověk 3 (Czech Republic, AD 801.label: raný středověk 3
raný středověk 3 (Czech Republic, AD 801.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 801–AD 930] raný středověk 3. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The age of Great Moravia, whose rulers built large fortified centres such as Mikulčice and Staré Město, minted no coins but accumulated remarkable metalwork, and in 863 received the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius with its Slavonic liturgy and Glagolitic script. Moravia collapsed under Magyar pressure early in the tenth century, and leadership passed to the Přemyslids of Prague, whose duke Wenceslas was murdered in 935.

rané středohradištní období (Czech Repub.label: rané středohradištní období
rané středohradištní období (Czech Repub.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 801–AD 850] rané středohradištní období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Fortified hilltop centres multiplied across Moravia and Bohemia as local rulers gathered followers and wealth. Frankish expansion after the destruction of the Avar Khaganate brought armies, missionaries and traded weapons into the region, and Moravian elites began accepting Christianity. These strongholds were the seeds of the Moravian polity that would dominate the following century.

vyspělé středohradištní období (Czech Re.label: vyspělé středohradištní období
vyspělé středohradištní období (Czech Re.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 851–AD 900] vyspělé středohradištní období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The high point of Great Moravia, when fortified centres such as Mikulčice, Staré Město and Pohansko held churches, workshops and princely graves furnished with gilded spurs, swords and fine jewellery. The mission of Constantine and Methodius brought Slavonic liturgy and the first Slavic script, giving the region a literary culture of its own. It was the first large Slavic polity in central Europe, and its collapse a few decades later left Bohemia to take the lead.

pozdní středohradištní období (Czech Rep.label: pozdní středohradištní období
pozdní středohradištní období (Czech Rep.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 901–AD 930] pozdní středohradištní období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A brief, decisive generation in which Great Moravia collapsed under Magyar pressure and its network of fortified centres was abandoned or destroyed. Power shifted north to the Přemyslid strongholds around Prague, where a new Bohemian duchy was being assembled from formerly independent tribal territories. The period ends with the murder of Duke Wenceslas, an event that gave the emerging state its patron saint.

raný středověk 4 (Czech Republic, AD 931.label: raný středověk 4
raný středověk 4 (Czech Republic, AD 931.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 931–AD 1150] raný středověk 4. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Under the Přemyslids, Bohemia became a coherent state: a network of ducal castles administered the countryside, silver denars were struck from the 950s, and the bishopric of Prague was founded in 973. Stone rotundas and basilicas appeared, monasteries were endowed, and chroniclers such as Cosmas began recording the dynasty's past. By the end of the period the duchy was a recognised power within the Holy Roman Empire.

rané mladohradištní období (Czech Republ.label: rané mladohradištní období
rané mladohradištní období (Czech Republ.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 931–AD 950] rané mladohradištní období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Two decades of consolidation after the murder of Duke Wenceslas, when Boleslav I broke the power of rival chiefs and welded central Bohemia into a single principality. Old tribal strongholds were destroyed and replaced by a network of ducal hillforts garrisoned by the duke's retinue, the archaeological signature of a state being built by force.

vyspělé mladohradištní období (Czech Rep.label: vyspělé mladohradištní období
vyspělé mladohradištní období (Czech Rep.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 951–AD 1050] vyspělé mladohradištní období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Přemyslid dukes turned a cluster of strongholds into a functioning state, with Prague Castle at its centre and a network of administrative castles collecting tribute and service. Silver denars were minted, a bishopric was established, and churches replaced pagan cult sites. Burial shifted decisively to Christian graveyards with simple, standardised graves.

pozdněhradištní období (Czech Republic,.label: pozdněhradištní období
pozdněhradištní období (Czech Republic,.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1051–AD 1150] pozdněhradištní období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The old timber-and-earth hillfort system gave way to a state organised around ducal castles, churches and the beginnings of chartered towns. Přemyslid dukes minted coins, endowed monasteries and tied Bohemia into the Holy Roman Empire, while village settlement spread into previously wooded uplands. Pottery, building techniques and burial customs all shift, marking the end of the early medieval world and the start of the high medieval one.

přechod raný/vrcholný středověk (Czech R.label: přechod raný/vrcholný středověk
přechod raný/vrcholný středověk (Czech R.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1151–AD 1250] přechod raný/vrcholný středověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Přemyslids won a hereditary royal crown, confirmed by the Golden Bull of Sicily in 1212, and set about reorganising their lands. Colonists, many German-speaking, were settled on cleared land and in newly chartered towns with market rights and regular street plans, while the older wooden hillforts gave way to stone castles and Romanesque churches yielded to Gothic. Silver strikes and a reformed coinage paid for it all and made the Bohemian crown one of the richer powers in the Empire.

vrcholný středověk–novověk (Czech Republ.label: vrcholný středověk–novověk
vrcholný středověk–novověk (Czech Republ.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1201–AD 1800] vrcholný středověk–novověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A broad bracket for material that can only be placed somewhere between the age of castle-building and the end of the eighteenth century. It covers the founding of chartered towns and silver mining, the Hussite wars, the Habsburg takeover and the Thirty Years' War, and finally Baroque estates and early manufacture. Finds dated this loosely are usually long-lived pottery, brick or ironwork.

vrcholný–pozdní středověk (Czech Republi.label: vrcholný–pozdní středověk
vrcholný–pozdní středověk (Czech Republi.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1201–AD 1500] vrcholný–pozdní středověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Three centuries that took the Czech lands from Přemyslid prosperity to the age of Charles IV, when Prague became an imperial capital with a university and a new town. The Hussite revolution then split society, destroyed monasteries and produced a religiously divided kingdom unlike any other in Europe. Towns, castles and rural churches from these centuries still dominate the historic landscape.

vrcholný středověk (Czech Republic, AD 1.label: vrcholný středověk
vrcholný středověk (Czech Republic, AD 1.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1201–AD 1300] vrcholný středověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Bohemia's boom century: royal towns were founded by charter, German-speaking settlers cleared new farmland, and the silver of Jihlava and later Kutná Hora made the Přemyslid kings among the richest in central Europe. Stone castles, Gothic churches and regular street grids replaced older timber settlements. The dynasty's extinction in 1306 opened the way for the Luxembourgs.

pozdní středověk (Czech Republic, AD 130.label: pozdní středověk
pozdní středověk (Czech Republic, AD 130.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1301–AD 1500] pozdní středověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Prague became an imperial capital under Charles IV, with a new university, a stone bridge and a cathedral, while silver from Kutná Hora funded one of Europe's richest kingdoms. The Hussite revolution then shattered that order: monasteries were burned, armies with war wagons defeated crusades, and a reformed Utraquist church survived a century before Luther. Under the later Jagiellonians the towns and nobility, not the crown, held the real power.

přechod pozdní středověk/novověk (Czech.label: přechod pozdní středověk/novověk
přechod pozdní středověk/novověk (Czech.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1451–AD 1550] přechod pozdní středověk/novověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Bohemia emerged from the Hussite wars as a kingdom with a Utraquist majority and an elective throne, ruled by the Jagiellonians and, from 1526, by the Habsburgs. Late Gothic building reached its most inventive in the vaults of Vladislav's Prague, even as Italian Renaissance forms began appearing in noble residences. Silver from Kutná Hora and the new mines at Jáchymov, whose coin gave the world the word dollar, financed much of it.

novověk (Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 1800.label: novověk
novověk (Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 1800.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 1800] novověk. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The centuries after the Middle Ages brought the Reformation, the Habsburg dynasty, and the Thirty Years' War, which devastated the Bohemian countryside and reduced its population. Estates were reorganised into large aristocratic domains worked by serfs, and towns and villages were rebuilt in Renaissance and then Baroque styles. Archaeologically it is the age of glassworks, ironworks, brick manors and mass-produced ceramics.

novověk 1 (Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 16.label: novověk 1
novověk 1 (Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 16.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 1650] novověk 1. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Renaissance building, humanist learning and a largely Protestant Bohemian nobility gave way to confessional conflict. The Bohemian Revolt of 1618 opened the Thirty Years' War, ending in defeat at White Mountain, the execution of rebel leaders, wholesale confiscation of estates and enforced Catholicism. Sites from these decades range from ornate chateaux to burnt villages and battlefield debris.

novověk 2 (Czech Republic, AD 1651–AD 18.label: novověk 2
novověk 2 (Czech Republic, AD 1651–AD 18.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1651–AD 1800] novověk 2. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Bohemia and Moravia emerged from war under a Catholic, German-speaking aristocracy that rebuilt the land with Baroque churches, pilgrimage sites and vast manorial estates. Serf labour underpinned an expanding economy of glass, iron, textiles and brewing, while Enlightenment reforms under Maria Theresa and Joseph II abolished serfdom's harshest bonds and dissolved many monasteries. The material record shifts towards standardised, industrially produced goods.

industriální období (Czech Republic, AD.label: industriální období
industriální období (Czech Republic, AD.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1801–AD 2000] industriální období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

The Czech lands turned from a farming province into the industrial engine of the Habsburg monarchy and later of Czechoslovakia: coal from Ostrava and Kladno, textile mills in the north, sugar refineries, Škoda's engineering works and a dense railway network. Cities swelled, a Czech national movement grew out of the new urban middle class, and the region passed through independence, Nazi occupation and four decades of communist heavy industry. Landscapes of slag heaps, mill chimneys and workers' housing date from this stretch.

industriální období 1 (Czech Republic, A.label: industriální období 1
industriální období 1 (Czech Republic, A.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1801–AD 1900] industriální období 1. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Steam power, coal and railways transformed Bohemia and Moravia into the workshop of the Habsburg empire, with textile towns in the north and ironworks and machine shops around Prague, Plzeň and Ostrava. Rural people poured into new industrial suburbs, and the Czech national revival gathered strength among the literate townspeople the factories helped create. The 1848 revolution and the abolition of serf labour obligations belong to this stretch.

industriální období 2 (Czech Republic, A.label: industriální období 2
industriální období 2 (Czech Republic, A.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1901–AD 2000] industriální období 2. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A century in which the same industrial base survived four political systems: the late Habsburg empire, the first Czechoslovak republic, Nazi occupation, and communist rule. Between the wars Czechoslovakia was one of the world's most industrialised states, with Škoda, Baťa's shoe empire and a large arms industry; after 1948 the economy was reorganised around heavy industry and mining, at heavy environmental cost. It closes with the Velvet Revolution and the return to market economics.

novověk–industriální období (Czech Repub.label: novověk–industriální období
novověk–industriální období (Czech Repub.prose:
[Czech Republic, AD 1501–AD 2000] novověk–industriální období. Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

A long sweep from the post-medieval world to the twentieth century, covering the Habsburg centuries, the rise of coal, iron and textile industry, and the factory towns of Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia. Archaeology here deals with mines, furnaces, railways, workers' housing and the debris of two world wars. Landscapes were reshaped more thoroughly in these centuries than in all preceding millennia.

střední/mladší doba laténská (LtC1–2) (C.node: střední/mladší doba laténská (LtC1–2) (Czech Republic, 250 BC–120 BC)
střední/mladší doba laténská (LtC1–2) (C.label: střední/mladší doba laténská (LtC1–2)
střední/mladší doba laténská (LtC1–2) (C.prose:
[Czech Republic, 250 BC–120 BC] střední/mladší doba laténská (LtC1–2). Period definition from AMCR Periods Vocabulary — Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic, 2025.

Celtic society here reached its peak of complexity, with specialised craft production in iron, glass and enamel, wheel-thrown pottery and rotary querns in everyday use. Large open agglomerations and, later, fortified oppida concentrated people and trade, and locally minted coins circulated widely. Classical writers name the Boii, whose presence gave Bohemia its Latin name, Boiohaemum.

Historic (Europe, AD 1–AD 2000).label: Historic
Historic (Europe, AD 1–AD 2000).prose:
[Eurasia, AD 1–AD 2000] Historic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. General term for later phases of complex civilizations. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

Opens with the first European descent of the Mississippi and covers French lead mining and river villages, Spanish administration, and then American statehood, steamboats and railroads. Sites from these centuries include trading posts, farmsteads, Civil War fortifications and industrial works, and are studied with documents and maps alongside the ground itself. Native communities persisted and were pushed out during the same span, so the archaeology records both settlement and dispossession.

Smithfield (Botswana, AD 1000–AD 1800).label: Smithfield
Smithfield (Botswana, AD 1000–AD 1800).prose:
[Southern Africa, AD 1000–AD 1800] Smithfield. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Smithfield used specifically without a following letter designation includes assemblages with backed bladelets, long end scrapers at end of sequence from Karoo. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

A Later Stone Age stone-tool tradition of the southern African interior, marked by small scrapers and microliths worked from local rocks, and associated with the hunter-gatherer ancestors of San communities. Its makers left rock paintings and engravings across the region and, in later centuries, traded and intermarried with incoming herders and farmers.

Ceramic Wilton (Botswana, AD 100–AD 1800.label: Ceramic Wilton
Ceramic Wilton (Botswana, AD 100–AD 1800.prose:
[Southern Africa, AD 100–AD 1800] Ceramic Wilton. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Wilton, probably hunter-gatherers, but with pottery. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

The later stretch of the Wilton stone-tool tradition, when hunter-gatherer groups using small crescent-shaped microliths began to use pottery as well. It overlaps with the arrival of herders and Iron Age farming villages, and the mixed assemblages record foragers trading, borrowing and living alongside their food-producing neighbours rather than simply vanishing.

Herder (Botswana, AD 1–AD 1800).label: Herder
Herder (Botswana, AD 1–AD 1800).prose: [Southern Africa, AD 1–AD 1800] Herder. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Herders are pastoralists with fat-tailed sheep, cows and Khoekhoe pottery. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

Strandloper (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1800).label: Strandloper
Strandloper (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1800).prose: [Southern Africa, 2000 BC–AD 1800] Strandloper. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. coastally adapted hunter-gatherers with few formal tools, large untrimmed flakes. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

LSA (Africa, 28000 BC–AD 1800).label: LSA
LSA (Africa, 28000 BC–AD 1800).prose:
[Africa, 28000 BC–AD 1800] LSA. ArchStrat LSA includes those assemblages that are of non-specific LSA attribution.

Only use this ArchStrat if you have no further information. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

The Later Stone Age brought small blade and microlith toolkits, bows and poisoned arrows, bone points and harpoons, and ostrich eggshell beads traded across long distances. Rock paintings and engravings from the Drakensberg to the Sahara belong to this span, along with the first evidence for fishing, snaring and highly specialised hunting. In many regions its way of life continued unchanged until farmers, herders and eventually European colonists arrived.

Iron Age (Europe, 1600 BC–AD 1).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Europe, 1600 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Eurasia, 1600 BC–AD 1] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Farming societies, agriculturalists with metal, animals, farming, generally defined. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Post-Wilton (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1).label: Post-Wilton
Post-Wilton (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Southern Africa, 2000 BC–AD 1] Post-Wilton. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Small hafted scrapers, associated with backed bladelets but few to no segments, younger than Wilton.

Based on Deacon HJ, Deacon J, 1999. Human Beginnings in South Africa. David Philip Publishers, Cape Town. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

The later stages of the Later Stone Age in the Kalahari region, following the small-tool Wilton industries, when microlithic scraper and segment kits continued in use alongside new elements. Pottery appears, and toward the end of the span sheep, cattle and goats spread into southern Africa, so hunting and gathering communities began living alongside - and sometimes adopting - herding. Sites of this age set the stage for the Iron Age farming settlements that follow.

Smithfield N (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1).label: Smithfield N
Smithfield N (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1).prose: [Southern Africa, 2000 BC–AD 1] Smithfield N. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. concave scrapers for wood working, from Natal (N). Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

Smithfield P (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1).label: Smithfield P
Smithfield P (Botswana, 2000 BC–AD 1).prose: [Southern Africa, 2000 BC–AD 1] Smithfield P. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. small hafted straight-sided scrapers with steep retouch for wood working, from Pongoland (P). Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

Smithfield General (Botswana, 10000 BC–A.label: Smithfield General
Smithfield General (Botswana, 10000 BC–A.prose:
[Southern Africa, 10000 BC–AD 1] Smithfield General. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Smithfield, with no clarification, was used before the time when Smithfield was divided into sub-divisions (A, B, C).

Smithfield without a clear definition of time. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

A Later Stone Age tool tradition of the southern African interior, defined by small scrapers and other microlithic implements made by hunter-gatherer communities. The name comes from a South African type site, and the label is used broadly for surface finds that share this technology.

Indian Microlithic (India, 46000 BC–1000.label: Indian Microlithic
Indian Microlithic (India, 46000 BC–1000.prose:
[South Asia, 46000 BC–1000 BC] Indian Microlithic. Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Asia, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan. Sites with microlithic technologies including backed pieces, microblades, microblade cores. In India the definition of microlithic begins at length of 3 cm (width not defined).

Age range based on max age for Mehtakheri and general min age for late hunter gatherers. Often the younger appearance of microlithic cultures is termed Mesolithic in India but we do not differentiate these in ROAD. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

Tiny geometric blades and bladelets - trapezes, triangles, lunates - hafted in rows to make composite arrows, knives and sickles, found across the subcontinent from rockshelters in the Vindhyas to coastal dunes. The technology tracks a shift toward flexible, mobile hunting and gathering, and in some regions persisted alongside farming villages for thousands of years. Sites such as Bhimbetka and Sarai Nahar Rai pair these tools with rock art and cemetery burials.

Bronze Age (Europe, 3300 BC–1500 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Europe, 3300 BC–1500 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 3300 BC–1500 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Approximate beginning of the Bronze Age in Levant, through the beginning of the Iron Age in the Hittite Empire. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Wilton (Botswana, 6000 BC–2000 BC).label: Wilton
Wilton (Botswana, 6000 BC–2000 BC).prose:
[Southern Africa, 6000 BC–2000 BC] Wilton. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Long and narrow scrapers for leather working, associated with backed bladelets but not segments.

Classic Wilton, microlithic assemblage with high incidence of backed bladelets and especially segments or crescents, borers, small scrapers on truncated flakes and blades, oval double scrapers with steep retouch along both margins (= double segments), ornaments, polished bone tools.

Based on Deacon HJ, Deacon J, 1999. Human Beginnings in South Africa. David Philip Publishers, Cape Town.

See Lombard et al. 2012 for age. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

A Later Stone Age tradition known from rock shelters and open sites across southern Africa, marked by tiny crescent-shaped and backed microliths set into wooden shafts as arrows and knives. Wilton assemblages also include ostrich-eggshell beads and water flasks, bone tools and grindstones, evidence of foragers exploiting a wide range of plants and small game. The toolkit and the way of life it represents lasted into recent centuries among Kalahari hunter-gatherers.

Chalcolithic (Europe, 5000 BC–3000 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Europe, 5000 BC–3000 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 5000 BC–3000 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Generally defined. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Neolithic (Europe, 9500 BC–3000 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Europe, 9500 BC–3000 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 9500 BC–3000 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Early farming societies, dates based on early start in Levant and late end in Europe. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Mesolithic (Europe, 9600 BC–4500 BC).label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (Europe, 9600 BC–4500 BC).prose:
[Europe, 9600 BC–4500 BC] Mesolithic. Does not include Epipaleolithic. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Capsian (Algeria, 8000 BC–5000 BC).label: Capsian
Capsian (Algeria, 8000 BC–5000 BC).prose:
[North Africa, 8000 BC–5000 BC] Capsian. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, South Sudan, Sudan, Tunisia. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

A way of life built around hunting, gathering and above all land snails in the high steppes of the Maghreb, leaving behind vast shell middens known as escargotières. Capsian toolkits of small backed bladelets and burins are accompanied by decorated ostrich eggshell containers, ground pigment and some of North Africa's earliest evidence of deliberate burial and bodily ornament. These communities were still in place when the first herds and cultivated plants reached the region.

Albany (Botswana, 10000 BC–5000 BC).label: Albany
Albany (Botswana, 10000 BC–5000 BC).prose:
[Southern Africa, 10000 BC–5000 BC] Albany. Spatial coverage: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa. Albany and Oakhurst assemblages contain few or no microliths, scrapers (round end, D-shaped, duckbill), polished bone tools.

Lockshoek is the Karoo variant.

Smithfield A: large round or rectangular scrapers > 30mm for leather working.

Based on Deacon HJ, Deacon J, 1999. Human Beginnings in South Africa. David Philip Publishers, Cape Town.

See Lombard et al. 2012 for age. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

A Later Stone Age tradition that replaced the tiny bladelets of the preceding Robberg industry with big, plain flakes and chunky scrapers, made mostly on coarse local stone. It spans the warming centuries after the last glacial maximum, when rising seas drowned the coastal plains and hunters shifted to new game and shellfish, before microliths returned with the Wilton.

Holocene (Europe, 9700 BC–AD 2000).label: Holocene
Holocene (Europe, 9700 BC–AD 2000).prose:
[Eurasia, 9700 BC–AD 2000] Holocene. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. General term for undefined, probably Holocene assemblages. Period definition from ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD) — The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) research center, 2020.

The warm interval since the last glaciation, in which rising seas cut Britain off from the continent and drowned the plain now beneath the North Sea. Tundra gave way to birch, pine and then dense mixed woodland; hunter-gatherers were followed by farmers, and every monument, field system, town and road in the country belongs to this sliver of geological time. Its later part is marked worldwide by human alteration of climate, soils and species.

Intihuasi I (Argentina, AD 500–AD 1500).label: Intihuasi I
Intihuasi I (Argentina, AD 500–AD 1500).prose: [Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), AD 500–AD 1500] Intihuasi I. Period definition from La estratigrafía de la gruta de Intihuasi (Prov. de San Luis, R.A.) y sus relaciones con otros sitios precerámicos de Sudamérica — González, A. R., 1960.
Intihuasi I (Argentina, AD 500–AD 1500).source: La estratigrafía de la gruta de Intihuasi (Prov. de San Luis, R.A.) y sus relaciones con otros sitios precerámicos de Sudamérica

Ayampitinense II (Argentina, 4000 BC–300.label: Ayampitinense II
Ayampitinense II (Argentina, 4000 BC–300.prose: [Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), 4000 BC–3000 BC] Ayampitinense II. Period definition from La estratigrafía de la gruta de Intihuasi (Prov. de San Luis, R.A.) y sus relaciones con otros sitios precerámicos de Sudamérica — González, A. R., 1960.
Ayampitinense II (Argentina, 4000 BC–300.source: La estratigrafía de la gruta de Intihuasi (Prov. de San Luis, R.A.) y sus relaciones con otros sitios precerámicos de Sudamérica

Período Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina,.label: Período Prehispánico Tardío
Período Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina,.prose:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), AD 450–AD 1650] Período Prehispánico Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de la Región Montañosa Central de Argentina. Avances en el Conocimiento de la Historia Prehispánica Tardía — Pastor, S., 2012.

A broad late pre-Columbian sequence covering the growth of farming villages, the rise of regional chiefdoms in the valleys, Inca annexation and the first violent decades of Spanish presence. Terraced fields, irrigation canals, hilltop strongholds and cemeteries of decorated funerary urns are its most visible remains. It ends with the destruction and forced resettlement of the valley communities.
Período Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina,.source: Arqueología de la Región Montañosa Central de Argentina. Avances en el Conocimiento de la Historia Prehispánica Tardía

Ayampitinense (Argentina, 6000 BC–2500 B.label: Ayampitinense
Ayampitinense (Argentina, 6000 BC–2500 B.prose:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), 6000 BC–2500 BC] Ayampitinense. Period definition from Esquema de la prehistoria argentina — Schobinger, Juan, 1959.

Early Holocene hunter-gatherers of the Argentine sierras, known above all for the Ayampitín point: a slender, leaf-shaped bifacial spearhead flaked on both faces. These bands hunted guanaco and deer and ground wild seeds with milling stones in rock shelters such as Intihuasi, whose excavation first defined the tradition. The type is one of the anchors of Andean and Pampean chronology, appearing across a wide swathe of southern South America.

Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico (A.node: Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico (Argentina, 12000 BC–500 BC)
Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico (A.label: Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico
Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico (A.prose:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), 12000 BC–500 BC] Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico. Period definition from Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino) — Antonio Serrano, 1967.

The long era before pottery, opening with the first hunters who tracked now-extinct megafauna across Patagonia and the Andean highlands. Over thousands of years groups adapted to changing climates, exploited camelids and wild plants, painted rock shelters such as Cueva de las Manos, and eventually began herding llamas and cultivating crops. The gradual shift toward settled life set the stage for everything that followed.
Primer Período Cultural o Precerámico (A.source: Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino)

Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico (Arg.node: Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico (Argentina, 500 BC–AD 1534)
Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico (Arg.label: Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico
Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico (Arg.prose: [Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), 500 BC–AD 1534] Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico. Period definition from Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino) — Antonio Serrano, 1967.
Segundo Período Cultural o Cerámico (Arg.source: Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino)

Primer Período Cerámico (Argentina, 400.label: Primer Período Cerámico
Primer Período Cerámico (Argentina, 400.prose:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), 400 BC–AD 800] Primer Período Cerámico. Period definition from Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino) — Antonio Serrano, 1967.

Pottery, cultivated crops and settled village life took hold in the valleys and puna of northwest Argentina. Households combined maize and quinoa farming with llama herding, and long-distance exchange moved obsidian, shell and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia across the Andes. The distinctive painted and modelled ceramics of these communities are among the most striking artefacts of the region.
Primer Período Cerámico (Argentina, 400.source: Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino)

Segundo Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD.label: Segundo Período Cerámico
Segundo Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD.prose: [Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), AD 800–AD 1534] Segundo Período Cerámico. Period definition from Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino) — Antonio Serrano, 1967.
Segundo Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD.source: Historia cultural del Tucumán Prehispánico (Una introducción a la Arqueología del Noroeste argentino)

San Lorenzo Phase (Panama, AD 800–AD 110.label: San Lorenzo Phase
San Lorenzo Phase (Panama, AD 800–AD 110.prose: [Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama, AD 800–AD 1100] San Lorenzo Phase. “The next occupation in the Chiriquí Gulf is the San Lorenzo Phase which I have tentatively placed between A.D. 800 and A.D. 1100… An estimate for the end of this phase is around A.D. 1100, based on estimates for the beginning of the next phase.” (p. 86). Period definition from Cultural chronology of the Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1968.
San Lorenzo Phase (Panama, AD 800–AD 110.source: Cultural chronology of the Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama

Chiriquí Phase (Panama, AD 1100–AD 1500).label: Chiriquí Phase
Chiriquí Phase (Panama, AD 1100–AD 1500).prose:
[Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama, AD 1100–AD 1500] Chiriquí Phase. “The beginnings of our Chiriquí Phase should be placed in the Gulf at around A.D. 1100… A terminal date for the Chiriquí Phase should be placed at the time of the Conquest (A.D. 1500) or slightly later.” (p. 86). Period definition from Cultural chronology of the Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1968.

Chiefdoms in the highlands and Pacific slopes of western Panama produced the region's most recognisable material: fine buff-coloured 'biscuit' ware, boldly painted polychrome vessels with animal motifs, and cast gold pendants of eagles, frogs and shamanic figures. Burials in stone-lined graves, richly furnished, show ranked societies that traded metalwork widely across the isthmus. These were the communities Spanish expeditions met in the sixteenth century, and their cemeteries were among the first in the Americas to be systematically looted for gold.
Chiriquí Phase (Panama, AD 1100–AD 1500).source: Cultural chronology of the Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama

Aguas Buenas (Panama, AD 300–AD 900).label: Aguas Buenas
Aguas Buenas (Panama, AD 300–AD 900).prose:
[Western Panama, AD 300–AD 900] Aguas Buenas. “For decades, the A.D. 600  eruption of Volcán Barú was assumed to have been catastrophic enough to have ended Aguas Buenas settlements across much of the region (Linares 1977:313, 1980e:245; Sheets 2004)”, but “it appears that both the A.D. 600 eruption and assumptions about the lack of early populations in the Caribbean watershed need to be rethought. Like the rest of Gran Chiriquí, the Aguas Buenas in Gran Chiriquí might have lasted until A.D. 800 or later (Corrales 2000).” (pp 74-75) 

“In Western Panama, the Aguas Buenas has three different names. The most used is the Bugaba (with early and late halves), coined by Spang et al. (1980) to refer to ceramics in highland Chiriquí and the Caribbean coast (Kudarauskas et al. 1980). The second is the Burica (A.D. 400-600), used by Linares (1968) to describe Aguas Buenas materials on the Pacific coast. The least used is the Barriles phase (400  B.C. to A.D. 200), described by Haberland  (1976).” (p. 75). Period definition from The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama — Palumbo, Scott, 2009.

Communities in the highlands and Pacific slopes of western Panama and southern Costa Rica lived in villages of round houses on stone-faced terraces, farming maize and root crops. Their pottery — tripod vessels, appliqué and modelled figures — and their carved stone statues and petroglyphs are the region's signature, and the first goldwork in the isthmus appears here. These settlements laid the ground for the chiefdoms encountered by Europeans centuries later.
Aguas Buenas (Panama, AD 300–AD 900).source: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama

San Lorenzo Phase (Panama, AD 700–AD 110.label: San Lorenzo Phase
San Lorenzo Phase (Panama, AD 700–AD 110.prose: [Western Panama, AD 700–AD 1100] San Lorenzo Phase. “San Lorenzo ceramics have been described as a temporal phase by Linares (1968a, 1968b)” (p. 76). Period definition from The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama — Palumbo, Scott, 2009.
San Lorenzo Phase (Panama, AD 700–AD 110.source: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama

Early Bugaba phase (Panama, AD 300–AD 60.label: Early Bugaba phase
Early Bugaba phase (Panama, AD 300–AD 60.prose: [Western Panama, AD 300–AD 600] Early Bugaba phase. Period definition from The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama — Palumbo, Scott, 2009.
Early Bugaba phase (Panama, AD 300–AD 60.source: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama

Late Bugaba Phase (Panama, AD 600–AD 900.label: Late Bugaba Phase
Late Bugaba Phase (Panama, AD 600–AD 900.prose: [Western Panama, AD 600–AD 900] Late Bugaba Phase. Period definition from The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama — Palumbo, Scott, 2009.
Late Bugaba Phase (Panama, AD 600–AD 900.source: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama

Concepción Phase (Panama, 299 BC–AD 400).label: Concepción Phase
Concepción Phase (Panama, 299 BC–AD 400).prose: [Western Panama, 299 BC–AD 400] Concepción Phase. "... pottery appears relatively late in the Chiriquí sequence with the introduction of Concepción wares around 300 B.C. The Concepción represents the adoption or introduction of ceramic technology in Western Panama." (p. 68). Period definition from The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama — Palumbo, Scott, 2009.
Concepción Phase (Panama, 299 BC–AD 400).source: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama

Chiriquí Phase (Panama, AD 900–AD 1500).label: Chiriquí Phase
Chiriquí Phase (Panama, AD 900–AD 1500).prose:
[Western Panama; parts of Costa Rica, AD 900–AD 1500] Chiriquí Phase. Spatial coverage: Costa Rica, Panama. “The Chiriquí phase (also called the Boruca, Palmer, or Sierpe in parts of Costa Rica) is the best known of all the Gran Chiriquí time periods.” (p. 77). Period definition from The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama — Palumbo, Scott, 2009.

Chiefdoms in the highlands and Pacific slopes of western Panama produced the region's most recognisable material: fine buff-coloured 'biscuit' ware, boldly painted polychrome vessels with animal motifs, and cast gold pendants of eagles, frogs and shamanic figures. Burials in stone-lined graves, richly furnished, show ranked societies that traded metalwork widely across the isthmus. These were the communities Spanish expeditions met in the sixteenth century, and their cemeteries were among the first in the Americas to be systematically looted for gold.
Chiriquí Phase (Panama, AD 900–AD 1500).source: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama

Talamanca Phase (Panama, 4599 BC–2299 BC.label: Talamanca Phase
Talamanca Phase (Panama, 4599 BC–2299 BC.prose: [Rio Chiriquí region, 4599 BC–2299 BC] Talamanca Phase. This definition is provided in a contribution by Ranere to the edited volume: A. Ranere, “Preceramic shelters in the Talamancan Range”, pp. 16-43. Period definition from Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1980.

Boquete Phase (Panama, 2299 BC–299 BC).label: Boquete Phase
Boquete Phase (Panama, 2299 BC–299 BC).prose: [Rio Chiriquí region, 2299 BC–299 BC] Boquete Phase. This definition is provided in a contribution by Ranere to the edited volume: A. Ranere, “Preceramic shelters in the Talamancan Range”, pp. 16-43. Period definition from Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1980.

Tropical Forest Archaic (Panama, 4799 BC.label: Tropical Forest Archaic
Tropical Forest Archaic (Panama, 4799 BC.prose:
[Chiriquí region, 4799 BC–499 BC] Tropical Forest Archaic. This definition is provided in Linares' concluding chapter, but makes reference to the preceding chapters, including Ranere's: O. Linares, "Conclusions", pp. 233-247. Period definition from Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1980.

Preceramic foragers in the Panamanian lowlands hunted, fished and gathered palm nuts while gradually taking up cultivation, burning clearings in the forest for early maize, manioc and arrowroot. Traces come mostly from rockshelters and their charred plant remains and starch grains, which push the beginnings of tropical farming back much earlier than pottery-using villages. The slow shift from foraging to gardening here helped carry domesticated crops between the Americas.

Talamanca phase (Panama, 5999 BC–2999 BC.label: Talamanca phase
Talamanca phase (Panama, 5999 BC–2999 BC.prose: [Greater Chiriqui, 5999 BC–2999 BC] Talamanca phase. Spatial coverage: Costa Rica, Panama. The older of the two preceramic phases, Talamanca, has been dated by Ranere (1975b: 177) to before 3000 B.C., while Cooke (1976a:22) suggested a dating between 5000 and 3000 B.C. Taking the corrected C14 dates into account, 6000 to 3000 B.C. seems appropriate.” (p. 236). Period definition from The Archaeology of Greater Chiriqui — Wolfgang Haberland, 1984.

Boquete phase (Panama, 2999 BC–999 BC).label: Boquete phase
Boquete phase (Panama, 2999 BC–999 BC).prose: [Greater Chiriqui, 2999 BC–999 BC] Boquete phase. Spatial coverage: Costa Rica, Panama. The Boquete lithic assemblage “stratigraphically overlies the Talamanca phase at the Casita de Piedra and Trapiche rockshelters (Ranere 1975b: 176-77). The single C14 date, slightly later than 3000 B.C. when adjusted, came from the top of layer D at Casita de Piedra and either antedates the Boquete phase or reflects its very beginning (Linares and Ranere 1971: 350). The end should be around 1000 B.C., since SI-1844 is said to date the transition to the following ceramic phase at Casita de Piedra. Boquete represents a gradual development out of the Talamanca phase.” (p. 237). Period definition from The Archaeology of Greater Chiriqui — Wolfgang Haberland, 1984.

Prehistoria Reciente (Europe, 5550 BC–11.label: Prehistoria Reciente
Prehistoria Reciente (Europe, 5550 BC–11.prose:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–1150 BC] Prehistoria Reciente. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

Galicia's landscape filled with monuments: megalithic tombs under earthen mounds, then, in the Bronze Age, thousands of open-air rock carvings of deer, weapons and cup-marks on granite outcrops. Metalworkers produced flat axes, halberds and remarkable gold ornaments, some deposited in hoards or bogs. By the end of the period people were gathering into fortified hilltop settlements, the seeds of the castro culture.

Neolítico (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC).label: Neolítico
Neolítico (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–3050 BC] Neolítico. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

The first farmers in the peninsula grew cereals and pulses and kept sheep, goats and cattle, spreading along the Mediterranean coast with distinctive shell-impressed Cardial pottery and inland through cave and open-air settlements. Burial in caves and, increasingly, in megalithic tombs marks a new concern with ancestors and place. Rock art and the earliest large communal monuments belong to these centuries.

Calcolítico (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC).label: Calcolítico
Calcolítico (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 3350 BC–1850 BC] Calcolítico. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

Copper metallurgy spread across the Iberian peninsula alongside the first walled settlements, such as Los Millares in the southeast, with bastioned enclosures, collective tholos and megalithic tombs, and rich grave goods of ivory, ostrich eggshell and Atlantic amber. Communal burial and long-distance exchange point to societies growing more unequal and more organised, while irrigation and metalworking reshaped the countryside. Near its end came the Bell Beaker phenomenon, whose distinctive drinking vessels and archer's kit turn up from Portugal to central Europe. The fortified towns and copper daggers of these centuries set the stage for the Bronze Age El Argar culture.

Edad del Bronce (Asia, 1850 BC–1150 BC).label: Edad del Bronce
Edad del Bronce (Asia, 1850 BC–1150 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 1850 BC–1150 BC] Edad del Bronce. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

Metalworking in copper and tin spread across the peninsula, and in the southeast the El Argar culture built fortified hilltop towns with rectangular houses, buried its dead in jars beneath house floors, and marked out sharp differences of wealth in silver and bronze grave goods. Elsewhere communities raised cairns and stelae, worked gold, and traded along Atlantic and Mediterranean routes. It was the first period in Iberia with clearly stratified societies controlling metal and land.

Roman Climate Optimum (Roman Empire, 199.label: Roman Climate Optimum
Roman Climate Optimum (Roman Empire, 199.prose:
[Roman Empire, 199 BC–AD 150] Roman Climate Optimum. Spatial coverage: Europe, Roman Empire. "The empire reached its maximal extent and prosperity in the folds of a late Holocene climate period called the Roman Climate Optimum (RCO)." (p.14). Period definition from The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire — Kyle Harper, 2019.

A long stretch of warm, wet and unusually stable conditions across the Mediterranean, when glaciers retreated and farming pushed into higher and drier ground. Reliable harvests underpinned dense cities, big armies and the grain fleets that fed Rome. The end of this favourable spell coincided with epidemics, harvest failure and political strain, a reminder of how closely the empire's economy tracked its weather.
Roman Climate Optimum (Roman Empire, 199.source: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire

Roman Transitional Period (Roman Empire,.label: Roman Transitional Period
Roman Transitional Period (Roman Empire,.prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 150–AD 450] Roman Transitional Period. Spatial coverage: Europe, Roman Empire. "... a period of climate disorganization covering three centuries (AD 150-450) set in, which we will propose to call the Roman Transitional Period." (p.15). Period definition from The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire — Kyle Harper, 2019.

A phase of unsettled climate between the reliable warmth of the earlier empire and the sharp cold of late antiquity, marked by shifting rainfall and repeated bad harvest years. It coincides with the Antonine plague, the third-century civil wars and the movements of peoples along the northern frontiers. Historians debate how far the weather drove these crises, but the correlation makes it one of the most argued-over episodes in climate history.
Roman Transitional Period (Roman Empire,.source: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire

Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empir.node: Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empire, AD 450–AD 700)
Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empir.label: Late Antique Little Ice Age
Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empir.prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 450–AD 700] Late Antique Little Ice Age. Spatial coverage: Europe, Roman Empire. "... from the later fifth century, we sense the stirrings of a decisive reorganization that culminated in the Late Antique Little Ice Age. A spasm of volcanic activity in the AD 530s and 540s brought on the most frigid spell in the entire Late Holocene." (p. 15). Period definition from The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire — Kyle Harper, 2019.

A cluster of massive volcanic eruptions beginning in 536 dimmed the sun and pushed temperatures down across the northern hemisphere for well over a century, a cooling recorded in tree rings and ice cores. Contemporaries described a year without summer, failed harvests and famine, and in 541 the Justinianic plague arrived to kill a large share of the Mediterranean population. Historians link the combined shock to the collapse of Justinian's reconquest, the weakening of Rome and Persia, and upheavals from the steppe to Scandinavia.
Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empir.source: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire

Pre-Christian Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–A.label: Pre-Christian Iceland
Pre-Christian Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–A.prose:
[Iceland, AD 870–AD 1000] Pre-Christian Iceland. Iceland was Christianized in the year 1000 CE, when Christianity became the religion by law. In Icelandic, this event is known as the kristnitaka (literally, "the taking of Christianity"). (from. Period definition from The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries — Gunnar Karlsson, 2019.

Norse and Hiberno-Norse settlers claimed an uninhabited island during the landnám, clearing birch woods, building turf longhouses and running sheep and cattle over land that eroded quickly under them. Without a king, chieftains (goðar) organised law and feud through local assemblies and, from about 930, the annual Althing at Þingvellir. Farmsteads of this era preserve pagan burials with horses and weapons, and the memory of the period shaped the sagas written centuries later.
Pre-Christian Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–A.source: The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries

Settlement Period, Iceland (Iceland, AD.label: Settlement Period, Iceland
Settlement Period, Iceland (Iceland, AD.prose:
[Iceland, AD 870–AD 930] Settlement Period, Iceland. Traditionally, the Icelandic Age of Settlement is considered to have lasted from 874 to 930, at which point most of the island had been claimed and Alþingi (Althingi), the assembly of the Icelandic Commonwealth, was founded at Þingvellir (Thingvellir). (from. Period definition from The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries — Gunnar Karlsson, 2019.

Norse and Hiberno-Norse families, many arriving via Norway, the Hebrides and Ireland, claimed land across an uninhabited island, felling birch woods and turning livestock loose on fragile volcanic soils. Within two generations the best land was taken and the settlers established a system of local chieftains that culminated in the founding of the Althing assembly. The period is unusually well documented for an early medieval migration, thanks to the Book of Settlements and the family sagas written down later.
Settlement Period, Iceland (Iceland, AD.source: The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries

Cenozoic Era (World, 65998050 BC–AD 1950.label: Cenozoic Era
Cenozoic Era (World, 65998050 BC–AD 1950.prose:
[World, 65998050 BC–AD 1950] Cenozoic Era. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The era that began when the asteroid impact and its aftermath wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs, leaving mammals and birds to fill the empty ecological space. India collided with Asia to raise the Himalaya, grasslands spread as the world cooled, and by the last few million years ice sheets were advancing and retreating across the northern continents. Primates evolved within it, and every human being who has ever lived belongs to its final sliver.

Holocene Epoch (World, 9750 BC–AD 1950).label: Holocene Epoch
Holocene Epoch (World, 9750 BC–AD 1950).prose:
[World, 9750 BC–AD 1950] Holocene Epoch. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The current warm interglacial, beginning as ice sheets retreated and sea levels rose by more than a hundred metres, flooding continental shelves and land bridges. Within a few thousand years people in several unconnected regions began cultivating plants and herding animals, leading to villages, cities, writing and states. Almost all of recorded human achievement, and the mass extinctions and atmospheric change of recent centuries, fall inside this single epoch.

Meghalayan Age (World, 2250 BC–AD 1950).label: Meghalayan Age
Meghalayan Age (World, 2250 BC–AD 1950).prose:
[World, 2250 BC–AD 1950] Meghalayan Age. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The most recent slice of geological time, defined by a severe drought roughly 4,200 years ago that is recorded in a stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave in northeast India. The same climate shift is blamed for the collapse or reorganisation of early civilisations in Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus valley and China. It is the first geological unit whose starting point is tied to a cultural event, and it runs up to the mid-twentieth century.

Northgrippian Age (World, 6250 BC–2250 B.label: Northgrippian Age
Northgrippian Age (World, 6250 BC–2250 B.prose:
[World, 6250 BC–2250 BC] Northgrippian Age. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The middle stage of the Holocene, bracketed by two abrupt climate events recorded in Greenland ice — the cold, dry 8.2-kiloyear pulse at its start and the 4.2-kiloyear drying at its end. It covers the warmest part of the present interglacial, when the Sahara was green and grassland, sea levels stabilised, and farming spread across Eurasia.
