Cities, writing, metallurgy and the first states all appear within it.

Quaternary Period (World, 2578050 BC–AD.label: Quaternary Period
Quaternary Period (World, 2578050 BC–AD.prose:
[World, 2578050 BC–AD 1950] Quaternary Period. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

Begins with the onset of the great northern ice ages, when the world's climate swung between glacial and interglacial states roughly every hundred thousand years, reshaping coastlines, rivers and the distribution of every living thing. Our own genus spread out of Africa across the globe during it, and everything humans have made lies within its deposits.

Post-Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1375–AD.label: Post-Classic Period
Post-Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1375–AD.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1375–AD 1450] Post-Classic Period. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

The last pre-contact century in southern Arizona saw the great Hohokam irrigation communities come apart: platform-mound villages and multi-storey compounds such as Casa Grande were abandoned, canal systems fell out of use, and populations dispersed into smaller settlements. Flooding, drought and canal failure are all argued as causes, along with social strain within crowded valley communities. When Spanish explorers arrived, they found the O'odham living among the ruins of those earlier towns.
Post-Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1375–AD.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375.label: Classic Period
Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375] Classic Period. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

Hohokam communities in the Sonoran Desert moved into walled adobe compounds and built platform mounds, while the older ballcourts fell out of use - signs of a more hierarchical society. The vast irrigation canal networks of the Salt and Gila valleys reached their greatest extent, and multi-storey great houses such as Casa Grande were raised, aligned to solar and lunar events. Within a few generations the canal systems and the large settlements were abandoned.
Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

Late Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1200–AD 127.label: Late Soho Phase
Late Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1200–AD 127.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1200–AD 1275] Late Soho Phase. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

Hohokam Classic-period communities of the Salt and Gila valleys, living in walled adobe compounds clustered around earthen platform mounds instead of the older ballcourts. Ceramics shift to plain and red wares with Salado polychromes arriving from outside, and burial practice moves from cremation toward inhumation. The changes point to a more hierarchical society and closer ties with peoples to the east and north.
Late Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1200–AD 127.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

Early Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 12.label: Early Soho Phase
Early Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 12.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1200] Early Soho Phase. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

Hohokam settlement changed shape: ballcourts fell out of use and people moved into walled adobe compounds clustered around platform mounds, with above-ground houses replacing the older pit dwellings. The change suggests tighter control by a small elite over land, water and ritual, and a more inward-looking, defensive kind of village. Irrigation continued on a huge scale, setting the stage for the great houses of the following century.
Early Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 12.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

Early Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–A.label: Early Classic Period
Early Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–A.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1275] Early Classic Period. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

In the Hohokam world of southern Arizona, ballcourts fell out of use and platform mounds became the focus of communities, suggesting a more hierarchical society with restricted ritual space. Above-ground adobe compounds replaced pithouses, and populations concentrated along the great irrigation canal systems of the Salt and Gila valleys.
Early Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–A.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

Sedentary Period (Arizona, AD 950–AD 110.label: Sedentary Period
Sedentary Period (Arizona, AD 950–AD 110.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 950–AD 1100] Sedentary Period. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam settlements in the Salt and Gila valleys reached their widest reach, sustained by hundreds of kilometres of hand-dug irrigation canals that watered maize, beans, cotton and agave. Ball courts served as gathering places across a network of villages, and craftspeople made red-on-buff pottery, carved shell jewellery etched with acid, and traded for macaws and copper bells from Mexico. Around 1100 the ball courts fell out of use and platform mounds took their place.
Sedentary Period (Arizona, AD 950–AD 110.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Late Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1070–AD.label: Late Sacaton Phase
Late Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1070–AD.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1070–AD 1100] Late Sacaton Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

The final stretch of Hohokam Sedentary-period life in the Phoenix and Gila basins, when red-on-buff pottery, ballcourts and vast hand-dug irrigation canals were at their height. Within a generation or two the ballcourt network collapsed and communities began building walled adobe compounds and platform mounds instead, opening the Classic period. Visitors can see the scale of the canal systems, some tens of kilometres long, that supported one of North America's largest desert farming populations.
Late Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1070–AD.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Middle Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1000–A.label: Middle Sacaton Phase
Middle Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1000–A.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1000–AD 1070] Middle Sacaton Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam farmers in the Salt and Gila valleys maintained the largest irrigation canal systems in prehistoric North America, some running for tens of kilometres. Villages centred on oval ballcourts, which drew people together for games, ritual and exchange, and craftworkers produced red-on-buff pottery, carved stone bowls and shell jewellery etched with acid. The ballcourt network linked settlements across much of southern Arizona before this way of life was reorganised around platform mounds.
Middle Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1000–A.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Early Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 950–AD.label: Early Sacaton Phase
Early Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 950–AD.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 950–AD 1000] Early Sacaton Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam villages along the Gila and Salt rivers reached their widest reach, tied together by ballcourts where communities gathered and traded, and fed by irrigation canals dug for kilometres across the desert. Red-on-buff pottery, shell jewellery worked with acid etching, and copper bells and macaws from Mesoamerica circulated through the network. Population and canal systems were at their peak before the shift to walled compounds and platform mounds.
Early Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 950–AD.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Colonial Period (Arizona, AD 750–AD 950).label: Colonial Period
Colonial Period (Arizona, AD 750–AD 950).prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 750–AD 950] Colonial Period. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam communities in the Sonoran Desert expanded rapidly, extending their irrigation canals across the Salt and Gila valleys and settling new districts. This is when ballcourts appear in numbers, hosting gatherings that linked scattered villages, alongside red-on-buff pottery, carved stone palettes, shell jewellery traded from the Gulf of California and cremation burial. Visitors can see the distinctive Gila Butte and Santa Cruz style pottery that defines the phase.
Colonial Period (Arizona, AD 750–AD 950).source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Santa Cruz Phase (Arizona, AD 850–AD 950.label: Santa Cruz Phase
Santa Cruz Phase (Arizona, AD 850–AD 950.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 850–AD 950] Santa Cruz Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A high point of the Hohokam Colonial period in southern Arizona, when villages spread out from the Gila and Salt river cores and the great irrigation canals were extended. Oval ballcourts became standard village features, tying scattered settlements into a network of gatherings and exchange, and potters produced finely painted red-on-buff vessels covered in tiny repeated human and animal figures. Shell from the Gulf of California, some of it etched with acid, moved widely through the region.
Santa Cruz Phase (Arizona, AD 850–AD 950.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Late Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 800–A.label: Late Gila Butte Phase
Late Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 800–A.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 800–AD 850] Late Gila Butte Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A Hohokam phase in the Gila and Salt river valleys, when irrigation canals lengthened, ballcourts spread between villages, and red-on-buff pottery carried repeating scroll and life-form designs. Trade brought shell from the Gulf of California, worked into bracelets and pendants in astonishing quantities.
Late Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 800–A.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Early Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 750–.label: Early Gila Butte Phase
Early Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 750–.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 750–AD 800] Early Gila Butte Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A Hohokam phase in the Phoenix Basin when desert farmers extended their canal systems and began building the large oval ballcourts that drew people together for games and exchange. Red-on-buff pottery, carved shell jewellery from the Gulf of California and cremation burial are its hallmarks.
Early Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 750–.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Pioneer Period (Arizona, AD 450–AD 750).label: Pioneer Period
Pioneer Period (Arizona, AD 450–AD 750).prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 450–AD 750] Pioneer Period. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

The earliest recognised stage of Hohokam life in the Sonoran Desert, when villages of shallow pit houses clustered around central plazas along the Salt and Gila rivers. Farmers began digging the irrigation canals that would eventually water thousands of acres, and potters produced plain and red-slipped wares before the buff pottery of later centuries. These small settlements were the foundation of the largest indigenous canal system in North America.
Pioneer Period (Arizona, AD 450–AD 750).source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Snaketown Phase (Arizona, AD 650–AD 750).label: Snaketown Phase
Snaketown Phase (Arizona, AD 650–AD 750).prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 650–AD 750] Snaketown Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Named for the great village on the Gila River, this phase of the Hohokam sequence saw settlements grow larger and more formally arranged, with clusters of pithouses around open plazas and the dead cremated with offerings. Distinctive red-on-buff painted pottery came into its own, and irrigation canals were extended across the desert floor — the engineering that made dense settlement possible in one of North America's harshest environments.
Snaketown Phase (Arizona, AD 650–AD 750).source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Sweetwater Phase (Arizona, AD 600–AD 650.label: Sweetwater Phase
Sweetwater Phase (Arizona, AD 600–AD 650.prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 600–AD 650] Sweetwater Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A phase of the early Hohokam sequence in the Sonoran Desert, when villages of shallow pithouses clustered around plazas and farmers extended irrigation canals off the Gila and Salt rivers. Potters began decorating buff and gray wares with red painted designs, an early step toward the distinctive red-on-buff tradition of later centuries. Shell ornaments from the Gulf of California show trade links already in place.
Sweetwater Phase (Arizona, AD 600–AD 650.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Estrella Phase (Arizona, AD 500–AD 600).label: Estrella Phase
Estrella Phase (Arizona, AD 500–AD 600).prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 500–AD 600] Estrella Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

An early stage of Hohokam life in the Phoenix Basin, when small groups of pit-house dwellers farmed the Salt and Gila floodplains and dug the first substantial irrigation canals. It is recognised chiefly by its pottery, plain and red-on-gray wares whose painted designs are among the earliest decorated ceramics in the Sonoran Desert. Everything the later Hohokam became famous for, ballcourts, vast canal systems, shell jewellery traded from the Gulf of California, grew out of these modest beginnings.
Estrella Phase (Arizona, AD 500–AD 600).source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Vahki Phase (Arizona, AD 450–AD 500).label: Vahki Phase
Vahki Phase (Arizona, AD 450–AD 500).prose: [South-Central Arizona, AD 450–AD 500] Vahki Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.
Vahki Phase (Arizona, AD 450–AD 500).source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

Red Mountain (Arizona, AD 50–AD 450).label: Red Mountain
Red Mountain (Arizona, AD 50–AD 450).prose:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 50–AD 450] Red Mountain. Listed in source as unknown started date. For these purposes a tentative start date for the Red Mountain period can be based off of the end date of the Early Agricultural Period (EAP). Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

The earliest recognised phase of Hohokam settlement in the Phoenix Basin, when scattered clusters of shallow pit houses appeared along the Salt and Gila rivers. Villagers grew maize, made undecorated brown pottery and began the small-scale ditching that would later grow into the largest canal systems in prehistoric North America. Because the remains are deeply buried under later occupations and modern Phoenix, the phase is known from only a handful of excavated sites.
Red Mountain (Arizona, AD 50–AD 450).source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

縄文時代 (Honshu, 10999 BC–299 BC).label: 縄文時代
縄文時代 (Honshu, 10999 BC–299 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州・北海道, 10999 BC–299 BC] 縄文時代. Spatial coverage: Hokkaidō, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Added alternative spelling with macrons. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

One of the world's longest-lasting hunter-gatherer cultures, sustained by acorns, chestnuts, salmon, deer and rich coastal shellfish beds rather than farming. Its people made some of the earliest pottery anywhere, built settled villages with pit dwellings and vast shell middens, and left striking clay figurines and flame-shaped vessels. The sheer stability of the way of life challenges the assumption that agriculture is a necessary step toward complex society.
縄文時代 (Honshu, 10999 BC–299 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC).node: 縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC)
縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC).label: 縄文時代早期
縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 8999 BC–4999 BC] 縄文時代早期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. start確認. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

As the last glaciation ended and the islands were cut off by rising seas, people adapted to new forests of oak and chestnut with bows, pit traps, fish hooks and a growing reliance on shellfish. Pointed-base and rounded pots suited to cooking over hearths appear, and the first large shell middens begin to accumulate along the drowned coastlines.
縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC).node: 縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC)
縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC).label: 縄文時代前期
縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 4999 BC–2999 BC] 縄文時代前期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Sea levels reached their highest point and warm waters pushed deep inland, leaving shell mounds now stranded far from the coast. Settlements grew larger and more permanent, with horseshoe-shaped arrangements of pit houses, and pottery shifted to flat-bottomed, cylindrical forms decorated with rolled cord impressions.
縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC).node: 縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC).label: 縄文時代中期
縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 2999 BC–1999 BC] 縄文時代中期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

The warm, resource-rich centuries when Jomon population peaked in central and eastern Honshu, with large villages laid out around open plazas and monumental sites like Sannai-Maruyama. Potters produced the most exuberant vessels of the whole era, including the flame-rimmed jars of the Shinano basin, alongside numerous clay figurines and stone rods that suggest an active ritual life.
縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC).node: 縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC)
縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC).label: 縄文時代後期
縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 1999 BC–999 BC] 縄文時代後期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

A cooling climate scattered the large inland villages, and people moved toward the coasts and river valleys. Ritual activity became more visible: stone circles such as Oyu, elaborate burial grounds, and finely finished pottery and lacquerware suggest communities investing heavily in ceremony as conditions grew harder.
縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC).node: 縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC)
縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC).label: 縄文時代晩期
縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 999 BC–299 BC] 縄文時代晩期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

The final Jomon centuries saw exquisitely crafted Kamegaoka pottery and the famous goggle-eyed dogu figurines in the north, while in the west rice agriculture was already taking hold. The overlap of the two worlds - foragers and the first farmers - marks the transition into the Yayoi era.
縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC).node: 弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC)
弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC).label: 弥生時代前期
弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 299 BC–199 BC] 弥生時代前期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. stopの期間はおおよそ. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Wet-rice paddy farming, spread from the Korean peninsula through northern Kyushu and up into western Honshu, along with bronze and iron tools, weaving and new burial customs using jars and dolmen-like stone markers. Villages became permanent and were often ditched or palisaded, a sign that stored grain surpluses were worth fighting over. The plain, wheel-finished pottery that gives the era its name replaced the elaborate cord-marked wares of the preceding age.
弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

弥生時代中期 (Honshu, 199 BC–AD 1).label: 弥生時代中期
弥生時代中期 (Honshu, 199 BC–AD 1).prose:
[本州・四国・九州, 199 BC–AD 1] 弥生時代中期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. startの期間はおおよそ。. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Rice farming was now well established across Honshu, supporting large moated settlements, storehouses on stilts and the first clear signs of hereditary rank. Bronze was used for display rather than tools: ritual bells cast in the east, weapon-shaped objects in the west, deliberately buried on hillsides. Imported Chinese mirrors and coins in elite graves show communities plugged into networks reaching the Han commanderies in Korea, while defensive ditches and injured skeletons point to competition between them.
弥生時代中期 (Honshu, 199 BC–AD 1).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC.node: 旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC)
旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC.label: 旧石器時代
旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC.prose:
[沖縄, 31999 BC–4999 BC] 旧石器時代. 大陸から現生人類が日本列島に渡り、居住を始める
炭素14年代測定法による校正年代では、Start label：B.C.36000. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Hunter-gatherers occupied the limestone caves and fissures of the Ryukyus, leaving some of the oldest human skeletal remains in Japan, including the Minatogawa and Shiraho-Saonetabaru finds. The islands' limestone preserves bone far better than the acidic soils of the main islands, which is why so much of what is known about Pleistocene people in Japan comes from here. Sea crossings were required to reach these islands, implying seafaring capability tens of thousands of years ago.
旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC.node: 貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC)
貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC.label: 貝塚時代前期
貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC.prose:
[沖縄, 10999 BC–999 BC] 貝塚時代前期. Added alternative translation. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

The long era in which Ryukyuan islanders lived off coral-reef fish, shellfish and wild plants, leaving huge accumulations of discarded shell. Pottery and stone tools followed their own island trajectory, distinct from the Jomon sequence of the main islands, showing how differently the subtropical south developed.
貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

貝塚時代中期 (Okinawa Islands, 999 BC–99 BC).node: 貝塚時代中期 (Okinawa Islands, 999 BC–99 BC)
貝塚時代中期 (Okinawa Islands, 999 BC–99 BC).label: 貝塚時代中期
貝塚時代中期 (Okinawa Islands, 999 BC–99 BC).prose:
[沖縄, 999 BC–99 BC] 貝塚時代中期. stopの期間はおおよそ Added alternative translation. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

While the main islands took up rice farming, people in the Ryukyus stayed with fishing, shellfish gathering and foraging along the reefs, leaving the deep shell middens that name the era. Their shell ornaments and tools travelled north into Kyushu, showing long-distance exchange between the islands and the emerging Yayoi world.
貝塚時代中期 (Okinawa Islands, 999 BC–99 BC).source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

Early period (Roman Noricum) (Austria, 1.label: Early period (Roman Noricum)
Early period (Roman Noricum) (Austria, 1.prose:
[Noricum, 14 BC–AD 117] Early period (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. Adapted from the source. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. The Celtic kingdom of Noricum, long a friendly trading partner supplying Rome with its prized iron, was absorbed into the empire under Augustus. Roman administration replaced hillfort centres with planned towns such as Virunum, and roads over the Alpine passes tied the region to Italy and the Danube. Latin, coinage and Mediterranean building styles spread quickly among a population that kept much of its Celtic identity.

Nero's suicide opened a scramble for the throne in which Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each held power within a year. The provinces learned, as Tacitus put it, that an emperor could be made outside Rome, and legions on the Rhine and Danube became kingmakers. Vespasian and his sons reorganised the Alpine and Danubian provinces, granting municipal status to towns such as Flavia Solva and boosting Virunum, Teurnia and Iuvavum. Stone building, road improvement and formal town charters replaced the older Celtic settlement pattern, and the iron and salt trade drew the region firmly into the imperial economy. Diocletian split the province into Noricum ripense along the Danube and Noricum mediterraneum in the Alpine interior, backed by a chain of forts facing pressure from beyond the river. As security frayed, people moved from open valley towns to fortified hilltop settlements, and Christianity spread with bishops and early churches. The Life of Saint Severinus describes the last decades of Roman life here, ending when Odoacer ordered the remaining Roman population evacuated to Italy.

Under Trajan, Hadrian and the Antonines, the Alpine province of Noricum enjoyed its most prosperous stretch, exporting its famous iron and supplying recruits to the legions. Towns such as Virunum and Ovilava gained forums, baths and stone monuments, and Roman law and Latin spread among the descendants of the Celtic Norici. The peace broke with the Marcomannic Wars under Marcus Aurelius, when Germanic raiders crossed the Danube and permanent legionary garrisons were installed.

Emperors were made and unmade by the army, dozens of them in half a century, while plague, debased coinage and invasion tore at the frontiers. In the Alpine and Danube provinces this meant raids across the river, hoards buried and never recovered, and communities pulling back from open valley towns onto defensible hilltops. Diocletian's accession ended the chaos and brought a reorganised, more militarised province.

Frontier garrisons went unpaid and unreplaced, low-lying towns shrank, and populations shifted to fortified hilltop settlements and church complexes. The Germanic commander who deposed the last western emperor in 476 ruled Italy as king, and the Roman provincials of Noricum along the Danube fell within his orbit. Frontier life there is vividly recorded in the Life of Saint Severinus: shrinking garrisons, unpaid soldiers, raids and towns emptying out. In 488 Odoacer ordered the remaining Romans evacuated south to Italy, effectively ending Roman civil administration on this stretch of the Danube.

Rome absorbed the Celtic kingdom of Noricum without a fight and conquered Pannonia by force, pushing the frontier to the Danube and turning the region into a corridor between Italy and the northern provinces. Legions and auxiliary forts appeared along the river, the amber road carried Baltic goods south, and native hilltop centres such as the Magdalensberg gave way to Roman towns. It was the foundation of four centuries of Roman life in the eastern Alps and the Vienna basin.

Under Claudius the Alpine kingdom of Noricum was formally organised as a procuratorial province and its main native centres — Virunum, Celeia, Teurnia, Aguntum, Iuvavum — were promoted to Roman municipia. Local elites gained citizenship and adopted Latin, monumental building and Roman religion, while iron and salt continued to flow south. Provincial administration and urban life arrived here largely by agreement rather than conquest.

As Rome expanded across the Mediterranean, its republican institutions buckled under the strain of army commanders, civil wars and vast new wealth. In the eastern Alps this was the era of the kingdom of Noricum, whose famous iron drew Italian merchants to the trading settlement on the Magdalensberg long before the region was formally annexed. Roman goods, coinage and inscriptions appear here generations ahead of Roman troops.

Timber camps on the Danube were rebuilt in stone as the frontier hardened into a permanent military zone, with legions installed at Carnuntum and a new fortress at Vindobona, the seed of Vienna. Trajan divided Pannonia into two provinces in 106 and drew troops from the region for his Dacian wars, while veteran settlement and trade turned garrison towns into civilian cities. The road and fort network laid down here shaped settlement in the area for centuries.

The high imperial period on the Danube frontier, when Carnuntum and Vindobona grew into major garrison towns with amphitheatres, baths and civilian settlements, and Noricum's iron and Pannonia's grain fed the army. Prosperity was interrupted by the Marcomannic Wars, when Germanic groups broke across the river and Marcus Aurelius spent years campaigning from Carnuntum, where he is said to have written part of his Meditations. The wars, and the plague that came with them, marked the point at which the frontier stopped being simply a place of profit.

Carnuntum was where the Pannonian legions proclaimed their governor, Septimius Severus, emperor in 193, and the province was rewarded with favour for the rest of the dynasty. Towns received city charters, soldiers' pay and privileges rose, and the Danube settlements reached their greatest extent, with stone amphitheatres, baths and imported cults such as Mithras and Jupiter Dolichenus. It was the high point of provincial prosperity before the crises of the mid-third century.

Roman emperors were made and unmade by their armies at bewildering speed, while invasions, plague and a collapsing silver coinage strained the empire to breaking point. Along the Danube in Noricum the pressure was felt directly: towns contracted behind walls, hilltop sites were reoccupied and rural villas were abandoned or fortified. Diocletian's accession ended the cycle and imposed a new, more militarised order.

Diocletian's reforms redrew the provinces and stiffened the Danube defences with new forts, watchtowers and river fleets, while Christianity spread and bishoprics appeared in the Alpine towns. From the fourth century the frontier came under mounting pressure, and the Life of Saint Severinus paints a vivid picture of shrinking towns, unpaid garrisons and negotiated survival among barbarian neighbours. The Roman population was evacuated to Italy in 488, and Bavarians, Lombards, Slavs and Avars filled the space that remained.

The moment when a Germanic officer of the imperial army removed Romulus Augustulus and sent the western regalia to Constantinople, taking the title of king rather than emperor. For the Danube provinces it meant the last thread of imperial authority snapped, leaving communities to negotiate with barbarian neighbours on their own, as the Life of Saint Severinus describes.

The first generation of Spanish town-founding, land grants and forced labour drafts, met by fierce indigenous resistance in the Andean valleys. Native settlements were relocated to mission towns, populations collapsed under epidemics and warfare, and European livestock, wheat and vines began transforming the landscape.
Período Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD.source: Las sociedades indígenas y su incorporación al proceso de producción de textiles en el período colonial temprano (Córdoba, 1573-1620)

Mesolithic (Portugal, 9999 BC–4999 BC).prose:
[Portugal, 9999 BC–4999 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Neolithic (Portugal, 4999 BC–2999 BC).prose:

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Chalcolithic (Portugal, 2999 BC–2199 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Portugal, 2999 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[Portugal, 2999 BC–2199 BC] Chalcolithic. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Bronze Age (Portugal, 2199 BC–700 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Portugal, 2199 BC–700 BC).prose:
[Portugal, 2199 BC–700 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Iron Age (Portugal, 799 BC–25 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Portugal, 799 BC–25 BC).prose:
[Portugal, 799 BC–25 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Roman Period (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 476).label: Roman Period
Roman Period (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 476).prose:

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

Early Roman Empire (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 3.label: Early Roman Empire
Early Roman Empire (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 3.prose:
[Portugal, 25 BC–AD 305] Early Roman Empire. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Augustus reorganised the far west of Iberia into provinces, and the territory that would become Portugal was drawn into a network of roads, towns and taxation centred on new foundations such as Bracara Augusta and Emerita Augusta. Villas, mines, fish-salting works and garum factories tied the Atlantic coast into Mediterranean markets, while local elites took Roman names, Roman citizenship and Roman gods. Latin, urbanism and the road system left permanent marks on the landscape.

Late Roman Empire (Portugal, AD 305–AD 4.label: Late Roman Empire
Late Roman Empire (Portugal, AD 305–AD 4.prose:
[Portugal, AD 305–AD 476] Late Roman Empire. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Diocletian's and Constantine's reforms reorganised the provinces, taxation and army, and Christianity moved from persecuted sect to favoured religion, leaving churches and Christian burials across the region. Wealth concentrated in large rural estates whose villas were decorated with elaborate mosaics, while towns contracted behind new walls. In the fifth century the frontier gave way and Suebic and Visigothic groups took control of the peninsula's west.

Late Antiquity (Portugal, AD 401–AD 800).label: Late Antiquity
Late Antiquity (Portugal, AD 401–AD 800).prose:
[Portugal, AD 401–AD 800] Late Antiquity. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The Roman provinces along the lower Danube and in Thrace became a frontier zone under constant pressure, with Goths, Huns and other groups crossing the river while emperors fortified cities and roads. Christianity spread fast: basilicas and bishoprics appeared at Serdica, Philippopolis and elsewhere, and Serdica hosted a major church council. After the empire split, these lands fell to the eastern half, setting up their long Byzantine future.

Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1415).label: Middle Ages
Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1415).prose:
[Portugal, AD 601–AD 1415] Middle Ages. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman rule in the west and the Renaissance saw Latin Christendom take shape: monasteries preserved and reworked classical learning, kingdoms hardened into states, and lords, peasants and towns settled into new legal relationships. Population and cultivated land grew steadily until plague and famine reversed it in the fourteenth century. Cathedrals, universities, guilds, parliaments and the vernacular literatures of Europe all date from this span.

Late Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 1100–AD 1.label: Late Middle Ages
Late Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 1100–AD 1.prose:

A frontier county broke away from León to become a kingdom, and its rulers pushed south with Templar and Cistercian help until the capture of the Algarve completed the Reconquest and fixed borders that have barely moved since. Lisbon and Porto grew on Atlantic trade, and Portuguese replaced Latin in royal documents. A succession crisis brought the House of Aviz to power at Aljubarrota, and the seizure of Ceuta in 1415 opened the era of overseas expansion.

Early Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1.label: Early Middle Ages
Early Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1.prose:

The Visigothic kingdom governed the west of Iberia until Muslim armies crossed from North Africa in 711, making the region the Gharb of al-Andalus, with Islamic administration, agriculture and urban life in the south. From the ninth century Christian rulers from the north pushed the frontier back down the Douro and Mondego, repopulating Braga, Porto and Coimbra. The county of Portucale that emerged from this frontier zone became the kingdom of Portugal in the twelfth century.

Medieval Islamic Period (Portugal, AD 71.label: Medieval Islamic Period
Medieval Islamic Period (Portugal, AD 71.prose:
[Portugal, AD 711–AD 1249] Medieval Islamic Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Umayyad armies crossed from North Africa in 711 and within a few years held most of the Iberian peninsula; the western territories became al-Andalus's Gharb, with Silves, Mértola and Lisbon as centres of irrigated agriculture, ceramics and Mediterranean trade. New crops, water-lifting technology and urban forms arrived, and Arabic left a deep mark on Portuguese vocabulary and place names. Christian kings pushed south over three centuries, and Afonso III's capture of Faro in 1249 completed the conquest and fixed Portugal's modern borders.

Medieval Christian Period (Portugal, AD.label: Medieval Christian Period
Medieval Christian Period (Portugal, AD.prose: [Portugal, AD 1200–AD 1415] Medieval Christian Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Modern Age (Portugal, AD 1415–AD 1789).label: Modern Age
Modern Age (Portugal, AD 1415–AD 1789).prose:
[Portugal, AD 1415–AD 1789] Modern Age. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Beginning with the seizure of Ceuta, Portugal pushed south along the African coast and then round it, reaching India and Brazil and building a seaborne empire of trading forts stretching to Macau. Wealth from spices, sugar, gold and the Atlantic slave trade poured through Lisbon, funding Manueline architecture and a court culture of global reach, even as the crown passed to Spain for sixty years and the empire's centre shifted to Brazil. The 1755 earthquake levelled Lisbon and gave the Marquis of Pombal his chance to rebuild the city and remake the state along Enlightenment lines.

Contemporary Period (Portugal, AD 1789–A.label: Contemporary Period
Contemporary Period (Portugal, AD 1789–A.prose:
[Portugal, AD 1789–AD 2021] Contemporary Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Napoleonic invasion drove the Portuguese court to Brazil, and the country came back to a liberal revolution, civil war and the loss of its largest colony. A republic replaced the monarchy in 1910, gave way to Salazar's long authoritarian Estado Novo, and the Carnation Revolution of 1974 ended both the dictatorship and the African empire, opening the way into Europe.

弥生時代 (Japan, 299 BC–AD 300).label: 弥生時代
弥生時代 (Japan, 299 BC–AD 300).prose:
[Japan, 299 BC–AD 300] 弥生時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Wet-rice agriculture arrived from the Asian mainland along with bronze and iron, transforming a foraging society into one of paddy fields, granaries and permanent villages. Surpluses meant inequality: some settlements were ringed with ditches and palisades, and skeletons show wounds from organised fighting. Chinese histories record dozens of small kingdoms sending envoys to the Han and Wei courts, among them Queen Himiko's Yamatai.
弥生時代 (Japan, 299 BC–AD 300).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

大和時代 (Japan, AD 300–AD 600).label: 大和時代
大和時代 (Japan, AD 300–AD 600).prose:
[Japan, AD 300–AD 600] 大和時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Rulers based in the Nara basin built enormous keyhole-shaped burial mounds, the largest earthworks ever raised in Japan, filled with mirrors, armour, horse gear and clay haniwa figures. This was when a paramount lineage extended control over much of the archipelago and maintained close ties with the kingdoms of the Korean peninsula. Immigrants brought iron working, horses, sericulture, writing and eventually Buddhism, laying the groundwork for a Chinese-style state.
大和時代 (Japan, AD 300–AD 600).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

飛鳥時代 (Japan, AD 600–AD 709).label: 飛鳥時代
飛鳥時代 (Japan, AD 600–AD 709).prose:
[Japan, AD 600–AD 709] 飛鳥時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Buddhism, Chinese writing, Chinese law and continental court ritual took hold as the Yamato rulers reshaped themselves into an emperor's government. Prince Shotoku's reforms and the Taika edicts introduced ranked officials, registered land and taxation, and the first great temples such as Horyuji rose with the oldest surviving wooden architecture in the world.
飛鳥時代 (Japan, AD 600–AD 709).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

奈良時代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 794).label: 奈良時代
奈良時代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 794).prose:
[Japan, AD 710–AD 794] 奈良時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Japan's first lasting capital, Heijo-kyo, was laid out on a Chinese grid, and the state ran on the ritsuryo law codes, censuses and rice taxes. Emperor Shomu poured national resources into Buddhism, casting the colossal bronze Buddha at Todai-ji and founding provincial temples. The court's earliest books date from these years: the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and the Man'yoshu poetry anthology, alongside the treasures still preserved in the Shosoin storehouse.
奈良時代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 794).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

平安時代 (Japan, AD 794–AD 1192).label: 平安時代
平安時代 (Japan, AD 794–AD 1192).prose:
[Japan, AD 794–AD 1192] 平安時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

With the capital settled at Heian-kyo, the Fujiwara family ruled through marriage alliances with emperors while the formal Chinese-style administration decayed. Court life produced the kana syllabary and a literature largely written by women, including The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book, alongside esoteric Tendai and Shingon Buddhism and a widespread belief in Amida's paradise. In the provinces, warrior clans grew strong enough to fight the Genpei War and hand real power to the samurai.
平安時代 (Japan, AD 794–AD 1192).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

古代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 1192).label: 古代
古代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 1192).prose:
[Japan, AD 710–AD 1192] 古代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Japan's classical age, governed by an imported Chinese-style legal code with a capital first at Nara and then at Heian-kyo, modern Kyoto. Buddhism was state-sponsored and monumental, but courtiers also developed a distinctly Japanese culture: kana writing, waka poetry, and prose such as The Tale of Genji. Behind the elegance, tax-free private estates and provincial warrior bands were quietly draining the court's power.
古代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 1192).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

鎌倉時代 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333).label: 鎌倉時代
鎌倉時代 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333).prose:
[Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333] 鎌倉時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Power shifted from the court in Kyoto to a warrior government in the east, with the shogun and later the Hojo regents ruling through networks of vassals. The two Mongol invasions were beaten back with the help of storms later called the kamikaze, though the cost strained the regime. Zen Buddhism and the popular Pure Land and Nichiren movements took root, and a stark, muscular style appeared in sculpture and war tales.
鎌倉時代 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

室町時代 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573).label: 室町時代
室町時代 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573).prose:
[Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573] 室町時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The Ashikaga shoguns governed from Kyoto, close to the imperial court, presiding over a lucrative trade with Ming China and over steadily weakening central control. Their patronage produced some of Japan's most enduring culture: noh drama, linked verse, ink landscape painting, flower arranging, and the Golden and Silver Pavilions. The Onin War of 1467 wrecked the capital and unleashed a century of provincial warfare in which retainers routinely overthrew their lords.
室町時代 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

中世 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573).label: 中世
中世 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573).prose:
[Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573] 中世. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Power passed from the court aristocracy to warrior houses ruling from Kamakura and later Kyoto, with the emperor reduced largely to a ceremonial role. Estates, temples and armed leagues carved up authority; Zen, Pure Land and Nichiren Buddhism spread among ordinary people; and the Mongol invasions were beaten off with help from storms remembered as the kamikaze. The era ends in a century of open civil war among regional warlords, which also produced the tea ceremony, noh theatre and ink painting.
中世 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

安土・桃山時代 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603).label: 安土・桃山時代
安土・桃山時代 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603).prose:
[Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603] 安土・桃山時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Three decades of dramatic unification, as Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi broke the power of independent warlords, monasteries and free cities. Hideyoshi's sword hunt and land surveys froze the boundary between samurai and peasants, and his two invasions of Korea ended in costly failure. The mood shows in the art: soaring stone-based castles, gold-leaf screens, and by contrast the deliberate rusticity of Sen no Rikyu's tea ceremony.
安土・桃山時代 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

江戸時代 (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868).label: 江戸時代
江戸時代 (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868).prose:
[Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868] 江戸時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Under the Tokugawa shoguns Japan enjoyed two and a half centuries without major war, with the country closed to most foreign contact and society divided into fixed hereditary ranks. Cities boomed - Edo became one of the largest in the world - and with them came kabuki, woodblock prints, popular fiction and a widely literate merchant public. The order finally cracked under fiscal strain and the arrival of American warships.
江戸時代 (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

近世 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868).label: 近世
近世 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868).prose:
[Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868] 近世. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The age from the warlord reunification under Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi through the Tokugawa peace: castles, cadastral surveys, disarmed peasants and a fixed status order. Cities, road networks and a money economy grew rapidly, producing a rich urban culture even as contact with the outside world was tightly restricted.
近世 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

明治時代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).label: 明治時代
明治時代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).prose:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912] 明治時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

In little more than four decades Japan dismantled the samurai order, built railways, factories, a conscript army and a written constitution, and turned itself from a country forced open by foreign gunboats into a power that defeated Russia. Domains became prefectures, commoners took surnames, and Western dress, science and law were adopted wholesale while Shinto was reworked into a state ideology around the emperor. The speed of the change made it a model, and a warning, for modernisers everywhere.
明治時代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

大正時代 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).label: 大正時代
大正時代 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).prose:
[Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926] 大正時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

A brief, liberal-feeling interlude often called Taisho democracy: party cabinets, universal male suffrage in 1925, mass-circulation newspapers, cafés, cinema and the 'modern girl'. Japan profited from the First World War and joined the great powers at Versailles, while labour unrest, rice riots and socialist agitation grew at home. The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 flattened Tokyo and Yokohama and killed over a hundred thousand people, and the same year's security laws pointed towards the harder decades ahead.
大正時代 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

昭和時代 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).label: 昭和時代
昭和時代 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).prose:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989] 昭和時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The longest imperial reign in Japanese history spanned militarism, empire, catastrophic defeat, occupation and then the fastest sustained economic growth the world had seen. A visitor can trace the same country from the invasion of Manchuria and the atomic bombings to bullet trains, transistor radios and the Tokyo Olympics within a single lifetime.
昭和時代 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

近代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989).label: 近代
近代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989).prose:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989] 近代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Japan's era as a modern state, from the Meiji reforms and industrialisation through empire-building in Korea, Taiwan and China, to war, defeat and postwar reconstruction. The whole arc - constitution, conscription, factories, colonies, ruin and recovery - unfolded in barely more than a century.
近代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

昭和時代戦前 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945).label: 昭和時代戦前
昭和時代戦前 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945).prose:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945] 昭和時代戦前. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Economic crisis, assassinations of politicians and the growing independence of the army pushed Japan from party government toward military domination. Expansion into Manchuria and China led into the Pacific War, ending with firebombed cities, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and unconditional surrender. Material from these years - propaganda posters, rationing goods, air-raid gear - shows how thoroughly civilian life was mobilised.
昭和時代戦前 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

昭和時代戦後 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988).label: 昭和時代戦後
昭和時代戦後 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988).prose:
[Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988] 昭和時代戦後. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Occupation reforms brought a new constitution renouncing war, land redistribution, votes for women and the dissolution of the great business combines. From the ruins came decades of double-digit growth built on steel, shipbuilding, cars and electronics, producing the consumer society of televisions, apartment blocks and commuter trains that still shapes Japan.
昭和時代戦後 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

平成時代 (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019).label: 平成時代
平成時代 (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019).prose:
[Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019] 平成時代. The source did not have an end label for the Heisei era because the era ended 5 years after its publication. I added the date because it is undisputed. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The era opened just as the asset bubble burst, ushering in the 'lost decades' of stagnant wages, deflation and an ageing, shrinking population. It saw the Kobe earthquake, the Tokyo subway sarin attack, and the 2011 tsunami and Fukushima nuclear disaster, alongside the global spread of Japanese games, anime and food. It ended with the first abdication of a Japanese emperor in two centuries.
平成時代 (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

現代 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019).label: 現代
現代 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019).prose:
[Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019] 現代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Postwar Japan under a pacifist constitution became the world's second-largest economy, then faced the bursting of its asset bubble, an ageing population and disasters like Kobe and Fukushima. It is also the era of Japanese cultural export - cameras, cars, video games, manga and anime reaching a global audience.
現代 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019).source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 20.label: Período Alfarero Temprano
Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 20.prose:
[Neuquén Province, 200 BC–AD 1400] Período Alfarero Temprano. Period definition from  Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina. — Pérez, Alberto E., 2020.

Farming hamlets appear with pottery, stone hoes, grinding equipment and pens for llamas, set among field walls and irrigation channels. Households were largely self-sufficient but exchanged obsidian, shell, metal and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia over long distances, laying the agricultural and technological groundwork for the crowded towns of later centuries.
Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 20.source: Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina.

Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.label: Período Alfarero Tardío
Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.prose:
[Neuquén Province, AD 1001–AD 1900] Período Alfarero Tardío. Period definition from  Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina. — Pérez, Alberto E., 2020.

Communities consolidated into large agglomerated towns of stone-walled rooms, often perched on defensible spurs above terraced fields, with cemeteries of urns holding infant burials. Painted Santa María and Belén jars, metalwork and evidence of raiding point to competition between valley polities, which were later drawn into the Inca road system and then shattered by the Spanish invasion and the Calchaquí wars.
Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.source: Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina.

Período Alfarero (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1.label: Período Alfarero
Período Alfarero (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1.prose:
[Neuquén Province, 200 BC–AD 1900] Período Alfarero. Period definition from Crono-categorías culturales Argentina. Base de Datos. — Izeta, Andrés Darío, 2021.

The long stretch in which fired pottery, cultivated crops and llama herding became the basis of life across northwestern Argentina. Scattered hunting camps gave way to permanent villages with storage, irrigation and cemeteries, and later to large fortified towns that were absorbed first by the Inca and then by Spain. Ceramics are the backbone of the chronology here: styles change often enough that a broken bowl can date a site to within a century or two.
Período Alfarero (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1.source: Crono-categorías culturales Argentina. Base de Datos.

Recent Prehistory (Europe, 5550 BC–1150.label: Recent Prehistory
Recent Prehistory (Europe, 5550 BC–1150.prose:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–1150 BC] Recent Prehistory. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The stretch from the spread of farming to the end of the Bronze Age, when Europe filled with villages, fields and herds, and communities began raising megaliths and burial mounds over their dead. Copper and then bronze metallurgy created long-distance trade in ore, amber and finished weapons, and with it visible differences of wealth and rank. By its close, fortified centres, chariots, warrior burials and shared prestige styles linked much of the continent to the Mediterranean palace world.
Recent Prehistory (Europe, 5550 BC–1150.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

Neolithic (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–3050 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.
Neolithic (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC).source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

Calcolithic (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC).label: Calcolithic
Calcolithic (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 3350 BC–1850 BC] Calcolithic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The centuries when copper working spread across Europe alongside continued heavy use of stone tools, bringing the first metal axes, daggers and ornaments and the first specialised miners. Ploughs, wheeled vehicles, wool sheep and horses transformed farming and travel, while megalithic tombs, richly furnished individual graves and hilltop enclosures point to sharpening inequality and conflict. It is the world of the Iceman, of Corded Ware and Bell Beaker pottery, and of the population movements that reshaped the continent's ancestry before bronze became standard.
Calcolithic (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC).source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

Bronze Age (Europe, 1850 BC–1150 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Europe, 1850 BC–1150 BC).prose:
[Eurasia, 1850 BC–1150 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Europe, 1850 BC–1150 BC).source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

Holocene (Europe, 9050 BC–AD 2021).label: Holocene
Holocene (Europe, 9050 BC–AD 2021).prose:
[Eurasia, 9050 BC–AD 2021] Holocene. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The warm interval since the last glaciation, in which rising seas cut Britain off from the continent and drowned the plain now beneath the North Sea. Tundra gave way to birch, pine and then dense mixed woodland; hunter-gatherers were followed by farmers, and every monument, field system, town and road in the country belongs to this sliver of geological time. Its later part is marked worldwide by human alteration of climate, soils and species.
Holocene (Europe, 9050 BC–AD 2021).source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

MIS 1 (Earth, 12050 BC–AD 1950).label: MIS 1
MIS 1 (Earth, 12050 BC–AD 1950).prose:
[World, 12050 BC–AD 1950] MIS 1. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The current warm interval in the ocean-sediment record, beginning as the last ice age ended, ice sheets melted and sea level rose more than a hundred metres, drowning coastlines and land bridges such as Doggerland and Beringia. Stable, comparatively mild conditions accompanied the spread of farming, cities, writing and every recorded civilisation. It is the climatic stage humans still live in.
MIS 1 (Earth, 12050 BC–AD 1950).source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

Quaternaire (France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000).label: Quaternaire
Quaternaire (France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000).prose:
[France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000] Quaternaire. Le Quaternaire est la troisième période géologique de l'ère du Cénozoïque et la plus récente sur l'échelle des temps géologiques. Cette période se caractérise par le retour des glaciations, l'extension du genre Homo et l'extinction des faunes de l'Holocène. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The most recent stretch of geological time, defined by repeated ice ages in which glaciers advanced and retreated across northern Europe, sea levels rose and fell by more than a hundred metres, and mammoth, reindeer and woolly rhinoceros ranged over the continent. It is also the age of humanity: the whole story of stone tools, cave painting, farming and cities falls inside it.
Quaternaire (France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Chronologie américaine (France, 23000 BC.prose: [France, 23000 BC–AD 1492] Chronologie américaine. Employer ce terme pour les périodes entre la préhistoire et l'arrivée des Espagnols (BL). Holocène (France, 9700 BC–AD 2000).label: Holocène
Holocène (France, 9700 BC–AD 2000).prose:
[France, 9700 BC–AD 2000] Holocène. L'Holocène (du grec ancien holos - ὅλος : entier, et kainos - καινός : récent) est une époque géologique s'étendant sur les 10 000 dernières années, toujours en cours de nos jours. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The postglacial warm period in which the ice caps withdrew, the Atlantic rose to something near its present level, and reindeer-hunting steppe gave way to oak and hazel forest. Mesolithic foragers adapted to the new woodlands and coasts before farming spread from the Mediterranean and the Danube, bringing megaliths, metal, and eventually towns. Everything from the painted caves' aftermath to the present belongs to this interval.
Holocène (France, 9700 BC–AD 2000).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Préhistoire (France, 800000 BC–3001 BC).label: Préhistoire
Préhistoire (France, 800000 BC–3001 BC).prose:
[France, 800000 BC–3001 BC] Préhistoire. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The long arc from the first hominins in Europe - the half-million-year-old skull from Tautavel, the Neanderthal burials of the Dordogne - to the eve of metal and writing. Its most famous legacy is the painted caves of Chauvet, Lascaux and Pech Merle, made by Ice Age hunters with charcoal and ochre. After the glaciers retreated, farming spread up the Rhône and along the Mediterranean, and communities began raising the megaliths and standing stones of Brittany, including the thousands of alignments at Carnac.
Préhistoire (France, 800000 BC–3001 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Néolithique (France, 6000 BC–2201 BC) [p.prose:
[France, 6000 BC–2201 BC] Néolithique. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Herding of sheep, goats and cattle, together with pottery and cultivated grain, spread across the Moroccan coast, the Rif and the Atlas, taking hold among populations descended from earlier hunter-gatherers. Cardial-impressed pottery in the north points to contact across the Strait with Iberia, while cave sites and shell middens show a mixed economy of farming, herding, fishing and gathering. Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.
Néolithique (France, 6000 BC–2201 BC) [p.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Néolithique moyen (France, 5300 BC–4501.label: Néolithique moyen
Néolithique moyen (France, 5300 BC–4501.prose:
[France, 5300 BC–4501 BC] Néolithique moyen. English label not present in original source but required for data entry via  client. Obtained via Google translate. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Farming communities across France moved beyond the tightly uniform longhouse villages of the first settlers into a patchwork of regional groups with their own pottery and burial customs. In the west, people began raising long earthen mounds and stone chambered tombs – among the earliest monumental architecture in Europe – while enclosures ringed by ditches and palisades appeared in the north and the Paris basin. Cattle herding, flint mining and long-distance movement of polished stone axes tied these communities together.
Néolithique moyen (France, 5300 BC–4501.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Néolithique récent (France, 4500 BC–2201.label: Néolithique récent
Néolithique récent (France, 4500 BC–2201.prose:
[France, 4500 BC–2201 BC] Néolithique récent. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Farming communities across France grew denser and more organised, raising megalithic tombs and long stone alignments, digging flint mines, and building enclosures ringed by ditches and palisades. Pottery styles and burial customs became strongly regional, from the collective gallery graves of the Paris Basin to the passage tombs of Brittany. Toward the end, copper objects and the first Beaker pottery signal the shift into the metal ages.
Néolithique récent (France, 4500 BC–2201.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Néolithique final (France, 4500 BC–3951.label: Néolithique final
Néolithique final (France, 4500 BC–3951.prose:
[France, 4500 BC–3951 BC] Néolithique final. Correspond au Chalcolithique sans métal. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The closing stage of the Neolithic in France, when the landscape filled with people: hilltop and ditched enclosures, large collective tombs and rock-cut hypogea, extensive flint mines and polished-axe workshops. Copper was worked in the south, and networks moving axes, flint and ornaments stretched across the country. These societies, denser and more competitive than what came before, were the ones absorbed into the Bell Beaker world at the threshold of the Bronze Age.
Néolithique final (France, 4500 BC–3951.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Sub-boréal (France, 3710 BC–851 BC).label: Sub-boréal
Sub-boréal (France, 3710 BC–851 BC).prose:
[France, 3710 BC–851 BC] Sub-boréal. Avant-dernier étage paléoclimatologique de l'Holocène, le Subboréal s'étend de - 5000 ans à - 2500 ans avant le présent. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

A climatic phase in the northern European sequence, drier and somewhat cooler than the warm Atlantic period that preceded it, traced through shifts in pollen: beech and hornbeam spreading, lime declining, and clear signals of forest clearance for fields and pasture. It spans the arrival and consolidation of farming, the megalith builders and the whole of the Bronze Age. Peat bogs and lake cores from this interval are the main archive for reconstructing how much of the landscape change was climate and how much was people.
Sub-boréal (France, 3710 BC–851 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Chronologie antillaise (France, 3000 BC–.prose: [France, 3000 BC–AD 1915] Chronologie antillaise. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC).label: Chalcolithique
Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC).prose:
[France, 3000 BC–2201 BC] Chalcolithique. Parfois appelé Énéolithique, ou encore plus rarement Épinéolithique, période de la protohistoire originellement définie comme une transition entre le Néolithique et l'âge du bronze. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Copper working spread through late Neolithic communities in France, while the great megalithic tomb-building traditions continued and collective burial in hypogea and gallery graves reached its height. Toward the close of the period, Bell Beaker pottery and archery equipment arrived from the wider European network, bringing new metalworking skills and burial customs that led into the Bronze Age.
Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Protohistoire (France, 2200 BC–51 BC).label: Protohistoire
Protohistoire (France, 2200 BC–51 BC).prose:
[France, 2200 BC–51 BC] Protohistoire. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Covers the Bronze and Iron Ages in Gaul, from the first metal-using communities through the tumulus and urnfield traditions to Hallstatt princely burials and the La Tène world of the Celts. These societies built hillforts and oppida, minted coins and traded wine with the Mediterranean, but wrote almost nothing about themselves, so they are known through excavation and through what Greeks and Romans said about them. The sequence ends with Caesar's conquest, which brought Gaul into recorded history.
Protohistoire (France, 2200 BC–51 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

âge du Bronze (France, 2200 BC–801 BC) [.prose:

Copper and tin alloyed into bronze pulled the region into long-distance exchange networks running from Cornwall and Brittany to central Europe and the Mediterranean. Warrior elites were buried under tumuli with daggers and axes, and later centuries produced enormous hoards of scrap and finished metalwork, deliberately buried or thrown into rivers. By the closing phase, cremation in urnfields, fortified hilltop sites and mass-produced socketed axes point to the more crowded, competitive world that iron would inherit.

Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–1601 BC).prose:
[France, 2200 BC–1601 BC] Bronze ancien. Correspond à l’apparition de la métallurgie, avant le Ve millénaire av. J.‑C. en Anatolie mais vers le IIe millénaire av. J.‑C. en Europe occidentale comme en France. (Wikipédia).
