The first true tin bronze came into general use in France, made into flanged axes, triangular daggers and pins. Elite burials under mounds appear in Brittany and the Rhône valley, stocked with weapons, gold ornaments and amber that show long-distance contacts with Wessex and central Europe. Settlement remained dispersed, but control of metal and its trade routes was starting to create visible social ranks.
Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–1601 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque mycénienne (France, 1650 BC–1101.label: époque mycénienne
époque mycénienne (France, 1650 BC–1101.prose:
[France, 1650 BC–1101 BC] époque mycénienne. après 1400 av. J.-C.- vers 1200 av. J.-C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Fortified palace citadels at Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns ruled mainland Greece, administering their territories with Linear B tablets in an early form of Greek. Their shaft graves and beehive tombs held gold masks, weapons and imports showing wide Mediterranean contacts. The palaces burned around 1200 BC and writing was lost for centuries, but the memory of these kings survives in Homer.
époque mycénienne (France, 1650 BC–1101.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–1401 BC).label: Bronze moyen
Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–1401 BC).prose:
[France, 1600 BC–1401 BC] Bronze moyen. Appelé aussi l’« âge du Bronze véritable », il correspond à la culture des tumulus protoceltiques ce qui en Europe centrale se situe vers le IIe millénaire av. J.-C. et vers 1500 av. J.-C. en France. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Tumulus burial with weapons and ornaments spread widely, and metalworkers turned out palstave axes, torcs, bracelets and the first long swords. Regional workshops in Brittany, the Rhône and the north each developed recognisable styles while sharing forms with central Europe and Britain. Deliberate deposition of metal in rivers and hoards became a regular practice.
Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–1401 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–801 BC).label: Bronze final
Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–801 BC).prose:
[France, 1400 BC–801 BC] Bronze final. Marqué par le début des grandes invasions, principalement celtiques, il se confond en Europe centrale avec la culture des champs d’urnes. Il commence en Europe occidentale comme en France vers le XIIe siècle av. J.-C. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Cremation replaced inhumation across much of France as the Urnfield tradition spread from central Europe, leaving large cemeteries of ash-filled pots. Bronze production reached industrial levels, with sheet-metal vessels, leaf-shaped swords and enormous scrap hoards along the Atlantic and Rhône corridors. Hilltop sites were fortified, and by the closing generations the first iron objects appear, leading directly into the Hallstatt Iron Age.
Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–801 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Hallstatt (France, 1200 BC–475 BC).label: Hallstatt
Hallstatt (France, 1200 BC–475 BC).prose:
[France, 1200 BC–475 BC] Hallstatt. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Central Europe's Early Iron Age, named after the Austrian salt-mining village whose cemetery yielded a thousand richly furnished graves. Iron replaced bronze for weapons and tools, while chieftains were buried under great mounds with four-wheeled wagons, horse harness, and wine-drinking gear imported from Greek and Etruscan traders. Hilltop "princely seats" such as the Heuneburg and Mont Lassois show wealth concentrating in a few hands before the whole system gave way to the La Tène world.
Hallstatt (France, 1200 BC–475 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bronze récent (France, 1200 BC–1001 BC).label: Bronze récent
Bronze récent (France, 1200 BC–1001 BC).prose:
[France, 1200 BC–1001 BC] Bronze récent. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last phase of bronze-working in France, when Urnfield practices spread west: cremation in urn cemeteries largely replaced inhumation, and metalworkers turned out sheet-bronze vessels, socketed axes and slashing swords in huge numbers. Enormous hoards of scrap and finished tools were buried across the country, evidence of long-distance exchange in copper, tin and finished goods. Hillforts and fortified settlements multiplied, foreshadowing the iron-using societies of the Hallstatt world.
Bronze récent (France, 1200 BC–1001 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bronze récent I (France, 1200 BC–1101 BC.label: Bronze récent I
Bronze récent I (France, 1200 BC–1101 BC.prose: [France, 1200 BC–1101 BC] Bronze récent I. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.
Bronze récent I (France, 1200 BC–1101 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bronze récent II (France, 1100 BC–901 BC.label: Bronze récent II
Bronze récent II (France, 1100 BC–901 BC.prose: [France, 1100 BC–901 BC] Bronze récent II. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.
Bronze récent II (France, 1100 BC–901 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque orientalisante (France, 1000 BC–7.label: époque orientalisante
époque orientalisante (France, 1000 BC–7.prose:
[France, 1000 BC–701 BC] époque orientalisante. de 750 à 600 pour les archéologues. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Contact with Phoenician and Near Eastern traders flooded the Greek and Italian world with new imagery — griffins, sphinxes, lions, palmettes — and new techniques in ivory, gold and bronze. Greek potters and metalworkers absorbed these motifs and made them their own, and the alphabet arrived by the same routes. It marks the point at which the Mediterranean became a single connected cultural zone.
époque orientalisante (France, 1000 BC–7.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bronze récent III (France, 900 BC–801 BC.label: Bronze récent III
Bronze récent III (France, 900 BC–801 BC.prose: [France, 900 BC–801 BC] Bronze récent III. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.
Bronze récent III (France, 900 BC–801 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Subatlantique (France, 850 BC–AD 2000).label: Subatlantique
Subatlantique (France, 850 BC–AD 2000).prose:
[France, 850 BC–AD 2000] Subatlantique. Sur l'échelle des temps géologiques, le Subatlantique est le dernier étage géologique de l'Holocène. Succédant au Subboréal, il s'étend depuis environ -850 (tant que la proposition de création de l'Anthropocène n'est pas retenue). (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The current climatic phase, opening with a cool, wet downturn around the start of the Iron Age that raised bog surfaces and pushed settlement off some upland ground. Beech and hornbeam dominate the pollen record where woodland survives, but the overwhelming story is human: sustained clearance, cereal and weed pollen, and eventually a landscape more managed than natural. It covers everything from Celtic Europe through the Roman world and the medieval warm period to the Little Ice Age and industrialisation.
Subatlantique (France, 850 BC–AD 2000).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–51 BC) [p02ch.label: âge du Fer
âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–51 BC) [p02ch.prose:
[France, 800 BC–51 BC] âge du Fer. Période chronologique caractérisée par l'usage de la métallurgie du fer et faisant généralement suite à l'âge du bronze. Cependant, les limites chronologiques de l'âge du fer varient considérablement selon l'aire culturelle et géographique considérée. Ainsi peut-il être considéré comme appartenant à la Préhistoire, à la Protohistoire ou l'Histoire selon les aires géographiques considérées. L'âge du fer débute vers 1100 av. J.-C. dans le monde méditerranéen, vers 800 à 700 av. J.-C. dans le nord de l'Europe et vers 500 av. J.-C. en Afrique. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Iron, cheap and widely available, replaced bronze for tools and weapons and changed who could arm and equip themselves. Princely burials, Mediterranean wine imports and later the fortified oppida trace the rise of Celtic chiefdoms with coinage, towns and craft specialisation. It ends with Caesar's conquest, which folded Gaul into the Roman world.
âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–51 BC) [p02ch.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Italie archaïque (France, 800 BC–401 BC).label: Italie archaïque
Italie archaïque (France, 800 BC–401 BC).prose:
[France, 800 BC–401 BC] Italie archaïque. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Archaic Italy, when Etruscan city-states dominated the centre of the peninsula, Greek colonies ringed the south, and Rome was still ruled by kings. Etruscan bronze vessels, black-glaze pottery and wine amphorae travelled north and west along trade routes to southern Gaul, where they turn up in native settlements and princely graves.
Italie archaïque (France, 800 BC–401 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 B.node: Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 BC)
Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 B.label: Premier âge du Fer
Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 B.prose:
[France, 800 BC–451 BC] Premier âge du Fer. Correspondant à la culture de Hallstatt, le Premier âge du Fer est une culture du centre-ouest de l'Europe qui dure d'environ -1200 à -500. Elle succède à l'âge du bronze final et précède la période de La Tène ou Second âge du Fer (fin de la Protohistoire). (D'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Iron working spread through Gaul, and with it a new social order: chieftains buried under great mounds with wagons, gold torcs and imported Mediterranean bronzes. The Vix krater and the princely seat at Mont Lassois show how Greek and Etruscan traders reached deep into the interior in exchange for tin, salt and slaves. Hillfort strongholds controlled the river routes, laying the groundwork for the Celtic societies Caesar would later meet.
Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 B.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

interglaciaire Riss-Würm (France, 800 BC.label: interglaciaire Riss-Würm
interglaciaire Riss-Würm (France, 800 BC.prose:
[France, 800 BC–451 BC] interglaciaire Riss-Würm. Avant-dernière période interglaciaire du Quaternaire. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last warm interval before the final glaciation, when temperatures in Europe briefly ran warmer than today. Deciduous forest spread to the far north and animals now associated with Africa and the Mediterranean, including hippopotamus, straight-tusked elephant and lion, lived in the river valleys of France. Neanderthals were the human population of the time, and their tool assemblages and butchered animal bones from this interval show them hunting large game in dense woodland.
interglaciaire Riss-Würm (France, 800 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque archaïque (France, 800 BC–481 BC).label: époque archaïque
époque archaïque (France, 800 BC–481 BC).prose:
[France, 800 BC–481 BC] époque archaïque. Ne concerne que le monde grec : de 800 à 480 pour les historiographes et de 600 à 480 pour les archéologues. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The Greek world recovered from its dark age and remade itself: the polis emerged, the alphabet was adopted, colonies were planted from the Black Sea to Marseille, and monumental stone temples and kouros statues appeared. Coinage, written law and the first philosophers date from these centuries. Everything the Classical period is famous for was invented, in rough form, here.
époque archaïque (France, 800 BC–481 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Transition Bronze/Fer (France, 775 BC–72.label: Transition Bronze/Fer
Transition Bronze/Fer (France, 775 BC–72.prose:
[France, 775 BC–725 BC] Transition Bronze/Fer. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The generations in which iron working spread through Gaul and the bronze-hoarding world of the Late Bronze Age gave way to the early Hallstatt chieftains. Cremation urnfields continue, but a new elite marks itself out with long iron slashing swords, horse harness and four-wheeled wagons buried under mounds - the beginning of the princely burial tradition that would culminate at Vix and Hochdorf.
Transition Bronze/Fer (France, 775 BC–72.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499) [p02ch.label: Antiquité
Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499) [p02ch.prose:
[France, 600 BC–AD 499] Antiquité. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The long stretch in which Gaul moved from Iron Age chiefdoms trading with Mediterranean merchants to a fully Roman province and then to a Christianised, increasingly fragmented late-imperial society. It covers Greek colonial contact on the southern coast, Caesar's conquest, the Gallo-Roman towns with their forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, and the arrival of Frankish and Visigothic settlers. Most of France's monumental ancient remains, from Nîmes to Vienne, belong to it.
Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499) [p02ch.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Antiquité gréco-romaine (France, 600 BC–.label: Antiquité gréco-romaine
Antiquité gréco-romaine (France, 600 BC–.prose:
[France, 600 BC–AD 499] Antiquité gréco-romaine. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

A combined label for the classical Mediterranean world as it reached and reshaped Gaul, from the first Greek colonies on the coast to the end of Roman rule. It spans the shared culture of city life, temple architecture, sculpture and inscribed stone that Greeks established and Romans spread across the whole of western Europe. Museum collections use it for material that sits on either side of that continuum.
Antiquité gréco-romaine (France, 600 BC–.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Antiquité grecque (France, 600 BC–229 BC.label: Antiquité grecque
Antiquité grecque (France, 600 BC–229 BC.prose:
[France, 600 BC–229 BC] Antiquité grecque. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Greek traders and colonists from Phocaea founded Massalia and a string of coastal settlements, bringing wine, olive oil, coined money and writing to southern Gaul. Their goods travelled far inland up the Rhône, and Greek imports turn up in the richest Celtic burials of the interior. The category also covers Greek objects held in French collections, from painted vases to sculpture.
Antiquité grecque (France, 600 BC–229 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

République romaine (France, 509 BC–27 BC.label: République romaine
République romaine (France, 509 BC–27 BC.prose:
[France, 509 BC–27 BC] République romaine. 509 av. J.-C. - 27 av. J.-C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last generation of the Roman Republic, when Caesar's newly conquered Gaul was absorbed into a state tearing itself apart in civil war. Gallic communities were reorganised, taxed and drawn into Roman military recruitment, and local elites began the shift to Latin, coinage and Roman-style towns that would define the provinces under the empire that followed.
République romaine (France, 509 BC–27 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque pré-classique grecque (France, 49.label: époque pré-classique grecque
époque pré-classique grecque (France, 49.prose:
[France, 490 BC–461 BC] époque pré-classique grecque. Abbreviation ép (for époque) not present in PACTOLS thesaurus, but present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Included as it is a commonly used alternative in French language. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The generation after the Persian Wars, when Greek sculptors abandoned the fixed archaic smile for the sober, weight-shifting figures of the Severe Style. Athens, its city sacked and rebuilt, emerged at the head of a naval league that would become an empire. The bronze Charioteer of Delphi and the Riace warriors belong to these decades.
époque pré-classique grecque (France, 49.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque classique grecque (France, 480 BC.label: époque classique grecque
époque classique grecque (France, 480 BC.prose:
[France, 480 BC–323 BC] époque classique grecque. L’Époque classique est une période de l'histoire de la Grèce antique, située entre l'époque archaïque et l'époque hellénistique. Elle correspond à la majeure partie des ve et ive siècles av. J.-C., c'est-à-dire depuis la victoire athénienne de Salamine contre les Perses en -480 jusqu'à la mort d'Alexandre le Grand en -323. (WP le 07/11/18). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The century and a half between the repulse of Persia and the death of Alexander, when Athens built the Parthenon, staged its tragedies and experimented with democracy. Sculpture reached the idealised naturalism later ages kept copying; Socrates, Plato and Thucydides worked in these decades. It was also an age of ruinous warfare between Greek cities that left them open to Macedonian takeover.
époque classique grecque (France, 480 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque étrusque (France, 470 BC–351 BC).label: époque étrusque
époque étrusque (France, 470 BC–351 BC).prose: [France, 470 BC–351 BC] époque étrusque. Abbreviation ép (for époque) not present in PACTOLS thesaurus, but present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Included as it is a commonly used alternative in French language. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.
époque étrusque (France, 470 BC–351 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

La Tène (France, 450 BC–51 BC) [p02chr4q.label: La Tène
La Tène (France, 450 BC–51 BC) [p02chr4q.prose:
[France, 450 BC–51 BC] La Tène. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Named after a votive deposit of weapons in a Swiss lake, this culture spread across Gaul with a new elite of horse-riding warriors buried with chariots, swords and imported wine services. Its curvilinear art, all tendrils, palmettes and hidden faces, is the most recognisable Celtic style. By the final century large fortified towns, coinage and mass production were emerging, and it all ended with the Roman conquest.
La Tène (France, 450 BC–51 BC) [p02chr4q.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC).node: Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC)
Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC).label: Second âge du Fer
Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC).prose:
[France, 450 BC–51 BC] Second âge du Fer. Correspondant à la culture de La Tène, le Second âge du Fer se développe en Europe entre environ 450 av. J.-C. et 25 av. J.-C. Considéré comme l'apogée de la civilisation celtique, il succède au Premier âge du Fer (Hallstatt, 1300-400 av. J.-C.) et s'achève avec la conquête romaine et les migrations germaniques. Son nom provient du site archéologique de La Tène découvert en 1857 à Marin-Epagnier, sur les bords du lac de Neuchâtel en Suisse. (D'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The La Tène era, when Gaulish societies produced the swirling curvilinear art found on scabbards and torcs, struck their own coinage, and built fortified towns, the oppida, with markets and workshops. Trade with the Mediterranean brought wine by the amphora-load, and Gaulish warbands raided as far as Italy and Greece. It closed with Caesar's conquest and the siege of Alesia.
Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

La Tène A (France, 450 BC–261 BC).label: La Tène A
La Tène A (France, 450 BC–261 BC).prose:
[France, 450 BC–261 BC] La Tène A. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The opening phase of the La Tène Iron Age, when a wealthy elite in the Rhine, Moselle and Marne regions buried its dead with two-wheeled chariots, gold neck-rings and imported Etruscan and Greek wine service. Out of contact with those Mediterranean imports came the Early Style of Celtic art, which took palmettes, lotus buds and lion masks and reworked them into the swirling, ambiguous designs seen on the Glauberg and Reinheim finds. The old Hallstatt hillfort centres further west collapsed at about this time, and power shifted north.
La Tène A (France, 450 BC–261 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque hellénistique (France, 323 BC–30.label: époque hellénistique
époque hellénistique (France, 323 BC–30.prose:
[France, 323 BC–30 BC] époque hellénistique. 323-31 av. J.C. - Période de l'Antiquité qui suit la conquête d’une partie du monde méditerranéen et de l’Asie par Alexandre le Grand jusqu’à la période romaine. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Alexander's conquests scattered Greek cities and Greek as a common language from Egypt to the Indus, and his generals carved the empire into rival kingdoms. Alexandria and Pergamon became centres of scholarship, libraries and mathematics; art turned dramatic, emotional and often colossal. Rome absorbed these kingdoms one by one, inheriting their culture along with their territory.
époque hellénistique (France, 323 BC–30.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

IIIe siècle av. J.-C. (France, 300 BC–20.node: IIIe siècle av. J.-C. (France, 300 BC–201 BC)
IIIe siècle av. J.-C. (France, 300 BC–20.label: IIIe siècle av. J.-C.
IIIe siècle av. J.-C. (France, 300 BC–20.prose:
[France, 300 BC–201 BC] IIIe siècle av. J.-C.. Alternative punctuation for av J-C was present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul in the full La Tène Iron Age: warrior aristocracies, elaborate metalwork with curving abstract ornament, and farming communities scattered across the countryside. Gallic bands raided deep into Italy, Greece and Asia Minor, and mercenary service brought home Macedonian gold coins that local smiths began to copy, launching the first native coinages. Trade in wine, salt and metals with the Mediterranean world grew steadily, laying the ground for the fortified towns and Roman contact of the following century.
IIIe siècle av. J.-C. (France, 300 BC–20.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

La Tène B (France, 260 BC–151 BC).label: La Tène B
La Tène B (France, 260 BC–151 BC).prose:
[France, 260 BC–151 BC] La Tène B. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The phase of the great Celtic migrations, when war bands from the north moved into the Po valley, the middle Danube and the Balkans; the sack of Rome and the raid on Delphi belong to these generations. Large flat cemeteries of inhumations replace the earlier princely tumuli, with men buried with sword, spear and shield and women with brooches and rings. Metalworkers developed the Waldalgesheim or Vegetal Style, a flowing tendril ornament that spread across Europe with astonishing uniformity.
La Tène B (France, 260 BC–151 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

La Tène D (France, 150 BC–51 BC).label: La Tène D
La Tène D (France, 150 BC–51 BC).prose:
[France, 150 BC–51 BC] La Tène D. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The final Iron Age phase, dominated by the oppida: huge walled towns with streets, workshops, mints and imported Roman wine. Political life sharpened into named tribes with magistrates and coinage, and the archaeological record ends with the Gallic Wars and the absorption of the region into the Roman world.
La Tène D (France, 150 BC–51 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

La Tène C (France, 150 BC–51 BC).label: La Tène C
La Tène C (France, 150 BC–51 BC).prose:
[France, 150 BC–51 BC] La Tène C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The middle La Tène, when the long slashing sword hung from an iron chain belt becomes the standard warrior's equipment and cremation begins to replace inhumation over much of the region. Large open settlements and craft centres grew, gold and silver coinage struck in imitation of Macedonian and Roman types came into use, and trade with the Mediterranean intensified. The decorated scabbards of this phase, in the so-called Sword Style, are among the finest Celtic metalwork.
La Tène C (France, 150 BC–51 BC).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque tardo-républicaine (France, 133 B.label: époque tardo-républicaine
époque tardo-républicaine (France, 133 B.prose:
[France, 133 BC–27 BC] époque tardo-républicaine. Abbreviation ép (for époque) not present in PACTOLS thesaurus, but present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Included as it is a commonly used alternative in French language. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Rome's last century as a republic, and the century in which Gaul became Roman. Armies moved north to protect the route to Spain, the province of Gallia Transalpina was organised around Narbo, and Caesar's campaigns of the 50s BC brought the rest of the territory under Roman control. Towns, roads, coinage and villa estates spread quickly, and the civil wars that ended the Republic were fought partly with Gallic manpower and money.
époque tardo-républicaine (France, 133 B.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Ier siècle av. J.-C. (France, 100 BC–1 B.node: Ier siècle av. J.-C. (France, 100 BC–1 BC)
Ier siècle av. J.-C. (France, 100 BC–1 B.label: Ier siècle av. J.-C.
Ier siècle av. J.-C. (France, 100 BC–1 B.prose:
[France, 100 BC–1 BC] Ier siècle av. J.-C.. Alternative punctuation for av J-C was present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Caesar's campaigns between 58 and 51 BC broke the Gallic confederations, ending with Vercingetorix's defeat at Alesia and the loss of enormous numbers of lives and captives. What followed was rapid reorganisation: new provincial boundaries, roads, taxation and colonies of veterans. Gaulish oppida gave way to Roman towns, and the local elite began the shift to Latin and Roman citizenship.

Antiquité romaine (France, 50 BC–AD 499).prose:
[France, 50 BC–AD 499] Antiquité romaine. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

After Caesar's conquest, Gaul was reorganised into provinces, laid out with roads, and filled with towns modelled on Rome; local elites adopted Latin, togas and civic office while keeping many indigenous gods. Aqueducts, arenas, theatres and villa estates transformed the landscape, and cities such as Lugdunum became imperial centres in their own right. The Gallo-Roman synthesis that resulted underlies later French language, law and settlement patterns.
Antiquité romaine (France, 50 BC–AD 499).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Gaul under the Principate, when Roman rule turned a patchwork of Celtic peoples into a network of chartered towns linked by paved roads. Cities like Lugdunum, Nemausus and Arelate acquired forums, aqueducts, amphitheatres and Latin inscriptions, while villa estates reorganised the countryside for grain, wine and pottery export. Local gods were paired with Roman ones and native aristocrats bought into imperial careers, leaving the monumental ruins that still anchor southern French towns.

Empire romain d'Occident (France, 27 BC–.prose:
[France, 27 BC–AD 476] Empire romain d'Occident. jusqu'en 476. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul spent five centuries as a set of Roman provinces, and the transformation was thorough: grid-planned cities with forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, a road network binding the Rhine frontier to the Mediterranean, villa estates exporting grain and wine, and Latin displacing Gaulish speech. Lyon, Arles, Nîmes and Trier became major imperial centres, and Christianity spread through them from the third century on. When central authority collapsed in the west, the bishops, estates and Latin language it left behind became the foundations of Frankish Gaul.

époque augustéenne (France, 27 BC–AD 14).prose:

The reign of Rome's first emperor, when the machinery of the Republic was quietly repurposed into one-man rule. Augustus rebuilt Rome in marble, sponsored Virgil and Horace, and imposed a long peace that let provincial cities be laid out on Roman lines with forums, theatres and aqueducts. In Gaul the period saw an intense burst of urban foundation and road building whose grid plans still shape modern towns.
époque augustéenne (France, 27 BC–AD 14).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Ier siècle (France, AD 1–AD 100).label: Ier siècle
Ier siècle (France, AD 1–AD 100).prose:
[France, AD 1–AD 100] Ier siècle. De l'an 1 à l'an 100. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul, conquered only decades earlier, became thoroughly Roman: new cities laid out on grids, aqueducts, amphitheatres and roads, with Lugdunum as the administrative hub and the site of the annual assembly of the Gallic provinces. Local aristocracies took Roman names and citizenship while Gaulish gods were paired with Roman ones. The pottery, glass and wine trades made the region one of the wealthiest parts of the western empire.
Ier siècle (France, AD 1–AD 100).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

IIe siècle (France, AD 100–AD 199).label: IIe siècle
IIe siècle (France, AD 100–AD 199).prose:
[France, AD 100–AD 199] IIe siècle. De l'an 101 à l'an 200. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul at the peak of Roman prosperity, with no wars on its soil and cities like Lugdunum, Nemausus and Arelate building amphitheatres, baths and aqueducts. Wealth came from grain, wine, pottery and river trade, and it shows in the sprawling villas and their mosaics. Latin, Roman gods and Roman dress mixed with Gallic traditions to make a distinctly Gallo-Roman culture.
IIe siècle (France, AD 100–AD 199).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

IIIe siècle (France, AD 200–AD 299).label: IIIe siècle
IIIe siècle (France, AD 200–AD 299).prose:
[France, AD 200–AD 299] IIIe siècle. De l'an 201 à l'an 300. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Roman Gaul went from prosperity to crisis: plague, civil war, currency collapse and Germanic raiding across the Rhine. For fourteen years the region broke away as a separate Gallic Empire under Postumus and his successors, and towns that had sprawled unwalled for two centuries pulled back behind hastily built ramparts made partly of tombstones and monuments. The century also brought the first Christian communities and bishops to Gaul, and the peasant Bagaudae revolts that Diocletian's reforms were meant to end.
IIIe siècle (France, AD 200–AD 299).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Antiquité tardive (France, AD 300–AD 499.label: Antiquité tardive
Antiquité tardive (France, AD 300–AD 499.prose:
[France, AD 300–AD 499] Antiquité tardive. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Imperial authority thinned, cities shrank behind hastily built walls, and bishops emerged as the effective leaders of urban communities. Christianity became the dominant religion, with the first basilicas and pilgrimage cults, while Franks, Burgundians and Visigoths settled and formed kingdoms out of the western provinces. It is the period in which Roman Gaul becomes medieval France, more by transformation than by sudden collapse.
Antiquité tardive (France, AD 300–AD 499.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bas-Empire romain (France, AD 300–AD 499.prose:
[France, AD 300–AD 499] Bas-Empire romain. Il constitue avec le Haut-Empire une des deux découpes historiographiques de l'Empire romain dans l'historiographie romaine vue par les historiens français. Ces termes sont des concepts très usuels, mais leurs limites chronologiques respectives ne sont pas fixées de façon unanime. On fixe la plupart du temps cette période entre les années 284 et 476.(Wikipédia). A militarised, heavily taxed empire, defended by field armies and frontier troops that increasingly included Germanic recruits. In Gaul the countryside consolidated into great estates while walled towns became administrative and episcopal centres, and imperial authority weakened until it dissolved into successor kingdoms.

IVe siècle (France, AD 300–AD 399).label: IVe siècle
IVe siècle (France, AD 300–AD 399).prose:
[France, AD 300–AD 399] IVe siècle. De l'an 301 à l'an 400. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Late Roman Gaul was a frontier province turned political centre, with emperors residing at Trier and armies stationed along the Rhine. Cities shrank behind thick new walls while great rural estates flourished. Christianity became the official religion and spread fast in the countryside under figures like Martin of Tours, and by the century's end Germanic peoples were settling inside the frontier as often as raiding across it.
IVe siècle (France, AD 300–AD 399).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Ve siècle (France, AD 400–AD 499).label: Ve siècle
Ve siècle (France, AD 400–AD 499).prose:
[France, AD 400–AD 499] Ve siècle. De l'an 401 à l'an 500. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Roman authority in Gaul dissolved over four generations: the Rhine was crossed in 406, the field armies withdrew, and Visigoths, Burgundians, Alans and Franks settled as federates who soon ruled in their own names. Villas were abandoned or fortified, cities shrank behind late walls, and bishops became the leading figures in urban life. By the end of the century Clovis had defeated the last Roman commander in the north and begun assembling the Frankish kingdom.
Ve siècle (France, AD 400–AD 499).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Empire byzantin (France, AD 476–AD 1453).prose: [France, AD 476–AD 1453] Empire byzantin. 395-1453. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

époque mérovingienne (France, AD 481–AD.label: époque mérovingienne
époque mérovingienne (France, AD 481–AD.prose:
[France, AD 481–AD 751] époque mérovingienne. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The first Frankish dynasty, descended from Clovis, ruled Gaul as it shifted from a Roman province to a Germanic kingdom. Its cemeteries are famous: the dead buried dressed, with weapons, belt buckles and garnet-inlaid brooches, giving archaeologists an unusually rich picture of costume and status. Real power drifted to the mayors of the palace, one of whose families eventually took the crown outright.

époque carolingienne (France, AD 751–AD.label: époque carolingienne
époque carolingienne (France, AD 751–AD.prose:
[France, AD 751–AD 999] époque carolingienne. De 751 à 987 en France ou 911 en Germanie (Rob.). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Under Charlemagne and his heirs a Frankish dynasty assembled an empire spanning much of western Europe and revived the title of emperor in the West. Monastic scriptoria produced a legible new script, Carolingian minuscule, and copied the classical texts that survive today largely because of it. The empire split among his grandsons, sketching the outlines of later France and Germany.
époque carolingienne (France, AD 751–AD.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque médiévale (France, AD 500–AD 1500.label: époque médiévale
époque médiévale (France, AD 500–AD 1500.prose:
[France, AD 500–AD 1500] époque médiévale. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The thousand years between the end of Roman rule in the West and the Renaissance, when Christianity, feudal landholding and the manor structured European life. Towns revived after the year 1000, cathedrals and castles rose in stone, universities were founded, and plague in the fourteenth century killed perhaps a third of the population. Most of Europe's villages, parish churches and field boundaries were laid down in these centuries.
époque médiévale (France, AD 500–AD 1500.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Haut Moyen Âge (France, AD 500–AD 999) [.prose:

The centuries between the collapse of Roman authority and the year 1000, when Frankish kings — first Merovingian, then Carolingian — built kingdoms out of the western provinces. Charlemagne's coronation in 800 revived the idea of a western empire and sponsored a revival of Latin learning and manuscript production in monastic scriptoria. Viking, Muslim and Magyar raids and the break-up of the Carolingian inheritance then shifted real power to counts and castellans, laying the ground for feudal society.
