VIe siècle (France, AD 500–AD 599).label: VIe siècle
VIe siècle (France, AD 500–AD 599).prose:
[France, AD 500–AD 599] VIe siècle. De l'an 501 à l'an 600. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Clovis's sons and grandsons carved Gaul into competing Merovingian kingdoms, absorbed Burgundy and Provence, and fought long dynastic feuds that Gregory of Tours recorded in vivid, gossipy detail. Roman civic institutions faded while bishops, drawn from the surviving senatorial families, took over the running of towns. Gold coinage, villa estates and long-distance trade in Mediterranean goods persisted, but on a shrinking scale.
VIe siècle (France, AD 500–AD 599).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

VIIe siècle (France, AD 600–AD 699).label: VIIe siècle
VIIe siècle (France, AD 600–AD 699).prose:
[France, AD 600–AD 699] VIIe siècle. De l'an 601 à l'an 700. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul was divided among rival Merovingian kingdoms — Neustria, Austrasia and Burgundy — whose queens and factions fought bitter civil wars; Dagobert I briefly reunited them. Afterwards effective power drained to the mayors of the palace, the aristocratic officials who would become the Carolingians. Irish and Frankish monasticism spread rapidly in the wake of Columbanus, planting abbeys such as Luxeuil and Corbie that became centres of learning and landholding.
VIIe siècle (France, AD 600–AD 699).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque islamique (France, AD 622–AD 750).label: époque islamique
époque islamique (France, AD 622–AD 750).prose:
[France, AD 622–AD 750] époque islamique. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Beginning with the Hijra, the community founded by Muhammad in Arabia expanded within a century across Syria, Egypt, Iran, North Africa and Spain, absorbing the Sasanian empire and half of Byzantium's territory. A new religion, a new script and a new political order spread through cities that were often the old Roman and Persian ones under new management. Raids reached as far as southern Gaul before being checked in the eighth century.
époque islamique (France, AD 622–AD 750).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque des Omeyyades (France, AD 661–AD.label: époque des Omeyyades
époque des Omeyyades (France, AD 661–AD.prose:
[France, AD 661–AD 750] époque des Omeyyades. époque du règne de la dynastie arabe des Omeyyades sur le monde musulman de 661 à 750. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The first hereditary Islamic dynasty, ruling from Damascus over an empire that stretched from Spain to Central Asia within a single lifetime of conquest. Arabic became the language of administration, the first Islamic coinage was struck, and the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus set the template for mosque architecture. Overthrown by the Abbasids in 750, a surviving branch went on to rule al-Andalus.
époque des Omeyyades (France, AD 661–AD.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

VIIIe siècle (France, AD 700–AD 799).label: VIIIe siècle
VIIIe siècle (France, AD 700–AD 799).prose:
[France, AD 700–AD 799] VIIIe siècle. De l'an 701 à l'an 800. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Real power had passed from the Merovingian kings to the Carolingian mayors of the palace: Charles Martel checked an Arab raiding army near Poitiers, and his son Pippin deposed the last Merovingian and had himself anointed king with papal blessing. That alliance between the Frankish crown and Rome culminated in Charlemagne's conquests of Lombardy, Saxony and Bavaria, and his imperial coronation at the century's end. Monastic scriptoria began producing the clear Caroline minuscule script that preserved much of Latin literature.
VIIIe siècle (France, AD 700–AD 799).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque abbasside (France, AD 750–AD 1258.label: époque abbasside
époque abbasside (France, AD 750–AD 1258.prose:
[France, AD 750–AD 1258] époque abbasside. Epoque du califat sunnite qui gouverna le monde musulman de 750 à 1258. Sous les Abbassides, le centre de gravité de l'islam se déplace de la Syrie vers l'Irak où une nouvelle capitale est fondée en 762 : Bagdad. (d'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The caliphate that overthrew the Umayyads and moved the centre of Islamic power east to Baghdad, a new round city built to be the hub of an empire. Its early centuries saw an extraordinary flowering of science, translation of Greek learning, and long-distance trade linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean. Political control fragmented long before the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, but Abbasid art, ceramics and scholarship set the standards imitated everywhere.
époque abbasside (France, AD 750–AD 1258.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Xe siècle (France, AD 900–AD 999).label: Xe siècle
Xe siècle (France, AD 900–AD 999).prose:
[France, AD 900–AD 999] Xe siècle. De l'an 901 à l'an 1000. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last Carolingian kings ruled little beyond a shrinking royal domain while counts and dukes in Flanders, Normandy, Aquitaine and Toulouse governed as they pleased and castles multiplied. Viking raiders settled as the Normans, and bishops began promoting the Peace of God to restrain private warfare. In 987 the nobles elected Hugh Capet, founding the dynasty that would rule France for centuries.
Xe siècle (France, AD 900–AD 999).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Moyen Age classique (France, AD 1000–AD.label: Moyen Age classique
Moyen Age classique (France, AD 1000–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1000–AD 1299] Moyen Age classique. Période qui comprend les XIe, XIIe et XIIIe siècles, située entre le Haut Moyen Âge et le Bas Moyen Âge. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Population, ploughland and towns all expanded, the Capetian kings turned a small domain around Paris into the strongest monarchy in Europe, and cathedral builders invented the Gothic style at Saint-Denis, Chartres and Amiens. Universities took shape in Paris, fairs in Champagne linked Flemish cloth to Mediterranean trade, and knights left for the crusades. It is the France of Philip Augustus, Louis IX and the troubadours - confident, expanding, and not yet touched by plague.
Moyen Age classique (France, AD 1000–AD.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XIe siècle (France, AD 1000–AD 1099).label: XIe siècle
XIe siècle (France, AD 1000–AD 1099).prose:
[France, AD 1000–AD 1099] XIe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Royal power meant little beyond the Île-de-France while castle-holding lords fought their own wars; bishops and abbots responded with Peace of God assemblies to limit the violence. Cluny and its network of monasteries drove a wave of reform, and stone churches in the Romanesque manner went up everywhere as forests were cleared and population grew. Normans conquered England and southern Italy, and the century ended with a French pope calling the First Crusade at Clermont.
XIe siècle (France, AD 1000–AD 1099).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XIIe siècle (France, AD 1100–AD 1199).label: XIIe siècle
XIIe siècle (France, AD 1100–AD 1199).prose:
[France, AD 1100–AD 1199] XIIe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The Capetian kings, still weak at the century's start, gained ground against the Anglo-Norman and Angevin lords who held more of France than they did, a rivalry sharpened when Eleanor of Aquitaine left Louis VII for Henry II. Saint-Denis under Abbot Suger produced the first Gothic architecture, and the schools of Paris, Chartres and Laon drove the intellectual revival associated with Abelard. Cistercian abbeys spread across the countryside while troubadour and chivalric literature took shape in the southern and western courts.
XIIe siècle (France, AD 1100–AD 1199).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XIIIe siècle (France, AD 1200–AD 1299).label: XIIIe siècle
XIIIe siècle (France, AD 1200–AD 1299).prose:
[France, AD 1200–AD 1299] XIIIe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The Capetian monarchy became the strongest in Europe: Philip Augustus stripped the English kings of Normandy and Anjou, the Albigensian crusade brought Languedoc under northern control, and Louis IX gave the crown a reputation for justice and piety that survived his failed crusades. Paris and its university were the intellectual capital of Latin Christendom, where Aquinas taught and scholastic theology took shape. It was also the great age of Gothic building, with Chartres, Reims, Amiens and the Sainte-Chapelle rising in a few decades.
XIIIe siècle (France, AD 1200–AD 1299).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Empire ottoman (France, AD 1299–AD 1923).label: Empire ottoman
Empire ottoman (France, AD 1299–AD 1923).prose: [France, AD 1299–AD 1923] Empire ottoman. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.
Empire ottoman (France, AD 1299–AD 1923).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Bas Moyen Âge (France, AD 1300–AD 1499).label: Bas Moyen Âge
Bas Moyen Âge (France, AD 1300–AD 1499).prose:
[France, AD 1300–AD 1499] Bas Moyen Âge. Époque distinguée par l'historiographie pour désigner la fin du Moyen Âge en France, en particulier les XIVe et XVe siècles. Elle précède ainsi la Renaissance en succédant au Moyen Âge classique. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

War with England, recurring plague and rural depopulation dominated these generations, yet they also produced a stronger royal state: standing armies, permanent taxation and a crown that emerged from the Hundred Years' War far more powerful than before. Towns rebuilt in flamboyant Gothic, printing arrived in the 1470s, and the marriage politics of the 1490s folded Brittany into the kingdom.
Bas Moyen Âge (France, AD 1300–AD 1499).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XIVe siècle (France, AD 1300–AD 1399).label: XIVe siècle
XIVe siècle (France, AD 1300–AD 1399).prose:
[France, AD 1300–AD 1399] XIVe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

War with England became the defining fact of French life: Edward III's claim to the crown opened a conflict that would run for over a century, and the defeats at Crécy and Poitiers, with the king himself taken prisoner, shook confidence in the nobility. Famine early on and then plague in 1348 killed perhaps a third of the population, emptying villages and pushing up wages for those who survived. Peasant revolt in the Beauvaisis, mercenary companies roaming the countryside and a papacy installed at Avignon all belong to the same unsettled world.
XIVe siècle (France, AD 1300–AD 1399).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XVe siècle (France, AD 1400–AD 1499).label: XVe siècle
XVe siècle (France, AD 1400–AD 1499).prose:
[France, AD 1400–AD 1499] XVe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The Hundred Years' War ended with the English expelled from all France but Calais, after Joan of Arc's intervention turned the war and Charles VII rebuilt royal finances and a standing army. Louis XI then outmanoeuvred and destroyed the rival power of Burgundy, and the crown absorbed Provence, Anjou and eventually Brittany. By the century's close a recovered, consolidated France was invading Italy and importing the Renaissance.
XVe siècle (France, AD 1400–AD 1499).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque moderne (France, AD 1492–AD 1815).label: époque moderne
époque moderne (France, AD 1492–AD 1815).prose:
[France, AD 1492–AD 1815] époque moderne. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Atlantic voyages, printing and the Reformation broke apart the medieval order, and European states began building overseas empires and standing armies. Absolute monarchy, gunpowder fortifications and global trade in sugar, silver and enslaved people define the era's material world. It closes with the French Revolution and Napoleon, which swept away the old regime of estates and privileges.
époque moderne (France, AD 1492–AD 1815).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Renaissance (France, AD 1500–AD 1699).label: Renaissance
Renaissance (France, AD 1500–AD 1699).prose:
[France, AD 1500–AD 1699] Renaissance. Période de l'époque moderne associée à la redécouverte de la littérature, de la philosophie et des sciences de l'Antiquité. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

French armies invading Italy came home dazzled, and kings from Charles VIII to Francis I imported Italian architects, painters and gardeners wholesale — the result is the Loire châteaux, Fontainebleau, and Leonardo da Vinci dying near Amboise. Print shops in Lyon and Paris spread humanist scholarship and the French vernacular, which Francis I made the language of law in 1539. The same presses spread Calvin, and the century closed in the Wars of Religion, resolved only by Henry IV and the Edict of Nantes.
Renaissance (France, AD 1500–AD 1699).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XVIe siècle (France, AD 1500–AD 1599).label: XVIe siècle
XVIe siècle (France, AD 1500–AD 1599).prose:
[France, AD 1500–AD 1599] XVIe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

France spent decades fighting the Habsburgs in Italy and absorbing Renaissance art and architecture in return - the châteaux of the Loire and the arrival of Leonardo at Amboise. Then the spread of Calvinism split the kingdom, and eight Wars of Religion, including the St Bartholomew's Day massacre, tore it apart for a generation. Henri IV ended the bloodshed by converting to Catholicism and granting the Huguenots toleration in the Edict of Nantes.
XVIe siècle (France, AD 1500–AD 1599).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XVIIe siècle (France, AD 1600–AD 1699).label: XVIIe siècle
XVIIe siècle (France, AD 1600–AD 1699).prose:
[France, AD 1600–AD 1699] XVIIe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The century of Richelieu, Mazarin and Louis XIV, when the French crown broke the power of the great nobles and the Protestant strongholds, crushed the Fronde revolts, and built a centralised state run by intendants and royal bureaucrats. Versailles turned the aristocracy into courtiers, while French armies made the kingdom the dominant power on the continent and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes drove Huguenots into exile. It was also the age of Descartes, Pascal, Molière and Racine, when French became the language of European elites.
XVIIe siècle (France, AD 1600–AD 1699).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XVIIIe siècle (France, AD 1700–AD 1799).label: XVIIIe siècle
XVIIIe siècle (France, AD 1700–AD 1799).prose:
[France, AD 1700–AD 1799] XVIIIe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The Enlightenment made Paris the intellectual capital of Europe, with Voltaire, Rousseau, Diderot's Encyclopédie and salons where new ideas circulated faster than censors could suppress them. Wealth grew through Atlantic trade and colonial sugar, even as France lost Canada and India to Britain in the Seven Years' War. Debt, a rigid privileged order and bad harvests brought the monarchy down in 1789, and the Revolution rewrote law, property, religion and the map of the country.
XVIIIe siècle (France, AD 1700–AD 1799).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Révolution française (France, AD 1789–AD.label: Révolution française
Révolution française (France, AD 1789–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1789–AD 1799] Révolution française. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Fiscal crisis and the calling of the Estates-General set off the destruction of the old order: the storming of the Bastille, the abolition of feudal privilege, the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and the execution of Louis XVI. War, the Terror and the fall of Robespierre followed, ending with the Directory and Bonaparte's coup. The Revolution exported the ideas of citizenship, nation and popular sovereignty across Europe and set the terms of political argument for the next two centuries.
Révolution française (France, AD 1789–AD.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

époque contemporaine (France, AD 1800–AD.label: époque contemporaine
époque contemporaine (France, AD 1800–AD.prose:
[France, AD 1800–AD 2000] époque contemporaine. Du XIXe siècle à nos jours. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Industrialisation, railways and mass politics reshaped daily life more thoroughly than anything since farming. Empires expanded and collapsed, two world wars killed on an unprecedented scale, and by the end most people lived in cities and worked away from the land. The material record shifts from handmade to mass-produced, and archaeology of this period deals as much with factories and battlefields as with settlements.
époque contemporaine (France, AD 1800–AD.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XIXe siècle (France, AD 1800–AD 1899).label: XIXe siècle
XIXe siècle (France, AD 1800–AD 1899).prose:
[France, AD 1800–AD 1899] XIXe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

France cycled through empire, restored monarchy, republic and empire again before the Third Republic settled in after defeat by Prussia — five regimes and three revolutions in eighty years. Railways, coal and steel transformed the economy, Paris was rebuilt with wide boulevards, and a second colonial empire was assembled in Africa and Indochina. It was also the age of Balzac and Zola, of Impressionism, and of the shift from a peasant country to an urban one.
XIXe siècle (France, AD 1800–AD 1899).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

XXe siècle (France, AD 1900–AD 1999).label: XXe siècle
XXe siècle (France, AD 1900–AD 1999).prose:
[France, AD 1900–AD 1999] XXe siècle. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Two world wars fought largely on or near French soil cost the country a generation of men, brought occupation, collaboration and Resistance, and ended the Third Republic. Decolonisation stripped away the empire, most painfully in Indochina and Algeria, and returned de Gaulle to power at the head of a new Fifth Republic. Postwar decades of rapid growth transformed daily life, and France became a founding architect of the European Community.
XXe siècle (France, AD 1900–AD 1999).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Antiquité égyptienne (France, 3150 BC–30.label: Antiquité égyptienne
Antiquité égyptienne (France, 3150 BC–30.prose:
[France, 3150 BC–30 BC] Antiquité égyptienne. 8000 av. J.-C.-30 ap. J.-C. : du Prédynastique ancien à la mort de Cléopâtre. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The span of pharaonic civilisation from the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt to the death of Cleopatra, taking in the pyramid builders, the New Kingdom empire and the long Greek-ruled Ptolemaic epilogue. French collections acquired vast quantities of Egyptian material in the nineteenth century, and Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822 gave the field its founding key. Visitors encounter it as mummies, coffins, papyri and monumental stone sculpture.
Antiquité égyptienne (France, 3150 BC–30.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Atlantique (palynozone) (France, 7500 BC.label: Atlantique (palynozone)
Atlantique (palynozone) (France, 7500 BC.prose:
[France, 7500 BC–3801 BC] Atlantique (palynozone). L'Atlantique est une palynozone et une chronozone de l'Holocène. Elle correspond à un optimum climatique entre -7500 et -3800. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

A warm, wet phase of the Holocene identified in pollen cores, when mixed oak forest with elm, lime and alder reached its greatest extent across northwestern Europe and sea levels rose to near modern heights. Pollen diagrams from this interval show the first clearances and cereal grains that mark the arrival of farming. It is the climatic optimum against which later, cooler phases are measured.
Atlantique (palynozone) (France, 7500 BC.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Royaumes francs (France, AD 400–AD 899).label: Royaumes francs
Royaumes francs (France, AD 400–AD 899).prose:
[France, AD 400–AD 899] Royaumes francs. Royaumes barbares qui se sont succédé ou ont cohabité en Europe occidentale (France, Belgique, Pays-Bas, Allemagne) après le déclin de l'Empire romain d'Occident et la conquête de ces territoires par les Francs au cours du Ve siècle. Ces royaumes ont perduré pendant tout le Haut Moyen Âge, du Ve au IXe siècle.(d'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Frankish warbands who had settled inside the collapsing Roman provinces built kingdoms that eventually swallowed most of Gaul, with Clovis converting to Catholic Christianity and Merovingian rulers dividing and redividing the realm among heirs. Roman taxation and towns decayed, while bishops, monasteries and aristocratic estates became the framework of power. The Carolingians displaced the old dynasty and, under Charlemagne, turned the kingdom into an empire before it fragmented again into the ancestors of France and Germany.
Royaumes francs (France, AD 400–AD 899).source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

Medieval (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1550).label: Medieval
Medieval (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1550).prose: [Iceland, AD 870–AD 1550] Medieval. The period is defined as starting with the settlement of Iceland c. 870 and ending with Reformation in 1550. Period definition from Inngangur að miðöldum — Gunnar Karlsson, 2007.

Pre-Modern (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1902).label: Pre-Modern
Pre-Modern (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1902).prose:
[Iceland, AD 870–AD 1902] Pre-Modern. “Nevertheless, the installation of an engine in the Stanley in 1902 began a new era in Icelandic history, since the successful mechanization of the Icelandic fishing fleet, which was to modernize the whole society and form the economic basis for the Icelandic welfare state followed from it.” Ch. 51, para. 2. Period definition from Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society — Gunnar Karlsson, 2020.

Runs from the Norse settlement of the island to the threshold of the twentieth century, a millennium in which most Icelanders lived on isolated turf farms raising sheep and cutting hay. Independence gave way to Norwegian and then Danish rule, and the royal trade monopoly, volcanic eruptions such as the Laki fires, and cooling climate brought famine and emigration. Archaeologically the period is read from turf building layers, middens and volcanic ash horizons that date them precisely.
Pre-Modern (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1902).source: Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society

Modern (Iceland, AD 1902–AD 2100).label: Modern
Modern (Iceland, AD 1902–AD 2100).prose:
[Iceland, AD 1902–AD 2100] Modern. “Nevertheless, the installation of an engine in the Stanley in 1902 began a new era in Icelandic history, since the successful mechanization of the Icelandic fishing fleet, which was to modernize the whole society and form the economic basis for the Icelandic welfare state followed from it.” Ch. 51, para. 2. Period definition from Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society — Gunnar Karlsson, 2020.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.
Modern (Iceland, AD 1902–AD 2100).source: Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society

WWII Occupation (Iceland, AD 1940–AD 194.label: WWII Occupation
WWII Occupation (Iceland, AD 1940–AD 194.prose:
[Iceland, AD 1940–AD 1946] WWII Occupation. On 10th May 1940 Iceland was invaded by Britain. They were replaced by American forces in 1941 but “It was not until the late summer of 1946 that Ólafur Thors made a treaty with the United States government, whereby the American army was to leave Iceland [...].” Ch. 56. Period definition from Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society — Gunnar Karlsson, 2020.

British troops landed in 1940 to forestall a German move on the island, and were replaced by American forces in 1941, at times outnumbering the adult Icelandic male population. The occupiers built airfields, roads, harbours and Nissen-hut camps that transformed a poor rural economy almost overnight, and wartime wages pulled people into Reykjavík. Iceland declared full independence from Denmark in 1944, and the wartime infrastructure became the foundation of the modern state.
WWII Occupation (Iceland, AD 1940–AD 194.source: Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society

Post-Medieval (Iceland, AD 1550–AD 1902).label: Post-Medieval
Post-Medieval (Iceland, AD 1550–AD 1902).prose:
[Iceland, AD 1550–AD 1902] Post-Medieval. “Nevertheless, the installation of an engine in the Stanley in 1902 began a new era in Icelandic history, since the successful mechanization of the Icelandic fishing fleet, which was to modernize the whole society and form the economic basis for the Icelandic welfare state followed from it.” Ch. 51, para. 2. Period definition from Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society — Gunnar Karlsson, 2020.

The centuries after 1500 brought the Reformation, overseas empire, and the shift from an agrarian to an industrial society, all leaving dense archaeological traces. Sites of this age are full of dateable mass-produced material - clay pipes, glass bottles, glazed and printed pottery - which makes them unusually precise chronological anchors. Field boundaries, mills, docks, mines and workers' housing from this span still form the framework of the modern landscape.
Post-Medieval (Iceland, AD 1550–AD 1902).source: Iceland's 1100 years : the history of a marginal society

Pre-Writing (Mesopotamia, 8499 BC–3499 B.label: Pre-Writing
Pre-Writing (Mesopotamia, 8499 BC–3499 B.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 8499 BC–3499 BC] Pre-Writing. Spatial coverage: Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The long stretch of Mesopotamian prehistory before cuneiform, running from the first farming hamlets through the Hassuna, Samarra, Halaf and Ubaid cultures to the eve of the Uruk city. People learned to irrigate the southern floodplain, built temples that were rebuilt on the same spot for generations, and kept accounts with clay tokens and stamp seals. Everything known about it comes from excavation alone, and it ends when those tokens and seals gave rise to the world's first written records.

Uruk V (Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–3349 BC).label: Uruk V
Uruk V (Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–3349 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–3349 BC] Uruk V. Spatial coverage: Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The earlier phase of Uruk's great expansion, when the Eanna precinct was first laid out on a monumental scale and mass-produced bevel-rim bowls became ubiquitous across the south. Administration was still handled with seals, sealings and clay tokens rather than tablets. The demographic and organisational groundwork for the first writing was already being laid.

Uruk IV (Mesopotamia, 3349 BC–3199 BC).label: Uruk IV
Uruk IV (Mesopotamia, 3349 BC–3199 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3349 BC–3199 BC] Uruk IV. Spatial coverage: Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The level in the Eanna precinct at Uruk that yielded the world's earliest known writing: thousands of clay tablets recording grain, beer, livestock and labour in pictographic signs. Monumental buildings decorated with cone mosaics were repeatedly built and demolished on the site. Writing here begins as accountancy, not literature, and it took centuries before it recorded anything a modern reader would call a text.

Uruk III (Mesopotamia, 3199 BC–2999 BC).label: Uruk III
Uruk III (Mesopotamia, 3199 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3199 BC–2999 BC] Uruk III. Spatial coverage: Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Also known as the Jemdet Nasr phase, this level at Uruk produced archaic tablets in which proto-cuneiform signs become more standardised and begin to record personal names and professions alongside commodities. Painted polychrome pottery and a distinctive glyptic style mark the period. It leads directly into the Early Dynastic city-states of Sumer.

Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC).label: Proto-Elamite
Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC).prose:
[Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Proto-Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Cities on the Iranian plateau adopted urban administration and produced their own still-undeciphered script, written on clay tablets recording livestock, grain and workers. Susa, Tepe Yahya and Shahr-i Sokhta shared this bureaucratic culture, evidence of an interaction network stretching from Mesopotamia to the edge of the Indus. Its cylinder seals, showing animals acting as humans, are among the most inventive images of early Iran.

ED I-II (Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2699 BC).label: ED I-II
ED I-II (Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2699 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2699 BC] ED I-II. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Sumer's city-states took mature form: Uruk, Ur, Kish, Lagash and their neighbours, each with its temple, its god and its ruler, competing for land and water. Writing moved beyond accounting towards recording names and events, and monumental palaces appear alongside temples. The world's oldest urban political landscape is on display here.

ED IIIa (Iraq, 2599 BC–2499 BC).label: ED IIIa
ED IIIa (Iraq, 2599 BC–2499 BC).prose:
[Iraq, 2599 BC–2499 BC] ED IIIa. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The richest phase of Sumerian city culture, contemporary with the Royal Cemetery of Ur and its spectacular burials of gold headdresses, inlaid lyres and a retinue interred alongside the dead. Archives from Shuruppak show a bureaucracy managing grain, labour and land in detail. Kings began styling themselves rulers of more than one city.

ED IIIb (Iraq, 2499 BC–2339 BC).label: ED IIIb
ED IIIb (Iraq, 2499 BC–2339 BC).prose:
[Iraq, 2499 BC–2339 BC] ED IIIb. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Rival dynasties at Lagash and Umma fought over a border strip for generations, leaving the earliest detailed war narratives and treaty texts, including the Stele of the Vultures. Urukagina of Lagash issued what is often called the first recorded reform decree. The struggle ended with conquest by Lugalzagesi and then by Sargon of Akkad.

Ebla (Syria, 2349 BC–2249 BC).label: Ebla
Ebla (Syria, 2349 BC–2249 BC).prose:
[Syria, 2349 BC–2249 BC] Ebla. Spatial coverage: Middle East, Syria. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

A wealthy Syrian city commanding the trade in textiles, timber and metals between Mesopotamia, Anatolia and the Mediterranean. Excavation of its palace uncovered some 17,000 clay tablets — administrative records, treaties and word-lists written in Sumerian script for a previously unknown Semitic language — proving that literate state power extended far west of the Tigris and Euphrates earlier than anyone expected. The palace was burned, most likely by an Akkadian army under Sargon or Naram-Sin, which baked and preserved the archive.

Old Akkadian (Mesopotamia, 2339 BC–2199.label: Old Akkadian
Old Akkadian (Mesopotamia, 2339 BC–2199.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2339 BC–2199 BC] Old Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East, Syria. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Sargon of Akkad brought the Sumerian city-states under a single ruler and campaigned from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, creating what is usually called the first empire. Akkadian, a Semitic language, was written in cuneiform for administration alongside Sumerian, and royal art under Naram-Sin depicted the king as a god. The empire's collapse after roughly a century and a half was long remembered in Mesopotamian literature as divine punishment.

Linear Elamite (Iran, 2199 BC–2199 BC).label: Linear Elamite
Linear Elamite (Iran, 2199 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[Iran, 2199 BC–2199 BC] Linear Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

A script used briefly in southwestern Iran, known from only a couple of dozen inscriptions, most connected with the ruler Puzur-Inshushinak of Susa. Its signs are neither cuneiform nor Proto-Elamite but a separate experiment in writing, cut into stone monuments and silver vessels. It resisted reading for more than a century, and recent claimed decipherments remain debated — one of the last near-silent scripts of the ancient Near East.

Lagash II (Mesopotamia, 2199 BC–2099 BC).label: Lagash II
Lagash II (Mesopotamia, 2199 BC–2099 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2199 BC–2099 BC] Lagash II. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

After the collapse of the Akkadian empire, the city-state of Lagash flourished independently under rulers who rebuilt temples and traded for stone, timber and metals from Magan and the Levant. Its most famous ruler, Gudea, left dozens of hard diorite statues and inscribed clay cylinders describing the building of the god Ningirsu's temple — among the finest Sumerian sculpture and literature to survive. The city was soon absorbed into the Third Dynasty of Ur.

Harappan (Pakistan, 2199 BC–1899 BC).label: Harappan
Harappan (Pakistan, 2199 BC–1899 BC).prose:
[Pakistan, 2199 BC–1899 BC] Harappan. Spatial coverage: Indus Valley Civilization, Pakistan. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The mature phase of the Indus civilisation, with brick-built cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa laid out on grids, equipped with covered drains, wells and great public baths. Standardised weights, fired bricks and a still-undeciphered script on carved seals show a society of remarkable uniformity across a territory larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, trading with the Gulf and Sumer. What is missing is as striking as what survives: no palaces, no temples, no royal tombs.

Ur III (Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC).label: Ur III
Ur III (Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC] Ur III. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The Third Dynasty of Ur built a tightly administered state that reached across the Iranian lowlands, holding Susa and planting garrisons and governors in the Zagros foothills. Its scribes produced tens of thousands of accounting tablets recording livestock, labour and grain in obsessive detail, the densest bureaucratic archive of the ancient world. The empire fell when Elamite forces sacked Ur, an event lamented in Sumerian poetry for centuries afterwards.

Early Old Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 1999.label: Early Old Babylonian
Early Old Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 1999.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Early Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East, Syria. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

After the Third Dynasty of Ur collapsed, Mesopotamia broke into rival city-states ruled largely by dynasties of Amorite origin—Isin, Larsa, Eshnunna, Assur and a then-minor Babylon. Kings issued law collections and debt cancellations, temples and merchants ran long-distance trade, and Akkadian steadily displaced Sumerian as the everyday written language. The competition among these states ended with Hammurabi's conquests.

Old Assyrian (Iraq, 1949 BC–1849 BC).label: Old Assyrian
Old Assyrian (Iraq, 1949 BC–1849 BC).prose:
[Iraq, 1949 BC–1849 BC] Old Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East, Syria. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Merchants from Assur ran a long-distance trade network carrying tin and woollen textiles by donkey caravan into Anatolia, exchanging them for silver and gold. Their archives at the Kanesh trading colony preserve thousands of clay letters, contracts and lawsuits, including those of women managing textile production at home. Shamshi-Adad I briefly welded northern Mesopotamia into a kingdom before Hammurabi's Babylon overshadowed it.

Old Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 1899 BC–159.label: Old Babylonian
Old Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 1899 BC–159.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1899 BC–1599 BC] Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East, Syria. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.

Middle Hittite (Anatolia, 1499 BC–1099 B.label: Middle Hittite
Middle Hittite (Anatolia, 1499 BC–1099 B.prose:
[Anatolia, 1499 BC–1099 BC] Middle Hittite. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Levant, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The Hittite state recovered from a long stretch of dynastic murder and territorial loss, tightening the succession, codifying law and reorganising the army under kings such as Tudhaliya I. Treaties with Kizzuwatna brought strong Hurrian religious and artistic influence into Hattusa, while Kaska raiders from the Pontic mountains remained a constant threat. These reforms set up the imperial expansion that would make the Hittites rivals of Egypt and Assyria.

Middle Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–.label: Middle Babylonian
Middle Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–1099 BC] Middle Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Under the Kassite dynasty Babylonia enjoyed unusual stability, its kings corresponding as equals with the pharaohs and the Hittites and rebuilding the great temples of Nippur and Babylon. Land grants were recorded on kudurru boundary stones carved with divine symbols, and scribes fixed the classic versions of Babylonian literature, including Gilgamesh. Elamite invaders sacked Babylon and carried off the statue of Marduk; Nebuchadnezzar I later won it back.

Middle Assyrian (Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–99.label: Middle Assyrian
Middle Assyrian (Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–99.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1399 BC–999 BC] Middle Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Assyria emerged from vassalage to Mitanni to become a great power, its kings conquering northern Mesopotamia and, under Tukulti-Ninurta I, briefly capturing Babylon itself. An efficient provincial administration, meticulous royal archives and the Middle Assyrian Laws - unusually harsh, especially toward women - date from this era. Weakened by Aramaean pressure after 1100 BC, the kingdom nevertheless kept the institutions that its Neo-Assyrian successors used to build an empire.

Middle Elamite (Iran, 1299 BC–999 BC).label: Middle Elamite
Middle Elamite (Iran, 1299 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Iran, 1299 BC–999 BC] Middle Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Elam's most powerful era, when kings ruling from Susa and Anshan wrote in Elamite rather than Akkadian and built on a monumental scale. Untash-Napirisha founded the sacred city of Chogha Zanbil with its huge stepped ziggurat, still the best-preserved in the world, and later Shutrukid rulers sacked Babylon and carried off the stele of Hammurabi's laws and the victory monument of Naram-Sin as trophies for Susa. Assyrian and Babylonian counterattacks eventually broke the dynasty.

Neo-Assyrian (Mesopotamia, 910 BC–611 BC.label: Neo-Assyrian
Neo-Assyrian (Mesopotamia, 910 BC–611 BC.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 910 BC–611 BC] Neo-Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Levant, Mesopotamia. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Assyrian armies pushed repeatedly into the Zagros in these centuries, campaigning for horses, tribute and control of the trade routes across the Iranian plateau, and leaving royal inscriptions and reliefs that give the first written glimpses of the Medes and Persians. Local fortified centres and elite burials, such as those at Hasanlu and Ziwiye, reflect both Assyrian pressure and the wealth it drew in. The eventual Median coalition that helped destroy Assyria grew out of this long confrontation.

Neo-Elamite (Iran, 769 BC–538 BC).label: Neo-Elamite
Neo-Elamite (Iran, 769 BC–538 BC).prose:
[Iran, 769 BC–538 BC] Neo-Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Elam re-emerged in southwestern Iran after a long dark age, its kings ruling from Susa and the Zagros valleys and playing a dangerous game of alliance with Babylon against Assyria. Assyrian armies sacked Susa in 646 BC, but Elamite scribes, art and administrative practice survived to be absorbed by the Persians, who took over Elamite script and bureaucracy at Persepolis. The period is the bridge between ancient Elam and the Achaemenid Empire.

Neo-Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 625 BC–538.label: Neo-Babylonian
Neo-Babylonian (Mesopotamia, 625 BC–538.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 625 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Ancient Egypt, Babylonia, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Judah under Babylonian rule was a diminished, largely rural province, its capital and temple in ruins and its royal house deported. Excavations show towns in the south and the Shephelah abandoned or shrunken while some settlements north of Jerusalem, around Benjamin, carried on. This bleak interval ended when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and permitted exiles to return.

Achaemenid (Mesopotamia, 546 BC–330 BC).label: Achaemenid
Achaemenid (Mesopotamia, 546 BC–330 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 546 BC–330 BC] Achaemenid. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Mesopotamia, Middle East, State of Palestine. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Cyrus the Great and his successors welded Iran, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Egypt into the largest empire the world had yet seen, governed through satraps, royal roads and a standardised silver coinage. Persepolis and Susa displayed the empire's wealth in carved processions of tribute-bearers from every subject people. Alexander's invasion brought it down, but its administrative model outlived it.

Hellenistic (Mesopotamia, 322 BC–62 BC).label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Mesopotamia, 322 BC–62 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 322 BC–62 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Babylonia, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Mesopotamia, Middle East, State of Palestine. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

Parthian (Mesopotamia, 246 BC–AD 224).label: Parthian
Parthian (Mesopotamia, 246 BC–AD 224).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 246 BC–AD 224] Parthian. Spatial coverage: Babylonia, Iran, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The Arsacid empire out of Iran pressed to the Euphrates, making Syria the frontier zone of a rivalry with Rome that lasted nearly three centuries. Crassus lost his army and his head at Carrhae in 53 BC, and later Parthian raids and Roman counter-invasions repeatedly swept the caravan cities between the two powers. That contested ground was also enormously profitable: Palmyra, Dura-Europos and the Euphrates routes grew rich handling silk and spices moving between the empires, and their art blends Greek, Iranian and Semitic styles.

Sassanian (Iran, AD 224–AD 641).label: Sassanian
Sassanian (Iran, AD 224–AD 641).prose:
[Iran, AD 224–AD 641] Sassanian. Spatial coverage: Babylonia, Iran, Iraq, Mesopotamia, Middle East. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.

Egyptian 0 (Egypt, 3299 BC–2999 BC).label: Egyptian 0
Egyptian 0 (Egypt, 3299 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 3299 BC–2999 BC] Egyptian 0. Spatial coverage: Ancient Egypt, Egypt. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

In the generations before the First Dynasty, rival centres in Upper Egypt such as Abydos and Hierakonpolis grew into small kingdoms whose rulers were buried with imported goods and labelled storage jars. Writing appears here in its earliest Egyptian form, on bone tags and pot marks, alongside the royal imagery later standard in pharaonic art. These "Dynasty 0" rulers laid the groundwork for the unification of the Nile valley into a single state.

Uruk (Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–2999 BC).label: Uruk
Uruk (Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–2999 BC] Uruk. Spatial coverage: Mesopotamia, Middle East. General period extrapolated from subordinated periods in original source, but not included in original source. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

Southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities in this period, with Uruk itself swelling to a size no settlement had reached before. Monumental temple platforms, mass-produced bevel-rim bowls for rationed labour, cylinder seals for accounting and finally the earliest writing all appear together, the machinery of a society organised around institutions rather than kin. Uruk-style material spread up the Euphrates into Syria and Anatolia, whether by colony, trade or imitation.

ED I-III (Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2339 BC).label: ED I-III
ED I-III (Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2339 BC).prose:
[Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2339 BC] ED I-III. Spatial coverage: Mesopotamia, Middle East. General period extrapolated from subordinated periods in original source, but not included in original source. Period definition from Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) — Robert Englund, 2016.

The age of the Sumerian city-states, when southern Mesopotamia was a patchwork of rival walled cities each centred on a temple estate. Cuneiform developed from pictures into a flexible script capable of literature and law; the Royal Cemetery of Ur, with its gold, lyres and sacrificed attendants, dates from its later part. It ended when Sargon of Akkad welded the cities into a single empire.

Jōmon period (Honshu, 13999 BC–799 BC).label: Jōmon period
Jōmon period (Honshu, 13999 BC–799 BC).prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, Hokkaidō, 13999 BC–799 BC] Jōmon period. Spatial coverage: Hokkaidō, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Named for the cord-marked patterns pressed into its pottery — among the oldest ceramics anywhere in the world — Jōmon culture supported large, settled villages of hunters, fishers and gatherers without farming, an unusual combination. Visitors notice the flamboyant flame-rimmed vessels and the dogū, small clay figurines with goggle eyes and swollen bodies. Shell middens, lacquerwork and the timber circles of sites like Sannai Maruyama show a society of striking complexity over more than ten millennia.
Jōmon period (Honshu, 13999 BC–799 BC).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Asuka period (Honshu, AD 592–AD 710).label: Asuka period
Asuka period (Honshu, AD 592–AD 710).prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 592–AD 710] Asuka period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Named for the valley south of Nara where the court sat, this era saw Buddhism arrive from Korea and take root under the patronage of Prince Shōtoku and the Soga clan, along with Chinese writing, calendars and bureaucratic ideas. The Taika Reforms and later legal codes tried to remake a clan-based society into a Chinese-style centralised state with the emperor at its head. Hōryū-ji, with the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the world, dates from this time.
Asuka period (Honshu, AD 592–AD 710).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Nara period (Honshu, AD 710–AD 794).label: Nara period
Nara period (Honshu, AD 710–AD 794).prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 710–AD 794] Nara period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Japan's first long-lasting capital, Heijō-kyō, was laid out on a Chinese grid plan and administered through imported law codes that registered land and people for taxation. State Buddhism reached a peak with provincial temples and the great bronze Buddha at Tōdai-ji, while the earliest surviving Japanese chronicles and poetry were compiled. The Shōsōin treasury still preserves silks, glass and instruments that travelled the Silk Road to the court.
Nara period (Honshu, AD 710–AD 794).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Heian period (Honshu, AD 794–AD 1185).label: Heian period
Heian period (Honshu, AD 794–AD 1185).prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 794–AD 1185] Heian period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

With the capital moved to Heian-kyō, the imperial court settled into four centuries of elaborate ceremony, poetry competitions and Fujiwara regency politics. Chinese models were absorbed and reworked into something distinctly Japanese — kana writing, the yamato-e painting style, courtly prose fiction. Meanwhile tax-free estates and provincial warrior families eroded central control, setting up the samurai age that followed.
Heian period (Honshu, AD 794–AD 1185).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Kamakura period (Honshu, AD 1185–AD 1333.label: Kamakura period
Kamakura period (Honshu, AD 1185–AD 1333.prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 1185–AD 1333] Kamakura period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Japan's first sustained military government ruled from a seaside town far from the imperial capital, with the Hōjō family holding real authority behind figurehead shoguns. It produced a hard, realistic style in sculpture and portraiture, the epic tales of the Heike, and popular Buddhist sects that spread among farmers and fighters alike. The Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 defined the age and drained the treasury that sustained it.
Kamakura period (Honshu, AD 1185–AD 1333.source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Nanbokuchō period (Honshu, AD 1333–AD 13.label: Nanbokuchō period
Nanbokuchō period (Honshu, AD 1333–AD 13.prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 1333–AD 1392] Nanbokuchō period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Emperor Go-Daigo's attempt to restore direct imperial rule collapsed when his general Ashikaga Takauji turned against him, installed a rival emperor in Kyoto and drove the old court into the mountains at Yoshino. For nearly sixty years two imperial lines each claimed legitimacy, and warriors chose sides according to local advantage. The courts were reunited in 1392, but the long conflict had transferred lasting power to provincial military governors and hollowed out the throne.
Nanbokuchō period (Honshu, AD 1333–AD 13.source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Muromachi period (Honshu, AD 1392–AD 157.label: Muromachi period
Muromachi period (Honshu, AD 1392–AD 157.prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 1392–AD 1573] Muromachi period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

The Ashikaga shoguns ruled from Kyoto's Muromachi district, a government that was culturally brilliant and politically weak. Zen monasteries, ink painting, the tea ceremony, Noh theatre and the dry rock garden all took mature form here, while trade with Ming China brought in copper cash and continental goods. Central authority collapsed after the Onin War of 1467 turned the capital into a battlefield, and the provinces slid into a century of warlord conflict that ended only with the shogunate's abolition.
Muromachi period (Honshu, AD 1392–AD 157.source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Azuchi-Momoyama period (Honshu, AD 1573–.label: Azuchi-Momoyama period
Azuchi-Momoyama period (Honshu, AD 1573–.prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 1573–AD 1603] Azuchi-Momoyama period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi broke the power of the warring provincial lords and brought most of Japan under one command, backed by massed firearms and vast stone-based castles like Azuchi and Osaka. Hideyoshi's land survey and sword hunt froze the social order, separating peasants from warriors. It was a flamboyant age of gold-leaf screen painting, grand tea gatherings under Sen no Rikyu, and the disastrous invasions of Korea.
Azuchi-Momoyama period (Honshu, AD 1573–.source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Edo period (Honshu, AD 1603–AD 1868).label: Edo period
Edo period (Honshu, AD 1603–AD 1868).prose:
[Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, AD 1603–AD 1868] Edo period. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Tokugawa rule brought peace and tight social control after generations of warfare, with domain lords bound to the shogun's court and overseas contact restricted to a few licensed channels. Cities swelled, a money economy and merchant culture flourished, and popular arts such as kabuki, ukiyo-e prints and haiku reached wide audiences. The order ended when foreign pressure and rebellious domains restored imperial rule.
Edo period (Honshu, AD 1603–AD 1868).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Meiji era (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).label: Meiji era
Meiji era (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).prose:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912] Meiji era. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

The restoration of imperial rule in 1868 swept away the shogunate and the feudal domains, replacing them with prefectures, a national tax and a conscript army. Foreign engineers, teachers and advisers were hired en masse while thousands of Japanese students went abroad; factories, banks and shipyards followed. Traditional crafts were reoriented for export markets, and the objects made for Western buyers in this period fill museum collections today.
Meiji era (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Taishō era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).label: Taishō era
Taishō era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).prose:
[Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926] Taishō era. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Japan's brief experiment with liberal politics, when party cabinets replaced rule by the Meiji oligarchs and the vote was extended to all adult men. The First World War brought an export boom and colonial gains in China and the Pacific, followed by rice riots, labour unrest and the devastating 1923 earthquake. The same laws that granted suffrage also created the machinery for policing political thought.
Taishō era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Shōwa era (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).label: Shōwa era
Shōwa era (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).prose:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989] Shōwa era. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Hirohito's reign spanned Japan's descent into military rule and total war and its rebirth as an industrial democracy. Army officers murdered prime ministers, Japan seized Manchuria and invaded China, attacked the United States and Britain, and ended in ruins under Allied occupation, which imposed a new constitution renouncing war. From the 1950s the same country produced the growth miracle of cars, steel and electronics that reshaped world markets.
Shōwa era (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Heisei era (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019).label: Heisei era
Heisei era (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019).prose:
[Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019] Heisei era. Period definition from Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions — Rebekah Harmon, 2022.

Emperor Akihito's reign, bracketed by the collapse of the bubble economy at its start and his abdication, the first in two centuries, at its end. Japan grappled with stagnation, banking crises, an ageing society and the triple disaster of 2011, while its popular culture found a worldwide audience. Akihito redefined the modern monarchy through disaster visits and gestures of reconciliation over the war.
Heisei era (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019).source: Style Manual for English Texts: General Conventions

Prehistoric (Ireland, 12699 BC–AD 400).label: Prehistoric
Prehistoric (Ireland, 12699 BC–AD 400).prose:
[Island of Ireland, 12699 BC–AD 400] Prehistoric. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

Late Chalcolithic communities on the Iranian plateau and in Khuzestan used mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, copper metallurgy and clay tokens and seals to track goods. Susa emerged as a major centre in close contact with Mesopotamian Uruk, and the accounting systems developed here fed directly into the invention of writing.
Prehistoric (Ireland, 12699 BC–AD 400).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Mesolithic (Ireland, 7999 BC–4000 BC).label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (Ireland, 7999 BC–4000 BC).prose:
[Island of Ireland, 7999 BC–4000 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.
Mesolithic (Ireland, 7999 BC–4000 BC).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Neolithic (Ireland, 3999 BC–2500 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Ireland, 3999 BC–2500 BC).prose:
[Island of Ireland, 3999 BC–2500 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.
Neolithic (Ireland, 3999 BC–2500 BC).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Chalcolithic (Ireland, 2499 BC–2200 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Ireland, 2499 BC–2200 BC).prose:
[Island of Ireland, 2499 BC–2200 BC] Chalcolithic. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.
Chalcolithic (Ireland, 2499 BC–2200 BC).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Bronze Age (Ireland, 2199 BC–800 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Ireland, 2199 BC–800 BC).prose:
[Island of Ireland, 2199 BC–800 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Ireland, 2199 BC–800 BC).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Iron Age (Ireland, 799 BC–AD 399).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Ireland, 799 BC–AD 399).prose:
[Island of Ireland, 799 BC–AD 399] Iron Age. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Ireland, 799 BC–AD 399).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Medieval (Ireland, AD 400–AD 1600).label: Medieval
Medieval (Ireland, AD 400–AD 1600).prose: [Island of Ireland, AD 400–AD 1600] Medieval. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.
Medieval (Ireland, AD 400–AD 1600).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Early Medieval (Ireland, AD 400–AD 1099).label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (Ireland, AD 400–AD 1099).prose:
[Island of Ireland, AD 400–AD 1099] Early Medieval. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.
Early Medieval (Ireland, AD 400–AD 1099).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Late Medieval (Ireland, AD 1100–AD 1599).label: Late Medieval
Late Medieval (Ireland, AD 1100–AD 1599).prose:
[Island of Ireland, AD 1100–AD 1599] Late Medieval. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

Bulgaria spent much of this stretch inside the Byzantine Empire after the fall of the First Bulgarian state, then broke free in 1185 to build a Second Empire ruled from Tarnovo, whose churches, painted tombs and silver coinage mark a confident revival. Ivan Asen II briefly made it the dominant power in the Balkans before Mongol raids, noble feuding and territorial splintering wore it down. Ottoman armies took Tarnovo and then Vidin, ending Bulgarian independence for nearly five centuries.
Late Medieval (Ireland, AD 1100–AD 1599).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Post Medieval (Ireland, AD 1600–AD 1750).label: Post Medieval
Post Medieval (Ireland, AD 1600–AD 1750).prose:
[Island of Ireland, AD 1600–AD 1750] Post Medieval. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

Beginning with the dissolution of the monasteries and the Reformation's stripping of parish churches, these centuries carried England through civil war, the growth of an Atlantic empire, enclosure of open fields, and industrialisation. Excavations of the period yield mass-produced goods - tin-glazed and transfer-printed pottery, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes, machine-made nails - that let sites be dated to within a decade or two. Landscapes changed as thoroughly as objects: hedged fields, canals, railways, mines and terraced workers' housing all belong to this span.
Post Medieval (Ireland, AD 1600–AD 1750).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

Modern (Ireland, AD 1750–AD 2000).label: Modern
Modern (Ireland, AD 1750–AD 2000).prose:
[Island of Ireland, AD 1750–AD 2000] Modern. Period definition from Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland — Carlin, Neil, 2022.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.
Modern (Ireland, AD 1750–AD 2000).source: Archaeological periods for the island of Ireland

The long stretch of the Old and Middle Stone Age, when small bands of hunters followed herds across a landscape repeatedly transformed by advancing and retreating ice. Britain was periodically abandoned altogether and repopulated, at times joined to the continent by the dry plain of Doggerland. The traces are flint tools, butchered animal bone and rare human remains — the evidence of half a million years of intermittent occupation before farming.

Later Prehistoric (Scotland, 4300 BC–AD.label: Later Prehistoric
Later Prehistoric (Scotland, 4300 BC–AD.prose:
[Scotland, 4300 BC–AD 800] Later Prehistoric. For monuments or objects that can be identified only to a date range from the introduction of agriculture in the Neolithic to the Iron Age. Use more specific term where appropriate. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

This long stretch covers the arrival of farming, the raising of Stonehenge and thousands of barrows, the spread of bronze and then iron, and the hillforts and tribal kingdoms the Romans found on arrival. Landscapes were permanently reshaped: forests cleared, fields laid out, boundaries dug that still show in aerial photographs. Metalwork hoards dropped into rivers and bogs, and richly furnished burials, hint at beliefs and hierarchies that left no written record.

Mesolithic (Scotland, 9800 BC–4000 BC).label: Mesolithic
Mesolithic (Scotland, 9800 BC–4000 BC).prose:
[Scotland, 9800 BC–4000 BC] Mesolithic. The Middle Stone Age, falling between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic; marks the beginning of a move from a hunter gatherer society towards food producing society. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Late Mesolithic (Scotland, 7000 BC–4000.label: Late Mesolithic
Late Mesolithic (Scotland, 7000 BC–4000.prose:
[Scotland, 7000 BC–4000 BC] Late Mesolithic. The Late Mesolithic is characterised by more elaborate stone tools including more elaborately retouched 'narrow blade' microliths and other edge-blunted forms. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Hunter-gatherers in dense post-glacial woodland made tiny geometric microliths set into composite arrows and worked the coasts, rivers and clearings with fire to draw in game. Rising seas finally drowned Doggerland during this period, cutting Britain off from the Continent and leaving its foragers on an island. Their world ended with the arrival of farming, and the debate over how much they contributed to what came next is still unresolved.

Neolithic (Scotland, 4300 BC–2500 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Scotland, 4300 BC–2500 BC).prose:
[Scotland, 4300 BC–2500 BC] Neolithic. The Neolithic, or New Stone Age, sees the transition from hunter gatherer economies to farming. Monumental architecture, including chambered cairns, develops. Pottery is first used and stone tool technologies become more sophisticated. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Early Neolithic (Scotland, 4300 BC–3500.label: Early Neolithic
Early Neolithic (Scotland, 4300 BC–3500.prose:
[Scotland, 4300 BC–3500 BC] Early Neolithic. The earliest subdivision of the Neolithic. Characterised include large rectangular houses, cursus monuments. Burial monuments include long and round barrows and cairns. The first pottery forms appear and artefact types include polished stone axeheads. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Farming, pottery and domesticated animals arrived in Britain, and within a few generations people were building monuments: earthen long barrows over the bones of the dead, ditched causewayed enclosures for gatherings and feasts, and deep flint mines. Woodland was cleared for cereals and pasture, beginning the long transformation of the British landscape. These communities laid the groundwork for the great henge and stone circle building that followed.

Middle Neolithic (Scotland, 3500 BC–2900.label: Middle Neolithic
Middle Neolithic (Scotland, 3500 BC–2900.prose:
[Scotland, 3500 BC–2900 BC] Middle Neolithic. The second subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Communal long barrows and causewayed enclosures fell out of use, and people began building cursus monuments – enormous parallel-ditched avenues running for miles across the landscape – along with the first great henges. Pottery grew heavier and more elaborately decorated, and forest clearance and herding reshaped the countryside. The earthwork phase of Stonehenge belongs to the end of this stretch of time.

Late Neolithic (Scotland, 3000 BC–2500 B.label: Late Neolithic
Late Neolithic (Scotland, 3000 BC–2500 B.prose:
[Scotland, 3000 BC–2500 BC] Late Neolithic. The third subdivision of the Neolithic sees the widespread appearance of novel burial practices and novel material culture, including Grooved Ware pottery, carved stone balls and maceheads. Monument types include Stone Circles and Henges, and rock art. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.

Chalcolithic (Scotland, 2500 BC–2200 BC).label: Chalcolithic
Chalcolithic (Scotland, 2500 BC–2200 BC).prose:
[Scotland, 2500 BC–2200 BC] Chalcolithic. The transitional period at the end of the Neolithic when metal is first used to make tools and weapons. New burial rites and artefacts appear at the same time as these copper implements appear. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

Bronze Age (Scotland, 2200 BC–800 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Scotland, 2200 BC–800 BC).prose:
[Scotland, 2200 BC–800 BC] Bronze Age. After the Neolithic and the first use of metal in the Chalcolithic, the Bronze Age is defined by advances in metal working to produce durable Bronze tools and weapons, accompanied by societal change. New architectural styles and burial practices appear. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
