Early Bronze Age (Scotland, 2200 BC–1500.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Scotland, 2200 BC–1500.prose:
[Scotland, 2200 BC–1500 BC] Early Bronze Age. The earliest subdivision of the Bronze Age often defined by artefact types. Pottery includes late Beakers, Food vessels, Collared and Cordoned Urns while the metal work evolves from simple to more complex forms. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

Middle Bronze Age (Scotland, 1500 BC–110.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Scotland, 1500 BC–110.prose:
[Scotland, 1500 BC–1100 BC] Middle Bronze Age. The second subdivision of the Bronze Age. New forms of metalwork appear, including louped spearheads, dirks and rapiers. Bucket urns appear in the pottery record. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

Late Bronze Age (Scotland, 1100 BC–800 B.label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Scotland, 1100 BC–800 B.prose:
[Scotland, 1100 BC–800 BC] Late Bronze Age. The third and latest subdivision of the Bronze Age. The earliest hillforts appear. Sophisticated metal working forms emerge including sheet metal working and complex casting processes. Flat-rimmed ware appears in the pottery record. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Iron Age (Scotland, 800 BC–AD 500).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Scotland, 800 BC–AD 500).prose:
[Scotland, 800 BC–AD 500] Iron Age. Tribal centres and elites appear in society at the end of the Bronze Age. There is a wide range of monumental buildings including brochs, duns and crannogs. Iron is used for tool making. The fall of Rome traditionally marks the end of the period. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Early Iron Age (Scotland, 800 BC–300 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Scotland, 800 BC–300 BC).prose:
[Scotland, 800 BC–300 BC] Early Iron Age. The earliest subdivision of the Iron Age in Scotland. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

Middle Iron Age (Scotland, 300 BC–AD 300.label: Middle Iron Age
Middle Iron Age (Scotland, 300 BC–AD 300.prose:
[Scotland, 300 BC–AD 300] Middle Iron Age. The second subdivision of the Iron Age in Scotland. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Hillforts, enclosed farmsteads and grain storage pits dominated the landscape, and roundhouse communities produced increasingly regionalised pottery and fine metalwork in flowing La Tène style. Many hillforts were abandoned or slimmed down to fewer, larger centres, hinting at the consolidation of the tribal groupings Roman writers would later name. Bodies and objects placed deliberately in disused pits offer a glimpse of ritual life.

Late Iron Age (Scotland, AD 300–AD 500).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (Scotland, AD 300–AD 500).prose:
[Scotland, AD 300–AD 500] Late Iron Age. The third sub-division of the Iron Age in Scotland. The label is applied variously to the last part of the Iron Age up to the end of the Roman incursions or from the end of the Roman incursions to the 9th Century Norse incursions. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Long Iron Age (Scotland, 800 BC–AD 800).label: Long Iron Age
Long Iron Age (Scotland, 800 BC–AD 800).prose:
[Scotland, 800 BC–AD 800] Long Iron Age. The Long Iron Age reflects the continuity and evolution of society, breaking down the perceived barriers between the Late Bronze Age, the Iron Age and much of the Early Medieval Period ending with the Norse incursions of the 9th century. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A term used for the whole stretch of Scottish prehistory and early history from the first ironworking to the Viking arrival, treated as one long continuum rather than broken into Roman and post-Roman halves. It covers the building of brochs, duns and crannogs, the brief Roman incursions that never took hold, and the emergence of the Picts and their symbol stones. The continuity of settlement forms across a thousand years is what makes the label useful.

Roman (Scotland, AD 75–AD 400).label: Roman
Roman (Scotland, AD 75–AD 400).prose:
[Scotland, AD 75–AD 400] Roman. A term applied to physical traces of the Roman military incursions into Scotland and objects made within the Roman Republic or Empire from the late 1st century until the 4th century BCE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

Flavian (Scotland, AD 69–AD 96).label: Flavian
Flavian (Scotland, AD 69–AD 96).prose:
[Scotland, AD 69–AD 96] Flavian. Referring to the Flavian dynasty who were Emperors of Rome in 69-96 BCE. In Scotland, evidence usually dates from the early 70s until the mid 80s CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Under Vespasian, Titus and Domitian, Roman armies pushed conquest to its furthest extent in Britain: Wales and northern England were subdued, legionary fortresses built at Chester, Caerleon and York, and Agricola campaigned deep into Scotland, winning at Mons Graupius. Towns acquired forums, baths and street grids, and Fishbourne-style villas appeared in the south. Much of the province's characteristic pottery and coin dating hinges on this well-documented building boom.

Antonine (Scotland, AD 138–AD 192).label: Antonine
Antonine (Scotland, AD 138–AD 192).prose:
[Scotland, AD 138–AD 192] Antonine. The Antonine dynasty were Emperors of Rome between 138 and 192 CE. In Scotland the period covers Roman reoccupation in Scotland including the construction of the Antonine Wall in the early 140s until its abandonment in the early 160 CEs. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Roman Britain under Antoninus Pius and his successors, when the frontier was pushed north to the newly built turf-and-timber Antonine Wall between the Forth and Clyde before being pulled back to Hadrian's Wall a generation later. Towns and villas flourished, and the era's distinctive samian pottery and coin issues make it one of the most closely dated horizons in British archaeology. It ends with the disorder following Commodus's assassination.

Severan (Scotland, AD 208–AD 211).label: Severan
Severan (Scotland, AD 208–AD 211).prose:
[Scotland, AD 208–AD 211] Severan. Referring to the Severan dynasty who were Emperors of Rome in 193-235 C.E. In Scotland, Severan relates to the campaigns of the Emperor Septimius Severus and his sons between 208-211 C.E. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Septimius Severus brought a huge army to Britain, campaigned deep into Scotland and died at York in 211, and the province was afterwards split in two to limit the power of its governors. Frontier forts along Hadrian's Wall and the northern roads were rebuilt in stone, and York and London flourished as provincial capitals. It was a boom time for the towns and villas of the south, funded by military spending and a garrison whose soldiers could now legally marry.

Post Roman (Scotland, AD 401–AD 1900).label: Post Roman
Post Roman (Scotland, AD 401–AD 1900).prose:
[Scotland, AD 401–AD 1900] Post Roman. Loosely defined as the centuries after the breakdown of the Roman Empire. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

With the withdrawal of Roman power, the north was left to Picts, Gaels of Dál Riata, Britons of Strathclyde and Angles of Bernicia, whose rivalries were reshaped by Christian missions and, from the late 700s, by Norse raiding and settlement. Out of that competition emerged the kingdom of Alba and eventually a unified Scotland. Used as a broad label, the term covers everything from carved Pictish symbol stones and duns to medieval burghs, castles and improvement-era farmsteads.

Pictish (Scotland, AD 300–AD 850).label: Pictish
Pictish (Scotland, AD 300–AD 850).prose:
[Scotland, AD 300–AD 850] Pictish. A cultural term derived from Picti - painted or tattooed people - was applied by the Romans to the peoples living north of the Forth and Clyde rivers. The distinctive art of the Symbol Stones documents the adoption of Christianity. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The peoples north of the Forth who resisted Rome and later coalesced into kingdoms such as Fortriu. They left hundreds of carved symbol stones covered in enigmatic emblems and, after conversion, elaborate Christian crosses, plus fortified hilltop centres like Burghead. Victory over Northumbria at Dunnichen in 685 secured their independence, but Viking pressure and dynastic union with Dál Riata dissolved Pictish identity into the new kingdom of Alba.

Viking (Scotland, AD 751–AD 1000).label: Viking
Viking (Scotland, AD 751–AD 1000).prose:
[Scotland, AD 751–AD 1000] Viking. Defined as the period of initial settlement following on from a period of Viking (raiding) activities and initial contact. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Raids on coastal monasteries from the 790s turned into invasion: the Great Heathen Army destroyed most English kingdoms, and only Wessex under Alfred survived, dividing the country with the Danelaw. Scandinavian settlers reshaped the north and east — place-names, land divisions, law and everyday speech — and made York a booming trading city. Later came a second wave and a Danish king, Cnut, ruling England as part of a North Sea empire.

Saxon (Scotland, AD 410–AD 1000).label: Saxon
Saxon (Scotland, AD 410–AD 1000).prose:
[Scotland, AD 410–AD 1000] Saxon. A cultural term. It is applied to the distinctive culture and artistic styles that evolved from the merging of native traditions with those of Germanic tribes who had migrated from northern Europe. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A label borrowed from English archaeology for the centuries between the end of Roman Britain and the eve of the Norman age. In Scotland these were the centuries of the Picts and their symbol stones, of Gaelic Dál Riata and the monastery on Iona, of the Britons of Strathclyde and Anglian settlers in Lothian, ended by Viking raids and settlement that reshaped the north and west. Out of these competing kingdoms the united realm of Alba emerged.

Anglo-Saxon (Scotland, AD 410–AD 1000).label: Anglo-Saxon
Anglo-Saxon (Scotland, AD 410–AD 1000).prose:
[Scotland, AD 410–AD 1000] Anglo-Saxon. Both a political and cultural term: applied to the distinctive culture and artistic styles that evolved from the merging of native traditions with those of Germanic tribes who had migrated from northern Europe. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

After Roman administration collapsed, settlers from across the North Sea — Angles, Saxons, Jutes and others — mixed with the British population and built a patchwork of small kingdoms that gradually consolidated into Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria. Missionaries from Rome and Ireland converted the elites, bringing literacy, monasteries and works like Bede's history and Beowulf. Viking invasions from the 790s nearly swept the kingdoms away before Alfred and his heirs forged a single English realm, which fell to William of Normandy in 1066.

Anglian (Scotland, AD 600–AD 1000).label: Anglian
Anglian (Scotland, AD 600–AD 1000).prose:
[Scotland, AD 600–AD 1000] Anglian. A cultural term for groups of people from northern Germany who occupied large parts of eastern England after the Romans left. The Anglian kingdom of Northumbria included much of the eastern side of Scotland up to the Firth of Forth. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Northumbrian Angles pushed north of the Tweed and ruled the Lothians and much of the south-east, planting English speech in what would become Scotland. Their expansion was checked in 685 at Nechtansmere, where the Picts destroyed a Northumbrian army and the bishopric at Abercorn was abandoned. The period's finest survivals are stone crosses such as Ruthwell, carved with vine-scroll and runic verse, evidence of a wealthy monastic culture on the northern frontier.

Medieval (Scotland, AD 1093–AD 1603).label: Medieval
Medieval (Scotland, AD 1093–AD 1603).prose: [Scotland, AD 1093–AD 1603] Medieval. The Medieval period or Middle Ages arbitrarily begins with the death of Malcolm III Canmore in 1093 until James VI inherited the English throne in 1603. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Early Medieval (Scotland, AD 400–AD 1100.label: Early Medieval
Early Medieval (Scotland, AD 400–AD 1100.prose:
[Scotland, AD 400–AD 1100] Early Medieval. Early medieval Scotland can be defined by the adoption of Christianity and emergence of identity from cultural groupings leading to state formation after the end of the Roman Empire. Overlaps with the end of the Long Iron Age. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Late Early Medieval (Scotland, AD 900–AD.label: Late Early Medieval
Late Early Medieval (Scotland, AD 900–AD.prose:
[Scotland, AD 900–AD 1100] Late Early Medieval. Used in some areas to describe the transition from the Long Iron Age to the Medieval period, following the Norse invasions of the 9th century. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Viking armies overran most of the English kingdoms until Alfred of Wessex held out, and his successors then conquered the Danelaw to forge a single kingdom of England with shires, burhs and a silver coinage. Danish kings including Cnut later ruled it as part of a North Sea empire. The period ends abruptly at Hastings.

Post Medieval (Scotland, AD 1603–AD 1900.label: Post Medieval
Post Medieval (Scotland, AD 1603–AD 1900.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1603–AD 1900] Post Medieval. Arbitrarily commences with the accession of James VI to the English throne until the start of the 20th century. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Beginning with the dissolution of the monasteries and the Reformation's stripping of parish churches, these centuries carried England through civil war, the growth of an Atlantic empire, enclosure of open fields, and industrialisation. Excavations of the period yield mass-produced goods - tin-glazed and transfer-printed pottery, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes, machine-made nails - that let sites be dated to within a decade or two. Landscapes changed as thoroughly as objects: hedged fields, canals, railways, mines and terraced workers' housing all belong to this span.

Georgian (Scotland, AD 1714–AD 1837).label: Georgian
Georgian (Scotland, AD 1714–AD 1837).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1714–AD 1837] Georgian. Dating to the reign of Kings George I, George II, George III, George IV, covering the overall period 1714 CE to 1830-37 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The century of the four Georges gave England sash windows, brick terraces, classical proportion and squares laid out to speculative plans, from Bath to Bloomsbury. Beneath the elegance ran rapid change: turnpikes and canals, coal, iron and cotton mills, a booming consumer market in ceramics and tea, and a slave-based Atlantic trade that funded much of it. Excavated Georgian sites are rich in mass-produced tablewares, clay pipes and imported goods.

Victorian (Scotland, AD 1837–AD 1901).label: Victorian
Victorian (Scotland, AD 1837–AD 1901).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1837–AD 1901] Victorian. Dating to the reign of Queen Victoria. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The age that gave England most of its familiar built landscape: red-brick terraces, mills and pumping stations, railway viaducts, board schools and Gothic Revival churches and town halls. Archaeologically it is a period of mass-produced things — transfer-printed ceramics, glass bottles, clay pipes, tinned food — that let sites be dated almost to the decade. It is also the period when antiquarianism hardened into archaeology, with the first systematic excavations and county societies.

Industrial (Scotland, AD 1750–AD 1850).label: Industrial
Industrial (Scotland, AD 1750–AD 1850).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1750–AD 1850] Industrial. Industrial relates to the mechanisation of manufacturing process, following the Industrial Revolution in the mid 18th century. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Steam engines, coal and iron turned Glasgow and the Clyde into one of the workshops of the world, while cotton mills and chemical works drew people off the land into fast-growing, overcrowded towns. In the countryside, improved farming and the Highland clearances pushed families to the cities or onto emigrant ships. The same decades produced Scottish engineering and shipbuilding traditions, tenement housing, and the first serious campaigns over factory conditions and the vote.

First World War (Scotland, AD 1914–AD 19.label: First World War
First World War (Scotland, AD 1914–AD 19.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1914–AD 1919] First World War. Used to record buildings, defensive monuments and sites dating to, and associated with, the First World War. For other types of building, such as houses, built during this period use EARLY 20TH CENTURY. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Britain's first experience of industrialised total war: conscription from 1916, Zeppelin and Gotha raids on civilian towns, rationing, and women entering munitions factories and transport in huge numbers. Nearly three-quarters of a million British servicemen died, and almost every town has a war memorial dating from the years just after. Trench systems, practice grounds, aerodromes and shell-filling factories left archaeological traces across the countryside.

Second World War (Scotland, AD 1939–AD 1.label: Second World War
Second World War (Scotland, AD 1939–AD 1.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1939–AD 1946] Second World War. Used to record buildings, defensive monuments and sites dating to, and associated with, the Second World War. For other types of building, such as houses, built during this period use MID 20TH CENTURY. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Britain fought from the first day to the last: evacuation at Dunkirk, the air battle over southern England, and the Blitz that gutted city centres from London to Coventry. Rationing, conscription of women into war work, and the evacuation of children reshaped everyday life, while cracking German codes at Bletchley Park quietly changed the war at sea. Victory came at the cost of exhaustion, debt and the beginning of the end of empire.

Crofting (Scotland, AD 1850–AD 2100).label: Crofting
Crofting (Scotland, AD 1850–AD 2100).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1850–AD 2100] Crofting. A system of working the land through small holdings called crofts. Following the highland clearances and the 1884 Crofters War, the Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886, or Crofters' Charter, granted crofters' rights over rents, security of tenure etc. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A distinctively Highland and Island system of small rented landholdings, worked alongside fishing, weaving and seasonal labour, which took its modern shape in the aftermath of the Clearances and the potato famine. Agitation by the Land League and the "crofters' war" of rent strikes and land raids forced the Crofters Holdings Act of 1886, granting security of tenure, fair rents and the right to pass a croft on. Crofting law still governs much of the northwest, and the townships it created remain the backbone of Gaelic-speaking rural settlement.

Pre-Improvement (Scotland, AD 1058–AD 18.label: Pre-Improvement
Pre-Improvement (Scotland, AD 1058–AD 18.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1058–AD 1800] Pre-Improvement. In Archaeology, largely applied to traces of the rural settlement and landscape documented or surviving the sweeping agricultural changes of the Age of Improvement. Indicate using the date range MEDIEVAL - 18TH CENTURY. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The centuries of Scottish rural life before agricultural Improvement, when townships of a few families farmed intermixed runrig strips, shared draught oxen and grazed livestock on common hill pasture. Houses were low, thick-walled and thatched, rebuilt often, and settlement clustered on the better ground with shieling huts used in summer uplands. The surviving field banks, corn-drying kilns and abandoned fermtouns are the landscape that Improvement, enclosure and clearance swept away after 1800.

Improvement (Scotland, AD 1750–AD 1850).label: Improvement
Improvement (Scotland, AD 1750–AD 1850).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1750–AD 1850] Improvement. Between about 1750 and 1850 rural, urban commercial and industrial Scotland underwent a dramatic transformation modernising society.
Use a range of 18th - 19th century instead of this term. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Landowners redrew the Scottish countryside: enclosed fields, drainage, crop rotations, new breeds, planned villages and straight roads replaced runrig farming and joint tenancies. In the Highlands the same logic produced the Clearances, with families moved off inland straths to make room for sheep and pushed to the coast or onto emigrant ships. The surplus labour and capital fed Glasgow's cotton mills and the Lanarkshire coal and iron trades, while Edinburgh's literati theorised the whole process.

House of Alpin (Scotland, AD 848–AD 1034.label: House of Alpin
House of Alpin (Scotland, AD 848–AD 1034.prose:
[Scotland, AD 848–AD 1034] House of Alpin. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The line descended from Kenneth mac Alpin, which fused Gaelic Dal Riata and Pictish territory into a single kingdom that came to be called Alba. Ruling by alternating succession between branches, its kings spent generations fighting Norse settlers and raiders while pushing the frontier south into Lothian and Strathclyde. By the death of Malcolm II the shape of a recognisable Scotland was in place.

Amlaib (Scotland, AD 973–AD 977).label: Amlaib
Amlaib (Scotland, AD 973–AD 977).prose:
[Scotland, AD 973–AD 977] Amlaib. King of the House of Alpin. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A short and shadowy reign in the kingdom of Alba, known almost entirely from terse king-lists and annal entries. Amlaíb, apparently a son of the earlier king Illulb, held or contested the kingship against Cinaed II, who killed him. The episode illustrates how the Scottish succession alternated violently between rival royal branches.

Kenneth II (Scotland, AD 971–AD 995).label: Kenneth II
Kenneth II (Scotland, AD 971–AD 995).prose:
[Scotland, AD 971–AD 995] Kenneth II. King of the House of Alpin. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Cináed mac Maíl Coluim ruled the young kingdom of Alba as it pressed south into Lothian and the Anglo-Scottish frontier took something like its later shape; chroniclers record him raiding into Northumbria and receiving lands from the English king. He was killed in 995 in a feud among the competing royal kindreds, a reminder that the crown still alternated violently between branches of the ruling house rather than passing from father to son.

Constantine III (Scotland, AD 995–AD 997.label: Constantine III
Constantine III (Scotland, AD 995–AD 997.prose:
[Scotland, AD 995–AD 997] Constantine III. King of the House of Alpin. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A short and violent reign in the long feud between rival branches of the Scottish royal kindred, ended when he was killed by his successor. Such contested successions were normal in a kingdom still consolidating its hold over Picts, Gaels and the lands taken from the Britons and Norse.

Kenneth III (Scotland, AD 997–AD 1005).label: Kenneth III
Kenneth III (Scotland, AD 997–AD 1005).prose:
[Scotland, AD 997–AD 1005] Kenneth III. King of the House of Alpin. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Cináed mac Duib held the kingship of Alba during the murderous rivalry between the two branches of the royal family, and was killed in battle at Monzievaird by his cousin Malcolm II, who then broke the pattern of alternating succession. His descendants kept a claim to the throne: his granddaughter Gruoch married Macbeth, and that claim helped justify Macbeth's own seizure of power.

Malcolm II (Scotland, AD 1005–AD 1034).label: Malcolm II
Malcolm II (Scotland, AD 1005–AD 1034).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1005–AD 1034] Malcolm II. King of the House of Alpin. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A long-reigning king of Alba who fought hard to extend his realm southwards, winning at Carham on the Tweed in 1018 and confirming Lothian in Scottish hands. He left no son, and by clearing rivals from his path he ensured the succession of his grandson Duncan — the manoeuvring that lies behind the later Macbeth story.

House of Dunkeld (Scotland, AD 1034–AD 1.label: House of Dunkeld
House of Dunkeld (Scotland, AD 1034–AD 1.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1034–AD 1286] House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The line running from Duncan I to Alexander III turned a patchwork of Gaelic provinces into something recognisable as a medieval kingdom: sheriffs and royal castles, chartered burghs trading with Flanders, reformed monasteries, and Anglo-Norman families like the Bruces and Stewarts settled on Scottish land. David I in particular imported feudal tenure wholesale. When Alexander III fell from his horse in 1286 with no surviving son, the dynasty ended and the succession crisis opened the door to English intervention.

Duncan I (Scotland, AD 1034–AD 1040).label: Duncan I
Duncan I (Scotland, AD 1034–AD 1040).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1034–AD 1040] Duncan I. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Grandson of Malcolm II, he came to the throne by inheritance rather than the older system of alternating succession, and united Strathclyde with the Scottish kingdom. His short reign was marked by a failed raid on Durham and defeat in the north; he was killed in battle by Macbeth, his own general. Shakespeare's portrait of a venerable king murdered in his bed bears little relation to the young, unlucky war leader of the sources.

Macbeth (Scotland, AD 1040–AD 1057).label: Macbeth
Macbeth (Scotland, AD 1040–AD 1057).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1040–AD 1057] Macbeth. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Mac Bethad mac Findlaích, ruler of Moray, killed King Duncan I in battle and held the Scottish throne for seventeen years, secure enough to leave the kingdom for a pilgrimage to Rome where he reportedly scattered money to the poor. He was defeated and killed by Duncan's son Malcolm, backed by Northumbrian troops. The murderous tyrant of Shakespeare's play bears little resemblance to a king remembered by contemporaries as generous and effective.

Lulach (Scotland, AD 1057–AD 1058).label: Lulach
Lulach (Scotland, AD 1057–AD 1058).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1057–AD 1058] Lulach. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Stepson of Macbeth, he was made king after Macbeth fell in battle and lasted only months before being killed by Malcolm III. Nicknamed 'the Unfortunate' or 'the Simple', he is remembered mainly as the last of the line that Malcolm's dynasty displaced.

Malcolm III (Scotland, AD 1058–AD 1093).label: Malcolm III
Malcolm III (Scotland, AD 1058–AD 1093).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1058–AD 1093] Malcolm III. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Known as Canmore, he took the throne after the fall of Macbeth and Lulach and ruled for thirty-five years of raiding into northern England. His marriage to the English princess Margaret brought southern churchmen, customs and refugees to his court, opening Scotland to Anglo-Norman influence; his submission to William the Conqueror at Abernethy in 1072 set up centuries of argument over English overlordship. He died in ambush at Alnwick.

Donald III (Scotland, AD 1093–AD 1097).label: Donald III
Donald III (Scotland, AD 1093–AD 1097).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1093–AD 1097] Donald III. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Donald Bán seized the Scottish throne on his brother Malcolm III's death and expelled the English and Norman courtiers Malcolm's queen Margaret had gathered, a deliberate turn back toward older Gaelic ways. He was ousted within a year by his nephew Duncan II, regained power, then was finally overthrown by Edgar with English backing, blinded and imprisoned. He was the last Scottish king buried on Iona, and the last to rule against the Anglo-Norman tide.

Duncan II (Scotland, AD 1094–AD 1094).label: Duncan II
Duncan II (Scotland, AD 1094–AD 1094).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1094–AD 1094] Duncan II. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Son of Malcolm III by his first marriage, he had spent years as a hostage at the English court and returned with Norman knights to take the throne from his uncle Donald Bán. Scottish resentment at his foreign backers forced him to send them away, leaving him exposed; he was killed after about six months. His reign is a marker of how far English and Norman power now reached into Scottish succession disputes.

Edgar (Scotland, AD 1097–AD 1107).label: Edgar
Edgar (Scotland, AD 1097–AD 1107).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1097–AD 1107] Edgar. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Edgar took the Scottish throne with an English army at his back, driving out his uncle Donald III, and ruled as a client of the Anglo-Norman kings. He and his brothers, sons of Malcolm III and the saintly Margaret, pushed Scotland toward continental church practice and Norman-style kingship. He also surrendered the Hebrides and Kintyre to Magnus Barelegs of Norway, an admission of how far the Norse still reached into the west.

Alexander I (Scotland, AD 1107–AD 1124).label: Alexander I
Alexander I (Scotland, AD 1107–AD 1124).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1107–AD 1124] Alexander I. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Son of Malcolm III and Saint Margaret, he ruled Scotland north of the Forth while his brother David governed the south, earning the nickname 'the Fierce' for crushing a rising in Moray. He founded houses of reformed monks at Scone and Inchcolm and fought off the archbishop of York's claim to authority over the Scottish church.

David I (Scotland, AD 1124–AD 1153).label: David I
David I (Scotland, AD 1124–AD 1153).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1124–AD 1153] David I. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The reign that reshaped Scotland along Anglo-Norman lines: David introduced feudal landholding for incoming knightly families, founded burghs with trading privileges, struck the first Scottish coinage, and endowed great abbeys such as Melrose, Jedburgh and Holyrood. He also reorganised the church into territorial dioceses and pushed royal authority into Moray and the south. Historians call the whole package the Davidian Revolution, and it set the framework of the medieval Scottish kingdom.

Malcolm IV (Scotland, AD 1153–AD 1165).label: Malcolm IV
Malcolm IV (Scotland, AD 1153–AD 1165).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1153–AD 1165] Malcolm IV. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A boy of twelve when he succeeded his grandfather David I, and dead of illness at twenty-three, which earned him the nickname "the Maiden". He was pressed by Henry II into surrendering Northumberland, Cumberland and Westmorland, and spent his short reign putting down revolts in Galloway, Moray and the west while continuing his grandfather's introduction of feudal landholding and reformed monasteries.

William I (Scotland, AD 1165–AD 1214).label: William I
William I (Scotland, AD 1165–AD 1214).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1165–AD 1214] William I. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

William the Lion's forty-nine-year reign was the longest in medieval Scotland. Captured at Alnwick in 1174 while raiding Northumberland, he was forced by the Treaty of Falaise to accept English overlordship — a humiliation he bought back fifteen years later for 10,000 marks when Richard I needed crusade money. He founded Arbroath Abbey, won papal recognition of the Scottish church's independence, and is traditionally credited with the rampant lion of the royal arms.

Alexander II (Scotland, AD 1214–AD 1249).label: Alexander II
Alexander II (Scotland, AD 1214–AD 1249).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1214–AD 1249] Alexander II. King of the House of Dunkeld. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Turned a fractious realm into a stable kingdom, putting down risings in Galloway, Argyll and Moray and settling the English border on roughly its modern line by the Treaty of York. He died on Kerrera while campaigning to wrest the Hebrides from Norwegian control, a project his son completed.

Alexander III (Scotland, AD 1249–AD 1286.label: Alexander III
Alexander III (Scotland, AD 1249–AD 1286.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1249–AD 1286] Alexander III. Alexander III was born at Roxburgh on 4 September 1241 and was inaugurated as king of Scots on 13 July 1249 at Scone. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Remembered as presiding over a golden age of peace and prosperity, he beat back Haakon IV's fleet at Largs and secured the Hebrides and Man for Scotland by treaty. His death in a fall from his horse at Kinghorn, with all his children already dead, left only an infant granddaughter as heir and led directly to the disputed succession and the Wars of Independence.

House of Sverre (Scotland, AD 1286–AD 12.label: House of Sverre
House of Sverre (Scotland, AD 1286–AD 12.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1286–AD 1290] House of Sverre. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Alexander III's only surviving descendant was his granddaughter Margaret, a small child in Norway, and for four years Scotland was ruled in her name by guardians while Edward I arranged her marriage to his son. She died on the voyage west, in Orkney, before ever reaching her kingdom. With no clear heir, thirteen competitors claimed the crown and Edward was invited to arbitrate - the opening move of the Wars of Independence.

Margaret (Scotland, AD 1286–AD 1290).label: Margaret
Margaret (Scotland, AD 1286–AD 1290).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1286–AD 1290] Margaret. Queen of the House of Sverre (1286-1290). Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A child queen who never set foot in her kingdom as ruler: the granddaughter of Alexander III, she was to be shipped from Norway and married to the heir of England, uniting the crowns. Her death in Orkney on the voyage left thirteen competitors claiming the Scottish throne and invited Edward I to arbitrate, a intervention that turned into invasion and the Wars of Independence.

First Interregnum (Scotland, AD 1286–AD.label: First Interregnum
First Interregnum (Scotland, AD 1286–AD.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1286–AD 1292] First Interregnum. The period between the rules of Alexander III and John Balliol. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Alexander III died without a surviving adult heir, and his infant granddaughter, the Maid of Norway, died on the voyage to Scotland. Thirteen claimants pressed for the crown, and the Scottish guardians invited Edward I of England to arbitrate - a decision that let him claim overlordship. His choice of John Balliol as king set up the confrontations that became the Wars of Independence.

House of Balliol (Scotland, AD 1292–AD 1.label: House of Balliol
House of Balliol (Scotland, AD 1292–AD 1.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1292–AD 1296] House of Balliol. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

John Balliol was chosen as king by Edward I of England, who had been invited to arbitrate between rival claimants after the Scottish royal line died out. Edward then treated him as a vassal, summoning him to answer legal appeals in England; when the Scots allied with France instead, Edward invaded, stripped Balliol of his regalia and removed him. The humiliation left Scotland without a king and set off the Wars of Independence.

John Balliol (Scotland, AD 1292–AD 1296).label: John Balliol
John Balliol (Scotland, AD 1292–AD 1296).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1292–AD 1296] John Balliol. King of the House of Balliol. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Chosen as king of Scots by Edward I of England, who had been invited to arbitrate a disputed succession and used the role to claim overlordship. Balliol's resistance, sealed by the first treaty of the Auld Alliance with France in 1295, brought English invasion, his humiliating deposition, and the stripping of his coat of arms that earned him the nickname Toom Tabard, 'empty coat'. The vacuum that followed launched the Wars of Scottish Independence.

Second Interregnum (Scotland, AD 1296–AD.label: Second Interregnum
Second Interregnum (Scotland, AD 1296–AD.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1296–AD 1306] Second Interregnum. The period between the rules of John Balliol and Robert I. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Edward I stripped John Balliol of his kingship in 1296, carried off the Stone of Scone and the royal records, and ruled Scotland as a conquered land. For a decade the country had no crowned king: Wallace and Moray won at Stirling Bridge, lost at Falkirk, and the guardians fought on in Balliol's name until resistance collapsed. The vacancy ended when Robert Bruce killed his rival John Comyn and had himself enthroned at Scone in 1306.

House of Bruce (Scotland, AD 1306–AD 137.label: House of Bruce
House of Bruce (Scotland, AD 1306–AD 137.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1306–AD 1371] House of Bruce. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Robert I seized the throne after murdering a rival in a church, was excommunicated and hunted, then rebuilt his position and destroyed an English army at Bannockburn. The Declaration of Arbroath asserted Scottish independence to the pope, and by 1328 England recognised it. His son David II reigned long but childless, and the crown passed to his nephew, beginning the Stewart dynasty.

Robert I (Scotland, AD 1306–AD 1329).label: Robert I
Robert I (Scotland, AD 1306–AD 1329).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1306–AD 1329] Robert I. King of the House of Bruce. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Robert the Bruce killed his rival, took the crown in defiance of Edward I, and spent years as a hunted guerrilla before turning the tide. His victory at Bannockburn in 1314 and the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320 secured recognition of Scottish independence, sealed by treaty in 1328, and made him the founding hero of the Scottish national story.

David II (Scotland, AD 1329–AD 1371).label: David II
David II (Scotland, AD 1329–AD 1371).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1329–AD 1371] David II. King of the House of Bruce. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Robert the Bruce's son came to the throne as a child and spent much of his reign in flight or captivity — exiled in France while Edward Balliol and the English pressed their claims, then held eleven years in England after his capture at Neville's Cross. His ransom saddled Scotland with crushing taxation and gave the burghs a permanent voice in parliament. He died without children, handing the crown to his nephew Robert Stewart and beginning the Stewart dynasty.

House of Stewart (Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1.label: House of Stewart
House of Stewart (Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1.prose:
[Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1567] House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Descended from the royal stewards and from Robert the Bruce's daughter, the Stewarts spent two centuries wrestling with over-mighty nobles, long royal minorities and violent deaths - James I murdered, James II killed by his own cannon, James IV cut down at Flodden. They also brought Renaissance building at Stirling and Falkland, the first Scottish universities, and printing. The Reformation of 1560 and the forced abdication of Mary, Queen of Scots in 1567 left an infant king and a Protestant kirk.

Robert II (Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1390).label: Robert II
Robert II (Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1390).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1371–AD 1390] Robert II. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Grandson of Robert the Bruce through his daughter, he came to the throne in late middle age as the first of the Stewart kings, a line that would hold Scotland until 1714 and later England as well. His reign saw renewed border warfare with England, culminating in the Scottish victory at Otterburn, while much of the day-to-day governing fell to his numerous and quarrelsome sons.

1st Century (Scotland, AD 1–AD 100).label: 1st Century
1st Century (Scotland, AD 1–AD 100).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1–AD 100] 1st Century. Century encompassing years 1 CE to 100 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Roman armies landed in AD 43 and turned southern Britain into a province, meeting fierce resistance — most famously Boudica's revolt, which burned Colchester, London and St Albans. Within a generation there were paved roads, planned towns with forums and baths, coinage and a Latin-using elite, while much of rural life carried on in roundhouses as before. It is the moment written history begins for Britain.

2nd Century (Scotland, AD 101–AD 200).label: 2nd Century
2nd Century (Scotland, AD 101–AD 200).prose:
[Scotland, AD 101–AD 200] 2nd Century. Century encompassing years 101 CE to 200 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Britain was a settled Roman province: Hadrian's Wall was built across the north from AD 122, the Antonine Wall briefly pushed the frontier to the Forth-Clyde line, and towns like London, York and Cirencester acquired forums, baths and masonry walls. Villas, roads, coinage and imported pottery spread through the lowlands while the army held the north and Wales. Much of what visitors recognise as 'Roman Britain' - inscriptions, mosaics, writing tablets - dates from these hundred years.

3rd Century (Scotland, AD 201–AD 300).label: 3rd Century
3rd Century (Scotland, AD 201–AD 300).prose:
[Scotland, AD 201–AD 300] 3rd Century. Century encompassing years 201 CE to 300 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Roman Britain grew rich and comparatively quiet while the rest of the empire lurched through civil wars, plague and invasion; villas, mosaics and walled towns spread across the south. The province was split in two for easier control, and coastal forts went up against seaborne raiders. For a decade Britain broke away entirely under Carausius and Allectus, who struck their own coins and ruled an independent North Sea empire before Constantius reconquered it.

4th Century (Scotland, AD 301–AD 400).label: 4th Century
4th Century (Scotland, AD 301–AD 400).prose:
[Scotland, AD 301–AD 400] 4th Century. Century encompassing years 301 CE to 400 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Roman Britain's most prosperous and most anxious century: grand mosaic-floored villas were built in the west and south while towns shrank and coastal forts were strengthened against Saxon, Irish and Pictish raiders. Christianity became the official religion, leaving behind chi-rho mosaics, lead baptismal tanks and hoards like Water Newton, though pagan temples were still being built. The raids of 367 and the steady withdrawal of troops for continental wars left the province exposed by the century's end.

5th Century (Scotland, AD 401–AD 500).label: 5th Century
5th Century (Scotland, AD 401–AD 500).prose:
[Scotland, AD 401–AD 500] 5th Century. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Roman government ended and Britain fragmented into small territories run by warlords, bishops and surviving town elites; coinage, pottery industries and stone building largely disappeared within a generation. Germanic-speaking settlers from across the North Sea established farms and cremation cemeteries in the east, while British kingdoms held the west and north. Almost everything we know comes from archaeology and from Gildas's furious sermon about the ruin of Britain — the shadowy period that later produced the Arthur legends.

6th Century (Scotland, AD 501–AD 600).label: 6th Century
6th Century (Scotland, AD 501–AD 600).prose:
[Scotland, AD 501–AD 600] 6th Century. Century encompassing years 501 CE to 600 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Small Anglo-Saxon kingdoms took shape across eastern and central Britain, their elites buried with weapons, brooches and imported glass, while British kingdoms survived in the west and Ireland's monasteries flourished. Plague swept the post-Roman world in the 540s and the climate downturn of 536 hit harvests hard. The century closed with Augustine's mission landing in Kent in 597 and the beginning of the conversion.

7th Century (Scotland, AD 601–AD 700).label: 7th Century
7th Century (Scotland, AD 601–AD 700).prose:
[Scotland, AD 601–AD 700] 7th Century. Century encompassing years 601 CE to 700 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

England's kings converted to Christianity, some more than once, bringing literacy, stone churches and monasteries founded from both Rome and Iona; the Synod of Whitby in 664 settled the contest in Rome's favour. The Sutton Hoo ship burial captures the wealth and long-distance connections of these new dynasties. Northumbria and Mercia emerged as the dominant powers, and the first English law codes were written down.

8th Century (Scotland, AD 701–AD 800).label: 8th Century
8th Century (Scotland, AD 701–AD 800).prose:
[Scotland, AD 701–AD 800] 8th Century. Century encompassing years 701 CE to 800 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Northumbrian monasteries produced Bede's history and manuscripts such as the Lindisfarne Gospels, and English missionaries like Boniface and scholars like Alcuin carried that learning to the Continent. Offa of Mercia dominated southern England, minted a reformed silver coinage, dealt with Charlemagne as an equal and built the great dyke facing Wales. Trading settlements at London, Ipswich and Hamwic grew — and in 793 Viking raiders sacked Lindisfarne.

9th Century (Scotland, AD 801–AD 900).label: 9th Century
9th Century (Scotland, AD 801–AD 900).prose:
[Scotland, AD 801–AD 900] 9th Century. Century encompassing years 801 CE to 900 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Viking raids became conquest: the Great Heathen Army destroyed the kingdoms of Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia, and Scandinavian settlers took land across the north and east under the Danelaw. Alfred of Wessex survived, bought time, built fortified burhs and a navy, and promoted translation of Latin works into English. Out of that emergency came the framework of a single English kingdom and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

10th Century (Scotland, AD 901–AD 1000).label: 10th Century
10th Century (Scotland, AD 901–AD 1000).prose:
[Scotland, AD 901–AD 1000] 10th Century. Century encompassing years 901 CE to 1000 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The kings of Wessex turned their military recovery against the Vikings into a single kingdom of England, with Æthelstan the first to rule the whole country and a network of fortified burhs, shires and royal mints binding it together. A monastic reform movement led by Dunstan and Æthelwold rebuilt the great abbeys and produced some of the finest manuscript art of the age. Renewed Danish raids at the century's end undid much of the stability the West Saxon kings had built.

11th Century (Scotland, AD 1001–AD 1100).label: 11th Century
11th Century (Scotland, AD 1001–AD 1100).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1001–AD 1100] 11th Century. Century encompassing years 1001 CE to 1100 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

England changed hands twice in fifty years: first to the Danish king Cnut, who ruled it as part of a North Sea empire, then to William of Normandy in 1066. The conquest replaced almost the entire landholding class, brought castles and a French-speaking aristocracy, and was recorded in the extraordinary land survey of Domesday Book. Stone cathedrals and abbeys were rebuilt on a vast scale, and England was pulled firmly into the orbit of continental Europe.

12th Century (Scotland, AD 1101–AD 1200).label: 12th Century
12th Century (Scotland, AD 1101–AD 1200).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1101–AD 1200] 12th Century. Century encompassing years 1101 CE to 1200 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

After the civil war between Stephen and Matilda known as the Anarchy, Henry II built an empire stretching from Northumberland to the Pyrenees and laid the foundations of the English common law with itinerant royal justices and juries. Towns and markets multiplied, Cistercian monks colonised the uplands with sheep runs, and the first stirrings of Gothic architecture appeared. The murder of Thomas Becket in 1170 made Canterbury one of Europe's great pilgrimage destinations.

13th Century (Scotland, AD 1201–AD 1300).label: 13th Century
13th Century (Scotland, AD 1201–AD 1300).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1201–AD 1300] 13th Century. Century encompassing years 1201 CE to 1300 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Conflict between kings and barons produced Magna Carta and then, after Simon de Montfort's rebellion, the first parliaments to include knights and townsmen. Edward I conquered Wales and ringed it with castles, and began the long wars with Scotland. Friars arrived to preach in the fast-growing towns, and the wool trade tied English farming to Flemish looms.

14th Century (Scotland, AD 1301–AD 1400).label: 14th Century
14th Century (Scotland, AD 1301–AD 1400).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1301–AD 1400] 14th Century. Century encompassing years 1301 CE to 1400 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

The Black Death of 1348-49 killed perhaps a third to a half of the population, shattering the old manorial economy, driving up wages and helping provoke the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. War with France dragged on for decades, paid for by new taxes and fought by archers whose victories at Crécy and Poitiers became national legend. English replaced French in the courts and, in Chaucer's hands, became a literary language, while Wycliffe's followers began questioning the church.

15th Century (Scotland, AD 1401–AD 1500).label: 15th Century
15th Century (Scotland, AD 1401–AD 1500).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1401–AD 1500] 15th Century. Century encompassing years 1401 CE to 1500 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Defeat in France ended the long war with almost nothing to show for it, and the aristocracy turned on itself in the dynastic conflict remembered as the Wars of the Roses, ending with Henry Tudor's victory at Bosworth in 1485. Wool gave way to woven cloth as the country's great export, and gentry and merchants built the grand parish churches and timber houses that still survive. Caxton set up a printing press at Westminster in 1476, putting books in English into circulation for the first time.

16th Century (Scotland, AD 1501–AD 1600).label: 16th Century
16th Century (Scotland, AD 1501–AD 1600).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1501–AD 1600] 16th Century. Century encompassing years 1501 CE to 1600 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Henry VIII's break with Rome dissolved the monasteries, transferred enormous wealth to the crown and gentry, and began a century of religious upheaval that swung between Protestant and Catholic before settling under Elizabeth I. Population rose sharply, prices soared, and enclosure of common land pushed people towards the towns. The defeat of the Spanish Armada, the first ventures across the Atlantic, and the London playhouses of Shakespeare and Marlowe all belong to the reign's later years.

17th Century (Scotland, AD 1601–AD 1700).label: 17th Century
17th Century (Scotland, AD 1601–AD 1700).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1601–AD 1700] 17th Century. Century encompassing years 1601 CE to 1700 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Quarrels between crown and parliament over money and religion escalated into civil war, the execution of Charles I in 1649 and a decade of republican rule, before the monarchy returned in 1660 and was again reshaped by the Glorious Revolution of 1688. Plague and the Great Fire devastated London in the 1660s, and the rebuilt city became a commercial capital served by joint-stock companies, coffee houses and the new Bank of England. The Royal Society gave institutional form to experimental science, and colonies in the Caribbean and North America made England a slave-trading Atlantic power.

18th Century (Scotland, AD 1701–AD 1800).label: 18th Century
18th Century (Scotland, AD 1701–AD 1800).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1701–AD 1800] 18th Century. Century encompassing years 1701 CE to 1800 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Georgian England grew rich on Atlantic trade, colonial expansion and a booming market in consumer goods, while enclosure and new crop rotations remade the countryside and pushed people toward the towns. Canals, coke-smelted iron, steam engines and mechanised spinning laid the groundwork for industrial production in the century's later decades. Everyday material culture changed dramatically: tea drinking, cheap printed cottons, mass-produced Staffordshire ceramics and clay pipes turn up in enormous quantities on sites of the period. Politically it was the century of the Union with Scotland, Hanoverian rule, the Jacobite risings and the loss of the American colonies.

19th Century (Scotland, AD 1801–AD 1900).label: 19th Century
19th Century (Scotland, AD 1801–AD 1900).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1801–AD 1900] 19th Century. Century encompassing years 1801 CE to 1900 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Steam, iron and coal turned England into the world's first industrial society: railways spread across the country from the 1830s, factory towns swelled, and by mid-century most people lived in urban places. Reform came in fits and starts, through the Reform Acts, factory and public health legislation, and the growth of trade unions, alongside grinding poverty, cholera and the workhouse. Britain's empire and global trade reached their greatest extent, and mass-produced goods, from transfer-printed china to bottled patent medicines, fill archaeological deposits of the period.

20th Century (Scotland, AD 1901–AD 2000).label: 20th Century
20th Century (Scotland, AD 1901–AD 2000).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1901–AD 2000] 20th Century. Century encompassing years 1901 CE to 2000 CE. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Two world wars drained the country's wealth and manpower, and the empire that had underwritten its power was dismantled within two decades of 1945. Out of the wars came the welfare state and the National Health Service; out of decolonisation came migration from the Caribbean and South Asia that remade Britain's cities. Heavy industry and coal collapsed, seaside and mill towns emptied, and the country reinvented itself around finance, services and pop culture.

Robert III (Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406).label: Robert III
Robert III (Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406] Robert III. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Lamed by a horse-kick and reckoned unfit to rule, he left government largely to his brother and other kinsmen while the kingdom slid towards factional violence; his heir David died in suspicious captivity at Falkland. His surviving son James was captured by the English at sea in 1406, news that reportedly killed the king and left Scotland under regents for eighteen years.

James I (Scotland, AD 1406–AD 1437).label: James I
James I (Scotland, AD 1406–AD 1437).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1406–AD 1437] James I. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Held prisoner in England for eighteen years, he came home determined to make royal authority felt, executing rival kinsmen, seizing earldoms and pushing a flood of legislation through parliament. He reorganised royal finances and taxation and imported English administrative habits, alienating the nobility in the process. A conspiracy of aggrieved nobles murdered him in a Perth friary; he is also credited with the poem 'The Kingis Quair'.

James II (Scotland, AD 1437–AD 1460).label: James II
James II (Scotland, AD 1437–AD 1460).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1437–AD 1460] James II. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

He took power in his own right after a childhood dominated by feuding magnates, then broke the overmighty Black Douglases, stabbing the eighth earl himself at Stirling and annexing their lands. Fascinated by artillery, he besieged English-held Roxburgh Castle in 1460 and was killed when one of his own great guns burst beside him. He was twenty-nine, and Scotland was left once more with a boy king.

James III (Scotland, AD 1460–AD 1488).label: James III
James III (Scotland, AD 1460–AD 1488).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1460–AD 1488] James III. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

An unmilitary and unpopular king who preferred artists, musicians and low-born favourites to his nobles, and who tried unsuccessfully to make peace and alliance with England. His one great gain came by marriage: Orkney and Shetland were pledged for his Danish bride's dowry and never redeemed, completing Scotland's modern shape. Rebel lords, fighting in the name of his own son, defeated and killed him at Sauchieburn.

James IV (Scotland, AD 1488–AD 1513).label: James IV
James IV (Scotland, AD 1488–AD 1513).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1488–AD 1513] James IV. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

A confident Renaissance monarch who brought the Lordship of the Isles firmly under crown control, patronised poets and scholars, licensed Scotland's first printing press, and built the enormous warship Great Michael. His marriage to Margaret Tudor in 1503 sealed a treaty of perpetual peace with England — and eventually gave his descendants the English throne. The peace did not hold: he invaded England in support of France and died with much of his nobility at Flodden.

James V (Scotland, AD 1513–AD 1542).label: James V
James V (Scotland, AD 1513–AD 1542).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1513–AD 1542] James V. King of the House of Stewart. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Came to the throne as an infant after Flodden and spent his youth as a pawn of rival noble factions before seizing control in his own right. He squeezed money from the church and the nobility to fund lavish Renaissance building at Stirling and Falkland, established the College of Justice, and married twice into French royalty, keeping Scotland tied to France against Henry VIII. His death days after the rout at Solway Moss left the week-old Mary, Queen of Scots, on the throne.

James VI (Scotland, AD 1567–AD 1625).label: James VI
James VI (Scotland, AD 1567–AD 1625).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1567–AD 1625] James VI. King of the House of Stewart. Also James I of England. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

King from infancy after his mother's forced abdication, he outlasted a series of regents to become a shrewd, bookish ruler who wrote on kingship, witchcraft and the evils of tobacco, and asserted royal authority over a fractious kirk and nobility. In 1603 he inherited the English throne and moved south, joining the two crowns in one person. His reign gave the world the King James Bible and the plantation of Ulster, with consequences still visible today.

Late Roman Iron Age (Scotland, AD 69–AD.label: Late Roman Iron Age
Late Roman Iron Age (Scotland, AD 69–AD.prose:
[Scotland, AD 69–AD 300] Late Roman Iron Age. Synonymous with Middle Iron Age. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Roman armies campaigned repeatedly into the north, building marching camps, the Antonine Wall and forts along the Highland fringe, but never held the territory for long. Native communities went on living in brochs, duns, roundhouses and souterrains, taking in Roman glass, pottery and silver through trade, tribute and raiding. The pressure of this frontier helped weld local groups into the larger confederations – later called Picts – that Rome faced by the fourth century.

Mary (Scotland, AD 1542–AD 1567).label: Mary
Mary (Scotland, AD 1542–AD 1567).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1542–AD 1567] Mary. Queen of the House of Stewart. Known as Mary, Queen of Scots. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Queen from six days old, she was sent to France as a child and returned a Catholic widow to a country that had just turned Protestant. Her marriages to Darnley and then to Bothwell, and Darnley's murder, wrecked her authority; the nobles deposed her and she fled to England, where Elizabeth held her prisoner for nineteen years before executing her. Her infant son became James VI, and eventually king of England too.

Modern (Scotland, AD 1901–AD 2100).label: Modern
Modern (Scotland, AD 1901–AD 2100).prose:
[Scotland, AD 1901–AD 2100] Modern. Non-preferred term for monuments and objects from the start of the 20th century to the present. Use the specific century. Period definition from Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA) — Historic Environment Scotland, 2018.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

Presencia Inca (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 15.label: Presencia Inca
Presencia Inca (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 15.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1536] Presencia Inca. Period definition from Arqueología del Valle de Uspallata. Provincia de Mendoza (sinopsis preliminar). — Schobinger Juan , 1971.

Cuzco's armies pushed the southern edge of Tawantinsuyu into the Andean valleys and puna of northwest Argentina, the far end of Qollasuyu. Roads, waystations, storehouses and high-altitude mountaintop shrines were built, and local communities were reorganised for labour service and moved as colonists. Sixty years later Spanish forces arrived, and the imperial infrastructure became the framework for colonial conquest.
Presencia Inca (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 15.source: Arqueología del Valle de Uspallata. Provincia de Mendoza (sinopsis preliminar).

Época Colonial (Argentina, AD 1600–AD 17.label: Época Colonial
Época Colonial (Argentina, AD 1600–AD 17.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1600–AD 1768] Época Colonial. Period definition from Arqueología del Valle de Uspallata. Provincia de Mendoza (sinopsis preliminar). — Schobinger Juan , 1971.

Spanish settlement in the region ran on encomienda labour, cattle and mule breeding for the Andean silver economy, and the transport corridor from Buenos Aires to Potosí. Jesuit estates and missions were among the largest enterprises, and Córdoba's university made it a centre of learning; the order's expulsion in 1767 abruptly redistributed that wealth. Buenos Aires, restricted by Spanish trade monopoly, grew rich on contraband — a tension that would help drive later demands for free trade and independence.
Época Colonial (Argentina, AD 1600–AD 17.source: Arqueología del Valle de Uspallata. Provincia de Mendoza (sinopsis preliminar).

Período 8 (Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1900).prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1900] Período 8. Period definition from Poblaciones indígenas de Malargüe: Su arqueología e historia — Durán Víctor, 2004.

Cazadores-Recolectores Tardíos (Argentin.label: Cazadores-Recolectores Tardíos
Cazadores-Recolectores Tardíos (Argentin.prose: [San Juan, Argentina, 5899 BC–2199 BC] Cazadores-Recolectores Tardíos. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Agrícola Incipiente (Argentina, 1799 BC–.label: Agrícola Incipiente
Agrícola Incipiente (Argentina, 1799 BC–.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, 1799 BC–AD 50] Agrícola Incipiente. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Groups still living largely by hunting guanaco and gathering wild plants began tending crops and keeping the first domesticated llamas, moving between seasonal camps and increasingly permanent dwellings. Early pottery, grinding stones and storage features mark the slow shift from foraging to food production. It is a long transitional stretch rather than a sudden revolution, and its uneven pace varied from valley to valley.

Agropecuario Temprano (Argentina, AD 50–.label: Agropecuario Temprano
Agropecuario Temprano (Argentina, AD 50–.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 50–AD 750] Agropecuario Temprano. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Communities that had long combined hunting with small-scale planting settled into permanent villages built around maize, quinoa and beans and herds of llamas. Pottery, ground-stone hoes, storage pits and rectangular house compounds appear together, along with the first metalwork in copper. The economic foundations laid here — irrigation, herding and stored surplus — supported every later society in the Andean northwest.

Agropecuario Medio (Argentina, AD 750–AD.label: Agropecuario Medio
Agropecuario Medio (Argentina, AD 750–AD.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 750–AD 1050] Agropecuario Medio. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Village agriculture and llama herding were now the backbone of life, supported by irrigation canals and terraced fields, with surpluses stored and exchanged. Craft production in ceramics and copper alloys became more skilled and more standardised, and burial goods start to show clear differences in rank. This is the horizon on which the Aguada style and its feline-and-sacrificer imagery spread across the northwest.

Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina, AD 1200–.label: Agropecuario Tardío
Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina, AD 1200–.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1490] Agropecuario Tardío. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Populations concentrated in large agricultural settlements, often walled or set on ridges, farming terraced slopes and herding llamas between valley and puna. Distinctive painted funerary urns, bronze axes and plaques, and dense clusters of house compounds characterise the regional groups of these centuries. The period closes with Inca annexation, which reorganised labour, roads and storage across the whole region.

Conquista Incaica (Argentina, AD 1490–AD.label: Conquista Incaica
Conquista Incaica (Argentina, AD 1490–AD.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 1490–AD 1530] Conquista Incaica. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Inca armies pushed south from Cuzco into the northwest valleys and as far as central Chile, absorbing local chiefdoms into the province of Collasuyu. They built roads, way-stations and administrative centres, moved populations as colonists, worked mines, and left high-altitude mountaintop shrines including child sacrifices preserved by the cold. The system was barely a few decades old when the Spanish arrived.

Indígena Local (Argentina, AD 1530–AD 15.label: Indígena Local
Indígena Local (Argentina, AD 1530–AD 15.prose: [San Juan, Argentina, AD 1530–AD 1562] Indígena Local. Period definition from Prehistoria de San Juan — Gambier Mariano, 2000.

Ayampitín (Argentina, 5999 BC–499 BC).label: Ayampitín
Ayampitín (Argentina, 5999 BC–499 BC).prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, 5999 BC–499 BC] Ayampitín. Period definition from Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan. — Nardi Ricardo L. J., 1966-1967.

Named for a lanceolate, willow-leaf spearpoint found across the sierras of central Argentina and beyond, this tradition belongs to mobile bands hunting guanaco and deer and grinding wild plant foods. Rock shelters like Intihuasi in San Luis, excavated in the 1950s, provided the stratigraphy and radiocarbon dates that made it a benchmark for early South American prehistory.
