Calingasta (Argentina, AD 1–AD 700).label: Calingasta
Calingasta (Argentina, AD 1–AD 700).prose: [San Juan, Argentina, AD 1–AD 700] Calingasta. Period definition from Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan. — Nardi Ricardo L. J., 1966-1967.
Calingasta (Argentina, AD 1–AD 700).source: Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan.

Aguada (Argentina, AD 700–AD 900).label: Aguada
Aguada (Argentina, AD 700–AD 900).prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 700–AD 900] Aguada. Period definition from Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan. — Nardi Ricardo L. J., 1966-1967.

A distinctive art style spread through the valleys of Catamarca and La Rioja, best known from grey incised and polychrome ceramics covered with felines, masked warriors and figures holding severed heads. Bronze plaques and axes, elaborate snuff trays for hallucinogens, and rich burials point to ritual specialists and emerging elites within farming and herding communities. The imagery links the Argentine northwest to the wider Andean religious world of the same centuries.
Aguada (Argentina, AD 700–AD 900).source: Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan.

Inca (Argentina, AD 1473–AD 1551).label: Inca
Inca (Argentina, AD 1473–AD 1551).prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 1473–AD 1551] Inca. Period definition from Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan. — Nardi Ricardo L. J., 1966-1967.

Tawantinsuyu was the largest state the Americas ever produced, run without money or writing through labour tribute, storehouses, knotted-cord khipu records and thousands of kilometres of paved road. Pizarro's capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca broke the imperial centre, and Spanish rule, epidemic disease and resettlement into reducciones transformed Andean life within a couple of generations - though the neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba held out for decades and Inca stonework still underpins Cusco.
Inca (Argentina, AD 1473–AD 1551).source: Contribuciones a la arqueología de San Juan.

Momentos Prehispánicos Tardíos (Argentin.label: Momentos Prehispánicos Tardíos
Momentos Prehispánicos Tardíos (Argentin.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1460] Momentos Prehispánicos Tardíos. Period definition from Tumbas y textiles preincaicos en una zona andina meridional. — Michieli Catalina Teresa, 2009.

In the last centuries before the Spanish arrival, northwestern Argentina was occupied by dense agricultural communities farming irrigated terraces and living in stone-walled villages, many of them hilltop strongholds. Regional pottery styles, metalwork and communal storage point to competing local chiefdoms and recurrent conflict. From the later fifteenth century the Inca incorporated much of the region, building roads, waystations and administrative centres over the existing settlements.

Angualasto (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480).label: Angualasto
Angualasto (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480).prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Angualasto. Period definition from Consideraciones sobre el primer fechado de C¹⁴ y la secuencia arqueológica de la provincia de San Juan. — González Alberto Rex, 1967.

Farming communities in the dry Andean valleys of northwestern San Juan, living in small settlements supported by irrigated fields and herding, and known archaeologically for a distinctive painted pottery style. Their territory was drawn into the Inca empire in the late fifteenth century, when imperial roads and installations reached the region.

Período Aguada Local (Argentina, AD 650–.label: Período Aguada Local
Período Aguada Local (Argentina, AD 650–.prose:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 650–AD 1100] Período Aguada Local. Period definition from Reconstruyendo el arte rupestre del tramo precordillerano del río San Juan. — García Alejandro, 2017.

The Aguada tradition dominated the valleys of Catamarca and La Rioja, known for lustrous black pottery incised with felines, masked figures and sacrificial scenes, and for skilled copper and bronze casting. Its imagery, tied to jaguar symbolism and psychoactive snuff paraphernalia, suggests ritual specialists who held real authority; trophy heads and weapons hint that violence was part of that power. Local variants show communities adapting the shared style to their own valleys before the tradition dissolved into the regional cultures that followed.
Período Aguada Local (Argentina, AD 650–.source: Reconstruyendo el arte rupestre del tramo precordillerano del río San Juan.

Bloque Temporal Tardío (Argentina, 50 BC.prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, 50 BC–AD 950] Bloque Temporal Tardío. Period definition from Organización tecnológica y biogeografía humana en La Payunia, sur de la provincia de Mendoza. — Salgán Laura, 2012.

Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional (Ar.label: Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional
Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional (Ar.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1650] Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional. Period definition from "No tan simples": Pesca y horticultura entre grupos originarios del Norte de Mendoza. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2013.

The final centuries of independent valley societies, marked by nucleated settlements, defensive locations and strongly regional ceramic styles. Populations here experienced Inca conquest and then the Spanish invasion within a few generations, and their sites often contain the debris of both. Indigenous life continued at these places until the mid-seventeenth-century deportations emptied them.
Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional (Ar.source: "No tan simples": Pesca y horticultura entre grupos originarios del Norte de Mendoza.

Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1301–.label: Prehispánico Tardío
Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1301–.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1301–AD 1500] Prehispánico Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

Densely populated valleys of the northwest supported farming communities that terraced hillsides, irrigated fields and built stone villages, some perched on defensible ridges as pukaras. Painted urns of the Santa María style, used to bury children beneath house floors, are the signature artefacts. Warfare and competition among these polities were cut short by Inca conquest and then by Spanish arrival.
Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1301–.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1501–AD.label: Colonial Temprano
Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1501–AD.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1501–AD 1601] Colonial Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

Spanish expeditions pushed in from Peru and Chile, founding towns like Santiago del Estero, Mendoza and Córdoba and imposing the encomienda on indigenous communities. Native populations collapsed under warfare, forced labour and epidemic disease, though groups in the Calchaquí valleys and the southern plains resisted for generations. European livestock and metal goods spread far beyond the reach of actual Spanish settlement.
Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1501–AD.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

Colonial Medio (Argentina, AD 1601–AD 17.label: Colonial Medio
Colonial Medio (Argentina, AD 1601–AD 17.prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1601–AD 1701] Colonial Medio. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.
Colonial Medio (Argentina, AD 1601–AD 17.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1.label: Colonial Tardío
Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1800] Colonial Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

Bourbon reforms reorganised Spanish administration, and the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776 turned Buenos Aires from a smuggling outpost into a legal port of empire. Cattle hides, mules and silver routed from Potosí drove the economy, while Jesuit expulsion in 1767 broke up the mission system. Creole grievances built here toward the revolutions that followed.
Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

Republicano (Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861).label: Republicano
Republicano (Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861).prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861] Republicano. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

The decades after Argentina broke with Spain, when the question was not independence but what kind of country would follow. Buenos Aires and the interior provinces fought a long series of civil wars between centralists and federalists, dominated for two decades by the caudillo Juan Manuel de Rosas, and settled only after Rosas fell and the province of Buenos Aires was reconciled with the Confederation. Out of this came the constitutional framework and territorial shape of the modern Argentine state.
Republicano (Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861).source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 135.label: Alfarero Medio
Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 135.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1350] Alfarero Medio. Period definition from Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina). — Ots María José, 2020.

The centuries when farming villages in the Argentine northwest became fully settled and hierarchical, relying on irrigated maize, llama herding and long-distance exchange across the Andes. This is the era of Ciénaga and Aguada pottery, with its dense feline and shamanic imagery, and of the first substantial stone-built settlements in the valleys of Catamarca and La Rioja.
Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 135.source: Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina).

Tardío-Incaico (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 15.label: Tardío-Incaico
Tardío-Incaico (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 15.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1550] Tardío-Incaico. Period definition from Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina). — Ots María José, 2020.

The last pre-Hispanic phase in northwest Argentina, joining the era of local valley chiefdoms with their conquest by the Inca, who made the region the far southern edge of Collasuyu. Inca roads, storehouses, high-altitude shrines and administrative centres were grafted onto existing towns, and the arrangement lasted barely a lifetime before Spanish expeditions arrived.
Tardío-Incaico (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 15.source: Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina).

Período Colonial (Argentina, AD 1551–AD.label: Período Colonial
Período Colonial (Argentina, AD 1551–AD.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1700] Período Colonial. Period definition from Articulaciones del Corredor Trasandino Meridional: El río Tunuyán en el Valle de Uco Mendoza, Argentina. — Ots María José, 2015.

Spanish towns, encomiendas and Catholic missions were imposed on indigenous societies, with native labour drafted for farming, textile workshops and the mule trade supplying the silver mines of Potosí. Epidemics, warfare and forced relocations dismantled the old valley communities, while African slavery and mixed-descent populations reshaped who lived where. Colonial-era sites often show indigenous cooking pots sitting alongside Spanish majolica and iron.
Período Colonial (Argentina, AD 1551–AD.source: Articulaciones del Corredor Trasandino Meridional: El río Tunuyán en el Valle de Uco Mendoza, Argentina.

Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media (Arge.label: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media
Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media (Arge.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 401–AD 1400] Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media. Period definition from Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2013.

The long middle stretch of village farming life in the Argentine Northwest, when maize and quinoa agriculture, llama herding and pottery-making supported permanent settlements in the valleys and puna. Craftwork became strikingly ambitious: bronze and copper metallurgy, elaborate painted and engraved ceramics, and the feline and warrior imagery associated with the Aguada tradition. Communities grew larger and more differentiated, setting the stage for the fortified chiefdoms of later centuries.
Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media (Arge.source: Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza).

Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía (Arg.label: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía
Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía (Arg.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1401–AD 1700] Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía. Period definition from Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2013.

The final centuries of indigenous village society in the Argentine Northwest, when dense settlements clustered on defensible hilltops and irrigated terraces climbed the valley slopes. Local chiefdoms with distinctive painted urn styles were absorbed into the Inca empire in the later 1400s, then confronted by Spanish colonists, whose arrival brought decades of resistance in the Calchaquí valleys.
Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía (Arg.source: Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza).

Precerámico (Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC).label: Precerámico
Precerámico (Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC).prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC] Precerámico. Period definition from Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2005.

A catch-all label for communities that had not yet taken up pottery, known instead from stone tools, grinding equipment, hearths and burials. Hunting, foraging and, in some regions, early herding and small-scale cultivation supported these groups, and their camps and rockshelters — some with painted walls — are the main evidence of the deep human past across Argentina.
Precerámico (Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC).source: Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza).

Agroalfarero Tardío Local (Argentina, AD.label: Agroalfarero Tardío Local
Agroalfarero Tardío Local (Argentina, AD.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1201–AD 1700] Agroalfarero Tardío Local. Period definition from Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2005.

Farming and llama-herding communities in the Andean northwest consolidated into large, densely packed settlements, many perched on defensible hilltops behind walls, a sign of chronic conflict over land and water. Painted urns and bowls, metalwork in bronze, and irrigated terraces mark the local chiefdoms of these centuries. Their independence ended in stages, first under Inca provincial rule and then under Spanish encomienda and forced resettlement.
Agroalfarero Tardío Local (Argentina, AD.source: Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza).

Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local (Argen.label: Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local
Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local (Argen.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 501–AD 1200] Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local. Period definition from Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2005.

Settled villages of farmers and camelid herders produced their own pottery and worked copper and bronze, living in scattered residential compounds beside irrigated fields. Long-distance exchange moved obsidian, shell, metal and hallucinogenic snuffs across the Andes, tying local groups into wider networks. The elaborate iconography of the period — felines, masked figures, trophy heads — shows a shared religious language spreading well beyond any one valley.
Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local (Argen.source: Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza).

Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 25.label: Período Alfarero Temprano
Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 25.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 250 BC–AD 450] Período Alfarero Temprano. Period definition from Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.  — Carosio Sebastián, 2020.

Farming hamlets appear with pottery, stone hoes, grinding equipment and pens for llamas, set among field walls and irrigation channels. Households were largely self-sufficient but exchanged obsidian, shell, metal and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia over long distances, laying the agricultural and technological groundwork for the crowded towns of later centuries.
Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 25.source: Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.

Período Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 45.label: Período Alfarero Medio
Período Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 45.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1500] Período Alfarero Medio. Period definition from Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.  — Carosio Sebastián, 2020.

The centuries when village societies in the northwest grew denser, more hierarchical and more artistically ambitious. This is the era associated with La Aguada imagery — jaguar-faced figures, sacrificed and trophy heads, finely burnished black ceramics and cast bronze — followed by the breakup of that tradition into regional chiefdoms with their own valley identities.
Período Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 45.source: Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.

Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.label: Período Alfarero Tardío
Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1450–AD 1600] Período Alfarero Tardío. Period definition from Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.  — Carosio Sebastián, 2020.

Communities consolidated into large agglomerated towns of stone-walled rooms, often perched on defensible spurs above terraced fields, with cemeteries of urns holding infant burials. Painted Santa María and Belén jars, metalwork and evidence of raiding point to competition between valley polities, which were later drawn into the Inca road system and then shattered by the Spanish invasion and the Calchaquí wars.
Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.source: Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.

Expansión Inkaica (Argentina, AD 1480–AD.label: Expansión Inkaica
Expansión Inkaica (Argentina, AD 1480–AD.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533] Expansión Inkaica. Period definition from La presencia inka en el extremo suroriental del Kollasuyo. Investigaciones en las tierras bajas de Mendoza y San Juan y el Valle de Uco -Rca. Argentina-. — Cahiza Pablo Andrés, 2002.

The Inca state pushed south into the valleys of northwest Argentina, absorbing local chiefdoms into the province of Collasuyu. Roads, waystations, storehouses and administrative centres were laid out, high mountain summits received capacocha sacrifices, and populations were resettled as mitmaqkuna to work fields and mines. The whole arrangement lasted barely two generations before Spanish conquest dismantled it.
Expansión Inkaica (Argentina, AD 1480–AD.source: La presencia inka en el extremo suroriental del Kollasuyo. Investigaciones en las tierras bajas de Mendoza y San Juan y el Valle de Uco -Rca. Argentina-.

Dominación Inka (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1.label: Dominación Inka
Dominación Inka (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533] Dominación Inka. Period definition from Ictioarqueología de las Lagunas de Guanacache (Mendoza, Argentina). Identificación y estacionalidad de captura a partir de análisis de otolitos sagitales. — Cahiza Pablo Andrés, 2003.

The southernmost expansion of the Inca empire, reaching the Andean valleys and the edge of the Cuyo region as part of Collasuyu. Roads, storehouses and garrison-like installations tied scattered local chiefdoms into a tribute system, and metalworkers and farmers were relocated to serve state projects. High-altitude mountain shrines, including capacocha burials on peaks above 6,000 metres, mark the frontier of imperial ritual. Spanish conquest cut the system short within two generations.
Dominación Inka (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1.source: Ictioarqueología de las Lagunas de Guanacache (Mendoza, Argentina). Identificación y estacionalidad de captura a partir de análisis de otolitos sagitales.

Período Incaico (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1.label: Período Incaico
Período Incaico (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1533] Período Incaico. Period definition from Sinopsis de investigaciones arqueológicas en el N.O. de la Provincia de Mendoza: Secuencias estratigráficas y cronología absoluta. — Bárcena Joaquín Roberto, 1982.

Under Inca rule the valleys and puna were tied into an imperial network of highways, waystations, farmland and metal production feeding Cuzco. Local Diaguita, Omaguaca and other groups kept their own pottery styles but adopted imperial forms, and some populations were resettled outright. The period closes with the collapse of Inca authority as the Spanish advanced from Peru.
Período Incaico (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1.source: Sinopsis de investigaciones arqueológicas en el N.O. de la Provincia de Mendoza: Secuencias estratigráficas y cronología absoluta.

Período Precerámico (Argentina, 5999 BC–.label: Período Precerámico
Período Precerámico (Argentina, 5999 BC–.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 5999 BC–AD 1] Período Precerámico. Period definition from Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza. — Bárcena Joaquín Roberto, 1974.

Millennia of hunting and gathering before pottery, from the first peopling of the region through Holocene camelid hunters using caves, rockshelters and open camps. Stone projectile points, grinding tools and vivid rock art record shifting prey and expanding social networks. Towards its end, the taming of llamas and cultivation of highland crops began the slow move to settled village life.
Período Precerámico (Argentina, 5999 BC–.source: Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza.

Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD 1–AD 153.label: Período Cerámico
Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD 1–AD 153.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1–AD 1536] Período Cerámico. Period definition from Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza. — Bárcena Joaquín Roberto, 1974.

Defined by the appearance and spread of fired clay vessels, which accompanied settled farming villages, storage of maize and beans, and camelid herding. Pottery styles, burial urns and metal ornaments allow archaeologists to trace regional traditions right up to the Spanish conquest.
Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD 1–AD 153.source: Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza.

Período A (Argentina, AD 150–AD 550).prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 150–AD 550] Período A. Period definition from El aprovechamiento de camélidos y ambientes de altura en sociedades agropastoriles prehispánicas del noroeste de Mendoza (Argentina). — Durán Víctor, 2020.

Período B (Argentina, AD 550–AD 750).prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 550–AD 750] Período B. Period definition from El aprovechamiento de camélidos y ambientes de altura en sociedades agropastoriles prehispánicas del noroeste de Mendoza (Argentina). — Durán Víctor, 2020.

Período C (Argentina, AD 1050–AD 1350).prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1050–AD 1350] Período C. Period definition from El aprovechamiento de camélidos y ambientes de altura en sociedades agropastoriles prehispánicas del noroeste de Mendoza (Argentina). — Durán Víctor, 2020.
Período C (Argentina, AD 1050–AD 1350).source: El aprovechamiento de camélidos y ambientes de altura en sociedades agropastoriles prehispánicas del noroeste de Mendoza (Argentina).

Período D (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1520).label: Período D
Período D (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1520).prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1520] Período D. Period definition from El aprovechamiento de camélidos y ambientes de altura en sociedades agropastoriles prehispánicas del noroeste de Mendoza (Argentina). — Durán Víctor, 2020.
Período D (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1520).source: El aprovechamiento de camélidos y ambientes de altura en sociedades agropastoriles prehispánicas del noroeste de Mendoza (Argentina).

Período Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina,.label: Período Agropecuario Tardío
Período Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina,.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1480] Período Agropecuario Tardío. Period definition from Barrio Ramos I: prácticas funerarias en el inicio del período de dominación inca del valle de Uspallata (Mendoza, Argentina). — Durán Víctor, 2018.

Farming and herding communities in the northwest lived in large agglomerated stone settlements, often perched on defensible high ground above terraced and irrigated fields. Regional ceramic styles, extensive bronze metallurgy and burials in painted urns mark the period, along with signs of frequent conflict between neighbouring valley groups. It closes with Inca expansion into the region.
Período Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina,.source: Barrio Ramos I: prácticas funerarias en el inicio del período de dominación inca del valle de Uspallata (Mendoza, Argentina).

Período de Dominación Incaica (Argentina.label: Período de Dominación Incaica
Período de Dominación Incaica (Argentina.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1532] Período de Dominación Incaica. Period definition from Estudios Arqueológicos sobre sus ocupantes prehispánicos. — Durán Víctor, 2011.

The southern reach of Tawantinsuyu, administered through the road system, provincial centres and the resettlement of labourers far from their homelands. The Inca were drawn by metals - copper, silver, gold - and by the region's farmland, and left mountaintop sanctuaries at extraordinary altitudes. Their rule collapsed with the Spanish capture of Atahualpa, leaving local groups to face a new conqueror.
Período de Dominación Incaica (Argentina.source: Estudios Arqueológicos sobre sus ocupantes prehispánicos.

Período Agroalfarero Medio (Argentina, A.label: Período Agroalfarero Medio
Período Agroalfarero Medio (Argentina, A.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 750–AD 1050] Período Agroalfarero Medio. Period definition from Variabilidad alfarera y procesos ambientales en un sitio de límite cultural. Estilos tecnológicos de la cerámica del río Desaguadero (PA68) (Mendoza, centro-oeste argentino). — Prieto Olavarría Cristina, 2016.

Village farming societies in the northwest valleys grew denser and more hierarchical, with the Aguada tradition setting the tone: finely burnished black pottery incised with feline and dancing-warrior figures, bronze axes and plaques, and imagery hinting at shamanic ritual and hallucinogenic snuff use. Ceremonial precincts and the movement of goods across the Andes point to leaders who drew authority from ritual as much as farmland.

Período Agroalfarero (Argentina, AD 350–.label: Período Agroalfarero
Período Agroalfarero (Argentina, AD 350–.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 350–AD 1650] Período Agroalfarero. Period definition from Resultados preliminares del análisis petrográfico de la cerámica de los períodos agroalfarero medio y tardío del Norte de Mendoza. — Prieto Olavarría Cristina, 2015.

The long era in northwest Argentina when people lived in permanent villages, farmed maize, beans and squash, herded llamas and made pottery. Irrigation canals, terraced fields and stone-walled house compounds spread through the valleys, and copper, bronze and gold metallurgy developed alongside elaborate painted and incised ceramics. It ends with the Inca annexation of the region and the Spanish invasion that followed.
Período Agroalfarero (Argentina, AD 350–.source: Resultados preliminares del análisis petrográfico de la cerámica de los períodos agroalfarero medio y tardío del Norte de Mendoza.

Etapa Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 15.label: Etapa Hispano-Indígena
Etapa Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 15.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1850] Etapa Hispano-Indígena. Period definition from La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 2004.

The centuries after Spanish forces subdued the Northwest, when indigenous communities were resettled into reducciones, granted as encomiendas and drawn into the labour economy supplying Potosí. Native pottery and building traditions persisted alongside imported glazes, iron tools and Christian ritual, producing a distinctly hybrid material culture. Prolonged resistance in the Calchaquí valleys ended in mass deportations, permanently reshaping the region's population.
Etapa Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 15.source: La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel

Premapuche (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650).label: Premapuche
Premapuche (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650).prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650] Premapuche. Period definition from La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 2004.

The generations in northern Patagonia and the Pampas before Mapuche language and culture spread east of the Andes. Local hunting peoples were already being reshaped by two forces arriving from outside: the horse, which transformed mobility and warfare, and the pressure of Spanish colonial settlement to the north.
Premapuche (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650).source: La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel

Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche (Argentina,.label: Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche
Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche (Argentina,.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1850] Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche. Period definition from La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 2004.

Mapuche groups spread east of the Andes into the Argentine plains and northern Patagonia, absorbing or reshaping earlier local societies in the process known as araucanización. Horses transformed everything: mounted raiding, long-distance cattle droving to Chile, large chiefdoms and a frontier trade in silver, textiles and captives. Archaeological sites from this time mix traditional pottery and stone tools with European glass, metal and horse gear, and the era closed with the Argentine and Chilean military campaigns of the later nineteenth century.

Cultura Agrelo (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100.label: Cultura Agrelo
Cultura Agrelo (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100] Cultura Agrelo. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

Early farming and herding communities of the Mendoza valleys, identified by dark incised pottery and by pit dwellings and storage features. Their appearance marks the shift in the region from mobile foraging to settlements combining cultivation, camelid herding and continued hunting.
Cultura Agrelo (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100.source: Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante.

Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial (Argen.label: Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial
Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial (Argen.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 100–AD 700] Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

The first centuries of settled village life with pottery: modest clusters of circular houses, agricultural terracing, llama herds and burials accompanied by simple modelled and incised vessels. Exchange networks moving obsidian, metal and coastal shell were already in place, linking the valleys to the puna and the eastern lowlands.
Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial (Argen.source: Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante.

Perído Cerámico Medio (Argentina, AD 700.prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 700–AD 1000] Perído Cerámico Medio. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

Período Cerámico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.label: Período Cerámico Tardío
Período Cerámico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450] Período Cerámico Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

Dispersed hamlets gave way to dense, walled settlements on defensible ground, surrounded by terraces and irrigated fields. Painted urns, bronze axes and disc-shaped ornaments circulated widely, and the fortified layouts and weapon finds suggest chronic conflict between valley groups in the generations before Inca expansion.
Período Cerámico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.source: Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante.

Etapa Arcaica (Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 B.label: Etapa Arcaica
Etapa Arcaica (Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 B.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 BC] Etapa Arcaica. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Hunter-gatherer bands ranged across the puna, valleys and steppe, hunting guanaco and vicuña, gathering wild plants and camping repeatedly in rock shelters whose walls they sometimes painted. Over these millennia the tools grew more specialised and the first steps were taken towards herding camelids and tending useful plants. These slow shifts are what made the later farming villages possible.
Etapa Arcaica (Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 B.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Etapa de proto-productores (Argentina, 2.label: Etapa de proto-productores
Etapa de proto-productores (Argentina, 2.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 2050 BC–350 BC] Etapa de proto-productores. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

A long transitional stage in which people still hunted and gathered but increasingly tended plants and managed camelid herds, moving less and storing more. Rock shelters show repeated seasonal occupation, and the first cultivated species and evidence of domesticated llamas appear. It is the slow groundwork for the fully agricultural villages that followed.

Etapa de Productores de Alimentos (Argen.node: Etapa de Productores de Alimentos (Argentina, 300 BC–AD 250)
Etapa de Productores de Alimentos (Argen.label: Etapa de Productores de Alimentos
Etapa de Productores de Alimentos (Argen.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 300 BC–AD 250] Etapa de Productores de Alimentos. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The point at which food production, rather than hunting and gathering, became the basis of life: cultivated fields, stored harvests and herded camelids supporting settled communities. Pottery, weaving and permanent dwellings accompany the change, and populations grew denser than ever before.
Etapa de Productores de Alimentos (Argen.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Atuel II (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100).label: Atuel II
Atuel II (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100).prose: [Mendoza, Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100] Atuel II. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Etapa Agroalfarera (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1.label: Etapa Agroalfarera
Etapa Agroalfarera (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1–AD 1551] Etapa Agroalfarera. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The span in which farming and pottery-making defined life across much of what is now Argentina, from early village communities through to the Spanish conquest. Maize, beans and squash agriculture, llama caravans, weaving and metalwork underpinned settlements that grew from scattered hamlets into large, defended towns. It ends abruptly with European invasion, which cut short indigenous political development and reorganised the countryside around encomiendas and missions.
Etapa Agroalfarera (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Temprano (Argentina, AD 1–AD 650.label: Período Temprano
Período Temprano (Argentina, AD 1–AD 650.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1–AD 650] Período Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Farming villages became the normal way of life: people settled in one place, grew maize, beans and squash, herded llamas, made pottery and began working copper and gold. Small clusters of round or rectangular houses spread through the valleys, with grinding stones, carved stone menhirs and the first metal ornaments. The social groundwork for the later valley chiefdoms was laid here.
Período Temprano (Argentina, AD 1–AD 650.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Medio (Argentina, AD 650–AD 950).label: Período Medio
Período Medio (Argentina, AD 650–AD 950).prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 650–AD 950] Período Medio. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.
Período Medio (Argentina, AD 650–AD 950).source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Tardío (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 14.label: Período Tardío
Período Tardío (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 14.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450] Período Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.
Período Tardío (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 14.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Inca (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551.label: Período Inca
Período Inca (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551] Período Inca. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Cuzco's armies incorporated the Northwest into Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, roughly a lifetime before the Spanish arrived. Roads, tambos, storage complexes and administrative centres were built, local lords were co-opted, and mitmaqkuna colonists were moved in to work fields and mines. Cuzco-style polychrome pottery and bronze appear in local villages, and mountain summits were turned into shrines.
Período Inca (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista (Argent.label: Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista
Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista (Argent.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1875] Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The colonial and early national economy, when the Argentine interior was tied into long-distance trade: mules and textiles moving north to the mines, hides and later wool moving out through the Atlantic ports. Towns, haciendas, sugar mills and cart roads reorganised the landscape, and imported ceramics, glass and metal goods appear throughout archaeological deposits. It ends as railways and mass immigration transformed the country's economy again.
Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista (Argent.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD.label: Período Hispano-Indígena
Período Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650] Período Hispano-Indígena. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The generation after the Spanish arrival, when conquistadors, missionaries and encomenderos imposed themselves on the agricultural communities of the Andean Northwest. Native settlements continued to be lived in, but their rubbish now mixes local pottery with imported glaze, metal blades and European livestock. Epidemics, forced labour and repeated rebellion reshaped populations that the Inca had ruled only decades earlier.
Período Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.label: Período Colonial Tardío
Período Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1750] Período Colonial Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

A settled colonial order of estancias, obrajes and mission towns, tied into the long mule and cart routes that linked the Río de la Plata with Upper Peru. Indigenous survivors of earlier wars and resettlements lived as tributaries and labourers, and material culture becomes increasingly hybrid — local earthenware beside imported glazed wares, glass and metal tools.
Período Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Histórico Institucional Temprano.label: Período Histórico Institucional Temprano
Período Histórico Institucional Temprano.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1750–AD 1810] Período Histórico Institucional Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Late colonial decades reshaped by the Bourbon reforms and the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, which turned Buenos Aires into a legal port and drew the interior into wider Atlantic commerce. Jesuit expulsion emptied major mission complexes, while cattle ranching, mule trade and mining supply routes structured rural settlement. Excavated sites from these years are full of imported European tableware, clay pipes and bottle glass among locally made wares.
Período Histórico Institucional Temprano.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Período Histórico Institucional Tardío (.label: Período Histórico Institucional Tardío
Período Histórico Institucional Tardío (.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1810–AD 1875] Período Histórico Institucional Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The break with Spain, followed by decades of caudillo warfare between Buenos Aires and the interior provinces before a national state was consolidated. Old colonial towns, estancias and mission sites were rebuilt, abandoned or absorbed by new frontier forts and immigrant settlement. Material culture shifts sharply towards mass-produced British ceramics and glass arriving through expanding river and later rail trade.
Período Histórico Institucional Tardío (.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

The great age of Bronze Age palaces and empires: Hammurabi's Babylon, Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs, the Hittites in Anatolia, Mycenaean citadels in Greece and the Shang in the Yellow River valley, all linked by long-distance trade in copper, tin and luxury goods. Writing spread and simplified, with the first alphabets appearing among Semitic workers in the Levant. Around 1200 BC much of this network collapsed within a generation, destroying kingdoms and scripts and clearing space for the smaller iron-using societies that followed.

The Third Dynasty of Ur had collapsed, and its bureaucratic empire gave way to competing Amorite kingdoms at Isin, Larsa and elsewhere, with Sumerian surviving as a scholarly language. In Egypt the Twelfth Dynasty restored strong central rule, colonised Nubia and reorganised the provinces. The Indus cities were losing population and their script and seals fell out of use, while Anatolia became the destination for a booming Assyrian tin and textile trade.

Hammurabi turned Babylon from a modest kingdom into the dominant power of Mesopotamia, leaving a stone-cut law code that remains one of the most famous documents of the ancient world. In Egypt the central authority of the late Middle Kingdom weakened, and Levantine settlers in the Delta laid the groundwork for Hyksos rule. On Crete, the palaces destroyed a generation earlier were being rebuilt on a grander scale, opening the most brilliant phase of Minoan civilisation.

The high point of the Late Bronze Age, when Egypt, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon and Mitanni dealt with one another as rival great powers, exchanging gold, brides and complaints in Akkadian on clay tablets. Egypt saw Akhenaten's religious revolution and its rapid undoing under Tutankhamun; Mycenaean lords fortified their citadels in Greece and traded across the Aegean. Bronze, tin and prestige goods moved along routes stretching from Afghanistan to the Atlantic, a network whose fragility would show itself two centuries later.

Egypt was at its wealthiest, and Akhenaten used that wealth to abolish the old gods, promote the sun-disc Aten, and build a new capital in the desert - an experiment undone almost immediately after his death. The clay letters left there record kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Assyria and Hatti bargaining with pharaoh as equals over gold and marriage. Under Suppiluliuma the Hittites broke Mitanni and became the dominant power in Syria.

Clay letters from that capital preserve the diplomatic correspondence of a whole interconnected world of great kings. The Hittites under Suppiluliuma seized Syria, Assyria emerged as an independent power, and Mycenaean Greece reached its peak.

The peak and last confident phase of the Late Bronze Age world, when Egypt under Ramesses II, the Hittite empire, Assyria, Mycenaean Greece and the Levantine port cities were bound together by diplomacy, royal marriages and trade in copper, tin and luxury goods. Kadesh was fought and then settled by the first surviving international peace treaty. By the century's end fires, abandonments and vanished palace archives mark the beginning of the collapse that ended the whole system.

The great powers of the Bronze Age - Egypt, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon - operated as a connected diplomatic system, trading gold, copper and royal brides. Ramesses II and the Hittite king fought to a draw at Kadesh and then signed the earliest surviving international peace treaty, a copy of which hung in both capitals. Mycenaean Greece built its cyclopean citadels and shipped pottery across the Mediterranean, unaware how soon the whole network would fail.

The eastern Mediterranean's palace civilisations were at their most interconnected and most fragile: Ramesses II's long reign ended, the Hittite empire entered its final decades, and Merneptah's victory stele of 1207 gives the earliest mention of Israel. Mycenaean rulers fortified their citadels with cyclopean walls, a sign of growing insecurity. Within a couple of generations most of these palaces would burn, in the collapse that ended the Bronze Age.

The Bronze Age palace world came apart: Hittite Hattusa burned, Mycenaean citadels were destroyed and abandoned, Ugarit vanished, and Egypt fought off the coalitions it called the Sea Peoples before losing its Asian empire. Writing systems, long-distance trade in tin and the palace bureaucracies disappeared over much of the eastern Mediterranean. Out of the wreckage came smaller societies, the spread of iron working, and the Philistine, Aramaean, Phoenician and Israelite polities of the following centuries.

The Bronze Age world system collapsed. The Hittite empire vanished, Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces burned, trade in tin and copper broke down, and Egypt fought off the seaborne coalitions its scribes called the Sea Peoples before sliding into decline. Writing was lost in Greece for centuries. Out of the wreckage came smaller societies, the spread of iron working, and new peoples - Philistines, Israelites, Arameans - in the Levant.

The aftermath of the Bronze Age collapse: Egypt's New Kingdom slid into weakness after Ramesses III, the Hittite empire was gone, and Elamite armies sacked Babylon and carried off its monuments. Small kingdoms and city-states filled the vacuum, Phoenician ports took over long-distance trade, and iron gradually replaced bronze for tools and weapons. Greece entered its illiterate 'dark age', with populations scattered into small villages.

The world after the Bronze Age collapse: palace kingdoms had fallen, writing lapsed in Greece, and iron gradually replaced bronze for everyday tools. Phoenician cities took over Mediterranean seaborne trade and spread an alphabet that would become the ancestor of Greek and Latin letters. In China the Zhou overthrew the Shang and set up a feudal order justified by the Mandate of Heaven; in the Levant, small kingdoms including early Israel emerged in the space left by imperial retreat.

The great Bronze Age powers were gone: Egypt split under the Twenty-first Dynasty with priests ruling Thebes, Hittite Anatolia had vanished, and Assyria contracted to its core. Across the Aegean, writing and palaces had been abandoned for two centuries, though iron working was spreading and Greek speakers were settling the coast of Asia Minor. In the Levant small kingdoms and Phoenician trading cities filled the vacuum, and in China the newly established Zhou were parcelling out lands to their kin.

The Zhou overthrew the Shang in China and set up a system of feudal grants under a 'mandate of heaven' that would justify dynastic change for three thousand years. Egypt fragmented into the Third Intermediate Period, biblical tradition places Saul and David's kingdom in these decades, and Phoenician cities like Tyre grew rich on Mediterranean trade. Ironworking spread widely and Greek potters began the disciplined Protogeometric style.

It is the millennium of the Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, Roman and Han empires, and of the thinkers - the Hebrew prophets, the Buddha, Confucius, the Greek philosophers - whose ideas still structure the world's religions and politics. Coinage, the alphabet and monumental city life spread from the Mediterranean to China.

Small Iron Age kingdoms filled the space left by the collapse of the Bronze Age empires: Tyre and the Phoenician ports grew rich on trade, Aramaean states spread across Syria, and the biblical tradition places Solomon's reign and the split of Israel and Judah in these decades. In Egypt, Libyan-descended pharaohs founded the 22nd Dynasty at Tanis. Neither Assyria nor Egypt yet dominated the Levant, leaving room for these local powers.

Assyrian kings began the campaigns that would rebuild their state into the Near East's dominant military power. Egypt, fragmented under the Libyan pharaohs of the Twenty-Second Dynasty, briefly reasserted itself in the Levant with Shoshenq I's raid into Palestine. Phoenician cities were expanding their seaborne trade westward, and in Greece the Iron Age villages that produced Geometric pottery were slowly growing into the first city-states.

In the southern Levant this is the era assigned by tradition to Solomon and the split of the kingdom, and it remains the most fiercely debated stretch of biblical archaeology, with scholars arguing over whether monumental gates and palaces belong here or a century later. Pharaoh Shoshenq I campaigned through Palestine around 925 BC, leaving a list of captured towns at Karnak. Egypt itself was ruled by Libyan dynasts, and Assyria was beginning the recovery that would make it a superpower.

Solomon's kingdom split into rival Israelite states, and the Egyptian pharaoh Shoshenq I campaigned through the Levant, an event recorded both on temple walls at Karnak and in the Bible. Assyria began the slow military recovery that would make it the region's superpower, while Phoenician merchants from Tyre and Sidon pushed their trade westward across the Mediterranean. In China the Zhou kings still held nominal authority over their vassals.

The Assyrian kings pushed west with a professional army, siege engines and deliberate terror, building the first empire to dominate the whole Near East. Phoenician traders were founding colonies along the Mediterranean, carrying the alphabet with them, while Greek communities were re-emerging from their dark age with new settlements and long-distance contacts. In China the Western Zhou kings were losing grip on their vassals.

Assyria came roaring back under Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III, deporting populations, carving stone reliefs of siege and hunt across the palaces of Nimrud, and forcing the small kingdoms of Syria and the Levant into coalitions - the alliance that met Assyria at Qarqar included Ahab of Israel. Phoenician traders were pushing west toward Cyprus, Sardinia and North Africa. In Greece, still without writing, geometric pottery and the first sanctuaries mark communities beginning to knit back together.

In the Levant, Omri founded Samaria as the capital of Israel, and Phoenician merchants from Tyre and Sidon were spreading their alphabet and their trading posts westward. Greece was emerging from its long post-Mycenaean dark age.

Assyria under Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III turned conquest into a system, moving the capital to Kalhu (Nimrud) and driving campaigns west toward the Mediterranean; the coalition that met Shalmaneser at Qarqar in 853 BC included Ahab of Israel and Damascene and Arab contingents. In the Levant, the Omride dynasty built at Samaria and Phoenician merchants pushed further west across the sea. The tribute lists and carved palace reliefs of these decades are among the first detailed records of a Near Eastern empire at work.

Assyrian armies under Shalmaneser III campaigned annually into Syria and the Levant, extracting tribute and leaving the first outside references to Israelite kings. Phoenician traders were planting settlements across the Mediterranean, and tradition dates the founding of Carthage to 814 BC. In Greece, population and trade were recovering, the alphabet was being adopted from Phoenician script, and the poems that became the Iliad and Odyssey were taking shape.

Assyria under Shalmaneser III and his successors pressed repeatedly into Syria and the Levant, and rulers such as Jehu of Israel are shown on the Black Obelisk bowing with tribute. Small Aramaean and Israelite kingdoms rose and fell in the gaps between campaigns, while Phoenician merchants pushed further west across the Mediterranean toward Sardinia, Spain and North Africa. In the Aegean, communities were growing again after the long post-Mycenaean slump, with Geometric pottery and the first stirrings of overseas settlement.

Assyria turned inward after civil war, ruled for a time through the regency of the queen Shammuramat, remembered later in Greek legend as Semiramis. The mountain kingdom of Urartu grew strong in the Armenian highlands, and Damascus dominated Syria in Assyria's absence. Tradition places the founding of Carthage in these years, while Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet and began writing again.

A century of new beginnings across the Old World: the Neo-Assyrian empire under Tiglath-Pileser III built the first true standing army and deportation state, Greeks adopted the alphabet and began founding colonies from Sicily to the Black Sea, and Rome traced its own foundation to these decades. The Homeric epics took written form, the first Olympiad was later dated to 776 BC, and Kushite kings from Nubia took the Egyptian throne. In China the Zhou court fled east, beginning the long slide into rule by competing states.

Rome's traditional founding date falls here. Assyria's temporary weakness let Urartu and the Syrian states breathe, until Tiglath-Pileser III seized the throne and rebuilt the empire on a new professional footing.

Rome expelled its last king and became a republic, Athens overthrew its tyrants and adopted Cleisthenes' citizen assemblies, and the Ionian Greek cities rose in revolt against Persia, setting up the wars that followed. In India and China, the teachings attributed to the Buddha and to Confucius were beginning to circulate.

Sparta's brief dominance began, Persian gold decided Greek quarrels, and in China the Warring States were consolidating into a handful of rival kingdoms.

It was also the century of Plato's Academy and Aristotle's biology and logic, of Rome's mastery of central Italy, and of Chandragupta's founding of the Mauryan empire in India.

The precedent that a general could march on his own capital was set here, and Caesar would follow it.

Augustus rebuilt the state as a monarchy in republican dress, bringing peace, a standing army and a building programme that reshaped Rome and its provinces. Egypt became Roman, Herod ruled Judaea, and the Han Empire in China entered a period of court intrigue.

Endless deaths in the family made the succession an unsolved problem, and by tradition Jesus was born in these final years.

The high point of Roman prosperity broke: the Antonine plague swept the empire from the 160s, war on the Danube occupied Marcus Aurelius for years, and the reign of Commodus ended in murder and civil war. Trade linking Rome, India and Han China was at its height, and the first Roman embassy is recorded in Chinese sources. In China itself, court factionalism and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 began the collapse of the Han.

The Antonine plague had thinned populations and armies, and frontier pressure grew along the Danube. In China the Yellow Turban rebellion shattered Han authority and began the slide toward the Three Kingdoms.

Rome nearly came apart: emperors were made and killed by their armies, the currency collapsed, plague and invasion crossed the frontiers, and provinces from Gaul to Palmyra broke away before being reconquered. In the east a resurgent Persia under the Sasanians captured a Roman emperor alive, while in China the Han dynasty dissolved into the Three Kingdoms. Christianity grew fast enough to attract empire-wide persecution, and in Mesoamerica the Maya entered their Classic era of dated stelae and dynastic cities.

The Severan emperors extended Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire in 212, a landmark act that also broadened the tax base, but army mutinies were becoming the normal means of imperial succession. In Persia the Sasanians overthrew the Parthians in 224 and set up an aggressive, Zoroastrian state that would challenge Rome for four centuries. China's Han dynasty formally ended in 220, splitting into the Three Kingdoms whose wars became legend.

The Roman Empire was at its most settled and prosperous, ruled by Hadrian and then Antoninus Pius, with frontiers marked by walls in Britain and consolidated rather than expanded. In Alexandria Ptolemy wrote the astronomical and geographical works that would govern European and Islamic science for over a millennium, while the Kushan empire linked Rome, India and China along the Silk Roads.

The Roman world passed through its worst crisis: rapid turnover of soldier-emperors, breakaway Gallic and Palmyrene states, plague, debased coinage and invasions across the Rhine, Danube and eastern frontier. Aurelian reunited the empire, and Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy from 284 rebuilt it as a more bureaucratic, militarised state. In Iran the Sasanians were at their most aggressive, capturing the emperor Valerian himself.

The Roman empire nearly came apart: emperor Valerian was captured alive by the Persian king Shapur in 260, plague swept the provinces, and Gaul and Palmyra broke away under their own rulers. Aurelian reconquered both within five years and ringed Rome itself with new walls, an admission that the capital was no longer safe. Coinage debased, cities fortified, and the army became the real arbiter of power.

After fifty years of usurpers, invasions and debased coinage, Diocletian restored order by remaking the state: an emperor for each half of the empire plus junior colleagues, new provinces, a bigger army and a reformed tax system. Prices, mints and bureaucracy were all overhauled, and the imperial court became a remote, ceremonial thing. The same reforming energy would soon turn on the Christians in the last and fiercest persecution.

Constantinople was founded as a new capital, the Roman world split into eastern and western administrations, and Gothic and Hunnic pressure on the frontiers began the movements that would break the west apart. Constantine reunited the Roman Empire, legalised Christianity and founded a new capital on the Bosphorus, turning a persecuted sect into the religion of emperors; the Council of Nicaea tried to fix what Christians must believe. Diocletian's reforms had already remade the state into a bureaucratic, heavily taxed machine with mobile field armies. Elsewhere the Gupta dynasty began its rise in northern India, Shapur II built Sasanian power in Iran, and Axum's kings converted and struck their own coinage.

At Nicaea in 325 bishops from across the empire hammered out a creed, making Christian doctrine an imperial concern. Within a single generation a persecuted sect became the religion of the emperor.

Italy fell to the Lombards, the Sui reunified China after three centuries of division, and the Turkic khaganate emerged across the steppe.

The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, ending the Roman Empire in the East and pushing Europeans to seek sea routes around the Muslim world; Portuguese caravels rounded Africa and Columbus crossed the Atlantic. Printing with movable type spread from Mainz across Europe within a few decades, transforming how ideas travelled. In the same century Ming fleets swept the Indian Ocean before being recalled, and the Inca built the largest empire the Americas had seen.

Spanish and Portuguese ships joined the hemispheres into one trading world, and the Aztec and Inca empires fell to conquistadors and epidemic disease while American silver flooded into Europe and Asia. Luther's protest fractured Western Christianity into rival confessions that Catholic reform and religious war could not reunite. In the same span the Ottomans, Safavids, Mughals and Ming ruled the wealthiest and most populous states on earth.

A century of religious warfare and state-building: the Thirty Years' War devastated central Europe, England executed its king, the Ming dynasty fell to the Manchus, and the Ottoman advance stalled at Vienna's gates. European trading companies planted permanent footholds in the Americas, Africa and Asia, and the Atlantic slave trade expanded sharply to feed sugar plantations. Galileo, Kepler and Newton meanwhile remade the understanding of the physical universe.

Enlightenment thinkers argued that reason, not tradition or revelation, should govern politics and knowledge — and revolutions in America and France put the argument into practice, producing constitutions and declarations of rights. Qing China and Mughal India reached their greatest extent before the latter fragmented and European trading companies moved in. Atlantic slavery peaked, plantations reorganised the economies of three continents, and in Britain steam engines and mechanised spinning began the shift to industrial production.

Steam power, factories and railways spread outward from Britain, multiplying output and pulling millions into cities and across oceans as migrants. European states used industrial wealth and weapons to take control of most of Africa and much of Asia, while Atlantic slavery was dismantled and serfdom abolished in Russia. Germany and Italy became unified nations, world population surged, and telegraphs, photography and Darwin's theory changed how people understood distance, time and themselves.

The bloodiest century on record: two world wars, industrialised genocide, and nuclear weapons, followed by a half-century standoff between the United States and the Soviet Union. Europe's empires dissolved and dozens of new states emerged across Asia and Africa. At the same time antibiotics, vaccines, mechanised farming and electronics roughly quadrupled the human population and lengthened lives everywhere, while people first left the planet.

Néolithique (France, 6499 BC–2200 BC).prose:
[Parts of central continental western Europe, 6499 BC–2200 BC] Néolithique. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, England, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy. This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a general chronology from the Paleolithic to the present day, of a central-western part of continental Europe. It is based on the periodization set up by INRAP and PACTOLS.
The territory covered by this chronology extends from the eastern part of France in the west to Moldavia in the east, and from the south of the UK through southern Germany to Slovenia and central France on a north/south axis.

Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie générale du Paléolithique à nos jours, d'une partie centrale-occidentale de l'Europe continentale. Elle se fonde sur la périodisation mise en place par l'INRAP et PACTOLS.
Le territoire recouvert par cette chronologie s'étend de la partie orientale de la France, à l'ouest, jusqu'à la Moldavie à l'est, et du sud du Royaume-Uni en passant par l'Allemagne méridionale jusqu'à la Slovénie et le centre de la France sur un axe nord/sud. Herding of sheep, goats and cattle, together with pottery and cultivated grain, spread across the Moroccan coast, the Rif and the Atlas, taking hold among populations descended from earlier hunter-gatherers. Cardial-impressed pottery in the north points to contact across the Strait with Iberia, while cave sites and shell middens show a mixed economy of farming, herding, fishing and gathering. Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.

Farming communities across France moved beyond the tightly uniform longhouse villages of the first settlers into a patchwork of regional groups with their own pottery and burial customs. In the west, people began raising long earthen mounds and stone chambered tombs – among the earliest monumental architecture in Europe – while enclosures ringed by ditches and palisades appeared in the north and the Paris basin. Cattle herding, flint mining and long-distance movement of polished stone axes tied these communities together.

Farming communities across France grew denser and more organised, raising megalithic tombs and long stone alignments, digging flint mines, and building enclosures ringed by ditches and palisades. Pottery styles and burial customs became strongly regional, from the collective gallery graves of the Paris Basin to the passage tombs of Brittany. Toward the end, copper objects and the first Beaker pottery signal the shift into the metal ages.

In the Aegean this is the age of Europe's first literate, palace-based societies: Minoan Crete with its labyrinthine complexes, frescoes and Linear A script; the marble-figurine cultures of the Cyclades; and the Mycenaean citadels of the mainland with their shaft graves, gold masks and Linear B archives. Long-distance trade carried Aegean pottery and metalwork across the Mediterranean and brought in copper, tin and ivory. The collapse of the palaces around 1200 BC ended writing and centralised rule for centuries, but left the legends that Homer later drew on.

The first true tin bronze came into general use in France, made into flanged axes, triangular daggers and pins. Elite burials under mounds appear in Brittany and the Rhône valley, stocked with weapons, gold ornaments and amber that show long-distance contacts with Wessex and central Europe. Settlement remained dispersed, but control of metal and its trade routes was starting to create visible social ranks.

The opening stage of the French Bronze Age, when Bell Beaker traditions faded and copper-tin alloys became standard for axes and daggers. Metalwork is still simple and often deposited in hoards or in single graves under small mounds. The rich Armorican tumulus burials of Brittany begin in this stage, with daggers, arrowheads and occasional gold.

The mature Early Bronze Age, with more varied metalwork: flanged axes, ogival daggers, spiral ornaments and the distinctive pin types of the Rhône culture. Amber, gold and imported forms show exchange with Britain, the Alps and central Europe. Burial under barrows with weapon sets continues, marking out a warrior elite.

Tumulus burial with weapons and ornaments spread widely, and metalworkers turned out palstave axes, torcs, bracelets and the first long swords. Regional workshops in Brittany, the Rhône and the north each developed recognisable styles while sharing forms with central Europe and Britain. Deliberate deposition of metal in rivers and hoards became a regular practice.

The early Middle Bronze Age, when tumulus burial with bronze grave goods became widespread and palstave axes replaced older flanged forms. Ornament sets of pins, bracelets and torcs dominate the finds. Exchange with the central European Tumulus cultures is clear in shared types.

Metalwork grew more elaborate, with decorated palstaves, ribbed bracelets and the first true cut-and-thrust swords in France. Hoards and river deposits of weapons multiplied, suggesting ritual as well as economic motives. The period runs straight into the changes that brought urnfield cremation to the region.

Marqué par le début des grandes invasions, principalement celtiques, il se confond en Europe centrale avec la culture des champs d’urnes. Il commence en Europe occidentale comme en France vers le XIIe siècle av. J.-C. (Wikipédia). Cremation replaced inhumation across much of France as the Urnfield tradition spread from central Europe, leaving large cemeteries of ash-filled pots. Bronze production reached industrial levels, with sheet-metal vessels, leaf-shaped swords and enormous scrap hoards along the Atlantic and Rhône corridors. Hilltop sites were fortified, and by the closing generations the first iron objects appear, leading directly into the Hallstatt Iron Age.

The transition into the Late Bronze Age, when urn cremation burials began to spread west from the Danube. Rixheim-type swords and new pin and razor forms mark the change in metalwork. Older tumulus burial customs survive alongside the new rite in many regions.

Urnfield cemeteries became the dominant burial form over much of eastern and southern France, some holding hundreds of cremations. Bronzesmiths mastered sheet-metal work, producing beaten cups, shields and helmets, while leaf-shaped slashing swords became the standard weapon. Hoarding of scrap and finished bronze increased sharply.

The first stage of the developed Urnfield period in France, with large cremation cemeteries and grave goods of pins, knives and razors. Metalwork follows central European fashions closely, particularly along the Rhine and Rhône. Sheet bronze vessels begin to appear in elite deposits.

A phase of intensified bronze production and deposition, with distinctive pin and sword types and growing regional workshops. Hoards of broken metal suggest organised recycling and metal circulating almost as currency. Contacts along the Atlantic seaboard and across the Alps both strengthened.

The last stage of the French Bronze Age, dominated by the Rhin-Suisse-France orientale group in the east and Atlantic networks in the west. Bronze was abundant and often buried in vast hoards, including the carp's-tongue sword complex of the north-west. Fortified hilltop settlements multiplied, and the earliest iron objects arrived shortly before the Hallstatt Iron Age began.

Fine incised and channelled pottery of the Rhin-Suisse-France orientale style spread across eastern France, alongside a rich repertoire of bronze ornaments. Atlantic France exchanged sword and axe types with Britain and Iberia. Cremation in urnfields remained the standard burial rite.

The closing generations of the Bronze Age, marked by enormous hoards of socketed axes and broken metal, especially in Brittany and the north-west. Bronze had become so plentiful that much of it seems to have circulated as bullion rather than as tools. Iron begins to appear in small quantities, and the burial and settlement patterns shift toward those of the early Hallstatt world.

After the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, Greece rebuilt from small, scattered communities — the era once called the Dark Age. Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons, cremation burials and Protogeometric then Geometric pottery mark a new visual language, and by its end the alphabet had been adapted from Phoenician, the first monumental temples were rising, and the polis was taking shape. Population growth pushed Greeks overseas as colonists and traders, setting the stage for the Archaic world.

Iron becomes the ordinary metal for weapons and tools, and a new warrior display emerges: long iron slashing swords, and burials under mounds containing four-wheeled wagons and horse gear. Salt extraction at Hallstatt reached its height, and the goods buried in its miners' graves show trade reaching to the Mediterranean and the Baltic.

The later early Iron Age in eastern France, defined by changing brooch and weapon types in tumulus burials. Long iron swords give way gradually to daggers as the mark of rank, anticipating the wealthy princely graves of the following Hallstatt D phases.

The climax and collapse of Hallstatt society. Fortified "princely seats" like the Heuneburg, with its Mediterranean-style mudbrick wall, controlled trade in Greek wine, bronze vessels and coral, while nearby mounds held spectacular burials such as the woman of Vix with her huge Greek bronze krater. Long swords gave way to short daggers, and by the end of the phase the centres were abandoned and the La Tène style was taking shape.

Wealth concentrates at a handful of fortified hilltop centres in eastern France and southern Germany, supplied with wine and bronze vessels through Greek Massalia. Daggers replace long swords in male graves, and chariot and wagon burials under large mounds mark out an aristocracy.

The opening phase of the La Tène Iron Age, when a wealthy elite in the Rhine, Moselle and Marne regions buried its dead with two-wheeled chariots, gold neck-rings and imported Etruscan and Greek wine service. Out of contact with those Mediterranean imports came the Early Style of Celtic art, which took palmettes, lotus buds and lion masks and reworked them into the swirling, ambiguous designs seen on the Glauberg and Reinheim finds. The old Hallstatt hillfort centres further west collapsed at about this time, and power shifted north.

The earliest horizon of the La Tène world in France, best known from the chariot and warrior graves of Champagne, where long iron swords, coral-inlaid brooches and beaked flagons appear together. The phase of the great Celtic migrations, when war bands from the north moved into the Po valley, the middle Danube and the Balkans; the sack of Rome and the raid on Delphi belong to these generations. Large flat cemeteries of inhumations replace the earlier princely tumuli, with men buried with sword, spear and shield and women with brooches and rings. Metalworkers developed the Waldalgesheim or Vegetal Style, a flowing tendril ornament that spread across Europe with astonishing uniformity.

The high point of the Vegetal Style, whose scrolling plant ornament runs over scabbards, torcs and bracelets from Champagne to Hungary. Celtic groups were now settled in the Po valley and along the Danube, and mercenaries served in the armies of Hellenistic kings.

The middle La Tène, when the long slashing sword hung from an iron chain belt becomes the standard warrior's equipment and cremation begins to replace inhumation over much of the region. Large open settlements and craft centres grew, gold and silver coinage struck in imitation of Macedonian and Roman types came into use, and trade with the Mediterranean intensified. The decorated scabbards of this phase, in the so-called Sword Style, are among the finest Celtic metalwork.

A time of dense, well-organised settlement and of Celtic mercenary service across the Hellenistic world. Burials contain iron sword-belt chains, shield bosses and brooches with the foot clamped back onto the bow, and the first locally struck gold coins appear.

The final Iron Age phase, dominated by the oppida: huge walled towns with streets, workshops, mints and imported Roman wine. Political life sharpened into named tribes with magistrates and coinage, and the archaeological record ends with the Gallic Wars and the absorption of the region into the Roman world.

The generation before Caesar, when large fortified towns — oppida — dominated Gaul, minting coins, mass-producing wheel-thrown pottery and ironwork, and trading heavily in Italian wine. Amphora sherds and Roman republican coins pile up on native sites, marking the deep economic pull of the Mediterranean world well before any legion arrived. Archaeologists date this phase closely using brooch types and imported wine containers.

The final phase of independent Gallic material culture, spanning the Roman conquest and its immediate aftermath. Oppida were abandoned or reorganised, new Roman-style towns and road stations appeared, and Italian pottery, glass and coin standards spread rapidly through everyday assemblages. It is the archaeological seam where Gaul becomes Gallo-Roman.
