The decades of Caesar's campaigns, when Gallic oppida were besieged, burned or surrendered and coinage was struck in huge quantities to fund war. Sites such as Alesia and Gergovia preserve the debris of these years — sling bullets, ballista points, military fittings — alongside wholly native craft traditions still in full production.

The years after the conquest, when Gaul was reorganised under Roman administration. Old hillfort centres were run down in favour of new lowland towns, Roman weights, measures and coin denominations took hold, and Italian tableware became ordinary household equipment. Native brooch and pottery styles survive alongside them, giving the period its hybrid character.

Gaul spent five centuries as a set of Roman provinces, and the transformation was thorough: grid-planned cities with forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, a road network binding the Rhine frontier to the Mediterranean, villa estates exporting grain and wine, and Latin displacing Gaulish speech. Lyon, Arles, Nîmes and Trier became major imperial centres, and Christianity spread through them from the third century on. When central authority collapsed in the west, the bishops, estates and Latin language it left behind became the foundations of Frankish Gaul.

Augustus turned victory in civil war into a durable one-man rule dressed in republican forms, creating the Principate that governed Rome for the next three centuries. Peace at home paid for a rebuilt capital of marble, a professional standing army, new provinces to the Danube and Spain, and the poetry of Virgil, Horace and Ovid. The disaster in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 fixed the empire's northern limit and ended the dream of conquering Germany.

The closing years of Augustus's long reign, when the machinery of one-man rule was settling into routine and the Mediterranean world enjoyed a peace it had not known for a century. Deaths in the imperial family forced the ageing princeps to adopt Tiberius as heir, and the annihilation of three legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 halted expansion beyond the Rhine for good. Augustus's death in AD 14 tested whether the position he had invented could actually be inherited.

Haut-Empire (Roman Empire, AD 15–AD 235).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 15–AD 235] Haut-Empire. Il constitue, avec le Bas-Empire, une des deux découpes historiographiques de l'Empire romain telle que vue par les historiens français. Ces termes sont des concepts très usuels, mais leurs limites chronologiques respectives ne sont pas fixées de façon unanime. Elle désigne la première période de l’Empire romain, qui débute en 27 av. J.-C. avec le principat d'Auguste, et inclut le règne idéalisé des Antonins. (Wikipédia). The high point of the Principate, from the settled succession of Augustus's heirs through the Antonines and Severans. Frontiers were fixed on the Rhine, Danube and Euphrates, citizenship was gradually extended to the provinces until Caracalla granted it to nearly everyone, and a single currency and legal system let goods and people move from Britain to Syria. This is the Rome of monumental building, long-distance trade and provincial cities, before the political and military crises of the third century.

The Augustan settlement hardened into a hereditary monarchy under the Julio-Claudians, survived the bloody year of four emperors in 69, and continued under the Flavians. Britain was invaded, the Rhine and Danube frontiers were fortified, and Judaea rose in revolt and was crushed. For most inhabitants it meant peace, tax, Roman law and a building boom of forums, baths and theatres from Syria to Spain.

The Julio-Claudian emperors turned Augustus's improvised settlement into a working system: a professional standing army on fixed frontiers, salaried provincial governors, imperial cult temples in every town, and roads and aqueducts built to a common template. Provincial elites bought into Roman citizenship and Latin, and mass-produced goods like Gallic red-gloss tableware and Spanish oil amphorae moved across the whole Mediterranean. The conquest of Britain under Claudius showed the machine still expanding.

The Severan emperors leaned openly on the army, raising pay and courting the legions while the Senate's influence shrank. In 212 Caracalla extended Roman citizenship to almost every free inhabitant of the empire, ending a distinction that had shaped provincial life for centuries. The murder of Severus Alexander in 235 opened the door to fifty years of military anarchy.

Bas-Empire (Roman Empire, AD 236–AD 395).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 236–AD 395] Bas-Empire. Période de l’histoire européenne et méditerranéenne qui commence à la fin du IIIe siècle mais dont le terme est beaucoup plus flou. Elle n’est employée qu’en référence aux pays ayant appartenu au monde romain : les régions d’Europe occidentale, orientale et méridionale, d’Asie et d’Afrique autour du bassin méditerranéen mais se prolonge bien au-delà de la fin de l’Empire romain d’Occident en 476. The reforms of Diocletian and Constantine reshaped Gaul into smaller provinces run by an expanded bureaucracy, with Trier serving as an imperial capital. Cities shrank behind hastily built walls, villas were fortified or abandoned, and Christianity moved from tolerated cult to the religion of the state, leaving bishops as the effective leaders of urban life. By the end of the period Frankish and Visigothic settlers were established inside the frontier.

Fifty years of soldier-emperors, assassinations, debased coinage and frontier breaches nearly destroyed the empire, and for a time separate Gallic and Palmyrene states ruled its edges. Cities across the west threw up hasty defensive walls, often built from the rubble of their own monuments. Aurelian and then Diocletian pulled the pieces back together, dividing rule between four emperors and rebuilding the army, taxation and administration on new, more rigid lines.

The decades when the empire's political stability broke down: soldier-emperors were raised and killed by their own troops, coinage was steadily debased, and pressure mounted on the Rhine, Danube and eastern frontiers. Decius ordered the first empire-wide requirement to sacrifice to the gods, producing the first general persecution of Christians. Towns began to invest in walls, and coin hoards from these years are a common archaeological marker of the insecurity.

The last decades of imperial rule in Gaul, beginning with the Rhine crossing of 406 and the collapse of the northern frontier. Visigoths were settled in Aquitaine in 418, Burgundians on the Rhône, and the emperors' authority came to depend on generals bargaining with these kings; Attila was checked near Chalons in 451. Coin circulation thins out, villas are abandoned, and towns contract inside their walls before the western title lapses in 476.

The last decades of Roman rule in Gaul: after Attila's Huns were checked on the Catalaunian Plains in 451, imperial authority north of the Alps became a fiction maintained by treaties with Visigoths, Burgundians and Franks. Roman landowners and bishops kept the machinery of towns and estates running while generals like Aegidius and Syagrius governed in the emperor's name with no emperor left behind them. Villas contract, cemeteries change, and Christian basilicas become the new focus of urban life.

A thousand years running from the collapse of Roman authority through Merovingian and Carolingian kingdoms to the age of cathedrals, and on into the plague, the Hundred Years' War and recovery under Charles VII and Louis XI. Latin Christianity, feudal lordship and the manorial countryside gave the era its framework, while towns, guilds and universities gradually grew inside it. By its end a recognisably French kingdom, language and royal state had emerged.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman authority and the year 1000, when Frankish kings — first Merovingian, then Carolingian — built kingdoms out of the western provinces. Charlemagne's coronation in 800 revived the idea of a western empire and sponsored a revival of Latin learning and manuscript production in monastic scriptoria. Viking, Muslim and Magyar raids and the break-up of the Carolingian inheritance then shifted real power to counts and castellans, laying the ground for feudal society.

The Roman order in Gaul is gone and the Frankish kings are the new power: Clovis defeated Syagrius at Soissons in 486 and pushed south and east against Alamanni, Burgundians and Visigoths. Burials of this generation are furnished with weapons, belt fittings and brooches in a new Germanic taste, while Gallo-Roman bishops kept churches, Latin and civic memory alive. It is the hinge between the ancient world and Merovingian Gaul.

Justinian tried to put the Roman Empire back together, retaking Africa and Italy, codifying Roman law into a text that would shape European legal systems for a millennium, and building Hagia Sophia. Then plague arrived from the east and killed a vast share of the Mediterranean population, wrecking the effort. In the west the Franks consolidated Gaul, India's Gupta order broke up under Hunnic pressure, and Buddhism reached Japan.

Justinian's reconquest of Italy and Africa proved brittle: plague had emptied the cities, and the Lombards overran much of Italy within a generation. Avars and Turks reshaped the steppe, Byzantium and Persia bled each other in endless war, and the Sui dynasty reunified China after centuries of division. Muhammad was born around 570; Gregory the Great sent missionaries to England in 597.

Byzantium and Sasanian Persia fought a war so exhausting that it hollowed out both; into the gap came the armies of the new Muslim community, taking Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Iran within twenty years of Muhammad's death. A single religion and Arabic administration now stretched from the Nile to the Iranian plateau. In East Asia the Tang dynasty was founded and grew into the era's model empire, while Harsha briefly reunited much of northern India.

Arab armies finished off the Sasanian empire and pressed across North Africa, while civil war among Muslims produced the Sunni-Shi'a split and the Umayyad caliphate at Damascus. Constantinople survived repeated sieges with the help of Greek fire, and the Dome of the Rock announced the new faith in monumental stone. In East Asia, Tang China expanded deep into Central Asia and Silla unified the Korean peninsula.

Arab armies reached their furthest limits - into Spain, across the Indus, and repeatedly against Constantinople - before the Umayyad dynasty was overthrown by the Abbasid revolution and the capital of Islam shifted east. Tang China under Xuanzong enjoyed a brilliant, cosmopolitan peak; Japan built its first permanent capital at Nara. In Byzantium the emperor banned religious images, starting a century of bitter iconoclast controversy.

The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads and built Baghdad, shifting the Islamic world's centre east toward Persia and opening an age of translation, mathematics and paper-making. In the west Pepin and then Charlemagne turned the Frankish kingdom into an empire crowned by the pope, reviving Latin learning. Tang China reeled from the An Lushan rebellion, and the first Viking raids struck the coasts of Britain.

Charlemagne's empire reached its height and then split apart among his grandsons at Verdun, drawing the rough outlines of France and Germany. In Baghdad the Abbasid court of Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun funded translations of Greek science into Arabic and made the city the richest in the world. Viking ships turned from raiding to overwintering and conquest along the coasts of Britain, Ireland and Francia, while in Java the vast Buddhist terraces of Borobudur were rising.

The last Carolingian kings competed with the Robertian family for the throne while real authority drained away to counts, dukes and castle-holding lords. Viking raiders settled at the mouth of the Seine in 911, creating what became Normandy, and fortified stone castles began to dot the countryside. The result was a patchwork of territorial principalities that would define French politics for generations.

Large empires broke into pieces: the Tang fell in 907 and China entered the Five Dynasties period, the Abbasid caliph became a figurehead under Buyid soldiers, and Carolingian Europe fragmented under Viking, Magyar and Saracen raids. New powers filled the gaps, with the Fatimids proclaiming a rival caliphate in North Africa and Abd al-Rahman III another at Córdoba. In England the house of Wessex forged a single kingdom, and in Central Asia Turkic dynasties began converting to Islam.

Otto I's imperial coronation in 962 revived an emperorship in the Latin West, and the Song reunified China after decades of warlordism, ushering in an era of printing, paper money and commercial growth. Vladimir's baptism drew the Rus into the Orthodox world, the Fatimids founded Cairo, and Córdoba under al-Mansur was among the largest cities on earth. Norse sailors settled Greenland and touched North America; in France the Capetian line took the throne.

The last Carolingian kings ruled a realm where real power had passed to counts and castellans who held their lands as hereditary property and fought their own wars. Royal authority barely reached beyond a few northern estates, while the Robertian family accumulated the resources that would soon carry Hugh Capet to the throne. Monastic reform spreading from Cluny was one of the few forces working across this fragmented landscape.

Universities took shape in Paris, fairs in Champagne linked Flemish cloth to Mediterranean trade, and knights left for the crusades. It is the France of Philip Augustus, Louis IX and the troubadours - confident, expanding, and not yet touched by plague.

Royal power at this point was thin, effective mainly around Paris and Orléans, while counts and castellans ruled their own territories in practice. The kingdom's slow reassembly around this small Capetian core is the foundation of medieval France.

Song China's cities, paper money and printed books made it the richest society on earth, while Mahmud of Ghazni raided repeatedly into northern India. Cnut ruled a North Sea empire from England, Norse sailors briefly settled Newfoundland, and the Chola fleet carried Tamil power across the Bay of Bengal. Fatimid Cairo and Byzantine Constantinople stood at their peak, though Greek and Latin churches were drifting toward the rupture of 1054.

Latin and Greek Christianity broke apart in 1054, and the reforming papacy fought emperors over who appointed bishops, forcing Henry IV to wait barefoot at Canossa. The Normans conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy, Seljuk Turks shattered a Byzantine army at Manzikert in 1071 and opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement, and in 1095 the pope's response set the First Crusade marching to take Jerusalem. Song China, meanwhile, argued over Wang Anshi's sweeping state reforms.

The crusader states settled into Levantine politics and the Second Crusade failed to save them. Song China lost its northern half and capital to the Jin and rebuilt itself in the south as a maritime, commercial power. In Europe this was the twelfth-century renaissance: Aristotle and Arabic science translated in Spain and Sicily, law and logic taught at new schools, and the first Gothic choir at Saint-Denis.

Europe's twelfth-century renaissance was in full flow: Gothic cathedrals rose, universities took institutional form, and Roman law and Greek science reached the Latin west through translations from Arabic. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187, provoking the Third Crusade; Angkor built its great temples under Jayavarman VII; Ghurid armies conquered northern India; and in Japan the Minamoto victory created the first shogunate.

A crusade aimed at Egypt sacked Christian Constantinople instead, crippling Byzantium permanently. Out of Mongolia, Genghis Khan and his heirs assembled the largest land empire in history, destroying the Khwarazmian and Jin states and reaching the edge of central Europe. In the west, English barons forced Magna Carta on their king, friars preached in the growing towns, and universities and Gothic cathedrals took the shape they still hold.

The Mongol empire reached its greatest extent and then fractured: Baghdad was sacked in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate, the Mamluks halted the advance at Ain Jalut, and Kublai Khan completed the conquest of Song China in 1279. Merchants and envoys like Marco Polo travelled the length of Eurasia along routes the Mongols secured. In the west, crusader Acre fell in 1291, universities flourished under Aquinas and scholastic theology, and a small Turkish emirate in Anatolia began the rise that became the Ottoman Empire.

The last stretch of Capetian confidence, when Philip the Fair humiliated the papacy, moved it to Avignon and destroyed the Templars to seize their wealth. Royal lawyers built up an administration and a treasury that treated the kingdom as a state rather than a bundle of lordships. Then came catastrophic harvest failures and famine, and in 1328 the direct male line ran out — opening the succession dispute that led to war with England.

War with England, recurring plague and rural depopulation dominated these generations, yet they also produced a stronger royal state: standing armies, permanent taxation and a crown that emerged from the Hundred Years' War far more powerful than before. Towns rebuilt in flamboyant Gothic, printing arrived in the 1470s, and the marriage politics of the 1490s folded Brittany into the kingdom.

A new Valois dynasty inherited a kingdom that quickly ran into disaster: English victories, a captured king, a ransom that drained the treasury, and plague returning in waves. Royal taxation became permanent and standing companies of soldiers appeared, but so did peasant and urban revolts against the cost. Charles V clawed back much of the lost territory before the century closed with a king descending into madness.

The Capetian direct line failed in 1328, bringing the Valois to the throne and giving Edward III of England a pretext to claim it; open war followed from 1337. French armies were shattered at Crécy in 1346 and Calais fell the next year, and in 1348 plague swept up from Marseille through a countryside already weakened by famine and heavy war taxation. Villages emptied, wages and prices lurched, and the confident growth of the previous two centuries came to an abrupt end.

A century that began in crisis: torrential rains brought the Great Famine of 1315–17 to northern Europe, and the Black Death arrived from Central Asia in 1347, killing perhaps a third of Europeans within a few years. England and France began the long dynastic struggle later called the Hundred Years' War, while the popes ruled from Avignon rather than Rome. Elsewhere Mansa Musa's Mali made its legendary pilgrimage to Cairo, the Mongol Yuan grip on China loosened, and Giotto's frescoes signalled a new naturalism in painting.

Europe lived through the aftershocks of the Black Death: labour shortages raised wages and broke old obligations, and revolts swept France, Flanders and England. The papacy split into rival lines in 1378, the Hundred Years' War ground on, and Chaucer wrote in English rather than French or Latin. In Asia the Ming expelled the Mongols from China in 1368 and Timur carved out an empire from Central Asia to Delhi.

Charles VII and Louis XI rebuilt the state with permanent taxation and a professional army, then broke Burgundy and drew Provence and Anjou into the royal domain. Population and villages slowly recovered from plague and war.

In Mainz Gutenberg's press went to work, while the Aztec and Inca states were building their imperial systems in the Americas.

The Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Roman Empire in the east and pushed Europeans to seek sea routes around the Muslim world, leading to Columbus's landfall in 1492 and Vasco da Gama's arrival in India in 1498. Gutenberg's printing press spread across Europe within a generation, multiplying books and ideas at unheard-of speed. Spain completed the Reconquista and expelled its Jews, Italy's cities funded the height of the Renaissance, and the Aztec and Inca empires reached their peak just before contact.

Louis XI outmanoeuvred and destroyed the power of Burgundy, absorbing great fiefs into the royal domain, and the marriage that brought Brittany into the kingdom completed the territorial core of France. Independence was declared in 1912 amid the Balkan Wars, but the new state's borders left large Albanian populations outside them, and the interwar years under Ahmet Zogu were poor and unstable. Spanish expeditions destroyed the Aztec and Inca empires and began shipping American silver across the world, while Portuguese fleets seized the chokepoints of the Indian Ocean. Suleiman's Ottomans besieged Vienna, Babur founded the Mughal empire, and Copernicus set the earth in motion around the sun.

American silver flowed through Seville and Manila to China, knitting the first genuinely global economy, while Akbar's Mughal empire and Ottoman power under Suleiman's successors dominated southern Asia and the Mediterranean. In East Asia the Ming dynasty fell to the Manchus in 1644, and Tokugawa Japan settled into more than two centuries of enforced stability.

Louis XIV's France set the European standard for centralised absolute monarchy, while England took the opposite path through civil war, restoration and the constitutional settlement of 1688. It was the decisive half-century of the Scientific Revolution, crowned by Newton's Principia, and of chartered trading companies that pushed European commerce and slaving deep into Asia, Africa and the Americas. The Ottoman failure at Vienna in 1683 and the Qing consolidation of China redrew the balance of the two greatest Eurasian empires.

France under Louis XV and Louis XVI grew rich on Atlantic trade and colonial sugar while the monarchy sank ever deeper into debt from wars with Britain, losing Canada and India but helping the American revolutionaries win. In salons and cafés the philosophes - Voltaire, Diderot, Rousseau - argued for reason, tolerance and natural rights, and the Encyclopédie put that thinking into print. Peter the Great dragged Russia toward the Baltic, Qing China under Kangxi and Yongzheng reached unprecedented extent and wealth, and Mughal authority in India collapsed after Aurangzeb, opening the way for European trading companies. Enlightenment writers challenged inherited authority even as the Atlantic slave trade reached its most intense phase.

Enlightenment ideas about reason, rights and government moved out of books and into politics, producing the American Revolution and then the French Revolution. Britain's global wars against France left it dominant in India and North America, while coal, steam and mechanised spinning began transforming manufacturing in a way no one yet had a name for. It is the half-century in which the modern categories of citizen, nation and industry took recognisable shape.

The last decades of the Ancien Régime: defeat in the Seven Years' War stripped away Canada and India, the monarchy's finances never recovered, and support for the American rebels finished the job. Meanwhile the Encyclopédie, salons and a booming print trade spread criticism of privilege and absolute power among an expanding reading public. Bankruptcy forced Louis XVI to summon the Estates-General, and the old order ended.

Morocco moved from a sovereign sultanate courted and squeezed by European powers to a French and Spanish protectorate imposed in 1912, then back to independence in 1956 under the Alaouite monarchy. The period saw Tangier as an international zone, the Rif war, huge growth of coastal cities like Casablanca, and rural depopulation as migration to Europe began.

In a single decade France abolished noble privilege and the guilds, sold off church lands, executed its king and queen, and redrew itself as departments governed by uniform law. The Terror, war against most of Europe, and mass conscription remade the state's reach over ordinary lives; the metric system and a new calendar were part of the same impulse to start from scratch. It closed with Bonaparte seizing power, carrying the Revolution's institutions forward under one man's rule.

Napoleon's wars remade the map of Europe before his defeat in 1815, and in their wake Spain's American empire dissolved into independent republics. Steam power, factory towns and the first railways transformed Britain and spread across the Atlantic and the Channel, while the British Empire abolished slavery in its colonies and pressed China open by force in the Opium War. The revolutions of 1848 showed how far nationalism and demands for constitutional government had spread among Europe's new urban classes.

Industrial technology, railways, steamships and the telegraph knitted the world into a single market, while millions emigrated across oceans. New nation-states appeared in Italy and Germany, the United States abolished slavery through civil war, Japan remade itself in the Meiji Restoration, and European powers partitioned nearly all of Africa. Darwin's theory of evolution, germ theory and electric power transformed how people understood and lived in the world.

Two world wars killed tens of millions, toppled the Russian, Ottoman, Habsburg and German empires, and ended with the atomic bombing of Japan. Between them came the Russian Revolution, the Great Depression, fascism and the Holocaust; after them came the United Nations, the Cold War and the first successes of decolonisation in Asia. It was also the age of flight, radio, antibiotics and mass production, which changed daily life as thoroughly as the politics.

Computers, antibiotics, jet travel, television and spaceflight reshaped daily life faster than in any comparable span, and the world's population more than doubled. The Soviet Union's fall left a single superpower and a rapidly globalising economy, with China's reopening setting up the century that followed.

The Abbasid caliphate lost effective control of its provinces to Turkish soldiers and local dynasties, and Tang China was shattered by the Huang Chao rebellion.

The Rhine garrisons were being drawn south to fight in Italy, leaving the frontier exposed. The great crossing of the Rhine in 406 and the loss of the Gallic provinces were only a few years away.

A century of dramatic reinvention: Diocletian's reforms and Constantine's rise remade imperial government, the capital shifted east to Constantinople, and Christianity went from illegal to official. Coinage was stabilised, the army restructured, and a vast new bureaucracy grew up around the emperor. It ended badly, with the disastrous defeat at Adrianople in 378 and Gothic groups settled inside the frontiers as armed communities.

Julian's brief pagan revival failed, the defeat at Adrianople in 378 forced the settlement of Goths inside the frontiers, and Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the state religion while suppressing the old cults. His death in 395 left the east and west under separate courts, a split that proved permanent.

The Greek world emerged from its dark age with an explosion of energy: the alphabet was adopted, cities sent out colonies from Spain to the Black Sea, coinage spread, and the polis became the basic unit of political life. Monumental stone temples, life-size kouros statues and the poetry of Sappho and Homer's written text all belong here, as do the first tyrants and the first experiments in citizen government at Athens. It ends with the Persian invasions, which the Greeks improbably survived.

Between the defeat of the Persian invasion and the death of Demosthenes, the Greek city-states reached their political and artistic peak and then exhausted themselves. Athens built the Parthenon, staged the great tragedies and experimented with direct democracy while fighting Sparta in the Peloponnesian War; Plato and Aristotle founded schools that shaped philosophy for two thousand years. Macedonian victory at Chaeronea ended the independence of the city-states and opened the Hellenistic age.

In the far west of Iberia, communities lived in fortified hilltop settlements, working iron and trading with Punic merchants who ran the Atlantic and Mediterranean coastal routes. Greek and Carthaginian goods reached these towns long before any Roman soldier did, and local elites adopted foreign luxuries while keeping their own burial customs and script traditions. It is the last stretch of independence before Carthaginian and then Roman armies made the peninsula a battlefield.

Alexander's successors divided his conquests into large monarchies, and Greek culture, language and city planning spread far beyond the Aegean. Old Greek city-states kept their institutions but lost real independence, while new capitals in Egypt and Asia became the centres of scholarship, sculpture and royal patronage. Rome's piecemeal conquest of the Mediterranean brought the era to a close.

After 395 the empire's eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the west by a thousand years, keeping Roman law, taxation and a professional army while conducting its business increasingly in Greek. Under Justinian its fleets and armies pushed back into the western Mediterranean, taking North Africa, Italy and a strip of southern Spain, so that imperial garrisons stood again on the Iberian coast until the Visigoths expelled them in the 620s.

When Theodosius I died in 395 the empire passed to his two young sons, and the division between east and west became permanent. The western provinces, including the Atlantic edge of Iberia, still functioned as Roman territory with villas, towns and bishops, but the army guarding the Rhine was already stretched thin. Within a decade the frontier would break and the western provinces would begin slipping out of imperial control.

The last Byzantine footholds in the Iberian southwest were squeezed out by Visigothic kings, and with Suintila's campaigns the peninsula came under a single crown for the first time since Rome. Visigothic Hispania then developed its own Catholic church councils at Toledo and its own legal code, while Isidore of Seville compiled the encyclopaedia that would teach medieval Europe most of what it knew of antiquity.

Lithique (Bahamas, 4599 BC–3000 BC).label: Lithique
Lithique (Bahamas, 4599 BC–3000 BC).prose:
[Antilles, 4599 BC–3000 BC] Lithique. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge lithique est marqué par un mode de vie nomade, vivant de chasse et de pêche, sans cultures végétales identifiées, sans utilisation de céramique, et avec une utilisation d’outils en pierre taillés et non polis.
Les sites sont concentrés uniquement dans les Grandes Antilles et à Trinidad.

The Lithic Age is marked by a nomadic lifestyle, living from hunting and fishing, with no identified plant crops, no use of ceramics, and the use of carved and unpolished stone tools.
Sites are concentrated only in the Greater Antilles and Trinidad. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Caribbean archaeologists use this label for the earliest human presence in the islands, when small bands of foragers who made chipped stone blades and used no pottery moved out from the mainland by sea. They lived on shellfish, fish, land crabs and wild plants, leaving thin scatters of flint and shell rather than villages. It marks the moment when island chains that had never seen people were first entered.

Archaïque (Bahamas, 2999 BC–500 BC).label: Archaïque
Archaïque (Bahamas, 2999 BC–500 BC).prose:
[Antilles, 2999 BC–500 BC] Archaïque. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge Archaïque est caractérisé par un peuplement de nomades vivant de chasse et de pêche, mais est aussi marqué par l’introduction de plantes depuis le continent, et par les premières utilisations de céramiques, bien que rares. Les productions lithiques intègrent des techniques diverses, débitage et polissage.
Les sites se situent majoritairement dans les Grandes Antilles et à Trinidad, et aussi dans les Petites Antilles du Nord.

The Archaic Age is characterised by a nomadic population living from hunting and fishing, but is also marked by the introduction of plants from the continent, and by the first uses of ceramics, although rare. The lithic productions integrate various techniques, cutting and polishing.
The sites are mainly located in the Greater Antilles and Trinidad, and also in the Lesser Antilles of the North. The Greek world emerged from its dark age with an explosion of energy: the alphabet was adopted, cities sent out colonies from Spain to the Black Sea, coinage spread, and the polis became the basic unit of political life. Monumental stone temples, life-size kouros statues and the poetry of Sappho and Homer's written text all belong here, as do the first tyrants and the first experiments in citizen government at Athens. It ends with the Persian invasions, which the Greeks improbably survived.
Archaïque (Bahamas, 2999 BC–500 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Céramique (Bahamas, 499 BC–AD 1491).label: Céramique
Céramique (Bahamas, 499 BC–AD 1491).prose:
[Antilles, 499 BC–AD 1491] Céramique. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge Céramique correspond à l’occupation formative des Antilles par une migration depuis le bassin de l’Orénoque. L’utilisation de la Céramique se développe très fortement, ainsi que l’horticulture. Si la première phase ne concerne que les Petites Antilles et Puerto Rico, les phases suivantes concernent l’ensemble de l’arc caribéen.

The Ceramic Age corresponds to the formative occupation of the West Indies by a migration from the Orinoco basin. The use of ceramics developed very strongly, as did horticulture. If the first phase concerns only the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico, the following phases concern the whole Caribbean arc. Céramique ancien (Bahamas, 499 BC–AD 400.label: Céramique ancien
Céramique ancien (Bahamas, 499 BC–AD 400.prose:
[Antilles, 499 BC–AD 400] Céramique ancien. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. Les occupations du Céramique ancien sont caractérisées par une localisation côtière de villages de taille modeste, dont la subsistance se base essentiellement sur la pêche, ainsi que l’horticulture et la chasse d’espèces importées du continent. Les productions matérielles tranchent avec l’âge précédent et son plutôt homogène sur l’aire concernée, en particulier à travers les céramique de type Saladoïde (huecan et cedrosan), la production importante d’éléments de parure en pierres diverses, et un outillage sur coquille de lambi.

The Early Ceramic occupations are characterised by a coastal location of modest-sized villages, whose subsistence is based essentially on fishing, as well as horticulture and the hunting of species imported from the continent. The material production contrasts with the previous age and is rather homogeneous in the area concerned, in particular through Saladoid type ceramics (huecan and cedrosan), the important production of various stone ornaments, and lambi shell tools. Céramique moyen (Bahamas, AD 401–AD 800).label: Céramique moyen
Céramique moyen (Bahamas, AD 401–AD 800).prose:
[Antilles, AD 401–AD 800] Céramique moyen. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. Le Céramique moyen montre une évolution essentiellement endogène des pratiques des sociétés amérindiennes. L’appropriation du territoire se fait plus intense, avec un nombre de sites plus importants dont certains plus à l’intérieur des terres. Les céramiques se modifient, et l’expression symbolique également, avec l’apparition des trois-pointes et, probablement, des premières représentations rupestres.

The Middle Ceramic period shows an essentially endogenous evolution of the practices of Amerindian societies. The appropriation of the territory was more intense, with a greater number of sites, some of which were further inland. Ceramics were modified, as was symbolic expression, with the appearance of the three-pointed stick and, probably, the first rock representations. Céramique récent (Bahamas, AD 801–AD 120.label: Céramique récent
Céramique récent (Bahamas, AD 801–AD 120.prose:
[Antilles, AD 801–AD 1200] Céramique récent. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. Le Céramique récent montre une occupation plus large de l’archipel antillais, ainsi que le début d’une régionalisation, visible en particulier sur les productions céramiques, qui se distinguent géographiquement, et qui perdent également en investissement technique par rapport aux périodes précédentes. La société se complexifie, devient plus hiérarchisée, et l’on retrouve des sites spécialisés, y compris des centres cérémoniels, en particulier dans les Grandes Antilles.

The Recent Ceramic period shows a wider occupation of the Antillean archipelago, as well as the beginning of a regionalization, visible in particular in the ceramic productions, which are geographically distinct, and which also lose in technical investment compared to the previous periods. Society became more complex and hierarchical, and specialised sites, including ceremonial centres, were found, particularly in the Greater Antilles. Céramique final (Bahamas, AD 1201–AD 149.label: Céramique final
Céramique final (Bahamas, AD 1201–AD 149.prose:
[Antilles, AD 1201–AD 1491] Céramique final. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. Le développement de sociétés complexes se poursuit au Céramique final, à l’échelle de l’archipel entier. La régionalisation se poursuit également, avec des différences marquées entre les Grandes Antilles et les Petites Antilles. 

The development of complex societies continues in the Late Ceramic period, on the scale of the entire archipelago. Regionalization also continued, with marked differences between the Greater Antilles and the Lesser Antilles. Historique (Bahamas, AD 1492–AD 2050).label: Historique
Historique (Bahamas, AD 1492–AD 2050).prose:
[Antilles, AD 1492–AD 2050] Historique. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge Historique début avec les premiers contacts entre les colons européens et les Amérindiens et se poursuit jusqu’à l’actuel, en passant par la période coloniale. Ces quelques siècles ont vu une révolution démographique, culturelle, environnementale, se dérouler dans cette région du monde, qui, d’un point de vue archéologique, reste encore largement à étudier, afin de s’affronter aux connaissances textuelles très importantes dont nous disposons sur cette période.

The Historical Age begins with the first contacts between the European settlers and the Amerindians and continues until the present day, passing through the colonial period. These few centuries have seen a demographic, cultural and environmental revolution take place in this region of the world, which, from an archaeological point of view, remains largely unstudied, in order to confront the very important textual knowledge that we have on this period. European contact begins here: Columbus's first Atlantic landfall was on a Lucayan island, and within about twenty-five years Spanish slave raiding for labour in Hispaniola's mines and pearl fisheries had emptied the archipelago of its indigenous people. The islands lay largely abandoned until English settlers arrived in the seventeenth century, followed by wreckers, pirates, and Loyalist planters with enslaved Africans after the American Revolution. The archaeology of this span is one of ruined plantations, harbour defences, shipwrecks and colonial towns rather than of continuity with the Lucayan past.

Farming villages spread to the last corners of temperate Europe while, in the Balkans, metalworkers began smelting and casting copper on a serious scale – the goldwork of the Varna cemetery comes from the end of this millennium. In southern Mesopotamia the Ubaid culture built temple platforms and irrigated fields that set the template for the first cities. Elsewhere, rice cultivation deepened in China and the Sahara was still green enough to support cattle herders who left rock paintings across it.

Farming villages across the Old World grew into something denser and more organised. In southern Mesopotamia the Ubaid culture drained marshes, irrigated fields and built successive mud-brick temples on the same sacred spots - the seed of the later city. Balkan smiths were casting heavy copper axes, Atlantic Europe began raising megalithic tombs, and millet farmers of the Yangshao culture painted their pottery along the Yellow River.

Farming villages across Eurasia grew denser and more unequal, and the first substantial metalworking appears: the Varna cemetery on the Black Sea holds more worked gold than the rest of the world combined at that date. In Mesopotamia the Ubaid culture spread temple-centred towns across the plain; in Europe, Cucuteni-Trypillia settlements and the first megalithic tombs went up. Ploughs, wool-bearing sheep, dairying and wheeled transport were beginning to change what farming could support.

Southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities, with Uruk's temples, mass-produced pottery and accounting tokens turning into the earliest writing. The wheel, the plough and the donkey caravan reshaped work and trade, and copper metallurgy spread widely. Egypt moved towards unification under a single king, while in Atlantic Europe communities raised megalithic tombs and stone circles.

Cities took shape in southern Mesopotamia, and the accounting needs of Uruk's temples produced the first writing; the wheel, the plough and mass-produced pottery spread from the same world. In Egypt competing Nile chiefdoms consolidated into the kingdom unified around 3100 BC. Northern Europe was building megalithic tombs and causewayed enclosures, and the Alpine iceman known as Ötzi died in these centuries.

The centuries in which the earliest cities and states became a lasting fact of life across much of Eurasia and North Africa. Egypt's Old Kingdom built the Giza pyramids, Sumerian city-states gave way to Sargon's Akkadian empire, the Indus civilisation laid out Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, and writing, bronze metallurgy and long-distance trade in tin, lapis and copper linked them all. Farther west and north, societies without writing raised megalithic tombs and stone circles and began working copper.

The world's first territorial empire, Akkad, rose and fell in Mesopotamia, Egypt's pyramid-building Old Kingdom gave way to the fragmented First Intermediate Period, and the Indus cities reached their mature planned form. In Europe, Bell Beaker pottery and early metalwork spread rapidly along with populations of steppe ancestry. Around 2200 BC a phase of drought and instability, often called the 4.2 ka event, coincided with political collapse across several of these regions.

IIIe millénaire AEC – Fin Néolithique (F.prose:
[Parts of central continental western Europe, 3299 BC–2200 BC] IIIe millénaire AEC – Fin Néolithique. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, England, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy. This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a general chronology from the Paleolithic to the present day, of a central-western part of continental Europe. It is used to connect the relative chronology to the gregorian calendar.
The territory covered by this chronology extends from the eastern part of France in the west to Moldavia in the east, and from the south of the UK through southern Germany to Slovenia and central France on a north/south axis.

Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie générale du Paléolithique à nos jours, d'une partie centrale-occidentale de l'Europe continentale. Elle est utilisée pour rattachée la chronologie relative au calendrier grégorien.
Le territoire recouvert par cette chronologie s'étend de la partie orientale de la France, à l'ouest, jusqu'à la Moldavie à l'est, et du sud du Royaume-Uni en passant par l'Allemagne méridionale jusqu'à la Slovénie et le centre de la France sur un axe nord/sud. The closing centuries of the Neolithic, when farming villages spread across the whole country and communities built collective tombs — passage graves, gallery graves and hypogea — in which hundreds of ancestors were laid together. Copper working appears, flint mining and axe production reach an industrial scale, and fortified and ditched enclosures suggest growing competition over land. It ends with the arrival of Bell Beaker pottery, archery equipment and metalwork, the prelude to the Bronze Age.

The last Neolithic centuries in France, when collective tombs, hypogea and allées couvertes were still being used and copper objects circulated more widely. Late in the period Bell Beaker pottery, archery equipment and individual burial rites appear, marking the transition toward Bronze Age societies. Regional groups such as the Artenacien and Seine-Oise-Marne define the archaeology of the time.

Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–61.node: Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–616 BC)
Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–61.label: Rois latins et sabins
Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–61.prose:
[Latium, 752 BC–616 BC] Rois latins et sabins. Durant cette première période 4 rois tour à tour Latin et Sabin mettent sur pied les fondations des institutions politiques et religieuses de la ville.
La ville est organisée en **curies**, le **Sénat** et les **comices** deviennent officiels. Les 4 premiers rois sont élus.

During this first period, 4 kings, in turn Latin and Sabine, laid the foundations of the city's political and religious institutions. The city was organised into **curies**, and the **Senate** and **comices** became official. The first 4 kings were elected. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The first four kings of Rome in legend — Romulus the founder, Numa the lawgiver of religion, the warlike Tullus Hostilius and Ancus Marcius — belong to a tradition that Romans themselves told to explain their institutions. Archaeology shows a real village cluster on the hills growing into a town in these centuries, but the named kings and their deeds are later reconstruction rather than record.
Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–61.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Romulus (Latium, 752 BC–714 BC).label: Romulus
Romulus (Latium, 752 BC–714 BC).prose:
[Latium, 752 BC–714 BC] Romulus. **Romulus** : Petit-fils du roi d'Albe-la-Longue, il fonde Rome et organise l’enlèvement des Sabines, agrandissant ainsi son territoire sur le Quirinal, colline appartenant à l’origine aux Sabins. Régna de -753 à -715 (38 ans).

**Romulus**: Grandson of the king of Alba-Longa, he founded Rome and organised the abduction of the Sabine women, thus extending his territory onto the Quirinal, a hill originally belonging to the Sabines. Reigned from 753 BC to 715 BC (38 years).

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The reign ascribed by tradition to Rome's legendary founder, who was said to have marked out the city's boundary, killed his brother Remus, seized wives from the Sabines and created the Senate and the first legions. No archaeology confirms the man, but early huts on the Palatine and a defensive wall show a real settlement forming at just this time. Romans treated the story as their charter myth, endlessly reworked to explain their institutions and their appetite for absorbing outsiders.
Romulus (Latium, 752 BC–714 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Numa Pompilius (Latium, 714 BC–671 BC).label: Numa Pompilius
Numa Pompilius (Latium, 714 BC–671 BC).prose:
[Latium, 714 BC–671 BC] Numa Pompilius. **Numa Pompilius** : roi d’origine sabine, pacifique et religieux, il crée le collège des Pontifes, fait construire le temple de Janus et fixe les fêtes religieuses dans un calendrier de douze mois.
Régna de -715 à -673 (42 ans).

**Reigned from 715 BC to 673 BC (42 years)**. A peaceful and religious king of Sabine origin, he created the College of Pontiffs, built the Temple of Janus and established religious festivals in a twelve-month calendar.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The second of Rome's legendary kings, remembered as the peaceful counterpart to the warlike Romulus. Roman tradition credited him with inventing the city's religious framework: the priestly colleges, the Vestal Virgins who tended the sacred fire, the office of pontifex maximus, and a reformed twelve-month calendar. Whether or not he existed, later Romans used him to explain why their state religion looked the way it did.
Numa Pompilius (Latium, 714 BC–671 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Tullus Hostilius (Latium, 671 BC–640 BC).label: Tullus Hostilius
Tullus Hostilius (Latium, 671 BC–640 BC).prose:
[Latium, 671 BC–640 BC] Tullus Hostilius. **Tullus Hostilius** : roi romain, guerrier, il organise l’armée, détruit Albe-la-Longue et conquiert tout le Latium.
Régna de -672 à -641 (31 ans).

**Reigned from 672 BC to 641 BC (31 years).** A Roman king and warrior, he organised his army, destroyed Albe-la-Longue and conquered the whole of Lazio.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Rome's legendary third king, remembered as a warrior in contrast to the pious Numa. Tradition credits him with the destruction of Alba Longa — decided, in the story, by the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii triplets — and the transfer of its people to Rome, along with the building of the first senate house, the Curia Hostilia. The tales are later constructions, but they encode how Rome absorbed its Latin neighbours and grew by incorporation.
Tullus Hostilius (Latium, 671 BC–640 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Ancus Marcius (Latium, 639 BC–615 BC).label: Ancus Marcius
Ancus Marcius (Latium, 639 BC–615 BC).prose:
[Latium, 639 BC–615 BC] Ancus Marcius. **Ancus Marcius** : roi sabin, petit-fils de Numa Pompilius, il est pacifique et religieux. C’est un bâtisseur : Rome ayant intégré les peuples latins, il fait construire un mur et un pont sur le Tibre, fait fonder **Ostie** vers -640 et favorise l’essor du commerce.
Régna de -640 à -616 (24 ans).

Reigned from 640 BC to 616 BC (24 years). A Sabine king and grandson of Numa Pompilius, he was a peaceful and religious man. He was a builder: as Rome had integrated the Latin peoples, he built a wall and a bridge over the Tiber, founded Ostia around 640 BC and encouraged the growth of trade.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The fourth of Rome's legendary kings, remembered as a builder rather than a conqueror. Tradition credits him with the first bridge over the Tiber, a prison on the Capitoline, the port of Ostia at the river mouth, and the resettlement of defeated Latins on the Aventine — a step that shaped Rome's later habit of absorbing its enemies as citizens. The details come from writers centuries later, so the man is half history, half national myth.
Ancus Marcius (Latium, 639 BC–615 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Rois étrusques (Latium, 615 BC–509 BC).label: Rois étrusques
Rois étrusques (Latium, 615 BC–509 BC).prose:
[Latium, 615 BC–509 BC] Rois étrusques. Durant cette seconde période, 3 rois étrusques entament une politique de conquête, et la monarchie devient héréditaire.

During this second period, 3 Etruscan kings began a policy of conquest, and the monarchy became hereditary. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Roman tradition assigns the city's last three kings to an Etruscan-influenced line, credited with the great drainage of the Forum, the Circus, the Capitoline temple and the first city walls — the works that turned Rome into a real urban centre. The expulsion of Tarquin the Proud became the founding myth of the Republic and of Roman hostility to monarchy.
Rois étrusques (Latium, 615 BC–509 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Tarquin l'Ancien (Latium, 615 BC–577 BC).label: Tarquin l'Ancien
Tarquin l'Ancien (Latium, 615 BC–577 BC).prose:
[Latium, 615 BC–577 BC] Tarquin l'Ancien. **Tarquin l'Ancien** : roi étrusque, tuteur des enfants d'Ancus Marcius, il est un grand bâtisseur : il embellit Rome en agrandissant ses murailles, en créant le forum , il fait commencer la construction du Capitole, équipe la Ville de la Cloaca Maxima, grand égout qui traverse Rome, et du Circus Maximus, le grand Cirque. Il est cependant assassiné car il veut transmettre son pouvoir à l’un de ses protégés, Servius Tullius, alors que les descendants d’Ancus Martius revendiquent sa succession.
Régna de -616 à -578 (38 ans).

Reigned from 616 BC to 578 BC (38 years). An Etruscan king and tutor to the children of Ancus Marcius, he was a great builder: he embellished Rome by extending its walls, creating the Forum, starting construction of the Capitol, equipping the city with the Cloaca Maxima, the great sewer that runs through Rome, and the Circus Maximus, the great Circus. However, he was assassinated because he wanted to pass on his power to one of his protégés, Servius Tullius, while the descendants of Ancus Martius claimed his succession.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The reign of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the first of Rome's Etruscan kings in the traditional list, remembered for turning a hill settlement into a city: draining the forum valley, laying out the Circus Maximus and beginning the great Capitoline temple. Whether or not the details are historical, they reflect a real period when Etruscan wealth and engineering reshaped early Rome.
Tarquin l'Ancien (Latium, 615 BC–577 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Servius Tullius (Latium, 577 BC–533 BC).label: Servius Tullius
Servius Tullius (Latium, 577 BC–533 BC).prose:
[Latium, 577 BC–533 BC] Servius Tullius. **Servius Tullius** : roi étrusque, c’est un grand administrateur. Il divise le peuple en quatre tribus territoriales et en sept classes en fonction de leur fortune, le cens. Il organise l'armée en centuries et fait construire la muraille de Rome, dite « de Servius Tullius ». Il crée aussi la première Constitution romaine. Il est cependant assassiné par sa propre fille et son gendre.
Régna de -578 à -534 (44 ans).

Reigned from 578 BC to 534 BC (44 years). This Etruscan king was a great administrator. He divided the people into four territorial tribes and seven classes according to their wealth, the cens. He organised the army into centuries and built the walls of Rome, known as the ‘walls of Servius Tullius’. He also created the first Roman Constitution. However, he was assassinated by his own daughter and son-in-law.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The sixth king in Rome's traditional list, remembered as a reformer who reorganised citizens into classes based on wealth rather than birth and created the assembly that voted by centuries. Tradition also credits him with the city's first great defensive wall and the census. Whether or not the man is historical, the institutions attributed to him structured Roman voting and military service for centuries.
Servius Tullius (Latium, 577 BC–533 BC).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Tarquin le Superbe (Latium, 533 BC–508 B.label: Tarquin le Superbe
Tarquin le Superbe (Latium, 533 BC–508 B.prose:
[Latium, 533 BC–508 BC] Tarquin le Superbe. **Tarquin le Superbe** : roi étrusque, fils de Tarquin l’Ancien, il achève l'œuvre de son père en poursuivant sa politique de grands travaux, fait bâtir le temple de Jupiter. Il est cependant guerrier et, son fils étant impliqué dans le viol de Lucrèce, la femme de Tarquin Collatin (neveu du roi), il est renversé, à cause de ses violences, par le peuple. Après vingt-cinq ans de règne, il est exilé et remplacé par deux consuls : Tarquin Collatin et Brutus, l’un de ses proches.
Régna de -534 à -509 (25 ans).

Reigned from 534 BC to 509 BC (25 years). Etruscan king, son of Tarquin the Elder, he completed his father's work by continuing his policy of major works, building the temple of Jupiter. However, he was a warrior and, as his son was involved in the rape of Lucrezia, the wife of Tarquin Collatin (the king's nephew), he was overthrown by the people because of his violence. After reigning for twenty-five years, he was exiled and replaced by two consuls: Tarquin Collatin and Brutus, one of his relatives.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The reign of Tarquinius Superbus, Rome's seventh and last king, cast by later writers as a tyrant who ruled by murder and fear. His overthrow — triggered in legend by his son's rape of Lucretia — ended the monarchy and founded the Republic, and Romans afterwards treated the very word 'king' as a political insult.
Tarquin le Superbe (Latium, 533 BC–508 B.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia (Rome, 50.node: Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia (Rome, 508 BC–287 BC)
Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia (Rome, 50.label: Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia
Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia (Rome, 50.prose:
[Rome, 508 BC–287 BC] Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Tite-Live rapporte qu’apres l'expulsion de Tarquin le Superbe deux consuls furent élus par les comices centuriates présidés par le préfet de la Ville, conformément aux commentarii de Servius Tulli. Selon la tradition antique, qui est unanime sur ce point, la premiere loi votée par les comices centuriates sous la présidence d'un consul fut la Lex Valeria de prouocatione, qui interdisait à tout magistrat de faire exécuter ou de faire fouetter un citoyen romain sans lui laisser le droit d'en appeler au peuple“. Comme le dit Cicéron dans le De legibus (Leg. 3, 6), la prouocatio ad populum avait pour róle de limiter le pouvoir de coercitio des magistrats supérieurs, pouvoir qui les autorisait à punir les citoyens qui refusaient de leur obéir. C'est aussi Cicéron qui fait dans le De oratore l’éloge de la prouocatio qu'il qualifie de sauvegarde de la cité et de rempart de la liberté“. 

Titus Livius reports that after the expulsion of Tarquin the Superb, two consuls were elected by the centuriate comices presided over by the prefect of the city, in accordance with the commentarii of Servius Tulli. According to ancient tradition, which is unanimous on this point, the first law passed by the comices centuriates under the presidency of a consul was the **Lex Valeria de prouocatione**, which prohibited any magistrate from executing or whipping a Roman citizen without giving him the right to appeal to the people’. As Cicero says in De legibus (Leg. 3, 6), the purpose of prouocatio ad populum was to limit the coercive power of the higher magistrates, which allowed them to punish citizens who refused to obey them. It was also Cicero who, in his De oratore, praised the prouocatio as a safeguard for the city and a bulwark of freedom. -

Ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–367 BC).label: Ère patricienne
Ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–367 BC).prose:
[Rome, 508 BC–367 BC] Ère patricienne. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Ère patricienne (-509 -367 AEC)
Durant la période consécutive à la révolution ayant entraîné la chute du dernier roi de Rome, le Sénat et les assemblées ont aussi peu de pouvoirs que sous la Royauté. La devise traditionnelle de la république est **Senatus populusque Romanus (SPQR)**, « le Sénat et le peuple romain ». Elle symbolise l'union consensuelle du Sénat, où siègent les sénateurs (patres) à l'origine les familles de l'élite économique et politique de la cité, et de l'ensemble des citoyens romains, qui par son vote adopte les lois, confère leurs pouvoirs aux magistrats, et consent au versement des impôts et à la levée des armées.

During the period following the revolution that led to the fall of the last king of Rome, the Senate and the Assemblies had as few powers as they did under the monarchy. The traditional motto of the republic is **Senatus populusque Romanus (SPQR)**, ‘the Senate and the Roman people’. It symbolises the consensual union of the Senate, where the senators (patres), originally the families of the city's economic and political elite, sit, and all Roman citizens, who by voting pass laws, confer their powers on magistrates, and consent to the payment of taxes and the raising of armies. In the first century and a half of the Republic, the patrician clans monopolised the consulship, the priesthoods and the interpretation of law, while the plebeians organised their own tribunes and assemblies to push back. The long 'Conflict of the Orders' produced the Twelve Tables and a series of concessions, ending when the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 BC forced the consulship open to plebeians. Rome in these years was still a modest central-Italian city fighting its neighbours, and was sacked by the Gauls in 390 BC.

Début de l'ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC.node: Début de l'ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–500 BC)
Début de l'ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC.label: Début de l'ère patricienne
Début de l'ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC.prose:
[Rome, 508 BC–500 BC] Début de l'ère patricienne. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. D'après la tradition, Junius Brutus, le neveu du dernier roi, Tarquin le Superbe, aurait été le fondateur de la République romaine, en 509 av. J.-C., aux côtés de Tarquin Collatin, membre de la famille des Tarquins et mari de Lucrèce, dont le viol par Sextus Tarquin, fils du roi, est l'élément déclencheur de la révolution. La tradition mentionne deux noms supplémentaires : Lucretius Tricipitinus, père de la victime, et Valerius Publicola, dont l'existence est attestée par la découverte d'une inscription sur un bloc de tuf (le lapis Satricanus). Selon les annalistes, Tarquin le Superbe est renversé parce qu'il use de ses pouvoirs pour instituer une tyrannie (il multiplie les exécutions arbitraires) et qu'il gouverne seul sans tenir compte du Sénat. C’est cette atteinte à la souveraineté du Sénat, plutôt qu’une tyrannie intolérable, qui pousse les patriciens - d’avantage que le peuple entier - à chasser le dernier roi. Comme le suggère la légende, cette monarchie historique est probablement très vite remplacée et les changements les plus importants qui ont lieu immédiatement après concernent le responsable de l’exécutif. Le Sénat décide d'élire deux chefs, appelés « préteurs » (les magistrats romains qui deviennent le consulat républicain). Les consuls possèdent les mêmes pouvoirs que le roi, avec deux limitations : chacun a un droit de veto sur les actes de son collègue et le mandat de leur magistrature est limité à une seule année. Ces deux restrictions limitent leur pouvoir et réduisent les risques d'établissement d'une autre tyrannie.

According to tradition, Junius Brutus, the nephew of the last king, Tarquin the Superb, was the founder of the Roman Republic in 509 BC, along with Tarquin Collatin, a member of the Tarquin family and husband of Lucrezia, whose rape by Sextus Tarquin, the king's son, was the catalyst for the revolution. Tradition mentions two more names: Lucretius Tricipitinus, the victim's father, and Valerius Publicola, whose existence is attested by the discovery of an inscription on a block of tufa (lapis Satricanus). According to the annalists, Tarquin the Superb was overthrown because he used his powers to institute a tyranny (he increased the number of arbitrary executions) and ruled alone without taking the Senate into account. It was this infringement of the Senate's sovereignty, rather than an intolerable tyranny, that prompted the patricians - rather than the people as a whole - to oust the last king. As the legend suggests, this historic monarchy was probably replaced very quickly and the most important changes that took place immediately afterwards concerned the head of the executive. The Senate decided to elect two chiefs, known as ‘praetors’ (the Roman magistrates who became the republican consulate). The consuls had the same powers as the king, with two limitations: each had the right to veto the actions of his colleague and their term of office was limited to a single year. These two restrictions limited their power and reduced the risk of another tyranny being established. The first years after the expulsion of the last king, when Rome replaced monarchy with two annually elected consuls and a Senate dominated by a closed circle of patrician families. Power over priesthoods, law and office was monopolised by that group, and plebeian resentment at debt-bondage and exclusion soon produced the long Conflict of the Orders. The traditions of this moment, from Brutus to the war with Lars Porsenna, were later told as founding legends of Roman liberty.

Years of blocked elections and agitation ended with the Licinio-Sextian laws, which required that one consul each year be a plebeian and capped how much public land any citizen could hold. The patrician monopoly on Rome's highest office was broken, and over the following decades plebeians gained access to the other magistracies and priesthoods. The result was not democracy but a new mixed nobility of office-holding families that would govern the Republic through its conquest of the Mediterranean.

Crises patricio-plébéiennes (Rome, 366 B.label: Crises patricio-plébéiennes
Crises patricio-plébéiennes (Rome, 366 B.prose:
[Rome, 366 BC–287 BC] Crises patricio-plébéiennes. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. **Guerre des ordres patriciens et plébéiens (-367 à -287 AEC)**
Cette période voit l’émergence de tendances alarmantes pour l'équilibre politique de l’État, tel que le rapprochement continu des tribuns et des sénateurs. Le Sénat commence à donner aux tribuns un réel pouvoir, tel que la reconnaissance officielle de leur droit de veto. Les tribuns se sentent alors redevables au Sénat. Comme les tribuns et les sénateurs se rapprochent de plus en plus, les sénateurs plébéiens sont souvent en mesure de réserver le tribunat aux membres de leurs propres familles. De plus, en 342 av. J.-C., deux lois importantes sont ratifiées : la première rend illégal le fait de cumuler les magistratures, la deuxième impose un délai de dix ans avant la réélection à une même magistrature. Ces deux lois introduisent un nouveau point faible dans le fonctionnement des institutions, qui peut éventuellement être interprété comme l’amorce du déclin de la République et facilite l’avènement de l’Empire.

War between the patrician and plebeian orders (-367 to -287 AEC) This period saw the emergence of alarming trends for the political balance of the state, such as the continued rapprochement of the tribunes and senators. The Senate began to give the tribunes real power, such as the official recognition of their right of veto. The tribunes then felt indebted to the Senate. As tribunes and senators became increasingly close, plebeian senators were often able to reserve the tribune seat for members of their own families. In addition, in 342 BC, two important laws were ratified: the first made it illegal to hold more than one magistracy, and the second imposed a ten-year time limit on re-election to the same magistracy. These two laws introduced a new weakness into the functioning of the institutions, which could be interpreted as the beginning of the decline of the Republic and facilitated the advent of the Empire. The closing rounds of the struggle between patricians and plebeians, opened by the Licinio-Sextian laws that reserved a consulship for plebeians and capped holdings of public land. Successive measures abolished debt-bondage, opened the priesthoods, and finally, with the Lex Hortensia, made resolutions of the plebeian assembly binding on all Romans. The outcome was not democracy but a merged patrician-plebeian nobility that would govern Rome through its wars of conquest.

Lois licinio-sextiennes (Rome, 366 BC–35.label: Lois licinio-sextiennes
Lois licinio-sextiennes (Rome, 366 BC–35.prose:
[Rome, 366 BC–350 BC] Lois licinio-sextiennes. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Les **lois licinio-sextiennes (Leges Liciniae Sextiae)** sont des lois romaines votées en -367 AEC. et qui prennent effet l'année suivante, en -366. Ces lois portent le nom de leurs deux auteurs, les tribuns de la plèbe Caius Licinius Stolon et Lucius Sextius Lateranus.
Elles restaurent définitivement le consulat, dont obligatoirement un des deux magistrats suprêmes doit être plébéien, elles imposent une limitation des possessions de l'ager publicus, et elles comprennent sûrement quelques dispositions pour diminuer les charges pesant sur les débiteurs.

The **Licinio-Sextian Laws (Leges Liciniae Sextiae)** were Roman laws passed in -367 BC and came into effect the following year, -366. These laws were named after their two authors, the tribunes of the plebs Caius Licinius Stolon and Lucius Sextius Lateranus. They definitively restored the consulship, in which one of the two supreme magistrates had to be a plebeian, they imposed a limit on the possessions of the ager publicus, and they certainly included a few provisions to reduce the burdens on debtors. After a decade of obstruction by two plebeian tribunes, Rome adopted laws opening the consulship to plebeians, capping the amount of public land any one man could hold, and easing debts. They broke the patrician monopoly on the highest office and set the shape of Republican politics, in which a mixed noble class competed for annual magistracies. The land clauses would be invoked again by the Gracchi two centuries later.

Lex Ogulnia (Rome, 299 BC–287 BC).label: Lex Ogulnia
Lex Ogulnia (Rome, 299 BC–287 BC).prose:
[Rome, 299 BC–287 BC] Lex Ogulnia. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Vers un statut politique égal entre plébéiens et patriciens.
La **lex Ogulnia** est une loi romaine adoptée en 300 av. J.-C. qui a ouvert les différents sacerdoces aux plébéiens (aux fonctions religieuses de pontifes et d’augures).  Elle fut une étape importante dans la longue lutte entre les plébéiens (plebs) et les patriciens (patricii) et vit l'abolition d'un des derniers privilèges des patriciens. Elle constitue une étape majeure dans l'élaboration des institutions patricio-plébéiennes de la République romaine.

Towards equal political status for plebeians and patricians. The **lex Ogulnia** was a Roman law passed in 300 BC that opened up the various priesthoods to plebeians (to the religious functions of pontiffs and augurs).  It was an important step in the long struggle between the plebeians (plebs) and the patricians (patricii) and saw the abolition of one of the last privileges of the patricians. It was a major stage in the development of the patricio-plebeian institutions of the Roman Republic. Thanks to Polybius, Titus Livius and Cicero, supplemented and sometimes corrected by numerous other authors and inscriptions, the institutions of republican Rome are well known to us from the Lex Hortensia of 287 BC, which made the laws enacted by the assembly of the plebs binding on all citizens. Despite certain changes and various disorders that arose from the Gracchus tribunate in 133 BC onwards, the general principles that governed Roman political life and the management of the Empire remained fairly stable until Caesar's dictatorship and his assassination in 44 BCE.

Institutions patricio-plébéiennes (Rome,.prose:
[Rome, 286 BC–133 BC] Institutions patricio-plébéiennes. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Promulguée en -287, la **Lex Hortensia**, connue également sous l'appellation de lois hortensiennes, est le résultat d'un conflit entre les patriciens et les plébéiens nommé le conflit des ordres.
La plèbe se retire sur le Janicule pour obtenir l’assignation des terres sabines nouvellement conquises. Quintus Hortensius, nommé dictateur et soutenu par Manius Curius Dentatus, promulgue les lois Hortensiennes qui favorisent la plèbe pour qu’elle revienne dans la cité. Elles amnistient et allègent les dettes et donnent aux plébiscites décidés par les concilia plebis force de loi pour le peuple entier (suppression de la ratification sénatoriale traditionnelle, l’auctoritas patrum[réf. Nécessaire]).
Le conseil de la plèbe obtient le droit de faire voter un **plébiscite** ( proclamé ou discuter sur une loi par le peuple sans passer par les autres ordres ).
Gräce à Polybe, Tite-Live et Cicéron, complétés et parfois corrigés par de nombreux autres auteurs et par des inscriptions, les institutions de la Rome républicaine nous sont bien connues depuis la /ex Hortensia de 287 av. J.-C. qui rendit contraignantes pour tous les citoyens les lois promulguées par l'assemblée de la plébe. En dépit de certains changements et de divers désordres survenus à partir du tribunat de Ti. Gracchus en 133 av. J.-C., les principes généraux qui régissaient la vie politique romaine et la gestion de l'Empire restèrent assez stables jusqu'à la dictature de César et à son assassinat en 44.

Promulgated in 287 BC, the **Lex Hortensia**, also known as the Hortensian Laws, was the result of a conflict between the patricians and plebeians known as the Conflict of Orders. The plebs withdrew to the Janiculum to obtain the assignment of the newly conquered Sabine lands. Quintus Hortensius, appointed dictator and supported by Manius Curius Dentatus, promulgated the Hortensian laws, which favoured the plebs to return to the city. They granted amnesty and debt relief and gave the plebiscites decided by the concilia plebis the force of law for the entire people (abolition of the traditional senatorial ratification, the auctoritas patrum [ref. Necessary]). The council of the plebs obtained the right to vote a **plebiscite** (proclaimed or discussed on a law by the people without going through the other orders). Thanks to Polybius, Titus Livius and Cicero, supplemented and sometimes corrected by numerous other authors and inscriptions, the institutions of republican Rome are well known to us from the /ex Hortensia of 287 BC, which made the laws enacted by the assembly of the plebs binding on all citizens. Despite certain changes and various disorders that arose from the time of Ti. Gracchus in 133 BC, the general principles governing Roman political life and the management of the Empire remained fairly stable until Caesar's dictatorship and his assassination in 44.

After the last of the plebeian secessions, decisions of the plebeian assembly became binding on all Romans, formally ending the long struggle between the orders. In practice power settled on a mixed nobility of patrician and rich plebeian families who monopolised the consulship and the Senate. Under this arrangement Rome conquered Italy, defeated Carthage and took over the eastern Mediterranean, until the strains of empire broke into open violence with the Gracchi.
