Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie qui présente les institutions et leurs représentants dans le monde romain-byzantin. À partir de l'année de la fondation de Rome par Romulus (l'Ab Urbe Condita a été définie par le moine Denys le Petit). Jusqu'au jour de la chute de Constantinople et à la mort de Constantin XI Paléologue, Dragasès.

Les 3 régimes successifs la Monarchie, la République, puis l'Empire sont présentés en différentes périodes.
Ces périodes sont thématiques suivant les différents critères que sont l'origine et la famille du régnant, l’évolution du droit et la modification des institutions du régime en place.
Cette chronologie n'est pas exhaustive. Les mandats annuels des consuls, les règnes de moins d'un an ou dans une succession chaotique ne sont pas présentés.
Cette chronologie est numérique. Pour des raisons techniques, certaines dates de fin son différentes des dates historiques pour donner la priorité de la date à la date de début de la période suivante. Les dates historiques sont indiquées dans les descriptions des périodes.

Les informations assemblées et présentées sont issues des sources ouvertes suivantes : Adalberto GIOVANNINI, Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, Library of Congress, Ministère de l'éducation nationale, Wikipedia. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

In the years between the destruction of Carthage and Corinth and the tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus, Rome mastered the Mediterranean and began to be pulled apart by its own success. Plunder and slaves poured in, great estates squeezed out smallholders who were also the army's recruiting pool, and a slave war erupted in Sicily. Gracchus's land bill and his murder in 133 BC opened a century of political violence that would end the Republic.
Vers la crise de la République (Rome, 14.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43.node: Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43 BC)
Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43.label: Crise de la République
Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43.prose:
[Rome, 132 BC–43 BC] Crise de la République. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Rome est devenue la première puissance du bassin méditerranéen, mais les guerres longues et lointaines et les conquêtes sont sources de tensions sociales : le système du paysan-soldat n’est plus adapté, le blé à bas prix qui afflue de Sicile, de Sardaigne, puis d'Afrique ruine les petits propriétaires, les classes populaires s’appauvrissent.
Le clivage patricien/plébéien s’est effacé de la vie politique, mais la classe sénatoriale monopolise le pouvoir politique et la richesse foncière, et s’oppose aux affairistes de l’ordre équestre, négociants, publicains et banquiers enrichis par l’exploitation des provinces.

Rome had become the leading power in the Mediterranean basin, but long and distant wars and conquests were a source of social tension: the peasant-soldier system was no longer appropriate, cheap wheat from Sicily, Sardinia and Africa was ruining small landowners, and the working classes were becoming poorer. The patrician/plebeian divide had disappeared from political life, but the senatorial class monopolised political power and land wealth, and opposed the businessmen of the equestrian order, merchants, publicans and bankers enriched by the exploitation of the provinces.

Credit : Adalberto Giovannini « Les institutions de la République romaine des origines à la mort d’Auguste ». (2015). Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Beginning with the murder of Tiberius Gracchus, Roman politics turned repeatedly to street violence, proscription and civil war as generals with loyal armies—Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar—outgrew the institutions meant to contain them. Land hunger, the demands of Italian allies and slave revolts strained a city-state constitution now governing a Mediterranean empire. The killing of Caesar solved nothing, and the triumvirs' proscriptions of 43 BC closed the era of genuine republican rule.
Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Tribunats des Gracques (Rome, 132 BC–120.label: Tribunats des Gracques
Tribunats des Gracques (Rome, 132 BC–120.prose:
[Rome, 132 BC–120 BC] Tribunats des Gracques. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. **Gracques** est le nom donné à deux frères et hommes d'État romains, Tiberius Gracchus et Caius Gracchus, connus pour leur tentative infructueuse de réformer le système social romain durant la deuxième moitié du IIe siècle av. J.-C. : Tiberius en 133 av. J.-C., puis Caius entre 123 et 121.

**Grachicus** is the name given to two brothers and Roman statesmen, Tiberius Gracchus and Caius Gracchus, who were known for their unsuccessful attempts to reform the Roman social system during the second half of the 2nd century BC: Tiberius in 133 BC, then Caius between 123 and 121. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Tiberius and then Gaius Gracchus used the tribunate to push land redistribution, grain subsidies and court reform past a hostile Senate, appealing directly to the popular assembly. Both were killed by their opponents, Tiberius clubbed down on the Capitol and Gaius dying in a bloodbath on the Aventine. Political murder had entered Roman public life, and the split between populares and optimates opened here would run all the way to the civil wars and the end of the Republic.
Tribunats des Gracques (Rome, 132 BC–120.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Nerva (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98).label: Nerva
Nerva (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98] Nerva. **Règne du 18 septembre 96 au 27 janvier 98 (1 an)**.
Proclamé empereur par le Sénat après le meurtre de Domitien.

**Reigned from 18 September 96 to 27 January 98 (1 year)**.
Proclaimed emperor by the Senate after the murder of Domitian. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An elderly senator raised to the throne after Domitian's assassination, he governed briefly and uneasily, hemmed in by a Praetorian Guard that forced him to hand over Domitian's killers. His lasting act was to adopt the general Trajan as his heir, a choice that steadied the state and gave Rome its succession of "adoptive" emperors. The precedent — merit rather than birth, at least in appearance — shaped nearly a century of comparatively stable rule.
Nerva (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Lucius Aurelius Verus (Roman Empire, AD.label: Lucius Aurelius Verus
Lucius Aurelius Verus (Roman Empire, AD.prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 161–AD 169] Lucius Aurelius Verus. **Règne du 7 mars 161 à janvier 169 (~ 7 ans)**.
Fils adoptif et héritier d'Antonin le Pieux. Co-empereur avec Marc Aurèle jusqu'à sa mort.

**Reigned from 7 March 161 to January 169 (~ 7 years)**.
Adopted son and heir of Antoninus the Pious. Co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius until his death. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Adopted alongside Marcus Aurelius, he became Rome's first co-emperor, an experiment in shared rule that would be repeated for centuries. He nominally commanded the long war against Parthia in the east, whose returning armies carried back the devastating Antonine Plague. He died of a stroke while campaigning on the Danube.
Lucius Aurelius Verus (Roman Empire, AD.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Caracalla (Roman Empire, AD 211–AD 216).label: Caracalla
Caracalla (Roman Empire, AD 211–AD 216).prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 211–AD 216] Caracalla. **Règne de 198 au 8 avril 217 (~ 19 ans)**.
Coempereur avec **Sévère** depuis 198, avec Sévère et **Geta** de 209 à février 211, avec Geta jusqu'en décembre 211.

**Reigned from 198 to 8 April 217 (~ 19 years)**.
Co-emperor with **Severus** from 198, with Severus and **Geta** from 209 to February 211, with Geta until December 211. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

He came to power alongside his brother Geta and secured it by having him murdered, then bought the army's loyalty with huge pay rises. His Antonine Constitution granted Roman citizenship to nearly every free inhabitant of the empire, ending a distinction that had shaped provincial life for centuries. He also left Rome its most spectacular bath complex, and was cut down by his own soldiers on campaign in the east.
Caracalla (Roman Empire, AD 211–AD 216).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère.label: Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère (Orient)
Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère.prose:
[Roman Empire, AD 305–AD 306] Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère (Orient). Constance Chlore : **Règne du 1er mai 305 au 25 juillet 306 (~1 an)**. Adopté en tant que « César » de l'Occident et héritier par Maximien en 293 « Auguste » de l'Occident jusqu'en 306.
Galère : **Règne du 1er mai 305 – mai 311 (~ 6 ans)**. Adopté en tant que « César » de l'Orient et héritier par Dioclétien de 293 à 305 « Auguste » de l'Orient de 305 à 307.

Constantius Chlorus: **Reigned from 1 May 305 to 25 July 306 (~1 year)**. Adopted as ‘Caesar’ of the West and heir by Maximian in 293 ‘Augustus’ of the West until 306.
Galerius: **Reign from 1 May 305 - May 311 (~ 6 years)**. Adopted as ‘Caesar’ of the East and heir by Diocletian from 293 to 305 ‘Augustus’ of the East from 305 to 307. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The tetrarchy's first test: after Diocletian and Maximian stepped down together, power passed to their deputies, who divided the empire between a western and an eastern Augustus. It lasted barely a year. When Constantius died at York in 306 his troops proclaimed his son Constantine, wrecking the orderly succession Diocletian had designed and opening two decades of civil war.
Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient.node: Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient (Byzantine Empire, AD 477–AD 517)
Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient.label: Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient
Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 477–AD 517] Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient. **Empire byzantin - Empire romain d’Orient** : À l'Est, l'Empire romain d'Orient fut confronté aux migrations de nombreux peuples venus d'Asie et d'Europe du Nord. Toutefois, la partie orientale de l'empire n'avait pas connu l'exode qui avait dépeuplé les villes de la partie occidentale et sa prospérité économique lui permit d'acheter la paix. Théodose II (401-450) fortifia les murailles de Constantinople. Elles résistèrent à tous les assauts jusqu'en 1204.
**Antiquité tardive** : Période de l’histoire européenne et méditerranéenne qui commence à la fin du IIIe siècle mais dont le terme est beaucoup plus flou. Elle n’est employée qu’en référence aux pays ayant appartenu au monde romain : les régions d’Europe occidentale, orientale et méridionale, d’Asie et d’Afrique autour du bassin méditerranéen mais se prolonge bien au-delà de la fin de l’Empire romain d’Occident en 476.

**Byzantine Empire - Eastern Roman Empire**: In the east, the Eastern Roman Empire was faced with the migration of many peoples from Asia and Northern Europe. However, the eastern part of the empire had not experienced the exodus that had depopulated the cities of the western part, and its economic prosperity enabled it to buy peace. Theodosius II (401-450) fortified the walls of Constantinople. They withstood all assaults until 1204. **Late Antiquity**: A period in European and Mediterranean history that began at the end of the 3rd century, but for which the term is much more vague. It is only used in reference to countries that once belonged to the Roman world: the regions of Western, Eastern and Southern Europe, Asia and Africa around the Mediterranean basin, but extends well beyond the end of the Western Roman Empire in 476. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

With the western provinces gone, the eastern half of the Roman Empire carried on from Constantinople with its taxes, bureaucracy and Latin legal tradition intact. Emperors such as Anastasius left a full treasury while the church tore itself apart over the nature of Christ, splitting Egypt and Syria from the capital. This was the platform from which Justinian would launch his attempt to reunite the Roman world.
Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Empire byzantin - Empire romain universe.node: Empire byzantin - Empire romain universel (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 716)
Empire byzantin - Empire romain universe.label: Empire byzantin - Empire romain universel
Empire byzantin - Empire romain universe.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 716] Empire byzantin - Empire romain universel. Justinien est parfois considéré comme le dernier empereur romain, avant que l'Empire byzantin (Empire romain d'Orient) ne commence à se différencier de l'Empire romain dont il est le continuateur direct. Il est le dernier empereur à chercher à rétablir l'unité et l'universalité de l'Empire romain, ce qui l'amène à mener des guerres expansionnistes, principalement en Italie et en Afrique, tout en défendant victorieusement les frontières contre les Perses ou les Slaves. 
Jusqu'à l'avènement d'Héraclius en 610, l'Empire romain d'Orient est la continuation directe de l'Empire romain qu'il tente de reconstituer, guidé dans cette politique par la volonté de retrouver son imperium (« emprise, contrôle, souveraineté ») sur l’Orbis romana (« monde romain »). Toutefois, le fait que l'Empire romain d'Orient règne principalement sur des régions où c'est le grec qui sert de langue commune et qui sont profondément christianisées, en fait un État original combinant structure romaine de l'État, culture hellénique et foi chrétienne.

Justinian is sometimes regarded as the last Roman emperor, before the Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) began to differentiate itself from the Roman Empire, of which he was the direct successor. He was the last emperor to seek to re-establish the unity and universality of the Roman Empire, which led him to wage expansionist wars, mainly in Italy and Africa, while successfully defending the borders against the Persians and Slavs. 
Until the advent of Heraclius in 610, the Eastern Roman Empire was a direct continuation of the Roman Empire, which it attempted to reconstitute, guided in this policy by the desire to regain its imperium (‘hold, control, sovereignty’) over the Orbis romana (‘Roman world’). However, the fact that the Eastern Roman Empire reigned mainly over regions where Greek was the common language and which were deeply Christianised made it an original state combining Roman state structure, Hellenic culture and Christian faith. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Justinian's reconquests briefly restored Roman rule over Italy, North Africa and southern Spain, and his jurists compiled the Corpus Juris Civilis that became the foundation of European law. Hagia Sophia was raised in five years as the largest domed interior in the world. Plague, exhaustion and then the Persian and Arab wars stripped away most of these gains within a century, leaving an empire fighting for survival.
Empire byzantin - Empire romain universe.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Dynastie Justiniens (Byzantine Empire, A.label: Dynastie Justiniens
Dynastie Justiniens (Byzantine Empire, A.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 609] Dynastie Justiniens. La dynastie justinienne est une dynastie ayant régné sur l'Empire byzantin de 518 à 610. Fondée par Justin Ier, elle se termine avec Maurice. Les prénoms « Justin », « Justinien » et « Germanus » y sont courants.

The Justinian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 518 to 610. Founded by Justin I, it ended with Maurice. The first names ‘Justin’, ‘Justinian’ and ‘Germanus’ were common. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Justinian I dominates the period: he codified Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots, and reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, at ruinous cost and just before the plague of 541 emptied the treasury and the countryside. His successors, Justin II, Tiberius, and the capable Maurice, struggled to hold Italy against the Lombards and the Balkans against Avars and Slavs while fighting Persia. Maurice's murder by the soldier Phokas opened the crisis that ended the dynasty.
Dynastie Justiniens (Byzantine Empire, A.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Justin Ier (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD.label: Justin Ier
Justin Ier (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 526] Justin Ier. **Règne du 10 juillet 518 au 1er août 527 (9 ans)**.
Général de basse extraction proclamé empereur par acclamation sur proposition du Sénat à la suite de la mort sans héritier d'Anastase Ier. Associa à son trône son neveu Justinien.

**Reigned from 10 July 518 to 1 August 527 (9 years)**. General of low extraction proclaimed emperor by acclamation on the proposal of the Senate following the death of Anastasius I without heir. He associated his nephew Justinian with his throne. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An illiterate Balkan peasant who rose through the palace guard and was acclaimed emperor in his late sixties, Justin ended the Acacian Schism and restored communion between Constantinople and Rome after nearly forty years of rupture. His most consequential act was promoting his nephew Justinian, who effectively ran the government and succeeded him.
Justin Ier (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Phocas (Byzantine Empire, AD 602–AD 609).label: Phocas
Phocas (Byzantine Empire, AD 602–AD 609).prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 602–AD 609] Phocas. **Règne du 23 novembre 602 au 5 octobre 610 (7 ans)**.
Soldat dans l'armée des Balkans, usurpateur désigné par ses troupes révoltées.

**Reigned from 23 November 602 to 5 October 610 (7 years)**.
Soldier in the Balkan army, usurper appointed by his revolting troops. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A junior officer raised to the throne by mutinying Danube troops, whose reign began with the murder of Emperor Maurice and ended with his own public dismemberment. The Balkans were abandoned to Slavs and Avars while the Persians overran the eastern provinces, using Maurice's death as their pretext. His overthrow by Heraclius left an empire in crisis that would soon face the Arab conquests.
Phocas (Byzantine Empire, AD 602–AD 609).source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Dynastie Héraclides (Byzantine Empire, A.label: Dynastie Héraclides
Dynastie Héraclides (Byzantine Empire, A.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 610–AD 694] Dynastie Héraclides. La dynastie des Héraclides (610 – 711) a vu se succéder six empereurs qui ont régné pendant un siècle, allant du fondateur de la dynastie, Héraclius (610–641), jusqu’au deuxième renversement de Justinien II en 711.

The Heraclian dynasty (610 - 711) was succeeded by six emperors who reigned for a century, from the founder of the dynasty, Heraclius (610-641), to the second overthrow of Justinian II in 711. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Heraclius overthrew Phokas, fought a desperate war that destroyed Sasanian Persia and recovered the True Cross, and then watched the exhausted empire lose Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa to the Arab conquests within a generation. What survived was a smaller, poorer, more militarised state organised around the themes, with Greek replacing Latin as the language of government and Constantinople twice holding off Arab siege. The religious compromises attempted in these years, monothelitism above all, deepened the split with Rome and the eastern churches.
Dynastie Héraclides (Byzantine Empire, A.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Constantin IV Pogonate (Byzantine Empire.label: Constantin IV Pogonate
Constantin IV Pogonate (Byzantine Empire.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 668–AD 684] Constantin IV Pogonate. **Règne du 15 septembre 668 au 14 septembre 685 (16 ans)**.
Règne après l'assassinat de son père Constant II, défait l'usurpateur Mézézios en Sicile.

**Reigned from 15 September 668 to 14 September 685 (16 years)**.
Reigns after the assassination of his father Constant II, defeats the usurper Mezezios in Sicily. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Constantinople survived years of Arab attack, and Greek fire, the empire's incendiary secret weapon, made its terrifying debut against enemy fleets. With the eastern threat blunted, the emperor summoned the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which condemned monothelitism and healed the rift with Rome. In the Balkans, though, he was forced to recognise a new Bulgar state south of the Danube.
Constantin IV Pogonate (Byzantine Empire.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Anarchie impériale (Byzantine Empire, AD.label: Anarchie impériale
Anarchie impériale (Byzantine Empire, AD.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 695–AD 716] Anarchie impériale. L’expression « Anarchie impériale » est utilisée en français pour désigner la période de grande instabilité politique à laquelle fut confrontée l’Empire byzantin lorsque plusieurs empereurs se succédèrent sur le trône entre la dynastie des Héraclides et la dynastie des Isauriens entre 695 et 717.

The Twenty Years' Anarchy is a historiographic term used by some modern scholars for the period of acute internal instability in the Byzantine Empire marked by the rapid succession of several emperors to the throne between the first deposition of Justinian II in 695 and the ascent of Leo III the Isaurian to the throne in 717, marking the beginning of the Isaurian dynasty. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Between the overthrow of Justinian II and the rise of Leo III, seven emperors seized and lost the Byzantine throne in barely twenty years, most ending blinded, mutilated or dead. Arab armies exploited the chaos, taking Carthage and raiding deep into Anatolia, and the empire lost North Africa for good. The turmoil ended only when Leo III took power and beat off the great Arab siege of Constantinople in 717-718.
Anarchie impériale (Byzantine Empire, AD.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénis.node: Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénisé (Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 1203)
Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénis.label: Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénisé
Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénis.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 1203] Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénisé. Cette période s’étend du début du VIIIe siècle jusqu’à la prise de Constantinople par les croisés en 1204 lors de la quatrième croisade. Elle vit une succession de reculs et d’expansions de l’Empire sous cinq dynasties : les Isauriens, les Amoriens, Macédoniens, les Comnènes et les Anges. Durant cette période, seuls les hellénophones des côtes, des grandes villes, de l'Hellade et d'Asie mineure occidentale (Grecs), les romanophones des Balkans (Dalmates, Valaques) et les arménophones d'Asie mineure orientale (Arméniens) se considérèrent encore comme des Romains (en grec Ρωμαίoί ou « Romées »). L'état empire multinational se transforma ainsi en un empire plus homogène ethniquement, tandis que les institutions subirent de profondes transformations pour faire face aux diverses menaces.

This period stretched from the beginning of the 8th century until the capture of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204 during the Fourth Crusade. It saw a succession of retreats and expansions of the Empire under five dynasties: the Isaurians, the Amorians, the Macedonians, the Comnenes and the Angels. During this period, only the Greek-speaking people of the coasts, large cities, Helladia and western Asia Minor (Greeks), the Roman-speaking people of the Balkans (Dalmatians, Vlachs) and the Armenian-speaking people of eastern Asia Minor (Armenians) still considered themselves Romans (in Greek Ρωμαίoί or ‘Romées’). The multinational empire state was thus transformed into a more ethnically homogenous empire, while institutions underwent profound transformations to cope with the various threats. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The empire that emerged from the Arab onslaught was smaller, Greek-speaking and organised around military provinces, its army and administration rebuilt for permanent defence. It fought out the iconoclast controversy over religious images, then under the Macedonian emperors recovered territory in the Balkans and Syria and sent missionaries who brought Slavic peoples into Orthodox Christianity. The schism with Rome in 1054 and the defeat at Manzikert in 1071 opened the way to the Crusades and to the catastrophe of 1204.

His early death left his widow Irene as regent for their young son, and it was she who summoned the council that restored icon veneration.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 802–AD 812] Dynastie Nicéphoriens. La dynastie nicéphorienne de l'Empire byzantin a débuté après la déposition de l'impératrice Irène d'Athènes. Le trône de l'Empire byzantin passe à une dynastie relativement éphémère, la dynastie des Niképhores, du nom de son fondateur, Nicéphore Ier . 

The Nikephorian dynasty of the Byzantine Empire began following the deposition of the Empress Irene of Athens. The throne of the Byzantine Empire passed to a relatively short-lived dynasty, the Nikephorian dynasty, named after its founder, Nikephoros I. Nikephoros I seized power from the empress Irene and set about repairing state finances with unpopular new taxes and land registers, while resettling populations in the Balkans to reassert control there. His campaign against the Bulgar khan Krum ended in ambush and his own death in 811, his skull reportedly made into a drinking cup. His short-lived successors, including Michael I Rangabe, could not stop Krum and the throne passed to Leo the Armenian.

The imperial treasurer who overthrew the empress Irene and set about repairing Byzantine finances with a battery of unpopular new taxes and fiscal controls that chroniclers, mostly monks he had also taxed, remembered as 'vexations'. He resettled populations in the Balkans to rebuild imperial control there and refused to buy peace with the Bulgars. His army was ambushed and annihilated at the Vărbica pass, and Khan Krum had his skull mounted in silver as a drinking cup.

A pious, generous emperor raised to the throne after his father-in-law Nikephoros I was killed in battle against the Bulgars, Michael I spent his short reign trying and failing to contain Khan Krum. To win Frankish recognition of Byzantine rights in the Adriatic he acknowledged Charlemagne as basileus — a landmark concession that effectively admitted a second emperor in the West. His army's collapse at Versinikia ended him: he abdicated, was tonsured as a monk, and lived on quietly for decades while Leo V reopened the war on icons.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 867] Dynastie Amoriens (phrygienne). La dynastie amorienne fut fondée par Michel l’Amorien en 820. Elle règnera sur l'Empire byzantin jusqu’à l'assassinat de Michel III par son chambellan Basile le Macédonien en 867.

The Amorian dynasty was founded by Michael the Amorian in 820. It ruled the Byzantine Empire until Michael III was assassinated by his chamberlain Basil the Macedonian in 867. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Three emperors from Amorion in Phrygia presided over the last phase of iconoclasm and its abandonment: in 843 the empress Theodora restored the veneration of images in the ceremony still marked as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Militarily the period was hard, with the loss of Crete to Arab corsairs and the slow Muslim conquest of Sicily, yet Constantinople saw a revival of learning around Leo the Mathematician and dispatched Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs. It ended when Basil the Macedonian murdered his patron Michael III and seized the throne.

A rough-spoken soldier from Amorion who came to the throne by having his former comrade Leo V murdered in the palace chapel, founding a dynasty that lasted three generations. He spent his first years fighting the massive revolt of Thomas the Slav, which besieged Constantinople itself, and could not prevent Arab forces from seizing Crete and beginning the long conquest of Sicily. In religion he kept a moderate iconoclast line, persecuting little but refusing to restore the images.

Theophilos was the last emperor to enforce iconoclasm, banning religious images while presiding over a court famous for its luxury — golden automata, mechanical birds and a roaring lion beside the throne. He fought a grinding war with the Abbasid caliphate that culminated in the sack of Amorion, his family's ancestral city, and he rebuilt Constantinople's walls and founded new palaces. Within a year of his death his widow Theodora restored the icons for good, ending the controversy that had split the church for over a century.

Remembered by hostile later historians as 'the Drunkard', Michael presided over a genuine Byzantine revival. Iconoclasm was formally abandoned in 843, the empire went on the offensive against the Arabs, and the missions of Cyril and Methodius carried Slavonic Christianity to Moravia and Bulgaria while Patriarch Photios opened a lasting rift with Rome. He was assassinated in 867 by his favourite Basil the Macedonian, who took the throne and whose dynasty had every reason to blacken his memory.

Dynastie Macédoniens (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 867–AD 1057] Dynastie Macédoniens. La dynastie macédonienne régna pendant presque deux siècles à Constantinople, soit de 867 à 1057.
Elle doit son nom à son fondateur, Basile Ier qui naquit dans le thème byzantin de Macédoine (district administratif correspondant à la région d'Andrinople en Thrace). Elle a compté plus de vingt souverains.

The Macedonian dynasty ruled Constantinople for almost two centuries, from 867 to 1057. It owes its name to its founder, Basil I, who was born in the Byzantine theme of Macedonia (an administrative district corresponding to the region of Andrinople in Thrace). It has had more than twenty sovereigns. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Under Basil I's line the empire went on the offensive, retaking Crete, Antioch and much of Syria, and Basil II destroyed the Bulgarian state after decades of campaigning. It was also an age of law and letters, with the Basilika code, encyclopaedic compilations and a revival of classical art known as the Macedonian Renaissance, while missionaries drew the Rus and the Slavs into the Orthodox world. The dynasty's last decades saw the frontier armies neglected and the schism with Rome of 1054, leaving problems that broke out under its successors.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 1028–AD 1050] Zoé Porphyrogénète. **Règne du 11 novembre 1028  à juin 1050 (22 ans)**.
Fille du précédent. Après que Basile II ait tenté sans succès de la marier à l'empereur romain germanique Otton III, Constantin VIII l'oblige à épouser Romain Argyre. A la mort de ce dernier en 1034, elle épouse Michel le Paphlagonien, puis adopte le neveu de celui-ci Michel le Calfat, et épouse enfin Constantin Monomaque en 1042.

**Reigned from 11 November 1028 to June 1050 (22 years)**. Daughter of the previous king. After Basil II tried unsuccessfully to marry her off to the Germanic Roman Emperor Otto III, Constantine VIII forced her to marry Roman Argyre. On his death in 1034, she married Michael the Paphlagonian, then adopted his nephew Michael the Calfat, and finally married Constantine Monomachus in 1042. Born in the purple chamber as an emperor's daughter, Zoe inherited the Byzantine throne in middle age and passed imperial legitimacy to three successive husbands and an adopted son, none of whom could rule without her. A popular uprising in Constantinople restored her when one of them tried to shut her away in a convent, and she ended up reigning jointly with her sister Theodora. Her reign is famous for court intrigue, lavish spending, and the vivid, gossipy portrait left by the historian Michael Psellos.

An emperor of court intrigue, lavish building and learned patronage, who refounded the law school at Constantinople and endowed churches while the army was allowed to decay. [Byzantine Empire, AD 1056–AD 1057] Michel VI Bringas. **Règne du 31 août 1056 au 30 août 1057 (1 an)**.
Issu d'une famille de hauts fonctionnaires, logothète des armées, il est désigné comme le successeur de Théodora. Une rébellion militaire conduite par Isaac Comnène met un terme définitif à la dynastie macédonienne, après quoi l'empereur abdique pour finir ses jours dans un monastère.

**Reign from 31 August 1056 to 30 August 1057 (1 year)**. Born into a family of high-ranking civil servants and a logothete of the armies, he was designated as Theodora's successor. A military rebellion led by Isaac Comnenus put a definitive end to the Macedonian dynasty, after which the emperor abdicated to end his days in a monastery. An elderly palace treasurer handed the throne by the dying Empress Theodora, Michael VI was the last ruler of the Macedonian line's political settlement and the last chosen by the civil bureaucracy against the army's wishes. He insulted a delegation of generals seeking promotions and rewards, and they proclaimed Isaac Komnenos emperor within months. His forced abdication marked the moment the military aristocracy of Anatolia seized control of the empire's destiny.

As commander of the army of the East, he led a conspiracy of generals and defeated Michael VI's troops. He was crowned emperor by Patriarch Michael Cerularius after the latter had forced Michael VI to abdicate. A general raised to the purple by a revolt of the Anatolian military aristocracy against the civil bureaucracy of Constantinople, and the first of the Komnenos family to rule. He cut court expenditure, confiscated church and monastic property to refill the treasury, and forced the removal of the overmighty patriarch Michael Keroularios. Ill and politically isolated, he abdicated to a monastery after barely two years, but his family would return to dominate the empire for a century.

Dynastie Doukas (Byzantine Empire, AD 10.label: Dynastie Doukas
Dynastie Doukas (Byzantine Empire, AD 10.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1060–AD 1080] Dynastie Doukas. Les Doukas (en grec, masculin : Δούκας, féminin : Δούκαινα, pluriel : Δούκαι) forment une ou plusieurs familles ayant appartenu à l'aristocratie byzantine. Le nom apparaît dans les textes au IXe siècle, mais son origine est incertaine. Une branche régna sur l'Empire de 1059 à 1081. Le nom devint avec le temps synonyme de noblesse et fut associé à d'autres noms comme celui des Comnène et Doukas d'Épire et de Thessalonique. Les liens de parenté entre les générations sont souvent difficiles à établir ou douteux, de telle sorte qu'il est impossible d'affirmer avec certitude que tous les personnages ayant porté ce nom aient effectivement appartenu à une seule famille.

The Doukas (Greek, masculine: Δούκας, feminine: Δούκαινα, plural: Δούκαι) are one or more families who belonged to the Byzantine aristocracy. The name appears in texts in the ninth century, but its origin is uncertain. One branch ruled the Empire from 1059 to 1081. Over time, the name became synonymous with nobility and was associated with other names such as the Comnenes and Doukas of Epirus and Thessalonica. Intergenerational links are often difficult to establish or doubtful, so it is impossible to say with certainty that all the people who bore this name belonged to a single family. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A short, troubled dynasty of civilian aristocrats whose reduced spending on the army coincided with disaster: in 1071 the emperor Romanos IV was defeated and captured by the Seljuks at Manzikert, and Bari, the last Byzantine city in Italy, fell to the Normans the same year. Under Michael VII the coinage was debased, Anatolia was lost piecemeal to Turkish bands, and rival generals rose in revolt. The crisis ended only with the accession of Alexios I Komnenos.

Released by the sultan, he was overthrown, blinded and left to die, while the resulting civil wars let Turkish groups settle across Anatolia, permanently shrinking Byzantine power.

Michael VII took power in the wreckage of Manzikert and presided over the loss of Anatolia, as Turkish warbands settled the interior unopposed and Bari fell to the Normans, ending five centuries of Byzantine rule in Italy. Bookish and dominated by his ministers, he debased the coinage so badly that grain measures shrank and Constantinople nicknamed him "Parapinakes" — "minus a quarter." Revolts on every frontier drove him into a monastery, and his reign is usually taken as the low point from which the Komnenian recovery had to begin.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 1078–AD 1081] Nicéphore III Botaniatès. **Règne du 4 mars 1078 au 4 avril 1081 (3 ans)**.
Chef militaire ayant déjà participé au soulèvement de 1057 contre Michel VI, il se rebelle à nouveau en 1071 face à la dégradation de la situation en Anatolie à la suite de la bataille de Manzikert. Il se fait couronner empereur, contraint Michel Doukas à rentrer dans un monastère, et épouse Marie d'Alanie.

**Reigned from 4 March 1078 to 4 April 1081 (3 years)**.
A military leader who had already taken part in the 1057 uprising against Michael VI, he rebelled again in 1071 in the face of the deteriorating situation in Anatolia following the battle of Manzikert. He was crowned emperor, forced Michael Doukas to return to a monastery and married Mary of Alania. An elderly Anatolian general who marched on Constantinople and unseated Michael VII, inheriting an empire hollowed out after Manzikert. He faced constant revolts, bought off Turkish warbands with land and titles, and debased the coinage still further as Norman attacks began in the west. Alexios Komnenos deposed him within three years and packed him off to a monastery, beginning a dynasty that would stabilise the empire.

A boy emperor whose brief reign collapsed into factional struggle around his regent mother, the Latin princess Maria of Antioch. Resentment of Western merchants exploded in the 1182 massacre of Constantinople's Italian residents, and his cousin Andronikos seized power and had the child strangled. The murder ended the stable Komnenian succession and began the slide towards 1204.

Andronic Ier Comnène (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1183–AD 1185] Andronic Ier Comnène. **Règne de septembre 1183 au 12 septembre 1185 (2 ans)**.
Fils d'Isaac Komnenos, fils d'Alexios Ier. Renverse la régence d'Alexios II en avril 1182, est couronné co-empereur en 1183 et fait assassiner Alexios II peu après.

**Reign from September 1183 to September 12, 1185 (2 years)**.
Son of Isaac Komnenos, a son of Alexios I. Overthrew the regency of Alexios II in April 1182, crowned co-emperor in 1183 and shortly thereafter had Alexios II murdered. Andronikos I Komnenos seized power as regent for a child emperor and made himself sole ruler amid the massacre of Constantinople's Latin merchants. He terrorised the great landowning families with executions and confiscations while posing as a defender of the provincial poor. When a Norman army sacked Thessalonica, the city turned on him and he was torn apart by a mob — the violent end of the Komnenian dynasty that had held the empire together for a century.

Isaac II Ange (Byzantine Empire, AD 1185.label: Isaac II Ange
Isaac II Ange (Byzantine Empire, AD 1185.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1195] Isaac II Ange. **Règne du 12 septembre 1185 au 8 avril 1195 (9 ans)**.
Arrière-petit-fils d'Alexis Ier. Résiste à l'ordre d'arrestation d'Andronikos Ier, après quoi il est proclamé empereur par le peuple de Constantinople. Capture et tue Andronikos Ier.

**Reign from 12 September 1185 to 8 April 1195 (9 years)**.
Great-grandson of Alexios I. Resisted an order of arrest issued by Andronikos I, after which he was proclaimed emperor by the people of Constantinople. Captured and killed Andronikos I. Isaac II came to the throne when a Constantinople mob lynched the tyrannical Andronikos I. His reign saw a heavy tax revolt in Bulgaria that succeeded, re-establishing an independent Bulgarian state, and the awkward passage of Frederick Barbarossa's crusading army through Byzantine territory. Blinded and deposed by his own brother, his cause later gave the Fourth Crusade its pretext for turning on Constantinople.

Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée (Byzan.node: Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée (Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1260)
Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée (Byzan.label: Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée
Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée (Byzan.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1260] Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée. Vestige de l’Empire byzantin ayant résisté à la prise de Constantinople par les croisés en 1204, l’empire de Nicée, le plus étendu des États grecs, occupait, en Asie Mineure occidentale, une large bande de terre s’étendant de la mer Égée à la mer Noire. Si Nicée demeura sa capitale et le siège du patriarcat pendant toute sa brève histoire (1204-1261), les empereurs établirent leur résidence et le siège du gouvernement à Nymphaion (aujourd’hui Kemalpaşa), ville de Lydie, moins exposée aux armées ennemies.
Les historiens modernes reconnaissent la lignée des empereurs de la dynastie des Laskaris, régnant à Nicée, comme les empereurs romains légitimes pendant cette période, car l'Empire nicéen a fini par reprendre Constantinople. Pour d'autres lignées d'empereurs prétendants, voir Liste des empereurs trapézantins et Liste des empereurs thessaliens.

A remnant of the Byzantine Empire that resisted the capture of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204, the Empire of Nicaea, the largest of the Greek states, occupied a wide strip of land in western Asia Minor stretching from the Aegean Sea to the Black Sea. While Nicaea remained its capital and the seat of the patriarchate throughout its brief history (1204-1261), the emperors established their residence and seat of government at Nymphaion (today's Kemalpaşa), a city in Lydia that was less exposed to enemy armies.
Modern historians recognize the line of emperors of the Laskaris dynasty, reigning in Nicaea, as the legitimate Roman emperors during this period because the Nicene Empire eventually retook Constantinople. For other lines of claimant emperors, see List of Trapezuntine emperors and List of Thessalonian emperors. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204 and carved the empire into Latin fiefs, driving the Byzantine court into exile. At Nicaea a rump state rebuilt an army, a treasury and a patriarchate, outmanoeuvred its rivals at Epirus and Trebizond, and cultivated learning at its provincial capital. In 1261 its troops walked into a lightly guarded Constantinople and restored the empire, though it never recovered its former strength.

Théodore Ier Lascaris (Byzantine Empire,.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1222] Théodore Ier Lascaris. **Règne du 19 mars 1205 à novembre 1222 (16 ans)**.
Gendre d'Alexis III. Époux d'Anna Komnène Angelina, fille d'Alexios III. Organise la résistance contre l'Empire latin à Nicée et est proclamé empereur en 1205 après la bataille d'Adrianople, couronné par le patriarche Michel IV le 6 avril 1208.

**Reigned from 19 March 1205 to November 1222 (16 years)**.
Son-in-law of Alexis III. Husband of Anna Komnene Angelina, a daughter of Alexios III. Organized resistance against the Latin Empire in Nicaea and proclaimed emperor in 1205 after the Battle of Adrianople, crowned by Patriarch Michael IV on 6 April 1208. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

After the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, he gathered Byzantine refugees in western Anatolia and built a functioning state at Nicaea, having himself crowned emperor by a patriarch in exile. He fought off the Latin emperors, the Seljuks of Rum and rival Greek claimants, defeating and killing the sultan in single combat at Antioch on the Meander. The realm he founded became the base from which the Byzantines retook their capital in 1261.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 1222–AD 1254] Jean III Doukas Vatatzès. **Règne du 15 décembre 1222 au 3 novembre 1254 (32 ans)**.
Gendre du précédent. Époux d'Irene Laskarina, fille de Théodore I.

**Reigned from 15 December 1222 to 3 November 1254 (32 years)**.
Son-in-law of the former. Husband of Irene Laskarina, a daughter of Theodore I. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Ruling the Empire of Nicaea while Latin crusaders held Constantinople, he expanded into Thrace, Macedonia and the Aegean islands, reducing the Latin emperors to little more than their capital. He is remembered for careful economic management — encouraging farming, limiting luxury imports, filling the treasury — and for founding schools and hospitals. His work made the recapture of Constantinople a few years after his death possible, and the Orthodox Church later venerated him as a saint.

Emperor of the exiled Byzantine state at Nicaea, a scholar-ruler who wrote philosophy and promoted men of talent over the great landed families. He held off Bulgarian and Epirote challenges and strengthened the army, but chronic illness and quarrels with the aristocracy dogged his short reign. His death left a child heir, whom Michael Palaiologos pushed aside before recapturing Constantinople.

A boy emperor of Nicaea who never really ruled: the general Michael Palaiologos made himself co-emperor and monopolised power. After Michael's forces retook Constantinople in 1261, he had the eleven-year-old blinded and shut away in a fortress. The patriarch excommunicated him for it, and the crime shadowed the legitimacy of the Palaiologan dynasty for generations.

Empire byzantin tardif (Byzantine Empire.label: Empire byzantin tardif
Empire byzantin tardif (Byzantine Empire.prose:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1261–AD 1453] Empire byzantin tardif. L'Empire byzantin a été gouverné par la dynastie des Paléologues entre 1261 et 1453, depuis la restauration de l'autorité byzantine à Constantinople par l'usurpateur Michel VIII Paléologue après sa reprise à l'Empire latin, fondé après la quatrième croisade (1204), jusqu'à la chute de Constantinople aux mains de l'Empire ottoman. Cette période est connue sous le nom d'Empire byzantin tardif.

The Byzantine Empire was ruled by the Palaiologos dynasty in the period between 1261 and 1453, from the restoration of Byzantine rule to Constantinople by the usurper Michael VIII Palaiologos following its recapture from the Latin Empire, founded after the Fourth Crusade (1204), up to the Fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire. This period is known as the late Byzantine Empire. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

After the recapture of Constantinople from the Latins, the restored empire under the Palaiologos dynasty was a shrunken state hemmed in by Serbs, Venetians and the rising Ottomans, wracked by civil wars and unable to pay for its own defence. Attempts to buy Western aid by submitting to the pope were rejected by most of the clergy and people. Yet these were decades of extraordinary art, learning and theological debate, and scholars fleeing westward carried Greek manuscripts into Italy, feeding the Renaissance.

History (Austria, AD 1–AD 2000).label: History
History (Austria, AD 1–AD 2000).prose:
[Austria, AD 1–AD 2000] History. History as opposed to prehistory. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The span in which the region enters the written record, first through Roman authors and inscriptions from the provinces of Noricum, Raetia and Pannonia, then through medieval charters and chronicles. Roman roads, forts and towns gave way to migration-period kingdoms, Carolingian marches, the Babenberg and Habsburg lands, and finally the modern republic. Archaeology here works alongside archives, so sites can often be tied to named people and events.

Prehistory (Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1).label: Prehistory
Prehistory (Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1).prose:
[Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1] Prehistory. Prehistory as opposed to history. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Runs from the earliest Palaeolithic occupation of the Danube corridor — including the mammoth hunters who carved the Venus of Willendorf — through Neolithic farming, copper mining in the Alps and the salt-and-iron wealth of the Hallstatt cemetery. Austria's Iron Age communities grew rich controlling Alpine salt and metal routes, and their culture was absorbed into the Roman Empire at the end of the period.
Prehistory (Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1).source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Early Middle Ages (Austria, AD 500–AD 11.prose:

The Visigothic kingdom governed the west of Iberia until Muslim armies crossed from North Africa in 711, making the region the Gharb of al-Andalus, with Islamic administration, agriculture and urban life in the south. From the ninth century Christian rulers from the north pushed the frontier back down the Douro and Mondego, repopulating Braga, Porto and Coimbra. The county of Portucale that emerged from this frontier zone became the kingdom of Portugal in the twelfth century.

Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 822).label: Avar Period
Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 822).prose:
[Austria, AD 568–AD 822] Avar Period. Period of Avar burials in Austria. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Horse-riding nomads from the Eurasian steppe built a khaganate centred on the Carpathian basin, drawing tribute from Byzantium and pressing Slavic peoples westward into the Alpine lands. Their graves are unmistakable: warriors buried with their mounts, cast bronze belt fittings covered in griffins and tendrils, stirrups and composite bows. Charlemagne's Frankish campaigns from 791 broke the khaganate and plundered its legendary treasure ring, leaving the region open to Frankish and Slavic settlement.
Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 822).source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Early Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 63.label: Early Avar Period
Early Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 63.prose:
[Austria, AD 568–AD 630] Early Avar Period. Early Avar Period in Austria. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Steppe horsemen from Inner Asia seized the Carpathian Basin after the Lombards left for Italy and built a khaganate that extracted tribute and gold from Constantinople for decades. Their graves are unmistakable: warriors buried with their horses, stirrups, composite bows and pressed gold ornaments, alongside farming Slavic and local populations they dominated. The failed siege of Constantinople in 626 broke Avar prestige and ended the period of expansion.
Early Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 63.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Middle Avar Period (Austria, AD 630–AD 6.label: Middle Avar Period
Middle Avar Period (Austria, AD 630–AD 6.prose:
[Austria, AD 630–AD 680] Middle Avar Period. Dated after P. Stadler 2010. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

After the failed Avar siege of Constantinople in 626 cut off the flow of Byzantine tribute, burial customs in the Carpathian Basin changed: gold gave way to different ornaments and new metalwork styles, and fresh groups from the eastern steppe appear to have arrived. Graves from this phase are a key argument in the long debate over whether the Avar realm was reinforced by newcomers. It bridges the early Avar khaganate and the later griffin-and-tendril horizon.
Middle Avar Period (Austria, AD 630–AD 6.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Late Avar Period (Austria, AD 680–AD 822.label: Late Avar Period
Late Avar Period (Austria, AD 680–AD 822.prose:
[Austria, AD 680–AD 822] Late Avar Period. Dated after P. Stadler 2010. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The Avar khaganate in the Carpathian basin settled into a dense agricultural society, buried with the cast bronze belt sets whose griffin and tendril ornament defines the era. Cemeteries of thousands of graves show a mixed population of steppe descendants and local farmers. Charlemagne's campaigns from 791 destroyed the khaganate's power and looted its treasure, opening the region to Frankish and later Slavic control.

Carolingian Era (Austria, AD 751–AD 919).label: Carolingian Era
Carolingian Era (Austria, AD 751–AD 919).prose:
[Austria, AD 751–AD 919] Carolingian Era. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Frankish armies destroyed the Avar khaganate and pushed the frontier down the Danube, organising the conquered lands into marches settled by Bavarian colonists. Bishoprics at Salzburg and Passau took charge of converting the Slavs of Carantania and Pannonia, tying the region to the Latin west rather than Byzantium. Magyar raids from the east wrecked this frontier order in the early tenth century.
Carolingian Era (Austria, AD 751–AD 919).source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Merovingian Era (Austria, AD 450–AD 750).label: Merovingian Era
Merovingian Era (Austria, AD 450–AD 750).prose:
[Austria, AD 450–AD 750] Merovingian Era. Time span in which Merovingian period finds occur in grave finds from Austria. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

With Roman authority gone from the Danube provinces, Bavarian and Slavic settlers moved into the valleys and buried their dead in row-grave cemeteries furnished with weapons, brooches and glass beads. Irish and Frankish missionaries such as Rupert and Virgil worked out of Salzburg, and the Agilolfing dukes of Bavaria drew the region into the Frankish orbit. It is the period when the ethnic and religious map of the eastern Alps was redrawn, setting up the later Carolingian conquest of Carantania.
Merovingian Era (Austria, AD 450–AD 750).source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Arpadian Age (Austria, AD 890–AD 1250).label: Arpadian Age
Arpadian Age (Austria, AD 890–AD 1250).prose:
[Austria, AD 890–AD 1250] Arpadian Age. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin, raided deep into western Europe until crushed at the Lechfeld, then converted to Christianity and built a kingdom under Stephen I. Their descendants ruled a realm of stone churches, royal counties and market towns whose western frontier ran along the Austrian borderlands, a zone of repeated warfare with the German rulers. The dynasty's Mongol catastrophe of 1241 forced a wave of castle-building that reshaped the landscape.
