Group C3 (Austria, AD 900–AD 1050).prose: [Austria, AD 900–AD 1050] Group C3. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.
Group C3 (Austria, AD 900–AD 1050).source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

Пре династије Немањића (Serbia, AD 700–A.label: Пре династије Немањића
Пре династије Немањића (Serbia, AD 700–A.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Vlastimirović Dynasty, Vojislavljević Dynasty, Vukanović Dynasty, AD 700–AD 1167] Пре династије Немањића. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Slavic groups settled the Balkan interior after Byzantine control lapsed, organising into župas and small principalities such as Raška, Duklja, Zahumlje and Travunija. Christianisation from the 9th century tied the region to Constantinople and to the Cyrillic literacy spreading from Bulgaria, and the Miroslav Gospel and Duklja's brief kingship under Mihailo mark its high points. Overlordship shifted repeatedly between Byzantium, Bulgaria and Hungary until the rise of the Nemanjići.

Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина (Ser.node: Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина (Serbia, AD 1167–AD 1267)
Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина (Ser.label: Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина
Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина (Ser.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Serbian Grand Principality, Rascia, Byzantine Empire, AD 1167–AD 1267] Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Stefan Nemanja united the Serbian lands and founded the dynasty that would rule for two centuries, endowing monasteries at Studenica and Hilandar and retiring as a monk. His son Sava secured an autocephalous Serbian church in 1219 and his brother a royal crown in 1217, binding church and monarchy together. The frescoed monastery churches of this era — Mileševa's White Angel, Sopoćani — are among the finest Byzantine-style painting anywhere.

Од краља Милутина до распада Српског цар.node: Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства (Serbia, AD 1267–AD 1371)
Од краља Милутина до распада Српског цар.label: Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства
Од краља Милутина до распада Српског цар.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Kingdom of Serbia, Byzantine Empire, AD 1267–AD 1371] Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Milutin pushed the frontier deep into Byzantine Macedonia and spent lavishly on churches, marrying into the imperial family; his successors continued the expansion. Stefan Dušan conquered Albania, Epirus and Thessaly, had himself crowned emperor of Serbs and Greeks in 1346 and issued a famous law code. His empire outgrew its foundations, and after his death in 1355 it fragmented among quarrelling lords — a collapse sealed by the Ottoman victory on the Marica in 1371.

Од распада Српског царства до пада под т.node: Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт (Serbia, AD 1371–AD 1459)
Од распада Српског царства до пада под т.label: Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт
Од распада Српског царства до пада под т.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Serbian Empire, Serbian Despotate, Byzantine Empire, AD 1371–AD 1459] Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Regional lords replaced the empire, and Prince Lazar's stand against the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389 — where both rulers died — became the founding tragedy of Serbian memory. Under Stefan Lazarević and Đurađ Branković the Despotate survived as an Ottoman and Hungarian vassal, prospering from the Novo Brdo silver mines and producing a late flowering of literature and art. Belgrade was rebuilt as a capital, then given up; the fall of Smederevo in 1459 extinguished the state.

Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе.node: Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1690)
Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе.label: Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба
Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Ottoman Empire, AD 1459–AD 1690] Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

With Smederevo's surrender the Serbian state disappeared and the land became Ottoman provincial territory, its nobility gone, its peasants paying tithe and the child-levy. The Orthodox Church, its Patriarchate at Peć restored in 1557, became the main institution holding a Serbian identity together. Austro-Ottoman wars repeatedly swept the region, and the failed Habsburg advance of 1689–90 ended in reprisals and mass flight northward.

Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског ус.node: Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка (Serbia, AD 1690–AD 1804)
Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског ус.label: Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка
Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског ус.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Ottoman Empire, Habsburg Monarchy, AD 1690–AD 1804] Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Patriarch Arsenije III led tens of thousands of Serbs north into Habsburg territory as Ottoman armies returned, shifting the demographic centre of the nation into what became Vojvodina. There, under imperial privileges, Serbs served as military frontiersmen and developed printing, schools and a merchant class, while the lands under Ottoman rule grew poorer and more violent. Abuses by renegade janissaries at the end of the period pushed the peasantry of the Belgrade Pashalik towards revolt.

Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светск.node: Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата (Serbia, AD 1804–AD 1914)
Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светск.label: Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата
Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светск.prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Principality of Serbia, Kingdom of Serbia, Ottoman Empire, Habsburg Monarchy, Austrian Empire, Austro-Hungarian Empire , AD 1804–AD 1914] Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Karađorđe's 1804 rising and Miloš Obrenović's second uprising won autonomy from the Sultan, and a modern state was assembled — a constitution, ministries, a capital at Belgrade, and the departure of Ottoman garrisons in 1867. Full independence came at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and a kingdom was proclaimed in 1882, though the rival Obrenović and Karađorđević dynasties fought bitterly, ending in the regicide of 1903. Victories in the Balkan Wars doubled Serbia's territory and sharpened the confrontation with Austria-Hungary that led to Sarajevo.

Камено доба (Serbia, 2599999 BC–3499 BC).label: Камено доба
Камено доба (Serbia, 2599999 BC–3499 BC).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, 2599999 BC–3499 BC] Камено доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Neanderthals and then modern humans hunted the Danube valley and Balkan uplands for hundreds of millennia before farming arrived from Anatolia. Along the Iron Gates gorge, the fisher-foragers of Lepenski Vir built trapezoidal houses and carved boulders into fish-faced human figures. Later Starčevo and Vinča farming villages grew into some of Europe's largest, producing distinctive burnished pottery, figurines and inscribed signs, and digging copper ore at Rudna Glava.

Метално доба (Serbia, 3499 BC–AD 150).label: Метално доба
Метално доба (Serbia, 3499 BC–AD 150).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, 3499 BC–AD 150] Метално доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Copper, then bronze, then iron reshaped the Balkans: metal wealth concentrated in the hands of chiefs, hillforts appeared, and hoards of bronze weapons and ornaments were buried across the Danube plain. Iron Age tribes — Triballi, Dardanians, Autariatae — were joined after 300 BC by Celtic Scordisci, who founded a settlement at the site of Belgrade. Rome absorbed the whole region by the early 1st century AD, ending local independence and knitting it into a provincial economy.

Енеолит (Serbia, 3499 BC–2199 BC).label: Енеолит
Енеолит (Serbia, 3499 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Baden Culture, Kostolac Culture, Vučedol Culture, 3499 BC–2199 BC] Енеолит. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Copper metallurgy became routine across the central Balkans, with cast axes and hammer-axes replacing the small ornaments of earlier centuries. The great tell villages of the Vinča world gave way to the Baden, Kostolac and Vučedol cultures, who often chose fortified hilltops and produced boldly incised, encrusted pottery. Kurgan burials and new pastoral practices signal contact with steppe populations moving up the Danube, foreshadowing the Bronze Age.

Бронзано доба (Serbia, 2199 BC–1099 BC).label: Бронзано доба
Бронзано доба (Serbia, 2199 BC–1099 BC).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Urnfield Culture, Vatin Culture, Somogyvár-Vinkovci Culture, Mureș Culture, Cruceni-Belegiš Culture, 2199 BC–1099 BC] Бронзано доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Farming and herding communities along the Danube, Sava and Morava adopted bronze metallurgy, and groups such as the Vatin culture built substantial settlements and buried their dead under mounds. Enormous hoards of bronze axes, sickles and ornaments testify to a region sitting on the trade routes that carried metal and amber between the Aegean, the Carpathians and central Europe. Fortified sites and the growing quantity of weaponry point to increasingly hierarchical, warlike societies.

Гвоздено доба (Serbia, 1099 BC–AD 150).label: Гвоздено доба
Гвоздено доба (Serbia, 1099 BC–AD 150).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Bosut Culture, Brnjica Culture, 1099 BC–AD 150] Гвоздено доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons among the hillfort communities of the central Balkans, ancestors of the tribes the Greeks and Romans knew as Triballi, Dardani and Autariatae. Princely burials with imported Greek bronzes and jewellery show elites plugged into Mediterranean trade, and from the 3rd century BC the Celtic Scordisci settled around the mouth of the Sava and struck their own coinage. The era closes with the Roman conquest and the absorption of the region into the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia.

Стари век (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 700).label: Стари век
Стари век (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 700).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, 299 BC–AD 700] Стари век. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Celtic Scordisci and Illyrian and Thracian tribes held the Danube and Morava valleys before Roman armies absorbed the area into the empire, founding cities, roads and river fortresses that made it a strategic corridor between Italy and the East. Mining, military recruitment and imperial patronage brought prosperity, and Christianity arrived early enough for local bishops to matter in church councils. The era ends as the Danube defences collapsed and Avar and Slavic groups settled the countryside.

Предримско доба (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 100).label: Предримско доба
Предримско доба (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 100).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Triballi, Dardani, Autariatae, Scordisci, Moesi, 299 BC–AD 100] Предримско доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Celtic Scordisci settled the Danube–Sava confluence after the failed Balkan invasion of 279 BC, founding Singidunum and minting their own coinage alongside the older Triballi and Dardanian communities. Hillforts, imported Greek wine and Italian bronze vessels show a trading world linked to the Mediterranean. Roman campaigns from the late 1st century BC broke local power and created the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia, bringing roads, legionary camps and Latin.

Римско доба (Serbia, AD 100–AD 700).label: Римско доба
Римско доба (Serbia, AD 100–AD 700).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, Ancient Rome, Byzantine Empire, AD 100–AD 700] Римско доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia, ancient Rome. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Roman armies pushed the frontier to the Danube, and the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia became one of the empire's most militarised and productive zones, with legionary bases, silver and lead mines, and paved roads carrying troops toward the east. Sirmium, Viminacium and Naissus grew into major cities, and the region produced a remarkable run of emperors, Constantine the Great among them. Mosaics, tombs painted with Christian imagery and the ruins of Danube fortresses show both the wealth and the anxiety of the later centuries, before Avar and Slavic incursions ended provincial life.

Средњи век (Serbia, AD 700–AD 1459).label: Средњи век
Средњи век (Serbia, AD 700–AD 1459).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, AD 700–AD 1459] Средњи век. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Slavic settlement and gradual conversion to Christianity gave way to competing principalities, then to the Nemanjić dynasty, which built an independent kingdom with its own archbishopric and endowed monasteries such as Studenica and Dečani, whose frescoes rank among the finest in Byzantine art. Under Stefan Dušan the state briefly reached the Aegean before fragmenting after his death. Ottoman pressure grew after the battle on the Kosovo field, and the period ends with the fall of the fortress capital of Smederevo.

Нови век (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1914).label: Нови век
Нови век (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1914).prose:
[Serbia, Balkans, AD 1459–AD 1914] Нови век. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Ottoman rule after the fall of Smederevo turned the Serbian lands into a frontier province, fought over repeatedly by Istanbul and Vienna and drained by migrations north. The Patriarchate of Peć and village life preserved a distinct identity through centuries without a state. From 1804 uprisings won autonomy, then full independence in 1878 and a kingdom that expanded in the Balkan Wars — ambitions that helped ignite a world war.

Iron I / II (Levant, 999 BC–899 BC).label: Iron I / II
Iron I / II (Levant, 999 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Levant, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron I / II. Transitional period, usually subsumed within Iron Ib or Iron IIA. Period definition from Levantine Chronology — Ilan Sharon, 2013.

The transitional century when highland villages began to consolidate into territorial polities and coastal and inland centres were rebuilt with fortifications and public buildings. Traditionally the era of Israel's early monarchy, its dating is one of the most fiercely contested problems in Levantine archaeology, with radiocarbon results pulling against the biblical chronology.

Iron III/Persian (Levant, 529 BC–329 BC).label: Iron III/Persian
Iron III/Persian (Levant, 529 BC–329 BC).prose:
[Levant, 529 BC–329 BC] Iron III/Persian. The historical end date (332 BCE) falls within the Persian/Hellenistic transition period. Period definition from Levantine Chronology — Ilan Sharon, 2013.

Achaemenid rule reorganised the Levant into satrapal provinces, with Phoenician cities like Sidon and Tyre prospering as naval and commercial powers and Jerusalem rebuilt on a small scale as the temple city of Yehud. Greek pottery and locally minted silver coins circulate widely, evidence of a coast integrated into Mediterranean trade well before Alexander arrived in 332 BC.

Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 474 BC–329 BC).label: Cypro-Classical
Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 474 BC–329 BC).prose:
[Cyprus, 474 BC–329 BC] Cypro-Classical. Period definition from Levantine Chronology — Ilan Sharon, 2013.

Under Persian suzerainty the island's kings played Greek and Persian interests against each other, most famously Evagoras I of Salamis, who fought a long war for independence and promoted Greek language and art. Cypriot syllabic writing survived alongside the Greek alphabet and Phoenician, and royal tombs at Salamis were furnished with chariots, horses and Homeric-looking grave goods. The kingdoms ended when Ptolemy I abolished them and absorbed Cyprus into his empire.

Early Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 168–AD.label: Early Mithraeum
Early Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 168–AD.prose:
[Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 168–AD 210] Early Mithraeum. End of pre-mithraeum phase, start of EM phase determined by inscription YUAG accession # 1935.97, WD QID Q98270560; end of EM and start of MM phase determined by the inscription referring to the rebuilding of a temple to mithras under Antonius Valentinus (CIMRM 1.53; AE 1940.220; PR VII + VIII no. 847, p. 85). Period definition from  Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935 — M. I. Rostovtzeff, 1939.

A small private shrine to Mithras installed in a house in a Roman garrison town, apparently by Palmyrene archers serving in the army—one of the very few mithraea whose whole history can be traced. Its dated reliefs of Mithras slaying the bull, set up by Palmyrene officers, are among the earliest firmly dated Mithraic monuments anywhere. The building was later enlarged and painted, then buried when the city's defences were reinforced, which is why it survives.
Early Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 168–AD.source: Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935

Middle Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 210–A.label: Middle Mithraeum
Middle Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 210–A.prose: [Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 210–AD 240] Middle Mithraeum. End of EM and start of MM phase determined by the inscription referring to the rebuilding of a temple to mithras under Antonius Valentinus (CIMRM 1.53; AE 1940.220; PR VII + VIII no. 847, p. 85). Period definition from  Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935 — M. I. Rostovtzeff, 1939.
Middle Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 210–A.source: Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935

Late Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 240–AD.label: Late Mithraeum
Late Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 240–AD.prose:
[Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 240–AD 256] Late Mithraeum. Date for the destruction of the building determined by the date of Sasanian siege c. 256 CE; Mithraeum went out of use when commandeered for the construction of a defensive embankment along wall street. Period definition from  Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935 — M. I. Rostovtzeff, 1939.

The final rebuilding of the temple of Mithras in a Roman garrison town on the Euphrates, enlarged and richly painted before the city was destroyed by Sasanian attack. Its frescoes show Mithras hunting on horseback and robed magi, and its walls carry graffiti left by soldiers of the Roman army. Buried in the defensive embankment thrown up during the final siege, it survived almost intact for excavators to find in the 1930s.
Late Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 240–AD.source: Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935

Brief period of Roman control (Dura-Euro.node: Brief period of Roman control (Dura-Europos, AD 116–AD 117)
Brief period of Roman control (Dura-Euro.label: Brief period of Roman control
Brief period of Roman control (Dura-Euro.prose:
[Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 116–AD 117] Brief period of Roman control. The brief period of Roman control of the site under Trajan is attested by an inscription from a triumphal arch dedicated to Trajan whose remains were excavated outside the walls of Dura--see Preliminary Report 7/8: 128–129, no. 868; Baird also notes: "While historical sources outside Dura are silent on Rome’s intervention at the site under Trajan, a single Greek inscription tells us that it was not a quiet nor unnoticed handover: in 116/17 CE, the inscription records that a man called Alexander (he was also known as Ammaios, it reports), who was the son of one Epinicus, renovated the naos of a temple, as his father had, and that he replaced at his own expense the temple doors, the originals having been taken away by the Romans. So, there was damage to the site (and the seizure of booty) by Roman forces, and the Romans were recorded by name as having desecrated a temple, all within Dura’s Arsacid period; this was an explicit judgement against the Romans" (p. 23). Period definition from  Dura-Europos — Jennifer A. Baird , 2018.

Trajan's Parthian campaign carried Roman armies down the Euphrates and briefly placed the caravan city under Roman command. The occupation collapsed almost immediately: Hadrian abandoned the new eastern conquests on his accession, and the city returned to Parthian hands for another sixty years.

Phase A (Dura-Europos, AD 180–AD 200).label: Phase A
Phase A (Dura-Europos, AD 180–AD 200).prose: [Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 180–AD 200] Phase A. One of at least two wall painting phases belonging to Mithraeum I; authors note that phases of wall decoration and structural changes to buildings do not always correspond to the same moment of intervention (169, 176). Note 33 to p. 169: "If the final decoration is dated to 209/10, the other two phases are perhaps to be dated to around 200 and 180 CE respectively.". Period definition from Rethinking the Dura-Europos Mithraeum — Lucinda Dirven, 2020.

Middle Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5799 BC.label: Middle Neolithic Greece
Middle Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5799 BC.prose:
[Greece, 5799 BC–4749 BC] Middle Neolithic Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Farming villages in Thessaly and central Greece grew into tells, occupied so long that the debris of mud-brick houses piled into artificial hills. This is the era of Sesklo, with rectangular houses, red-on-white painted pottery and finely made stone tools, and of the small clay figurines that fill museum cases. The settlements show a settled, prosperous farming society centuries before anything resembling a town appeared in the Aegean.
Middle Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5799 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC.node: Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4799 BC)
Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC.label: Late Neolithic I Greece
Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC.prose:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4799 BC] Late Neolithic I Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Thessalian villages such as Arapi and Otzaki flourished, producing the painted and black-burnished wares that define the phase, while similar communities spread through Macedonia and southern Greece. Farmers kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs and grew cereals and pulses, living in mudbrick houses on tells. Melian obsidian moved widely, evidence of regular seafaring around the Aegean.
Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 B.node: Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 BC–4499 BC)
Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 B.label: Late Neolithic II Greece
Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 B.prose:
[Greece, 4799 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic II Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The era of Dimini in Thessaly, with its concentric enclosure walls and central court, and of the elaborate incised and polychrome wares that bear its name. Settlements were denser and more differentiated than before, and copper and gold objects begin to appear in small numbers. These developments set the stage for the Final Neolithic dispersal of settlement and the start of the Bronze Age.
Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4.label: Late Neolithic Greece
Late Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4.prose:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Villages across Thessaly, Macedonia and the south expanded, some into substantial tell settlements with enclosure ditches and walls, while distinctive regional pottery styles proliferated. Obsidian from Melos and Spondylus shell ornaments circulated over long distances. Copper working and increasingly elaborate figurines point to social changes that would culminate in the Final Neolithic and Bronze Age.
Late Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Neolithic Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–449.label: Late Neolithic Crete
Late Neolithic Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–449.prose:
[Crete, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic Crete. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Crete remained thinly settled, with the long-lived village at Knossos its best-documented community, along with cave sites used for shelter and burial. Pottery turned to dark burnished wares with incised and pattern-burnished decoration. The deep Neolithic mound at Knossos became the foundation on which the Bronze Age palace would later rise.
Late Neolithic Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–449.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4.node: Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4899 BC)
Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4.label: Late Neolithic I Crete
Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4.prose:
[Crete, 5299 BC–4899 BC] Late Neolithic I Crete. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Occupation on Crete stayed concentrated at a few places, above all the growing settlement mound at Knossos, with caves used episodically elsewhere. Dark burnished pottery with incised and rippled decoration is characteristic. The island's isolation kept its material culture distinct from mainland Greek assemblages.
Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Neolithic Northern Greece (Greece,.node: Late Neolithic Northern Greece (Greece, 5499 BC–3249 BC)

Late Neolithic Northern Greece (Greece,.prose:
[Northern Greece, 5499 BC–3249 BC] Late Neolithic Northern Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Farming villages in Thessaly and Macedonia grew into long-lived tells, their mudbrick houses rebuilt on the rubble of earlier ones until settlements like Sesklo and Dimini stood as low mounds above the plain. Potters produced fine painted and burnished wares, and obsidian from Melos and Spondylus-shell ornaments moved along exchange routes reaching deep into the Balkans. It is the phase in which village life in the southern Balkans reached its densest and most settled form, setting the stage for the metal-using societies that followed.

Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece (.node: Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece (Greece, 4499 BC–2999 BC)
Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece (.label: Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece
Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece (.prose:
[Greece, 4499 BC–2999 BC] Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

A long transitional stretch between the settled farming villages of the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, when copper and silver working took hold, settlement scattered into caves and small upland sites, and seafaring links across the Aegean grew stronger. Burial and craft practices become more varied, and some communities began to show clearer differences in wealth. It is the seedbed of the Early Bronze Age societies of the mainland and islands.

Final Neolithic IV Crete (Crete, 3299 BC.prose:
[Crete, 3299 BC–2999 BC] Final Neolithic IV Crete. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The last stretch of the Cretan Neolithic, immediately preceding the Early Minoan period, when settlement spread well beyond the long-occupied mound at Knossos to new sites across the island, including defensible hilltops and coastal spots.
Final Neolithic IV Crete (Crete, 3299 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Bronze Age (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Greece, 3199 BC–1049 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 B.label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 B.prose:
[Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Bronze Age (Greece, 2099 BC–1549.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Greece, 2099 BC–1549.prose:
[Greece, 2099 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Greece, 2099 BC–1549.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Bronze Age Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–107.label: Bronze Age Cycladic
Bronze Age Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–107.prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–1079 BC] Bronze Age Cycladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The small marble islands produced the folded-arm figurines that have made Cycladic art famous, mostly found in cist graves and originally painted. Island communities grew wealthy as middlemen in the obsidian and metal trade, building fortified towns like Chalandriani and, at Akrotiri on Thera, a multi-storey town with frescoes and drainage that was buried by a volcanic eruption. Cycladic independence faded as first Minoan Crete and then Mycenaean Greece drew the islands into their orbit.
Bronze Age Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–107.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Cycladic
Early Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Cyclades, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Cycladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The islands of the Aegean supported small farming and fishing communities that became skilled sailors and metalworkers, moving obsidian, copper and marble around the sea. They are best known for the marble folded-arm figurines placed in graves, pared down to abstract simplicity and much admired by modern artists. Their trading networks laid the groundwork for the later Minoan and Mycenaean maritime world.
Early Cycladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Cycladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.label: Early Cycladic I
Early Cycladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.prose:
[Cyclades, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Early Cycladic I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The earliest phase of island culture in the Bronze Age Aegean, known largely from small cist-grave cemeteries of the Grotta-Pelos type rather than from settlements. Grave goods include schematic 'violin-shaped' marble figurines and simple dark burnished pottery, the beginnings of a distinctive Cycladic tradition.
Early Cycladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Cycladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.label: Early Cycladic II
Early Cycladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.prose:
[Cyclades, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Early Cycladic II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The high point of Cycladic culture, when settlements such as Chalandriani on Syros grew and fortified sites appeared. Craftsmen produced the famous canonical folded-arm figurines, marble bowls, and metal tools and weapons, while frying-pan vessels engraved with ships attest to long-distance voyaging.
Early Cycladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Cycladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.label: Early Cycladic III
Early Cycladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.prose:
[Cyclades, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Early Cycladic III. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The islands lost their earlier prominence as trade shifted toward Crete and the mainland; many cemeteries went out of use and figurine production largely ceased. Settlement contracted onto fewer, often defensible sites, a reorganisation that preceded the rise of Minoan influence in the Aegean.
Early Cycladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Cycladic
Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Cyclades, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Cycladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After the fragmented villages of the earlier islands, Cycladic life concentrated into a few substantial, sometimes walled towns — Phylakopi on Melos, Ayia Irini on Kea, Akrotiri on Thera — living off obsidian, trade and the sea. Potters produced matt-painted jars and beaked jugs decorated with birds and spirals, and Cretan goods and habits arrived in growing quantity. The Minoan connection deepened until the islands became cultural satellites of Crete, setting the stage for the frescoed town buried by the Thera eruption.
Middle Cycladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.label: Middle Cycladic I
Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.prose:
[Cyclades, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Middle Cycladic I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The islands settle into fewer, larger communities as the scattered hamlets of the Early Bronze Age are abandoned. Local potters develop matt-painted wares with dark geometric designs on pale slip, while imports show contact with Crete and the Greek mainland is still modest.
Middle Cycladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.label: Middle Cycladic II
Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.prose:
[Cyclades, 1899 BC–1699 BC] Middle Cycladic II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The mature phase of island town life, when Phylakopi, Ayia Irini and Akrotiri were compact, densely built settlements with organised streets and defences. Painted pottery, including jugs decorated with birds and flowers, shows Cycladic workshops absorbing Cretan taste while keeping their own style, and Melian obsidian and trade in metals kept the islands prosperous.
Middle Cycladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.label: Middle Cycladic III
Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.prose:
[Cyclades, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Cycladic III. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Cretan influence becomes overwhelming: Minoan pottery, weights, loomweights and even Linear A writing appear in island towns, and local products imitate palatial styles. The transformation carries directly into the frescoed, richly furnished Akrotiri destroyed by the eruption of Thera in the following period.
Middle Cycladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).label: Late Cycladic
Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).prose:
[Cyclades, 1599 BC–1079 BC] Late Cycladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The Bronze Age islands at their most connected, when Cretan influence in architecture, script, fresco and fashion gave way after about 1450 BC to Mycenaean control from the mainland. Towns like Akrotiri on Thera, Phylakopi on Melos and Ayia Irini on Keos were substantial harbour settlements with shrines, drainage and painted rooms. The eruption of Thera, the rise of Mycenaean palatial trade and the upheavals around 1200 BC all fall within this span.
Late Cycladic (Greece, 1599 BC–1079 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.label: Late Cycladic I
Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.prose:
[Cyclades, 1599 BC–1499 BC] Late Cycladic I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The moment captured at Akrotiri on Thera: a prosperous multi-storey town with paved streets, plumbing and walls painted with boxing boys, saffron gatherers and a fleet of ships. Cretan weights, script and pottery shapes show how deeply the islands were tied into the Minoan world, without being ruled by it. A volcanic eruption buried the town under metres of pumice, preserving it and ending the phase abruptly.
Late Cycladic I (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1389 B.label: Late Cycladic II
Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1389 B.prose:
[Cyclades, 1499 BC–1389 BC] Late Cycladic II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The generations after the Theran eruption, when island settlements rebuilt on a smaller scale and Minoan influence gave way to Mycenaean. Pottery, burial customs and imports increasingly point towards the mainland palaces rather than Crete. Phylakopi and Ayia Irini remained the main harbours, now nodes in a Mycenaean-run trade network.
Late Cycladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1389 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1389 BC–1079.label: Late Cycladic III
Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1389 BC–1079.prose:
[Cyclades, 1389 BC–1079 BC] Late Cycladic III. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The islands under mainland Mycenaean culture, with megaron-plan buildings and a sanctuary at Phylakopi holding clay idols, and fortification walls going up as conditions worsened. Around 1200 BC the palatial system collapsed and many sites were burned, abandoned or reduced to villages. Scattered communities carried on into the early Iron Age, with new cemeteries and the first signs of the later island city-states.
Late Cycladic III (Greece, 1389 BC–1079.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Bronze Age Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–104.label: Bronze Age Helladic
Bronze Age Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–104.prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–1049 BC] Bronze Age Helladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Mainland Greece moved from village farming through the shaft-grave wealth of early Mycenae to the palace states of Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns, with their cyclopean walls, chariot warfare and Linear B accounts of a tightly administered economy. These are the societies later Greeks remembered as the age of heroes and set the Trojan War in. Around 1200 BC the palaces burned, writing ceased, and Greece entered several centuries of poverty and depopulation.
Bronze Age Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–104.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Helladic
Early Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The mainland Greek Bronze Age begins: bronze tools and weapons, donkeys and sailing craft, and settlements engaged in Aegean-wide exchange. Its most striking buildings are the 'corridor houses' such as the House of the Tiles at Lerna — large, tiled, administratively organised structures, sealed storerooms and all — which suggest emerging central authority. Widespread destructions and abandonments end the period, and the mainland enters the poorer Middle Helladic era.
Early Helladic (Greece, 3099 BC–1999 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Helladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.label: Early Helladic I
Early Helladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.prose:
[Greece, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Early Helladic I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Small farming hamlets in the southwest Peloponnese take up metal and new pottery shapes, the first mainland stage of the Bronze Age. Settlements were modest and scattered, with burials in simple pits and cists rather than monumental tombs. It provides the baseline against which the wealthier, more centralised communities of the following centuries stand out.
Early Helladic I (Greece, 3099 BC–2699 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Helladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.label: Early Helladic II
Early Helladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.prose:
[Greece, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Early Helladic II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The most prosperous stage of the early mainland Bronze Age in Messenia, marked by larger settlements, standardised wheel-influenced pottery and active exchange around the Aegean. Elsewhere in the Peloponnese this is the age of monumental corridor houses and sealing systems, and Messenian sites participate in the same expanding economy. Its end came with disruption and abandonment at many sites.
Early Helladic II (Greece, 2699 BC–2199.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Helladic IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399.label: Early Helladic IIA
Early Helladic IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399.prose:
[Greece, 2699 BC–2399 BC] Early Helladic IIA. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The high point of the early mainland Bronze Age. Communities at Lerna, Tiryns, Kolonna and Thebes built large tiled "corridor houses", stamped hundreds of clay sealings to control stored produce, and imported obsidian, metal and finished goods from the islands and Anatolia. Historians see here the first attempts at centralised authority on the Greek mainland, several centuries before Mycenaean palaces.
Early Helladic IIA (Greece, 2699 BC–2399.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Helladic IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199.label: Early Helladic IIB
Early Helladic IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199.prose:
[Greece, 2399 BC–2199 BC] Early Helladic IIB. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

A short, unsettled phase in which new pottery of the Lefkandi I–Kastri type, with Anatolian-looking shapes such as tankards and depas cups, spreads across the Aegean. It closes with the burning of the House of Tiles at Lerna and destructions at other major sites, ending the corridor-house world.
Early Helladic IIB (Greece, 2399 BC–2199.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Helladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.label: Early Helladic III
Early Helladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.prose:
[Greece, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic III. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After the destructions, Messenian settlements were smaller and simpler, with apsidal houses and new dark-on-light painted pottery of the Tiryns type. Population and long-distance contacts contracted sharply. The pottery and building traditions of this phase carry directly into the Middle Helladic period.
Early Helladic III (Greece, 2199 BC–1999.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Helladic
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Helladic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Mainland Greece at its poorest and plainest: modest villages of mudbrick houses, burials in simple cist graves and tumuli, and the grey wheel-made pottery known as Minyan ware. Messenia's communities were small and dispersed, with little sign of the wealth or hierarchy to come. Towards its end, richer graves and imported Cretan goods signal the emergence of the warrior elites who would build the Mycenaean palace at Pylos.
Middle Helladic (Greece, 1999 BC–1599 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.label: Middle Helladic I
Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.prose:
[Greece, 1999 BC–1899 BC] Middle Helladic I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The opening of a subdued era on the Greek mainland, following widespread destruction and abandonment at the end of the Early Bronze Age. Settlements are small and simply built, grave goods are few, and the characteristic burnished grey Minyan pottery becomes standard — a material culture that gives little hint of the Mycenaean wealth to come.
Middle Helladic I (Greece, 1999 BC–1899.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.label: Middle Helladic II
Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.prose:
[Greece, 1899 BC–1699 BC] Middle Helladic II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Mainland Greek villages of small mudbrick houses, cist-grave cemeteries and plain, wheel-made grey 'Minyan' pottery, materially far poorer than Minoan Crete across the sea. Communities like Lerna, Asine and Kolonna on Aegina were farming settlements with modest hierarchies, though Aegina's fortified town shows some were already trading widely. The apparent simplicity is deceptive: this is the society out of which Mycenaean Greece grew.
Middle Helladic II (Greece, 1899 BC–1699.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.label: Middle Helladic III
Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.prose:
[Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC] Middle Helladic III. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The moment mainland Greece began to pull ahead. Warrior burials filled with bronze weapons, gold and imported Cretan goods — above all Grave Circle B at Mycenae — reveal families accumulating wealth and advertising it in death for the first time. Within a couple of generations these lineages would build the shaft-grave dynasties and palatial citadels of the Mycenaean world.
Middle Helladic III (Greece, 1699 BC–159.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Bronze Age Minoan (Crete, 3099 BC–1049 B.label: Bronze Age Minoan
Bronze Age Minoan (Crete, 3099 BC–1049 B.prose:
[Crete, 3099 BC–1049 BC] Bronze Age Minoan. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Crete's palace societies at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros ran redistributive economies recorded first in hieroglyphs, then in the still-undeciphered Linear A. Their frescoes of bull-leapers, dolphins and processions, their fine polychrome pottery and their trade in oil, wine and metals spread Cretan taste across the eastern Mediterranean. Earthquakes, the eruption of Thera and finally Mycenaean Greek takeover ended the system, leaving Linear B tablets in Greek at a Knossos ruled from the mainland.
Bronze Age Minoan (Crete, 3099 BC–1049 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Old Palace period (Crete, 1899 BC–1599 B.label: Old Palace period
Old Palace period (Crete, 1899 BC–1599 B.prose:
[Crete, 1899 BC–1599 BC] Old Palace period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The building of the first monumental palaces marks the point at which Cretan society became recognisably Minoan, with centralised storerooms, workshops and courts for public ceremony. Administrative sealings and the first Aegean scripts appear alongside brilliantly painted Kamares pottery exported as far as Egypt. Their destruction and rebuilding opened the way to the more famous Neopalatial age.
Old Palace period (Crete, 1899 BC–1599 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

New Palace period (Crete, 1599 BC–1389 B.label: New Palace period
New Palace period (Crete, 1599 BC–1389 B.prose:
[Crete, 1599 BC–1389 BC] New Palace period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After earthquakes levelled the first Cretan palaces, they were rebuilt on a grander scale at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, with light-wells, colonnaded halls and vast storage magazines. This was Minoan civilisation at its height: bull-leaping frescoes, gold-and-crystal seal stones, Linear A administration, and pottery and metalwork traded across the Aegean and to Egypt. It ended in a wave of destructions, after which Mycenaean Greeks ruled from Knossos and kept their accounts in Linear B.
New Palace period (Crete, 1599 BC–1389 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Final Palatial period (Crete, 1449 BC–12.label: Final Palatial period
Final Palatial period (Crete, 1449 BC–12.prose:
[Crete, 1449 BC–1299 BC] Final Palatial period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Knossos alone still functioned as a palace, but the administration was now run by Greek speakers who kept their accounts in Linear B, listing sheep, chariots, textiles and offerings to gods. Warrior burials with bronze weapons appear around the town, and Minoan art continued under Mycenaean patronage. When the Knossos archive burned, Crete's palatial system ended for good and the island became a province of the mainland Mycenaean world.
Final Palatial period (Crete, 1449 BC–12.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Post-palatial period (Crete, 1389 BC–106.label: Post-palatial period
Post-palatial period (Crete, 1389 BC–106.prose:
[Crete, 1389 BC–1069 BC] Post-palatial period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

With the palaces no longer functioning as administrative centres, Crete lost its writing-based bureaucracy and its tightly organised storage economy. Communities became more numerous and more scattered, some perched in defensible hill locations, and material culture aligned with broader Mycenaean Aegean fashions in pottery, tombs and weaponry. The gradual unravelling of eastern Mediterranean trade at the end of the Bronze Age carries the island into the Iron Age.
Post-palatial period (Crete, 1389 BC–106.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Minoan I (Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC).label: Early Minoan I
Early Minoan I (Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC).prose:
[Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC] Early Minoan I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The opening phase of the Cretan Bronze Age, when new burial customs appeared: circular stone tholos tombs in the south and burial caves elsewhere, used by whole communities over generations. Dark burnished Pyrgos ware and red-on-buff Agios Onouphrios pottery mark the period, alongside the first regular use of copper. Change came gradually from the preceding Neolithic, with some sites showing signs of newcomers arriving on the island.
Early Minoan I (Crete, 3099 BC–2999 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Minoan II (Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC).label: Early Minoan II
Early Minoan II (Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC).prose:
[Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC] Early Minoan II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The most prosperous stretch of prepalatial Crete, when craftsmen produced mottled orange-and-black Vasiliki ware, translucent stone vases and fine gold ornaments. Excavated settlements such as Myrtos Fournou Korifi and the House on the Hill at Vasiliki show planned, agglomerated buildings with storage and workshop space. Seals came into common use for marking goods, an early hint of the record-keeping that would underpin the palaces.
Early Minoan II (Crete, 2649 BC–2199 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Minoan IIA (Crete, 1799 BC–1749 B.label: Middle Minoan IIA
Middle Minoan IIA (Crete, 1799 BC–1749 B.prose:
[Crete, 1799 BC–1749 BC] Middle Minoan IIA. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Crete's first palaces were fully operating, concentrating storage, craft workshops and ritual in complexes around a central court. Administrators used stamped clay sealings and the Cretan Hieroglyphic script, and potters produced the earliest fine Kamares wares.
Middle Minoan IIA (Crete, 1799 BC–1749 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Minoan IIB (Crete, 1749 BC–1699 B.label: Middle Minoan IIB
Middle Minoan IIB (Crete, 1749 BC–1699 B.prose:
[Crete, 1749 BC–1699 BC] Middle Minoan IIB. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The last and richest phase of the first palaces, with eggshell-thin polychrome Kamares pottery, elaborate seal engraving, and Cretan exports reaching Egypt and the Syrian coast. It ended in destructions at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, usually blamed on earthquake, which cleared the way for the grander second palaces.
Middle Minoan IIB (Crete, 1749 BC–1699 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Iron Age (Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.
Early Iron Age (Greece, 1099 BC–699 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Sub-Mycenean (Greece, 1099 BC–1049 BC).label: Sub-Mycenean
Sub-Mycenean (Greece, 1099 BC–1049 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–1049 BC] Sub-Mycenean. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The transitional horizon between the fall of the Mycenaean palaces and the Protogeometric style, recognised chiefly from poor, small-scale burials with degenerate versions of Mycenaean pottery shapes. Craft standards, trade and literacy all fell away. Its brevity and poverty make it one of the most argued-over slices of Aegean chronology.
Sub-Mycenean (Greece, 1099 BC–1049 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Sub-Minoan (Crete, 1069 BC–1014 BC).label: Sub-Minoan
Sub-Minoan (Crete, 1069 BC–1014 BC).prose:
[Crete, 1069 BC–1014 BC] Sub-Minoan. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The last phase of Cretan Bronze Age culture, after the palaces had gone: pottery still recognisably Minoan in shape but coarser and looser in decoration, made by communities that had largely withdrawn to defensible upland refuges such as Karphi. Metal is scarcer, settlements smaller, writing gone. Out of this thinned-out world came the Cretan communities of the Early Iron Age.
Sub-Minoan (Crete, 1069 BC–1014 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC).label: Protogeometric
Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC).prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Protogeometric. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

In the aftermath of the Mycenaean collapse, potters in Athens imposed a new discipline on their work: compass-drawn concentric circles and semicircles, crisp horizontal bands, and dark glaze over the vessel's shoulders. It is the first sign of confidence returning after the palaces fell, and it coincides with the spread of iron tools and weapons. The style travelled with Aegean settlers to the coast of Asia Minor and set the pattern for Geometric art that followed.
Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC) [p0ds9.label: Geometric
Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC) [p0ds9.prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Greece emerging from the post-Mycenaean dark age, its pottery covered in meanders, zigzags and banded panels, later giving way to silhouetted horses, chariots and mourners on the huge Dipylon grave markers of Athens. Communities coalesced into the first city-states, sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filled with dedications, the Phoenician alphabet was adapted to Greek, and settlers began sailing west to Italy and Sicily. The oral traditions that became the Iliad and Odyssey took shape in these years.
Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC) [p0ds9.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).label: Early Geometric
Early Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).prose:
[Greece, 899 BC–849 BC] Early Geometric. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian potters imposed strict order on their vessels — concentric circles, meanders and bands drawn with compass and multiple brush, on tall silhouetted shapes. It marks the recovery of Greek communities after the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, with iron working established and burials in cemeteries like the Kerameikos showing renewed wealth. The disciplined patterning would soon open up to include the human figure.
Early Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Geometric (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC).label: Middle Geometric
Middle Geometric (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC).prose:
[Greece, 849 BC–759 BC] Middle Geometric. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Greek communities recovering after the fall of the Mycenaean palaces grew steadily richer, and their pottery shows it: tall Attic amphorae and kraters covered in precisely drafted meanders, zigzags and bands of glazed black. Cemeteries at Athens and settlements like Lefkandi reveal imported gold, faience and eastern bronzes, evidence that Aegean traders were again working the Levantine coast. Figures of humans and horses start creeping into the ornament, pointing towards the narrative scenes and colonising ventures of the century that followed.
Middle Geometric (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).label: Late Geometric
Late Geometric (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).prose:
[Greece, 759 BC–699 BC] Late Geometric. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Greek vase painters abandoned pure pattern for people: funeral processions, chariots, warships and duelling warriors crowd the huge Dipylon grave markers of Athens. The same decades saw the alphabet adopted, sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filling with dedications, colonists sailing west to Italy and Sicily, and the emergence of the polis — the world in which the Homeric poems took shape.
Late Geometric (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric I (Greece, 759 BC–734 BC).label: Late Geometric I
Late Geometric I (Greece, 759 BC–734 BC).prose:
[Greece, 759 BC–734 BC] Late Geometric I. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian workshops, above all that of the Dipylon Master, produced monumental amphorae and kraters set over graves, their friezes showing the laying-out of the dead and processions of mourners. Figures return to Greek art after centuries of abstract ornament, and pottery in this style spread widely through the Aegean and beyond.
Late Geometric I (Greece, 759 BC–734 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric IA (Greece, 759 BC–749 BC.label: Late Geometric IA
Late Geometric IA (Greece, 759 BC–749 BC.prose:
[Greece, 759 BC–749 BC] Late Geometric IA. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The moment human figures reappear in Greek art on a grand scale: the Dipylon Master and his circle painted man-high grave vases with silhouetted mourners flanking the bier, framed by dense meander and zigzag bands.
Late Geometric IA (Greece, 759 BC–749 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric IB (Greece, 749 BC–734 BC.label: Late Geometric IB
Late Geometric IB (Greece, 749 BC–734 BC.prose:
[Greece, 749 BC–734 BC] Late Geometric IB. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Figured scenes multiply and diversify on Athenian vases — chariot processions, files of armed warriors, oared ships — while ornament thins out to make room for them. Painting of this kind spread to Argos, Corinth and the islands as Greeks were beginning to settle overseas.
Late Geometric IB (Greece, 749 BC–734 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric II (Greece, 734 BC–699 BC.label: Late Geometric II
Late Geometric II (Greece, 734 BC–699 BC.prose:
[Greece, 734 BC–699 BC] Late Geometric II. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The final flourish of Geometric vase painting, when the tight bands of meander and zigzag gave way to crowded scenes of warriors, ships and funerals, and eastern motifs began creeping in from Phoenician and Syrian imports. These same decades saw Greeks planting colonies in Sicily and southern Italy, the alphabet spreading, and the earliest sanctuaries filling with dedications. Pottery from this horizon is a key dating tool for the whole Mediterranean, because Greek cups turn up wherever Greeks settled or traded.
Late Geometric II (Greece, 734 BC–699 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric IIA (Greece, 734 BC–719 B.label: Late Geometric IIA
Late Geometric IIA (Greece, 734 BC–719 B.prose:
[Greece, 734 BC–719 BC] Late Geometric IIA. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian and Corinthian workshops pushed figured scenes further, with stick-like men, horses and mourners filling the panels of grave markers and drinking vessels. The style spread widely as colonists carried it west, so a sherd of this pottery in an Italian or Sicilian site fixes the settlement's date.
Late Geometric IIA (Greece, 734 BC–719 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Geometric IIB (Greece, 719 BC–699 B.label: Late Geometric IIB
Late Geometric IIB (Greece, 719 BC–699 B.prose:
[Greece, 719 BC–699 BC] Late Geometric IIB. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The last phase before the Orientalizing revolution, when Greek painters started abandoning strict geometry for curving florals, lions and sphinxes borrowed from Near Eastern imports. Corinth in particular moved fastest, and its new fine wares would dominate Mediterranean trade for the next century.
Late Geometric IIB (Greece, 719 BC–699 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Archaic (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).label: Archaic
Archaic (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–479 BC] Archaic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.
Archaic (Greece, 699 BC–479 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Archaic (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC).label: Early Archaic
Early Archaic (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–619 BC] Early Archaic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.
Early Archaic (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Archaic (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).label: Middle Archaic
Middle Archaic (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).prose:
[Greece, 619 BC–559 BC] Middle Archaic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.
Middle Archaic (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Sub-Geometric (Greece, 699 BC–599 BC).label: Sub-Geometric
Sub-Geometric (Greece, 699 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–599 BC] Sub-Geometric. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

In several regions the tight meanders, zigzags and banded panels of Geometric pottery carried on being painted well after Corinthian and Athenian workshops had moved to orientalising floral and animal designs. The overlap is useful to archaeologists as a marker of conservative local workshops and of how unevenly new styles spread. It coincides with the period of Greek colonial foundation in Sicily and Italy and the spread of the alphabet.
Sub-Geometric (Greece, 699 BC–599 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Orientalizing (Greece, 719 BC–599 BC).label: Orientalizing
Orientalizing (Greece, 719 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Greece, 719 BC–599 BC] Orientalizing. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Rich hillforts and enormous burial mounds in the Dolenjska region mark a wealthy Hallstatt-era elite trading with Italy and the eastern Alps. Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. The imagery borrows from Etruscan and Near Eastern art but tells local stories.
Orientalizing (Greece, 719 BC–599 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Daedalic (Greece, 659 BC–619 BC).label: Daedalic
Daedalic (Greece, 659 BC–619 BC).prose:
[Greece, 659 BC–619 BC] Daedalic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

A distinctive style in early Greek sculpture and terracotta: small figures with flat-topped heads, triangular faces, large eyes and stiff wig-like hair falling in horizontal waves, borrowed in part from Syrian and Egyptian models. Crete and the Peloponnese produced it in quantity, and it gave Greek artists their first repeatable formula for the human figure, leading directly to the life-size kouroi and korai of the following century.
Daedalic (Greece, 659 BC–619 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Protoattic (Greece, 699 BC–629 BC).label: Protoattic
Protoattic (Greece, 699 BC–629 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–629 BC] Protoattic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian potters abandoned the tight geometric grid and filled their vases with sphinxes, lions and floral scrolls borrowed from the Near East, drawn at a bold, sometimes clumsy scale. For the first time Greek myth was told in paint — Odysseus blinding Polyphemos, Perseus and the Gorgons. These experiments in narrative are the direct ancestors of Athenian black- and red-figure painting.
Protoattic (Greece, 699 BC–629 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Protoattic (Greece, 699 BC–674 BC).label: Early Protoattic
Early Protoattic (Greece, 699 BC–674 BC).prose:
[Greece, 699 BC–674 BC] Early Protoattic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian potters broke away from the tight geometric grids of the previous century and began drawing large, loose, outlined figures — monsters, chariots, mythological scenes — in an experimental style influenced by imported Near Eastern imagery. Compositions grew ambitious and often eccentric, with grotesque creatures filling whole panels. It is the moment Greek vase painting starts to tell stories rather than pattern surfaces.
Early Protoattic (Greece, 699 BC–674 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Protoattic (Greece, 674 BC–649 BC.label: Middle Protoattic
Middle Protoattic (Greece, 674 BC–649 BC.prose:
[Greece, 674 BC–649 BC] Middle Protoattic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian vase painters abandoned neat geometric ordering for huge, freely drawn figures, adding white slip and outline drawing to tell mythological stories – Perseus and the Gorgons, Odysseus blinding Polyphemus. The vessels are large, experimental and often crude by later standards, but they show Greek artists learning to render narrative for the first time. This is the workshop tradition out of which Athenian black-figure painting emerged.
Middle Protoattic (Greece, 674 BC–649 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Protoattic (Greece, 649 BC–629 BC).label: Late Protoattic
Late Protoattic (Greece, 649 BC–629 BC).prose:
[Greece, 649 BC–629 BC] Late Protoattic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Athenian vase painters worked at large scale in a bold, sketchy style, filling amphorae and funerary vessels with monsters, myths and orientalising floral ornament – the Eleusis amphora with the blinding of Polyphemos belongs here. Outline drawing gradually gave way to incised black-figure technique borrowed from Corinth. It is the moment Athenian painting first commits to telling stories.
Late Protoattic (Greece, 649 BC–629 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Protocorinthian (Greece, 719 BC–624 BC).label: Protocorinthian
Protocorinthian (Greece, 719 BC–624 BC).prose:
[Greece, 719 BC–624 BC] Protocorinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Corinth's workshops perfected a miniature style, above all the small globular aryballos that carried perfumed oil to markets all round the Mediterranean. Painters here developed the black-figure technique — silhouettes incised with fine detail and touched with added colour — and used it for friezes of hoplites, animals and monsters. Corinthian pots turn up from Sicily to Syria, making them one of archaeology's best dating tools for the whole eighth and seventh centuries.
Protocorinthian (Greece, 719 BC–624 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Protocorinthian (Greece, 719 BC–68.label: Early Protocorinthian
Early Protocorinthian (Greece, 719 BC–68.prose:
[Greece, 719 BC–689 BC] Early Protocorinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Corinthian workshops perfected a small, finely made perfume flask and covered it with miniature animals, sphinxes and warriors drawn in silhouette with incised detail — the technique that would become black-figure. These tiny vessels travelled everywhere Greek ships went, turning up in Italy, Sicily and the Levant, and they are among archaeology's most useful dating tools for the eighth and seventh centuries. Corinth's commercial reach and its absorption of Near Eastern motifs are visible in a single hand-sized pot.
Early Protocorinthian (Greece, 719 BC–68.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Protocorinthian (Greece, 689 BC–6.label: Middle Protocorinthian
Middle Protocorinthian (Greece, 689 BC–6.prose:
[Greece, 689 BC–649 BC] Middle Protocorinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Corinthian potters perfected the tiny perfume flasks that carried their city's oils across the Mediterranean, decorating them with miniature animal friezes and incised black-figure detail. The technique of cutting lines through silhouette to show anatomy was worked out here and later borrowed by Athens. Some of the finest pieces show ranks of hoplites advancing to the music of pipes, the earliest images of the phalanx.
Middle Protocorinthian (Greece, 689 BC–6.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Protocorinthian (Greece, 649 BC–624.label: Late Protocorinthian
Late Protocorinthian (Greece, 649 BC–624.prose:
