[Greece, 649 BC–624 BC] Late Protocorinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Corinthian workshops perfected miniature painting on small perfume flasks, packing hoplite ranks, animal friezes and hunting scenes into bands only centimetres high using incision and added colour. These aryballoi and alabastra travelled everywhere Greek ships went, from Etruria to the Levant, making Corinth the dominant pottery exporter of its day. The black-figure technique refined here was taken up and eventually surpassed by Athens.
Late Protocorinthian (Greece, 649 BC–624.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Corinthian (Greece, 624 BC–534 BC).label: Corinthian
Corinthian (Greece, 624 BC–534 BC).prose:
[Greece, 624 BC–534 BC] Corinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Corinth's potters dominated Mediterranean markets with small perfume flasks and jugs painted in a distinctive style: rows of lions, sphinxes and goats set against a field of incised rosettes, worked in black silhouette with fine engraved detail. Their exports turn up from Etruria to the Levant and are one of the best dating tools archaeologists have for the seventh and sixth centuries. Athenian workshops eventually took the trade away.
Corinthian (Greece, 624 BC–534 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Transitional to Corinthian (Greece, 624.label: Transitional to Corinthian
Transitional to Corinthian (Greece, 624.prose:
[Greece, 624 BC–609 BC] Transitional to Corinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The short phase in which Corinth's exquisite miniaturist Protocorinthian vase painting broadened into the mass-produced Corinthian style. Painters gave up fine incised narrative for rows of lions, panthers and sphinxes filled out with rosettes, and shipped the resulting perfume flasks and drinking vessels across the Mediterranean in such numbers that they now date sites from Sicily to the Levant.
Transitional to Corinthian (Greece, 624.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Corinthian (Greece, 609 BC–579 BC).label: Early Corinthian
Early Corinthian (Greece, 609 BC–579 BC).prose:
[Greece, 609 BC–579 BC] Early Corinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Corinthian workshops were the leading exporters of fine painted pottery in the Greek world, and their small perfume flasks travelled to Etruria, Sicily and the Levant. Painters filled vessels with friezes of lions, sphinxes and hoplites in black-figure silhouette with incised detail. The pottery is one of archaeology's most useful clocks for dating early colonial sites across the Mediterranean.
Early Corinthian (Greece, 609 BC–579 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Corinthian (Greece, 579 BC–554 BC.label: Middle Corinthian
Middle Corinthian (Greece, 579 BC–554 BC.prose:
[Greece, 579 BC–554 BC] Middle Corinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The peak and turning point of Corinth's pottery industry, whose small perfume flasks and wine jugs, crowded with lions, panthers and grazing deer in incised black silhouette, were shipped across the Mediterranean from Etruria to the Black Sea. Painters increasingly added human myth scenes and named figures, borrowing techniques Athens would soon perfect. Within a generation Attic black-figure had captured the export market and Corinthian production went into decline.
Middle Corinthian (Greece, 579 BC–554 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Corinthian (Greece, 554 BC–534 BC).label: Late Corinthian
Late Corinthian (Greece, 554 BC–534 BC).prose:
[Greece, 554 BC–534 BC] Late Corinthian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The closing phase of Corinth's once-dominant figured pottery, whose small perfume flasks and animal-frieze vases had been exported all over the Mediterranean for a century. Painters increasingly imitated Athenian black-figure, even coating their pale clay with a red slip, but Attic workshops had captured the market. Corinth stayed rich as a trading city, yet its potters largely abandoned figured decoration.
Late Corinthian (Greece, 554 BC–534 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Classical (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).label: Classical
Classical (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).prose:
[Greece, 479 BC–322 BC] Classical. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.
Classical (Greece, 479 BC–322 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC) [.label: High Classical
High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC) [.prose:
[Greece, 449 BC–399 BC] High Classical. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The decades after the Persian wars when Athens, funded by its maritime empire, rebuilt the Acropolis and put up the Parthenon under Pheidias's direction. Sophocles and Euripides were writing for the theatre, Socrates was arguing in the agora, and sculptors worked out an idealised human figure that European art would copy for two thousand years. The same era brought the Peloponnesian War, plague, and the collapse of Athenian power in 404.
High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC) [.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC) [p0ds.label: Hellenistic
Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC) [p0ds.prose:
[Greece, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.
Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC) [p0ds.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Hellenistic (Greece, 329 BC–219 BC.label: Early Hellenistic
Early Hellenistic (Greece, 329 BC–219 BC.prose:
[Greece, 329 BC–219 BC] Early Hellenistic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Following Alexander's conquest, the region fell under Ptolemaic and then Seleucid rule, with Greek-style cities, coinage and administration layered over older Transjordanian communities. The Nabataeans of Petra were meanwhile building wealth from the incense trade. Greek architectural forms, imported amphorae and new fortified estates mark the change on the ground.
Early Hellenistic (Greece, 329 BC–219 BC.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Hellenistic (Greece, 219 BC–149 B.label: Middle Hellenistic
Middle Hellenistic (Greece, 219 BC–149 B.prose:
[Greece, 219 BC–149 BC] Middle Hellenistic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Greece became a battleground for Rome's wars against Philip V and Perseus of Macedon, with the Achaean and Aetolian leagues manoeuvring between the two. Roman victories at Cynoscephalae and Pydna dismantled Macedonian power and left the leagues as clients rather than partners. The period closes on the eve of the sack of Corinth, after which Greece was governed from Rome.
Middle Hellenistic (Greece, 219 BC–149 B.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Hellenistic (Greece, 149 BC–30 BC).label: Late Hellenistic
Late Hellenistic (Greece, 149 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Greece, 149 BC–30 BC] Late Hellenistic. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Seleucid armies took the region from the Ptolemies at the start of this stretch, but imperial control soon frayed: Hasmonean rulers pushed east of the Jordan, the Greek-styled cities that would become the Decapolis asserted themselves, and the Nabataeans of Petra grew rich taxing incense and spice caravans. Greek language, coinage and civic architecture spread widely while local Semitic culture persisted underneath. The period closes as Rome moves into Syria and begins rearranging the whole region.
Late Hellenistic (Greece, 149 BC–30 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Graeco-Roman (Greece, 149 BC–30 BC).label: Graeco-Roman
Graeco-Roman (Greece, 149 BC–30 BC).prose:
[Greece, 149 BC–30 BC] Graeco-Roman. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Egypt after Alexander was ruled first by the Macedonian Ptolemies from their new capital at Alexandria, then, after Cleopatra's defeat, as the personal grain-basket of the Roman emperors. Greek became the language of administration while Egyptian temples were still built and decorated in pharaonic style, and the two worlds met in things like the painted mummy portraits from the Fayum. The papyri preserved in the dry sand make this one of the best-documented societies of the ancient world.
Graeco-Roman (Greece, 149 BC–30 BC).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Roman (Greece, 30 BC–AD 324).label: Roman
Roman (Greece, 30 BC–AD 324).prose:
[Greece, 30 BC–AD 324] Roman. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.
Roman (Greece, 30 BC–AD 324).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Roman (Greece, AD 250–AD 600).label: Late Roman
Late Roman (Greece, AD 250–AD 600).prose:
[Greece, AD 250–AD 600] Late Roman. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.
Late Roman (Greece, AD 250–AD 600).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Antique (Greece, AD 306–AD 610).label: Late Antique
Late Antique (Greece, AD 306–AD 610).prose:
[Greece, AD 306–AD 610] Late Antique. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The western empire dissolved into barbarian kingdoms: Ostrogothic rule under Theoderic preserved much of Roman administration at Ravenna, until Justinian's twenty-year Gothic War devastated the peninsula and the Lombards seized the north in 568. Cities shrank, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and bishops and monasteries took over civic leadership. It was also an age of extraordinary art - Ravenna's mosaics - and of the Rule of St Benedict.
Late Antique (Greece, AD 306–AD 610).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 1453).label: Byzantine
Byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 1453).prose:
[Greece, AD 324–AD 1453] Byzantine. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.
Byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 1453).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Christian (Greece, AD 175–AD 625).label: Early Christian
Early Christian (Greece, AD 175–AD 625).prose:
[Greece, AD 175–AD 625] Early Christian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Christianity spread through the Greek cities and then, under imperial patronage, became the dominant religion, remaking the urban landscape. Temples were abandoned, quarried or converted, and large basilicas with mosaic floors rose in towns from Thessaloniki to Crete. The old civic centres shrank while bishops became the leading local figures, a change visible in almost every excavated Greek town.
Early Christian (Greece, AD 175–AD 625).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).label: Early Byzantine
Early Byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).prose:
[Greece, AD 324–AD 610] Early Byzantine. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The island prospered as a wealthy province of the Eastern Roman Empire, its cities rebuilt with grand basilicas whose floors were laid with mosaics and whose bishops claimed independence from Antioch. Salamis, refounded as Constantia, and Kourion and Paphos flourished despite earthquakes. Arab naval raids from the 640s ended this security and opened centuries in which Cyprus was contested and shared between Byzantium and the caliphate.
Early Byzantine (Greece, AD 324–AD 610).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Byzantine (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204.label: Middle Byzantine
Middle Byzantine (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204.prose:
[Greece, AD 610–AD 1204] Middle Byzantine. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After the disruptions of the early medieval centuries, imperial administration and the church reasserted control over the southwest Peloponnese, and new bishoprics, monasteries and small cross-in-square churches were built. Settlement and agriculture expanded, and Slavic-speaking populations in the interior were gradually Christianised and absorbed. The period ends with the Fourth Crusade, after which Frankish lords carved up the Morea.
Middle Byzantine (Greece, AD 610–AD 1204.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Byzantine (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453).label: Late Byzantine
Late Byzantine (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453).prose:
[Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453] Late Byzantine. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Nikephoros Phokas's reconquest in 965 ended centuries of contested Arab-Byzantine condominium and made Cyprus a securely imperial province again, governed from Nicosia and Famagusta. Wealth from grain, sugar and trade paid for the mountain monasteries and churches whose frescoes are the island's greatest medieval treasure. It ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island in 1191, beginning three centuries of Latin rule.
Late Byzantine (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1453).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Medieval/Frankish (Greece, AD 323–AD 145.label: Medieval/Frankish
Medieval/Frankish (Greece, AD 323–AD 145.prose:
[Greece, AD 323–AD 1453] Medieval/Frankish. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Greece spent most of these centuries as the heartland of the Byzantine Empire, its cities and countryside organised around Orthodox Christianity and Constantinople. The Fourth Crusade's sack of the capital in 1204 shattered that order, and Frankish knights, Venetians and Catalans carved out duchies and principalities across the Peloponnese and central Greece, building castles that still crown many hills. Byzantine successor states clawed some territory back, but Ottoman armies took Constantinople in 1453.
Medieval/Frankish (Greece, AD 323–AD 145.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Venetian (Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650).label: Venetian
Venetian (Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650).prose:
[Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650] Venetian. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Venice took formal control of the island after the last Lusignan queen, Caterina Cornaro, was persuaded to abdicate, running it as a colony geared to sugar, cotton and grain exports. Facing the Ottoman threat, Venetian engineers threw up the massive walls of Nicosia and Famagusta that still ring both cities. The Ottoman invasion of 1570 took Nicosia in weeks; Famagusta held out for nearly a year before falling in 1571.
Venetian (Greece, AD 1200–AD 1650).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Ottoman (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).label: Ottoman
Ottoman (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).prose:
[Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821] Ottoman. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.
Ottoman (Greece, AD 1453–AD 1821).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Modern period (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).label: Modern period
Modern period (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).prose:
[Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000] Modern period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The revolt against Ottoman rule that began in 1821 produced Europe's first successful nationalist secession and, by 1830, a small independent kingdom under foreign monarchs and great-power tutelage. Territorial expansion drove Greek politics for a century until the disastrous Asia Minor campaign ended in 1922 with the population exchange that brought over a million refugees. Occupation, a savage civil war, dictatorship until 1974 and then entry into the European Community shaped the modern state, while Athens grew from a provincial town into a city of millions.
Modern period (Greece, AD 1821–AD 2000).source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Early Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–89.label: Early Protogeometric
Early Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–89.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Early Protogeometric. This sub-period is used to categorize information in BSA collections, but has not been assigned specific dates because of the depth of scholarly disagreement about the internal divisions of the Protogeometric period. It is therefore associated generally with the entire time-span of the Protogeometric period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

After the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, Athenian potters produced a disciplined new style: fast-wheel shapes decorated with compass-drawn concentric circles and semicircles in lustrous dark paint. The order and precision of the pottery contrasts with a period of depopulation, lost writing and shrunken settlement, and marks the point at which Greek material culture begins to recover and diverge regionally. Burial in single cist graves and cremation urns replaces older communal tombs.
Early Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–89.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Middle Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–8.label: Middle Protogeometric
Middle Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–8.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Middle Protogeometric. This sub-period is used to categorize information in BSA collections, but has not been assigned specific dates because of the depth of scholarly disagreement about the internal divisions of the Protogeometric period. It is therefore associated generally with the entire time-span of the Protogeometric period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

In the centuries after the Mycenaean palaces collapsed, potters in Athens and Euboea developed a disciplined new style, using a fast wheel and compass-drawn concentric circles on dark-glazed vessels. Communities were small and largely illiterate, but cremation burials with iron weapons and imported goods – above all at Lefkandi – show elites re-establishing contact with Cyprus and the Levant. These are the first stirrings of recovery that led to the Geometric period and the emergence of the Greek city-states.
Middle Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–8.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Late Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–899.label: Late Protogeometric
Late Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–899.prose:
[Greece, 1099 BC–899 BC] Late Protogeometric. This sub-period is used to categorize information in BSA collections, but has not been assigned specific dates because of the depth of scholarly disagreement about the internal divisions of the Protogeometric period. It is therefore associated generally with the entire time-span of the Protogeometric period. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

In the centuries after the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, potters at Athens and elsewhere imposed strict order on their vases with compass-drawn concentric circles and semicircles set against glossy dark paint. Iron working became routine, cremation burial spread, and sites like Lefkandi show elite households with contacts reaching to Cyprus and the Levant. The taut geometry of these pots is the first sign of the visual discipline that would define later Greek art.
Late Protogeometric (Greece, 1099 BC–899.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

Wadi Suq (Oman, 1999 BC–1599 BC).label: Wadi Suq
Wadi Suq (Oman, 1999 BC–1599 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Wadi Suq. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Wadi Suq and Late Bronze Age in the Oman Peninsula — Velde, Christian, 2003.

Following the collapse of the Umm an-Nar order, settlement in southeastern Arabia became more dispersed and mobile, with a stronger emphasis on herding alongside oasis farming. Communal round tombs gave way to long above-ground burial chambers, and grave goods include distinctive soft-stone vessels and bronze weapons showing continued contact with Mesopotamia and the Indus world.
Wadi Suq (Oman, 1999 BC–1599 BC).source: Wadi Suq and Late Bronze Age in the Oman Peninsula

Late Bronze Age (Oman, 1599 BC–1299 BC).label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Oman, 1599 BC–1299 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1599 BC–1299 BC] Late Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Wadi Suq and Late Bronze Age in the Oman Peninsula — Velde, Christian, 2003.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Oman, 1599 BC–1299 BC).source: Wadi Suq and Late Bronze Age in the Oman Peninsula

Iron Age I (Oman, 1299 BC–1099 BC).label: Iron Age I
Iron Age I (Oman, 1299 BC–1099 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1299 BC–1099 BC] Iron Age I. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age — Magee, Peter, 1996.

The Hittite empire disappeared and Anatolia fragmented into small, often illiterate societies, with monumental hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions kept alive only by the Neo-Hittite successor states of the south-east. Phrygians moved into the central plateau and settlement clustered on defensible mounds, while in the east the tribal groups later unified as Urartu began to coalesce. From this fractured landscape came the kingdoms - Phrygia, Urartu, Lydia and the Syro-Hittite city-states - that dominated the following centuries.
Iron Age I (Oman, 1299 BC–1099 BC).source: The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age

Iron Age II (Oman, 1099 BC–599 BC).label: Iron Age II
Iron Age II (Oman, 1099 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1099 BC–599 BC] Iron Age II. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age — Magee, Peter, 1996.

Greek settlers pushed out from Syracuse and Naxos to found a chain of colonies around the coast, while Phoenicians held the western tip at Motya and Panormus. The indigenous Sikels, Sikanians and Elymians adopted Greek pottery, building styles and writing even as they lost land, and Sikel resistance culminated in Ducetius' short-lived confederation. Sicily's grain, its tyrants and its rivalry with Carthage made the island a major player in the wider Mediterranean world.
Iron Age II (Oman, 1099 BC–599 BC).source: The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age

Iron Age III (Oman, 599 BC–299 BC).label: Iron Age III
Iron Age III (Oman, 599 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 599 BC–299 BC] Iron Age III. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age — Magee, Peter, 1996.

Lydia rose to dominate western Anatolia from Sardis, striking some of the world's first coins and drawing wealth from the Pactolus river, while Phrygia declined after Cimmerian raids. In the east, Urartu was worn down and the Assyrian empire fell, leaving Medes and Babylonians to divide the spoils. The era closed abruptly when Cyrus the Great took Sardis and made Anatolia Persian.
Iron Age III (Oman, 599 BC–299 BC).source: The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age

Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–299 BC).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1299 BC–299 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age — Magee, Peter, 1996.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–299 BC).source: The Chronology of the Southeast Arabian Iron Age

Late Iron Age (Oman, 299 BC–AD 300).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (Oman, 299 BC–AD 300).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 299 BC–AD 300] Late Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Cross-roads Early and Late Iron Age South-eastern Arabia — Paul Yule, 2017.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.
Late Iron Age (Oman, 299 BC–AD 300).source: Cross-roads Early and Late Iron Age South-eastern Arabia

Rumeilah I (United Arab Emirates, 1299 B.node: Rumeilah I (United Arab Emirates, 1299 BC–999 BC)
Rumeilah I (United Arab Emirates, 1299 B.label: Rumeilah I
Rumeilah I (United Arab Emirates, 1299 B.prose:
[Rumeilah, 1299 BC–999 BC] Rumeilah I. Period definition from Datations absolues de Rumeilah et chronologie de l'âge du Fer dans la Péninsule d'Oman — Boucharlat, Rémy, 1991.

Iron Age oasis settlement in the interior of southeastern Arabia, with mudbrick houses and columned halls built beside date-palm gardens. The key innovation of the age was the falaj, a gently sloping underground channel tapping groundwater and carrying it to fields, which allowed permanent villages far from the coast and reshaped settlement across the region.
Rumeilah I (United Arab Emirates, 1299 B.source: Datations absolues de Rumeilah et chronologie de l'âge du Fer dans la Péninsule d'Oman

Rumeilah II (United Arab Emirates, 999 B.node: Rumeilah II (United Arab Emirates, 999 BC–299 BC)
Rumeilah II (United Arab Emirates, 999 B.label: Rumeilah II
Rumeilah II (United Arab Emirates, 999 B.prose:
[Rumeilah, 999 BC–299 BC] Rumeilah II. Period definition from Datations absolues de Rumeilah et chronologie de l'âge du Fer dans la Péninsule d'Oman — Boucharlat, Rémy, 1991.

The later Iron Age at the Al Ain oases, when falaj-fed villages continued alongside communal tombs, soft-stone vessels and distinctive painted pottery. Contacts reached out to Mesopotamia and eventually the Achaemenid world, before the settlement pattern thinned in the centuries preceding the caravan and coastal trade of the later pre-Islamic era.
Rumeilah II (United Arab Emirates, 999 B.source: Datations absolues de Rumeilah et chronologie de l'âge du Fer dans la Péninsule d'Oman

Classic Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates,.node: Classic Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates, 1999 BC–1449 BC)
Classic Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates,.label: Classic Wadi Suq
Classic Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates,.prose:
[Kalba, 1999 BC–1449 BC] Classic Wadi Suq. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Defining the Late Bronze Age in Southeast Arabia : ceramic evolution and settlement during the Second Millennium. — Robert Andrew Carter, 1998.

After the collapse of the monumental Umm an-Nar tradition, communities in south-east Arabia adopted a more mobile, pastoral way of life with smaller settlements. Burial shifted from great circular tombs to long, above-ground collective graves, furnished with fine painted pottery, softstone vessels and bronze weapons. Copper production and trade with Mesopotamia and the Indus continued, but on a reduced and reorganised scale.
Classic Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates,.source: Defining the Late Bronze Age in Southeast Arabia : ceramic evolution and settlement during the Second Millennium.

Late Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates, 144.node: Late Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates, 1449 BC–1299 BC)
Late Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates, 144.label: Late Wadi Suq
Late Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates, 144.prose:
[Kalba, 1449 BC–1299 BC] Late Wadi Suq. Period definition from Defining the Late Bronze Age in Southeast Arabia : ceramic evolution and settlement during the Second Millennium. — Robert Andrew Carter, 1998.

Following the collapse of the walled Umm an-Nar towns, people lived in smaller, more dispersed settlements and herded as much as they farmed. The dead were placed in long, low collective tombs alongside distinctive soft-stone vessels, painted pottery and bronze daggers and arrowheads. These centuries bridge the Bronze Age copper-trading world and the Iron Age, when falaj irrigation would allow settlement to expand again.
Late Wadi Suq (United Arab Emirates, 144.source: Defining the Late Bronze Age in Southeast Arabia : ceramic evolution and settlement during the Second Millennium.

Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2799 BC–1999 BC).label: Umm an-Nar
Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2799 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Bat, 2799 BC–1999 BC] Umm an-Nar. Period definition from Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia — Swerida, Jennifer, 2021.

Named after an island near Abu Dhabi, this Bronze Age culture built distinctive round communal tombs of dressed white stone, holding hundreds of dead together, alongside fortified circular towers and mudbrick villages. Its people smelted the copper that Mesopotamian texts call the product of Magan, trading it for goods from Sumer and the Indus valley - Harappan pottery and weights turn up on Omani sites. Date cultivation and irrigated oasis farming took hold here, setting the pattern of settlement for millennia.
Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2799 BC–1999 BC).source: Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia

Early Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2799 BC–2499 BC).label: Early Umm an-Nar
Early Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2799 BC–2499 BC).prose:
[Bat, 2799 BC–2499 BC] Early Umm an-Nar. Period definition from Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia — Swerida, Jennifer, 2021.

Coastal and inland communities in southeastern Arabia began building the distinctive circular, above-ground stone tombs that give the culture its name, holding the collective remains of whole communities. Copper from the Omani mountains was smelted and shipped out to Mesopotamia, where the region was known as Magan, and imported Indus and Iranian goods travelled back. Mudbrick and stone towers with wells appear at settlements, marking a shift to permanent, organised village life sustained by oasis farming and the sea.
Early Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2799 BC–2499 BC).source: Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia

Middle Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2499 BC–2199 BC.label: Middle Umm an-Nar
Middle Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2499 BC–2199 BC.prose:
[Bat, 2499 BC–2199 BC] Middle Umm an-Nar. Period definition from Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia — Swerida, Jennifer, 2021.

Southeast Arabia's Bronze Age communities buried their dead in monumental circular tombs of dressed stone, each holding hundreds of individuals, and built round mud-brick and stone towers beside date-palm oases. Copper mined in the Omani mountains was smelted and exported to Mesopotamia, where this land was known as Magan. Imported Indus and Iranian pottery in the tombs shows how far these maritime connections reached.
Middle Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2499 BC–2199 BC.source: Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia

Middle Umm an-Nar 1 (Oman, 2499 BC–2399.label: Middle Umm an-Nar 1
Middle Umm an-Nar 1 (Oman, 2499 BC–2399.prose:
[Bat, 2499 BC–2399 BC] Middle Umm an-Nar 1. Period definition from Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia — Swerida, Jennifer, 2021.

The mature phase of southeast Arabia's Bronze Age, when circular communal tombs became larger and more finely built, with carefully fitted ashlar facing and carved reliefs of animals and human figures. Oasis settlements clustered around monumental towers, and copper production for export to Mesopotamia was at its height.
Middle Umm an-Nar 1 (Oman, 2499 BC–2399.source: Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia

Middle Umm an-Nar 2 (Oman, 2399 BC–2199.label: Middle Umm an-Nar 2
Middle Umm an-Nar 2 (Oman, 2399 BC–2199.prose:
[Bat, 2399 BC–2199 BC] Middle Umm an-Nar 2. Period definition from Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia — Swerida, Jennifer, 2021.

Copper mining and long-distance exchange continued at full strength, with Indus Valley goods and traders reaching the Oman peninsula. Tombs remained the great communal investment, reused over generations and filled with pottery, softstone vessels and beads that record the reach of the region's seaborne connections.
Middle Umm an-Nar 2 (Oman, 2399 BC–2199.source: Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia

Late Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2199 BC–1999 BC).label: Late Umm an-Nar
Late Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2199 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Bat, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Late Umm an-Nar. Period definition from Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia — Swerida, Jennifer, 2021.

The closing centuries of the oasis towns of the Oman peninsula, known to Mesopotamian scribes as Magan and prized as a source of copper. Communities built stone defensive towers and buried their dead collectively in circular, finely faced tombs holding hundreds of individuals, along with Indus Valley and Mesopotamian imports. As long-distance trade shifted, these towns were abandoned and settlement fragmented into the smaller, more mobile pattern of the Wadi Suq period.
Late Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2199 BC–1999 BC).source: Settlement and Chronology in the early Bronze Age of Southeastern Arabia

Early Bronze Age (Oman, 3099 BC–1999 BC).label: Early Bronze Age
Early Bronze Age (Oman, 3099 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 3099 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.
Early Bronze Age (Oman, 3099 BC–1999 BC).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Bronze Age (Oman, 3099 BC–1299 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Oman, 3099 BC–1299 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 3099 BC–1299 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.
Bronze Age (Oman, 3099 BC–1299 BC).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Middle Bronze Age (Oman, 1999 BC–1599 BC.label: Middle Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age (Oman, 1999 BC–1599 BC.prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.
Middle Bronze Age (Oman, 1999 BC–1599 BC.source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Late Bronze Age (Oman, 1599 BC–1299 BC).label: Late Bronze Age
Late Bronze Age (Oman, 1599 BC–1299 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1599 BC–1299 BC] Late Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.
Late Bronze Age (Oman, 1599 BC–1299 BC).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Hafit (Oman, 3099 BC–2699 BC).label: Hafit
Hafit (Oman, 3099 BC–2699 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Hafit. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

The beginning of the Bronze Age in southeastern Arabia, marked by thousands of stone beehive-shaped tombs strung along ridgelines above the oases, often with a single burial and a few pots inside. Imported Mesopotamian jars found in them show that this coast was already tied into Gulf trade networks, and the copper of these mountains is very likely the metal Sumerian texts credit to the land of Magan. Falaj-fed oasis settlement and date cultivation begin to take hold here.
Hafit (Oman, 3099 BC–2699 BC).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2699 BC–1999 BC).label: Umm an-Nar
Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2699 BC–1999 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 2699 BC–1999 BC] Umm an-Nar. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Named after an island near Abu Dhabi, this Bronze Age culture built distinctive round communal tombs of dressed white stone, holding hundreds of dead together, alongside fortified circular towers and mudbrick villages. Its people smelted the copper that Mesopotamian texts call the product of Magan, trading it for goods from Sumer and the Indus valley - Harappan pottery and weights turn up on Omani sites. Date cultivation and irrigated oasis farming took hold here, setting the pattern of settlement for millennia.
Umm an-Nar (Oman, 2699 BC–1999 BC).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–AD 300).label: Iron Age
Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–AD 300).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 1299 BC–AD 300] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.
Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–AD 300).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Islamic Period (Oman, AD 630–AD 1970).label: Islamic Period
Islamic Period (Oman, AD 630–AD 1970).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, AD 630–AD 1970] Islamic Period. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Oman converted early, and by the eighth century had adopted Ibadi Islam and begun electing its own imams, a tradition that set it apart from the wider Muslim world. Its ports thrived on the monsoon trade to India, East Africa and China, its interior on falaj irrigation and date gardens; later the Ya'ariba and Al Bu Said rulers expelled the Portuguese and built a maritime empire that reached Zanzibar. Forts, watchtowers and mud-brick towns from these centuries still dominate the landscape.
Islamic Period (Oman, AD 630–AD 1970).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Early Islamic (Oman, AD 630–AD 1055).label: Early Islamic
Early Islamic (Oman, AD 630–AD 1055).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, AD 630–AD 1055] Early Islamic. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Arab armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and under the Umayyads it lay close to the heart of the new empire, dotted with the rural palaces and bath-houses known as the desert castles. Village life, churches and mosaic workshops carried on with surprising continuity, though the devastating earthquake of AD 749 wrecked many towns. When the Abbasids moved the capital to Iraq, the area slipped from imperial centre to provincial backwater.
Early Islamic (Oman, AD 630–AD 1055).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Middle Islamic (Oman, AD 1055–AD 1650).label: Middle Islamic
Middle Islamic (Oman, AD 1055–AD 1650).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, AD 1055–AD 1650] Middle Islamic. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Jordan sat between Crusader lordships, Ayyubid armies and finally the Mamluk sultanate, whose castles, sugar mills and postal routes reshaped the countryside. Karak and Shobak changed hands amid the wars of Saladin and his successors, and villages prospered on sugar cane, pottery and the pilgrimage road to Mecca. Handmade geometric-painted wares are the characteristic find of the period.
Middle Islamic (Oman, AD 1055–AD 1650).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Late Islamic (Oman, AD 1650–AD 1970).label: Late Islamic
Late Islamic (Oman, AD 1650–AD 1970).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, AD 1650–AD 1970] Late Islamic. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Mamluk administration gave way to Ottoman rule, and much of the countryside shifted from villages to a more mobile, tribally organised way of life based on herding and seasonal cultivation. State attention concentrated on the pilgrimage road to Mecca, guarded by a chain of forts with cisterns where caravans watered. Handmade painted pottery and clay tobacco pipes are the period's most common archaeological markers.
Late Islamic (Oman, AD 1650–AD 1970).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Modern (Oman, AD 1970–AD 2020).label: Modern
Modern (Oman, AD 1970–AD 2020).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, AD 1970–AD 2020] Modern. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.
Modern (Oman, AD 1970–AD 2020).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Sasanian (Oman, AD 300–AD 630).label: Sasanian
Sasanian (Oman, AD 300–AD 630).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, AD 300–AD 630] Sasanian. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.
Sasanian (Oman, AD 300–AD 630).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Neolithic (Oman, 8499 BC–3099 BC).label: Neolithic
Neolithic (Oman, 8499 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 8499 BC–3099 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah — Conrad Schmidt, 2021.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.
Neolithic (Oman, 8499 BC–3099 BC).source: Die Entstehung komplexer Siedlungen im Zentraloman Archäologische Untersuchungen zur Siedlungsgeschichte von Al-Khashbah

Early Holocene (Oman, 8499 BC–4999 BC).label: Early Holocene
Early Holocene (Oman, 8499 BC–4999 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 8499 BC–4999 BC] Early Holocene. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Hunter-gatherers of the "empty quarter of the early Holocene" to the last Neolithic societies: chronology of the late prehistory of south-eastern Arabia (8000-3100 BC) — Charpentier, Vincent, 2008.

As the last ice age ended, monsoon rains pushed north and southeast Arabia became far greener, with lakes, grassland and productive coasts. People fished, gathered shellfish in huge middens, hunted and eventually kept domestic animals, leaving distinctive Arabian Neolithic stone tools and shell ornaments. The gradual drying that followed pushed communities toward the oases and coastal settlements that shaped later Omani life.
Early Holocene (Oman, 8499 BC–4999 BC).source: Hunter-gatherers of the "empty quarter of the early Holocene" to the last Neolithic societies: chronology of the late prehistory of south-eastern Arabia (8000-3100 BC)

Middle Holocene (Oman, 4999 BC–3099 BC).label: Middle Holocene
Middle Holocene (Oman, 4999 BC–3099 BC).prose:
[Eastern Arabia, 4999 BC–3099 BC] Middle Holocene. Spatial coverage: Oman, United Arab Emirates. Period definition from Hunter-gatherers of the "empty quarter of the early Holocene" to the last Neolithic societies: chronology of the late prehistory of south-eastern Arabia (8000-3100 BC) — Charpentier, Vincent, 2008.

A wetter climate supported herders, fishers and shell-gatherers along the Arabian coast and in the interior, leaving huge shell middens, stone-built tombs and finely made bifacial arrowheads. Domestic cattle, sheep and goats spread, and communities traded with Mesopotamia across the Gulf. As monsoon rains retreated toward the end, populations concentrated at oases and the coast, setting the pattern for later Bronze Age settlement.
Middle Holocene (Oman, 4999 BC–3099 BC).source: Hunter-gatherers of the "empty quarter of the early Holocene" to the last Neolithic societies: chronology of the late prehistory of south-eastern Arabia (8000-3100 BC)

Late Neolithic (Oman, 4499 BC–3099 BC).label: Late Neolithic
Late Neolithic (Oman, 4499 BC–3099 BC).prose:

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.

The founding phase of a settlement in the Al Ain oasis, contemporary with the Hafit-period cairn tombs that dot the nearby hills. Excavation here produced some of the earliest evidence anywhere for cultivated date palms, alongside wheat, barley and melon — proof that oasis farming, not just herding and fishing, underpinned early settled life in south-eastern Arabia.

Copper from the Omani mountains, exported to Mesopotamia as the metal of 'Magan', paid for imported pottery and beads, and communities buried their dead together in round stone tombs. The layered sequence of rebuildings here is the backbone of Bronze Age chronology for the whole Oman peninsula.

The tower settlement's final occupation, coinciding with the Wadi Suq period, when the great collective tombs and monumental round towers of the preceding centuries fell out of use. Settlement across the Oman peninsula became more dispersed and mobile, with a heavier emphasis on herding, and burial shifted to smaller family graves. The site was eventually abandoned, ending nearly a millennium and a half of continuous life at the oasis.

Early Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–599 BC).label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–599 BC).prose:
[Sultanate of Oman, 1299 BC–599 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from Iron Age chronology in South East Arabia and new data from Salut, Sultanate of Oman — Phillips, Carl, 2010.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.
Early Iron Age (Oman, 1299 BC–599 BC).source: Iron Age chronology in South East Arabia and new data from Salut, Sultanate of Oman

Late Iron Age (Oman, 599 BC–299 BC).label: Late Iron Age
Late Iron Age (Oman, 599 BC–299 BC).prose:
[Sultanate of Oman, 599 BC–299 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from Iron Age chronology in South East Arabia and new data from Salut, Sultanate of Oman — Phillips, Carl, 2010.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.
Late Iron Age (Oman, 599 BC–299 BC).source: Iron Age chronology in South East Arabia and new data from Salut, Sultanate of Oman

Late Islamic 1a (United Arab Emirates, A.label: Late Islamic 1a
Late Islamic 1a (United Arab Emirates, A.prose:
[Al-Ain , AD 1650–AD 1720] Late Islamic 1a. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

The Portuguese had been driven from the Gulf ports and the Omani Ya'ariba imams built a maritime power that traded and raided as far as East Africa. Coastal communities lived on pearling, fishing and date gardens, with imported Chinese and Persian ceramics reaching quite modest households. Watchtowers and mud-brick forts of this era still stand across the region's oases.
Late Islamic 1a (United Arab Emirates, A.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 1b (United Arab Emirates, A.label: Late Islamic 1b
Late Islamic 1b (United Arab Emirates, A.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1720–AD 1790] Late Islamic 1b. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Civil war in Oman weakened the old order and opened the way for new powers: the Qawasim built a fleet based on the northern coast and the Bani Yas moved out of the interior toward the coast and its pearl banks. Trade drew in Iranian, Indian and European goods, while glazed and mass-produced imported wares increasingly displaced local pottery.
Late Islamic 1b (United Arab Emirates, A.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 1c (United Arab Emirates, A.label: Late Islamic 1c
Late Islamic 1c (United Arab Emirates, A.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1790–AD 1820] Late Islamic 1c. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Qawasim shipping dominated the lower Gulf and clashed repeatedly with British and Omani interests, a conflict the British recast as piracy. Punitive naval expeditions culminated in the destruction of Ras al-Khaimah and a general treaty that ended the era of independent local sea power. Pearling and date cultivation remained the economic backbone throughout.
Late Islamic 1c (United Arab Emirates, A.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 2a (United Arab Emirates, A.label: Late Islamic 2a
Late Islamic 2a (United Arab Emirates, A.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1820–AD 1870] Late Islamic 2a. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Maritime truces brokered by Britain gave the coastal sheikhdoms a stable framework, and the pearl trade boomed as demand rose in India and Europe. Coastal towns grew around pearling fleets, with barasti palm-frond housing, coral-stone merchant houses and new forts. Political authority consolidated in the ruling families that would later govern the Trucial States.
Late Islamic 2a (United Arab Emirates, A.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 2b (United Arab Emirates, A.label: Late Islamic 2b
Late Islamic 2b (United Arab Emirates, A.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1870–AD 1920] Late Islamic 2b. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Pearling reached its peak: hundreds of boats sailed each summer to the banks, financing the growth of towns like Dubai and Abu Dhabi and drawing in migrant divers and merchants from Iran, India and Africa. Dubai's tax-free port attracted traders displaced from the Persian coast, and imported European and Asian goods filled local markets. Britain's treaties tightened into formal protection over the sheikhdoms' external affairs.
Late Islamic 2b (United Arab Emirates, A.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 2c (United Arab Emirates, A.label: Late Islamic 2c
Late Islamic 2c (United Arab Emirates, A.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1920–AD 1970] Late Islamic 2c. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Japanese cultured pearls and the world depression destroyed the pearling economy within a decade, causing hardship, emigration and the abandonment of coastal quarters. Oil concessions and then production transformed the picture from mid-century, funding harbours, roads, schools and concrete construction. The period closes with Britain's withdrawal and the founding of a federal state.
Late Islamic 2c (United Arab Emirates, A.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 1 (United Arab Emirates, AD.label: Late Islamic 1
Late Islamic 1 (United Arab Emirates, AD.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1650–AD 1820] Late Islamic 1. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Late Mamluk sugar estates and villages contracted, and after 1516 the region passed to the Ottomans, who surveyed it for taxation and reorganised the annual Hajj caravan route through it. Fortified way-stations, cisterns and khans were built or refurbished along that road. Many settled sites were abandoned as tribal groups took control of the land.
Late Islamic 1 (United Arab Emirates, AD.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Late Islamic 2 (United Arab Emirates, AD.label: Late Islamic 2
Late Islamic 2 (United Arab Emirates, AD.prose:
[Al-Ain, AD 1820–AD 1970] Late Islamic 2. Period definition from A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf — Power, Timothy, 2015.

Ottoman authority over the region was mostly exercised through subsidies to tribal leaders and control of the Hajj route rather than direct administration. Settlement was sparse and largely pastoral, with seasonal camps, small fortified farms and pilgrimage forts making up most of the built record. Coffee and tobacco consumption spread, leaving distinctive clay pipe bowls at almost every site.
Late Islamic 2 (United Arab Emirates, AD.source: A First Ceramic Chronology for the Late Islamic Arabian Gulf

Achaemenid/Iron Age IV (Iran, 550 BC–330.label: Achaemenid/Iron Age IV
Achaemenid/Iron Age IV (Iran, 550 BC–330.prose:
[Iran, 550 BC–330 BC] Achaemenid/Iron Age IV. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Cyrus the Great and his successors welded the Iranian plateau into the largest empire the world had yet seen, running from the Aegean to the Indus. Provincial satraps, a royal road system, standardised coinage and an Aramaic bureaucracy held it together, while Persepolis and Pasargadae advertised royal power in stone. It ended with Alexander's invasion, but its administrative model shaped every later Near Eastern empire.

Bronze Age, Akkadian (Iraq, 2400 BC–2150.label: Bronze Age, Akkadian
Bronze Age, Akkadian (Iraq, 2400 BC–2150.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 2400 BC–2150 BC] Bronze Age, Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Sargon of Akkad welded the Sumerian city-states into the first large territorial empire in Mesopotamia, campaigning from the Gulf to the Mediterranean and installing his own governors and his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess at Ur. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the language of government alongside Sumerian, and royal art turned to naturalistic victory monuments such as Naram-Sin's stele. The empire's collapse under Gutian pressure became a lasting theme in Mesopotamian literature about the fragility of kingship.

Bronze Age (Bahrain, 3200 BC–1500 BC).label: Bronze Age
Bronze Age (Bahrain, 3200 BC–1500 BC).prose:
[Arabia, 3200 BC–1500 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Bahrain, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Yemen. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Bronze Age, Early Dynastic I (Iraq, 2900.node: Bronze Age, Early Dynastic I (Iraq, 2900 BC–2750 BC)
Bronze Age, Early Dynastic I (Iraq, 2900.label: Bronze Age, Early Dynastic I
Bronze Age, Early Dynastic I (Iraq, 2900.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 2900 BC–2750 BC] Bronze Age, Early Dynastic I. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Southern Mesopotamia settles into a landscape of rival walled city-states after the Uruk expansion faded, each with its temple, its god and its ruler. Cities grew as villages emptied into them, and monumental mudbrick fortifications became a defining feature of the plain. Writing continued to develop from accounting notations toward a script capable of recording names, titles and eventually language itself.

Bronze Age, Early Dynastic II (Iraq, 275.node: Bronze Age, Early Dynastic II (Iraq, 2750 BC–2600 BC)
Bronze Age, Early Dynastic II (Iraq, 275.label: Bronze Age, Early Dynastic II
Bronze Age, Early Dynastic II (Iraq, 275.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 2750 BC–2600 BC] Bronze Age, Early Dynastic II. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The age to which later Mesopotamians assigned their heroic kings, Gilgamesh of Uruk among them, when city walls, palaces and competitive rulership took firm shape. Temples grew richer, craft specialists multiplied, and rival cities fought over land and water in the irrigated south. Cylinder seals of this time are crowded with contest scenes of heroes, bulls and lions.

Bronze Age, Early Dynastic III (Iraq, 26.node: Bronze Age, Early Dynastic III (Iraq, 2600 BC–2350 BC)
Bronze Age, Early Dynastic III (Iraq, 26.label: Bronze Age, Early Dynastic III
Bronze Age, Early Dynastic III (Iraq, 26.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 2600 BC–2350 BC] Bronze Age, Early Dynastic III. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The high point of Sumerian city-state civilisation, known from the Royal Cemetery of Ur with its lyres, gold headdresses and mass burials, and from the archives of Girsu and Ebla. Cuneiform now recorded literature, law and administration fully, and the long war between Lagash and Umma produced the earliest detailed war narratives and boundary treaties. Kings claimed hegemony over several cities, foreshadowing the empire Sargon would build.

Bronze Age, Jemdat Nasr (Iraq, 3100 BC–2.node: Bronze Age, Jemdat Nasr (Iraq, 3100 BC–2900 BC)
Bronze Age, Jemdat Nasr (Iraq, 3100 BC–2.label: Bronze Age, Jemdat Nasr
Bronze Age, Jemdat Nasr (Iraq, 3100 BC–2.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 3100 BC–2900 BC] Bronze Age, Jemdat Nasr. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

A short transitional phase named for a small site near Kish, marked by distinctive black-and-red painted jars and by mass-produced plain wares. Proto-cuneiform tablets from this time list officials, rations and city names, showing an administrative system already binding southern cities together. Trade reached the Gulf and Iran, and the temple economies that would define Sumer were taking their classic form.

Bronze Age, Kaftari/Yahya IVA (Iran, 230.node: Bronze Age, Kaftari/Yahya IVA (Iran, 2300 BC–1500 BC)
Bronze Age, Kaftari/Yahya IVA (Iran, 230.label: Bronze Age, Kaftari/Yahya IVA
Bronze Age, Kaftari/Yahya IVA (Iran, 230.prose:
[Southern Iran, 2300 BC–1500 BC] Bronze Age, Kaftari/Yahya IVA. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

A revival of settled life in highland Fars, centred on Anshan (Tal-e Malyan), whose buff pottery painted in dark bands gives the Kaftari phase its name. The city was large and walled, and its administrative sealings tie it to the Elamite political world of the lowlands. At Tepe Yahya in Kerman the contemporary occupation shows the same highland networks reaching toward the southeast.

Bronze Age, Kassite (Iraq, 1550 BC–1100.label: Bronze Age, Kassite
Bronze Age, Kassite (Iraq, 1550 BC–1100.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 1550 BC–1100 BC] Bronze Age, Kassite. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

A dynasty of outsiders took over Babylonia after the Hittite raid destroyed Hammurabi's line, and then ruled for longer than any other in Mesopotamian history. They founded a new capital at Dur-Kurigalzu, corresponded as equals with Egypt in the Amarna letters, and introduced the kudurru, a carved stone recording land grants under the protection of divine symbols. Under them Babylon became the cultural centre of the Near East, where scribes fixed the classic versions of Mesopotamian literature.

Bronze Age (Iran, 3100 BC–1100 BC).prose:

Bronze Age, Late Banesh/Yayha IVB (Iran,.label: Bronze Age, Late Banesh/Yayha IVB
Bronze Age, Late Banesh/Yayha IVB (Iran,.prose:
[Southern Iran, 2900 BC–2300 BC] Bronze Age, Late Banesh/Yayha IVB. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

In highland Fars the Proto-Elamite centre of Anshan shrank and its administrative system faded, while in Kerman the settlement at Tepe Yahya became a workshop for carved chlorite bowls in the so-called intercultural style. Those dark stone vessels, decorated with intertwined snakes, scorpions and architectural facades, travelled from the Iranian plateau to temples in Sumer and to the Gulf. The period shows Iranian communities supplying raw materials and finished luxuries to Mesopotamian cities without being ruled by them.

Bronze Age, Middle Babylonian (Iraq, 140.label: Bronze Age, Middle Babylonian
Bronze Age, Middle Babylonian (Iraq, 140.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 1400 BC–1100 BC] Bronze Age, Middle Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The later Kassite centuries, when Babylonia was one of several great powers exchanging gold, brides and letters with Egypt, Hatti and Assyria. Akkadian in its Babylonian dialect served as the diplomatic language of the whole eastern Mediterranean, taught to scribes from Amarna to Anatolia. Babylonian scholars codified omen series, medical texts and epics into the forms later copied for a thousand years.

Bronze Age, Middle Elamite (Iran, 1500 B.node: Bronze Age, Middle Elamite (Iran, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
Bronze Age, Middle Elamite (Iran, 1500 B.label: Bronze Age, Middle Elamite
Bronze Age, Middle Elamite (Iran, 1500 B.prose:
[Khuzestan, 1500 BC–1100 BC] Bronze Age, Middle Elamite. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Elamite kings ruling from Susa and Anshan built on a scale not seen before, above all Untash-Napirisha's temple city of Chogha Zanbil with its huge stepped ziggurat. Royal inscriptions switched from Akkadian to the Elamite language, asserting a distinct identity. Raids into Babylonia carried off famous monuments, including Hammurabi's law stele and the Naram-Sin victory stele, which archaeologists later found at Susa.

Bronze Age, Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1900 B.node: Bronze Age, Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1900 BC–1550 BC)
Bronze Age, Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1900 B.label: Bronze Age, Old Babylonian
Bronze Age, Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1900 B.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 1900 BC–1550 BC] Bronze Age, Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Amorite dynasties ruled competing kingdoms across Mesopotamia until Hammurabi of Babylon absorbed his rivals and had his laws inscribed on a black stone stele beneath an image of the sun god. The palace archives of Mari preserve thousands of letters about diplomacy, prophecy and the movement of armies, giving an unusually intimate view of ancient politics. Scribal schools of this era produced the mathematics, Sumerian literature and Gilgamesh poems that later ages inherited.

Bronze Age, Qaleh/Shogha-Teimuran (Iran,.label: Bronze Age, Qaleh/Shogha-Teimuran
Bronze Age, Qaleh/Shogha-Teimuran (Iran,.prose:
[Southwest Iran, 1500 BC–1000 BC] Bronze Age, Qaleh/Shogha-Teimuran. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Phases in the Kur River basin of Fars named after distinctive painted pottery styles, following the decline of the large Kaftari-period settlement at Anshan. Life became more dispersed and village-based, with smaller sites scattered across the plain. The wares bridge the late Bronze Age and the Iron Age cultures of southwestern Iran.

Bronze Age, Susa III/Proto-Elamite (Iran.node: Bronze Age, Susa III/Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3100 BC–2675 BC)
Bronze Age, Susa III/Proto-Elamite (Iran.label: Bronze Age, Susa III/Proto-Elamite
Bronze Age, Susa III/Proto-Elamite (Iran.prose:
[Khuzestan, 3100 BC–2675 BC] Bronze Age, Susa III/Proto-Elamite. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Susa turned away from Mesopotamia and toward the Iranian plateau, adopting a writing system of its own that remains undeciphered. Proto-Elamite tablets and their vivid animal-figure seals turn up from Susa to Tepe Yahya and Shahr-i Sokhta, evidence of a shared accounting culture stretching across Iran. It is the first sign of a distinctly Iranian political and economic world operating alongside Sumer.

Bronze Age, Susa IV/ Old Elamite I (Iran.node: Bronze Age, Susa IV/ Old Elamite I (Iran, 2675 BC–2200 BC)
Bronze Age, Susa IV/ Old Elamite I (Iran.label: Bronze Age, Susa IV/ Old Elamite I
Bronze Age, Susa IV/ Old Elamite I (Iran.prose:
[Khuzestan, 2675 BC–2200 BC] Bronze Age, Susa IV/ Old Elamite I. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Susa and the lowland plain were repeatedly fought over by Mesopotamian kings, and the Akkadian empire installed governors there. The Awan dynasty of Elamite rulers appears in Mesopotamian king lists, and a treaty between Naram-Sin and an Elamite king survives in the earliest text written in the Elamite language. Susa's material culture in these years is strongly Mesopotamian in style even as its politics remained separate.

Bronze Age, Susa V/ Old Elamite II (Iran.node: Bronze Age, Susa V/ Old Elamite II (Iran, 2200 BC–1800 BC)
Bronze Age, Susa V/ Old Elamite II (Iran.label: Bronze Age, Susa V/ Old Elamite II
Bronze Age, Susa V/ Old Elamite II (Iran.prose:
[Khuzestan, 2200 BC–1800 BC] Bronze Age, Susa V/ Old Elamite II. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Elamite rulers of the Shimashki line ended the Third Dynasty of Ur, sacking the city and carrying off its last king, a disaster mourned in Sumerian lament poetry. Their successors, the sukkalmah, governed Susa and highland Anshan together in one of Elam's most powerful eras, trading with Babylonia and Central Asia. Susa in this period produced fine bronzes, cylinder seals and family archives written in Akkadian.

Bronze Age, Susa VI/ Old Elamite III (Ir.node: Bronze Age, Susa VI/ Old Elamite III (Iran, 1900 BC–1500 BC)
Bronze Age, Susa VI/ Old Elamite III (Ir.label: Bronze Age, Susa VI/ Old Elamite III
Bronze Age, Susa VI/ Old Elamite III (Ir.prose:
[Khuzestan, 1900 BC–1500 BC] Bronze Age, Susa VI/ Old Elamite III. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Susa was the lowland capital of Elam under the sukkalmah or "Grand Regent" dynasty, whose rulers held a loose federation of highland and lowland territories together through a system of co-regents. Thousands of clay tablets in Akkadian record sales, loans and adoptions sworn by Elamite gods, giving an unusually intimate view of family and property law. Susa's craftsmen worked bitumen, glazed ceramics and bronze, and the city traded with Mesopotamia, Dilmun and the Iranian plateau while remaining politically independent of Babylon.

Bronze Age, Ur III Period (Iraq, 2150 BC.node: Bronze Age, Ur III Period (Iraq, 2150 BC–2000 BC)
Bronze Age, Ur III Period (Iraq, 2150 BC.label: Bronze Age, Ur III Period
Bronze Age, Ur III Period (Iraq, 2150 BC.prose:
[Southern Mesopotamia, 2150 BC–2000 BC] Bronze Age, Ur III Period. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Third Dynasty of Ur rebuilt southern Mesopotamia into a tightly run state, with the great stepped ziggurat of Ur, a standardised calendar and weights, and an army of scribes who recorded almost every sheep and shekel. The surviving archives run to tens of thousands of tablets, the densest bureaucratic record from the ancient world. Shulgi and his successors also issued one of the earliest known law collections, before the dynasty collapsed under Amorite pressure and an Elamite sack of Ur.

Byzantine (Libya, AD 400–AD 640).label: Byzantine
Byzantine (Libya, AD 400–AD 640).prose:
[Cyrenaica/Egypt, AD 400–AD 640] Byzantine. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Libya. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.
