Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

These finds are among the earliest evidence for seaborne exchange in the Gulf, the beginning of a maritime network that later made Bahrain the hub of Dilmun.

A short but pivotal phase in highland Fars and Kerman, when population concentrated at Tal-e Malyan — the future Elamite city of Anshan — and pottery, sealing and administrative practices shifted sharply. It is the immediate prelude to the Proto-Elamite expansion, when accounting tablets and a shared bureaucratic culture spread across the Iranian plateau.

The heyday of the Bakun painted pottery tradition in southern Iran, whose thin buff vessels carry stylised ibexes, birds and dazzling geometric designs. Excavated villages contain copper-smelting debris and large numbers of stamp seals and sealings, showing that small farming communities were already keeping track of stored and moving goods long before writing.

Farming villages across southern Mesopotamia coalesced into larger settlements with tripartite mudbrick houses and, at Eridu, a sequence of small temples rebuilt on the same spot for centuries. Distinctive pale greenish pottery painted with dark geometric motifs, mass-produced on the slow wheel, spread from the marshes of Iraq to Anatolia, Iran and the shores of the Gulf, marking one of the first broad cultural horizons in the Near East. Irrigation, sailing boats and the beginnings of social ranking here laid the groundwork for the cities of Uruk.

In the Fars highlands the elaborate painted pottery of the preceding Bakun tradition gave way to plain burnished red wares, and many village sites were abandoned as populations apparently shifted toward more mobile herding. The thinning of settlement makes this one of the more elusive stretches of Iranian prehistory, immediately before the rise of the Proto-Elamite centre at Tal-e Malyan.

The end of the Ubaid horizon in northern Mesopotamia, when painted pottery traditions faded and communities such as Tepe Gawra began to build monumental structures and use stamp seals to control stored goods. The period sets the stage for the northern towns that would later confront expanding Uruk influence from the south.

Chalcolithic, Late 2 (Iraq, 4200 BC–3800.label: Chalcolithic, Late 2
Chalcolithic, Late 2 (Iraq, 4200 BC–3800.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 4200 BC–3800 BC] Chalcolithic, Late 2. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Northern Mesopotamian centres like Tepe Gawra and Tell Brak grew into substantial towns with temples, seal-impressed administrative controls and evidence of craft specialisation, developing complexity independently of southern Sumer. Mass-produced coarse bowls and clay sealings show that institutions were now feeding and monitoring labour.

Chalcolithic, Late 3 (Iraq, 3800 BC–3600.label: Chalcolithic, Late 3
Chalcolithic, Late 3 (Iraq, 3800 BC–3600.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 3800 BC–3600 BC] Chalcolithic, Late 3. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Tell Brak and other northern centres reached urban scale, with the famous Eye Temple's forerunners and dense industrial quarters, at the same time that Uruk in the south was expanding. The two regions were converging on city life at once, a discovery that overturned the older assumption that urbanism radiated outward from Sumer alone.

Chalcolithic, Late 4 (Iraq, 3600 BC–3300.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 3600 BC–3300 BC] Chalcolithic, Late 4. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Uruk expansion: southern Mesopotamian material culture, from bevelled-rim bowls to cylinder seals, appears at colonies and outposts along the Euphrates and into Iran and Anatolia. Habuba Kabira and similar planned settlements look like transplanted southern towns, evidence of long-distance trade networks reaching for timber, metal and stone.

Chalcolithic, Late 5 (Iraq, 3300 BC–3000.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 3300 BC–3000 BC] Chalcolithic, Late 5. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The climax of the Uruk world and its abrupt collapse. In the city of Uruk itself, the vast Eanna precinct was rebuilt on a monumental scale and administrators began pressing signs into clay tablets, producing the earliest writing; then the northern colonies were abandoned and the network dissolved, leaving southern Mesopotamia to develop into the Sumerian city-states.

Clay sealings and standardised storage rooms show householders and communities keeping track of goods, an early step toward the administrative systems of highland Iran.

On the Susiana plain settlement clustered around a few larger centres, and Susa itself emerged with a massive terrace platform crowned by public buildings and surrounded by a cemetery of over a thousand graves. The elaborate painted beakers placed with the dead are among the masterpieces of Iranian prehistoric art.

The Proto-Elamite horizon in highland Iran, when Tal-e Malyan grew into a walled centre of some 50 hectares and scribes at Malyan, Susa and Tepe Yahya kept accounts on tablets in an undeciphered script of their own. Standardised sealings and tablets found across hundreds of kilometres reveal an interlinked network of highland trade in metals and stone.

Susa began as a monumental platform on the Khuzestan plain, a place of assembly and burial rather than an ordinary village. Thousands of graves yielded tall painted goblets decorated with elongated ibexes and running dogs, alongside copper axes and stamp seals that hint at emerging elites.

Chalcolithic, Susa II/Uruk (Iran, 3700 B.label: Chalcolithic, Susa II/Uruk
Chalcolithic, Susa II/Uruk (Iran, 3700 B.prose:
[Khuzestan, Iran, 3700 BC–3100 BC] Chalcolithic, Susa II/Uruk. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Susa was drawn into the orbit of southern Mesopotamia, adopting bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and numerical clay tablets almost identical to those of Uruk. The accounting devices used here, including hollow clay balls filled with tokens, are central evidence in the debate over how writing began.

Chalcolithic, Transitional (Iran, 5200 B.prose: [Northern Iran, 5200 BC–4300 BC] Chalcolithic, Transitional. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Classical (Libya, 500 BC–350 BC).prose:
[Cyrenaica, 500 BC–350 BC] Classical. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.

Classical/Pre-Islamic (Israel, 330 BC–AD.label: Classical/Pre-Islamic
Classical/Pre-Islamic (Israel, 330 BC–AD.prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia/Iran/Northern Arabia, 330 BC–AD 640] Classical/Pre-Islamic. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Saudi Arabia. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

From Alexander's conquest to the Arab conquest, the region passed through Hellenistic kingdoms, Hasmonean independence, Herodian and Roman rule, and finally Byzantine Christian administration. These centuries saw the Second Temple rebuilt and destroyed, the birth of rabbinic Judaism and of Christianity, and the revolts that scattered Jewish populations across the empire. Byzantine pilgrimage transformed the landscape with churches, monasteries and mosaic-floored villages, many abandoned soon after 640.

Classical/Protohistoric/Pre-Islamic (Alg.label: Classical/Protohistoric/Pre-Islamic
Classical/Protohistoric/Pre-Islamic (Alg.prose:
[North Africa, 500 BC–AD 640] Classical/Protohistoric/Pre-Islamic. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Berber kingdoms such as Numidia and Mauretania emerged in the shadow of Carthage, then were absorbed after Rome destroyed its rival and turned North Africa into a granary. Cities like Timgad, Djemila and Tipasa were laid out with forums, theatres and olive-oil presses, and the region produced Latin writers and bishops including Augustine of Hippo. Vandal and Byzantine rule followed before the Arab armies arrived in the seventh century.

Contemporary Islamic (Algeria, AD 1900–A.label: Contemporary Islamic
Contemporary Islamic (Algeria, AD 1900–A.prose:
[MENA, AD 1900–AD 2023] Contemporary Islamic. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

A century of upheaval in Algeria: French settler colonialism at its height, a brutal eight-year war of independence, and then a nation-state built on oil and gas revenues, one-party rule and Arabisation policies. The violent 1990s and the mass protests of 2019 are the most recent chapters.

Contemporary Islamic, Modern (Algeria, A.label: Contemporary Islamic, Modern
Contemporary Islamic, Modern (Algeria, A.prose:
[MENA, AD 1950–AD 2023] Contemporary Islamic, Modern. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The war launched in 1954 ended 132 years of French rule and drove out almost the entire settler population; independence in 1962 brought a socialist, hydrocarbon-funded state under the FLN. Cancelled elections in 1991 triggered a decade of insurgency and mass killing, after which the country settled into an uneasy stability shaped by gas exports and a young, largely urban population.

Dynastic Egypt (Egypt, 3000 BC–350 BC).label: Dynastic Egypt
Dynastic Egypt (Egypt, 3000 BC–350 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 3000 BC–350 BC] Dynastic Egypt. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

From the unification of the Nile valley under a single king, Egypt maintained a state, a script and a religion of remarkable continuity for close to three millennia, punctuated by intermediate periods of collapse. Its rulers built the pyramids of Giza, the temples of Karnak and the tombs of the Valley of the Kings, and at its height the New Kingdom empire reached into Syria and Nubia. Later centuries brought Libyan, Kushite, Assyrian and Persian rulers, and the tradition of pharaonic kingship was taken over rather than abolished by Alexander and the Ptolemies.

Early Bronze Age, 1-3 (Lebanon, 3400 BC–.label: Early Bronze Age, 1-3
Early Bronze Age, 1-3 (Lebanon, 3400 BC–.prose:
[Northern Levant, 3400 BC–2500 BC] Early Bronze Age, 1-3. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Byblos grew from a village into a walled town whose temples and harbour served a steady trade in cedar timber and resin with Old Kingdom Egypt; Egyptian stone vessels bearing pharaohs' names were dedicated in its sanctuaries. Copper and bronze tools, mass-produced pottery and monumental temple architecture mark the coast's first urban age. These coastal towns became the seed of the later Phoenician cities.

Early Bronze Age 1 (Israel, 3600 BC–3000.label: Early Bronze Age 1
Early Bronze Age 1 (Israel, 3600 BC–3000.prose:
[Southern Levant, 3600 BC–3000 BC] Early Bronze Age 1. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Village farming communities in the southern Levant grew larger and denser, some covering many hectares, though still without walls. Copper working expanded, olive and vine cultivation spread, and Egyptian goods — and eventually Egyptian settlers and administrators in the southern coastal plain — appear in quantity. These were the immediate foundations of the region's first walled towns.

Early Bronze Age 2 (Israel, 3000 BC–2800.label: Early Bronze Age 2
Early Bronze Age 2 (Israel, 3000 BC–2800.prose:
[Southern Levant, 3000 BC–2800 BC] Early Bronze Age 2. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The first true urban phase in the southern Levant: towns such as Arad, Megiddo and Beth Yerah acquired massive mudbrick fortifications, planned streets, temples and public storage. Trade with Egypt of the First and Second Dynasties was intense — Canaanite jars of oil and wine travelled south, and vessels bearing Narmer's name turn up in Canaan. Town life, once begun here, would define the region for the next thousand years.

Early Bronze Age 3 (Israel, 2800 BC–2500.label: Early Bronze Age 3
Early Bronze Age 3 (Israel, 2800 BC–2500.prose:
[Southern Levant, 2800 BC–2500 BC] Early Bronze Age 3. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Walled towns reached their greatest extent, with monumental buildings such as the great circular granary at Beth Yerah and temple complexes at Megiddo. A striking new pottery, the burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, arrives with influences from the north, hinting at movement of people from Anatolia and the Caucasus. By the end of the period, one town after another was abandoned.

Early Bronze Age, 4 (Lebanon, 2500 BC–20.label: Early Bronze Age, 4
Early Bronze Age, 4 (Lebanon, 2500 BC–20.prose:
[Northern Levant, 2500 BC–2000 BC] Early Bronze Age, 4. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The prosperous coastal towns faltered as Egypt's Old Kingdom weakened and long-distance trade thinned; Byblos suffered destruction and rebuilding, and many smaller sites were left empty. Settlement became more dispersed and pastoral, with new pottery styles and shaft-grave burials shared across the wider Levant. The disruption ended with the rise of the Amorite-ruled Middle Bronze Age cities.

Early Bronze Age 4 (Israel, 2500 BC–2000.label: Early Bronze Age 4
Early Bronze Age 4 (Israel, 2500 BC–2000.prose:
[Southern Levant, 2500 BC–2000 BC] Early Bronze Age 4. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Urban life in the southern Levant collapsed. Fortified towns were deserted and people dispersed into small unwalled villages, seasonal camps and pastoral groups, leaving cemeteries of shaft tombs as their most conspicuous remains. Often called the Intermediate Bronze Age, it is the gap between two urban worlds — and a long-running argument among archaeologists about whether drought, invasion or the failure of trade brought the first cities down.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

Early Bronze Age, Early (Iraq, 3100 BC–2.label: Early Bronze Age, Early
Early Bronze Age, Early (Iraq, 3100 BC–2.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 3100 BC–2600 BC] Early Bronze Age, Early. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Sumer's cities took recognisable shape: Uruk, Ur, Kish and their neighbours built walls and monumental temples, and rival rulers began fighting over land and water. The pictographic script of the Uruk tablets hardened into cuneiform capable of recording names, laws and stories. Metalworkers turned increasingly to tin bronze, and the potter's wheel and mass-produced ware supplied growing urban populations.

Early Bronze Age/Early Transcaucasian (I.node: Early Bronze Age/Early Transcaucasian (Iran, 3100 BC–1600 BC)
Early Bronze Age/Early Transcaucasian (I.label: Early Bronze Age/Early Transcaucasian
Early Bronze Age/Early Transcaucasian (I.prose:
[Northwest Iran, 3100 BC–1600 BC] Early Bronze Age/Early Transcaucasian. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Communities using Kura-Araxes material culture — glossy black-and-red burnished pottery, portable horned hearths, round houses — spread from the South Caucasus across northwestern Iran and eventually as far as the Levant. They were mobile herders and farmers with no palaces, temples or writing, yet remarkably uniform in their household goods over a huge area. Their movement is one of the clearest archaeological cases of a way of life travelling across mountains and borders.

Early Bronze Age, Late (Iraq, 2600 BC–20.node: Early Bronze Age, Late (Iraq, 2600 BC–2000 BC)
Early Bronze Age, Late (Iraq, 2600 BC–20.label: Early Bronze Age, Late
Early Bronze Age, Late (Iraq, 2600 BC–20.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 2600 BC–2000 BC] Early Bronze Age, Late. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The age of the Sumerian city-states peaked — the Royal Cemetery of Ur, with its gold headdresses, lyres and sacrificed retainers, dates here — before Sargon of Akkad welded the region into the world's first empire. Akkadian became a written language alongside Sumerian, and royal art turned to portraying kings as victorious and semi-divine. After the empire's collapse, the Third Dynasty of Ur rebuilt centralised rule with ziggurats, standardised weights and vast bureaucratic archives, only to fall around 2000 BC.

Early Bronze Age (Iran, 3100 BC–2200 BC).prose:
[Northeast Iran, 3100 BC–2200 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3000 BC–2700 BC).label: Early Dynastic
Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3000 BC–2700 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 3000 BC–2700 BC] Early Dynastic. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

Early Iron Age (Bahrain, 1500 BC–1000 BC.label: Early Iron Age
Early Iron Age (Bahrain, 1500 BC–1000 BC.prose:
[Arabia, 1500 BC–1000 BC] Early Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Bahrain, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Yemen. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

Early South Arabian (Yemen, 800 BC–100 B.prose:
[Southern Arabia, 800 BC–100 BC] Early South Arabian. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The incense kingdoms — Saba, Ma'in, Qataban and Hadramawt — grew rich controlling the overland caravan route that carried frankincense and myrrh north to the Mediterranean. They built stone temples and city walls, wrote in the elegant angular musnad script, and irrigated their fields with engineering works of which the great dam at Marib is the most famous. Their wealth made 'Arabia Felix' a byword in the classical world.

First Intermediate (Egypt, 2150 BC–2050.label: First Intermediate
First Intermediate (Egypt, 2150 BC–2050.prose:
[Egypt, 2150 BC–2050 BC] First Intermediate. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Central authority at Memphis broke down after the long reign of Pepi II, and provincial governors ruled their nomes as effectively independent lords, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Tomb art becomes rougher and more regional, but funerary texts and coffins once reserved for kings now appear for ordinary officials. Theban victory under Mentuhotep II ended the split and began the Middle Kingdom.

First World War (Algeria, AD 1914–AD 191.label: First World War
First World War (Algeria, AD 1914–AD 191.prose:
[MENA, AD 1914–AD 1918] First World War. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Britain's first experience of industrialised total war: conscription from 1916, Zeppelin and Gotha raids on civilian towns, rationing, and women entering munitions factories and transport in huge numbers. Nearly three-quarters of a million British servicemen died, and almost every town has a war memorial dating from the years just after. Trench systems, practice grounds, aerodromes and shell-filling factories left archaeological traces across the countryside.

Hellenistic/Ptolemaic (Libya, 350 BC–30.label: Hellenistic/Ptolemaic
Hellenistic/Ptolemaic (Libya, 350 BC–30.prose:
[Cyrenaica/Egypt, 350 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic/Ptolemaic. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Libya. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Cyrenaica's five Greek cities came under the rule of the Ptolemies of Egypt, exporting grain, horses and the celebrated medicinal plant silphium. Cyrene remained a wealthy centre of philosophy, medicine and monumental building, with a large Jewish community alongside Greeks and Libyans. The last Ptolemaic ruler bequeathed the region to Rome in 96 BC.

Hellenistic/Seleucid, Late (Israel, 160.label: Hellenistic/Seleucid, Late
Hellenistic/Seleucid, Late (Israel, 160.prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia, 160 BC–50 BC] Hellenistic/Seleucid, Late. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Seleucid attempts to impose Greek cult practice in Jerusalem triggered the Maccabean revolt, and the Hasmonean family turned resistance into an independent Jewish kingdom that expanded across Judaea, Galilee and beyond. Fortresses, ritual baths and the first Jewish coinage appear in the archaeology, alongside continued use of Greek architectural and administrative forms. Hasmonean infighting opened the door to Roman intervention.

Iron Age 1 (Israel, 1200 BC–1000 BC).label: Iron Age 1
Iron Age 1 (Israel, 1200 BC–1000 BC).prose:
[Southern Levant, 1200 BC–1000 BC] Iron Age 1. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The unsettled aftermath of the Bronze Age collapse: Egyptian garrisons withdrew, great Canaanite cities such as Hazor and Lachish were burned or shrank, and Philistine settlers with Aegean-style pottery took over the southern coastal plain. Hundreds of small unwalled villages appeared in the central hill country, farming terraces and keeping livestock, the archaeological setting for early Israel. Out of these scattered communities came the territorial kingdoms of the following centuries.

Iron Age 2 (Israel, 1000 BC–700 BC).label: Iron Age 2
Iron Age 2 (Israel, 1000 BC–700 BC).prose:
[Southern Levant, 1000 BC–700 BC] Iron Age 2. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The age of consolidated kingdoms: Jerusalem and Samaria grew into royal capitals with monumental gates, palaces and water systems, and Hebrew, Moabite, Ammonite and Aramaic inscriptions multiply. Trade in olive oil, wine and horses linked the region to Phoenicia, Egypt and Arabia. Assyrian expansion under Tiglath-Pileser III and his successors ended it, destroying the northern kingdom of Israel and deporting its people in 722 BC.

Iron Age 3 (Israel, 700 BC–550 BC).label: Iron Age 3
Iron Age 3 (Israel, 700 BC–550 BC).prose:
[Southern Levant, 700 BC–550 BC] Iron Age 3. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Palestine. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Judah survived as an Assyrian vassal after Sennacherib devastated the Shephelah, and Jerusalem swelled with refugees, becoming a genuine city. When Assyria fell, Egypt and Babylon fought over the corridor until Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, destroyed the temple in 586 BC and deported its elite. The exile that followed reshaped Judaean religion and produced much of the literature later gathered as the Hebrew Bible.

Iron Age (Bahrain, 1500 BC–100 BC).prose:
[Arabia, 1500 BC–100 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Bahrain, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Yemen. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

Iron Age, Early (Algeria, 1000 BC–800 BC.label: Iron Age, Early
Iron Age, Early (Algeria, 1000 BC–800 BC.prose:
[Maghreb, 1000 BC–800 BC] Iron Age, Early. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Communities across the Maghreb interior lived by farming and stock-raising, burying their dead in stone tumuli and dolmens whose ruins still dot the landscape. Iron working spread slowly, and the first Phoenician sailors began touching along the coast, opening the contacts that would reshape North African life.

Iron Age I (Iran, 1250 BC–1050 BC).label: Iron Age I
Iron Age I (Iran, 1250 BC–1050 BC).prose:
[Northwest Iran, 1250 BC–1050 BC] Iron Age I. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Hittite empire disappeared and Anatolia fragmented into small, often illiterate societies, with monumental hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions kept alive only by the Neo-Hittite successor states of the south-east. Phrygians moved into the central plateau and settlement clustered on defensible mounds, while in the east the tribal groups later unified as Urartu began to coalesce. From this fractured landscape came the kingdoms - Phrygia, Urartu, Lydia and the Syro-Hittite city-states - that dominated the following centuries.

Iron Age II (Iran, 1050 BC–800 BC).label: Iron Age II
Iron Age II (Iran, 1050 BC–800 BC).prose:
[Northwest Iran, 1050 BC–800 BC] Iron Age II. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Greek settlers pushed out from Syracuse and Naxos to found a chain of colonies around the coast, while Phoenicians held the western tip at Motya and Panormus. The indigenous Sikels, Sikanians and Elymians adopted Greek pottery, building styles and writing even as they lost land, and Sikel resistance culminated in Ducetius' short-lived confederation. Sicily's grain, its tyrants and its rivalry with Carthage made the island a major player in the wider Mediterranean world.

Iron Age III/Late Iron Age (Iran, 800 BC.node: Iron Age III/Late Iron Age (Iran, 800 BC–550 BC)
Iron Age III/Late Iron Age (Iran, 800 BC.label: Iron Age III/Late Iron Age
Iron Age III/Late Iron Age (Iran, 800 BC.prose:
[Northern Iran, 800 BC–550 BC] Iron Age III/Late Iron Age. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Assyrian and later Urartian campaigns pushed repeatedly into the Zagros, where Median and Persian chiefdoms were coalescing amid columned halls and fortified strongholds such as Godin Tepe and Nush-i Jan. Elam, the old power of the southwest, was crushed by Assyria and never recovered. The consolidation of the Medes and then Cyrus the Great's takeover turned this fragmented highland world into the core of the first Persian empire.

[Mesopotamia, 950 BC–600 BC] Iron Age, Late/Neo-Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Assyria expanded from a north Mesopotamian kingdom into the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Nimrud, Khorsabad and finally Nineveh. Its kings built palaces lined with carved stone reliefs, assembled libraries, moved whole populations to break resistance, and ran an efficient system of provinces and royal roads. Overstretched and torn by civil war, the empire collapsed when Medes and Babylonians sacked Nineveh in 612 BC.

Iron Age, Late (Lebanon, 550 BC–330 BC).label: Iron Age, Late
Iron Age, Late (Lebanon, 550 BC–330 BC).prose:
[Northern Levant, 550 BC–330 BC] Iron Age, Late. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Under Achaemenid Persian rule the Phoenician cities kept their own kings, temples and coinage, and supplied the fleets that fought the Greeks. Sidon in particular grew rich, leaving the royal necropolis whose carved sarcophagi are masterpieces of the age. The period ended with Alexander's brutal seven-month siege of Tyre in 332 BC.

Phoenician and then Carthaginian traders established anchorages and towns along the North African coast, linking the Maghreb into a Mediterranean network of metals, purple dye and grain. Inland Numidian communities took up new goods, gods and eventually a written script, while keeping their own tumulus burials and tribal structures.

Iron Age, Middle Assyrian (Iraq, 1200 BC.node: Iron Age, Middle Assyrian (Iraq, 1200 BC–950 BC)
Iron Age, Middle Assyrian (Iraq, 1200 BC.label: Iron Age, Middle Assyrian
Iron Age, Middle Assyrian (Iraq, 1200 BC.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 1200 BC–950 BC] Iron Age, Middle Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

After a brief imperial peak, Assyria was thrown back on its heartland along the Tigris as Aramaean groups moved into the countryside and the wider Near East entered a long recession. Tiglath-Pileser I briefly campaigned to the Mediterranean, but his successors lost ground for generations. The administrative texts, law collections and royal annals of these centuries laid the bureaucratic and ideological groundwork for the Neo-Assyrian empire that followed.

Iron Age, Middle (Lebanon, 900 BC–550 BC.label: Iron Age, Middle
Iron Age, Middle (Lebanon, 900 BC–550 BC.prose:
[Northern Levant, 900 BC–550 BC] Iron Age, Middle. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Freed from Egyptian overlordship, Tyre, Sidon and Byblos turned to the sea, planting trading posts and colonies as far as Spain and North Africa and carrying their alphabet with them. Their craftsmen supplied ivories, metalwork and purple cloth to the courts of the Near East. Prosperity came at the price of heavy tribute to Assyria, and later a thirteen-year Babylonian siege of Tyre.

Iron Age, Neo-Babylonian (Iraq, 650 BC–5.label: Iron Age, Neo-Babylonian
Iron Age, Neo-Babylonian (Iraq, 650 BC–5.prose:
[Mesopotamia, 650 BC–550 BC] Iron Age, Neo-Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Kuwait, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Babylon's last native dynasty, founded by Nabopolassar, who joined the Medes to destroy Nineveh and inherit the Assyrian empire. Under Nebuchadnezzar II the city was rebuilt on a colossal scale — glazed-brick gates, ziggurat, and processional way — while campaigns in the west destroyed Jerusalem and deported its elite, setting the Babylonian Exile in motion. Temple archives and astronomical diaries from these decades are among the richest documentary sources from the ancient Near East. The dynasty fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC.

Iron Age, Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 1100 BC–7.node: Iron Age, Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 1100 BC–725 BC)
Iron Age, Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 1100 BC–7.label: Iron Age, Neo-Elamite I
Iron Age, Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 1100 BC–7.prose:
[Khuzestan/Southwest Iran, 1100 BC–725 BC] Iron Age, Neo-Elamite I. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

A thinly documented stretch after the collapse of the Middle Elamite kingdom, when written sources from Susa and the highlands almost dry up. Elam persists as a political entity but leaves little monumental record, and much of what is known comes from pottery sequences and scattered Mesopotamian references. Iranian-speaking groups were settling the Zagros during these centuries, reshaping the region's population.

Iron Age, Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 725 BC–5.node: Iron Age, Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 725 BC–520 BC)
Iron Age, Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 725 BC–5.label: Iron Age, Neo-Elamite II
Iron Age, Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 725 BC–5.prose:
[Khuzestan/Southwest Iran, 725 BC–520 BC] Iron Age, Neo-Elamite II. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Elam re-emerges into history as a player in the wars between Assyria and Babylon, backing Babylonian rebels against Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal. The result was catastrophic: Ashurbanipal sacked Susa around 646 BC and carried off its gods and treasures. In the aftermath Elamite territory was absorbed into the rising Persian orbit, though Elamite script, administrative practice and craft traditions carried directly into the Achaemenid empire.

Iron Age, Post-Assyrian/Achaemenid/Persi.label: Iron Age, Post-Assyrian/Achaemenid/Persian
Iron Age, Post-Assyrian/Achaemenid/Persi.prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia, 550 BC–330 BC] Iron Age, Post-Assyrian/Achaemenid/Persian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Under Persian rule the region was organised as small provinces within the satrapy Beyond the River, among them Yehud, where returning exiles rebuilt the Jerusalem temple and compiled much of the Hebrew Bible. Settlement was modest and rural compared with the Iron Age kingdoms, but Greek imported pottery, Attic coinage and Phoenician trade show the coast drawn into a wider Mediterranean economy. The period closes with Alexander's conquest.

Iron Age, Pre-Achaemenid (Iran, 650 BC–5.label: Iron Age, Pre-Achaemenid
Iron Age, Pre-Achaemenid (Iran, 650 BC–5.prose:
[Southeast Iran, 650 BC–500 BC] Iron Age, Pre-Achaemenid. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The centuries between Assyrian collapse and the rise of Cyrus, when Median and other Iranian elites dominated the western Zagros. Excavated sites such as Nush-i Jan, Godin Tepe and Baba Jan reveal fortified manors, columned halls and stepped fire altars — architectural ideas that Achaemenid builders would later monumentalise at Pasargadae and Persepolis. Written sources are almost entirely foreign, so archaeology carries most of the story.

Iron Age, Yahya III (Iran, 800 BC–650 BC.node: Iron Age, Yahya III (Iran, 800 BC–650 BC)
Iron Age, Yahya III (Iran, 800 BC–650 BC.label: Iron Age, Yahya III
Iron Age, Yahya III (Iran, 800 BC–650 BC.prose: [Southeast Iran, 800 BC–650 BC] Iron Age, Yahya III. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Islamic, Early [Early Caliphate/Umayyad].label: Islamic, Early [Early Caliphate/Umayyad]
Islamic, Early [Early Caliphate/Umayyad].prose:
[Iraq, AD 640–AD 750] Islamic, Early [Early Caliphate/Umayyad]. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Arab armies destroyed Sasanian power at Qadisiyya and the region became the heartland of a caliphate ruled from Damascus. New garrison cities — Basra, Kufa, Wasit — grew into major towns, Arabic replaced Persian and Greek in administration, and coinage was reformed to carry Quranic inscriptions rather than portraits. Discontent among non-Arab converts and the Shi'a here eventually fuelled the revolution that toppled the Umayyads.

Islamic, Early [Tahirid/Saffarid/Samanid.label: Islamic, Early [Tahirid/Saffarid/Samanid/Buyids]
Islamic, Early [Tahirid/Saffarid/Samanid.prose:
[Iran, AD 800–AD 1000] Islamic, Early [Tahirid/Saffarid/Samanid/Buyids]. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

As the Abbasid caliphs lost real power, regional dynasties took over the east: Tahirid and Saffarid governors, the Samanids of Bukhara and Samarkand, and finally the Buyids, who occupied Baghdad and kept the caliph as a figurehead. Persian re-emerged as a written literary language — Rudaki and, at the end of the era, Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Cities such as Nishapur and Rayy became centres of glazed pottery, glass and long-distance trade in silver.

Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid/Fatimid].label: Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid/Fatimid]
Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid/Fatimid].prose:
[Levant/Arabia, AD 640–AD 1070] Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid/Fatimid]. Spatial coverage: Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Byzantine rule ended in the 630s and the land became a frontier province of successive caliphates, with Jerusalem gaining the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa as monumental statements of the new faith. Umayyad governance brought new towns and desert estates; the shift of the caliphate to Baghdad and later Cairo left the region provincial, shaken by earthquakes and rival armies. Christian, Jewish and Samaritan communities persisted, while Arabic and Islam spread gradually rather than at once.

Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid] (Algeri.label: Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid]
Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid] (Algeri.prose:
[North Africa, AD 640–AD 900] Islamic, Early [Umayyad/Abbasid]. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Arab conquest brought the Maghreb into the caliphate, and the Berber population converted while frequently rebelling against Arab governors — Kharijite revolts carved out independent states in the interior. Kairouan and Tahert became inland capitals, and caravan routes across the Sahara began carrying gold and slaves north. By the ninth century the region was effectively ruled by local dynasties rather than distant caliphs.

The Sasanian empire collapsed and Iran was absorbed into the caliphate, first governed from Damascus and then, after 750, from a newly founded Baghdad on the edge of the Iranian plateau. Persian administrators, scribes and families such as the Barmakids shaped Abbasid government, and Zoroastrianism gradually gave way to Islam. Excavated towns show new mosque plans, fresh ceramic traditions and the reorientation of trade towards the Persian Gulf.

The Almohad empire broke apart into competing Berber sultanates — Hafsids at Tunis, Zayyanids at Tlemcen, Marinids at Fez — that fought each other while trading grain, wool and gold with Genoa, Pisa and Catalonia. Cities gained madrasas and elaborate tile and stucco decoration, and refugees from the Christian conquest of Spain brought Andalusi crafts and music with them. Corsairing and Iberian raiding along the coast set the stage for Ottoman and Spanish intervention.

Mamluk sultans ruling from Cairo held the Levant after expelling the last Crusaders, dismantling coastal ports to deny the Franks a landing place and shifting life inland. They invested in roads, bridges, caravanserais and a fast postal system, and endowed madrasas and mausolea whose striped stonework still stands in Jerusalem and Hebron. Plague, Bedouin unrest and the collapse of the sugar industry marked the era's later years.

Islamic, Late [Ottoman] (Iraq, AD 1500–A.label: Islamic, Late [Ottoman]
Islamic, Late [Ottoman] (Iraq, AD 1500–A.prose:
[Iraq, AD 1500–AD 1900] Islamic, Late [Ottoman]. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Ottoman and Safavid armies fought over Baghdad and Basra for a century before the Ottomans secured them, ruling through pashas, tribal shaykhs and, for a long spell, a self-perpetuating Mamluk elite. Irrigation and population were much reduced from medieval levels, and the great shrine cities of Najaf and Karbala drew pilgrims and Persian influence. Nineteenth-century reforms, steamships on the Tigris and the telegraph pulled the provinces into world markets shortly before British occupation.

Spanish garrisons seized coastal towns and Ottoman corsair captains, the Barbarossas among them, drove them out and made the region a province of Istanbul ruled by deys and janissaries. For three centuries privateering, captive-taking and treaties with European powers defined its relations with the Mediterranean world. A French invasion in 1830 began a violent conquest and settler colonisation that reorganised land, agriculture and society.

Islamic, Late [Post-Abbasid] (Iraq, AD 1.label: Islamic, Late [Post-Abbasid]
Islamic, Late [Post-Abbasid] (Iraq, AD 1.prose:

The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 killed the caliph and ended five centuries of Abbasid rule, and the Ilkhanid conquerors governed from Iran rather than Iraq. Neglected canals silted up, farmland shrank and Baghdad became a provincial town; Timur's campaigns and Turkmen confederations brought further destruction. By the end of the era the region was a contested borderland between two rising empires, Ottoman and Safavid.

Islamic, Late [Timurid/Safavid/Qajar] (I.label: Islamic, Late [Timurid/Safavid/Qajar]
Islamic, Late [Timurid/Safavid/Qajar] (I.prose:
[Iran, AD 1400–AD 1900] Islamic, Late [Timurid/Safavid/Qajar]. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Timur's descendants made Herat and Samarkand centres of miniature painting, poetry and astronomy, and then the Safavids imposed Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion, permanently changing Iran's religious identity. Shah Abbas rebuilt Isfahan with its vast maidan, mosques and bridges and traded silk directly with Europe and India. Afghan invasion and civil war ended the dynasty; the Qajars restored unity from Tehran but lost territory to Russia and ceded control of resources to foreign concessions.

Power moved from Damascus to a new round city at Baghdad, which grew into perhaps the largest city on earth, with paper mills, hospitals, and translators turning Greek science into Arabic. Wealth came from an irrigated Sawad and Gulf trade reaching India and China, and left behind lustre pottery and the stucco and spiral minaret of Samarra. Central authority faded as Turkish soldiers, the Zanj revolt and Buyid and Seljuk overlords took control, until the Mongols ended the line.

The central Maghreb passed through a rapid succession of dynasties: the Fatimids launched their conquest of Egypt from Ifriqiya, leaving Berber vassals, the Zirids and Hammadids, who built new princely capitals such as the Qal'a of the Banu Hammad. Berber reform movements from the desert and the Atlas, the Almoravids and then the Almohads, swept north and briefly united the Maghreb with Muslim Spain under a single authority. The centuries left fortified hilltop cities, great congregational mosques at Tlemcen and Algiers, and a lasting Maliki religious culture.

Islamic, Middle [Ghaznavid/Seljuq/Khwara.label: Islamic, Middle [Ghaznavid/Seljuq/Khwarazmshah]
Islamic, Middle [Ghaznavid/Seljuq/Khwara.prose:
[Iran, AD 1000–AD 1200] Islamic, Middle [Ghaznavid/Seljuq/Khwarazmshah]. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Turkish military dynasties took over the Iranian world from the Persian emirates that preceded them, ruling in the caliph's name while patronising Persian letters — this is the age of Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and Omar Khayyam. Seljuq viziers like Nizam al-Mulk built madrasas and a bureaucratic order, and architects worked out the four-iwan mosque and the brick dome, seen at Isfahan's Friday Mosque. The Khwarazmshahs inherited the empire just in time to provoke Genghis Khan.

Islamic, Middle [Mongol/Ilkhanid/Muzaffa.label: Islamic, Middle [Mongol/Ilkhanid/Muzaffarid/Jalayrid]
Islamic, Middle [Mongol/Ilkhanid/Muzaffa.prose:
[Iran, AD 1200–AD 1400] Islamic, Middle [Mongol/Ilkhanid/Muzaffarid/Jalayrid]. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Mongol invasions shattered Iran's cities and ended the Abbasid caliphate, but within decades the Ilkhanid rulers converted to Islam and became patrons of an extraordinary hybrid art: Chinese motifs in Persian miniature painting, huge illustrated Shahnamehs, and monumental tombs such as Oljeitu's at Sultaniyya. Land was reorganised, observatories and histories were commissioned, and Iran was plugged into a trans-Asian trade and information network. When the Ilkhanate fragmented, the Muzaffarids and Jalayrids carried the artistic traditions forward until Timur arrived.

[Levant, 1600 BC–1400 BC] Late Bronze Age 1. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

After the destruction of the great Middle Bronze Age walled towns, Canaan came under the direct shadow of Egypt's New Kingdom, whose armies campaigned north after Thutmose III's victory at Megiddo. Cities were fewer, smaller and largely unfortified, ruled by local kings who paid tribute; imported Cypriot and Mycenaean pottery in their tombs shows how deeply the region was plugged into Mediterranean trade.

Late Bronze Age 1/Mittani (Iraq, 1600 BC.label: Late Bronze Age 1/Mittani
Late Bronze Age 1/Mittani (Iraq, 1600 BC.prose:
[Northern Mesopotamia, 1600 BC–1400 BC] Late Bronze Age 1/Mittani. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Hurrian kingdom of Mittani dominated northern Mesopotamia and Syria, its chariot aristocracy and horse-training expertise making it a great power alongside Egypt, Babylon and Hatti. Assyria was for a time its vassal. Archives from provincial towns such as Nuzi give an unusually intimate view of family law, adoption and land sales, even though Mittani's capital has never been found.

Late Bronze Age 2 (Israel, 1400 BC–1200.label: Late Bronze Age 2
Late Bronze Age 2 (Israel, 1400 BC–1200.prose:
[Levant, 1400 BC–1200 BC] Late Bronze Age 2. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The age of the Amarna letters, when Canaanite rulers wrote to the Egyptian court in cuneiform Akkadian, begging for troops and denouncing their neighbours. Egyptian garrisons and governors' residences sat among the towns, and international trade reached its peak, as the cargo of the Uluburun shipwreck attests. The period ends with widespread destruction and the collapse of the whole system around 1200 BC.

Assyria emerged from Mittani's shadow to become an empire in its own right, conquering the Khabur region and, under Tukulti-Ninurta I, even sacking Babylon. Its kings built a bureaucracy of provincial governors and issued the harsh Middle Assyrian Laws, while a distinctive plain, mass-produced pottery marks Assyrian control across the north.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

Late Dynastic (Egypt, 650 BC–350 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 650 BC–350 BC] Late Dynastic. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Egypt's last centuries as an independent kingdom, opening with the Saite revival — a deliberate, self-conscious return to Old Kingdom art and script — and closing under Persian rule punctuated by brief native dynasties. Greek merchants and mercenaries became a fixture at Naukratis and in the army, and Egypt's temples, mummies and priests began to fascinate visiting Greeks like Herodotus. Alexander's arrival soon after ended pharaonic rule for good.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

Late South Arabian (Yemen, AD 300–AD 640.prose:
[Southern Arabia, AD 300–AD 640] Late South Arabian. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Himyarite kings from Zafar absorbed Saba, Hadramawt and the old caravan kingdoms, unifying the highlands and coasts under one rule for the first time. Polytheistic temple religion gave way to monotheism, with a Jewish-leaning royal court, an Aksumite Christian invasion in 525, and then Sasanian Persian control. Irrigation works decayed and the great Marib dam finally broke, and within a few decades the region was absorbed into the new Islamic state.

Median (Iran, 800 BC–585 BC).label: Median
Median (Iran, 800 BC–585 BC).prose:
[Central Zagros, Iran, 800 BC–585 BC] Median. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Medes of the Iranian plateau consolidated under their own kings and, allied with Babylon, destroyed the Assyrian Empire by sacking Nineveh in 612 BC. Their realm stretched across western Iran into Anatolia until Cyrus the Great absorbed it into the Persian Empire, taking over its administration, court practices and much of its aristocracy. Archaeologically they remain elusive: fortified hilltop sites like Godin Tepe and Nush-i Jan, with its remarkable fire temple, are the main evidence against Herodotus's colourful narrative.

Middle Bronze Age 1 (Israel, 2000 BC–180.label: Middle Bronze Age 1
Middle Bronze Age 1 (Israel, 2000 BC–180.prose:
[Levant, 2000 BC–1800 BC] Middle Bronze Age 1. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Urban life returned to the southern Levant after the long rural interlude that followed the collapse of the Early Bronze Age cities. New towns were laid out on the coastal plain and in the valleys, with strong links to Byblos and the Syrian coast, and the potter's wheel and tin-bronze metallurgy came back into wide use. The Canaanite city-state pattern that shaped the region for the next millennium begins here.

Canaanite cities reached their greatest extent, ringed by massive earthen ramparts and defended by monumental gateways at places like Hazor, Megiddo and Ashkelon. Palaces, temples and rich warrior burials show a stratified society trading with Egypt, Cyprus and Syria. Population from this region moving into the Nile Delta contributed to the rise of the Hyksos rulers of Egypt, and the eventual Egyptian reconquest brought the period to a violent close.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

Middle Bronze Age I (Iran, 2100 BC–1900.prose:
[Northwest Iran, 2100 BC–1900 BC] Middle Bronze Age I. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Towns and cities were re-established across the southern Levant after centuries of largely village and pastoral life, with fortifications, wheel-made pottery and true bronze metallurgy returning. Coastal sites looked north to Byblos and the Syrian world for trade and inspiration. This revival set the framework of Canaanite city-states that Egyptian and biblical sources would later describe.

Middle Bronze Age II (Iran, 1900 BC–1600.node: Middle Bronze Age II (Iran, 1900 BC–1600 BC)
Middle Bronze Age II (Iran, 1900 BC–1600.label: Middle Bronze Age II
Middle Bronze Age II (Iran, 1900 BC–1600.prose:
[Northwest Iran, 1900 BC–1600 BC] Middle Bronze Age II. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The high point of Canaanite urbanism, when cities were surrounded by huge sloping ramparts and fosses, and palaces, temples and craft workshops flourished. Trade connected the region to Egypt, Cyprus and inland Syria, and scarabs, cylinder seals and fine painted pottery circulated widely. Cities of this era, such as Hazor, were among the largest ever built in the southern Levant.

Middle Bronze Age III (Iran, 1600 BC–145.node: Middle Bronze Age III (Iran, 1600 BC–1450 BC)
Middle Bronze Age III (Iran, 1600 BC–145.label: Middle Bronze Age III
Middle Bronze Age III (Iran, 1600 BC–145.prose:
[Northwest Iran, 1600 BC–1450 BC] Middle Bronze Age III. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The last phase of Canaanite urban splendour, when the great fortified towns were still functioning but increasingly under pressure. Egyptian expulsion of the Hyksos and subsequent campaigns into Asia brought destructions and abandonments at many sites. What followed was a Canaan of smaller towns under Egyptian imperial control.

Middle Iron Age (Bahrain, 1000 BC–600 BC.prose:
[Arabia, 1000 BC–600 BC] Middle Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Bahrain, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Yemen. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Hillforts, enclosed farmsteads and grain storage pits dominated the landscape, and roundhouse communities produced increasingly regionalised pottery and fine metalwork in flowing La Tène style. Many hillforts were abandoned or slimmed down to fewer, larger centres, hinting at the consolidation of the tribal groupings Roman writers would later name. Bodies and objects placed deliberately in disused pits offer a glimpse of ritual life.

Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2050 BC–1650 BC).label: Middle Kingdom
Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2050 BC–1650 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 2050 BC–1650 BC] Middle Kingdom. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

Middle South Arabian (Yemen, 100 BC–AD 3.label: Middle South Arabian
Middle South Arabian (Yemen, 100 BC–AD 3.prose:
[Southern Arabia, 100 BC–AD 300] Middle South Arabian. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The old incense kingdoms of Saba, Qataban and Hadramawt were gradually eclipsed by Himyar, rising from the southern highlands to unify most of Yemen. Maritime routes through the Red Sea began to carry trade that had once gone overland by camel, reshaping the economy that had built the great dam at Marib. Thousands of monumental inscriptions in the South Arabian alphabet survive from these centuries, recording temples, wars and dedications.

Nabataean (Israel, 100 BC–AD 400).label: Nabataean
Nabataean (Israel, 100 BC–AD 400).prose:
[Levant/Northern Arabia, 100 BC–AD 400] Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Saudi Arabia, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Arab caravan merchants grew rich moving frankincense, myrrh and spices from southern Arabia to Mediterranean ports, and turned the profits into rock-cut tombs, temples and elaborate water systems in the desert. Their fine, eggshell-thin painted pottery is one of the most distinctive wares of the ancient Near East. Rome absorbed the kingdom in AD 106, but Nabataean towns, farms and script continued for centuries afterwards.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

As the Sahara passed through a wet, green phase, herders spread across what is now Algerian desert with cattle, sheep and goats, camping by lakes and seasonal rivers. They left thousands of engravings and paintings on the rock walls of the Tassili n'Ajjer and Ahaggar, showing cattle herds, hunts, dances and animals - giraffe, elephant, hippo - that could not survive there today. Pottery and ground stone tools appear early here, and the imagery is the best record anywhere of a landscape that later dried out completely.

Villages were smaller and more scattered than in the preceding Pre-Pottery period, with a stronger emphasis on herding, and clay figurines with coffee-bean eyes are among their most distinctive products.

Small groups along the Gulf shore lived by fishing, netting and gathering shellfish, moving between coastal camps and using fine flaked arrowheads of an Arabian bifacial tradition. Their middens of fish bone and shell, and the first imported Mesopotamian pottery, record the earliest sustained occupation of the island.

New Kingdom (Egypt, 1550 BC–1050 BC).label: New Kingdom
New Kingdom (Egypt, 1550 BC–1050 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 1550 BC–1050 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2700 BC–AD 2150).label: Old Kingdom
Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2700 BC–AD 2150).prose:
[Egypt, 2700 BC–AD 2150] Old Kingdom. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

Parthian (Israel, 250 BC–AD 225).label: Parthian
Parthian (Israel, 250 BC–AD 225).prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia/Iran/Northern Arabia, 250 BC–AD 225] Parthian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Saudi Arabia. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Arsacid empire out of Iran pressed to the Euphrates, making Syria the frontier zone of a rivalry with Rome that lasted nearly three centuries. Crassus lost his army and his head at Carrhae in 53 BC, and later Parthian raids and Roman counter-invasions repeatedly swept the caravan cities between the two powers. That contested ground was also enormously profitable: Palmyra, Dura-Europos and the Euphrates routes grew rich handling silk and spices moving between the empires, and their art blends Greek, Iranian and Semitic styles.

Post-Achaemenid/Hellenistic/Seleucid, Ea.label: Post-Achaemenid/Hellenistic/Seleucid, Early
Post-Achaemenid/Hellenistic/Seleucid, Ea.prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia/Iran, 330 BC–160 BC] Post-Achaemenid/Hellenistic/Seleucid, Early. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian administration with Macedonian rule, and the region became a border zone fought over by Ptolemies in Egypt and Seleucids in Syria until the Seleucids took it around 200 BC. Greek city foundations, coinage, imported amphorae and architecture spread, and Judaean elites divided over how far to embrace Hellenistic culture. The tension broke into the Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV, which closes the phase and creates an independent Hasmonean state.

Pre-Dynastic, Early (Egypt, 4400 BC–3500.label: Pre-Dynastic, Early
Pre-Dynastic, Early (Egypt, 4400 BC–3500.prose:
[Egypt, 4400 BC–3500 BC] Pre-Dynastic, Early. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Farming communities of the Badarian and early Naqada cultures buried their dead in simple pits with combs, ivory figurines, slate cosmetic palettes and glossy black-topped red pottery. Copper was being hammered into small tools, flint knapping reached a high standard, and goods moved along the river and across the Red Sea hills. Differences in grave wealth are already visible, the first sign of the ranked society that would produce Egypt's kings.

Pre-Dynastic (Egypt, 4400 BC–3000 BC).label: Pre-Dynastic
Pre-Dynastic (Egypt, 4400 BC–3000 BC).prose:
[Egypt, 4400 BC–3000 BC] Pre-Dynastic. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Village societies along the Nile and in the still-habitable desert margins grew from small farming communities into competing chiefdoms with rich cemeteries, fine painted and polished pottery, copper tools and imported lapis and Levantine goods. Elite burials became steadily more elaborate, and boat and hunting scenes on pots and palettes carry the imagery that would become pharaonic art. By its close a handful of centres, above all Abydos and Hierakonpolis, had absorbed their rivals and produced the first hieroglyphs, kings and a unified state.

The Naqada II and III phases, when a few Upper Egyptian centres grew into towns, mass-produced pottery, and buried their rulers in mudbrick tombs stocked with gold, ivory and imported goods. Long-distance contact with the Levant and Nubia intensified, writing appeared on labels and jar seals, and ceremonial palettes and maceheads depict rulers smiting enemies in the poses later used for pharaohs. It ends with the first dynasty and a single kingdom stretching from the Delta to the First Cataract.

In the highlands and desert fringes of Yemen, oasis communities mastered flood irrigation and began building the great dams and sluices that would water the plain of Marib. Control of the frankincense and myrrh routes north to the Mediterranean concentrated wealth, and a distinctive monumental script appeared. Out of these settlements grew the kingdoms of Saba, Ma'in and Qataban.

Carthage's commercial and cultural reach along the North African coast, felt inland among the Numidian kingdoms through Punic language, gods like Baal Hammon and Tanit, and urban planning. Local rulers adopted Punic script and building styles even as they played Carthage and Rome against each other. Rome's destruction of Carthage in 146 BC ended the political order, but Punic culture persisted here for centuries afterwards.

Beginning with Herod's client kingdom and its vast building programmes at Caesarea, Jerusalem and Masada, the period runs through two catastrophic Jewish revolts, the destruction of the Temple and the refounding of Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina. Rabbinic Judaism took shape in Galilee while Christianity, once imperial, filled the land with churches, monasteries and pilgrims. It closes with the Muslim conquest in the 630s.

Roman Imperial, Early (Israel, 31 BC–AD.label: Roman Imperial, Early
Roman Imperial, Early (Israel, 31 BC–AD.prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia, 31 BC–AD 200] Roman Imperial, Early. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Herod's client kingdom gave way to direct Roman rule, and with it came monumental building at Caesarea, Masada and the Jerusalem Temple. Two catastrophic revolts followed: the destruction of the Temple in AD 70 and the crushing of Bar Kokhba's rising, after which Jerusalem was refounded as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina. Jewish life shifted to Galilee and to rabbinic study, while a Jewish sect centred on Jesus spread across the empire.

With the Temple gone, Judaism was remade around rabbis and text; the Mishnah was compiled and the Galilee filled with study centres and richly carved synagogues. Imperial conversion under Constantine transformed the region into the Christian Holy Land, with pilgrim churches at Jerusalem and Bethlehem and a wave of imperial patronage. Villages and terraced farmland expanded, making these among the most densely settled centuries in the region's history.

The African provinces became one of the richest parts of the empire, shipping grain and olive oil to Rome from a landscape crowded with towns, olive presses and great mosaic-floored houses. Christianity here produced Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, and the bitter Donatist schism. Vandal conquest and a Byzantine reconquest ended the era before the Arab armies arrived.

Roman, Republican (Algeria, 150 BC–50 BC.label: Roman, Republican
Roman, Republican (Algeria, 150 BC–50 BC.prose:
[Maghreb, 150 BC–50 BC] Roman, Republican. Spatial coverage: Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

The Republic destroyed Carthage in 146 BC and inherited its African hinterland, ruling the rest through Numidian client kings – an arrangement that collapsed into the war against Jugurtha. Roman merchants, tax farmers and veteran settlers moved in, and Caesar's victory at Thapsus finished off the last independent kingdom. Grain and oil from these lands soon fed the city of Rome.

Sasanian (Israel, AD 225–AD 640).label: Sasanian
Sasanian (Israel, AD 225–AD 640).prose:
[Levant/Mesopotamia/Iran/Northern Arabia, AD 225–AD 640] Sasanian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Palestine, Saudi Arabia. Period definition from EAMENA Database — University of Oxford, 2021.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.
