[Câmpia Careilor, 2899 BC–2299 BC] grupul Sănislău. Gogâltan, F., 2017, p. 32. Este datat în Bronzul Timpuriu III sau 2300 - 1950 a. Chr, conform cronologiei propuse de Florin Gogâltan (F. Gogâltan 2017, p. 32). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Bronze Age group of the sandy Nyírség borderland of north-west Romania, closely tied to related groups across the Hungarian plain. Its low settlement mounds and cremation burials, with textile-impressed and incised pottery, mark the period when herding communities of the Tisza lowlands took on a distinctly Bronze Age character.

Vučedol (Timiș County, 2499 BC–2299 BC).label: Vučedol
Vučedol (Timiș County, 2499 BC–2299 BC).prose:
[Banat, Valea inferioară a Mureșului, 2499 BC–2299 BC] Vučedol. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Hunedoara County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 71-72. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A late Copper Age culture of the middle Danube known for dark burnished pottery with white-encrusted geometric designs, including the famous vessel long read as a calendar. Its people worked copper on a substantial scale using two-piece moulds and lived in fortified hilltop settlements, and their expansion and ceramic styles fed into the early Bronze Age cultures of central Europe.

grupul Orlea-Gornești (Timiș County, 229.label: grupul Orlea-Gornești
grupul Orlea-Gornești (Timiș County, 229.prose: [Banat, Valea inferioară a Mureșului, 2299 BC–2149 BC] grupul Orlea-Gornești. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Hunedoara County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 72-73. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Wietenberg (Sălaj County, 1999 BC–1499 B.label: Wietenberg
Wietenberg (Sălaj County, 1999 BC–1499 B.prose:
[Transilvania, 1999 BC–1499 BC] Wietenberg. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Bistrița-Năsăud County, Brașov County, Cluj County, Covasna County, Harghita County, Hunedoara County, Mureș County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 255-258. Studiul lui Gabriel Bălan, Collin Quinn și Gregory Hodgins propune  o periodizare a culturii Wietenberg în trei faze distincte bazate pe formele și ornamentele ceramice: timpurie, clasică și târzie. ornamentele ceramice: timpurie, clasică și târzie. Faza timpurie se clasifică  printr-o ceramică cu tradiții în bronzul timpuriu final  și este similară fazelor I-II potrivit periodizării lui N. Chidioșan și fazelor A1-2 definite de N. Borofka.  Conform datelor C14, această fază poate fi datată în invervalul secolelor XX-XVIII a. Chr. Faza clasică prezintă noi forme și ornamente ceramice, evidențiate în ultimele două niveluri din așezarea de la Derșida. Vase bogat ornamentate, care au stat la baza definirii culturii. Similară fazelor III Chidioșan și B-C Boroffka și poate fi datată în intervalul secolelor XVIII- XVI a. Chr conform datelor C14. Faza târzie prezintă forme și ornamente ceramice diferite de cele din faza clasică. Faza de locuire este restrânsă în jumătatea de vest a spațiului locuit anterior, fapt ce poate fi pus în legătură cu apariția culturii Noua. Este similară fazelor IV Chidioșan și D Boroffka. Conform datelor C14 perioada este cuprinsă între secolele XVI și XV a. Chr. In Ciugudean, H., Quinn, C., 2015, p. 147-178 si Palincaș, N., et all 2019, p. 38-51 este realizata o impartire in patru faze; N. Palincaș propune incheierea fazei a IV-a din Cultura Wietenberg dupa 1400 a.Chr. Dupa Gogâltan, F.,  2009, p. 45-70 este datata faza a patra a culturii Wietenberg in secolul XIII a.Chr. In Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 73-78. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of the Transylvanian basin, best known for pottery covered in tightly incised spirals, meanders and running scrolls — some of the most elaborate ornament of Bronze Age Europe. Its communities lived in hilltop and terrace settlements, worked local gold and copper, and exchanged goods along routes that link them to the Carpathian and Mycenaean worlds.

Wietenberg faza timpurie (Mureș County,.node: Wietenberg faza timpurie (Mureș County, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
Wietenberg faza timpurie (Mureș County,.label: Wietenberg faza timpurie
Wietenberg faza timpurie (Mureș County,.prose:
[Centrul Transilvaniei - bazinul carpatic, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Wietenberg faza timpurie. Spatial coverage: Brașov County, Mureș County, Sibiu County. Bălan, G., Quinn, C.,  Hodgins G., 2016, p. 67-92. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The formative stage of the Transylvanian Bronze Age culture, when its settlements and pottery styles emerged out of the preceding Early Bronze Age communities of the region. Decoration is simpler than in the later phases, with the incised spiral ornament that would define the culture still developing.

Wietenberg faza clasică (Mureș County, 1.node: Wietenberg faza clasică (Mureș County, 1799 BC–1599 BC)
Wietenberg faza clasică (Mureș County, 1.label: Wietenberg faza clasică
Wietenberg faza clasică (Mureș County, 1.prose:
[Centrul Transilvaniei - bazinul carpatic, 1799 BC–1599 BC] Wietenberg faza clasică. Spatial coverage: Brașov County, Mureș County, Sibiu County. Bălan, G., Quinn, C.,  Hodgins G., 2016, p. 67-92. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The mature stage of the Transylvanian Bronze Age culture, when its characteristic spiral and meander ornament on dark burnished pottery reached its most complex form, including hearths and vessels decorated with sun and wheel motifs. Metalwork and gold objects from this horizon show wide-ranging contacts across the Carpathian basin.

Wietenberg faza târzie (Mureș County, 15.node: Wietenberg faza târzie (Mureș County, 1599 BC–1499 BC)
Wietenberg faza târzie (Mureș County, 15.label: Wietenberg faza târzie
Wietenberg faza târzie (Mureș County, 15.prose:
[Zona de ocupație se restrânge la Mureșul Mijlociu, Someșul Cald și Someșul Rece., 1599 BC–1499 BC] Wietenberg faza târzie. Spatial coverage: Cluj County, Mureș County. Bălan, G., Quinn, C.,  Hodgins G., 2016, p. 67-92. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The closing stage of the Transylvanian Bronze Age culture, when decoration becomes sparser and vessel forms shift, and settlement patterns change under pressure from new groups moving into the Carpathian basin. It gives way to the Noua culture and its very different herding-oriented ash-mound settlements.

Otomani (Arad County, 1699 BC–1249 BC).label: Otomani
Otomani (Arad County, 1699 BC–1249 BC).prose:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1699 BC–1249 BC] Otomani. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Vulpe, Al. 2001, p. 249-250, 258-260; Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Cultura Otomani- Fuzesabony a  apărut în zona bazinului Tisei, extinzându-se spre vestul României, Slovacia de est, nord-estul Ungariei, Ucraina Transcarpatică și sud-estul Poloniei (Gankarski 2002, p. 8).  Pe teritoriul României: nordul Crișanei, bazinul inferior al Someșului, Câmpia de Vest. Întregul areal cultural este încadrat între 2150 a. Chr și 1250 a. Chr.. Maria Gimbutas încadrează faza timpurie a culturii Otomani la începutul mileniului II î.Chr, faza clasică între 1550- 1400 î.CHr, și faza finală până la 1100 î.Chr. (Gimbutas 1965; Fazecaș 1999, p. 53). Dumitru Berciu (1965) împărțea cultura Otomani în patru faze. (Fazecaș 1999). Ordenlitch revine asupra acestei probleme și împarte prima fază în două subfaze: Ia, încadrată în Br A1 și Ib în Br A2, menținând pentru  celelalte încadrarea propusă anterior. (Ordenlitch 1973, 15, Fazecaș 1999). T. Bader pornește de la cronologia  lui Ordenlitch și propune împărțirea în patru etape menținând limitele Br A-D (Bader 1978, 61; Fazecaș 1999). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age culture of the Carpathian Basin, known for tightly packed settlements protected by ditches and ramparts, some of them built up into tells occupied for generations. Its metalworkers produced bronze weapons, ornaments and horse gear traded far across central Europe, and its fortified sites suggest chiefly elites competing for control of the routes carrying copper, tin and gold. Excavated houses, storage pits and rich metal hoards make it one of the best-documented Bronze Age societies of the region.

Otomani A (Arad County, 1699 BC–1549 BC).label: Otomani A
Otomani A (Arad County, 1699 BC–1549 BC).prose:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1699 BC–1549 BC] Otomani A. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Br. A2 Central European (Reinecke). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The formative stage of the culture, when communities in the Tisza and Mureș lowlands settled into long-lived villages and began enclosing them with ditches and banks. Pottery styles and the first substantial bronze working mark a break with the preceding Early Bronze Age groups.

Periam-Pecica (Mureș County, 2199 BC–169.label: Periam-Pecica
Periam-Pecica (Mureș County, 2199 BC–169.prose:
[Valea inferioara a Muresului, 2199 BC–1699 BC] Periam-Pecica. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 261-265; Vulpe, Al., 2010, p. 257; Nicodemus,  O`Shea, J.,  2015, p. 691-702. Datări C14 din cimitirul Mokrin, din Banatul sârbesc, sugerează un interval de timp între 2200 și 1700 a. Chr. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Bronze Age farmers of the lower Mureș valley who lived in long-occupied tell settlements, rebuilding house on house until the mounds stood metres above the floodplain. Excavations at Pecica revealed workshops for bronze casting and bone working, horse gear, and imported goods showing links to the Mycenaean world and the Carpathian metal trade. Their fine burnished pottery with knobs and spiral decoration is a hallmark of the Maros culture.

Vatina (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1499 BC).label: Vatina
Vatina (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Banat, 1899 BC–1499 BC] Vatina. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Ljustina, M., Dmitrovic, K., 2015, p. 37-47;Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79. Cultura Vatin s-a întins din sudul Câmpiei Panonice până în nord-vestul Peninsulei Balcanice, în Banatul sârbesc și Banatul românesc. Cronologia generală pentru întreg arealul cultural este cuprinsă între 2000 și 1500 a. Chr.; Dupa Ljustina, M., Dmitrovic, K., 2015, p. 37-47aceasta cultura avea 3 faze, dupa Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79 exista doua faze. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of the Banat plain and the middle Danube, known from long-lived tell settlements and cemeteries with cremation urns. Its fine dark burnished pottery, incised and channelled with spirals and encrusted with white paste, is among the most distinctive of the region. Bronze weapons and ornaments in its graves show it was plugged into exchange networks running from the Carpathians towards the Aegean.

Vatina faza timpurie (Timiș County, 1899.node: Vatina faza timpurie (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1649 BC)
Vatina faza timpurie (Timiș County, 1899.label: Vatina faza timpurie
Vatina faza timpurie (Timiș County, 1899.prose: [Banat, 1899 BC–1649 BC] Vatina faza timpurie. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Ljustina, M., Dmitrovic, K., 2015, p. 37-47;Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79. Bronz A2 central European, Helladicul târziu (mormintele cu puț). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Vatina faza clasică (Timiș County, 1649.node: Vatina faza clasică (Timiș County, 1649 BC–1499 BC)
Vatina faza clasică (Timiș County, 1649.label: Vatina faza clasică
Vatina faza clasică (Timiș County, 1649.prose: [Banat, 1649 BC–1499 BC] Vatina faza clasică. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79. O parte din A3 central european și Bronz B1 european. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Verbicioara (Gorj County, 1899 BC–1499 B.label: Verbicioara
Verbicioara (Gorj County, 1899 BC–1499 B.prose:
[Oltenia , 1899 BC–1499 BC] Verbicioara. Spatial coverage: Dolj County, Gorj County, Mehedinți County, Olt County, Vâlcea County. 3-5 faze. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 265-267; Vulpe, Al., 2010, p. 261. B. Hansel contestă existența fazelor IV și V ale culturii Verbicioara pe care le include în grupul Govora, atestat mai ales în nordul și estul Olteniei. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age culture of Oltenia and the Danube valley in south-western Romania, known chiefly from its settlements and its dark, highly burnished pottery decorated with incised spirals and meanders, often filled with white paste. Its people farmed and herded in small tell-like and open villages, and their bronze- and goldwork shows links running down the Danube to the Balkans and the Aegean world.

Tei (Călărași County, 2199 BC–1499 BC).label: Tei
Tei (Călărași County, 2199 BC–1499 BC).prose:
[Muntenia  si sud-estul Transilvaniei, 2199 BC–1499 BC] Tei. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Brașov County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County, Covasna County, Călărași County, Dâmbovița County. primele 3 faze. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2),, p. 267-269; Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Fazele IV și V prezintă multe discrepanțe față de cele precedente, precum și strânse asemănări cu grupul Govora din Oltenia, încât cercetătoarea Nona Palincaș a propus denumirea grupului cultural Govora-Fundeni, care evoluează în Bronzul târziu sub forma unei sinteze sub ceramica de tradiția Verbicioara și Tei. (N. Palincaș 1996, p. 239-295). Dupa A. Laszlo (Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300) faza a cincea a culturii Tei se prelungeste pana pe la 1100 a.Chr.. Dupa Gavrilă, E., 2013, p. 153-168; Leahu, V., 2003, p. 42-43, 202-208 cultura Tei ar fi situata intre 2000/1900 a.Chr. si 1520/1410 a.Chr. iar aria de raspandire este sud-estul României și Bulgaria între Stara Planina (sud) și Carpații Meridionali în nord, bazinul superior al Ialomiței și Mostiștea în est și râul Vedea în Vest. Descoperiri și în sud-estul Transilvaniei. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of the lower Danube plain, known from settlement mounds and cemeteries around Bucharest and the Wallachian lowlands. Its people farmed and herded on the plain and made dark burnished pottery with incised and encrusted geometric decoration, part of the network of Carpathian-Balkan communities linked by bronze exchange.

Monteoru (Buzău County, 2499 BC–1099 BC).label: Monteoru
Monteoru (Buzău County, 2499 BC–1099 BC).prose:
[Nord-estul Munteniei, sudul Moldovei, 2499 BC–1099 BC] Monteoru. Spatial coverage: Brăila County, Buzău County, Galați County, Vrancea County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 250-254; Motzoi-Chicideanu, I., Șandor-Chicideanu, M.,  2015, p. 9-53. 2500 a. Chr. posibil si mai devreme; data de final post 1500 a. Chr.. Ocupă un spațiul cuprins între curbura Carpaților, până spre câmpie, pentru ca în faza de maximă expansiune, să ocupe cea mai mare parte a sudului și centrului Moldovei, cu unele pătrunderi spre est, dincolo de Prut, unde intră în contact cu manifestările culturale Mnogovalikovaja. (Bolohan 2016, p. 98). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age culture of the sub-Carpathian hills, known for terraced hilltop settlements defended by ditches and ramparts, and for cemeteries of crouched inhumations. Its pottery, with spiral and channelled decoration, and its bronze and bone ornaments show contacts stretching from the Carpathian Basin to the steppe. The type site at Sărata Monteoru, with its long stratified sequence, remains the yardstick for dating the Bronze Age of eastern Romania.

Gârla Mare (Caraș-Severin County, 1649 B.label: Gârla Mare
Gârla Mare (Caraș-Severin County, 1649 B.prose:
[Sudul Banatului și Oltenia, 1649 BC–1249 BC] Gârla Mare. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Dolj County, Gorj County, Mehedinți County, Vâlcea County. are patru faze. Șandor-Chicideanu, M., 2003. cultura Zuto-Brdo-Gârla Mare; Ion Motzoi Chicideanu in  2009,  consideră că prima etapă a culturii Gârla Mare începe cu faza a III-a a culturii Verbicioara. El propune o cronologie intre 1900 si 1400 a.Chr. Sfârșitul este marcat de apariția grupului cultural Bistreș-Ișalnița. Verbicioara III. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age community of the lower Danube, best known for cremating its dead in urns and for extraordinary clay figurines: bell-shaped female statuettes covered in incised spirals and meanders that seem to record costume, jewellery and tattooing. The pottery is richly decorated and often encrusted with white paste. The figurines remain the fullest picture we have of how people in this region dressed and adorned themselves.

Suciu (Satu Mare County, 1599 BC–1199 BC.label: Suciu
Suciu (Satu Mare County, 1599 BC–1199 BC.prose:
[Tara Lapusului, Maramuresul istoric, 1599 BC–1199 BC] Suciu. Spatial coverage: Bistrița-Năsăud County, Maramureș County, Mureș County, Satu Mare County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (1), p. 224; Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 261; Petrescu-Dȋmboviţa, M. 2001 (3), p.280-281; Petrescu-Dȋmboviţa, M., 2019, p. 274. Unii cercetători o denumesc faza a treia a culturii Suciu cultura Culciu Mare. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Late Bronze Age culture of the upper Tisza basin, recognised above all by its dark burnished pottery covered in incised spirals and meander patterns. Its people cremated their dead, worked bronze on a large scale, and left hoards of tools, weapons and ornaments that show them plugged into the metal trade networks running between the Carpathians and central Europe.

Coslogeni (Călărași County, 1349 BC–1049.label: Coslogeni
Coslogeni (Călărași County, 1349 BC–1049.prose:
[Sud-estul Munteniei, Dobrogea, 1349 BC–1049 BC] Coslogeni. Spatial coverage: Constanța County, Călărași County, Ialomița County, Tulcea County. 3 faze. Sabatinovka-Noua-Coslogeni/Noua-Sabatinovka-Coslogeni sau grupul Coslogeni-Yagnilo. Petrescu-Dȋmboviţa, M. 2001 (3), p.285-286; Bojadziev, J., 1992, p. 17;Bolohan 2016, p, 160. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Late Bronze Age herding culture of the lower Danube and Dobrudja, part of the wider Noua-Sabatinovka-Coslogeni complex that stretched east across the steppe. Its most recognisable sites are the so-called ash mounds, low heaps of grey settlement debris packed with cattle and sheep bone, that mark seasonal camps of a heavily pastoral economy.

Otomani B (Arad County, 1549 BC–1399 BC).label: Otomani B
Otomani B (Arad County, 1549 BC–1399 BC).prose:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Otomani B. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Br. B Central European (Reinecke). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The classic stage, with heavily fortified settlements and tell mounds, dense house plots and a flourishing bronze industry producing weapons, ornaments and harness fittings. Wealth differences visible in burials and hoards point to an established warrior elite controlling metal supply and trade.

Otomani C (Arad County, 1399 BC–1249 BC).label: Otomani C
Otomani C (Arad County, 1399 BC–1249 BC).prose:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1399 BC–1249 BC] Otomani C. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Br. C Central European (Reinecke). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The late stage, when the great fortified tells were abandoned or reduced and material culture shifted under influence from the Tumulus groups spreading through central Europe. Metalwork remained abundant, but settlement broke up into smaller, more dispersed sites as the Middle Bronze Age order gave way.

Cehăluț (Cluj County, 1299 BC–1199 BC).label: Cehăluț
Cehăluț (Cluj County, 1299 BC–1199 BC).prose:
[între Câmpia Careiului și Colinele Tășnadului, în nord și râurile Crasna și Barcău, în sud, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Cehăluț. Spatial coverage: Bihor County, Cluj County, Satu Mare County, Sălaj County. grupul cultural Cehăluț-Pișcolt-Hajdúbagos. Gogâltan, F., 2009, p. 45-70; Nemeti, J., 2008, p. Este contemporan Bronzului C/D din cronologia lui Reinecke. T. Bader considera grupul cultural Cehăluț-Pișcolt faza a IV-a a culturii Otomani. Suciu de Sus II și Lăpuș I. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Late Bronze Age group of northwestern Romania and the neighbouring Hungarian plain, usually paired with the Hajdúbagos finds across the border. It is known mainly from cremation cemeteries with urns and from dark burnished pottery with channelled and knobbed decoration, part of the wider shift in the Carpathian basin towards urnfield burial rites.

Gava (Timiș County, 1349 BC–999 BC).label: Gava
Gava (Timiș County, 1349 BC–999 BC).prose:
[Maramureș, Banat, 1349 BC–999 BC] Gava. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County, Timiș County. complexul cultural Gava-Holihrady. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A late Bronze Age world of the eastern Carpathian Basin recognised by its channelled pottery, black and glossy outside with a deep orange interior, and by cremation burials in urnfields. Its communities buried enormous hoards of bronze and were among the first in the region to work iron, forming a bridge between the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age cultures of the Danube and Transylvania.

Poienesti-Lukasevka (Romania, 199 BC–19.label: Poienesti-Lukasevka
Poienesti-Lukasevka (Romania, 199 BC–19.prose:
[Romania, 199 BC–19 BC] Poienesti-Lukasevka. Babes, M. 2001, p. 522-528; Iarmulschi 2018, p. 36. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An archaeological culture of the lands between the Carpathians and the Dniester whose cremation cemeteries, brooches and pottery show strong links to the Jastorf world of northern Europe. It is generally identified with the Bastarnae, Germanic-speaking migrants who moved southeast and appear in Greek and Roman accounts as mercenaries and raiders in the Balkans. Its remains document one of the earliest large-scale Germanic migrations into southeastern Europe.

cultura geto-dacica clasica (Romania, 17.label: cultura geto-dacica clasica
cultura geto-dacica clasica (Romania, 17.prose:
[Romania, 174 BC–AD 106] cultura geto-dacica clasica. Babes, M. 2010, p. 805-808. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The height of Dacian civilisation, when Burebista and later Decebalus welded the tribes north of the Danube into a kingdom powerful enough to alarm Rome. Its centre was the mountain complex around Sarmizegetusa Regia, with stone-walled citadels, circular sanctuaries, ironworking on an industrial scale and hoards of silver ornaments and Greek and Roman coin. Trajan's two wars ended it, and the conquered kingdom became the Roman province of Dacia.

The culture marks contact between the settled Carpathian populations and Scythian groups from the east.

These communities are generally seen as ancestors of the Getae who later confronted Greeks and Persians on the lower Danube.

The group belongs to the northern Thracian world of the later Hallstatt period, when iron working, mounted warriors and contacts with the steppe and the Greek Black Sea coast reshaped local society.

Tuscany was the heartland of the Etruscans, whose independent cities, Volterra, Chiusi, Populonia, Vetulonia and Arezzo among them, grew wealthy on the iron of Elba, copper mining and Mediterranean trade. Their painted and chamber tombs, banqueting scenes, bronze mirrors and alabaster urns give an unusually vivid picture of daily life and belief, and their inscriptions preserve a language still only partly understood. Roman conquest and, finally, the grant of citizenship after the Social War dissolved them into Italy.

Etruria was absorbed into the Roman state after the Social War, its cities granted citizenship and its language and script fading within a few generations. Roman roads, centuriated field systems, colonies like Florentia and Luca, and coastal villas producing wine and oil reshaped the landscape; marble from Luni was shipped across the empire. Much of what survives above ground in Tuscan towns - street grids, theatres, aqueducts, baths - dates from these centuries.

Tuscany in these centuries shifted from a landscape of Roman villas and municipal towns to one of fortified hilltop settlements, shrinking cities and Christian basilicas. Estates were consolidated, coinage and long-distance pottery imports thinned out, and bishops took over much of the administrative role once held by civic magistrates. The Gothic War of the mid-sixth century wrecked much of the region, and the Lombard arrival at its close reshaped who held the land.

Following the Gothic wars, Tuscany passed to the Lombards, who made Lucca a ducal seat, and then to the Carolingian counts and the powerful margraves who succeeded them. Roman towns shrank, but monasteries, rural parish churches and the first fortified hilltop villages took shape, laying the settlement pattern still visible today. Trade never disappeared entirely: pilgrims and merchants moving along the Via Francigena kept the region connected to the wider world.

Tuscan towns broke free of feudal lords and organised themselves as communes, growing rich on wool, banking and long-distance trade; Florence, Siena, Pisa and Lucca fought each other as much as they fought outsiders. The florin became an international currency, and merchant wealth paid for cathedrals, town halls and the first generation of painters and poets who would define the Renaissance. Plague in 1348 killed perhaps half the population and permanently altered the balance between the surviving cities.

The Medici turned Florence into a hereditary duchy and then a grand duchy, draining marshes, developing the free port of Livorno and governing a unified Tuscan state. The dynasty died out in 1737 and the Habsburg-Lorraines took over, bringing Enlightenment reform - most famously the abolition of the death penalty in 1786, the first anywhere. Meanwhile the region's political weight in Europe steadily faded even as its art and science drew visitors from everywhere.

Railways, land reclamation in the Maremma, marble and mining industries, and mass emigration transformed a largely agricultural region, while sharecropping estates that had shaped the countryside for centuries were finally dismantled after the Second World War.

The height of Etruscan power, when cities like Vulci, Volterra, Chiusi and Populonia controlled the Tyrrhenian sea and traded intensively with Greeks and Carthaginians. Painted tombs, monumental temples with terracotta decoration, black bucchero ware and imported Attic vases fill the archaeological record; writing in the Etruscan alphabet becomes common. Etruscan kings ruled Rome for much of this period, until their expulsion around 509 BC.

Naval defeat at Cumae in 474 BC and pressure from Celts in the north cost the Etruscans their sea power and their northern colonies, and coastal cities declined while inland centres such as Chiusi, Volterra and Perugia held on. Art absorbed Greek classical models, and rising Rome began the long series of wars that would end Etruscan independence.

City by city the Etruscan states fell to Rome, keeping local institutions and language while losing political freedom. Wealthy families built family tombs filled with carved alabaster and terracotta ash urns, and Volterra and Chiusi produced some of the most distinctive sculpture of the period; the era closes with the granting of Roman citizenship and the swift Latinisation of the region.

After the Social War, the Etruscan towns received Roman citizenship, and Latin, Roman law and Roman coinage rapidly displaced Etruscan civic life. Sulla's veteran colonies at places like Arretium and Faesulae redistributed land, while the countryside filled with slave-run villa estates producing wine and oil for wider markets. Visitors see the last Etruscan-language inscriptions and urns alongside the first thoroughly Roman townscapes.

Augustus turned the exhausted Roman Republic into a monarchy in all but name, and his Julio-Claudian heirs ruled to Nero's fall. Etruria was reshaped by veteran colonies, new road building and vast senatorial estates worked by slaves, while its old cities became comfortable Roman municipia. Marble public buildings, imperial portrait statues and mass-produced Arretine red-gloss pottery from Arezzo, exported as far as India, define the material world of these decades.

The Flavians and the Antonines brought stability after the civil wars of 69, with the Empire at its widest extent under Trajan and a long stretch of peace under Hadrian and the Antonines. In Etruria this shows in prosperous villas, brick-stamped building booms, and the exploitation of marble and terracotta industries feeding Rome's construction. Roman citizenship spread widely through the provinces, and the era closes with Commodus's murder and a return to civil war.

From the Severan emperors through the third-century crisis to Constantine, the Roman world weathered civil war, inflation, plague and frontier collapse, and re-emerged reorganised under Diocletian and his successors. In Italy, coastal villas were fortified or abandoned, town councils buckled under fiscal pressure, and large estates absorbed smallholders. The period ends with a Christian emperor and a new capital in the east, leaving Italy politically sidelined.

Tuscany lay under Lombard rule, governed from ducal seats such as Lucca and Chiusi by warrior elites whose weapon-filled graves are among the region's most distinctive finds. Roman towns shrank to a fraction of their former size, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and settlement shifted toward hilltops and rural estates. The Lombards gradually converted from Arianism to Catholicism, setting up the church networks that would organise the countryside for centuries.

Lombard Tuscany reached its most organised phase, with Lucca a wealthy ducal capital, a revival of stone church building, and a boom in monastic foundations that generated the parchment archives historians still rely on. In 774 Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom, and Frankish counts replaced Lombard dukes, tying the region into a north-European empire. Written wills, land charters and craft workshops show an economy reviving after two centuries of contraction.

Under Carolingian rule Tuscany was governed as a march from Lucca, with Frankish and Lombard counts holding land alongside powerful bishops and monasteries. Church building, land charters and monastic estates shaped the countryside, while coastal towns had to cope with Saracen raiding from the sea. The great families who emerged here would dominate Italian politics for the next two centuries.

Bishops and monasteries such as those around Lucca and Arezzo held huge estates and acted as centres of law and literacy. The century's castle-building set the settlement pattern that still shapes the Tuscan landscape.

The march of Tuscany reached its height under the Canossa family, culminating in Countess Matilda, whose castle hosted the emperor's submission to the pope in 1077 during the investiture struggle. Pisa turned to the sea, raiding Muslim ports and building a fleet that would make it a Mediterranean power, and began its marble cathedral in 1063. Church reform, growing towns and new markets were loosening the old rural order.

Tuscan towns turned themselves into self-governing communes, run by elected consuls and bound by oath rather than by counts or bishops, and promptly began fighting each other over land and roads. Pisa and Genoa contested the sea; Florence, Siena, Lucca and Arezzo expanded into their countryside and pulled down rival castles. Money economy, long-distance cloth trade and the Romanesque churches of the period all date from this surge of urban confidence.

Tuscan cities became European financial centres, with Sienese and Florentine bankers handling papal revenues and Florence minting the gold florin in 1252, a coin trusted from London to Constantinople. Guelf and Ghibelline factions split the region in wars that ended with Florence's dominance after Benevento, and popular guilds pushed the old nobility out of government. The same decades produced Dante's early years, Giotto's teachers, and the great mendicant churches and civic palaces still standing in Florence and Siena.

Florence became the workshop of the Renaissance: Brunelleschi raised a dome no one knew how to build, Masaccio and Donatello reinvented perspective and the human figure, and scholars hunted down Greek and Latin manuscripts. Banking wealth, above all the Medici's, paid for it, and Cosimo and then Lorenzo ran the republic without ever holding a crown. The city also absorbed Pisa and gained a sea outlet, before Savonarola's brief theocracy and French invasion upended everything at century's end.

The republic finally died: Medici dukes returned with imperial backing, and Cosimo I built a centralised state, crushed Siena and had himself made Grand Duke. Vasari laid out the Uffizi and wrote the first history of art, while Michelangelo, Cellini and Giambologna worked for princely patrons rather than guilds. Livorno was developed as a free port open to Jews, Greeks and other outsiders, and the Tuscan countryside settled into the sharecropping pattern that lasted for centuries.

The old wool and banking wealth drained away as northern Europeans took over Mediterranean trade, and plague in 1630–31 hit the cities hard. Grand-ducal Florence nonetheless kept a scientific edge: Galileo worked under Medici patronage, and the Accademia del Cimento pioneered experimental method with thermometers and barometers. Livorno thrived as a cosmopolitan port while the rural economy stagnated, and the last Medici rulers grew increasingly devout and indebted.

Land was drained and redistributed, and economists in Florence argued about free trade with an audience across Europe. The reforms ended abruptly with French armies and a peasant backlash at the century's close.

French occupation under Napoleon swept away the old Grand Duchy before the Lorraine dynasty returned, ruling a quiet, largely agricultural state famous for its mild government and its foreign residents. Marsh drainage in the Maremma and Val di Chiana, new roads and the first railways reshaped the countryside, while Livorno remained the region's commercial window. Tuscany voted itself into the new Italian kingdom, and Florence briefly served as its capital, gaining boulevards and piazzas at the cost of its medieval centre.

Tuscany passed from a united Italy's liberal monarchy through Fascism, wartime occupation and the bitter fighting along the Gothic Line, which shattered Florence's bridges and many hill towns. Postwar reconstruction brought industry to the Arno valley, mass emigration from the countryside, and the 1966 flood that swamped Florence's libraries and galleries and launched a global rescue of its art. Densely populated valleys of the northwest supported farming communities that terraced hillsides, irrigated fields and built stone villages, some perched on defensible ridges as pukaras. Painted urns of the Santa María style, used to bury children beneath house floors, are the signature artefacts. Warfare and competition among these polities were cut short by Inca conquest and then by Spanish arrival.

Late Prehispanic Period (Córdoba, AD 600.prose:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 600–AD 1600] Late Prehispanic Period. Period definition from Colonial rock art: A reflection on resistance and cultural change (16th and 17th century-Córdoba, Argentina) — Andrea Recalde, 2014-09-11.

The hills and plains of central Argentina were occupied by groups later known to the Spanish as Comechingones and Sanavirones, who lived in semi-subterranean pit dwellings, grew maize, beans and squash, and hunted and gathered alongside their crops. They made plain and incised pottery, ground stone tools and mortars in bedrock outcrops, and left painted rock art in the sierras. The period closes with Spanish colonisation and the collapse of these communities under encomienda.

Mesolithic (Poland, 9150 BC–2950 BC).prose:
[Poland, 9150 BC–2950 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 1, 500 000 - 5500 BC — 2016.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

Late Mesolithic (Poland, 6050 BC–2950 BC.label: Late Mesolithic
Late Mesolithic (Poland, 6050 BC–2950 BC.prose:
[Poland, 6050 BC–2950 BC] Late Mesolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 1, 500 000 - 5500 BC — 2016.

Hunter-gatherers in dense post-glacial woodland made tiny geometric microliths set into composite arrows and worked the coasts, rivers and clearings with fire to draw in game. Rising seas finally drowned Doggerland during this period, cutting Britain off from the Continent and leaving its foragers on an island. Their world ended with the arrival of farming, and the debate over how much they contributed to what came next is still unresolved.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

Early Neolithic (Poland, 5499 BC–4099 BC.prose:

Farming, pottery and domesticated animals arrived in Britain, and within a few generations people were building monuments: earthen long barrows over the bones of the dead, ditched causewayed enclosures for gatherings and feasts, and deep flint mines. Woodland was cleared for cereals and pasture, beginning the long transformation of the British landscape. These communities laid the groundwork for the great henge and stone circle building that followed.

Communal long barrows and causewayed enclosures fell out of use, and people began building cursus monuments – enormous parallel-ditched avenues running for miles across the landscape – along with the first great henges. Pottery grew heavier and more elaborately decorated, and forest clearance and herding reshaped the countryside. The earthwork phase of Stonehenge belongs to the end of this stretch of time.

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

Farming communities on the Polish lowlands began using copper — mostly small ornaments and tools traded in from the south — while stone remained the working material. Villages of Funnel Beaker and related groups cleared woodland with ard ploughs and cattle traction, and began building the long earthen barrows and communal monuments that mark the landscape.

Late Eneolithic (Poland, 3799 BC–2799 BC.prose:

Farming communities across the Polish lands shifted towards herding, wagons and copper metallurgy, with Funnel Beaker settlements giving way to Globular Amphora groups and then the widely dispersed Corded Ware culture. Burial changes are striking: single graves under barrows, men with stone battle-axes, women with beads. This is the horizon linked to steppe-derived ancestry spreading into central Europe.

Bronze Age (Poland, 1999 BC–749 BC).prose:
[Poland, 1999 BC–749 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

Middle Bronze Age (Poland, 1299 BC–1099.prose:
[Poland, 1299 BC–1099 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

[Poland, 1099 BC–899 BC] Younger Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Lusatian communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large, orderly cemeteries, some holding thousands of graves. Settlements grew larger and some were ringed with timber-and-earth ramparts; bronze was plentiful enough to be deposited in hoards in rivers and bogs. The pottery, sheet-bronze vessels and pins show close links across a broad Central European world stretching from the Elbe to the Carpathians.

[Poland, 899 BC–749 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

The Przeworsk and Wielbark cultures flourished on the amber route running from the Baltic to the Danube, and Roman coins, glass, bronze vessels and sigillata reached Polish lands in quantity. Wielbark cemeteries with stone circles and unburnt burials are linked to the Goths, whose southward movement in the third century reshaped the region. Local iron smelting, notably in the Holy Cross Mountains, worked on a scale rarely matched in barbarian Europe.

Communities of the Przeworsk and Wielbark cultures in the Vistula and Oder basins were still tied to the Roman world by the amber route, importing coins, glass, bronze vessels and weaponry, and burying their dead with them. Local ironworking and pottery production reached an industrial scale in places, notably the smelting centres of the Holy Cross Mountains. The arrival of the Huns on the Black Sea steppe at the end of the fourth century broke these networks and pushed groups westward.

The Late Roman period opens with the aftermath of the Marcomannic Wars, when the frontier trade that had funnelled Roman coin, bronze vessels and glass into the Vistula basin was disrupted and reorganised. Przeworsk communities kept burying their dead with weapons, while Wielbark groups pushed south-east towards the Black Sea — the movement that ancient writers describe as the migration of the Goths. Grave goods from this phase are the richest in Polish Iron Age cemeteries.

A short, unsettled phase matching the crisis decades of the Roman Empire, when the flow of denarii northwards dried up and local craftsmen copied Roman forms rather than importing them. Barbarian raiding across the Danube and Black Sea coasts brought new booty and new fashions in brooches and belt fittings back to the Vistula. Settlement in some areas thins out as populations shifted south and east.

Mesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 9299 BC–389.label: Mesolitikum
Mesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 9299 BC–389.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 9299 BC–3899 BC] Mesolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. This is a wider term encompassing all the source's Mesolithic sub-periods. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

As the ice retreated and the sea flooded the land bridges, Denmark's hunter-gatherers passed through the Maglemose, Kongemose and Ertebølle traditions, moving from inland lake and bog camps to a rich life on the coast. Waterlogged sites preserve an extraordinary record: dugout canoes, leister prongs, bows, fish weirs, and huge shell middens of oyster and cockle. Ertebølle communities were settled enough to build cemeteries and make pottery while still living entirely by hunting and fishing, and they traded with farming neighbours for generations before taking up farming around 4000 BC.
Mesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 9299 BC–389.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Neolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699.label: Neolitikum
Neolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699 BC] Neolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. This is a wider term encompassing all the source's Neolithic sub-periods. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Farming reached the Oslofjord region only patchily; for most of these millennia people continued to hunt, fish and gather while adopting pottery, polished axes and, eventually, small-scale cereal growing and stockkeeping. Funnel Beaker influences appear early along the coast, followed by Battle Axe/Corded Ware groups with their distinctive shafthole axes and burials. It shows how the agricultural package thinned out and changed shape at the northern edge of Europe.
Neolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Seinmesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC.label: Seinmesolitikum
Seinmesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 6299 BC–3899 BC] Seinmesolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Hunter-fisher groups worked the rising, rebounding coastline of the Oslo fjord, living off seals, fish and wild game and leaving shore-bound camps that are now stranded well inland. Ground and pecked stone axes of Nøstvet type appear alongside blade tools, and sites become larger and more repeatedly used, hinting at a more settled rhythm of life. Farming had not yet arrived.
Seinmesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Mesolitikum, Fase 3 (Eastern Norway, 629.label: Mesolitikum, Fase 3
Mesolitikum, Fase 3 (Eastern Norway, 629.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC] Mesolitikum, Fase 3. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Along a coast still rising rapidly from the sea, hunter-fisher groups settled on shorelines that shifted with every few centuries of land uplift, leaving beach terraces stacked like a staircase inland. This phase is marked by ground stone adzes of greenstone and a heavy reliance on marine resources, seals, fish and sea birds. The strandline dating of these sites gives Norwegian archaeologists an unusually precise chronological tool.
Mesolitikum, Fase 3 (Eastern Norway, 629.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Mesolitikum, Fase 4 (Eastern Norway, 449.label: Mesolitikum, Fase 4
Mesolitikum, Fase 4 (Eastern Norway, 449.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC] Mesolitikum, Fase 4. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

The last hunter-gatherer centuries in eastern Norway, when coastal settlements grew larger and more repeatedly occupied, and contacts reached south towards the pottery-using fishers of the Baltic and Denmark. Ground stone tools and specialised marine hunting continued right up to the point when farming and Neolithic material culture began to filter northwards.
Mesolitikum, Fase 4 (Eastern Norway, 449.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Nøstvetfasen (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–44.label: Nøstvetfasen
Nøstvetfasen (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–44.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC] Nøstvetfasen. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Coastal hunter-fisher groups along the Oslo Fjord, named for the Nøstvet site, worked greenstone into distinctive pecked and ground core axes—the first heavy woodworking tools in the region. Settlements cluster on what were then shorelines, now stranded well inland by land uplift, and shell and bone refuse points to seal hunting, fishing and boat use. The technology marks a Middle Mesolithic world of stable, resource-rich coastal life before pottery and farming reached Scandinavia.
Nøstvetfasen (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–44.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Kjeøyfasen (Eastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899.label: Kjeøyfasen
Kjeøyfasen (Eastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899.prose: [Southeastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC] Kjeøyfasen. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.
Kjeøyfasen (Eastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Tidligneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 B.label: Tidligneolitikum
Tidligneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 B.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 3899 BC–3299 BC] Tidligneolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Farming reached the interior and coastlands of eastern Norway in a piecemeal way: cereals, domestic animals and polished flint axes appear alongside continuing hunting, fishing and sealing. Pottery and burial customs echo the Funnel Beaker world of southern Scandinavia, but settlement stayed mobile and small-scale, and many communities kept living much as their Mesolithic ancestors had. The interest lies in the mixture — a frontier zone where the Neolithic package arrived as an option rather than a replacement.
Tidligneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 B.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Mellomneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3299 B.label: Mellomneolitikum
Mellomneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3299 B.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 3299 BC–2349 BC] Mellomneolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

In the Oslofjord region farming and Funnel Beaker traditions took hold, while inland and along the coast hunting, fishing and pecked-slate technology continued much as before. The later part of the period brought the Battle Axe culture, with single graves, corded pottery and polished boat-shaped axes, and with it new connections south to Denmark and east to Sweden. The mix makes eastern Norway a frontier zone where farmers and foragers lived side by side.
Mellomneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3299 B.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Mellomneolitikum A (Eastern Norway, 3299.label: Mellomneolitikum A
Mellomneolitikum A (Eastern Norway, 3299.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 3299 BC–2849 BC] Mellomneolitikum A. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Funnel Beaker influence reached the Oslofjord, bringing pottery, polished flint axes and the first traces of cultivation and stock-keeping to eastern Norway. Away from the fjord, communities kept to hunting, fishing and a rich slate and quartzite tool tradition, so the archaeological picture is one of contrast rather than a clean transition to farming.
Mellomneolitikum A (Eastern Norway, 3299.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Mellomneolitikum B (Eastern Norway, 2849.label: Mellomneolitikum B
Mellomneolitikum B (Eastern Norway, 2849.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 2849 BC–2349 BC] Mellomneolitikum B. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

The Battle Axe culture arrived, recognisable from its cord-decorated beakers and polished boat-shaped stone axes, buried with individuals rather than in collective tombs. Herding and a more mobile, cattle-centred economy spread through the lowlands, part of the wider Corded Ware expansion that reshaped populations across northern Europe.
Mellomneolitikum B (Eastern Norway, 2849.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Seinneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 2349 BC–.label: Seinneolitikum
Seinneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 2349 BC–.prose:
[Southeastern Norway, 2349 BC–1699 BC] Seinneolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Farming and herding took firm hold in eastern Norway, along with a new material culture centred on finely pressure-flaked flint daggers imitating the metal blades of the Continent. Two-aisled longhouses appear, along with burials under cairns and the first regular use of bronze objects obtained through southern Scandinavian networks. The groundwork for the Nordic Bronze Age was laid here.
Seinneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 2349 BC–.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena (Tu.label: Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena
Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena (Tu.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1660] Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena. Period definition from Investigations at Pichao: Introduction to Studies in the Santa María Valley, North-western Argentina — Acreche Noemí, 2001.

Spanish entradas from Peru and Chile pushed into the valleys of the Northwest, founding short-lived towns and imposing encomienda tribute on Diaguita and other communities. Resistance was fierce and prolonged, culminating in the Calchaquí wars; defeat brought forced relocation of whole populations, and settlement sites from these decades mix indigenous pottery with European glass, iron and glazed ware.
Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena (Tu.source: Investigations at Pichao: Introduction to Studies in the Santa María Valley, North-western Argentina

Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Tucum.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales
Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Tucum.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1500] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Desarrollo del asentamiento del sitio STucTav 5 (El Pichao), provincia de Tucumán, comentarios sobre dataciones de 14C y luminiscencia — Cornell Per, 1993.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Tucum.source: Desarrollo del asentamiento del sitio STucTav 5 (El Pichao), provincia de Tucumán, comentarios sobre dataciones de 14C y luminiscencia

Spanish Native Period (Tucumán, AD 1530–.label: Spanish Native Period
Spanish Native Period (Tucumán, AD 1530–.prose: [Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1600] Spanish Native Period. Period definition from The excavation of the cemeteries 1991-1992 — Johansson Nils , 2001.

Late Pre-agricultural Period (Tucumán, 5.label: Late Pre-agricultural Period
Late Pre-agricultural Period (Tucumán, 5.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 5999 BC–499 BC] Late Pre-agricultural Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

Mobile hunting and gathering groups worked the valleys, high puna and eastern forest margins of northwest Argentina, hunting camelids and deer with stone-tipped weapons and returning repeatedly to rock shelters and open camps. Their traces are chipped stone tools, grinding equipment, hearths and painted or engraved rock art. Over these millennia people began cultivating and herding, gradually leading into the settled farming villages of the region.
Late Pre-agricultural Period (Tucumán, 5.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

Archaic Period (Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC).label: Archaic Period
Archaic Period (Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC).prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC] Archaic Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

The island's many small city-states — Knossos, Gortyn, Dreros, Lyktos — produced the earliest surviving Greek law inscribed on stone, and a strong tradition of hammered bronze work and Daedalic sculpture that influenced sculptors on the mainland. Votive deposits in the Idaean Cave and the temples of Dreros and Prinias show a distinctive local blend of Greek and Near Eastern forms. Crete then turned inward, staying out of the Persian Wars and playing little part in the classical politics that followed.
Archaic Period (Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC).source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

Regional Development Period (Tucumán, AD.label: Regional Development Period
Regional Development Period (Tucumán, AD.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1480] Regional Development Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

After the collapse of the wide-reaching Aguada style, the valleys of the Argentine northwest split into competing local polities with their own pottery, dress and burial customs. Populations concentrated in dense hillside settlements and fortified pukaras, farming irrigated terraces and burying infants in painted funerary urns. The Inca conquest at the end of the period absorbed these chiefdoms into Collasuyu, resettling populations and building roads and administrative centres among them.
Regional Development Period (Tucumán, AD.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

Imperial Period (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 153.label: Imperial Period
Imperial Period (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 153.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1536] Imperial Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

Inca armies pushed south into the valleys of northwest Argentina, absorbing local chiefdoms into the province of Qollasuyu. Roads, waystations, hilltop administrative centres and relocated groups of settlers changed how people lived, and imperial-style pottery and metalwork appear alongside older local wares. Spanish entradas arrived while this system was still young, and it collapsed quickly.
Imperial Period (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 153.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

Spanish Contact Periods (Tucumán, AD 153.label: Spanish Contact Periods
Spanish Contact Periods (Tucumán, AD 153.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1536–AD 1660] Spanish Contact Periods. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

Spanish expeditions pushing south from Peru and east from Chile met dense, fortified farming communities in the valleys of northwest Argentina. Encomienda demands, mission settlement and forced resettlement provoked the long Calchaquí wars, which kept parts of the region outside colonial control for over a century. Sites of the period mix indigenous pottery with glass beads, iron and European animal bone, before whole populations were deported and dispersed.
Spanish Contact Periods (Tucumán, AD 153.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

Formativo (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800).label: Formativo
Formativo (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800).prose: [Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800] Formativo. Period definition from Consideraciones acerca de la variabilidad formal en el diseño de las plantas de arquitectura en el NOA durante las Etapas Formativa y de Desarrollos Regionales — Giani Laura Margarita, 1999.
Formativo (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800).source: Consideraciones acerca de la variabilidad formal en el diseño de las plantas de arquitectura en el NOA durante las Etapas Formativa y de Desarrollos Regionales

Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Region.node: Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1470)
Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Region.label: Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales
Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Region.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1470] Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Nuevos avances en las prospecciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de los Cardones — Rivolta Gustavo Mario, 2005.

After the collapse of earlier region-wide styles, distinct local polities emerged across the Northwest, each with its own pottery and territory. Populations concentrated in large settlements and hilltop pukarás, irrigation and terracing expanded, and warfare left its mark in fortifications and weapons. Painted funerary urns for infant burials are among the most recognisable objects of the era, which closed with the Inca annexation of the region.
Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Region.source: Nuevos avances en las prospecciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de los Cardones

Período Arcaico (Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC.label: Período Arcaico
Período Arcaico (Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC] Período Arcaico. Period definition from Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina) — Gómez Augier Julián Patricio , 2020-11-30.

Small mobile bands hunted guanaco and deer, gathered algarrobo pods and chañar, and camped in rockshelters and open sites across the ranges and valleys. Over these millennia grinding stones, storage and the first tended plants and camelids appear, marking the slow shift from foraging to food production that made settled village life possible.
Período Arcaico (Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC.source: Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina)

Período Formativo (Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 75.label: Período Formativo
Período Formativo (Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 75.prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 750] Período Formativo. Period definition from Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina) — Gómez Augier Julián Patricio , 2020-11-30.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.
Período Formativo (Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 75.source: Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina)

Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500).label: Período Tardío
Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500).prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500] Período Tardío. Period definition from Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina) — Gómez Augier Julián Patricio , 2020-11-30.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.
Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500).source: Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina)

Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1535).label: Período Inca
Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1535).prose:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1535] Período Inca. Period definition from Distribución espacial de los asentamientos de los Períodos de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca en el tercio central de la Sierra de Quilmes (Valle de Yocavil-Tucumán — Maldonado Mario Gabriel, 2014.

Cuzco's armies incorporated the Northwest into Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, roughly a lifetime before the Spanish arrived. Roads, tambos, storage complexes and administrative centres were built, local lords were co-opted, and mitmaqkuna colonists were moved in to work fields and mines. Cuzco-style polychrome pottery and bronze appear in local villages, and mountain summits were turned into shrines.

Cultura Tafí (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 500).label: Cultura Tafí
Cultura Tafí (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 500).prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 500] Cultura Tafí. Period definition from Investigaciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de la Ciénaga (Dpto. Tafí, Tucumán) — Cremonte María Beatriz, 1996.

The first settled farming villages of the Tucumán highlands, whose people lived in circular stone houses grouped around patios and grew maize on terraced slopes. They are best known for carved stone menhirs, some over two metres tall, bearing stylised faces - among the earliest monumental sculpture in northwest Argentina.
Cultura Tafí (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 500).source: Investigaciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de la Ciénaga (Dpto. Tafí, Tucumán)

Etapa Formativa (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800).label: Etapa Formativa
Etapa Formativa (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800).prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800] Etapa Formativa. Period definition from Análisis funcional de una unidad doméstica de la etapa Formativa del valle de Tafí (Pcia. de Tucumán- Rep. Argentina) — Berberián Eduardo Enrique, 1988.

Farming villages took root in the valleys of Tucumán, with stone-walled house compounds, cultivated terraces and llama herds. The Tafí communities of the highland valleys left standing menhirs and carved stone monuments, while the Candelaria groups of the wooded eastern slopes made distinctive modelled pottery. Pottery, weaving and early metalwork all appear here for the first time in the region.
Etapa Formativa (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800).source: Análisis funcional de una unidad doméstica de la etapa Formativa del valle de Tafí (Pcia. de Tucumán- Rep. Argentina)

Etapa agrícola-aldeana del noroeste arge.label: Etapa agrícola-aldeana del noroeste argentino
Etapa agrícola-aldeana del noroeste arge.prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800] Etapa agrícola-aldeana del noroeste argentino. Period definition from Reflexiones en torno a un proyecto de Parque. Arqueológico en el valle de Tafi (Pcia. de Tucumán -Rep. Argentina) — Berberián Eduardo Enrique, 1988.

The stage when people in the Argentine Northwest settled into permanent farming hamlets, growing maize and other crops on terraced slopes and keeping llamas. Circular stone house compounds, grinding stones, ceramic vessels and the carved menhirs of the Tafí valley all belong to this world. It marks the shift from mobile foraging to the rooted village life on which all later Andean societies in the region were built.
Etapa agrícola-aldeana del noroeste arge.source: Reflexiones en torno a un proyecto de Parque. Arqueológico en el valle de Tafi (Pcia. de Tucumán -Rep. Argentina)

Período Formativo (Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 80.prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 800] Período Formativo. Period definition from Llama offerings in an early village landscape: new data from northwestern Argentina (200 b.c.–a.d. 800) — Franco Salvi Valeria Leticia, 2014-11-13.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.
Período Formativo (Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 80.source: Llama offerings in an early village landscape: new data from northwestern Argentina (200 b.c.–a.d. 800)

Formative Period (Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 850.label: Formative Period
Formative Period (Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 850.prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 850] Formative Period. Period definition from Dynamic places, durable structures: Early Formative agropastoral settlements of the southern Andes, Argentina — Salazar Julián, 2016-11-21.

Farming villages took hold in the valleys and piedmont of northwestern Argentina, with maize, beans and squash cultivated alongside herds of llamas. People built permanent stone and adobe houses, made pottery and ground-stone tools, and buried their dead beneath house floors and in stone cists. Exchange along the mountain corridors moved obsidian, shell and snuff-taking equipment over long distances, laying the base for the later fortified towns of the region.
Formative Period (Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 850.source: Dynamic places, durable structures: Early Formative agropastoral settlements of the southern Andes, Argentina

Regional Developments Period (Tucumán, A.label: Regional Developments Period
Regional Developments Period (Tucumán, A.prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1480] Regional Developments Period. Period definition from Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis — Páez María Cecilia, 2014-05-14.

After the collapse of the wide-reaching Aguada style, the valleys of the Argentine northwest split into competing local polities with their own pottery, dress and burial customs. Populations concentrated in dense hillside settlements and fortified pukaras, farming irrigated terraces and burying infants in painted funerary urns. The Inca conquest at the end of the period absorbed these chiefdoms into Collasuyu, resettling populations and building roads and administrative centres among them.
Regional Developments Period (Tucumán, A.source: Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis

Inca Period/Late Horizon (Tucumán, AD 14.label: Inca Period/Late Horizon
Inca Period/Late Horizon (Tucumán, AD 14.prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1530] Inca Period/Late Horizon. Period definition from Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis — Páez María Cecilia, 2014-05-14.

The Inca state absorbed the valleys and puna of the far south, tying them to Cusco through roads, tambos and administrative centres and reorganising labour for farming and mining. Imperial pottery styles and architecture appear at local sites, mixed with long-established regional traditions. The arrangement lasted barely two generations before Spanish expeditions arrived from Peru and Chile.
Inca Period/Late Horizon (Tucumán, AD 14.source: Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis

Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430).label: Período Tardío
Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430).prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430] Período Tardío. Period definition from Desafiando esencialismos. Las vasijas globulares negro sobre rojo del Valle de Tafí (Tucumán, Argentina) — Páez María Cecilia, 2023-02-10.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.
Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430).source: Desafiando esencialismos. Las vasijas globulares negro sobre rojo del Valle de Tafí (Tucumán, Argentina)

Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1430–AD 1530).label: Período Inca
Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1430–AD 1530).prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 1430–AD 1530] Período Inca. Period definition from Desafiando esencialismos. Las vasijas globulares negro sobre rojo del Valle de Tafí (Tucumán, Argentina) — Páez María Cecilia, 2023-02-10.

Cuzco's armies incorporated the Northwest into Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, roughly a lifetime before the Spanish arrived. Roads, tambos, storage complexes and administrative centres were built, local lords were co-opted, and mitmaqkuna colonists were moved in to work fields and mines. Cuzco-style polychrome pottery and bronze appear in local villages, and mountain summits were turned into shrines.
Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1430–AD 1530).source: Desafiando esencialismos. Las vasijas globulares negro sobre rojo del Valle de Tafí (Tucumán, Argentina)

Tafí Culture (Tucumán, 359 BC–AD 800).prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 359 BC–AD 800] Tafí Culture. Period definition from Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina — Sampietro Vattuone María Marta, 2009.

The first settled farming villages of the highland valleys of northwest Argentina, whose people grew maize and herded llamas around clusters of circular stone-walled house compounds. They are best known for carved stone menhirs, some over two metres tall, set up in ceremonial spaces and marked with stylised human and feline faces. Their terraces and field walls laid the groundwork for the later, larger societies of the region.
Tafí Culture (Tucumán, 359 BC–AD 800).source: Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina

Santa María Culture (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD.label: Santa María Culture
Santa María Culture (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD.prose:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1400] Santa María Culture. Period definition from Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina — Sampietro Vattuone María Marta, 2009.

A society of the Calchaquí valleys of northwest Argentina, known above all for its large painted funerary urns, which held the remains of infants and are decorated with staring faces, toads, snakes and rheas. Its people lived in dense stone-built towns, many perched on defensible hilltops behind walls, farming maize on terraces and herding llamas. The fortified settlements point to endemic warfare; the Inca absorbed the region in the fifteenth century, and its descendants fought the Spanish for over a hundred years.
Santa María Culture (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD.source: Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina
