Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín (Catam.prose: [Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 950–AD 1000] Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.
Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín (Catam.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

Fase XII o Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 1300–.label: Fase XII o Guanchín
Fase XII o Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 1300–.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1300–AD 1480] Fase XII o Guanchín. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

The late pre-Inca centuries in the Abaucán valley, when farming communities lived in dispersed stone-walled settlements, irrigated the desert bottomlands and buried their dead with painted vessels. It was a time of local chiefdoms without any overarching state, the world the Inca armies would encounter when they pushed south into the Argentine Northwest.
Fase XII o Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 1300–.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

Fase XIII o Guatungasta (Catamarca, AD 1.label: Fase XIII o Guatungasta
Fase XIII o Guatungasta (Catamarca, AD 1.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1535] Fase XIII o Guatungasta. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

Incorporation into the Inca empire brought the valley roads, way-stations and a new administrative overlay on communities that had been independent. Imperial pottery styles and reorganised labour appear alongside older local traditions, marking the far southern edge of Tawantinsuyu.
Fase XIII o Guatungasta (Catamarca, AD 1.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

Fase XIV o Tinogasta (Catamarca, AD 1535.label: Fase XIV o Tinogasta
Fase XIV o Tinogasta (Catamarca, AD 1535.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1535–AD 1630] Fase XIV o Tinogasta. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

Spanish expeditions crossing from Chile and Peru broke the Inca order and imposed encomiendas, mission priests and tribute on the valley's inhabitants. Indigenous households kept making their own pottery while European animals, metal and disease reshaped everyday life.
Fase XIV o Tinogasta (Catamarca, AD 1535.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD.node: Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD 1630–AD 1637)
Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD.label: Fase XV o Cerro Encantado
Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1630–AD 1637] Fase XV o Cerro Encantado. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

A few violent years coinciding with the great indigenous uprising that swept the Calchaquí and neighbouring valleys, when communities abandoned lowland sites for defensible heights and Spanish control briefly collapsed. The revolt was crushed and its leaders executed, and the region never regained that measure of independence.
Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

Fase XVI o Abaucán (Catamarca, AD 1637–A.label: Fase XVI o Abaucán
Fase XVI o Abaucán (Catamarca, AD 1637–A.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1637–AD 1690] Fase XVI o Abaucán. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

The decades after the failed rebellion, when surviving communities were resettled, put to work under encomenderos and steadily absorbed into colonial parish and estate life. Indigenous ceramic traditions thinned out and the distinctive archaeological record of the valley effectively comes to an end.
Fase XVI o Abaucán (Catamarca, AD 1637–A.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.node: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1200–AD 1400)
Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío
Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1400] Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío. Period definition from Colores y surcos: Una propuesta metodológica para el análisis de las representaciones plásticas de la región de Fiambalá (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina) — Mara Basile, 2011.

A time of assertive local polities between the collapse of the Aguada horizon and Inca conquest, each valley producing its own recognisable pottery and settlement pattern. People concentrated in fortified villages overlooking terraced land, and craft production in ceramics and bronze intensified. The archaeology suggests competition over land and water in an increasingly crowded landscape.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.source: Colores y surcos: Una propuesta metodológica para el análisis de las representaciones plásticas de la región de Fiambalá (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina)

Período Formativo (Catamarca, 1999 BC–AD.label: Período Formativo
Período Formativo (Catamarca, 1999 BC–AD.prose:
[Valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina, 1999 BC–AD 200] Período Formativo. Period definition from Continuidad y ruptura en procesos de diferenciación social en comunidades aldeanas del valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina (s. IV-X dC) — Laguens Andrés Gustavo, 2006-12.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.
Período Formativo (Catamarca, 1999 BC–AD.source: Continuidad y ruptura en procesos de diferenciación social en comunidades aldeanas del valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina (s. IV-X dC)

Período de Integración Regional (Catamar.label: Período de Integración Regional
Período de Integración Regional (Catamar.prose:
[Valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 300–AD 1000] Período de Integración Regional. Period definition from Continuidad y ruptura en procesos de diferenciación social en comunidades aldeanas del valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina (s. IV-X dC) — Laguens Andrés Gustavo, 2006-12.

Farming villages across the western valleys grew denser and more organised, tied together by shared styles of decorated pottery, textiles and cast bronze. This is the horizon of the Aguada tradition, whose black incised vessels carry stylised feline and warrior imagery that suggests shamanic ritual and an emerging elite. Metallurgy, llama herding and irrigation agriculture all became firmly established, setting the economic base for the later chiefdoms of the region.
Período de Integración Regional (Catamar.source: Continuidad y ruptura en procesos de diferenciación social en comunidades aldeanas del valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina (s. IV-X dC)

Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 500–AD 1000.label: Período Medio
Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 500–AD 1000.prose:
[Valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 500–AD 1000] Período Medio. Period definition from Metalurgia prehispánica en el sitio La Rinconada (dpto. Ambato, Catamarca) - Argentina — Gordillo Inés, 2007.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.
Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 500–AD 1000.source: Metalurgia prehispánica en el sitio La Rinconada (dpto. Ambato, Catamarca) - Argentina

Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional.node: Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional (Catamarca, AD 700–AD 1100)
Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional.label: Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional
Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional.prose:
[Valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 700–AD 1100] Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional. Period definition from Prácticas mortuorias entre las poblaciones Aguada del valle de Ambato (Catamarca, Argentina) — Gordillo Inés, 2009.

Named for the way distant valley communities came to share one visual language – the feline and shaman imagery of the Aguada style – on pottery, bronze and rock walls. Farming villages grew, irrigation and llama herding expanded, and metalworkers produced fine cast plaques and axes. The unity dissolved towards the end of the period, giving way to more localised, competitive societies.
Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional.source: Prácticas mortuorias entre las poblaciones Aguada del valle de Ambato (Catamarca, Argentina)

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.

Known for dark, polished pottery and bronze plaques covered in feline and jaguar-man imagery, this was the great artistic tradition of northwest Argentina. Its craftsmen mastered metallurgy, its iconography suggests shamanic ritual and human sacrifice, and its motifs echo those of Tiwanaku far to the north, hinting at long-distance religious connections across the Andes.

Farming villages took hold in the valleys and piedmont of northwestern Argentina, with maize, beans and squash cultivated alongside herds of llamas. People built permanent stone and adobe houses, made pottery and ground-stone tools, and buried their dead beneath house floors and in stone cists. Exchange along the mountain corridors moved obsidian, shell and snuff-taking equipment over long distances, laying the base for the later fortified towns of the region.

Settled valley communities in the Argentine northwest coalesced into larger, more organised societies, best known through the Aguada tradition. Metalworkers produced cast bronze plaques and axes, and potters covered black burnished vessels with jaguar-headed figures and sacrificing warriors – imagery that hints at shared ritual beliefs across a wide region. Irrigated fields and llama herding supported growing populations that later fragmented into the fortified settlements of the following era.

This is the era of Aguada art, with its jaguar-men, sacrificers and severed heads incised on black polished pottery and cast in bronze plaques – imagery suggesting warfare, hallucinogen use and a shared religious world stretching across the Andean foothills.

Catamarca's valleys were the heartland of Aguada, whose distinctive engraved and painted ceramics and jaguar iconography spread across the Northwest. Villages of agriculturalists and llama herders grew, metalworkers produced elaborate bronze objects, and ritual paraphernalia points to a shared belief system uniting scattered communities. Its breakdown gave way to the more fragmented, fortified societies of later centuries.

Farming villages in the valleys of the Argentine northwest grew denser, with irrigated fields, llama herding, and stone-walled compounds. This is the era of Ciénaga and then Aguada, whose potters and metalworkers produced dark engraved vessels and cast bronze plaques covered in feline and sacrificer imagery, evidence of a shared religious world and of emerging social ranking. Long-distance exchange carried goods across the Andes and down to the lowlands.

The dominant culture of northwest Argentina's valleys during the Middle Period, unified less by political control than by a shared and unmistakable art style. Its black incised pottery, carved stone and cast bronze plaques are covered with feline and jaguar-man imagery, warriors and trophy heads, hinting at ritual specialists and hallucinogen use. Irrigated fields, llama caravans and metalworking supported dense settlement before the style dissolved around AD 1000.

[Valle del Bolsón, Catamarca, Argentina, 550 BC–AD 850] Formativo a nivel regional. Period definition from Arte Rupestre en El Bolsón—Las Cuevas (Catamarca, Argentina): Formulando hipótesis de cambio y conflicto. — Korstanje María Alejandra, 1996.

Village farming and herding communities across the valleys of Catamarca, living in round stone-walled houses with adjoining fields and corrals. This is the era of the Condorhuasi, Ciénaga and Alamito traditions, known for modelled and polychrome pottery, carved stone bowls, early copper metallurgy and elaborate equipment for taking hallucinogenic snuff. Long-distance llama caravans tied the valleys to the puna and the eastern lowlands.

[Valle del Bolsón, Catamarca, Argentina, 899 BC–AD 900] Formativo larga duración. Period definition from Procesos sociales prehispánicos en el sur andino: La vivienda, la comunidad y el territorio. — Korstanje María Alejandra, 2007.

A long era of continuity in the valleys of Catamarca, when dispersed farming and herding hamlets, stone-walled fields and household craft production persisted with only gradual change. Ceramic styles shifted through the Condorhuasi, Ciénaga and Aguada traditions, copper and bronze working developed, and ritual objects such as carved stone bowls and snuff tablets circulated widely. Treating it as one long span emphasises how slowly, rather than how dramatically, these societies were transformed.

Dense agricultural settlements of stacked stone rooms, terraces and canals filled the valleys, associated with the Belén and Santa María pottery traditions and their tall painted funerary urns. Metalworking in bronze reached its height, producing axes, discs and plaques. Rising population and visible fortification suggest competition between valley polities, a landscape the Inca would later reorganise rather than replace.

The centuries of the Santa María and Belén traditions, when the valleys of Catamarca filled with large agglomerated settlements of stone-walled houses, extensive terraced fields and hilltop pukaras. Painted funerary urns, bronze working and evidence of raiding mark a crowded, competitive landscape that was eventually taken over by the Inca and then dismantled by the Spanish.

After the long era of village farming, populations in the valleys and puna of northwest Argentina gathered into larger, often defended settlements with dense stone architecture and terraced fields. Distinctive painted urns and black-on-red wares mark regional polities that were later absorbed into the Inca empire, which built roads, waystations and high-altitude shrines here. Spanish conquest and the long indigenous resistance close the sequence.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.

Local chiefdoms in the valleys built dense villages, extensive field systems and hilltop refuges, each with recognisable pottery and burial customs. Long-distance caravan traffic kept them supplied with obsidian, metals and altiplano goods, while competition over land and water drove fortification. Their leaders were the intermediaries through whom the Inca later governed.

recent Colonial period (Catamarca, AD 16.prose:
[Valle del Bolsón, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1800] recent Colonial period. Period definition from An Early Hispanic-Indigenous Contact Event at the Los Viscos Archaeological Site in the South-Central Andes: A Zooarchaeological Perspective — Árias María Florencia, 2021-10-16.

Following the long Calchaquí Wars and the forced deportation of surviving indigenous communities, the valleys of northwestern Argentina were reorganised around Spanish towns, encomiendas and haciendas. Estates raised cattle and mules for the mining economy of Upper Peru, adobe chapels and rural churches spread, and indigenous, Spanish and mestizo populations merged into a new rural society. Excavated sites of the era show European ceramics and metal goods used alongside persisting local pottery traditions.

[Campo del Pucará, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 240–AD 360] Fase I de Alamito. Period definition from  Aproximación a la funcionalidad de un determinado tipo de recintos presentes en campo del Pucará (Depto Andalgalá, Catamarca), desde una perspectiva geoarqueológica.  — Gianfrancisco María Soledad, 2005.

The earliest layer of the distinctive Alamito settlements on the Campo del Pucará, where houses were arranged as a ring of low mounds around an open plaza with paired ceremonial mounds and a sunken patio. The plan is one of the most formalised village layouts in the pre-Hispanic Argentine northwest, and the workshops found in it show craftspeople working stone and copper for exchange with neighbouring valleys.

Fase II de Alamito (Catamarca, AD 360–AD.label: Fase II de Alamito
Fase II de Alamito (Catamarca, AD 360–AD.prose:
[Campo del Pucará, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 360–AD 480] Fase II de Alamito. Period definition from  Aproximación a la funcionalidad de un determinado tipo de recintos presentes en campo del Pucará (Depto Andalgalá, Catamarca), desde una perspectiva geoarqueológica.  — Gianfrancisco María Soledad, 2005.

The full flowering of the Alamito settlement pattern, with its ring of dwelling mounds facing a plaza and ceremonial precinct. Stone sculpture, notably the crouching 'suplicante' figures, and intensive craft production in stone and metal belong to this stretch, before the sites were abandoned and the region's population shifted towards the emerging Aguada world.

Fase La Manga (Ciénaga I) (Catamarca, AD.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 200–AD 300] Fase La Manga (Ciénaga I). Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

The opening stage of the Ciénaga tradition in the valleys of Catamarca, when small farming and herding hamlets took shape and potters began producing the incised dark ware with hatched geometric designs that defines the culture. It marks the transition out of the earlier Condorhuasi world and the beginning of a sequence that would culminate in Aguada.

[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 300–AD 450] Fase Guiyischi (Ciénaga II). Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

The later stage of the Ciénaga tradition, when farming hamlets of the Catamarca valleys were well established and their potters were turning out the dark burnished bowls incised with hatched geometric panels and stiff, stylised human and feline figures that make Ciénaga ware instantly recognisable. Copper working, llama herding and maize agriculture all deepen in this stretch, setting the stage for the more hierarchical Aguada society that followed.

Cultura de la Aguada (Catamarca, AD 600–.label: Cultura de la Aguada
Cultura de la Aguada (Catamarca, AD 600–.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 600–AD 800] Cultura de la Aguada. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

Known for dark, polished pottery and bronze plaques covered in feline and jaguar-man imagery, this was the great artistic tradition of northwest Argentina. Its craftsmen mastered metallurgy, its iconography suggests shamanic ritual and human sacrifice, and its motifs echo those of Tiwanaku far to the north, hinting at long-distance religious connections across the Andes.
Cultura de la Aguada (Catamarca, AD 600–.source: Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.

Cultura Hualfín (Catamarca, AD 800–AD 11.prose: [Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 800–AD 1100] Cultura Hualfín. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

Belén I (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1300).label: Belén I
Belén I (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1300).prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1300] Belén I. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

Farming and herding communities of the Catamarca valleys developed the bold black-on-red pottery — tall urns with stylised faces and geometric bands — that gives this culture its name. Villages of stone-walled compounds sat near irrigated fields of maize and quinoa, with llama caravans linking the valleys to the puna and beyond.
Belén I (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1300).source: Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.

Belén II (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480).label: Belén II
Belén II (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480).prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1300–AD 1480] Belén II. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

A time of growing conflict and concentration, when communities moved onto defensible hilltops and built walled settlements overlooking their fields. Belén urns and metalwork circulated widely across northwestern Argentina, and local chiefly leaders emerged in the valleys of Hualfín and Abaucán.
Belén II (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480).source: Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.

Belén III (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1535).label: Belén III
Belén III (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1535).prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1535] Belén III. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

The Inca empire absorbed the Catamarca valleys, imposing roads, storehouses and administrative centres and resettling labour for state mines and fields. Local Belén pottery continued but now alongside imperial Cuzco-style vessels. Spanish invaders arrived within a generation, touching off the long Calchaquí wars that ended with the forced removal of the valley populations.
Belén III (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1535).source: Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.

The mature phase of Ciénaga village life in the Hualfín and neighbouring valleys, marked by incised grey-black pottery covered in fine hatched geometry and schematic human and animal figures. Its farming, herding and copper metallurgy formed the base on which the later Aguada culture, with its jaguar imagery and sharper social divisions, was built.

Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 14.label: Período Tardío
Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 14.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1480] Período Tardío. Period definition from La cultura de La Ciénaga y el período temprano. — Sempé María Carlota, 2005.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.
Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 14.source: La cultura de La Ciénaga y el período temprano.

Período Formativo (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD.label: Período Formativo
Período Formativo (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, 199 BC–AD 650] Período Formativo. Period definition from Contextos temáticos y ordenamientos funerarios en el cementerio Aguada orilla norte. — Sempé María Carlota, 2002.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.
Período Formativo (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD.source: Contextos temáticos y ordenamientos funerarios en el cementerio Aguada orilla norte.

Período de Integración (Catamarca, AD 65.label: Período de Integración
Período de Integración (Catamarca, AD 65.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 650–AD 950] Período de Integración. Period definition from Contextos temáticos y ordenamientos funerarios en el cementerio Aguada orilla norte. — Sempé María Carlota, 2002.

The Aguada tradition spread a shared visual language across the valleys - felines, sacrificers and geometric designs incised on fine black pottery and cast in bronze. Ceremonial spaces, elaborate burials and the circulation of prestige goods point to emerging ranked societies and shared ritual practice over a wide area. Its breakdown gave way to the fragmented regional polities of later centuries.
Período de Integración (Catamarca, AD 65.source: Contextos temáticos y ordenamientos funerarios en el cementerio Aguada orilla norte.

Período de Desarrollos Regionales del No.node: Período de Desarrollos Regionales del Noroeste argentino (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1480)
Período de Desarrollos Regionales del No.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales del Noroeste argentino
Período de Desarrollos Regionales del No.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período de Desarrollos Regionales del Noroeste argentino. Period definition from La Loma de Ichanga: Visibilidad, defensibilidad y abandono en el valle de Hualfín (Depto. De Belén, Prov. De Catamarca, Argentina). — Balesta Bárbara, 2010.

Valley communities developed strongly local identities visible in ceramics, burial practice and architecture, building agglutinated stone villages and extensive terrace systems. Painted urns holding infant burials, worked bronze and defensive site placement are the period's signature finds. These regional polities were the political units the Inca later incorporated as provinces.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales del No.source: La Loma de Ichanga: Visibilidad, defensibilidad y abandono en el valle de Hualfín (Depto. De Belén, Prov. De Catamarca, Argentina).

Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka (.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1536] Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka. Period definition from La configuración del paisaje Belén (valle de Hualfín, Catamarca). — Balesta Bárbara, 2011.

Spans the era of independent valley chiefdoms and their incorporation into Tawantinsuyu. Local Belén and Santa María communities continued to make their own pottery and bury children in urns while working within Inca demands for labour, metal and maize. Imperial roads and installations laid over older villages make the two phases hard to separate in the ground.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka (.source: La configuración del paisaje Belén (valle de Hualfín, Catamarca).

Temprano Inicial (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD 2.label: Temprano Inicial
Temprano Inicial (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD 2.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, 199 BC–AD 200] Temprano Inicial. Period definition from Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín. — Salceda Susana, 2005.

The beginnings of settled village life in the valleys of Catamarca, when small farming hamlets with stone-walled houses and fields replaced more mobile ways of living. Pottery, llama herding and the cultivation of maize and quinoa take hold, laying the base for everything that follows in the northwest Argentine sequence.
Temprano Inicial (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD 2.source: Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín.

Temprano Propiamente Dicho (Catamarca, A.label: Temprano Propiamente Dicho
Temprano Propiamente Dicho (Catamarca, A.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 200–AD 600] Temprano Propiamente Dicho. Period definition from Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín. — Salceda Susana, 2005.

The mature Early Period, when villages grew, funerary traditions became elaborate and workshops turned out the modelled Condorhuasi figures, Cienaga incised wares and the first copper and bronze ornaments of the region. Exchange linked these valleys to the puna and the Pacific slopes, moving obsidian, shell and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia over long distances.
Temprano Propiamente Dicho (Catamarca, A.source: Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín.

Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 600–AD 1000.label: Período Medio
Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 600–AD 1000.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 600–AD 1000] Período Medio. Period definition from Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín. — Salceda Susana, 2005.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.
Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 600–AD 1000.source: Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín.

Período Tardío-Incaico (Catamarca, AD 10.label: Período Tardío-Incaico
Período Tardío-Incaico (Catamarca, AD 10.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1500] Período Tardío-Incaico. Period definition from Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín. — Salceda Susana, 2005.

Covers the flourishing of local valley polities and their absorption into Tawantinsuyu. Painted funerary urns, terraced hillsides and tightly packed stone villages mark the earlier centuries; imperial roads, waystations and mining installations mark the last decades. Objects from the transition often blend Andean imperial motifs with stubbornly local styles.
Período Tardío-Incaico (Catamarca, AD 10.source: Cronología y paleodemografía en el Valle del Hualfín.

Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NO.node: Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NOA (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1480)
Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NO.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NOA
Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NO.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1480] Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NOA. Period definition from Tendencias morfométricas y caracterización composicional de la cerámica Belén en el valle de Hualfín (Belén, Catamarca). — Wynveldt Federico, 2007.

Across northwest Argentina, regional pottery styles - Belén, Santa María, Sanagasta - replaced the earlier shared iconography, marking a landscape of independent valley societies. Populations concentrated in walled hilltop settlements above terraced fields, and bronze axes and plaques circulated as markers of status. The period ends with Inca conquest, which found these communities already politically organised and agriculturally productive.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales del NO.source: Tendencias morfométricas y caracterización composicional de la cerámica Belén en el valle de Hualfín (Belén, Catamarca).

Late and Inka times (Catamarca, AD 1400–.label: Late and Inka times
Late and Inka times (Catamarca, AD 1400–.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1400–AD 1500] Late and Inka times. Period definition from Palo Blanco: a village in Late and Inka landscapes in Hualfín Valley (Catamarca, Argentina) — Wynveldt Federico, 2016-05-26.

Densely settled valley communities in the Argentine Northwest, farming with terraces and irrigation and making the bold black-on-red urns of the Belén and Santa María traditions. Cuzco's armies then absorbed the region into the empire's southern province, building the road system and an administrative centre at El Shincal with plazas, storehouses and a ceremonial hill. Inka rule reorganised labour, mining and settlement here for only a few decades before Spanish arrival.
Late and Inka times (Catamarca, AD 1400–.source: Palo Blanco: a village in Late and Inka landscapes in Hualfín Valley (Catamarca, Argentina)

Tiempos Formativos Inferiores o Período.node: Tiempos Formativos Inferiores o Período Temprano (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD 500)
Tiempos Formativos Inferiores o Período.label: Tiempos Formativos Inferiores o Período Temprano
Tiempos Formativos Inferiores o Período.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, 499 BC–AD 500] Tiempos Formativos Inferiores o Período Temprano. Period definition from Réquiem por Watungasta. — Raffino Rodolfo, 1996.

Villages of circular houses and terraced fields spread through the valleys and puna, supported by maize, quinoa and llama herding. Potters made the modelled and painted wares of the Condorhuasi, Ciénaga and Tafí traditions, stone carvers raised menhirs, and the first copper and bronze metallurgy in the region appeared. Long-distance caravan routes already linked these communities to the Pacific coast and the eastern lowlands, moving obsidian, shell and hallucinogenic snuffs.

Tiempos Formativos Superiores o Período.node: Tiempos Formativos Superiores o Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 500–AD 900)
Tiempos Formativos Superiores o Período.label: Tiempos Formativos Superiores o Período Medio
Tiempos Formativos Superiores o Período.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 500–AD 900] Tiempos Formativos Superiores o Período Medio. Period definition from Réquiem por Watungasta. — Raffino Rodolfo, 1996.

The Aguada tradition drew the valleys into a shared religious style dominated by the feline: snarling jaguar-men engraved on black burnished pottery, bronze plaques and axes, and carved stone. Metalworking became genuinely skilled, and craft and ritual specialists emerged in denser, more hierarchical settlements. The imagery connects the region to Tiwanaku and the wider Andean world, and its collapse opened the way to the fortified valley chiefdoms of later centuries.

Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.node: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1470)
Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Tardío
Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Perí.prose:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1470] Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Tardío. Period definition from Réquiem por Watungasta. — Raffino Rodolfo, 1996.

Regional traditions such as Belén and Santa María replaced earlier shared styles, and settlement shifted towards large, tightly built stone villages and defensible heights. Terraces, canals and storage structures show intensified farming; painted urns and bronze objects fill the graves. These were the societies whose leaders negotiated with, or resisted, Inca expansion.

Período Hispano-Indígena (Catamarca, AD.label: Período  Hispano-Indígena
Período Hispano-Indígena (Catamarca, AD.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1536–AD 1660] Período  Hispano-Indígena. Period definition from El Sinchihuasi de El Shincal de Quimivíl. — Raffino Rodolfo, 2001.

Spanish expeditions from Chile and Peru founded and repeatedly lost towns in the valleys of northwest Argentina, imposing encomienda labour on Diaguita and Calchaquí communities. Indigenous resistance was fierce and prolonged: the great Calchaquí uprisings culminated in campaigns that ended only with the forced removal of whole populations, the Quilmes among them, to the outskirts of Buenos Aires. Sites from these years mix native pottery with European glass, iron and glazed wares, and show villages relocating to defensible ground.
Período Hispano-Indígena (Catamarca, AD.source: El Sinchihuasi de El Shincal de Quimivíl.

Período Formativo Inferior (Catamarca, 4.label: Período Formativo Inferior
Período Formativo Inferior (Catamarca, 4.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, 499 BC–AD 400] Período Formativo Inferior. Period definition from El Shincal de Quimivil. — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 2004.

The earliest settled farming communities of the Catamarca valleys, living in small dispersed houses among fields and camelid pens. Their modelled and painted ceramics, early copper and gold work and long-distance exchange in obsidian and shell mark the beginning of the region's distinctive craft traditions.

Horizonte Inka (Catamarca, AD 1471–AD 15.label: Horizonte Inka
Horizonte Inka (Catamarca, AD 1471–AD 15.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1471–AD 1536] Horizonte Inka. Period definition from El Shincal de Quimivil. — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 2004.

The decades when the Inca state absorbed the valleys of northwest Argentina, its southernmost frontier. Roads, waystations and administrative centres such as El Shincal were built, local lords were co-opted, whole communities were resettled as mitmaqkuna, and mountain summits became sites of high-altitude sacrifice. Spanish entradas ended Inca authority here, but the labour-tribute system the Inca imposed shaped how the colonists organised the region.

Formativo Superior (Catamarca, AD 400–AD.label: Formativo Superior
Formativo Superior (Catamarca, AD 400–AD.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 400–AD 800] Formativo Superior. Period definition from El Shincal de Quimivil. — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 2004.

The later stage of village farming society in the Argentine Northwest, when settlements grew larger and more clustered, agricultural terraces and irrigation spread, and craft production in ceramics and metal became more specialised. Distinct regional pottery styles emerged, and differences in burial goods hint at growing inequality. These communities are the direct ancestors of the fortified towns and chiefdoms of the following Regional Development period.

La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regio.node: La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regional (Catamarca, AD 500–AD 1000)
La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regio.label: La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regional
La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regio.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 500–AD 1000] La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regional. Period definition from Las representaciones de la muerte en el Shincal y la Aguada. — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 2008.

A distinctive art style spread across the valleys of northwest Argentina, its polished black pottery and cast bronze plaques covered with feline-human figures, sacrificers and trophy heads. Settlements in the Ambato valley combined farming terraces with ceremonial architecture, and metalworkers produced some of the finest bronze casting in the southern Andes. The imagery suggests ritual specialists, hallucinogenic snuff use and violence bound up in the same ceremonies.
La Aguada del Perío­do Floreciente Regio.source: Las representaciones de la muerte en el Shincal y la Aguada.

Período de ocupación Inka (Catamarca, AD.label: Período de ocupación Inka
Período de ocupación Inka (Catamarca, AD.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1471–AD 1536] Período de ocupación Inka. Period definition from La etnobotánica de «El Shincal» (Catamarca) y su importancia para la arqueología 1: Recursos combustibles y madereros. — Capparelli Aylén, 1997.

Imperial administration arrived in the form of planned centres like El Shincal de Quimivil, with plazas, ushnu platforms, storehouses and stretches of the Qhapaq Ñan road. Local lords were co-opted, workers drafted for state farms and mines, and populations sometimes transplanted far from home. Cuzco polychrome pottery, aríbalos and imperial masonry mark the sites, but the whole episode lasted only about sixty years before Spanish conquest.
Período de ocupación Inka (Catamarca, AD.source: La etnobotánica de «El Shincal» (Catamarca) y su importancia para la arqueología 1: Recursos combustibles y madereros.

Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 147.label: Período Tardío
Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 147.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1470] Período Tardío. Period definition from Características de la relación local-estatal en Hualfín Inca (depto Belén, prov. De Catamarca, Argentina). Inferencias a partir del análisis cerámico.  — Lynch Julieta, 2011.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.
Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 147.source: Características de la relación local-estatal en Hualfín Inca (depto Belén, prov. De Catamarca, Argentina). Inferencias a partir del análisis cerámico.

Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regional.node: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1480)
Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regional.label: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales
Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regional.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1480] Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Una aproximación cronológica al centro administrativo Hualfín Inka, Catamarca, Argentina — Lynch Julieta , 2012-12-10.

Local chiefdoms in the valleys built dense villages, extensive field systems and hilltop refuges, each with recognisable pottery and burial customs. Long-distance caravan traffic kept them supplied with obsidian, metals and altiplano goods, while competition over land and water drove fortification. Their leaders were the intermediaries through whom the Inca later governed.
Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regional.source: Una aproximación cronológica al centro administrativo Hualfín Inka, Catamarca, Argentina

Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regio.node: Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1470)
Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regio.label: Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales
Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regio.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1470] Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from La vida en el valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, antes de la llegada española. — Lynch Julieta, 2015.

After the collapse of the Aguada horizon, the valleys of northwest Argentina fragmented into competing local polities that built defensive hilltop settlements and dense agglomerated villages with terraced fields. This is the era of Belén and Santa María pottery, of children buried in painted urns, and of chronic conflict visible in fortified pukaras. It ended when Inca armies absorbed the region into Collasuyu.
Intermedio Tardío o de Desarrollos Regio.source: La vida en el valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, antes de la llegada española.

Época Tardía (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1430.label: Época Tardía
Época Tardía (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1430.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1430] Época Tardía. Period definition from El Inca antes de la llegada española en el valle de Hualfín, Catamarca. — Lynch Julieta, 2015.

After the collapse of the earlier regional polities, populations concentrated in large agricultural settlements and fortified hilltop pukarás overlooking terraced valleys. Santa María and Belén pottery, including the tall painted funerary urns used to bury infants beneath house floors, is the signature of the period, along with metalwork in bronze and evidence of recurrent conflict. These chiefdoms were the societies the Inca encountered and subdued.
Época Tardía (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1430.source: El Inca antes de la llegada española en el valle de Hualfín, Catamarca.

Época Incaica (Catamarca, AD 1430–AD 153.label: Época Incaica
Época Incaica (Catamarca, AD 1430–AD 153.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1430–AD 1532] Época Incaica. Period definition from El Inca antes de la llegada española en el valle de Hualfín, Catamarca. — Lynch Julieta, 2015.

Inca armies absorbed the valleys of the southern Andes into the empire's Collasuyu province, linking them by the Qhapaq Ñan road with waystations, storehouses and administrative centres. Local populations were resettled as mitmaqkuna, set to work in mines and on state fields, and Inca ceramic and architectural styles appear alongside older regional traditions. High mountain summits were converted into sanctuaries, some holding capacocha sacrifices, until Spanish arrival dismantled the system.
Época Incaica (Catamarca, AD 1430–AD 153.source: El Inca antes de la llegada española en el valle de Hualfín, Catamarca.

Período Formativo (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD.label: Período Formativo
Período Formativo (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, 499 BC–AD 900] Período Formativo. Period definition from Estudio tecno-morfológico de palas y/o azadas líticas del sector norte del valle de Hualfín (Catamarca, Argentina) — Bentivenga Emiliano, 2021-07-02.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.
Período Formativo (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD.source: Estudio tecno-morfológico de palas y/o azadas líticas del sector norte del valle de Hualfín (Catamarca, Argentina)

Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Catam.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales
Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Catam.prose:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1430] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Estudio tecno-morfológico de palas y/o azadas líticas del sector norte del valle de Hualfín (Catamarca, Argentina) — Bentivenga Emiliano, 2021-07-02.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Catam.source: Estudio tecno-morfológico de palas y/o azadas líticas del sector norte del valle de Hualfín (Catamarca, Argentina)

Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino (.node: Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino (Catamarca, AD 1471–AD 1536)
Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino (.label: Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino
Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino (.prose:
[Sierra de Zapata, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1471–AD 1536] Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino. Period definition from El “Tambillo Nuevo” de la Sierra de Zapata (Provincia de Catamarca). — Moralejo Reinaldo Andrés, 2009.

Inca administration reached the Catamarca valleys with installations such as roads, tambos and mining and metallurgical centres exploiting local copper and gold. Existing Belén and Santa María communities were reorganised around imperial demands for labour and tribute, and imperial ceramic shapes and designs blended with local traditions. Imperial control lasted only a few generations before Spanish invasion.
Período Incaico del Noroeste Argentino (.source: El “Tambillo Nuevo” de la Sierra de Zapata (Provincia de Catamarca).

Período Temprano (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD 4.label: Período Temprano
Período Temprano (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD 4.prose:
[Sierra de Zapata, Catamarca, Argentina, 499 BC–AD 400] Período Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología y paisaje en el interfluvio de Zapata, Catamarca, Noroeste Argentino — Moralejo Reinaldo, 2017.

Farming villages became the normal way of life: people settled in one place, grew maize, beans and squash, herded llamas, made pottery and began working copper and gold. Small clusters of round or rectangular houses spread through the valleys, with grinding stones, carved stone menhirs and the first metal ornaments. The social groundwork for the later valley chiefdoms was laid here.
Período Temprano (Catamarca, 499 BC–AD 4.source: Arqueología y paisaje en el interfluvio de Zapata, Catamarca, Noroeste Argentino

Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales.node: Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1470)
Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales.label: Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales
Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales.prose:
[Sierra de Zapata, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1470] Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Arqueología y paisaje en el interfluvio de Zapata, Catamarca, Noroeste Argentino — Moralejo Reinaldo, 2017.

Independent valley polities, identified archaeologically by ceramic styles such as Belén and Santa María, dominated the region. They farmed terraced hillsides, herded llamas, buried infants in painted urns and built or occupied fortified pukaras overlooking their fields. Their political fragmentation ended when the Inca imposed imperial rule.
Período Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales.source: Arqueología y paisaje en el interfluvio de Zapata, Catamarca, Noroeste Argentino

Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 600–AD 900).label: Período Medio
Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 600–AD 900).prose:
[Valle de Catamarca, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 600–AD 900] Período Medio. Period definition from Petrología Cerámica Comparativa del tipo Aguada Portezuelo: Aportes Preliminares para su Estudio en el Valle de Catamarca. — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2005.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.
Período Medio (Catamarca, AD 600–AD 900).source: Petrología Cerámica Comparativa del tipo Aguada Portezuelo: Aportes Preliminares para su Estudio en el Valle de Catamarca.

Settled village life took hold in the valleys of the Argentine Northwest: people built stone-walled houses and terraces, herded llamas, grew maize and made the first pottery of the region, including the modelled and painted wares of Condórhuasi and Ciénaga. Carved stone masks, menhirs and early copper and gold work show growing ritual and craft specialisation, laying the groundwork for the larger societies that followed.

Andean valleys of the northwest were drawn into the Inca empire, with roads, waystations, agricultural terracing and provincial centres imposed on communities that had been organised as independent chiefdoms and fortified villages. Imperial pottery, tunics and metalwork spread among local elites who administered tribute on Cusco's behalf. High-altitude mountaintop shrines, including capacocha burials, belong to this horizon.

Momentos Tardíos (Catamarca, AD 1250–AD.prose:

Dense farming villages of stone-walled compounds and terraced fields spread through the valleys, with fortified hilltop settlements suggesting frequent warfare between neighbouring groups. Painted urns and bowls of the Belén and Santa María styles, along with copper and bronze working, are the hallmark of the period. Inca conquest in the later fifteenth century added roads, storehouses and high-altitude shrines before the Spanish invasion brought the sequence to an end.

Inka Horizon (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1532.prose:
[Valle de Chaschuil, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1532] Inka Horizon. Period definition from Technological characterization of Inka and pre-Inka pottery: A ceramic petrology approach. — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2004.

The Inca state absorbed the valleys of the Argentine northwest into Qollasuyu, the empire's southern quarter, running roads, waystations and high-altitude shrines through the mountains. Local lords were left in place but bound by tribute and labour service, and colonists were resettled to work fields and mines. Inca-style pottery and architecture appear suddenly in local sites, layered directly beneath the arrival of the Spanish.
Inka Horizon (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1532.source: Technological characterization of Inka and pre-Inka pottery: A ceramic petrology approach.

Late Period (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1380).label: Late Period
Late Period (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1380).prose:
[Valle de Chaschuil, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1380] Late Period. Period definition from Technological characterization of Inka and pre-Inka pottery: A ceramic petrology approach. — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2004.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.
Late Period (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1380).source: Technological characterization of Inka and pre-Inka pottery: A ceramic petrology approach.

People built permanent stone and adobe houses, made pottery and ground-stone tools, and buried their dead beneath house floors and in stone cists. Exchange along the mountain corridors moved obsidian, shell and snuff-taking equipment over long distances, laying the base for the later fortified towns of the region.

The span in which farming and pottery-making defined life across much of what is now Argentina, from early village communities through to the Spanish conquest. Maize, beans and squash agriculture, llama caravans, weaving and metalwork underpinned settlements that grew from scattered hamlets into large, defended towns. It ends abruptly with European invasion, which cut short indigenous political development and reorganised the countryside around encomiendas and missions.

Late Intermediate Period (Catamarca, AD.prose:

With no overarching state, communities in the northwestern Andean valleys built dense hilltop settlements and defensive pukaras, a sign of chronic conflict over land and water. Santa María painted urns, irrigated terracing and llama caravan trade tie the valleys into a wide exchange network. Inca armies absorbed the whole region at the close of the period, imposing roads, garrisons and forced resettlement.

Farming villages became the normal way of life: people settled in one place, grew maize, beans and squash, herded llamas, made pottery and began working copper and gold. Small clusters of round or rectangular houses spread through the valleys, with grinding stones, carved stone menhirs and the first metal ornaments. The social groundwork for the later valley chiefdoms was laid here.

Formative Period (Catamarca, 1499 BC–AD.prose:
[Valle del Cajón, Catamarca, Argentina, 1499 BC–AD 600] Formative Period. Period definition from Built landscapes of everyday life: a house in an early agricultural village of north-western Argentina — Scattolin María Cristina , 2009-09.

Farming villages took hold in the valleys and piedmont of northwestern Argentina, with maize, beans and squash cultivated alongside herds of llamas. People built permanent stone and adobe houses, made pottery and ground-stone tools, and buried their dead beneath house floors and in stone cists. Exchange along the mountain corridors moved obsidian, shell and snuff-taking equipment over long distances, laying the base for the later fortified towns of the region.

[Valle del Cajón, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1436] Late Period. Period definition from Built landscapes of everyday life: a house in an early agricultural village of north-western Argentina — Scattolin María Cristina , 2009-09.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.
Late Period (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1436).source: Built landscapes of everyday life: a house in an early agricultural village of north-western Argentina

The transition from mobile hunting and gathering to settled life in the valleys of the Argentine Northwest. People began cultivating maize, beans and quinoa, herding llamas, storing crops in pits and cists, and making the region's first pottery, while continuing to hunt guanaco and vicuña. Small, widely spaced hamlets of round houses replaced the earlier rock-shelter camps.

Bronze casting, llama caravans and long-distance exchange linked these communities across the Andes. The period closes with the arrival of Inca administration, which reworked local labour and land without erasing regional identities.

Local polities in the Calchaquí and neighbouring valleys built agglomerated stone settlements, some heavily fortified, and farmed terraced slopes with irrigation. Each group developed its own ceramic style, and bronze ornaments and weapons became widespread. Population growth and visible defence works point to sustained competition before Inca rule imposed a new order.
Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Tard.source: Bloques y Arte Rupestre en la Quebrada de Miriguaca (Depto. Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina).

[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período Agroalfarero Tardío o Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from La ocupación Inca en la Puna Meridional Argentina: Departamento de Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca.  — Olivera Daniel Enzo, 1991.

With no single dominant tradition, the northwest broke into rival valley polities, each with its own pottery style and territory, most famously the Santa María and Belén groups. People clustered in large stone-built towns and defensible hilltop pukaras above irrigated terraces, buried infants in painted urns, and traded metal, textiles and Andean goods over long distances. Inca conquest in the later fifteenth century brought roads, garrisons and mountaintop shrines.
Período Agroalfarero Tardío o Desarrollo.source: La ocupación Inca en la Puna Meridional Argentina: Departamento de Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca.

Período Inka (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1532.prose:
[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1532] Período Inka. Period definition from La ocupación Inca en la Puna Meridional Argentina: Departamento de Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca.  — Olivera Daniel Enzo, 1991.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.
Período Inka (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1532.source: La ocupación Inca en la Puna Meridional Argentina: Departamento de Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca.

Herding, farming and pottery-making took root in the valleys of Catamarca, and scattered camps gave way to permanent villages with terraced fields and irrigation. Metalworking in copper and bronze, elaborate painted ceramics and carved stone objects show growing craft specialisation and long-distance exchange with the Andean highlands. These communities laid the demographic and technological foundation for the later fortified towns of the region.

The last phase of village farming life before the rise of Aguada, with substantial house compounds, intensive agriculture and camelid herding. Copper and bronze casting, fine polished ceramics and ritual paraphernalia for hallucinogenic snuff indicate specialists at work and social distinctions hardening within these communities.

Formativo (Catamarca, 1050 BC–AD 850).prose: [Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, 1050 BC–AD 850] Formativo. Archaic Times (Catamarca, 8050 BC–1550 B.label: Archaic Times
Archaic Times (Catamarca, 8050 BC–1550 B.prose:
[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, 8050 BC–1550 BC] Archaic Times. Period definition from Obsidian circulation in south-central Andes after ca. 1100 BP: A contribution based on geochemical studies in Argentinean Southern Puna Plateau — Elías Alejandra Mercedes, 2018-10.

Small bands moved through the high puna and valleys of northwest Argentina, hunting guanaco and vicuña with spearthrowers and camping repeatedly in rock shelters. Over time they came to manage and finally domesticate camelids, laying the economic foundation for the later herding and farming villages of the Andes. Their painted and engraved rock art, showing hunts and processions of animals, is among the region's most striking early remains.
Archaic Times (Catamarca, 8050 BC–1550 B.source: Obsidian circulation in south-central Andes after ca. 1100 BP: A contribution based on geochemical studies in Argentinean Southern Puna Plateau

Regional Late Period (Catamarca, AD 950–.label: Regional Late Period
Regional Late Period (Catamarca, AD 950–.prose:
[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 950–AD 1530] Regional Late Period. Period definition from Of Hunting and Herding: Isotopic evidence in wild and domesticated camelids from the Southern Argentine Puna (2120–420 years BP) — Grant Jennifer , 2017-02.

Local groups such as the Belén and Santa María peoples dominated the valleys, each with distinctive painted ceramics and a pattern of large agglutinated villages, hilltop strongholds and terraced fields. Warfare and competition over land shaped settlement, and children were buried in tall decorated urns beneath house floors. The period closes with Inca annexation and then Spanish invasion, which met fierce and prolonged resistance in these valleys.
Regional Late Period (Catamarca, AD 950–.source: Of Hunting and Herding: Isotopic evidence in wild and domesticated camelids from the Southern Argentine Puna (2120–420 years BP)

Período Arcaico (Catamarca, 8050 BC–1050.label: Período Arcaico
Período Arcaico (Catamarca, 8050 BC–1050.prose:
[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, 8050 BC–1050 BC] Período Arcaico. Period definition from Arqueobotánica de Quebrada Seca 3: Recursos vegetales utilizados por cazadores-recolectores durante el período Arcaico en la Puna Meridional Argentina. — Rodríguez María Fernanda, 1998.

Small mobile bands hunted guanaco and deer, gathered algarrobo pods and chañar, and camped in rockshelters and open sites across the ranges and valleys. Over these millennia grinding stones, storage and the first tended plants and camelids appear, marking the slow shift from foraging to food production that made settled village life possible.
Período Arcaico (Catamarca, 8050 BC–1050.source: Arqueobotánica de Quebrada Seca 3: Recursos vegetales utilizados por cazadores-recolectores durante el período Arcaico en la Puna Meridional Argentina.

Formativo (Catamarca, 1050 BC–AD 450).label: Formativo
Formativo (Catamarca, 1050 BC–AD 450).prose: [Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, 1050 BC–AD 450] Formativo. Period definition from Contexto paleoambiental para la ocupación arqueológica en Corral Grande (Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina). — Tchilinguirian Pablo, 2018.
Formativo (Catamarca, 1050 BC–AD 450).source: Contexto paleoambiental para la ocupación arqueológica en Corral Grande (Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina).

Tardío-Inka (Catamarca, AD 850–AD 1500).label: Tardío-Inka
Tardío-Inka (Catamarca, AD 850–AD 1500).prose:
[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 850–AD 1500] Tardío-Inka. Period definition from Contexto paleoambiental para la ocupación arqueológica en Corral Grande (Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina). — Tchilinguirian Pablo, 2018.

Groups together the long florescence of local valley societies in Catamarca — nucleated stone-built settlements, terraced agriculture, distinctive painted urns and metalwork — with their final absorption into the Inca empire. Visitors can see how imperial pottery and architecture appear suddenly on top of centuries-old local traditions.
Tardío-Inka (Catamarca, AD 850–AD 1500).source: Contexto paleoambiental para la ocupación arqueológica en Corral Grande (Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina).

Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcai.node: Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcaicos (Catamarca, 4050 BC–1050 BC)
Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcai.label: Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcaicos
Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcai.prose:
[Puna Meridional, Catamarca, Argentina, 4050 BC–1050 BC] Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcaicos. Period definition from Contexto paleoambiental para la ocupación arqueológica en Corral Grande (Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina). — Tchilinguirian Pablo, 2018.

Small mobile bands used caves and rockshelters in the highlands and valleys, hunting guanaco and vicuña with spearthrowers and gathering algarrobo pods and other wild plants. Their camps preserve grinding stones, basketry, cordage and rock art, and in the driest sites remarkable organic remains. Over these millennia camelids were brought under human control and the first cultivated plants appear, laying the groundwork for later herding and farming villages.
Momentos de cazadores-recolectores arcai.source: Contexto paleoambiental para la ocupación arqueológica en Corral Grande (Antofagasta de la Sierra, Catamarca, Argentina).

Prehispánico Tardío Final (Córdoba, AD 9.label: Prehispánico Tardío Final
Prehispánico Tardío Final (Córdoba, AD 9.prose:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1550] Prehispánico Tardío Final. Period definition from Conflicto y violencia en las Sierras de Córdoba durante el Período Prehispánico: Una discusión basada en información arqueológica y etnohistórica. — Iván Díaz, 2015.

In the Córdoba sierras, small groups combined hunting and gathering of algarrobo pods with maize and bean cultivation, living in semi-subterranean pit dwellings clustered near streams. They made simple pottery, ground food in bedrock mortars, and left painted and engraved images in rockshelters. Spanish colonists encountered their descendants — the peoples recorded as Comechingones and Sanavirones — in the sixteenth century.
Prehispánico Tardío Final (Córdoba, AD 9.source: Conflicto y violencia en las Sierras de Córdoba durante el Período Prehispánico: Una discusión basada en información arqueológica y etnohistórica.

Tardocolonial (Córdoba, AD 1770–AD 1970).label: Tardocolonial
Tardocolonial (Córdoba, AD 1770–AD 1970).prose:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 1770–AD 1970] Tardocolonial. Period definition from Sitios arqueológicos rurales en campos serranos del suroeste de la provincia de Córdoba, Argentina — Flavio Ribero, 2020-08-25.

The late colonial horizon in the Argentine interior, opening in the decades after the Jesuits were expelled from their Córdoba estancias and the Bourbon reforms redrew trade and administration, and running on through independence and the republican era. Material culture from these centuries — imported English ceramics, glass, mass-produced metal goods alongside surviving criollo and indigenous traditions — is what archaeologists use to track the region's shift from colonial outpost to modern provincial society.
Tardocolonial (Córdoba, AD 1770–AD 1970).source: Sitios arqueológicos rurales en campos serranos del suroeste de la provincia de Córdoba, Argentina

Etapa Arcaica (Mendoza, 6050 BC–2050 BC).label: Etapa Arcaica
Etapa Arcaica (Mendoza, 6050 BC–2050 BC).prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 BC] Etapa Arcaica. Periods for the Northern Patagonian Subregion of Mendoza and Neuquén. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Hunter-gatherer bands ranged across the puna, valleys and steppe, hunting guanaco and vicuña, gathering wild plants and camping repeatedly in rock shelters whose walls they sometimes painted. Over these millennia the tools grew more specialised and the first steps were taken towards herding camelids and tending useful plants. These slow shifts are what made the later farming villages possible.
Etapa Arcaica (Mendoza, 6050 BC–2050 BC).source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Periodo Hispano-Criollo (Mendoza, AD 140.label: Periodo Hispano-Criollo
Periodo Hispano-Criollo (Mendoza, AD 140.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1400–AD 1850] Periodo Hispano-Criollo. Periods for the Northern Patagonian Subregion of Mendoza and Neuquén. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Covers the arrival of Spaniards in the Cuyo region and the centuries of colonial and creole settlement that followed, when Huarpe communities were drawn into encomienda labour, irrigation farming and stock-raising around the new town of Mendoza. Archaeologically it shows up as glazed and wheel-thrown pottery, glass, metal and European animal bones mixed with older indigenous material.
Periodo Hispano-Criollo (Mendoza, AD 140.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Contactos Mapuches Tempranos (Mendoza, A.label: Contactos Mapuches Tempranos
Contactos Mapuches Tempranos (Mendoza, A.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1750] Contactos Mapuches Tempranos. Periods for the Northern Patagonian Subregion of Mendoza and Neuquén. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The first sustained movement of Mapuche people and Mapuche influence across the Andes into the eastern piedmont, part of the wider process often called araucanización. Horses, acquired from the Spanish, transformed mobility and warfare, and indigenous groups east of the cordillera absorbed Mapuche language, goods and social ties while colonial towns on the frontier watched uneasily.
Contactos Mapuches Tempranos (Mendoza, A.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

Contactos Mapuches Tardíos (Mendoza, AD.label: Contactos Mapuches Tardíos
Contactos Mapuches Tardíos (Mendoza, AD.prose:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1750–AD 1850] Contactos Mapuches Tardíos. Periods for the Northern Patagonian Subregion of Mendoza and Neuquén. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Mapuche groups from west of the Andes were by now deeply established in the eastern plains and valleys, moving stock, salt, textiles and captives along long-distance routes between Chile and the Buenos Aires frontier. Mounted raiding parties and trading alliances made these networks a real political force that colonial and then Argentine authorities negotiated with rather than controlled, until the military campaigns of the later nineteenth century ended them.
Contactos Mapuches Tardíos (Mendoza, AD.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

okres plemienny (Poland, AD 400–AD 950).label: okres plemienny
okres plemienny (Poland, AD 400–AD 950).prose:
[Central Poland, AD 400–AD 950] okres plemienny. Period definition from Studia i materiały do osadnictwa Wielkopolski wczesnohistorycznej, — W. Hensel, 1950.

Before any Polish state existed, Slavic populations lived in dispersed settlements and small tribal territories, each clustered around timber-and-earth strongholds. Pottery was simple and handmade, cremation was the usual burial rite, and no coins or writing anchor the record. Out of the competition between these tribal units, the Polanie eventually built the polity that became Poland.
okres plemienny (Poland, AD 400–AD 950).source: Studia i materiały do osadnictwa Wielkopolski wczesnohistorycznej,

okres wczesnopaństwowy (Poland, AD 950–A.label: okres wczesnopaństwowy
okres wczesnopaństwowy (Poland, AD 950–A.prose:
[Central Poland, AD 950–AD 1250] okres wczesnopaństwowy. Period definition from Studia i materiały do osadnictwa Wielkopolski wczesnohistorycznej, — W. Hensel, 1950.

The Piast dukes welded tribal territories into a Christian kingdom, ringing the country with earth-and-timber strongholds at Gniezno, Poznań, Kraków and Wrocław. Bishoprics, stone churches, minted coins and the first written chronicles appear; the earlier cremation rite disappears entirely. Fragmentation among the dukes after 1138 gradually undid the unity the period had built.
okres wczesnopaństwowy (Poland, AD 950–A.source: Studia i materiały do osadnictwa Wielkopolski wczesnohistorycznej,

podokres przedpiastowski (Poland, AD 570.label: podokres przedpiastowski
podokres przedpiastowski (Poland, AD 570.prose:
[Poland, AD 570–AD 950] podokres przedpiastowski. Period definition from Pradzieje Polski — J. Kostrzewski, 1965.

Slavic-speaking communities filled the lands between the Oder and the Bug, living in small unfortified villages of sunken-floored huts with plain handmade pottery and little metal. Over these centuries tribal groupings coalesced, the first timber-and-earth strongholds went up, and local chieftains began extracting tribute from surrounding settlements. Out of this patchwork of tribes the Polanie of Greater Poland emerged as the power that would build the Polish state.

podokres wczesnopiastowski (Poland, AD 9.label: podokres wczesnopiastowski
podokres wczesnopiastowski (Poland, AD 9.prose:
[Poland, AD 950–AD 1250] podokres wczesnopiastowski. Period definition from Pradzieje Polski — J. Kostrzewski, 1965.

Mieszko I's baptism in 966 and the coronation of Bolesław the Brave in 1025 turned a tribal confederation into a Christian kingdom with bishoprics, silver coinage and a chain of great strongholds at Gniezno, Poznań and Kraków. Stone churches and palatia appear, long-distance trade in silver and slaves flourishes, and written records begin. The period ends amid the dynastic fragmentation that followed Bolesław Wrymouth's division of the realm.

wędrówka ludów (Poland, AD 400–AD 700).label: wędrówka ludów
wędrówka ludów (Poland, AD 400–AD 700).prose:
[Northern Poland, AD 400–AD 700] wędrówka ludów. Period definition from Kultura Pomorza we wczesnem średniowieczu na podstawie wykopalisk — W. Łęga, 1930.

Old Germanic settlement in the Polish lands dissolved as groups moved towards the collapsing Roman frontier, leaving a landscape that archaeologists find strikingly empty of finds. Into this thinly occupied country came Slavic communities with simple sunken-floored huts and plain hand-made pottery. How complete the break was, and where the newcomers came from, remains one of the most argued questions in Polish archaeology.
wędrówka ludów (Poland, AD 400–AD 700).source: Kultura Pomorza we wczesnem średniowieczu na podstawie wykopalisk

faza F (Poland, AD 700–AD 900).label: faza F
faza F (Poland, AD 700–AD 900).prose:
[Northern Poland, AD 700–AD 900] faza F. Period definition from Kultura Pomorza we wczesnem średniowieczu na podstawie wykopalisk — W. Łęga, 1930.

The tribal centuries of the Polish lands, before any state existed: scattered Slavic communities farming small plots, cremating their dead, and beginning to raise the timber-and-earth ring-forts that would dominate the landscape. Handmade pottery gives way to wheel-finished wares, and Arab silver dirhams start arriving along the Baltic trade routes, evidence of contact with the wider world.
faza F (Poland, AD 700–AD 900).source: Kultura Pomorza we wczesnem średniowieczu na podstawie wykopalisk

faza G (Poland, AD 900–AD 1050).label: faza G
faza G (Poland, AD 900–AD 1050).prose:
[Northern Poland, AD 900–AD 1050] faza G. Period definition from Kultura Pomorza we wczesnem średniowieczu na podstawie wykopalisk — W. Łęga, 1930.

The decisive phase in which the Piast dynasty welded the tribal territories of Greater Poland into a single realm, marked archaeologically by a wave of huge new strongholds at Gniezno, Poznań and Kraków. Mieszko I's baptism in 966 brought churches, stone building and Latin literacy; silver hoards of coin and hacksilver from these decades show how far the new state reached into international trade.

After the crisis and pagan reaction of the 1030s, the Polish realm was rebuilt around new centres, with stone churches, monastic foundations and the beginnings of chartered towns. Coinage of local mints replaced imported silver, castellan strongholds organised the countryside, and the division of the kingdom among Bolesław III's sons at the end of the period opened two centuries of fragmentation.

Roman-era settlement patterns had collapsed and the archaeological record thins dramatically, with far fewer sites, no more imported goods and simple hand-made pottery replacing the wheel-turned wares of earlier centuries. Into this landscape came the earliest Slavic-speaking communities, whose small sunken-floored huts, Prague-type pots and cremation burials mark the beginning of a new cultural order. Debates about how far the land was actually emptied, and how much of the older population remained, are among the liveliest in Polish archaeology.

Scandinavian raiders, traders and settlers turned the Baltic into a connected trading zone, and the southern coast held major emporia such as Wolin and Truso where Slavic, Scandinavian and Baltic goods changed hands. Arab silver dirhams reached these ports in huge quantities, and hoards of hacksilver are a signature find. The wealth and contacts of this trade fed directly into the rise of the early Polish state.
