The last generations before and during Christianisation, when cremation, sacred groves and offerings at springs and hilltops were still living practice. Mieszko I's baptism in 966 began a slow replacement of these rites by churchyard inhumation, though pagan customs persisted in the countryside and flared into revolt in the 1030s. Archaeology catches the overlap in cemeteries mixing old grave goods with new Christian orientation.

[Poland, AD 375–AD 450] wczesna faza okresu wędrówek ludów. Period definition from The Chronology — M. Mączyńska, 2020.

The Przeworsk world that had traded with Rome for centuries began to unravel as populations moved south and west in the wake of Hunnic pressure. Settlements and cemeteries thin out, but spectacular gold and silver finds appear, including polychrome-style ornaments in the fashion of the steppe elites. It is the beginning of a profound break in the settlement history of the Polish lands.

[Poland, AD 375–AD 410] okres wędrówek ludów D1. Period definition from The Chronology — M. Mączyńska, 2020.

The decades after the Huns broke into Europe, when Germanic groups moved west across the Rhine and Danube and the Roman frontier system unravelled. In Polish lands the long-established Przeworsk culture began to break down, with settlements abandoned and supplies of Roman imports drying up. Rich individual burials with polychrome cloisonné metalwork mark a new, mobile warrior elite.

okres wędrówek ludów D2 (Poland, AD 410–.label: okres wędrówek ludów D2

[Poland, AD 410–AD 450] okres wędrówek ludów D2. Period definition from The Chronology — M. Mączyńska, 2020.

The high point of Hunnic power under Attila and the years of its collapse, felt across Central Europe as populations shifted and older settlement patterns vanished. Finds are sparse but striking: gold sheet ornaments, garnet-inlaid buckles, and the artificially deformed skulls associated with steppe elites. Much of the Polish lowland appears thinly occupied by the period's end, before Slavic settlement expanded into the gap.

The Przeworsk culture that had dominated much of the region for centuries broke apart, its cemeteries and settlements falling silent as Germanic groups moved south and west toward the crumbling Roman frontier. Finds thin out dramatically, leaving a poorly populated landscape known mainly from scattered hoards and imported goods carrying Danubian and Hunnic-era styles. The emptiness matters: it is the gap into which Slavic-speaking communities moved over the following century, resetting the ethnic map of the region.

Dynastia Piastów (Poland, AD 963–AD 1370.label: Dynastia Piastów
Dynastia Piastów (Poland, AD 963–AD 1370.prose:
[Poland, AD 963–AD 1370] Dynastia Piastów. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

The dynasty that made Poland a state: Mieszko I accepted Latin Christianity in 966, and his son Boleslaw the Brave was crowned king, tying the country to western Europe rather than Byzantium. After 1138 the realm splintered into quarrelling duchies open to Mongol raids and German colonisation, until Wladyslaw the Short reunited a crown that Casimir the Great then consolidated with law codes, castles, and the founding of Krakow's university. Casimir died without a son in 1370, ending the line.

Dynastia Andegawenów (Poland, AD 1370–AD.label: Dynastia Andegawenów
Dynastia Andegawenów (Poland, AD 1370–AD.prose:
[Poland, AD 1370–AD 1386] Dynastia Andegawenów. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

With no male heir to the Piasts, the crown passed to Louis of Anjou, king of Hungary, who ruled Poland largely through regents from Buda. To secure the succession for a daughter he granted the Privilege of Koszyce, cutting the nobility's taxes and setting the pattern by which the szlachta extracted concessions from every later monarch. The reign of his daughter Jadwiga ended the line in 1386, when her marriage to Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania joined the two states.

Dynastia Jagiellonów (Poland, AD 1386–AD.label: Dynastia Jagiellonów
Dynastia Jagiellonów (Poland, AD 1386–AD.prose:
[Poland, AD 1386–AD 1572] Dynastia Jagiellonów. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

Begun by the marriage of Jadwiga to the Lithuanian grand duke Jogaila, baptised as Wladyslaw II, the dynasty joined Poland to the vast pagan-turned-Christian Grand Duchy and broke the Teutonic Order at Grunwald in 1410. Jagiellonian princes at times also wore the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary, while at home Renaissance culture flourished at Wawel and Krakow's university produced Copernicus. The Union of Lublin of 1569 turned the dynastic link into a single Commonwealth; three years later the last Jagiellon died childless and the throne became elective.

Monarchia elekcyjna (Poland, AD 1573–AD.label: Monarchia elekcyjna
Monarchia elekcyjna (Poland, AD 1573–AD.prose:
[Poland, AD 1573–AD 1795] Monarchia elekcyjna. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

After the last Jagiellon king died without an heir, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth's nobles took the right to choose each new monarch by open vote on a field outside Warsaw, binding him to a contract of conditions. It produced one of Europe's most nobility-dominated states, with a parliament so protective of its members that a single deputy's veto could dissolve it, and foreign powers openly bought elections. The system's paralysis, and belated reform attempts like the 1791 constitution, ended with the partitions that erased the state from the map.

Okres rozbiorów (Poland, AD 1795–AD 1914.label: Okres rozbiorów
Okres rozbiorów (Poland, AD 1795–AD 1914.prose:
[Poland, AD 1795–AD 1914] Okres rozbiorów. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

Erased from the map by Russia, Prussia and Austria, Poland existed for over a century as language, church and memory rather than a state. Repeated insurrections in 1830 and 1863 were crushed and answered with Russification and confiscations, while emigres in Paris made Polish Romanticism a European cause. Industrialisation and mass emigration reshaped society before the First World War reopened the question of independence.

Pierwsza wojna światowa (Poland, AD 1914.label: Pierwsza wojna światowa
Pierwsza wojna światowa (Poland, AD 1914.prose:
[Poland, AD 1914–AD 1918] Pierwsza wojna światowa. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

Polish lands, split between Russia, Germany and Austria-Hungary, became a battlefield fought over by the very empires that had partitioned them, and Poles were conscripted to fight one another. Piłsudski's Legions, the Blue Army in France and diplomatic work abroad kept the question of statehood alive. The collapse of all three partitioning powers in 1918 allowed an independent Poland to be declared after 123 years.

Dwudziestolecie międzywojenne (Poland, A.label: Dwudziestolecie międzywojenne
Dwudziestolecie międzywojenne (Poland, A.prose:
[Poland, AD 1918–AD 1939] Dwudziestolecie międzywojenne. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

Poland reappeared on the map after 123 years of partition, and had to fuse three legal systems, three rail gauges and several currencies into one state while fighting border wars, most dramatically against the Red Army outside Warsaw in 1920. Parliamentary democracy gave way in 1926 to Jozef Pilsudski's coup and the authoritarian Sanacja regime, though the era also produced the port of Gdynia, the Central Industrial Region, and a brilliant literary and mathematical scene. It ended with the German invasion of September 1939 and the Soviet entry two weeks later.

Druga wojna światowa (Poland, AD 1939–AD.label: Druga wojna światowa
Druga wojna światowa (Poland, AD 1939–AD.prose:
[Poland, AD 1939–AD 1945] Druga wojna światowa. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

Invaded from the west by Germany and from the east by the Soviet Union, the country was partitioned, its state dismantled and its people subjected to mass deportation, forced labour and extermination. It became the site of the Holocaust's main killing centres; roughly six million citizens died, half of them Jews, and Warsaw was deliberately levelled after the 1944 uprising. An underground state and home army fought on throughout, but liberation brought Soviet domination and borders shifted hundreds of kilometres west.

Rzeczpospolita Ludowa (Poland, AD 1945–A.label: Rzeczpospolita Ludowa
Rzeczpospolita Ludowa (Poland, AD 1945–A.prose:
[Poland, AD 1945–AD 1989] Rzeczpospolita Ludowa. Period definition from Dzieje Polski : Kalendarium — 2000.

Communist Poland, installed under Soviet auspices after the war and held together by the ruling party, censorship and a security apparatus – though the Catholic Church and private farming survived in a way they did not elsewhere in the bloc. Repeated revolts in 1956, 1970 and 1976 culminated in the Solidarity movement of 1980, ten million strong, met by martial law in 1981. Negotiations at the Round Table in 1989 produced the first semi-free elections in the bloc and began the unravelling of communist Europe.

Neolithic 8000–4000 BC. (Afghanistan, 79.label: Neolithic 8000–4000 BC.
Neolithic 8000–4000 BC. (Afghanistan, 79.prose:
[Afghanistan, 7999 BC–3999 BC] Neolithic 8000–4000 BC.. Period definition from Archaeological Gazetteer of Afghanistan — Warwick Ball, 2019-07-18.

Caves and open sites in northern Afghanistan, notably the Aq Kupruk group near the Balkh river and Darra-i-Kur in Badakhshan, hold some of the region's earliest evidence for herded sheep and goats. The area sat between the farming worlds of Iran and the Indus, and its early villages foreshadow the irrigated oasis settlements of the Bronze Age.

Bronze Age 4000–1500 BC (Afghanistan, 39.label: Bronze Age 4000–1500 BC
Bronze Age 4000–1500 BC (Afghanistan, 39.prose:
[Afghanistan, 3999 BC–1499 BC] Bronze Age 4000–1500 BC. Period definition from Archaeological Gazetteer of Afghanistan — Warwick Ball, 2019-07-18.

This is the era of the Oxus civilisation, or Bactria–Margiana complex, when irrigated oases in the north supported monumental mudbrick citadels, and of southern centres such as Mundigak. Afghan lapis lazuli from Badakhshan travelled as far as Mesopotamia and Egypt, making the region a crucial node in the earliest long-distance luxury trade. Its distinctive stone and metal figurines and compartmented seals turn up across Iran and into the Indus valley.

Iron Age 1500–700 BC (Afghanistan, 1499.label: Iron Age 1500–700 BC
Iron Age 1500–700 BC (Afghanistan, 1499.prose:
[Afghanistan, 1499 BC–699 BC] Iron Age 1500–700 BC. Period definition from Archaeological Gazetteer of Afghanistan — Warwick Ball, 2019-07-18.

Fortified oasis settlements and irrigation agriculture spread across the Bactrian plains and river valleys after the fall of the Bronze Age Oxus civilisation, marked by handmade painted wares of Yaz type. This was the world in which the Avestan hymns took shape and eastern Iranian pastoral and settled populations mixed. It ended as the region was absorbed into the great western empires, with Bactria becoming one of the richest satrapies of Achaemenid Persia.

Achaemenid c.530–330 BC (Afghanistan, 54.label: Achaemenid c.530–330 BC
Achaemenid c.530–330 BC (Afghanistan, 54.prose:
[Afghanistan, 549 BC–329 BC] Achaemenid c.530–330 BC. Period definition from Archaeological Gazetteer of Afghanistan — Warwick Ball, 2019-07-18.

Under the Persian kings the lands around the Hindu Kush became wealthy satrapies supplying gold, lapis lazuli and cavalry to the imperial armies. Irrigated oases supported walled towns, and Aramaic served as the language of administration. The satrap Bessus made his last stand here against Alexander.
